scenario_stem:
TimberCraft is a sole trader forestry business founded 8 years ago in Country X, supplying raw logs to construction firms. It employs 35 full-time loggers felling timber in the primary sector. Country X saw rapid industrialization, with secondary and tertiary sectors growing as the primary sector contracts.

A $250,000 processing mill turning logs into pre-cut wooden beams for house builders would raise added value. Management must decide whether to convert to a Private Limited Company by selling shares, while environmental protesters oppose increased felling.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'factors of production'.
questions.model_answer: The resources that a business needs to produce goods or services, consisting of land, labor, capital, and enterprise [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Country X's economy might be experiencing a shift from the primary sector to the secondary sector.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Industrialization and technological growth [k], allowing higher efficiency when turning raw logs into processed products [app]. Reason 2: Higher profit potential and added value [k], as selling pre-cut wooden beams yields greater revenue than selling raw timber [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to TimberCraft of using division of labor in its new processing mill.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Increased worker speed and operational efficiency [k], as employees specialize solely in operating automated log-cutting machinery [app], which increases output per hour [an]. Benefit 2: Reduced training time and costs [k], since loggers only need to master one specific task in processing timber into beams [app], lowering operational errors and unit production costs [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think the advantages to TimberCraft of converting into a Private Limited Company are greater than the disadvantages? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An advantage is gaining limited liability protection [k], which safeguards personal assets if the $250,000 processing mill expansion fails [app], significantly reducing personal financial risk [an]. A disadvantage is the legal incorporation fees and administrative formalities [k], which increase initial startup expenses [app] and delay setting up the timber processing operations [an]. Overall, the advantages are greater because investing $250,000 in industrial sawmill machinery carries substantial financial risk [eval], making limited liability essential to safeguard personal wealth when expanding [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs asset protection against legal costs in expansion context

scenario_stem:
A commercial gym network is a private limited company operating 4 health centers. it employs 12 location managers and 48 hourly fitness trainers, generates $1.2m sales and spends $450,000 on labor.

Trainer turnover has reached 30% because wages are unpredictable and income insecure. Staff feel demotivated off-peak, causing poor engagement and complaints about cancelled classes. HR is weighing fixed monthly salary against a $50 'Employee of the Month' bonus, while 2 new gym centers need head trainers.

questions.question_text: Define 'job enrichment'.
questions.model_answer: Adding tasks that require higher responsibility and complexity to make work more rewarding [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why high employee turnover might be a problem for this business.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Increased recruitment expenses [k] to advertise and hire replacement fitness trainers [app]. Reason 2: Reduced customer satisfaction [k] as gym members lose familiarity with class instructors [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to this business of offering fixed monthly salaries instead of hourly wages.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Improved income security for instructors [k], reducing financial anxiety during off-peak gym seasons [app], which increases motivation and lowers resignation rates [an]. Benefit 2: Better budget predictability [k], allowing labor expenses of $450,000 to be calculated accurately across 4 health centers [app], reducing cash flow uncertainty [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think introducing fixed monthly salaries is a better motivation method for this business than an 'Employee of the Month' bonus scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A fixed monthly salary provides guaranteed income security [k], motivating hourly-paid gym trainers during off-peak seasons [app] and reducing trainer turnover costs [an]. However, an 'Employee of the Month' bonus scheme creates competitive drive [k] for individual instructors teaching gym classes [app], but may demotivate non-winning staff who feel the $50 award is unfairly distributed [an]. Overall, fixed salaries are better because 30% turnover stems from basic financial insecurity [eval], which a small $50 bonus cannot resolve [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs basic financial security against small individual bonus in high-turnover gym context

scenario_stem:
A boutique beverage manufacturer is a private limited company producing organic cold-pressed juices in 250ml glass bottles sold at $4.00 to 45 health food stores. After 4 years it earns $600,000 with a 5% regional juice share and a $35,000 marketing budget.

Launching wellness shots, it must choose a niche of gym members or mass supermarket distribution. It also decides between $20,000 of social media video ads targeting urban consumers aged 18–35 and in-store taste testing trials.

questions.question_text: Define 'market segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Dividing a total market into distinct groups of consumers who share similar characteristics or needs [2].

knowledge_max_2: dividing a total market into distinct groups

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to this business of targeting a niche market for its wellness shots.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Less direct competition [k] from large commercial beverage brands in specialized health food stores [app]. Advantage 2: Ability to charge higher premium prices [k] to health-conscious gym members willing to pay above $4.00 per bottle [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to this business of conducting primary market research before launching the new beverage line.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Collects up-to-date and specific consumer feedback [k] regarding flavor preferences for wellness shots [app], allowing recipe adjustments that increase initial sales volume [an]. Benefit 2: Gauges accurate customer price tolerance [k] for 250ml glass bottles [app], reducing the financial risk of setting an uncompetitive launch price [an].

knowledge_max_2: gauges price tolerance/reduces product failure risk
analysis_max_2: allows recipe adjustments to boost sales volume

questions.question_text: Do you think social media video advertising is a better promotional method for this business than in-store taste testing trials? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Social media video advertising allows wide reach among target urban consumers aged 18–35 [k] within the $20,000 budget [app], building brand awareness rapidly before store launches [an]. However, in-store taste testing trials allow potential buyers to sample the organic cold-pressed juice directly [k], encouraging immediate impulse purchases in health food stores [app] despite higher staffing costs per trial [an]. Overall, in-store taste trials are better because flavor acceptance is critical for organic beverages [eval], making direct sampling more effective at converting shoppers than online video ads [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs online brand awareness against direct sampling conversion in organic beverage context

scenario_stem:
BoxPack Ltd is a private limited company making custom packaging boxes in one factory with 80 workers. Using batch production, it makes 100,000 cardboard boxes weekly, incurring $15,000 fixed and $45,000 variable costs, selling each box at $0.80.

Manual assembly errors create a 4% defect rate, causing waste, raw-material loss and customer complaints. The manager is choosing between investing $350,000 in automated flow production and adopting Lean Production with Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management to cut raw-material storage costs and cardboard waste.

questions.question_text: Calculate the total cost per box. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Total Cost = Fixed Costs ($15,000) + Variable Costs ($45,000) = $60,000 [1]. Average Cost per box = $60,000 / 100,000 units = $0.60 per box [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by the 4% defect rate in box manufacturing.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Wasted raw materials [k], increasing unit costs for cardboard paper supplies [app]. Problem 2: Damage to brand reputation [k], leading to lost orders from packaging clients [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to this business of introducing Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Reduced warehouse storage costs [k], as cardboard rolls are delivered only when needed for production [app], lowering fixed overheads across the factory [an]. Benefit 2: Reduced risk of inventory damage [k], as fewer raw packaging materials sit in storage [app], minimizing wasted stock and improving cash flow [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think introducing automated flow production is better for this business than relying on Lean Production techniques? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Automated flow production reduces reliance on manual assembly workers [k], eliminating the 4% defect rate in cardboard boxes [app] and lowering average unit costs below $0.60 over time [an]. However, automated machinery requires a heavy capital investment of $350,000 [k], increasing initial financial risk for the factory [app] and creating downtime during installation [an]. Overall, automated flow production is better because fixing manual assembly errors at high volumes (100,000 boxes weekly) requires machine precision [eval], making technological automation more reliable at scale than procedural lean changes [eval].

analysis_max_2: lowers average unit costs over time
evaluation_max_2: weighs high capital outlay against high-volume precision needs in packaging context

scenario_stem:
Northline Apparel Ltd is a private limited company running 8 clothing stores. Annual sales revenue is $1,500,000, cost of sales $900,000 and operating expenses $450,000. Current assets of $350,000 (inventory $220,000, receivables $80,000, cash $50,000) are set against current liabilities of $250,000 (payables $170,000, overdraft $80,000).

To fund a $200,000 winter stock expansion, the finance manager is preparing a cash-flow forecast, comparing a 5-year bank loan at 7% interest with 90-day trade credit from fabric suppliers.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Gross Profit Margin for this business. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Gross Profit = Revenue ($1,500,000) - Cost of Sales ($900,000) = $600,000 [1]. Gross Profit Margin = ($600,000 / $1,500,000) x 100 = 40% [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the Acid-Test Ratio for this business and explain what this result indicates.
questions.model_answer: Acid-Test Ratio = (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities [k] = ($350,000 - $220,000) / $250,000 = 0.52 : 1. The business has only $0.52 of liquid assets for every $1.00 of short-term liabilities [app], meaning it would struggle to pay the $80,000 bank overdraft and trade payables immediately [app]. Such a very low ratio signals a serious short-term liquidity risk that the business must manage carefully [k].

knowledge_max_2: explanation of liquid assets vs short-term debt

questions.question_text: Explain two ways this business could improve its cash flow position over the next 6 months.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Negotiate extended payment terms with fabric suppliers [k], delaying cash outflows for trade payables [app] and keeping cash in the bank for operational needs [an]. Way 2: Offer early payment discounts to retail trade receivables [k], encouraging faster cash inflows from credit customers [app] and reducing the reliance on the $80,000 bank overdraft [an].

analysis_max_2: keeps cash in bank for operational needs

questions.question_text: Do you think taking out a 5-year bank loan is a better source of finance for the $200,000 winter stock expansion than securing extended trade credit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A 5-year bank loan provides a structured long-term capital sum [k] to purchase the $200,000 winter stock upfront [app], spreading repayments over 5 years so current liquidity is not immediately drained [an]. However, the loan incurs 7% interest expenses [k], increasing annual overheads beyond the current $450,000 operating expenses [app] and creating long-term debt liabilities [an]. Extended 90-day trade credit avoids interest charges but requires fast-selling inventory to pay fabric suppliers within 90 days. Overall, the 5-year bank loan is better because purchasing seasonal stock requires long-term repayment stability [eval], whereas relying on 90-day trade credit with a low acid-test ratio of 0.52:1 risks severe insolvency if winter sales stall [eval].

knowledge_max_2: spreads capital repayment over long term
incurs interest expenses / risk of default
evaluation_max_2: weighs interest cost against insolvency risks given low 0.52:1 acid-test ratio in retail context

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Vista Juices plc is a public limited company mass-producing premium fruit juices in plastic bottles, with 250 employees. It exports 60% of output to 15 foreign countries, earning $4,500,000 annual revenue.

The government raised corporate profit tax from 22% to 26% and interest rates from 3% to 7%, while inflation reached 8%. A $150 per tonne carbon penalty hits plastic lines and a 6% currency appreciation threatens exports. Management must choose between raising prices and cutting operating expenses.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: A sustained increase in the average price level of goods and services in an economy over time [2].

knowledge_max_2: sustained increase in average price level

questions.question_text: Explain two impacts on this business of the government increasing corporate profit tax from 22% to 26%.
questions.model_answer: Impact 1: Lower retained profit [k], leaving less internal finance available to invest in upgrade equipment for plastic bottle manufacturing lines [app]. Impact 2: Reduced dividends for shareholders [k], lowering returns for investors in a Public Limited Company with 250 factory employees [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways an increase in interest rates from 3% to 7% could affect this business.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Cost of borrowing increases [k], raising interest payments on loans taken out to fund fruit juice production facilities [app] and reducing overall net profit margins [an]. Way 2: Consumer disposable income falls [k] because mortgage and loan repayments rise across domestic households [an], causing demand for premium fruit juices to decline [app].

analysis_max_2: raises loan repayment costs / reduces profit margin

questions.question_text: Do you think raising product prices is a better response to an 8% inflation rate for this business than cutting operating expenses? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising product prices passes higher unit costs directly to customers [k], protecting profit margins during 8% inflation [app] and maintaining cash flow for fruit juice production [an]. However, price increases may lead to lost sales volume as foreign buyers in 15 countries face a 6% currency appreciation, making products uncompetitive. Cutting operating expenses [k], such as reducing factory energy usage or workforce expenses for 250 employees [app], lowers total production costs directly without driving away price-sensitive buyers [an]. Overall, cutting operating expenses is better because raising prices in an inflationary market where export currency has appreciated by 6% risks severe sales drops across $4,500,000 revenue [eval], making expense reduction a safer strategy for long-term profit retention [eval].

knowledge_max_2: passes cost increases to customers / protects margins
analysis_max_2: risks loss of sales volume / reduced competitiveness
evaluation_max_2: weighs price increases against cost reduction in light of appreciation and revenue risks

scenario_stem:
Artisan Bakes is a partnership bakery in a busy town center owned by Elena and Sophia. 8 skilled bakers produce hand-crafted sourdough bread and fresh pastries using organic flour, generating $180,000 annual sales.

Rising organic flour costs have cut profit margins. The partners must choose between a $90,000 second shop funded by a bank loan requiring a business plan, internal expansion of their bakery kitchen, or a takeover of a nearby struggling cafe through horizontal integration.

questions.question_text: Identify two key elements contained within a business plan.
questions.model_answer:
1. Financial forecasts / cash flow forecast [1].
2. Marketing strategies / market research data [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why preparing a business plan is important to Artisan Bakes when applying for finance.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Helps convince commercial banks to approve loan funding [k] by proving that $180,000 in revenue can cover the $90,000 expansion cost [app]. Reason 2: Helps clarify business objectives and targets [k] to manage rising organic flour expenses and ensure loan repayments are met on time [app].

knowledge_max_2: helps convince lenders/banks to provide finance

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Artisan Bakes could increase the added value of its products.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Creating an attractive, premium packaging design [k] for hand-crafted sourdough bread and pastries [app], allowing the bakery to charge higher retail prices to customers [an]. Way 2: Establishing a strong, recognized high-quality brand image [k] emphasizing locally sourced organic flour ingredients [app], which increases customer willingness to pay and improves profit margins [an].

analysis_max_2: increases willingness to pay/improves profit margins

questions.question_text: Do you think the advantages to Artisan Bakes of expanding through horizontal integration are greater than expanding through internal growth? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Horizontal integration by buying a rival cafe immediately removes a competitor [k], giving the 8 skilled bakers direct access to an established customer base [app] and rapidly increasing market share [an]. However, taking over another business involves higher acquisition costs than $90,000 [k] and risks cultural clashes between bakery and cafe staff [app], leading to poor coordination [an]. Overall, horizontal integration offers greater advantages because acquiring an existing town-center cafe location avoids startup delays [eval], making it easier to generate immediate sales revenue to repay the bank expansion loan [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs immediate revenue against integration risks in retail context

scenario_stem:
A custom furniture manufacturing enterprise is a partnership with 2 workshop facilities, employing 35 skilled carpenters and 10 warehouse staff, earning $2.1m on piece-rate at $45 per wooden table.

Rushing to earn more, carpenters ignore safety and inspection checks, so product returns have risen 25%. Hygiene factors are failing and motivators such as recognition are absent, per Herzberg. The partners must choose profit-sharing or job enrichment, giving carpenters whole projects from raw timber to final polish.

questions.question_text: Define 'piece-rate payment'.
questions.model_answer: A payment system where workers are paid a fixed amount for each unit of output produced [2].

knowledge_max_2: wage tied directly to output volume

questions.question_text: Explain two hygiene factors according to Herzberg's theory that might be demotivating workers in this workshop.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Poor working conditions and safety [k], as carpenters ignore safety guidelines in workshop facilities [app]. Factor 2: Unfair wage structure [k], as $45 piece-rate wages encourage rushing rather than fair compensation for quality woodworking [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to this business of introducing job enrichment for its carpenters.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher job satisfaction and pride in work [k], as carpenters oversee entire custom furniture projects from raw timber to final polish [app], leading to greater attention to detail and higher craftsmanship quality [an]. Benefit 2: Reduced customer returns [k] by eliminating rushed assembly of wooden tables [app], which lowers waste expenses and protects business reputation [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think this business should replace piece-rate wages with profit-sharing schemes or implement job enrichment to reduce product quality returns? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Implementing job enrichment gives carpenters responsibility for full furniture design and assembly [k], encouraging pride in completed wooden tables [app] and reducing product return rates [an]. Replacing piece-rate pay with profit-sharing encourages teamwork and quality focus [k] across 35 workshop staff [app], but individual workers may feel their personal effort does not directly alter total firm profit [an]. Overall, job enrichment is better because the 25% increase in product returns stems directly from rushed work under piece-rate pay [eval], making complete project responsibility more effective at restoring craftsmanship than sharing annual profits [eval].

knowledge_max_2: promotes teamwork/lack of direct link to individual effort
evaluation_max_2: weighs direct quality ownership against collective financial incentives in craft manufacturing context

scenario_stem:
An eco-friendly footwear company is a public limited company making sustainable sneakers from recycled ocean plastics. After 5 years it sells 40,000 pairs at $80 each for $3.2m revenue, holding 8% of the sustainable athletic footwear market with a $180,000 marketing budget.

Directors are choosing demographic segmentation by income and age or psychographic targeting of environmentally conscious urban commuters, and a mass market billboard campaign or targeted influencer marketing on photo-sharing platforms.

questions.question_text: Define 'niche market'.
questions.model_answer: A small, specialized segment of a larger market where customers have specific needs and characteristics [2].

questions.question_text: Outline two reasons why segmenting the market by demographic factors might benefit this footwear business.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Helps tailor pricing strategy [k] to target income groups capable of paying $80 per pair of sneakers [app]. Reason 2: Improves advertising placement [k] by focusing promotional media on specific age groups interested in athletic footwear [app].

knowledge_max_2: tailors pricing strategy to income levels

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to this business of targeting environmentally conscious urban commuters through psychographic segmentation.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher brand loyalty [k], as consumers who value sustainable sneakers made from recycled ocean plastics identify strongly with the eco-friendly mission [app], leading to repeat purchases [an]. Benefit 2: Reduced wasted advertising expenditure [k] by focusing the $180,000 budget on eco-conscious lifestyle channels rather than uninterested mass audiences [app], increasing marketing return on investment [an].

knowledge_max_2: reduced wasted ad spend/higher marketing ROI

questions.question_text: Do you think targeted influencer marketing on photo-sharing platforms is a better promotional strategy for this footwear company than a mass market billboard campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Influencer marketing on photo-sharing platforms engages environmentally conscious urban commuters directly [k], showing eco-influencers wearing sneakers made from recycled ocean plastics [app] and driving online store traffic efficiently [an]. Conversely, mass market billboards create high visual exposure across major cities [k] to expand beyond an 8% market share [app], but suffer from high advertising costs and wasted views from non-eco consumers [an]. Overall, targeted influencer marketing is better because sustainable footwear relies on authentic credibility [eval]; visual proof from eco-influencers builds trust far more effectively than generic billboard ads [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs targeted social media credibility against mass market visual exposure in eco-footwear context

scenario_stem:
Oakcraft Workshop is a partnership handcrafting wooden dining tables with 12 skilled carpenters. Using job production, it completes 50 bespoke tables weekly, with $8,000 fixed and $22,000 variable costs; each table sells at $800.

Manual woodworking causes a 5% defect rate requiring costly rework as restaurant orders rise. The partners must choose between switching to batch production with Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) equipment costing $120,000 and expanding job production by hiring 8 more carpenters under Total Quality Management.

questions.question_text: Define 'job production'.
questions.model_answer: A production method where single, unique products are made one at a time to meet specific customer requirements [2].

knowledge_max_2: producing single unique products one at a time

questions.question_text: Calculate the weekly profit per dining table. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Total weekly cost = Fixed costs ($8,000) + Variable costs ($22,000) = $30,000 [k]. Average cost per table = $30,000 / 50 tables = $600 [app]. Weekly profit per table = $800 retail price - $600 average cost = $200 [app], so weekly profit = $200 x 50 tables = $10,000 [k].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to this workshop of transitioning from job production to batch production.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Higher output volume [k], enabling 12 carpenters to manufacture more than 50 wooden tables weekly for commercial restaurants [app], increasing sales revenue [an]. Advantage 2: Lower average costs per unit [k], as buying timber materials in larger batches reduces variable costs below $22,000 total [app], improving profit margins [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think investing in Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) equipment is a better strategy for this workshop than hiring additional carpenters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in CAM equipment standardizes cutting processes [k], reducing the 5% defect rate in handcrafted dining tables [app] and lowering unit manufacturing costs [an]. However, purchasing CAM machinery requires $120,000 in capital outlay [k] and risks losing the unique hand-carved appeal valued by custom buyers [app], creating financial strain [an]. Overall, investing in CAM equipment is better because meeting commercial restaurant orders requires consistent table dimensions and speed [eval]; machine precision eliminates rework expenses far more effectively than hiring more manual carpenters [eval].

knowledge_max_2: high capital cost/loss of custom craftsmanship
evaluation_max_2: weighs capital cost and lost craftsmanship against precision and speed for commercial expansion

scenario_stem:
Harrowfield Bakery Ltd is a private limited company producing packaged artisan breads for regional supermarkets. Annual operating overheads are $600,000. Current assets of $400,000 include $150,000 inventory, $180,000 receivables and $70,000 cash; current liabilities of $300,000 comprise $220,000 payables and $80,000 bank borrowings, with $500,000 non-current liabilities.

To fund a $600,000 automated baking ovens project, management is choosing between issuing new ordinary share capital to existing shareholders and taking a 10-year bank loan at 6% annual interest.

questions.question_text: State two reasons why a business requires long-term finance.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To purchase non-current assets such as machinery or premises [1]. Reason 2: To finance long-term business expansion or capital development projects [1].

questions.question_text: Calculate the Working Capital for this commercial bakery and outline what this figure represents.
questions.model_answer: Working Capital = Current Assets ($400,000) - Current Liabilities ($300,000) = $100,000 [k]. This positive working capital means the bakery's current assets comfortably exceed its current liabilities [app], suggesting it can settle its $220,000 trade payables and $80,000 short-term borrowings as they fall due [app]. It also indicates healthy short-term liquidity for day-to-day trading operations [k].

questions.question_text: Explain one internal source and one external source of finance suitable for purchasing short-term raw material supplies.
questions.model_answer: Internal Source: Retained profit from previous trading years [k] can be used without paying interest [an], drawing on the cash balance of $70,000 to buy ingredients for the artisan breads [app]. External Source: Trade credit from flour and ingredient suppliers [k] allows the bakery to delay payment while it awaits supermarket invoices being settled [an], easing pressure on its current liabilities of $300,000 [app].

questions.question_text: Consider whether issuing new ordinary shares or taking out a 10-year bank loan is the better source of finance for the $600,000 automated baking oven project. Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer: Issuing new ordinary shares brings permanent equity capital [k] for the $600,000 automated baking ovens [app], which never has to be repaid and incurs zero interest charges [an]. However, selling shares dilutes ownership control and requires paying dividends from profit for the year. A 10-year bank loan preserves ownership structure [k], but adds 6% annual interest expenses to existing overheads of $600,000 [app] and increases non-current liabilities beyond $500,000 [an]. Overall, issuing shares is recommended because adding a $600,000 loan to existing non-current liabilities of $500,000 significantly increases fixed-interest debt risk [eval], whereas equity finance provides safe funding for fixed capital without burdening monthly cash flow with interest repayments [eval].

knowledge_max_2: no repayment / no interest for equity
loan interest costs / increased financial risk
evaluation_max_2: weighs fixed-interest financial risk against ownership dilution in capital expansion context

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Oakline Furniture Ltd is a private limited company making budget wooden furniture, employing 120 carpenters. It generates $2,800,000 revenue, with 20% from exports.

A recession has cut GDP growth to -2.5% and raised unemployment from 4% to 9%. Personal income tax rose from 18% to 22%, reducing disposable income, while interest rates hit 6.5%. A 15% timber tariff and falling orders for furnishings squeeze sales. Management must weigh a cheaper flat-pack furniture range against expanding export sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A period of negative Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth lasting for two or more consecutive quarters in an economy [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two impacts on this business of an increase in national unemployment from 4% to 9%.
questions.model_answer: Impact 1: Easier recruitment of staff [k], allowing the wooden furniture manufacturer to hire skilled carpenters from a larger labor pool [app]. Impact 2: Decreased consumer spending [k], as unemployed households reduce non-essential purchases, lowering domestic orders for home furnishings [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways an increase in personal income tax from 18% to 22% affects this business.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Reduces consumer disposable income [k], leaving households with less money to spend on wooden furniture items [app], which leads to falling sales revenue across domestic retail markets [an]. Way 2: Workers may demand higher wage increases [k] to maintain their living standards after tax increases, raising operating costs for the 120 skilled carpenters [app] and reducing net profit margins [an].

analysis_max_2: raises operating costs / reduces net profit margins

questions.question_text: Do you think introducing a cheaper range of flat-pack furniture is a better strategy during a recession with -2.5% GDP growth than increasing export sales to overseas markets? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Introducing cheaper flat-pack furniture targets budget-conscious domestic consumers [k], appealing to households with falling disposable income during a -2.5% GDP recession [app] and maintaining sales volume [an]. However, developing flat-pack products requires new equipment and machinery investment [k], increasing capital costs when 6.5% interest rates make borrowing expensive [app]. Expanding export sales to overseas markets taps into foreign demand unaffected by the domestic slump, bringing in foreign currency revenue to support $2,800,000 total turnover and reducing reliance on the home market [an]. Overall, introducing flat-pack furniture is better because 80% of sales are domestic, and overcoming a 15% timber tariff on exports makes international expansion less profitable during a global downturn [eval], making local product adaptation crucial for business survival [eval].

knowledge_max_2: taps into foreign demand / diversifies revenue
analysis_max_2: reduces reliance on depressed home market
evaluation_max_2: weighs domestic focus against export expansion considering high tariffs and domestic sales share

scenario_stem:
Solis Energy Solutions is a private limited company providing solar panel installation and maintenance services for commercial and residential property owners. It employs 42 certified technicians and has $1.2 million capital employed.

The municipal government has invited tenders for a $400,000 public sector contract to install solar systems across fifteen state schools. Management wants to bid for rapid growth, but shareholders worry that bidding low to beat commercial competitors will cut profit margins and annual dividend payouts.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'public sector'.
questions.model_answer: The part of the economy owned and controlled by the government or state to provide services to the public [2].

questions.question_text: Outline two methods that could be used to measure the size of Solis Energy Solutions.
questions.model_answer: Method 1: Number of employees [k], as Solis employs 42 certified technicians [app]. Method 2: Capital employed [k], as Solis has total capital invested amounting to $1.2 million [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two differences in objectives between private sector businesses and public sector organizations.
questions.model_answer: Difference 1: Private sector businesses focus on maximizing financial profit [k] to pay dividends to solar company shareholders [app], whereas public sector organizations focus on providing affordable essential services to society [an]. Difference 2: Private sector businesses aim for market growth and competitive share [k] among commercial solar installers [app], while public sector organizations aim to satisfy community social welfare targets within public budgets [an].

knowledge_max_2: profit maximization vs public service provision
market growth vs social welfare/budget targets
analysis_max_2: enables dividend payments to private owners
ensures affordable service delivery to citizens

questions.question_text: Do you think Solis Energy Solutions should bid for the $400,000 municipal contract? Justify your answer by considering shareholder objectives and business growth.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for this healthcare software company. Show your working.

The acid-test ratio shows whether liquid assets cover short-term liabilities without selling inventory [k]. This result shows $1.40 of liquid assets per $1.00 owed [app], indicating healthy solvency to settle $1,800,000 trade payables and the $700,000 overdraft [app].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Ironvale Fasteners Co is a private limited company making steel bolts and nuts, employing 96 workers. Output hit 1.8 million units, up 12%. Pay is $9.50 hourly, yet 34% of bolts failed March checks and two line supervisors resigned over overtime.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Maslow's hierarchy of needs'.
questions.model_answer: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a theory that arranges human needs in five levels — physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation — where lower-level needs must be met before higher-level needs can motivate employees [2].

knowledge_max_2: Needs are arranged in a hierarchy or levels (physiological to self-actualisation)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a well-motivated workforce is important to Ironvale Fasteners Co.
questions.model_answer: A well-motivated workforce matters because motivated workers produce more output per hour, raising productivity so Ironvale can grow beyond 1.8 million units with the same 96 workers [k]. Higher productivity spreads fixed costs over more bolts, lowering the average cost per unit and protecting the margin needed to fund the $18,000 scheme [app]. Second, motivated workers take greater care and make fewer mistakes [k]. Fewer errors mean the 34% defect rate seen in March should fall, so fewer bolts are scrapped and Ironvale's reputation with its new contract customer is protected [app].

application_max_2: Reference to 1.8 million units output / 96 workers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ironvale Fasteners Co might face if it introduces the piece rate (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, a problem is that piece rate can reduce quality [k]. Paying $0.09 per approved bolt pushes workers to produce bolts as fast as possible, so defect rates could climb above the 34% recorded in March [app], and higher defects would damage Ironvale's standing with clients, leading to lost orders and rework costs [an]. Second, piece rate rewards individual speed, not teamwork [k]. Taylor's scientific management treats each worker separately, so experienced staff may refuse to help the slower of the 60 line workers [app], and the friction could trigger more disputes like the one that cost the factory two supervisors, raising labour turnover [an].

analysis_max_2: Chain from rushing to more defects to lost orders / rework costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironvale Fasteners Co should switch to the piece rate (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A follows Taylor's scientific management: paying $0.09 per approved bolt links pay directly to output, so the 60 line workers would be driven to maximise production and Ironvale could lift output above 1.8 million units [k]. Because only approved bolts are paid, workers also carry the quality risk themselves, creating a direct incentive to avoid the defects that reached 34% in March [app]. Higher throughput would spread fixed costs over more units, improving efficiency and competitiveness [an]. However, Option B targets Herzberg's theory and Maslow's esteem needs [k]. Monthly certificates and a $150 team bonus reward the whole team for the lowest defect rate while keeping the $9.50 per hour base pay unchanged, so the $18,000 cost is predictable [app]. This addresses the overtime dispute and low morale directly, whereas piece rate could inflame them further [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because Ironvale's central problem is quality — a 34% failure rate — and Herzberg shows pay alone does not remove dissatisfaction; recognition and team effort do [eval].

scenario_stem:
Wrenford Bakery is a private limited company running 4 bakery shops, founded 7 years ago by the Wren family. Profit after tax was $210,000 in 2025. Shareholders want a $58,000 dividend; the family a 5th shop costing $260,000. A $92,000 contingency reserve covers emergencies.

Directors compare reinvesting $152,000 of retained profit in the 5th shop with paying the dividend and financing expansion later. Two fitting contractors' quotes differ by $18,000; the new shop adds $95,000 a year to operating profit.

questions.question_text: Define 'retained profit'.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit is the profit kept in the business after tax and after dividends or drawings have been paid, available for reinvestment [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of using retained profit to finance the new shop.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Retained profit is an internal source, so no external lender needs to be approached [k]; the Wren family avoids interest charges on the $260,000 expansion [app]. Advantage 2: Reinvesting keeps ownership and control with the Wren family [k]; the business does not need to issue new shares to open the 5th shop [app].

knowledge_max_2: internal source: no repayment or interest obligation
retains ownership and control, no new shares needed
application_max_2: no new shares required for the 5th shop

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of reinvesting $152,000 of retained profit in the 5th shop.

Disadvantage 2: Reinvesting means shareholders may receive no dividend [k]; they were expecting $58,000 this year [app] and missing the payment could damage the Wren family's relationship with shareholders [an].

However, paying the $58,000 dividend [k] rewards shareholders who have backed the business for 7 years and keeps the family shareholders satisfied [app]; the shop could be financed later once the $18,000 difference between the two contractor quotes is resolved [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brackenhill Home Furnishings is a private limited company selling mid-market furniture from 3 stores with 64 staff. Revenue rose from $7.4 million to $8.6 million in the growth stage of the business cycle; unemployment fell to 5% and consumer spending rose.

The government plans to cut income tax from 22% to 19%. The directors must decide whether to open a fourth store in the southern suburbs at a cost of $1.2 million, or hold the cash in reserve against a slowdown.

questions.question_text: Define 'business cycle'.
questions.model_answer: The business cycle is the regular pattern of fluctuations (ups and downs) in economic activity over time, typically moving through stages such as growth, boom, recession and slump. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the regular pattern/cycle of fluctuations in economic activity over time
Names at least two stages, e.g. growth, boom, recession, slump

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenhill Home Furnishings' revenue rose.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer spending rises during the growth stage of the business cycle, so households are more willing to buy big items such as sofas and dining tables. [k] This is shown by revenue rising from $7.4 million to $8.6 million. [app] Reason 2: Unemployment has fallen to 5%, so more people have jobs and disposable income, and can afford mid-market furniture; rising demand explains why the directors are considering a fourth store. [k] [app]

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brackenhill Home Furnishings might face if it opens the fourth store in the southern suburbs.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The new store costs $1.2 million, so cash reserves would be greatly reduced and the firm may need to borrow, adding extra costs to the business. [k] With revenue of $8.6 million, spending $1.2 million is a large commitment that could strain cash if sales disappoint. [app] The extra fixed costs of rent and wages for a fourth outlet must be covered before profit rises, so profit could fall in the short term. [an] Problem 2: Opening in the southern suburbs is risky if the economy slows; a growth stage can end in a boom followed by a recession or slump. [k] The 3 stores already employ 64 staff, and a fourth store would add more staff and costs before demand in the suburbs is proven. [app] If income tax is not cut from 22% to 19% as hoped, consumer spending could weaken and the new store could make losses. [an]

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenhill Home Furnishings should open the fourth store now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, opening now lets Brackenhill Home Furnishings capture demand in the growth stage, when consumer spending is rising and unemployment is just 5%. [k] Revenue has already risen from $7.4 million to $8.6 million, showing strong demand for the sofas and furniture the new store would sell. [app] A fourth store in the southern suburbs would widen the customer base, spread fixed costs over more sales and raise profit further. [an] However, the fourth store would cost $1.2 million, and the growth stage can turn into a boom followed by a slowdown. [k] If income tax is not cut from 22% to 19%, or the economy slows, the new store's wages and rent would still need paying and the money held in reserve would be gone. [app] Keeping the cash in reserve would protect the 64 staff's wages and the existing 3 stores if the cycle turned down, but it would mean losing sales to competitors that expand first. [an] Overall, the firm should open the fourth store, but only once the income tax cut is confirmed, because acting on strong demand now gains a first-mover advantage while the condition limits the risk to cash flow. [eval] This is justified by the rise in revenue from $7.4 million to $8.6 million; spending $1.2 million is safer once demand and government policy are both confirmed. [eval]

scenario_stem:
Hazelbrook Dairy is a primary sector family farm in Country X with 85 cows producing 26,000 litres of milk monthly. It sells 20,000 litres of raw milk to a processor at $0.55 per litre; the 6,000 litres surplus is discarded.

The family considers $95,000 cheese and yogurt equipment to turn surplus into products earning $1.40 per litre-equivalent. A rival farm now sells yogurt, and the processor may cut prices 8%.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'primary sector'.
questions.model_answer: The part of the economy that extracts or harvests natural resources and raw materials from the land or the sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and quarrying [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hazelbrook Dairy might consider processing its milk into cheese and yogurt.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To use the surplus milk currently wasted [k], the remaining 6,000 litres are discarded each month even though they could become cheese and yogurt [app]. Reason 2: To reduce reliance on one buyer [k], after the hinted 8% price cut would reduce income from the 20,000 litres of raw milk sold at $0.55 per litre [app].

application_max_2: 20,000 litres sold raw at $0.55 per litre

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Hazelbrook Dairy of producing cheese and yogurt.

Benefit 2: Use of waste [k], the 6,000 surplus litres currently discarded each month [app], would turn from a disposal problem into extra income without buying more cows [an].

However, the risks have grown [k]: a rival farm already sells yogurt locally, and the processor's hinted 8% price cut would reduce raw-milk income to about $0.51 per litre [app], squeezing the cash available to repay the $95,000 investment [an]. Overall, investing is the stronger option because $1.40 is about 2.5 times the raw price and the discarded 6,000 litres are free raw material for the new products [eval], but the family should confirm demand with local supermarkets before committing the full $95,000 [eval].

scenario_stem:
Copperfield Electronics Assembly is a public limited company making circuit boards, with 210 workers and 18 quality inspectors. Revenue is $26 million, but turnover on the assembly line hit 22% as 58 workers left in 12 months. The $1,450 salary feels repetitive.

Elena Brooks chooses: Option A, a 10-week training programme and a $2.10 piece rate under Taylor's scientific management, or Option B, job rotation between three assembly stations every 4 hours plus a $90 monthly attendance bonus.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Taylor's scientific management'.
questions.model_answer: Taylor's scientific management is the theory that workers are motivated principally by money, using time-and-motion studies to find the one best way to do each job and paying a piece rate linked to how much each worker produces [2].

knowledge_max_2: Workers motivated mainly / principally by money
Time-and-motion studies identify the one best way / pay linked to output via piece rate

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why labour turnover on the assembly line is high at Copperfield Electronics Assembly.
questions.model_answer: One reason is that the work is repetitive, so workers become bored and see no challenge in the job [k]. Repeating the same assembly stations all day adds no variety or new skills, removing Herzberg's motivators such as responsibility, so the 210 production-line workers drift towards quitting — 58 left in the last 12 months [app]. A second reason is that pay does not reward effort [k]. A salary of $1,450 per month is paid regardless of output, so productive and unproductive workers earn the same, and turnover has hit 22% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Repetitive work causes boredom / removes Herzberg's motivators
Salary is fixed regardless of output, so effort is not rewarded
application_max_2: Reference to 58 workers leaving in 12 months / 210 production-line workers
Reference to $1,450 per month salary / 22% turnover

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Copperfield Electronics Assembly of introducing Option B (job rotation).
questions.model_answer: One benefit is reduced boredom [k]. Moving each worker between three assembly stations every 4 hours adds variety and fresh skills to a repetitive job [app], and less boredom means fewer errors and fewer absences, helping the 210 production-line workers sustain daily output [an]. A second benefit is greater flexibility [k]. With every worker trained on three stations, cover is available whenever colleagues are absent, so the 18 quality inspectors receive a steadier flow of comparable boards [app], reducing bottlenecks and protecting the $26 million annual revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Job rotation adds variety / reduces boredom
Job rotation makes workers multi-skilled / flexible cover
application_max_2: Reference to three assembly stations every 4 hours / repetitive work
Reference to 210 production-line workers / 18 quality inspectors / $26 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Chain from variety to lower boredom to fewer errors / absences / sustained output
Chain from multi-skilling to flex cover to steady flow / protected revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperfield Electronics Assembly should introduce Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is built on Taylor's theory that money drives effort: a piece rate of $2.10 per tested board would reward fast workers, so tested output per worker should rise above current levels [k]. Time-and-motion studies and a 10-week training programme would also standardise methods for new hires, helping stabilise a workforce that lost 58 workers in 12 months [app]. Higher tested output spreads overheads over more boards, improving cost efficiency [an]. However, Option B tackles why people are leaving — repetitive, unchallenging work [k]. Job rotation between three assembly stations every 4 hours adds variety, and the $90 monthly attendance bonus rewards presence without raising the $1,450 basic salary bill unpredictably [app]. Retention of skilled assemblers also protects quality, which the 18 inspectors police on every board before it reaches home-appliance clients [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the stronger choice [eval] because 58 workers left in 12 months mainly from monotony, and Herzberg's theory shows adding variety keeps people better than paying more for the same dull job [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Taylor's scientific management: link pay to output via piece rate
Herzberg: hygiene factors vs motivators / variety reduces dissatisfaction
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $2.10 per tested board / 10-week training programme
Reference to Option B: three assembly stations every 4 hours / $90 monthly attendance bonus / $1,450 salary
analysis_max_2: Chain from piece rate to higher tested output to lower unit overheads
Chain from rotation to retention of skilled assemblers to protected quality / fewer leavers
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem evidence (58 leavers, 22% turnover, salary vs piece rate)

scenario_stem:
Old Harbour Biscuits, a partnership, makes digestive biscuits. Its best-seller sells 120,000 packs yearly at $2.40; sales are flat after 3 years in a saturated market, with profits down from $96,000 to $70,000, across 55 independent grocers and 8 cafes.

They must choose a relaunch with three new flavours and a modern wrapper costing $45,000, or a 15% price cut to $2.04. A rival's cut won 8% market share; they cannot fund both and must decide by month-end.

questions.question_text: Define 'saturation' in the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: Saturation is the stage of the product life cycle when the market is full of the product, sales stop rising and competition is intense, so revenue flattens [2].

knowledge_max_2: market is full / market no longer growing
sales flatten and competition is intense

questions.question_text: Explain two problems a saturated market creates for Old Harbour Biscuits.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Flat sales cap revenue [k], because digestive biscuit sales have been stuck at 120,000 packs a year for 3 years [app]. Problem 2: Rivals undercut and take share [k], because the main competitor cut prices and gained 8% market share [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Old Harbour Biscuits of relaunching with three new flavours and new packaging.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A relaunch can re-stimulate demand [k], because three new flavours and a modern wrapper give existing buyers a reason to try the biscuits again [app], which can reverse 3 years of flat sales supplied to 55 grocers and 8 cafes [an]. Benefit 2: Fresh packaging can support a better price [k], because buyers link modern packaging with improved quality [app], lifting margins as profits eased from $96,000 to $70,000 and offsetting the $45,000 wrapper cost [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Old Harbour Biscuits should relaunch with new flavours rather than cut the price by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that relaunching refreshes the product [k], because three new flavours and a modern wrapper costing $45,000 give buyers a reason to repurchase [app], reviving the 120,000-pack-a-year business and rebuilding profits that eased from $96,000 to $70,000 [an]. On the other hand, the 15% price cut to $2.04 is simpler and faster [k]: it directly answers the competitor that gained 8% market share and could lift volume quickly [app], but each pack earns $0.36 less, so profit per pack falls [an]. Overall, the relaunch is the better choice because cutting price only matches a rival and erodes margins, while new flavours defend share properly and could restore the $96,000 peak profit level [eval], but the partners should track sales weekly and switch to pricing action if the relaunch has not lifted packs within 3 months [eval].

questions.question_text: Identify two disadvantages of batch production.
