unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppermere Brick and Cement Co is a public limited company supplying bricks and cement from 2 plants, employing 180 workers. It made 9.5 million bricks last year; revenue rose from $11.8 million to $14.2 million, and its order book is full for 12 months.

The economy is in a boom. The government may raise corporation tax from 24% to 28% to cool it. The board must decide whether to invest $3 million in a third plant, or delay expansion until the boom ends.

questions.question_text: Define 'boom'.
questions.model_answer: A boom is the peak stage of the business cycle, when economic activity is at its highest, demand is strong, output is high and unemployment is low. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the boom as the peak/high point of the business cycle
Identifies high demand, output or employment / strong economic activity

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of a boom on Coppermere Brick and Cement Co.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Demand for bricks and cement rises sharply in a boom, so the firm sells more and revenue grows; it produced 9.5 million bricks and revenue reached $14.2 million. [k] [app] Effect 2: In a boom labour is scarce and wages tend to rise, so keeping 180 workers paid may squeeze margins even as sales increase and the order book stays full. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that demand/output rise in a boom
Identifies that labour is scarce / wages rise in a boom
application_max_2: References 9.5 million bricks and/or revenue of $14.2 million
References 180 workers, the full order book or the construction sector expansion

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of investing $3 million in a new third plant during the boom.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Construction costs and wages are high in a boom, so the $3 million budget could overrun and the firm may need to borrow more. [k] With revenue of $14.2 million, extra borrowing at this point would still cut profit, especially if corporation tax rises from 24% to 28%. [app] Higher fixed costs from a third plant must be paid even if orders fall, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes more fragile. [an] Problem 2: When the boom ends, demand for bricks falls; a new plant built now may be underused, leaving excess capacity and heavy fixed costs. [k] Orders are full for the next 12 months, but the business cycle will eventually move into a slowdown, and the extra workers taken on cannot be avoided easily. [app] Underused capacity spreads fixed costs over fewer bricks, raising average costs and reducing competitiveness. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that costs are high in a boom / the budget may overrun
Identifies that demand will fall when the boom ends, leaving excess capacity
application_max_2: References the $3 million cost against $14.2 million revenue or the 24% to 28% tax rise
References the full 12-month order book or the boom eventually ending
analysis_max_2: Explains that higher fixed costs raise the break-even point and fragile profit
Explains that underused capacity raises average cost per brick (diseconomy/under-absorption)

questions.question_text: Do you think Coppermere Brick and Cement Co should invest $3 million in a third plant now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: in a boom, demand is strong and delaying expansion means losing orders to rivals. [k] Revenue has already climbed from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the order book is full for 12 months, so more capacity is needed urgently. [app] A third plant would let the firm serve all its housing-developer customers and raise profit despite the possible rise in corporation tax from 24% to 28%. [an] However, booms do not last forever; the business cycle will eventually turn to a downturn. [k] If the economy slows after the boom, the third plant's $3 million cost and the wages of extra workers would leave the firm with excess capacity and weaker cash to pay its 180 workers. [app] Delaying expansion until the boom ends would reduce this risk but would hand orders to competitors at the peak of demand. [an] Overall, the board should invest in the third plant now but phase the building over 18 to 24 months, keeping a cash reserve in case the cycle turns, because the revenue evidence strongly justifies expansion. [eval] This is justified by the $2.4 million revenue increase and the full order book; phasing the spend limits the damage if the boom ends sooner than expected. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies strong demand / capacity shortage in a boom
Identifies that the boom will end and demand will fall (cycle risk)
application_max_2: References revenue growth from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the full order book
References the $3 million cost, 180 workers or the 24% to 28% corporation tax rise
analysis_max_2: Explains how extra capacity raises profit when demand is strong
Explains how excess capacity and fixed costs hurt the firm after the boom
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. invest now but phase it)
Weighs opportunity cost of delay against the risk of over-expansion

scenario_stem:
Calder Steel Works is a secondary sector steel rolling mill in Country X employing 240 workers. It makes steel beams and had $9 million turnover. The secondary sector's employment share fell from 31% to 19% amid de-industrialisation.

The owners weigh two options. Option one spends $1.5 million on machinery making higher-value finished sections for export, with government grants up to $400,000 requiring 200 jobs kept. Option two sells the site to a developer for $6 million and closes.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'de-industrialisation'.
questions.model_answer: The decline in the importance of the secondary (manufacturing) sector in a country's economy, with manufacturing employment and output falling as services grow in importance [2].

knowledge_max_2: decline in importance/share of the secondary (manufacturing) sector
manufacturing employment and output fall as services grow

questions.question_text: Explain two problems de-industrialisation creates for Calder Steel Works.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A shrinking customer base [k], with the secondary sector's share of employment down from 31% to 19%, construction demand for the mill's steel beams could weaken [app]. Problem 2: Skills shortages [k], as fewer school leavers enter manufacturing, the mill's 240 steelworker roles may become harder and more costly to fill [app].

knowledge_max_2: reduced demand for manufactured goods as secondary sector shrinks
labour/skills shortage as fewer workers enter manufacturing
application_max_2: secondary sector employment fell from 31% to 19%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the local economy if Calder Steel Works chooses option one.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Preserved jobs [k], investing would keep 240 workers employed in an area where the secondary sector has fallen to 19% of employment [app], sustaining local spending and tax revenues [an]. Benefit 2: Export earnings [k], the new machinery would let the mill sell higher-value finished sections abroad [app], bringing foreign currency into Country X and supporting further industrial growth [an].

knowledge_max_2: jobs preserved sustains local spending and tax revenue
export sales earn foreign currency and support industry
analysis_max_2: sustains local shops/services and tax base
foreign currency inflow supports Country X's industrial base

questions.question_text: Do you think Calder Steel Works should invest $1.5 million rather than sell the site for $6 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing protects the mill and jobs [k]: keeping 240 workers employed in a region hit by de-industrialisation would preserve the $9 million turnover and satisfy the grant condition of at least 200 jobs [app], and a possible $400,000 grant plus export sales of finished sections could make the $1.5 million pay back over time [an]. Selling is the safer short-term route [k]: the $6 million sale gives certain cash now, freeing the owners from a shrinking secondary sector while workers receive redundancy payments [app], but it would leave 240 people without work where secondary jobs have already fallen to 19% of employment [an]. Overall, investing is the better option because the $1.5 million cost, minus any $400,000 grant, is far smaller than the $6 million opportunity forgone, yet it keeps a viable $9 million turnover business alive [eval]; however, if export orders cannot be secured soon, the certain $6 million sale would be the wiser choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: investment keeps jobs, turnover and possible grant support
sale gives certain cash but ends the mill and costs jobs
application_max_2: $1.5 million machinery investment vs $6 million sale
$400,000 grant requiring at least 200 jobs kept
analysis_max_2: grant and exports spread the cost and secure payback
sale removes risk but destroys jobs in a declining sector
evaluation_max_2: weighs certain $6 million against long-term viability of the mill
conditional recommendation based on securing export orders

scenario_stem:
Halcyon Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company employing 78 workers at its pottery, producing 3,400 hand-decorated plates monthly. Workers earn $11.20 per hour and eat in a cramped canteen with no heating. Absenteeism reached 9%, and 11 workers resigned in 6 months.

Production director Marcus Vale must decide this month: Option A, $40,000 on hygiene factors, or Option B, $40,000 on motivators - job enrichment, recognition boards and team leaders with quality responsibility on each kiln line.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Herzberg's two-factor theory'.
questions.model_answer: Herzberg's two-factor theory states that job satisfaction and dissatisfaction come from different factors: hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as recognition, responsibility and advancement create satisfaction and encourage effort [2].

knowledge_max_2: Job satisfaction and dissatisfaction arise from different factors
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction

questions.question_text: Explain two hygiene factors Halcyon Ceramics Ltd should improve.
questions.model_answer: One hygiene factor is working conditions [k]. The canteen has no heating and lockers are poor, so making these comfortable would remove a daily irritation, helping to cut the 9% absenteeism recorded last winter [app]. A second hygiene factor is rest and recovery space [k]. A quiet rest room for the 78 workers would ease fatigue during long kiln shifts, so people return to work on the 3,400 hand-decorated plates with more care rather than after a miserable break [app].

knowledge_max_2: Working conditions are a hygiene factor
Rest or facilities are hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction
application_max_2: Reference to cramped canteen with no heating / lockers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halcyon Ceramics Ltd of spending the $40,000 on motivators (Option B).
questions.model_answer: One benefit is greater responsibility and esteem [k]. Giving team leaders responsibility for quality on each kiln line meets Maslow's esteem level and gives workers a real voice in standards [app], so workers take ownership of each batch and defect rates on the 3,400 plates should fall [an]. A second benefit is recognition of good performance [k]. Monthly recognition boards make strong performance visible and job enrichment adds variety to decorating work [app], and motivated workers are more productive and less likely to join the 11 who resigned in the last 6 months [an].

knowledge_max_2: Responsibility and esteem are motivators / create satisfaction
Recognition and job enrichment are motivators
application_max_2: Reference to team leaders on each kiln line / responsibility for quality
Reference to monthly recognition boards / job enrichment / 11 workers resigned
analysis_max_2: Chain from responsibility to ownership to lower defect rates
Chain from recognition to motivation to higher productivity / lower turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Halcyon Ceramics Ltd should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is strongly supported by Herzberg: hygiene factors like a heated canteen and better lockers do not motivate on their own, but when they are poor they create dissatisfaction that blocks everything else [k]. The $40,000 would immediately improve daily life for all 78 workers, directly tackling the discomfort behind last winter's 9% absenteeism and the 11 resignations in 6 months [app]. Fixing dissatisfaction first stabilises the team before a demanding export order [an]. However, Option B adds only true motivators — job enrichment, recognition boards and team-leader responsibility — which Herzberg argues create genuine satisfaction and extra effort [k]. The pay of $11.20 per hour is presumably adequate, so further comfort may simply become the new normal, whereas motivators keep adding satisfaction [app]. Motivators build long-term engagement and quality ownership across the export order's production run [an]. Overall, I think Halcyon should choose Option A first [eval] because Herzberg is explicit that hygiene factors must be adequate before motivators can work — you cannot enrich jobs for workers shivering in an unheated canteen [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction / are prerequisites
Herzberg: motivators create satisfaction / extra effort
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: heated canteen / lockers / rest room / $40,000
Reference to Option B: job enrichment / recognition boards / $11.20 per hour
analysis_max_2: Chain from removing dissatisfaction to stabilised team / export readiness
Chain from motivators to long-term engagement / quality ownership
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem evidence (9% absenteeism, 11 resignations vs $11.20 pay adequacy)

scenario_stem:
Everline Audio, a private limited company, made DVD players and MP3 players for 11 years. Sales fell from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units in 2025, a decline stage, with 38 employees, $260,000 unsold stock and revenue halved to $1.2m in 3 years.

Directors weigh an extension strategy: $120,000 retooling for a DVD/MP3 media centre with smart streaming, or discontinuing the range and selling machinery for about $180,000. Either affects 38 employees; shareholders vote next month.

questions.question_text: Define 'decline stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The decline stage is when sales fall steadily because the product is outdated or replaced by alternatives, and revenue and profit shrink [2].

knowledge_max_2: product is outdated/replaced so revenue and profit shrink

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Everline Audio's products are in the decline stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Technology is outdated [k], because DVD players and MP3 players have been replaced by streaming and online content [app]. Reason 2: Unit sales keep shrinking [k], with sales falling from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units in 2025 [app].

knowledge_max_2: products become outdated as technology moves on
sales fall steadily in the decline stage
application_max_2: DVD/MP3 players replaced by modern alternatives
sales fell from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units in 2025

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Everline Audio of launching the media centre as an extension strategy.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It can win back lapsed customers [k], because a DVD/MP3 media centre with smart streaming updates the old range for existing owners [app], slowing the slide from 30,000 units to 9,000 units a year and protecting the 38 staff [an]. Benefit 2: It keeps the factory productive [k], because $120,000 of retooling reuses the plant and 11 years of manufacturing experience [app], preserving $1.2 million of annual revenue instead of shutting down for a machinery sale [an].

knowledge_max_2: extension strategies extend a declining product life
application_max_2: media centre with smart streaming for $120,000 of retooling
analysis_max_2: can slow the sales slide and protect jobs and revenue
cheaper than starting from scratch; keeps plant productive

questions.question_text: Do you think Everline Audio should launch the media centre rather than discontinue the range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that the extension strategy buys time [k], because the media centre with smart streaming refreshes an outdated range for only $120,000 of retooling [app], which could recover some of the fall from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units and keep the 38 staff employed [an]. On the other hand, discontinuing is cleaner [k], because selling the machinery for about $180,000 frees cash and ends the $260,000 unsold-stock problem [app], letting shareholders redeploy money instead of backing a shrinking DVD/MP3 market [an]. Overall, Everline should discontinue the range because four years of decline, down to 9,000 units from a 30,000 peak, show demand is structurally gone; taking the $180,000 is safer than risking $120,000 of further losses [eval], but if confirmed pre-orders for the media centre top 12,000 units the board should approve the launch instead [eval].

knowledge_max_2: extension strategies can prolong but not reverse structural decline
discontinuing releases cash and ends losses
application_max_2: $120,000 retooling vs selling machinery for about $180,000
sales fell from 30,000 units (2021) to 9,000 (2025); $260,000 of unsold stock
analysis_max_2: media centre may recover some demand but DVD/MP3 market keeps shrinking
discontinuing frees $180,000 and stops cash drain on dead stock
evaluation_max_2: weighs extension risk against clean exit
justified exit recommendation with a clear trigger for reversal

scenario_stem:
SoftWeave Paper Products Ltd, a private limited company, makes paper tissues and kitchen roll on one continuous flow line running 16 hours a day, 6 days weekly, at 1,200 packs per hour with 38 machine operators and 6 maintenance staff.

Last year it sold 9.6 million packs at $2.40 each. Demand rises, so directors compare adding a second line for $1.15 million, doubling capacity to 2,400 packs per hour, against overtime, while deepening reliance on a single supplier of recycled paper pulp.

questions.question_text: State two advantages of flow production.
questions.model_answer: Flow production can produce very large quantities quickly through a continuous process [1]. Unit costs are low because output is high and machinery keeps running, spreading fixed costs [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Low unit cost / fixed costs spread over huge output

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why flow production suits SoftWeave Paper Products Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Paper tissues are a standardised, identical product sold in huge volumes, which suits continuous production [k]. The line already outputs 1,200 packs per hour and SoftWeave sold 9.6 million packs last year, volumes that job or batch production could not match economically [app]. Reason 2: Flow production uses capital equipment intensively with very few changeovers [k]. With only tissues and kitchen roll to make, the single line and its 38 machine operators can run 16 hours a day without costly resetting [app].

knowledge_max_2: Standardised, identical products suit flow production
Capital intensive, few changeovers / machinery used continuously
application_max_2: 1,200 packs per hour; 9.6 million packs sold; $2.40 per pack
38 machine operators; 16 hours a day line running tissues and kitchen roll

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of adding a second flow production line.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: The $1.15 million investment raises fixed costs sharply [k]. If demand dipped below the doubled capacity of 2,400 packs per hour, the new line would still incur machine and building costs [app], squeezing profit margins and lengthening the time needed to recoup the money invested [an]. Risk 2: A second line deepens dependence on a single supplier of recycled paper pulp [k]. Any disruption to pulp deliveries would halt twice as much output as before, stopping both lines together [app], which could lose key supermarket customers to rivals during the outage [an].

knowledge_max_2: High capital cost / fixed costs rise with a second line
Dependence on one supplier / supply disruption risk
application_max_2: $1.15 million cost; doubled capacity of 2,400 packs per hour
Single supplier of recycled paper pulp; both lines depend on pulp
analysis_max_2: Idle capacity squeezes margins / delays recouping the investment
Losing pulp supply halts all output, risking customers

questions.question_text: Do you think SoftWeave should add the second production line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for adding the line: demand is rising and the present line already runs 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, so it has no spare capacity [k]. A second line doubling capacity to 2,400 packs per hour could lift sales beyond 9.6 million packs without overtime or outsourcing premiums [app]. Higher output would lower average costs and could win new supermarket contracts [an]. Arguments against: outsourcing overflow is flexible, so SoftWeave pays only for the output it needs and avoids the $1.15 million outlay and the single-supplier pulp risk [k]. If demand fell, outsourcing could simply be cut back [app]. Keeping cash free also funds marketing and shields the firm from over-commitment to one pulp supplier [an]. Overall, if rising demand is confirmed by firm supermarket orders, the second line offers the lowest long-run unit cost and is worth funding [eval]. However, if demand is seasonal or unproven, outsourcing overflow first limits risk until the trend is certain [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Flow production lowers unit cost at high volumes / justifies investment
Outsourcing offers flexibility without capital outlay
application_max_2: 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, 1,200 packs per hour, 9.6 million packs
$1.15 million cost; 2,400 packs per hour capacity; single pulp supplier
analysis_max_2: Lower average costs and new contracts from expanded capacity
Flexibility of outsourcing vs fixed commitment and supplier risk
evaluation_max_2: Justified conditional judgement based on evidence of demand
Reversal condition stated if demand is unproven

scenario_stem:
Boxhaven Packaging Ltd is a private limited company making cardboard boxes for 3 food manufacturers. Last year's operating profit was $185,000; retained profit is $140,000. A $160,000 box-folding machine would raise output 25% and cut labour costs $2,800 monthly; one buyer is 60% of sales; demand rises before the busy season.

Monthly wages and materials cost $48,000, so cash must cover the next payroll. Directors choose between buying now, draining most retained profit, or delaying 12 months as the balance rebuilds from $15,000 monthly profits.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital expenditure'.
questions.model_answer: Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets that will benefit the business for more than one year, such as machinery, vehicles and buildings [2].

knowledge_max_2: assets used for more than one year

questions.question_text: Explain two needs for finance that Boxhaven Packaging Ltd has.
questions.model_answer: Need 1: The $160,000 box-folding machine is capital expenditure [k]; buying it now would raise output by 25% and cut labour costs by $2,800 a month [app]. Need 2: Day-to-day running costs must still be met [k]; wages and raw materials absorb $48,000 a month, so the business needs working capital to cover every payroll [app].

knowledge_max_2: capital expenditure need: long-term asset purchase
working capital need: day-to-day running costs
application_max_2: $160,000 machine raising output by 25% with $2,800 monthly labour saving
$48,000 a month on wages and raw materials must be covered

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of using retained profit to buy the machine now.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Spending the $140,000 retained profit leaves almost no internal cushion [k]; with wages and raw materials costing $48,000 a month, one late payment from the largest customer could strain the payroll [app], forcing the directors to borrow quickly at short notice [an]. Disadvantage 2: Buying now commits the business before the busy season is fully tested [k]; if orders from the 3 food manufacturers soften, the extra 25% capacity may go unused [app], wasting part of the $160,000 outlay [an].

knowledge_max_2: drains internal funds, leaving little reserve for working capital
commits capital before demand is confirmed
application_max_2: $140,000 retained profit against $48,000 monthly wage and material costs
extra 25% capacity relies on the 3 food manufacturers
analysis_max_2: late customer payment could force emergency short-term borrowing
unused capacity would waste part of the $160,000 spent

questions.question_text: Do you think Boxhaven Packaging Ltd should buy the box-folding machine now or delay 12 months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying now [k] would capture the $2,800 monthly labour saving, about $33,600 a year, and raise output by 25% precisely when the busy season arrives [app]; with operating profit of $185,000 last year, the extra capacity could be funded from retained profit without external borrowing [an]. Delaying 12 months [k] would let the retained profit balance rebuild through monthly profits of about $15,000, keeping the payroll safe [app]; however, the business would forgo the full year of labour savings, roughly $33,600, and risk disappointing the largest customer that accounts for 60% of sales [an]. On balance, the business should buy now [eval], because the annual saving and protected customer base outweigh the strain on reserves, provided a separate payroll buffer is ring-fenced [eval].

knowledge_max_2: buying now gains labour savings and capacity immediately
delaying preserves working capital and internal reserves
application_max_2: $2,800 a month labour saving (about $33,600 a year) with 25% more output
$185,000 operating profit vs $140,000 retained profit and monthly payroll protection
analysis_max_2: extra capacity matches rising demand and the largest 60%-of-sales customer
delaying forgoes about $33,600 of labour savings over the year
evaluation_max_2: overall justified judgement balancing savings against reserve risk
recommendation references the trade-off with a ring-fenced payroll buffer

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches is a partnership selling luxury watches and jewellery from 2 boutiques with 14 specialist sales staff. Takings per boutique fell from $130,000 to $95,000 a month in a slump; footfall dropped by a third and two luxury retailers closed.

With consumer confidence low, the government has cut VAT from 20% to 15% for 12 months. The partners must decide whether to cut prices by 10% to attract buyers, or hold prices to protect the brand's exclusive image.

questions.question_text: Define 'slump'.
questions.model_answer: A slump is the lowest point of the business cycle, when economic activity, output, incomes and employment are at their weakest and consumer spending is very low. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the slump as the lowest/weakest stage of the business cycle
Identifies very low output, incomes, employment and/or consumer spending

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sales of luxury watches and jewellery fall during a slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In a slump, consumer incomes and confidence are very low, so households postpone non-essential high-price purchases such as luxury watches. [k] This is shown by takings per boutique falling from $130,000 to $95,000 a month. [app] Reason 2: In a slump, people fear for their jobs, so they prioritise essentials over luxury goods. [k] Footfall has fallen by a third and two nearby luxury retailers have closed, confirming the collapse in demand. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies low consumer incomes/confidence as the cause of weak luxury demand
Identifies job insecurity/fear of unemployment causing postponement of big non-essential purchases
application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 per boutique a month
References footfall falling by a third / two nearby luxury retailers closing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 10%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 10% price cut shrinks the profit margin on every watch sold, yet the boutiques still have to pay 14 specialist sales staff and rent. [k] Takings are already down to $95,000 per boutique a month, so lowering prices could erode profit further unless sales volume rises sharply. [app] Lower margins reduce the cash available to ride out the slump and could force staff hour cuts. [an] Problem 2: Heavy discounting can damage the exclusive brand image that convinces customers to pay high prices. [k] Keeping prices unchanged protects that exclusive image, but cutting prices by 10% may teach buyers to wait for discounts rather than pay full price. [app] If the exclusive image weakens, takings may never recover to $130,000 a month even when the slump ends. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut reduces profit margins per unit
Identifies that discounting damages an exclusive/premium brand image
application_max_2: References takings of $95,000 vs $130,000 or the 14 specialist sales staff
References the exclusive brand image / 10% discount
analysis_max_2: Explains the margin/volume trade-off and its effect on cash (staff cuts)
Explains how a weakened brand image undermines long-term takingsRecovery

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches should cut prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: No: cutting prices by 10% would shrink margins on all watches and risk destroying the exclusive brand image. [k] Takings per boutique have fallen from $130,000 to $95,000, but a 10% discount would erode what profit remains and encourage buyers to delay purchases. [app] The VAT cut from 20% to 15% already lowers shelf prices by about 4% if passed on, which stimulates demand without the firm cutting its own prices. [an] Yes: a 10% cut could attract cautious buyers who feel they are getting value, especially during the 12 months the VAT cut lasts. [k] Takings of $95,000 a month per boutique show demand is weak; a well-advertised 10% discount could clear slow-moving stock and draw customers back into the 2 boutiques. [app] More sales at lower margin could raise total profit if enough extra customers are attracted, but it is uncertain whether a slump can be discounted away. [an] Overall, the partners should keep headline prices unchanged and pass on the VAT cut instead of cutting prices by a full 10%, because protecting the brand and margin matters most for luxury goods in a slump. [eval] This is justified by the collapse in takings from $130,000 to $95,000; discounting heavily rarely restores luxury demand, so a modest VAT-linked saving is the safer move. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the margin/brand-image argument against a 10% price cut
Identifies the demand-stimulation argument in favour of a 10% price cut
application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 and the VAT cut from 20% to 15%
References the 2 boutiques, 12-month VAT window or footfall fall
analysis_max_2: Explains the VAT pass-on as a softer demand stimulus (roughly 4% shelf-price fall)
Explains the margin/volume/brand trade-off and its effect on profit
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. keep prices, pass on VAT saving)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

scenario_stem:
Willowbank Textiles is a secondary sector weaving mill producing grey cotton fabric sold to garment factories at $4.10 per metre. It sold 1.6 million metres, earning $6.56 million revenue, with a 6% margin.

They consider $800,000 in dyeing and finishing machinery to supply ready-to-use coloured fabric at $6.40 per metre. Overseas garment exporters offer two-year contracts if colours match specifications. The alternative is continued grey fabric on shorter orders; Daniel expects around 400,000 metres yearly.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'secondary sector'.
questions.model_answer: The part of the economy that manufactures and processes raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods, and includes construction [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Willowbank Textiles could add value to its fabric.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Further processing [k], by using the $800,000 dyeing and finishing machinery to sell ready-to-use coloured fabric at $6.40 per metre instead of grey fabric at $4.10 [app]. Way 2: Meeting customer specifications [k], by matching the colour specifications required by overseas garment exporters to win two-year contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: further processing/conversion of raw materials into finished goods
application_max_2: coloured fabric at $6.40 per metre vs grey at $4.10

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Willowbank Textiles might face if it invests in dyeing and finishing.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Cost pressure and debt [k], the $800,000 machinery must be repaid while the profit margin is only 6% [app], so any order shortfall could push the mill into losses [an]. Problem 2: Skills and quality risk [k], workers must learn to colour-match to the garment exporters' specifications [app], and rejected batches could breach the two-year contracts and trigger penalties [an].

knowledge_max_2: high capital outlay must be repaid from thin margins
new skills/quality control needed for specialised products
application_max_2: two-year contracts and shorter lower-margin orders

scenario_stem:
Suncourt Flowers is a family-owned private limited company growing roses and lilies for 3 national supermarket chains. It harvests daily and stores up to 4 days of unsold flowers in a chilled store costing $3,600 weekly; at peak it holds $28,000 of flowers.

questions.question_text: State two advantages of low inventory levels for a business.

Benefit 2: Just-in-time also reduces waste [k]. The 9% of output lost to unsold stock should fall because flowers are cut only to known demand [app].

Risk 2: JIT depends on reliable partners and offers no protection against cancellations [k]. scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting is a private limited company casting 240,000 brake housings, employing 84 machine operators and 12 inspectors across 2 shifts at $12.40 hourly. Last year 27 accidents, more than double the 13 two years ago, with noise at 95 decibels and burns from molten metal.

Viktor Lam decides before a safety audit in 8 weeks: Option A, invest $55,000 for Maslow's safety needs, or Option B, raise 96 workers' pay 8% to $13.39 hourly.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'motivation'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting should invest in safety before raising pay.
questions.model_answer: One reason is Maslow's hierarchy of needs [k]. With 27 accidents last year, noise at 95 decibels and fear of burns from molten metal, workers cannot move up the hierarchy towards esteem and self-actualisation while they feel physically unsafe [app]. A second reason is that accidents destroy productivity and cost money [k]. Every injury means lost shifts and investigation time across the 2 shifts, so preventing injuries is cheaper and more reliable than enduring them [app].

questions.model_answer: One benefit is fewer accidents [k]. Extraction fans, heat shields and quieter machines would cut exposure to fumes, burns and noise, so the 27 accidents reported last year should fall towards the 13 seen 2 years ago [app], keeping the 84 machine operators productive and the 2 shifts running on schedule [an]. A second benefit is a stronger audit outcome [k]. The improvements directly answer the safety audit due in 8 weeks and show the workforce that management takes its duties seriously [app], which should lift confidence, morale and willingness to stay at the plant [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting should choose Option A? Justify your answer.

Maslow's hierarchy shows safety needs must be met before higher motivation is possible, and with 27 accidents more than double the 13 recorded 2 years ago, plus 95 decibel noise, no pay rise makes molten metal safer [app]. The $55,000 covers physical safeguards used by all 96 workers, and passing the 8-week safety audit protects production of the 240,000 brake housings a year [an]. Option B is simpler — 8% more pay, $13.39 per hour for every worker, no machinery changes [k]. Herzberg would class this as a hygiene factor: welcome, but it prevents dissatisfaction rather than creating motivation, so the fear of burns persists [app]. It also permanently raises the wage bill by $0.99 per hour per worker regardless of safety outcomes [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the right choice [eval] because the stem's own evidence — double the accidents and dangerous noise — points to unmet safety needs that Option B cannot fix, however welcome $13.39 per hour feels [eval].

scenario_stem:
Rushton Paper Mill Ltd is a private limited company producing 26,000 tonnes of kraft paper a year on a 10-year-old machine with 120 workers on 3 shifts. Last year it scrapped 2,080 tonnes, or 8% of output, and spent $150,000 disposing of waste.

questions.question_text: Identify two ways kaizen can reduce waste in a factory.

Benefit 2: A 25% waste cut frees up machine capacity [k]. questions.question_text: Do you think Rushton Paper Mill Ltd should adopt kaizen instead of buying the laser trimmer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for kaizen: it attacks the same 8% wastage at low cost, avoiding the $250,000 trimmer outlay [k]. Weekly team meetings and a suggestion scheme build a culture of continuous improvement and lift morale on the shop floor [app]. Because kaizen is gradual, savings build over 12 months without debt or long machine downtime [an]. Arguments for the trimmer: it would cut trimming waste by 40% at once, beating the 25% kaizen target in year one [k]. Kaizen also demands sustained management commitment, whereas the trimmer is a one-off purchase [an]. Overall, kaizen is the better first step given its low cost, morale gains and 25% target, with the trimmer deferred until 12-month results are visible [eval]. However, if the board demands a guaranteed, fast 40% waste cut and cash is available, buying the trimmer now is the stronger choice [eval].

scenario_stem:
Baobab Sewing Cooperative is a rural cooperative making school uniforms. It sells 210 uniforms a month at $18 each and wants a $5,400 industrial sewing machine to fulfil a local school contract for 500 uniforms.

A government enterprise grant of $2,000 is available to rural start-ups creating at least 3 jobs. A micro-finance lender offers $5,400 over 24 months at 12% interest. Members have saved $900 and add $300 a month from profits, but work part-time around farming.

questions.question_text: Define 'micro-finance'.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance is the provision of very small loans and financial services to people who cannot access traditional bank finance, typically to start or grow a very small business [2].

knowledge_max_2: very small loans for people excluded from bank finance

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the government enterprise grant for the cooperative.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The $2,000 grant does not need to be repaid [k], so it directly reduces the amount the cooperative must borrow for the $5,400 machine [app]. Advantage 2: The grant supports rural start-ups that create jobs [k], helping the cooperative fund its plan to hire at least 3 local women when it signs the school contract [app].

knowledge_max_2: grant is not repayable — free funding
grant encourages job creation in rural areas
application_max_2: $2,000 reduces the $5,400 machine cost needing finance
at least 3 local jobs requirement links to the school contract

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of relying only on the cooperative's own savings.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: The members' savings total only $900 [k], exactly one sixth of the $5,400 machine [app], so saving alone cannot fund the school contract in time and the cooperative risks losing the 500-uniform order [an]. Limitation 2: Accumulating savings is slow [k]; even with the $2,000 grant, covering the remaining $3,400 at $300 a month would take about 11 months, and 18 months without the grant [app], by which time the school may have sourced its uniforms elsewhere [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think the cooperative should take the micro-finance loan or wait and save from profits? Justify your answer.

Waiting to save $300 a month [k] avoids all interest and keeps the cooperative debt-free [app]; but saving the full amount would take 18 months, and even after the $2,000 grant about 11 months, risking the school contract entirely [an]. On balance, the cooperative should take the micro-finance loan and still apply for the $2,000 grant [eval], because the machine's revenue gain far outweighs roughly $1,296 of interest over 2 years [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Penny & Thread is a private limited company running 3 discount clothing stores in low-income areas, selling own-brand clothing and basics, with 27 staff and revenue of $4.9 million. The government raised weekly benefits by $30 per child and cut income tax for low-income households to 10%.

Footfall has risen 12% in 3 months and shelves empty faster. The directors must decide whether to open a fourth store in a deprived estate for $600,000, or refurbish the existing 3 stores for $250,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'redistribution of income'.
questions.model_answer: Redistribution of income is the transfer of income from higher-income groups to lower-income groups, for example through taxes and benefits, to make the distribution of income more equal. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the transfer of income from richer to poorer groups
Identifies the mechanism (taxes and benefits) or the aim (greater equality)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the government's redistribution of income on Penny & Thread.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Low-income households have more money to spend, so demand for discount clothing rises; footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months. [k] [app] Effect 2: Higher benefits of $30 per child per week and an income tax rate of just 10% raise disposable income, increasing sales of own-brand clothing and school uniforms at low prices. [k] [app]

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of refurbishing the existing 3 stores instead of opening a fourth.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Refurbishment at $250,000 costs less than half of the $600,000 needed for a new store, so the firm avoids heavy borrowing and keeps a cash cushion. [k] With revenue of only $4.9 million, committing $600,000 to an untested estate is a big financial risk. [app] Lower capital spending means lower financial risk and a quicker return on the investment, protecting profit and the 27 jobs. [an] Advantage 2: Upgrading the existing 3 stores keeps proven locations and customer bases while adding space and better displays to handle the 12% footfall rise. [k] The stores already sell own-brand clothing and uniforms that low-income families depend on, so improvements will directly serve current customers. [app] Refurbishment raises capacity where demand is already proven, so sales can rise with far less risk than opening in an untested estate. [an]

questions.question_text: Do you think Penny & Thread should open the fourth store in the deprived estate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: opening the fourth store puts Penny & Thread directly in front of the low-income families who have just gained from the redistribution of income. [k] Benefits up by $30 per child per week, an income tax rate of just 10% and a 12% rise in footfall all point to durable demand that the existing 3 stores cannot absorb. [app] A fourth store in a deprived estate would capture this demand, spread fixed costs across 4 stores and lift revenue beyond $4.9 million. [an] However, the new store costs $600,000, more than twice the $250,000 refurbishment, and the benefit increase could be reduced in a future budget. [k] If demand falls back, the fourth store's rent and wages would burden the business, whereas refurbishing the existing 3 stores copes with growth at lower cost and lower risk. [app] Staying small protects the 27 staff and the proven customer base, but shelves are already emptying faster and customers may switch to rivals. [an] Overall, the directors should open the fourth store, because the 12% rise in footfall and the ongoing benefit increase justify expanding into underserved areas. [eval] This is justified by the demonstrated rise in low-income spending; staging the opening over 12 months would manage the risk of a future policy reversal. [eval]

scenario_stem:
Greystone Quarry Partners is a primary sector limestone quarry employing 38 people. It sells raw crushed stone to builders at $18 per tonne; last year it supplied 55,000 tonnes. Housing demand is rising, and builders request graded stone for concrete.

The partners weigh a $275,000 crushing, grading and washing plant producing processed aggregates at $44 per tonne. It must meet environmental standards with dust controls, installation takes 8 months, interrupting output, and 3 regular builders hold standing orders.

questions.question_text: State two ways a business can increase the added value of its products.
questions.model_answer: Any two of: processing or manufacturing raw materials into finished goods; improving packaging and presentation; building a strong brand image; providing better customer service or after-sales support [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Greystone Quarry Partners of installing the crushing and grading plant.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A higher selling price [k], processed aggregates sell at $44 per tonne against $18 per tonne for raw stone [app]. Advantage 2: Stronger customer relationships [k], local builders repeatedly ask for graded stone, sand and chippings ready for concrete production [app].

meeting customer specifications builds loyal repeat demand
application_max_2: processed aggregates at $44 per tonne vs raw stone at $18

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Environmental compliance costs [k], the plant needs dust controls to meet Country X's environmental standards [app], adding to the $275,000 cost and risking fines if emissions breach the rules [an]. Problem 2: Interrupted output and cash flow [k], the 8-month installation period will interrupt crushed stone production [app], so deliveries to regular builders may pause and revenue could stall [an].

However, it carries execution risks [k]: dust controls must meet Country X's environmental standards, and the 8-month installation will interrupt output and cash flow just when builders need stone [app], leaving the partners committed to $275,000 before the first tonne of aggregates is sold [an]. Overall, installing the plant is the better choice because builders are already asking for graded stone and the $26 per tonne uplift across 55,000 tonnes dwarfs the $275,000 cost [eval], but the partners should agree supply contracts and obtain the environmental permit before work begins [eval].

scenario_stem:
Clearway Glassworks is a private limited company making glass tubing, with 52 glass-blowers and 14 packers. Output averages 9,500 metres at a defect rate of 4%. Blowers earn a $1,380 salary, but quit rates reach 15% yearly; Helena Ortiz blames low pay.

Helena chooses: Option A, profit sharing - 3% of annual profit, $70,000, split among 66 staff - or Option B, an individual bonus of $60 while the defect rate stays under 2%, for 5 months yearly.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'teamworking'.
questions.model_answer: Teamworking is organising employees into groups that share responsibility for a task or goal, pooling skills, supporting one another and taking collective ownership of the result [2].

knowledge_max_2: Employees organised into groups sharing responsibility for a task/goal
Pool skills / support one another / collective ownership

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Clearway Glassworks could use Maslow's hierarchy of needs to motivate its glass-blowers.
questions.model_answer: One way is to meet safety needs [k]. Glass-blowing involves molten glass, so better heat-resistant gloves and face protection would reduce the 15% annual quit rate among young blowers by making the workshop feel safe [app]. A second way is to meet esteem needs [k]. Recognising blowers whose defect rate is under 2% with a certificate would make them feel respected and valued, matching the pride Herzberg says esteem-level recognition creates [app].

knowledge_max_2: Safety needs must be met (protection, equipment, safe conditions)
application_max_2: Reference to molten glass / 15% annual quit rate among young blowers
Reference to defect rate under 2% / recognition with a certificate

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of Option B (an individual bonus of $60 per month for defects under 2%).
questions.model_answer: One drawback is weakened teamwork [k]. Paying $60 only for personal sub-2% months rewards individual effort over group success [app], so experienced blowers may stop helping juniors whose defect rates run closer to 4%, eroding the shared skills the workshop needs [an]. A second drawback is the temptation to hide defects [k]. Blowers chasing $60 could pass flawed tubes on to the 14 packers for shipment [app], and faulty laboratory tubing reaching hospitals would mean returns, lost contracts and a damaged reputation far costlier than the bonus pool [an].

knowledge_max_2: Individual rewards can undermine teamwork / helping colleagues
Individual rewards can encourage hiding defects / cutting corners
application_max_2: Reference to $60 per month / sub-2% defect target / juniors near 4%
Reference to 14 packers / laboratory tubing reaching hospitals
analysis_max_2: Chain from individual reward to rivalry to lost shared learning / rising 4% rate
Chain from hiding defects to faulty tubes to returns / lost contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Clearway Glassworks should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is straightforward and equal: 3% of annual profit, about $70,000 this year, split equally among all 66 staff, gives blowers and packers the same stake [k]. On Herzberg's view, financial reward is a hygiene factor — a profit share will not by itself create lasting drive — but it signals the firm values everyone and costs nothing until profits exist [app]. Equal sharing, however, links blower effort only weakly to the payout: each of the 66 staff receives roughly $1,060 whether or not their own defects fell [an]. Option B ties $60 per qualifying month directly to quality: under 2% defects, up to 5 months a year, worth $300 extra for top blowers [k]. It attacks the actual 4% defect rate with a clear personal target and leaves the $1,380 salary untouched [app]. But it ignores the packers entirely, may breed rivalry among the 52 blowers, and does not address why quit rates hit 15% a year [an]. Overall, I think Clearway should choose Option A first, then layer Option B on next year [eval] because equal profit sharing builds firm-wide loyalty at predictable cost, while the individual bonus can be added once defect data is reliable [eval].

Equal profit sharing links pay weakly to individual effort

Chain from personal quality target to lower 4% defect rate but rivalry risk / packers excluded
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem evidence ($70,000 pool, 4% defect rate, 15% quit rate)

scenario_stem:
Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd is a private limited company making hand trowels, forks and rakes, moving parts between 3 separate buildings, where changeovers take 55 minutes. Scrap cost $95,000 last year and late deliveries $30,000, with 38,000 units forecast and 4 retailers on the order book.

The owner considers lean production—cutting waste, reorganising into a single flow and involving workers in improvement—at $60,000 for training and layout changes, versus continuing with a new sales manager aiming to boost revenue within 6 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'lean production'.
questions.model_answer: Lean production is an approach to production that aims to reduce or eliminate waste of all kinds, such as time, materials, stock, movement and defects, from the production process [1]. It also aims to produce only what is needed, when it is needed, using fewer resources [1]. [2]

Cutting the $95,000 metal-offcut scrap through tighter layouts and worker suggestions would directly improve profit [app]. Benefit 2: Lean production shortens changeover times [k]. questions.model_answer: Way 1: Lean removes delays between processes [k]. Reorganising into a single flow instead of 3 separate buildings cuts transport time and waiting between stages [app], so throughput rises without overtime and the 38,000 units forecast becomes achievable [an]. Way 2: Lean reduces late deliveries [k]. Smoother flow and faster 55-minute changeovers mean orders ship on time, helping avoid repeat $30,000 penalty fees [app], which keeps key retail customers loyal and protects future orders [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd should adopt lean production? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for adopting lean: it tackles waste directly, with $95,000 scrap, 55-minute changeovers and $30,000 penalty fees all reducible [k]. A one-off $60,000 for training and layout changes could recover its cost within a year and lift capacity towards 38,000 units [app]. Involving workers in continuous improvement should raise motivation and ownership on the shop floor [an]. Arguments for the sales-manager alternative: that route could boost revenue quickly without reorganising production or spending $60,000 upfront [k]. If workers resist change or meetings fade, lean savings may not materialise [app]. A new sales manager may also open new retail accounts that increase orders immediately [an]. Overall, lean production attacks the root causes of waste and should underpin sustainable growth towards 38,000 units, so adopting it now is justified if the owner commits to training and follow-through [eval]. However, if cash is tight, rolling the changes out gradually, department by department, limits risk while still capturing savings [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Meadowgate Grocers is a private limited company operating 5 neighbourhood supermarkets, each with 6,000 product lines. Employing 88 staff, it had revenue of $16.4 million; inflation reached 6%, above the government's 2% stable prices target.

Costs have risen 8%; suppliers demand more and the government has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively. The directors must decide whether to raise shelf prices by 6%, the first across-the-board rise in 3 years, or absorb costs by cutting staff hours and promotions.

questions.question_text: Define 'stable prices'.
questions.model_answer: Stable prices means the general price level in the economy rises only slowly, i.e. inflation is low and predictable, so money keeps its value. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Meadowgate Grocers of inflation rising to 6%.

[k] [app] Effect 2: Customers' purchasing power falls as prices rise, so shoppers become more price-sensitive and may switch to cheaper goods; with about 6,000 product lines to re-price, the workload and pressure on staff increase. [k] [app]

application_max_2: References the 8% rise in costs / the 6% price rise under consideration

[k] Suppliers of milk, bread and fresh produce have raised prices by 8%, but passing on 6% of that still erodes margins while risking lower footfall across the 5 neighbourhood supermarkets. [app] Lower volumes would spread the 88 staff's wages over fewer sales, raising the average cost per transaction and squeezing profit. [an] Problem 2: Raising prices conflicts with the government's stable prices objective, and the government has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively; bad publicity could harm the brand. [k] The 6% rise would be the first across-the-board increase in 3 years, drawing customer attention to higher bills. [app] Reputational damage could outlast any short-term margin gain, especially if lower inflation arrives soon. [an]

scenario_stem:
Goldenacre Orchard Processing is a secondary sector business buying 500 tonnes of apples at $1,200 per tonne yearly. It presses them into 400,000 bottles of juice sold to supermarkets at $2.50 per bottle. Costs are $300 per tonne.

scenario_stem:
Marlin Rope & Twine Factory is a private limited company producing marine rope, with 44 spinners and 16 finishers. Output is 820,000 metres on $3.1 million revenue. Spinners earn $9.80; absenteeism reached 11% and 3 experienced spinners retired in 2 years.

scenario_stem:
Spinwell Vinyl Ltd is a private limited company pressing vinyl records in batches of 2,000, changing labels and jackets between runs. The machine presses 4,000 records per working day and sold 820,000 records last year, with independent artists ordering 500-1,000 at premium prices.

High capital investment / needs high volumes to break even

Runs of 500-1,000 records for independent artists need different labels and jackets, and changing over between batches makes these variations practical [app]. Reason 2: Batch production suits premium-priced, lower-volume work [k]. scenario_stem:
Redwood Retail Group is a private limited company running 11 discount stores. It plans a $350,000 refit of its largest store over 18 months and $80,000 of stock before the December trading season. Profit after tax was $420,000; retained profit is $260,000.

Directors choose between retained profit for December stock plus a long-term refit loan, or retained profit for the refit plus short-term stock finance. Suppliers offer 60 days' trade credit; refit bank loans cost 8% over 6 years.

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The December stock is needed for only a few weeks [k]; a short-term source such as 60 days' trade credit matches this, as the stock will sell before the refit finishes [app]. Reason 2: Short-term finance avoids paying 8% interest for 6 years on a purchase recovered within weeks [k]; the $80,000 stock will generate cash during December, making a 6-year loan wasteful [app].

Factor 2: Control [k]; using retained profit keeps ownership fully with the existing shareholders [app], whereas outside long-term finance could dilute control or add conditions [an].

scenario_stem:
Redbank Paper Mill is a public limited company producing corrugated cardboard, with 118 workers on 3 shifts at $10.10 hourly. Output is 1.4 million square metres quarterly, but fibre waste reached 8.5% of materials; recycling recovered 3%.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'hygiene factors'.
questions.model_answer: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, hygiene factors are job-related conditions such as pay, working conditions, company policy and supervision; if they are inadequate they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them does not by itself create motivation [2].

Raising wages to $10.61 per hour stops dissatisfaction but soon becomes the expected norm, so the extra motivation fades after the first few pay packets [app]. A second limitation is that pay does not change behaviour at the machine [k]. scenario_stem:
Northpeak Outdoor, a private limited company, makes hiking jackets. Its Northpeak Pro sells 8,500 units at $145, with 45% reordering from 40 specialist outdoor shops across the highlands, built on durability and a premium image.

A budget rival entered at $95 and sales fell 18% last quarter. Directors debate cutting the Northpeak Pro to $110 or holding $145 and spending $60,000 on athlete sponsorship and a 'buy once, last forever' campaign defending the premium image.

Problem 2: It removes margin per unit [k], because each jacket earns $35 less than at $145 [app], which across 8,500 units a year strips about $297,500 of revenue [an].

scenario_stem:
CaseCraft Ltd is a private limited company moulding phone cases under contract for 2 smartphone brands. It adopted just-in-time, holding almost no stock, and orders moulded parts from one overseas supplier with a 12-week lead time and no local alternative.

Two supplier failures halted assembly for 3 days each, costing $96,000 and forcing air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment, while net-30 terms squeeze cash flow. The manager debates rebuilding a 3-week stock for $120,000 or keeping just-in-time and qualifying a second supplier.

questions.question_text: Outline two disadvantages of just-in-time production.
questions.model_answer: If suppliers fail to deliver on time, production must stop because there is no stock to fall back on [1]. The business becomes heavily dependent on reliable suppliers, and any disruption can halt output completely [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Supply delays halt / stop production with no stock fallback

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of just-in-time shown by CaseCraft's experience.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Just-in-time leaves no stock to absorb supplier disruption [k]. Both halts followed supplier failures, and with a 12-week lead time CaseCraft could not quickly replace moulded parts from scratch [app]. Risk 2: A single overseas supplier creates dangerous dependence [k]. The need to air-freight parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment shows how one failing source can sharply raise costs and stress the two smartphone brands [app].

Dependence on a single/unreliable supplier is risky

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of qualifying a second overseas supplier while keeping just-in-time.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A second supplier reduces the chance of a halted line [k]. If one supplier fails, CaseCraft can switch orders across, avoiding 3-day stoppages like the two that cost $96,000 in lost output [app], protecting the two smartphone contracts and future renewals [an]. Benefit 2: A second supplier keeps the benefits of just-in-time [k]. Just-in-time still avoids the $120,000 needed to rebuild a 3-week stock, plus storage costs [app], so the firm keeps its lean cash flow while gaining resilience [an].

questions.model_answer: Arguments for abandoning: two supplier failures in 8 months stopped the line for 6 days in total and cost $96,000 in lost output plus $18,000 air-freight bills [k]. Predictability and customer trust may outweigh stock-holding costs [an]. Arguments against abandoning: a 3-week stock ties up $120,000 that could be used elsewhere and adds storage costs, eroding the savings just-in-time created [k]. Qualifying a second overseas supplier attacks the same risk at lower cost while keeping working capital free [app]. Large stock also raises obsolescence risk for phone-specific parts [an]. Overall, abandoning just-in-time entirely is not justified; qualifying a second supplier plus a small emergency stock of critical parts is cheaper and safer than either extreme [eval]. However, if no second supplier can be qualified within 3 months, rebuilding the 3-week stock is a necessary stopgap [eval].

scenario_stem:
Anchorline Hotel is a private limited company with 48 guest rooms. Revenue was $1,150,000, profit after tax $230,000, and occupancy averaged 74%. The board paid a dividend of $85,000 and holds $96,000 of retained profit brought forward.

The hotel wants to refurbish the kitchen for $140,000 and replace its shuttle vans for $54,000. The finance manager proposes funding the kitchen from retained profit and selling 2 vans for $14,000, but shareholders are divided between higher dividends and investment.

questions.question_text: Calculate the retained profit Anchorline Hotel added this year. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit = Profit after tax − Dividends paid = $230,000 − $85,000 = $145,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: correct formula: profit after tax − dividends

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of using retained profit to fund the kitchen refurbishment.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Retained profit is an internal source of finance [k], so the hotel avoids interest charges on the $140,000 kitchen cost [app]. Advantage 2: Reinvesting retained profit keeps ownership unchanged [k]; no new shares need to be issued and existing shareholders retain full control [app].

knowledge_max_2: internal source: no interest or repayment required
application_max_2: no interest on the $140,000 kitchen cost
no new shares issued; control stays with current shareholders

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of relying only on retained profit to fund both projects.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The two projects total $194,000 [k], more than this year's $145,000 retained profit [app], so the hotel must draw on its $96,000 brought-forward balance, leaving nothing in reserve for next year [an]. Disadvantage 2: Retained profit is finite and may disappoint shareholders [k]; the board already paid $85,000 [app], and shareholders expecting an increase may resent an unchanged or lower dividend while funds are locked into the kitchen and vans [an].

using retained profit may reduce or prevent a dividend

Paying a higher dividend [k] would reward shareholders who backed a 74% occupancy year and satisfy those shareholders wanting immediate returns [app]; however, it would leave the kitchen and vans unfunded, pushing the board towards borrowing or delaying investment that grows future profits [an]. scenario_stem:
Ashford Grain Co-operative is a primary sector partnership of 14 wheat farmers in industrialising Country X. They sell 9,000 tonnes of wheat yearly to exporters at $240 per tonne. Manufacturing grew 8.2% last year, and domestic bakeries import $30 million of flour annually.

questions.question_text: Outline why the primary sector's share of employment falls as a country develops.

questions.model_answer: Batch production allows a range of different products to be made on shared machines, keeping some flexibility between runs [1]. Unit costs are lower than job production because larger quantities spread fixed and setup costs [1]. [2]

Lower unit cost than job production / setup costs spread over batch

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why batch production might help Calloway Rods.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Batch production lowers unit costs for standard lines [k]. Making 3 standard models in batches of 40 would spread labour and machine time across 120 rods, cutting average cost per rod compared with one-off builds [app]. Reason 2: Batch production can supply local angling shops reliably [k]. Stocking 3 standard models in predictable batches of 40 matches exactly what the shops have asked for and relieves the 6-week waiting list [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower unit cost from larger runs / shared fixed costs
application_max_2: 3 standard models x 40 = 120 rods per batch cycle
Angling shops asked for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Calloway Rods could face if it switched fully to batch production.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Unique bespoke work would disappear [k]. Dropping custom orders means giving up the $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods and the loyal customers behind the 6-week waiting list [app], shrinking the firm's premium reputation with serious anglers [an]. Problem 2: Batch production risks unsold stock [k]. If the 3 standard models do not sell in batches of 40, capital is tied up in rods that angling shops cannot shift [app], raising storage costs and waste if designs fall out of fashion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loss of custom/bespoke work and premium reputation
Risk of unsold stock / capital tied up in batches

3 standard models in batches of 40 held as stock

questions.question_text: Do you think Sam should switch the three standard models to batch production alongside the bespoke work? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for switching: producing 3 standard models in batches of 40 spreads setup costs, frees capacity for bespoke rods and shortens the 6-week waiting list [k]. Supplier discounts on identical hand-built cork grips ordered in batches cut material costs further [app]. The angling shops' request widens the market beyond the 260 rods sold last year [an]. Arguments against: splitting production could dilute the bespoke reputation that supports $340 pricing [k]. Batch runs of 40 unsold models tie up cash, and savings only materialise if grips are ordered for proven demand [app]. Overproducing one design would leave expensive unsold stock [an]. Overall, adding 3 standard batch models alongside bespoke work captures shop demand and supplier discounts without abandoning the firm's identity, so the partial switch is justified [eval]. However, Sam should keep batches small and monitor sell-through before expanding, protecting workshop flexibility [eval].

Risks: diluted bespoke identity, unsold stock, tied-up capital

Supplier discounts on identical cork grips; $340 bespoke price
