scenario_stem:
Foxglove Lodge is a partnership guest house with 14 letting rooms, founded by Mark and Leanne Doyle. Revenue was $310,000. Bookings peak in summer. They want a self-catering annexe costing $120,000, adding 8 family rooms, and must repair the kitchen roof for $26,000 while keeping $9,400 a month for wages.

Internal sources are $74,000 of retained profit, an unused minibus worth $22,000, and $30,000 of personal savings. Both owners work full-time and must decide which project to fund first and from which source.

questions.question_text: Identify two needs for finance that Foxglove Lodge has.
questions.model_answer: Capital expenditure for the annexe and the kitchen roof repair [1] and working capital to pay the monthly wages [1].

knowledge_max_2: working capital for day-to-day costs such as wages

questions.question_text: Explain two internal sources of finance available to Foxglove Lodge.
questions.model_answer: Source 1: Retained profit [k]; the lodge has accumulated $74,000 from past profits, which could pay the $26,000 roof repair in full and still leave $48,000 towards the annexe [app]. Source 2: Sale of the unused minibus [k] would raise $22,000 towards the project without borrowing or repaying interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: retained profit — internal reinvestment of past earnings
sale of existing assets — selling unused property or equipment
application_max_2: minibus valued at $22,000 sold to fund part of the annexe

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the owners face when choosing between these sources.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Each source is finite [k]; internal sources total $126,000 but the annexe and the roof cost $146,000 together, a shortfall of $20,000 [app], so something must be delayed, reduced or financed from outside the business [an]. Problem 2: Using personal savings carries a heavy opportunity cost [k]; the $30,000 is also the family's safety cushion [app], and spending it on the annexe would leave them exposed if bookings fell or another repair was needed [an].

knowledge_max_2: internal sources combined may be insufficient for both needs
personal savings involve opportunity cost and lost security
application_max_2: $30,000 personal savings double as the family safety cushion
analysis_max_2: projects cannot both be funded internally — delay, cut scope or borrow
spending savings leaves the family exposed to falling bookings or emergencies

questions.question_text: Do you think the Doyles should build the annexe now or delay it and repair only the roof? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the annexe now [k] would add 8 family rooms and could lift revenue beyond the $310,000 earned last year [app]; internal sources total $126,000, so after the $26,000 roof repair the couple could put $100,000 towards the $120,000 annexe, leaving only $20,000 to find [an]. Delaying the annexe and repairing only the roof [k] would protect the $30,000 personal savings and keep wages of $9,400 a month secure [app]; however, the lodge would forfeit a full summer of extra family-room income and might lose guests to rival guest houses [an]. On balance, the Doyles should build the annexe now [eval], using retained profit, the minibus sale and savings, and covering the $20,000 gap with a small short-term bank loan only if strictly needed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: building now captures new revenue and growth
delaying protects personal security and cash stability
application_max_2: 8 new family rooms could lift revenue beyond $310,000
$126,000 internal sources; $100,000 available after the $26,000 roof, leaving a $20,000 gap
analysis_max_2: extra summer bookings would be forfeited by delaying
savings and $9,400 monthly wages stay protected if the annexe waits
evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation with a clear order of preference
judgement covers how the $20,000 gap would be handled

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Harwick Appliances Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing washing machines and ovens for retailers and export customers in 6 countries, employing 210 workers. Revenue rose from $16.1 million to $18.5 million; wages rose 7%.

The economy is close to full employment; corporation tax has risen from 21% to 25% and skilled workers are scarce. The directors must decide whether to spend $1.5 million automating 2 production lines, cutting the need for 30 assembly workers, or keep manual lines and accept slower output.

questions.question_text: Define 'full employment'.
questions.model_answer: Full employment is a situation in which everyone who is willing and able to work at the prevailing wage rate can find a job, i.e. unemployment is kept at a very low level. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that everyone willing and able to work can find a job
Identifies that unemployment is kept very low

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Harwick Appliances Ltd of the economy being close to full employment.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Skilled assembly workers are hard to find, so Harwick cannot recruit the workers it needs and output cannot grow; it already employs 210 workers at one factory. [k] [app] Effect 2: Wages across the economy are rising fast — Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year — pushing up costs and squeezing profit after the 25% corporation tax. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies labour shortages/recruitment difficulty near full employment
Identifies upward pressure on wages (and costs)
application_max_2: References 210 workers at one factory / inability to recruit assembly workers
References the 7% wage rise or the 25% corporation tax

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of automating the 2 production lines at a cost of $1.5 million.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $1.5 million investment must come from profit or borrowing, so cash is tied up and financial risk rises. [k] With corporation tax now at 25%, profit retained after tax is lower, making the $1.5 million harder to fund internally. [app] High upfront costs must be recovered through higher output, so the automated lines need to run at high capacity for years. [an] Problem 2: Automation would cut the need for 30 assembly workers, causing possible redundancies and lower morale among the remaining 210 workers. [k] Cutting jobs could damage Harwick's reputation as a stable employer in the 6 countries where it sells. [app] Low morale and industrial relations problems could disrupt production and offset the wage savings from automation. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/cash flow risk of $1.5 million or funding difficulty
Identifies redundancies/low morale/reputation risk from automation
application_max_2: References the $1.5 million cost or the 25% corporation tax (reduced retained profit)
References the 30 assembly workers, 210 workers or 6 countries
analysis_max_2: Explains how upfront costs must be recovered through high utilisation
Explains how job losses/morale problems can offset automation savings

questions.question_text: Do you think Harwick Appliances Ltd should automate the 2 production lines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: automating solves the underlying problem — near full employment means labour is scarce and Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year. [k] Harwick employs 210 workers, cannot recruit assembly staff and faces 25% corporation tax, so cutting unit labour costs protects profit. [app] The $1.5 million spent on 2 lines would stabilise output of washing machines and ovens and remove the 30 hard-to-fill vacancies. [an] However, $1.5 million is a major commitment and automating may cut jobs and lower morale among the workforce. [k] Keeping manual lines preserves all 210 jobs and avoids upfront debt, but slower output and rising wages would hold Harwick back while revenue grows from $16.1 million to $18.5 million. [app] Redundancies could also hurt the brand's reputation in 6 markets, though retraining affected workers onto the new lines would soften this. [an] Overall, Harwick should automate the 2 lines, because chronic labour shortages near full employment make the current approach unsustainable. [eval] This is justified by 7% wage growth and the recruitment gap; spending $1.5 million now is cheaper long-term than permanent wage inflation, provided some workers are retrained. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies automation as the fix for labour scarcity/wage inflation
Identifies the job losses/morale/upfront cost risks of automation
application_max_2: References 210 workers, 7% wage rise, 25% corporation tax or the 30 assembly workers
References the $1.5 million cost, revenue growth from $16.1 million to $18.5 million or 2 production lines
analysis_max_2: Explains how automation cuts unit labour costs and stabilises output
Explains the morale/reputation risk and how retraining mitigates it
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. automate with retraining)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

scenario_stem:
Kestrel Construction Ltd is a private limited company building houses and warehouses in Marlow. It owns one plot near the ring road large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse. The houses would earn $900,000 over 18 months; the warehouse $650,000 over 14 months.

With only $120,000 saved for materials, Daniel must choose, since land prices have risen 20% since 2023 and delays could raise costs 15%. Scarcity means every choice carries an opportunity cost.

questions.question_text: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Land refers to all natural resources used to produce goods and services, such as the plot near the ring road in Marlow and materials like timber and sand. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Land = all natural resources used in producing goods and services, e.g. the building plot, timber, sand or land itself
Reward any example of a natural resource input used to make goods or services (2 marks for a clear definition with reference to nature)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why land is important to Kestrel Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Land is a basic factor of production that provides natural resources for making goods [k]. Kestrel's only plot near the ring road is large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse worth $900,000 or $650,000 of revenue [app]. Reason 2: Without suitable land the business cannot produce or sell anything [k]. With no plot to build on, the $900,000 house scheme and the $650,000 warehouse scheme would both be impossible and Kestrel would earn nothing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Land provides natural resources / site / raw materials needed for production
Without land the firm cannot produce or generate sales revenue
application_max_2: Reference to the single plot being large enough for 12 houses or the warehouse
Reference to the $900,000 (houses) and $650,000 (warehouse) revenue figures / the Marlow site

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which opportunity cost affects Kestrel Construction Ltd's decision.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made [k]. By choosing the 12 houses, Kestrel gives up the chance to earn $650,000 from the warehouse, so the true cost of the houses includes the lost warehouse revenue [app]. This means Daniel must compare both revenue streams carefully before spending the $120,000 of scarce materials money [an]. Point 2: Scarcity of the single plot means the land cannot serve both projects [k]. Committing the plot to the housing scheme removes the chance to use it for the warehouse, so every scarce input carries a sacrifice [app]. This forces Daniel to recognise that scarcity creates opportunity cost in all of his decisions, not only in this one [an].

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone when a decision is made
Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants, forcing economic choices
application_max_2: Reference to forgoing the $650,000 warehouse revenue if the 12 houses are chosen (or vice versa)
Reference to the single plot / the $120,000 materials finance as scarce resources
analysis_max_2: Analysis of how foregone revenue or profits changes the true cost of each option
Analysis chain linking scarcity -> choice -> sacrifice -> better decision-making

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrel Construction Ltd should build the 12 houses rather than the warehouse? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the houses: Building 12 houses suits Kestrel's construction skills and could earn $900,000 in revenue [k]. That is $250,000 more than the warehouse's $650,000, even though it takes 18 months rather than 14 [app]. However, the scheme ties up $120,000 of scarce materials money and any delay could raise costs by 15%, squeezing the margin for error on a fixed plot [an]. Argument for the warehouse: The warehouse earns $650,000 within 14 months, releasing cash faster for future projects [k]. Land prices have risen 20% since 2023, so completing quickly protects the value of the Marlow plot [app]. But $650,000 is $250,000 less revenue and would leave Kestrel dependent on a single buyer in a weaker warehouse market [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the housing project offers the higher revenue of $900,000 and matches Kestrel's house-building specialism, so it should proceed only if Daniel secures firm buyer contracts and a contingency for the 15% cost risk [eval]. Otherwise the quicker, lower-risk warehouse would be the wiser choice for a business holding just $120,000 in materials finance [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Houses give higher total revenue ($900,000 vs $650,000)
Warehouse gives faster cash return (14 vs 18 months) and matches 20% land price rise
application_max_2: Uses $900,000 / $650,000 / $120,000 / 12 houses / 18 months vs 14 months figures from the stem
Reference to the single Marlow plot and the 15% cost-overrun or 20% price-rise risk
analysis_max_2: Analysis of revenue, cash-flow timing and cost-risk trade-offs between the two schemes
Analysis of how the decision affects scarce materials finance and future projects
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that is conditional on contracts/cost risk, or favours the warehouse, supported by stem figures
Balanced judgement recognising the risk of the houses scheme vs the security of the warehouse

scenario_stem:
Northgate Fashion Stores is a private limited clothing chain with 5 stores, 26 assistants and 4 managers. Revenue is $3.1m; assistants earn a time-rate wage of $13 per hour. Turnover reached 28%, and customer feedback cited slow fitting rooms.

Directors choose for peak season: Option one, 4% commission on sales, lifting top sellers about $300; Option two, keep time-rate pay and add non-financial methods - job enrichment through window-display styling, teamworking incentives and training to promotion to supervisor.

questions.question_text: Define 'motivation'.
questions.model_answer: Motivation is the willingness of people to work hard and apply effort in their jobs, driven by internal and external factors [2].

knowledge_max_2: employees' willingness to work hard and apply effort
driven by internal and external factors

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Northgate Fashion Stores of introducing a 4% commission for sales assistants.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Higher sales revenue [k], as commission-based pay pushes assistants to sell more in the 5 stores during the peak season [app]. Advantage 2: Lower fixed wage cost for weak sellers [k], as 4% commission lifts top sellers' pay by $300 a month while poor performers earn less than the $13 per hour wage [app].

knowledge_max_2: pay linked to output lowers fixed wage cost

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to this business of the non-financial package instead of commission.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Improved customer service [k], as training and window-display styling give assistants the skills customers asked for in feedback [app], which should lift customer satisfaction and loyalty [an]. Benefit 2: Better retention and a promotion pipeline [k], as job enrichment and training leading to promotion to supervisor motivate ambitious assistants [app], reducing the 28% staff turnover and its recruitment costs [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Fashion Stores should introduce the 4% commission rather than keep the time-rate wage with the non-financial package? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Commission rewards high sellers [k], lifting top pay by around $300 a month and driving sales across the 5 stores during the peak season [app], which could push revenue beyond $3.1m [an]. On the other hand, the non-financial package attacks the root causes [k]: job enrichment, teamworking incentives and training leading to promotion address the feedback about styling advice [app], building loyalty and cutting the 28% turnover [an]. Overall, Northgate should keep the time-rate wage with the non-financial package rather than introduce commission [eval], because its service and retention problems stem from low engagement rather than low pay; the package protects experienced assistants and the $3.1m revenue base more reliably than commission pressure, though a small peak-season bonus could be added later to sharpen effort [eval].

knowledge_max_2: commission drives sales but income varies
non-financial package tackles engagement and retention
evaluation_max_2: weighs engagement-led problems against pay-led incentives; recommends retention-first approach with optional seasonal bonus

scenario_stem:
Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie, a family-run deli, serves about 420 roast-chicken meals weekly. Each costs $8 and, with 25% cost-plus pricing, sells at $10, giving $4,200 revenue and $840 weekly mark-up profit.

A new supermarket deli nearby charges $9.50, attracting price-sensitive shoppers. The owner must keep 25% cost-plus pricing and promote quality, or adopt competitive pricing at $9.50, reviewing the decision in September after 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'mark-up'.
questions.model_answer: A mark-up is the amount added to the cost of a product to arrive at its selling price, usually expressed as a percentage of cost; for example, adding 25% to the $8 cost gives a price of $10 [2].

knowledge_max_2: the amount added to the cost of a product to set the selling price
usually expressed as a percentage of cost

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie of keeping cost-plus pricing.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A guaranteed profit margin [k], as the 25% mark-up on the $8 cost gives $2 per meal and about $840 a week at 420 meals [app]. Advantage 2: Simplicity [k], as the owner can set prices in minutes without tracking the supermarket's $9.50 price every day [app].

knowledge_max_2: guarantees a profit margin on every unit sold
simple and quick way to set selling prices
application_max_2: 25% mark-up on the $8 cost gives $2 per meal
$840 weekly mark-up profit at 420 meals; supermarket charges $9.50

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of keeping 25% cost-plus pricing instead of switching to competitive pricing.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A price above the rival [k], as cost-plus ignores the supermarket's $9.50 meal and leaves the deli at $10 [app], so price-sensitive shoppers may switch, cutting weekly volume and the $840 mark-up profit [an]. Problem 2: No signal from the market [k], as cost-plus only covers the $8 cost plus 25% and ignores what shoppers will pay [app], so falling demand may go unnoticed until the September trading review [an].

knowledge_max_2: cost-plus ignores competitors' prices and market demand
price set above the rival loses sales
application_max_2: $9.50 supermarket meal versus the deli's $10 price
price-sensitive shoppers; 8 weeks of trading data by September
analysis_max_2: cuts weekly volume and the $840 mark-up profit
prevents early detection of falling demand until the review

questions.question_text: Do you think Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie should keep 25% cost-plus pricing rather than switch to competitive pricing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Keeping cost-plus protects the margin [k]: the 25% mark-up yields $2 per meal and about $840 a week at 420 meals [app], and dropping to $9.50 would wipe out $0.50 per meal and roughly $210 a week of profit at 420 meals [an]. However, competitive pricing matches shopper expectations [k]: aligning to the supermarket's $9.50 would win back the price-sensitive lunch trade lost since March [app], potentially restoring volume and protecting the deli's footfall [an]. Overall, Queensbridge should keep cost-plus at $10 rather than match $9.50 for now [eval], because its speed, quality and market-square location remain proven at $10 and a $0.50 cut costs $210 a week before extra sales are guaranteed [eval]. The owner should promote quality and convenience, and review the September trading data before switching.

knowledge_max_2: cost-plus protects a planned unit margin
competitive pricing defends share against a rival
application_max_2: 25% mark-up gives $2 per meal / $840 weekly profit
$9.50 supermarket price; $0.50 cut costs about $210 a week at 420 meals
analysis_max_2: cutting to $9.50 immediately reduces profit even before sales response
matching $9.50 could win back price-sensitive shoppers and restore volume
evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed margin against competitive threat; recommends keeping cost-plus with a review
quantifies $210 a week at risk from a $0.50 price cut

scenario_stem:
Brackenhill Biscuits Ltd is a family-owned private limited company making shortbread and cream crackers, which invested $480,000 in an automated wrapping and packing line using robotic arms to seal 120 packs per minute, replacing 3 benches and 15 jobs.

Since March, output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs weekly and faulty seals fell from 4% to 1%; payback is under 3 years. Yet 15 redundant packers got only statutory pay and morale among 60 factory workers has dipped.

questions.question_text: Define 'automation'.
questions.model_answer: Automation is the use of machines and technology to control and carry out production processes with little or no human input [2].

knowledge_max_2: Use of machines/technology to carry out tasks or control processes
Little or no human involvement or intervention in the process

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brackenhill Biscuits of automating its packing line.
questions.model_answer: First, the line raised productivity [k], sealing 120 packs per minute and lifting weekly output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs [app]. Second, product quality improved [k], as faulty seals fell from 4% to 1% of packs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Improved and more consistent product quality or fewer errors
application_max_2: Line seals 120 packs per minute and weekly output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs
Faulty seals fell from 4% to 1% of packs

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Brackenhill Biscuits of introducing the automated line.
questions.model_answer: First, redundancies [k]: the business made 15 packers redundant, so they received only statutory pay [app], and lower morale among the remaining 60 factory workers could raise absenteeism and errors [an]. Second, high capital outlay [k]: $480,000 had to be spent before the estimated payback of under 3 years [app], so if weekly output falls short of 52,000 packs the family may struggle to recover the cost and stay competitive against imports [an].

knowledge_max_2: High initial capital cost of the investment
application_max_2: 15 packers made redundant and paid only statutory pay; morale dipped among the remaining 60 factory workers
$480,000 was invested with payback estimated at under 3 years
analysis_max_2: Poorer morale could increase absenteeism and mistakes on the line
If demand or output falls below 52,000 packs per week, repaying the investment becomes harder and threatens competitiveness

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenhill Biscuits should invest in automated mixing and baking equipment as well? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, further automation should raise productivity [k]; the packing line lifted output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week and cut faulty seals from 4% to 1% [app]; extending the same technology to mixing and baking could remove more errors, lower unit costs and keep biscuits cheaper than imports [an]. However, automation destroyed jobs [k]; this project cost $480,000, made the 15 redundant packers leave on statutory pay and soured morale among the remaining 60 factory workers [app]; repeating that scale of disruption in mixing and baking, where timing and temperature need judgement, could deepen absenteeism and hurt consistency [an]. Overall I recommend phased investment in automated mixing first, with skilled staff retrained and supervising [eval]; baking should keep human oversight for now, so automating both stages fully would be premature given the morale damage already seen [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automation raises productivity and reduces errors
Automation causes redundancies, high capital cost and morale problems
application_max_2: Output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week; faulty seals fell from 4% to 1%
$480,000 invested, 15 packers redundant on statutory pay, morale dipped among 60 remaining workers
analysis_max_2: More automation could cut unit costs and errors and improve competitiveness against imports
Over-automation in baking could damage morale and product consistency, risking mistakes
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation
Conditional decision (phased approach) supported by stem figures

scenario_stem:
Silverbirch Aerospace Plc is a public limited company making small aircraft components in Country X, with 240 workers and revenue of $18 million last year. It wants a $6.5 million plant to cut delivery times and meet overseas orders.

The Board is choosing between issuing 2.5 million new shares at $2.60 each and a bank loan of $6.5 million over 8 years at 8.5%, costing $552,500 yearly. Its 40 million existing shares make shareholders fear dilution of control.

questions.question_text: Define 'issue of shares' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: An issue of shares is the sale of shares (small ownership stakes) in a company to investors in exchange for capital. It is a long-term source of external finance available to limited companies, and the money raised does not have to be repaid. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sale of shares (ownership stakes) to investors for capital
Money raised does not have to be repaid; long-term external finance for limited companies

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of issuing new shares rather than taking a bank loan to finance the new plant.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: issuing shares provides the $6.5 million of capital without adding fixed repayments, so $552,500 a year of interest is saved and cash flow is eased while the 240 workers are paid [k], which suits a company whose revenue is already $18 million and whose overseas orders are rising [app]. Second advantage: shares carry no obligation to repay the capital, unlike the 8-year bank loan at 8.5%, so the risk of insolvency is reduced if profits fall [k], and the $2.60 issue price means 2.5 million new shares raise exactly the $6.5 million needed without increasing the company's debt [app].

knowledge_max_2: No repayment obligation and no interest to pay on share capital
Reduces insolvency risk compared with fixed loan repayments
application_max_2: $6.5 million raised matches the cost of the new plant

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing new shares for the existing shareholders of Silverbirch Aerospace Plc.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: existing shareholders' ownership would be diluted, because issuing 2.5 million shares to new investors reduces the percentage held by the owners of the existing 40 million shares [k], meaning each share receives a smaller slice of any future dividends and has weaker voting power over how the new $6.5 million plant is run [app], so existing investors may resist the issue or demand a higher share price [an]. Second disadvantage: control of the company could change hands, because new shareholders voting at the AGM may outvote current holders on key decisions [k], for example whether the $6.5 million raised is reinvested to cut delivery times or paid out as dividends [app], so the original owners risk losing their ability to steer the company's long-term strategy [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dilution of existing shareholders' ownership percentage
Possible loss of control; weaker voting power over decisions
application_max_2: 2.5 million new shares compared with existing 40 million shares
Dividend per share and voting strength reduced for current holders
Decisions on spending the $6.5 million / cutting delivery times
analysis_max_2: Dilution leads to smaller dividends and weaker influence, causing shareholder resistance
Loss of control means original owners cannot direct company strategy

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverbirch Aerospace Plc should issue new shares rather than take the 8-year bank loan to finance the new plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Issuing shares would raise the full $6.5 million needed for the plant without creating fixed repayments, saving $552,500 a year of interest and keeping cash flow healthy while orders grow [k], and because revenue is already $18 million with 240 workers, the company can afford to dilute the 40 million existing shares by issuing 2.5 million new ones at $2.60 [app], so the business avoids the risk of defaulting on the loan if overseas demand weakens [an]. However, the bank loan would keep ownership and control unchanged and protect the existing 40 million shares from dilution, costing only $552,500 per year of interest, which a business with $18 million revenue could comfortably cover [k], and loan interest is tax-deductible whereas share dividends are not, and unlike share issues the loan does not permanently reduce shareholders' claim on profits [app], so the loan is less damaging to owners in the long run [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppermill Furniture Ltd is a private limited company making oak dining tables and chairs. It made $2.6 million sales; a 2023 $400,000 loan at 5% leaves $300,000 outstanding.

The base rate has risen from 5% to 9%, adding $12,000 yearly. Priya Raman wants a $180,000 second workshop via a 10% loan costing $18,000 yearly. The order book is full, but customers may spend less if rates stay high; she must decide whether to expand now or wait.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a rise in interest rates on a business with a bank loan.
questions.model_answer: One effect is higher interest payments on the outstanding loan, which reduce profit. A second effect is less cash available to fund other spending or expansion, which may force the business to delay plans. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest payments on an existing loan reduce profit
Higher borrowing costs make new loans more expensive

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the interest rate rise on Coppermill Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Higher interest costs: the rise from 5% to 9% on the $300,000 outstanding balance adds $12,000 a year, which will reduce Coppermill's profit [k], and this extra cost arrives while the machinery loan taken out in 2023 is still being repaid [app]. More expensive expansion finance: the proposed second workshop would need a further loan at 10%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [k], which may make the $180,000 expansion hard to justify if customers spend less while rates stay high [app].

knowledge_max_2: Interest payments on an existing loan increase when rates rise
New borrowing becomes more expensive when rates rise
application_max_2: The outstanding balance is $300,000, so the rise from 5% to 9% adds $12,000 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why rising interest rates might reduce demand for Coppermill's furniture.
questions.model_answer: Higher mortgage and loan payments: rising interest rates increase the cost of borrowing for households [k], so buyers of oak dining furniture already stretched by higher monthly repayments have less money to spend [app]. As buyers postpone big-ticket purchases, Coppermill's order book may shorten from its current 6 months, cutting future revenue [an]. Attractive savings returns: higher rates make saving more rewarding, so households save rather than spend [k], meaning demand for non-essential items like oak furniture falls [app], which would leave Coppermill with unsold stock and lower cash inflow [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for consumers
Higher interest rates make saving more attractive than spending

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya Raman should proceed with the $180,000 expansion now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Proceeding now would let Coppermill open the second workshop while its order book is full for the next 6 months [k], spreading the $18,000 a year interest on a $180,000 loan across higher sales [app], so profit could rise and the firm could win customers from rivals [an]. However, the rise from 5% to 9% already adds $12,000 a year to existing loan costs, and customers may spend less so demand could drop below the order book's promise [k], leaving the new loan hard to repay on only $2.6 million of sales [app], and serving two loans at once could push the business into debt it cannot service [an]. scenario_stem:

This raises productivity so the $580,000 wage bill is spread over more units and average labour cost per table falls [an]. Point 2: Specialised workers become faster and more skilled at their single stage [k]. Each of the 4 stations such as cutting or finishing would develop deep expertise, keeping quality complaints below the 3% target [app]. scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Bluewater Frozen Foods, a discount retailer, opened 3 stores with $900,000 capital. Its frozen vegetables sell at $3.50 using penetration pricing, against $6.00 at the national chain; $2.75 unit costs leave $0.75 per bag, and first-month sales hit 9,000 bags.

scenario_stem:
Cinderford Brickworks is a private limited company supplying facing and engineering bricks to housebuilders, which spent $250,000 on a mechanised extrusion machine and automatic wire-cutter. The yard employs 74 workers, 30 of whom run the machines.

scenario_stem:
Bramblehurst Joinery Co is a private limited company making bespoke fitted kitchens and bedroom furniture, with revenue of $3.2 million and profit of $290,000. It needs $850,000 for a CNC routing machine to reduce production from 9 days to four per kitchen.

questions.question_text: Define 'bank loan' as a source of finance.

Second reason: although the $76,500 annual interest is a fixed cost, the machine should cut cutting times from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and win more orders, lifting revenue above $3.2 million so the interest is comfortably covered [k], and the 5-year term spreads repayment instead of demanding one large up-front sum the business cannot fund from profit of $290,000 alone [app].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

However, raising to $1.49 adds guaranteed profit [k]: a $0.04 rise on 950,000 annual litres would add around $38,000 a year to fuel margin if volume holds [app], though losing only modest footfall to the 2 rivals within 2 kilometres could erase it through lost shop sales [an]. Overall, Harrington should keep $1.45 [eval], because the shop is the real profit centre and a $0.04 rise risks the footfall that makes the whole site viable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: matching price protects footfall and shop-dependent profit
raising price adds direct margin if volume holds
application_max_2: $1.45 matched price; 1,400 weekly shoppers; $86,000 shop revenue
$1.49 gives $0.04 rise; 950,000 litres = about $38,000 a year
analysis_max_2: shop margins far healthier than fuel's $0.06, so footfall protects total profit
lost footfall could wipe out the $38,000 gain through lost shop sales
evaluation_max_2: recommends keeping $1.45 to protect the shop profit centre
quantifies the $38,000 gain against footfall risk from 2 rivals within 2 kilometres

scenario_stem:
Dunmere Plastics Ltd is a private limited company injection-moulding plastic housings for appliances, running two shifts and 8 moulding machines controlled by $320,000 CAM software. Set-up fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes and scrap from 9% to 4%.

Annual output is 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries, but orders from 2 plants are 80% of output. Extending CAM to the final assembly robot would displace 12 of the 120 employees; the managing director must decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'CAM (computer-aided manufacturing)'.
questions.model_answer: CAM is the use of computer software to control machines and manufacturing processes directly during production [2].

knowledge_max_2: Used to plan and run manufacturing directly in production

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of CAM for Dunmere Plastics Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, faster set-ups [k]; machine set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes [app]. Second, less waste [k]; scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output [app].

application_max_2: Set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes
Scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Dunmere Plastics may face if it extends CAM to the final assembly robot.
questions.model_answer: First, job losses and morale [k]: extending CAM to assembly would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app], which could damage motivation, raise turnover and harm the business's reputation as an employer [an]. Second, high extra cost and risk [k]: after spending $320,000 on moulding CAM, another system must be bought and integrated [app], so if exports to the 3 countries slow, the investment may take longer to repay and strain cash flow [an].

knowledge_max_2: Redundancies/job losses harming morale and reputation
High additional capital cost and repayment risk
application_max_2: Assembly CAM would displace 12 of the 120 employees
$320,000 already spent on the moulding CAM system
analysis_max_2: Displaced workers may leave, reducing goodwill and raising training costs for remaining staff
Extra investment is risky if export demand in the 3 countries weakens, delaying payback

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunmere Plastics should extend CAM to the final assembly robot? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, assembly CAM would compound the gains [k]; moulding CAM already cut set-ups from 45 to 12 minutes and scrap from 9% to 4%, with 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries [app]; extending computer control to assembly could deliver the same consistency at the final stage and help win larger export contracts [an]. However, assembly CAM would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app]; the moulding system already cost $320,000 [k], and forcing 12 redundancies could lower morale, raise absenteeism and increase long-run labour costs among those remaining [an]. Overall I recommend extending CAM to assembly only if the 12 affected workers are retrained or redeployed [eval]; the quality and export benefits justify the move, but rushing it without reskilling would risk the workforce goodwill the business still needs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CAM improves consistency, speed and waste reduction
application_max_2: Set-up fell 45 to 12 minutes; scrap fell 9% to 4%; 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries
Assembly robot would displace 12 of 120 employees; moulding CAM cost $320,000
analysis_max_2: Consistent final assembly could win larger export contracts and cut customer complaints
Forcing 12 redundancies could reduce morale and raise long-run labour costs
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation
Conditional decision supported by stem figures

scenario_stem:
Aldermoor Engineering Ltd is a private limited company making precision metal castings for export, employing 320 workers with revenue of $24 million. It needs $10 million for a finishing facility to double overseas sales from 15% to 30%.

The Board weighs converting to a Plc and issuing 2 million new shares at $5.00, raising $10 million with $400,000 listing costs, against a 7-year bank loan costing $800,000 yearly and $5.6 million total interest. Twelve family shareholders holding 80% fear losing control.

questions.question_text: Define 'share capital' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: Share capital is the money raised by a company through the issue of shares to shareholders, who become part-owners of the company. It is shown in the statement of financial position and is a long-term source of finance for limited companies. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Money raised by issuing shares to shareholders
Shareholders become part-owners; shown in statement of financial position

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of converting to a Plc and issuing shares rather than taking the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: issuing 2 million shares at $5.00 each raises the full $10 million needed for the export finishing facility without creating any repayment obligation [k], so unlike the 7-year bank loan costing $800,000 per year ($5.6 million in total), the company keeps more cash to fund the plan to double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output [app]. Second advantage: a public listing raises the company's profile and makes future share issues and borrowing easier and cheaper [k], and the $400,000 listing cost is a one-off fee, far smaller than $5.6 million of interest over 7 years [app].

knowledge_max_2: Share capital need not be repaid; no interest is payable
Public listing raises profile and eases future fundraising
application_max_2: $5.6 million total interest avoided ($800,000 per year)
$400,000 one-off listing cost compared with $5.6 million interest

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing public shares for Aldermoor Engineering and its family shareholders.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: the existing twelve family shareholders fear losing control, since selling 2 million new shares to the public could reduce the family's combined 80% holding below 50% [k], giving outside investors power to influence decisions on the new export finishing facility and on dividends [app], so the founding family could lose the final say over the company's direction just as overseas sales are set to double [an]. Second disadvantage: public companies face much heavier legal and reporting duties, including publishing audited accounts and informing the stock exchange [k], costing time and about $400,000 just to list, money a 320-worker company could otherwise spend on the $10 million facility [app], reducing the finance actually available for the expansion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dilution of family control; possible loss of majority ownership
Heavier legal disclosure and reporting requirements for public companies
application_max_2: Family's 80% combined holding could fall below 50%
$400,000 listing cost reduces funds for the $10 million facility
analysis_max_2: Loss of control means outside investors steer strategy at a critical moment
Listing and disclosure costs reduce capital available for the expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Aldermoor Engineering should convert to a public limited company and issue shares rather than remain private and take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Converting to a Plc would raise the $10 million needed through 2 million shares at $5.00 each, with no interest to pay and no $800,000 annual charge for 7 years ($5.6 million saved) [k], and the issue would give the family easier access to large sums of capital for its plan to double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output [app], removing the fixed repayment burden that a $24 million-revenue private company must carry even in weak trading years [an]. However, selling public shares could cut the family's 80% holding below 50%, so they would lose control of the company they built [k], and public status brings audit costs, listing fees of about $400,000 and ongoing disclosure duties that a 320-worker private limited company has so far avoided [app], which may outweigh the interest saving if the family values control above growth [an]. Overall, I think Aldermoor should remain a private limited company and take the 7-year bank loan, because preserving 80% family control and avoiding the disclosure burden matters more than saving $5.6 million of interest, provided profits can cover the $800,000 annual interest [eval]. If the family wanted to grow faster and share the risk with outside investors, the public share issue would be the bolder and cheaper long-term choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Plc share issue raises capital with no repayment or interest obligation
Public status brings disclosure duties; loan keeps company private and control intact
application_max_2: 2 million shares at $5.00 raises $10 million; $5.6 million interest avoided
$400,000 listing cost and disclosure burden for a 320-worker business
analysis_max_2: No fixed repayments protect cash flow in weak trading years
Loss of majority control gives outside investors influence over strategy
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing control against interest savings
Acknowledges conditions under which the public issue would be preferable

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Saltwood Coffee Roasters is a private limited company supplying roasted coffee beans to 240 independent cafés. With 16 staff, it produced 320,000 bags last year. Inflation has reached 9.5%, lifting green bean costs 40%, roasting energy 22% and packing wages 8%.

Cost per bag rose from $17.50 to $21.00. Tomás Ibero must choose: raise the $24.00 price to $27.50 (14.6%) next month, or hold it to keep loyal café customers. Two key café customers complained about smaller rises in 2025.

questions.question_text: Outline two ways high inflation can affect a business.
questions.model_answer: One way is that input costs such as raw materials, energy and wages rise, squeezing profit margins. A second way is that consumers' purchasing power falls, so demand may drop as customers spend less. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises the cost of inputs such as materials, energy and wages
Inflation reduces consumers' purchasing power, lowering demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Saltwood's profit margin has fallen.
questions.model_answer: Rising input costs: inflation of 9.5% has pushed green coffee bean costs up 40% and roastery energy up 22% [k], so the cost of producing a 1kg bag has climbed from $17.50 to $21.00 [app]. Wage increases: packing staff wages have risen 8% [k], adding to costs that cannot be passed on while the wholesale price is held at $24.00 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Rising input costs reduce profit margins
Rising wage costs increase production expenses
application_max_2: Green coffee bean costs are up 40% and roasting energy up 22%
Production cost per bag has risen from $17.50 to $21.00 with wages up 8%

questions.question_text: Explain two risks for Saltwood of raising the wholesale price to $27.50.
questions.model_answer: Loss of café customers: raising prices by 14.6% may push price-sensitive cafés to cheaper suppliers [k], while two key café customers already complained about Saltwood's smaller 2025 price rises [app], so losing their weekly orders would cut volume across the 240 café network [an]. Reduced demand: higher wholesale prices may force cafés to raise their own prices, reducing café footfall [k], which passes inflation pressure onto end customers [app], shrinking Saltwood's sales and making the recovery of its 12.5% margin harder [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices may push customers to cheaper suppliers
application_max_2: Two key café customers already complained about smaller price rises in 2025
Saltwood supplies 240 independent cafés and a 14.6% rise is proposed
analysis_max_2: Losing café customers cuts sales volume and revenue
Passing costs on to cafés may reduce end-consumer demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltwood should raise the wholesale price from $24.00 to $27.50? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising the price would restore Saltwood's margin: at $27.50 against a $21.00 cost, margin would rise from 12.5% to about 24% [k], and with bean costs up 40%, holding $24.00 would destroy profit on 320,000 bags a year [app], threatening the jobs of 16 staff [an]. However, a 14.6% increase may drive loyal café customers to rivals [k], and Saltwood has already faced complaints from two key customers in 2025 [app], so volume could fall and erase the benefit of the higher price [an]. On balance, Saltwood should raise the price, but by a smaller amount or with advance notice and quality assurances [eval], because the margin evidence shows it cannot absorb another year at 12.5% [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Raising price can restore profit margins when costs rise
Raising price risks losing customers to competitors
application_max_2: Production cost per bag rose from $17.50 to $21.00 while the price is held at $24.00
Two key café customers complained about the smaller 2025 price rises
analysis_max_2: A higher price protects profit and staff jobs
Volume loss from unhappy cafés could erase the margin gain
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the $27.50 price
Judgement weighs margin recovery against customer loyalty risk

scenario_stem:
Sunvalley Foods Ltd is a food processing company freezing mixed vegetables for supermarket own-brands. It employs 46 production staff producing 30,000 bags weekly across five stages: sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing.

Aoife wants permanent specialisation so each worker does one stage. Similar factories raised output 40%, but staff fear boredom, and 2 workers left after a 3-month trial last year. Training one worker costs $800, and rejection rates stand at 6%.

questions.question_text: Define 'division of labour'.
questions.model_answer: Division of labour is where production is split into separate tasks and each worker specialises in one task, such as sorting, washing, cutting, blanching or packing mixed vegetables. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Division of labour = splitting production into small distinct tasks
Each worker specialises in just one repeated task / stage

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why businesses use division of labour.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Division of labour breaks production into small tasks so workers specialise [k]. Sunvalley splits its line into five stages — sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing — across 46 production staff [app]. Reason 2: It raises productivity and speeds up output [k]. In similar factories specialisation raised output by 40%, which would push Sunvalley well beyond its current 30,000 bags per week [app].

knowledge_max_2: Workers specialise in one repeated task rather than all tasks
Specialisation speeds up work / raises productivity through practice
application_max_2: Reference to the five stages and 46 production staff
Reference to the 40% output gain and 30,000 bags per week from the stem

valid_app_words: sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Sunvalley Foods Ltd might face after introducing specialisation.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Repetitive specialist work causes boredom and lowers motivation [k]. Sunvalley already lost 2 workers after a 3-month specialisation trial last year, showing that single-stage work can demoralise the 46 production staff [app]. This raises recruitment and training costs at $800 per replacement and disrupts the 30,000-bag weekly target [an]. Point 2: Over-dependence on key specialists creates bottlenecks [k]. If the cutting specialist is absent, the whole line can stall because each worker masters only one stage [app]. This risks raising rejection rates above the current 6% and jeopardising supermarket own-brand contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Monotony/boredom reduces motivation and can raise labour turnover
Over-specialisation creates dependency on individuals, risking bottlenecks
application_max_2: Reference to the 2 workers lost after the 3-month trial and $800 retraining cost
Reference to the 6% rejection rate / possible contract loss
analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from boredom -> resignations -> higher costs and disrupted output
Analysis chain from absence of a specialist -> line stoppage -> missed orders

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunvalley Foods Ltd should introduce permanent specialisation on its production line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for specialisation: Giving each of the 46 production staff one of the five stages could raise output by 40%, easing the strain on the 30,000-bag week [k]. Trained specialists make fewer mistakes, which should help push rejection rates below the present 6% [app]. However, boredom could worsen turnover, following the 2 resignations seen in the 3-month trial [an]. Argument against: Keeping job rotation preserves motivation and flexibility [k], and retraining everyone at $800 each would be wasted if staff keep leaving or demand shifts between stages like blanching and packing [app]. But rotation means slower throughput and caps output at 30,000 bags a week for a growing own-brand range [an]. Overall, permanent specialisation is justified if Aoife combines it with job rotation, structured training at $800 per head and close monitoring of the 6% rejection rate, because the 40% output gain is too large to ignore for supermarket contracts [eval]. Imposing rigid single-task roles without staff consultation would only repeat last year's resignations [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation can raise output by 40% and reduce mistakes
Rotation preserves motivation; rigid tasks risk turnover and training waste
application_max_2: Uses the 40% figure, 30,000 bags, 6% rejections, $800 training cost and the 2 resignations
Reference to the five stages and 3-month trial from the stem
analysis_max_2: Analysis of productivity gains vs turnover/retraining costs
Analysis of quality and flexibility trade-offs for the supermarket range
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on rotation/consultation/monitoring
Balanced judgement weighing the 40% gain against boredom and resignations

scenario_stem:
Curl & Co Hair Studio is a sole trader unisex salon with 11 stylists and 2 receptionists. Revenue is $420,000, retail products 15%. Stylists earn 6% commission, averaging $1,900 monthly but $650 in quiet months, and turnover reached 27%.

Lena Ortiz wants motivation: option one raises commission to 9% with a $250 quarterly bonus; option two keeps 6% commission but builds teamworking with shared stylist stations, joint client consultations, colour techniques training and promotion after 18 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'teamworking'.
questions.model_answer: Teamworking is organising employees into groups to work cooperatively on shared tasks or goals, rather than working entirely alone [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of raising commission to 9% with the $250 quarterly bonus.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Stronger individual selling incentive [k], as 9% commission on cuts, colour and treatments lifts earnings above the current $1,900 average month [app]. Advantage 2: Extra reward for top performers [k], as the quarterly $250 bonus singles out the top-selling stylist and pushes everyone to compete for it [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of option two for Curl & Co Hair Studio.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Better client experience and loyalty [k], as shared stylist stations and joint client consultations help the 11 stylists share ideas and solve problems together [app], encouraging repeat visits and extra retail sales [an]. Benefit 2: Lower stylist turnover [k], as weekly training in colour techniques plus promotion to senior stylist after 18 months give staff a future [app], reducing the 27% turnover rate and recruitment costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: improved retention through training and promotion
analysis_max_2: repeat visits and extra retail sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Curl & Co Hair Studio should choose the teamworking option rather than raise commission to 9%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising commission to 9% would boost individual earnings [k], lifting sellers above the $1,900 monthly average and rewarding colour treatment sales [app], which could lift takings during busy weeks [an]. However, quiet months already see takings fall to $650 [k], and a bigger commission plus the $250 bonus may widen rivalry between the 11 stylists rather than cooperation [app], doing little to fix the 27% turnover rate [an]. Overall, Curl & Co should choose the teamworking option rather than raise commission to 9% [eval], because low, unpredictable income and 27% turnover point to disengagement rather than weak incentives; shared stations, joint consultations, weekly training and promotion after 18 months protect loyalty and client experience while the 6% base commission keeps some link between pay and effort [eval].

knowledge_max_2: turnover suggests disengagement needing non-financial action
analysis_max_2: rivalry may worsen turnover and cooperation
evaluation_max_2: recommends teamworking justified by income variability and turnover root cause

scenario_stem:
Willowmere Home & Furniture runs an out-of-town warehouse. Each bank holiday, promotional pricing cuts lines 20% for 4 days; a $1,200 sofa goes for $960. April drew 3,800 visitors and 420 sofas, lifting revenue to $980,000 from $610,000 in March.

As 55% of sales came from repeat bargain-hunters, the board is choosing between extending promotional pricing to every weekend in July and August or keeping just 6 bank holidays, with 2,900 sofas in stock.

questions.question_text: Define 'promotional pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Promotional pricing is reducing the selling price of a product for a short period to boost sales, attract customers or clear stock; the price returns to normal after the promotion ends [2].

knowledge_max_2: reducing the price for a short period
used to boost sales, attract customers or clear stock; price returns to normal afterwards

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Willowmere Home & Furniture of promotional pricing.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A strong short-term sales boost [k], as the April event sold 420 sofas at $960 and lifted April revenue to $980,000 against $610,000 in March [app]. Advantage 2: Attracts new and repeat visitors [k], as the event drew 3,800 visitors, widening Willowmere's customer base [app].

knowledge_max_2: boosts sales quickly during the promotion
application_max_2: April event sold 420 sofas; revenue rose to $980,000 from $610,000
3,800 visitors attended the April event; $960 sale price

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of extending promotional pricing to every summer weekend for Willowmere.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Lost margin on every sale [k], as the $1,200 sofa sells at $960, giving up $240 per sofa [app], so 2,900 summer sofas at 55% bargain-hunter reliance could forfeit deep margin [an]. Problem 2: Customers wait for discounts [k], as 55% of event sales already came from repeat bargain-hunters [app], so everyday $1,200 prices may stop selling at full price [an].

knowledge_max_2: margin is sacrificed on every discounted unit
customers become trained to wait for sales, damaging full-price demand
application_max_2: $1,200 sofa sells at $960, losing $240 per unit
55% of event sales from repeat bargain-hunters; 2,900 sofas in stock
analysis_max_2: extending discounts across the summer could cost a very large share of margin
full-price sales collapse once bargain behaviour becomes the norm

questions.question_text: Do you think Willowmere Home & Furniture should extend promotional pricing to every summer weekend rather than keep bank-holiday events only? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Every-weekend discounting would shift summer stock fast [k]: sale events could clear part of the 2,900-sofa stock at $960, adding weekly volume, as April's event pushed revenue to $980,000 against a $610,000 March [app], converting floor stock to cash before the autumn delivery cycle [an]. However, constant sales would damage the everyday price [k]: with 55% of event sales from repeat bargain-hunters, extending discounts risks training customers to never pay $1,200, and margin lost at $240 per sofa across 2,900 sofas amounts to $696,000 [app], wiping out the April-style revenue gain if full prices stop selling [an]. Overall, Willowmere should not discount every weekend [eval]; it should keep bank-holiday promotions and add at most one mid-summer event, protecting the everyday $1,200 price while still capturing some impulse volume [eval].

knowledge_max_2: frequent promotions clear stock and lift short-term cash
constant promotions destroy everyday price integrity and margin
application_max_2: April event sold 420 sofas, revenue $980,000 vs $610,000 March
55% of event sales from repeat bargain-hunters; 2,900 sofas at $240 off = $696,000 at risk
analysis_max_2: summer volume converts stock to cash before the autumn cycle
loss of full-price sales outweighs the promotion revenue gain
evaluation_max_2: rejects every-weekend discounting; recommends keeping bank holidays plus one mid-summer event
quantifies $696,000 margin at risk across 2,900 sofas

scenario_stem:
Aldercroft Auto Components is a private limited company making suspension brackets and exhaust flanges for 2 car assembly plants, with 240 workers and a $1.2 million CIM system linking 14 CNC machines and quality scanners.

Defects fell from 6% to 1.5% and lead time from 21 to 9 days, cutting buffer stock, but CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries and the loan must be repaid. The board debates rolling CIM into a second hall.

questions.question_text: Define 'CIM (computer-integrated manufacturing)'.
questions.model_answer: CIM is the use of a single computer system to link and control all stages of production, from design through manufacture to quality and stock control [2].

knowledge_max_2: Computer systems link and control production stages together
Covers design, manufacture, quality and stock/inventory control in one integrated system

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of CIM for Aldercroft Auto Components.
questions.model_answer: First, better product quality [k]; defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5% after the system was installed [app]. Second, faster delivery [k]; average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days, helping both assembly plants cut buffer stock [app].

application_max_2: Average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days

questions.question_text: Explain two risks or costs of CIM for Aldercroft Auto Components.
questions.model_answer: First, dependence on specialist staff [k]: CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app], so if they leave, the whole production line could stall until replacements are found and trained [an]. Second, financial risk [k]: the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan [app], so the business must keep the 2 assembly plants' orders profitable enough to meet interest payments, or face cash-flow pressure if orders fall [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dependence on scarce specialist IT staff
High capital cost financed by borrowing
application_max_2: 2 full-time IT technicians required on $38,000 salaries
$1.2 million financed by a bank loan
analysis_max_2: If technicians leave or the system fails, production stops and deliveries to both assembly plants are jeopardised
Loan repayments strain cash flow; falling orders would make the debt harder to service

questions.question_text: Do you think Aldercroft Auto Components should roll CIM out to a second production hall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, rolling CIM out to a second hall would replicate proven gains [k]; defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5% and lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days [app]; a second hall could cut buffer stocks for both assembly plants, win more orders and spread the fixed costs of the CIM system [an]. However, the first $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan and the system already needs 2 IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app]; duplicating it doubles loan pressure, and one technical failure could halt even more limited IT capacity [an], even though integration usually lifts productivity [k]. Overall I recommend a phased second-hall rollout funded from operating surplus rather than new borrowing [eval], because the 4.5-point defect fall and 12-day lead-time cut are compelling, but only once the 2 technicians confirm the system is stable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CIM raises quality and speed across production
High capital cost and dependence on specialist staff
application_max_2: Defects fell from 6% to 1.5%; lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days
$1.2 million financed by bank loan; 2 IT technicians on $38,000 salaries
analysis_max_2: Second hall would spread fixed costs, cut buffer stock and win more assembly-plant orders
New borrowing or a single system failure could strain cash and halt production
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation
Conditional decision supported by stem figures

scenario_stem:
Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative is a small co-operative handloom weaving enterprise in Country X employing 18 artisan weavers, with $9,000 saved and sales of $210,000. It wants $45,000 for two new looms and training to raise output from 120 to 180 pieces a month.

Members compare a $45,000 micro-finance loan at 12% over 3 years, costing $5,400 yearly and $16,200 interest, with rewards-based crowdfunding aiming for $45,000 at a 6% platform fee, which may fail to reach its target.

questions.question_text: Define 'micro-finance' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance is the provision of very small loans and other financial services to small businesses or individuals who cannot access traditional bank finance. It is usually delivered by specialist local institutions and supports micro-enterprises and start-ups. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Very small loans provided to those excluded from bank finance
Provided by specialist local institutions to micro-enterprises or start-ups

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of micro-finance for Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: micro-finance guarantees the full $45,000 the co-operative needs for the two new looms and training [k], unlike the crowdfunding option whose target may never be met [app]. Second advantage: the micro-finance institution specialises in rural enterprises and can offer financial advice and support [k], helping 18 artisan weavers run the co-operative professionally as output rises from 120 to 180 pieces a month [app].

knowledge_max_2: Guaranteed access to the required funds if approved
Tailored to small/rural enterprises, often with business advice and support
application_max_2: $45,000 needed for two looms and training
Output to rise from 120 to 180 pieces a month
Members' savings of $9,000 are insufficient alone

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: the micro-finance loan adds fixed repayments of $5,400 of interest per year for 3 years ($16,200 in total) [k], which is heavy for a business with sales of only $210,000 and members' savings of $9,000 [app], so a fall in orders could put the looms and the co-operative's future at risk [an]. Second disadvantage: $45,000 is still a small sum, so Mwangaza cannot use micro-finance to fund much larger expansion or exporting later [k], meaning that if the two looms succeed and output reaches 180 pieces a month, the co-operative will soon outgrow this source of finance [app], limiting its ability to scale up production [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest and repayments burden small cash flows
Micro-finance provides only small sums, limiting expansion scope
application_max_2: $5,400 per year interest; $16,200 in total over 3 years
Sales of $210,000 and members' savings of $9,000
analysis_max_2: Weak cash flow raises default and insolvency risk

Better decisions weigh all alternatives, not only immediate gains

analysis_max_2: Analysis linking foregone alternative to true cost of each option

questions.question_text: Do you think Maria should launch the sugar-free range rather than buy the new kettle line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the sugar-free range: Launching costs $26,000 and taps proven demand, with chutney sales growing 30% and customers explicitly asking for sugar-free jars [k]. Healthier ingredients cost only $0.40 more per jar, preserving margins while unmet demand is captured [app]. However, $26,000 for ingredients and jars is a near-total commitment of the $30,000 budget and the range has never sold at Copperfield before [an]. Argument for the kettle line: The $28,000 boiling kettle line would raise capacity and protect supply of the existing chutney, safeguarding the 30% growth already in evidence [k]. It is a known product so the investment feels safer, but it creates no new demand and yields no extra revenue by itself [app]. By contrast the range could add $90,000 in sales if it succeeds, more than three times its launch cost [an]. Overall, Maria should launch the sugar-free range because the $90,000 upside against a $26,000 cost and explicit customer demand is compelling, provided she trials small batches to limit risk within her $30,000 budget [eval]. The kettle line can be bought later once range sales prove themselves [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ember & Oak Bistro is a sole trader restaurant in a market town with 24 staff: 9 servers, 10 kitchen brigade and 5 managers. It made $96,000 profit. Turnover is 29%, and chefs feel underappreciated despite 46-hour weeks.

Marta Ellison decides in 3 weeks: proposal one, share ownership of 3% of shares for staff with 2 years' service, worth $28,800; proposal two, a $500 loyalty bonus for staff with 1 year's service, costing $9,000 for 18 eligible staff.

questions.question_text: Define 'share ownership'.
questions.model_answer: Share ownership is a financial reward where employees receive shares in the business, giving them a stake in its performance and sometimes dividends [2].

knowledge_max_2: employees receive shares in the business
stake in performance and possible dividends

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the share ownership proposal for Ember & Oak Bistro.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Long-term commitment and loyalty [k], as only staff with at least 2 years of service receive shares valued at $28,800 in total [app]. Advantage 2: Aligned incentives with profit [k], as employee-shareholders benefit when the bistro's $96,000 profit grows [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the one-off $500 loyalty bonus for this bistro.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Immediate morale boost [k], as every staff member with at least 1 year of service feels valued straight away [app], easing tension after busy 46-hour weeks [an]. Benefit 2: Lower, predictable cost [k], as $9,000 for the 18 eligible staff is far cheaper than the $28,800 share distribution [app], protecting cash for kitchen repairs and menu upgrades [an].

analysis_max_2: protects cash for kitchen repairs and menu upgrades

questions.question_text: Do you think Ember & Oak Bistro should offer share ownership rather than the one-off $500 loyalty bonus? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The one-off $500 loyalty bonus is cheap and certain [k], costing $9,000 for the 18 eligible staff this year [app], which lifts mood quickly while turnover sits at 29% [an]. Share ownership is slower to feel [k], yet it binds experienced staff into the bistro's future: 3% of shares worth $28,800 rewards those with 2 years of service [app], aligning the team with the $96,000 profit and deepening the loyalty the kitchen and front-of-house lack [an]. Overall, Ember & Oak should offer share ownership rather than only a one-off bonus [eval], because a one-off payment fades quickly and does not change why staff leave; tying a stake to tenure targets the 29% turnover directly, although pairing it with modest annual recognition would be sensible [eval].
