shares build long-term loyalty and alignment
analysis_max_2: bonus lifts mood fast but fades
ownership targets turnover and aligns with profit
evaluation_max_2: recommends share ownership targeting retention root cause; suggests pairing with annual recognition

scenario_stem:
Hartley & Rye Artisan Bakery runs 2 shops in a market town, with 14 bakers and 1,100 loyal weekly customers. It sells a staple cottage loaf at $3.20 and a premium heritage-grain sourdough at $5.50.

Last year, 10% on the staple cut sales 2%, but 10% on the premium loaf cut them 14%. As sourdough makes 38% of revenue, the owner must choose between raising all prices 10% or only the staple.

questions.question_text: Define 'price elasticity of demand'.
questions.model_answer: Price elasticity of demand describes how responsive demand for a product is to a change in its price: demand is price-elastic when a price change leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded, and price-inelastic when quantity changes proportionately less [2].

knowledge_max_2: describes how responsive demand is to a change in price
elastic = quantity changes proportionately more than price; inelastic = proportionately less

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why demand for Hartley & Rye's staple cottage loaf is price-inelastic.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Bread is a necessity [k], as everyday bread is a staple bought weekly by around 1,100 loyal customers, so the 10% price rise last year cut sales by only 2% [app]. Reason 2: Limited local choice [k], as with only 2 shops in the market town, weekly routines kept shoppers buying despite the rise [app].

knowledge_max_2: everyday bread is a necessity or habit purchase
limited local substitutes keep customers buying
application_max_2: 10% rise last year cut staple sales by only 2%
around 1,100 loyal weekly customers; 2 shops in the market town

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why demand for the premium heritage-grain sourdough is price-elastic.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It is a luxury, not a necessity [k], as the $5.50 heritage-grain loaf is a premium choice, so buyers are more price-aware than cottage-loaf buyers [app], making demand fall sharply when price rises [an]. Reason 2: Substitutes are close at hand [k], as shoppers can switch to the $3.20 cottage loaf or other bread options [app], so the 10% rise cut premium unit sales by 14% [an].

knowledge_max_2: premium products are luxuries that customers cut back on when prices rise
application_max_2: 10% rise cut premium sales by 14%; cottage loaf at $3.20
analysis_max_2: premium spend is discretionary and drops sharply with price rises
easy substitution drives the 14% fall in sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Hartley & Rye should raise all bread prices by 10% rather than only the staple loaf? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising everything rides on the inelastic staple [k]: cottage-loaf sales fell just 2% on a 10% rise last year, so lifting $3.20 to $3.52 would hold volume and lift revenue from around 1,100 weekly customers [app], protecting margin on the highest-volume line [an]. However, lifting the premium sourdough ignores its elasticity [k]: the premium loaf generates 38% of revenue and its sales already fell 14% on the last 10% rise, so a further rise risks steeper losses on the line that matters most [app], eroding revenue despite the higher unit price [an]. Overall, Hartley & Rye should raise only the staple loaf and leave the premium sourdough at $5.50 [eval], because the data shows a price-inelastic staple and a price-elastic premium line, exactly the opposite of what an across-the-board rise needs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: inelastic demand allows price rises with little volume loss
elastic demand means price rises cause steep volume losses
application_max_2: staple fell 2% on a 10% rise; $3.20 to $3.52
premium loaf generates 38% of revenue; sales fell 14% on the last 10% rise
analysis_max_2: staple rise protects margin on the highest-volume line
premium rise erodes revenue and risks losing the line generating 38% of revenue
evaluation_max_2: recommends staple-only increase, leaving the premium sourdough at $5.50
grounds the recommendation in the opposite elasticities shown by the sales data

scenario_stem:
Tannersley Glassworks is a private limited company supplying soft-drink bottlers for 16 years, where 120 workers once made 240,000 bottles weekly, or 2,000 bottles per worker. After 2 furnaces and a forming machine costing $900,000, 96 workers make 288,000 bottles.

That is 3,000 bottles per worker, a 50% productivity rise, with annual output near 15 million. The $900,000 was borrowed; overtime costs $16 per hour time-and-a-half, a furnace takes 18 months to install but lasts 25 years, and bottlers want 40,000 bottles more weekly.

questions.question_text: Define 'productivity'.
questions.model_answer: Productivity is the output produced per worker, or per other input, over a given time period [2].

knowledge_max_2: Measured over a period of time

questions.question_text: Explain two differences between production and productivity.
questions.model_answer: First, what they measure [k]; production is total output, which rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week, while productivity is output per worker, which rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker [app]. Second, how each is increased [k]; production can be raised by adding workers or overtime, while productivity rose because 96 workers replaced 120 after the new machines arrived [app].

knowledge_max_2: Production = total output; productivity = output per worker/per input
Production can be raised by more inputs; productivity by more efficient use of inputs
application_max_2: Total output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week
Output per worker rose from 2,000 to 3,000 after the workforce fell from 120 to 96

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tannersley Glassworks of the rise in productivity.
questions.model_answer: First, lower labour cost per bottle [k]; output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while the workforce fell from 120 to 96 [app], so fixed costs are spread over more units and the business can improve profit to help repay the $900,000 loan [an]. Second, stronger competitiveness [k]; each of the 96 remaining workers now produces 3,000 bottles per week [app], so unit costs fall and Tannersley can undercut rivals to win the contract for an extra 40,000 bottles a week [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher output per worker lowers average cost per unit
application_max_2: Output rose 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while staff fell from 120 to 96
Each worker now produces 3,000 bottles per week
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs are spread over more bottles, improving profit and ability to repay the bank loan
Lower unit costs strengthen competitiveness and support winning the extra 40,000 bottles contract

questions.question_text: Do you think Tannersley Glassworks should raise output further by overtime or by buying a third furnace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, a third furnace would replicate the gains [k]; productivity already rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after the 2 new furnaces were installed [app]; a third furnace would last 25 years and help supply bottlers the extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract [an]. However, overtime is more flexible right now [k]; the $900,000 was borrowed and overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half adds capacity without new long-term debt [app]; but overtime raises labour cost per bottle and cannot match machine efficiency or consistent quality [an]. Overall I recommend buying the third furnace, financed partly from retained profit, because the proven 50% productivity rise shows machines outperform overtime [eval]; if demand softens before contracts are signed, delay the furnace and use overtime as a stop-gap [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Investment in capital machinery raises productivity long term
Overtime adds capacity quickly but at higher unit cost
application_max_2: Productivity rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after 2 new furnaces
$900,000 loan outstanding; overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half; furnace would take 18 months and last 25 years
analysis_max_2: A third furnace locks in capacity and consistency to fulfil the 40,000 bottles weekly contract
Overtime protects cash flow now but erodes unit economics and quality consistency
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options and reaches a clear, justified recommendation
Conditional decision supported by stem figures

scenario_stem:
Drummond Alloys Ltd is a private limited company producing copper and aluminium alloys, with 150 workers and $9 million revenue. A $2 million furnace is needed as ageing plant breaks down 12 times a year.

The Finance Manager compares a $2 million bank loan over 5 years at 8%, costing $160,000 a year, with a $2 million debenture at 7.5%, redeemable after 10 years: holders gain no ownership but first claim on assets, and interest falls $10,000 to $150,000.

questions.question_text: Calculate the total interest payable on the bank loan over its 5-year term.
questions.model_answer: Annual interest = $2,000,000 × 8% = $160,000 per year; total interest over 5 years = $160,000 × 5 = $800,000 [2]

knowledge_max_2: Annual interest = principal × rate = $160,000 per year

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of issuing a $2 million debenture rather than taking the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: the debenture carries 7.5% interest, only $150,000 per year against $160,000 on the bank loan, saving $10,000 per year [k], and debenture interest can be planned around the $2 million furnace project without the early-repayment pressure a bank might apply when plant breaks down 12 times a year [app]. Second advantage: debenture holders are not owners, so control of the company remains with the existing shareholders, and the 10-year repayment profile is gentler than repaying over 5 years [k], giving Drummond Alloys a longer, steadier repayment window for a $2 million furnace that will transform alloy output [app].

knowledge_max_2: Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, so control is retained
Interest fixed and predictable; repayable over a longer term
application_max_2: 7.5% debenture = $150,000 per year vs $160,000 loan, saving $10,000 per year
$2 million furnace needed to stop 12 breakdowns a year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing a $2 million debenture.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: although debenture holders have no vote, they rank ahead of shareholders for repayment and have first claim on the company's assets if it fails [k], and with revenue of only $9 million and a $2 million furnace, assets pledged as security could leave the business with little cushion if alloy orders fall [app], discouraging banks and suppliers from offering further credit on good terms [an]. Second disadvantage: debenture interest of $150,000 per year must be paid even if profits fall, for 10 years, twice as long as the 5-year bank loan [k], so a prolonged downturn in copper and aluminium alloy orders would still leave the company paying $150,000 every year with no flexibility to pause [app], locking the business into high fixed costs for a decade [an].

knowledge_max_2: Debenture holders rank ahead of shareholders; first claim on assets if the company fails
Interest is a fixed charge payable in all years, for a long period
application_max_2: $2 million furnace against revenue of $9 million
$150,000 per year for 10 years versus $160,000 for 5 years
Statement of financial position carries the debenture for twice as long
analysis_max_2: Weak asset cushion increases insolvency risk and deters further credit
Decade-long fixed charge locks cash flow and limits flexibility

questions.question_text: Do you think Drummond Alloys Ltd should issue the debenture rather than take the bank loan to finance the furnace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Issuing the debenture saves $10,000 of interest every year ($150,000 versus $160,000) and stretches repayment to 10 years instead of 5 [k], easing the burden on a company with $9 million revenue that needs the $2 million furnace to stop the roughly 12 breakdowns a year and stabilise output [app], so cash flow under the debenture is more predictable and safer in weak months [an]. However, the debenture ties the company up for 10 years and gives holders first claim on assets if it fails, unlike a 5-year bank loan that would be cleared in half the time [k], and total interest over 10 years ($1,500,000) far exceeds the bank loan's $800,000 [app], so the debenture is cheap per year but expensive overall [an]. Overall, I think Drummond Alloys should take the 8% bank loan, because clearing the debt in 5 years and saving $700,000 of total interest ($1,500,000 minus $800,000) outweighs the $10,000 annual saving [eval]. If preserving cash flow over the next 5 years is the priority, the debenture would be the better choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Debenture: lower annual interest but repaid over a longer term
Bank loan: higher annual interest but cleared sooner and cheaper overall
application_max_2: 10-year debenture vs 5-year loan; $1,500,000 vs $800,000 total interest
$9 million revenue; furnace to stop 12 breakdowns a year
analysis_max_2: Debenture eases annual cash flow but raises total interest cost
Loan clears debt sooner and reduces long-term asset claims by creditors
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing annual saving against total interest
Acknowledges the alternative choice and when it would be preferable

scenario_stem:
Ainsworth Active Leisure runs 2 leisure centres. It has 3,800 members paying $42 monthly, earning $2.7 million. Inflation is 8.5% and rates 7%; confidence fell from 105 to 88, and 620 members cancelled in 6 months.

Lucy Hammond can cut membership from $42 to $35, losing $26,600 monthly, or launch an off-peak $25 membership for retirees and job-seekers, mornings only, without cutting standard prices. Renewals are due for 1,500 members next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'consumer confidence'.
questions.model_answer: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel about the economy and their own finances. Higher confidence encourages spending; low confidence makes consumers save instead of spend. [2]

High confidence encourages spending; low confidence encourages saving

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why gym membership at Ainsworth has fallen recently.
questions.model_answer: High inflation reduces real incomes: inflation of 8.5% means wages buy less, so consumers cut non-essential spending [k]; Ainsworth has lost 620 members in 6 months [app]. Low consumer confidence: the index has fallen from 105 to 88, so households feel pessimistic about their finances [k], and a $42 monthly leisure membership is an easy budget item to cancel [app].

Protects standard fees: standard members keep paying $42, avoiding the $26,600 monthly loss a full cut would cause [k], while the off-peak tier widens the market to price-sensitive groups [app], building the membership base to offset the 620 cancellations [an].

However, cutting the fee reduces income by $26,600 a month before any new members sign up [k], and an off-peak membership at $25 targets price-sensitive customers without discounting everyone [app], so a full cut may be unnecessarily deep while 1,500 renewals are due next quarter [an]. scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Redhill Everyday Value, a discount chain with 4 stores, makes own-brand tomato soup. At $1.10 per tin, a 20% cost-plus mark-up sets $1.32, below the market leader's $1.49 but above the cheapest rival's $1.19.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.

scenario_stem:
Vantage Cold Storage Plc is a public limited company operating 8 refrigerated warehouses, employing 260 workers with revenue of $31 million. It needs $12 million for 3 new automated cold rooms to win a medicines storage contract.

The Board compares $12 million of debentures at 6%, redeemable in 12 years and costing $720,000 yearly, with 3 million new shares at $4.00. Debentures demand fixed payments regardless of profit; shares cut the existing 25 million holders from 100% to about 89%.

questions.question_text: Define 'debenture' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: A debenture is a long-term loan to a company, usually secured on the company's assets, paying fixed interest to debenture holders. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, and are repaid on a set date. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Long-term loan to a company, usually secured on assets
Fixed interest; holders are creditors not owners; repaid on a set date

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of selling debentures rather than issuing new shares.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: debenture holders are not owners, so existing shareholders keep 100% of the 25 million shares and full control of the company [k], avoiding the dilution to about 89% that would follow issuing 3 million new shares at $4.00 each [app]. Second advantage: debenture interest of $720,000 per year is fixed, predictable and tax-deductible, and may be cheaper than paying dividends to 3 million new shareholders [k], which suits a profitable medicines-storage contract where the Board knows the $12 million will be repaid over 12 years [app].

knowledge_max_2: Control is retained because debenture holders are creditors, not owners
Interest is fixed, predictable and tax-deductible; can be cheaper than dividends
application_max_2: 100% of the 25 million shares preserved versus dilution to about 89%
3 million new shares at $4.00 each raises $12 million

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of selling debentures to raise the $12 million.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: the $720,000 fixed interest must be paid every year for 12 years, whatever profit the company earns [k], so if the medicines-storage contract underperforms, this fixed charge could push Vantage close to insolvency even though revenue was $31 million last year [app], and debenture holders could enforce their claim on the 8 refrigerated warehouses if payments are missed [an]. Second disadvantage: debentures add a long-term liability that stays on the statement of financial position for 12 years, limiting future share issues or loans [k], so when the $12 million medicines contract finishes or trade weakens, the company may struggle to raise further long-term finance for new cold rooms [app], constraining growth and financial flexibility [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid regardless of profit; fixed charge for many years
Added long-term liability limits future borrowing capacity

8 refrigerated warehouses could be at risk of a security claim
analysis_max_2: Fixed charge in a weak year leads to insolvency risk and asset claims

questions.question_text: Do you think Vantage Cold Storage Plc should sell debentures rather than issue new shares? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Selling debentures would raise the $12 million needed for the 3 new automated cold rooms while keeping the existing 25 million shareholders in complete control (100% instead of about 89%) [k], and the fixed interest of $720,000 per year can be comfortably covered by a company with revenue of $31 million and 260 workers serving a new medicines-storage contract [app], avoiding the need to pay dividends to 3 million new shareholders who dilute ownership [an]. However, debenture interest of $720,000 must be paid for 12 years regardless of profit, and missing payments could put the 8 refrigerated warehouses used as security at risk [k], whereas new shares at $4.00 would bring in permanent capital with no repayment date or fixed charge [app], suiting a business taking on long-term medicines-storage work where financial flexibility is valuable [an]. Overall, I think Vantage should sell the $12 million debentures, because retaining 100% control and a predictable $720,000 annual cost is preferable while revenue and the medicines contract remain strong [eval]. If the Board fears trade could weaken or wants to remove the fixed charge entirely, issuing new shares would be the safer long-term choice [eval].

Share issue brings permanent capital with no fixed repayment obligation

scenario_stem:
Emmer & Oak Bakery is a family-run partnership supplying bread and rolls to 140 schools under a 12-month, $1.6 million fixed-price contract. It has 48 staff and made 2.1 million loaves. Inflation of 10% pushed flour up 35%, packaging 18% and energy 25%.

Mira Castellanos expects a $90,000 loss over the remaining 5 months. She can renegotiate with the caterer now, risking cancellation if it uses a rival bakery, or wait and quote higher at renewal; a 3-month notice applies.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by a 'fixed-price contract'.

Fixed-price contracts give the buyer certainty but shift cost risk onto the supplier

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Emmer & Oak's costs have increased.
questions.model_answer: Rising raw material costs: inflation of 10% has pushed flour prices up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18% [k], so every one of the 2.1 million loaves costs more to produce [app]. Higher energy bills: oven energy costs have risen 25% [k], which is significant for a bakery running ovens throughout the day [app].

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises energy and utility costs

questions.model_answer: Loss of the contract: if the caterer refuses and invokes the 3-month notice period, the bakery could lose a $1.6 million contract to a rival [k], cancelling roughly $133,000 of monthly revenue and putting 48 jobs at risk [app], leaving the ovens idle and fixed costs uncovered [an]. Damaged relationships: challenging a signed contract may make the caterer distrust future deals [k], and the schools' caterer may warn other public buyers about the bakery [app], making it harder to win the renewal or new contracts [an].

questions.model_answer: Renegotiating now could stop the bakery losing $90,000 over its remaining 5 months [k], and with flour up 35% and oven energy up 25%, continuing at the agreed price is unsustainable for 48 staff [app], so an honest conversation backed by cost evidence might be accepted by the caterer [an]. However, renegotiation risks cancellation under the 3-month notice period, losing $1.6 million a year [k], and the caterer could simply switch to a rival bakery rather than pay more mid-contract [app], leaving the bakery with idle ovens and wages it cannot cover [an]. scenario_stem:
Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd is a private limited woodworking business founded 9 years ago. It employs 10 woodworkers making hand-carved walnut cabinets at $1,900 each (16 hours) and flat-pack pine shelves at $85 each (40 minutes), with $720,000 revenue.

Specialising in walnut cabinets would cut waste 12% and attract boutique retailers, but walnut costs $9 per board foot and demand is uncertain with 60 firm cabinet orders. The 3,000 flat-pack shelves keep cash flowing.

questions.question_text: Outline one way specialisation can add value to furniture.

Cedar & Co could let its 10 woodworkers master cabinet-making instead of dividing time with flat-pack pine shelves [app]. Reason 2: Specialisation raises efficiency and adds value [k]. Dedicated cabinet staff could cut waste by 12% and justify premium $1,900 pricing to boutique retailers [app].

questions.model_answer: Point 1: Specialised workers develop deeper skills and waste less material [k]. Full-time cabinet makers could cut walnut waste by 12% while mastering the 16-hour build [app]. This lowers unit cost and raises the value added per $1,900 cabinet sold [an]. Point 2: Specialisation enables a stronger brand and premium pricing [k]. Boutique retailers pay more for expert joinery than for general furniture [app]. This helps Cedar & Co capture more value from each of the 60 firm orders for next year, instead of relying on $85 shelves with thin margins [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd should specialise fully in hand-carved walnut cabinets? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for full specialisation: Concentrating on walnut cabinets lets each of the 10 woodworkers master one craft, cutting waste by 12% and sharpening the brand for boutique retailers [k]. Cabinets at $1,900 each could lift average revenue well beyond the current $720,000 if the 60 firm orders convert and expand [app]. However, with walnut at $9 per board foot and only 60 firm cabinet orders for next year, volume would sit far below the 3,000 flat-pack shelves sold annually [an]. Specialising too soon could leave the workshop underused and Cedar & Co short of working capital [app]. But splitting focus dilutes craftsmanship, keeps waste high and weakens the added-value story boutique retailers will pay for [an]. Overall, Cedar & Co should specialise fully only once the 60 firm orders are converted into deposits covering at least a full year's production, because the 12% waste saving and $1,900 pricing reward mastery [eval]. scenario_stem:
Greenfield Community Pharmacy is a sole trader chemist with 2 pharmacists, 7 dispensing technicians and 2 assistants, dispensing 1,900 prescriptions monthly. Technicians earn $14 per hour on a 40-hour week, but waits reach 12 minutes and turnover is 24%.

questions.question_text: Define 'non-financial motivation'.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of raising technician pay to $15.50 per hour.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Stronger recruitment and retention [k], as $15.50 per hour beats the current $14 and may cut the 24% technician turnover [app]. Advantage 2: Simple, predictable cost [k], as the rise costs about $21,840 a year for all 7 technicians, which is easy to budget [app].

questions.question_text: Analyse two benefits of option two for Greenfield Community Pharmacy.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Greater flexibility across the pharmacy [k], as job rotation between dispensary, counter and home-delivery duties lets technicians cover each other [app], cutting the 12-minute counter waiting times [an]. Benefit 2: Higher competence and loyalty [k], as training technicians as pharmacy accuracy checkers with a pay step motivates them to qualify [app], lowering errors and reducing the 24% turnover [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Greenfield Community Pharmacy should choose option two (non-financial motivation) rather than raise pay to $15.50 per hour? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising pay to $15.50 per hour is certain and simple [k], costing about $21,840 a year and lifting the 7 technicians above the current $14 rate [app], which may ease the 24% turnover quickly [an]. However, money alone does not fix monotony [k]: the 12-minute counter queues and turnover suggest technicians need variety and progression [app], which a flat pay rise will not deliver [an]. Option two keeps wages at $14 and adds job rotation, weekly huddles and accuracy-checker training with a pay step. Overall, Greenfield should choose option two [eval], because it develops multi-skilled technicians and a qualification pathway far more cheaply than $21,840 a year, directly attacking boredom and the retention problem; if turnover still lags after a review period, the owner can revisit the $1.50 rise [eval].

scenario_stem:
Cindervale Ceramic Company, a private limited company, makes a premium artisan pizza oven. At $380 production cost and $260,000 development over 4 years, Priya must choose a spring launch price: price skimming at $950 or penetration at $520, below the market leader's $640.

Forecasts show 900 units at $950, earning $570 margin, or 1,700 at $520, earning $140 each ($238,000 total). Capacity is 1,800 yearly; Priya wants quick recovery, but Marco Diaz argues share comes first.

questions.question_text: Define 'penetration pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Penetration pricing is setting an initially low price for a new product to attract customers quickly, build market share fast, and discourage rivals from entering the market [2].

aims to build market share quickly and deter rival entry

Advantage 2: Deters rival entry [k], as a low price makes the premium back-garden oven niche unattractive to competitors watching from the sidelines [app].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Meridian Ceramic Tiles is a private limited company making glazed ceramic floor tiles in Country X. Boxes sell for $30 with variable costs of $18 per box and fixed costs of $72,000; annual output is 9,000 boxes.

Priya Raman weighs a $40,000 new kiln cutting costs to $14 per box but raising fixed costs to $96,000, versus keeping the old kiln and charging $33. She wants break-even output for both, fearing the price rise to $33 may deter builders' merchants.

questions.question_text: Define 'total costs'.
questions.model_answer: Total costs are the full cost of producing a given level of output, found by adding fixed costs to total variable costs (Meridian's $72,000 fixed costs plus the variable cost of every box made). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs do not change with output, e.g. rent and salaries
Total costs = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x output)

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Priya of calculating break-even output before deciding on the new kiln.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: break-even output shows Priya the minimum number of boxes she must sell before making a profit [k]; with the new kiln, fixed costs of $96,000 divided by the $16 contribution gives 6,000 boxes, so she can check whether the current 9,000 boxes a year still leaves a safe cushion [app]. Benefit 2: it lets her compare the options on equal terms [k]; keeping the current kiln needs $72,000 divided by $12 = 6,000 boxes, while the $33 selling price option needs $72,000 divided by $15 = 4,800 boxes, so she can see which option leaves the biggest margin of safety [app].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even output identifies the output needed to cover all costs
Break-even can be used to compare options / assess risk before investing
application_max_2: Applies figures: $96,000 fixed costs, $16 contribution, 6,000 boxes break-even
Applies figures: $72,000 / $12 = 6,000 boxes; $72,000 / $15 = 4,800 boxes at the $33 price

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis for Priya's investment decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes all output is sold, which may not happen [k]; if builders' merchants buy fewer boxes than the 9,000 a year forecast, revenue will fall short while the $96,000 fixed costs of the new kiln remain unchanged, so the calculated break-even output gives false comfort [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes costs and revenue move in straight lines [k]; if the new kiln cuts variable costs to $14 per box only at full efficiency, or if discounts push the $33 selling price lower than expected, the $16 contribution would shrink and the true break-even output would be higher than the 6,000 boxes calculated [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes all output is sold
Break-even assumes linear (straight-line) costs and revenue
application_max_2: Applies to builders' merchants buying fewer than 9,000 boxes with fixed costs unchanged
Applies to the $14 per box variable cost and $33 price risk shifting the $16 contribution
analysis_max_2: Explains that unsold output means the break-even figure overstates safety
Explains that a lower contribution pushes the break-even output above 6,000 boxes

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should invest in the new kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Priya could invest in the new kiln because it lowers the cost of every box made [k]. Cutting variable costs to $14 per box lifts contribution to $16, so break-even output stays at 6,000 boxes ($96,000 divided by $16) and profit rises from $36,000 to $48,000 a year (9,000 boxes x $16, minus $96,000) [app][an]. However, the $40,000 must be paid up front and fixed costs would rise to $96,000; if sales slip below 6,000 boxes the loss would be deeper than before, and the 3,000-box margin of safety is thin [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the current kiln and raising the price to $33 would cut break-even output to 4,800 boxes ($72,000 divided by $15) and could yield $63,000 profit (9,000 x $15, minus $72,000), but only if builders' merchants accept the higher price [k][eval]. Overall, because variable-cost savings are under Priya's control while a price rise depends on uncertain demand in a competitive market, the evidence favours the kiln - provided she is confident of holding at least 9,000 boxes of annual sales; otherwise the safer short-term move is the price rise, whose 4,800-box break-even output is more forgiving [eval].

application_max_2: New kiln profit $48,000 vs current $36,000 at 9,000 boxes
Current kiln fixed costs $72,000 and 3,000-box margin of safety
analysis_max_2: Identifies that higher fixed costs deepen losses if sales fall below 6,000 boxes
Analyses that the price-rise option depends on demand holding at $33
evaluation_max_2: Justified overall recommendation tied to Priya's demand confidence and control over costs

scenario_stem:
Amberley Farm Shop is a private limited company selling home-grown vegetables, eggs and preserves to 210 weekly customers. Current assets are $48,000. June inflows of $9,400 against outflows of $11,200 give net cash flow of -$1,800.

July opens with $2,600, with inflows of $12,750 and outflows of $8,900. Jenny fears the shop cannot cover a $26,000 cold room due in August. Options: an overdraft, asking 60 debtors to pay sooner, or postponing the purchase by six months.

questions.question_text: Define 'net cash flow'.
questions.model_answer: Net cash flow is the difference between a business's total cash inflows and its total cash outflows over a period of time (for Amberley Farm Shop, $12,750 inflows minus $8,900 outflows gives a net cash flow of +$3,850 in July). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Net cash flow is total inflows minus total outflows over a period
A positive net cash flow means more cash came in than went out during the period

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Amberley Farm Shop could overcome its short-term cash shortfall in June.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Amberley Farm Shop could arrange an overdraft with its bank [k]; the June forecast shows outflows of $11,200 against inflows of only $9,400, so a facility of roughly $2,000 would cover the gap until July, when inflows of $12,750 are forecast to exceed outflows of $8,900 [app]. Way 2: the shop could ask its 60 debtors to settle sooner [k]; pulling those payments forward would lift June inflows above $11,200, removing the -$1,800 deficit without borrowing [app].

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft lets a business spend more than its bank balance up to an agreed limit
Asking debtors to pay faster speeds up cash inflows
application_max_2: Applies the June figures: $11,200 outflows vs $9,400 inflows, roughly a $2,000 gap
Applies the 60 debtors and the -$1,800 June net cash flow to the faster-payment option

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Amberley Farm Shop of preparing a cash-flow forecast.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: a forecast shows the shortfall before it happens [k]; because the June deficit of $1,800 would be visible in advance, Jenny can arrange an overdraft or chase the 60 debtors before wages and supplier bills fall due [app][an]. Benefit 2: it helps decide whether the $26,000 cold-room purchase in August is affordable [k]; the July closing balance will be about $6,450 (opening $2,600 plus net cash flow of +$3,850), far below the purchase price, so the forecast tells her extra finance or a postponement is essential [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A cash-flow forecast highlights periods of expected shortage or surplus in advance
It supports decisions about large or irregular purchases
application_max_2: Applies the June deficit of $1,800 and the 60 debtors as early-warning use
Applies the July closing balance of about $6,450 against the $26,000 cold-room price
analysis_max_2: Explains that early warning allows action before the shortfall hits

questions.question_text: Do you think Jenny should buy the cold room now using an overdraft, or postpone it by six months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Jenny could argue the cold room should be bought now so it is ready for the August vegetable peak [k]. However, the forecast shows only $2,600 opening in July and a +$3,850 net cash flow, so a $26,000 payment would swallow all available cash and push the shop deeper into overdraft while June is already forecast at -$1,800 [app][an]. Postponing six months protects the thin position and lets the shop build its balance from the stronger July forecast of $12,750 inflows, though it delays the extra capacity a growing shop with 210 customers may need [app][an]. Because postponement is reversible and cheap, whereas an overdraft is not guaranteed [k][eval], the sensible decision is to postpone the cold room until autumn sales are banked and only then confirm the purchase [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying now secures the equipment before the August peak
Postponement is a reversible, low-cost way to manage cash shortage
application_max_2: Applies the $2,600 July opening balance and +$3,850 net cash flow against the $26,000 price
Applies the June -$1,800 deficit and the $12,750 July inflows to the postponement option
analysis_max_2: Explains that a $26,000 payment cannot be funded from a $6,450 July closing balance
Explains that postponement lets cash rebuild from July inflows before committing
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to the reversibility of postponing and the risk of overdraft reliance
Recognises the trade-off with the August capacity need

scenario_stem:
Copper Kettle Preserves is a partnership making artisan strawberry jam in Millbrook, Country X. Jars sell for $6 with variable costs of $2.50 per jar and fixed costs of $21,000; it makes 7,000 jars a year.

questions.question_text: Calculate the break-even output for Copper Kettle Preserves. You are advised to show your working.
questions.model_answer: Break-even output = Fixed costs / (Price - Variable cost) = $21,000 / ($6.00 - $2.50) = $21,000 / $3.50 = 6,000 jars per year. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Nadia and Theo should calculate the margin of safety before signing the supermarket contract.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the margin of safety shows how far sales can fall before the partnership makes a loss [k]; at 7,000 jars a year and a break-even output of 6,000 jars, the cushion is only 1,000 jars, so relying on the bulk contract's lower price could be risky if the supermarket cuts orders [app]. Reason 2: it tests whether the contract improves security [k]; selling 17,000 jars in total (7,000 plus the 10,000 bulk jars) against the same 6,000-jar break-even output would lift the margin of safety to 11,000 jars, reducing the chance of losses [app].

A larger margin of safety means lower risk of losses
application_max_2: Applies figures: combined 17,000 jars gives an 11,000-jar margin of safety

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using break-even analysis for the contract decision.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: break-even analysis shows the output at which total revenue equals total costs [k]; the $4.50 bulk jar leaves only $2.00 contribution ($4.50 - $2.50), so 10,500 jars at the bulk price alone would be needed to cover the $21,000 fixed costs - warning the partners that the deal is only worthwhile alongside their existing sales [app][an]. Benefit 2: break-even analysis supports a like-for-like comparison of options [k]; selling 10,000 bulk jars adds $20,000 contribution (10,000 x $2.00) to the current $3,500 profit (7,000 x $3.50 - $21,000), showing the total profit would rise to $23,500 [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even compares fixed and variable costs with revenue
Break-even allows objective comparison of options
application_max_2: Applies figures: $2.00 contribution, 10,500 bulk jars to cover $21,000 fixed costs
Applies figures: $20,000 added contribution, profit rising from $3,500 to $23,500
analysis_max_2: Explains the bulk deal only covers fixed costs if existing premium sales continue
Explains the contract lifts total profit despite a lower per-jar margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Copper Kettle Preserves should accept the supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the contract would secure a guaranteed weekly outlet for 10,000 jars and spread the $21,000 fixed costs over far more units [k]. Selling 10,000 bulk jars at $4.50 adds $20,000 contribution (10,000 x $2.00) to the current $3,500 profit, lifting the total to around $23,500, and the combined margin of safety would rise to 11,000 jars [app][an]. However, the bulk price of $4.50 leaves only $2.00 contribution per jar, far below the $3.50 earned on premium jars; 10,500 bulk jars would be needed merely to cover the $21,000 fixed costs, and the supermarket may demand an even lower price after the first year [app][an]. Conversely, keeping only premium farmers' market sales protects the brand but caps growth and leaves the 1,000-jar margin of safety exposed to poor weather and festival cancellations [k][eval]. Overall, the partnership should accept the contract only if production capacity and jar quality can be maintained at 17,000 jars a year and the $4.50 price and shelf-life terms are written into a fixed two-year agreement; if the supermarket's price or volume is uncertain, Nadia and Theo should negotiate first rather than sign [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Bulk contribution $2.00 per jar vs $3.50 premium contribution
application_max_2: Applies figures: 10,000 x $2.00 = $20,000 added contribution, profit ~$23,500
Applies figures: combined 17,000 jars gives 11,000-jar margin of safety
analysis_max_2: Analyses that fixed costs are spread thinner at 17,000 jars but the margin per jar falls
Analyses the risk of price pressure or order cuts from the supermarket
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on capacity, quality and a fixed contract

scenario_stem:
Bluewater Surf School is a sole trader run by Kai Delgado, teaching surf lessons to 480 pupils a season. July inflows are $18,600; August $15,200 against $14,750; September only $6,800 against $9,900.

September opens with $7,900, and current assets of $22,000 against liabilities of $14,500 leave working capital of $7,500. Kai wants two new rescue boards at $3,400 each in October but fears the quiet winter. Options: delay to the spring term or take a small bank overdraft.

questions.question_text: Define 'opening balance'.
questions.model_answer: Opening balance is the cash a business has available at the start of a period, brought forward from the previous period's closing balance (Bluewater Surf School begins September with $7,900). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Opening balance is the cash held at the start of a period
The opening balance equals the previous closing balance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why September is the hardest month of the season for Bluewater Surf School's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: demand collapses once the season ends [k]; the forecast shows September inflows of only $6,800 against $18,600 in July and $15,200 in August [app]. Reason 2: outflows are slower to fall than inflows [k]; September outflows of $9,900 still exceed inflows, giving a net cash flow of -$3,100 and leaving a September closing balance of only $4,800 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Seasonal businesses see demand fall sharply when the season ends
Fixed-style outflows (wages, storage) continue when revenue falls
application_max_2: Applies the fall in inflows from $18,600 (July) and $15,200 (August) to $6,800 (September)
Applies September outflows of $9,900 vs inflows of $6,800, i.e. -$3,100 and closing $4,800

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Kai could overcome the cash-flow problem he expects in September.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Kai could ask his bank for an overdraft [k]; this covers the September shortfall of $3,100 so the school keeps paying instructors and boat maintenance while it waits for next season's deposits [app][an]. Way 2: he could delay buying the two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each until spring [k]; postponing this $6,800 capital item protects the $7,500 working capital and keeps September liquid [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft or bank loan provides short-term finance for a cash-flow gap
Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflow

Explains that delaying a discretionary purchase is a cheaper way to protect cash

questions.question_text: Do you think Kai should buy the two rescue boards in October, or delay until the spring term? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Kai could argue the boards should be bought now, before the winter, because they are essential safety equipment for a school teaching 480 pupils and because October prices may rise [k]. The forecast offers little room: September closes at $4,800, already below the $6,800 cost of the boards, so both would be paid for out of a $7,500 working capital, cutting it to under $1,000 [app][an]. However, delaying to spring protects the cash position through the worst months, risks only a seven-month delay to the purchase and still lands in time for next season [app][an]. Because the boards are important but not needed until lessons restart [k], the evidence favours delaying to the spring term unless the bank confirms an overdraft in writing [eval]; overcommitting in the off-season would jeopardise instructor wages [eval].

Explains that delay costs reputation little but protects instructor wages and bills

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
PalmCrest Estates is a private limited company running palm oil plantations with 520 workers and $6,800,000 in exports. To double output it plans to clear 1,500 hectares of forest for an extra $3,200,000.

Environmental groups say the forest holds endangered primates and a petition has 45,000 signatures. The government requires an environmental impact assessment, with $500,000 fines for illegal logging. Alternatively it could buy 800 hectares of degraded land for $2,100,000, with lower yields for 6 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'deforestation'.
questions.model_answer: The clearing and permanent removal of trees and forest cover from land, usually to make way for farming, logging or development [2].

knowledge_max_2: clearing and permanent removal of trees and forest cover
to make way for farming, logging or development

questions.question_text: Explain two problems that clearing 1,500 hectares of forest could cause for PalmCrest Estates.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Legal penalties [k], the government now requires an environmental impact assessment and illegal logging brings fines of $500,000 [app]. Problem 2: Reputational damage and lost sales [k], the petition signed by 45,000 people shows strong opposition to clearing the forest [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for PalmCrest Estates of buying the 800 hectares of degraded land instead of clearing the forest.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: No legal risk [k], already-cleared degraded land avoids the environmental impact assessment problem and the $500,000 illegal logging fine [app], removing the risk of losing the expansion programme [an]. Advantage 2: Protects reputation and exports [k], replanting degraded land keeps the $6,800,000 export business safe from the 45,000-signature petition [app], supporting continued sales growth [an].

analysis_max_2: removing the risk of losing the expansion programme

questions.question_text: Do you think PalmCrest Estates should buy the degraded land instead of clearing the 1,500 hectares of forest? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the degraded land avoids fines and rejection [k], because the government requires an environmental impact assessment and illegal logging brings fines of $500,000 [app], protecting the company's legal position and expansion plan [an]. It also safeguards the $6,800,000 export business, since buyers increasingly prefer sustainable palm oil while 45,000 people have signed the petition [app], securing long-term contracts [an]. However, clearing the forest could unlock $3,200,000 in extra sales quickly [k], boosting growth for 520 workers. Overall, buying the degraded land is wiser because the $2,100,000 price is outweighed by avoiding the $500,000 fine risk and reputational harm [eval], and sustainable replanting keeps the estates compliant and attractive to export buyers for years to come [eval].

knowledge_max_2: avoids fines and rejection / legal compliance
clearing forest unlocks extra sales quickly
analysis_max_2: protecting the company's legal position and expansion plan
evaluation_max_2: weighs $2,100,000 purchase price against $500,000 fine and reputational harm
sustainable replanting keeps estates compliant and attractive to buyers

scenario_stem:
Meridian Care Homes is a private company running 3 care homes with 120 beds in the capital, charging $1,450 per week. It employs 78 nurses and carers and made $1.9 million profit last year.

The public National Care Trust runs a 200-bed facility, but its waiting list has reached 340 with 9-month waits. The government, which spent $28 million on public care, is considering paying Meridian $6 million to run 40 extra beds instead of building a $15 million public ward.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'private sector'.
questions.model_answer: The part of the economy owned and controlled by private individuals and businesses rather than the government, usually aiming to make a profit. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Owned and controlled by private individuals or businesses
Usually aims to make a profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Country X has a mixed economy in care provision.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Private firms add capacity and choice [k], as Meridian Care Homes runs 3 homes with 120 beds and its $6 million contract would open 40 more beds faster than a $15 million public ward [app]. Reason 2: Public provision protects those who cannot pay [k], since the National Care Trust operates 200 beds funded by $28 million of government spending for patients facing 9-month waits [app].

knowledge_max_2: Private sector adds capacity and choice
Public sector guarantees access regardless of ability to pay
application_max_2: 120 beds across 3 homes; $6 million for 40 contracted beds versus a $15 million public ward
200-bed National Care Trust funded by $28 million with 9-month waits

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why stakeholder objectives may conflict in Country X's care sector.
questions.model_answer: Conflict 1: Residents want quality care at fair prices but owners want profit [k], because Meridian charges $1,450 per week and earned $1.9 million profit from 120 beds with 78 staff [app], so cost control may reduce staffing levels and care quality [an]. Conflict 2: Taxpayers want value for money while patients want short waits [k], yet the government must choose between a $6 million contract with Meridian and a $15 million public expansion to clear the 340-person waiting list [app], and funding one option limits money for the other [an].

knowledge_max_2: Owners' profit objective conflicts with residents' quality objective
Taxpayers' value-for-money objective conflicts with patients' access objective
application_max_2: $1,450 weekly fees and $1.9 million profit from 120 beds with 78 staff
Choice between $6 million contract and $15 million ward to clear 340 waiting patients
analysis_max_2: Cost pressure may lower staffing and care quality
Limited public funds force trade-offs between options

questions.question_text: Do you think the government should sign the $6 million contract with Meridian Care Homes? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the contract is that it is cheaper and faster [k], costing $6 million instead of $15 million for a new public ward and adding 40 beds to cut the 340-person waiting list sooner [app], improving care access without raising taxes [an]. However, one argument against is that public money would enrich a profit-making firm [k], whose $1,450 weekly fees and $1.9 million profit show a private objective that may conflict with affordable care for poorer residents [app], weakening long-term public provision [an]. Overall, the government should sign the contract [eval], because $6 million is less than half the public alternative and 9-month waits harm vulnerable people now, provided the contract enforces quality standards and fee caps [eval].

Private profit motive may conflict with affordable public care

Meridian charges $1,450 per week and earned $1.9 million profit

Profit orientation may raise long-term costs or reduce equity
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the private contract and public expansion
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Riverstone Building Supplies is a partnership selling timber and cement from 4 depots, with 68 people. Sales were $9.3m, its largest customer buys $1.1m. Its tall structure has 5 layers: managing partner, 2 branch managers per depot, section leaders and staff.

A 5th depot adds $1.8m revenue but needs restructuring before the lease in 6 weeks: keep the tall structure with a narrow span of 6 staff, or a flat structure with owners managing 15 staff per depot.

questions.question_text: Define 'tall organisational structure'.
questions.model_answer: An organisational structure with many levels of management, a narrow span of control and a long chain of command [2].

knowledge_max_2: narrow span of control/long chain of command

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Riverstone Building Supplies of a tall organisational structure.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Slow communication [k] as messages pass through 5 layers between the managing partner and yard staff across 4 depots [app]. Disadvantage 2: Higher overheads [k] because 2 branch managers per depot plus section leaders add salary costs against $9.3m sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: higher salary/overhead costs of multiple tiers

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of a flat organisational structure for the proposed 5th depot.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Faster decisions [k] because the owners directly approve purchases and credit for 15 staff per depot [app], avoiding delays through 5 layers [an]. Advantage 2: Lower management costs [k] as no branch managers are needed at the $1.8m depot [app], leaving more margin on builders' materials [an].

application_max_2: owners directly managing 15 staff per depot
analysis_max_2: leaves more margin on materials sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Riverstone Building Supplies should adopt a flat structure for the 5th depot rather than keep the tall structure? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A flat structure would let each owner manage 15 staff per depot directly [k], cutting the cost of branch managers and section leaders [app] and protecting margin on the $1.8m extra revenue [an]. Fewer layers would also speed decisions on stock such as timber and cement [app], improving responsiveness to house-builders [an]. However, keeping the tall structure gives each manager a narrow span of control of 6 staff [k], protecting supervision of yard safety and credit control across the 4 depots, at the cost of higher overheads. Overall, the flat structure suits the new 5th depot [eval] because the tall chain of 5 layers already slows approvals, and 68 staff across 4 depots prove the partners can coordinate wider spans with clear job roles [eval].

knowledge_max_2: narrow span/supervision advantage of tall structure
application_max_2: branch managers and section leaders cost
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation based on burden of 5 layers and partners' demonstrated ability to coordinate

scenario_stem:
BrightBuy Supermarkets runs 14 stores in Country X, with $9.6 million annual revenue and a $18,000 weekly marketing budget. Cereal sales are slow at 300 boxes per store, 25% below target, so the manager is choosing between two own-brand cornflakes promotions.

Option 1 is BOGOF, costing about $7,500 weekly and expected to double sales. Option 2 is a 20% cut from $4.00 to $3.20 per box, costing $5,800 with modest growth; the board wants volume without sacrificing margins.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Short-term incentives designed to encourage customers to purchase a product, such as price reductions, BOGOF offers, competitions or free gifts [2].

knowledge_max_2: short-term incentives to encourage product purchase
examples include price reductions, BOGOF offers, competitions or free gifts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why BrightBuy Supermarkets might use sales promotion to increase breakfast cereal sales.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Sales promotion can encourage immediate purchases and product trial [k], helping the supermarket lift its 300 boxes per store per week, currently 25% below target across 14 stores [app]. Reason 2: Promotions can pull customers away from rival supermarkets [k], which matters when BrightBuy generates $9.6 million in revenue and wants to protect its share of household grocery spending [app].

knowledge_max_2: encourages immediate purchases and product trial
pulls customers away from rival supermarkets

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to BrightBuy Supermarkets of using BOGOF on its own-brand cornflakes.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: BOGOF reduces the profit earned on each promotional sale [k], because the second box is given free, and with cornflakes priced at $4.00 per box the supermarket sacrifices half the revenue per promotional pack [app], squeezing the margin that covers store and staffing costs [an]. Disadvantage 2: Customers may become conditioned to expect free offers [k], damaging sales of regular-priced lines once the $7,500 weekly promotion ends [app], leaving the 25% shortfall to reappear without continual discounting [an].

knowledge_max_2: reduces profit per promotional sale because the second unit is free
customers become conditioned to expect free offers
analysis_max_2: squeezes the margin that covers store and staffing costs
post-promotion sales drop back without continual discounting

questions.question_text: Do you think a BOGOF offer or a 20% price reduction to $3.20 is the better sales promotion for this supermarket? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: BOGOF is widely understood and doubles the perceived value of each pack [k], and at an estimated $7,500 per week it should lift cereal volume well above 300 boxes per store per week across the 14 stores [app], clearing slow stock and closing the 25% gap to target [an]. However, a 20% price reduction from $4.00 to $3.20 costs only $5,800 per week [k], is simpler to operate on shelf and keeps customers paying something for every box [app], preserving more margin than giving a full box away [an]. Overall, BOGOF is the better promotion because the board's key objective is restoring sales volume, and the extra $1,700 per week is justified if double-unit sales are achieved [eval], though a shorter trial period would limit the conditioned-expectation risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: BOGOF doubles perceived value and is easy to understand
price reduction is simpler, cheaper and preserves per-unit margin
analysis_max_2: lifts volume, clears slow stock and closes the 25% target gap
protects margin and avoids customers expecting free goods
evaluation_max_2: weighs volume-driving impact of BOGOF against margin protection of the price cut
justifies the choice against the board's volume objective while noting the extra cost risk

scenario_stem:
Silverline Window Frames is a public limited company making triple-glazed window units in Country X. Units sell for $450 with variable costs of $270 per unit and fixed costs of $810,000; it sold 6,000 units to housebuilders.

The board weighs an automated cutting line raising fixed costs to $1,050,000, cutting variable costs to $240 per unit and lifting capacity to 7,500 units. Directors want break-even figures for both: lower unit costs versus higher break-even output if sales slip.

questions.question_text: State what is meant by 'average cost'.
questions.model_answer: Average cost is the total cost of producing a given output divided by the number of units produced - the cost per unit (at 6,000 units with total costs of $2,430,000, the average cost is $405). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Average cost includes both fixed and variable elements per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the board wants break-even figures for both options.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: to judge the extra risk from higher fixed costs before approving the machine [k]; the automated cutting line raises fixed costs to $1,050,000, so break-even output climbs to 5,000 units ($1,050,000 / $210) compared with 4,500 units today ($810,000 / $180), showing sales must hold above 5,000 units [app]. Reason 2: to protect shareholders' funds and dividends [k]; at 6,000 units the margin of safety would fall from 1,500 units to 1,000 units, so the board can decide whether the risk of dividend cuts is acceptable [app].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even figures reveal the sales needed to avoid losses
Higher fixed costs raise break-even output and risk
application_max_2: Applies figures: margin of safety falls from 1,500 to 1,000 units at 6,000 sales

questions.question_text: Analyse two ways the board could use a break-even chart to present the options.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: the chart's total revenue line (units sold x $450) and total cost line show exactly where they cross for each option [k]; the machine option's cost line starts at $1,050,000 and rises less steeply (variable cost $240 vs $270), so the crossing moves from 4,500 to 5,000 units, and directors can see the shift at a glance [app][an]. Way 2: the vertical gap between the two lines at 6,000 units shows profit and margin of safety [k]; the current set-up shows a profit of $270,000 at 6,000 units against $210,000 with the machine, and the loss zone above 5,000 units is visible immediately, making the comparison persuasive to shareholders [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even chart plots total revenue and total cost against output
The intersection shows break-even output; the gap shows profit or loss
application_max_2: Applies figures: revenue line $450 per unit, cost line rising $240 vs $270 per unit
Applies figures: profit $270,000 current vs $210,000 with machine at 6,000 units
analysis_max_2: Explains why the flatter cost line moves the intersection right to 5,000 units
Explains that the chart makes profit differences visible to non-financial directors

questions.question_text: Do you think the board should approve the automated cutting line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The board could approve the line because it cuts variable costs to $240 per unit and lifts capacity to 7,500 units, helping Silverline win larger housebuilder contracts [k]. At full capacity of 7,500 units the machine would earn $525,000 profit (7,500 x $210 contribution, minus $1,050,000 fixed costs) compared with about $540,000 today at the same volume - so the case rests on winning more orders, not on lower costs alone [app][an]. However, at the current 6,000 units the machine would cut profit from $270,000 to $210,000, average cost rises from $405 to $415, and break-even output climbs to 5,000 units with only a 1,000-unit margin of safety [app][an]. Conversely, approve the line too late and a rival with cheaper units could undercut Silverline, whose current $405 average cost and thin 1,500-unit cushion leave little room against leaner competitors [k][eval]. Overall, the board should not approve the line now: the figures show it only beats the current option above 8,000 units, which exceeds its own 7,500-unit capacity, so no realistic output justifies it yet; the directors should wait until housebuilders sign firm orders for at least 7,000 units a year, or renegotiate the machine's price or financing, before voting in favour [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Machine option: contribution $210, break-even 5,000 units, profit $210,000 at 6,000
Current option: contribution $180, break-even 4,500 units, profit $270,000 at 6,000
application_max_2: Applies figures: machine profit at 7,500 units = $525,000
Applies figures: average cost $405 current vs $415 with machine
analysis_max_2: Identifies the indifference output of 8,000 units lies beyond the 7,500-unit capacity
Links higher fixed costs to a deeper loss zone below 5,000 units
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: delay approval until contracted volume or price improves

scenario_stem:
Redbank Construction Ltd is a private limited company building houses in Country X. Current assets include $34,000 owed by debtors; its housing association client pays 60 days late. March outflows of $29,300 exceed inflows of $21,500.

April opens with $5,100; inflows of $27,800 against outflows of $22,400. Marta must decide before the April payroll: offer the housing association a 2% early-payment discount, take a $20,000 bank loan, or delay the $32,000 cement mixer order.

questions.question_text: Define 'closing balance'.
questions.model_answer: Closing balance is the cash a business has at the end of a period, found by adding the net cash flow to the opening balance (Redbank begins April with $5,100 and April's forecast net cash flow is +$5,400, giving a closing balance of $10,500). [2]

Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redbank Construction of offering the 2% early-payment discount to the housing association.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: the discount should pull cash in sooner [k]; the housing association is 60 days late and owes $34,000, so pulling even half into April would more than cover the $22,400 of April outflows [app]. Benefit 2: a 2% discount is cheap finance [k]; giving up $680 on $34,000 costs far less than the interest on a $20,000 bank loan and still lands before the April payroll [app].

A small discount can be cheaper than interest on borrowed finance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order could help Redbank's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: delaying postpones a very large capital outflow [k]; moving the $32,000 mixer out of April keeps April outflows at $22,400 and lets the forecast opening balance of $5,100 recover to about $10,500 without new borrowing [app][an]. Reason 2: it avoids committing before the association pays [k]; with the client 60 days late on $34,000, delaying the purchase means Redbank is not forced into a $20,000 loan before knowing when cash will actually arrive [app][an].

Avoiding new long-term borrowing reduces interest costs and insolvency risk

Applies the association's 60-day lateness and the $34,000 owed to the loan alternative
analysis_max_2: Explains that delaying pushes the large outflow beyond the strained month
Explains that commitment before payment risks inability to fund the April payroll

questions.question_text: Do you think Marta should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $20,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marta could argue for the 2% early-payment discount because it tackles the root problem [k]. Because the discount is cheap and non-binding while the mixer delay alone does not guarantee cash [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the discount first and taking the $20,000 loan only if the association refuses [eval]; the decision should be made before the April payroll, not after it.

A bank loan gives certain finance but adds interest and repayment obligations

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
BrightKiln Cement Works is a private limited company running a cement plant at Alderney with 150 workers and $11,000,000 revenue. Night grinding creates noise of 60 decibels, dust and lorry traffic past 200 homes; 1,200 signatures demand action.

A $750,000 noise barrier and enclosed conveyor would cut noise by 25 decibels. Shareholders want a $1,400,000 expansion doubling output, but the council warns of enforcement notices and closure. Alternatively, moving night shifts to daytime cuts capacity by 20%.

questions.question_text: Define 'noise pollution'.
questions.model_answer: Unwanted or excessive sound that harms the health and quality of life of people living or working near its source, such as machinery or lorry traffic [2].

knowledge_max_2: harms the health and quality of life of people nearby

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs the BrightKiln Cement Works plant creates for the local community.
questions.model_answer: External cost 1: Noise disturbing homes [k], night-time grinding of around 60 decibels disturbs residents near the Alderney plant [app]. External cost 2: Dust and traffic pollution [k], lorries passing up to 200 homes and dust from the plant have driven 1,200 residents to sign the association's petition [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to BrightKiln Cement Works of installing the $750,000 noise barrier and enclosed conveyor.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Avoids closure [k], cutting noise by 25 decibels answers the council's warning over the 60 decibels night-time breaches [app], protecting $11,000,000 of annual revenue and 150 jobs [an]. Benefit 2: Repairs community relations [k], easing the complaints of the 1,200-signature residents' association [app], strengthening the plant's licence to operate and planning position [an].

strengthening the plant's licence to operate and planning position

questions.question_text: Do you think BrightKiln Cement Works should install the $750,000 noise barrier and enclosed conveyor or move night shifts to daytime? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The barrier permanently cuts noise by 25 decibels [k], removing the 60 decibels night-time breach that risks the council's enforcement notice and closure [app], safeguarding $11,000,000 annual revenue and 150 jobs [an]. However, moving night shifts to daytime avoids the $750,000 cost entirely [k], preserving short-term cash, though cutting capacity by 20% reduces sales. Overall, installing the barrier is the stronger option because avoiding closure and the 20% capacity loss outweighs the one-off $750,000 [eval], and permanent noise control protects the $1,400,000 expansion and community support the plant needs [eval].

scenario_stem:
Rivermart Stores PLC is a public limited company operating 26 supermarkets across Country X. It employs 1,900 people, reports $310 million revenue and made $14 million profit last year, paying $6 million in dividends.

Managers propose automating checkouts in 18 stores, a $6 million investment cutting 150 jobs. Employees demand a $0.75 hourly rise costing $2.9 million a year; customers want lower prices. Shareholders vote at the AGM on automation versus the pay rise.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'shareholders'.
questions.model_answer: People or organisations that own shares in a company and are therefore part-owners of it. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Shareholders own shares in the company
Shareholders are part-owners of the business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why objectives at Rivermart Stores PLC conflict.
questions.model_answer: Conflict 1: Shareholders want higher dividends but employees want higher pay [k], because a $0.75 hourly rise costing $2.9 million a year would cut the $14 million profit available for the $6 million dividend and the automation plan [app]. Conflict 2: Customers want lower prices while owners want profit [k], so with revenue of $310 million across 26 stores, cutting prices to please customers would squeeze the returns shareholders expect [app].

knowledge_max_2: Shareholder returns objective conflicts with employee pay objective
Customer low-price objective conflicts with owner profit objective
application_max_2: $0.75 hourly rise costing $2.9 million against $14 million profit and $6 million dividend

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Rivermart Stores PLC if it automates instead of granting the pay rise.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: 150 employees would lose their jobs [k], because the automation plan cuts roles across 18 of Rivermart's 26 stores [app], damaging morale and increasing recruitment and training costs [an]. Problem 2: Industrial action by the union becomes more likely [k], as workers demanding $0.75 per hour see $2.9 million redirected into a $6 million machine investment [app], risking strikes, higher absenteeism and lost sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: Automation causes redundancies and job insecurity
Automation provokes union resistance and industrial action

questions.question_text: Do you think Rivermart Stores PLC should invest in automation rather than approve the pay rise? Justify your answer.

Overall, Rivermart should not automate now [eval], because the $2.9 million pay rise is cheaper than $6 million machines, protects 1,900 jobs and motivates workers to serve customers better [eval].

Worsened morale risks industrial action and lost revenue

Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Aurelia Hotels Group is a public limited company owning 9 hotels and 420 staff. Revenue fell to $18.5m from $21m, average occupancy dropped to 68% and satisfaction to 74% after a $2.4m refurbishment.

A flat structure would remove 3 layers and widen spans to 14 staff, saving $520,000 after the $2.5m revenue drop; keeping the tall structure protects 240 housekeeping and front-desk staff despite slow decisions across 7 levels. Shareholders vote in 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'flat organisational structure'.
questions.model_answer: An organisational structure with few levels of management and a wide span of control [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of a flat organisational structure for Aurelia Hotels Group.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Lower costs [k] from removing 3 layers, saving an estimated $520,000 a year [app]. Advantage 2: Faster communication [k] between the 240 housekeeping and front-desk staff through fewer than the 7 levels [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Aurelia Hotels Group of widening spans of control to 14 staff per manager.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Reduced supervision [k], making it harder for each manager to check the work of 14 staff across 9 hotels [app], risking guest service quality in kitchens and housekeeping [an]. Problem 2: Manager overload [k] as wider spans leave little time to motivate or train 420 staff [app], increasing errors and absenteeism [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Aurelia Hotels Group should remove 3 layers and adopt the flat structure proposal? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Removing 3 layers [k] would save an estimated $520,000 a year [app], helping after revenue fell from $21m to $18.5m [an]. Communication through fewer levels would help the 240 housekeeping and front-desk staff coordinate in busy seasons [app], improving guest satisfaction [an]. However, keeping the tall structure protects close supervision [k] across 9 hotels, avoiding quality lapses that could push revenue down further. Overall, shareholders should back the flat structure proposal [eval] because the $2.5m two-year revenue drop shows delay is already costly, and checklists, duty managers and training can replace lost layers of supervision [eval].

close supervision advantage of tall structure
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation based on revenue decline and feasibility of replacing supervision with checklists, duty managers and training

scenario_stem:
Crunchy Harvest Snacks, a partnership, makes baked oat bars for 8 supermarket chains, with 16 workers and $640,000 sales. Trials with 300 shoppers scored a new peanut-butter bar 4.5 out of 5, and partners have a $15,000 promotional budget.

They must choose free samples—10,000 bars over 4 weekends, converting at 20%—or a lunchbox gift with every 6-bar multipack, costing $9,000 for 5,000 boxes and lifting sales 30% over the 6-week campaign.

questions.question_text: Define 'free sample'.
questions.model_answer: A small quantity of a product given to consumers at no cost so they can try it before deciding to buy [2].

knowledge_max_2: small quantity of a product given at no cost
lets consumers try the product before buying

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Crunchy Harvest Snacks of giving away free samples of the new oat bar.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Free samples let unsure customers taste the bar at no risk [k], which suits a new peanut-butter flavour buyers have not yet tried, handed out at supermarket entrances [app]. Reason 2: They can convert trial into repeat purchase [k], and at an expected 20% trial-to-purchase rate on 10,000 samples the partners could gain around 2,000 new buyers [app].

knowledge_max_2: lets customers taste a new product at no risk

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Crunchy Harvest Snacks of promoting the new bar with a reusable lunchbox gift.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Gifts add cost to every multipack sale [k], because $9,000 buys 5,000 lunchboxes, cutting the profit per 6-bar multipack just as the campaign launches [app], directly shrinking the margin that funds the $15,000 budget [an]. Disadvantage 2: Some customers may buy only to collect the gift [k], so when the 6-week campaign ends and the 30% uplift fades, underlying repeat demand may be far lower [app], wasting much of the $9,000 gift spend [an].

knowledge_max_2: gifts add cost per sale and cut profit margin
customers may buy only to collect the gift
analysis_max_2: shrinks the margin funding the $15,000 budget

questions.question_text: Do you think free samples or the lunchbox gift promotion is the better choice for the new oat bar? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Free samples put the product directly into shoppers' hands [k], and with 10,000 samples over 4 weekends at busy supermarket entrances and a 20% conversion rate, the partners could gain around 2,000 new peanut-butter bar buyers [app], building genuine product awareness at manageable cost within the $15,000 budget [an]. However, the lunchbox gift with the 6-bar multipack should lift multipack sales by 30% during the 6-week campaign [k], appealing to family shoppers already buying Crunchy Harvest products across the 8 supermarket chains [app], which may lift immediate revenue more than small samples [an]. Overall, free samples are the better choice because a new flavour depends on taste acceptance, and mouth-to-mouth persuasion drives repeat purchase better than a giveaway [eval], although briefly running both would maximise launch impact [eval].

gift promotion should lift multipack sales by 30% and appeal to families
