TV campaign guarantees 1.5 million viewer exposure with a controlled message
analysis_max_2: free word-of-mouth the money cannot buy
certainty and controlled message reduce the sharing gamble
evaluation_max_2: weighs low-cost targeted viral reach against guaranteed TV exposure
judges fit to the tight budget and young demographic and recommends risk insurance

scenario_stem:
Northgate Paper Bags is a partnership making recycled paper shopping bags in Country X. Batches sell for $90 with variable costs of $55 per batch and fixed costs of $52,500; it sold 2,500 batches last year.

The partners weigh larger premises adding $17,500 to fixed costs and lifting output to 3,200 batches, against a six-month bulk order from a wholesaler at $80 per batch. Both are risky; they want effects on break-even output and margin of safety.

questions.question_text: State what is meant by 'total fixed cost'.
questions.model_answer: Total fixed cost is the sum of all costs that do not vary with output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and salaries - Northgate's $52,500 a year stays the same whether 1 or 3,200 batches are made. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run
Examples include rent, insurance and salaries

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the partners should calculate break-even output for the two options.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: to see how the extra premises cost changes the sales needed to avoid losses [k]; the larger site lifts fixed costs to $70,000, so break-even output rises to 2,000 batches ($70,000 / $35) against 1,500 batches today, showing the business must gain around 500 extra batches just to stand still [app]. Reason 2: to compare the bulk order honestly [k]; at $80 per batch contribution is only $25, giving a 2,100-batch break-even ($52,500 / $25), so the partners can see that filling the order with bulk sales alone would leave only a thin cushion at 2,500 batches [app].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit
Comparison of break-even across options reveals relative risk
application_max_2: Applies figures: larger premises $70,000 / $35 = 2,000 batches vs 1,500 today
Applies figures: bulk order contribution $25, break-even 2,100 batches

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis when comparing the premises and the bulk order.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes output is sold at one constant price, yet the two options use different prices [k]; blending $90 supermarket batches with $80 wholesale batches changes the average contribution, so a single break-even figure misleads the partners about true safety ($25 contribution on bulk batches versus $35 normally) [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes all output is sold and costs stay linear [k]; moving to a larger premises assumes supermarkets actually buy 3,200 batches, and costs such as transport, storage and extra power on a bigger site may rise faster than output, so the 2,000-batch break-even is only a guide and unsold batches would turn the expansion into a loss [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes constant price; multiple products/prices distort it
Break-even assumes all output sells and costs are linear
application_max_2: Applies figures: $25 bulk contribution vs $35 normal contribution
Applies figures: 3,200 batches assumed; larger-site costs may exceed $70,000
analysis_max_2: Explains blended pricing makes one break-even figure unreliable for the mix
Explains demand shortfall at 3,200 batches or non-linear costs create losses

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Paper Bags should move to the larger premises? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The partners could move because supermarket demand is growing and capacity is the constraint [k]; the larger premises raises fixed costs to $70,000 and lifts capacity to 3,200 batches, giving a 2,000-batch break-even output and, at 3,200 batches, a margin of safety of 1,200 batches and profit of $42,000 (3,200 x $35 - $70,000) [app][an]. However, at last year's 2,500 batches the bigger site would earn only $17,500 profit (2,500 x $35 - $70,000), halving the current $35,000 profit, and the partners would need around 3,000 batches just to match today's earnings - unproven demand for a business employing nine staff [app][an]. Conversely, the six-month bulk order at $80 per batch is safer in the short run: contribution of $25 per batch still beats doing nothing new, and it would build the cash and track record needed to support the premises move later, without betting $17,500 extra every year on untested capacity [k][eval]. Overall, the partners should move to the larger premises only if at least one or two supermarkets sign volume commitments consistent with 3,000-3,200 batches a year; if not, they should take the bulk order first, bank the $25-per-batch contribution, and revisit the move in 12 months when the extra demand is proven rather than hoped for [eval].

scenario_stem:
Marigold Bakery & Patisserie is a private limited company supplying 14 supermarkets with bread and celebration cakes. Invoices are paid 30 days late. questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.

Benefit 2: the discount is cheaper than the alternative finance [k]; a 4% discount costs $940, while a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest costs $2,250 a year, so the discount saves about $1,310 [app].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Hillybrook Honey Farm is a family partnership bottling wildflower honey in 500g jars in Country X. Jars sell for $8 with variable costs of $3.00 per jar and fixed costs of $36,000; it filled 9,000 jars.

Owners weigh a new bottling line raising fixed costs to $60,000 but cutting costs to $2.00 per jar, or lifting the price to $9. A wet summer makes them wary: honey sales swing with weather and tourism, so break-even figures may mislead.

questions.question_text: Define 'total variable cost'.
questions.model_answer: Total variable cost is the sum of all costs that change directly with output, found by multiplying variable cost per unit by units made (Hillybrook last year: $3.00 x 9,000 jars = $27,000 - more jars means proportionally higher variable costs). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Variable costs change directly with output
Total variable cost = variable cost per unit x output

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the owners want break-even figures for the new bottling line.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: to check whether the line is affordable at current demand [k]; the bottling line raises fixed costs to $60,000 and cuts variable costs to $2.00 per jar, so contribution becomes $6.00 and break-even output jumps to 10,000 jars ($60,000 / $6.00) - 1,000 jars more than the 9,000 filled last year [app]. Reason 2: to compare the line fairly against the certification price rise [k]; raising the price to $9 also gives $6.00 contribution but keeps fixed costs at $36,000, so break-even output would be 6,000 jars - a far safer cushion than the line offers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit
Higher fixed costs raise break-even output even when variable costs fall
application_max_2: Applies figures: line break-even $60,000 / $6.00 = 10,000 jars vs 9,000 filled
Applies figures: $9 price gives $6.00 contribution, break-even 6,000 jars

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why break-even analysis has limitations for a weather-dependent honey farm.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes all jars produced are sold [k]; a wet summer reduces both the honey crop and tourist footfall at farm shops and markets, so if only, say, 6,000 jars are sold, the $36,000 fixed costs would outstrip revenue and the calculated 7,200-jar break-even would never reveal that risk [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes prices and unit costs stay constant [k]; a poor harvest raises honey cost per jar, and discounting to shift slow-moving stock narrows the $5.00 contribution, dragging break-even above 7,200 jars and eroding the 1,800-jar margin of safety precisely when demand is weakest [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes all output is sold
Break-even assumes constant prices and costs (straight lines)
application_max_2: Applies figures: weak sales of 6,000 jars leave $36,000 fixed costs uncovered
Applies figures: narrower $5.00 contribution lifts break-even above 7,200 jars

questions.question_text: Do you think the owners should buy the new bottling line? Justify your answer.

However, at last year's 9,000 jars the line would raise fixed costs to $60,000 and give break-even output of 10,000 jars ($60,000 / $6.00), producing a loss of about $6,000 (9,000 x $6.00 - $60,000) and a negative margin of safety of 1,000 jars - it cannot pay for itself without finding 1,000 extra jars a year [app][an]. Conversely, raising the jar price to $9 to fund quality certification also yields $6.00 contribution but keeps fixed costs at $36,000, so break-even output falls to 6,000 jars, the margin of safety widens to 3,000 jars and profit rises from $9,000 to $18,000 at unchanged volume [k][eval]. scenario_stem:
Kiriti Kitchens is a meal-delivery start-up founded 8 months ago by Priya Raman after her banking job. She invested $9,500 savings, delivers 340 meals weekly to 12 office blocks at $6 each, and employs 2 drivers.

To reach 30 office blocks she needs $14,000 for a second delivery van and 2 cooks. The Youth Enterprise Programme offers a $10,000 grant plus 8 weeks free training for 6 months, but requires a business plan; otherwise she reinvests $800 monthly.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'entrepreneur'.
questions.model_answer: A person who takes the risk of starting and running a business, organising resources to produce goods or services in the hope of making a profit [2].

knowledge_max_2: person who takes the risk to start/run a business
organises resources to produce goods/services for profit

questions.question_text: Explain two characteristics of a successful entrepreneur shown by Priya when founding Kiriti Kitchens.
questions.model_answer: Characteristic 1: Risk-taking [k], shown when Priya left her secure banking job and invested $9,500 of her savings [app]. Characteristic 2: Determination [k], shown by working to deliver 340 meals a week across 12 office blocks only 8 months after launch [app].

application_max_2: 340 meals a week / 12 office blocks / 8 months

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kiriti Kitchens of completing the detailed business plan required by the Youth Enterprise Programme.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Clear objectives and direction [k], because the plan forces Priya to cost her expansion to 30 office blocks, including $14,000 for a second van and 2 cooks [app], reducing the risk of running out of cash during growth [an]. Benefit 2: Easier access to finance [k], because the plan sets out how she will use the $10,000 grant and her $800 monthly profits [app], making approval by the government lender more likely [an].

analysis_max_2: reduces risk of cash-flow problems during growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should accept the $10,000 grant and expand to 30 office blocks, or keep Kiriti Kitchens small and reinvest $800 a month? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the grant gives Priya $10,000 plus 8 weeks of free business training [k], which covers most of the $14,000 expansion cost to reach 30 office blocks [app], lowering the financial risk of rapid growth [an]. However, the grant demands a completed business plan and monthly mentoring for 6 months [k], pulling time away from managing 12 office blocks and 340 weekly deliveries [app], which could strain a founder already working with only 2 part-time drivers [an]. Overall, Priya should accept the grant [eval], because a $10,000 boost plus free training outweighs the mentoring time cost, given her proven demand of 340 meals a week [eval].

knowledge_max_2: grant conditions: business plan + 6 months mentoring
evaluation_max_2: weighs grant benefits against time costs
recommendation justified using demand and figures

scenario_stem:
Redcliff Brickworks is a private limited company making clay bricks with 70 production workers and 6 drivers. Vera Okafor sets a daily target of 48,000 bricks and approves overtime; workers have no staff body.

A $900,000 contract for a supermarket development needs 60,000 bricks per day for 9 weeks. A union organiser cites 2 forklift accidents from rushed instructions. The board must keep Vera's autocratic speed or introduce democratic briefings.

questions.question_text: Define 'autocratic leadership'.
questions.model_answer: An autocratic leader makes all decisions alone, without consulting employees [2].

knowledge_max_2: leader makes all decisions alone/without consulting employees
employees expected to follow instructions without input

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of autocratic leadership for Redcliff Brickworks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Decisions are made quickly [k], allowing 60,000 bricks per day to reach the supermarket development within 9 weeks [app]. Reason 2: One clear authority [k] keeps 70 production workers focused on Vera's 48,000 bricks daily target [app].

knowledge_max_2: single clear authority/clear direction for staff

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of autocratic leadership for Redcliff Brickworks.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Workers feel ignored [k], which is why a union organiser has approached the 70 production workers [app], increasing the risk of disruption and lost output [an]. Disadvantage 2: Risks are missed by one person [k], as rushed instructions were linked to 2 forklift accidents last year [app], threatening the 9 weeks supermarket deadline [an].

knowledge_max_2: workers feel ignored/low morale and engagement
no input from workers who see risks first-hand
analysis_max_2: risk of union disputes/disruption and lost output
accidents threaten the deadline and safety record

questions.question_text: Do you think Redcliff Brickworks should replace Vera's autocratic leadership with democratic leadership on the supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Democratic leadership would give workers a voice [k] through daily briefings for the 60,000 bricks per day supermarket order [app], improving safety and morale so fewer accidents occur [an]. However, autocratic control gives one decisive decision-maker [k], letting Vera hit the tight 9 weeks deadline for the $900,000 contract [app], which lengthy democratic debates might delay [an]. Overall, democratic leadership is the better choice [eval] because consulting workers directly addresses the 2 forklift accidents and union pressure [eval] while still meeting the agreed deadline.

knowledge_max_2: democratic leadership consults/involves workers in decisions
autocratic leadership gives fast single decision-maker
analysis_max_2: consultation improves safety/morale and reduces accidents
democratic debates could delay output and risk the deadline
evaluation_max_2: weighs speed of autocratic control against safety and union pressure
justified recommendation tied to the accidents and deadline

scenario_stem:
Meadowsweet Skincare, a private limited company founded by Priya Nair, makes organic facial moisturisers with $410,000 sales through 3 high-street beauty shops. A supermarket offers shelf space in 25 stores, ordering 2,400 units monthly at $9 per unit.

But the supermarket pays 60 days late and charges $1,200 yearly in listing fees. An online marketplace takes 5% commission; her own website costs $6,800 to build. Directors must choose the channel protecting margins and growth.

questions.question_text: Define 'retailer'.
questions.model_answer: A retailer is a business that buys goods from producers or wholesalers and sells them in small quantities to final consumers [2].

knowledge_max_2: sells goods to final consumers in small quantities
buys from producers/wholesalers rather than manufacturing

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Meadowsweet Skincare might sell through the supermarket chain.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Supermarkets attract very large numbers of shoppers [k], so shelf space in 25 stores would expose her moisturisers to far more buyers than 3 high-street beauty shops [app]. Reason 2: Supermarkets are trusted, convenient places to buy everyday items [k], and an order of 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit would give a predictable, regular flow of revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: regular bulk orders give predictable demand and revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Meadowsweet Skincare would face by selling through supermarkets.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The supermarket pays 60 days late [k], so selling 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit means waiting 2 months for around $21,600 in income [app], which could create cash-flow difficulties [an]. Problem 2: Supermarkets squeeze suppliers on price [k], charging $1,200 a year in listing fees on top of a low unit price [app], reducing the profit available to reinvest in the brand [an].

knowledge_max_2: late payment/long credit terms strain cash flow
supermarkets negotiate low prices and may charge listing fees
analysis_max_2: lower margins reduce funds for marketing and growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowsweet Skincare should launch its own website to sell directly to consumers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Selling direct through its own website would give Meadowsweet Skincare full control over pricing, branding and customer data [k], avoiding the supermarket's 60-day late payment and $1,200 a year listing fees on the 2,400-unit monthly order [app], allowing more profit to be reinvested in marketing and quality [an]. However, a supermarket chain would give her instant access to shoppers in 25 stores [k], and an order of 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit would generate around $21,600 a month before fees [app], which a new website with unknown traffic may take years to match [an]. Overall, launching her own website is the better option [eval] because the $6,800 build cost is small next to a year's listing fees and it builds a direct customer relationship the brand needs [eval], while she can still approach supermarkets later with better terms.

knowledge_max_2: direct channel gives control of price, brand and customer relationships
indirect channel gives instant reach and sales volume through established retailers
analysis_max_2: more profit reinvested and stronger brand without intermediaries
a new website may take years to match supermarket volume
evaluation_max_2: weighs control/independence against instant supermarket reach
justified recommendation tied to the $6,800 build cost and listing fees

scenario_stem:
Hartwell Flour Milling Co is a private limited company milling flour in Country X with 45 workers. Last year revenue was $3.6 million and profit $420,000; it mills 600 tonnes monthly.

Daniel wants 900 tonnes monthly for a national bakery chain, buying grain in bulk at $240 a tonne instead of $310, saving $70 a tonne. Widening the warehouse costs $95,000, needed before the first delivery in four months; option B stays at 600 tonnes for local bakeries.

questions.question_text: Define 'purchasing economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Purchasing economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains by buying inputs in large quantities, because suppliers offer bulk discounts so the cost of each unit of materials purchased falls [2].

knowledge_max_2: Buying inputs in large quantities / bulk
Suppliers offer discounts, so cost per unit of materials falls

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Hartwell Flour Milling Co of purchasing economies of scale.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is lower grain costs [k]. Buying at $240 a tonne instead of $310 saves $70 a tonne, a saving of $63,000 a month on 900 tonnes, which cuts Hartwell's average cost per tonne of flour [app]. A second benefit is stronger competitiveness [k]. With cheaper flour, Hartwell can price its bid for the national bakery chain contract more aggressively than its larger rival, protecting its $3.6 million revenue base [app].

knowledge_max_2: Buying in bulk lowers the cost of inputs
Lower input costs can improve competitiveness / prices
application_max_2: Reference to $240 a tonne vs $310, saving $70 a tonne
Reference to $63,000 a month saved on 900 tonnes / national bakery chain contract

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Hartwell Flour Milling Co might face if it expands output to 900 tonnes a month.
questions.model_answer: One problem is the strain on cash [k]. Widening the mill warehouse costs $95,000, and grain must be paid for before the first delivery arrives, so Hartwell's cash position could tighten even though profit was $420,000 last year [app], and if the contract start is delayed the mill would carry the extra debt without the expected revenue [an]. A second problem is diseconomies of scale [k]. Running at 900 tonnes means more lorries, more staff and busier shifts each day [app], and without additional supervisors, miscommunication could raise flour waste and breach the bakery chain's quality requirements [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large expansion strains cash / requires upfront finance
Diseconomies of scale: coordination and communication problems as output rises
application_max_2: Reference to $95,000 warehouse cost / payment before first delivery
Reference to 900 tonnes output / $420,000 profit last year
analysis_max_2: Chain from $95,000 upfront spend to tight cash to risk if contract delayed
Chain from larger scale to miscommunication/waste to quality risk with national bakery chain

questions.question_text: Do you think Hartwell Flour Milling Co should sign the contract and expand to 900 tonnes a month? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, signing the contract gives Hartwell a reliable national customer and protects its $3.6 million revenue base [k]. Bulk grain at $240 a tonne instead of $310 saves $70 a tonne, worth $63,000 a month on 900 tonnes [app]. Lower input costs create purchasing economies of scale, so average cost falls and profit can rise above the $420,000 earned last year, making Hartwell more competitive against its rival [an]. However, expanding is not risk-free [k]. Widening the warehouse costs $95,000 before the first delivery in 4 months, cash must be found while the mill pays for grain up front, and running a bigger mill could bring poor communication and flour waste [app]. If the bakery chain delays or cancels, Hartwell would carry high fixed costs with sales below 900 tonnes, squeezing profit and possibly threatening the mill's future [an]. Overall, I think Hartwell should sign the contract [eval]. The $63,000 monthly saving is large next to the $95,000 one-off warehouse cost, which would be recovered in about 6 weeks of running at the new volume, and purchasing economies at this size clearly outweigh the coordination risks for a well-established mill [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Purchasing economies of scale reduce average cost when buying in bulk
Growth carries risks such as diseconomies of scale and cash strain
application_max_2: Reference to $240 vs $310 a tonne, $70 saving worth $63,000 a month on 900 tonnes
Reference to $95,000 warehouse cost, delivery in 4 months, $3.6 million revenue, $420,000 profit
analysis_max_2: Chain from bulk saving to lower average cost to higher profit and competitiveness
Chain from $95,000 upfront spend and bigger scale to cash strain or waste to risk if contract lost
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on signing the contract
Weighs both options using stem figures ($63,000 saving vs $95,000 cost and 4-month delay)

scenario_stem:
Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd is a private limited company milling oats into breakfast cereal for supermarket chains. Its income statement showed Revenue $486,000, Cost of Sales $312,000, Gross Profit $174,000, Expenses $96,000 and Profit for the year $78,000; after a $30,000 dividend, Retained Profit was $48,000.

With current assets of $210,000, working capital of $120,000 and shareholders' equity of $500,000, directors must choose between Option 1, a special dividend of $20,000, and Option 2, using the $48,000 retained profit towards a $120,000 dehuller.

questions.question_text: Define 'Revenue'.
questions.model_answer: Revenue is the total income a business earns from selling its goods or services during a trading period, before deducting any costs [2].

knowledge_max_2: Total income earned from selling goods and/or services
Earned during a trading period, before any costs are deducted

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit is important to Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit can be retained and reinvested, funding growth such as the new dehuller without extra borrowing [k], and the $48,000 Retained Profit shows that such funds are genuinely available [app]. Reason 2: Profit rewards shareholders for their risk, enabling the $30,000 dividend paid this year [k], which helps maintain investor confidence in the $500,000 of equity [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit can be retained and reinvested to fund growth without borrowing
Profit rewards owners/shareholders and enables dividends to be paid
application_max_2: $48,000 Retained Profit is available towards the dehuller
$30,000 dividend paid, rewarding shareholders in a company with $500,000 equity

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the income statement is useful to the directors when choosing between the special dividend and the dehuller.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The income statement confirms the company earned a Profit for the year of $78,000 after Expenses of $96,000, so the business is genuinely profitable and not just cash-rich [k], which tells directors that either option is genuinely affordable rather than a gamble on one good quarter [app][an]. Reason 2: It shows Retained Profit of $48,000 after the ordinary dividend of $30,000, indicating exactly how much could be committed towards the dehuller [k], so directors know Option 2 would use only two-fifths of the machine's cost and a further funding route would still be needed [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Confirms the business is profitable after deducting expenses
Shows retained profit available after dividends
application_max_2: $48,000 Retained Profit vs the dehuller's $120,000 cost
analysis_max_2: Sustainable profit means either option is affordable, not dependent on a windfall
$48,000 covers only two-fifths of the cost, so a further funding plan is required

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should pay the $20,000 special dividend (Option 1) or use the retained profit towards the dehuller (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 rewards shareholders for their risk and signals confidence in the company, returning part of the profit directly to investors [k], and it would be affordable given current assets of $210,000 and working capital of $120,000 [app], which should keep shareholders loyal ahead of the expansion [an]. Option 2 keeps the $48,000 inside the business and directs it towards the dehuller, protecting the future Gross Profit base rather than distributing it once [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the stronger choice because the dehuller should improve milling efficiency and lift future profits for every shareholder, whereas the special dividend is a one-off reward that shrinks the funds available for growth; the directors can revisit a dividend next year once the machine's returns are proven [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Retained profit can fund productive investment for long-term growth
application_max_2: Option 1 special dividend of $20,000 affordable from $210,000 current assets / $120,000 working capital
Option 2 keeps $48,000 retained towards the $120,000 dehuller
analysis_max_2: Dividend boosts loyalty now but leaves nothing for the machine
Dehuller should improve efficiency and protect/lift future Gross Profit
evaluation_max_2: For: immediate reward and signal of strength / option 2 costs shareholders cash
Against/Overall: Option 2 maximises long-term value; dividends can be paid once returns are proven

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Redmire Snack Foods is a private limited company in Country X producing savoury snack packs. It sells 240,000 packs yearly at $1.80 each, earning $432,000 revenue, with 35 staff; sales flat for 18 months.

Nordvik Foods, a Country Z multinational, offers Redmire a 3-year deal as Country X (host country) supplier: 300,000 packs a year at $1.45 each, four annual audits. Redmire needs $90,000 for a packing line (20% grant) and must choose the contract or domestic retailers.

questions.question_text: Define 'host country'.
questions.model_answer: The country in which a multinational company locates production, offices or sales operations, which is different from the country where the multinational was originally based [2].

knowledge_max_2: a multinational locates production/sales/operations in another country
that country is different from the multinational's home/origin country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redmire Snack Foods of accepting the Nordvik Foods contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A 3-year deal gives Redmire predictable, large-scale orders [k], with Nordvik wanting 300,000 packs a year, 60,000 more than the 240,000 packs Redmire currently sells [app]. Benefit 2: The government grant cuts the cost of the new packing line [k], covering 20% of the $90,000 investment, a saving of $18,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: guaranteed/regular large orders / stable demand from the multinational
government grants/support reduce the cost of investment
application_max_2: 300,000 packs a year vs 240,000 packs currently (60,000 more)
20% grant on $90,000 = $18,000 saving on the packing line

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Redmire Snack Foods could face if it accepts the Nordvik Foods contract.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The contract price is much lower [k], at $1.45 per pack versus $1.80 for domestic retailers [app], so revenue per pack falls by about 19% and profits may shrink unless Redmire raises output efficiency [an]. Problem 2: Redmire could become too dependent on one buyer [k], because Nordvik's 300,000 packs would exceed Redmire's entire current output of 240,000 [app], leaving Redmire vulnerable if Nordvik ends the 3-year deal or demands price cuts later [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower contract prices squeeze profit margins
application_max_2: 300,000 packs would exceed all current output of 240,000 packs
analysis_max_2: profits shrink unless efficiency/output rises to offset lower prices
vulnerable if the 3-year contract ends or prices are renegotiated downward

questions.question_text: Do you think Redmire Snack Foods should accept the Nordvik Foods contract or keep supplying domestic retailers at current prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the contract gives Redmire predictable, high-volume sales [k], with 300,000 packs at $1.45 bringing in $435,000 a year, close to the $432,000 it earns domestically now [app], and the 20% grant saves $18,000 on the $90,000 packing line, so unit costs should fall as volume rises [an]. However, the price is well below the $1.80 domestic rate [k], so Redmire must check that higher volumes still cover costs and the four quality audits a year [app]; failing an audit could lose the 3-year deal after Redmire has committed $72,000 of its own money [an]. On balance, Redmire should accept the contract, because secured volume growth and the grant outweigh the margin risk for a firm whose sales have been flat for 18 months [eval]; it should also keep some domestic retail sales so no single buyer ever dominates [eval].

knowledge_max_2: multinational contracts offer large, predictable volumes and scale
lower prices and single-buyer dependence are risks of such deals
application_max_2: $1.80 domestic vs $1.45 contract price; four quality audits a year; flat sales for 18 months
analysis_max_2: economies of scale and falling unit costs from higher output and the grant
margin risk and audit failure could strand the $72,000 investment
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on accepting the contract or not
recognises the continuing value of domestic retail sales as diversification

scenario_stem:
Marigold Mobile Hairdressing is a mobile hairdressing start-up founded by Jane Okafor with $6,000 savings. She serves 150 clients monthly at $18 a cut, but monthly costs of $3,400 exceed revenue of $2,700.

She has missed sales forecasts by 30% for 4 consecutive months and has no business plan. The Enterprise Reboot scheme offers free 10-week training and help renegotiating supplier credit; alternatively she could close, repay her $4,200 overdraft and seek work.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons why new businesses fail.
questions.model_answer: Poor planning and cash-flow problems caused by weak financial control [2].

knowledge_max_2: poor planning / lack of a business plan
cash-flow problems / poor financial or management control

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marigold Mobile Hairdressing may be failing.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Poor planning [k], because Jane has no written business plan and missed her sales forecast by 30% for 4 consecutive months [app]. Reason 2: Weak cash-flow control [k], because monthly costs of $3,400 exceed revenue of $2,700 [app].

application_max_2: no written business plan / sales forecast missed by 30%

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the government's Enterprise Reboot scheme could help Marigold Mobile Hairdressing.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Free 10-week business training [k], teaching Jane to write a business plan and set realistic targets for 150 clients a month [app], reducing the chance of repeating her planning mistakes [an]. Way 2: A dedicated mentor with supplier credit help [k], supporting her to renegotiate credit so costs stop exceeding revenue [app], easing Marigold's cash-flow pressure [an].

application_max_2: renegotiating credit to close the $700 monthly gap
analysis_max_2: reduces likelihood of repeated planning failure
relieves cash-flow pressure / stops losses growing

questions.question_text: Do you think Jane should try to revive Marigold Mobile Hairdressing using the Enterprise Reboot scheme, or close the business? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Reviving through Enterprise Reboot gives Jane free 10-week training and a mentor [k], tackling the planning failures behind her 30% sales miss and $700 monthly shortfall [app], which could return Marigold to profit without new capital [an]. Closing now would stop mounting losses and let Jane clear her $4,200 overdraft [k], but it abandons 150 monthly clients and the $6,000 she already invested [app], wasting her remaining potential [an]. Overall, Jane should revive the business [eval], because the free support directly targets her two biggest problems at no cash cost, unlike closing and restarting elsewhere [eval].

knowledge_max_2: closing stops losses and clears overdraft
analysis_max_2: could restore profit without new capital
closing wastes invested capital and client base
evaluation_max_2: weighs free revival support against certain losses
justified recommendation based on figures and support offered

scenario_stem:
Sunfield Vineyards is a partnership with 140 hectares of vines and 45 staff: 15 cellar hands and 30 seasonal pickers. Revenue is $2.6 million, bottles sell for $18. Marta Ilyenko uses democratic leadership, with weekly meetings and a profit bonus.

After a heatwave, 70% of the crop must be picked in 14 days, not 4 weeks, and $120,000 of grapes risk over-ripening. Two partners urge autocratic control, but Marta recalls staff flagging mildew early last year, saving $95,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'democratic leadership'.
questions.model_answer: A democratic leader involves employees in decision-making and consults them before deciding [2].

knowledge_max_2: decisions may be made collectively/by vote

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of democratic leadership for Sunfield Vineyards.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Staff feel valued [k], so 30 seasonal pickers contribute ideas at weekly meetings on pruning and shifts [app]. Benefit 2: Better-informed decisions [k], as cellar hands flagged mildew early last year, saving a $95,000 crop [app].

application_max_2: weekly meetings on pruning and shifts

questions.question_text: Explain two problems democratic leadership might cause Sunfield Vineyards during the heatwave.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Slower decisions [k], so 70% of the grape crop may over-ripen within the 14 days instead of the planned 4 weeks [app], risking the season's $2.6 million revenue [an]. Problem 2: Too many conflicting opinions [k], as 45 staff vote on shift patterns each week [app], delaying the urgent picking arrangements [an].

analysis_max_2: risk of over-ripening crop and lost revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunfield Vineyards should switch to autocratic leadership until the heatwave harvest ends? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Autocratic control gives one decisive leader [k], which could mobilise 30 seasonal pickers fast enough to save 70% of the crop within 14 days [app], preventing the $120,000 over-ripening loss [an]. However, democratic leadership keeps expert input flowing [k], letting the 15 cellar hands spot mildew and adjust picking priorities [app], which last year saved a $95,000 crop [an]. Overall, a temporary switch to autocratic leadership for the 14 days is justified [eval] because speed now decides the season's crop, though Marta should restore democratic meetings once harvest ends [eval].

knowledge_max_2: autocratic leadership gives fast single decision-maker
democratic leadership draws on staff expertise
analysis_max_2: fast autocratic action can save the over-ripening grapes
democratic input improves quality but may delay the emergency pick
evaluation_max_2: weighs crisis speed of autocratic control against proven value of consultation
temporary measure with return to democratic meetings justified

scenario_stem:
Copperdell Outdoor Furniture, a partnership, makes garden dining sets with 18 carpenters. Sets cost $410 and sell for $720 through 35 independent retailers keeping a 28% margin; delivering 220 sets a year costs $85 each, absorbed by Copperdell.

A wholesaler offers 750 sets a year at $470, collecting from the factory and reselling in 120 shops, removing delivery risk. A website would keep the full price but pay $85 each way and risk returns of 90 kg sets.

questions.question_text: Define 'wholesaler'.
questions.model_answer: A wholesaler is a business that buys goods in bulk from producers or manufacturers and sells them in smaller quantities to retailers [2].

knowledge_max_2: buys goods in bulk from producers/manufacturers
sells in smaller quantities to retailers/other businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Copperdell Outdoor Furniture might accept the wholesaler's offer.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The wholesaler would collect the sets from the factory [k], so Copperdell could stop absorbing the $85 lorry cost on 220 sets a year [app]. Reason 2: The wholesaler guarantees a regular bulk order [k], buying 750 sets a year at $470 each and reselling them in 120 shops [app].

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler takes over transport/delivery from the factory
regular bulk orders give steady, predictable demand

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Copperdell Outdoor Furniture of selling direct through a website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Selling direct removes the retailers' 28% margin [k], so Copperdell keeps the full $720 per set instead of sharing the price with 35 independent retailers [app], increasing the profit per set available to reinvest in the workshop [an]. Benefit 2: Selling direct builds a direct relationship with households [k], letting Copperdell collect feedback on its hardwood sets from buyers nationwide [app], which can improve future designs and strengthen loyalty [an].

knowledge_max_2: direct sales keep the full price/higher margin per unit
direct contact builds customer relationships and feedback
analysis_max_2: more profit per set to reinvest in the workshop

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperdell Outdoor Furniture should accept the wholesaler's contract rather than launch its own website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the wholesaler would remove all delivery risk [k], guaranteeing collection of 750 sets a year at $470 each and ending the $85 lorry charge absorbed on 220 sets a year [app], giving steady cash flow to run the workshop of 18 carpenters [an]. However, selling direct keeps the full $720 price and avoids the 28% retailer margin [k], and would build direct household customers rather than let the wholesaler resell under its own brand in 120 shops [app], protecting Copperdell's brand identity and long-term margin [an]. Overall, accepting the wholesaler is the safer short-term option [eval] because a guaranteed order of 750 sets a year outweighs the higher online price for a firm currently paying $85 lorry costs [eval], although a website could be added once cash flow improves.

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler gives a guaranteed order and removes transport risk
direct sales keep the full price and the brand
analysis_max_2: steady cash flow lowers risk for the workshop
risk of losing brand identity to the reseller's own brand
evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed wholesaler order against higher direct margins
justified recommendation tied to the $85 lorry burden

scenario_stem:
Sunvale Soft Drinks is a private limited company making premium sparkling fruit drinks. It makes 2 million bottles a year, earning $3.1 million revenue and $280,000 profit; last year's $150,000 advertising bought radio adverts.

Managing director Priya Raman wants a national brand. Option A is a $600,000 national television and billboard campaign for 1.2 million bottles and $1.8 million revenue; option B is a $120,000 regional campaign for 400,000 bottles and $600,000 revenue. The board has three months.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Marketing economies of scale are cost advantages where the cost of advertising and promotion is spread over a larger volume of sales, so the marketing cost per unit falls as the business grows [2].

knowledge_max_2: Advertising/promotion cost is spread over more units sold
Marketing cost per unit falls as output and sales rise

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Sunvale Soft Drinks of using a national campaign.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is a much wider audience [k]. A $600,000 national television and billboard campaign would put Sunvale's drinks in front of customers across the whole country, far more than the $150,000 a year now spent on three cities [app]. A second benefit is spreading the advertising cost over more sales [k]. Adding 1.2 million bottles to the 2 million already sold would spread the campaign cost over far more units, lowering the marketing cost per bottle [app].

knowledge_max_2: National advertising reaches a much wider audience
Marketing cost is spread over more units sold / cost per unit falls
application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 national campaign vs $150,000 spent on three cities
Reference to 1.2 million extra bottles added to 2 million current sales

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Sunvale Soft Drinks might face if it spends $600,000 on the television and billboard campaign.
questions.model_answer: One problem is the high upfront cost [k]. Paying $600,000 is four times Sunvale's $150,000 advertising budget and more than twice its $280,000 profit, so financial strain is a serious risk [app]. If sales do not rise as expected, cash flow would suffer and other investment plans would be delayed [an]. A second problem is poor targeting [k]. A national television and billboard campaign cannot be tailored to specific towns or income groups [app], so money could be wasted on viewers who never buy premium fruit drinks, lowering the return on the campaign spend [an].

knowledge_max_2: A large upfront campaign strains cash flow and profit
Mass campaigns cannot be targeted precisely / risk wasted spend
application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 vs $150,000 budget and $280,000 profit
Reference to national television and billboard campaign / premium sparkling fruit drinks
analysis_max_2: Chain from $600,000 spend to cash-flow strain to delayed investment if sales disappoint
Chain from broad targeting to wasted spend to lower return on the campaign

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunvale Soft Drinks should launch the national campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, the $600,000 campaign could transform Sunvale from a regional seller into a national brand [k]. It would add about 1.2 million bottles a year, worth $1.8 million in extra revenue, three times the campaign cost [app], and the higher volume would spread advertising and fixed costs over more units, lowering the marketing cost per bottle through marketing economies of scale [an]. On the other hand, the risk is real [k]. The campaign costs four times the $150,000 advertising budget of last year and over twice the $280,000 profit Sunvale earned, so if extra sales fall short of 1.2 million bottles the money would be wasted and cash flow could be damaged [app]. A safer route is the $120,000 regional campaign, expected to add 400,000 bottles worth $600,000 in extra revenue, growing the brand without crippling the business [an]. Overall, I think Sunvale should launch the national campaign [eval]. The expected $1.8 million extra revenue dwarfs the $600,000 cost, and without national visibility the brand may never escape regional obscurity; spend can be trimmed later if the response disappoints [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Marketing economies of scale: cost per unit falls as advertising is spread over more sales
Large campaigns carry cash-flow and targeting risks
application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 cost, 1.2 million extra bottles, $1.8 million expected revenue
Reference to $150,000 budget, $280,000 profit, $120,000 regional alternative with 400,000 extra bottles
analysis_max_2: Chain from higher volume to marketing cost spread over more units to lower cost per bottle
Chain from $600,000 upfront cost to cash-flow risk to potential harm if sales disappoint
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on the national campaign
Weighs both options using stem figures ($1.8 million vs $600,000; $120,000 alternative)

scenario_stem:
Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd is a private limited company servicing refrigeration units for supermarket and restaurant chains. Revenue was $1,150,000, Cost of Sales $690,000 and Profit for the year $110,000.

Its statement of financial position shows current assets of $300,000, including inventories of $95,000, current liabilities of $130,000, working capital of $170,000, capital employed of $990,000 and shareholders' equity of $690,000, with a $300,000 bank loan. Directors weigh Option 1, repaying $100,000 early to save $6,000 interest, against Option 2, buying a $92,000 delivery van.

questions.question_text: Define 'Current Assets'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets are assets a business expects to convert into cash, sell or use within one year, such as inventories, trade receivables and cash at bank [2].

knowledge_max_2: Assets expected to be sold, used or turned into cash within 12 months
Examples: inventories, trade receivables, cash at bank

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why positive working capital is important to Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Working capital pays the day-to-day running costs such as engineers' wages and supplier invoices, and Fenwick's $170,000 of working capital keeps its service visits operating smoothly [k][app]. Reason 2: Working capital shows whether current assets exceed current liabilities, and with $300,000 against $130,000 the company can meet its short-term debts on time [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Covers day-to-day operating outflows such as wages and supplier bills
Indicates ability to meet short-term debts as they fall due
application_max_2: $170,000 working capital funds the servicing operation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the bank would study this statement of financial position before restructuring the loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bank checks whether current assets can absorb an early $100,000 repayment, and with $300,000 available (including $95,000 of inventories) the cover looks adequate [k][app][an]. Reason 2: The bank assesses how the $300,000 long-term loan sits against the $990,000 capital employed and the $690,000 of shareholders' equity backing it, judging whether rescheduling keeps the loan secure [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Bank assesses liquidity/capacity to absorb extra or early repayments
Bank checks solvency: loan size relative to capital employed and equity
application_max_2: $300,000 current assets including $95,000 inventories vs $100,000 repayment
analysis_max_2: After repayment, roughly $200,000 of current assets would remain, still ahead of $130,000 current liabilities
Equity of $690,000 gives the bank confidence restructuring adds no meaningful default risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd should repay $100,000 of the loan early (Option 1) or buy the delivery van (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 would cut non-current liabilities from $300,000 and save $6,000 of interest, improving the balance sheet the bank assesses and freeing future cash flow for debt service [k][app][an]. Option 2's van would let the company reach more supermarket and restaurant contracts, protecting the $1,150,000 Revenue base and the servicing margin it generates [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the better decision because the guaranteed $6,000 saving is modest beside the Revenue the van could win, and with $300,000 of current assets covering $130,000 of current liabilities a $92,000 purchase still leaves working capital positive; the loan can be rebalanced next year once retained profits have rebuilt equity [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Early repayment cuts interest costs and improves the balance sheet
Investing in assets can generate additional revenue
application_max_2: Option 2 costs $92,000 and supports the $1,150,000 Revenue base
analysis_max_2: Lower debt improves future cash flow and bank relations
Van increases capacity to service more contracts; purchase still leaves working capital positive
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: guaranteed $6,000 saving and lower risk / frees no new income
Overall: Option 2 wins on revenue generation; balance sheet remains healthy afterwards

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Wharfdale Cement Co is a private limited company in Country X producing cement. It made 180,000 tonnes at $38 a tonne, sold at $52, employing 64 workers, while Country Z imports undercut prices.

Options: a $2.4 million grinding plant in Country Y, where labour is 30% cheaper and demand is 400,000 tonnes, or a $1.1 million upgrade of the Country X plant for export. Country Y needs expatriates for 2 years and brings political and currency risks.

questions.question_text: Outline one benefit to a business of becoming a multinational company.
questions.model_answer: It can access larger markets abroad, increasing sales and spreading risk across countries rather than relying on one domestic economy [2].

knowledge_max_2: spreads risk / less dependence on the home economy

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wharfdale Cement Co of building the Country Y plant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A Country Y plant would give Wharfdale access to a much bigger market [k], where projected demand is 400,000 tonnes a year, more than double its current 180,000 tonnes in Country X [app]. Benefit 2: Producing locally in Country Y would cut costs [k], because labour there is 30% cheaper, widening the $14 margin on each $52 tonne sold [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets / more customers
lower operating costs from cheaper labour/inputs
application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand vs 180,000 tonnes produced now
labour 30% cheaper in Country Y; cost $38 vs price $52

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wharfdale Cement Co could face if it builds the Country Y plant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The overseas plant demands heavy capital [k], at $2.4 million versus just $1.1 million for the export-upgrade option [app], so cash is tied up for years and any fall in Country Y demand would sharply reduce returns [an]. Problem 2: Operating abroad brings unfamiliar risks [k], including the 2 years of expatriate management and the political risks the board foresees [app], which could disrupt production and make budgeting very difficult [an].

knowledge_max_2: very high capital cost / large upfront investment
application_max_2: $2.4 million for Country Y vs $1.1 million for export upgrade
2 years expatriate team; political and currency risks noted by the board
analysis_max_2: capital tied up; a fall in Country Y demand cuts returns
disruption risk and difficult budgeting in an unfamiliar country

questions.question_text: Do you think Wharfdale Cement Co should build the Country Y plant or upgrade the Country X plant for export? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building in Country Y would let Wharfdale capture 400,000 tonnes of projected demand right at the customer [k], helped by 30% cheaper labour and the booming construction market [app], raising margins on each $52 tonne and spreading risk across two countries [an]. However, it costs $2.4 million, more than double the $1.1 million export upgrade [k], and needs 2 years of expatriate managers with political and currency risks [app], so a downturn in Country Y construction could leave an idle plant and stretched cash flow [an]. On balance, Wharfdale should upgrade the Country X plant and export through the southern port first [eval], because it is cheaper, reversible and tests overseas demand using existing strengths [eval].

knowledge_max_2: multinational location in growth markets brings scale and lower costs
overseas investment carries heavy capital and country risks
application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand; 30% cheaper labour; $52 per tonne
$2.4 million vs $1.1 million export option; 2 years expatriate team
analysis_max_2: higher margins and risk spreading via Country Y production
idle-plant/cash-flow risk if Country Y demand falters; export route is reversible
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (export first vs Y plant)
recognises staged/conditional logic: revisit Country Y after export proves demand

scenario_stem:
Amber Fox Games is an educational board-game start-up founded by Leo and Marcus Grant. They spent $7,500 on a prototype, have 3 trial schools but no business plan, and their $11,000 savings are nearly gone, leaving $4,000.

They must choose how to spend it: $1,500 for market research surveying 200 parents, or $3,800 for 100 printed copies to demonstrate at a schools exhibition in 6 weeks. Either could win the first 20 paid school orders.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'start-up'.
questions.model_answer: A newly established business, usually small, which is still developing and has not yet built a stable position in the market [2].

knowledge_max_2: small business still developing, not yet stable

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a business plan could help Amber Fox Games.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: It sets clear objectives [k], helping the brothers decide whether to spend their remaining $4,000 on research or samples before the 6-week exhibition deadline [app]. Way 2: It helps secure finance [k], showing schools or backers how the $7,500 prototype can become 20 paid orders [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two contents of a business plan that would be most important for Amber Fox Games, and why.
questions.model_answer: Content 1: Market research section [k], surveying 200 parents and teachers about the game [app], showing whether any school will actually pay for it before the brothers print 100 copies [an]. Content 2: Financial section [k], setting out the $3,800 cost of printed copies against their nearly exhausted $11,000 savings [app], avoiding running out of cash before orders arrive [an].

analysis_max_2: validates demand before committing to production
avoids running out of cash / poor financial control

questions.question_text: Do you think Amber Fox Games should spend their remaining $4,000 on market research, or on producing 100 printed copies of the game? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Market research costing $1,500 would reveal demand from 200 parents and teachers before committing further [k], protecting the remaining $2,500 of their savings [app], reducing the risk of producing a game schools will not buy [an]. Printed copies costing $3,800 would let the brothers demonstrate the game at the exhibition in 6 weeks [k], impressing the 3 trial schools and other buyers face to face [app], turning interest into early orders [an]. Overall, they should spend $3,800 on printed copies [eval], because a physical game at the exhibition can convert trial interest into the 20 paid orders they need, while research alone produces no sales [eval].

analysis_max_2: reduces risk of producing an unwanted game
evaluation_max_2: weighs information gain against sales potential
justified recommendation based on figures and timing

scenario_stem:
Aster and Grey Design Studio is a private limited company with 25 designers on $1.9 million fees. Leon Parks uses laissez-faire leadership: designers set their own hours and approve their own final work.

Growth strains: three clients worth $420,000 complained of inconsistent branding, two junior designers resigned, and deadlines slipped 4 times in 12 months. The board proposes a democratic style operations manager with weekly reviews, but Leon fears losing the senior designers producing 80% of fee income.

questions.question_text: Define 'laissez-faire leadership'.
questions.model_answer: A laissez-faire leader gives employees freedom to make their own decisions with minimal interference [2].

knowledge_max_2: minimal supervision or interference by the leader

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why laissez-faire leadership suited Aster and Grey Design Studio.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It empowers creative specialists [k], letting designers set their own hours and approve their own work [app]. Reason 2: It suits highly skilled talent [k], as the 6 senior designers producing 80% of fee income work best without close supervision [app].

knowledge_max_2: empowers creative/skilled staff to decide their own work

questions.question_text: Explain two problems laissez-faire leadership is now causing Aster and Grey Design Studio.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: No consistent standards [k], so 3 clients worth $420,000 complained about inconsistent branding [app], threatening future repeat business and referrals [an]. Problem 2: Junior staff lack direction [k], leading two junior designers to resign and brief deadlines to be missed 4 times in 12 months [app], raising recruitment costs and client delays [an].

knowledge_max_2: no consistent standards/control over work quality
application_max_2: brief deadlines missed 4 times in 12 months
analysis_max_2: risk of losing repeat business and referrals

questions.question_text: Do you think Aster and Grey Design Studio should replace laissez-faire leadership with democratic leadership? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Democratic leadership would add structured consultation [k] through weekly reviews and quality standards on the work of the $420,000 of unhappy clients [app], reducing branding complaints and keeping clients [an]. However, laissez-faire freedom drives the studio's core value [k], and 6 senior designers producing 80% of fee income may resist losing autonomy [app], risking resignations and lost income [an]. Overall, democratic leadership is the better choice [eval] because complaints, resignations and missed deadlines show freedom now needs limits [eval], though Leon should preserve autonomy for the 6 senior designers.

knowledge_max_2: laissez-faire freedom motivates top creative talent
analysis_max_2: standardised reviews reduce complaints and lost clients
removing autonomy risks losing senior talent and fee income
evaluation_max_2: weighs need for standards against creative freedom driving fee income
justified partial replacement preserving senior autonomy

scenario_stem:
Crimson Chilli Foods, a private limited company, makes Crimson Reaper hot sauce in 250ml bottles. Daniel Okoro sells 4,500 bottles weekly at $5.20 locally and wants to export to 2 neighbouring countries.

An agent at the northern port charges 9% commission, leaving shipping and paperwork with the firm. A foreign wholesaler offers 60,000 bottles yearly at $3.40, collected monthly—below the $3.75 local wholesale rate but transferring all transport risk.

questions.question_text: Define 'agent'.
questions.model_answer: An agent is a person or business that acts on behalf of a producer or seller to sell goods in a market, usually in return for a commission, without taking ownership of the goods [2].

knowledge_max_2: acts on behalf of the producer/seller
earns commission and does not own the goods

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Crimson Chilli Foods might export through the agent.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The agent works on commission [k], so Crimson Chilli pays 9% only on completed orders, never on unsold stock [app]. Reason 2: The agent is based at the northern port [k], giving access to buyers in the 2 neighbouring countries without setting up overseas [app].

knowledge_max_2: commission is paid only on completed sales
agent has local knowledge/contacts in foreign markets

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Crimson Chilli Foods of accepting the wholesaler's offer.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The wholesaler would buy 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 [k], adding a confirmed export order on top of the 4,500 bottles sold locally each week [app], making production planning easier [an]. Benefit 2: The wholesaler collects the bottles monthly from the factory [k], so Crimson Chilli avoids shipping costs, transport risk and import paperwork [app], protecting its local operation's margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler provides a large regular order
wholesaler takes on transport and collection risk
analysis_max_2: confirmed order eases production planning and scheduling

questions.question_text: Do you think Crimson Chilli Foods should export through the agent rather than the wholesaler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The agent would charge only 9% commission on completed orders [k], keeping Crimson Chilli in full control of its price, brand and paperwork in the 2 neighbouring countries [app], preserving the margin on each of the 4,500 bottles it could sell each week and beyond [an]. However, the wholesaler offers a guaranteed 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 with monthly collection from the factory [k], removing all transport risk and giving a predictable export order Daniel Okoro can plan around [app], which would support investment in extra production capacity [an]. Overall, the agent is the better first step into the export market [eval] because it limits financial risk while the firm tests demand in the 2 new countries [eval], although the wholesaler may suit the firm once the market is proven.

knowledge_max_2: agent = low-risk market testing, commission-only payment
wholesaler = guaranteed volume with transport risk passed on
analysis_max_2: keeps control, margins and brand while testing markets
guaranteed volume supports planning and investment
evaluation_max_2: weighs agent's lower risk against the wholesaler's guaranteed order
justified recommendation tied to testing the two new markets

scenario_stem:
Wexford Steel Co is a private limited company supplying rolled steel in Country X, employing 84 staff at one depot. It made 4,000 tonnes with revenue of $11.5 million and profit of $900,000.

Aaron Blake wants an electric furnace lifting capacity to 6,500 tonnes. The bank lends $2.5 million at 7% against rivals' 11%, with $175,000 annual interest. Option A fits it and sells the extra 2,500 tonnes under a 5-year supply deal; option B keeps 4,000 tonnes.

questions.question_text: Define 'financial economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Financial economies of scale are cost advantages where large businesses can borrow money at lower interest rates and on better terms than smaller businesses, because lenders view them as less risky [2].

knowledge_max_2: Large businesses pay lower interest rates on loans
Lenders see larger, safer businesses as less risky

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wexford Steel Co of financial economies of scale.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is cheaper borrowing [k]. Wexford would pay 7% interest rather than the 11% typical for smaller rivals, saving $100,000 a year on a $2.5 million loan [app]. A second benefit is funding expansion from outside savings [k]. Access to a $2.5 million loan lets Wexford buy the electric furnace and raise output from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes without waiting years to save the cash from revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Larger firms borrow at lower interest rates
Cheaper, easier finance funds growth and investment
application_max_2: Reference to 7% vs 11%, saving $100,000 a year on $2.5 million
Reference to electric furnace / capacity lifted from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes

questions.question_text: Explain two risks to Wexford Steel Co of borrowing $2.5 million at 7% interest.
questions.model_answer: One risk is the fixed interest cost [k]. Interest of $175,000 a year must be paid even in a downturn [app], so if steel orders fall, Wexford could struggle to cover payments and last year's $900,000 profit would shrink fast, raising the danger of insolvency [an]. A second risk is over-committing to one customer [k]. The 5-year supply deal depends on the extra 2,500 tonnes being sold [app], and if demand does not materialise, Wexford would be left paying for an underused furnace while still owing the bank $2.5 million [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid regardless of trading conditions
Debt creates repayment/insolvency risk if revenue falls
application_max_2: Reference to $175,000 a year interest / $900,000 profit last year
Reference to 5-year supply deal / extra 2,500 tonnes / $2.5 million loan
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed interest to pressure on profit to risk of insolvency in a downturn
Chain from reliance on one deal to underused capacity to cash strain while still owing the bank

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexford Steel Co should borrow the $2.5 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, borrowing at 7% shows a clear financial economy of scale [k]. Paying $175,000 interest a year instead of $275,000 at the 11% rate rivals typically pay saves $100,000 a year, and the furnace lifts capacity from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes under a 5-year supply deal [app]. That extra scale would spread fixed costs, such as the depot and management, over more tonnes, lowering average cost and helping Wexford win further building-sector contracts [an]. On the other hand, debt adds pressure [k]. Even at 7%, Wexford commits $175,000 a year for many years, and profit of $900,000 last year could evaporate if construction demand falls or the 5-year deal is renegotiated smaller [app]. Staying at 4,000 tonnes avoids any risk to the 84 staff and keeps Wexford flexible if orders drop [an]. Overall, I think Wexford should borrow the $2.5 million [eval]. The guaranteed 5-year supply deal secures the extra 2,500 tonnes of sales, and the four percentage point interest advantage saves $100,000 a year, making expansion decisively worthwhile for an established supplier [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Financial economies of scale: larger firms borrow at lower interest rates
Debt increases fixed financial commitments and risk
application_max_2: Reference to 7% vs 11%, $175,000 vs $275,000 interest, saving $100,000 a year
Reference to 5-year supply deal, 6,500 tonnes vs 4,000 tonnes, $900,000 profit, 84 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower interest and extra scale to lower average cost to more competitiveness
Chain from fixed interest commitments to pressure on $900,000 profit to insolvency risk if demand falls
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on borrowing the $2.5 million
Weighs both options using stem figures ($100,000 saving vs fixed $175,000 interest risk)

scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is a private limited company weaving wool fabrics for tailoring businesses. With Expenses of $87,000, Profit was $65,000, yet only $18,000 lay in the bank; a major customer pays 60 days late.

Current assets of $208,000 include $120,000 owed by customers and $70,000 of inventories; current liabilities of $150,000 include $112,000 owed to suppliers, leaving working capital of $58,000. Directors weigh Option 1, an overdraft, against Option 2, asking suppliers to extend terms by 30 days.

questions.question_text: Outline the difference between profit and cash.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the surplus remaining after all costs are deducted from Revenue in the income statement, whereas cash is the money actually received and paid; a credit sale counts as profit before the cash arrives [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit = Revenue minus all costs, as reported in the income statement
Cash = money actually received and paid; timing differences make the two diverge

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is profitable but short of cash.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Much of its earnings is tied up as $120,000 owed by customers, some of whom pay around 60 days late, so Revenue is recognised before the cash arrives [k][app]. Reason 2: The company must still pay Expenses of $87,000 and suppliers the $112,000 it owes, so cash goes out before the corresponding income is collected [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Credit sales create profit before cash is received
Costs must be paid when incurred, regardless of when cash arrives
application_max_2: $120,000 owed by customers, one pays about 60 days late
$87,000 expenses and $112,000 owed to suppliers still must be paid

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the statement of financial position shows how Carrowmore Weavers Ltd could improve its cash position.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The $120,000 of receivables inside current assets could be collected faster with firmer payment terms, immediately lifting the $18,000 cash balance without any new finance [k][app][an]. Reason 2: Suppliers are owed $112,000, so Option 2's extra 30 days would defer cash outflow, protecting working capital of $58,000 while the receivables are collected [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Convert receivables to cash faster through stronger credit control
Defer payments to suppliers by negotiation
application_max_2: $120,000 receivables vs only $18,000 in the bank
$112,000 owed to suppliers could be stretched 30 days under Option 2
analysis_max_2: Faster collection rebuilds the cash balance with no borrowing cost
Deferring outflow bridges the timing gap, keeping the business solvent month to month

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should take the overdraft (Option 1) or ask suppliers to extend terms by 30 days (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft would cover the immediate gap and is simple to arrange, but it is repayable on demand and its interest would eat into the $65,000 profit [k][app][an]. Option 2 defers the $112,000 supplier outflow at no direct cost and suits a profitable company with $58,000 of working capital waiting on $120,000 of receivables [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is preferable in the short term because Carrowmore is profitable and its problem is timing, not solvency; the directors should chase the $120,000 receivables firmly and keep the overdraft only as a backup if a major customer defaults [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Overdrafts give immediate cash but are repayable on demand and carry interest
Extending supplier terms is cost-free short-term finance
application_max_2: Overdraft interest would reduce the $65,000 profit
Option 2 stretches the $112,000 supplier bill while awaiting $120,000 of receivables
analysis_max_2: Option 1 solves the gap quickly but increases financing cost and dependency
Option 2 aligns outflow with expected inflow, stabilising the $58,000 working capital
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: certainty and immediacy / for Option 2: no cost but relies on supplier goodwill
Overall: Option 2, with the overdraft as backup — collect receivables and the cash crisis passes

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Dunharrow Woollen Mills is a private limited company in Country X weaving woollen cloth. It makes 60,000 metres with 110 weavers, exporting 25%. Trade barriers removed, deals with 9 countries and shipping cut delivery from 6 weeks to 10 days.

A Country Y group offers 1.2 million metres if Dunharrow meets its specification within 12 months. It can export from Country X or joint-venture in Country Y, yet the partner may copy designs and home production limits speed.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff (tax on imports) or a quota (limit on the quantity of imports), used to protect domestic industry [2].

knowledge_max_2: a government-imposed restriction on international trade
examples include tariffs (import taxes) and quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities that the removal of trade barriers has created for Dunharrow Woollen Mills.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Lower trade barriers open larger export markets [k], and the Country Y tailoring group alone wants 1.2 million metres a year, far more than the 60,000 metres Dunharrow makes each month [app]. Opportunity 2: Faster, cheaper shipping widens Dunharrow's reach [k], because delivery times have fallen from 6 weeks to 10 days, making overseas orders practical [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets after barriers removed
improved transport/communications make global trade faster and cheaper
application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year wanted by Country Y vs 60,000 metres a month made
delivery times cut from 6 weeks to 10 days; deals with 9 countries

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Dunharrow Woollen Mills could face if it forms the joint venture with the Country Y partner.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Dunharrow risks losing its designs [k], because the Country Y partner would see its specification and could copy it once the 12 months are up [app], damaging Dunharrow's competitive advantage in woven cloth [an]. Problem 2: A joint venture splits control [k], so decisions about quality, output and price must be agreed with the partner [app], which can slow responses to faults and disappoint the tailoring group [an].

knowledge_max_2: risk of ideas/designs being copied by the partner
shared control slows decisions and creates friction
application_max_2: specification visible to partner; risk after the 12 months agreement
shared decisions on quality, output and price versus 1.2 million metres commitment
analysis_max_2: losing design secrecy destroys Dunharrow's competitive advantage
slower quality/fault responses risk breaching the order's standards

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunharrow Woollen Mills should serve the Country Y order by exporting from Country X or by forming the joint venture? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting from Country X keeps Dunharrow in full control of its designs and quality [k], letting it earn the whole margin on 1.2 million metres a year through the 10-day container route [app], protecting the jobs of its 110 weavers and avoiding the risk of a partner copying its work [an]. Forming the joint venture would share the cost of weaving to specification and speed up the ramp-up within 12 months [k], giving local knowledge but splitting profits and ceding control of quality and price decisions [app], with the real danger of a future competitor armed with Dunharrow's specification [an]. On balance, Dunharrow should export from Country X [eval], because design protection and full margins outweigh shared setup costs, accepting a tight 12-month capacity challenge [eval].

joint ventures share cost/resources but split control and profits

capacity strain under 12-month deadline vs faster local ramp-up
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between exporting and the joint venture
