scenario_stem:
Harbour & Pine Boat Tours is a guided fishing-trip start-up run by Tom Weaver. It carries 28 passengers weekly in summer and 6 in winter at $45 a ticket, earning $58,000, though the boat lies idle 4 months yearly.

Tom wants a second boat costing $26,000. The Coastal Enterprise Scheme offers a $13,000 tourism grant, or he could refit the existing boat for $3,500 during the shutdown and accept slower growth.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'determination'.
questions.model_answer: A quality of successful entrepreneurs meaning the willingness to persist and keep working towards goals despite setbacks, obstacles or failure [2].

knowledge_max_2: quality of successful entrepreneurs / pursuing goals

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the government Coastal Enterprise Scheme could help Harbour & Pine Boat Tours.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: A $13,000 grant towards a second boat [k], cutting the cash Tom needs for the $26,000 expansion by half [app]. Way 2: Reduced tax for firms employing local staff [k], lowering fixed costs during the 4 idle winter months each year [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Harbour & Pine Boat Tours of receiving the $13,000 grant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lower personal financial risk [k], because the grant halves the $26,000 price of the second boat [app], making Tom's own cash stretch further [an]. Benefit 2: Faster expansion [k], funding capacity for 28 weekly summer passengers to rise as demand grows [app], building extra $45-per-ticket revenue sooner [an].

analysis_max_2: revenue grows sooner from higher capacity

questions.question_text: Do you think Tom should buy a second boat with the grant, or refit the existing boat for $3,500? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying a second boat with the $13,000 grant halves Tom's outlay on the $26,000 expansion [k], doubling capacity for 28 weekly summer passengers and capturing peak-season demand [app], which could lift his $58,000 annual revenue well above current levels [an]. Alternatively, refitting for $3,500 preserves his cash but leaves the boat idle for 4 months each year and caps growth [k], limiting earnings from just 6 winter passengers a week [app], so the business stays stuck at one boat's capacity [an]. Overall, Tom should buy the second boat using the grant [eval], because the $13,000 halves his risk and proven peak demand of 28 summer passengers justifies doubling capacity now [eval].

knowledge_max_2: grant halves expansion cost / doubles capacity
$3,500 refit preserves cash but caps growth
application_max_2: 28 weekly summer passengers / $58,000 revenue / 6 winter passengers
analysis_max_2: captures peak demand and lifts revenue
refit leaves idle months and caps capacity
evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion risk against cautious refit
justified by seasonal demand and grant figures

scenario_stem:
Kestrel House Care Home is a private limited company caring for 90 residents, with 85 staff including 55 carers on $13.20 hourly. Turnover is $4.4 million. 52 carers joined the union Caring Together to negotiate collectively.

The union demands $14.50, adding $150,000 to wages. Owner Priya Raman, never having recognised a union, must recognise Caring Together or handle carers separately; refusal risks a strike ballot, with 18 shifts unfilled last quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'collective bargaining'.
questions.model_answer: Negotiation between an employer and a trade union representing employees to agree pay and working conditions [2].

knowledge_max_2: negotiation between employer and trade union/employees collectively
to agree pay and working conditions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kestrel House of recognising the union for collective bargaining.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: One negotiating channel [k], letting management settle pay with the 52 carers 'Caring Together' represents at once [app]. Benefit 2: A more stable workforce [k], reducing the strike risk that left 18 shifts unfilled last quarter [app].

knowledge_max_2: single channel/simpler negotiation for many employees

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Kestrel House of conceding the $14.50 demand.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Higher wage costs [k], adding about $150,000 a year to the wage bill for 55 carers [app], squeezing the margin on $4.4 million turnover [an]. Drawback 2: Less individual flexibility [k], as pay must be settled collectively with 52 union carers [app], risking further demands the home cannot afford [an].

knowledge_max_2: less flexibility in pay decisions per individual

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrel House should recognise 'Caring Together' and bargain collectively? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Recognising the union enables collective bargaining [k], settling pay for all 52 carers in one process [app], which builds trust and reduces strike risk around 90 vulnerable residents [an]. However, conceding $14.50 per hour costs about $150,000 a year [k], pressuring a care home with $4.4 million turnover [app], and may set a precedent for further claims Kestrel cannot fund [an]. Overall, recognition is preferable [eval] because a strike ballot and 18 unfilled shifts threaten resident care more than the extra cost [eval], provided any deal is phased in over time.

analysis_max_2: improves trust, reduces strike risk and unfilled shifts
higher costs and precedent may strain finances
evaluation_max_2: weighs strike risk and resident safety against wage cost increase
justified recommendation preferring recognition with phased deal

scenario_stem:
Foxhollow Dairy Farm, a family partnership, bottles 3,200 litres weekly for 3 village shops. A third goes to supermarkets at $0.85 per litre, but they return cartons and pay 30 days late; the family is considering a farm gate shop and website at $1.60 per litre.

A wholesaler offers 4,000 litres weekly at $0.95 but demands a $14,000 upgrade. Farm gate and website buyers pay up front, with next-day delivery for $4 per order, yet weekend sales average 900 litres; the family must decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct selling'.
questions.model_answer: Direct selling is when a producer sells its goods straight to the final customer without using any intermediary such as a wholesaler or retailer [2].

knowledge_max_2: producer sells straight to the final consumer

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Foxhollow Dairy Farm of selling through its own farm gate shop and website.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The farm keeps the full $1.60 per litre [k], almost double the $0.85 per litre that retail supermarkets pay [app]. Reason 2: Farm gate customers pay up front [k], so the farm avoids the 30-day wait for supermarket payment and the cost of returned unsold cartons [app].

knowledge_max_2: producer keeps the full price/no share taken by intermediaries

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of accepting the wholesaler's offer.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The wholesaler would collect 4,000 litres a week [k], more than the 3,200 litres the farm currently bottles, so spare capacity on the refrigerated van would be used [app], increasing total weekly revenue [an]. Benefit 2: The wholesaler pays $0.95 per litre [k], which is higher than the $0.85 per litre supermarkets pay [app], improving the return on every litre collected [an].

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler offers a larger, more stable weekly volume
wholesaler pays more than the supermarkets
analysis_max_2: spare capacity is used, raising total revenue
better price improves margin per litre

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxhollow Dairy Farm should accept the wholesaler's offer rather than expand direct selling? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The wholesaler offers to collect 4,000 litres a week at $0.95 per litre [k], using the 800 litres of spare capacity and paying more than the $0.85 supermarkets pay [app], providing stable, growing revenue after the $14,000 upgrade [an]. However, direct selling at $1.60 per litre nearly doubles the price per litre [k], and customers pay up front with $4 delivery per order [app], building cash flow and brand loyalty that a wholesaler cannot match [an]. Overall, the farm should accept the wholesaler [eval] because 4,000 litres at $0.95 (around $3,800 a week) beats direct sales of 900 litres at $1.60 (around $1,440 a week) while weekend demand remains small [eval], keeping the farm gate shop open for loyal customers.

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler gives volume, capacity use and stable revenue
direct selling gives a higher price and up-front payment
analysis_max_2: stable growing revenue using spare capacity
direct selling builds cash flow and loyalty but demand is limited
evaluation_max_2: quantified comparison: about $3,800 vs $1,440 a week
justified recommendation linked to weekend demand of 900 litres

scenario_stem:
Carrick Pharmaceuticals is a private limited company in Country X making generic painkillers with 120 workers. It produces 80,000 packs, earning $8.4 million revenue and $950,000 profit; late deliveries have doubled.

General managers juggle marketing, planning and finance. Option A hires three specialists — marketing director, production manager and finance analyst — for $260,000, aiming to cut pack wastage from 9% (about $90,000 lost) to 3%. Option B waits until profit passes $1.1 million; the two owners disagree.

questions.question_text: Define 'managerial economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Managerial economies of scale are cost advantages where a larger business can afford specialist managers for particular functions, whose expertise reduces waste and improves decisions as the business grows [2].

knowledge_max_2: Large businesses can afford specialist managers
Specialist expertise reduces waste and improves decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Carrick Pharmaceuticals of hiring specialist managers.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is better decisions in each function [k]. A dedicated marketing director, production manager and finance analyst would each give expert attention to their area instead of roles being covered by stretched generalists at a business employing 120 workers [app]. A second benefit is lower wastage [k]. Targeting wastage from 9% to 3% would cut roughly $60,000 of the $90,000 lost each year, protecting part of the $950,000 profit [app].

knowledge_max_2: Specialist managers make better decisions in their function
Specialists reduce waste and errors in the business
application_max_2: Reference to 120 workers / general managers covering marketing, production planning and finance
Reference to wastage cut from 9% to 3% / $90,000 lost a year / $950,000 profit

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Carrick Pharmaceuticals might face from hiring the three specialists.
questions.model_answer: One problem is the salary cost [k]. The three specialists cost $260,000 a year, which would cut profit from $950,000 to roughly $690,000 before any savings are made [app]. If wastage does not fall as planned, Carrick would carry the extra payroll with no financial benefit in return [an]. A second problem is duplicated authority [k]. Adding a production manager above existing supervisors could create conflict over who makes decisions [app], and slow early coordination between new and existing managers could delay the very efficiency gains the hires are meant to deliver [an].

knowledge_max_2: Senior specialists are expensive and reduce short-term profit
New managers can create conflict or duplication of authority
application_max_2: Reference to $260,000 combined annual salaries / profit $950,000 to about $690,000
Reference to a production manager above existing supervisors / current generalist structure
analysis_max_2: Chain from $260,000 salary cost to lower profit to pressure if savings do not materialise
Chain from overlapping authority to conflict or slow coordination to delayed efficiency gains

questions.question_text: Do you think Carrick Pharmaceuticals should hire the three specialists now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, managerial economies of scale apply as Carrick grows [k]. At 120 workers producing 80,000 packs a year, general managers are stretched across marketing, production planning and finance; specialists could cut wastage from 9% to 3%, saving about $60,000 a year of the $90,000 now lost [app]. Expert coordination would also reduce late deliveries and missed orders, protecting the $8.4 million revenue and supporting further efficient growth [an]. On the other hand, the cost is heavy [k]. Paying $260,000 a year would drop profit from $950,000 to about $690,000, and the two owners disagree; if savings fall short, waiting until annual profit passes $1.1 million, as Option B suggests, would be the safer route [app]. Duplicated authority and slow decisions between new and existing managers are also possible at this size [an]. Overall, I think Carrick should hire the three specialists now [eval]. The wastage saving plus better marketing and financial control make $260,000 good value against a $950,000 profit, and postponing to $1.1 million simply lets more waste accumulate [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale: specialists improve decisions and reduce waste as firms grow
Hiring costs reduce short-term profit and carries integration risks
application_max_2: Reference to 120 workers, 80,000 packs, wastage cut from 9% to 3%, about $60,000 of the $90,000 saved
Reference to $260,000 salaries, profit $950,000 to about $690,000, Option B threshold of $1.1 million, $8.4 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Chain from specialist expertise to less waste and fewer errors to protected revenue and margin
Chain from $260,000 payroll to lower profit to risk if savings fall short / postponed hiring
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on hiring now versus Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($260,000 vs $950,000 profit and 9% to 3% wastage)

scenario_stem:
Hollyhock Nurseries Ltd is a private limited company growing ornamental plants for garden centres. Profit for the year was $68,000; after a proposed $25,000 dividend, Retained Profit is $43,000. Its statement of financial position shows non-current liabilities of $120,000 and shareholders' equity of $320,000.

To fund a $200,000 expansion the board chooses between Option 1, issuing new shares to investors, and Option 2, expanding gradually from retained profits of about $43,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'Shareholders' Equity'.
questions.model_answer: Shareholders' equity (shareholders' funds) is the owners' stake in the business, equal to capital employed minus non-current liabilities, made up of share capital plus retained profit and reserves [2].

knowledge_max_2: The owners'/shareholders' stake in the business
Equals share capital + retained profit, or capital employed − non-current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why retained profit is an attractive way to fund the expansion.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Retained profit is finance the business already owns, so it does not have to be repaid — keeping non-current liabilities at $120,000 unchanged [k][app]. Reason 2: Using retained profit avoids issuing new shares, so existing shareholders keep their proportional control of the $320,000 of equity [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Retained profit is permanent, internal finance — not repayable
Retained profit avoids diluting existing shareholders' control
application_max_2: Existing $320,000 equity remains in the same hands

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on shareholders' equity and on the expansion if Option 1 is chosen rather than Option 2.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Issuing new shares for $200,000 would raise shareholders' equity immediately from $320,000 to $520,000, providing the whole expansion fund at once [k][app][an]. Point 2: Option 2 adds only about $43,000 to equity each year, so building a similar fund would take around five years of retained profits while the expansion waits [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A new share issue increases share capital and equity by the amount raised
Retained profit builds equity gradually through reserves
application_max_2: Equity would jump from $320,000 to $520,000 under Option 1
$43,000 a year means around five years to approach $200,000 under Option 2
analysis_max_2: Option 1 lets the expansion proceed immediately and shares risk with new investors
Option 2 delays the project and keeps ownership unchanged, but growth is slow

questions.question_text: Do you think the board should issue new shares (Option 1) or expand gradually from retained profits (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 provides the full $200,000 immediately, letting Hollyhock respond to garden centre demand at once and lifting shareholders' equity to $520,000 without adding interest-bearing debt [k][app][an]. Option 2 avoids dilution and keeps every decision with the current owners, but at $43,000 a year the company would need roughly five years to match the fund, risking lost seasonal sales [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 1 is justified because Profit of $68,000 and Retained Profit of $43,000 prove trading strength, but not enough speed to seize the opportunity; new investors would enlarge the equity that backs the expansion and share the risk, so long as dividend expectations are negotiated carefully to protect existing owners [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: New share issues raise finance quickly and share risk with investors
Retained profit is the cheapest internal finance and preserves control
application_max_2: Option 2 yields about $43,000 a year — around five years to build a similar fund
analysis_max_2: Option 1 enables immediate expansion and faster growth in Revenue
Option 2 preserves control but loses the timing advantage of the opportunity
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 1: dilution and dividend expectations may pressure profits
Overall: Option 1, since retained profits alone are too slow to fund a time-sensitive expansion

scenario_stem:
Stormont Electronics Ltd is a public limited company in Country X assembling set-top boxes and routers. Its Country Z subsidiary (480 workers) repatriated $4.5 million to Country X and retained $1.7 million locally, drawing criticism.

The board weighs repatriating $5 million of the expected $6.8 million subsidiary profit to pay a special dividend in Country X and fund a factory upgrade, or reinvesting in a $5.5 million Country Z plant where reinvestment may earn preferential tax treatment.

questions.question_text: Define 'repatriation of profits'.
questions.model_answer: The transfer of profits earned by a multinational's subsidiary or branch in a foreign country back to the parent company in its home country [2].

knowledge_max_2: profits earned abroad are returned to the home/parent company
typically by a multinational's subsidiary or branch

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Country Z of Stormont repatriating $5 million of subsidiary profits.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country Z loses funds that could support local growth [k], because returning $5 million of the $6.8 million expected profit would leave only $1.8 million to reinvest or tax locally [app]. Problem 2: The host country gains less from foreign investment [k], so the planned assembly hall and its construction orders for local suppliers could be postponed [app].

knowledge_max_2: less money remains in the host country for reinvestment
fewer local benefits (jobs, supplier orders, taxes) from the MNC's presence
application_max_2: $5 million repatriated out of $6.8 million expected profit leaves $1.8 million
assembly hall ($5.5 million) postponed / local construction orders lost

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Stormont Electronics Ltd might choose to repatriate the profits to Country X.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Shareholders expect rewards from abroad [k], and paying a special dividend from repatriated profits boosts returns and may support the share price [app], which is why the board lists repatriation despite criticism from Country Z [an]. Reason 2: The parent company urgently needs funds at home [k], so repatriating $5 million could part-finance the Country X factory upgrade without new borrowing [app], improving productivity where head office and most owners are based [an].

application_max_2: special dividend planned to be paid in Country X
$5 million earmarked toward the Country X factory upgrade
analysis_max_2: shareholder approval and share-price support despite host-country criticism
improved home productivity / avoids interest on new loans

questions.question_text: Do you think Stormont Electronics Ltd should repatriate $5 million or reinvest it in the Country Z assembly hall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Repatriating $5 million rewards shareholders and helps fund the Country X factory upgrade [k], continuing last year's pattern of sending $4.5 million home while keeping $1.7 million locally [app], though taking $5 million of the expected $6.8 million could worsen relations with the Country Z government and invite punitive taxes [an]. Reinvesting $5.5 million in the Country Z hall would secure the 480 workers' jobs, win the hinted preferential tax treatment and expand capacity near the market [k], but it leaves the Country X factory underfunded and Country X shareholders without their special dividend [app], tying scarce cash to one overseas site that faces political risk [an]. On balance, Stormont should reinvest in the assembly hall [eval], because the tax preference and host-country goodwill are worth more than this year's dividend, provided the board explains the decision clearly to shareholders [eval].

reinvestment secures host-country relations, jobs and possible tax benefits

scenario_stem:
Keystone Tutoring is a one-to-one tuition start-up founded 11 months ago by Aisha and Zainab Rahman. It serves 90 students at $25 per hour, using a self-designed app to track progress. It earns $4,600 monthly and holds $22,000.

In their business plan they weigh spending $7,000 on marketing to recruit 150 new students against hiring a tutor at $2,000 a month for 60 more students. Both options risk their saved cash while the start-up is young.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'innovation'.
questions.model_answer: The introduction of new ideas, products, services or methods into a business, creating something new or improving an existing offering [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the Rahman sisters show the characteristics of successful entrepreneurs.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Innovation [k], shown by developing their own app to track the progress of 90 students after every lesson [app]. Way 2: Initiative [k], shown by founding Keystone Tutoring and building a digital tracking system before any competitor offered one [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Keystone Tutoring of preparing a business plan.

questions.question_text: Do you think the Rahman sisters should spend $7,000 on marketing, or hire an additional tutor at $2,000 a month? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Silverdale Adventure Park if it concedes the $13.50 demand.

scenario_stem:
VoltEdge Electronics, a private limited company, runs 2 high-street shops, with $1.9 million revenue including $640,000 online. Only 4 in 10 buyers trust paying unseen, and 18% of online orders return within 14 days.

questions.question_text: State two benefits of e-commerce for businesses.
questions.model_answer: Businesses can sell to a wider market, reaching customers across the country or the world [1], and businesses can trade 24/7 without the costs of running staffed physical shops at all hours [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for VoltEdge Electronics of switching to online-only sales.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Trading online only would remove the shops' fixed costs [k], saving $220,000 a year in rent and wages [app]. Reason 2: A website is open at all hours [k], serving customers nationwide and supporting the $640,000 of online revenue already achieved [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems VoltEdge Electronics would face by closing its 2 shops.

scenario_stem:
Silverline Electronics is a private limited company in Country X assembling circuit-breaker panels with 30 workers. Manual assembly pays $11 an hour for 40 hours weekly, producing 6,000 units a month at about $13,200 weekly labour cost; profit was $700,000.

Demand exceeds capacity. Option A buys an automated assembly line for $1.8 million, run by 8 operators, lifting output to 14,000 units; option B stays manual, hiring 12 workers at $11 an hour for 8,500 units.

questions.question_text: Define 'technical economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Technical economies of scale are cost advantages where a large business can afford advanced machinery and production techniques that lower the average cost per unit as output rises [2].

knowledge_max_2: Large businesses can afford advanced/automated machinery
Specialist techniques lower average cost per unit as output rises

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Silverline Electronics of buying the automated assembly line.

scenario_stem:
Redhall Textiles Ltd is a private limited company weaving upholstery fabric for furniture manufacturers. Revenue of $500,000, Cost of Sales of $300,000 and Gross Profit of $200,000 in 2025 became Revenue $650,000, Cost of Sales $455,000 and Gross Profit $195,000 in 2026, with Expenses $140,000 leaving Profit of only $55,000.

With current liabilities of $95,000 and working capital of $85,000, directors weigh Option 1, raising prices by 8%, against Option 2, a cheaper yarn supplier cutting Cost of Sales by 10% but risking quality.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Gross Profit fell even though Revenue rose.

Reason 2: Higher yarn and material costs raised the cost of each metre of fabric, so although the company sold more, every sale contributed a lower margin [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: When cost of sales grows faster than revenue, gross profit is squeezed
Higher direct input costs reduce the surplus on each unit sold

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the falling Gross Profit creates for the directors.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: With Expenses already at $140,000, the smaller Gross Profit of $195,000 leaves Profit for the year of only $55,000, so there is almost no cushion if input costs rise further [k][app][an]. Reason 2: Less Gross Profit means less is available to retain from earnings, so while working capital is only $85,000 against $95,000 of current liabilities, funding growth or replacing looms becomes very difficult [k][app][an].

Lower retained profit restricts internal funding for growth

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should raise the selling price by 8% (Option 1) or switch to the cheaper yarn supplier (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 would lift Revenue to about $702,000 if sales volume holds, restoring Gross Profit to roughly $247,000 with no change in fabric quality [k][app][an]. Option 2 would cut Cost of Sales by about $45,500 a year (10% of $455,000), lifting Gross Profit to roughly $240,500 but risking the quality reputation that wins upholstery contracts [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 1 is the safer recommendation because Expenses of $140,000 and the falling $55,000 Profit leave no room for returns or complaints; working capital of $85,000 cannot absorb a quality dispute with a furniture manufacturer, so protecting the product matters more than the modest $6,500 difference in year-one Gross Profit [eval][eval].

scenario_stem:
Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making brake discs and hub assemblies. It employs 88 workers, sells 500,000 discs a year and had $9.6 million revenue.

Kestrel Mobility Group, a foreign multinational opening a Country X plant, offers a 4-year deal for 700,000 discs annually. questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd of winning the Kestrel contract.

Benefit 2: Trevelyan gains new technology and skills [k], because Kestrel's engineers would help install the $800,000 automated grinding equipment, lifting quality and productivity [app].

questions.question_text: Do you think Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd should accept the Kestrel contract or keep supplying domestic customers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the Kestrel deal offers 700,000 discs a year of secured sales, well above Trevelyan's 500,000 output, plus technology transfer as Kestrel's engineers help install the grinding equipment [k]; the $800,000 cost is steep, but the 4-year contract spreads it and domestic demand of 300,000 discs cannot fill the line alone [app], so productivity and worker skills should jump [an]. scenario_stem:
Silverline Security Systems is a sole trader alarm-installation business run by Derek Hale for 7 years with 9 technicians. Revenue reached $380,000 but profit only $9,000, amid 4 missed-site visits weekly, 2 of 9 technicians leaving and a 15% complaint rate.

Derek avoids delegation. The Skills for Enterprise programme funds 70% of a 12-week management course costing $8,000. Alternatively he could sell his contracts and vans to a national firm for $140,000 and start afresh.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'initiative'.

knowledge_max_2: spotting and acting on opportunities / proactive quality

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Silverline Security Systems may be failing despite being established.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Poor management [k], because Derek avoids delegation, causing 4 missed-site visits a week and 2 of 9 technicians leaving [app]. Reason 2: Weak customer focus [k], because a complaint rate of 15% of jobs is damaging reputation and repeat business [app].

application_max_2: 4 missed-site visits a week / 2 of 9 technicians left

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the government's Skills for Enterprise programme could help Derek.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: 70% funding of a 12-week management course [k], cutting Derek's cost to $2,400 of the $8,000 fee [app], making professional training affordable [an]. Way 2: Teaching delegation, scheduling and customer care [k], directly reducing the 4 missed-site visits a week and technician turnover [app], lifting profit from just $9,000 [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Derek should undertake the management training, or sell the business for $140,000? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Citybasket Grocery, a private limited company, runs 3 supermarkets and online delivery. The average basket is $54 and each van route costs $68; customers pay $5 delivery, but 60% abandon at that fee.

Owners propose a $65 minimum for free delivery within 8 kilometres. Fuel rose 19%, and of 240 deliveries weekly only 80 of them reach $65; punctuality complaints rose 15%, so they must weigh margins against customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'logistics'.
questions.model_answer: Logistics is the planning and management of the movement and storage of goods, including transport, warehousing and delivery from producer to consumer [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Citybasket Grocery of offering free delivery on orders above $65.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Free delivery encourages customers to add items to their basket [k], lifting the average $54 order toward $65 or more [app]. Reason 2: Larger orders spread the $68 delivery cost across more items [k], improving the margin on each of the 240 deliveries made weekly [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Citybasket Grocery would face with the $65 free-delivery rule.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Only 80 of them reach $65 or more among the 240 deliveries made weekly [k], so two-thirds of current customers would not qualify for free delivery [app], risking lost orders and more abandoned baskets [an]. Problem 2: Fuel prices have risen 19% this year and driver wages absorb half of route costs [k], so a $65 order may not cover the $68 cost of each route [app], wiping out the delivery margin [an].

However, only 80 of them reach $65 or more among the 240 weekly deliveries [k], so two-thirds of customers gain nothing, and with 60% already abandoning baskets at the $5 charge, some may switch to rivals [app], risking a fall in delivery volume [an]. Overall, the owners should introduce the $65 rule [eval] because raising basket sizes is the best lever to offset the 19% fuel cost rise [eval], provided they monitor abandoned baskets closely after the change.

scenario_stem:
Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative is a co-operative owned by 60 member farms in Country X, collecting 150,000 litres daily with 55 staff. Revenue was $9.8 million and the surplus paid to members $640,000.

Option A builds a $4 million central plant, cutting average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre and raising capacity to 240,000 litres daily. Option B upgrades for $1.2 million to 190,000 litres. Members fear late payments, coordination problems and slow decisions across a doubled site.

questions.question_text: Define 'scale of production'.
questions.model_answer: Scale of production is the size of a business's output, meaning how large the operation is and the volume of goods or services it produces [2].

knowledge_max_2: Scale of production refers to the size of output / the volume produced
It shows how large the business operation is

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Meadowlark of increasing its scale of production.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. A new central plant would cut average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre, saving 9 cents on every one of 240,000 litres processed each day [app]. A second benefit is greater capacity for member farms [k]. Capacity rising from 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day means all 60 member farms can sell more milk through the co-operative instead of seeking outside buyers [app].

Larger scale gives more capacity and output

Reference to capacity 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day / 60 member farms

questions.question_text: Explain two diseconomies of scale Meadowlark might face at a large central plant.
questions.model_answer: One diseconomy is poor communication [k]. A bigger site with more drivers, engineers and member farms means messages travel further, and a quality problem in one shift could reach the board days late [app]. Slow reaction would waste more milk than the current 150,000-litres-a-day operation, hitting the $9.8 million revenue [an]. A second diseconomy is slow decision-making [k]. More layers of approval at a plant nearly twice the size mean routine decisions, such as buying parts or changing shifts, take longer [app], so the co-operative becomes sluggish just as larger rivals cut their prices [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative should build the large central plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, bigger scale brings real economies [k]. A plant 60% larger could bring poor communication and slower decisions across 60 farms, and if 240,000 litres cannot be sold profitably, member milk could be paid late, as some members fear [app]. Option B, upgrading the existing line for $1.2 million to reach 190,000 litres a day, is a cheaper and safer step that still adds capacity and avoids a doubled site [an]. Overall, I think Meadowlark should build the central plant [eval]. The $0.49 average cost and an extra 90,000 litres of daily capacity offer savings far beyond the $1.2 million upgrade, provided the board appoints extra supervisors to keep communication clear [eval].

scenario_stem:
Dunmore Cheese Co Ltd is a private limited company making farmhouse cheese from locally collected milk. Point 2: Most of the current assets are tied up as $85,000 of inventories and $95,000 of trade receivables, leaving $10,000 of cash, so one slow-paying customer could create an immediate cash crisis [k][app][an].

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should cut inventories to $55,000 (Option 1) or ask the bank to convert the $60,000 overdraft into a long-term loan (Option 2)? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Do you think Brentmoor Steel Plc should lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting costs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lobbying for the 15% tariff would narrow the 18% import gap, lifting Brentmoor's $610 competitiveness and defending its 22% market share and 320 workers [k], but it risks alienating the two construction groups that buy much of its 90,000 tonnes a year and invites retaliation against Country X exporters [app], while discouraging the efficiency drive needed on the $540 cost [an]. Cutting costs to compete freely keeps customers loyal and prepares Brentmoor for any removal of protection [k], but trimming $540 per tonne below import prices 18% under $610 is hard and may mean wage or job cuts [app], with no guarantee of success [an]. On balance, Brentmoor should lobby for the tariff in the short term while committing to an internal efficiency programme [eval], because defending 320 jobs now matters and protection cannot be permanent [eval].

knowledge_max_2: tariffs protect domestic industry from cheaper imports
protection raises customer costs and breeds complacency
application_max_2: 15% tariff vs 18% import gap; $540 cost and $610 price; 22% share
two construction groups oppose; 90,000 tonnes a year; 320 workers
analysis_max_2: tariff defends jobs/share but risks losing customers and retaliation
efficiency focus keeps loyalty but is hard and may cut wages/jobs
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified position (short-term lobbying with long-term efficiency)
recognises protection is temporary, not permanent

scenario_stem:
Tansy Lane Plant Nursery is a plant-growing start-up run by Elise Moreau. It sells to 6 garden centres and 40 households, with $74,000 revenue and one weekend worker. She wants a full-time assistant grower at $1,900 a month.

The First Steps Employment Scheme offers a tax incentive of 20% of wages for 2 years plus a $5,000 grant for tools and a greenhouse vent system. With $16,000 cash and last autumn's frost cutting stock 18%, Elise fears hiring before the spring peak.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'tax incentive'.
questions.model_answer: A reduction or exemption in the tax a business has to pay, offered by the government to encourage activities such as hiring staff or investing [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why governments support start-ups like Tansy Lane Plant Nursery.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To reduce unemployment [k], by encouraging Elise to hire her first full-time assistant grower [app]. Reason 2: To boost regional economic growth [k], helping the nursery add $74,000 of revenue while serving 6 garden centres and 40 households locally [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tansy Lane Plant Nursery of the government's First Steps Employment Scheme.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lower wage costs [k], with a tax incentive of 20% of her first full-time employee's $1,900 monthly wages for 2 years [app], saving around $380 a month [an]. Benefit 2: A $5,000 tools and greenhouse grant [k], contributing towards tools and a greenhouse vent system without draining her $16,000 cash reserve [app], preserving working capital before spring [an].

analysis_max_2: preserves working capital before spring peak

questions.question_text: Do you think Elise should hire her first full-time employee now, or wait until after the spring sales peak? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring now lets Elise claim the 20% tax incentive and $5,000 tools grant immediately [k], offsetting about $380 of the $1,900 monthly wage and equipping her before orders peak [app], which strengthens the business for spring [an]. However, her cash reserve is only $16,000 and the autumn frost already cut stock by 18% [k], so committing $1,900 a month before spring revenue arrives risks a cash-flow strain [app], leaving little buffer if sales disappoint [an]. Overall, Elise should hire now [eval], because the $5,000 grant plus 20% tax relief discounts the wage cost and 6 garden centres need reliable hedging supply through the spring peak [eval].

knowledge_max_2: hiring now unlocks tax incentive + tools grant
waiting protects cash reserve until demand confirmed
analysis_max_2: grant and relief cut effective wage cost
evaluation_max_2: weighs incentive timing against cash risk
justified recommendation using figures and demand

scenario_stem:
Juniper Botanicals is a private limited company distilling craft gin, bottling 240,000 bottles yearly with 28 staff including 10 distillers, on $1.5 million. Elena Marchetti leads democratically, consulting on recipes, batch sizes and shift patterns.

A second bottling line needs 12 new staff and faster shift coverage decisions. COO candidate Darek Stone offers autocratic discipline, while union membership has risen to 18 of 28 staff. Elena must give Darek an autocratic brief or promote a democratic leader.

questions.question_text: Define 'leadership style'.
questions.model_answer: The way a manager behaves and makes decisions, for example autocratic, democratic or laissez-faire [2].

knowledge_max_2: manner/approach of a leader when making decisions and treating staff

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Elena's democratic leadership has worked at Juniper Botanicals so far.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Skilled distillers contribute expertise [k], improving recipes and batch sizes discussed in team consultations [app]. Reason 2: Staff feel valued [k], which suits a small 28-staff firm where morale drives output [app].

knowledge_max_2: consultation boosts morale and motivation in small teams

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why appointing Darek Stone as an autocratic operations manager might help Juniper Botanicals.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Faster decisions [k], covering rosters for the second bottling line's 12 new staff without delay [app], keeping 240,000 bottles a year on schedule [an]. Benefit 2: Tighter discipline [k], enforcing consistent shift coverage across both lines [app], reducing errors and wastage [an].

analysis_max_2: avoids growth bottlenecks/keeps production on schedule

questions.question_text: Do you think Juniper Botanicals should appoint Darek Stone with an autocratic brief? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Appointing Darek brings rapid, clear decisions [k], which suits the second bottling line needing 12 new staff and faster shift coverage [app], avoiding bottlenecks as output heads past 240,000 bottles [an]. However, 18 of 28 staff are union members wanting formal consultation [k], and an autocratic brief could trigger grievances or resignations among the 10 distillers [app], undermining the morale behind $1.5 million revenue [an]. Overall, promoting an internal democratic team leader is the safer choice [eval] because losing distillers would cost more than slower decisions [eval].

knowledge_max_2: democratic option preserves consultation and morale
analysis_max_2: autocratic brief aids growth but risks grievances/turnover
losing distillers harms quality and revenue growth
evaluation_max_2: weighs speed for the second line against morale and union relations
justified preference for internal democratic leader

scenario_stem:
Petalpost Florists, a partnership, runs 2 shops. Walk-in bouquets average $46; online orders average $52, but 12% are refunded within 48 hours as flowers arrive bruised. Courier delivery costs $7, and online brings 40% of revenue.

Spring weddings will bring 340 online bouquets over 3 months, yet 9 complaints cited misleading photos. With a rival accused of fake reviews, the partners must decide whether to keep promoting delivery or focus on the 2 shops.

questions.question_text: Define 'intermediary'.
questions.model_answer: An intermediary is a person or business, such as a wholesaler, retailer or agent, that links the producer of a product with the final consumer in the channel of distribution [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Petalpost Florists of promoting online bouquet orders.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Online orders average $52 per bouquet [k], which is $6 more than the $46 walk-in average [app]. Reason 2: A website is open all day and night [k], capturing sales during the spring wedding season, which will bring 340 online bouquets over the next 3 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: online orders have a higher average value

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Petalpost Florists of delivering online orders.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers before dispatch [k], and 12% are refunded within 48 hours because the flowers arrive bruised or smaller than the photographs suggest [app], adding courier and refund costs [an]. Disadvantage 2: Each courier delivery costs the firm $7 [k], while 9 complaints last month mentioned misleading photos [app], damaging the firm's reputation and future sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: refunds and damaged goods erode margins
analysis_max_2: refund and courier costs reduce profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Petalpost Florists should keep promoting online delivery rather than concentrate on its 2 shops? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Keeping delivery would exploit the 40% of monthly bouquet revenue already coming online at an average of $52 per order [k], capturing the 340 wedding bouquets over the coming 3 months with round-the-clock ordering [app], growing sales beyond what the 2 shops can handle [an]. However, 12% of online orders are refunded within 48 hours and each delivery costs $7 [k], while online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers and 9 complaints mentioned misleading photos [app], eroding profit and risking the reputational damage that fake-review accusations against rivals also show [an]. Overall, Petalpost should keep promoting delivery while tightening quality control [eval] because higher online revenue outweighs refund costs if it photographs honestly and packs carefully [eval], while refusing to buy fake reviews at all times.

knowledge_max_2: online channel already substantial and higher value
refunds, delivery cost and reputation risks
evaluation_max_2: weighs online growth against refund and reputation risks
justified recommendation tied to honest photography and quality control

scenario_stem:
Quickhaul Courier Services is a private limited company delivering parcels for online retailers in Country X. It grew to 210, handling 15,000 parcels a day, $6.3 million revenue; late deliveries rose from 5% to 12%.

Option A is a $1.4 million national contract pushing staff to about 400. Option B splits Quickhaul into 3 regional divisions of about 70 staff each. Jess Marino decides within six weeks, as head-office messages arrive too late and meeting notes go missing.

questions.question_text: Identify two diseconomies of scale.
questions.model_answer: Poor communication, such as instructions from head office arriving late or being lost between depots [1]; slow decision-making, as more layers of management delay each approval [1].

knowledge_max_2: Poor communication as the business grows larger
Slow decision-making as more management layers are added

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Quickhaul Courier Services of splitting into regional divisions.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is better communication [k]. Divisions of around 70 staff would have shorter chains of command, so messages between depots and drivers would arrive on time and fewer parcels would be missed [app]. A second benefit is faster decision-making [k]. Each division's operations manager could approve routes and shifts without waiting for head office, helping to cut the 12% late-delivery rate back toward 5% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Delegated decisions are made faster at division level
application_max_2: Reference to divisions of around 70 staff / lost messages between depots
Reference to 12% late deliveries vs 5% / operations manager per division

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Quickhaul Courier Services of signing the national contract.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is secure revenue [k]. The national contract is worth $1.4 million a year, giving Quickhaul predictable income on top of its current $6.3 million revenue [app]. Guaranteed volume would spread fixed costs, such as vehicles and depots, over more parcels a day, lowering average cost per delivery [an]. A second benefit is stronger market position [k]. With about 400 staff and 15,000-plus parcels a day, Quickhaul could win more online-retail contracts from rival couriers [app], and greater scale could unlock purchasing economies when buying fuel, tyres and packaging [an].

knowledge_max_2: A large contract secures predictable revenue
Greater scale spreads fixed costs and unlocks purchasing economies
application_max_2: Reference to $1.4 million a year contract / $6.3 million revenue
Reference to about 400 staff / 15,000 parcels a day
analysis_max_2: Chain from guaranteed volume to spread fixed costs to lower average cost per delivery
Chain from national scale to purchasing economies and stronger negotiating position

questions.question_text: Do you think Quickhaul Courier Services should sign the national contract worth $1.4 million a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, signing the contract secures $1.4 million of annual revenue [k]. It would push the workforce from 210 to about 400 and lock in a large online retailer, helping Quickhaul spread fixed costs over 15,000-plus parcels a day and benefit from purchasing economies on fuel and vehicle parts [app]. This scale could secure Quickhaul's position as a national courier and lift profit above its current level [an]. On the other hand, growing to about 400 staff risks serious diseconomies of scale [k]. Deliveries are already 12% late, up from 5%, and drivers say head-office messages arrive too late; expanding to near double today's 210 as one organisation would likely worsen communication further [app]. Splitting into 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff, each with its own operations manager, would shorten chains of command and speed up decisions before capacity is stretched [an]. Overall, I think Quickhaul should sign the national contract only after splitting into regional divisions [eval]. The $1.4 million revenue is too valuable to refuse, but the rise from 5% to 12% late shows the current structure is already failing; divisions protect service quality while keeping the contract's scale [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Large contracts secure revenue and scale economies (purchasing, fixed cost spreading)
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decisions as firms grow
application_max_2: Reference to $1.4 million a year contract, workforce 210 to about 400, 15,000 parcels a day
Reference to deliveries 5% to 12% late, 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from contract volume to fixed costs spread over more parcels to lower average cost and higher profit
Chain from larger single organisation to worse communication to rising late deliveries
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation combining or choosing between the options
Weighs both options using stem figures ($1.4 million vs 5% to 12% late deliveries)

scenario_stem:
Hedgerow Launderette Ltd is a private limited company operating two high-street launderettes. Profit for the year rose to $75,000 from $52,000, all retained with no dividend. Its statement of financial position shows current assets of $190,000, including cash of $130,000, current liabilities of $75,000 and working capital of $115,000.

Capital employed and shareholders' equity both stand at $395,000. The board weighs Option 1, opening a third launderette for $150,000 from retained profits, against Option 2, holding a $150,000 cash reserve against a downturn.

questions.question_text: Outline why profit is important to a business.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the reward to owners for taking the risk of investing; it provides internal funds for growth, enables dividends to be paid and creates a cushion against future losses [2].

knowledge_max_2: Rewards owners/shareholders for the risk they take (return on investment)
Provides internal funds for growth and a buffer against losses

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits profit has brought Hedgerow Launderette Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit rose from $52,000 to $75,000, an increase of about 44%, showing the two shops are trading increasingly successfully [k][app]. Reason 2: Because no dividend is paid, all profit is retained — building the $130,000 cash balance and the $395,000 of shareholders' equity that could fund future growth [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit can be retained to finance growth internally
Retained profit strengthens reserves, equity and the cash position
application_max_2: All profit retained, building $130,000 cash and $395,000 equity

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit figures alone cannot tell the board whether Option 1 is safe.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit is not cash — the company records $75,000 of annual profit but holds only $130,000 of cash, and the $150,000 cost of a third shop exceeds that balance [k][app][an]. Reason 2: Paying for Option 1 would drain working capital of $115,000, since current assets of $190,000 would no longer comfortably cover current liabilities of $75,000 once the cash is spent [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Profit differs from cash — it is an accounting figure, not spendable money
Spending funds reduces liquidity shown in the statement of financial position
application_max_2: Working capital $115,000 and current assets $190,000 would be drained against $75,000 current liabilities
analysis_max_2: The board would need at least $20,000 of extra finance for the gap
After spending, the business could not absorb a downturn in either existing shop

questions.question_text: Do you think the board should open the third launderette now (Option 1) or build up a cash reserve (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 would extend a proven, profitable concept — Profit jumped to $75,000 — and would create a third income stream funded from accumulated retained profits rather than new debt [k][app][an]. Option 2 protects the position, keeping $130,000 of cash, $190,000 of current assets and working capital of $115,000 available if either existing shop suffers a downturn [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the more responsible decision now because Option 1 costs $150,000 against $130,000 of cash, so opening immediately would strain liquidity when current liabilities of $75,000 already absorb part of the assets; the board should build the reserve first and fund the third shop in a year or two from retained profits [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Expansion can raise future profit if the concept is proven
Cash reserves protect the business against downturns
application_max_2: Option 2 preserves $190,000 current assets and $115,000 working capital
analysis_max_2: Option 1 risks liquidity strain and may need external finance
Option 2 forfeits early growth but guarantees the existing shops survive a shock
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 2: idle cash earns little and competitors may move first
Overall: Option 2 first — rebuild cash, then expand from retained profits

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Solway Preserves Co is a private limited company in Country X making jam and chutney. It produces 800,000 jars a year with 46 staff, exporting 15%. Container shipping and online ordering brought enquiries from supermarkets in 6 countries and ads reaching 2 million people.

Owners weigh a $150,000 filling line to double export output, funded from $220,000 reserves or a 9% bank loan, against keeping output unchanged and selling in Country X, where two rivals launched discount jams.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons for globalisation.
questions.model_answer: Improvements in transport and communications technology, making international trade faster and cheaper; the removal or reduction of trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas [2].

knowledge_max_2: improvements in transport/communications (e.g. container shipping, internet)
removal/reduction of trade barriers such as tariffs or quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation is creating opportunities for Solway Preserves Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cheaper, faster transport lets Solway reach distant buyers [k], and supermarkets in 6 countries have already enquired about importing its jars [app]. Reason 2: The internet and global media spread product awareness [k], with Solway's social media adverts reaching 2 million people and pulling in overseas interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: global media/internet spread brand awareness worldwide
application_max_2: social media adverts reaching 2 million people

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Solway Preserves Co could face if it doubles production for export.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Doubling output needs heavy spending [k], with $150,000 for the bigger filling line on top of $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan [app], so interest and repayments strain cash if export orders lag [an]. Problem 2: Overseas buyers may demand changes [k], such as different labels, recipes or health regulations [app], raising costs and risking rejected shipments [an].

knowledge_max_2: high expansion cost financed by reserves or loans
foreign markets demand adaptation (labels, tastes, regulations)
application_max_2: $150,000 line vs $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan offer
enquiries from 6 countries with differing requirements
analysis_max_2: interest/repayment strain if export orders arrive slowly
higher adaptation costs and risk of rejected shipments

questions.question_text: Do you think Solway Preserves Co should invest in the new filling line to double output for export, or keep production the same and sell more in Country X? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing $150,000 would let Solway exploit enquiries from 6 countries and its reach to 2 million people on social media, doubling 800,000 jars of annual production [k]; with $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan, the line is affordable, and it would grow exports beyond the current 15% of output [app], spreading risk beyond a home market under attack from two discount rivals [an]. Keeping production steady avoids debt and the risk of unsold jars if overseas buyers prove slow [k], but it blocks growth and leaves Solway fighting discount jams at home with stagnant margins [app], likely losing share in Country X as well [an]. On balance, Solway should invest in the filling line [eval], taking the 9% loan only if confirmed export orders cover the repayments comfortably [eval].

knowledge_max_2: globalisation opens overseas demand through transport and media
expansion financed by reserves/loans carries repayment risk
application_max_2: $150,000 line; $220,000 reserves; 9% loan; 6 countries; 2 million reach
two discount rivals at home; exports at 15%; 800,000 jars a year
analysis_max_2: risk spreading beyond the embattled home market vs export order risk
domestic price war undermines the stand-still strategy
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (invest vs stay at current output)
conditional logic: loan only when confirmed orders cover repayments

scenario_stem:
Larkspur Linens is a handmade linen bedding start-up founded by Naomi Carter with her $13,000 redundancy payment. She works 2 days weekly at a shop earning $240 a week, and sells sets at $120 made from flax from 4 farms.

Her business plan, including lender-required market research, shows fabric flaws cause most returns: 30 of 95 sets sold last month came back with stitching complaints, from $11,400 revenue, after making 200 samples. She must decide whether to resign and run it full-time.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'risk-taking'.
questions.model_answer: A characteristic of successful entrepreneurs meaning being willing to make decisions where the outcome is uncertain, including investing money that could be lost [2].

knowledge_max_2: willingness to invest money that could be lost

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Naomi shows risk-taking when running Larkspur Linens.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Investing her redundancy payment [k], spending $13,000 on a sewing contract, fabric and 200 samples [app]. Way 2: Trading secure income for an unproven idea [k], launching a handmade linen range before knowing whether sets at $120 will sell consistently [app].

knowledge_max_2: launching unproven product / leaving secure income

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Larkspur Linens of including market research in its business plan.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Identifying customer preferences [k], such as which sets failed on stitching and why 30 of 95 were returned [app], guiding fabric and supplier choices to cut future returns [an]. Benefit 2: Forecasting demand [k], using last month's sales of 95 sets and $11,400 revenue to plan stock from 4 local farms [app], avoiding costly stockouts or overstock [an].

application_max_2: 30 of 95 sets returned with stitching complaints
analysis_max_2: reduces returns by fixing supplier issues

questions.question_text: Do you think Naomi should resign from her part-time retail job, or keep it while building Larkspur Linens? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Resigning would free Naomi's full attention for Larkspur Linens [k], letting her resolve the stitching problem behind 30 of 95 returns and rebuild $11,400 monthly revenue faster [app], accelerating growth of a brand she fully controls [an]. However, quitting costs her a guaranteed $240 a week [k], leaving the business as her only income while nearly a third of sets are returned and the supplier issue persists [app], which could push the fragile start-up into a cash crisis [an]. Overall, Naomi should keep her part-time job [eval], because $240 a week still covers essential fabric purchases while she fixes quality and proves repeat sales before committing full-time [eval].

analysis_max_2: full-time focus could fix quality and grow faster
quitting risks cash crisis while returns persist
evaluation_max_2: weighs time commitment against income security
justified by return rate and wage figures

scenario_stem:
Northwind Fishing is a private limited company running 6 trawlers with 54 crew, earning $8.2 million. The union Sea Workers United claims rest hours on the newest trawler fell below 6, and 2 near-miss accidents were logged in March.

The union balloted 54 crew; 41 voted to strike in peak prawn season, forfeiting $600,000. The firm offers $300,000 for bunks; the union wants the trawler stood down for checks. Markus Hale decides.

questions.question_text: Define 'strike'.
questions.model_answer: A form of industrial action in which employees refuse to work to pressure the employer to meet their demands [2].

knowledge_max_2: a form of industrial action to pressure the employer

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why 41 of 54 crew voted to strike.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rest-break failures [k], with rest hours on the newest trawler dropping below 6 between trips [app]. Reason 2: Safety incidents [k], including 2 near-miss accidents logged in March [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why settling the dispute quickly would benefit Northwind Fishing.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Protects revenue [k], avoiding about $600,000 in lost catch during peak prawn season [app], safeguarding the $8.2 million annual turnover [an]. Benefit 2: Protects crew safety [k], addressing rest hours on the newest trawler after 2 near-miss accidents [app], reducing the risk of a serious injury and future disruption [an].

knowledge_max_2: avoids lost revenue/catch during peak season
analysis_max_2: reduces risk of serious injury and further industrial action

questions.question_text: Do you think Northwind Fishing should stand down the offending trawler until safety is independently checked, rather than only improve bunks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Standing down the trawler removes the immediate risk [k], protecting the 54 crew after 2 near-miss accidents in March [app], which is what the union's 41-vote strike mandate demands [an]. However, the $300,000 bunk improvement [k] would fix rest-hour shortages across all 6 trawlers [app], whereas a stand-down risks part of the $600,000 peak-season catch [an]. Overall, Northwind should stand the trawler down [eval] because crew safety outweighs one vessel's season profit [eval], ideally paired with the $300,000 rotation investment.

knowledge_max_2: standing down removes risk pending independent safety check
bunk improvements address rest shortages across fleet
analysis_max_2: eliminates risk of serious injury and forced shutdown later
stand-down may forfeit catch while bunks fix all vessels
evaluation_max_2: weighs immediate safety against lost catch revenue
justified stand-down recommendation prioritising safety

scenario_stem:
Nettlemead Jewellery, a sole trader, handcrafts silver rings. Elena Marchetti sells 210 pieces monthly at $48 through craft fairs and 2 boutique gift shops paying $26 per piece wholesale, and is considering online sales.

A marketplace charging 15% commission plus $300 monthly reaches 3 million buyers but has 900 similar sellers. Her own $2,400 website has 2% card fees and just 60 visitors daily; six loyal customers refuse to buy jewellery unseen.

questions.question_text: State two limitations of selling through an online marketplace.
questions.model_answer: The marketplace charges a commission on every sale [1], and the seller's products appear alongside many competing sellers, reducing control over branding and pricing [1].

little control over branding/direct customer relationships

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Nettlemead Jewellery of joining the online marketplace.

Reason 2: The marketplace provides advertising and ready-made demand [k], so Elena could start selling online without first paying $2,400 to build her own website [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Nettlemead Jewellery of building its own website.

Benefit 2: A personal website gives full control over branding and presentation [k], letting her tell her handcrafted story to buyers instead of competing with 900 similar sellers [app], strengthening loyalty and repeat purchases [an].

knowledge_max_2: full control of brand and customer experience
analysis_max_2: more profit per piece at volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Nettlemead Jewellery should build its own website rather than join the marketplace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Her own website would avoid the 15% commission and $300 a month [k], saving about $7.20 per $48 piece, roughly $1,500 a month on 210 pieces [app], keeping more margin and full control of her brand and customer list [an]. However, the marketplace offers 3 million ready buyers compared with her estimate of 60 visitors a day on a new site [k], and six loyal customers have said they would not buy jewellery online without seeing it first [app], so a personal site may mean slow sales and a poor return on the $2,400 build cost [an]. new site may be too quiet to pay back its cost

justified recommendation: own website plus craft fairs

scenario_stem:
Driftwood Timber Co is a private limited company turning pine logs into fence panels with 64 workers. It made 120,000 panels with $1.92 million revenue and $210,000 profit. Total production costs were $1.71 million, an average cost of $14.25 per panel.

Builders' merchants want 30% more panels. Option A invests $350,000 in a larger kiln and conveyor for 200,000 panels, cutting timber waste from 12% to 5%, with bank lending at 8%. Option B repairs the kiln for $40,000; Ellison fears straining supervision.

questions.question_text: Define 'efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: Efficiency is producing the maximum possible output from a given amount of inputs, or minimising waste of time, materials and money in the production process [2].

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency means maximum output from given inputs
Efficiency means minimising waste of resources

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Driftwood Timber Co could improve its efficiency.
questions.model_answer: One way is investing in a larger kiln and conveyor [k]. Automating the movement of panels would lift output from 120,000 to 200,000 panels a year using the same 64 workers [app]. A second way is cutting timber waste [k]. Reducing waste from 12% to 5% of timber would get far more panels from each log, so the same raw materials would produce more saleable output [app].

knowledge_max_2: Automation can raise output from the same inputs
Reducing waste increases usable output from the same materials
application_max_2: Reference to output lifted from 120,000 to 200,000 panels / 64 workers unchanged
Reference to waste cut from 12% to 5% of timber

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Driftwood Timber Co might face if it expands to 200,000 panels a year.
questions.model_answer: One problem is higher supervisory strain [k]. A works operating at two-thirds more output needs tighter supervision, and without it the quality of fence panels could fall [app]. Defects found by the two national builders' merchants would damage Driftwood's reputation and future orders [an]. A second problem is larger fixed costs [k]. The $350,000 kiln and conveyor add to overheads at a works that currently earns $210,000 profit, and if demand from builders' merchants falls short of target, the extra capacity would be underused [app], leaving high fixed costs spread over fewer panels and raising average cost instead of lowering it [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rapid growth strains supervision and can reduce quality
Extra capacity raises fixed costs, which must be justified by demand
application_max_2: Reference to two national builders' merchants / output rose 120,000 to 200,000 panels
analysis_max_2: Chain from weaker supervision to defects to damaged reputation and lost orders
Chain from extra capacity to underused fixed costs to rising average cost if demand disappoints

questions.question_text: Do you think Driftwood Timber Co should invest $350,000 in the kiln and conveyor? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, the investment lifts efficiency at a bigger scale [k]. Output would rise from 120,000 to 200,000 panels a year and waste would fall from 12% to 5%, so far more usable timber comes from each log and the average cost of $14.25 per panel should fall [app]. Technical economies like this lower average cost as output rises, and the bank would lend at 8% under Option A, so the extra capacity can be financed affordably [an]. On the other hand, expansion carries real risk [k]. Driftwood earned only $210,000 profit on revenue of $1.92 million, so $350,000 is about 1.7 times last year's profit [app]. If the two national builders' merchants do not take the extra 30% of panels, fixed costs would be spread over too few panels, profit would fall and the loan would be hard to repay [an]. Overall, I think Driftwood should invest the $350,000 [eval]. The 12% to 5% waste saving and automated output gain are decisive for a business facing a 30% demand increase, and the 8% bank loan is affordable; Option B only delays an inevitable decision [eval].

Large investments raise fixed costs and financing risk

scenario_stem:
Tamarind Soap Co Ltd is a private limited company making handmade botanical soaps. Gross Profit was $168,000 on Revenue of $260,000, and Expenses of $118,000 left Profit of $50,000. A supermarket chain offers a contract adding $60,000 of Revenue for $38,000 of extra materials.

With current liabilities of $48,000, directors weigh Option 1, accepting it to lift Revenue to $320,000 and Gross Profit to $190,000, against Option 2, keeping boutique sales and a premium gift range adding $30,000 to Gross Profit at no extra cost.

questions.question_text: Define 'Cost of Sales'.
questions.model_answer: Cost of sales is the direct cost of producing or purchasing the goods a business sells during the period, such as raw materials and direct labour [2].

knowledge_max_2: Direct costs directly linked to the goods/services sold
Examples: raw materials, components, direct labour

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of Tamarind Soap Co Ltd's high Gross Profit.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Gross Profit of $168,000 — about 65% of Revenue — comfortably covers Expenses of $118,000 and still leaves Profit of $50,000 [k][app]. Reason 2: A strong Gross Profit shows each product creates substantial added value, giving the business room to fund the premium gift range without external finance [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: High gross profit covers expenses and secures net profit
Shows products create real added value, enabling self-funding of projects
application_max_2: $168,000 gross profit vs $118,000 expenses leaves $50,000 profit
~65% margin gives headroom to fund the gift range internally

questions.question_text: Explain two implications of the supermarket contract for the income statement.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Revenue would rise by $60,000 to $320,000, but Cost of Sales would rise by $38,000 too, so Gross Profit would reach only $190,000 [k][app][an]. Point 2: The contract earns just $22,000 of Gross Profit on $60,000 of Revenue — about 37%, well below the boutique margin — so the company's overall Gross Profit margin would fall even as total profit rises [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Both revenue and cost of sales rise under a new contract; gross profit is the difference
A contract margin below the business average dilutes overall margin
application_max_2: Revenue $320,000 and Gross Profit $190,000 under Option 1
Contract contributes about $22,000 on $60,000 (~37% vs ~65% boutique margin)
analysis_max_2: Total profit rises while margin percentage falls — volume growth at low margin
Each contract sale generates less cash to cover Expenses and risk

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should accept the supermarket contract (Option 1) or develop the premium gift range (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 guarantees Revenue of $320,000 and Gross Profit of $190,000, securing volume for the soap room and using spare capacity at low added capital cost [k][app][an]. Option 2 should add $30,000 of Gross Profit at the full boutique margin with no extra materials risk, lifting Gross Profit towards $198,000 while preserving exclusivity [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the better fit for this business because it protects the ~65% margin that defines the brand, requires no $38,000 materials outlay against current liabilities of $48,000, and keeps the premium positioning that supermarket own-label supply would gradually erode [eval][eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fenwick Wind Components Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing towers and nacelles. With 74 workers it makes 120 towers and earns $14 million. Local content rules require 45% of wind farm project value from Country X firms.

NordAero plans a $30 million turbine plant and wants Fenwick as supplier for 200 towers under a 5-year deal. It needs $3.2 million for pressing equipment, making NordAero 80% of revenue; domestic customers order 90 towers.

questions.question_text: Define 'local content rules'.
questions.model_answer: Government rules requiring that a minimum share of a product's value or materials be made in the host country, used to boost domestic industry and jobs [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Fenwick Wind Components Ltd of supplying the NordAero plant.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The deal would more than double Fenwick's output [k], with NordAero wanting 200 towers a year against 120 made now and only 90 ordered by domestic customers [app]. Advantage 2: Five years of contracted orders give Fenwick stable demand [k], supporting investment in the new pressing equipment and protecting the jobs of its 74 workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: much larger orders / rapid output growth
long-term stable contracts aid planning and investment
application_max_2: 200 towers a year wanted vs 120 made now and 90 domestic orders
5-year deal; 74 workers; $3.2 million pressing equipment supported

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Fenwick Wind Components Ltd could face if it supplies NordAero.

Problem 2: The $3.2 million pressing equipment strains finances [k], especially while relying on NordAero for 80% of revenue [app], so if NordAero's $30 million plant is delayed Fenwick still carries the debt [an].

knowledge_max_2: over-dependence on a single large customer
application_max_2: $3.2 million pressing equipment; NordAero's $30 million plant may be delayed
analysis_max_2: cancellation or price cut would threaten the whole business

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenwick Wind Components Ltd should sign the NordAero supply deal or stay with its domestic customers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing gives Fenwick 200 towers a year of contracted demand from a $30 million world-class plant, lifting output well beyond 120 towers, with valuable experience built under the 45% local content rule [k]; the $3.2 million equipment is affordable against $14 million revenue, especially spread over 5 years [app], and positions Fenwick as the leading local supplier [an]. However, 80% reliance on NordAero is dangerous [k]: if the plant is delayed or the deal is cancelled, Fenwick carries $3.2 million of debt with empty capacity [app], threatening its 74 workers and the firm's future [an]. On balance, Fenwick should sign the deal [eval], but only with safeguards such as staged payments and a minimum monthly order written into the contract [eval].

dependence and capital risk come with a single large customer

analysis_max_2: scale and leadership gains vs single-buyer dependence
debt risk with empty capacity if the plant is delayed/cancelled
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (sign vs stay domestic)
