scenario_stem:
Beacon Digital Marketing is a social-media marketing agency start-up run by Aaron Silva from his spare bedroom. He manages 8 client accounts at $900 monthly, employs no staff and earns $7,200 a month, but wants 20 more clients.

City-centre office rent is $1,600 a month. The Founders' Incubator Programme offers shared space at $320 a month, weekly mentoring and meeting rooms for 2 years, requiring a business plan and 30 hours of client work monthly.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'business incubator'.
questions.model_answer: An organisation, often supported by government, that provides start-up businesses with low-cost premises, advice, training and shared services to help them survive and grow [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why governments provide business incubators.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To reduce start-up failure rates [k], by giving firms like Beacon Digital Marketing space at $320 a month instead of $1,600 city-centre rent [app]. Reason 2: To encourage entrepreneurship and job creation [k], helping agencies grow beyond 8 client accounts and hire staff [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Beacon Digital Marketing of joining the Founders' Incubator Programme.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Cheap premises [k], at $320 a month for 2 years instead of $1,600 city-centre rent [app], saving $1,280 a month to reinvest in growth [an]. Advantage 2: Weekly mentoring and meeting rooms [k], helping Aaron pitch to new clients beyond his 8 current accounts [app], improving his credibility and win rate [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Aaron should move Beacon Digital Marketing into the incubator, or stay working from home? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The incubator offers Aaron office space at $320 a month with mentoring and meeting rooms [k], saving $1,280 a month against $1,600 city-centre rent and letting him host clients professionally [app], which can accelerate signings beyond his current 8 accounts [an]. However, acceptance requires a written business plan and 30 hours of client work per month [k], and leaving home means fixed obligations for 2 years [app], reducing flexibility while revenue is only $7,200 a month [an]. Overall, Aaron should join the incubator [eval], because $320 a month is affordable within $7,200 revenue and professional premises plus mentoring should win more clients faster than a radio campaign alone [eval].

knowledge_max_2: acceptance requires business plan and monthly hours
evaluation_max_2: weighs low cost against reduced flexibility
justified recommendation based on revenue figures

scenario_stem:
Dovecote Poultry is a family partnership processing 25,000 chickens weekly with 40 staff and $2.9 million revenue. Owner Ray Dodds splits an $18,000 bonus pool alone, leaving 2 shifts understaffed.

Three key line workers resigned, citing 'no voice', and a union is recruiting. A supermarket offers a 260-store contract worth $1.1 million but demands consultation and safety standards. Ray must choose democratic shift briefings with $9,000 or autocratic rule with $250 bonuses.

questions.question_text: State two advantages of autocratic leadership for a business.
questions.model_answer: Decisions are made quickly [1]. Clear direction and control over employees [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dovecote Poultry's workforce is unhappy with Ray Dodds's autocratic approach.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: No consultation [k], shown by 3 key line workers resigning this quarter citing 'no voice' [app]. Reason 2: Secret bonus decisions [k], with the $18,000 pool split by Ray without any staff input [app].

knowledge_max_2: pay/reward decisions made secretly without staff involvement

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why introducing democratic weekly shift briefings could help Dovecote Poultry win the supermarket contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Documented consultation [k], exactly what the 2-year, 260-store contract worth $1.1 million a year requires before signing [app], raising the chance of securing it [an]. Benefit 2: Engaged, safety-aware staff [k], meeting the required safety standards [app], reducing accidents and audit failures [an].

analysis_max_2: increases likelihood of winning/keeping the contract
reduces accidents and helps pass audits

questions.question_text: Do you think Dovecote Poultry should introduce democratic weekly shift briefings? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Democratic briefings give staff a real voice [k], reversing the 'no voice' complaints behind 3 resignations [app], and deliver the documented consultation the 260-store, $1.1 million a year contract requires [an]. However, autocratic bonus appeals keep control with Ray [k], rewarding 40 staff at $250 each without changing how decisions are made [app], and suit his directive style [an]. Overall, the briefings are the right decision [eval] because a customer demanding consultation cannot be satisfied by one-off bonuses [eval], while the unionisation risk also falls.

knowledge_max_2: bonuses reward staff without changing decision-making
analysis_max_2: consultation required to win the contract and rebuild trust
bonuses cost money but do not meet consultation requirements
evaluation_max_2: weighs quick bonus appeal against structural consultation change

scenario_stem:
Gleamwheels Mobile Car Wash, a private limited company, washes 620 cars monthly at $18 from 2 vans. Sam Whitmore uses leaflets; 4 car dealerships offer referrals at 25% of sales, bringing 150 extra washes monthly.

Dealers could promote it at vehicle handover, but Gleamwheels keeps just $13.50 per wash and Sam fears relying on 1 partner. His booking app costs $3,900 plus $110 monthly, while 45% of customers already book by phone.

questions.question_text: Identify two benefits of selling services directly to consumers.
questions.model_answer: Selling direct lets a business build a personal relationship with its customers and earn loyalty [1], and direct sales avoid paying commission to intermediaries such as dealerships [1].

knowledge_max_2: no commission or revenue shared with intermediaries

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Gleamwheels of accepting the dealership referral offer.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The dealerships would refer about 150 extra washes a month [k], lifting monthly volume from 620 to roughly 770 [app]. Reason 2: Referrals come through the 4 car dealerships at vehicle handover [k], bringing steady weekday work with no extra advertising spend such as leaflets [app].

knowledge_max_2: promotion at no advertising cost to the business

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of the dealership referral arrangement.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Gleamwheels keeps only $13.50 of each $18 wash after the 25% commission [k], losing $4.50 on every referred wash [app], so the extra 150 washes add much less profit than expected [an]. Problem 2: The offer creates dependence on 1 partner [k], and if any of the 4 car dealerships stops referring, Gleamwheels could lose bookings overnight [app], threatening the business's stability [an].

knowledge_max_2: commission reduces profit per referred sale
dependence on a single partner chain
analysis_max_2: referred washes earn less, limiting profit growth
loss of the partner means loss of volume and stability

questions.question_text: Do you think Gleamwheels Mobile Car Wash should accept the dealerships' referral offer rather than build its own booking app? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The referral offer would deliver about 150 extra washes a month through 4 car dealerships [k], lifting Gleamwheels towards 770 washes a month and keeping the vans busy on weekdays with no advertising cost [app], improving cash flow quickly [an]. However, the 25% commission leaves only $13.50 of each $18 wash [k], and dependence on 1 partner is risky, whereas the app costs $3,900 plus $110 a month and would suit the 45% of customers already booking by phone [app], creating a direct branded channel that Gleamwheels owns outright [an]. Overall, Gleamwheels should accept the referral offer short-term [eval] because immediate extra weekday volume at zero marketing cost beats waiting for an unproven app to attract users [eval], while keeping the app as a longer-term goal to cut commission dependence.

knowledge_max_2: referrals bring volume without marketing spend
an app gives an owned direct channel with no commission
analysis_max_2: quick cash-flow gain and weekday utilisation
commission dependence versus a long-term owned channel
evaluation_max_2: weighs immediate zero-cost volume against app ownership
staged recommendation: referral now, app later

scenario_stem:
Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd is a private limited company producing industrial cleaning granules with 150 workers. It made 220,000 kg, $1.9 million revenue, $1.32 million total costs and $580,000 profit, averaging $6.00 per kg.

Option A spends $2.2 million on a third production hall for 330,000 kg, average cost near $5.10 per kg. Option B keeps two halls and 220,000 kg to protect the $580,000 profit. Managers report slow decisions, and bank lending runs eight years at 6%.

questions.question_text: Calculate the average cost per kg last year when total costs were $1.32 million and output was 220,000 kg.
questions.model_answer: Average cost = total cost / output = $1,320,000 / 220,000 kg = $6.00 per kg [2].

knowledge_max_2: Average cost = total cost divided by output

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd of building the third production hall.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. Lifting output from 220,000 to 330,000 kg a year would spread fixed costs over 50% more units, projecting average cost near $5.10 per kg instead of $6.00 [app]. A second benefit is greater capacity to accept orders [k]. A third hall would let Saltmarsh take on larger contracts from industrial customers without turning work away to rival suppliers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Larger scale spreads fixed costs, lowering average cost
More capacity enables larger orders / new customers
application_max_2: Reference to output 220,000 to 330,000 kg / average cost $6.00 to $5.10 per kg
Reference to third production hall / industrial cleaning granules customers

questions.question_text: Explain two diseconomies of scale Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd might face after building the third production hall.
questions.model_answer: One diseconomy is slow decision-making [k]. With three halls, approvals for maintenance, shifts and purchases would pass through more managers, so routine decisions take longer [app]. That could delay urgent repairs and cut availability of the halls below plan [an]. A second diseconomy is poor communication [k]. A workforce expanding beyond 150 workers would need clearer reporting lines [app], and without them mistakes in handling industrial cleaning granules could cause accidents or rejected batches [an].

knowledge_max_2: Slow decision-making as more management layers are added
Poor communication as the workforce grows larger
application_max_2: Reference to three halls / more managers for decisions
Reference to 150 workers / handling industrial cleaning granules
analysis_max_2: Chain from more approval layers to slower decisions to delayed repairs and lost output
Chain from unclear reporting lines to mistakes/accidents to rejected batches and higher cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd should build the third production hall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, greater scale would cut average cost [k]. Output would rise from 220,000 to 330,000 kg a year, with average cost projected near $5.10 per kg against $6.00 now; on 330,000 kg that is roughly $297,000 saved each year [app]. The 6% bank loan over 8 years is manageable against a $580,000 profit, and the extra capacity strengthens Saltmarsh's position with industrial buyers [an]. On the other hand, the risk is concentrated [k]. Paying $2.2 million for the hall with only $580,000 a year of profit means it pays for itself slowly, and fixed interest of about $132,000 a year at 6% would bite hard if orders stall [app]. Diseconomies such as slow decisions across three halls and weaker communication could also erode the projected $5.10 saving [an]. Overall, I think Saltmarsh should build the third hall [eval]. The $297,000 annual saving is about half of the $580,000 profit, the 6% loan is affordable and Option B locks in $6.00 average cost forever; with clear reporting lines, the risks are controllable [eval].

Large investments raise fixed financial commitments and financing risk
application_max_2: Reference to output 220,000 to 330,000 kg, average cost $6.00 to $5.10, saving about $297,000 a year
Reference to $2.2 million cost, $580,000 profit, 6% loan over 8 years
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower average cost at larger scale to about $297,000 annual saving to stronger profit
Chain from fixed interest of about $132,000 a year to pressure on profit if orders stall
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on building the third hall
Weighs both options using stem figures ($297,000 saving vs $2.2 million cost and $580,000 profit)

scenario_stem:
Hazelbeck Vegetables Co Ltd is a private limited company packing frozen mixed vegetables for supermarket own-label ranges. Revenue was $900,000 and Gross Profit $340,000, but Expenses of $300,000, including $70,000 of advertising and $85,000 of freezer electricity, left Profit of just $40,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'Expenses'.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marlowe Bicycles is a private limited company in Country X making steel-framed commuter bicycles. With 28 workers it sells 9,000 bicycles at $210 for $1.9 million revenue. Multinational retailers sell imports at $150, so sales fell 20% and market share dropped from 12% to 9%.

questions.question_text: Identify two threats of globalisation for businesses.

downward price pressure and loss of market share for local firms

questions.question_text: Explain two ways globalisation is threatening Marlowe Bicycles.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why governments create enterprise zones in rural areas.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Red Kite Falconry Centre of locating in the enterprise zone.

Benefit 2: 100% relief on start-up equipment purchases [k], softening the impact of her $30,000 investment in 4 trained birds of prey [app], protecting scarce cash [an].

analysis_max_2: eases early losses while revenue builds
protects scarce cash / lowers barriers to entry

questions.question_text: Do you think Sylvia should open a second display site, or invest $9,000 in a school education programme at the existing site? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A second site costing $24,000 would double display capacity and open a fresh market area [k], building on $46,000 revenue from 60 groups in year one [app], potentially boosting long-term growth [an]. The education programme costs only $9,000 [k], and tourism officers estimate it could add $18,000 a year in school bookings [app], returning twice its cost within a single year [an]. Overall, Sylvia should invest $9,000 in the education programme [eval], because it costs less than half the expansion, adds $18,000 a year and suits a business still absorbing its early losses [eval].

education programme costs $9,000 with estimated uplift

programme returns twice its cost in one year
