justified by estimated uplift against early losses

scenario_stem:
Willowbank Stables Riding Centre is a private limited company with 60 horses, 7 riding instructors, 4 grooms and 7 yard staff on $1.1 million. Josie Bennett uses laissez-faire leadership, letting instructors plan their own lessons.

Freedom is fraying: 9 complaints about inconsistent lessons in 3 months, 2 junior instructors missed certification deadlines, and a near-miss when a child entered the yard. Josie must keep laissez-faire or introduce democratic weekly training with clear standards at $28,000.

questions.question_text: Outline two reasons why laissez-faire leadership may suit some businesses.
questions.model_answer: It empowers highly skilled specialists to work autonomously [1]. It encourages creativity and independence in motivated teams [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Willowbank Stables has gained from laissez-faire leadership so far.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Instructors enjoy autonomy [k], planning their own lessons across 60 horses [app]. Benefit 2: Experienced instructors stay motivated [k], sustaining $1.1 million in annual revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: self-direction can sustain service quality and revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the laissez-faire approach is now causing Willowbank Stables.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Inconsistent lesson quality [k], shown by 9 complaints arriving in 3 months [app], damaging the centre's reputation with parents [an]. Problem 2: Unsupported junior staff [k], as 2 junior instructors have missed certification deadlines [app], weakening lesson standards and safety [an].

knowledge_max_2: no consistent standards leads to variable quality
analysis_max_2: damages reputation and risks losing members
weakens standards and raises safety risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Willowbank Stables should replace laissez-faire leadership with democratic weekly training sessions? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Democratic weekly sessions would standardise quality [k], addressing the 9 complaints in 3 months across the 7 instructors [app], and protect children in the yard [an]. However, laissez-faire freedom keeps senior instructors motivated [k], sustaining $1.1 million revenue from riding lessons and livery [app], and removing it could push talented staff to rival centres [an]. Overall, Willowbank should introduce the democratic sessions [eval] because a $28,000 training cost is small against lost reputation and injury risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: democratic sessions create shared standards and consistency
laissez-faire retains autonomy and motivation of experts
analysis_max_2: standardised training reduces complaints and safety incidents
removing autonomy may lose senior instructors and revenue
evaluation_max_2: weighs creative freedom against quality control and safety
justified adoption of democratic sessions at modest cost

scenario_stem:
Cobbled Lane Books, a private limited company, runs one bookshop with $680,000 sales. Some 30% of revenue comes from an online marketplace charging 14% commission; events draw 900 visitors monthly, and 55% of buyers join its email club.

Leaving for a sole website costs $5,300 yearly with 2% card fees but loses its 4.8-star rating from 1,900 reviews and 3,500 unique visitors monthly, though the email club could recover many buyers.

questions.question_text: Calculate the commission paid to the marketplace on a $350 order.
Explain two benefits for Cobbled Lane Books of leaving the marketplace and selling only through its own website.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Its own website charges just 2% card fees [k], saving most of the 14% commission charged on the 30% of revenue currently earned online [app]. Reason 2: The shop would pay only $5,300 a year to run its own site [k], and the email club of past buyers could be marketed to directly [app].

knowledge_max_2: own channel means far lower selling costs/fees
own customer list enables direct marketing

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Cobbled Lane Books of staying on the online marketplace.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The marketplace brings 3,500 unique visitors a month [k], exposing the bookshop to thousands of readers who would otherwise never find it [app], sustaining online sales growth [an]. Benefit 2: The marketplace provides trusted payment and delivery systems [k], saving the $5,300 a year running cost of the shop's own website [app], protecting cash flow and avoiding technical risks [an].

knowledge_max_2: marketplace brings traffic/reach beyond the local area
marketplace handles infrastructure, trust and payment
analysis_max_2: sustains online revenue from new customers
saves running cost and avoids technical risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Cobbled Lane Books should leave the online marketplace and sell only through its own website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Leaving the marketplace would cut selling costs from 14% to 2% [k], and on the online share of revenue (about $204,000 a year) the saving after $5,300 running costs would be roughly $19,200 [app], boosting profit the owners can invest in stock and events [an]. However, the marketplace brings 3,500 unique visitors a month who would otherwise never find the shop [k], and losing its 4.8-star rating built from 1,900 reviews, plus the trust holding the 55% email club together, may cut sales [app], costing far more than the commission saving [an]. Overall, the owners should stay on the marketplace while building the website in parallel [eval], because $680,000 annual revenue leans on marketplace traffic and the shop's 900 monthly event visitors [eval], shifting more sales to its own site only as the email club grows.

knowledge_max_2: marketplace provides traffic, trust and an established rating
analysis_max_2: annual saving of roughly $19,200 boosts profit
lost traffic/trust may cost more than the saving
evaluation_max_2: weighs fee savings against dependence on marketplace traffic
hybrid recommendation justified by the $680,000 revenue dependence

scenario_stem:
Clayborne Tiles Ltd is a private limited company making ceramic floor tiles with 92 workers. Output is 400,000 tiles, with fixed costs of $480,000 and variable cost $2.60; revenue $1.6 million and profit $80,000.

Demand rises 20% yearly. Option A builds a fourth kiln for $1.5 million, lifting output to 550,000 tiles with fixed costs $640,000, variable cost $2.60 and average $3.76. Option B keeps three kilns and uses overtime for 460,000 tiles at $2.85 and average $3.89.

questions.question_text: Calculate the total variable cost when output is 400,000 tiles and the variable cost is $2.60 per tile.
questions.model_answer: Total variable cost = variable cost per unit x output = $2.60 x 400,000 = $1,040,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Total variable cost = variable cost per unit multiplied by output

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Clayborne Tiles Ltd of building the fourth kiln.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. Holding variable cost at $2.60 while fixed costs rise only to $640,000 gives an average cost of about $3.76 a tile, below Option B's $3.89 [app]. A second benefit is extra capacity to fill the order book [k]. Output of 550,000 tiles a year would let Clayborne meet builder demand growing by 20% a year without turning orders away [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher output with stable variable cost lowers average cost
Extra capacity allows the business to accept more orders
application_max_2: Reference to $2.60 variable cost held / fixed costs $640,000 / $3.76 vs $3.89
Reference to output 550,000 tiles / demand rising 20% a year / order book full until spring

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Clayborne Tiles Ltd might face if it keeps three kilns and uses overtime under Option B.
questions.model_answer: One problem is the higher variable cost [k]. Overtime raises the variable cost from $2.60 to $2.85 a tile, adding 25 cents on every one of 460,000 tiles, about $115,000 a year of extra cost [app]. That would wipe out the $80,000 profit unless prices rise, which could lose sales to rivals [an]. A second problem is worker fatigue and low morale [k]. Sustained overtime lowers motivation and concentration [app], so defects could rise and deliveries to builders could slip, damaging Clayborne's reputation just as the order book is fullest [an].

knowledge_max_2: Overtime raises variable cost per unit
Overtime lowers morale and motivation, risking defects and delays
application_max_2: Reference to variable cost $2.60 to $2.85 / 25 cents x 460,000 tiles / about $115,000 a year
Reference to $80,000 profit / order book full until spring / three kilns
analysis_max_2: Chain from higher variable cost to $115,000 extra cost to loss of the $80,000 profit or higher prices
Chain from overtime fatigue to defects and late deliveries to damaged reputation with builders

questions.question_text: Do you think Clayborne Tiles Ltd should build the fourth kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, the fourth kiln delivers real economies of scale [k]. Output rises from 400,000 to 550,000 tiles, fixed costs climb from $480,000 to $640,000, yet average cost falls to about $3.76 a tile against $3.80 now and $3.89 under overtime [app]. Spreading higher fixed costs over 37.5% more tiles lowers average cost, and $1.5 million buys durable capacity for a business whose orders are full until spring and whose demand is growing 20% a year [an]. On the other hand, $1.5 million is a large commitment for a firm earning $80,000 profit [k]. The fourth kiln probably needs borrowing, and if builder demand slows, output near 550,000 tiles would not materialise, leaving Clayborne with underused fixed costs of $640,000 [app]. Option B costs nothing up front, keeps flexibility and lifts output to 460,000 tiles, though at $2.85 a tile its average cost is worse [an]. Overall, I think Clayborne should build the fourth kiln [eval]. Average cost of $3.76 against $3.89, plus capacity for 20% annual demand growth, outweighs the $1.5 million outlay; the firm should negotiate the loan before committing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Larger scale spreads fixed costs, lowering average cost (economies of scale)
Large investments raise financing risk and fixed cost commitments
application_max_2: Reference to output 400,000 to 550,000 tiles, fixed costs $480,000 to $640,000, average cost $3.76 vs $3.89, $1.5 million kiln
Reference to $80,000 profit, demand rising 20% a year, order book full until spring, Option B with overtime at $2.85
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed costs spread over 37.5% more tiles to lower average cost to stronger profit per tile
Chain from $1.5 million outlay to financing strain to risk if demand slows and capacity lies underused
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on building the fourth kiln
Weighs both options using stem figures ($3.76 vs $3.89 average cost; $1.5 million vs $80,000 profit)

scenario_stem:
Wrenmore Garage Ltd is a private limited company running a car repair workshop servicing family cars and vans. Profit was $130,000. Its statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $520,000, current assets of $230,000, current liabilities of $110,000, working capital of $120,000, capital employed of $640,000, non-current liabilities of $200,000 and shareholders' equity of $440,000.

The landlord offers the freehold for $640,000. The board weighs Option 1, a $550,000 long-term bank loan plus $90,000 cash, against Option 2, renting at $60,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'Retained Profit'.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit is the profit left in the business after dividends (and tax) have been paid, accumulated over time in reserves as part of shareholders' equity [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit kept in the business after dividends/tax are paid
Accumulates in reserves within shareholders' equity

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why capital employed is a useful figure for anyone judging Wrenmore Garage Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Capital employed of $640,000 shows the total long-term funds invested in the business — non-current assets of $520,000 plus working capital of $120,000 [k][app]. Reason 2: Comparing Profit of $130,000 with capital employed of $640,000 indicates how effectively the invested funds are being used to generate returns for investors [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Shows the total long-term finance invested (non-current assets + working capital)
Enables judging how effectively invested funds generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on the statement of financial position if the directors buy the freehold (Option 1).
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Non-current assets would rise by $640,000 to $1,160,000 and non-current liabilities by $550,000 to $750,000, so capital employed would rise to $1,190,000 [k][app][an]. Point 2: Using $90,000 of cash cuts current assets to $140,000 while current liabilities stay at $110,000, so working capital falls to just $30,000 — a very thin cushion [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Buying property increases non-current assets and total assets
Financing the purchase with a loan increases non-current liabilities and capital employed
application_max_2: Cash −$90,000 leaves current assets $140,000 and working capital $30,000
analysis_max_2: The statement of financial position still balances: $1,190,000 employed = $750,000 loan + $440,000 equity
Working capital of $30,000 against $110,000 current liabilities leaves almost no short-term slack

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should buy the freehold using the loan (Option 1) or continue to rent (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 secures the workshop for the long term, removes the risk of rent increases and turns the $640,000 freehold into a company asset, though non-current liabilities rise to $750,000 and working capital falls towards $30,000 [k][app][an]. Option 2 keeps $230,000 of current assets and $120,000 of working capital intact, avoids extra interest and preserves flexibility, but the $60,000 annual rent never builds ownership [k][app][an]. Overall, continuing to rent (Option 2) is the wiser short-term decision because Profit of $130,000 covers the rent comfortably, and the thin $30,000 of working capital after purchase would leave the garage unable to absorb a shock; the board can revisit buying once retained profits rebuild the cash position [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying property builds ownership and fixes premises cost long term
Renting preserves liquidity and flexibility but builds no asset
application_max_2: Option 1: non-current liabilities rise to $750,000; working capital about $30,000
Option 2: keeps $230,000 current assets and $120,000 working capital
analysis_max_2: Option 1 adds ownership and stability but concentrates risk in a thinner liquidity position
Option 2 avoids interest and preserves cash, but rent is a permanent cost with no equity built
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 2: rent never converts to ownership and may rise
Overall: Option 2 now — rebuild cash from retained profits, then buy later

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Drummond Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making truffles and bars. It sells 1.5 million bars at $3.50 with 57 staff and $5.25 million revenue. A free trade agreement removed 8% tariff on cocoa and chocolate exports.

Board weighs a $1.8 million export factory for 2.6 million bars across the region, needing 25 extra workers and two years to capacity, with revenue $9.1 million, or keeping single factory for premium domestic sales (18% share).

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade'.
questions.model_answer: International trade between countries without tariffs, quotas or other restrictions, allowing goods and services to cross borders freely [2].

knowledge_max_2: goods and services move freely across borders

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities the free trade agreement creates for Drummond Chocolates Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Removing the 8% export tariff makes Drummond's bars cheaper in neighbouring countries [k], supporting sales of up to 2.6 million bars a year across the region [app]. Opportunity 2: Removing the 8% tariff on cocoa cuts Drummond's input costs [k], improving margins on every bar sold at home and in the region [app].

knowledge_max_2: export tariffs removed, so market access is cheaper/easier abroad
input tariffs removed, so production costs fall
application_max_2: 2.6 million bars a year possible under the regional plan
8% tariff gone on cocoa bought from Country Y

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Drummond Chocolates Ltd could face if it builds the export factory.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $1.8 million factory strains finances [k], with only $5.25 million current revenue and two years before full capacity [app], so Drummond may need loans and face heavy interest during the ramp-up [an]. Problem 2: Regional competition is unfamiliar [k], with established local brands and price-sensitive shoppers [app], risking slow sales of the extra bars and wasted capacity [an].

knowledge_max_2: high capital cost with a slow ramp-up creates financing risk
unfamiliar foreign competition and price sensitivity
application_max_2: $1.8 million factory; $5.25 million revenue; two years to full capacity
2.6 million bars a year target vs 1.5 million bars now
analysis_max_2: loan/interest burden during the slow ramp-up period
slow uptake risks wasted capacity and weak returns

questions.question_text: Do you think Drummond Chocolates Ltd should build the export factory for the free trade region, or keep the single factory focused on domestic premium sales? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the export factory exploits free trade: with the 8% tariff gone, Drummond could sell 2.6 million bars a year and lift revenue from $5.25 million to $9.1 million [k], with cocoa also cheaper and 25 extra workers strengthening production [app], achieving larger scale and spreading risk beyond an 18%-share home market [an]. Keeping the single factory avoids $1.8 million of debt and protects the proven premium domestic position [k], but it ignores a revenue rise of about $3.85 million and leaves capacity trapped while regional rivals expand [app], risking long-term decline [an]. On balance, Drummond should build the export factory [eval], staged so the loan is only drawn once confirmed regional orders justify it [eval].

knowledge_max_2: free trade removes tariffs, opening markets and cutting input costs
expansion carries heavy capital cost and ramp-up risk
application_max_2: 8% tariff gone; 2.6 million bars a year; revenue $5.25 million to $9.1 million
$1.8 million factory; two years to capacity; 18% domestic share; 25 extra workers
analysis_max_2: larger scale and risk spreading vs $1.8 million debt and ramp-up risk
ignoring a ~$3.85 million opportunity vs protecting the premium domestic niche
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (build vs stay single factory)
staged/conditional approach tied to confirmed regional orders

scenario_stem:
Harborlight Bakery is a sole trader business owned by Priya, baking sourdough loaves and buttery pastries in a rented high-street shop. She invested $25,000, works 60 hours weekly with 4 part-time assistants and made $180,000 sales, using a second-hand oven.

As a sole trader she carries unlimited liability for all debts. Her friend Sofia, a qualified pastry chef, wants to invest $20,000 as an equal partner. Priya must weigh extra capital and shared workload against sharing profits and control.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'sole trader'.
questions.model_answer: A business owned and controlled by one person who keeps all the profits but bears unlimited liability for the business's debts [2].

knowledge_max_2: business owned and controlled by one person
keeps all profits / unlimited liability for debts

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Priya Raman of remaining a sole trader rather than forming a partnership.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Priya keeps all the profits [k], retaining the full benefit of $180,000 in annual sales rather than giving half to Sofia [app]. Advantage 2: She keeps complete control of the business [k], deciding menu, opening hours and suppliers herself without needing Sofia's agreement [app].

knowledge_max_2: keeps all profits rather than sharing them
full control of decisions / no partner agreement needed
application_max_2: equal partner taking half of profits

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Priya Raman of remaining a sole trader.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Unlimited liability [k], meaning her $25,000 savings and personal possessions could be seized to pay business debts if the bakery fails [app], leaving her in severe financial difficulty [an]. Disadvantage 2: Limited access to capital [k], because she can only invest what she has and cannot invite outside investors or issue shares [app], so expansion such as buying a second-hand oven is hard to fund [an].

knowledge_max_2: unlimited liability / personal assets at risk
limited access to capital for expansion
application_max_2: unlimited liability for all business debts
analysis_max_2: personal assets could be seized to pay creditors
restricted ability to fund expansion and grow

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya Raman should form a partnership with Sofia Marino? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An advantage of a partnership is the extra capital [k], since Sofia's $20,000 investment would raise total funds to $45,000 for new ovens and recipe development [app], spreading the financial risk across two owners [an]. A disadvantage is the loss of full control and shared profits [k], because Sofia would take half of future profits and a say in menu and hour decisions [app], reducing Priya's independence over the bakery she built over 6 years [an]. Overall, Priya should form the partnership [eval] because the $20,000 injection and Sofia's pastry expertise would ease the 60 hours workload and strengthen sales beyond $180,000 more than losing sole control would cost her [eval].

knowledge_max_2: extra capital and shared risk from partnership
loss of sole control / profits shared with partner
analysis_max_2: shared risk eases financial pressure on Priya
loss of independence and half of profits retained
evaluation_max_2: weighs extra capital and skills against reduced control and shared profits in her bakery context

scenario_stem:
Coral Ridge Hotel is a private limited company, a 4-star resort with 120 rooms and 3 restaurants and 95 staff. The $54,000 chef left. A regional newspaper advert costing $350 drew 24 applications in 2 weeks: 9 staff, 15 outside.

It pays $55,000. The manager must promote Marco, a section chef on $42,000 with 5 years' service who knows the kitchen brigade, or recruit externally. Summer lasts 14 weeks at 90% occupancy, with a $2.4 million wage bill.

questions.question_text: Define 'external recruitment'.
questions.model_answer: External recruitment is the process of hiring new workers from outside the business, for example through job advertisements, instead of promoting existing employees. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Hiring new workers from outside the business
Attracting outside candidates, for example through job advertisements, rather than promoting existing staff

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Coral Ridge Hotel placed a job advertisement in the regional newspaper.
questions.model_answer: Placing a job advertisement informs potential candidates outside the hotel about the head chef vacancy, widening the pool beyond the 9 internal applicants [k]. Advertising at a cost of $350 attracted 15 external applications within 2 weeks, giving the manager a wider choice of experienced chefs [app]. An advertisement can set out the salary and the requirements of the role [k], which filters for candidates willing to lead 3 restaurants at the advertised salary of $55,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: The advert informs potential candidates that a vacancy exists, widening the applicant pool
The advert sets out the salary and requirements, attracting suitable applicants and filtering out unsuitable ones
application_max_2: The advert cost $350 and attracted 15 external applications within 2 weeks
$55,000 salary is advertised for managing 3 restaurants

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Coral Ridge Hotel of promoting Marco to head chef.
questions.model_answer: Promoting Marco is cheaper and quicker than external recruitment [k], because the hotel avoids the $350 advertising cost and the time spent interviewing unknown applicants [app], so the new head chef can be in post before the 14-week summer season and the wage bill of $2.4 million is not strained further [an]. Internal promotion also rewards loyalty and motivates other staff [k]. Marco has 5 years' service and knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu, so service can continue smoothly across the 3 restaurants [app]. Because guests will find familiar quality during a season when occupancy averages 90%, reviews and repeat bookings are more likely to hold up [an].

knowledge_max_2: Internal promotion is cheaper and quicker than external recruitment
Promoting internally rewards and motivates loyal existing staff
application_max_2: $350 advertising avoided; Marco has 5 years' service
Marco knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu across the 3 restaurants
analysis_max_2: Head chef in post before the 14-week peak, avoiding disruption at high occupancy
Continuity of quality protects reputation, reviews and revenue during the 90% occupancy season

questions.question_text: Do you think Coral Ridge Hotel should promote Marco or recruit a new head chef externally? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Promoting Marco is cheaper and faster [k]. Marco has 5 years' service, knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu, and the promotion costs about $13,000 a year more ($55,000 minus $42,000) rather than $350 of advertising plus weeks of interviews [app]. Staying with Marco protects food quality and cover during the 14-week peak when occupancy averages 90% [an]. However, Marco has never run a whole kitchen, and external candidates may bring broader experience across several kitchens and fresh menu ideas [k]. The 15 external applications include chefs prepared to accept $55,000; a stronger outsider could lift standards and motivate the brigade across the 3 restaurants [app]. An external hire might also introduce new routines that improve standards, but risks upsetting established staff and losing continuity during the busiest season [an]. Overall, the hotel should promote Marco because the risk and cost of external hiring so close to the 14-week season are too high, and his 5 years here make him the safest pair of hands [eval]. If the board wanted a long-term transformation of the menu, an external search after the summer would be wiser, but this vacancy must be filled immediately [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Internal promotion: cheaper, faster, known candidate, motivates staff
External recruitment: wider pool, fresh skills/experience, but costlier and riskier
application_max_2: Marco: 5 years' service; knows brigade and menu; promotion costs about $13,000 a year more
analysis_max_2: Internal pick protects quality and continuity during peak season
External pick could raise standards but disrupt staff and delay the start date
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement justified by timing, cost and risk
Recognises when external recruitment would become the better option

scenario_stem:
Coppertree Bakery is a family-owned partnership with 6 outlets in Country X, 34 staff and $780,000 revenue. Office workers aged 25-45 buy lunchtime rolls, but sales of rolls and salads fell 12% in 18 months as more firms let staff work from home.

The owners plan a gluten-free range and must choose: spend $15,000 on a secondary research report or survey 300 regular customers; launch in all 6 outlets at once or trial in 2 outlets first.

questions.question_text: Define 'market research'.
questions.model_answer: The systematic process of collecting, analysing and interpreting information about a market, including customer needs and demand [2].

knowledge_max_2: collecting and analysing information about a market

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Coppertree Bakery of carrying out primary market research before launching its gluten-free range.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It provides specific, up-to-date information [k] about whether office workers aged 25-45 want gluten-free baked goods [app]. Benefit 2: It reduces the risk of failure [k] by testing demand in 2 outlets before launching in all 6 outlets [app].

knowledge_max_2: reduces the risk of product failure
application_max_2: trial in 2 outlets before all 6 outlets

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations to Coppertree Bakery of relying only on secondary market research data.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Secondary data may be out of date [k] and not specific to its 6 outlets [app], so the owners could launch a gluten-free range that local customers do not want [an]. Limitation 2: Secondary data cannot reveal the taste preferences of office workers [k] aged 25-45 who buy lunchtime rolls [app], so recipes may miss local demand and sales may disappoint [an].

knowledge_max_2: secondary data may be out of date or not specific
cannot reveal specific local customer preferences
analysis_max_2: risk of launching an unwanted gluten-free range
recipes miss local demand so sales disappoint

questions.question_text: Do you think Coppertree Bakery should spend $15,000 on a secondary research report before launching its gluten-free range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The secondary research report would give broad, national market data within weeks [k] for $15,000 [app], showing whether the gluten-free market is large enough before the owners commit stock to all 6 outlets [an]. However, primary research with 300 regular customers would give specific, current feedback [k] from people who actually buy lunchtime rolls from Coppertree Bakery [app], cutting the risk of unsold gluten-free stock after launch [an]. Overall, the owners should first carry out primary research [eval] because it directly reflects their own customers [eval], buying the report only if national expansion is pursued later.

knowledge_max_2: secondary data gives broad national market picture
primary research gives specific current customer feedback
analysis_max_2: shows market size before committing stock to 6 outlets
reduces risk of unsold gluten-free stock after launch
evaluation_max_2: weighs broad national data against specific local evidence
justified recommendation to do primary research first

scenario_stem:
Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company employing 42 workers making premium boxed chocolates. It sold 1.4 million boxes for $11.2 million revenue; broken-praline complaints reached 240 a month.

Some 18% of boxes failed final inspection in May. Before the Christmas gifting range ships in 10 weeks, Carla Ferreira chooses quality control — an end-of-line inspection team costing $60,000 a year — or quality assurance building checks into every stage and training 30 workers, at $95,000.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'quality assurance'.
questions.model_answer: Quality assurance is a system of building quality into every stage of production, from raw materials to dispatch, so that faults are prevented rather than just detected [2].

knowledge_max_2: Quality is built into every stage of production
Faults are prevented rather than just detected

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why quality is important to Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, quality is important because high-quality chocolates satisfy customers and build loyalty [k]. With complaints already at 240 a month, fixing quality would protect the Christmas gifting range and encourage shoppers to reorder Hazelmere boxes [app]. Second, quality is important because poor quality wastes resources [k]. The 18% of boxes failing final inspection contain wasted ingredients and labour, so improving quality lowers costs and protects the $11.2 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality builds customer satisfaction and loyalty
Quality reduces waste, rework and costs
application_max_2: Reference to 240 complaints a month / Christmas gifting range
Reference to 18% failing final inspection / $11.2 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd might face if it introduces quality control (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, quality control checks products at the end of production, so faults are only detected after costs have been added [k]. With 18% of boxes already failing final inspection, even a larger inspection team would simply find more faulty boxes without stopping them being made, raising rework and scrap [app]. This would increase costs rather than remove the root cause of the defect problem, squeezing profit [an]. Second, quality control adds a permanent wage bill for inspectors [k]. The extra team costs $60,000 a year on top of existing wages for 42 workers, and that money cannot also train 30 production workers [app]. The ongoing expense reduces funds available for improvements such as Option B, limiting long-term competitiveness [an].

knowledge_max_2: Quality control checks at the end of production; faults detected late
Quality control adds a permanent staffing cost
application_max_2: Reference to $60,000 a year / 42 workers / 30 workers to train
analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to rework and scrap to higher costs and squeezed profit
Chain from inspector wages to fewer funds for training to weaker long-term competitiveness

questions.question_text: Do you think Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd should introduce quality assurance (Option B) rather than quality control (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A, quality control, would catch faulty boxes at the end of the line, protecting customers quickly before dispatch [k]. At $60,000 a year it is cheaper up front and would visibly cut complaints during the 10 weeks before the Christmas gifting range ships [app]. This rapid protection is valuable given the reputation risk at peak season [an]. However, Option B, quality assurance, prevents defects at every stage rather than detecting them afterwards [k]. Training 30 of the 42 workers to check recipes, enrobing and packaging costs $95,000 to set up, but it attacks the rework behind the 18% failure rate directly [app]. Preventing faults earlier reduces wasted ingredients, rework and complaints, protecting Hazelmere's $11.2 million revenue more sustainably than end-of-line checks [an]. Overall, I think Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd should choose Option B [eval] because prevention is cheaper than failure: the $95,000 is less than two years of Option A at $60,000 a year, after which Option B is cheaper and errors fall further [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Quality control detects faults at end of production
Quality assurance prevents faults at every stage
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $60,000 a year / 10 weeks / Christmas gifting range
Reference to Option B: $95,000 / 30 of 42 workers / 18% failure rate / $11.2 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Chain from end-of-line detection to rapid reputation protection at peak season
Chain from prevention at source to less rework/waste to protected revenue and lower long-run cost
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($60,000 vs $95,000, 18% failure, 240 complaints)

scenario_stem:
Marlbrook Outfitters is a private limited company running 3 clothing stores in Country X. Year to 30 June: revenue $840,000, gross profit $378,000, expenses $252,000, profit $126,000; last year revenue $780,000, gross profit $304,200, profit $97,500 on premium lines.

Naomi must choose between a cheaper own-brand range against value retailers and keeping the premium lines loyal customers prefer. Her accountant is preparing ratio analysis for the board, meeting in 6 weeks to approve the own-brand range and set pricing.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Gross profit margin is the percentage of revenue remaining as gross profit after deducting the cost of sales, calculated as gross profit divided by revenue multiplied by 100; for Marlbrook Outfitters this year, $378,000 divided by $840,000 multiplied by 100 gives 45.0%, up from 39.0% last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin = gross profit / revenue x 100
It shows the percentage of each dollar of revenue kept after cost of sales

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Naomi should use gross profit margin when judging the own-brand proposal.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: gross profit margin shows the percentage of revenue left after the cost of sales, so it reveals how efficiently Marlbrook buys or makes its goods [k]; the margin improved from 39% ($304,200 divided by $780,000) last year to 45% ($378,000 divided by $840,000) this year, evidence that cost control on premium lines is strong [app]. Reason 2: gross profit margin lets Naomi compare lines and judge whether a cheaper own-brand range would still cover the cost of sales [k]; if the range runs near the current 45% margin while revenue passes $840,000, it adds profitable sales rather than diluting margins [app].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin shows profitability after cost of sales, before expenses
Gross profit margin can be compared across periods or product lines to judge cost control
application_max_2: Applies last year's 39% from $304,200 / $780,000 and weighs margin against $840,000 revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using gross profit margin alone to judge the own-brand proposal.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: gross profit margin ignores operating expenses [k]; with expenses of $252,000, the profit margin is only 15% ($126,000 divided by $840,000), so judging the range on the $378,000 gross profit alone could approve a proposal that actually cuts final profit [app][an]. Limitation 2: gross profit margin is calculated from historic figures and ignores other evidence [k]; last year's $304,200 and this year's $378,000 say nothing about how customers respond to cheaper own-brand clothing in one of the 3 stores, so sales and cash forecasts must also be studied [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin ignores expenses / overhead costs
Gross profit margin is historic and ignores non-financial evidence
application_max_2: Applies $252,000 expenses to show profit margin is only 15% ($126,000 / $840,000)
Applies historic figures such as $304,200 and $378,000 and the 3 stores context
analysis_max_2: Explains a proposal can raise gross profit yet cut final profit once expenses are charged
Explains historic margins cannot predict customer response to the cheaper range

questions.question_text: Do you think Naomi should launch the cheaper own-brand range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Naomi could launch the range because demand from price-sensitive customers is often strong in clothing retail [k]. Revenue growing from $780,000 to $840,000 with a 45% gross profit margin shows Marlbrook can price own-brand lines below the premium tier and still cover the cost of sales, potentially lifting volume and profit together [app][an]. However, expenses of $252,000 leave a profit margin of only 15% ($126,000 divided by $840,000), so heavy discounting on the own-brand range could cut overall profit even as sales rise [app][an]. Conversely, keeping premium lines protects the margin gain from 39% to 45% and the rise from $97,500 to $126,000, but cedes the value segment to rivals [k][eval]. Overall, Naomi should trial the own-brand range in one of the 3 stores for one quarter, comparing its margin against 45% before wider roll-out; expand only if final profit holds above this year's $126,000, because the thin 15% profit margin leaves little room for error [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin improved from 39% to 45%; profit margin is 15% ($126,000 / $840,000)
Revenue grew from $780,000 to $840,000; expenses remain high at $252,000
application_max_2: Applies the 45% margin headroom and 15% profit margin to the range pricing decision
Applies revenue growth from $780,000 to $840,000 as evidence of demand
analysis_max_2: Explains that value demand and margin headroom could lift volume and profit together
Explains that discounting could cut final profit even if sales rise because expenses are fixed at $252,000
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighing margin protection against new demand, tied to a one-store trial and the $126,000 profit benchmark

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Suncrest Olive Estate is a private limited company producing gourmet olive oil for export. It sells 400,000 bottles a year at $9 each, earning $3.6 million; 60% (240,000 bottles) go to Country W. A 12% appreciation means Country W buyers now pay $10.08 unless prices are cut.

The June price list is due. Option A cuts the Country W price to $8.10, 10% off, to hold volumes. Option B keeps $9 and accepts orders falling, shifting marketing to domestic supermarkets.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so a currency buys more foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A rise in the value of a currency
Compared with other currencies / buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 12% appreciation on Suncrest Olive Estate.
questions.model_answer: First, appreciation makes Suncrest's oil more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. Each $9 bottle now costs Country W customers the equivalent of $10.08, so demand for the 240,000 bottles a year they buy may fall [app]. Second, appreciation weakens Suncrest's competitiveness against rival suppliers [k]. Country W supermarkets may switch to locally bottled olive oil instead, so Suncrest risks losing listings and part of its $3.6 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports more expensive abroad
Appreciation reduces export competitiveness versus foreign rivals
application_max_2: Reference to Country W 240,000 bottles / $3.6 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Suncrest Olive Estate might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the price by 10% reduces the revenue earned on every Country W bottle [k]. At $8.10 instead of $9, Suncrest loses 90 cents on each of its 240,000 Country W bottles, which is $216,000 a year less export revenue [app]. If volumes do not rise enough to replace this, profit falls and less money is available to reinvest in groves and bottling lines [an]. Second, a lower export price can trigger a price war with Country W rivals [k]. Rival producers may match the $8.10 offer to keep their supermarket listings, so Suncrest gains little extra shelf space [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across a market that takes 60% of sales, making the business less able to absorb future cost rises [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting price reduces revenue per unit
Lower prices risk competitor price matching / price war
application_max_2: Reference to Country W / 60% of sales / supermarket listings
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to lower revenue to reduced profit and less funds for reinvestment
Chain from rival price matching to no extra volume and permanently lower margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Suncrest Olive Estate should cut the Country W price to $8.10 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the Country W price by 10% to $8.10 to hold order volumes steady [k]. This keeps Suncrest competitive now that its bottles cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08, helping to protect the 240,000-bottle order book that supplies 60% of its $3.6 million revenue [app]. Retaining shelf space prevents listings being lost to local Country W rivals, which would be hard and expensive to win back [an]. However, Option B holds the $9 price [k]. Refusing to discount protects the 90-cent margin on each bottle, so Suncrest avoids the $216,000 annual revenue loss built into Option A and keeps strong cash flow for the supermarkets [app]. The danger is that orders fall sharply as the 12% appreciation pushes Country W buyers towards cheaper local oil [an]. Overall, I think Suncrest should choose Option A [eval] because the appreciation was caused by currency markets rather than by Suncrest, and volume and shelf presence in Country W matter more than the margin; it can review the $8.10 price each season and raise it if the dollar weakens [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut price by 10% to $8.10 to defend volume
Option B: hold $9 and protect margin
application_max_2: Reference to $10.08 equivalent / 12% appreciation / 10% price cut
Reference to 240,000 bottles / 60% of sales / $3.6 million revenue / $216,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to retained competitiveness and protected Country W shelf space
Chain from holding price to preserved margin but risk of order losses to local rivals
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($8.10 vs $9, $216,000, 240,000 bottles)

scenario_stem:
Kestrel Cycle Works is a bicycle repair and assembly partnership run by brothers Danny and Aaron Cole. With 6 mechanics, it assembled bikes for local retailers, made $240,000 sales and splits profits equally, but the brothers are personally liable for debts.

They want a second workshop across town costing $90,000. The bank offers only a $45,000 loan without more security, so they must choose between staying a partnership or incorporating as a private limited company and issuing shares for the $90,000.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'partnership'.
questions.model_answer: A business owned by two or more people (usually up to 20) who share capital, profits, workload and liability, commonly governed by a deed of partnership [2].

knowledge_max_2: owned by two or more people
shared profits, workload and liability / deed of partnership

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to the brothers of remaining a partnership rather than incorporating.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The brothers keep all the profits between them [k], splitting the $240,000 in sales revenue equally rather than paying dividends to outside shareholders [app]. Advantage 2: A partnership has few legal formalities [k], so it is cheap to run without registering a company or filing public accounts [app].

knowledge_max_2: profits kept and shared only between partners
few legal formalities / no public filing of accounts

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to the brothers of remaining a partnership.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: They remain personally liable for all business debts [k], so Danny and Aaron's personal savings and property could be used to pay the lift equipment and rent arrears [app], risking serious personal financial loss [an]. Disadvantage 2: Difficulty raising large sums of capital [k], so funding the $90,000 second workshop through a single $45,000 loan is risky [app], potentially leaving the expansion underfunded or abandoned [an].

analysis_max_2: personal assets exposed to business creditors
expansion may be underfunded or cancelled

questions.question_text: Do you think the brothers should convert Kestrel Cycle Works into a private limited company? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An advantage of incorporating is limited liability [k], because Danny and Aaron would risk only their investment and shares could raise the full $90,000 without further personal borrowing [app], protecting their homes while funding the second workshop [an]. A disadvantage is the extra legal paperwork and disclosure [k], because private limited companies must register and file accounts [app], adding costs that eat into profits from $240,000 of sales [an]. Overall, the brothers should incorporate [eval] because the expansion depends on raising $90,000 and limited liability protects them if the new workshop fails in its first year [eval].

knowledge_max_2: extra formalities / filed accounts and costs
analysis_max_2: personal homes protected while expansion proceeds
compliance costs reduce profits available for reinvestment
evaluation_max_2: weighs funding need and liability protection against disclosure and compliance costs

scenario_stem:
BrightPath Logistics is a private limited company parcel depot with 78 staff: 50 full-time on $15 an hour, 28 part-time on $12 an hour. Volumes rise 45% in the 10-week peak to 9,600 parcels weekly; 140 were damaged last year.

The manager must hire 20 additional part-time for the peak or 10 full-time at $31,200 with 6 weeks' training. Part-timers cannot drive heavy vehicles or forklifts. Advertising costs $180 per vacancy; the budget is $4,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'part-time employment'.
questions.model_answer: Part-time employment is a job in which the employee works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee, often on flexible or reduced shifts, and is paid for the hours worked. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee
Paid for the hours worked, often on flexible or reduced shifts

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to BrightPath Logistics of hiring 20 additional part-time workers for the peak.
questions.model_answer: Part-time workers are paid only for the hours they work [k], so during the 10-week pre-Christmas peak, when volumes rise by 45% to 9,600 parcels a week, the depot pays extra wages only when the extra capacity is actually needed [app]. Additional part-time staff reduce the overload on the existing 78 staff [k], helping to prevent repeats of the 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels that occurred last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Pay only for the hours worked; labour cost flexes with demand
Extra staff relieve pressure and reduce errors/losses
application_max_2: 10-week peak; volumes rise 45% to 9,600 parcels a week; $12 an hour
140 damaged and 12 lost parcels last year; 78 existing staff

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of employing 10 additional full-time staff all year.
questions.model_answer: Full-time staff can be trained and trusted with demanding tasks [k]. The 50 current full-time drivers and operatives already handle heavy vehicles and forklifts, and new full-time hires would receive 6 weeks of training [app], widening the pool of skilled staff available all year, not just in December [an]. Full-time staff remain after the peak, giving the depot stable capacity [k]. Ten full-time salaries cost $312,000 a year (10 x $31,200), but these staff can cover quieter months and stand in for absences [app], reducing reliance on agency cover and repeated seasonal recruitment every December [an].

knowledge_max_2: Full-time staff can receive full training and handle more demanding tasks
Full-time staff provide year-round stable capacity and continuity
application_max_2: 6 weeks of training; heavy vehicles and forklifts; 50 current full-time staff
10 x $31,200 = $312,000 a year; stays after the peak ends
analysis_max_2: Wider skilled pool all year reduces bottlenecks and dependence on December cover
Year-round presence lowers agency costs and re-recruitment effort

questions.question_text: Do you think BrightPath Logistics should hire 20 additional part-time workers for the peak or 10 additional full-time staff all year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring 20 part-time workers is cheaper and more flexible [k]. At $12 an hour part-timers cost less than the $15 full-time rate and are paid only for hours worked, and 20 vacancies at $180 each total $3,600, still inside the $4,000 recruitment budget [app]. Bringing in extra hands should stop the 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels that overstretched staff caused last year [an]. However, part-time staff cannot drive heavy vehicles or operate forklifts [k], so the depot would still rely on its 50 full-time staff for the hardest tasks and might repeat the same overload in January returns or other peaks [app]. Full-time hires at $31,200 each would stay year-round, receive 6 weeks of training and cut the need to re-recruit every December [an]. Overall, the depot should hire the 20 part-time peak workers because demand is temporary and $312,000 of annual salary for year-round cover is hard to justify for a peak that lasts 10 weeks [eval]. If volumes stayed high all year, or forklift-certified full-time staff were urgently needed, the full-time option would become worth the extra cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Part-time: flexible, cheaper per hour, suits short peaks
Full-time: permanent, trained, versatile but costly year-round
application_max_2: $12 vs $15 an hour; $180 per vacancy; 20 vacancies = $3,600 inside $4,000 budget
10 x $31,200 = $312,000; 10-week peak; 9,600 parcels; 140 damaged and 12 lost
analysis_max_2: Cheap flexible capacity matched to a known 10-week peak reduces overload and parcel losses
Full-time gives year-round skill and stability but overspends for a temporary need
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement justified by the temporary nature of the peak and the cost arithmetic
Recognises the circumstances in which the full-time option would be preferable

scenario_stem:
Northgate Electrical is a family-run partnership with 2 stores in Country X, 26 staff and $2.4 million sales. It stocks 1,800 product lines, mainly televisions and washing machines. Since a national chain opened nearby, sales fell 9% and footfall keeps dropping.

The owners must choose: use market research to identify local demand for smart home devices and restructure the range, or keep the range and cut prices 15% to match the national chain. Unsold televisions fill the shelves.

questions.question_text: Define 'market-orientated business'.
questions.model_answer: A business that bases its decisions on the needs and wants of customers identified through market research, rather than on what it currently produces [2].

knowledge_max_2: bases decisions on customer needs and wants
uses market research to guide decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Northgate Electrical of being a market-orientated business.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Products would better match local customer needs [k], so stock such as smart home devices would appeal to country town buyers [app]. Benefit 2: Customer satisfaction and loyalty would improve [k], helping the 2 stores win back sales lost since the national chain opened [app].

application_max_2: smart home devices as example stock
2 stores recovering from the 9% sales fall

questions.question_text: Explain two difficulties Northgate Electrical might face in becoming more market-orientated.
questions.model_answer: Difficulty 1: Market research costs money and staff time [k], so interviewing customers across both stores takes staff off the shop floor [app], leaving less cash for new stock purchases [an]. Difficulty 2: Customer tastes change quickly [k], so research done this year may not show what customers want next year [app], meaning the restructured range of 1,800 lines could still miss demand [an].

knowledge_max_2: market research costs money and time
analysis_max_2: less cash left for new stock purchases
range could still miss future demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Electrical should restructure its range based on market research rather than cut prices by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Market research would identify exactly what local customers want [k], letting Northgate stock profitable lines such as smart home devices instead of unsold televisions [app], differentiating the 2 stores from the national competitor and protecting margins [an]. However, cutting prices by 15% would produce an immediate sales boost [k], tempting country town customers to return [app], but it would slash profit on every one of its 1,800 product lines [an]. Overall, restructuring the range is the stronger strategy [eval] because differentiation builds loyalty that a price cut cannot [eval].

knowledge_max_2: market research identifies local customer wants
price cut gives immediate sales boost
application_max_2: smart home devices replacing unsold televisions
analysis_max_2: differentiation protects margins against the national chain
price cut slashes profit on every line
evaluation_max_2: weighs differentiation and loyalty against short-term sales boost
justified recommendation to restructure the range

scenario_stem:
Driftwood Toy Co is a private limited company owned by Daniel Reyes, designing wooden trains and puzzles. With 68 workers it made 900,000 units exported to 6 countries for $7.2 million; paint-defect returns hit 5%.

One retailer threatened to cancel a $400,000 order. Within eight weeks Daniel chooses Total Quality Management — every worker responsible, weekly meetings and a suggestion scheme, costing $30,000 in training — or keeps four end-of-line inspectors, costing nothing but leaving returns unchanged.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'Total Quality Management (TQM)'.
questions.model_answer: Total Quality Management is a business-wide approach in which every employee is responsible for quality, with continuous improvement of processes and products until zero defects are achieved [2].

knowledge_max_2: Every employee in the business is responsible for quality
Continuous improvement aiming for zero defects

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Driftwood Toy Co of producing high-quality toys.
questions.model_answer: First, high quality builds reputation and customer loyalty [k]. Export retailers in 6 countries rely on safe, well-made toys, so a good record would help secure the $400,000 order now at risk of cancellation [app]. Second, high quality reduces returns and rework costs [k]. With paint defects causing 5% of shipments to be returned, better quality would cut replacement costs and protect the $7.2 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality builds reputation and customer loyalty
Quality reduces returns, rework and replacement costs
application_max_2: Reference to 6 export countries / $400,000 order at risk
Reference to 5% paint defect returns / $7.2 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of introducing Total Quality Management (Option A) at Driftwood Toy Co.
questions.model_answer: First, TQM makes every worker responsible for quality [k]. Under weekly improvement meetings, all 68 workers can spot paint defects during production rather than after dispatch [app]. Catching faults at source reduces waste and rework, lowering production costs and raising profit margins [an]. Second, TQM encourages continuous improvement and employee involvement [k]. The suggestion scheme lets workers closest to the toys propose fixes, improving morale and ownership [app]. A motivated workforce checks its own work more carefully, so the 5% return rate falls and the $400,000 retailer order is protected [an].

knowledge_max_2: Every employee is responsible for quality; faults found at source
Continuous improvement / employee involvement through suggestions
application_max_2: Reference to 68 workers / weekly improvement meetings
Reference to suggestion scheme / 5% returns / $400,000 order
analysis_max_2: Chain from shared responsibility to fewer faults to lower waste and rework costs
Chain from employee involvement to morale to fewer returns and a secured order

questions.question_text: Do you think Driftwood Toy Co should introduce Total Quality Management (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A costs $30,000 to train all 68 workers, but TQM builds quality into every stage, so paint defects would be prevented before toys reach export markets [k]. This directly addresses the root cause of the 5% return rate and would reassure the retailer ahead of the $400,000 order review [app]. Preventing defects also cuts rework and scrap, improving profit over time rather than just inspecting faults after they occur [an]. However, Option B keeps 4 end-of-line inspectors at no extra cost, so Daniel could redeploy the $30,000 to sales or new toy designs [k]. Inspection does catch faulty toys before dispatch, but returns would likely stay at 5% and the retailer could still cancel the $400,000 order [app]. Losing that order would cost far more than $30,000, and it does nothing to fix the paint process itself [an]. Overall, I think Daniel should choose Option A [eval] because $30,000 is small next to the $400,000 order and the $7.2 million revenue at stake; prevention beats detection [eval].

knowledge_max_2: TQM builds quality into each stage / all employees responsible
End-of-line inspection detects faults but does not prevent them
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $30,000 / 68 workers / weekly meetings / suggestion scheme
Reference to Option B: no extra cost / 4 inspectors / 5% returns / $400,000 order
analysis_max_2: Chain from TQM prevention to fewer returns to protected profit and contract
Chain from inspection-only to persistent 5% returns to risk of losing $400,000
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($30,000 vs $400,000, 5% returns, $7.2 million revenue)

scenario_stem:
Halvern Castings Ltd is a private limited company casting iron brackets for farm machinery. At 30 June, current assets were $286,000, comprising inventories $150,000, trade receivables $96,000 and cash $40,000, against current liabilities of $104,000.

The steel supplier offers a 2% cash discount to settle the $60,000 debt early instead of usual 60-day terms. Marcus must decide whether to take a 90-day bank loan at 1.5% interest to pay early, or wait and risk upsetting the supplier before steel prices rise next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities with its current assets, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Halvern Castings holds $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities, a ratio of 2.75:1. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
It shows the liquidity of the business, i.e. its ability to pay short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marcus should check the current ratio before taking the loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities [k]; Halvern's $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities is 2.75:1, indicating comfortable cover today before taking on a 90-day loan [app]. Reason 2: the current ratio helps Marcus see whether paying $60,000 early still leaves the business able to meet its remaining bills [k]; paying early would use the $40,000 cash plus part of the $96,000 trade receivables, so he must confirm cover stays above 1:1 through the 90 days [app].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities
Current ratio indicates the liquidity buffer available before taking on new short-term debt
application_max_2: Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 trade receivables against the $60,000 early payment

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio alone for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the current ratio treats all current assets as equally quick to convert into cash [k]; Halvern holds $150,000 of inventories, the slowest asset, so excluding them (the acid test ratio) gives a more cautious picture of ($286,000 minus $150,000) divided by $104,000, about 1.31:1 [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio is a single snapshot at 30 June and ignores timing [k]; if $96,000 of trade receivables pay slowly, Halvern may not have the $60,000 in cash even though the 2.75:1 ratio looks strong, so cash-flow timing must also be checked [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio assumes all current assets convert to cash equally fast
Current ratio is a static snapshot and ignores cash-flow timing
application_max_2: Applies the $150,000 inventories exclusion giving an acid test of about 1.31:1
Applies the $96,000 trade receivables timing and the 2.75:1 snapshot
analysis_max_2: Explains inventories are the slowest asset so the current ratio overstates true liquidity
Explains that a strong snapshot figure can still hide a cash-timing shortfall in the 90 days

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should take the 90-day bank loan to pay the supplier early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marcus could take the loan because a strong steel supplier supports reliable deliveries for the farm-machinery brackets his factory casts [k]. The 2% discount on the $60,000 saves $1,200 against $900 of interest (1.5% for 90 days), a net gain of $300, and the current ratio of 2.75:1 plus an acid test of about 1.31:1 shows he can cover a short 90-day loan from $286,000 of current assets [app][an]. However, the cash buffer is only $40,000 and the $96,000 of trade receivables must convert to cash within 90 days, so if customers pay late the loan rolls over with fresh interest and the net gain turns into a loss [app][an]. Conversely, waiting for the normal 60-day settlement costs nothing but forfeits the $1,200 discount and leaves the supplier waiting [k][eval]. Overall, Marcus should take the loan only if receivables have a strong payment record and the supplier confirms the terms in writing; the acid test of about 1.31:1 supports it, but with only a $300 net saving he should walk away if any part of the arrangement looks uncertain [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Foxglove Denim Co is a private limited company weaving denim at its Glendale mill. It imports 30 tonnes of cotton monthly from Country Z; a 15% depreciation lifts the cost from $120,000 to $138,000 a month, or $4,600 per tonne. 40% of jeans are exported.

Prices must be set by 1 August. Option A raises jeans from $45 to $48, passing on the $18,000 monthly rise. Option B keeps $45 and absorbs $216,000 a year, hoping cotton costs fall or Country Z sales grow.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so the currency buys less foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of a currency

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 15% depreciation on Foxglove Denim Co.
questions.model_answer: First, depreciation raises the cost of imported cotton [k]. Cotton now costs $4,600 per tonne, so the monthly bill has jumped from $120,000 to $138,000, an extra $18,000 a month [app]. Second, depreciation makes Foxglove's jeans cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. With 40% of jeans exported to Country Z, the finished garments cost Country Z retailers fewer Country Z units, so export orders may rise and partly offset the higher cotton bill [app].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports
application_max_2: Reference to 40% exported to Country Z

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Foxglove Denim Co might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, absorbing the increase squeezes profit margins on every pair of jeans [k]. The extra $216,000 a year must come out of the margin on jeans sold at $45, leaving less for repairs, machinery or wages at the Glendale mill [app]. Lower retained profit means less money available for future investment, such as replacing weaving looms, which weakens competitiveness [an]. Second, Foxglove cannot know when cotton costs will fall back [k]. If the Country X dollar keeps depreciating beyond 15%, the $138,000 monthly cotton bill could rise further, so a fixed $45 price leaves the firm exposed to open-ended cost growth [app]. Continued absorption would eventually push certain lines into loss-making months, forcing emergency price changes or borrowing [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxglove Denim Co should raise its wholesale jean price from $45 to $48 (Option A)? Justify your answer.

Holding price may retain retailer loyalty and sales volume at home, and with 40% of jeans exported, stronger export volumes could offset the $216,000 absorbed [app]. The risk is that cotton costs keep rising if the dollar weakens further, so $45 may become unsustainable [an]. Overall, I think Foxglove should choose Option A [eval] because a $3 rise is only about 6.7% on a wholesale price and is caused by an external currency movement, so retailers are likely to accept it rather than lose supply; it should review the price each season in case cotton costs fall back [eval].

scenario_stem:
Meadowbrook Day Nursery is a sole trader nursery for 48 children, with 9 full-time practitioners on $26,000 and 5 part-time assistants. One resigned; the $250 advert drew 30 applications in 3 weeks for autumn term.

Of these, 18 enclosed a curriculum vitae and 12 completed the application form with 8 standard questions; CVs vary in layout, forms give consistent data. Panels cost $120 per candidate; the budget is $800. The owner must shortlist by CV or form.

questions.question_text: Define 'application form'.
questions.model_answer: An application form is a standard document produced by the business that applicants complete to provide details such as personal information, qualifications and experience, allowing the employer to compare candidates fairly. [2]

questions.model_answer: Application forms present every candidate's information in the same format [k]. With 30 applications received in 3 weeks, the owner can scan the 12 completed forms quickly against the 8 standard questions instead of comparing 18 different CV layouts [app]. Forms ensure the nursery gets the specific information it needs [k]. The form's questions on qualifications, experience and childcare training directly test whether applicants meet the requirements for caring for children aged 2 to 5 [app].

With $120 of staff time per candidate and a total budget of $800 (minus $250 already spent on the advertisement), the nursery can interview only the strongest candidates and check their claims face to face [app], which reduces the risk of hiring unsuitable staff for the 48 children [an]. Interviews also give candidates the chance to ask questions about the role [k]. Discussing the $26,000 full-time salary, the 9 existing full-time practitioners and daily duties helps both sides judge fit before the autumn term [app], lowering the chance of an early resignation and the $120 per-interview cost being wasted [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowbrook Day Nursery should shortlist using the CVs or the application forms? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Application forms give consistent information the nursery can compare quickly [k]. The 12 completed forms answer the 8 standard questions directly, so the owner can shortlist confidently before paying $120 per interview from the remaining budget [app]. This reduces the risk of hiring someone unsuitable to work with the 48 children aged 2 to 5 [an]. However, CVs reveal more about personality, motivation and experiences such as first-aid courses, and the 18 CVs received may contain stronger candidates than the forms show [k]. A detailed CV might reveal qualities the standard form cannot capture, and rejecting them all could leave the nursery choosing only from the form-fillers [app]. Over-reliance on the form alone could cause the nursery to miss the most enthusiastic applicant for the role [an]. Overall, the nursery should shortlist using the application forms because consistency and the 8 targeted questions suit a safeguarding-critical childcare role, and the budget does not stretch to interviewing widely from an unverified CV pool [eval]. If strong candidates emerge on the forms, CVs can be read as supporting evidence, but the form should remain the primary tool [eval].

scenario_stem:
Tidewater Leisure Pools Ltd is a private limited company operating 2 swimming and fitness venues. In the year to 31 August, profit was $180,000 and capital employed $900,000; last year profit was $135,000 on capital employed $900,000. A competitor's ROCE is 12%.

Rachel must decide whether to build a third venue costing $400,000 from retained profit, adding $52,000 in year one but $112,000 once established, or raise annual dividends of $60,000. She will announce this at the September annual general meeting.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for Tidewater Leisure Pools. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE is the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Tidewater Leisure Pools earns $180,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100 = 20.0% this year, up from 15.0% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: It shows how effectively capital is used to generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why ROCE is the key figure for the board's decision.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows how much profit each dollar of capital employed generates [k]; Tidewater's ROCE improved from 15% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000) to 20% this year ($180,000 divided by $900,000), well above the competitor's 12%, evidence that the existing venues earn strong returns [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the board compare the $400,000 third venue with leaving retained profit idle or paying dividends [k]; if the new venue lifts annual profit towards $292,000 in its third year, ROCE would reach about 22.5% ($292,000 divided by $1,300,000), beating the competitor and justifying the build [app].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE shows the return generated on capital employed
ROCE allows investment options to be compared on a percentage return basis
application_max_2: Applies 20.0% this year ($180,000 / $900,000) versus 15.0% last year and 12% competitor
Applies the $400,000 venue cost, $1,300,000 resulting capital employed and the $292,000 third-year profit potential

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ROCE is based on historic figures and profit only, not on how long the $400,000 takes to recover [k]; the venue adds only $52,000 in its first year, giving a first-year ROCE of about 17.8% on capital employed of $1,300,000, so early years dilute the ratio before the full benefit appears [app][an]. Limitation 2: ROCE ignores the other factors affecting the 2 existing venues [k]; occupancy, local competition and the $60,000 dividend expectation do not appear in the ratio, so customer demand and team capacity must also guide the board [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE is historic and does not show how an investment recovers its cost over time
ROCE ignores non-financial and contextual factors
application_max_2: Applies the $52,000 first-year contribution and the $1,300,000 resulting capital employed (about 17.8%)
Applies the $400,000 cost, $60,000 dividends and the 2 existing venues context
analysis_max_2: Explains that first-year returns dilute ROCE so the ratio looks worse than the long-run position
Explains that ROCE cannot capture demand, competition or shareholder expectations

questions.question_text: Do you think Rachel should build the third venue? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Rachel could approve the build because the business currently earns an ROCE of 20% ($180,000 divided by $900,000) against a competitor's 12%, proving the 2-venue model works well [k][app]. The third venue should add $52,000 in year one and $112,000 at maturity, lifting capital employed to $1,300,000 and reaching an ROCE of about 22.5% in year three, while also defending the venues' position in Country X [an]. However, first-year ROCE falls to about 17.8% ($232,000 divided by $1,300,000), and paying $400,000 from retained profit reduces dividends below the $60,000 shareholders currently expect [app][an]. Conversely, paying larger dividends rewards shareholders now but leaves $400,000 barely generating anything and loses the chance to outgrow the 12% competitor [k][eval]. Overall, Rachel should approve the third venue but phase the spending, because a long-run ROCE above the competitor matters more than short-term dilution, provided membership numbers stay strong and some dividend is maintained during construction [eval].

application_max_2: Applies the 20% current ROCE versus the competitor's 12% as evidence the model works

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ridgemont Electronics Ltd is a private limited company assembling smartphone accessories at its Darnwell factory with 85 workers. It imports circuit boards from Country W, paying €90,000 a month. The rate moved from $1.30 to $1.45 per euro, raising dollar costs.

Second, the movement reduces the reliability of Ridgemont's cost planning [k]. If the rate moves beyond $1.45 per euro, the $130,500 monthly import cost rises further, so the firm cannot confidently fix prices in its October supply contract [app].

If the dollar weakens past $1.45 per euro, the €90,000 payment will exceed the current $130,500 and could approach the $135,000 charged by the Country X supplier [app]. Open-ended cost growth makes it hard to quote firm prices to customers, risking lost orders [an]. Second, continued importing keeps Ridgemont dependent on one foreign supplier and its lead times [k]. Any delay or disruption at the Country W factory would halt the Darnwell line that employs 85 workers [app]. A line stoppage would push up costs and damage reputation with accessory customers [an].

scenario_stem:
Tekworks Electronics is a private limited company repairing computers at 2 workshops with 64 people, producing 1,100 repaired devices at $190. A new client needs 12 electronics assemblers in 6 weeks.

HR chooses: a practical assessment of soldering and fault-finding, 2 hours at $45, or a 30-minute panel interview at $25 per candidate; both cost $70. The line must reach 400 units in 4 months at 98% fault-free. With $3,000 budget, 55 applied and 35 applicants are invited.

questions.question_text: Define 'interview' in the context of selection.
questions.model_answer: An interview is a face-to-face meeting between a job applicant and the business, used to assess the applicant's suitability, skills and attitude for the role. [2]
