questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tekworks Electronics should test the 12 assemblers before hiring them.
questions.model_answer: Testing reveals the practical ability that an interview cannot show [k]. The assembly line needs soldering and fault-finding skill, so a $45 practical assessment shows exactly which of the 35 invited applicants can meet the 98% fault-free requirement [app]. Testing reduces the risk of costly mistakes and rework [k]. With the line due to reach 400 units a month within 4 months, hiring untested assemblers risks faulty devices and a damaged relationship with the new client [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tests measure actual job skills directly rather than claimed ability
Testing identifies unsuitable candidates and reduces hiring errors and rework
application_max_2: 35 invited applicants; $45 assessment; 400 units a month within 4 months

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using interviews as part of the selection process.
questions.model_answer: Interviews let the panel assess communication and teamwork [k], so the manager can check how applicants would fit into the team of 64 across the 2 workshops before devices priced at $190 are entrusted to them [app], improving team fit and reducing early turnover [an]. Interviews also let candidates ask about the job [k], so shortlisted applicants can understand the 400-unit monthly target, the 6-week hiring deadline and working patterns [app], meaning expectations match reality and the $3,000 recruitment budget is not wasted on someone who resigns quickly [an].

Realistic expectations reduce early resignations, saving recruitment cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Tekworks Electronics should use practical assessments or panel interviews to select the 12 assemblers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Practical assessments directly measure the exact skills the assembly line needs [k]. A $45 assessment for 35 applicants costs $1,575, leaving $1,425 of the $3,000 budget, and shows who can actually solder to the 98% fault-free standard [app]. Choosing by observed skill rather than talk minimises rework and protects delivery of 400 units a month within 4 months [an]. However, practical tests alone cannot show how candidates communicate under pressure or fit into the 64-person team [k]. The $25 interview would reveal reliability and willingness to start within 6 weeks; running both costs $70 per applicant, or $2,450 for 35, still within budget [app]. A brilliant solderer who quits after a week would leave the line short-staffed and waste selection time [an]. Overall, practical assessments are the essential tool because the role is skill-critical and the client's 98% fault-free clause leaves no margin for unsuitable technicians [eval]. Interviews should be added only as a brief final check for the chosen 12, not as the main basis of selection [eval].

scenario_stem:
Rosedale Knitwear is a private limited company employing 110 workers. It knitted 600,000 garments last year, averaging $15 each for $9 million revenue; complaints and returns over stitching faults reached 12,000 garments last quarter.

Its main overseas customer, taking 60% of output, demands a plan. Within 5 weeks, ahead of an audit, Sara Okafor chooses 6 more inspectors for $54,000 a year or quality assurance at every stage with retraining for all 110 workers, costing $80,000 once.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Rosedale Knitwear should reduce the number of faulty garments.
questions.model_answer: First, faulty garments create rework and returns costs [k]. With returns at 12,000 garments last quarter, each faulty item wastes yarn, machine time and labour, so fewer faults would lower production costs [app]. questions.question_text: Explain two problems Rosedale Knitwear might face if it hires 6 more inspectors (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, inspection at the end of production only detects faults; it does not prevent them [k]. Double-checking finished garments would not stop stitching faults occurring during linking, so the 12,000 returns might continue [app]. Rework and scrap costs would persist, squeezing profit margins [an]. Second, hiring 6 inspectors raises costs without fixing processes [k]. The extra $54,000 a year is a permanent wage bill that does not reduce the fault rate itself [app]. questions.question_text: Do you think Rosedale Knitwear should introduce quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B builds quality into every stage, from yarn inspection to pressing, preventing stitching faults rather than catching them afterwards [k]. Retraining all 110 workers costs $80,000 as a one-off but attacks the root cause of the 12,000 returns, protecting the relationship with the retail group taking 60% of output [app]. Fewer returns would cut rework costs and safeguard the $9 million revenue earned last year [an]. But the fault rate itself would persist, and two years of $54,000 totals $108,000 — more than Option B's single $80,000 payment [app]. scenario_stem:
Redfern Farm Kitchen Ltd is a private limited company making pasta sauce and pesto. Year to 30 April: revenue $610,000, gross profit $183,000, expenses $103,700, profit $79,300; last year revenue $520,000, expenses $88,400, profit $83,200.

Revenue rose $90,000 yet profit fell. The value range, launched 18 months ago, is now 60% of jars sold. Colin Marsh must decide whether to discontinue it and focus on premium sauces, or keep it for volume and shelf space in 3 chains.

questions.question_text: Calculate the profit margin for Redfern Farm Kitchen. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin (net profit margin) is the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all expenses are deducted, calculated as profit divided by revenue multiplied by 100; Redfern Farm Kitchen earned $79,300 divided by $610,000 multiplied by 100 = 13.0% this year, down from 16.0% last year ($83,200 divided by $520,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: It shows the percentage of each dollar of revenue left as final profit after expenses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Colin should study the profit margin before discontinuing the value range.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the profit margin shows the percentage of revenue left after all expenses, revealing whether the value range is truly profitable [k]; the margin fell from 16.0% last year ($83,200 divided by $520,000) to 13.0% this year ($79,300 divided by $610,000), a drop of 3 percentage points despite revenue growing by $90,000 [app]. Reason 2: the profit margin shows whether the value range dilutes overall profitability [k]; with the value range making 60% of jars sold and expenses rising from $88,400 to $103,700, overhead growth is eating into final profit even though gross profit held near 30% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin shows final profitability after expenses
Profit margin can be compared across periods to detect dilution of profit
application_max_2: Applies the 60% value-range share of jars and expenses rising from $88,400 to $103,700

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using profit margin to judge the value range.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the profit margin is a single blended figure that cannot split value-range performance from premium-sauce performance [k]; without product-level accounts, the 13.0% margin could hide a strong premium line subsidising a weak value line, so discontinuing the wrong lines would remove volume without lifting profit [app][an]. Limitation 2: the profit margin ignores the strategic value the range brings [k]; 60% of jars sold means the value lines fill factory capacity and support the $90,000 of revenue growth, and dropping them could strand overheads while gross profit margin stays at 30% [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin is a blended figure and cannot isolate product-line performance
Profit margin ignores strategic and volume effects
application_max_2: Applies the 13.0% blended margin and missing product-level breakdown
Applies the 60% of jars sold, the 30% gross profit margin and $90,000 revenue growth
analysis_max_2: Explains that without line-level data the wrong decision could be made
Explains that dropping the range could strand overheads and lose revenue growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Colin should discontinue the value range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Colin could keep the range because it accounts for 60% of jars sold and helped revenue grow by $90,000 (from $520,000 to $610,000), filling factory capacity and widening brand reach in Country X [k][app]. Dropping it might restore the profit margin above 16% but risks losing most of the volume that absorbs factory overheads [an]. However, the profit margin has fallen to 13.0% ($79,300) and expenses are $103,700 (up from $88,400), so the value range may be turning a healthy 30% gross profit margin into thin final profit while tying up cash in stock and distribution [app][an]. Conversely, focusing on premium sauces could restore profit above $83,200, but below that the value lines still absorb fixed overhead that premium sales alone may not carry [k][eval]. Overall, Colin should re-price the value range and cut its costs first rather than discontinue it outright, because 60% of volume is too important to drop without product-level profit evidence, but he should review discontinuation if margins do not recover within 12 months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin fell from 16.0% to 13.0% ($83,200 to $79,300); expenses rose $88,400 to $103,700
Revenue grew by $90,000; value range is 60% of jars sold; gross profit margin 30%
application_max_2: Applies the 60% volume share and $90,000 revenue growth to argue for keeping the range
Applies the 13.0% margin and $103,700 expenses to argue for discontinuation

Explains that the range converts 30% gross profit into thin final profit

scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Cider Co is a private limited company pressing craft cider in Country X. Of 150,000 cases a year, half are exported to Country W at €20 each, invoiced in euros. The rate moved from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, strengthening the dollar.

January export prices are due. Option A cuts the Country W price by 10% to €18 a case to defend 75,000 cases yearly. Option B holds €20 and accepts orders falling to 60,000, focusing on domestic farm shops and supermarkets.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar value of the annual export payments before and after the rate change.
questions.model_answer: Annual exports: 75,000 cases x €20 = €1,500,000. Before: €1,500,000 x $1.45 = $2,175,000. After: €1,500,000 x $1.30 = $1,950,000. The appreciation cuts dollar export revenue by $225,000 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Carrowmore Cider Co.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the dollar value of Carrowmore's euro export sales [k]. The same 75,000 cases at €20 now convert to $1,950,000 rather than $2,175,000, so dollar export revenue falls by $225,000 [app]. Second, the appreciation makes it harder to recover that revenue by raising the export price [k]. Lifting the €20 price to claw back the shortfall would make Country W buyers switch to cheaper local cider, so Gareth must plan marketing carefully [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation lowers the dollar value of euro receipts
Raising foreign prices to recover revenue weakens competitiveness
application_max_2: Reference to Country W buyers / €20 a case / local cider rivals

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Carrowmore Cider Co might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, holding price means giving up export volume [k]. Orders fall from 75,000 to 60,000 cases, so euro export revenue drops from €1,500,000 to €1,200,000, a loss of €300,000 a year [app]. Lower export volume may leave cider stockpiled for the domestic market, forcing farm-gate discounting [an]. Second, Option B shrinks Carrowmore's presence in Country W [k]. Once listings are lost to Country W rivals, winning them back is expensive, and farm shops and supermarkets at home may not absorb the extra 15,000 cases [app]. Domestic sales growth could lag, leaving the pressing plant underused and unsold stock [an].

knowledge_max_2: Holding price loses export volume and revenue
Lost listings are hard to recover / domestic market may not absorb displaced volume
application_max_2: Reference to farm shops and supermarkets / Hereford vale / 15,000 cases
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower export volume to unsold stock and farm-gate discounting
Chain from lost listings to higher re-entry cost and underused capacity

questions.question_text: Do you think Carrowmore Cider Co should cut its Country W price to €18 a case (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the export price by 10% to €18 to defend the 75,000-case order book [k]. Keeping 75,000 cases at €18 raises €1,350,000, which converts to $1,755,000 at the new $1.30 rate, well ahead of the 60,000-case alternative, and it keeps Carrowmore's cider listed in Country W stores [app]. Volume and shelf presence protect the brand abroad and spread fixed costs over more cases [an]. However, Option B holds €20 [k]. Orders fall to 60,000 cases, worth €1,200,000 or $1,560,000, but the margin per case is higher and the firm avoids cheapening its craft brand in its main overseas market [app]. The danger is losing momentum at the moment domestic farm shops and supermarkets are being asked to absorb extra cases [an]. Overall, I think Carrowmore should choose Option A [eval] because keeping 75,000 cases in front of Country W shoppers protects long-term export relationships while the firm builds domestic sales; it can restore €20 once the rate improves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut price by 10% to €18
Option B: hold €20, export volume falls to 60,000 cases
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to defended volume and protected shelf space and brand
Chain from holding price to higher per-case margin but lost listings and domestic pressure
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B

scenario_stem:
Aurora Cinema Group is a private limited company operating 5 cinemas in Country X. It sells 210,000 tickets a year at $9 each; attendance fell 8% last year. The group wants feedback on a proposed loyalty scheme and new food menu.

questions.question_text: Define 'questionnaire'.

Overall, the questionnaire is the better first step [eval] because a large, low-bias sample reduces risk before the loyalty scheme launch [eval], with interviews afterwards to dig deeper.

scenario_stem:
Bramblewick Honey is a sole trader business owned by Yusuf Rahman, bottling honey from 80 hives. He makes 36,000 jars a year at $5 each, earning $180,000 through farmers' markets and 14 local shops.

A supermarket chain wants 30 stores but requires batch testing after complaints of incorrectly blended honey. In four weeks Yusuf chooses laboratory batch testing for $8,000 a year, or a $6,000 refractometer with quality assurance checklists covering extraction, straining and jarring.

questions.question_text: State two costs of poor quality to a business.
questions.model_answer: Poor quality leads to customer complaints and returns, raising costs [1]. It damages reputation, losing customers and sales [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Damaged reputation / lost customers and sales

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramblewick Honey of improving quality before supplying the supermarket chain.
questions.model_answer: First, higher quality would help secure the new contract [k]. Listing in 30 stores would massively expand sales beyond his 14 local shops, multiplying market reach [app]. Second, consistent quality protects reputation [k]. With complaints of incorrectly blended honey already recorded, proving reliable jars to the supermarket would earn repeat, larger orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality helps secure new contracts / sales growth
application_max_2: Reference to 30 supermarket stores vs 14 local shops
Reference to incorrectly blended honey complaints

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Yusuf might face if he relies on laboratory testing of finished batches alone (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, testing finished batches detects faults but does not prevent them [k]. Blending and straining errors would already have happened by the time the laboratory approves a batch, so jars of incorrectly blended honey could still slip through to the 30 stores [app]. A rejected batch would destroy honey he has already paid to produce and jar [an]. Second, the laboratory fee is a permanent annual cost [k]. Paying $8,000 a year cuts into the $180,000 revenue from jars sold at $5 each, eroding his small margin [app]. Over two years the $16,000 total exceeds the $6,000 cost of Option B's equipment [an].

knowledge_max_2: Finished-product testing detects faults but does not prevent them
Laboratory testing is an ongoing annual cost
application_max_2: Reference to 30 stores / incorrectly blended honey / extraction, straining and jarring stages
Reference to $8,000 a year / $180,000 revenue / $5 per jar
analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to spoiled produced stock to lost value
Chain from $8,000 fee to lower margin to $16,000 two-year cost exceeding Option B

questions.question_text: Do you think Yusuf Rahman should choose quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $6,000 once and introduces quality assurance checklists at extraction, straining and jarring, preventing faults at source [k]. This directly prevents the incorrectly blended honey problem before jars reach the 30 stores, and the equipment remains his indefinitely with no recurring fee [app]. Over two years Option A costs $16,000 against $6,000 for Option B, leaving more cash for Yusuf to fund growth [an]. However, Option A uses an independent laboratory, which may reassure the supermarket more than self-checks [k]. Independent test certificates give the chain objective proof that each delivery meets its batch requirements, though waiting for approval could delay dispatch to stores [app]. The $8,000 a year fee is also ongoing, and a failed batch wastes both the fee and the production cost of that batch [an]. Overall, I think Yusuf should choose Option B [eval], provided the supermarket accepts documented QA procedures: it prevents faults, saves $10,000 over two years and builds lasting capability [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Quality assurance prevents faults at source at each stage
Independent laboratory testing offers objective third-party proof
application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $6,000 one-off / extraction, straining, jarring checklists / refractometer
Reference to Option A: $8,000 a year laboratory / 30 stores / batch testing requirement
analysis_max_2: Chain from QA checklists to prevention to fewer rejected batches and protected sales
Chain from independent testing to supermarket confidence vs recurring $8,000 fee and wasted batches
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($6,000 vs $8,000 a year, 30 stores, $180,000 revenue)

scenario_stem:
Thorne & Vale Toys Ltd is a private limited company running a toy shop. At 31 October, current assets were $340,000: inventories $224,000, trade receivables $88,000, cash $28,000, against current liabilities of $160,000. Last year's acid test ratio was 0.95:1; festive sales are 45% of annual sales.

Beth must choose between a full $180,000 festive stock order, backed by her forecast, or a reduced $120,000 order, waiting on December trading before reordering. Supplier prices rise 6% in November.

questions.question_text: Define 'acid test ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities using only its quick assets (excluding inventories), calculated as (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities; Thorne & Vale Toys has ($340,000 minus $224,000) divided by $160,000 = $116,000 divided by $160,000 = 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1 last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio = (current assets - inventories) / current liabilities
It measures immediate liquidity without relying on selling inventories

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Beth should consider the acid test ratio before placing the festive order.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the acid test ratio shows whether liquid assets alone can cover current liabilities, without counting inventories [k]; Thorne's quick assets are only $116,000 ($88,000 receivables plus $28,000 cash) against $160,000 of current liabilities, giving 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1 last year [app]. Reason 2: the acid test ratio signals whether the full $180,000 stock order would stretch the business through the festive peak [k]; festive sales make up 45% of annual toy sales, so stock must be right, but committing $180,000 against a $44,000 shortfall exposes the shop to supplier-payment risk [app].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio shows liquidity excluding inventories
Acid test ratio indicates the risk of committing to large stock purchases on credit
application_max_2: Applies the $116,000 quick assets against $160,000 liabilities = 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1
Applies the $180,000 order against only $28,000 cash and the $44,000 shortfall

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the acid test ratio for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the acid test ratio assumes inventories cannot be sold quickly, which is rarely true in a busy toy shop in December [k]; festive stock turns over fast, so excluding all $224,000 of inventories may understate Thorne's ability to generate cash from the 45% of annual toy sales that arrive in the season [app][an]. Limitation 2: the acid test ratio is a single snapshot and ignores the effect of order size on December sales [k]; a reduced order of $120,000 protects cash but could leave shelves empty in the peak fortnight when 45% of annual toy sales are made, losing revenue and emptying shelves [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio assumes inventories cannot be converted to cash quickly
Acid test ratio is a snapshot and ignores sales momentum and timing
application_max_2: Applies the $224,000 inventories exclusion and the 45% festive sales share
Applies the $120,000 reduced order versus the $180,000 full order scenario
analysis_max_2: Explains that fast-turning festive stock means the ratio understates real cash generation
Explains that a reduced order risks lost festive sales despite protecting cash

questions.question_text: Do you think Beth should place the full $180,000 festive order? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Beth could place the full order because festive season sales make up 45% of annual toy sales, and running out of stock in December would forfeit her biggest trading period of the year [k][app]. The overall current ratio of 2.125:1 ($340,000 divided by $160,000) shows comfortable cover, and festive stock should convert quickly to cash if December trading matches the 45% pattern [an]. However, the acid test ratio of 0.725:1 means quick assets of $116,000 fall $44,000 short of current liabilities, and a full $180,000 order on top of a cash balance of $28,000 means paying suppliers before festive revenue arrives, risking overdraft costs [app][an]. Conversely, a reduced order of $120,000 saves $60,000 of cash and protects the shop if festive sales disappoint, though re-ordering mid-season may delay delivery and cost late-December sales [k][eval]. Overall, Beth should place a staged order: most of the $180,000 now with a top-up in early December once first-week festive cash arrives; this balances the 0.725:1 acid test against the 45% of annual toy sales at stake [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Festive season sales make up 45% of annual toy sales; acid test 0.725:1 versus 0.95:1 last year
Current ratio 2.125:1; quick assets $116,000 vs liabilities $160,000 ($44,000 shortfall); cash only $28,000
application_max_2: Applies the 45% festive sales share and 2.125:1 current ratio to argue for ordering
Applies the 0.725:1 acid test, $44,000 shortfall and $28,000 cash to argue caution
analysis_max_2: Explains festive stock converts quickly to cash if December trading is normal
Explains supplier payments fall due before festive revenue arrives, risking overdraft
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of a staged order balancing acid test risk against the 45% festive revenue at stake

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Wren & Willow Fashion is a private limited company running 6 shops selling womenswear across Country X, with 34 full-time and part-time staff. It imports 4,000 winter coats a year from Country W at €40 each. Appreciation from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro cuts coat costs from $58 to $52.

Winter prices must be set. Option A cuts ticket prices by $6 to boost footfall and market share. Option B holds prices and keeps $24,000 extra a year to refurbish 2 shops.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a stronger currency on businesses that import goods.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods become cheaper in the home currency; importers can cut their selling prices or enjoy higher profit margins [2].

knowledge_max_2: Imports cost less in the home currency
Importers can cut prices or raise margins

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Wren & Willow Fashion.
questions.model_answer: First, each imported coat now costs $52 instead of $58, saving $6 [k]. On 4,000 winter coats a year the total saving is $24,000, which can fund refurbishment or wage rises [app]. Second, cheaper coats let Wren & Willow compete on price without cutting its margin [k]. Passing on the $6 would keep relative value attractive to Country X shoppers while protecting the mark-up the shops need to pay 34 staff for 6 stores [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cheaper import costs in home currency
Scope to cut retail prices or boost margins

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wren & Willow Fashion might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the ticket price sacrifices margin headroom [k]. Passing on the entire $6 import saving leaves no extra profit from the appreciation, so the $24,000 stays locked in lower prices rather than funding refurbishment of 2 shops [app]. If sales do not rise enough to offset the lower price, the business forgoes profit the currency change already delivered [an]. Second, price promotions can be matched by rival shops [k]. Competing Country X retailers importing from Country W will also face a $6 cost fall, so all may cut ticket prices together, leaving Wren & Willow with lower prices but little extra footfall [app]. Market-wide price cuts reduce revenue per coat and can squeeze cash flow during the crucial winter season [an].

knowledge_max_2: Passing on all the savings removes extra profit
application_max_2: Reference to Country X retailers importing from Country W / winter season
analysis_max_2: Chain from full price pass-through to forgone profit if volume flat
Chain from rival price matching to market-wide margin squeeze and weaker cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think Wren & Willow Fashion should cut the ticket price of the imported coats by $6 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A passes the $6 saving straight to customers as lower ticket prices [k]. This makes the 4,000 imported coats noticeably better value, which should boost footfall across the 6 shops and lift market share before the winter peak [app]. Higher volume spreads fixed costs such as rent and wages over more coats and builds loyalty for the rest of the range [an]. However, Option B keeps ticket prices and banks the $24,000 [k]. The shops keep their margin, and the money could refurbish 2 of the 6 stores to improve customer experience without touching price [app]. The risk is that rivals cut prices first, leaving Wren & Willow uncompetitive on the high street despite the $6 saving being available [an]. Overall, I think Wren & Willow should choose Option A [eval] because the $6 saving was a currency windfall rather than genuine efficiency, and giving it back as value wins loyalty and share while margins stay at their pre-appreciation level [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut ticket prices by $6
Option B: hold prices and keep $24,000
application_max_2: Reference to 6 shops / 2 shop refurbishment / 34 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from cut prices to footfall, market share and loyalty
Chain from held prices to funded refurbishment but risk of rivals undercutting
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($6, $24,000, 4,000 coats)

scenario_stem:
Brightpath Electrical Services is an unincorporated sole trader business run by electrician Tom Okoro for 9 years, wiring homes and shops. He employs 3 apprentices and invoiced $150,000 last year, with his house backing every contract.

Tom wants larger shop fit-outs worth $400,000, but clients demand liability protection and insurance certificates. He must decide whether to stay unincorporated or register as a private limited company with separate legal status.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'incorporated business'.
questions.model_answer: A business registered as a separate legal entity from its owners, able to own property, sue and be sued, with owners protected by limited liability [2].

knowledge_max_2: registered as separate legal entity from owners
owners enjoy limited liability / can own property, sue and be sued

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Tom Okoro of registering Brightpath Electrical Services as a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Limited liability [k], so Tom's house and savings would be protected if a contract worth up to $400,000 runs into trouble [app]. Advantage 2: A separate legal identity [k], which reassures commercial clients who already want proof of liability protection before signing fit-out contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: separate legal identity / greater client credibility
application_max_2: clients want proof of liability protection

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Tom Okoro of becoming a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Extra costs and paperwork [k], because registration fees and annual filed accounts reduce the $150,000 he invoiced last year [app], leaving less cash for wages and tools [an]. Disadvantage 2: Loss of privacy [k], because rival electricians can view his filed accounts showing his margins [app], making it easier for them to undercut his prices [an].

analysis_max_2: less cash available for wages and tools

questions.question_text: Do you think Tom Okoro should incorporate Brightpath Electrical Services as a private limited company? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An advantage of incorporation is limited liability [k], because clients demanding proof of protection could sign contracts up to $400,000, nearly three times the $150,000 invoiced last year [app], without risking Tom's home for every job [an]. A disadvantage is the added cost and disclosure [k], because registering and filing accounts adds fees and reduces privacy [app], eating into profits just as he expands [an]. Overall, Tom should incorporate [eval] because the $400,000 commercial contracts he wants are only safely possible with limited liability and separate legal status [eval].

registration fees and public disclosure disadvantages

scenario_stem:
Riverview Leisure Centre is a publicly owned facility with 2 swimming pools and a gym, employing 40 full-time staff. Attendances rose 18% to 210,000 visits, extending hours to 14 hours a day.

The manager must hire 8 part-time lifeguards at $11.50 an hour for evenings, each covering 1 pool on 30-minute shifts, or 4 full-time lifeguards at $24,500 who also do gym induction checks, with 5 weeks' leave. The $900 budget includes $280 advertising.

questions.question_text: Define 'full-time employment'.
questions.model_answer: Full-time employment is a job in which the employee works the standard number of hours each week set by the employer, usually around 35 to 40 hours, on an ongoing basis. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Works the full/standard working week (about 35-40 hours)
On an ongoing, usually permanent basis for the business

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of hiring 8 part-time lifeguards for the evening and weekend sessions.
questions.model_answer: Part-time cover matches staffing to demand [k], so the new 14-hour days can be covered at $11.50 an hour only when pools are busy, instead of paying $24,500 salaries all year [app]. Eight part-time lifeguards provide scheduling flexibility [k], covering 30-minute shifts and just 1 pool each across 2 pools, and they can cover for one another at short notice [app].

knowledge_max_2: Pay only for the hours needed; labour cost matches demand
Flexible shifts and more staff provide cover and resilience
application_max_2: $11.50 an hour; 14-hour days; evenings and weekends
1 pool each; 30-minute shifts; 2 pools; $24,500 full-time alternative

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of hiring 4 full-time lifeguards instead.
questions.model_answer: Full-time lifeguards can take on wider duties [k]. They would open and close the pools and complete gym induction checks, tasks that part-timers on 30-minute shifts cannot practically handle [app], giving consistent standards at both ends of the 14-hour day [an]. Four full-time staff are also easier to train and supervise than 8 part-timers [k]. At $24,500 each, totalling $98,000 a year, they receive 5 weeks of annual leave arranged around demand and stay year-round [app], which lowers induction and turnover costs and strengthens safety compliance [an].

knowledge_max_2: Full-time staff take on wider, end-to-end duties
Fewer staff are easier to train, supervise and retain
application_max_2: Open and close duties; gym induction checks; 30-minute shifts impractical
$24,500 each, $98,000 total; 5 weeks annual leave; 14-hour day

Lower turnover and training burden; stronger safety compliance

questions.question_text: Do you think Riverview Leisure Centre should hire 8 part-time lifeguards or 4 full-time lifeguards? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring 8 part-time lifeguards costs less and flexes with demand [k]. At $11.50 an hour, covering only evenings and weekends is cheaper than $98,000 a year of full-time salaries, and 30-minute shifts slot neatly around peak attendance from 210,000 visits [app]. Part-time cover keeps the pools staffed into busy sessions without exhausting the $900 recruitment budget [an]. However, part-time staff cannot open and close or complete gym induction checks properly [k], so the 14-hour day would still stretch the 40 existing full-time staff further, or require tighter supervision [app]. Four full-time lifeguards on $24,500 each would handle openings, closings and induction checks, with 5 weeks of leave rosterable around the summer peak [an]. Overall, the centre should hire the 4 full-time lifeguards because open/close and gym induction duties are essential to safe 14-hour days, and 8 part-timers would leave those duties uncovered [eval]. If attendances proved erratic after summer, some evening shifts could be converted to part-time once core full-time cover was secure [eval].

Full-time: committed, wider duties, end-to-end responsibility

Full-time option guarantees daily end-to-end safety cover

scenario_stem:
Harrowgate Homeware is an independent sole-trader furniture retailer with 3 stores in Country X and around 1,400 customers a week. The owner wants to redesign the layout to promote a new $850 sofa range arriving in September.

The options are observation, recording where 1,000 shoppers stop over 4 weeks, or a focus group of 8 loyal customers discussing styles and prices. Results as bar charts will guide spending on display fittings.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation'.
questions.model_answer: A primary research method in which researchers watch and record how consumers behave in real settings, without asking them questions [2].

knowledge_max_2: in a real setting, without asking questions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Harrowgate Homeware of using observation for the layout decision.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It shows what customers actually do [k], where the 1,000 shoppers stop inside the 3 stores [app]. Benefit 2: Customers behave naturally when they do not know they are watched [k], giving unbiased evidence for placing the $850 sofa range near the entrance [app].

knowledge_max_2: shows actual rather than stated behaviour
unobtrusive so behaviour is natural and unbiased
application_max_2: placing the $850 sofa range near the entrance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the owner should still consider the focus group before deciding.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Focus groups reveal opinions and reasons, not just behaviour [k], 8 loyal customers can explain why they would or would not buy the $850 sofa [app], guiding which models and colours to display [an]. Reason 2: Observation cannot explain why shoppers stop [k], it will not reveal that fabrics look unappealing [app], so a layout built only on observation might still fail to lift sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: focus groups give opinions and reasons
observation shows behaviour but not reasons
application_max_2: observation will not reveal unappealing fabrics
analysis_max_2: guides which sofa models and colours to display
layout based only on observation may still fail to lift sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Harrowgate Homeware should use observation rather than the focus group for the layout decision? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Observation of 1,000 shoppers over 4 weeks gives hard, unbiased evidence of real behaviour [k] across all 3 stores [app], showing exactly where to place the $850 sofa range [an]. However, the focus group of 8 loyal customers costs far less and gives detailed opinions on style and price tolerance [k] from customers who already trust the retailer [app], though their views may not represent the 1,400 weekly shoppers [an]. Overall, observation is the better choice for a layout decision [eval] because traffic flow needs behavioural evidence presented as bar charts [eval], with a focus group afterwards to refine the range.

knowledge_max_2: focus groups give detailed opinions cheaply

scenario_stem:
Starling Cosmetics is a private limited company formulating organic skincare creams with 54 workers. Last year it sold 210,000 jars at $30 each for $6.3 million; skin irritation complaints reached 320 in six months.

A contaminated batch forced recall of 4,000 jars costing $90,000, drawing regulator attention. Before the audit in eight weeks, Priya Nair adds 2 testers for $48,000 a year or adopts Total Quality Management across formulation and packing, with a suggestion scheme, costing $75,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'customer satisfaction'.
questions.model_answer: Customer satisfaction is the degree to which customers are pleased with a product or service and feel their needs and expectations have been met [2].

knowledge_max_2: Customers are pleased with a product or service
Their needs and expectations are met

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why high quality is important to Starling Cosmetics.
questions.model_answer: First, high quality protects customers' health and avoids recalls [k]. The contaminated face cream already forced a recall of 4,000 jars costing $90,000, and more recalls would destroy trust in the brand [app]. Second, high quality protects reputation and sales [k]. With 320 complaints of skin irritation in 6 months, quality failures would deter new buyers and cut the $6.3 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality protects customer safety / prevents recalls
application_max_2: Reference to recall of 4,000 jars / $90,000 recall cost

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of introducing Total Quality Management (Option B) at Starling Cosmetics.
questions.model_answer: First, TQM involves every department in quality [k]. Targets and monthly review meetings across formulation, filling, packaging and warehousing would catch errors such as contamination before batches are filled [app]. Preventing faults at source would cut recalls and scrap, saving money and protecting the brand [an]. Second, TQM encourages continuous improvement and employee suggestions [k]. The suggestion scheme empowers 54 workers to report risks and propose safer handling [app]. Engaged workers take greater care, reducing the 320 complaints and satisfying the regulator ahead of its audit [an].

knowledge_max_2: TQM involves every department / all employees share responsibility for quality
TQM encourages continuous improvement and employee suggestions
application_max_2: Reference to formulation, filling, packaging and warehousing / monthly review meetings

questions.question_text: Do you think Starling Cosmetics should introduce Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $75,000 to implement, more than the $48,000 a year cost of Option A, but TQM prevents defects across every department rather than only catching them in the laboratory before release [k]. Monthly review meetings and quality targets shared by 54 workers would tackle why the contaminated batch reached 4,000 jars in the first place [app]. Preventing contamination protects the $6.3 million revenue and helps satisfy the regulator at the 8-week audit, avoiding forced withdrawal or fines [an]. However, Option A, quality control, is quicker and cheaper in year one, adding 2 technicians who pass or fail every batch independently [k]. Laboratory testing would intercept faulty batches before dispatch, but the $48,000 fee recurs each year and does nothing to stop errors in filling or packaging [app]. Over two years Option A costs $96,000, exceeding Option B's $75,000, while Option B leaves the business a permanent quality culture [an]. Overall, I think Starling Cosmetics should choose Option B [eval] because TQM removes causes of failure system-wide and costs less over two years [eval].
