scenario_stem:
Fenland Woollens Ltd is a private limited company making woollen blankets. Year to 30 June: city mill revenue $540,000, gross profit $167,400, profit $59,400, capital employed $594,000; rural branch revenue $300,000, gross profit $66,000, profit $9,000, capital employed $225,000.

The board may close the rural branch if figures confirm this, yet it supplies the city mill with specialist yarn and employs 15 local weavers, affecting the community. The managing director must recommend at next month's board meeting.

questions.question_text: State two limitations of ratio analysis.
questions.model_answer: Two limitations of ratio analysis are firstly that ratios are based on historic figures and may not reflect future performance, and secondly that ratios ignore qualitative factors such as staff morale, customer loyalty and community impact, so they cannot tell the whole story about a business. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Ratios use historic data, so they may not predict future performance
Ratios ignore qualitative and non-financial factors

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the board has used ratio analysis on the two mills' figures.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: ratio analysis lets the board compare the two mills on a common basis [k]; the city mill produced a 31% gross profit margin ($167,400 divided by $540,000) against the rural branch's 22% ($66,000 divided by $300,000), showing the rural branch is weaker at the making or buying stage [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis highlights where profit leaks after expenses [k]; the rural branch returned only a 3% profit margin ($9,000 divided by $300,000) on capital employed of $225,000 (an ROCE of 4%) versus 11% and 10% for the city mill, flagging underperformance for the board [app].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis enables comparison of different parts of a business on a common basis
Ratio analysis identifies weaknesses in profitability and efficiency
application_max_2: Applies 31% vs 22% gross profit margins ($167,400/$540,000 vs $66,000/$300,000)
Applies 3% vs 11% profit margins and 4% vs 10% ROCE ($9,000/$225,000 vs $59,400/$594,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis that apply to this closure decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ratios ignore the qualitative factors behind the figures [k]; the rural branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill, so closing it could disrupt the city mill's 31% gross profit margin in ways that appear nowhere in the rural branch's own 3% profit margin [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratios are calculated from one year's figures and give no reasons for the poor result [k]; one weak year of $9,000 profit does not prove the branch cannot improve with new equipment or markets, and the value of 15 local weavers' skills to the Country X community is invisible to the ratios [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios ignore qualitative and interconnected business factors
Ratios are historic single-year snapshots with no explanation of causes
application_max_2: Applies the rural branch's yarn supply role versus the city mill's 31% gross profit margin
Applies the 15 local weavers, $9,000 profit and single-year data
analysis_max_2: Explains closure could damage the profitable city mill despite good city ratios
Explains that ratios cannot explain or reverse the underlying causes of weak performance

questions.question_text: Do you think the managing director should recommend closing the rural branch? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The director could recommend closure because the figures are stark: the rural branch returned a 3% profit margin ($9,000 divided by $300,000) and a 4% ROCE ($9,000 divided by $225,000), far below the city mill's 11% profit margin and 10% ROCE [k][app]. Closing would release the $225,000 of capital employed to be used in the city mill, which earns $167,400 of gross profit on $540,000 revenue [an]. However, the branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill; closure could raise city mill's costs and endanger its 31% gross profit margin, and making 15 local weavers redundant damages the yarn supply and community goodwill [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the branch open preserves the yarn supply and the weavers' skills, but it consumed management time for only $9,000 profit, while the same $225,000 employed in the city mill would earn about 10% [k][eval]. Overall, the director should not close the branch outright; she should set a 12-month turnaround plan targeting yarn costs and sales, because the supply dependency outweighs one year of weak ratios, but closure must follow if branch profit stays below, say, $30,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Rural branch: 3% profit margin, 4% ROCE ($9,000 / $225,000); city mill: 11% and 10%
City mill gross profit $167,400 on $540,000 revenue (31%)
application_max_2: Applies the stark 3%/4% rural versus 11%/10% city ratios to argue for closure
Applies the yarn supply role and 15 local weavers to argue against closure
analysis_max_2: Explains released capital employed could earn the city mill's higher return
Explains closure could disrupt the city mill and endanger its 31% gross profit margin
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of a 12-month turnaround with a profit trigger for closure

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brannock Construction Ltd is a private limited company building 40 homes a year around Millbrook in Country X. It imports structural steel and timber worth $1.2 million a year from Country W. An 8% depreciation adds about $96,000 a year to material costs.

Supplies must be secured before the spring building season. Option A uses Country X suppliers at 10% above import prices, costing $1.32 million a year in stable dollars. Option B keeps importing and raises homebuyers' prices to cover the extra $96,000.

questions.question_text: State two ways a business can plan for exchange-rate fluctuations.
questions.model_answer: Monitor exchange-rate movements and adjust prices or sourcing in advance; agree contracts priced in the home currency or keep a contingency fund [2].

knowledge_max_2: Monitor rate movements and adjust prices or sourcing
Contract in home currency / keep contingency funds or reserves

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 8% depreciation on Brannock Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, the depreciation raises the cost of imported steel and timber [k]. The $1.2 million annual import bill now costs about $96,000 more, putting pressure on the margins of the 40 homes it builds a year [app]. Second, the depreciation squeezes Brannock's building economics unless home prices change [k]. Adding $96,000 across 40 homes means roughly $2,400 extra cost per home, which Brannock must absorb or recover through pricing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports
Higher input costs squeeze margins / must recover through prices
application_max_2: Reference to 40 homes / $2,400 per home / spring building season

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brannock Construction Ltd might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, domestic supplies cost $120,000 a year more than even the current import bill [k]. At $1.32 million against $1.2 million, Brannock pays a premium of $120,000, which is more than the $96,000 the depreciation added [app]. Higher material costs cut the margin on each of the 40 homes unless house prices rise [an]. Second, Country X steel and timber suppliers may not meet Brannock's volume or quality needs [k]. Millbrook builders all want local supplies at once, so lead times for domestic steel could run past the spring start, delaying the 40 homes [app]. Delays trigger penalty clauses in buyer contracts and raise site overhead, eroding the benefit of fixed prices [an].

knowledge_max_2: Domestic suppliers charge more than imports
application_max_2: Reference to $1.32 million vs $1.2 million / $120,000 vs $96,000
Reference to 40 homes / spring building season / Millbrook
analysis_max_2: Chain from domestic premium to lower margin per home
Chain from local capacity limits to delays, penalties and overhead strain

questions.question_text: Do you think Brannock Construction Ltd should source steel and timber from Country X suppliers (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A locks in Country X supplies at $1.32 million a year with no exchange-rate risk [k]. Because Brannock sells homes on fixed prices, a further depreciation beyond 8% would otherwise destroy its margin on 40 homes, and $1.32 million gives complete cost certainty for the spring programme [app]. Certain costs make cash flow and profit planning reliable, protecting the business from open-ended import bills [an]. However, Option B keeps the cheaper import route [k]. The current $96,000 increase is smaller than Option A's $120,000 premium, and raising homebuyers' prices by about $2,400 a home might cover the extra while keeping imported materials [app]. Relying on homebuyers absorbing rises is risky if competing builders keep prices lower or the rate moves further against the dollar [an]. Overall, I think Brannock should choose Option A [eval] because its buyers have fixed-price contracts and cost certainty protects profit better than chasing a $24,000 saving that could vanish with one more rate move; it can return to imports if the dollar recovers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: domestic supplies at $1.32 million, fixed
Option B: keep imports and raise home prices by about $2,400
application_max_2: Reference to 40 homes / $2,400 per home / spring building season
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed domestic costs to reliable planning and protected margins
Chain from homebuyer price rises to risk of losing sales to rivals
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($1.32 million vs $1.2 million, $96,000)

scenario_stem:
Larkspur Dairy is a family partnership run for 12 years by sisters Hannah and Ruth Whitmore, farming 180 dairy cows and bottling milk sold to 25 local shops. It employs 8 workers, made $380,000 sales, and the sisters share profits and carry unlimited liability.

A retailer offers a $200,000 contract over 3 years, but new pasteurising equipment costs $120,000. They must decide whether to fund it personally as partners or form a private limited company for limited liability protecting their homes.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'limited liability'.
questions.model_answer: The protection enjoyed by owners of incorporated companies, who can only lose the money they invested and are not personally responsible for the company's debts [2].

knowledge_max_2: owners can only lose invested money
not personally responsible for business debts

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to the Whitmore sisters of forming a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Their homes and savings are protected [k], so if the $120,000 pasteurising equipment debt cannot be repaid, creditors can only claim company assets [app]. Advantage 2: The $200,000 supply contract looks more credible [k], as a limited company reassures the regional retailer they are a reliable, established supplier [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to the Whitmore sisters of forming a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: More paperwork and filing duties [k], so annual accounts and registration costs reduce the $380,000 sales revenue [app], leaving less for wages, feed and vet fees [an]. Disadvantage 2: Loss of privacy and informality [k], as the shops and rival dairies could view filed accounts showing their margins [app], weakening their negotiating position on milk prices [an].

application_max_2: feed supplier bills and vet fees
analysis_max_2: less cash for daily running costs

questions.question_text: Do you think limited liability is the most important reason for the Whitmore sisters to form a private limited company? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Limited liability does protect the sisters [k], because under unlimited liability their homes would back the $120,000 equipment loan and any shortfall on the $200,000 contract [app], risking family security for the business [an]. However, other reasons also matter [k], because a limited company's separate identity can win bigger retail contracts and easier bank finance [app], not just liability protection [an]. Overall, limited liability is the main reason in this case [eval] because the sisters' homes are directly exposed by the $120,000 purchase and the 3 years commitment, so incorporation is worthwhile [eval].

knowledge_max_2: limited liability protects home and personal savings
other incorporation benefits (credibility, finance access) also exist
analysis_max_2: personal assets directly at risk without incorporation
credibility and finance gains are helpful but secondary
evaluation_max_2: judges personal asset exposure as the decisive factor over status and finance benefits

scenario_stem:
Greenacres Garden Centre is a family-run sole trader with 22 staff selling plants and tools. Spring drives 60% of sales: 1,800 plants weekly at $9 over a 13-week season.

For March to May the owner needs 3 extra weekend assistants and must choose advertising: $400 for a local newspaper read mainly by those over 55, or $150 online with younger reach but no local targeting. A print advert drew 40 phone enquiries; the budget is $600.

questions.question_text: Identify two pieces of information a job advertisement could include.
questions.model_answer: A job advertisement could include the job title and key duties of the role, and the pay offered, working hours and how to apply. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Job title and key duties/responsibilities of the role
Pay offered, working hours, closing date or how to apply (any valid content)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Greenacres Garden Centre should include clear details in its job advertisement for the 3 weekend assistants.
questions.model_answer: Clear details attract applicants who can actually do the job [k], so stating the 13-week March to May weekend pattern and duties such as helping customers and loading purchases filters out anyone wanting permanent, full-time work [app]. Precise details reduce wasted applications [k], meaning the $150 online or $400 print advert pulls in relevant candidates the first time rather than forcing a costly re-advertisement [app].

knowledge_max_2: Clear details attract suitable applicants and set realistic expectations
Clear details screen out unsuitable applicants, saving time and money
application_max_2: 13-week March to May weekend contract; 3 extra weekend assistants
$150 online vs $400 print choice; loading large purchases; plant sales at $9

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of choosing the $150 online advert.
questions.model_answer: The online advert costs far less than print [k], saving $250 against the $400 newspaper advert and leaving $450 of the $600 budget for other recruitment tasks [app], which improves value for money across just 3 seasonal posts [an]. Online adverts also reach younger, mobile-first audiences quickly [k], going beyond the over 55 newspaper readership that dominated the last print campaign [app], which raises the chance of filling all 3 weekend roles before the 13-week season starts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Online advertising is cheaper than print
Online advertising reaches wider and younger audiences quickly
application_max_2: Over 55 newspaper readership; 13 weeks; March to May
analysis_max_2: Savings improve cost-effectiveness and free budget for other hiring needs
Wider reach accelerates filling the 3 roles before the peak season

questions.question_text: Do you think Greenacres Garden Centre should place the $400 newspaper advert or the $150 online advert? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The online advert is cheaper and reaches a broader, younger audience [k]. At $150 it leaves $450 of the $600 budget intact, and younger weekend applicants are more likely to be flexible, often browse mobile job sites and may know garden tools and tills, fitting a plant retail environment selling at an average of $9 [app]. Choosing online reduces cost per effective applicant and should fill the 3 roles before the 13 weeks begin [an]. However, the local newspaper is read mainly by residents over 55, who are the garden centre's core plant-buying customers and may be the most credible, knowledgeable weekend assistants [k]. The centre's last print advert generated 40 phone enquiries, proving its local pull, whereas the online advert offers no guaranteed local targeting [app]. Print might produce fewer but far better-suited local candidates, some with real horticultural knowledge for questions about 1,800 plants sold in a peak week [an]. Overall, the centre should place the online advert because it can be launched quickly, costs $250 less, and 3 seasonal roles can be filled from a wider pool without breaking the $600 budget [eval]. If the online response produces too few strong local candidates, a small print boost can follow, using the savings to reinforce the local message [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Online: cheap, fast, wide reach, younger audience
Print: local credibility, older readership, proven response (40 enquiries)
application_max_2: Over 55 local readers; 40 enquiries last print; 60% of sales in spring
analysis_max_2: Online wins on cost, speed and reach for short-term seasonal posts
Print wins on local credibility and quality of horticultural knowledge
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall recommendation (online) with reasons tied to cost and urgency
Acknowledges the fallback print option if online response is weak

scenario_stem:
Zephyr Mobile is a sole-trader phone retailer with 4 shops in Country X, selling $150 handsets mainly to adults aged 35-55 (62% of sales). A $220 handset for 16-24 year-olds sold 240 units in 2 months, 70% to under-25s.

The owner must choose: niche-target the 16-24 segment with student-focused advertising at $300 per campaign, or run one mass-market campaign for all ages costing $4,500. Money is tight after a $60,000 refit.

questions.question_text: Define 'demographic segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Dividing a market into groups based on demographic characteristics such as age, gender, income, occupation or family size [2].

knowledge_max_2: groups based on age, gender, income, occupation or family size

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Zephyr Mobile of segmenting its market by age.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Promotion can target the chosen age group directly [k], student advertising can focus on 16-24 year-olds [app]. Benefit 2: The marketing budget is spent more efficiently [k], focusing on the segment that bought 70% of the 240 pilot units [app].

application_max_2: the segment buying 70% of 240 pilot units

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of Zephyr Mobile targeting the 16-24 niche rather than a mass-market campaign.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A niche approach builds a strong reputation with young buyers [k], 240 units were sold in 2 months, 70% to under-25s [app], encouraging student word-of-mouth and repeat purchases [an]. Advantage 2: Niche advertising is cheaper than mass campaigns [k], adverts placed in student media rather than nationwide [app], so limited funds go further while prices hold at $220 [an].

knowledge_max_2: niche builds strong reputation with the segment
niche advertising is cheaper than mass campaigns
application_max_2: student media rather than nationwide advertising
analysis_max_2: word-of-mouth lifts repeat sales from students
limited budget goes further while holding the $220 price

questions.question_text: Do you think Zephyr Mobile should target the 16-24 niche rather than continue mass marketing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The pilot results of 240 units in 2 months, with 70% bought by under-25s, show strong demand from 16-24 year-olds [k], so niche student advertising would be targeted and cost-effective [app], building a loyal younger customer base for the $220 handset [an]. However, the 35-55 segment still provides 62% of sales [k], so abandoning mass marketing could alienate loyal customers across the 4 shops [app] and hand younger buyers to strong competitors there [an]. Overall, Zephyr should shift towards the 16-24 niche [eval] because the pilot data shows where growth is strongest [eval], while keeping basic mass coverage in its existing adverts.

knowledge_max_2: mass marketing protects existing customer base
application_max_2: 240 units in 2 months with 70% under-25 buyers
35-55 segment providing 62% of sales across 4 shops
analysis_max_2: targeted advertising builds loyal young customer base for the $220 handset
dropping mass marketing risks alienating core customers
evaluation_max_2: weighs pilot evidence of youth demand against existing 62% base
justified recommendation to shift towards the 16-24 niche

scenario_stem:
Ferndale Tiles is a private limited company making ceramic wall and floor tiles with 85 workers. It produced 2.2 million tiles at $2 each for $4.4 million; two containers cracked in transit and 4% failed finish inspection.

A hotel group offers $600,000 for proven quality. In six weeks the owners choose $45,000 for an external audit and 12-month certification, or building their own quality assurance system for clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing at $22,000 plus $5,000 yearly.

questions.question_text: Outline the difference between quality control and quality assurance.
questions.model_answer: Quality control checks finished products at the end of production and removes faulty items [1]. Quality assurance builds quality into every stage of production so faults are prevented before they occur [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Quality control = checks finished goods / removes faulty items at the end
Quality assurance = builds quality into every stage / prevents faults

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferndale Tiles of obtaining external certification (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, certification proves quality objectively to buyers [k]. The hotel group offering $600,000 wants proof before placing orders, and an external audit provides independent evidence [app]. Second, certification strengthens reputation and competitiveness [k]. Winning the $600,000 contract would lift revenue above the $4.4 million earned last year and open further large hotel projects [app].

application_max_2: Reference to $4.4 million revenue / 2.2 million tiles

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferndale Tiles of building its own quality assurance system (Option B).
questions.model_answer: First, quality assurance prevents faults at source [k]. Checking clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing would catch the flaws causing tiles to crack, rather than discovering them after dispatch [app]. Preventing the 4% finish failures would cut returns and rework, raising profit [an]. Second, a documented system makes quality consistent and trainable [k]. Written procedures let all 85 workers follow the same checks every shift, so quality does not depend on memory [app]. Consistent routines lower waste and help Ferndale keep the hotel contract worth $600,000 year after year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Quality assurance prevents faults at source at each stage
Documented procedures make quality consistent and trainable
application_max_2: Reference to clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing / 4% finish failures
analysis_max_2: Chain from stage-by-stage checks to fewer cracks/rejects to lower rework cost and higher profit
Chain from written procedures to consistent quality to lower waste and a stable $600,000 contract

questions.question_text: Do you think Ferndale Tiles should pay for external certification (Option A) rather than build its own quality assurance system (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A costs $45,000 and provides independent, audit-verified certification that the hotel group can trust as proof of consistent quality [k]. Because the hotel wants quality proven, the 12-month certificate converts directly into the $600,000 contract and renews credibility with other large buyers [app]. Securing $600,000 of annual revenue against $45,000 spent is a strong commercial return [an]. However, Option B costs $22,000 plus $5,000 a year and tackles the actual causes of the 4% finish failures and cracked tiles, rather than just reporting on them [k]. Owning the system keeps procedures for clay preparation to packing in-house permanently, and over three years Option B costs $37,000, less than the first $45,000 year of Option A [app]. Building internal capability also raises staff ownership of quality, not just audit paperwork [an]. Overall, I think Ferndale Tiles should choose Option B [eval], because it prevents faults permanently and costs less, unless the hotel group rejects uncertified systems, in which case Option A is a necessary $45,000 investment to secure the $600,000 contract [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Certification = independent external audit of quality
Own QA system = prevention-focused, held in-house
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $45,000 / external audit / 12-month certification / renewable annually
Reference to Option B: $22,000 plus $5,000 a year / clay preparation, glazing, firing, packing / 4% finish failures
analysis_max_2: Chain from certification to audit-proof to contract win and repeat credibility
Chain from own QA system to lower 3-year cost ($37,000) and fault prevention to sustainable quality
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($45,000 vs $22,000 + $5,000 a year, $600,000 contract, 4% failures)

scenario_stem:
Marrow Lane Catering Ltd is a private limited company providing event catering. At 30 September, current assets were $408,000, comprising cash $240,000, trade receivables $108,000 and inventories $60,000, against current liabilities of $120,000; last year's current ratio was 2.1:1.

A $300,000 bank loan carries 7% interest. Shareholders want Tom to repay $240,000 early from cash to save interest, or keep the cash as a buffer for a spring wedding contract needing $90,000 of supplies paid upfront by February.

questions.question_text: Calculate the current ratio for Marrow Lane Catering. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures current assets against current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Marrow Lane Catering holds $408,000 divided by $120,000 = 3.4:1, up from 2.1:1 last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
Expressing the answer as a ratio such as 3.4:1

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of a strong current ratio for the wedding contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: a strong current ratio shows Marrow Lane can pay its short-term obligations as they fall due [k]; with $408,000 of current assets against $120,000 of current liabilities (3.4:1), the business can comfortably cover the $90,000 of up-front wedding supplies and normal monthly bills [app]. Benefit 2: a healthy current ratio reassures suppliers and the lender of creditworthiness [k]; paying the $90,000 of catering supplies up front is easy when cash alone is $240,000, and the ratio gives the bank confidence about the $300,000 loan [app].

knowledge_max_2: A strong current ratio indicates the business can meet short-term obligations
A healthy current ratio strengthens credibility with suppliers and lenders
application_max_2: Applies $408,000 / $120,000 = 3.4:1 against the $90,000 up-front wedding supplies
Applies the $240,000 cash and the $300,000 bank loan context

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of a very high current ratio.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: a very high current ratio can mean resources are idle rather than productive [k]; $240,000 of cash earning nothing while the $300,000 loan still costs 7% interest ($21,000 a year) represents an opportunity cost shareholders rightly question [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio hides what the assets actually are [k]; if most of the $408,000 were slow-moving inventories or unpaid trade receivables of $108,000 rather than cash, the 3.4:1 ratio would overstate true short-term strength [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A high current ratio may indicate idle, unproductive resources
The current ratio does not show the composition or quality of current assets
application_max_2: Applies the $240,000 idle cash against the 7% interest on the $300,000 loan ($21,000 a year)
Applies the $60,000 inventories and $108,000 trade receivables composition of the $408,000
analysis_max_2: Explains idle cash loses value against the ongoing loan interest cost
Explains the ratio can flatter liquidity if assets are slow-moving

questions.question_text: Do you think Tom should repay $240,000 of the loan early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Tom could repay the $240,000 because it would save $16,800 of annual interest at 7%, directly lifting profit, and shareholders would see disciplined use of cash instead of a 3.4:1 idle balance [k][app]. The reduced current ratio of 1.4:1 ($168,000 divided by $120,000) still covers current liabilities, and the loan balance would fall to $60,000, lightening the balance sheet and reducing risk [an]. However, using all $240,000 of cash leaves nothing as a buffer if the spring wedding contract needs $90,000 of supplies up front or if receivables of $108,000 pay late, and Tom could face emergency borrowing at higher cost [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the cash protects the wedding contract and day-to-day operations, but shareholders would question why a 7% loan stays outstanding while cash sits idle [k][eval]. Overall, Tom should repay $180,000 now and keep $60,000 plus receivables as a buffer; this saves about $12,600 of interest, keeps the current ratio near 1.9:1 ($228,000 divided by $120,000), and still funds the wedding supplies, balancing shareholder pressure against operational safety [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Repaying $240,000 at 7% saves $16,800 a year; repaying $180,000 saves about $12,600
Post-repayment current ratio: 1.4:1 (full repayment) or about 1.9:1 ($228,000/$120,000) for $180,000
application_max_2: Applies the $16,800 interest saving and reduced 1.4:1 ratio to argue for repayment
Applies the $90,000 wedding supplies need and $108,000 receivables to argue for keeping cash
analysis_max_2: Explains repayment lifts profit and lightens the balance sheet
Explains zero cash risks emergency borrowing if the wedding contract is delayed or receivables pay late
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of a partial $180,000 repayment keeping a buffer and a near-1.9:1 ratio

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Thistledown Coffee Roasters is a private limited company importing and roasting green coffee from Country W for independent cafe chains. It buys 80 tonnes a year at €2,800 a tonne. Appreciation from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro cuts the bill from $324,800 to $291,200, saving $33,600.

Beans must be chosen. Option A signs a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne with the Country W supplier. Option B buys monthly at spot rates, saving more if the dollar reaches $1.25 per euro ($280,000).

questions.question_text: Define what is meant by a 'stronger currency'.
questions.model_answer: A stronger currency is one that has risen in value against other currencies, so it buys more foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: Buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Thistledown Coffee Roasters.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the annual green coffee bill [k]. At the new rate, 80 tonnes cost $291,200 rather than $324,800, saving $33,600 a year [app]. Second, the cheaper euros give Thistledown more room to compete and invest [k]. The $33,600 saving can be kept as extra profit or reinvested in roasting capacity without raising bean prices for cafe customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Import bill falls in the home currency
Savings can be kept as profit or reinvested
application_max_2: Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / cafe customers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Thistledown Coffee Roasters might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the contract locks the cost even if the dollar keeps strengthening [k]. If the rate reaches $1.25 per euro, spot buyers would pay only $280,000 a year, so Thistledown would overpay by $11,200 against spot purchases [app]. Overpaying weakens the margin on every bag of beans and wastes funds that could finance growth [an]. Second, a 12-month fixed contract removes flexibility to switch suppliers [k]. If the Country W supplier's quality or reliability slips, Thistledown cannot easily move its 80 tonnes to a rival roaster without renegotiating, and it is exposed for a full year [app]. Being locked in limits negotiating power on quality, delivery and payment terms during the peak season [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed contract overpays if the currency keeps strengthening
Long contracts reduce flexibility to switch suppliers
application_max_2: Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / Country W supplier
analysis_max_2: Chain from locked price to overpaying vs spot to weaker margin and wasted funds
Chain from reduced flexibility to weaker negotiating power and supplier risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Thistledown Coffee Roasters should sign the 12-month fixed-price contract (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A signs a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne [k]. This locks the bill at $291,200 equivalent regardless of rate movements, so planning, pricing and cash flow are predictable for the whole year [app]. Certainty matters because the bean bill is Thistledown's biggest cost, and locking it protects margin if the dollar weakens back towards $1.45, which would lift the bill to $324,800 [an]. However, Option B keeps monthly spot buying [k]. If the dollar strengthens to $1.25 per euro, the annual bill falls to $280,000, saving $11,200 more than the contract, and buying monthly avoids being locked into one supplier [app]. The trade-off is exposure to sudden reversals, which could add tens of thousands of dollars of cost overnight [an]. Overall, I think Thistledown should choose Option A [eval] because predictable input costs protect the business's narrow roaster margins and support firm pricing with cafe customers; the $11,200 possible extra saving is not worth the risk of a reversal [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne
Option B: spot buying saves more if the dollar strengthens to $1.25
analysis_max_2: Chain from certainty to predictable planning and protected margin
Chain from spot buying to extra saving but exposure to sudden reversals
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($291,200, $280,000, $1.25/$1.45)

scenario_stem:
Alderney Freight is a private limited company founded by the Duarte family, running 28 trucks carrying building materials nationwide. It employs 55 drivers, made $720,000 profit, and 60 shareholders hold 300,000 shares equally.

TransGlobal Freight Plc offers $4,200,000 for all shares, a 10% premium, but the offer expires in 30 days. The family must decide whether to sell and cash in, or reject it and keep managing the private company independently.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'dividend'.
questions.model_answer: A payment made to shareholders from a company's profits as a return on their investment, usually expressed per share and decided by the directors [2].

knowledge_max_2: return on investment / per share / decided by directors

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to the Duarte family of rejecting TransGlobal's offer and remaining a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The family keeps full control and independence [k], continuing to run the 28 trucks and national deliveries as it chooses [app]. Advantage 2: They keep future profits [k], retaining the $720,000 earned last year rather than exchanging it for one lump-sum offer [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to shareholders of rejecting the TransGlobal offer.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Missing a 10% premium [k], so refusing $4,200,000 now means shareholders forgo a guaranteed instant gain [app], with no certainty future profits will match that sum [an]. Disadvantage 2: Competing as a small firm [k], with only 28 trucks against TransGlobal's national network [app], price competition could cut the $720,000 profit and shareholder returns [an].

knowledge_max_2: missing the premium / opportunity cost of rejection
smaller scale versus a national competitor
analysis_max_2: forgone certain gain against uncertain future profits
price pressure erodes profit and returns

questions.question_text: Do you think the Duarte family should sell Alderney Freight to TransGlobal Freight Plc? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An advantage of selling is a guaranteed, premium payout [k], because $4,200,000 including a 10% premium gives immediate, risk-free value to all shareholders [app], freeing the family from fleet and driver risks [an]. A disadvantage is losing control and future upside [k], because Alderney earned $720,000 last year and independence lets the family keep growing it [app], surrendering that potential to TransGlobal [an]. Overall, the family should reject the offer [eval] because $720,000 annual profit and family control suggest lasting value greater than the one-off $4,200,000, although the 30 days deadline means they must decide quickly [eval].

analysis_max_2: independence preserves future growth and profits
evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed payout against control and future earnings

scenario_stem:
Northgate Coach Travel is a private limited company running 24 daily routes between 5 cities: 44 drivers on $34,000 a year and 26 staff. It won an airport shuttle contract needing 8 drivers in 8 weeks.

The director chooses two-round interviews - a 15-minute telephone screening and a 30-minute panel at $140 - or a 20-minute informal chat. Drivers need a 5-year clean driving record. With $1,400, 40 drivers applied; screening took 10 hours.

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of using interviews to select candidates.
questions.model_answer: Interviews let the panel assess communication and customer-service skills face to face, and allow candidates to explain their 5-year clean driving record and route knowledge. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Assesses communication and interpersonal skills directly
Allows candidates to explain experience and driving history

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using two-round interviews to select the 8 airport drivers.
questions.model_answer: Telephone screening cheaply filters out unsuitable applicants [k], so the 15-minute first round can eliminate anyone lacking a valid licence or the 5-year clean record before staff time is spent, narrowing the 40 applicants to a serious shortlist [app]. Structured panel interviews give every shortlisted driver the same 30-minute question set [k], making customer-service answers directly comparable and enabling a fair choice of the strongest 8 within the $1,400 budget [app].

knowledge_max_2: Screening removes unqualified applicants early at low cost
Structured interviews make assessments fair and comparable
application_max_2: 15-minute screening; 40 applicants in 2 weeks; 5-year clean record; valid licence
$140 per shortlisted candidate; $1,400 budget; 30-minute panel interview

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Northgate Coach Travel might face with a single informal chat.
questions.model_answer: Informal chats follow no fixed agenda [k], so each of the 40 applicants may be asked different questions and answers cannot be compared consistently when picking the 8 airport drivers [app], raising the risk of a biased or lucky selection for a safety-critical role [an]. A single chat also reveals little depth [k]. In 20 minutes the owner cannot verify driving records, licences or claim histories before trusting drivers with passengers on 24 daily routes [app], risking poor service that could damage, or even lose, the new airport contract [an].

knowledge_max_2: Informal chats lack standard questions, so comparisons are inconsistent and biased
A short chat cannot verify key facts or test judgement in depth
application_max_2: 40 applicants; 8 drivers; 20 minutes only; no record checks mentioned
24 daily routes; 5-year clean record required; airport contract at stake
analysis_max_2: Inconsistent comparison risks unsafe or unsuitable hires
Unverified selection risks reputational and contract loss

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Coach Travel should use two-round interviews or a single informal chat to select the 8 airport drivers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Two-round interviews cost a little but are far more reliable [k]. The 15-minute telephone screening clears the 40 applicants cheaply, and the $1,400 budget covers panel interviews for up to 10 finalists at $140 each (10 x $140 = $1,400), selecting the strongest 8 on merit [app]. Structured, recorded answers protect the company from unfair-selection claims and let panel members probe customer-service skills properly [an]. However, the 20-minute informal chat is free, fast and might secure drivers within days, which helps if routes must start within 8 weeks [k]. For internal candidates from the 44 existing drivers it could work, but it cannot test new applicants consistently against licence and the 5-year clean-record requirement [app]. Saving $1,400 means little if an unfit driver causes an incident on the 24 daily routes [an]. Overall, the company should run two-round interviews because the airport contract demands verified records and strong customer-service skill, and the process fits the $1,400 budget exactly [eval]. The informal chat could follow the panel decision as a courtesy introduction, but never as the selection method [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Two-round interviews: thorough, fair, verifiable, structured selection
Informal chat: free, fast, but unstructured and unreliable for unknown applicants
application_max_2: 15-minute telephone screening; $140 per finalist; $1,400 budget; 40 applicants
8 drivers; 8-week deadline; 24 daily routes; 5-year clean record; 44 existing drivers
analysis_max_2: Better evidence protects passengers, brand and the new contract
The free/fast appeal is outweighed by the risk of unsafe hires
evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation justified by contract requirements and budget arithmetic
Notes the limited legitimate role of an informal chat (courtesy, not selection)

scenario_stem:
Boreal Outdoor Gear is a private limited company in Country X selling waterproof jackets and boots from 6 branches: 3 northern branches and 3 southern coastal branches, plus an online store. Revenue is $1.6 million, with the north producing 65%.

The north averages 850 mm of rain a year, the south 480 mm and winter peaks. Directors must choose: launch a new $260 jacket nationwide using the online store, or focus only on the 3 northern branches.

questions.question_text: Define 'geographic segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Dividing a market into groups based on geographic factors such as region, climate, country or urban and rural area [2].

knowledge_max_2: groups based on region, climate, country or urban/rural area

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Boreal Outdoor Gear of geographic segmentation.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Products can be matched to local climate [k], heavy-duty jackets suit the 850 mm northern rainfall [app]. Benefit 2: Promotion can be focused where demand is proven [k], targeting the 3 northern branches and their online customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: matches products to local climate and conditions
focuses promotion where demand is proven
application_max_2: heavy-duty jackets for 850 mm northern rainfall

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Boreal Outdoor Gear should be cautious about launching the $260 jacket nationwide.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Southern demand is weaker [k], with only 480 mm of rain, coastal customers buy lighter jackets [app], so unsold $260 stock could pile up in the 3 southern coastal branches [an]. Reason 2: National promotion costs more [k], advertising across all 6 branches and the online store [app], so a weak southern launch would squeeze profit on the $1.6 million revenue [an].

application_max_2: 480 mm of rain means lighter jackets in coastal branches
advertising across 6 branches plus the online store
analysis_max_2: unsold $260 stock piling up in southern branches
weak southern launch squeezes profit on $1.6 million revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Boreal Outdoor Gear should launch the $260 jacket in only the 3 northern branches? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The 3 northern branches deliver 65% of $1.6 million revenue and face 850 mm of rain a year [k], so demand for a premium waterproof jacket is proven there [app], allowing a targeted, low-risk launch with focused promotion [an]. However, a nationwide launch would use all 6 branches plus the online store [k], spreading fixed costs over higher volumes and building national brand awareness [app], though it risks weak sales in the 480 mm south [an]. Overall, Boreal should launch in the 3 northern branches first [eval] because matching product and climate maximises early sell-through [eval], expanding south later if demand proves itself.

knowledge_max_2: northern launch is targeted and low risk
nationwide launch spreads fixed costs and builds awareness
application_max_2: 3 northern branches deliver 65% of $1.6 million revenue
all 6 branches plus the online store in a national launch
analysis_max_2: nationwide risks weak sales in the 480 mm south
evaluation_max_2: weighs targeted regional launch against national awareness
justified recommendation for the northern-only launch first

scenario_stem:
Amberleigh Dairies is a private limited company processing 90,000 litres of milk weekly, supplying 40 shops and 8 cafes. Last year revenue was $2.9 million; three deliveries contained sour milk and 2% of yoghurt pots were underweight.

Its largest customer, a 10-shop chain, is reviewing suppliers. In 5 weeks the owners choose 2 inspectors testing finished batches at packing for $30,000 a year, or quality assurance covering pasteurisation checks, calibrated fillers and hygiene training for $40,000 once.

questions.question_text: Define 'zero defects'.
questions.model_answer: Zero defects is the quality target that every product produced should have no faults, so production is right first time [2].

knowledge_max_2: Producing goods with no faults at all
Being right first time / continuous effort to eliminate errors

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why quality is important to Amberleigh Dairies.
questions.model_answer: First, quality is vital for food safety [k]. Sour milk in three deliveries last month risks making customers ill, which could lead to fines, product seizures and prosecution [app]. Second, quality protects customer relationships and sales [k]. The 10-shop chain, its largest customer, is reviewing suppliers, and repeated faults would push it to switch to a rival dairy [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality protects customer safety / avoids fines
Quality protects customer relationships and sales
application_max_2: Reference to sour milk in three deliveries last month
Reference to 10-shop chain reviewing suppliers / $2.9 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Amberleigh Dairies might face if it relies on inspection of finished batches alone (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, checking finished batches detects faults only after they occur [k]. Pasteurisation errors and underweight filling happen upstream, so inspectors would find but not fix the 2% below-weight pots [app]. Scrapped pots waste milk already processed, raising costs [an]. Second, sampling at packing can miss faulty items in a large batch [k]. With 90,000 litres processed weekly, sour milk could still slip through in untested pots reaching 40 shops and 8 cafes [app]. One case of food poisoning could cost the dairy its 10-shop chain and permanently damage its reputation [an].

knowledge_max_2: Finished-batch checks detect faults late / after value is added
Sampling can miss defective items in a batch
application_max_2: Reference to 2% below-weight pots / pasteurisation upstream
Reference to 90,000 litres weekly / 40 shops and 8 cafes / 10-shop chain risk
analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to scrapped pots to wasted milk and higher costs
Chain from undetected faulty batch to food poisoning to loss of largest customer and reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberleigh Dairies should choose quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $40,000 once and prevents faults at source: pasteurisation temperature and time checks, calibrated filling machines and hygiene training remove the causes of sour milk and below-weight pots [k]. Preventing failures before packing protects the 40 shops, 8 cafes and the 10-shop chain whose review is due within 5 weeks [app]. Over two years Option B costs $40,000 while Option A costs $60,000, so prevention is both safer and cheaper [an]. However, Option A hires 2 inspectors for $30,000 a year and starts immediately, giving early warning on every finished batch as an independent checkpoint [k]. But Option A recurs at $60,000 over two years, detects rather than prevents, and leaves pasteurisation faults unchecked at source [app]. A single missed batch could still end the 10-shop chain relationship, threatening $2.9 million of revenue [an]. Overall, I think Amberleigh Dairies should choose Option B [eval] because it addresses root causes, costs $20,000 less over two years and directly defends the largest customer contract [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option B = quality assurance preventing faults at source
Option A = inspection of finished batches / quality control
application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $40,000 one-off / temperature and time checks / calibrated filling machines / hygiene training
Reference to Option A: $30,000 a year / 2 inspectors / finished batches at packing
analysis_max_2: Chain from prevention to fewer sour batches and below-weight pots to protected contracts
Chain from recurring $30,000 fee to $60,000 two-year cost exceeding $40,000 plus unaddressed root cause
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($30,000 vs $40,000, 10-shop chain, $2.9 million revenue)

scenario_stem:
Pellham Bay Hotel Ltd is a private limited company running a 120-room coastal hotel. It borrowed $1.8 million to fund a new 30-room wing, raising capital employed from $2.0 million to $3.8 million; profit rose from $400,000 to $570,000, yet occupancy averaged just 62% while industry ROCE is 14%.

The managing director must choose between approving Phase 2, a $1.5 million extension adding 24 rooms, or pausing expansion until the wing fills and the original 90 rooms are upgraded.

questions.question_text: Define 'return on capital employed' (ROCE).
questions.model_answer: Return on capital employed measures the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Pellham Bay Hotel earned $570,000 divided by $3.8 million multiplied by 100 = 15.0% this year, down from 20.0% last year ($400,000 divided by $2.0 million). [2]

knowledge_max_2: It shows how efficiently capital invested in the business is turned into profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the managing director should worry about the falling ROCE before Phase 2.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows the return the hotel earns on each dollar of capital employed [k]; it fell from 20% last year ($400,000 divided by $2.0 million) to 15% ($570,000 divided by $3.8 million), even though profit rose, showing the borrowed $1.8 million wing is not yet earning its keep [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the director benchmark the hotel against the industry average of 14% [k]; at 15% Pellham barely beats that benchmark, so adding a further $1.5 million in Phase 2 without higher occupancy risks ROCE slipping below the industry average [app].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE measures the percentage return on capital employed
ROCE can be benchmarked against competitors or industry averages
application_max_2: Applies the 14% industry average and the $1.5 million Phase 2 cost

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE to judge the new wing's performance.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ROCE uses balance-sheet figures and historic carrying values, not what the wing could be worth now [k]; if property values have risen above the $3.8 million carrying value, the 15% ROCE understates the wing's true return [app][an]. Limitation 2: ROCE ignores non-financial measures that explain performance [k]; occupancy of only 62% and the cost of servicing the borrowed money do not appear in the ratio, so Phase 2 must also weigh occupancy trends and borrowing risk [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE uses carrying values that may differ from market values
ROCE ignores non-financial measures and financing details
application_max_2: Applies the $3.8 million carrying value versus possible market appreciation of the wing
Applies the 62% occupancy and the borrowed-money funding of the $1.8 million wing
analysis_max_2: Explains historic carrying values can understate the true return on the wing
Explains occupancy and borrowing costs drive the investment decision beyond the ratio

questions.question_text: Do you think the managing director should approve the Phase 2 extension? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The director could approve Phase 2 because the first wing lifted profit from $400,000 to $570,000 (up $170,000, or 42.5%) and the ROCE of 15% still edges the industry average of 14%, showing the strategy works once the rooms fill [k][app]. Adding 24 rooms for $1.5 million would spread fixed costs over more guests and could lift profit and ROCE if occupancy climbs above 62% [an]. However, occupancy of only 62% means the new 30-room wing is already under-filled; adding a further 24 rooms could push ROCE below 14% and deepen the exposure to borrowed money beyond the $1.8 million already owed [app][an]. Conversely, pausing Phase 2 delays expansion but protects the existing 15% ROCE and cash flow, letting the first wing fill until profit and ROCE recover toward 20% [k][eval]. Overall, the director should not approve Phase 2 yet; she should wait until occupancy exceeds about 75% and the wing proves it can hold an ROCE comfortably above the 14% industry average, because committing a further $1.5 million at 62% occupancy risks diluting shareholder returns further [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Profit rose $400,000 to $570,000 (up 42.5%); ROCE fell 20% to 15% but still beats the 14% industry average
Phase 2 costs $1.5 million for 24 rooms; occupancy is only 62%
application_max_2: Applies the $570,000 profit and 15% ROCE versus the 14% industry average to argue for approval
Applies 62% occupancy and the extra $1.5 million borrowed to argue against
analysis_max_2: Explains spreading fixed costs over more rooms could lift profit and ROCE
Explains adding rooms at 62% occupancy risks pushing ROCE below the industry average
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to defer Phase 2 until occupancy exceeds about 75% and ROCE holds above 14%

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brinemare Fisheries is a private limited company freezing prawns off Country X's north coast with 60 crew and 12 factory staff. It exports 2,400 tonnes a year, 70% to Country W supermarkets, at $4,000 a tonne, earning $9.6 million. A 10% depreciation makes its prawns cheaper abroad.

Country W orders rose 25% to 3,000 tonnes, beyond the 2,400-tonne capacity. Option A invests $250,000 in a second freezer adding 800 tonnes. Option B holds at 2,400 tonnes, quoting new buyers higher prices and later delivery.

questions.question_text: Identify two types of business that benefit when a currency depreciates.
questions.model_answer: Exporting businesses benefit because their goods become cheaper abroad; home businesses competing with imports benefit because imports become dearer [2].

knowledge_max_2: Home businesses competing with imports benefit (imports dearer)

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the depreciation for Brinemare Fisheries.
questions.model_answer: First, depreciation makes Brinemare's prawns cheaper for Country W supermarkets [k]. Orders have already risen by 25% to 3,000 tonnes, worth up to $12 million a year if the extra volume is met [app]. Second, the weaker dollar strengthens Brinemare's competitiveness against Country W prawn suppliers [k]. Country X product now undercuts rivals in Country W shops, so Brinemare can win longer-term listings rather than one-off orders on its 70% export share [app].

application_max_2: Reference to orders up 25% to 3,000 tonnes / $4,000 a tonne / $12 million
Reference to 70% of catch to Country W supermarkets / $9.6 million

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brinemare Fisheries might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the $250,000 investment is a heavy up-front cash outlay [k]. Brinemare earns $9.6 million a year, so $250,000 is about 2.6% of revenue, and it must be financed before the extra 800 tonnes can be handled [app]. If the money is borrowed, interest payments raise costs until the freezer pays back [an]. Second, the extra capacity depends on export demand lasting [k]. The 10% depreciation could be reversed, and a 25% order surge might fade; an 800-tonne freezer running half empty would burden Brinemare with labour and running costs [app]. Idle capacity would eat the profit from core 2,400 tonnes and could leave the firm overstretched [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large up-front investment must be financed
Demand surge may not last if the rate reverses
application_max_2: Reference to 25% order rise / 10% depreciation / 2,400-tonne capacity
analysis_max_2: Chain from investment to finance costs and payback pressure
Chain from rate reversal to idle capacity and wasted running costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Brinemare Fisheries should invest in a second blast freezer (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A invests $250,000 in a second blast freezer adding 800 tonnes of capacity [k]. Demand has already risen 25% to 3,000 tonnes, so the investment would let Brinemare capture up to $12 million a year of prawn sales instead of turning customers away [app]. Extra volume spreads the fixed costs of 60 crew and the factory over more tonnes, improving profit per tonne [an]. However, Option B holds capacity at 2,400 tonnes and manages scarcity with higher prices and later delivery dates [k]. This protects margins on current sales without new finance, and higher prices could lift revenue per tonne from the fixed 2,400 tonnes [app]. The risk is that Country W buyers turned away now sign with rival suppliers and do not return when the capacity arrives [an]. Overall, I think Brinemare should choose Option A [eval] because refusing orders above capacity risks the permanent loss of Country W listings, while $250,000 is recoverable through the margin on extra tonnes; it can phase the investment over two fishing seasons to limit the cash risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: invest $250,000 in 800 tonnes extra capacity
Option B: hold 2,400 tonnes, use higher prices and later deliveries
application_max_2: Reference to 3,000 tonnes vs 2,400 / $12 million potential
Reference to $250,000 / $4,000 a tonne / 70% Country W
analysis_max_2: Chain from new capacity to captured volume and spread fixed costs
Chain from refusing orders to permanent loss of listings
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($250,000, 3,000 vs 2,400 tonnes)

scenario_stem:
Northgate Water Corporation is a public corporation supplying 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses across a coastal region. It employs 600 staff, spent $50,000,000 upgrading pipes, and has prices set by a government regulator.

Private buyers promise $80,000,000 investment over 4 years, cutting leakage 30%, but warn bills may rise. The board and unions favour public ownership, arguing water is essential and should not be run for private profit.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'public corporation'.
questions.model_answer: A business owned and controlled by the government on behalf of the public, usually created by law to provide essential services without the aim of maximising profit [2].

knowledge_max_2: owned and controlled by the government on behalf of the public
provides essential services / not for profit maximisation

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to the region of Northgate remaining in public ownership.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Prices can be kept affordable [k], so the government water regulator can hold down bills for 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses [app]. Advantage 2: Investment focuses on service, not dividends [k], so the $50,000,000 spent on pipes and treatment plants prioritises reliability over shareholder returns [app].

knowledge_max_2: investment for service rather than profit

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to the region of Northgate remaining in public ownership.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Limited access to capital [k], so the promised $80,000,000 private investment across 4 years could not come from public funds [app], slowing the planned 30% leakage cut [an]. Disadvantage 2: Risk of inefficiency [k], because public corporations face weak competitive pressure and bureaucratic delays [app], leaving 600 staff potentially underdeployed and costs high [an].

knowledge_max_2: inefficiency / weak competitive pressure and bureaucracy
analysis_max_2: leakage cut delayed, water loss and costs rise
high costs passed to taxpayers and households

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Water Corporation should remain in public ownership? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An argument for public ownership is fairness of access [k], because a government-owned corporation can price water affordably for 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses [app], preventing the bill rises private buyers have warned about [an]. An argument for sale is faster funding [k], because $80,000,000 of private investment over 4 years could cut leakage by 30% far sooner [app], modernising ageing pipes quicker [an]. Overall, Northgate should remain in public ownership [eval] because water is an essential service and the regulator plus $50,000,000 of recent public upgrades show public delivery can work without private profit motives [eval].

private investment and efficiency argument for sale

scenario_stem:
The Reading Nook is a sole trader bookshop with 7 staff: the owner, 2 managers on $21,500 a year, 3 part-time assistants on $9.50 an hour and 1 weekend cashier. Sales are $780,000 a year, peaking at 900 customers.

The owner weighs a strict person specification requiring 2 years' retail experience and 5 qualifications against a flexible one for book-lovers working 12 Saturdays. Last year 11 of 25 applicants met the strict criteria, taking 4 weeks; advertising cost $240 and April sales fell 8%.

questions.question_text: Identify two qualities a person specification might include.
questions.model_answer: A person specification might include good communication and interpersonal skills, and relevant retail experience or availability on the required days. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Relevant experience, qualifications or availability for the role

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why The Reading Nook should use a person specification before advertising for the replacement assistant.
questions.model_answer: A person specification sets out exactly what the shop needs [k], so the owner can match candidates against a checklist instead of guessing; of the 25 applications last time, she could immediately set aside the 14 who lacked the 2 years' retail experience the shop wanted [app]. A clear specification makes shortlisting fair and consistent [k], so every applicant is judged against the same 5 school qualifications and the Saturday-availability requirement, reducing personal bias in a small independent team [app].

knowledge_max_2: Sets out the exact skills, qualities and qualifications required
Enables fair, consistent comparison and reduces bias when shortlisting
application_max_2: 25 applications last time; 11 of 25 met the strict criteria
5 school qualifications; 2 years' retail experience; Saturday availability

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with using a strict person specification.
questions.model_answer: A strict specification shrinks the pool of applicants [k]. Only 11 of 25 applicants met it last year, and the strict advert took 4 weeks to fill at a cost of $240 in advertising [app]. If the same happens again, April's short-staffed dip, when sales fell 8%, could recur [an]. It also excludes enthusiastic, book-loving applicants [k], who could learn stock knowledge quickly and engage Saturday's 900 customers despite lacking 2 years' experience [app], narrowing the shop's personality and wasting free enthusiasm the community shop thrives on [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shrinks the applicant pool and slows the hiring process
Excludes trainable, enthusiastic people who lack formal experience
application_max_2: 11 of 25 met the strict criteria; 4 weeks to fill; $240 advertising
900 Saturday customers; sales fell 8% in April when short-staffed
analysis_max_2: Repeat vacancy drag risks another 8% April sales fall
Rejecting trainable staff narrows character and service in a community bookshop

questions.question_text: Do you think The Reading Nook should use a strict person specification or a flexible one? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A flexible specification widens the pool and speeds hiring [k]. Dropping the 2-years'-experience rule in favour of Saturday availability, enthusiasm for books and trainability suits $9.50-an-hour staff who can engage the 900 Saturday customers driving $780,000 of annual sales [app]. Faster hiring avoids another April dip like last year's 8% fall and saves a repeat of the $240 advertising outlay [an]. However, the strict specification with 2 years' experience and 5 school qualifications guarantees a baseline of competence, stock knowledge and dependable service [k]. If sales hinge on expert recommendations, an inexperienced hire might underperform and pile more work onto the 2 full-time weekend managers [app]. Strict criteria also cut the owner's workload by pre-filtering the 14 of 25 applicants who failed the requirements last time [an]. Overall, the owner should adopt the flexible specification with a short trial-shift assessment, because the 8% April sales drop showed the real cost of an empty seat and stock can be learned within a month in a bookshop [eval]. If the best applicants are inexperienced, she should choose the one who connects with customers and train them on stock in the first weeks [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Flexible spec widens the pool, speeds hiring and values trainability
Strict spec guarantees baseline competence and reduces screening effort
application_max_2: 2 years' experience rule; only 11 of 25 met it; $240; 4 weeks; April fell 8%
$9.50 an hour; 900 Saturday customers; $780,000 a year; 3 part-time assistants
analysis_max_2: Faster fill avoids revenue loss and re-advertising costs
Risk of weaker service from inexperienced hire vs the saved screening time
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall recommendation (flexible plus brief assessment) with reasoning
Contingency if the shortlist is entirely inexperienced

scenario_stem:
Kettleworth Coffee Co is a private limited company with 7 coffee shops in Country X, serving 4,200 customers weekly at $4.80 average spend. Email members visit 11 times a year, double non-members; repeat visits fell 15% after a mall rival opened.

The manager must choose: a loyalty card with one free drink after 8 stamps, costing $18,000, or $9,500 on customer-service training across 7 shops. The rival has taken an estimated 20% of local lunch trade.

questions.question_text: Identify two ways a business can maintain customer loyalty.
questions.model_answer: Loyalty reward schemes such as stamp cards, and high-quality customer service [2].

knowledge_max_2: loyalty reward schemes such as stamp cards

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kettleworth Coffee Co of maintaining customer loyalty.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Loyal customers give repeat, predictable sales [k], email members visit 11 times a year [app]. Benefit 2: Retaining customers costs less than attracting new ones [k], cheaper than replacing the 20% lunch trade lost to the mall rival [app].

knowledge_max_2: cheaper to retain than attract new customers
application_max_2: email members visiting 11 times a year
20% lunch trade lost to the mall rival

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the loyalty card over staff training as a response to the lost trade.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: It directly rewards repeat visits [k], a free drink after 8 stamps gives 4,200 weekly customers a reason to return [app], quickly rebuilding visit frequency [an]. Advantage 2: It produces usable data [k], stamp redemptions show which of the 7 shops keep loyal customers [app], guiding future promotion spending [an].

application_max_2: free drink after 8 stamps for 4,200 weekly customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Kettleworth Coffee Co should introduce the loyalty card rather than invest in staff training? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The loyalty card costs $18,000 but directly incentivises repeat visits [k] from 4,200 weekly customers spending $4.80 each [app], quickly replacing the 15% fall in repeat visits since March [an]. However, staff training costs just $9,500 and tackles the root cause of service quality [k], improving experience across all 7 shops [app], building loyalty that stamps alone cannot buy, though its effect is slower [an]. Overall, introduce the loyalty card now [eval] because visit frequency must be rebuilt urgently while the mall rival gains ground [eval], adding training in the next quarter.

knowledge_max_2: loyalty card directly incentivises repeat visits
training tackles root cause of service quality
application_max_2: 4,200 weekly customers spending $4.80 each; 15% fall since March

training builds deeper loyalty across all 7 shops but slower
