scenario_stem:
Osprey Electronics is a private limited company assembling smart-home control panels. It made 24,000 units at $250 each for $6 million; bench tests show 7% fail, costing $180,000 yearly in rework.

Warranty claims rise, and a developer wants 8,000 panels but asks for a defect-reduction plan. In six weeks the owners add tester overtime for $25,000 yearly, or adopt Total Quality Management over 12 months with cross-functional teams, a suggestion scheme and a supplier quality programme, costing $85,000.

questions.question_text: Identify two costs a business might incur to improve quality.
questions.model_answer: Installing inspection and testing equipment is one cost of improving quality [1]. Training workers to check their own work at each stage is another cost [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Testing or inspection equipment / laboratory fees
Training costs for staff on quality checks

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why reducing the failure rate matters to Osprey Electronics.
questions.model_answer: First, a lower failure rate cuts rework costs [k]. Failures already cost $180,000 a year, so fixing processes would release funds for wages and materials [app]. Second, fewer defects build customer trust and win orders [k]. The developer weighing an 8,000-panel order, worth $2 million at $250 each, will favour a supplier with a credible defect-reduction plan [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower defects cut rework / waste costs
Lower defects build trust and help win orders
application_max_2: Reference to $180,000 a year rework cost
Reference to developer's 8,000-panel order / $250 per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of adopting Total Quality Management (Option B) at Osprey Electronics.
questions.model_answer: First, TQM prevents defects at source by making everyone responsible for quality [k]. Cross-functional teams covering assembly, testing and dispatch would find why 7% of units fail before panels are built [app]. Eliminating root causes would shrink the $180,000 rework bill and free capacity for new orders [an]. Second, TQM extends into the supply chain [k]. The supplier quality programme audits bought-in components, stopping faulty inputs reaching the test bench [app]. Fewer incoming faults raise first-pass test rates and strengthen the bid for the 8,000-panel order [an].

knowledge_max_2: TQM prevents defects at source / all employees responsible
TQM extends quality into supplier relationships
application_max_2: Reference to cross-functional teams / 7% unit failures / suggestion scheme
Reference to supplier quality programme / 8,000-panel order
analysis_max_2: Chain from root-cause elimination to lower rework bill to freed capacity and orders
Chain from supplier audits to fewer incoming faults to higher first-pass pass rates and contract wins

questions.question_text: Do you think Osprey Electronics should adopt Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $85,000 over 12 months, more than the $25,000 a year of Option A, but it prevents defects at source through cross-functional teams, a suggestion scheme and supplier checks [k]. The 7% failure rate and $180,000 rework cost both point to process faults, and only TQM removes those causes rather than managing a backlog [app]. Eliminating rework quickly offsets the $85,000 programme and makes the 8,000-panel, $2 million developer order far more secure [an]. However, Option A keeps end-of-line control with overtime at $25,000 a year, cheaper immediately and clears the inspection backlog within weeks [k]. But a year of $25,000 still leaves the 7% fail rate untouched, the $180,000 rework bill standing and customer confidence flat [app]. Clearing a backlog is not the same as curing the process disease, and the developer wants evidence of reduction that inspection alone does not provide [an]. Overall, I think Osprey Electronics should adopt Option B [eval], with Option A only as a temporary supplement; the $85,000 buys prevention, the $2 million contract and falling rework costs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: TQM = prevention across the whole business incl. suppliers
Quality control / inspection = detects faults at the end / short-run relief
application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $85,000 / 12 months / cross-functional teams / supplier quality programme
Reference to Option A: $25,000 a year / tester overtime / inspection backlog / 7% failures
analysis_max_2: Chain from root-cause prevention to lower rework to protected developer contract ($2 million)
Chain from inspection-only to unchanged 7% failure and $180,000 rework to weak customer confidence
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($25,000 vs $85,000, 7% failures, $180,000 rework, 8,000 panels)

scenario_stem:
Farlow Wholesale Foods Ltd is a private limited company supplying chilled foods to shops. At 30 June, current assets were $1,250,000, comprising inventories $980,000, trade receivables $180,000 and cash $90,000; current liabilities were $260,000. A competitor's acid test ratio is 1.6:1.

A supermarket chain offers a $400,000-a-year contract at a 17% gross margin if Farlow grants 60-day credit terms instead of 30 days. Debtors would rise about $130,000; Samira must decide before it starts in September.

questions.question_text: Calculate the acid test ratio for Farlow Wholesale Foods. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities using only its quick assets, calculated as (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities; Farlow Wholesale Foods has ($1,250,000 minus $980,000) divided by $260,000 = $270,000 divided by $260,000, about 1.04:1, below the competitor's 1.6:1. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio = (current assets - inventories) / current liabilities
Expressing the answer as a ratio such as about 1.04:1

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the acid test ratio matters for the 60-day credit offer.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the acid test ratio shows whether Farlow can meet current liabilities without selling inventories [k]; excluding the $980,000 of inventories, quick assets are $270,000 ($180,000 receivables plus $90,000 cash) against $260,000 of current liabilities, giving about 1.04:1, well below the competitor's 1.6:1 [app]. Reason 2: the acid test ratio reveals how tight cash is before granting longer credit [k]; granting 60-day terms on the $400,000 contract would add about $130,000 of debtors at any time, lifting the paper ratio but stranding the cash Farlow needs to pay its own suppliers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio shows liquidity without relying on inventory sales
Acid test ratio highlights how much cash is tied up in receivables
application_max_2: Applies the $270,000 quick assets / $260,000 liabilities = about 1.04:1 versus competitor's 1.6:1
Applies the $130,000 extra debtors on 60-day terms and the $90,000 cash

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of the acid test ratio for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the acid test ratio treats all receivables as equally collectable [k]; the national supermarket chain is almost certainly a reliable payer, so discounting its $130,000 from quick assets may understate Farlow's true liquidity under the new 60-day terms [app][an]. Limitation 2: the acid test ratio is a snapshot and ignores the timing and profit impact of the contract [k]; the $400,000 contract earns about $68,000 of annual gross profit at 17% and cash would arrive within 60 to 90 days, so the ratio alone cannot capture whether the deal strengthens the business [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio treats all receivables as equal, ignoring creditworthiness
Acid test ratio is a snapshot ignoring timing and profit effects
application_max_2: Applies the $130,000 new supermarket debtors against the reliable-payer assumption
Applies the $400,000 contract at 17% gross profit margin (about $68,000) and 60 to 90 day collection
analysis_max_2: Explains reliable supermarket debts make the ratio understate true liquidity
Explains the snapshot cannot weigh the profit and timing benefits of the contract

questions.question_text: Do you think Samira should accept the supermarket contract on 60-day terms? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Samira could accept because the $400,000 annual contract earns about $68,000 of gross profit at 17%, and 60-day terms are standard for supermarket supply deals, strengthening Farlow's credibility with a national chain [k][app]. Even with debtors rising by about $130,000, the acid test ratio would move from 1.04:1 to about 1.54:1, close to the competitor's 1.6:1, and the supermarket's payment record makes collection risk low [an]. However, cash of only $90,000 against $260,000 of current liabilities means Farlow relies on quick collection; if the supermarket pays late or queries invoices, suppliers pressing for cash could strain the business despite the profitable contract [app][an]. Conversely, declining keeps the 30-day terms and simple liquidity, but it forfeits $400,000 of revenue and the $68,000 gross profit, which would likely go to a rival supplier [k][eval]. Overall, Samira should accept the contract but negotiate a shorter first cycle (for example 45 days for the opening quarter) or a deposit as a condition, because the $68,000 gross profit outweighs the timing cost if collection risk is controlled up front [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Contract $400,000 at 17% gross profit margin = about $68,000 gross profit; 60-day vs 30-day terms
Acid test would rise from 1.04:1 to about 1.54:1 with $130,000 extra debtors; competitor 1.6:1
application_max_2: Applies the $68,000 gross profit and 1.54:1 projected acid test to argue for acceptance
Applies the $90,000 cash and $260,000 current liabilities to argue for caution
analysis_max_2: Explains supermarket reliability makes collection risk low and the ratio stays near competitor level
Explains late payment or invoice queries could strain suppliers despite profitability
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to accept with negotiated 45-day opening cycle or deposit to control collection risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Alderney Motors is a private limited company selling cars in Country X's capital city. It imports 18 cars a month from Country W at €26,000 each. Appreciation from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro cuts each car's cost from $37,700 to $33,800, saving $3,900 a car or $842,400 a year.

Prices must be set. Option A cuts prices by $2,000 per car to attract buyers and raise sales. Option B holds prices and keeps the extra $70,200 a month as profit to expand the service department.

questions.question_text: State two ways consumers benefit when their country's currency appreciates.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods become cheaper in home-currency terms; foreign holidays and imported products become more affordable [2].

knowledge_max_2: Foreign travel and imported products become more affordable

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Alderney Motors.
questions.model_answer: First, each imported car costs $3,900 less [k]. The monthly saving on 18 cars is $70,200, equal to $842,400 a year at the new rate [app]. Second, Alderney can choose how to use the saving [k]. A modest price cut of $2,000 a car would still leave most of the $3,900 saving intact while winning price-sensitive buyers from rival showrooms [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower import costs in home currency
Flexibility to cut prices or keep margin
application_max_2: Reference to $3,900 a car / $70,200 a month / $842,400

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Alderney Motors might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the price cut gives back $36,000 a month of the $70,200 saving immediately [k]. The margin per car falls from $3,900 to $1,900, so Alderney keeps only half the windfall and volumes may not rise enough to compensate [app]. Weaker margins squeeze the cash available for staff, stock and the showroom, risking losses if sales stay flat [an]. Second, rival dealers will also see the appreciation lift their margins [k]. If they match a $2,000 cut, no showroom gains share, and Alderney's prices fall with no extra cars sold [app]. Market-wide discounting lowers revenue across the whole market and trains customers to wait for promotions rather than buy [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices sacrifices margin without guaranteed volume
Rivals likely to match the cut
application_max_2: Reference to $2,000 / $36,000 of the $70,200 / $1,900 remaining margin
Reference to 18 cars / rival showrooms / the capital city
analysis_max_2: Chain from margin sacrifice to weaker cash flow if volumes stay flat
Chain from price matching to market-wide discounting and customers waiting for deals

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderney Motors should cut showroom prices by $2,000 per car (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts showroom prices by $2,000 a car to win buyers [k]. Because import costs fell to $33,800 from $37,700, this still leaves $1,900 of extra margin per car, and lower sticker prices should increase footfall and sales of the 18-car monthly quota [app]. More volume spreads overheads such as showroom staff and service bays, improving overall profit if sales respond [an]. However, Option B keeps prices unchanged and keeps the extra $70,200 a month [k]. Alderney banks a full $842,400 a year with zero risk to margin, which can expand the service department and deepen customer relationships after the sale [app]. The danger is that price-sensitive buyers drift to rivals who advertise lower prices, costing Alderney volume and long-term service work [an]. Overall, I think Alderney should choose Option B [eval] because the $70,200 monthly saving is certain while the volume gain from a $2,000 cut is not guaranteed; funding the service department strengthens the whole business, and selective promotions can target fence-sitters without a blanket cut [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut prices by $2,000 to boost volume
Option B: hold prices and keep $70,200 a month
application_max_2: Reference to $842,400 a year / 18 cars / service department
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to uncertain volume response and spread overheads
Chain from held prices to certain $842,400 margin funding service expansion
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($2,000, $70,200, $842,400)

scenario_stem:
Eastvale City Council runs refuse collection as a municipal service, employing 120 council workers to collect waste from 95,000 households weekly. It cost taxpayers $9,600,000 last year and missed 8% of collections during a staff shortage.

CleanRight Ltd offers to run it for $8,400,000 yearly with performance targets and fines, saving $1,200,000. The council must decide by December, weighing savings against job losses, lower wages and reduced local accountability.

questions.question_text: Identify two types of business organisation in the public sector.
questions.model_answer: Public corporations [1]; municipal services run by local authorities [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Eastvale residents of keeping refuse collection as a municipal service.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Direct accountability to residents [k], because the council must answer to voters at elections for the service used by 95,000 households [app]. Advantage 2: Local control of standards and jobs [k], so the 120 council workers can be directed to fix the 8% missed collections quickly [app].

knowledge_max_2: local control of standards and employment

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Eastvale City Council of keeping refuse collection in-house.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Higher cost to taxpayers [k], because $9,600,000 a year is $1,200,000 more than CleanRight's $8,400,000 offer [app], money unavailable for roads and parks [an]. Disadvantage 2: Capacity and staffing problems [k], shown by 8% missed collections during the staff shortage [app], damaging residents' health and satisfaction [an].

analysis_max_2: less money available for other council services

questions.question_text: Do you think Eastvale City Council should contract refuse collection to CleanRight Ltd? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An advantage of contracting out is the clear saving [k], because the $1,200,000 a year difference between $9,600,000 and $8,400,000 frees money for other services [app], and strict performance targets with fines should end missed collections [an]. A disadvantage is the loss of local control [k], because CleanRight is a private firm whose main aim is profit [app], risking job cuts, lower wages and weaker accountability to 95,000 households [an]. Overall, the council should contract to CleanRight [eval] because the $1,200,000 annual saving plus penalty-backed targets directly fix the 8% missed collections, provided the contract protects the 120 workers and service levels [eval].

knowledge_max_2: loss of local control / private profit motive
analysis_max_2: targets and fines should restore reliable collections
risk of job losses and weaker accountability
evaluation_max_2: weighs savings and performance targets against accountability and job risks

scenario_stem:
Kestrel Security Services is a private limited company supplying officers, employing 120: 80 full-time on $28,500 and 40 part-time. After 3 new contracts it needs 10 more officers in 8 weeks.

New duties - night patrols, radios and incident reports - are absent from last year's documents. Job analysis took 60 hours. The manager must update the job description. Advertising is $220 online and $500 in print; the last advert drew 75 enquiries; the budget is $1,200.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'job analysis'.
questions.model_answer: Job analysis is the process of studying a job in detail to identify the tasks, duties and responsibilities involved and the skills and qualifications required to perform it. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Studying the job in detail: tasks, duties and responsibilities
Identifying the skills and qualifications needed to perform it

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of carrying out a fresh job analysis before recruiting the 10 officers.
questions.model_answer: A job analysis reveals what the new contracts actually require [k]. The duties now include night car-park patrols, radio operation and incident reports, which are absent from the old documents, so the analysis defines the real job rather than a stale version [app]. It also produces an accurate job description and person specification [k], so the firm's 75 recent enquiries can be screened against the current demands before interviews are booked [app].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the actual, current duties of the job
Forms the basis of an accurate job description and person specification
application_max_2: Night car-park patrols; radio equipment; incident reports; duties absent from old documents
3 new contracts; 75 enquiries received; 10 officers needed within 8 weeks

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Kestrel Security Services would face if it re-used the old job description.
questions.model_answer: The old job description omits the new night duties [k], so selected officers may arrive unprepared for car-park patrols, radios and incident reporting across the 3 new contracts and 40 additional locations [app], risking complaints, client dissatisfaction and even loss of the contracts [an]. Re-using stale documents also wastes advertising spend [k]. Money spent on the $220 online and $500 print adverts would attract applicants unsuitable for night patrols, forcing a re-advertisement within the 8-week window [app] and doubling selection costs beyond the $1,200 budget [an].

knowledge_max_2: A stale job description misdescribes the job being recruited for
Attracts unsuitable applicants and wastes recruitment spend
application_max_2: Old documents miss patrols, radios and incident reports; 3 new contracts; 40 locations
analysis_max_2: Mismatched hires damage client relations and risk contract loss
Re-advertising and duplicate selection breach budget and deadline

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrel Security Services should carry out a fresh job analysis or re-use last year's job description and person specification? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A fresh job analysis is essential because the contracts changed [k]. The new duties (night car-park patrols, radio operation and incident reports across 3 contracts and 40 extra store locations) differ fundamentally from last year's role, so without analysis the job description would mislead both the 75 enquiries and the interview panel [app]. A small share of the $1,200 budget spent now prevents repeat hiring, client disputes and lost contracts later [an]. However, a fresh job analysis last time took 60 hours of staff time [k], time that could have covered billable patrols or officer training, and re-using old documents is free and fast [app]. If last year's specification were merely edited and re-published for $220 online, the 10 officers could be hired inside the 8-week window with minimal disruption [an]. Overall, the firm should carry out a fresh job analysis because the risk of appointing officers unsuited to night patrols and incident reporting far outweighs 60 staff-hours, and any cost gap can be closed by choosing the $220 online advert over print [eval]. Re-using old documents would be defensible only if the new contracts were identical to last year's, which they are not [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Fresh analysis: accuracy, correct person specification, lower mis-hire risk
Re-use: free and fast, but risky when the role has changed
application_max_2: New duties absent from old documents; 75 enquiries; $1,200 budget; $220 online
60 staff-hours cost; 8-week deadline; 3 new contracts; 120 officers
analysis_max_2: Prevents mismatched hiring, complaints and contract loss
Staff-time cost weighed against error cost; analysis still favourable
evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation justified by changed duties and risk balance
Notes the narrow condition under which re-use would be defensible

scenario_stem:
Maren Apparel is a women's clothing partnership with 9 shops in Country X and $3.1 million revenue. Over 2 years formal wear sales fell 25%, while casual and homewear reached 58% as more women work from home; online sales are just 12%.

Rivals offer delivery within 48 hours. Owners must choose: commission focus groups of 10 customers in each of 3 cities, or use internal records of 2 years' sales to steer the range towards casual wear now.

questions.question_text: State two reasons why consumer spending patterns change.
questions.model_answer: Changes in consumer incomes, and changes in tastes and lifestyles [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Maren Apparel could respond to changing consumer spending patterns.
questions.model_answer: Response 1: Steer the range towards casual wear [k], which already accounts for 58% of sales [app]. Response 2: Invest in online selling [k], lifting the 12% of sales currently generated by its online store [app].

knowledge_max_2: adapt the product range to consumer demand
application_max_2: online store only generating 12% of sales

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Maren Apparel of using focus groups to understand changing spending patterns.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Focus groups give detailed qualitative insight [k] into why formal office wear fell by 25% over 2 years [app], so the owners design lines customers genuinely want [an]. Benefit 2: They test reactions to new ranges before committing [k], 10 customers in each of 3 cities discussing casual designs [app], reducing unsold stock across the 9 shops [an].

10 customers in each of 3 cities discussing casual designs

reduces unsold stock across the 9 shops

questions.model_answer: Focus groups with 10 customers in each of 3 cities would reveal why tastes shifted [k], explaining the motivations behind the 58% casual-wear share that sales figures alone cannot show [app], helping the owners choose winning styles [an]. However, internal records are free and immediate [k], 2 years of sales by line across the 9 shops [app], pinpointing exactly which lines to drop and which to expand this season [an]. Overall, rely on internal records first [eval] because the evidence already points clearly to casual wear [eval], commissioning focus groups afterwards to refine the relaunched range.

scenario_stem:
Thornhill Vineyards is a family-owned partnership wine estate, producing 140,000 bottles from 60 hectares with 30 staff. Wines sell at $14 each for $1.96 million; inconsistent fermentation rejects 6% at bottling.

Two vintages scored poorly; a supermarket chain offers an own-label listing worth $800,000 yearly, conditional on quality and an external audit. In 9 weeks the family hires a $45,000 quality manager for end-of-line quality control, or adopts winery-wide quality assurance with TQM principles for $70,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'repeat business'.
questions.model_answer: Repeat business is when customers return to buy from the same business again, usually driven by satisfaction with the quality and service received [2].

knowledge_max_2: Customers return to buy from the same business again
Driven by satisfaction with quality and service

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why consistent quality is important for the supermarket listing at Thornhill Vineyards.
questions.model_answer: First, the supermarket listing would provide reliable, high-volume sales [k]. It is worth $800,000 a year, nearly a 41% uplift on the $1.96 million revenue, and guarantees a route to market for part of the 140,000 bottles [app]. Second, consistent quality protects reputation [k]. Two poorly scored vintages and a 6% rejection rate show how quickly standards can slip, risking withdrawal of the listing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Consistent quality secures large, stable sales contracts
Consistent quality protects reputation and avoids losing listings
application_max_2: Reference to $800,000 a year own-label listing / $1.96 million revenue
Reference to 6% rejected at bottling / poorly scored vintages

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of relying on end-of-line quality control at bottling only (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, bottling-stage checks detect faults after they have been created [k]. Fermentation and vineyard problems arise months earlier, so rejecting faulty bottles at the end still wastes wine, glass and labour [app]. 6% of 140,000 bottles is 8,400 bottles lost every year [an]. Second, a single quality manager is a single point of failure [k]. One hire cannot continuously cover vineyard, cellar and bottling, so errors outside those hours go unchecked [app]. Poor processes persist, critic scores stay low and the supermarket may cancel the $800,000 own-label deal [an].

knowledge_max_2: End-of-line control detects faults after they occur / after value added
Reliance on one manager creates a single point of failure / limited coverage
application_max_2: Reference to fermentation / vine-to-bottle stages / 6% rejection / 140,000 bottles
Reference to $800,000 own-label listing / critics / end-of-line quality control
analysis_max_2: Chain from late rejection to 8,400 wasted bottles a year to lost revenue and profit
Chain from incomplete coverage to unchecked faults to poor critic scores and lost listing

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornhill Vineyards should implement quality assurance and Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $70,000 once and rebuilds quality from vine to bottle, with procedures, staff training and lab checks at each stage, so fermentation faults are caught before bottling [k]. This directly targets the 6% rejection rate, 8,400 bottles a year, and gives the supermarket an audit-ready record for the $800,000 own-label listing [app]. Preventing rejects also saves wine, bottles and labour, protecting the $1.96 million revenue [an]. However, Option A hires a quality manager for $45,000 a year, $90,000 over two years, to run end-of-line checks at bottling and is simple to start within 9 weeks [k]. But it only filters faulty bottles after months of wasted work, leaves fermentation uncontrolled and does nothing for critic confidence [app]. The listing depends on an annual external audit, which a bottling-only filter cannot support [an]. Overall, I think Thornhill Vineyards should choose Option B [eval] because it removes the causes of rejects, satisfies the audit and costs less than two years of Option A [eval].

Option A = end-of-line quality control / filtering at bottling

Reference to Option A: $45,000 a year / end-of-line checks / 9 weeks / critic scores

scenario_stem:
Fallowfield & Dean Licensed Grocers Ltd is a private limited company running 2 convenience stores. Year to 30 April: revenue $800,000, gross profit $304,000, profit $72,000; capital employed $960,000; current assets $288,000, including inventories $128,000, against current liabilities $160,000.

The cousins want a $350,000 loan at 9% interest to refit both stores and add a chilled food counter, rather than refitting over 3 years from retained profit. Their bank requires ratio analysis before its December lending committee.

questions.question_text: Identify two uses of ratio analysis.
questions.model_answer: Two uses of ratio analysis are firstly to compare a business's performance over time and against competitors, and secondly to support applications for finance such as bank loans by showing lenders the business's profitability and liquidity. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis compares performance over time or against competitors
Ratio analysis supports decisions and finance applications by quantifying profitability and liquidity

questions.question_text: Explain two ways ratio analysis can support the bank loan application.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: ratio analysis gives the bank a standardised view of creditworthiness [k]; the current ratio of 1.8:1 ($288,000 divided by $160,000) and an acid test ratio of 1.0:1 show the stores can cover short-term debts, supporting the $350,000 loan request [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis shows the owners understand their business numbers [k]; a gross profit margin of 38.0% ($304,000 divided by $800,000) and a 7.5% ROCE ($72,000 divided by $960,000) give the bank evidence the stores are profitable and professionally run [app].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis provides standardised evidence of creditworthiness
Ratio analysis demonstrates the owners understand their business performance
application_max_2: Applies the 1.8:1 current ratio and 1.0:1 acid test ratio ($288,000, $128,000, $160,000)
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 7.5% ROCE ($304,000 / $800,000; $72,000 / $960,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis the cousins should consider.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ratio analysis is based on historic accounts and cannot prove the refit will pay back [k]; a 9.0% profit margin ($72,000 divided by $800,000) would fall to about 5.1% after paying $31,500 of interest on the $350,000 loan (leaving $40,500 of profit), squeezing margins exactly when the stores need cash for the chilled counter [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors and context [k]; neither the 38.0% gross profit margin nor the 1.8:1 current ratio captures customer loyalty, staffing stability or whether a chilled counter would actually lift sales, so the business plan matters as much as the figures [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis is historic and cannot prove future returns on investment
Ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors such as customers and staff
application_max_2: Applies the 9.0% margin falling to about 5.1% after $31,500 interest ($40,500 profit)
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 1.8:1 current ratio ignoring loyalty and the chilled counter
analysis_max_2: Explains interest costs sharply reduce final profit margin after borrowing
Explains figures alone cannot capture customer demand for the chilled counter

questions.question_text: Do you think the cousins should take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The cousins could take the loan because refitting both stores now, rather than over 3 years from retained profit, defends the 38.0% gross profit margin ($304,000) against rivals adding chilled counters and captures sales sooner [k][app]. Profit of $72,000 (9.0% margin) barely covers the $31,500 interest, leaving $40,500 (5.1%), so the refit must generate meaningful new sales to be worthwhile [an]. However, the acid test ratio of 1.0:1 leaves no slack for trading setbacks, and capital employed would rise to $1,310,000, cutting ROCE to about 3.1% ($40,500 divided by $1,310,000) unless profits recover quickly [app][an]. Conversely, refitting slowly from retained profit avoids interest entirely and keeps the 1.0:1 acid test intact, but it cedes competitive advantage for 3 years and may never deliver the chilled food counter at all [k][eval]. Overall, the cousins should take the loan only if the bank offers a grace period before full repayments begin, because a 5.1% post-interest margin leaves almost no room for error; otherwise they should refit from retained profit and accept the slower refit as the safer route [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Loan $350,000 at 9% = $31,500 interest; post-interest profit $40,500 (5.1% margin)
ROCE falls to about 3.1% on $1,310,000 capital employed; acid test 1.0:1

Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin defence and acid test 1.0:1 to argue for slow refit

evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to a bank grace period, otherwise slower retained-profit refit

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Tarnmoor Medical Supplies is a private limited company making surgical gloves for hospitals and clinics in Country X. It exports 500,000 boxes a year to Country W, worth about €9 million, 70% of revenue. The rate has swung between $1.30 and $1.45 per euro over 12 months.

A deal must be signed before the tender. Option A fixes prices at €18 a box for 12 months, priced around $1.40 per euro. Option B re-quotes quarterly at spot rates, shifting risk to Country W buyers.

questions.question_text: Outline why many businesses prefer exchange rates to remain stable.
questions.model_answer: Stable rates let businesses plan and budget with confidence because the home-currency value of export receipts and import costs does not keep changing [2].

knowledge_max_2: No unexpected shifts in export revenue or import costs

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tarnmoor Medical Supplies is worried about exchange-rate swings.
questions.model_answer: First, most of Tarnmoor's revenue comes from Country W exports [k]. With €9 million, 70% of revenue, invoiced in euros, a swing from $1.45 to $1.30 cuts export income from $13.05 million to $11.7 million, a loss of $1.35 million [app]. Second, the swing makes it hard to set prices and budgets [k]. Its costs in Country X, such as wages and materials, stay in dollars, so a $1.35 million revenue swing lands straight on profit, making the next year's plan unreliable [app].

knowledge_max_2: Most revenue is in foreign currency
Dollar costs against euro revenue create planning uncertainty
application_max_2: Reference to €9 million / 70% of revenue / $1.30 vs $1.45
Reference to 500,000 boxes / $13.05 million vs $11.7 million / $1.35 million swing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Tarnmoor Medical Supplies might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, quarterly re-quoting pushes risk onto Country W buyers but burdens them with uncertainty [k]. Buyers signing hospital supply contracts may switch to rivals offering fixed prices, especially as the rate swung a 15-cent range within a year [app]. Losing tendered contracts would damage Tarnmoor's market share precisely when it needs stable export income [an]. Second, re-quoting every quarter creates administrative work and disputes [k]. Four price lists a year, credit notes and contract changes would strain the small finance team, and buyers may query invoices whenever the $1.30 to $1.45 band bites [app]. Time spent renegotiating diverts management from production, and delayed or disputed payments would squeeze working capital while orders ship [an].

knowledge_max_2: Customers dislike unpredictable prices / risk of losing contracts
Admin burden and disputes from frequent re-quoting
application_max_2: Reference to quarterly re-quotes / Option B / Country W buyers
Reference to $1.30 to $1.45 / 500,000 boxes / hospital supply contracts
analysis_max_2: Chain from quarterly price changes to lost fixed-price tenders and export share
Chain from repeated renegotiation to admin strain and disputed payments

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarnmoor Medical Supplies should sign the 12-month fixed-price contract (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A fixes the euro export price at €18 a box under a 12-month contract built around $1.40 per euro [k]. Hospitals get one stable price all year, which protects Tarnmoor's 500,000-box order book and keeps its position against rivals in Country W [app]. Stable pricing encourages buyers to commit annual volumes rather than shop around every quarter, supporting reliable cash flow [an]. However, Option B re-quotes every quarter at the spot rate and pushes risk onto buyers [k]. If the dollar rises to $1.45, Tarnmoor would collect $13.05 million for the same €9 million, keeping $1.35 million more than at $1.30 [app]. But buyers may resist and demand fixed prices, so this theoretical gain may rarely be realised [an]. Overall, I think Tarnmoor should choose Option A [eval] because certainty wins long-term medical contracts and protects 70% of its revenue; $1.40 sits comfortably inside the $1.30-$1.45 band, so the deal is fair to both sides across a full year [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 12-month fixed price at €18, built around $1.40
Option B: quarterly spot re-quotes, risk passed to buyers
application_max_2: Reference to 500,000 boxes / €9 million / 70% of revenue
Reference to $1.30-$1.45 band / $13.05 million vs $11.7 million / $1.35 million
analysis_max_2: Chain from stable pricing to committed buyers and steady cash flow
Chain from quarterly re-quoting to buyer resistance and forgone certain volume
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures (€18, $1.40, $1.30/$1.45)

scenario_stem:
Meridian Can Works is a private limited company running an automated aluminium can plant. It employs 18 technicians, output is valued at $4.6 million, and capital employed is $6.9 million, mostly in imported pressing lines.

It considers investing $900,000 of retained profit in a second line. Bidding for a government supply contract, the board debates measuring size by headcount, output or capital, since rival Harbor Can & Bottle Co employs 120 workers at a labour-intensive plant.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital employed'.
questions.model_answer: Capital employed is the total long-term finance invested in a business to fund its operations and assets [2].

knowledge_max_2: total long-term finance invested in the business
non-current assets plus working capital (total assets minus current liabilities)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using number of employees to measure the size of Meridian Can Works.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Automation distorts the figure [k], as 18 technicians run lines that produce $4.6 million of cans while a 120-worker rival sells fewer cans [app]. Reason 2: It ignores asset intensity [k], because Meridian's $6.9 million of capital employed is invested in pressing lines rather than wages [app].

knowledge_max_2: employee count ignores asset or output scale

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using value of output to measure the size of Meridian Can Works.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Value of output ignores how the figure is achieved [k], as producing $4.6 million of cans came from costly automated lines funded by $6.9 million of capital employed [app], which inflates apparent size compared with labour-intensive rivals [an]. Problem 2: Output values can change with prices and stocks [k], so a rise or fall in the $4.6 million figure may reflect can price movements rather than more cans being made [app], giving an unreliable basis for comparing size with Harbor Can & Bottle Co [an].

knowledge_max_2: output value ignores asset input/method of production
output value can be distorted by price changes and stock movements
analysis_max_2: inflates apparent size relative to labour-intensive rivals
gives unreliable comparison over time or between firms

questions.question_text: Do you think Meridian Can Works should invest $900,000 in a second automated production line or continue operating at its current scale? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing $900,000 would double capacity [k] and allow Meridian to convert retained profit into more automated pressing lines [app], spreading fixed costs over more cans and raising long-term profit [an]. However, the rival Harbor Can & Bottle Co employs 120 workers and sells fewer cans at lower margins [k], showing that growth is no guarantee of sales [app], and a second line could leave the firm with surplus output it cannot sell, draining cash [an]. Overall, the investment is worthwhile because the firm can fund it from retained profit without new debt [eval], and doubling automated capacity is the fastest route to winning the government supply contract that would secure steady orders [eval].

knowledge_max_2: growth increases capacity/output and spreads fixed costs
expansion carries risk if demand does not materialise
analysis_max_2: spreads fixed costs and raises long-term profit
risk of surplus output/cash drain if sales lag
evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion benefits against demand and cash-flow risk, using retained profit and the government contract as the deciding factor

scenario_stem:
Harbourview Hotels Group is a private limited company operating 4 coastal resort hotels with 210 staff, including 36 housekeeping supervisors. Complaints rose from 42 to 78 after 2 housekeepers left, and staffing is 12% below budget.

The HR manager wants to dismiss 3 supervisors with the most complaints; others want support. The board chooses between dismissal or a 6-week retraining programme costing $18,000. Dismissal risks unfair claims, while retraining diverts cash from a $240,000 refurbishment loan.

questions.question_text: Define 'dismissal'.
questions.model_answer: When an employer terminates an employee's contract of employment, usually because of misconduct or poor performance [2].

knowledge_max_2: employer terminates the contract of employment
usually because of misconduct or poor performance / breach of contract

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Harbourview Hotels Group might choose to dismiss the 3 supervisors.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Removing the 3 supervisors whose teams receive the most complaints should lift room cleanliness standards quickly [k], improving guest satisfaction across the 4 hotels during peak season [app]. Reason 2: Dismissal signals that poor performance is not tolerated [k], which could motivate the remaining 207 staff and help reverse the rise to 78 complaints a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: motivates remaining staff / signals standards expected

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Harbourview Hotels Group could face if it dismisses the 3 supervisors.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Unfair dismissal claims [k] could follow if the 3 supervisors are dismissed without proper warnings or a hearing, and a tribunal award would hit cash at the same time as the $240,000 refurbishment loan [app], reducing funds available for improving guest facilities [an]. Problem 2: Losing experienced supervisors [k] stretches the remaining supervision team when staffing is already 12% below budget [app], so workloads rise and complaints may stay well above 42 per year [an].

knowledge_max_2: risk of unfair dismissal claims / tribunal costs
loss of experienced staff / recruitment and training costs
analysis_max_2: heavier workloads / complaints may remain high

questions.question_text: Do you think Harbourview Hotels Group should dismiss the 3 supervisors rather than retrain them? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Keeping the 3 supervisors and funding the 6-week retraining programme treats the underlying cause [k], because staffing is already 12% below budget and replacement recruitment across the 4 hotels would be costly and disruptive [app]. However, if complaints rose from 42 to 78 per year due to weak supervision, retaining the supervisors may simply let the problem grow [k], and the $18,000 cost diverts cash alongside the $240,000 refurbishment loan [app]. Retraining could lift cleanliness standards within 6 weeks [an], while dismissal is quicker but risks unfair dismissal compensation if procedures slip [an]. On balance, the board should retrain rather than dismiss, because the 12% staffing shortfall and the complaint trend suggest the supervisors need support [eval]; if retraining fails within 6 weeks, dismissal through a fair procedure remains a justified fallback [eval].

knowledge_max_2: dismissal is quicker / removes poor performers
analysis_max_2: retraining could raise standards within 6 weeks
dismissal risks compensation if procedures not followed
evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation based on staffing shortfall and complaint trend
conditional judgement: dismiss only if retraining fails within 6 weeks

scenario_stem:
Saffron Dune Spices is a private limited company in Country X packing saffron jars. It sells 42,000 jars at $6.50 each, earning $273,000, with 18 workers. Share fell from 15% to 11% as supermarkets launched cheaper own-brand blends.

A Country Y distributor offers 60,000 jars at $5.20 if the firm licenses its brand locally or joins a joint venture. Country Y has a 12% import tariff and prefers milder flavours. It must choose: domestic, licensing or joint venture.

questions.question_text: Define 'licensing'.
questions.model_answer: An agreement where a business (the licensor) grants another business (the licensee) the right to produce or sell its product using its brand, patent or process, usually in exchange for a fee or royalty [2].

knowledge_max_2: one business grants another the right to use its brand/patent/process
in exchange for a fee or royalty

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Saffron Dune Spices of expanding into Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Entering Country Y gives Saffron Dune access to a much larger customer base [k], because the distributor could sell 60,000 jars a year at $5.20, worth about $312,000 in extra revenue [app]. Opportunity 2: Selling abroad reduces dependence on the domestic market [k], which matters because Saffron Dune's domestic market share has already slipped from 15% to 11% [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to a larger market / more customers abroad
spreads risk / reduces reliance on the domestic market
application_max_2: 60,000 jars a year at $5.20 / about $312,000 extra revenue
domestic share fell from 15% to 11% / revenue $273,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Saffron Dune Spices could face if it expands into Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country Y shoppers prefer milder flavours [k], so the existing saffron blends may not appeal and recipes may need reformulating to win buyers [app], increasing costs and risking a launch that fails to cover the entry investment [an]. Problem 2: The 12% import tariff on finished spice jars [k] would add about $0.62 to each $5.20 jar [app], cutting margins or pushing prices up so local competitors stay cheaper [an].

knowledge_max_2: cultural differences / tastes differ between countries
tariffs raise the cost of selling abroad
application_max_2: Country Y prefers milder flavours / recipes need reformulating
12% import tariff on $5.20 jar / about $0.62 added per jar
analysis_max_2: higher costs / launch may fail to cover entry investment
margins squeezed or prices raised / lose competitiveness

questions.question_text: Do you think Saffron Dune Spices should enter Country Y through licensing or a joint venture? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Licensing its brand to a local bottler would let Saffron Dune sell in Country Y without paying the 12% import tariff, because the jars would be filled locally [k], and could generate 60,000 jars at $5.20, about $312,000 a year, with little capital at risk [app]. However, licensing gives limited control over quality and over the milder recipe adaptation [an]. A joint venture with the Country Y importer would share the risk and bring market knowledge for the milder-flavour demand [k], while giving closer oversight and shared decision-making over the 60,000-jar plan [app], yet it locks capital into a long-term partnership and exposes Saffron Dune to the partner's performance [an]. Overall, licensing is the better first step given the share slide to 11% at home, because it is quick and low-risk [eval]; if Country Y orders exceed 60,000 jars a year, converting to a joint venture would then protect the brand [eval].

knowledge_max_2: licensing = local firm produces/sells for a fee, low capital risk
joint venture = shared ownership/risk with local partner and shared knowledge
application_max_2: 60,000 jars at $5.20 / about $312,000 a year for licensing
12% import tariff avoided locally / milder flavours / share fell to 11%
analysis_max_2: licensing avoids tariff and keeps capital free but weakens quality control
joint venture shares risk and adds local knowledge but locks capital in
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two entry methods
conditions/sequence suggested (license first, convert to JV if successful)

scenario_stem:
Redbank Brickworks Ltd is a private limited company making clay bricks for housebuilders for 9 years. It operates one kiln 38 km from its clay quarry, pays $420,000 to haul 17,000 tonnes of clay, and serves 210 customers on $2.6 million sales.

The quarry owner offers 5 hectares beside the quarry at $30,000 yearly, 25% below current rent, but it is 60 km from the motorway and wages are $1,700 monthly against $2,100 now. The board must choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'raw materials'.
questions.model_answer: Raw materials are the basic inputs a business buys in and uses in the production of its goods or services, for example clay used to make bricks [2].

knowledge_max_2: raw materials are the basic inputs used in production
they are transformed into finished goods or services

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Redbank Brickworks might relocate the kiln beside the quarry.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Locating beside the quarry removes the 38 km haulage of 17,000 tonnes of clay each year, cutting the $420,000 fuel and road transport bill [k], which matters because diesel prices are rising and squeezing margins [app]. Reason 2: The quarry plot costs just $30,000 a year in rent, 25% below the current site, and wages there are $1,700 a month against $2,100 at the current site [k], saving money every month the kiln operates [app].

knowledge_max_2: removes or reduces transport costs of raw materials
lower rent or lower wages near the supplier
application_max_2: $420,000 transport per year / 17,000 tonnes of clay / 38 km
$30,000 rent, 25% below current site / $1,700 vs $2,100 wages

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Redbank Brickworks could face if it relocates beside the quarry.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The quarry plot is 60 km from the main motorway [k], so delivering finished bricks to 210 customers may take longer and cost more in fuel than today [app], eating into the $30,000 rent saving and squeezing the already-thin margins [an]. Problem 2: Moving an operating kiln means a costly shutdown and rebuild [k], during which Redbank could fail to deliver bricks to its 210 customers for weeks [app], risking lost orders and damage to customer relationships built over 9 years [an].

knowledge_max_2: longer delivery distances to customers from the remote site
shutdown and relocation costs / disruption to production
application_max_2: 60 km from the main motorway / 210 customers
kiln move / 9 years of customer relationships
analysis_max_2: higher transport costs erode the $30,000 rent saving and margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Redbank Brickworks should relocate the kiln beside the quarry? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relocating beside the quarry would eliminate 38 km of clay haulage per trip and cut the $420,000 annual transport bill on 17,000 tonnes of clay [k], while the subsidised $30,000 rent and $1,700 monthly wages add further savings [app]. However, staying put keeps the kiln close to the motorway and to the 210 customers, protecting delivery times [k], and it avoids the 60 km stretch to the motorway absorbing the $30,000 rent saving [app]. Relocation could strengthen competitiveness as diesel prices rise [an], but a kiln rebuild would halt production in the short term [an]. On balance, Redbank should relocate, because the $420,000 yearly transport saving outweighs the one-off move costs and the motorway distance [eval]; it should plan the move in stages to guarantee customer deliveries throughout [eval].

knowledge_max_2: relocation removes transport and lowers rent and wages
staying preserves customer proximity and avoids disruption

rebuild halts production and threatens customer deliveries

justified recommendation with a staged move to protect deliveries

scenario_stem:
Wexcombe Pottery Ltd is a private limited company making pottery, employing 58 workers at its Stokeham workshop. Final accounts show revenue of $2.4 million and profit of $310,000, up from $185,000, on a $1.6 million wage bill.

The Clay & Ceramics Union wants to see the final accounts, arguing its 6% pay claim, costing $96,000 a year, is affordable. Priya Nair must choose between granting 6% and holding to a 2% offer costing $32,000 that would fund a kiln replacement.

questions.question_text: Define 'final accounts'.
questions.model_answer: Final accounts are the financial statements a business prepares at the end of an accounting period to show its profit, revenue and financial position, helping stakeholders judge performance [2].

knowledge_max_2: Statements prepared at the end of the accounting period
Show profit, revenue and financial position to stakeholders

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Clay & Ceramics Union would want to see Wexcombe Pottery Ltd's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: First, the union wants to see whether the business can afford the 6% claim [k]. Profit rose to $310,000 on revenue of $2.4 million, so members argue the accounts prove the case for higher pay [app]. Second, the union uses the accounts to judge job security [k]. If profit fell back towards $185,000 or expenses spiked, jobs and future rises could be at risk, shaping whether to press for 6% or accept the $32,000 offer [app].

knowledge_max_2: Judge whether the business can afford the pay claim
Assess job security and the basis for negotiating

Reference to the 6% claim versus the 2% offer ($32,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the directors might face if they agree to the 6% claim.
questions.model_answer: First, agreeing the claim raises wage costs [k]. The extra $96,000 a year would come from profit of $310,000, leaving only about $214,000 before tax [app]. This squeezes the owners' return and could force price rises, risking orders from price-sensitive retailers [an]. Second, the claim absorbs funds for the kiln replacement [k]. The 2% offer costs $32,000, but 6% costs $96,000, a difference of $64,000 [app]. Without the new kiln, output and quality at Stokeham could deteriorate, hurting delivery reliability and customer trust [an].

Chain from no kiln to lower output and quality to lost customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should accept the 6% pay claim? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Granting the 6% claim would reward workers after a strong year [k]. It costs $96,000 a year, and with profit of $310,000 the business could pay it while keeping about $214,000, improving morale across all 58 workers and cutting the risk of strikes [app]. Better motivation could lift output and reduce labour turnover at the workshop, protecting revenue of $2.4 million [an]. However, the 6% claim absorbs the funds needed for the kiln replacement, unlike the 2% offer costing $32,000 [k]. Accepting 6% would also set a precedent the business cannot afford if profit falls back towards $185,000 [app]. Sustained higher wages could force price rises that lose customers to rivals, eroding the very profit that makes the claim affordable [an]. Overall, I think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should hold to the 2% offer plus a one-off profit-linked bonus [eval]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ironhart Steel Co, a private limited company, makes reinforcing bar for construction firms in Country X, with $9.6 million revenue. An import quota caps foreign bar at 40,000 tonnes, down from 95,000 tonnes; output rose 12% and 14 workers were hired.

GoldenHive Apiaries is a private limited company founded by Rosa and Emilio Varela, keeping bees on 2 farms. It manages 400 hives, employs 12 beekeepers, and has $520,000 sales, with supermarket demand exceeding supply by 30 per cent.

questions.question_text: Define 'external growth'.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to GoldenHive Apiaries of growing internally rather than through acquisition.

Second, shareholders use the accounts to assess the risk and growth prospects of their investment [k].
