scenario_stem:
Lumen & Co Fashion is a private limited company running 6 stores. Both flagship options need $180,000 of fit-out. Site A is on the high street with 9,500 daily footfall, $14,000 monthly rent and 45 parking spaces.

Site B is an out-of-town retail park with $8,500 rent, 320 free parking spaces and a cinema, but footfall of only 2,200. Site A sits two doors from a direct competitor; Site B has none. The board decides in March.

questions.question_text: Define 'footfall'.
questions.model_answer: Footfall is the number of people passing through or visiting a retail location during a given period, indicating the potential customer traffic for a shop [2].

knowledge_max_2: number of people passing through/visiting a location
indicates potential customer traffic for a shop

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Site A might suit the new flagship.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Site A offers footfall of 9,500 people a day against just 2,200 at Site B [k], giving the flagship far more natural exposure to fashion shoppers at no extra marketing cost [app]. Reason 2: Site A sits two doors from a direct competitor [k], so opening there lets Lumen defend its share of high street shoppers in the capital and respond to rival promotions [app].

knowledge_max_2: high footfall brings more potential customers
proximity to competitor supports defensive positioning
application_max_2: 9,500 people a day vs 2,200 at Site B
two doors from a direct competitor / high street / capital

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of opening at Site A.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Site A's rent of $14,000 a month exceeds Site B's $8,500 by $5,500 [k], adding $66,000 a year of extra fixed costs before the first garment is sold [app], which raises the sales the flagship needs to break even on its $180,000 fit-out [an]. Drawback 2: With only 45 parking spaces nearby, car-borne shoppers may choose Site B's 320 free spaces instead [k], diverting customers to the retail park with the cinema next door [app], weakening the flagship's early sales in March [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher rent raises fixed costs and break-even point
application_max_2: $14,000 vs $8,500, i.e. $5,500 more per month / $66,000 a year
45 parking spaces vs 320 at Site B / cinema next door / $180,000 fit-out
analysis_max_2: higher break-even sales needed to cover the fit-out
lost car-borne customers weaken early sales in March

questions.question_text: Do you think Lumen & Co Fashion should open the flagship at Site A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Site A delivers footfall of 9,500 people a day, more than four times Site B's 2,200 [k], which should drive far stronger walk-in sales for a fashion flagship investing $180,000 in fit-out [app]. However, Site A costs $14,000 a month in rent, $66,000 a year more than Site B's $8,500, and only 45 parking spaces may frustrate car-borne shoppers [k], who could defect to Site B's 320 free spaces and cinema destination [app]. Site A's two-door proximity to a direct competitor risks constant price comparison and discounting [an], while Site B offers lower overheads and exclusive trade nearby but far fewer passing shoppers [an]. On balance, Lumen should open at Site A, because footfall is the strongest driver of fashion retail revenue and outweighs the rent gap if the fit-out attracts attention [eval]; it should negotiate a rent reduction and arrange evening parking for shoppers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: rent and parking disadvantages of Site A
application_max_2: $14,000 vs $8,500 rent / 45 vs 320 parking spaces / two doors from a direct competitor / cinema next door
analysis_max_2: competitor proximity forces price comparison and discounting
Site B offers lower overheads but far less passing trade
evaluation_max_2: weighs 9,500 daily footfall against $66,000 extra yearly rent and 45 parking spaces
justified recommendation for Site A conditional on rent negotiation and parking solutions

scenario_stem:
Ternhill Dairy Ltd is a private limited company making cheese and butter for 14 regional supermarkets. Revenue was $5.1 million and profit $420,000; it has applied to Country X Bank for a $400,000 loan to buy three refrigerated vans.

Its statement of financial position shows current assets of $980,000, including inventories of $350,000 and debtors of $520,000, against current liabilities of $600,000 and cash of $110,000. The current ratio fell to 1.63 from 1.9, and the acid test ratio to 1.05 from 1.3.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due, using cash or assets that can quickly be turned into cash [2].

knowledge_max_2: Ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due
Using cash or assets quickly convertible to cash

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Country X Bank would examine Ternhill Dairy Ltd's statement of financial position before granting the loan.
questions.model_answer: First, the bank wants to judge whether short-term debts can be paid [k]. Current assets of $980,000 against current liabilities of $600,000 give a current ratio of 1.63, down from 1.9 two years ago, which tells the bank Ternhill has some cushion but a weakening one [app]. Second, the bank wants to know what can be turned into cash quickly [k]. With inventories of $350,000 the acid test ratio is 1.05, down from 1.3, and cash is only $110,000, so the bank would probe the $520,000 of debtors to see whether supermarkets pay on time [app].

knowledge_max_2: Judge ability to pay short-term debts
Assess how much is quickly convertible to cash
application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.63 vs 1.9; current assets $980,000 vs current liabilities $600,000
Reference to acid test 1.05 vs 1.3; inventories $350,000, debtors $520,000, cash $110,000

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio and the acid test ratio to judge Ternhill's ability to repay the loan.
questions.model_answer: First, ratios are a snapshot at one date [k]. Ternhill's current ratio of 1.63 and acid test ratio of 1.05 held at the year end, but a single late supermarket payment or a big stock delivery could change both quickly, so the figures may flatter the business on the day the $400,000 loan is decided [app]. Liquidity could be materially weaker exactly when the first instalments fall due [an]. Second, ratios ignore the quality of what the business owns [k]. Of the $980,000 of current assets, $350,000 is inventories and $520,000 is debtors; slow-paying or defaulting supermarkets, or damaged stocks, would shrink the real acid test well below 1.05 [app]. The bank could lend on the strength of figures that evaporate once debtors and inventories are properly valued [an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios are a snapshot at one date; figures change quickly
Ratios ignore the quality of assets (stock and debtors may be impaired)
application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.63 and acid test 1.05 at year end
Reference to inventories $350,000 and debtors $520,000 of $980,000 current assets
analysis_max_2: Chain from year-end snapshot to weaker instalment-date liquidity
Chain from impaired stock or debtors to an overstated acid test

questions.question_text: Do you think Country X Bank should grant the $400,000 loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Ternhill is profitable, with profit of $420,000 almost covering the $400,000 loan in a single year [k]. Revenue of $5.1 million and supply deals with 14 regional supermarkets suggest steady cash generation, and three refrigerated vans would cut spoilage and secure deliveries, supporting future sales [app]. Stronger distribution could widen margins and lift profit further, improving the bank's repayment prospects across the term of the loan [an]. However, liquidity is weakening: the current ratio has fallen from 1.9 to 1.63, the acid test from 1.3 to 1.05, cash is only $110,000 and debtors are $520,000 — more than half of current assets [k]. Granting cash before debtors are collected could leave Ternhill unable to meet early instalments, especially if one supermarket pays late [app]. A rushed approval could turn a good customer into an overdraft problem, adding risk and cost to the bank with no extra margin [an]. Overall, I think Country X Bank should grant the loan, but in staged instalments linked to milestones, with vans delivered and debtors collected down to agreed limits [eval]. The profit and revenue justify supporting the business, yet the weakening acid test and $110,000 cash balance demand controls rather than one upfront payout [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Profitable business; loan is close to one year of profit
Weakening current ratio, acid test and cash position
application_max_2: Reference to revenue $5.1 million, profit $420,000 and 14 supermarkets
Reference to cash $110,000, debtors $520,000, current ratio 1.63, acid test 1.05
analysis_max_2: Chain from new vans to lower spoilage and stronger sales to easier repayment
Chain from rushed approval to overdraft pressure and added risk
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to lend in stages
Weighs both sides with stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Rosewood Fashion, a private limited company, is a Country X clothing retailer with 14 stores. It imports 70% of $4.8 million stock ($3.36 million) from outside the Aster Trade Bloc, paying 18% tariff. Joining the bloc removes tariffs on clothing from the other 6 member countries.

Two bloc suppliers offer prices 15% below the current non-bloc supplier, saving $504,000 yearly. The current supplier has worked with Rosewood for 8 years, giving 60 days' credit. The director must decide whether to switch or keep it.

questions.question_text: Define 'member state'.
questions.model_answer: A member state is a country that has joined a trade bloc and agreed to follow its rules, such as trading without tariffs with other member countries [2].

knowledge_max_2: a country that has joined a trade bloc
agreed to follow the bloc's rules / trades on agreed terms with other members

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Rosewood Fashion of Country X joining the Aster Trade Bloc.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The 18% import tariff on clothing from the other 6 member countries is removed [k], so the imported garments that make up 70% of its $4.8 million stock become cheaper to buy [app]. Advantage 2: Bloc-based suppliers offered prices 15% below its current supplier [k], saving about $504,000 a year on the $3.36 million of imported garments [app].

application_max_2: 18% tariff / 6 member countries / 70% of $4.8 million stock
$504,000 a year saving on $3.36 million of imports

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Rosewood Fashion could face if it switches to these bloc-based suppliers.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Its current supplier gives 60 days' credit [k]; new bloc suppliers may demand payment on order, straining cash flow [app] across 14 stores stocking seasonal lines [an]. Problem 2: Switching after 8 years means unproven quality and reliability [k]; faulty garments would damage Rosewood's brand image [app], leading to lost customers and lower repeat sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: new suppliers may end 60 days' credit terms
switching risks unproven quality and reliability
application_max_2: 60 days' credit / 14 stores stocking seasonal lines
8 years with the current supplier / Rosewood's brand image
analysis_max_2: brand damage / lost customers and lower repeat sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Rosewood Fashion should switch to the bloc-based suppliers when Country X joins the Aster Trade Bloc, or keep its existing supplier? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching removes the 18% tariff and saves about $504,000 a year on $3.36 million of imports [k], lifting profit across its 14 stores [app] without raising prices for middle-income families [an]. However, keeping the current supplier preserves 60 days' credit and 8 years of trust [k]; unknown suppliers risk quality and cash-flow problems [app], which could hurt the brand more than the saving is worth [an]. Overall, Rosewood should switch to the bloc-based suppliers because $504,000 a year is a major saving and bloc membership gives lasting tariff-free access [eval], although it should negotiate credit terms close to the existing 60 days before committing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: switching cuts import costs / tariff removed
keeping the supplier preserves credit and trust
application_max_2: $504,000 a year saving on $3.36 million of imports / 14 stores
60 days' credit / 8 years with current supplier / 18% tariff
analysis_max_2: risk to brand and cash flow from unknown suppliers
evaluation_max_2: weighs switching for the saving against keeping the trusted supplier; justified recommendation with figures

scenario_stem:
Redstone Ceramic Tiles is a private limited company making wall and floor tiles at one factory for 11 years. It employs 55 technicians with 3 kilns, produced tiles worth $3.2 million, and sells almost all output through 3 wholesalers charging 12 per cent margin.

Founder Miriam Holt considers opening retail showrooms in 2 cities for $420,000 to sell direct, capturing the wholesalers' margin. Her adviser warns that showrooms need retail staff, stock systems and marketing experience she lacks.

questions.question_text: Define 'forward vertical integration'.
questions.model_answer: Forward vertical integration is when a business takes over or merges with a distributor or retailer that sells its products to the final customer [2].

knowledge_max_2: integration with a distributor/retailer/next stage towards the customer
opposite direction from backward vertical integration

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Redstone Ceramic Tiles of forward vertical integration.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Capturing the wholesaler margin [k], as selling direct through Redstone's own 2 showrooms would keep the 12 per cent each wholesaler charges [app]. Advantage 2: Better contact with final customers [k], as dealing with consumers, builders and architects directly gives feedback on which tiles sell, instead of relying on 3 distant wholesalers [app].

knowledge_max_2: direct contact with customers improves market feedback/control

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redstone Ceramic Tiles of achieving business growth.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher revenue [k], as opening 2 showrooms would tap direct sales from consumers and builders in addition to the $3.2 million already produced for wholesalers [app], increasing total sales and spreading income across more customers [an]. Benefit 2: Greater economies of scale [k], as higher output from the factory's 3 kilns would spread fixed costs over more tiles [app], lowering average cost per tile and improving profit on every unit sold [an].

knowledge_max_2: growth increases revenue/sales and customer base
growth enables economies of scale (lower average cost)
analysis_max_2: more revenue and spread risk across customers
fixed costs spread over more units, lowering average cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Redstone Ceramic Tiles should open its own retail showrooms or continue selling through wholesalers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening 2 showrooms at $420,000 would let Redstone capture the 12 per cent margin currently taken by 3 national wholesalers [k], raising profit on the $3.2 million of tiles produced each year [app], and giving direct contact with consumers, builders and architects to plan products [an]. However, showrooms are a tertiary activity requiring retail staff and stock systems Miriam Holt has never managed [k], which risks high costs and slow-moving stock that could erase the margin gain [app], and $420,000 of cash would be tied up with no guarantee of sales [an]. Overall, continuing with wholesalers for now is wiser [eval], because Redstone should test direct selling with one pilot showroom before committing fully [eval].

knowledge_max_2: forward integration captures margin and customer contact
forward integration adds cost/risk in an unfamiliar tertiary activity
analysis_max_2: margin capture raises profit and feedback improves products
cash tied up and weak retail skills risk losses
evaluation_max_2: weighs margin capture against unfamiliar retail risk, recommending a cautious pilot before full commitment

scenario_stem:
Ironhold Construction is a private limited company with 85 staff, 11 women, bidding for a $14m hospital refurbishment. Candidates: Priya, an engineer with 6 years, and an external man with 4 years' experience.

Some directors favour the outsider, preferring a familiar type; others call it discrimination. Priya is cheaper with no fees; external hire costs $9,500 and 8 weeks' notice. With a tender in 5 weeks and an equal opportunity contract, a claim could damage the bid.

questions.question_text: Define 'discrimination'.
questions.model_answer: Discrimination is treating an employee or job applicant unfairly because of a personal characteristic such as gender, age or race [2].

knowledge_max_2: unfair treatment of an employee / applicant
because of a personal characteristic such as gender, age or race

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Ironhold Construction must avoid discrimination when appointing the site supervisor.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Legal consequences [k]; Ironhold signed an equal opportunity contract and a tribunal could order compensation [app]. Reason 2: Reputation and the $14m bid [k]; favouring the external candidate because of gender would break that contract and could cost the hospital refurbishment tender [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Ironhold Construction can ensure the supervisor appointment is free from discrimination.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Use objective selection criteria [k]; an agreed person specification listing skills such as site management and safety would judge Priya on her 6 years against the external candidate's 4 years [app], removing personal bias from the decision [an]. Way 2: Hold structured interviews with the same questions for both [k]; a mixed interview panel scores each answer consistently [app], making the final choice defensible if challenged at a tribunal [an].

knowledge_max_2: structured interviews / mixed panel / consistent scoring
application_max_2: both candidates interviewed the same way
analysis_max_2: removes personal bias from the decision
defensible decision if challenged at tribunal

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironhold Construction should promote Priya rather than appoint the external candidate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Promoting Priya is faster and cheaper [k]; there are no $9,500 agency fees or 8 weeks of notice, and she knows Ironhold's sites and safety culture after 6 years [app]. However, promoting an internal candidate without objective testing could still look like favouritism [k], and only external advertising guarantees the widest pool for a $14m hospital project [app]. Fairly assessed against a person specification, Priya's 6 years outweigh the external candidate's 4 years [an], and the board avoids a discrimination claim that could wreck the hospital bid [an]. On balance, Ironhold should promote Priya provided she meets the specification in a structured interview [eval], since this is both the cheaper and the legally safer outcome for the tender [eval].

knowledge_max_2: risk of favouritism / external pool widens choice
analysis_max_2: Priya's 6 years outweigh 4 years if specification met
avoids discrimination claim wrecking the bid
evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: promote Priya if specification met
balanced view: external hiring justified only if she fails the assessment

scenario_stem:
Amber Brook Cheese is a private limited company in Country X making artisan hard cheeses. It produces 24,000 wheels at $28 each, earning $672,000, and employs 25 workers. Domestic sales flat for 3 years and milk costs rose 18%.

A supermarket chain in Country V will buy 15,000 wheels at $24 if food-safety certification is met within 9 months. Exporting brings a 10% import duty, $3 freight and unfamiliar labels. The board must decide: export or focus domestically.

questions.question_text: Define 'exporting'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods or services produced in one country to buyers located in another country [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling goods or services to buyers in another country
cross-border trade rather than domestic sales

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Amber Brook Cheese of exporting to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Exporting brings a firm order for 15,000 wheels a year [k], roughly $360,000 in extra revenue on top of its flat $672,000 domestic sales [app]. Opportunity 2: Selling in a second country spreads risk [k], so a downturn in Country X would no longer leave the 25 workers wholly dependent on the home market [app].

knowledge_max_2: larger market / additional sales revenue abroad
diversification / less dependence on the domestic economy
application_max_2: 15,000 wheels a year at $24 / about $360,000 extra revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Amber Brook Cheese could face if it exports to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 10% import duty plus $3 freight per wheel [k] would cut the $24 export price to an effective $18.60 [app], squeezing margins at exactly the time milk costs have risen 18% [an]. Problem 2: Country V requires its own food-safety certification and labelling rules [k], which take up to 9 months to complete [app], delaying the first export order and tying up cash in compliance before any revenue arrives [an].

knowledge_max_2: tariffs/import duties and transport costs reduce margins
foreign markets have unfamiliar regulations and standards
application_max_2: 10% duty plus $3 freight / $24 reduced to about $18.60
food-safety certification and labelling rules / up to 9 months
analysis_max_2: margins squeezed when milk costs already up 18%
compliance delays cash inflow and adds cost before sales begin

questions.question_text: Do you think Amber Brook Cheese should export to Country V or focus on the domestic market? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting would add $360,000 a year from 15,000 wheels [k], lifting revenue from $672,000 to roughly $1.03 million [app], vital while domestic sales have been flat for 3 years [an]. However, the 10% duty ($2.40 per wheel) and $3 freight leave about $18.60 per wheel [k], far below the $28 domestic price [app], and milk costs up 18% could make each export wheel barely profitable [an]. Overall, exporting is still worth pursuing if certification is secured within 9 months, because the extra volume should absorb fixed costs and offset the 18% milk-cost rise [eval]; if freight or duty terms cannot be improved, Amber Brook should delay exports and fix domestic sales first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: exporting gains extra revenue and volume in a new market
duties and freight reduce the effective export price and margin
application_max_2: 15,000 wheels / about $360,000 extra revenue (~$1.03 million total)
$2.40 duty and $3 freight / about $18.60 vs $28 domestic
analysis_max_2: extra volume helps absorb fixed costs and offset 18% milk-cost rise
weaker margin and certification delay risk cash flow
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation with conditions
recommendation sensitive to duty/freight negotiations

scenario_stem:
Goldengrain Bakery Ltd is a private limited company baking in Country X with 85 workers, making 11,000 loaves daily for 140 local shops. Night shifts run 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and neighbours complain of oven and lorry noise.

The council enforces 45 decibels after 9 p.m. unless the firm buys acoustic insulation for $120,000 or relocates. The current site has power at $0.09 per kWh; the industrial estate costs $35,000 more rent but meets the rules.

questions.question_text: Define 'planning permission'.
questions.model_answer: Planning permission is the formal approval granted by a local authority for a building or change of use, confirming the development complies with rules such as planning, noise and environmental controls [2].

knowledge_max_2: formal approval from a local authority for building/change of use
confirms compliance with planning and noise controls

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Goldengrain Bakery might choose acoustic insulation over relocation.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Acoustic insulation costs $120,000 once, far less than buying and fitting out a new bakery [k], and it keeps the current site's cheap power at $0.09 per kWh and its established position near 140 local shops [app]. Reason 2: Upgrading avoids any shutdown of the 11,000 loaves a day output [k], so customer deliveries to 140 local shops continue uninterrupted overnight [app].

knowledge_max_2: one-off upgrade costs less than relocation
avoids shutdown and preserves current site advantages
application_max_2: 11,000 loaves a day / 140 local shops / overnight delivery

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Goldengrain Bakery could face if it relocates to the industrial estate.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The estate site costs $35,000 a year more in rent [k], which squeezes the margin on every one of the 11,000 loaves produced daily [app], reducing cash available to replace ovens and maintain quality standards [an]. Problem 2: Relocating 85 workers and the delivery fleet would interrupt nightly production [k], so orders may be missed for weeks while the new site is commissioned [app], risking lost contracts with the 140 local shops [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher rent adds to annual fixed costs
application_max_2: $35,000 a year more in rent / 11,000 loaves a day
analysis_max_2: lower margins reduce cash for reinvestment
missed deliveries risk losing contracts with the 140 local shops

questions.question_text: Do you think Goldengrain Bakery should install acoustic insulation rather than relocate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Acoustic insulation at $120,000 is a one-off cost that keeps 11,000 loaves a day flowing overnight [k], protecting the $0.09 per kWh power advantage and the location near 140 local shops [app]. However, the council's 45 decibels limit may tighten further, and insulation may not solve noise from 10 p.m. delivery lorries [k], exposing the bakery to enforcement action if limits are breached [app]. Relocating to the industrial estate guarantees legal compliance and removes neighbour complaints permanently [an], but costs $35,000 a year extra for years and risks lost customers during the move [an]. On balance, Goldengrain should install the insulation first, since $120,000 once breaks even against $35,000 of extra annual rent in about 3.4 years [eval]; moving remains sensible only if noise still exceeds 45 decibels after the upgrade [eval].

knowledge_max_2: insulation is a one-off cost preserving the site
moving guarantees compliance but adds rent and disruption
application_max_2: $120,000 insulation / $0.09 per kWh / 140 local shops / 11,000 loaves
45 decibels limit / 10 p.m. delivery lorries / $35,000 extra rent
analysis_max_2: moving guarantees compliance but adds $35,000 yearly and disruption
enforcement risk remains if noise persists after insulation
evaluation_max_2: weighs $120,000 one-off vs $35,000 a year (break-even ~3.4 years)
justified recommendation to insulate first, relocate only if limits still breached

scenario_stem:
Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd is a private limited company supplying roofing, insulation and timber to the trade, with 28 staff. Hollowbrook Homes Ltd wants $180,000 of materials for a 24-house estate and asks for 60 days to pay.

Hollowbrook's accounts show revenue of $6.4 million, profit of $250,000, current assets of $550,000, including inventories of $250,000, and current liabilities of $500,000; current ratio 1.1, acid test 0.6, and slow payment to suppliers. Wicklow must choose between 60-day credit and 30-day terms, risking the order.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade credit'.
questions.model_answer: Trade credit is an arrangement allowing a customer to receive goods immediately and pay the supplier after an agreed period, such as 30 or 60 days [2].

knowledge_max_2: Payment made after an agreed period such as 30 or 60 days

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd would want to see Hollowbrook Homes Ltd's accounts before offering trade credit.
questions.model_answer: First, the accounts show whether Hollowbrook can pay [k]. Current assets of $550,000 against current liabilities of $500,000 give a current ratio of 1.1 and an acid test ratio of 0.6, so quick funds are thin for settling a $180,000 invoice [app]. Second, the accounts show whether the order is reasonable for the customer's size [k]. Revenue of $6.4 million and profit of $250,000 against a $180,000 order means the deal equals 72% of annual profit, so Wicklow must judge whether the margin justifies the exposure [app].

knowledge_max_2: Assess order size relative to the customer's resources
application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.1, acid test 0.6, current assets $550,000 vs current liabilities $500,000
Reference to $180,000 order = 72% of $250,000 profit on revenue of $6.4 million

questions.question_text: Explain two risks to Wicklow of granting 60-day credit.
questions.model_answer: First, Wicklow faces late or non-payment [k]. Hollowbrook's acid test of 0.6 and inventories of $250,000, nearly half its current assets, show cash is tight and it is already slow paying existing suppliers, so the $180,000 could sit unpaid well beyond 60 days [app]. Wicklow would then lack cash for its own stock and wages, possibly needing costly overdraft borrowing [an]. Second, a single large customer raises dependence [k]. The $180,000 order equals 72% of Hollowbrook's $250,000 profit, so one default or insolvency would be a heavy blow to a 28-staff merchant [app]. Losing that sum could wipe out Wicklow's margin on the whole estate deal and strain relations with its own suppliers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Risk of late payment or default
application_max_2: Reference to acid test 0.6, inventories $250,000 (nearly half of current assets) and slow payment of suppliers
analysis_max_2: Chain from late payment to Wicklow cash strain and overdraft costs
Chain from one default to lost margin and supplier strain

questions.question_text: Do you think Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd should grant the 60-day credit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Granting 60-day credit could win a $180,000 order for a 24-house estate and open a long-term relationship with a growing developer [k]. Hollowbrook is profitable at $250,000 on revenue of $6.4 million, and the deal equals 72% of its profit, so losing it to a rival merchant would hand over valuable future estate business [app]. Securing the account could bring regular orders and steady sales without new advertising spend [an]. However, Hollowbrook's liquidity is weak: acid test 0.6, current ratio 1.1, inventories of $250,000 and a record of slow payment to existing suppliers [k]. If payment slips beyond 60 days, Wicklow faces a cash gap of $180,000 on top of its own commitments, risking its ability to pay suppliers and staff [app]. One bad debt could erase months of Wicklow's margin, and repeated chasing strains the relationship the deal was meant to build [an]. Overall, I think Wicklow should not grant 60 days on the current terms [eval]; it should insist on 30-day terms, or staged payments with a deposit, because the acid test of 0.6 and the slow payment history do not justify open-ended 60-day credit, however attractive the order looks [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Winning the order builds a relationship and future business
Weak liquidity and slow payment history make 60 days risky
application_max_2: Reference to $180,000 order, $250,000 profit, 72% of profit, 24-house estate
Reference to acid test 0.6, current ratio 1.1, inventories $250,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from winning the account to regular future orders
Chain from late payment to a cash gap and bad-debt risk
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (30-day terms or staged payments instead)
Weighs both options with stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kibale Tea Co, a private limited company, runs 3 tea estates, exporting 60% of its tea in 20 kg sacks. As a member of the Tzara Free Trade Area, it trades tariff-free with members, each setting its own tariff on outside tea.

A new buyer market in another member country has demand for premium loose-leaf tea growing 9% annually. Entry costs $300,000 for distribution and marketing, projecting $750,000 in first-year sales. Flat non-member markets need no marketing spend. The director must choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade area'.
questions.model_answer: A free trade area is a group of countries that agree to trade goods between themselves without tariffs, while each member keeps its own tariff on goods imported from outside the area [2].

Consequence 2: Without understanding customer needs [k], the bookshop may stock unwanted titles and miss requests for events and recommendations [app], wasting shelf space and cash while customers defect to online sellers [an].

knowledge_max_2: ignoring needs loses sales and customers to rivals
poor marketing leads to wasted stock and missed opportunities
application_max_2: customers want events and recommendations / online rivals
analysis_max_2: revenue falls further without a response
wasted stock and cash; customers defect to online sellers

questions.question_text: Do you think The Paper Lantern Bookshop should employ a part-time marketing assistant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Employing an assistant for $14,000 a year [k] would put someone in place to identify customer needs and organise events and recommendations [app], directly tackling the 22% footfall decline and building customer loyalty [an]. However, the bookshop still owes $26,500 and wages cannot be used to repay that debt [k], so the $14,000 adds a fixed cost before any extra sales arrive [app], and if sales do not respond the hire strains cash further [an]. Overall, hiring the assistant is justified because $14,000 is under 4.5% of the $323,000 revenue and directly reverses the 22% slide by rebuilding the relationships that keep bookshops alive [eval]; the owners should set a 6-month sales target and review it to protect cash [eval].

knowledge_max_2: marketing builds loyalty and relationships that defend sales
extra wages are a fixed cost and compete with debt repayment
application_max_2: $14,000 a year assistant / tackles 22% footfall decline
analysis_max_2: assistant reverses footfall decline and builds loyalty

scenario_stem:
Crumb & Co Bakehouse is a sole trader bakery in Country X supplying 180 supermarket stores with 24 million rolls a year. A chilled warehouse storing up to 500,000 rolls costs $6,800 monthly.

For the December peak the owner builds 400,000 frozen rolls in October at $0.06 per roll monthly, or relies on just-in-time daily production, risking empty shelves. Last year stockouts cost $95,000. 2 production lines could raise November output 30%; capacity and cash are tight.

questions.question_text: Define 'inventory'.
questions.model_answer: Inventory is the stock of goods and materials a business holds to support production or sale, including raw materials, work in progress and finished goods [2].

knowledge_max_2: stock of goods and materials held by a business
includes raw materials, work in progress and finished goods

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Crumb & Co might build a festive inventory of 400,000 rolls.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Building an inventory of 400,000 extra rolls meets the sudden surge in December demand across 180 supermarket stores [k], avoiding stockouts that cost an estimated $95,000 of lost sales last year [app]. Reason 2: Holding finished rolls in chilled storage smooths production across the 2 lines [k], letting the bakery run steadily instead of chasing just-in-time orders daily at peak time [app].

knowledge_max_2: inventories meet sudden or seasonal demand spikes
finished goods stock smooths production and avoids stoppages
application_max_2: 400,000 extra rolls / 180 supermarket stores / $95,000 lost sales
2 production lines / December peak / just-in-time deliveries

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of holding the extra festive inventory.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Chilled storage costs $6,800 a month, and holding 400,000 rolls adds $0.06 per roll per month, about $24,000 a month [k], so the pre-Christmas build could add more than $30,000 of storage costs before January [app], cutting the margin on festive sales [an]. Problem 2: Storage capacity is limited to 500,000 rolls and unsold rolls tie up cash [k], so if December demand disappoints, rolls may be left in chilled storage needing to be sold later at a discount [app], reducing cash available for flour and January wages [an].

knowledge_max_2: storage and handling costs of holding inventories
cash tied up / risk of unsold stock needing discounting
application_max_2: $6,800 a month / $0.06 per roll per month / about $24,000 a month
analysis_max_2: storage costs above $30,000 erode festive margins
unsold rolls tie up cash needed for January expenses

questions.question_text: Do you think Crumb & Co should build the festive inventory rather than rely on just-in-time deliveries? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the 400,000-roll inventory protects the 180 stores from December stockouts [k], and last year empty shelves cost $95,000 of lost sales, far above the roughly $30,000 storage cost for the period [app]. However, relying on just-in-time production of around 24 million rolls a year would keep storage costs near zero and make the bakery leaner [k], leaving only the chilled warehouse's $6,800 a month within its 500,000-roll capacity [app]. A partial build covering the peak, combined with 30% higher output from the 2 lines in November, meets surge demand and limits excess stock [an], but if stores over-order, chilled capacity is wasted and cash is tied up in unsold rolls [an]. On balance, Crumb & Co should build the festive inventory, because the $95,000 loss risk outweighs about $30,000 of storage and capacity can absorb the surge [eval]; it should scale the order to each store's December forecast [eval].

knowledge_max_2: inventory guards against stockouts during demand spikes
application_max_2: just-in-time / 24 million rolls a year / $6,800 a month / 500,000-roll capacity
analysis_max_2: partial build with 30% extra November output meets the surge efficiently
over-ordering wastes chilled capacity and ties up cash
evaluation_max_2: weighs $95,000 stockout risk against about $30,000 storage cost and 500,000-roll capacity
justified recommendation to build stock scaled to store-level forecasts

scenario_stem:
Halcyon Reef Resorts Ltd is a private limited company running three eco-resorts. Comparing the accounts over two years, revenue rose from $9.6 million to $10.4 million, but gross profit margin fell from 52% to 47% and profit from $840,000 to $720,000; the current ratio was 1.8 and occupancy averaged 78%.

Option A raises room rates from $145 to $154, a $9 rise; Option B holds rates and cuts operating costs by re-tendering laundry and kitchen contracts, saving $120,000 a year but risking service consistency.

questions.question_text: Define 'ratio analysis'.
questions.model_answer: Ratio analysis is the use of financial ratios, such as gross profit margin, return on capital employed and the current ratio, to assess a business's performance and financial position, often compared over time [2].

knowledge_max_2: Using financial ratios to assess performance and financial position
Comparisons over time or against other businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why comparing the accounts over two years is useful to managers.
questions.model_answer: First, two years of ratios reveal trends that a single year cannot [k]. Revenue rising from $9.6 million to $10.4 million looks healthy on its own, but the gross profit margin falling from 52% to 47% shows growth is being bought with weaker pricing or higher input costs [app]. Second, trend analysis helps locate the problem precisely [k]. A current ratio steady at 1.8 alongside falling profit shows liquidity is fine, so managers should attack costs or pricing, and the profit drop of $120,000 matches the projected $120,000 saving exactly [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reveals trends that a single year cannot
Locates whether problems are cost, price or liquidity
application_max_2: Reference to revenue $9.6 million to $10.4 million; gross profit margin 52% to 47%
Reference to current ratio steady at 1.8; profit fall of $120,000 matching the $120,000 saving

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of comparing Halcyon's ratios over just two years.
questions.model_answer: First, two years is a short window and may catch one-off events [k]. Halcyon's profit fell from $840,000 to $720,000 partly because of higher laundry and kitchen costs, which the $120,000 saving would reverse, so the 47% margin may understate underlying performance [app]. Judging on a single cost shock could push directors into rushed rate rises or cuts that harm guests [an]. Second, ratios ignore qualitative factors [k]. Occupancy of 78% shows rooms are selling, but guest satisfaction, staff morale and brand reputation, all affected by Option B's service-consistency risk, sit outside the numbers [app]. Cutting the wrong contracts could save $120,000 yet damage the experience that drives occupancy and revenue of $10.4 million [an].

knowledge_max_2: Short window; one-off events distort the picture
Ratios ignore qualitative factors (service, morale, brand)
application_max_2: Reference to profit $840,000 to $720,000; 47% margin; $120,000 saving
Reference to occupancy 78% and revenue of $10.4 million
analysis_max_2: Chain from a short window to rushed, harmful decisions
Chain from blunt cost cuts to damaged occupancy and revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Halcyon Reef Resorts Ltd should choose Option B rather than Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises rates from $145 to $154, a $9 increase, restoring revenue from existing guests without restructuring operations [k]. With occupancy at 78%, even a modest rise lifts revenue across three resorts, but it may deter price-sensitive holidaymakers already facing higher costs elsewhere [app]. If even 5% of guests defect, the lost contribution could erase the extra $9 a night and push occupancy below break-even [an]. Option B keeps rates at $145 and cuts costs by $120,000 a year, exactly the profit lost, by re-tendering laundry and kitchen contracts [k]. This attacks the problem directly and protects the $145 rate that keeps the resorts competitive, provided service standards are monitored closely [app]. Well-run contracts could restore profit towards $840,000 without touching price or occupancy [an]. Overall, I think Halcyon should choose Option B, with strict service-level monitoring [eval]; it exactly offsets the $120,000 profit fall and avoids demand risk at 78% occupancy, whereas Option A remains a useful fallback if service complaints rise after the switch [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A restores revenue but risks demand at 78% occupancy
Option B targets the cost cause and protects price and occupancy
application_max_2: Reference to $145 to $154 ($9) and occupancy 78% at three resorts
Reference to $120,000 saving equalling the profit lost; profit back towards $840,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from a rate rise to guest defections and lower occupancy
Chain from cost re-tendering to protected price and margin recovery
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation for Option B with safeguards
Weighs both options with stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Vireo Bicycles Ltd, a private limited company, makes bicycles in Country X with 140 employees. After leaving the Aster Trade Bloc, a single market, exports of 55% of output ($8 million yearly) to the bloc face a new 8% tariff, adding $640,000 a year.

A $1.8 million final-assembly facility in the bloc would employ 50 workers, restore tariff-free access and tap 6% demand growth. The board must decide whether to invest or stay in Country X and absorb the 8% tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'single market'.
questions.model_answer: A single market is a trade bloc in which goods, services, workers and capital can move freely between member countries as if they were one internal market [2].

knowledge_max_2: trade bloc with free movement of goods, services, workers and capital
members act as one internal market / no internal tariffs

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Vireo Bicycles might build the final-assembly facility inside the bloc.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Assembly inside a member country keeps bloc exports tariff-free [k], avoiding the new 8% tariff on $8 million of exports, worth $640,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Bloc demand for bicycles is growing at 6% a year [k], so a tariff-free facility lets Vireo capture that growth with 50 local workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: keeps exports tariff-free / avoids the new tariff
application_max_2: 8% tariff on $8 million of exports / $640,000 a year
6% a year demand growth / 50 local workers

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Vireo Bicycles of the new 8% tariff if it stays in Country X.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Exports to bloc countries worth $8 million a year face the 8% tariff [k], adding $640,000 a year to costs [app] and squeezing profit margins on 55% of its output [an]. Disadvantage 2: Vireo must absorb the tariff or raise prices [k]; raising prices makes its bicycles dearer than bloc-made rivals [app], so bloc sales volume and market share could fall [an].

knowledge_max_2: choice between absorbing the tariff or raising prices
analysis_max_2: lost sales volume and market share

questions.question_text: Do you think Vireo Bicycles should build the $1.8 million final-assembly facility inside the bloc, or stay in Country X and absorb the 8% tariff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the facility keeps tariff-free access to the bloc [k], saving $640,000 a year against the 8% tariff on $8 million of exports [app], so the $1.8 million cost could be recovered in under 3 years [an]. Staying in Country X avoids that investment and its risks [k]; absorbing $640,000 a year or raising prices may erode bloc demand, which is growing at 6% a year [app], damaging a market that takes 55% of output [an]. Overall, Vireo should build the facility, because the tariff saving and access to a market growing at 6% a year outweigh the $1.8 million cost [eval], provided the $1.8 million can be financed without straining cash flow [eval].

knowledge_max_2: building inside the bloc restores tariff-free access
staying avoids the investment and its risks
application_max_2: $640,000 a year tariff / $8 million of exports / 55% of output
$1.8 million facility / 6% a year demand growth
analysis_max_2: tariff saving recovers the cost in under 3 years
absorbing or passing on the tariff erodes bloc demand
evaluation_max_2: weighs building the facility against absorbing the tariff; justified recommendation with figures

scenario_stem:
Saffron Lane Spice Merchants is a sole trader business owned by Priya Nair, grinding small-batch, hand-blended spices. With 3 part-time assistants it sells through 40 independent delicatessens and online, generating $180,000 yearly with loyal customers.

A supermarket offers a 3-year exclusive contract for its 120 stores, but Priya must buy a $150,000 industrial grinder, triple output and hire 8 staff. She fears mass production would dilute quality and relying on one customer is risky.

questions.question_text: Define 'business growth'.
questions.model_answer: Business growth is the increase in the size of a business over time, such as higher sales, more output, more employees or more assets [2].

knowledge_max_2: increase in size of the business over time

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why some businesses choose to remain small.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To keep quality and customer loyalty [k], as Priya Nair's hand-blended spices sold through 40 delicatessens earn $180,000 a year upheld by loyal customers [app]. Reason 2: To stay in owner's control [k], as remaining a sole trader with 3 part-time assistants keeps decision-making simple and avoids the $150,000 risk of mass expansion [app].

knowledge_max_2: small firms can focus on quality/customer loyalty/niche markets
owner retains control/avoids complexity and risk of growth

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Saffron Lane Spice Merchants of achieving growth.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher sales and revenue [k], as a 3-year contract supplying 120 stores would multiply the $180,000 annual sales well beyond current levels [app], sharply raising profit and allowing investment in new products [an]. Benefit 2: Greater economies of scale [k], as tripling output with an industrial grinder would spread fixed costs like rent and wages over more kilograms of spice [app], lowering average cost per kilogram and improving competitiveness [an].

knowledge_max_2: growth enables economies of scale (lower average cost)
analysis_max_2: fixed costs spread over more units, lowering average cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Saffron Lane Spice Merchants should accept the supermarket contract or remain a small specialist business? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the 3-year contract to supply 120 stores would transform the business [k], turning $180,000 annual sales into national volumes and justifying the $150,000 industrial grinder and 8 new staff [app], giving stable revenue and a platform for future growth [an]. However, mass production could dilute the hand-blended quality loyal customers love [k], risking the customer loyalty that supports $180,000 a year of sales [app], and over-dependence on one supermarket means losing the contract would leave spare capacity and a $150,000 asset [an]. Overall, remaining small is the wiser decision for now [eval], because protecting quality and independence better suits a sole trader with 40 delicatessen customers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: large contracts raise revenue and enable economies of scale
growth risks quality dilution and over-dependence on one customer
analysis_max_2: national volume raises revenue and spreads costs
quality dilution and single-customer risk threaten the niche brand
evaluation_max_2: weighs large-scale revenue against brand/quality risk and independence, favouring remaining small at this stage

scenario_stem:
Northgate Freight Services is a private limited haulage firm with 6 depots and 260 drivers. Last year's 46-page handbook and weekly emails covered safety rules. After a driver missed a loading note and $30,000 of goods were rejected, the board debated new rules.

The $18,000 handbook reaches all drivers but may go unread; 30-minute depot briefings at $25 per driver give feedback but clash with night runs. Insurers want proof all 260 were informed. It decides from June.

questions.question_text: Define 'written communication'.
questions.model_answer: Written communication is the exchange of information through written words, such as letters, emails, reports and handbooks [2].

knowledge_max_2: exchange of information through written words

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of written communication for Northgate Freight Services.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Permanent record [k]; the 46-page handbook and weekly emails prove to insurers that all 260 drivers received the safety rules [app]. Advantage 2: Consistent message [k]; every driver at the 6 depots reads the same fuel-saving and loading instructions regardless of shift pattern [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of written communication for Northgate Freight Services and how it could overcome each.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: No immediate feedback [k]; drivers cannot ask about the revised loading rules electronically, so misunderstanding like the missed loading note goes unnoticed [app], which is why a short question-and-answer session should follow each handbook update [an]. Limitation 2: Risk of being ignored [k]; a 46-page handbook translated into several languages is unlikely to be read in full [app], so key rules should be summarised on one page with a signature or reply email to confirm receipt [an].

knowledge_max_2: no immediate feedback / cannot ask questions
may not be read / ignored / too long
analysis_max_2: one-page summary with confirmation proves receipt

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Freight Services should rely on written communication rather than verbal depot briefings for the revised rules? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Written communication is the stronger primary method [k]; the $18,000 handbook gives insurers evidence that all 260 drivers received the rules, and reaches night-shift drivers that briefings miss [app]. However, the $30,000 rejected load shows written messages can simply be overlooked [k], and briefings at $25 per driver cost $6,500 per session but guarantee understanding and instant feedback [app]. A short briefing after each handbook update would close the feedback gap for high-risk rules [an], but weekly briefings for all content would be an expensive recurring cost for 6 depots [an]. On balance, Northgate should rely on written communication as the primary method with brief, targeted briefings for the safety-critical rules [eval], because the insurer evidence requirement outweighs the convenience of verbal sessions for 260 dispersed drivers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: written gives permanent record / insurer evidence
written can be overlooked / briefings guarantee understanding
analysis_max_2: targeted briefings close the feedback gap for critical rules
weekly briefings are a high recurring cost across 6 depots
evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: written primary plus targeted briefings
justified by insurer evidence and 260 dispersed drivers

scenario_stem:
Summit Grill Co is a private limited company in Country X making charcoal barbecues. It sold 9,500 units at $95 each, earning $902,500, and employs 31 workers. Advertisements claim the grills are smoke-free, but tests found smoke and the regulator calls the claim misleading.

The board must choose: keep the slogan and contest the regulator, risking a $50,000 fine, or withdraw the campaign and run honest adverts, costing $12,000 to reprint and redesign packaging to build trust.

questions.question_text: Define 'misleading promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Advertising, packaging or other promotion that is false or exaggerated, or leaves out important information, so consumers are deceived about a product's qualities, price or performance [2].

knowledge_max_2: promotion that is false or exaggerated
leaves out important information so consumers are deceived

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Summit Grill Co must obey legal controls over marketing.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Misleading claims can trigger a fine of up to $50,000 [k], more than four times the $12,000 cost of an honest campaign [app]. Reason 2: Legal controls protect consumers from being deceived [k], so complying preserves the public trust on which $902,500 of annual barbecue sales depend [app].

knowledge_max_2: legal controls prevent false/misleading claims to consumers
compliance avoids fines and reputational damage
application_max_2: $50,000 fine vs $12,000 cost of honest campaign
$902,500 annual revenue depends on consumer trust

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Summit Grill Co could face if it keeps the smoke-free claim.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The regulator could impose a $50,000 fine [k], equivalent to roughly 526 barbecues at $95 each [app], cancelling a large slice of annual profit [an]. Problem 2: Customers who discover the smoke-free claim is false may stop trusting the brand [k], cutting the 9,500 units sold last year [app], damaging reputation and making an honest relaunch far harder [an].

knowledge_max_2: regulators can fine businesses for misleading promotion
misleading claims destroy consumer trust and loyalty
application_max_2: 9,500 units sold last year at risk
analysis_max_2: fine wipes out profit on hundreds of units
lost trust cuts sales and complicates relaunch

questions.question_text: Do you think Summit Grill Co should withdraw the smoke-free campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Withdrawing the campaign and launching an honest low-smoke advertisement costs $12,000 [k], affordable against $902,500 of revenue and removing the threat of a $50,000 fine [app], which is more than four times the relaunch cost [an]. Keeping the slogan would save $12,000 today [k], but Summit Grill would risk the fine, possible legal action and a collapse in customer trust across its 31-worker operation [app], cutting into sales of 9,500 units [an]. Overall, withdrawing is clearly the right decision because honest promotion with redesigned packaging builds the trust and loyalty needed to protect future sales [eval]; the $12,000 is far cheaper than the regulator's fine and the long-term cost of a deceived customer base [eval].

knowledge_max_2: withdrawing and correcting misleading claims restores trust
keeping misleading claims risks fines and reputational damage
analysis_max_2: fine is over four times the relaunch cost; withdrawal is low risk
keeping the claim risks sales collapse and harder recovery
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation
honest low-smoke positioning builds long-term trust and loyalty

scenario_stem:
Stonebridge Builders Merchants is a sole trader supplier of cement, blocks and timber to 320 trade customers. It stores 260 tonnes in a warehouse rented at $2,400 a month, holding $210,000 of goods and turning over about 300 tonnes monthly.

The supplier offers 8% off orders above 900 tonnes, but cement older than 90 days hardens. Extra security costs $1,150 monthly, and $74,000 cash would delay a $28,000 forklift. The owner chooses the discount or smaller orders.

questions.question_text: Define 'obsolescence'.
questions.model_answer: Obsolescence is the process by which items lose usefulness or value because they become outdated or spoiled, for example cement hardening if stored too long [2].

knowledge_max_2: caused by becoming outdated or spoiled

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Stonebridge might accept the 8% bulk-buy discount.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: An 8% discount on 900 tonnes lowers the price of the merchant's key input for its 320 trade customers [k], improving margins or allowing it to pass savings on as sharper trade prices [app]. Reason 2: Buying in bulk reduces the frequency of deliveries and admin per tonne [k], freeing staff to serve trade counter customers during busy mornings [app].

knowledge_max_2: fewer, larger deliveries reduce admin and handling

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of holding 900 tonnes of cement at Stonebridge.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Extra security and insurance cost $1,150 a month on top of $2,400 a month of warehouse rent [k], so carrying the larger stock adds $3,550 a month of holding costs [app], which erodes the 8% discount if cement turns over slowly [an]. Problem 2: Cement older than 90 days hardens and must be written off [k], so stock bought in bulk could spoil before the merchant sells through its usual 300 tonnes a month [app], turning part of the $74,000 cash investment into waste [an].

knowledge_max_2: storage, security and insurance costs rise with stock size
perishable inventories can spoil and be written off
application_max_2: $1,150 extra security and insurance / $2,400 rent / $3,550 total
cement older than 90 days / 300 tonnes each month / $74,000 cash tied up
analysis_max_2: holding costs erode the 8% discount if turnover slows

questions.question_text: Do you think Stonebridge should accept the 8% bulk-buy discount? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the discount on 900 tonnes could cut the cost of cement for 320 trade customers and lift margins [k], and with turnover of around 300 tonnes each month, the store could clear 90 days' worth of stock if sales hold up [app]. However, extra security and insurance of $1,150 a month plus $2,400 rent make $3,550 a month of carrying costs [k], and cement older than 90 days hardens and must be written off [app]. The discount only pays if sales stay near 300 tonnes a month and stock moves within 90 days [an], but a slow quarter would leave Stonebridge paying $3,550 monthly for unsellable cement, while $74,000 of cash tied up would delay the $28,000 forklift replacement [an]. On balance, Stonebridge should accept the discount only with phased deliveries [eval]; if the supplier cannot split the order, it should keep smaller orders rather than risk spoilage [eval].

knowledge_max_2: bulk discount improves margin if turnover is steady
holding costs and spoilage risk can wipe out the saving
application_max_2: 8% discount on 900 tonnes / 320 trade customers / 300 tonnes a month / 90 days
$1,150 security and insurance + $2,400 rent = $3,550 a month / $74,000 cash tied up / $28,000 forklift
analysis_max_2: discount viable only if sales hold near 300 tonnes a month and stock moves within 90 days
slow quarter leaves unsellable cement and $3,550 monthly costs
evaluation_max_2: weighs 8% discount and margin gain against $3,550 monthly carrying costs and 90-day spoilage risk
justified recommendation for phased deliveries or smaller orders

scenario_stem:
Wrenfield Cider Ltd is a private limited company producing apple cider, with revenue of $4.1 million, gross profit margin of 39%, ROCE of 11% and a current ratio of 1.7. The board considers buying rival Fenwick Orchards Ltd for $2.6 million.

Fenwick's accounts show revenue of $3.2 million, gross margin 44%, ROCE 16% on $1.6 million capital employed and a current ratio of 1.4, but include a one-off $90,000 land sale. Its figures are 12 months old and inventories are valued differently.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio is a liquidity ratio that compares a business's current assets with its current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities [2].

knowledge_max_2: Compares current assets with current liabilities
Calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fenwick's higher ratios might not prove it is the better buy.
questions.model_answer: First, one-off items can flatter a single year's ratios [k]. Fenwick's 16% ROCE was helped by a $90,000 one-off land sale, so underlying profit is nearer $166,000; $2.6 million is more than fifteen years of that recurring profit [app]. Second, different accounting policies distort comparisons [k]. Fenwick values inventories on a different basis and its figures are already 12 months old, so its 44% gross profit margin and 1.4 current ratio are not directly comparable with Wrenfield's 39% and 1.7 accounts [app].

knowledge_max_2: One-off items can distort a single year's ratios
application_max_2: Reference to the $90,000 one-off land sale within the 16% ROCE; underlying profit nearer $166,000
Reference to Fenwick's inventory method and figures being 12 months old; 44% vs 39% gross profit margin; 1.4 vs 1.7 current ratio

questions.question_text: Explain two other checks Wrenfield should make before buying Fenwick.
questions.model_answer: First, Wrenfield should inspect Fenwick's physical assets and stock [k]. A current ratio of 1.4 tells nothing about condition; ageing cider, obsolete labels or tired bottling kit would force post-purchase write-downs, eroding the $2.6 million price [app]. Overstated assets would mean Wrenfield pays for value that no longer exists [an]. Second, Wrenfield should review Fenwick's customer contracts and forward orders [k]. Revenue of $3.2 million and a 44% gross profit margin mean little if pub and retail accounts are uncontracted, paying late, or reflecting a fading local cider trend captured in the 12-month-old figures [app]. Losing a key account after completion would cut the profit base that justified the price [an].

knowledge_max_2: Inspect physical assets and stock quality
Review customer contracts and forward orders
application_max_2: Reference to the current ratio of 1.4 and the $2.6 million price
Reference to revenue of $3.2 million at a 44% gross profit margin and 12-month-old figures
analysis_max_2: Chain from overstated stock to post-purchase write-downs
Chain from lost accounts to a collapsed profit rationale

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenfield Cider Ltd should buy Fenwick Orchards Ltd for $2.6 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying would remove a rival and add $3.2 million of revenue at a 44% gross profit margin to Wrenfield's $4.1 million, 39% operation [k]. Even with the $90,000 one-off stripped out, leaving nearer $166,000 of recurring profit, synergies in buying apples, bottling and distribution could lift both margins and make the $2.6 million pay back faster [app]. If Wrenfield shares distribution routes and negotiates bulk supply, the deal could raise its own 39% margin towards Fenwick's 44% [an]. However, Fenwick's figures are 12 months old, inventories are valued differently, and its 16% ROCE rests partly on the $90,000 land sale [k]. Paying $2.6 million on unaudited, mismatched evidence risks overpaying by a wide margin, with limited recourse after completion [app]. A bad deal could tie up Wrenfield's cash for years, weaken its own current ratio of 1.7 and leave it exposed to poor harvests [an]. questions.model_answer: Barrier 1: Staff without access [k]; 18% of staff, about 252 people, have no smartphone or home computer [app], so noticeboards and printed memos must remain for them alongside the app [an]. Barrier 2: IT failure [k]; a 6-hour outage delayed 38 deliveries worth $22,000 [app], so backup paper procedures and offline access to critical information are essential during week-one rollout [an].

knowledge_max_2: lack of staff access / digital divide
analysis_max_2: keep noticeboards and memos for those excluded
offline backups / paper fallback protects operations

questions.question_text: Do you think Cardinal Retail Group should replace noticeboards with a staff intranet? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An intranet reaches all 1,400 staff instantly [k], cuts $7,200 a year of printing and proves who read each announcement across 30 stores and 2 distribution centres [app]. However, about 252 staff (18%) have no smartphone or home computer [k], and a 6-hour IT outage already delayed $22,000 of deliveries, so removing noticeboards entirely would silence a fifth of the workforce and leave no fallback [app]. The intranet's $1,500 monthly cost is modest once set up, but only if most staff actually use it [an], while verbal huddles cost nothing yet cannot prove receipt [an]. On balance, Cardinal should install the intranet but keep noticeboards and huddles for the 252 excluded staff [eval], because replacing noticeboards outright ignores the 18% without access and the outage risk shown in practice [eval].
