removing noticeboards excludes 18% / no outage fallback
analysis_max_2: value only if most staff actually use the intranet
huddles cost nothing but cannot prove receipt
evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: intranet plus retained noticeboards and huddles
justified by the 18% excluded and the outage risk

scenario_stem:
Hearthside Foods is a private limited company in Country X producing chilled ready meals sold through 9 supermarkets. It sold 250,000 meals at $5.40 each, earning $1.35 million. It will enter Country U, three times larger, via a distributor.

The manager must devise the marketing mix: a premium range at $6.80 for affluent urban households in specialist shops, or a family value range at $4.40 for price-sensitive shoppers in large supermarket chains. The distributor favours family value.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing mix'.
questions.model_answer: The combination of elements a business uses to market its products, usually product, price, place and promotion, to achieve its marketing objectives [2].

knowledge_max_2: combination of elements used to market products

questions.question_text: Explain two elements of the marketing mix Hearthside Foods should consider for Country U.
questions.model_answer: Element 1: Price — the premium option charges $6.80 per meal while the family value option charges $4.40 [k], and Country U shoppers are reported to be price-sensitive, so pricing must match the target segment [app]. Element 2: Place — the meals could go through specialist shops or large supermarket chains [k], with the family value range gaining reach across a market three times the size of Country X [app].

knowledge_max_2: price must reflect costs and what the target segment will pay
place/distribution must reach the target customers
application_max_2: $6.80 premium vs $4.40 family value / price-sensitive shoppers
specialist shops vs supermarket chains / market three times the size

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Hearthside Foods could face entering Country U.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country U shoppers are price-sensitive [k], so premium $6.80 meals may sell slowly and stock could build up in the distributor's freezers [app], cutting margins and potentially ending the trial with unsold inventory [an]. Problem 2: Relying on a single import distributor [k] gives that partner control over pricing and shelf placement [app], so Hearthside loses direct contact with Country U customers and may struggle to build its brand or gather feedback [an].

knowledge_max_2: price-sensitivity limits demand for premium prices abroad
intermediaries control distribution and customer access
application_max_2: $6.80 premium meals may not sell to price-sensitive shoppers
analysis_max_2: excess stock and markdowns destroy trial economics
weak brand-building and no direct customer feedback

questions.question_text: Do you think Hearthside Foods should launch the premium or the family value range in Country U? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The family value range at $4.40 per meal [k] matches Country U's price-sensitive shoppers and the distributor's plan to list in supermarket chains [app], giving the best chance of high volume in a market three times the size of Country X [an]. The premium range at $6.80 [k] protects margins and suits affluent urban households, but the distributor doubts demand at that price and freezer stock could pile up unsold [app], forcing markdowns that destroy the premium positioning [an]. Overall, launching family value is the sensible first move because it maximises reach and builds operational scale in Country U, generating cash and brand recognition [eval]; a premium gift line can follow once the brand is established [eval].

knowledge_max_2: family value range fits price-sensitive mass markets
premium range protects margins but limits volume
application_max_2: $4.40 family value / distributor favours it / supermarket chains
$6.80 premium / affluent urban households / doubts over demand
analysis_max_2: family value maximises volume and reach at scale
premium risks unsold stock and markdowns
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options
sensible sequencing suggested (value range first, premium later)

scenario_stem:
Polar Toy Co is a private limited company selling educational toys in 9 stores. Festive sales reached $520,000, but in week 1 of December it ran out of its 3 best-selling puzzles and action figures, losing $86,000, while other lines needed 20% cuts in January.

Managers want to triple the order to $240,000, storing surplus in 2 distribution hubs at $3,100 monthly each for three months. The finance director worries cash stays tied up until January; the board decides this month.

questions.question_text: Outline two reasons why businesses hold inventories.
questions.model_answer: Businesses hold inventories to avoid production or sales stopping when supplies are delayed [1], and to meet sudden or seasonal increases in customer demand [1].

knowledge_max_2: avoids interruption to production or sales if supplies are delayed
meets sudden or seasonal increases in demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Polar Toy Co might triple its festive inventory order to $240,000.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It ran out of its 3 best-selling puzzles and action figures in week 1 last December [k], so a $240,000 order should keep the 9 stores stocked through the peak [app]. Reason 2: Lost sales were estimated at $86,000 last year [k], so extra inventory should recover far more than the $3,100 per month storage cost of the 2 distribution hubs [app].

knowledge_max_2: inventory prevents stockouts during peak demand
avoids losing sales from running out of best-sellers
application_max_2: 3 best-selling puzzles and action figures / week 1 / $86,000 lost sales

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with tripling the festive inventory order.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Cash would be tied up in $240,000 of stock until January [k], leaving less money for January costs while each of the 2 distribution hubs adds $3,100 per month [app], raising the risk of a short-term cash shortfall [an]. Problem 2: Unsold toys may need 20% price cuts to clear [k], and lines that did not sell last year sat in storage after the season ended [app], cutting the margin on the whole festive range [an].

knowledge_max_2: cash tied up in unsold inventory / storage costs add up
unsold stock may need discounting to clear
application_max_2: $240,000 tied up until January / 2 distribution hubs at $3,100 per month each
20% price cuts / last year's unsold lines / $520,000 festive sales
analysis_max_2: discounting erodes margins on the festive range

questions.question_text: Do you think Polar Toy Co should triple the festive inventory order? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Tripling the order to $240,000 would protect the week-1 peak that cost an estimated $86,000 of lost sales [k] and keep the 9 stores stocked in their 3 best-selling puzzles and action figures, supporting festive sales above last year's $520,000 [app]. However, tying up $240,000 until January strains cash flow just when the 2 distribution hubs add $3,100 per month each [k], and unsold lines would need 20% price cuts to clear [app]. If demand matches last year, the extra stock sells and cash recycles quickly [an], but over-ordering leaves the hubs full of discounted toys and exposes the cash warning [an]. On balance, Polar Toy should raise the order but by a smaller, forecast-based amount rather than tripling blindly [eval]; it should set reorder triggers and cap the order at predicted best-seller demand [eval].

knowledge_max_2: larger order prevents stockouts in best-sellers
larger order strains cash flow and risks discounting
application_max_2: $240,000 order / $86,000 lost sales / 3 best-selling puzzles and action figures / 9 stores
week 1 peak / $520,000 last year / 2 distribution hubs at $3,100 per month / 20% price cuts
analysis_max_2: if demand matches last year, cash recycles quickly
over-ordering forces discounting and strains cash
evaluation_max_2: weighs $86,000 stockout risk and $520,000 festive revenue against $240,000 tied-up cash and 20% discounting
justified recommendation to raise, not triple, the order, based on sales forecasts

scenario_stem:
Amberfield Fabrics Plc is a public limited company weaving fabrics at its Redmile mill, with 480 staff. To fund $3 million of new weaving machinery through a share issue, Country X rules require its accounts to be published for investors.

Option A publishes full accounts in a prospectus, showing revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, gross margin 34% and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares. Option B publishes minimum audited statements, keeping details confidential but risking a weak response.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'published accounts'.
questions.model_answer: Published accounts are the financial statements a limited company must make publicly available, showing its performance and financial position, so shareholders, lenders, employees, customers and the government can assess them [2].

knowledge_max_2: Financial statements a limited company must make publicly available
Used by shareholders, lenders, employees, customers and the government

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Amberfield Fabrics Plc's accounts are published.
questions.model_answer: First, publication is a legal requirement for a listed company [k]. Under Country X rules, a Plc on the Stock Exchange raising $3 million through a share issue must publish audited accounts so the offer is transparent to investors [app]. Second, publication lets stakeholders assess the business [k]. Investors can see revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a 34% gross profit margin and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares ($1.25 million), judging whether the new machinery justifies subscribing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Legal requirement for a listed Plc
Transparency so stakeholders can assess the business
application_max_2: Reference to $3 million share issue and Country X Stock Exchange rules
Reference to revenue $12 million, profit $1.5 million, 34% margin, 5c on 25 million shares = $1.25 million

questions.question_text: Explain two stakeholders, other than shareholders, who use Amberfield Fabrics Plc's published accounts and why.
questions.model_answer: First, employees use published accounts to judge job security and pay prospects [k]. With 480 staff at the Redmile mill and profit of $1.5 million on revenue of $12 million, the workforce can see the business is profitable and funded for new machinery, shaping wage negotiations and retention of skilled weavers [app]. If the accounts instead showed falling profit, staff could anticipate restructuring and plan accordingly [an]. Second, the government uses published accounts to assess tax and approve support [k]. Corporation tax on the $1.5 million profit is computed from these figures, and agencies licensing the machinery or granting support rely on the same audited numbers [app]. Accurate reporting funds public services and keeps Amberfield compliant, avoiding penalties and reputational damage [an].

knowledge_max_2: Employees use them to judge job security and pay
Government uses them to assess tax and approve grants or licences
application_max_2: Reference to 480 staff at the Redmile mill; profit $1.5 million on revenue of $12 million
Reference to corporation tax computed on $1.5 million profit and machinery licensing
analysis_max_2: Chain from visible profit to wage negotiations and retention
Chain from accurate reporting to compliance, public revenue and avoiding penalties

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfield Fabrics Plc should publish full accounts as part of the share issue prospectus? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Publishing full accounts gives investors the evidence to subscribe for the $3 million issue [k]. Transparent figures, showing revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a gross profit margin of 34% and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares worth $1.25 million, build trust, improving uptake and reducing the risk the issue fails [app]. Strong disclosure could attract institutional investors, securing the weaving machinery sooner and lifting output, sales and the share price [an]. However, full disclosure exposes margins and cost structures to rivals [k]. Rivals could undercut Amberfield or poach customers once the 34% margin and $1.5 million profit are public, and customers may press for lower prices on that evidence [app]. The competitive damage could exceed the financing benefit, making Option B's minimum publication tempting despite a weaker investor response [an]. Overall, I think Amberfield should publish the full accounts [eval]. As a listed Plc it already publishes audited statements, and the $3 million issue needs investor confidence; margins on shirting fabrics are hard to hide in a public offer anyway, and the certainty of funding outweighs the extra visibility, though customer lists should stay confidential [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Full accounts give investors evidence and build trust
Full disclosure exposes margins and cost structures to rivals
application_max_2: Reference to revenue $12 million, profit $1.5 million, 34% margin, 5c dividend on 25 million shares ($1.25 million)
Reference to rivals or customers using published margins to undercut or renegotiate
analysis_max_2: Chain from disclosure to investor uptake to secured machinery and growth
Chain from visibility to price pressure and competitive damage
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to publish in full
Weighs both options with stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Elmsgrove Apples is a private limited company apple grower in Country X, farming 45 hectares with 30 pickers. An import quota caps apples at 6,000 tonnes, lifting domestic prices from $1.40 to $1.85; revenue reached $1.1 million last season.

The ministry may raise the quota to 9,000 tonnes to cut prices. Supermarkets want it for lower prices and more choice, but Elmsgrove warns cheaper imports would flood the domestic market and force it to lay off 10 pickers. The owner must decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'domestic market'.
questions.model_answer: The domestic market is the market for goods and services sold within the business's own country, such as apples sold to buyers in Country X [2].

knowledge_max_2: the market for goods sold within the business's own country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the apple import quota for Elmsgrove Apples.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Capping imports at 6,000 tonnes a year restricts foreign competition [k], so domestic apple prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg [app]. Benefit 2: Higher prices lifted Elmsgrove's revenue to $1.1 million last season [k], helping it keep 30 seasonal pickers employed [app].

application_max_2: 6,000 tonnes cap / prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg
$1.1 million revenue last season / 30 seasonal pickers

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of the import quota for consumers in Country X.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: With imports capped at 6,000 tonnes a year [k], apple supply is restricted and prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg [app], so households spend more on fruit [an]. Disadvantage 2: Quotas reduce consumer choice [k]; shops stock fewer foreign apple varieties [app], leaving shoppers with less variety outside the season [an].

knowledge_max_2: supply is restricted by the quota
application_max_2: 6,000 tonnes cap / prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg
fewer foreign apple varieties in shops

questions.question_text: Do you think Elmsgrove Apples should support the ministry's proposal to raise the apple import quota from 6,000 to 9,000 tonnes? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Supporting the higher quota would raise import competition and push prices down [k]; raising the cap to 9,000 tonnes could cut prices back from $1.85 towards $1.40 per kg [app], eroding Elmsgrove's $1.1 million revenue [an]. Opposing the rise protects Elmsgrove's prices and its 30 seasonal pickers [k], keeping the quota at 6,000 tonnes as it stands today [app], but it looks self-interested while consumers pay more and get less choice [an]. Overall, Elmsgrove should oppose the quota increase, because its business depends on the $1.85 per kg price and $1.1 million revenue, and the 9,000-tonne cap could cost 10 pickers their jobs [eval], although the owner could offer to support a smaller increase in exchange for a phased rise [eval].

knowledge_max_2: higher quota increases import competition / pushes prices down
opposing the rise protects the grower's prices and pickers
application_max_2: raising the cap to 9,000 tonnes / prices back from $1.85 towards $1.40 per kg
$1.1 million revenue / 30 seasonal pickers / 10 pickers at risk / 6,000 tonnes today
analysis_max_2: looks self-interested / consumers pay more with the quota kept
evaluation_max_2: weighs supporting against opposing the quota rise; justified recommendation with figures

scenario_stem:
Goldenharvest Foods Plc is a public limited company producing dried pasta at 2 factories. It employs 850 staff, reported $46 million sales and has $30 million capital employed; 35 per cent of durum wheat is imported.

The board weighs buying Roma Pasta Co, with 210 staff and $9 million sales, for $12 million, or Durum Plains Wheat Farm, 1,800 hectares, for $9 million, securing supply for 10 years. It will recommend one to shareholders.

questions.question_text: Define 'integration'.
questions.model_answer: Integration is when 2 or more businesses join together or one buys another to form a larger single business [2].

knowledge_max_2: businesses joining/merging or one taking over another
creates external growth and a larger single business

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Goldenharvest Foods Plc of horizontal integration.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Instant market share [k], as buying Roma Pasta Co would add its $9 million of sales to Goldenharvest's $46 million [app]. Advantage 2: Removing a rival [k], as taking over Roma Pasta Co eliminates a direct competitor for durum pasta customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration adds market share/scale instantly
horizontal integration removes a competitor at the same stage

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Goldenharvest Foods Plc of external growth.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Faster expansion [k], as either acquisition adds capacity in weeks instead of the years needed to build a third factory [app], protecting market position while demand grows [an]. Benefit 2: Stronger bargaining power [k], as with 850 staff and $46 million sales plus an acquired rival or farm, Goldenharvest negotiates better deals on inputs and distribution [app], lowering average costs across both portfolios [an].

knowledge_max_2: external growth is fast (speed of expansion)
analysis_max_2: speed protects market share sooner than organic growth
larger scale lowers average costs and improves negotiating position

questions.question_text: Do you think Goldenharvest Foods Plc should acquire Roma Pasta Co or Durum Plains Wheat Farm? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Acquiring Roma Pasta Co for $12 million would add 210 staff and $9 million of sales [k], giving immediate horizontal integration and removing Goldenharvest's closest rival, lifting sales from $46 million towards $55 million [app], strengthening market leadership and sharing best practice across both factories [an]. However, acquiring Durum Plains Wheat Farm for $9 million would secure 35 per cent of durum imports from 1,800 hectares of owned land [k], cutting exposure to volatile overseas prices for the next 10 years [app], protecting margins and supply security [an]. Overall, Roma Pasta Co is the better buy [eval], because Goldenharvest already buys most wheat on contract and a 10-year supply deal could be negotiated instead of a $9 million purchase [eval].

knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration adds market share/removes rival quickly
backward vertical integration secures supply/price stability
analysis_max_2: rival purchase boosts market share and leadership
farm purchase secures supply and cuts price risk
evaluation_max_2: weighs horizontal vs backward vertical options, favouring the rival purchase on cost-effective growth grounds, given contracts can secure wheat instead

scenario_stem:
Brightstack Software is a private limited company that grew from 40 to 85 staff in 3 years, with $3.2m revenue. Turnover hit 22% and 3 product launches slipped. Founders send one-way email memos.

The director proposes monthly meetings, an anonymous suggestion box and surveys costing $9,000 yearly. Meetings cost $4,400 a session but build feedback; memos are free but ignored. Two founders resist before 20 new hires start in July.

questions.question_text: Define 'two-way communication'.
questions.model_answer: Two-way communication is communication in which the receiver can respond and give feedback to the sender [2].

knowledge_max_2: receiver can respond / feedback to sender

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of two-way communication for Brightstack Software.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Feedback highlights problems early [k]; pulse surveys would have surfaced the training needs behind the 3 slipped product launches [app]. Benefit 2: Staff feel valued [k]; giving 85 developers a voice could help reverse the 22% staff turnover [app].

knowledge_max_2: staff feel valued / higher motivation and retention

questions.question_text: Explain two barriers to two-way communication at Brightstack Software and how each could be overcome.
questions.model_answer: Barrier 1: Fear of the founders [k]; junior developers may not challenge two founders who favour email memos [app], so anonymous suggestion boxes and surveys let staff speak safely, surfacing problems early [an]. Barrier 2: Time pressure [k]; 85 busy developers lose 1 hour per monthly meeting, $4,400 per session [app], so keeping sessions short, focused and followed by written summaries protects coding time while still inviting feedback [an].

knowledge_max_2: hierarchy / fear of seniors silences staff
application_max_2: two founders favour email memos / anonymous suggestion box
analysis_max_2: anonymous channels let staff speak safely
short focused sessions plus written summary protect coding time

questions.question_text: Do you think Brightstack Software should introduce monthly two-way meetings and surveys rather than keep one-way email memos? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Two-way communication fixes the root problem [k]; with 22% turnover and 3 slipped launches, anonymous feedback would surface training needs and rebuild trust before 20 new hires arrive in July [app]. However, monthly meetings cost $4,400 per session plus $9,000 a year for surveys [k], and two founders argue email preserves coding time across a team grown from 40 to 85 in 3 years [app]. Meetings with a written summary give every voice a route into decisions [an], while memos remain free and fast but leave staff unheard and jumping ship [an]. On balance, Brightstack should introduce the meetings and surveys [eval], because reversing 22% turnover and protecting the July intake outweighs a $4,400 monthly time cost, with memos kept for routine updates only [eval].

knowledge_max_2: two-way fixes root problems / feedback channels
meetings cost staff time / memos are free and fast
application_max_2: 22% turnover / 3 slipped launches / 20 new hires / July
analysis_max_2: written summaries give every voice a route into decisions
evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: adopt meetings and surveys
justified against turnover, launch slips and 20 new hires; memos for routine updates

scenario_stem:
Ironwood Smokehouse is a private limited company in Country X producing smoked sausages and cured meats sold through 11 delicatessens. Revenue was $420,000 from 168,000 packs at $2.50, and it employs 14 workers. An importer in Country S is interested.

The importer offers 20,000 packs a year at $2.20, but exporting costs $90,000 to set up and needs local labelling. Owners must weigh this against $30,000 on a domestic loyalty scheme and tasting evenings with delicatessen partners.

questions.question_text: Define 'brand loyalty'.
questions.model_answer: The tendency of customers to keep buying the same brand repeatedly rather than switching to rivals, usually because of trust, satisfaction or attachment to it [2].

knowledge_max_2: customers repeatedly buy the same brand
rather than switching to rival brands / because of trust or satisfaction

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a domestic loyalty scheme could help Ironwood Smokehouse build customer loyalty.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Points or discounts for repeat purchases [k] reward the habit behind 168,000 pack sales a year [app]. Way 2: Tasting evenings for loyal customers [k] build personal relationships and give shoppers direct reasons to keep choosing the brand at $2.50 per pack over rivals [app].

knowledge_max_2: events build relationships and deepen attachment to the brand
application_max_2: $2.50 per pack / shoppers choose it over rivals

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ironwood Smokehouse could face if it exports to Country S.

Problem 2: The importer offers just $2.20 per pack [k], 30 cents below the domestic price of $2.50 [app], so margins thin exactly when new-market costs rise, risking losses on every export order [an].

knowledge_max_2: entering foreign markets requires significant upfront investment
exporters often accept lower prices/margins from intermediaries

analysis_max_2: cash drained before overseas sales begin
thin margins risk losses on export volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironwood Smokehouse should export to Country S or invest in a domestic loyalty scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting offers 20,000 packs a year at $2.20, about $44,000 in extra revenue [k], opening a new market beyond the 11 delicatessens [app], but the $90,000 setup would take more than 2 years of export revenue to recover [an]. The loyalty scheme costs just $30,000 [k] and should raise repeat purchases from the existing 168,000-pack base while deepening relationships with delicatessen partners [app], delivering steadier returns at lower risk [an]. Overall, investing in the domestic loyalty scheme is the better recommendation now [eval], because protecting and deepening the local 168,000-pack franchise is cheaper, faster and builds exactly the relationships that would make exporting viable later [eval].

loyalty scheme retains and deepens existing customers more cheaply

analysis_max_2: export investment recovers in over 2 years at $44,000 a year
loyalty delivers steadier returns at lower risk
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options

scenario_stem:
Silkharbour Garments Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making 420,000 shirts, exporting 70% to Asia and Europe. The dollar strengthened 14%, pushing margins from 11% to 6%, and Asian orders fell 18%.

The board weighs moving one of 3 factories to Country Y, where the currency is 20% weaker and wages 35% lower, against keeping all 3 in Country X and renegotiating. Staying retains domestic suppliers delivering within 3 days; the chief executive must choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'legal environment'.
questions.model_answer: The legal environment refers to the laws and regulations of a country, such as employment, safety and product standards, which a business relocating abroad must comply with [2].

knowledge_max_2: laws and regulations of a country a business must follow
includes employment, safety and product standards

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Silkharbour might relocate one factory to Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The currency in Country Y is 20% weaker [k], which would make shirts made there cheaper for Asia and Europe buyers and help restore margins lost when the dollar strengthened by 14% [app]. Reason 2: Wages are 35% lower in Country Y [k], significantly cutting labour cost on the relocated factory's share of the 420,000 shirts produced each year [app].

knowledge_max_2: weaker foreign currency lowers export prices
application_max_2: 20% weaker currency / 14% dollar strengthening / margins 11% to 6%
35% lower wages / 420,000 shirts a year / Asia and Europe buyers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of relocating one factory to Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Moving one of 3 factories means new permits, quality checks and management systems in Country Y [k], which could disrupt the 3-day domestic supplier deliveries and shipments to Asia and Europe buyers [app], risking penalties under existing buyer contracts [an]. Problem 2: The dollar's 14% strengthening may reverse [k], so relocating could prove premature if the currency falls back and export competitiveness returns [app], leaving the new factory underused with higher fixed costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: relocation disrupts supply chains and compliance
exchange rates can reverse, making relocation premature

questions.question_text: Do you think Silkharbour should relocate one factory to Country Y? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relocating one factory would let Silkharbour produce in a currency 20% weaker with wages 35% lower, directly countering the 14% dollar strengthening that squeezed margins from 11% to 6% [k], and would help defend its 70% export share to Asia and Europe buyers [app]. However, keeping all 3 factories in Country X preserves 3-day delivery from domestic suppliers [k], and relocating before the dollar move proves lasting could freeze capital in a factory that later proves unnecessary [app]. The relocation hedges against further dollar strength and restores export competitiveness [an], but the 18% fall in Asian orders could reflect changing buyer demand, which a new factory would not fix [an]. 70% export share / 3 factories / 3-day domestic deliveries / 18% fall in Asian orders

evaluation_max_2: weighs currency and wage advantage against 3-day supply security and risk of premature move

scenario_stem:
Carrow Insulation Plc is a public limited company making insulation boards. Daljit Singh owns 40,000 shares. Over three years, accounts show revenue of $14 million, $15 million and $15.5 million, while profit fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million and $1.2 million.

ROCE fell from 17% to 12% to 8%, the dividend from 6c to 2c, and gross profit margin from 33% to 24%; the current ratio stayed at 1.6. Daljit must decide whether to sell now or hold for a turnaround plan.

questions.question_text: Define 'acid test ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio is a liquidity ratio measuring whether a business can pay its short-term debts from its most liquid assets, calculated as current assets minus inventories, divided by current liabilities [2].

knowledge_max_2: A liquidity ratio using the most liquid assets
Formula: (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Daljit Singh would compare Carrow Insulation Plc's accounts over three years before deciding to sell.
questions.model_answer: First, one year can flatter or alarm [k]. Profit of $1.2 million alone looks merely weak, but set against $2.4 million and $1.9 million in prior years it confirms a steady decline, with ROCE falling from 17% to 12% and then 8% over the same period [app]. Second, trends show whether the dividend is sustainable [k]. The dividend has been cut from 6c to 2c per share, so Daljit's income on 40,000 shares has fallen from $2,400 to $800 a year, and the three-year figures reveal whether this is a temporary dip or a structural decline [app].

knowledge_max_2: A single year can mislead; the trend shows direction
Reveals whether the dividend is sustainable
application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.4 million to $1.9 million to $1.2 million; ROCE 17% to 12% to 8%
Reference to dividend cut from 6c to 2c; income falling from $2,400 to $800 on 40,000 shares

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE alone to judge Carrow Insulation Plc's performance.
questions.model_answer: First, ROCE ignores liquidity completely [k]. Carrow's current ratio held at 1.6 across all three years, genuinely stable, but ROCE of 8% says nothing about whether cash or debtors are under strain underneath that figure [app]. A shareholder judging by ROCE alone could miss early warning signs that a steady 1.6 can still conceal [an]. Second, ROCE does not show where the decline comes from [k]. Revenue actually grew from $14 million to $15.5 million, yet the gross profit margin slid from 33% to 24%, growth at worse pricing rather than weak demand [app]. Blind to margin detail, ROCE could mislabel Carrow's problem as a market dip rather than a cost or pricing failure, misleading sell decisions [an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE ignores liquidity (current ratio steady at 1.6)
ROCE hides the source of decline (margin compression vs demand)
application_max_2: Reference to the current ratio holding at 1.6 in all three years and ROCE of 8%
Reference to revenue rising $14 million to $15.5 million while gross profit margin slid 33% to 24%
analysis_max_2: Chain from a ROCE-only view to missed liquidity stress
Chain from margin detail to a misdiagnosed problem

questions.question_text: Do you think Daljit Singh should sell his 40,000 shares? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Selling now crystallises the reality of a three-year slide: profit fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million and then $1.2 million, ROCE from 17% to 8%, and the dividend from 6c to 2c, cutting Daljit's income from $2,400 to $800 a year [k]. Waiting for the turnaround risks further losses if plant modernisation and cost control underperform, and the share price already trades well below last year's level [app]. Selling frees cash to redeploy into higher-yielding investments while the margin trend of 33% to 24% remains unproven [an]. However, holding has merit [k]. Carrow's current ratio has stayed at 1.6 for three years and revenue grew from $14 million to $15.5 million, showing demand is intact under a new chief executive with a modernisation plan [app]. If he restores the gross profit margin from 24% towards 33%, ROCE could recover towards double digits and the share price would reward patient holders [an]. Overall, I think Daljit should sell his 40,000 shares [eval]. Three consecutive years of falling profit, ROCE and dividend, with no turnaround evidence yet delivered, make holding speculation rather than investment; he can re-enter if the plan shows two quarters of margin recovery, but discipline says sell now at the current weak price [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Selling crystallises losses and cuts risk exposure
Holding has merit if the turnaround delivers
application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.4 million to $1.9 million to $1.2 million; ROCE 17% to 8%; dividend 6c to 2c; income $2,400 to $800
Reference to current ratio steady at 1.6, revenue $14 million to $15.5 million and margin 33% to 24%
analysis_max_2: Chain from an unproven margin trend to a weak share price
Chain from a successful turnaround to recovering ROCE and price
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to sell
Weighs both options with stem figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

scenario_stem:
Thornwick Paper Mills Ltd is a private limited company running a newsprint mill in Aldervale, Country Y. It employs 210 workers, produced 18,000 tonnes of newsprint and earned $7.2 million, as cheaper imports flooded the market.

Managing director Helen Marsh weighs a $2.4 million conversion of line two to recycled packaging board, selling at $1,150 per tonne against $780 for newsprint. Overseas demand may fall 15%, but board orders from 2 food makers are signed.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'added value'.
questions.model_answer: The difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the inputs used to make it, so the business earns more than it spends on materials and labour [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Thornwick Paper Mills might add value by converting to packaging board.

Reason 2: Diversifying reduces dependence on a shrinking newsprint market [k], since overseas demand is forecast to fall a further 15% next year while 2 regional food manufacturers have already signed board orders [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Thornwick Paper Mills of adding value through a recycled packaging board line.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher revenue per unit sold [k], because board earns $1,150 per tonne while newsprint earns $780 [app], so each tonne converted adds value and repays the $2.4 million investment faster [an]. questions.question_text: Do you think Thornwick Paper Mills should convert line two to recycled packaging board rather than continue producing newsprint? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Corvid Electronics Ltd is a private limited company making smart-home controllers in Brannock, Country X. Its 140 production workers made 96,000 units worth $4.8 million last year. On a time rate of $9.50 hourly they average 25 controllers per hour, but absence reached 11%.

MD Priya Raman may replace the time rate with a piece rate of $0.38 per unit, lifting output 20% to 115,000 units. Yet 60 workers oppose it over safety and rushed work. She must decide before next month's cycle.

questions.model_answer: The internal desire and external incentives that encourage employees to work hard and commit to achieving a business's objectives [2].

knowledge_max_2: internal and external factors encouraging effort

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Corvid Electronics might want employees who are well motivated.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A motivated workforce raises output and productivity [k], because each of the 140 production workers currently completes only 25 controllers per hour and output stands at 96,000 units [app]. Reason 2: Motivation reduces absenteeism and disruption [k], because absenteeism on the line reached 11% last year [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Corvid Electronics Ltd of introducing piece rate payment.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Piece rate links pay directly to output [k], because workers earn $0.38 per completed unit instead of just $9.50 per hour [app], so faster assemblers are rewarded and output could rise by 20% towards 115,000 units [an]. Advantage 2: It encourages a stronger work pace on the line [k], because only 25 controllers per worker per hour are completed now [app], so beating that level adds revenue on every unit above the threshold [an].

each extra unit above 25 per hour adds revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Corvid Electronics Ltd should introduce piece rate payment rather than continue with the time rate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Introducing piece rate would directly reward effort [k], since at 25 units per hour a worker earns exactly $9.50 and every extra unit adds $0.38 [app], so faster assemblers earn more and output could rise by 20% [an]. However, piece rate risks quality and safety problems [k], because 60 of the 140 workers oppose the change and absenteeism is already 11% [app], so rushed work could raise defect rates and harm the reputation of the controllers [an]. Overall, piece rate should be introduced but with quality checks and a safety review [eval], because the output gains are substantial for a line already suffering 11% absence and low hourly output [eval].

analysis_max_2: faster assemblers earn more and output rises

scenario_stem:
Fernbrook Cleaning Co is a private limited company in Country X selling liquid laundry detergent to 18,000 households, with 34 staff and $2.3 million revenue. It is developing a concentrated refill tablet that dissolves in existing bottles.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'new product development'.
questions.model_answer: New product development is the process by which a business creates, tests and launches new products or significantly improves existing ones, moving from idea generation through design, testing and test marketing to commercial launch. [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fernbrook Cleaning Co might benefit from launching the refill tablet.

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Developing new products is costly and the outcome is uncertain [k]; Fernbrook has already spent $260,000 and needs a further $150,000 for the trial run, so a failed launch would write off $410,000 [app]; this matters because the loss would reduce retained profit and limit funds available to support the core liquid detergent range [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication is a private limited company making steel beams in Calderfield, Country X, with 85 welders. Output was 3,400 tonnes worth $6.1 million, but 3 minor accidents and 18% turnover have been recorded. Workers earn $11.00 per hour.

Operations Director Marcus Hale has a $120,000 budget: new washrooms, a canteen and safety guards, or a $1.25 hourly rise costing $221,000 a year. Only 34 of 85 welders like conditions, so he wants to fix dissatisfaction before experienced staff leave.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'hygiene factors'.
questions.model_answer: Aspects of work that do not actively motivate employees but, if poor, cause dissatisfaction; Herzberg argued these include pay, working conditions and job security [2].

knowledge_max_2: examples: pay, working conditions, job security

questions.question_text: Explain two hygiene factors that could be causing dissatisfaction at Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Poor working conditions and safety are hygiene factors [k], because the yard has recorded 3 minor accidents this year and pay is only $11.00 per hour [app]. Reason 2: Weak workplace facilities cause dissatisfaction [k], because a recent survey showed only 34 of the 85 welders were satisfied with yard conditions [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication of improving hygiene factors before raising pay.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Better safety reduces accidents and lost time [k], because the yard recorded 3 minor accidents this year [app], so improved guards and facilities cut injury risk and keep the 85 welders productive [an]. Benefit 2: Improving conditions tackles the root cause of low morale cheaply [k], because only 34 of the 85 welders are satisfied with yard conditions [app], so fixing washrooms and a canteen for $120,000 addresses dissatisfaction before an extra $221,000 a year wage bill is needed [an].

knowledge_max_2: safety improvements cut accidents and absence
conditions address root cause of dissatisfaction
analysis_max_2: guards cut injury risk and lost productive time
fixing facilities for $120,000 avoids a $221,000 annual wage increase

questions.question_text: Do you think Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication should spend the $120,000 on facilities and safety rather than raise hourly pay by $1.25? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Spending $120,000 on facilities would remove clear hygiene problems [k], because only 34 of the 85 welders are satisfied and the yard recorded 3 minor accidents this year [app], so better washrooms, a canteen and guards could cut turnover from 18% and protect the safety of the experienced crew [an]. However, a $1.25 hourly rise would raise every worker's pay now [k], because it costs about $221,000 per year across 85 welders earning $11.00 per hour [app], so it is expensive but directly competitive in a tight labour market [an]. Overall, the $120,000 should go on facilities and safety first [eval], because Herzberg showed hygiene factors must be fixed before pay motivates anyone, and accidents and turnover are the urgent problems [eval].

knowledge_max_2: hygiene factors must be fixed before motivation rises
analysis_max_2: facilities cut turnover and protect the experienced crew
pay rise is expensive but competitive in a tight labour market
evaluation_max_2: weighs one-off facility spend against ongoing wage cost
prioritises hygiene over pay as per Herzberg

scenario_stem:
Granary & Grain Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making traditional wheat pasta. It spent $340,000 developing VerdeProtein, a plant-based protein pasta. It employs 48 staff, and VerdeProtein earned just $75,000 in 6 months.

Stocked in 120 supermarkets, July sales reached 5,600 packs at $2.80, so it is in the introduction stage. Only 22% of shoppers could identify the brand. The manager controls a $60,000 promotion budget.

questions.question_text: Define the 'introduction stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The introduction stage is the first stage of a product's life cycle after launch, when the product is first offered to the market and sales are usually low because awareness is limited and customers have not yet tried it. Promotion and distribution are still being built up and the product often makes losses at this stage. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies it as the launch stage when sales are low
Notes that awareness or distribution is still being built

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sales of VerdeProtein are likely to be low during the introduction stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In the introduction stage the product is new to the market and customer awareness is low [k]; only 22% of shoppers surveyed by Granary & Grain could identify VerdeProtein [app]. Reason 2: Consumers are reluctant to buy an unfamiliar product without proof or promotion [k]; VerdeProtein is stocked in 120 supermarkets and July sales reached just 5,600 packs at $2.80 each, so customer habit and shelf presence are still developing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that awareness is low for a newly launched product
Recognises that customers are reluctant to try unknown products
application_max_2: Uses the 120 supermarkets or 5,600 July packs figure

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits VerdeProtein could gain from strong promotional support during the introduction stage.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Promotion increases awareness and trial among the target market [k]; allocating part of the $60,000 budget to social media and in-store tasting could lift the 22% recognition figure and persuade gym-goers to try VerdeProtein [app]; wider trial would generate word of mouth and repeat purchases, building early momentum as the product moves towards growth [an]. Benefit 2: Promotion can shift demand and help recover development costs [k]; with July sales of 5,600 packs at $2.80 producing only about $15,680 a month, stronger promotion could close the gap on the $340,000 development spend faster [app]; rising sales also reassure supermarkets to keep stocking the product and avoid delisting [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that promotion builds awareness and trial
Recognises that promotion can lift sales or recover costs
application_max_2: Uses the $60,000 promotional budget or 22% awareness figure
Uses the 5,600 July packs or $2.80 price figure
analysis_max_2: Explains how trial leads to repeat purchase and growth
Explains how rising sales support supermarket listings and faster recovery of costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Granary & Grain Foods Ltd should spend the full $60,000 promoting VerdeProtein during the introduction stage? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Spending now is justified because promotion matters most in the introduction stage [k]; with only 22% of shoppers recognising VerdeProtein and just $75,000 of revenue in 6 months, investment is needed before rivals copy the recipe [app]; allocating the $60,000 across social media and in-store tasting could build awareness and trial, moving VerdeProtein towards growth and protecting the $340,000 spent on development [an]. However, the introduction stage usually brings losses [k]; sales of 5,600 packs in July at $2.80 yield only around $15,680 a month [app], so committing all $60,000 at once could strain cash flow when returns are unproven, and poorly targeted spending aimed at gym-goers may be wasted [an]. Overall, Granary & Grain should spend the $60,000 but in stages, linked to awareness and sales milestones [eval]; this balances the need to build the new brand against financial prudence while the product is unproven [eval].

Understands introduction-stage losses and cash-flow pressure

Uses the $60,000 budget or $340,000 development cost figure

Analyses the risk of overspending or targeting errors draining cash flow

Considers a staged spending approach linked to milestones

scenario_stem:
Sunpepper Hot Sauce Co is a private limited company founded by Lena Ortiz with 14 staff. It cooks 6,000 litres in batches of 750 litres, selling 250 ml bottles at $6.40 for $153,600 monthly, across 12 varieties including smoky chipotle.

A supermarket lists smoky chipotle nationally, forecasting 72,000 bottles monthly, triple output. Lena installs a $480,000 continuous flow line, or buys 2 750-litre vats for $60,000 and hires 6 staff at $1,150 to triple batches. She decides shortly.

questions.question_text: Define 'batch production'.
questions.model_answer: Producing a set quantity of identical items, completing each stage for the whole batch before moving to the next batch [2].

knowledge_max_2: a batch is a set number of identical items produced together
each stage is completed for the batch before production switches

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of batch production for Sunpepper.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Batch production allows different varieties to be made [k], which suits Sunpepper's 12 varieties, since each 750-litre batch can focus on one recipe [app]. Reason 2: Batch production spreads set-up costs across many units [k], lowering the average cost per bottle across the 24,000 bottles sold each month at $6.40 [app].

knowledge_max_2: batch production can switch between varieties or recipes
batch production spreads set-up costs over many units
application_max_2: each 750-litre batch is devoted to one of the 12 varieties
24,000 bottles a month (6,000 litres at 250 ml) at $6.40 each

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Sunpepper of its current batch production.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Batch production needs downtime between batches [k], so cleaning and resetting vats across 12 varieties loses production hours in a factory making only 6,000 litres a month [app], leaving too little capacity to serve the supermarket listing [an]. Problem 2: One error can spoil a whole batch [k], and a faulty recipe could waste all 750 litres in a run before anyone notices [app], creating unsold stock and cash flow pressure against $153,600 monthly revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: batches need changeover time for cleaning and resetting
a single fault can ruin an entire batch
application_max_2: 12 varieties mean frequent vat changeovers in a small factory

analysis_max_2: changeover downtime prevents meeting the 72,000-bottle forecast

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunpepper Hot Sauce Co should install the $480,000 flow production line rather than expand batch capacity? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The supermarket forecasts 72,000 bottles a month, three times current output [k]; buying 2 additional 750-litre vats at $60,000 and hiring 6 staff at $1,150 adds only $6,900 a month in wages [app], far cheaper than $480,000 [an]. However, a flow line would cut unit costs and fill 72,000 bottles smoothly every month [k], avoiding 24 changeovers and protecting the national listing [app], building long-term volume beyond the chipotle sauce [an]. Overall, Sunpepper should expand batch capacity first [eval], keeping 12 varieties flexible for local shops while proving the supermarket volume before committing $480,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: flow production cuts unit cost for one standardised product at high volume
expanding batch capacity keeps variety and flexibility at lower cost
application_max_2: 72,000 bottles a month (three times current) vs 2 vats at $60,000 and 6 staff at $1,150
$480,000 line vs $6,900 a month extra wages (6 x $1,150)
analysis_max_2: capital cost difference between the two options and when each breaks even
variety flexibility versus single-product flow efficiency and listing security
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to cash flow, the 8-week decision window and listing risk

scenario_stem:
Foulsham Joinery is a partnership making bespoke oak furniture in Country X. It employs 24 craftspeople, earned $620,000 revenue and retained profit of $60,000. Doubled cabinet orders now exceed workshop capacity.

The partners want $110,000 of capital expenditure on an automated spray-finishing machine to cut finishing time and waste. With $50,000 in owners' savings available, they want internal finance only and must weigh retained profit against savings.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital expenditure'.
questions.model_answer: Capital expenditure is money spent on non-current assets such as machinery, vehicles or premises that the business will use for more than one year [2].

knowledge_max_2: assets used for more than one year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Foulsham Joinery wants to invest $110,000 of capital expenditure in the spray-finishing machine.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To increase efficiency [k], because the automated spray-finishing machine would cut finishing time and reduce waste on bespoke oak furniture [app]. Reason 2: To meet rising demand [k], since cabinet orders have doubled this year and orders now exceed workshop capacity [app].

knowledge_max_2: ability to meet rising demand / take on more orders
application_max_2: machine cuts finishing time and reduces waste on oak furniture
cabinet orders doubled and now exceed workshop capacity

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of Foulsham Joinery using retained profit to fund the machine.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It carries no interest or repayment obligation [k], so the $60,000 reinvests money the firm itself earned, protecting monthly cash [app], which keeps the workshop running smoothly [an]. Benefit 2: It is immediately available [k], already in hand after last year's $620,000 revenue [app], letting the partners order the machine without outside approval [an].

application_max_2: in hand after the $620,000 revenue year
analysis_max_2: protects monthly cash flow / steady workshop running
machine can be ordered without outside approval

questions.question_text: Do you think Foulsham Joinery should fund the $110,000 spray-finishing machine mainly from retained profit rather than owners' savings? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit is long-term internal finance with no repayment obligation [k], so using the $60,000 to help fund the $110,000 machine reinvests money the business earned itself [app], strengthening the partnership without adding financial pressure [an]. However, owners' savings of $50,000 are also immediately available and carry no interest [k], so together the two sources exactly cover the $110,000 [app], letting the partners decide the split without any shortfall [an]. Overall, retained profit should be used as the main source [eval], because the $60,000 came from the firm's own $620,000 revenue and keeps personal risk low, with the $50,000 savings topping up the balance [eval].

knowledge_max_2: retained profit is long-term internal finance with no repayment

application_max_2: the $60,000 came from the firm's $620,000 revenue
analysis_max_2: strengthens the firm without financial pressure

evaluation_max_2: weighs reinvesting business earnings against committing personal funds
justified recommendation to use retained profit with savings top-up

scenario_stem:
Sorrento Gelato Co is a sole trader making luxury ice cream in 9 parlours in Country X. It sold 420,000 tubs at $4.50 each for $1,890,000; fixed costs are $9,000 a month and ingredient costs rose 12%.

Country X is in a boom: spending up 6.1%, unemployment 2.8%, footfall up 25% and 74 staff struggling with demand. Lena Costa must decide by 1 June whether to raise prices 6% or absorb the costs before the peak summer season.

questions.question_text: Define 'a boom'.
questions.model_answer: The peak stage of the business cycle, when the economy is strongest, with very high demand and output, low unemployment and rising incomes [2].

knowledge_max_2: a boom is the peak stage of the business cycle with very high output
a boom brings high demand, high incomes and very low unemployment

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the boom benefits Sorrento Gelato Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A boom means very high consumer spending [k]; spending across Country X rose by 6.1% and Sorrento's parlour footfall is up 25% [app]. Reason 2: In a boom incomes are high [k], so customers can afford $4.50 tubs and Sorrento sold 420,000 tubs and made $1,890,000 of revenue last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: a boom brings very high consumer spending and demand
a boom brings high incomes and low unemployment
application_max_2: consumer spending up 6.1% and footfall up 25%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Sorrento Gelato Co faces during the boom.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A boom creates cost pressure as demand competes for scarce resources [k]; Sorrento's ingredient costs have risen by 12% this year [app], squeezing margins if tub prices stay at $4.50 [an]. Problem 2: Low unemployment makes hiring difficult [k]; with unemployment at just 2.8%, Sorrento's staff are struggling to serve 25% more footfall through its 9 parlours [app], so poor service could cost sales in the peak season [an].

knowledge_max_2: a boom pushes up business costs through resource competition
a boom makes recruiting and retaining staff difficult
application_max_2: unemployment at just 2.8% with staff struggling to meet demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Sorrento Gelato Co should raise prices by 6% for the summer season? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising prices by 6% would protect margins [k]; ingredient costs are up 12% and demand is strong with footfall up 25% while consumer spending rose 6.1% [app], so $1,890,000 of revenue can be defended and profits increased [an]. However, higher prices may test customer loyalty [k]; customers already face higher costs, and a rise from $4.50 may deter price-conscious buyers outside the summer peak [app], so sales volumes could fall and undo the gain [an]. Overall, Sorrento should raise prices by 6% [eval], because boom conditions with 6.1% spending growth and 2.8% unemployment mean demand is strong enough to absorb a modest rise [eval].

scenario_stem:
Amberfield Flour Mill is a partnership run by the Okafor family in Country Z. It employs 96 workers, milled 62,000 tonnes of wheat flour and earned $5.5 million selling to 38 bakeries and 4 catering suppliers.

With pasta and noodle demand up 26% in 3 years, the family considers a $1.9 million pasta line selling at $1,450 per tonne against $890 for flour. Supermarkets want own-brand pasta from January, but installation takes 6 months and 12 more staff by December.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'industrialisation'.
questions.model_answer: The growth in importance of the secondary manufacturing sector in an economy, with a rising share of total output and employment in factories [2].

knowledge_max_2: rising share of output or employment

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Amberfield might want to move into pasta production.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Growing domestic demand for pasta [k], with demand up 26% in 3 years across Country Z [app]. Reason 2: Committed retail buyers [k], as two national supermarkets have asked for own-brand dried pasta from January [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Amberfield might face if it installs the pasta line.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A heavy upfront cost [k], since the line costs $1.9 million [app], which may strain the partnership's cash flow and require borrowing [an]. Problem 2: Disruption to current output [k], as installation takes 6 months and needs 12 more staff [app], which could delay deliveries to its 38 bakeries and damage goodwill [an].

analysis_max_2: cash flow strain or extra borrowing

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfield Flour Mill should install the pasta line rather than continue selling bulk flour? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The pasta line should increase added value [k], because pasta sells at $1,450 per tonne against $890 for bulk flour [app], adding $560 per tonne on top of the $5.5 million flour-only revenue [an]. However, continuing with flour avoids disruption [k], as the mill already supplies 38 bakeries from 62,000 tonnes a year [app], and a 6-month installation plus 12 new staff could cause missed orders and harm the family's reputation if supermarkets do not commit formally [an]. Overall, installation is the better option because domestic pasta demand in Country Z has risen 26% in 3 years [eval], and two national supermarkets requesting own-brand dried pasta from January make new orders unusually secure for a start-up product [eval].

knowledge_max_2: higher added value vs continuity risk
analysis_max_2: missed orders and reputational damage during installation
evaluation_max_2: weighs rising pasta demand and supermarket interest against installation risk

scenario_stem:
Redbrook Food Processing Ltd is a private limited company canning vegetables in Vellamo, Country X, with 110 line workers and 12 supervisors. It made 5.2 million tins worth $3.9 million. A forklift incident in March injured 2 workers; an audit rated two lines high risk.

HR manager Daniel Okafor has $125,000: $80,000 on guarding and forklift safety, or $45,000 on leadership and esteem training for the 12 supervisors. Maslow ranks safety below esteem. The board meets next month.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Maslow's hierarchy of needs'.
questions.model_answer: Maslow's five-level model of motivation, which suggests people must satisfy lower-level needs such as safety before they can be motivated by higher-level needs such as esteem [2].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Meeting safety needs removes a source of fear and anxiety [k], because a forklift incident in March injured 2 workers and two lines were rated high risk [app]. Reason 2: Safe workers are more productive workers [k], because the factory employs 110 line workers canning 5.2 million tins a year [app].

Advantage 2: A safer workplace raises morale and trust [k], because the 110 line workers would see the company investing in their welfare [app], increasing their effort towards the 5.2 million tins target [an].

questions.model_answer: Spending $80,000 on safety would meet the most basic needs first [k], because a forklift incident injured 2 workers and two production lines are rated high risk [app], so safer lines would cut injuries, absences and lost output across the 110-worker workforce [an]. However, the leadership programme could still raise motivation [k], because for only $45,000 it would meet the esteem needs of the 12 supervisors [app], giving them recognition and responsibility that could cascade into better line management [an]. Overall, the safety upgrades should take priority [eval], because Maslow's hierarchy puts safety before esteem and the injured workers show the need is urgent [eval].

scenario_stem:
Wildroot Brew Co is a private limited company in Country X that launched fermented kombucha 18 months ago. Sales rose from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles, with 26 staff. The product is in the growth stage.

It sells through 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains at $3.20 per 500ml bottle; profit was $180,000. Rival Zing launches in 6 months. Owners must choose: invest $400,000 of retained profit in brewing tanks or raise the price to $3.60.

questions.question_text: Define the 'growth stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The growth stage is the phase in which a product's sales and profits rise rapidly as awareness spreads, the product is accepted by the market and distribution widens. Competitors often enter the market at this stage as the product proves successful. [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Wildroot Brew Co's kombucha sales are rising rapidly in the growth stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In the growth stage early buyers accept the product and word of mouth spreads awareness [k]; bottle sales have risen from 30,000 in Wildroot's first quarter to 190,000 in the latest quarter [app]. Reason 2: Wider distribution makes the product easy to buy [k]; Wildroot is stocked in 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains, so growing numbers of customers can buy a 500ml bottle at $3.20 [app].

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Extra capacity lets the business meet rising demand and avoid lost sales [k]; with quarterly sales up from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles, current tanks are stretched, so extra capacity would let Wildroot fill every order before rival Zing launches in 6 months [app]; this would strengthen supermarket relationships and secure shelf space that might otherwise go to competitors [an]. Benefit 2: Higher volume spreads fixed costs and lifts profit [k]; increasing output to serve the 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains at $3.20 per bottle would grow revenue above its current level and raise the $180,000 profit [app]; economies of scale on ingredients and bottling would further reduce unit costs and improve margins [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Wildroot Brew Co should invest $400,000 of retained profit in extra brewing tanks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing is attractive because the growth stage is the moment to capture market share [k]; sales have risen from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles per quarter and distribution spans 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains [app]; added capacity would let Wildroot supply demand fully, lock in volume and defend supermarket shelf space before Zing launches in 6 months, building on the $180,000 profit already achieved [an]. scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fernhill Orchard Farm faces working capital pressure before the harvest.

scenario_stem:
Brackenwood Rice Mill Ltd is a private limited company in the Riverton district. It employs 180 workers, mills 27,000 tonnes of rice yearly and earned $8.1 million, though its profit margin has narrowed to 4% as secondary employment fell from 31% to 22%.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenwood's profit margin might have narrowed to 4%.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brackenwood of investing in the roasted rice-cake line.

Benefit 2: Access to higher-growth retail demand [k], with local retailers already agreeing trial orders [app], broadening the mill beyond bulk export buyers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenwood Rice Mill should invest in the rice-cake line rather than continue supplying bulk milled rice to exporters? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Amberfields Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing QuickQuick instant noodle pots. Sales have been flat at 900,000 pots a year for 3 years, placing it at maturity. It employs 72 staff and earned $2.7 million.

questions.question_text: Define the 'maturity stage' of the product life cycle.
