questions.question_text: Do you think Brightstead Superstores should replace the time rate with a piece rate for warehouse pickers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching links pay to output [k]; at $0.11 per item an average picker earns about $440 a week, matching the current $437 time rate [app], so fast pickers are rewarded and productivity should rise [an]. However, piece rate can encourage rushing [k]; with errors already at 6% and costing $3,100 a month, paying per item could push accuracy below the 97% the bonus scheme demands [app], increasing refunds and damaging customer trust [an]. Overall, Brightstead should keep the time rate and add the $40 team bonus instead [eval], because online grocery fulfilment depends on correct orders, not just fast ones [eval].

knowledge_max_2: piece rate risks poor quality and rushing
analysis_max_2: output-linked pay should raise picker productivity
rushing increases errors, refunds and customer harm
evaluation_max_2: weighs higher output against order accuracy and fulfilment quality

scenario_stem:
Foxbury Flour Mills is a private limited company in Country X milling 9,000 tonnes of wheat into flour for 60 bakeries. It uses cost-plus pricing with a 25% markup; production cost rose from $0.80 to $0.88 and now $0.96.

The price moved from $1.00 to $1.10; keeping the 25% markup means $1.20. Rival Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 and two bakeries threaten to switch. Cole wants to hold at $1.10; Dana wants the full increase passed on.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing is a pricing method in which a business calculates the total cost of producing a product and then adds a percentage markup to set the selling price. This ensures all production costs are covered and a profit margin is built in [2].

knowledge_max_2: Business calculates the total cost of making the product
Adds a percentage markup to the cost to set the selling price

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Foxbury Flour Mills uses cost-plus pricing.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing ensures that all production costs are covered and a profit is made [k], which is vital when wheat costs have risen from $0.80 to $0.96 per kilogram [app]. It is also straightforward to calculate and easy to update as costs change [k], as shown by the price moving from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and possibly to $1.20 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Covers production costs and guarantees a profit margin
Simple to calculate and adjust when costs change
application_max_2: Wheat cost has risen from $0.80 to $0.88 and now $0.96 per kilogram
Price moved from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and could rise to $1.20 with the 25% markup

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Foxbury Flour Mills may face if it raises its price to $1.20 per kilogram.
questions.model_answer: A higher price could make Foxbury uncompetitive against rivals [k], because Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram [app], so the two large bakeries may switch suppliers, cutting Foxbury's sales volume [an]. A price rise could also damage Foxbury's relationships with long-standing customers [k], as two of its 60 bakery buyers have already warned they will switch [app], leaving capacity under-used across the 9,000 tonnes milled and reducing revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: May become uncompetitive / rivals may be cheaper
May damage customer relationships / lose goodwill and long-standing buyers
application_max_2: Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram, below the proposed $1.20
Two of Foxbury's 60 bakery customers have already warned they will switch suppliers
analysis_max_2: Sales volume and revenue fall if bakeries switch to Harborpoint
Under-used milling capacity across the 9,000 tonnes milled reduces recovery of fixed costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxbury Flour Mills should raise its price to $1.20 per kilogram, in line with cost-plus pricing, or hold the price at $1.10 per kilogram? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising the price to $1.20 maintains the 25% markup on the higher wheat cost of $0.96 [k], preserving the profit Foxbury earns on each of its 9,000 tonnes of flour [app], protecting cash flow and avoiding erosion of margins [an]. However, holding at $1.10 keeps Foxbury close to Harborpoint Flour's $1.15 price [k], helping Foxbury retain its 60 bakery customers and avoid losing the two large buyers who warned they will switch [app], protecting long-term revenue and market share [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to raise the price in line with cost-plus pricing [eval], because repeated input cost rises from $0.80 through $0.88 to $0.96 cannot be absorbed indefinitely without destroying profit, and the price must reflect true costs to remain sustainable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cost-plus keeps the markup intact and protects profit
Holding the price protects share and keeps the price close to the rival
application_max_2: $0.96 wheat cost with 25% markup gives $1.20; margin must cover 9,000 tonnes
Holding at $1.10 stays near Harborpoint Flour at $1.15; two of 60 bakeries threatening to switch
analysis_max_2: Raising preserves margin and protects cash flow
Holding protects long-term volume, share and customer relationships
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that costs rose repeatedly ($0.80 to $0.88 to $0.96) so absorption is unsustainable
Acknowledges the risk of losing the two large bakery buyers and weighs it against margin protection

scenario_stem:
Brackenfell Woodcraft is a sole trader furniture business founded by Helen Marchetti in Country X with 26 workers making handcrafted oak dining tables and chairs. Output is 140 tables a month on annual revenue of $620,000, sold to local hotels and homes.

The workshop has cutting, sanding and assembly areas with parts travelling 14 metres between them. Helen funds kaizen continuous improvement for $6,500 yearly, or a $95,000 computer-controlled sanding machine cutting sanding time 35%, before the new financial year.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'kaizen'.
questions.model_answer: A Japanese term meaning continuous, small, ongoing improvements to production processes, involving employees at every level rather than one-off large changes [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenfell Woodcraft might introduce kaizen.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Kaizen involves all employees in spotting small, ongoing improvements [k], which suits a 26-worker workshop where parts travel 14 metres between cutting, sanding and assembly [app]. Reason 2: Kaizen costs very little in capital spending [k], at about $6,500 a year compared with a $95,000 machine [app].

knowledge_max_2: continuous small improvements by all staff
low-cost approach needing no major capital outlay

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brackenfell Woodcraft of choosing kaizen rather than the computer-controlled sanding machine.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Kaizen preserves cash [k], because $6,500 a year is far cheaper than the $95,000 sanding machine [app], leaving money free for timber and wages [an]. Benefit 2: Kaizen builds a culture where all 26 workers contribute improvement ideas [k], applied across the 140 tables a month passing through cutting, sanding and assembly [app], cutting rework and defects over time [an].

knowledge_max_2: kaizen needs little capital, freeing cash flow
kaizen engages and motivates all employees
analysis_max_2: cash saved can be spent on materials and wages
ongoing employee ideas reduce defects and rework

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenfell Woodcraft should introduce kaizen instead of buying the computer-controlled sanding machine? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Kaizen spreads the cost at about $6,500 a year [k], engaging all 26 workers in improving the flow of 140 tables a month across workshop areas 14 metres apart [app], so savings build steadily while cash stays available for materials [an]. However, the sanding machine would cut sanding time by 35% immediately [k], lifting capacity on a $620,000 revenue business far faster than gradual kaizen steps [app], which could win larger hotel orders and raise output [an]. Overall, Brackenfell Woodcraft should introduce kaizen first [eval], because low-cost cultural change suits a family-run workshop better than a $95,000 commitment before waste is removed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: kaizen is low-cost and gradual with staff involvement
automation gives an immediate, measurable time saving
analysis_max_2: cash preserved funds materials and wages
faster sanding lifts capacity and wins larger orders
evaluation_max_2: weighs low-cost gradual improvement against immediate machine productivity gain

scenario_stem:
Thornfen Grain Milling Ltd is a private limited company milling wheat and maize at its Riverside mill. Founded 7 years ago, it earns $2.4 million annually and is owned by the Pryce brothers, who hold all 200,000 ordinary shares and want a $600,000 roller mill.

Options: issue 400,000 new ordinary shares to family shareholders at $1.50 each, or a $600,000 bank loan over 8 years at $36,000 interest yearly. The brothers must choose by 31 March.

questions.question_text: Define 'issue of shares'.
questions.model_answer: Selling new shares in the business to investors in return for capital, which the business does not have to repay [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling shares to investors raises capital for the business
share capital does not have to be repaid like a loan

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Thornfen of raising the $600,000 by issuing shares instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Issued share capital does not have to be repaid [k], so Thornfen avoids 8 years of fixed $36,000 annual interest payments the bank loan would require [app]. Reason 2: Share capital carries no mandatory interest cost [k], so Thornfen can keep more cash when revenue is only $2.4 million a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: share capital is not a loan and does not have to be repaid
shares carry no compulsory interest charge
application_max_2: the loan would cost $36,000 interest every year for 8 years
Thornfen currently earns revenue of $2.4 million a year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to the Pryce brothers of issuing 400,000 new ordinary shares.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Issuing shares dilutes the existing owners' control [k], because 400,000 new shares at $1.50 each would be added to the brothers' existing 200,000 ordinary shares [app], so their percentage ownership and say in decisions at the Riverside mill would fall [an]. Problem 2: Shareholders commonly expect dividends [k], and with annual revenue of only $2.4 million the brothers may have to share profits with new shareholders each year [app], weakening the family's claim on future earnings [an].

knowledge_max_2: issuing new shares reduces existing shareholders' percentage of ownership
ordinary shareholders usually expect dividends from profits
application_max_2: 400,000 new shares at $1.50 each would take total shares from 200,000 to 600,000
Thornfen earns revenue of $2.4 million a year
analysis_max_2: the brothers lose voting power and influence over the business
profit is spread across more shareholders, reducing what the family keeps

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornfen Grain Milling Ltd should issue the new ordinary shares rather than take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Issuing shares would raise the full $600,000 without any fixed repayment [k], since 400,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each add $600,000 of permanent capital with no $36,000 interest every year for 8 years [app], so Thornfen's cash position stays flexible while bakery demand rises [an]. However, taking the loan keeps the business entirely in family hands [k]; the brothers avoid new shareholders expecting dividends even in lean years when revenue slips below $2.4 million [app], protecting their control of the Riverside mill [an]. Overall, Thornfen should take the bank loan [eval], because Daniel's wish to protect family control matters more to a 7-year-old family business than saving $36,000 of interest each year [eval].

knowledge_max_2: share issue avoids fixed interest repayments and adds permanent capital
bank loan preserves existing ownership and control
application_max_2: 400,000 shares at $1.50 each raises $600,000 against $36,000 annual loan interest for 8 years
current revenue is $2.4 million a year
analysis_max_2: cash flexibility versus ownership dilution trade-off
control of the family business weighed against the cost of interest
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the family-business context

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramble & Rowan Outfitters is a private limited company running 5 stores selling mid-range men's and women's casual clothing. It employs 32 sales assistants, with revenue of $2,400,000 and a gross profit margin of 42%, competing on price and store location.

Income tax rises from 20% to 25% in April, cutting disposable income, and footfall has fallen 8% this year. Management must decide whether to cut prices to stimulate demand or hold prices steady and accept lower sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'income tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax that individuals pay on the income they earn, such as wages and salaries. The amount paid usually rises as income increases [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax paid by individuals on income/wages/salaries
amount rises as income increases / deducted by the government

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the rise in income tax on Bramble & Rowan Outfitters.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Lower disposable income for customers [k], so shoppers at the 5 stores keep less of their pay after tax and buy fewer mid-range casual clothes [app]. Effect 2: Falling sales revenue [k], adding to the 8% drop in footfall already seen this year across the company's stores [app].

knowledge_max_2: customers have less disposable income / reduced spending power

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the rise in income tax could affect Bramble & Rowan's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Customers have reduced disposable income [k], so after the basic rate of income tax rises to 25% they keep less of their wages [app], which means non-essential purchases like casual clothing are cut first [an]. Way 2: Customers become more price-sensitive [k], so shoppers compare Bramble & Rowan's mid-range prices against discounters [app], leading some to switch to cheaper stores and reducing the company's sales volumes [an].

knowledge_max_2: greater price sensitivity / switching to cheaper substitutes
application_max_2: basic rate of income tax rises from 20% to 25%
analysis_max_2: customers switch to discount retailers, reducing sales volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramble & Rowan Outfitters should cut its prices rather than hold prices steady? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting prices could stimulate demand [k] by attracting price-sensitive shoppers back to the 5 stores after footfall already fell by 8% [app], lifting sales volumes and using the 42% gross profit margin to cushion lower prices [an]. Holding prices steady protects the margin [k] and preserves profit per item on $2,400,000 of last year's revenue [app], avoiding a price war with competitors that could further erode profitability [an]. On one hand, holding prices steady risks further footfall declines [eval]; on the other hand, cutting prices may fail to offset lower margins if disposable incomes keep falling after the tax rise to 25% [eval]. Overall, cutting prices moderately is the stronger option because footfall has already dropped 8% and the business needs traffic through its stores to protect total profit, even though margins will narrow.

knowledge_max_2: price cut stimulates demand / attracts shoppers
holding prices protects margin / profit per item
analysis_max_2: lower prices lift volume using the margin cushion
holding prices risks further traffic decline and no volume recovery
evaluation_max_2: weighs price cut against price hold in light of the tax rise
justified recommendation referencing footfall and margin

scenario_stem:
Cardew Dairy Farm is a partnership owned by Helen and Marcus Cardew in Country X, keeping 60 cows producing 1,200 litres daily sold raw to a creamery at $0.55 per litre. Feed costs rose 15%, squeezing margins.

They consider $80,000 on cheese-making equipment for cheddar at $15 per kilogram, using 10 litres of milk and $4 extra costs per kilogram. The creamery offers a 2-year raw-milk contract at $0.60 per litre; cheese needs 4 extra workers.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by the 'primary sector'.
questions.model_answer: The primary sector is the part of the economy that extracts and harvests natural resources, such as farming, fishing and quarrying [2].

knowledge_max_2: extracts, grows or harvests raw materials from nature
examples include agriculture, fishing, forestry and quarrying/mining

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Cardew Dairy Farm might add value to its milk by making cheese.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cheese sells for far more than raw milk [k], because each kilogram of cheddar at $15 is made from 10 litres of milk that the farm currently sells raw at $0.55 per litre, about $5.50 per 10 litres [app]. Reason 2: Cheese lasts much longer [k], because matured cheddar can be stored for months and sold when prices are good, whereas 1,200 litres of raw milk a day must be collected daily or it spoils [app].

knowledge_max_2: processing raises the price received per input unit
processed products store longer, cutting waste and smoothing sales
application_max_2: 10 litres of milk per kilogram of cheese

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Cardew Dairy Farm of making its own cheese instead of selling raw milk.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A much higher return per litre [k], because cheese at $15 per kilogram uses 10 litres of milk and even after $4 of running costs keeps $11 per kilogram [app], far above the $6 return on the same 10 litres at $0.60 per litre on the 2-year contract, lifting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Greater control over where the product is sold [k], because the farm could sell its cheddar directly at markets and shops instead of depending on the large creamery [app], keeping the full retail margin and avoiding the creamery lowering its $0.55 per litre price [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing raises profit
selling directly keeps more of the final selling price
application_max_2: $4 of extra running costs per kilogram
analysis_max_2: $11 per kilogram retained far beats the $6 per 10-litre contract return
direct sales reduce dependence on the creamery's price decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Cardew Dairy Farm should make its own cheese rather than accept the 2-year raw-milk contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that cheese adds far more value [k], because each kilogram at $15 is made from 10 litres of milk, so keeping $11 after running costs is far above the $6 return on the same milk at $0.60 per litre [app], meaning the farm could build up capital quickly [an]. However, the 2-year contract is guaranteed income [k], worth about $720 a day from 1,200 litres at $0.60 per litre, with no $80,000 debt, no 4 extra workers to recruit and no risk that the unproven cheddar fails to sell [app]; with feed costs already up 15%, dependable cash matters [an]. Overall, making cheese is the better long-term choice if the partners have secured orders for their cheddar, since $11 per kilogram beats the $6 contract return [eval]; without signed orders, the safer 2-year raw-milk contract at $0.60 per litre is wiser until the cheese proves itself [eval].

knowledge_max_2: processing increases added value and margin
the 2-year contract offers certainty and avoids debt
application_max_2: $15 per kilogram cheddar with $4 running costs
analysis_max_2: $11 retained per kilogram far exceeds the contract return, aiding loan repayment
contract removes finance, staffing and market risk
evaluation_max_2: weighs superior margin against contract security and debt
justified conditional recommendation tied to feed costs and orders

scenario_stem:
The Marram Bay Hotel is a sole trader, a 3-star coastal hotel in Country X with 74 staff. Its weddings manager, 4 years in post, booked $875,000 of events last year on a $2,600 monthly salary with no commission. Two beach wedding packages launch in March, targeting $900,000.

Owner Priya Ramanthan chooses between 4% commission, about $35,000 last year, or raising salary to $3,100, an extra $6,000 a year. Front-desk staff also expect a rise.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'commission'.
questions.model_answer: A payment calculated as a percentage of the value of sales an employee makes, usually paid in addition to or instead of a basic wage [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Marram Bay Hotel might add 4% commission for its events manager.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Commission directly links reward to sales achieved [k], giving the manager a strong incentive to fill the calendar of two new beach wedding packages launched in March [app]. Reason 2: It ties the hotel's payment to confirmed events revenue [k], so the 4% commission would track the $900,000 target instead of committing a fixed $6,000 salary rise [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the manager of keeping a higher salary instead of taking the commission.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A salary gives a predictable income every month [k], so the manager can budget reliably rather than depend on whether the $900,000 booking target is met [app], reducing financial stress and improving focus on service quality [an]. Benefit 2: A raise to $3,100 is guaranteed pay [k], worth $6,000 more a year with no risk if few events are booked, such as after a weak January [app], making earnings more secure than a 4% commission that paid about $35,000 only at last year's level of $875,000 [an].

analysis_max_2: predictable pay reduces stress and supports service quality
guaranteed income protects against weak trading months

questions.question_text: Do you think the Marram Bay Hotel should add 4% commission rather than raise the manager's salary to $3,100 a month? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Commission ties reward to results [k]; at 4% of last year's $875,000 bookings the manager could earn about $35,000, far more than a $6,000 salary rise [app], so the manager is pushed to fill the two new beach wedding packages and hit $900,000 [an]. However, high commission can tempt over-promising to close sales [k], and the manager may neglect existing corporate clients worth $875,000 a year [app], damaging the hotel's reputation among loyal event bookers [an]. Overall, the hotel should add the commission [eval], because a results-linked cost rises only when revenue does and it most strongly motivates hitting the $900,000 target [eval].

knowledge_max_2: commission can distort behaviour and neglect existing clients
analysis_max_2: results-linked pay rises only with revenue
commission pressure may harm service and client coverage
evaluation_max_2: weighs higher potential earnings against behaviour risk and client neglect

scenario_stem:
Harborview Electrical is a private limited company in Country X selling televisions from two high-street shops, with 16 staff. It sold 2,400 televisions at $599 against a $410 unit cost, earning $1.44 million revenue and $0.30 million profit.

ValueMart has cut prices to $549 with match-any-price weekend deals. Matching would cut margin per television from $189 to $139, but holding $599 may lose 20% of sales. Priya must set the summer price.

questions.question_text: Define 'competitive pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Competitive pricing is a pricing method where a business sets its prices at or close to the prices charged by its competitors, rather than basing the price only on its own costs, so that it remains attractive to customers in the market [2].

knowledge_max_2: Price is set at or close to competitors' prices
Focus is on matching the market rather than the business's own costs

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of competitive pricing for Harborview Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Competitive pricing keeps Harborview's televisions attractive next to ValueMart, which has cut prices to $549 [k], helping Harborview defend its position against a rival running match-any-price weekend promotions [app]. It also helps prevent losing customers to cheaper competitors [k], protecting Harborview's 2,400 television sales and $1.44 million annual revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Keeps the product attractive against rivals' prices
Helps prevent loss of customers to cheaper competitors
application_max_2: ValueMart has cut television prices to $549 and runs match-any-price weekends
Harborview sold 2,400 televisions and earned $1.44 million in revenue last year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of competitive pricing for Harborview Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Matching ValueMart at $549 cuts the profit margin per television from $189 to $139 [k], meaning $50 is lost on every set while the cost stays at $410 [app], squeezing Harborview's $0.30 million profit across its 2,400 sales [an]. Competitive pricing also makes Harborview dependent on rivals' decisions [k], so ValueMart's match-any-price weekends may force repeated price cuts [app], eroding margins in the two shops without any guarantee of extra volume [an].

knowledge_max_2: Margins are squeezed because price is set by rivals
The business becomes dependent on competitors' pricing decisions
application_max_2: Matching $549 cuts the margin from $189 to $139 against a $410 unit cost
analysis_max_2: Profit is squeezed across the 2,400 televisions sold, threatening the $0.30 million profit
Repeated reactive price cuts erode margins without guaranteeing more volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Harborview Electrical should lower its television price to $549 to match ValueMart, or hold at $599? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Matching at $549 would cut the profit margin per television from $189 to $139 [k], reducing profit on the 2,400 sets sold and threatening the $0.30 million annual profit [app], limiting funds available for the free-delivery offer and in-store advice [an]. However, holding $599 risks losing customers to ValueMart and its match-any-price weekend promotions [k], potentially cutting television sales by the 20% Priya fears across the two shops [app], shrinking Harborview's market share in its local market [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to hold at $599 but add clearer value such as free delivery and expert advice [eval], because matching a national chain's discount triggers a price war Harborview cannot win on size, while superior service justifies the $50 premium for local buyers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Matching protects volume but erodes margin per unit
Holding the price risks losing customers / market share to the rival
application_max_2: Margin falls from $189 to $139 at $549 against $410 cost
2,400 televisions sold, $0.30 million profit, ValueMart match-any-price weekends, 20% feared sales fall
analysis_max_2: Matching funds shrink (delivery, advice) and erodes per-unit margin
Holding risks sales volume and local market share
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation balancing margin erosion against share loss
Recognises Harborview cannot win a price war on size against a national chain, so service must carry the premium

scenario_stem:
Selbrook Foods Ltd is a chilled ready-meal company and private limited company with 48 workers. It makes 9,500 meals a day, earning $1.8 million last year. Vegetables arrive weekly; the cold store holds 6 days of stock.

The store costs $4,300 monthly. Just-in-time deliveries four times a day would cut stock to half a day but add $900 monthly in transport, and any late load stops the line. Selbrook decides before signing a three-year supply contract.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'just-in-time'.
questions.model_answer: A stock management approach in which raw materials and components are delivered only when they are needed in production, rather than being held in inventory [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Selbrook Foods Ltd might introduce just-in-time deliveries.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: JIT reduces the cost of holding inventory [k], because cutting stock from 6 days to half a day would slash much of the $4,300 monthly cold-store cost [app]. Reason 2: JIT keeps ingredients fresher [k], which matters because chilled meals receive fresh vegetables in bulk every Monday and demand peaks before weekends [app].

knowledge_max_2: reduces inventory holding costs and space
perishable inputs arrive fresher and spoil less
application_max_2: fresh vegetables in bulk every Monday

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Selbrook Foods Ltd of introducing just-in-time deliveries.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lower storage costs [k], as cold-store stock falls from 6 days to half a day against a current $4,300 monthly bill [app], freeing cash for other uses [an]. Benefit 2: Fresh ingredients support consistent quality [k], protecting the chilled ready-meal reputation with supermarket buyers who receive 9,500 meals a day [app], which should secure loyal, repeat orders [an].

knowledge_max_2: JIT cuts storage and holding costs
analysis_max_2: cash tied up in stock is freed for other uses
better quality protects supermarket relationships and repeat orders

questions.question_text: Do you think Selbrook Foods Ltd should switch to just-in-time deliveries? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Just-in-time means vegetables arrive four times a day [k], cutting the cold store from 6 days of stock to half a day and reducing the $4,300 monthly cost [app], so cash tied up in stock drops and ingredients stay fresher [an]. However, deliveries add $900 a month in transport and any late arrival would stop a line producing 9,500 meals a day [k], so four trucks a day leave no buffer when traffic delays suppliers [app], risking lost sales and supermarket penalties [an]. Overall, Selbrook should adopt just-in-time from its main vegetable supplier [eval], because chilled meals spoil quickly and freshness outweighs the $900 delivery cost, provided late-delivery penalties are written into the three-year contract [eval].

knowledge_max_2: JIT cuts inventory cost and improves freshness
JIT creates vulnerability to supply delays with no buffer stock
analysis_max_2: less cash held in stock and fresher ingredients
a single late delivery halts output and loses sales
evaluation_max_2: weighs freshness and storage savings against transport cost and supply risk

scenario_stem:
Brackenridge Publishing Plc is a public limited company publishing textbooks and trade paperbacks. It reported $9.6 million revenue after a weak Christmas sales season. The board wants a $2 million distribution centre to cut delivery times.

It can sell a 10-year $2 million debenture at 7.5%, paying $150,000 interest yearly and tax-deductible, or make a rights issue of 500,000 new shares at $4.00 each, raising $2 million with no repayment. Shareholders vote on 18 June.

questions.question_text: Define 'debenture'.
questions.model_answer: A long-term loan sold by a company to investors, paying a fixed rate of interest and repaid on an agreed future date [2].

knowledge_max_2: a debenture is a long-term loan made to the company
debenture holders receive fixed interest and repayment at a set date

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenridge Publishing Plc might prefer selling debentures to a rights issue.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Debenture interest is tax-deductible [k], so Brackenridge can cut its tax bill while paying a predictable $150,000 each year on the $2 million raised [app]. Reason 2: Existing shareholders keep their full stake in the company [k], because no new shares are issued unlike the 500,000 new shares at $4.00 each under the rights issue [app].

knowledge_max_2: issuing shares dilutes existing shareholders' percentage of ownership
application_max_2: the 7.5% rate means $150,000 interest a year on $2 million
the rights issue would add 500,000 new shares at $4.00 each

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Brackenridge of a $2 million debenture issue at 7.5%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Debenture interest must be paid every year [k], and $150,000 a year reduces profit even while the new centre has not yet lifted revenue beyond $9.6 million after a weak Christmas [app], squeezing returns to existing shareholders [an]. Problem 2: The debenture must eventually be repaid [k], so $2 million falls due in a single payment after 10 years regardless of trading conditions [app], creating a huge cash demand in a year of weak sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is fixed and compulsory even in poor years

However, pure commission exposes junior staff [k]; the newest stylist who billed $3,200 would earn only about $1,120, below the current $1,450 [app], risking demotivation and departure precisely when training investment is highest [an]. Overall, the studio should keep the $1,450 salary with 8% retail commission [eval], because the mixed system keeps pay fair across the 9 stylists and still rewards effort [eval].

knowledge_max_2: commission is risky for juniors and low billers
analysis_max_2: higher commission drives upselling and fuller books
pay drop for juniors risks demotivation and exit
evaluation_max_2: weighs motivation of seniors against fairness and retention of juniors

scenario_stem:
Vertex Drone Works is a private limited company in Country X designing camera drones for surveyors, with 18 engineers. It sold 1,100 drones at $1,500 each for $1.65 million revenue, spending $220,000 on research and development.

The Vertex Pro X1 cost $180,000 to develop and $1,050 to produce. The board chooses price skimming at $2,400 for 12 months or penetration at $1,500. Pre-orders stand at 300 units at $2,400; the sales director prefers the lower price.

questions.question_text: Define 'price skimming'.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming is a pricing method where a new product is launched at a high price to earn high profits from early adopters and recover development costs, before the price is lowered later as the product becomes established [2].

knowledge_max_2: New product launched at a high price
High profits earned early / price lowered later as product establishes

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of price skimming for Vertex Drone Works.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming generates high profits from customers willing to pay a premium [k], because each Vertex Pro X1 sold at $2,400 earns $1,350 above its $1,050 production cost [app]. It also helps recover the $180,000 development cost of the new model quickly [k], turning the 300 pre-orders at $2,400 into $720,000 of early revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: High profit per unit / high margins from premium buyers
Recovers research and development costs quickly
application_max_2: $2,400 price versus $1,050 production cost gives a $1,350 margin
300 pre-orders at $2,400 worth $720,000 towards the $180,000 development cost

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of price skimming for Vertex Drone Works.
questions.model_answer: A high launch price attracts fewer buyers in the wider market [k], since many surveying firms may wait for a lower price rather than pay $2,400 for the Vertex Pro X1 [app], limiting sales beyond the 300 pre-orders and slowing revenue growth [an]. Competitors may also copy the drone quickly [k], because a high price with strong early margins signals a profitable market [app], forcing Vertex to cut prices sooner and reducing the benefit of skimming [an].

knowledge_max_2: High price limits the number of buyers / appeals only to early adopters
High profit signals attract competitor entry and copying
application_max_2: $2,400 price for the Vertex Pro X1 may deter surveying firms outside the 300 pre-orders
Strength of margins invites rivals to copy, ending the skimming window in the first 12 months
analysis_max_2: Slower adoption limits early revenue and delays cost recovery
Earlier-than-planned price cuts erode the expected skimming benefit

questions.question_text: Do you think Vertex Drone Works should launch the Vertex Pro X1 at $2,400 using price skimming or at $1,500 using penetration pricing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming at $2,400 would earn a $1,350 margin per unit [k], and the 300 pre-orders alone would deliver $720,000, helping recover the $180,000 development cost fast [app], funding future research and protecting Vertex's premium positioning through the first 12 months with early adopters [an]. However, penetration pricing at $1,500 would undercut rivals immediately [k], matching the company's volume drone already selling 1,100 units a year at $1,500 and protecting the $1.65 million revenue line [app], which reduces the risk of weak launch sales and speeds adoption [an]. Overall, the stronger choice is price skimming at $2,400 [eval], because Vertex's customers are professional surveyors who value survey-grade accuracy over price, and early adopters expect to pay a premium for a genuinely new flagship product [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Penetration undercuts rivals to win adoption quickly
Skimming earns premium margins from early adopters
application_max_2: 300 pre-orders at $2,400 worth $720,000 towards the $180,000 development cost; margin $1,350 per unit
1,100 drones a year already sold at $1,500; penetration matches the $1.65 million revenue line
analysis_max_2: Skimming funds future research and holds premium positioning for 12 months
Penetration cuts launch risk and speeds adoption but sacrifices margin
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation referencing the professional surveyor customer base and early adopters
Weighs survey-grade differentiation and pre-order evidence against the appeal of a lower launch price

scenario_stem:
Anderfell Paper Mill is a private limited company employing 84 workers making kraft paper sacks for the cement industry. It runs batches of 25,000 sacks; finished stock waits, costing $7,600 monthly; customers wait 21 days for delivery.

Cement works threaten to switch suppliers. The manager proposes lean production with demand-driven runs, cutting stock and lead time; the sales manager fears losing $45,000 in volume discounts. The board votes on $52,000 for reorganisation this quarter.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'batch production'.
questions.model_answer: A production method in which a quantity of identical products is made together as one group, with each stage completed for the whole batch before the next stage or product begins [2].

knowledge_max_2: a quantity of identical items made together
one stage completed for the whole batch before moving on

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Anderfell Paper Mill might switch to lean production.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lean cuts storage of finished stock [k], removing much of the $7,600 monthly warehouse cost holding batches of 25,000 sacks [app]. Reason 2: Lean shortens lead times [k], reducing the 21 days customers currently wait and the threat of losing orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: lean minimises inventory and storage cost
lean reduces order lead time and waste

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Anderfell Paper Mill of switching to lean production.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lower holding costs [k], saving much of the $7,600 a month spent storing batches of 25,000 sacks [app], freeing cash for other investment [an]. Benefit 2: Faster delivery [k], ending the 21-day wait that has two cement works threatening to switch [app], securing repeat orders and protecting future revenue [an].

analysis_max_2: cash saved on warehousing can fund other investment
shorter lead times protect contracts and future revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Anderfell Paper Mill should switch to lean production? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lean means smaller demand-driven runs [k], removing much of the $7,600 monthly warehouse cost on stored 25,000-sack batches and cutting the 21-day customer wait [app], protecting accounts from defection and improving cash flow [an]. However, bulk cement works currently earn volume discounts worth $45,000 a year [k], and smaller runs could forfeit some of this and raise unit costs [app], squeezing margins just when reorganisation costs $52,000 [an]. Overall, Anderfell should switch to lean [eval], because warehouse savings of about $91,200 a year ($7,600 x 12) outweigh $45,000 of possible lost discounts, and faster delivery secures customers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: lean reduces storage cost and lead time
smaller runs may sacrifice bulk-buying discounts and raise unit costs
analysis_max_2: cash saved and repeat orders strengthen finances
lost discounts and higher unit costs would squeeze margins
evaluation_max_2: weighs annual storage savings against lost volume discounts and reorganisation cost

scenario_stem:
Dunsley Renewables Plc is a public limited company listed on the Country X Stock Exchange, building and operating wind farms. It reported $18.5 million revenue and wants a 12-turbine extension costing $4.5 million, funded over 10 years.

A $4.5 million bank loan at 7% would be secured against its existing 30-turbine wind farm; alternatively, $4.5 million of debentures at 6% are unsecured. Dunsley has paid a 4 cent dividend for three years and plans to continue it.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest payable on the $4.5 million bank loan at 7% per year.
questions.model_answer: $4.5 million Ã— 7% = $315,000 per year [2].

knowledge_max_2: interest = loan amount Ã— annual interest rate

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Dunsley of issuing $4.5 million of debentures at 6% instead of taking the bank loan at 7%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The debenture rate is 1 percentage point lower [k], saving $45,000 a year compared with the $315,000 charge on the 7% loan [app]. Reason 2: The debentures are unsecured [k], so the existing 30-turbine wind farm is not offered as security for the $4.5 million [app].

knowledge_max_2: a lower interest rate reduces the annual finance cost
unsecured debentures need no asset as security
application_max_2: 6% on $4.5 million is $270,000 a year versus $315,000 at 7%
the bank loan would be secured on the 30-turbine wind farm

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Dunsley of issuing $4.5 million of debentures.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Debenture interest is fixed and compulsory [k], and $270,000 a year must be paid even if wind speeds cut output below revenue of $18.5 million [app], reducing profit left for dividends [an]. Problem 2: The debentures must be repaid after 10 years [k], so $4.5 million falls due in a single payment at the end of the term [app], a huge demand on cash for a company funding a 12-turbine extension [an].

knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is fixed and compulsory even in poor years
the principal is repaid at the end of the debenture term
application_max_2: $270,000 a year of interest at 6% on $4.5 million
the extension is a 12-turbine project on top of an existing 30-turbine farm
analysis_max_2: fixed interest reduces profit available for dividends
a single $4.5 million repayment after 10 years strains cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunsley Renewables Plc should issue debentures rather than take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Debentures are cheaper and unsecured [k]; at 6% the interest would be $270,000 a year instead of $315,000, and the existing 30-turbine wind farm stays safe [app], freeing cash for the 12-turbine extension [an]. However, the bank loan at 7% is quicker to arrange from one lender [k], with repayment terms negotiated over 10 years, whereas a failed payment on public debentures would damage Dunsley's Stock Exchange reputation and its streak of a 4 cent dividend per share [app], deterring future investors [an]. Overall, Dunsley should issue the debentures [eval], because a 1% saving of $45,000 a year and no charge on the wind farm outweigh the reputational risk for a company with $18.5 million revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: unsecured debentures at a lower rate cut finance cost and protect assets
bank loans are quicker to arrange but need security and may raise reputational stakes
application_max_2: 6% on $4.5 million is $270,000 a year versus $315,000 at 7%
existing 30-turbine farm would secure the loan; revenue last year was $18.5 million
analysis_max_2: cost saving and asset protection weighed against arrangement speed
reputational risk to dividends and future investor confidence
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the Stock Exchange context

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Greyfen Textiles Ltd is a private limited company weaving polyester fabric for garment makers. It employs 64 weavers on 3 lines, with revenue of $2,900,000, supplying 22 clothing factories.

A 15% import tariff now applies to fabric imports. Greyfen imports 70% of its raw fabric, with an $800,000 annual bill, so the tariff adds $120,000 yearly. A domestic fabric supplier charges 20% more but delivers within 2 weeks; management must decide whether to switch or absorb the cost.

questions.question_text: Define 'import tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tax placed on goods imported from other countries, paid by the importing business when the goods cross the border [2].

knowledge_max_2: paid by the importer at the border

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the import tariff on Greyfen Textiles Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Higher production costs [k], as the 15% tariff adds $120,000 a year on top of the $800,000 imported fabric bill [app]. Effect 2: Lower profit margin or higher prices [k], because Greyfen must either absorb the extra $120,000 cost from revenue of $2,900,000 or raise prices for its 22 clothing factory customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: lower profit margin or higher prices
application_max_2: 15% tariff adds $120,000 a year to the $800,000 fabric bill

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a government might impose import tariffs.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To protect domestic producers [k], for example a Country X fabric supplier would benefit if Greyfen switched from 70% imported fabric to local sources [app], helping domestic firms compete and keeping jobs in the country [an]. Reason 2: To raise government revenue [k], collecting the 15% tariff on Greyfen's $800,000 fabric imports would yield $120,000 a year [app], which the government can spend on public services [an].

application_max_2: Greyfen switched from 70% imported fabric to local sources

questions.question_text: Do you think Greyfen Textiles should switch to the domestic fabric supplier rather than absorb the tariff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to the domestic supplier avoids the $120,000 tariff [k], because domestic fabric priced 20% above imports removes the border tax on $800,000 of fabric [app], and deliveries within 2 weeks improve reliability for its 22 clothing factory customers [an]. However, the domestic price is 20% higher than imports [k], adding around $160,000 a year to the fabric bill [app], which exceeds the $120,000 cost of the tariff [an]. On one hand, absorbing the tariff keeps annual costs $40,000 lower [eval]; on the other hand, domestic sourcing supports Country X jobs and removes import risk [eval]. Overall, absorbing the tariff is the stronger short-term option, because $120,000 a year is cheaper than the domestic premium, but Greyfen should renegotiate with the domestic supplier and review its sourcing next year.

knowledge_max_2: switching avoids the tariff / domestic delivery is faster
domestic price is 20% higher / tariff is cheaper
analysis_max_2: absorbing keeps costs lower by $40,000 a year
domestic sourcing removes import risk and supports local jobs
evaluation_max_2: weighs tariff cost against domestic premium
justified recommendation with review next year

scenario_stem:
Woldgate Grain Farm is a partnership owned by Tom and Elsie Brauer in Country X, farming 900 hectares of wheat. It harvests 4,500 tonnes sold raw to a milling company at $280 per tonne, but a drought cut output 20%.

They consider $600,000 on a flour mill: each tonne yields 750 kilograms of flour sold at $0.80 per kilogram with $140 costs. The milling company offers a 2-year contract at $300 per tonne; milling needs 7 extra workers.

questions.question_text: State what is meant by 'industrialisation'.
questions.model_answer: Industrialisation is the process by which a country's economy shifts towards a larger secondary, manufacturing sector as it develops [2].

knowledge_max_2: growth in importance/size of the secondary manufacturing sector
typically involves investment in factories and industry as an economy develops

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Woldgate Grain Farm could add value to its wheat.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Milling the wheat into flour [k], by spending $600,000 on a flour mill to sell flour at $0.80 per kilogram instead of raw wheat at $280 per tonne [app]. Way 2: Selling branded, consistent-quality flour [k], by supplying bagged flour directly to artisan bakeries, which pay more than raw grain bought in bulk by the milling company [app].

knowledge_max_2: processing raw materials into a higher-priced finished product
branding and packaging can raise the price received
application_max_2: 750 kilograms of flour per tonne of wheat

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Woldgate Grain Farm of milling its own flour instead of selling raw wheat.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A higher income per tonne [k], because each tonne of wheat yields about 750 kilograms of flour at $0.80 per kilogram, worth $600 per tonne [app], and even after $140 of extra running costs the farm keeps $460 per tonne, $160 more than the $300 contract, lifting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Less dependence on one buyer [k], because flour can be sold to many bakeries and shops rather than only the milling company [app], spreading the 4,500 tonnes a year across more customers and protecting the farm if the contract price is renegotiated downwards [an].

knowledge_max_2: processing raises revenue per tonne and profit
selling to many buyers reduces reliance on a single customer
application_max_2: $600 per tonne of flour (750 kilograms at $0.80)
$140 of extra running costs per tonne
analysis_max_2: $460 per tonne retained beats the $300 contract by $160
wider customer base lowers single-buyer risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Woldgate Grain Farm should build its own flour mill rather than accept the 2-year wheat contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that milling captures much more value [k], because flour at $0.80 per kilogram from 750 kilograms per tonne is worth $600 per tonne, keeping $460 after $140 milling costs, beating the $300 contract by $160 per tonne [app], so across 4,500 tonnes a year the extra could approach $720,000 and clear the $600,000 loan [an]. On the other hand, the 2-year contract at $300 per tonne is guaranteed [k], needing no $600,000 loan, no 7 extra workers and no risk that the farm's flour fails to win bakery customers [app]; after drought cut the harvest by 20%, dependable cash is vital [an]. Overall, building the mill is the better choice if the Brauers have forward orders from bakeries, since $460 per tonne beats $300 [eval]; without confirmed buyers, the safer 2-year contract at $300 per tonne protects a drought-hit farm [eval].

knowledge_max_2: milling increases added value and margin per tonne
the 2-year contract offers certainty and avoids debt
application_max_2: flour at $0.80 per kilogram (750 kilograms per tonne)
analysis_max_2: about $720,000 extra a year could clear the $600,000 loan
contract removes finance, staffing and demand risk after the drought
evaluation_max_2: weighs superior milling margin against contract security
justified conditional recommendation linked to orders and the drought

scenario_stem:
UrbanPulse Fitness is a sole trader running 5 clubs in Country X with 60 staff, including 22 group-exercise instructors on $13 hourly and 30-hour weeks. They teach pre-set head-office classes and turnover hit 35%.

Owner Marcus Whitlam chooses between an 8% pay rise costing $35,700 a year, or job enrichment where instructors design classes, track members and run workshops, costing $6,000 once. Exit interviews cited boredom and no ownership, not pay, for leaving.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'job enrichment'.
questions.model_answer: A non-financial method of motivation where employees are given more demanding, varied or complex tasks and greater control over how they carry them out [2].

knowledge_max_2: greater control and responsibility for the worker

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why UrbanPulse Fitness might introduce job enrichment for its instructors.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Job enrichment makes work more challenging and meaningful [k], addressing the boredom cited in exit interviews at the same clubs with 35% turnover [app]. Reason 2: It is far cheaper than a pay rise [k], costing a one-off $6,000 instead of about $35,700 a year for the 8% increase [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the 8% pay rise for UrbanPulse Fitness.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A pay rise is simple to deliver and quick to feel [k], with about $35,700 a year shared across 22 instructors from the current $13 per hour [app], immediately lifting perceived fairness of pay [an]. Benefit 2: It can help retention in a competitive local labour market [k], where rival clubs recruit instructors at higher rates and turnover is already 35% [app], cutting the cost and disruption of hiring and retraining replacements [an].

analysis_max_2: lower turnover cuts recruitment and retraining costs

questions.question_text: Do you think UrbanPulse Fitness should introduce job enrichment rather than the 8% pay rise? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Job enrichment targets the real problem [k]; exit interviews blamed boredom and lack of ownership, not pay, and the programme costs a one-off $6,000 against about $35,700 a year for the rise [app], making it sustainable and motivating members as instructors design their own classes [an]. However, enrichment takes time to work and demands skill [k]; if instructors feel overloaded on top of current 30-hour weeks, enthusiasm could fade and the 35% turnover persist [app], while pay clearly answers any wage concerns at rival clubs [an]. Overall, UrbanPulse should introduce job enrichment first [eval], because it is cheaper and addresses the cause, reviewing pay after 12 months if turnover does not fall below 20% [eval].

knowledge_max_2: enrichment can overload staff if poorly managed
analysis_max_2: low one-off cost makes the fix sustainable
overload risk could sustain high turnover
evaluation_max_2: weighs targeted motivational fix against quick, safe financial reward

scenario_stem:
Ambertide Resort & Spa is a private limited company in Country X, a 120-room beach resort with a spa and restaurants employing 85 staff. Peak-season occupancy reaches 85% at $220 per night, while off-peak occupancy falls to 45%.

To lift trade, Ravi proposes promotional pricing: a three-night package at $150 a night with breakfast and a free $45 dinner, aiming to raise off-peak occupancy to 70% at $12,000 advertising cost. Meera prefers $220 to protect the image.

questions.question_text: Define 'promotional pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Promotional pricing is a pricing method where a business lowers its price for a limited time, or offers a special package or discount, to boost sales volume, often in a quiet period or to clear stock [2].

knowledge_max_2: Price is lowered for a limited time / special offer made
Aim is to boost sales volume, often in quiet periods or to clear stock

questions.question_text: Explain two aims of promotional pricing for Ambertide Resort & Spa.
questions.model_answer: Promotional pricing aims to increase sales during quiet periods [k], helping Ambertide lift off-peak occupancy from 45% towards the proposed 70% with its $150 three-night package [app]. It also aims to attract new customer groups such as families [k], using the free dinner worth $45 to make the deal more appealing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Increase sales / lift occupancy in a quiet period
Attract new customer groups to the business
application_max_2: Off-peak occupancy expected to rise from 45% to 70% with the three-night package
Free dinner worth $45 aimed at attracting families

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of promotional pricing for Ambertide Resort & Spa.
questions.model_answer: Selling rooms at $150 instead of the standard $220 reduces the profit earned per room per night [k], and breakfast and the free dinner worth $45 add further cost [app], so each guest contributes far less, weakening off-peak profit even if occupancy rises [an]. Frequent promotions also train customers to expect lower prices [k], as families wait for the deal rather than book at $220 [app], damaging the resort's premium image and long-run profit per room [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower price reduces profit per sale / margins are squeezed
Customers learn to expect discounts / brand image suffers
application_max_2: $150 package versus $220 standard rate; breakfast and a free dinner worth $45 add cost
Families may wait for the deal rather than book at $220
analysis_max_2: Weaker off-peak profit per room even if occupancy rises to 70%
Brand image damage reduces long-run pricing power and profit per room

questions.question_text: Do you think Ambertide Resort & Spa should run the promotional package ($150 per night with breakfast and a free dinner) or keep the standard $220 rate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The promotional package would lift off-peak occupancy from 45% towards 70% [k], filling more of the 120 rooms in June to September, where occupancy is just 45% at the standard $220 rate [app], raising total room revenue and keeping staff busy through the quiet season [an]. However, keeping $220 protects the premium image and profit per room [k], avoiding over-reliance on discounts and the $12,000 advertising spend, and avoiding training families to expect deals [app], which protects long-term margin and brand strength [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to run the promotional package for the off-peak months only [eval], because 70% occupancy across 120 rooms (84 rooms) earns far more than 45% (54 rooms) at $220, even with the added $45 dinner cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Promotion fills rooms in quiet periods and attracts new customers
Keeping the standard rate protects premium image and margin
application_max_2: Off-peak occupancy 45% to 70%; 120 rooms (84 versus 54 rooms filled); $150 rate with breakfast
$220 standard rate; $12,000 advertising spend; free dinner worth $45 per stay
analysis_max_2: Higher occupancy raises total room revenue and covers staff through quiet months
Holding rate avoids deal-expectation and protects long-run margin and brand
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighting 84 rooms at $150 against 54 rooms at $220
Recognises the dinner cost ($45) and advertising ($12,000) but still favours the promotion

scenario_stem:
Tallowmere Chocolates is a private limited company with 37 workers making 18,000 boxes of chocolates a month. Revenue is $1.1 million. Before Easter it made 60,000 boxes; 14,500 stayed unsold in a $2,100 monthly warehouse.

The owner proposes a make-to-order approach for seasonal lines, making boxes only against confirmed retailer orders. The sales director warns of empty peak shelves and lost impulse sales of about $48,000. The board chooses the system for next Easter, with planning in December.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'lean production'.
questions.model_answer: A production approach that aims to minimise waste at every stage of the production process, producing only what customers demand while using resources efficiently [2].

knowledge_max_2: aims to eliminate or minimise waste
produces only what is needed / matches customer demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tallowmere Chocolates might adopt a make-to-order approach for seasonal boxes.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Make-to-order prevents overproduction [k], avoiding a repeat of 14,500 unsold boxes from the 60,000 made in advance [app]. Reason 2: Make-to-order reduces storage needs [k], easing the $2,100 monthly cost of renting warehouse space for unsold stock [app].

knowledge_max_2: avoids overproduction, a key lean waste
cuts the cost of storing excess output

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tallowmere Chocolates of a make-to-order approach.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Less unsold stock [k], sparing the business another 14,500 boxes from the 60,000 made in advance sitting in storage [app], which cuts waste costs and protects the $1.1 million revenue margin [an]. Benefit 2: Better cash flow [k], because making against confirmed retailer orders avoids money being tied up each month in the output of 18,000 boxes [app], freeing cash for ingredients and wages [an].

knowledge_max_2: make-to-order removes the risk of unsold output
cash is not tied up in finished goods stock
analysis_max_2: lower storage and write-off costs raise margins
freed cash improves liquidity for wages and ingredients

questions.question_text: Do you think Tallowmere Chocolates should make seasonal boxes only against confirmed retailer orders? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A make-to-order approach means producing only against confirmed retailer orders [k], which would prevent a repeat of 14,500 of 60,000 pre-made Easter boxes going unsold and paying $2,100 a month for storage [app], releasing cash and cutting waste dramatically [an]. However, empty shelves in peak weeks could forfeit impulse sales of about $48,000 [k], and a strict make-to-order system cannot serve unplanned supermarket top-up orders when demand spikes [app], risking lost display space and goodwill [an]. Overall, Tallowmere should switch largely to make-to-order [eval], because the certain saving on 14,500 unsold boxes outweighs the speculative $48,000, provided a modest flexible reserve is kept for peak weeks [eval].

knowledge_max_2: make-to-order removes overproduction and storage waste
strict make-to-order risks empty shelves and lost impulse sales
analysis_max_2: freed cash and lower storage raise margins and liquidity
missed peak demand damages supermarket display and goodwill
evaluation_max_2: weighs certain waste savings against speculative impulse-sales losses

scenario_stem:
Southvale Pharma Plc is a public limited company manufacturing generic medicines. It reported $42 million revenue, but two rivals have cut prices. Southvale wants a $10 million research wing for new antibiotics, due to open by 2028.

The finance director proposes 4 million new ordinary shares at $2.50 each to raise $10 million. The chairman prefers a $10 million 8-year debenture at 6.5%, costing $650,000 yearly. Antibiotic demand is seasonal, making profits uneven. Decision before 30 September.

questions.question_text: Define 'external finance'.
questions.model_answer: Finance obtained from outside the business, such as bank loans, share issues or debentures, rather than from internal sources [2].

examples include loans, debentures, share issues and grants

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Southvale of issuing 4 million new ordinary shares at $2.50 each.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Issued shares carry no fixed interest cost [k], so Southvale avoids the certain $650,000 charge a 6.5% debenture would add every year [app]. Reason 2: Shares are permanent capital [k], meaning the $10 million raised from 4 million shares at $2.50 never has to be repaid [app].

knowledge_max_2: shares carry no compulsory interest payment
share capital is permanent and never has to be repaid
application_max_2: the 6.5% debenture would cost $650,000 a year
4 million shares at $2.50 each raise $10 million

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Southvale of the chairman's $10 million debenture issue at 6.5%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Debenture interest is fixed [k], and $650,000 a year must be paid even when seasonal demand makes yearly profits uneven [app], cutting the profit available to ordinary shareholders [an]. Problem 2: The debentures must be repaid after 8 years [k], so $10 million falls due in a single year even if antibiotic sales remain seasonal [app], creating refinancing pressure on the company [an].

knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is fixed and compulsory even in weak years
the principal is repaid in full at the end of the term
application_max_2: $650,000 a year of interest at 6.5% on $10 million
demand for antibiotics is seasonal and yearly profits are uneven
analysis_max_2: fixed interest reduces profit available to shareholders

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppergate Civil Engineering Ltd is a private limited company building roads, bridges and drainage schemes in Country X. It employs 120 engineers and site workers and reported revenue of $9,000,000.

The government has announced a $250 million infrastructure programme over 5 years. Coppergate could bid for a 2-year government contract worth $3,500,000 but must invest $800,000 in heavy equipment, financed by a bank loan. Management is deciding whether to bid or keep serving its private clients.

Benefit 2: Increased demand for its services [k], as government infrastructure spending raises orders for civil engineering firms like Coppergate, which already reported $9,000,000 of revenue [app].

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Interest payments increase costs [k], so repayments on the $800,000 bank loan reduce the profit earned from the $3,500,000 contract [app], squeezing cash flow in the early months of the project [an]. Problem 2: Risk if the bid fails [k], because winning is not guaranteed and Coppergate could be left with new heavy equipment and loan repayments without the government contract revenue [app], raising financial pressure on the business [an].

It also encourages off-peak travel with lower fares [k], which can lift off-peak occupancy from its 38% level [app].

knowledge_max_2: Raises fares when demand is highest / maximises peak revenue
Lower prices encourage off-peak travel / spread demand
application_max_2: Peak fares $15 and off-peak $9, versus 88% peak occupancy
Off-peak services run at just 38% occupancy

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of dynamic pricing for Quayside Ferry Co.
questions.model_answer: Regular commuters may resent fares changing between journeys [k], especially if peak fares reach $15, $3 above the current flat $12 [app], damaging loyalty among the 500,000 annual passengers and pushing them towards the rival speedboat at $13 [an]. Dynamic pricing also requires investment and ongoing cost [k], such as the $40,000 per year software licence [app], which must be paid even if off-peak demand stays at 38% occupancy [an].

knowledge_max_2: Requires investment in systems / ongoing software cost
application_max_2: Peak fare $15 is $3 above the flat $12 fare; rival speedboat charges $13
$40,000 per year software; off-peak occupancy stuck at 38%
analysis_max_2: Loyalty damage among 500,000 annual passengers pushes them to the rival speedboat
Software cost must be recouped; weak off-peak demand may not cover it

questions.question_text: Do you think Quayside Ferry Co should introduce dynamic pricing ($15 peak, $9 off-peak) or keep the flat $12 fare? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Dynamic pricing would raise total revenue from $6.0 million to $6.3 million [k], based on 300,000 peak passengers at $15 and 200,000 off-peak passengers at $9 [app], adding $300,000 that would more than cover the $40,000 software cost and offset the 25% fuel increase [an]. However, keeping the flat $12 fare protects predictability for regular commuters [k], avoiding the risk that they switch to the rival speedboat service at $13, which is only $1 more if peak fares rise to $15 [app], protecting Quayside's reputation and existing passenger base [an]. Overall, the stronger position is dynamic pricing [eval], because peak occupancy is 88% and fares should reflect that scarcity, while $9 off-peak fares will win price-sensitive passengers without abandoning peak revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Dynamic pricing monetises high-demand peak seats
Flat fare is predictable and protects loyalty
application_max_2: Revenue rises from $6.0 million to $6.3 million: 300,000 peak at $15 + 200,000 off-peak at $9
$40,000 software cost; 25% fuel increase; rival speedboat at $13 versus flat $12
analysis_max_2: Extra $300,000 covers software cost and fuel increase
Flat fare protects reputation and passenger base against the $13 rival
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation based on 88% peak occupancy signalling scarcity
Weighs rival switching risk and commuter preference for predictability against revenue gain

scenario_stem:
Anvilbrook Bottling Co is a private limited company with 33 workers on a lean line filling 15,000 bottles a week on demand, only 1.5% discarded as waste. Its range has six flavours.

A regional hotel group offers a one-off contract for 2,400 bottles of bespoke strawberry-elderflower cordial with a custom label at $6.50 each, worth $15,600. Sales wants to hand-finish it on a separate bench; operations warns this removes two shifts and breaks the flow. They reply Friday.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'job production'.
questions.model_answer: A production method in which a single item, or a small number of items, are made to an individual customer's specification rather than for general stock [2].

knowledge_max_2: one-off or small number of items made
made to a specific customer's specification/order

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Anvilbrook Bottling Co might accept the bespoke job production contract.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: High revenue per bottle [k], with the one-off contract paying $6.50 a bottle, worth $15,600 in total [app]. Reason 2: A new customer relationship [k], offering 2,400 bottles of bespoke strawberry-elderflower cordial to a regional hotel group that could place repeat orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: job production earns premium prices per unit
a bespoke job can win new customers and future orders

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Anvilbrook Bottling Co of hand-finishing the bespoke order on a separate bench.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Disrupted flow [k], because removing up to two shifts off the lean line breaks the standard flow that keeps bottle waste at 1.5% [app], raising waste and unit costs [an]. Problem 2: Lost standard output [k], as two removed shifts reduce the 15,000 bottles a week available to regular buyers [app], risking missed regular orders and revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: removing capacity disrupts the standard flow
less capacity means fewer regular units produced
analysis_max_2: broken flow raises waste and unit costs
lost regular output risks missed orders and revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Anvilbrook Bottling Co should accept the bespoke job production contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The contract pays $6.50 a bottle for 2,400 bottles, worth $15,600 [k], a high-margin one-off deal that could showcase the firm's cordials to a regional hotel group [app], potentially opening future contracts beyond the standard 15,000-bottle-a-week range [an]. However, hand-finishing removes up to two shifts from the lean line [k], risking waste above the usual 1.5% and delaying regular orders of 15,000 bottles a week [app], which could erode the reliability regular buyers rely on [an]. Overall, Anvilbrook should accept, but schedule the job after peak filling weeks [eval], securing $15,600 without sacrificing the lean flow that keeps waste at 1.5% [eval].

acceptance risks disrupting the standard flow and waste level

scenario_stem:
Keswickmoor Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company making ceramic tiles for hotels and restaurants. Revenue was $4.6 million with $1.1 million retained profit. Two chains want 300,000 extra tiles next year. Keswickmoor wants $750,000 for a glaze laboratory and automated kiln line.

A $750,000 bank loan at 5.5% over 6 years costs $41,250 yearly, but the bank gives no further credit while outstanding. Alternatively, 500,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 raise $750,000. Protecting glaze quality matters; the board votes on 20 February.

questions.question_text: Define 'ordinary shares'.
questions.model_answer: The standard voting shares of a company, giving holders ownership rights and a claim to dividends from profit [2].

knowledge_max_2: ordinary shares carry ownership and voting rights
ordinary shareholders receive dividends from profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Keswickmoor might take the bank loan rather than issue new shares.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Existing shareholders keep full ownership [k], because no 500,000 new ordinary shares are added to the current holding [app]. Reason 2: Loan interest is certain and tax-deductible [k], at $41,250 a year for 6 years, reducing the tax payable on profits from $4.6 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: a bank loan does not change ownership or control
loan interest is certain in advance and tax-deductible
application_max_2: the share option would add 500,000 new ordinary shares
the loan costs $41,250 a year at 5.5% over 6 years

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Keswickmoor of issuing the 500,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Shares are permanent capital [k], so the $750,000 raised never has to be repaid, unlike the loan due in full after 6 years [app], protecting cash flow while the glaze laboratory is built [an]. Advantage 2: No fixed interest [k], so dividends can fall if hotel orders below $4.6 million disappoint, whereas $41,250 a year interest would still fall due [app], giving flexibility in weak seasons [an].

knowledge_max_2: share capital is permanent and never has to be repaid
ordinary dividends can be reduced when profit falls
application_max_2: the loan at 5.5% costs $41,250 a year for 6 years
analysis_max_2: no repayment protects cash during the laboratory build
flexible dividends give room in weak seasons

questions.question_text: Do you think Keswickmoor Ceramics Ltd should take the bank loan rather than issue new ordinary shares? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The bank loan raises $750,000 quickly [k], preserves full ownership and costs a tax-deductible $41,250 a year, so Keswickmoor keeps control while hotel clients get their extra 300,000 tiles [app], and the 5.5% rate is affordable against $4.6 million revenue [an]. However, issuing 500,000 new shares at $1.50 brings $750,000 that never needs repaying [k], avoids the clause that the bank gives no further credit while the loan is outstanding and shields the glaze laboratory project if demand dips [app], reducing fixed obligations across the 6 years [an]. Overall, Keswickmoor should issue the new ordinary shares [eval], because the no-further-credit clause would cramp growth, making permanent share capital the safer route despite the $1.50 dilution [eval].

share issue raises permanent capital with no repayment obligation
application_max_2: loan costs $41,250 a year at 5.5% for 6 years; shares at $1.50 raise $750,000
two national hotel chains want 300,000 extra tiles; revenue was $4.6 million
analysis_max_2: speed and control weighed against the no-further-credit clause
permanent capital versus fixed annual obligations
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the hotel-chain order
