scenario_stem:
The Gilded Fork is a private limited company operating 4 casual restaurants. It employs 38 kitchen and floor staff, with sales of $2,070,000, an average meal bill of $45 and 46,000 meals served near full capacity.

VAT on hospitality is temporarily cut from 13.5% to 9% for 12 months to revive the restaurant sector. Management must decide whether to pass the cut to customers through lower menu prices or keep prices unchanged to rebuild cash reserves.

questions.question_text: Define 'indirect tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax charged on spending on goods and services, collected by the seller on behalf of the government, such as VAT [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax on spending / goods and services
collected by seller on behalf of government (e.g. VAT)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the VAT cut on The Gilded Fork.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Either a higher margin or lower prices [k], because the cut from 13.5% to 9% lets the restaurants keep more of the $45 average meal bill or pass savings to diners [app]. Effect 2: A potential boost to demand [k], as cheaper meals may lift sales above the 46,000 meals served last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: choice between higher margin or lower prices
application_max_2: cut from 13.5% to 9% / $45 average meal bill

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the VAT cut could affect the restaurant's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Lower prices if the cut is passed on [k], so customers pay less for their average $45 meal [app], stretching household budgets further during the difficult downturn [an]. Way 2: Better value for money [k], encouraging customers to dine out more than the 46,000 meals served last year [app], supporting the hospitality sector's recovery [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower prices if cut passed on
better value for money / more dining out

questions.question_text: Do you think The Gilded Fork should pass the VAT cut on to customers rather than keep menu prices unchanged? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Passing the cut on lowers dining-out costs [k], stretching the $45 average meal bill further for customers after a difficult downturn [app], which should increase meal covers above the 46,000 served last year and restore lost business [an]. However, keeping prices unchanged rebuilds cash [k], converting the 4.5 percentage point VAT cut straight into margin on $2,070,000 of sales [app], which strengthens the business after a difficult year [an]. On one hand, passing on the cut wins share and goodwill quickly [eval]; on the other hand, retaining margin protects jobs and supplier payments in a fragile sector [eval]. Overall, The Gilded Fork should pass on most of the cut through slightly lower prices, because the cut is temporary for 12 months and stimulating demand now is the fastest way to restore $2,070,000 or higher sales.

knowledge_max_2: passing on the cut lowers prices / stretches budgets
keeping prices rebuilds cash / protects jobs
application_max_2: 4.5 percentage point cut on $2,070,000 of sales
analysis_max_2: lower prices restore lost business quickly
retained margin strengthens cash and supplier payments
evaluation_max_2: weighs goodwill and share gains against cash rebuilding
justified recommendation referencing the 12-month window

scenario_stem:
Alderbrace Construction Ltd is a private limited company building 30 family homes a year. It owns 2 tower cranes and 14 lorries, and bought land for $2.1m. Output rose 11% after new machinery was installed.

The director must decide whether to buy a $380,000 mobile crane lifting loads 4 times faster, or hire 12 additional bricklayers at $520 a week for 3 years. Each lays 340 bricks a day, but 22 houses remain unsold.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Capital is the man-made resources used to produce goods and services, such as Alderbrace's 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 6 excavators and hoist, which are used to build homes. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made / human-made resources used to produce goods and services
Reward any suitable examples such as machinery, tools, vehicles, equipment or buildings

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why capital is important to Alderbrace Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Capital gives a business the man-made resources it needs to produce goods and services [k]. Alderbrace owns 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries and 6 excavators to build its 30 family homes a year [app]. Reason 2: Capital raises productivity because machines can work faster and longer than people alone [k]. After new machinery was installed last year, site output rose 11%, showing capital equipment measurably increased production [app].

knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made resources used in production (machinery, vehicles, tools)
Capital goods help raise output and productivity
application_max_2: Alderbrace's own assets: 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 6 excavators / 30 family homes a year
The 11% rise in site output after new machinery was installed

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of buying the $380,000 mobile crane for Alderbrace.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Capital equipment can increase the speed of production [k]. The crane would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist, allowing the firm to complete phases more quickly [app]. Faster lifting would reduce the time each house spends under construction, raising overall output and helping clear unsold stock sooner [an]. Benefit 2: Machinery raises efficiency by getting more output from existing inputs [k]. A $380,000 crane costs far less over 3 years than hiring 12 bricklayers at $520 a week, which would total $973,440 (12 x $520 x 156 weeks) [app]. Paying once for the crane instead of ongoing wages would cut production costs per house and improve profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: Machinery/capital equipment can increase speed and output
Machinery can reduce average costs / raise efficiency versus ongoing wages
application_max_2: Crane lifts loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist
Cost comparison: $380,000 crane versus $973,440 to hire 12 bricklayers over 3 years
analysis_max_2: Faster lifting shortens build time, raising output and sales turnover
Lower labour cost per house improves profit margins on the remaining houses

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderbrace Construction Ltd should buy the $380,000 mobile crane rather than hire 12 additional bricklayers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the crane: buying the $380,000 mobile crane gives Alderbrace more capital, which is a man-made resource for production [k]. It would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist, and site output already rose 11% after the previous machinery was installed [app]. This suggests further capital investment would raise productivity and shorten build times, helping shift the 22 houses that remain unsold [an]. Argument for hiring bricklayers: hiring 12 bricklayers at $520 a week is more flexible and avoids a large one-off outlay [k]. However, 12 bricklayers over the next 3 years would cost $973,440 (12 x $520 x 156 weeks), far more than the crane's one-off $380,000 [app]. Yet with 22 houses still unsold, committing cash to the crane is risky if demand weakens, because a specialised crane cannot easily be resold or redeployed [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the crane is cheaper over 3 years ($380,000 versus $973,440) and matches the 11% output gain from the earlier machinery, so Alderbrace should buy the crane if it can secure buyer interest in the remaining houses [eval]. If demand stays weak, flexible bricklayers would protect the firm's cash, so the decision depends on confirmed sales [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Crane = capital investment; bricklayers = labour, both are factors of production
Capital can raise productivity and reduce unit costs over time
application_max_2: $380,000 crane versus 12 x $520 x 156 weeks = $973,440 over 3 years
4 times faster lifting / 11% output rise / 22 houses remain unsold / $2.1m land purchase
analysis_max_2: Cost comparison over 3 years favours the crane if demand holds
Fixed capital carries resale/redeployment risk versus flexible labour given unsold stock
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on confirmed demand/buyer contracts for the remaining houses
Balanced judgement recognising flexibility of labour against the crane's cost saving

scenario_stem:
Brewhurst Bottling Co is a private limited company in Carrick, Country X, bottling craft soft drinks for 90 supermarket customers. It has 74 staff, including 64 bottling operatives; output was 1.5 million bottles. Supervisors manage 8 operatives each and quality checks take 3 hours a day per line.

The board proposes 12 operatives per supervisor, removing 2 supervisors to save $58,000 (2 x $29,000). A March trial lifted output per shift 4% while complaints rose from 11 to 22 monthly.

questions.question_text: Define 'span of control'.
questions.model_answer: Span of control is the number of subordinates that one manager is directly responsible for, such as Brewhurst's 8 supervisors each managing 8 bottling operatives. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Span of control = number of subordinates reporting directly to one manager
Can be wide (many staff per manager) or narrow (few staff per manager)

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brewhurst Bottling Co of widening the span of control to 12 operatives per supervisor.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A wider span of control means each supervisor manages more operatives, so fewer supervisors are needed [k]. Removing 2 supervisors would save $58,000 a year in wages (2 x $29,000) [app]. Benefit 2: Fewer supervisors can speed up communication between directors and operatives [k]. The March trial lifted output per shift by 4%, suggesting operatives can work well with less direct supervision [app].

knowledge_max_2: Wider span of control = more subordinates per manager, fewer managers needed overall
Fewer managers can reduce wage costs and speed up communication
application_max_2: Saving $58,000 a year by removing 2 supervisors (2 x $29,000)
March trial raised output per shift by 4%; 64 operatives would be covered by fewer supervisors at 12 each

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Brewhurst of widening the span of control to 12 operatives per supervisor.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Supervisors with more operatives to oversee have less time to monitor each one [k]. Quality checks already take 3 hours a day per line, so spreading one supervisor over 12 operatives could stretch supervision even further [app]. Weaker supervision may let defects reach dispatch, damaging relationships with the 90 supermarket customers [an]. Drawback 2: A wider span of control can leave operatives without enough support or guidance [k]. Customer complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month during the March trial [app]. Rising complaints could mean more returns and penalty charges, wiping out the $58,000 wage saving [an].

knowledge_max_2: Wider span gives each subordinate less supervision and support
Supervisors may become overloaded, so guidance and discipline weaken
application_max_2: Quality checks already take 3 hours a day per line; proposal is 12 operatives per supervisor
Complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month during the March trial; 90 supermarket customers
analysis_max_2: Less supervision raises the risk of defects reaching customers, harming supermarket relationships
Complaint and return costs could exceed the $58,000 wage saving

questions.question_text: Do you think Brewhurst should widen the span of control to 12 operatives per supervisor rather than keep 8 operatives each? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for widening: a wider span of control cuts the number of supervisors Brewhurst needs [k]. Removing 2 supervisors would save $58,000 a year in wages (2 x $29,000), and the March trial lifted output per shift by 4% with 64 bottling operatives working in teams [app]. Lower wage costs would raise profit on 1.5 million bottles a year, helping Brewhurst price competitively for its 90 supermarket customers [an]. Argument for keeping 8 supervisors: the current narrow span lets supervisors monitor quality checks that take 3 hours a day per line [k]. The March trial doubled complaints from 11 to 22 a month while output rose only 4%, showing operatives may need closer supervision [app]. Wider spans could overload supervisors, harm quality and lose supermarket contracts that depend on reliable supply [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Brewhurst should not widen the span yet, because complaints doubling to 22 a month and only a 4% output gain outweigh the $58,000 saving; it should fix the causes of complaints first [eval]. If complaint and quality data improve over the next 3 months, widening the span could then be reconsidered [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Wider span reduces manager numbers and wage costs
Narrower span allows closer supervision and support
application_max_2: $58,000 yearly saving from removing 2 supervisors (2 x $29,000); March trial output per shift up only 4%
Quality checks take 3 hours a day per line; complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month
analysis_max_2: Lower wages raise per-bottle profit and competitive pricing across 1.5 million bottles
Overloaded supervisors could damage quality and lose supermarket contracts
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation not to widen yet, tied to the 22 complaints per month and the 4% gain
Conditional reconsideration if complaint and quality data improve over 3 months

scenario_stem:
Wickmere Fruit Juices is a private limited company in Country X owned by Carla Jimenez, pressing juices sold to supermarkets. It sells 32,000 bottles a month for $920,000 yearly. Share is 4% against Purevale's 21%, and sales grew 9%.

With a $35,000 budget, Carla must choose: an informative campaign on the low-sugar recipe for $16,000, or a persuasive lifestyle campaign targeting switchers for $27,000. Both must build loyalty and support a 750ml family-size bottle.

questions.question_text: Define 'promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Promotion is communicating with customers to inform, persuade or remind them about a product in order to encourage sales [2].

knowledge_max_2: communicating with customers/informing or persuading them
to encourage sales or remind them of the product

questions.question_text: Explain two aims Wickmere Fruit Juices could have for its promotion.
questions.model_answer: Aim 1: To inform existing customers about the new low-sugar recipe [k], giving clear details of what has changed in the juices they already buy [app]. Aim 2: To persuade rival brand switchers to buy Wickmere juices instead [k], helping the company grow from its 4% market share against Purevale's 21% [app].

knowledge_max_2: to inform customers/explain the product or its changes
to persuade customers to buy or switch brands

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wickmere Fruit Juices of setting clear aims for its promotion.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Clear aims allow Carla to choose between the informative and persuasive proposals [k], so the $35,000 budget goes to the option that fits the business best [app], reducing wasted spending on the wrong method [an]. Benefit 2: Clear aims provide measurable targets, such as continued growth in bottles sold [k], letting Carla check whether sales stay ahead of the recent 9% rise [app], which helps judge whether the campaign succeeded [an].

knowledge_max_2: aims focus budget on a suitable promotional method
aims provide measurable targets to evaluate success
analysis_max_2: reduces wasted expenditure on an unsuitable method
enables the business to judge campaign success afterwards

questions.question_text: Do you think Wickmere Fruit Juices should choose the informative campaign or the persuasive campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The informative campaign explains the new low-sugar recipe to existing customers [k], targeting the buyers of the 32,000 bottles sold each month [app], which should protect repeat sales and the recent 9% growth [an]. However, the persuasive campaign uses lifestyle posters and television advertising to reach rival brand switchers [k], going beyond Wickmere's 4% share against Purevale's 21% [app], which could accelerate growth of the family-size bottle if it succeeds [an]. Overall, the informative campaign is the safer choice because Carla's first priority should be keeping existing customers as the recipe changes [eval], and with a budget of $35,000 the cheaper $16,000 option leaves headroom to support the 750ml family-size bottle launch [eval].

persuasive campaign: wider reach, can attract new customers
analysis_max_2: protects repeat sales and recent 9% growth
could accelerate family-size bottle success via switchers

justified choice given the $35,000 budget constraint

scenario_stem:
Wychwood Furniture Co, a private limited company, makes flat-pack wardrobe doors for 12 furniture retailers. Of 34 workers, 18 are on manual cutting benches. Last year's 240,000 doors saw 6% of doors fail quality checks, costing $95,000 in rework.

Option A keeps hand-cutting plus a second shift. Option B spends $900,000 on CAM-controlled CNC routers, replacing 10 cutting jobs, lifting output to 300,000 doors and cutting defects from 6% to 2%. Maintenance is $120,000 a year, yet $210,000 a year is saved in waste.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-aided manufacturing (CAM)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-aided manufacturing is the use of computer-controlled machines and software to carry out production processes such as cutting and assembly, rather than doing them by hand. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CAM = use of computers and software to control manufacturing machinery and processes
CAM programs guide machines such as CNC routers and edgebanders automatically

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wychwood Furniture Co of using CAM-controlled machines.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CAM machines cut and edge doors to the same measurements every time, removing human error [k]. The defect rate would fall from 6% of doors to 2%, saving costly rework [app]. Benefit 2: CAM-controlled routers work continuously and faster than hand cutting [k]. Output would rise from 240,000 doors a year to 300,000, helping Wychwood serve its 12 retailers [app].

knowledge_max_2: CAM gives consistent, accurate output and removes human error
CAM machines work faster and continuously, raising output
application_max_2: Defect rate falls from 6% to 2%, cutting rework costs
Output rises from 240,000 to 300,000 doors a year for 12 retailers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wychwood Furniture Co could face if it buys the CAM-controlled machines.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The machines are expensive to buy and run [k]. Option B costs $900,000 plus $120,000 a year in maintenance, a heavy outlay for one factory [app]. If sales stay flat, these fixed costs may take years to recover and strain cash flow [an]. Problem 2: CAM removes labour from the cutting benches [k]. Replacing 10 cutting jobs from 34 workers would make staff redundant [app]. Redundancy payments and lower morale among remaining workers could reduce productivity [an].

knowledge_max_2: High capital and running costs for CAM equipment
CAM machines replace manual jobs, leading to redundancies
application_max_2: Option B costs $900,000 plus $120,000 a year in maintenance
10 cutting jobs would be replaced from 34 workers
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs rise, squeezing profit and cash flow if sales do not grow
Redundancy costs and lower morale can reduce productivity and damage the workforce

questions.question_text: Do you think Wychwood Furniture Co should buy the CAM-controlled machines rather than add a second shift? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for Option B: CAM would make production faster and more accurate [k]. Output would rise from 240,000 to 300,000 doors a year while defects fall from 6% to 2%, and the $210,000 a year board saving less $120,000 a year maintenance still leaves about $90,000 a year before rework savings [app]. Lower unit costs would let Wychwood price competitively and win larger orders from its 12 retailers [an]. Case for Option A: keeping hand-cutting avoids the $900,000 investment and protects the 10 cutting jobs [k]. A second shift keeps 18 manual benches running with no redundancy costs, but the 6% defect rate would stay [app]. Staying manual would keep rework at $95,000 a year and leave Wychwood vulnerable to rivals with fewer defects [an]. Overall, Wychwood should buy the CAM machines because the defect saving and $210,000 annual board saving outweigh the maintenance cost and the 10 lost jobs [eval]. If retailer demand weakens, the company could lease rather than buy the machines outright [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CAM gives faster, more consistent production than hand methods
Keeping manual cutting avoids capital cost and redundancies
application_max_2: Output rises to 300,000 doors; defects fall from 6% to 2%; $210,000 board saving less $120,000 maintenance
Option A avoids $900,000 spend; $95,000 a year rework cost would continue; 18 manual benches kept
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs improve competitiveness and retailer orders
Manual operation preserves rework cost burden and weaker quality position
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation based on stem figures (defect saving and $210,000 outweigh costs)
Condition suggested for the alternative (lease if demand weakens)

scenario_stem:
Renwick Precision Ltd is a private limited company making metal brackets and gear housings for agricultural machinery in Country X. It employs 18 workers and wants an $80,000 CNC machining centre to win a contract worth $150,000 a year.

Owner Priya Raman compares factoring of debts with crowdfunding. Debtors owe $100,000; a factor offers 80% ($80,000) now for a 3% fee of $3,000. Crowdfunding targets $85,000 with a 5% fee ($4,250), but needs videos and rewards for backers.

questions.question_text: Define 'factoring of debts'.
questions.model_answer: Factoring of debts is when a business sells its unpaid customer invoices (debtors) to a specialist finance company, which pays an immediate cash advance and then collects the money owed, usually in return for a fee. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Selling unpaid invoices/debtors to a specialist company (factor)
Factor pays an advance and collects the debts for a fee

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Renwick Precision Ltd.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Alderford Kitchens Ltd is a private limited company selling and installing fitted kitchens in Redby. It employs 28 staff, with $3.9 million sales and $1.1 million of stock. An average kitchen costs $9,400; 65% of customers use a finance plan.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the rise in interest rates has reduced demand for Alderford Kitchens.

scenario_stem:
Vantara Logistics Ltd is a private limited fulfilment business in Hallwick. It employs 340 operatives, processes 1,150 orders a day for 40 retail clients, and splits work between 5 stations.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why division of labour increases output at Vantara's warehouse.

Since work was split into 5 stations, output per worker per hour has risen from 62 to 74 orders [app]. Reason 2: Specialisation reduces time lost switching between different tasks [k]. questions.question_text: Do you think Vantara should add a 6th quality-check station rather than train staff to rotate between all 5 stations? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the 6th station: adding a dedicated quality-check station would extend division of labour, a method that already raised output from 62 to 74 orders per worker per hour [k]. This should raise accuracy without disrupting the current specialisation that delivers 1,150 orders a day [an]. Argument for rotation: training staff to rotate between all 5 stations would make work more varied and less boring [k]. It would also let Vantara cover absences and peak periods without hiring, protecting client service while wages average $11 per hour [app]. However, rotating staff could reduce the task-specific skill that lifted output by 12 orders per worker per hour over 18 months [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, adding the 6th station builds on proven gains of 62 to 74 orders per hour and protects quality for 40 clients, so Vantara should add the quality-check station and offer limited job rotation to the most experienced operatives [eval]. If errors are rare and morale is the bigger problem, rotation would be better, so the final decision should depend on error-rate data [eval].

scenario_stem:
Hallowmere Furniture Co is a private limited company in Brantwell, Country X, making oak dining furniture for 35 furniture retailers with 84 staff. Orders pass through 5 management levels. Last year it lost 14 orders worth $96,000 because quotes took 9 days to approve.

Managing director Ruth Ellison proposes letting department heads approve quotes up to $4,000. The sales manager agrees, but 2 senior managers warn juniors may approve underpriced work and rushed sign-off could raise waste, already 7% of timber.

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Hallowmere Furniture Co of its long chain of command.

scenario_stem:
Aldermont Cycles is a private limited company in Country X selling electric bicycles at $1,850 from a single showroom, with $1.9 million revenue and 1,020 e-bikes sold last year. It employs 14 staff and spends $90,000 on marketing.

questions.model_answer: Difference 1: Informative advertising gives factual information about a product [k], such as the 90km battery range, the 2-year warranty and the crash-tested frame [app]. Difference 2: Persuasive advertising aims to convince customers by appealing to emotions and desires [k], using television and billboards showing freedom and prestige [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Aldermont Cycles of using persuasive advertising for the new commuter e-bike.

scenario_stem:
Ondara Convenience Stores is a private limited company running 4 convenience stores, employing 58 staff with $9.6 million annual sales. Handwritten stock books make each monthly stock-take take 2 days per store; theft and missing stock cost $84,000 a year.

Option A keeps manual records, hiring 1 part-time clerk per store at $19,000 a year each. Option B spends $260,000 on EPOS tills with a central stock database, scanning sales and reordering automatically, cutting shrinkage by 60% and stock-takes to 4 hours per store.

questions.question_text: Define 'electronic point of sale (EPOS)'.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ondara Convenience Stores of installing EPOS tills.

Benefit 2: EPOS creates a detailed sales record that helps ordering decisions [k]. Shrinkage of $84,000 a year would be expected to fall by 60%, saving about $50,400 a year [app].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marne Valley Dairies is a sole trader dairy farm in Country X selling milk to a processing plant. It earned $820,000 revenue and $46,000 profit, having borrowed $400,000 at a variable interest rate of 4% to replace its milking parlour.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a rise in interest rates increases the financial pressure on businesses with loans.

Way 2: Renegotiate the loan with its bank [k]. The $400,000 outstanding loan could be stretched over a longer repayment period or converted to a fixed rate [app], which spreads the cost more evenly and removes the risk of rates rising again [an].

scenario_stem:
Brackmoor Haulage Co is a road freight partnership in Fenwick running 28 HGVs on the northern industrial corridor. Its 34 drivers take 2 weeks of training and specialise on 3 fixed routes, carrying 1,900 tonnes monthly.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexmoor should create the senior carer grade rather than give all carers a 4% pay rise? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Bramfield Supermarket is a private limited company in Country X with 6 branches and 480 staff, earning $14.6 million. Breakfast cereals are 11% of sales. Annual marketing is $210,000, with $60,000 allocated to cereal promotions as discounters cut staple prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Short-term incentives used to encourage customers to buy a product or to boost sales of it, such as discounts or special offers [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Bramfield Supermarket of using a BOGOF offer on cereal.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: BOGOF can rapidly increase sales volume [k], helping the supermarket reach its target of a 20% rise in cereal sales across the 6 branches [app]. Advantage 2: BOGOF attracts customers into the supermarket [k], where they may buy other products alongside the 14 cereal brands [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramfield Supermarket of the suppliers funding half the promotion.

Benefit 2: Suppliers fund the activity because higher sales also benefit their own brands [k], so they share the risk on the 14 cereal brands [app], which strengthens the long-term trading relationship [an].

However, the 15% price reduction is simpler for staff and customers to understand [k], lowering the shelf price of every box without giving away extra units [app], protecting margins if BOGOF would halve the value of each sale at higher volume [an]. Overall, Bramfield should choose BOGOF because the suppliers fund half the cost either way, making the free extra units affordable [eval], and a dramatic offer is more likely to achieve a 20% quarterly uplift than a modest 15% discount during rival price cuts [eval].

scenario_stem:
Breckfield Pump Works, a private limited company, makes water pumps for farms. With 85 workers it produces 1,400 pumps a month and earns $11.2 million a year. Design errors mean 8% of pumps need reworking before dispatch.

Option A keeps separate CAD/CAM machines and 2 inspection stations. Option B spends $2.4 million on a CIM system linking design, 6 CNC machines, scanners and stock control, cutting rework from 8% to 3% and lifting output to 1,750 pumps a month; training 12 staff costs $36,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-integrated manufacturing is the linking of all production stages - design, machining, quality inspection and stock control - into one computer-controlled system that shares information automatically. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CIM links design, production, inspection and stock in one computer system
Information flows automatically between stages without manual paperwork

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Breckfield Pump Works of installing a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CIM shares design data directly with the machines, removing manual re-entry [k]. Rework would fall from 8% of pumps to 3%, saving materials and labour [app]. Benefit 2: Linking all stages in one system speeds up the whole production flow [k]. Output would rise from 1,400 pumps a month to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase [app].

knowledge_max_2: CIM removes manual data transfer errors between design and production
An integrated flow speeds up the process from planning to dispatch
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3% of pumps
Output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month (a 25% increase)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Breckfield Pump Works could face if it installs a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: CIM costs a great deal of money up front [k]. Option B requires $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff [app]. Borrowing that sum would add interest payments and raise financial risk for the company [an]. Problem 2: CIM depends on all its linked parts working together [k]. A fault in 1 of the 6 CNC machines or in the shared database could stop the whole line [app]. One breakdown could halt deliveries to farm customers and breach supply commitments [an].

knowledge_max_2: CIM requires very high capital investment and training spend
Integrated systems can fail as a whole if one component breaks
application_max_2: Option B costs $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff
6 CNC machines and one shared database are all linked together
analysis_max_2: High borrowing increases interest burden and financial risk
A single-point failure could stop production and lose farm customer contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Breckfield Pump Works should install the CIM system rather than keep the separate machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for CIM: CIM links design, machining, inspection and stock in 1 system [k]. It would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase on $11.2 million of revenue [app]. Fewer errors and higher output would raise profit and let Breckfield take on more farm contracts [an]. Case for keeping separate machines: Option A avoids the $2.4 million cost and the $36,000 training bill [k]. The existing CAD and CAM machines and 2 inspection stations already work, so there is no disruption or retraining [app]. Staying with separate machines keeps the 8% rework rate and the 1,400 pumps a month output limit [an]. Overall, Breckfield should install CIM, because cutting rework from 8% to 3% and lifting output by 25% outweighs the upfront cost over time [eval]. The directors could phase the system in over 12 months to limit disruption [eval].

Separate machines avoid capital cost and retraining
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3%; output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps (+25%) on $11.2 million revenue

analysis_max_2: Lower rework and higher output raise profit and capacity for farm contracts
Keeping separate machines preserves status quo inefficiencies and output ceiling
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (rework and 25% output gain outweigh cost)
Practical phasing suggestion to reduce risk (12-month phased rollout)

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

It would cut pattern preparation from 2 weeks to 2 days and reduce waste from 9% to 6%, saving about $27,000 a year on $900,000 of fabric [app]. Faster turnaround and less waste would raise profit on school uniform orders worth part of $7.3 million of revenue [an]. Case for hand-drawn patterns: Option A avoids the $140,000 cost and the $18,000 yearly licences [k]. The 3 pattern cutters already serve 20 schools and need no retraining or computers [app]. Hand methods keep the 2-week pattern cycle and the 9% waste rate, so savings stay slow to arrive [an]. Overall, Sorrel & Main should adopt CAD, because pattern time cut from 2 weeks to 2 days and about $27,000 a year in fabric savings outweigh licence costs [eval]. The directors could buy 1 workstation first to test staff acceptance [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CAD speeds up and improves accuracy of pattern design
Hand-drawn patterns avoid capital cost and retraining
application_max_2: Pattern time 2 weeks to 2 days; waste 9% to 6%; about $27,000 a year saved on $900,000 fabric
Option A avoids $140,000 and $18,000 yearly licences; 3 cutters serve 20 schools already
analysis_max_2: Faster turnaround and lower waste raise profit on $7.3 million revenue
Hand methods preserve slow 2-week cycle and 9% waste, limiting savings
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (time and $27,000 fabric saving)
Practical low-risk first step suggested (trial one workstation)

scenario_stem:
Gorse & Grain Preserves Ltd is a private limited company making chutneys, jams and pickles. It sells 40% of output at farmers' markets and has revenue of $95,000. Leah Montrose wants a copper jam kettle and jars costing $22,000 after the old kettle cracked.

She compares crowdfunding targeting $25,000, with a 6% success fee ($1,500) and rewards of preserves and named labels, with a $15,000 micro-finance loan at 14%, costing $2,100 a year over 5 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'crowdfunding'.
questions.model_answer: Crowdfunding is raising small amounts of money from a large number of people, usually through an online platform, to fund a business venture or project. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Raising finance from a large number of people
Usually via an online platform / small individual contributions

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of crowdfunding for Gorse & Grain Preserves Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: No interest or repayments are owed [k]; if Leah reaches the $25,000 target, the copper kettle and a year's supply of jars are funded by backers rather than by debt [app]. Advantage 2: A campaign raises publicity and sales [k]; named-label rewards turn backers into ambassadors, extending Leah's reach beyond the 40% of sales currently made at farmers' markets [app].

application_max_2: $25,000 target covers the $22,000 kettle and jars
40% of sales at farmers' markets / named labels / artisan food platform

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Gorse & Grain Preserves Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Interest must be paid on the loan [k]; the 14% rate costs $2,100 a year for 5 years, on annual sales revenue of only $95,000 [app], reducing the profit Leah can reinvest in the business [an]. Disadvantage 2: The loan on offer is too small [k]; only $15,000 is available against the $22,000 needed, leaving a $7,000 gap [app], and monthly repayments would strain cash flow in quiet trading months [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loan size limited / may be below the amount required
analysis_max_2: Interest reduces profit and reinvestment capacity
Shortfall and repayments strain cash flow, especially seasonally

questions.question_text: Do you think Gorse & Grain Preserves Ltd should use crowdfunding or micro-finance? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Crowdfunding could raise $25,000, more than the $22,000 required, with no interest and free publicity among Leah's farmers'-market customers; however, reaching the target is not guaranteed, and the 6% success fee costs $1,500 and producing hundreds of named-label jars adds work [k] [app] [an]. Micro-finance is more certain and simpler to administer [k], costing $2,100 a year in interest, but the $15,000 on offer leaves a $7,000 gap and monthly repayments for 5 years would pressure a small seasonal business [app] [an]. Overall, I think Gorse & Grain should try crowdfunding first [eval], because its loyal artisan-food customer base is a natural audience for a preserving campaign and the full cost would be covered without debt; micro-finance remains the sensible fallback if the campaign falls short [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Crowdfunding: no interest, publicity, uncertain target, platform fee
Micro-finance: certain small loan, interest, repayments
analysis_max_2: Campaign risk vs certainty of micro-finance
Effect of fees/interest on profit, cash flow and reinvestment capacity
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures
Fallback/sequencing argument or justified overall judgement

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Alcott Windows Ltd is a private limited company in Country X installing double glazing, windows and doors. It employs 22 staff, earned $2.6 million revenue and holds $400,000 of window and door stock.

The base rate rose from 3.5% to 6.5%. 75% of customers use a finance plan, and installations fell from 120 to 84 a quarter, a 30% drop, leaving the workshop at half its usual capacity. The owner must decide whether to cut prices by 10%.

questions.question_text: Define 'mortgage'.
questions.model_answer: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property such as a house or flat, repaid with interest over many years and usually secured against the property itself. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Long-term loan used to purchase property
Repaid with interest over many years, typically secured on the property

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why higher interest rates have reduced demand for Alcott Windows.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Finance to spread the cost of windows is now more expensive [k]. Around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, and with the base rate up at 6.5% the monthly repayments on new orders have risen [app]. Reason 2: Higher rates leave households with less disposable income [k]. Homeowners face bigger mortgage repayments, so installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates increase the cost of finance plans
Higher rates raise mortgage costs, reducing disposable income
application_max_2: 75% of customers pay by finance plan; base rate raised to 6.5%
Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the fall from 120 to 84 installations a quarter causes Alcott Windows.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Lower revenue and profit [k]. A drop of 30% means far fewer windows sold each quarter [app], so fixed costs such as warehouse rent and the interest on $400,000 of stock are spread over fewer jobs, squeezing margins [an]. Problem 2: Under-used labour and capacity [k]. The workshop is running at half its usual capacity, with 22 staff and much of the $400,000 stock sitting unsold [app], so the business may be forced to cut hours or make installers redundant [an].

knowledge_max_2: Falling orders reduce revenue and profit
Falling output leaves labour and stock underutilised
application_max_2: Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%
$400,000 of stock; workshop at half its usual capacity; 22 staff
analysis_max_2: Fewer sales spread fixed costs over less output, squeezing the profit margin
Idle capacity pressures the business into wage cuts or redundancy

questions.question_text: Do you think Alcott Windows should cut prices by 10% to win back orders? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A 10% price cut could win back price-sensitive customers [k]: installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%, so a discount might persuade cautious homeowners to proceed before the summer peak [app], lifting volume enough to cover fixed warehouse costs on $400,000 of stock [an]. However, the real barrier is the 6.5% base rate, not the price [k]: around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, so higher monthly repayments are stopping purchases, not the quoted price [app], meaning a blanket 10% cut would simply reduce margin on the 84 orders still coming in [an]. Overall [eval], Alcott should offer a targeted discount or contribution to finance costs on finance-plan sales rather than a blanket 10% cut [eval], because the demand fall is driven by borrowing costs rather than the headline price.

knowledge_max_2: Price cuts can attract price-sensitive customers
Demand driven by borrowing cost is not resolved by price cuts
application_max_2: Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%
75% of customers pay by finance plan; base rate raised from 3.5% to 6.5%
analysis_max_2: A discount could lift volume enough to cover fixed costs
Margins on remaining orders fall without fixing the real barrier
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified, conditional recommendation (targeted offer, not a blanket cut)

scenario_stem:
Brindle Wharf Logistics is a private limited distribution warehouse beside Alderquay port, storing goods for 38 clients. It owns 46 fork-lift trucks and 12 reach trucks, employs 150 staff on 3 shifts, and handles 2,400 pallet movements weekly.

Breakdowns hit 27 times last year, costing $3,800 monthly. Carl Whitmore is weighing an $85,000 in-house workshop, including two mechanics at $16 an hour, against an external contract at $2,900 a month with 48-hour response, to protect its 9% operating margin.

questions.question_text: Define 'efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: Efficiency means producing the maximum output from given inputs with minimum waste, such as Brindle getting the most deliveries from its 46 fork-lift trucks and 12 reach trucks with the least wasted time and money. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency = maximum output from inputs / minimum waste
Best use of resources to achieve output (accept efficiency defined in contrast to productivity if accurate)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why efficiency matters to Brindle Wharf Logistics.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Efficient operations lower costs and protect profit [k]. The fleet broke down 27 times last year, costing $3,800 a month in lost time and repairs [app]. Reason 2: Efficient use of equipment keeps goods moving on time for clients [k]. Brindle stores imported goods for 38 clients with 150 staff across 3 shifts, so wasted time directly delays dispatches [app].

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency lowers costs and waste, protecting profit
Efficient processes keep customer service reliable
application_max_2: 38 clients; 150 staff; 3 shifts; December peak of 2,400 pallet movements a week

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Brindle could improve its efficiency.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Regular preventive maintenance would reduce breakdowns [k]. The fleet broke down 27 times last year, and either an in-house workshop at $85,000 a year or an external contract at $2,900 a month would service trucks before they fail [app]. Fewer breakdowns would cut the $3,800 monthly losses and reduce idle staff time [an]. Way 2: Better shift planning would cut wasted waiting time [k]. With 150 staff across 3 shifts and goods for 38 clients, matching staffing to weekly pallet movements would reduce overtime and bottlenecks [app]. Smoother flow would raise throughput per worker and protect the 9% operating margin [an].

knowledge_max_2: Better planning/scheduling cuts waste of time and labour
application_max_2: 27 breakdowns; $3,800 a month; options of $85,000 a year or $2,900 a month
analysis_max_2: Fewer breakdowns cut losses and idle time, raising efficiency
Matching staffing to demand raises throughput and protects the operating margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Brindle should build the in-house maintenance workshop rather than sign the external service contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for in-house: an in-house workshop lets Brindle service trucks immediately, cutting the 27 breakdowns that cost $3,800 a month in lost time and repairs [k]. Including two mechanics paid $16 an hour, it costs $85,000 a year but keeps expertise on site for 46 fork-lift trucks and 12 reach trucks [app]. Faster repairs mean less downtime, higher throughput and more reliable service, protecting the 9% operating margin [an]. Argument for external: the $2,900 monthly contract costs $34,800 a year (12 x $2,900), less than half the in-house cost [k]. The guaranteed 48-hour response covers emergencies without paying two mechanics' fixed wages, though 48-hour delays could still disrupt dispatch for its 38 clients [app]. Slower response risks more lost pallet movements and strained client trust than the saving justifies [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Brindle should sign the external contract first because $34,800 a year is far cheaper than $85,000, which matters on a 9% operating margin, while it measures whether response times protect client service [eval]. If breakdowns persist or response times slip, the in-house workshop would become the better choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: External = cheaper outsourced service, slower response
application_max_2: $85,000 in-house including two mechanics at $16 an hour; $2,900 a month = $34,800 a year
27 breakdowns; $3,800 monthly losses; 46 fork-lift trucks; 12 reach trucks; 38 clients
analysis_max_2: Faster repairs reduce downtime and protect client service and the 9% margin
External contract saves money but 48-hour delay risks disruption and client trust
evaluation_max_2: Recommends the external contract with conditions, reviewing if breakdowns persist
Recognises margin pressure versus service-quality trade-off between the two options

scenario_stem:
Overbrook Farms Ltd is a private limited company, an arable farm in Country X growing wheat and barley with 18 workers. Owner Sarah Vane works 70-hour weeks approving every repair, seed order and holiday request. Output was $2.3m and overtime rose 18%.

She must decide whether to delegate to farm manager Tom Ilsley, approving repairs up to $1,500 and holiday requests, or hire an assistant for $38,000 a year. Tom has 6 years' experience and a management course, but Sarah recalls 2 costly repair mistakes.

questions.question_text: Define 'delegation'.
questions.model_answer: Delegation is the passing of authority down the hierarchy to subordinates to perform tasks and make decisions, such as Sarah letting Tom approve repairs up to $1,500 and all holiday requests. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Delegation = passing authority/tasks down from manager to subordinate
Subordinate is accountable for the task, manager remains responsible overall

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Sarah of delegating routine decisions to Tom Ilsley.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Delegation frees the manager's time for more important work [k]. Sarah works 70-hour weeks and personally approves every tractor repair, seed order and holiday request, so delegation would cut her workload [app]. Advantage 2: Delegation develops the subordinate's skills and motivation [k]. Tom has run the machinery fleet for 6 years and passed his management course in March, so trusted responsibility would build his judgement and confidence [app].

knowledge_max_2: Delegation frees managers to focus on strategic work
application_max_2: Sarah works 70-hour weeks, approving every repair, seed order and holiday request
Tom has 6 years running the fleet and passed his management course in March

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for the farm of delegating to Tom Ilsley.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The manager remains accountable for mistakes made by the subordinate [k]. Sarah recalls 2 costly repair mistakes last winter, so handing Tom repair sign-off up to $1,500 carries real financial risk [app]. A repeat mistake on a $1,500 repair could escalate into crop losses at the height of the season [an]. Disadvantage 2: Delegation can fail if the subordinate is not ready or supported [k]. Tom has passed his management course, but approving repairs across a $2.3m output still demands judgement under cost pressure [app]. Poor decisions could push overtime, already up 18%, even higher as errors are fixed late [an].

knowledge_max_2: Delegator remains accountable for subordinates' mistakes
Delegation may fail without the right skills, support and limits
application_max_2: 2 costly repair mistakes last winter; repairs delegated up to $1,500
Output worth $2.3m; overtime rose 18%; Tom passed his management course in March
analysis_max_2: A repeat repair mistake could escalate into crop losses at peak season
Poor decisions could push overtime above the existing 18% rise as errors are corrected

questions.question_text: Do you think Sarah should delegate routine decisions to Tom Ilsley rather than hire an assistant farm manager at $38,000 a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for delegating to Tom: delegation passes authority to a trusted subordinate at no wage cost [k]. Tom has run the machinery fleet for 6 years and passed his management course in March, and Sarah works 70-hour weeks with decisions waited on her [app]. Delegating repairs up to $1,500 and holiday requests would cut her workload and rebuild Tom's motivation without the $38,000 salary [an]. Argument for hiring an assistant: an assistant farm manager adds extra capacity rather than stretching existing staff [k]. Hiring at $38,000 a year would bring in fresh judgement while Tom keeps handling the machinery fleet he knows [app]. However, hiring raises fixed costs on output worth $2.3m, and 2 costly repair mistakes last winter suggest Sarah's approval bottleneck, not Tom's competence, is the real problem [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Sarah should delegate to Tom, because his 6 years of fleet experience and March management course make him ready, and $38,000 a year is better spent only if delegation fails [eval]. If Tom makes costly errors beyond $1,500 or turnover rises among the 18 full-time workers, she should reconsider the hire [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Delegation empowers existing trusted staff at little cost
Hiring adds capacity but raises fixed wage costs
application_max_2: Tom: 6 years on the machinery fleet, passed his management course in March; repairs up to $1,500
Assistant manager $38,000 a year; Sarah works 70-hour weeks; overtime rose 18%
analysis_max_2: Delegation cuts Sarah's workload and costs nothing beyond current wages
Hiring adds judgement and capacity but raises fixed costs on $2.3m output
evaluation_max_2: Recommends delegating to Tom based on his experience and course, with $38,000 held in reserve
Reconsider hiring if Tom errs above $1,500 or worker turnover rises

scenario_stem:
Kestrelmere Machine Tools is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing and servicing industrial metal presses at $85,000 each. It sells 24 units a year to factories, earning $2.05 million from presses and employing 26 engineers and 3 sales representatives.

It must raise press sales by 4 units to justify a factory extension: hire 2 more sales representatives on 3% commission, or exhibit at the National Manufacturing Show, costing $38,000 for a stand and demonstration rigs.

questions.question_text: Define 'personal selling'.
questions.model_answer: Direct, face-to-face communication between a salesperson and a customer with the aim of persuading that customer to buy a product [2].

knowledge_max_2: to persuade a customer to buy

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Kestrelmere Machine Tools of using personal selling.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Personal selling lets representatives explain the technical features of an $85,000 press in detail [k], answering factory buyers' questions directly [app]. Advantage 2: Representatives can build long-term relationships with industrial customers [k], supporting repeat press sales and servicing contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: can explain technical features/handle complex products

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kestrelmere Machine Tools of exhibiting at the National Manufacturing Show.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A trade show stand exposes Kestrelmere to many factory buyers in one place [k], reaching more qualified prospects in three days than 2 extra representatives could visit in months [app], generating a faster flow of sales leads [an]. Benefit 2: Live demonstrations of the demonstration rigs attract serious buyers [k], letting buyers see the industrial metal presses in action before committing to $85,000 [app], which can shorten the decision-making process [an].

knowledge_max_2: reaches many prospects in one concentrated venue
demonstrations build buyer confidence for high-value purchases
analysis_max_2: generates sales leads faster than territory visits

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrelmere Machine Tools should hire 2 additional sales representatives or exhibit at the National Manufacturing Show? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring 2 representatives on 3% commission means pay rises only when sales rise [k], protecting cash while directly targeting the 4 extra presses needed for the factory extension [app], and strengthening territory coverage for deepening relationships with factories [an]. However, the National Manufacturing Show costs $38,000 up front but concentrates dozens of serious factory buyers in one exhibition hall [k], letting Petra's team show the demonstration rigs, gather competitor intelligence and win orders that territory calls rarely secure quickly [app], which could deliver the 4 units in weeks rather than months [an]. Overall, Kestrelmere should exhibit at the show because the planned factory extension depends on landing a few large contracts quickly [eval], and the show offers a concentrated, time-bound route to qualified buyers that commission-based hiring cannot guarantee [eval].

knowledge_max_2: commission-only reps align pay with sales results
exhibition concentrates many qualified buyers in one place
application_max_2: 4 extra presses for the factory extension
analysis_max_2: protects cash flow but adds ongoing labour cost
show can compress a long sales cycle into days
evaluation_max_2: weighs steady territory coverage against concentrated exposure
justified choice given urgency of factory extension target

scenario_stem:
Warrenfield Farm Shops, a private limited company, runs 3 farm shops with 24 staff and monthly sales of $85,000 per shop. Fresh stock is ordered by hand from notebooks, and 12% of fresh stock becomes monthly unsold waste.

Option A keeps handwritten records, adding an ordering day weekly. Option B spends $96,000 on EPOS with stock control tracking sales in real time and suggesting reorders, cutting waste from 12% to 5% of stock and shrinkage by 40%; loyal cash customers rarely use cards.

questions.question_text: Define 'stock control'.
questions.model_answer: Stock control is the process of ordering, storing and monitoring a business's stock so it has enough to meet customer demand without holding too much. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Stock control = managing the ordering, holding and monitoring of inventory
Aim is the right stock at the right time with minimum waste

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Warrenfield Farm Shops of installing EPOS with stock control.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: EPOS records every sale as it happens [k]. Stock levels would update in real time, so notebook records are replaced and reordering becomes automatic [app]. Benefit 2: Live sales data shows exactly what sells [k]. Fresh-stock waste would fall from 12% to 5% of stock across the 3 farm shops [app].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS gives accurate, up-to-date stock records in real time
Sales data allows automated, needs-based reordering
application_max_2: Fresh-stock waste falls from 12% to 5% of stock
Real-time tracking replaces handwritten notebook records in 3 shops

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Warrenfield Farm Shops could face if it installs EPOS.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: EPOS tills cost money to buy and run [k]. Option B requires $96,000, a large sum for 3 rural shops earning $85,000 a month each [app]. The outlay may take years to recover from waste savings [an]. Problem 2: Some customers pay cash and rarely use cards [k]. EPOS could make loyal cash-paying customers feel unwelcome or unable to pay as before [app]. Lost goodwill in small rural communities could cut sales sharply [an].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS needs significant upfront and ongoing investment
EPOS may not suit customers who prefer paying cash
application_max_2: Option B costs $96,000 against 3 shops earning $85,000 a month each
Loyal cash-paying customers rarely use cards at these rural shops
analysis_max_2: High fixed outlay strains cash flow of small rural shops
Alienating cash customers risks losing loyal local sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Warrenfield Farm Shops should install EPOS rather than keep handwritten records? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for EPOS: EPOS links the till to live stock records [k]. It would cut monthly fresh-stock waste from 12% to 5% and shrinkage by 40% across 3 shops averaging $85,000 in sales each month [app]. Better stock data would cut waste costs and free staff from notebooks to serve customers [an]. Case for handwritten records: Option A costs nothing and keeps ordering simple for 24 staff [k]. Adding 1 ordering day per week per shop would catch waste earlier without new technology [app]. Handwritten records also keep personal contact with local suppliers, but waste would stay near 12% and shrinkage untracked [an]. Overall, Warrenfield should install EPOS, because waste falling from 12% to 5% saves far more than an extra ordering day costs [eval]. The owners could keep notebook records as backup and train staff gradually to retain loyal cash customers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS gives real-time stock visibility and automated reordering
Manual records cost nothing but keep errors and waste
application_max_2: Waste falls 12% to 5%, shrinkage cut by 40%, across 3 shops at $85,000 monthly sales each
Option A adds 1 ordering day per week per shop, no capital cost, 24 staff unchanged
analysis_max_2: Lower waste and shrinkage directly protect profit margins
Manual system leaves 12% waste and shrinkage untracked
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (waste saving outweighs ordering-day cost)
Suggestion to de-risk (keep notebook backup, train staff gradually)

scenario_stem:
Marigold & Rye Bakery Ltd is a private limited company running 3 outlets in Country X. It employs 24 staff. Wholesale clients buy on 45-day credit and owe $38,000; with $18,000 retained profit, the family wants a $45,000 van for a $95,000 supermarket contract.

A factoring company advances 80% of invoices ($30,400) for a 4% fee ($1,520). Crowdfunding targets $50,000 with early-bird bread subscriptions as rewards and a 5% fee ($2,500). Deliveries must start within 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: Working capital is the finance a business needs for day-to-day operations, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Marigold & Rye Bakery Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Cash is received immediately [k]; 80% of the $38,000 owed ($30,400) is paid now rather than after 45 days [app]. Advantage 2: The factor takes over debt collection [k], reducing administration for the 24 staff so the family can focus on the supermarket contract worth $95,000 a year, with deliveries starting within 8 weeks [app].

knowledge_max_2: Immediate cash advance from outstanding invoices
Factor takes over collecting the debts

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of crowdfunding for Marigold & Rye Bakery Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Success is uncertain [k]; if the campaign misses its $50,000 target, the early-bird bread subscriptions may not sell and the $45,000 van cannot be funded [app], putting the supermarket contract worth $95,000 a year at risk [an]. Disadvantage 2: Fees and rewards reduce the net benefit [k]; the 5% platform fee costs $2,500 and honouring the subscriptions adds ongoing delivery costs [app], cutting the cash left for the van purchase [an].

knowledge_max_2: Target may not be reached / success not guaranteed
Platform fee and reward fulfilment costs
analysis_max_2: Campaign failure risks losing the supermarket contract
Fees and fulfilment costs reduce net funds and future cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think Marigold & Rye Bakery Ltd should use factoring of debts or crowdfunding? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Factoring of debts [k] delivers $30,400 now, and together with the $18,000 retained profit it covers the $45,000 van ($48,400 in total), at a low fee of $1,520 (4%), with cash highly likely to arrive within the 8-week window before deliveries start [app] [an]. Crowdfunding could raise $50,000 and generate publicity and loyal bread subscribers [k], but success is not guaranteed, the 5% fee costs $2,500 and the family would owe subscriptions to donors for months [app] [an]. Overall, I think Marigold & Rye should use factoring of debts [eval], because certainty and speed matter most with deliveries due within 8 weeks and the cheaper fee preserves profit; crowdfunding could be run later, once the supermarket contract is won, purely as a marketing campaign [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Factoring: certain immediate advance, fee payable
Crowdfunding: uncertain target, fee, marketing/reward costs
analysis_max_2: Certainty and speed vs publicity and risk of failure
Fee costs vs ongoing subscription obligations; effect on profit and cash flow
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures
Recognition of crowdfunding's marketing upside or sequencing argument / justified overall judgement

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Elmcrest Farm Machinery is a sole trader tractor and combine dealer earning $5.4 million revenue. New tractor sales, usually 120 a year at $48,000 each, have fallen to 66 this year.

With the base rate up from 4% to 7%, most farmers use bank loans and many defer orders. A $500,000 overdraft funds showroom stock; interest rose from 6% to 9%, an extra $15,000 yearly. The dealer must decide whether to discount new tractors to clear stock.

questions.question_text: Define 'overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft is a bank facility that lets a business withdraw more money from its current account than it holds, up to an agreed limit and repaid with interest. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Facility allowing withdrawal beyond the account balance up to an agreed limit
Repayable with interest, often on demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why farmers may postpone buying new tractors when interest rates rise.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Loans to buy tractors become more expensive [k]. Most farmers finance purchases with bank loans, and with the base rate up from 4% to 7% the interest on financing a $48,000 tractor has jumped sharply [app]. Reason 2: Farmers are uncertain about future income while rates are high [k]. Tractor sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year, showing farmers are delaying major capital purchases [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest increases the cost of finance for capital purchases
Uncertainty and low confidence make buyers delay major investments
application_max_2: Base rate raised from 4% to 7%; average tractor price $48,000
New tractor sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Elmcrest Farm Machinery could reduce the cost of holding stock.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Reduce showroom stock and order to demand [k]. With sales down to 66 from 120 a year, fewer machines are needed on the forecourt [app], so the dealer can shrink its $500,000 overdraft and cut the interest it pays [an]. Way 2: Renegotiate the overdraft with its bank [k]. Overdraft interest has risen from 6% to 9%, costing an extra $15,000 a year [app], so even a 1% reduction in the margin would save $5,000 a year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower stock levels reduce financing needs and interest costs
Renegotiating bank facilities can cut interest margins
application_max_2: Sales fell from 120 a year to 66; overdraft of $500,000
Overdraft interest rose from 6% to 9%, an extra $15,000 a year ($30,000 to $45,000)
analysis_max_2: Less stock directly reduces the overdraft and its interest charge

questions.question_text: Do you think Pembroke should buy the used CNC machine rather than hire capacity from a rival foundry? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Harbour & Lark Streetwear of using social media to promote its products.

Overall, Zoe should choose the paid campaign because reliable, targeted reach matters more than lottery-odds virality [eval], and her limited budget cannot comfortably absorb $2,500 on a stunt that may never trend [eval].

scenario_stem:
Glen Carrick Water Co, a private limited company, bottles spring water with 28 workers on 2 shifts, producing 1.2 million litres monthly at $0.55 per litre. Hand capping and labelling leave 4% of bottles leaking.

Option A hires 8 workers at $16,000 a year each, raising output to 1.5 million litres monthly. Option B invests $1.1 million in an automated capping/labelling line, replacing 6 jobs, cutting leaks from 4% to under 1%, lifting output to 1.8 million litres and costing $85,000 a year.

scenario_stem:
Coveside Lodge Ltd is a private limited company running a coastal eco-lodge. It employs 41 staff, ran at 92% occupancy and made $1.15 million revenue. It plans $90,000 on solar panels to cut electricity bills by $14,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the tourism development grant for Coveside Lodge Ltd.

Advantage 2: It preserves cash for trading needs [k]; Coveside can keep its $1.15 million revenue flowing at 92% occupancy while still capturing the $14,000 a year saving on electricity [app].

scenario_stem:
Fernwood Café Ltd is a private limited company running a café in Marrowgate with 12 staff. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over 18 months after two factories closed, costing 240 jobs.

Unemployment rose from 4% to 9%, and the central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 3.5%, but footfall stays weak and January meal deals had little effect. The owner is considering a $150,000 second outlet or trimming staff hours at the single site.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a phase of the business cycle in which economic activity falls, usually shown by two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, with rising unemployment and falling consumer spending. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Period of falling economic output/negative GDP growth
Rising unemployment and weak consumer spending

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the cut in interest rates from 6% to 3.5% could help Fernwood Café.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Customers can afford to borrow and spend more [k]. Lower rates reduce the cost of personal loans and overdrafts, so office workers and families may return to the café at lunchtimes and weekends [app]. Reason 2: The café could finance a second outlet more cheaply [k]. With the base rate cut to 3.5%, a loan for the $150,000 neighbouring-town outlet would carry much lower interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower rates increase disposable income and the incentive to spend
Lower rates reduce the cost of business borrowing
application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; café serves office workers and families
A second outlet costing $150,000 in a neighbouring town

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fernwood Café may still struggle despite cheaper credit.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer confidence is low and unemployment is high [k]. Local unemployment has risen from 4% to 9% after two local factories closed with the loss of 240 jobs [app], so even cheap credit may not persuade cautious households to eat out [an]. Reason 2: The café's revenue has already collapsed [k]. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over the last 18 months [app], so fixed costs such as rent and the wages of 12 staff are spread over far fewer customers, squeezing profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: Low confidence and high unemployment suppress spending regardless of rates
Falling revenue against unchanged fixed costs erodes profit
application_max_2: Unemployment rose from 4% to 9%; two factories closed with 240 jobs lost
Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over 18 months; 12 staff
analysis_max_2: Fearful households save rather than spend, so the rate cut has limited effect
Fixed costs spread over fewer sales reduce margin and risk losses

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernwood Café should open the second outlet now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening now would give Fernwood a foothold in a neighbouring town before the market recovers [k]: a loan at the cut base rate of 3.5% would be relatively cheap for the $150,000 cost [app], and capturing customers early could help rebuild revenue towards the $420,000 it earned before the closures [an]. However, the café is already weakened by the recession [k]: revenue has fallen from $420,000 to $330,000 and local unemployment has risen to 9% with 240 jobs lost in two factory closures [app], so taking on $150,000 of new commitments while one site struggles could magnify losses and threaten the original café [an]. Overall [eval], Fernwood should wait rather than open now [eval], because opening in a recession with weak footfall and collapsed revenue risks compounding losses; it should hold the $150,000 and focus on restoring sales at the existing site.

knowledge_max_2: Early expansion can secure a new market when credit is cheap
Expanding while loss-making multiplies financial risk
application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; second outlet costing $150,000
Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000; unemployment rose to 9%; 240 jobs lost
analysis_max_2: Early mover advantage could rebuild revenue towards pre-closure levels
New fixed commitments in a downturn magnify losses at the existing site
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Clear, justified recommendation (wait; restore the existing site first)

scenario_stem:
Windover Housebuilding Ltd is a private limited housebuilder with 2 active sites and 38 skilled workers, building 46 houses a year on $16m turnover. It bought a 7-hectare greenfield plot for $3.4m, planning 120 houses over 5 years.

Director Ben Hollis must choose between that plot and an inner-city brownfield site at $5.9m, which saves 18 months of planning. Greenfield needs $700,000 of new road access, while brownfield may need $850,000 of contamination clean-up.

questions.question_text: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Land is all natural resources used to produce goods and services, including the 7-hectare greenfield plot Windover bought for $3.4m and the raw materials taken from building sites to make homes. [2]

Reward examples such as building plots, minerals, timber or land itself

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why land is important to Windover Housebuilding.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Land provides the natural space and raw materials needed for building [k]. Windover owns 2 active sites and recently bought a 7-hectare plot for $3.4m to build 120 houses [app]. Reason 2: Without land Windover cannot produce or sell homes [k]. The planned 120-house development over 5 years depends entirely on securing suitable building land [app].

knowledge_max_2: Land = site and natural resources needed for building

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of the greenfield plot compared with the brownfield site.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: The greenfield plot needs new road access, adding $700,000 to costs [k]. Together with the $3.4m purchase, Windover would commit $4.1m before construction, while the brownfield site already sits within existing roads and utilities [app]. Higher upfront costs reduce early cash flow and squeeze returns on the 120 planned houses [an]. Drawback 2: Greenfield development may face a longer planning process [k]. The brownfield site would save 18 months of planning time and sit closer to buyers' workplaces, advantages the greenfield plot lacks [app]. questions.question_text: Do you think Windover should buy the inner-city brownfield site rather than proceed with the greenfield plot? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for brownfield: the brownfield site costs $5.9m plus $850,000 of contamination clean-up, so $6.75m in total, but it saves 18 months of planning and sits closer to buyers' workplaces [k]. Faster sales of part of the 120 houses would bring in revenue sooner and cut holding costs [app]. Earlier revenue would also improve cash flow and reduce the need to borrow during construction [an]. Argument for greenfield: at $3.4m plus $700,000 road access, the greenfield plot costs $4.1m in total, $2.65m less than brownfield, and offers open space for all 120 houses [k]. However, delay would tie up capital and the 38 skilled workers and could strain cash before first sales [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Windover should proceed with the greenfield plot because at $4.1m it is $2.65m cheaper than brownfield at $6.75m, and the saving outweighs 18 months provided planning approval is likely for a 7-hectare plot outside the city [eval]. analysis_max_2: The $2.65m saving outweighs 18 months if approvals are obtainable

evaluation_max_2: Recommends greenfield based on the $2.65m saving, conditional on planning approval

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Define 'production'.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferrymead Packaging Ltd of using CAD and CAM.

scenario_stem:
Stanway Uniform Co is a private limited company making school and hospital uniforms in Country X. It employs 30 full-time production workers, with monthly wages of $28,000. Clients buy on 75-day credit and owe $84,000. Ruth Calloway needs $58,000 embroidery machines to keep a $120,000 hospital contract.

A factoring company advances 90% of invoices ($75,600) for a 2% fee ($1,680) and takes over credit control. A $25,000 micro-finance loan charges 13% over 3 years, costing $3,250 a year and $9,750 total interest.

questions.question_text: Define 'debtor'.
questions.model_answer: A debtor is a customer or organisation that owes money to a business, usually because goods or services were bought on credit and payment has not yet been made. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Bought on credit / payment not yet received

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Stanway Uniform Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Immediate cash is received [k]; 90% of the $84,000 owed ($75,600) is paid now, enough to buy the $58,000 embroidery machines without waiting 75 days [app]. Advantage 2: The factor takes over collecting the debts [k], removing the chasing workload from Ruth Calloway's 30 workers and helping to safeguard the hospital contract worth $120,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Immediate cash advance from outstanding invoices
Factor takes over debt collection/credit control

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Stanway Uniform Co.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The loan is far too small [k]; at $25,000 it leaves a $33,000 shortfall against the $58,000 machines [app], so the hospital contract worth $120,000 a year could be lost [an]. Disadvantage 2: Interest is expensive relative to the amount borrowed [k]; 13% costs $3,250 a year and $9,750 over 3 years [app], a heavy strain alongside monthly wages of $28,000 [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Stanway Uniform Co should use factoring of debts or micro-finance? Justify your answer.

Micro-finance would keep Stanway in full control of its customer relationships [k], but it supplies only $25,000, leaving a $33,000 gap, and costs $9,750 in interest over 3 years on top of $28,000 monthly wages [app] [an]. Overall, I think Stanway should use factoring of debts [eval], because the machines cannot wait and the fee is small beside a $120,000-a-year contract; micro-finance would make sense only if Stanway later improved collections and wanted to avoid further fees [eval].
