unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Corvale Deliveries Ltd is a private limited company providing parcel and grocery delivery. It employs 29 staff, serves 300 business customers with 8 diesel vans bought with a $240,000 loan, and earned $1.9 million.

As the base rate rose from 3% to 6%, interest rose from $7,200 to $14,400 yearly, an extra $7,200. Inflation reached 7%, lifting diesel and wage costs, with fuel up $38,000, yet customers resist surcharges. Should the owner raise prices 8% across all contracts?

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services, which reduces the purchasing power of money over time. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general price level
Reduces the purchasing power of money (each unit buys less)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems rising inflation causes for Corvale Deliveries.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Diesel and wage costs rise faster than revenue [k]. Inflation has reached 7%, the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year, and wages must keep pace to retain the firm's 29 staff [app]. Reason 2: Pressure on margins because customers resist surcharges [k]. Interest on the $240,000 van loan is also up $7,200 a year after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%, so the gap between costs and revenue keeps widening [app].

Inflation forces higher prices or squeezes profit margins
application_max_2: Inflation at 7%; fuel bill rose by $38,000; 29 staff

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Corvale Deliveries could respond to its rising costs.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Raise delivery prices to customers [k]. An 8% increase across all contracts would recover some of the extra $7,200 a year of interest and the $38,000 fuel increase [app], though the firm risks losing rounds to cheaper rivals [an]. Way 2: Improve route efficiency and cut empty miles [k]. Combining parcel routes across its 300-plus business customers would cut diesel use per drop [app], lowering costs without raising prices [an].

However, a flat 8% rise risks losing price-sensitive contracts [k]: customers resist surcharges and rivals that hold prices could win the firm's rounds [app], so Corvale could lose more revenue than it recovers [an]. Overall [eval], Corvale should raise prices by a smaller, cost-linked amount rather than a flat 8%, or add a transparent fuel surcharge [eval], because recovering proven cost increases is fairer and less likely to drive away the 300-plus business customers it serves.

Customers resist surcharges; 8% proposed across all contracts
analysis_max_2: An 8% rise broadly offsets the quantified cost increases
Losing contracts could outweigh the recovered costs
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified, qualified recommendation (smaller cost-linked rise or fuel surcharge)

scenario_stem:
Valecrest Logistics Ltd is a private limited delivery company in Ridgeline running 36 vans and 9 HGVs for 130 retail and e-commerce clients. Last year's fleet completed 48,000 deliveries, up 16%, but 2 HGVs need replacing at $110,000 each.

Managing director Sara Iqbal is choosing between a $720,000 same-day deal needing 4 dedicated vans and a 4-hour delivery window, and 3 bulk contracts worth $540,000 using existing vehicles. She has a $250,000 bank credit limit.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why customer wants matter to Valecrest Logistics.

Higher revenue would lift profits and help fund the 2 HGVs due for replacement at $110,000 each [an]. Benefit 2: The deal would strengthen Valecrest's reputation in e-commerce [k]. questions.model_answer: Argument for the same-day deal: the deal pays $720,000 a year, $180,000 more than the $540,000 total for the 3 bulk contracts [k]. scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Embergate Cinema of offering a 25% price reduction on Monday to Thursday tickets.

scenario_stem:

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eldercombe Toys Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing toys with 41 staff. Sales fell from $3.4 million in a boom to $2.6 million in the slump, profit reaching $120,000, with a third exported.

After the base rate fell from 6% to 3%, the economy grew 2.8% a year. Christmas brings 55% of sales and retailers are rebuilding stock, so orders are rising. A $350,000 expansion would add a moulding machine and 6 jobs. Should it expand now?

questions.question_text: Define 'business cycle'.

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Callowmere Supermarkets is a private limited company running 9 stores with 320 staff. Inflation climbed from 6.1% to 11.3%, food prices rose 14% but wages grew 6%. Revenue rose 9% to $48.5 million, yet items sold fell 4% as shoppers switched to own-label, now 44% of basket value.

Problem 2: Raising prices when real wages grew only 6% outstrips pay rises [k], and shoppers already cut items purchased by 4% as inflation hit 11.3% [app], so basket values could shrink despite the 8% rise [an].

Overall, Saltwick should not place the full order [eval], because the downside is far larger than the upside - losing $90,000 outweighs the $1,320 net annual benefit after storage costs [eval].

evaluation_max_2: asymmetric risk, reject the full order
justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

scenario_stem:
Thornwick Gifts Ltd is a private limited company running 3 gift shops selling toys, candles and cards, with revenue of $620,000, including $210,000 in November and December. Current assets are $95,000 against current liabilities of $70,000.

The directors want $45,000 for Christmas stock. They compare a bank overdraft at 11% interest, costing about $1,650 over 4 months, with extended 60 day trade credit from suppliers who normally require payment within 30 days but expect it before February.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: The finance used for day to day trading, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities [2].

knowledge_max_2: finance used for day to day trading
calculated as current assets minus current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why short term finance is suitable for the Christmas stock.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The need is temporary [k], because the $45,000 is tied up only from October until the stock is sold by the end of December [app]. Reason 2: Repayment matches seasonal cash flow [k], because about $210,000 of November and December revenue would pay off the overdraft or the suppliers before February [app].

knowledge_max_2: short term finance suits temporary needs
short term finance matches seasonal repayment cycles
application_max_2: $45,000 is tied up only from October until the end of December
about $210,000 of November and December revenue arrives before February

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of using a bank overdraft for the $45,000 Christmas stock.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Interest adds to seasonal costs [k], because 11% annual interest on $45,000 for 4 months costs around $1,650 [app], trimming the margin made on Christmas sales [an]. Problem 2: The overdraft can be withdrawn on demand [k], because the bank may reduce the limit and the shops hold only $95,000 of current assets against $70,000 of liabilities [app], pressuring the directors if December sales disappoint [an].

application_max_2: only $95,000 of current assets against $70,000 of liabilities
analysis_max_2: interest trims the profit margin on Christmas sales
a reduced limit would pressure the directors if December sales disappoint

questions.question_text: Do you think a bank overdraft is a better source than extended trade credit for the $45,000 Christmas stock? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Trade credit is interest free [k], so the shops avoid the $1,650 overdraft charge and keep the full margin on around $210,000 of seasonal sales [app], which suits the tight working capital of only $25,000 [an]. However, relying on extended 60 day credit is risky [k], because the two suppliers expect payment before February and may shorten terms or charge more if trading stays slow [app], straining the relationships behind 11 years of stock supply [an]. Overall, trade credit is the better, cheaper option for the Christmas stock because the zero interest cost directly helps profit [eval], but the overdraft should remain available as backup if December trading falls well short of $210,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: trade credit is interest free finance from suppliers
extended supplier credit carries a risk of tightened terms
application_max_2: avoids the $1,650 overdraft charge and keeps margin on $210,000 of seasonal sales
current assets of $95,000 against current liabilities of $70,000 leave tight working capital
analysis_max_2: zero interest directly protects profit and cash flow
strained supplier relationships could damage future stock supply
evaluation_max_2: recommends trade credit as the cheaper option for the Christmas stock
retains the overdraft as backup if December sales fall short

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Pennyroyal Café is an independent café serving breakfast, brunch and lunch with 14 staff. GDP grew 4.2%, unemployment fell to 3.8% and restaurant spending rose 11% over 2 years. Revenue reached $86,000 from $61,000; weekend waits average 25 minutes. Consumer confidence is at its highest for a decade.

The owners must choose between a second café in the retail park 3 km away, costing $240,000 and seating 55 customers, or refitting 40 seats at the current site, before the lease is allocated in 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'economic growth'.
questions.model_answer: An increase in the value of goods and services produced in an economy, measured by the rise in GDP [2].

knowledge_max_2: an increase in real GDP / output of goods and services
the economy produces more value over time

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Pennyroyal's revenue grew during the economic boom.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rising GDP lifts household incomes [k], and with unemployment down to 3.8% and GDP up 4.2%, more customers treat café meals as everyday spending rather than a luxury [app]. Reason 2: Strong consumer confidence encourages spending on leisure [k], and with restaurant spending up 11% over 2 years, Pennyroyal's monthly revenue rose from $61,000 to $86,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: economic growth raises household incomes and purchasing power
consumer confidence rises in a boom, boosting discretionary spending
application_max_2: GDP grew 4.2% and unemployment fell to 3.8%
restaurant spending rose 11% and monthly revenue climbed from $61,000 to $86,000

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Pennyroyal of opening the retail park café.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A second site widens the catchment [k], tapping the growing industrial estate and retail park trade instead of only the current street [app], so total revenue could rise beyond $86,000 a month [an]. Benefit 2: Two venues share customer goodwill and catering costs [k], and with 55 customers seated the $240,000 build cost can be spread across higher combined volume [app], improving overall profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: a new location reaches new customers and widens the catchment
expansion spreads fixed costs and shared resources across sites
application_max_2: retail park near a growing industrial estate, 3 km from the current site
new site seating 55 customers for $240,000 versus refitting 40 seats
analysis_max_2: higher combined volume lifts total revenue above $86,000 a month
fixed costs spread over two sites improve margins if demand holds

questions.question_text: Do you think Pennyroyal Café should open the retail park café rather than extend the current site? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening the retail park site would capture the boom at its peak [k]; with GDP up 4.2%, unemployment at 3.8% and restaurant spending up 11%, a café seating 55 customers near the industrial estate could reach a new market while the original site keeps the loyal crowd causing 25-minute weekend waits [app], so revenue could grow well past $86,000 a month [an]. However, extending the current site by refitting 40 seats is cheaper and less risky [k]; it costs far less than $240,000 and keeps one 14-person team focused on one location [app], so profit per café rises without duplicated management or split oversight while the boom lasts [an]. Overall, Pennyroyal should open the retail park café [eval], because demand fundamentals (GDP +4.2%, confidence at its highest for a decade) support two locations, and waiting 8 weeks risks losing the lease to a rival [eval].

knowledge_max_2: opening a second site captures new markets during rapid growth
extending the existing site is cheaper and keeps management simple
application_max_2: $240,000 new site seating 55 customers near a growing industrial estate
current site refit of 40 seats; weekend waits of 25 minutes at $86,000 monthly revenue
analysis_max_2: two-site revenue growth and capacity relief versus $240,000 outlay and execution risk
single-site efficiency and lower risk versus missing the retail park lease deadline
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 8-week lease deadline and boom-stage demand
recommendation links back to confidence at its highest for a decade

scenario_stem:
Olive Branch Kitchen Co is a private limited company preparing ready-to-cook meal kits, selling 52,000 kits at $12 each for $624,000 revenue. Ingredients cost $5.50 per kit, leaving $6.50 of added value on every sale.

Founder Marcus Vale is deciding how to raise added value: pre-chop ingredients and add recipe cards with 14 extra hours of labour weekly, or rebrand with premium packaging costing $0.85 extra per kit to target busy professionals and support a $2 price rise.

questions.question_text: Define 'added value'.
questions.model_answer: Added value is the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Difference between selling price and cost of bought-in materials/inputs
Value added by the business's own processes and services

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Olive Branch Kitchen Co adds value.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Transforming raw ingredients into meal kits changes their form and usefulness [k]; Olive Branch buys ingredients at $5.50 and sells each prepared kit for $12 [app]. Way 2: Convenient preparation saves customers time [k]; kits save busy buyers the effort of shopping and chopping across 52,000 kits a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Processing/transforming inputs into finished products adds value
Convenience, service or time-saving adds value for customers
application_max_2: Ingredients bought at $5.50, kits sold at $12
Kits save customers shopping/chopping time across 52,000 kits a year

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Olive Branch Kitchen Co could increase added value.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Improving the product with pre-chopped ingredients and recipe cards raises quality perception [k]; kits would appeal to time-poor customers who currently pay $12 each [app], allowing the business to charge more per kit without doubling ingredient costs [an]. Way 2: Better packaging and branding can raise the price customers will pay [k]; spending $0.85 extra per kit on premium packaging could support a $2 price rise [app], lifting added value per kit from $6.50 to $7.65 even after packaging costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: Product improvement/perceived quality can raise added value
Packaging, branding and convenience can raise the price customers pay
application_max_2: Pre-chopped ingredients and recipe cards appeal to time-poor customers at $12 per kit
Premium packaging at $0.85 extra per kit could support a $2 price rise
analysis_max_2: Higher perceived quality supports higher prices and repeat purchases
Added value per kit rises from $6.50 to $7.65 after the $0.85 packaging cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Olive Branch Kitchen Co should increase added value through premium packaging and rebranding rather than extra preparation? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for the rebrand is profit: spending $0.85 per kit on premium packaging could support a $2 price rise [k], taking added value from $6.50 to $7.65 per kit [app], an extra $1.15 per kit across 52,000 kits worth about $59,800 a year [an]. However, the pre-chop alternative deepens real product value [k]; recipe cards and chopped ingredients make every kit genuinely more convenient for Marcus's customers [app], which could build loyalty and repeat orders rather than relying on looks alone [an]. Overall, the rebrand is the smarter next step because it is quicker and cheaper than adding 14 hours of labour a week [eval], but Marcus should revisit deeper preparation changes if customers reject the $2 rise [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Packaging/branding can raise price without changing product
Product improvement (pre-chop, recipes) raises real convenience and quality
application_max_2: $0.85 packaging supports a $2 rise; added value rises from $6.50 to $7.65 per kit
Pre-chop recipe option adds 14 hours of labour a week but genuinely improves the kit
analysis_max_2: $1.15 extra per kit across 52,000 kits is about $59,800 more revenue-based value
Genuine convenience can build loyalty, but costs 14 extra labour hours weekly
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both rebrand vs prep options using stem figures
Reaches a justified recommendation with a fallback condition

scenario_stem:
Coppergrove Assembly Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making kitchen appliances. It has 54 workers on two production lines making 3,800 units monthly, with $2.1 million revenue. Supervisor Adam Kone used laissez-faire.

Output has fallen to 3,400 units and errors risen from 2% to 5%. New manager Lucia Ferreira wants a democratic style with 10-minute briefings, aiming to restore 3,800 units in 3 months. Adam, trusted after 6 years, defends freedom.

questions.question_text: Define 'motivation'.
questions.model_answer: Motivation is the internal desire or willingness of employees to work hard and perform well in order to achieve business objectives. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Motivation is the willingness/desire to work hard/perform well
Motivation drives effort towards business objectives

questions.question_text: Explain two ways motivation affects the performance of Coppergrove Assembly Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: A motivated workforce is more productive and achieves higher output [k]; this matters because output has fallen from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month [app]. Point 2: Motivated workers take more care and make fewer mistakes [k]; with the error rate up from 2% to 5%, fewer errors would save wasted appliances [app].

knowledge_max_2: Motivated workers are more productive/achieve higher output
Motivated workers make fewer errors/higher quality work
application_max_2: Output has fallen from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month
Error rate has risen from 2% to 5%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of laissez-faire leadership shown by Coppergrove Assembly Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders provide little guidance or control, so workers may lack direction and standards [k]; under Adam's freedom the lines slipped from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month [app], showing output was not being maintained [an]. Problem 2: Without intervention, quality drifts [k]; errors rose from 2% to 5% with nobody correcting working methods [app], increasing waste and eating into the $2.1 million revenue [an].

application_max_2: Lines slipped from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month
Error rate rose from 2% to 5% without correction
analysis_max_2: More waste/rework reducing revenue of $2.1 million

questions.question_text: Do you think Lucia should introduce democratic leadership at Coppergrove Assembly Ltd? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Democratic leadership involves workers in decisions through consultation and shared information [k]; Lucia's daily 10-minute briefings would let the 54 line workers discuss targets and contribute ideas [app], which should rebuild commitment and could return output to 3,800 units within 3 months [an]. However, Adam argues the experienced line staff value the freedom they already have and their motivation relies on it [k]; replacing freedom with daily briefings could resent workers who prefer autonomy [app], so motivation might fall further before it improves, with errors possibly worsening [an]. On balance, introducing democratic briefings while keeping some team freedom, and reviewing progress after 3 months against the 3,800-unit target, is the better choice [eval], because the democratic approach directly addresses why output fell without removing autonomy completely [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire = freedom/autonomy valued by experienced staff

evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (democratic briefings vs existing laissez-faire freedom)
Justified recommendation with review period/partial autonomy retained

scenario_stem:
Solmar Soft Drinks is a private limited company in Country X producing Solmar Fizz lemonade for supermarkets. Domestic sales are flat at $950,000 from 90,000 cases, and it employs 26 workers. A distributor in Neighbourland offers 25,000 cases at $8, worth $200,000 yearly.

Export labelling costs $12,000 and freight $1.50 per case, netting about $150,500. Alternatively, $60,000 on domestic marketing is predicted to lift sales 15%, worth $142,500. The board must choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'exporting'.
questions.model_answer: Exporting is selling goods or services produced in a business's home country to buyers in another country, for example through an overseas distributor. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Selling home-produced goods in another country

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Solmar Soft Drinks of entering the Neighbourland market.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Access to new demand [k]; the Neighbourland distributor offered to buy 25,000 cases at $8 each, worth $200,000 a year, easing the plateau at $950,000 domestic sales [app]. Opportunity 2: Higher output from existing capacity [k]; 25,000 extra cases would use spare capacity at the factory employing 26 workers, with scope to grow beyond the first order [app].

knowledge_max_2: Export growth can use idle capacity and diversify markets
application_max_2: 25,000 cases at $8 = $200,000 a year vs flat $950,000 domestic
Spare capacity at the factory with 26 workers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Solmar Soft Drinks might face in the Neighbourland market.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Exporting adds costs [k]; labelling costs $12,000 and freight adds $1.50 per case, absorbing $37,500 of the $200,000 deal, leaving about $150,500 before product costs [app], a thinner margin than domestic sales [an]. Problem 2: Unfamiliar market and reliance on one distributor [k]; Solmar has never sold in Neighbourland, so if the distributor underperforms after the $12,000 labelling spend, sales of Solmar Fizz could stall [app], leaving the firm unable to respond quickly to local tastes or rivals [an].

knowledge_max_2: Exporting adds logistical and compliance costs
Limited knowledge of foreign markets increases risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Solmar Soft Drinks should enter the Neighbourland market or spend $60,000 on a domestic marketing campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting brings in 25,000 cases at $8, worth $200,000, netting about $150,500 after $12,000 labelling and $37,500 freight [k]; this is new revenue on top of the flat $950,000 domestic business and builds exporting experience [app], though it commits Solmar to an unfamiliar market with dependence on one distributor [an]. However, the $60,000 domestic campaign is forecast to lift local sales by 15%, worth roughly $142,500 of extra revenue [k]; it builds on a proven home market with no export logistics or labelling costs [app], but the gain depends on the agency's forecast and may fade once the campaign ends [an]. On balance, Solmar should enter Neighbourland [eval], because $150,500 of contracted revenue beats a forecast $142,500, with scope for repeat export orders afterwards [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Exporting earns new revenue but adds costs and risk
Marketing investment aims to grow sales in the home market
application_max_2: $150,500 net export income vs $142,500 forecast domestic uplift
analysis_max_2: Export deal is contracted and diversifies markets
Domestic campaign is lower risk but gains may be temporary
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (exports vs domestic marketing spend)
Justified recommendation: enter Neighbourland

scenario_stem:
Brimfield Garments Ltd is a private limited company making clothing. It made 28,800 garments, 240 per machinist, with a profit of $108,000. Its main customer orders seasonal summer lines.

It needs 9,000 summer dresses by 1 June, worth $450,000. It could make them between March and May, stored in a rented warehouse at $1,800 per month plus $400 per month security, or produce in weekly batches in May and June, risking late delivery and dresses unsold after August.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: The ability to produce the maximum output from given inputs with minimum waste of resources such as time, labour and materials [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brimfield Garments Ltd holds finished goods before 1 June.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Finished goods allow Brimfield to meet sudden seasonal demand [k], because holding 9,000 summer dresses ready means it can fill the customer's order in full by 1 June [app]. Reason 2: Finished goods protect valuable orders [k], because the dresses are worth $450,000 at the selling price and being late risks the retailer cancelling the order [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of holding the 9,000 dresses in the warehouse from March to May.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Storage and security costs reduce profit [k]; the rented warehouse costs $1,800 per month and security $400 per month, around $6,600 over three months [app], which cuts the margin on the $450,000 order [an]. Cost 2: Obsolescence risk [k]; dresses unsold after August are difficult to sell [app], so if the summer range did not sell, stock worth far more than the $6,600 holding cost could be written off [an].

analysis_max_2: around $6,600 over three months cuts margin
write-off risk exceeds the holding cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Brimfield Garments Ltd should manufacture the 9,000 dresses before June and hold them in the warehouse? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Manufacturing the dresses early would secure the order [k]; 9,000 dresses ready in the warehouse guarantee on-time delivery to the customer by 1 June [app], protecting revenue of $450,000 that weekly batch production might fail to deliver [an]. However, holding them carries costs [k]; warehouse and security charges of $2,200 per month from March to May plus the risk that dresses unsold after August become obsolete [app], which adds cost to a business with an $108,000 annual profit [an]. Overall, Brimfield should manufacture the dresses in advance [eval], because missing the June deadline could cost the entire $450,000 order and the $6,600 three-month holding cost is small in comparison [eval].

knowledge_max_2: securing the order versus holding costs
late delivery risks losing the contract
analysis_max_2: weekly batches risk missing the deadline
$6,600 holding cost is small against the $450,000 order
evaluation_max_2: weighs deadline security against holding costs
justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

scenario_stem:
Norwyn Engineering Ltd is a private limited company repairing industrial gearboxes for farms and mines, employing 60 machinists, with revenue of $2.4 million. The founding family still works full time. It wants $800,000 for a second workshop.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'debenture'.

knowledge_max_2: a long term loan raised by a company from investors
usually fixed interest and repaid after an agreed period, often secured

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why control matters when Norwyn Engineering chooses between debentures and shares.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Shares transfer ownership [k], because 50,000 new shares at $16 each would dilute the founding family from 60% to 40% of the company [app]. Reason 2: Control shapes the direction of the firm [k], because debenture holders have no votes, so the family keeps full say over the 60 machinists and the second workshop plan [app].

knowledge_max_2: issuing shares transfers ownership and voting power
debenture holders have no voting rights
application_max_2: 50,000 new shares at $16 would dilute the founding family from 60% to 40%
debentures let the family keep full say over the 60 machinists and the workshop

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing new shares to raise the $800,000.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The family loses control [k], because its stake falls from 60,000 of 100,000 shares (60%) to 60,000 of 150,000 shares (40%) [app], so new investors could block key decisions about the workshop [an]. Disadvantage 2: Profit is shared among more owners [k], because $2.4 million revenue would be divided among 150,000 shares rather than 100,000, cutting the family's share of the profit [app], which could reduce the incentive to keep investing [an].

knowledge_max_2: issuing shares dilutes the ownership and control of existing owners
issuing shares spreads the same profit across more shareholders
application_max_2: stake falls from 60,000 of 100,000 shares (60%) to 60,000 of 150,000 shares (40%)
$2.4 million revenue would be divided among 150,000 shares instead of 100,000

smaller family share of profit could reduce the incentive to keep investing

questions.question_text: Do you think selling debentures is a better option than issuing shares for the $800,000 second workshop? Justify your answer.

debentures carry fixed interest payable regardless of profits

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Calder Vale Motors is a franchised car dealership with 38 staff. After 3 consecutive quarters of contraction, unemployment reached 9.4% and consumer confidence is at its lowest in 12 years. Sales fell 24% to 610 vehicles; 140 cars are unsold over 60 days and showroom visits are down 30%.

The dealer principal must choose between a 'Sale Days' promotion offering 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing, or making 5 sales staff redundant and cutting marketing spend by 40%.

questions.question_text: Define 'consumer confidence'.

confidence influences willingness to spend, especially on major purchases

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why car sales fell at Calder Vale.

rising unemployment reduces disposable income available for car purchases

Problem 2: Redundancy damages morale among remaining staff [k], leaving 33 employees facing the pressure of clearing 140 aged cars with 9.4% unemployment weighing on buyers [app], so motivation and customer service may decline [an].

redundancy harms morale and service quality among remaining staff

scenario_stem:
Kettleworth Canning Co is a company making tinned tomatoes and sweet corn. It produced 4.8 million tins, selling at $1.25 each to 9 supermarket chains. Its single tinplate supplier has a 12-week delivery lead time.

A 3-week supply interruption stopped line two, losing 40,000 tins worth $50,000. Raising the raw material reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks would cost $2,100 per month extra storage, $350 per month extra insurance and tie up $480,000 of working capital.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons why businesses hold inventories.
questions.model_answer: To keep production running without interruption if supplies are delayed; to meet sudden or unexpected demand from customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: helps meet sudden or unexpected demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Kettleworth Canning Co should increase its raw material reserve to 6 weeks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A larger reserve prevents production stoppages [k], because the single tinplate supplier has a 12-week delivery lead time and one 3-week interruption already stopped line two [app]. Reason 2: A larger reserve protects revenue [k], because last winter's interruption cost 40,000 tins of lost output, worth $50,000 at $1.25 a tin [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of raising the reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Extra storage costs reduce profit [k]; the 6-week reserve adds $2,100 per month of storage and $350 per month of insurance, about $29,400 a year [app], which is more than half of last winter's $50,000 loss repeated within a single year [an]. Cost 2: Capital tied up [k]; raising the reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks locks up $480,000 of working capital [app], which cannot be used for new lines or repairs and might have to be borrowed at interest [an].

analysis_max_2: about $29,400 a year, more than half the prior loss
capital unavailable for other uses or borrowing needed

However, the reserve is not free [k]; storage and insurance cost $2,450 per month and $480,000 of working capital would be tied up in tinplate and tomatoes [app], and the money could instead earn interest or fund line two while a second supplier is found [an]. Overall, Kettleworth should raise the reserve [eval], because one avoided stoppage saves $50,000 against $29,400 a year of holding costs, and with 12-week lead times another delay is likely, not rare [eval].

scenario_stem:
Rillwater Construction Ltd is a private limited company employing 78 construction workers. GDP grew 3.6%, unemployment fell to 4.1% and housebuilding approvals rose 17%. Its order book is worth $9.4 million, its fullest in 6 years, but it turned down 2 contracts worth $2.8 million for lack of bricklayers and electricians.

Effect 2: Recruiting from rivals costs more [k], and with GDP growth of 3.6% and three new housing estates due to start, keeping the 78 workers it has is harder [app].

Benefit 2: Better pay improves retention and morale [k], so the 78 workers are less likely to leave for rivals whose site wages already rose 12% [app], protecting site productivity and delivery dates [an].

However, subcontracting avoids permanent wage inflation [k]; paying 25% deposits upfront and accepting margins cut from 9% to 5% on the 2 contracts would still clear the workload if recruiting fails [app], so subcontracting protects cash while the labour market stays tight [an]. However, Cilento's own sales office keeps full control of recipes, quality and pricing [k]; it costs $180,000 in year 1 but captures the whole profit margin in Ostresh and builds direct customer relationships [app], delivering far more income long term if the market grows [an]. On balance, Cilento should license first and review after two years [eval], because $56,000 of low-risk income beats a $180,000 untested commitment in a foreign market Cilento knows little about [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Licensing gives low-risk entry using a local partner
Own operations keep full control and full margin but higher risk

analysis_max_2: Licensing protects cash and tests the market
Own office offers greater long-term profit and control
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (licensing vs own office)
Justified recommendation: license first, review later

scenario_stem:
Aldenbrook Print Co is a company producing catalogues and leaflets. It made 1.8 million catalogues, 60,000 per operator, with revenue of $720,000 at $0.40 per copy.

A national retailer offers 900,000 catalogues over 6 months, worth $360,000. Aldenbrook could use overtime at time and a half, costing $54,000 extra wages, or invest $150,000 in a second-hand press raising output per operator by 30%, but installation and training take a full year.

questions.question_text: Identify two ways a business could increase productivity.
questions.model_answer: Investing in new or better machinery and technology; training workers or improving their skills [2].

knowledge_max_2: new or better machinery and technology

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why higher productivity matters to Aldenbrook Print Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher productivity lowers cost per catalogue [k], because producing 60,000 catalogues per operator at $0.40 per copy spreads wages across more output [app]. Reason 2: Higher productivity wins more business [k], because raising output per operator by 30% helps Aldenbrook fulfil the retailer's 900,000-catalogue order worth $360,000 [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Aldenbrook Print Co of investing in the second-hand press.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The press raises productivity [k]; output per operator would rise by 30% to about 78,000 catalogues a year with no extra wages [app], which lowers unit costs and increases profit on every copy printed [an]. Benefit 2: The press adds long-term capacity [k]; once installed, the one-off $150,000 cost compares favourably with the $54,000 overtime premium that recurs whenever orders spike [app], so Aldenbrook can take repeat work such as the retailer's $360,000 order at lower marginal cost [an].

analysis_max_2: about 78,000 catalogues per operator lowers unit cost
one-off press cost versus recurring overtime premium

questions.question_text: Do you think Aldenbrook Print Co should invest in the second-hand press rather than use overtime? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in the press would raise productivity permanently [k]; output per operator would rise by 30% to about 78,000 catalogues a year [app], cutting the labour cost of future retailer work without time and a half on every shift [an]. However, overtime suits the immediate order better [k]; the press costs $150,000 and needs a full year to install and train staff, while the retailer needs 900,000 catalogues within 6 months [app], so the overtime premium of $54,000 is far cheaper now and keeps the presses busy immediately [an]. Overall, Aldenbrook should use overtime rather than rush into the press [eval], because the immediate order is only $360,000 and the $96,000 difference between the two options can be kept as cash now, with the press worth buying later if the retailer renews the contract [eval].

knowledge_max_2: timing of the order versus installation lead time
analysis_max_2: 30% rise means about 78,000 catalogues per operator
$96,000 difference keeps cash in the business now
evaluation_max_2: weighs short-term cash and timing against long-term productivity
justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

scenario_stem:
Rushmere Jam Co Ltd is a private limited company making fruit preserves for three supermarkets, with revenue of $2.1 million and energy costs of $310,000. It wants a $150,000 boiler cutting energy costs by $45,000 a year; the current boiler fails the supermarkets' green audits.

An environmental grant covers 40% ($60,000), requiring quarterly energy reports for 5 years and a 25% emissions cut. A bank loan of $150,000 at 7.5% interest over 6 years costs $11,250 yearly and must be repaid if savings slip.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: Financial help given by the government to a business to encourage a particular activity, such as cutting pollution or creating jobs [2].

knowledge_max_2: financial help given by the government to a business
used to encourage a particular activity such as cutting pollution

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Rushmere Jam Co Ltd should consider when choosing between the grant and the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: The cost of the finance [k], because the grant funds $60,000 without interest, while the loan adds $11,250 a year for 6 years [app]. Factor 2: The conditions attached [k], because the grant demands quarterly energy reports for 5 years and a 25% emissions cut, enforced even if the savings slip [app].

knowledge_max_2: the cost of the finance influences the choice
the conditions attached to a grant influence the choice
application_max_2: the grant funds $60,000 without interest while the loan adds $11,250 a year for 6 years
the grant requires quarterly energy reports for 5 years and a 25% emissions cut

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of using the environmental grant for the boiler.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: It cuts the amount to be financed [k], because $60,000 of the $150,000 boiler comes free, leaving $90,000 to fund, or less than $150,000 to borrow at 7.5% [app], keeping interest well below the $11,250 a year the full loan would cost [an]. Advantage 2: It supports green credentials [k], because cutting emissions by 25% and reporting energy use quarterly satisfy the supermarkets' environmental audits [app], helping retain three supermarket contracts worth $2.1 million a year [an].

grants can improve a firm's environmental standing

the 25% emissions cut and quarterly reports satisfy the supermarkets' audits

retaining three supermarket contracts worth $2.1 million a year protects revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think the environmental grant is a better choice than the bank loan to fund the boiler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The grant is free money [k], because it covers $60,000 of the $150,000 boiler with no 7.5% interest attached, saving about $4,500 a year of interest on that portion [app], freeing cash from the $310,000 energy budget for fruit purchases and wages [an]. However, it binds Rushmere to quarterly energy reports for 5 years and a 25% emissions cut [k], and if the paperwork slips the supermarkets may doubt the firm's green claims [app], wiping out the saving and damaging the three supermarket contracts behind $2.1 million revenue [an]. Overall, the grant is the better option because the $60,000 funding plus at least $27,000 of interest saved beats the paperwork burden, given $45,000 a year energy savings are expected [eval], though the firm should appoint an energy manager before signing the reporting conditions [eval].

grants carry binding conditions such as reporting and emissions cuts

quarterly energy reports for 5 years and a 25% emissions cut are required

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Skerry Bay Hotel is a 3-star hotel with 120 rooms and 64 employees. GDP fell 1.4%, unemployment reached 10.2% and holiday spending fell 16%. Revenue fell from $3.1 million to $2.4 million, occupancy from 71% to 58%, and international tourist numbers fell 9%. Corporate bookings, once 30% of revenue, have dried up completely.

The manager must choose between cutting room rates by 15% to attract domestic families, or keeping rates and closing the leisure wing, making 9 staff redundant. Rivals cut rates by 12%.

questions.question_text: Define 'slump'.
questions.model_answer: The lowest point of the business cycle, when GDP is stagnant or falling, demand is weak and unemployment is high [2].

knowledge_max_2: the lowest point of the business cycle
weak demand, high unemployment and stagnant or falling GDP

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Skerry Bay's occupancy fell during the slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher unemployment cuts discretionary travel spending [k], and with unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%, fewer families booked Skerry Bay, dropping occupancy from 71% to 58% [app]. Reason 2: Weak confidence and incomes reduce business tourism [k], and with GDP down 1.4% and corporate bookings dried up completely, international tourist numbers also fell 9% [app].

knowledge_max_2: high unemployment reduces disposable income for leisure travel
weak growth and confidence reduce business and overseas travel
application_max_2: unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%; occupancy fell from 71% to 58%
GDP down 1.4%, corporate bookings dried up completely and international visitors fell 9%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Skerry Bay Hotel of cutting room rates by 15%.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lower rates attract domestic families trading down from poor value overseas trips [k], directly targeting the 16% drop in overseas holiday spending [app], so occupancy can recover from 58% towards the previous 71% [an]. Benefit 2: Higher occupancy lifts on-site dining and bar revenue [k], and with 120 rooms each night filling at a 15% discount, add-on spend rises with volume [app], recovering part of the $700,000 revenue shortfall [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower prices attract price-sensitive domestic customers
higher occupancy increases ancillary revenue per occupied room
application_max_2: 15% rate cut targets families avoiding the 16% fall in overseas holiday spending
120 rooms at 58% occupancy versus 71% before the slump
analysis_max_2: occupancy recovery towards 71% restores room and add-on revenue
volume gains offset the lower rate per room towards the $700,000 gap

questions.question_text: Do you think Skerry Bay Hotel should cut room rates by 15% rather than close the leisure wing and make 9 staff redundant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting room rates by 15% would win price-sensitive domestic business [k]; with unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%, families switching from overseas trips are the realistic growth segment, and rivals have already cut rates by 12% [app], so matching the market could lift occupancy from 58% and protect the $2.4 million revenue base [an]. However, closing the leisure wing and making 9 staff redundant would cut overheads [k]; weak corporate demand (bookings dried up completely) means fixed leisure costs weigh on profit while revenue sits $700,000 below last year's $3.1 million [app], so closure stops losses if the 15% discount fails to fill rooms [an]. Overall, Skerry Bay should cut room rates by 15% [eval], because closing the leisure wing removes the facilities that differentiate the hotel, whereas a targeted discount rebuilds occupancy from 58%, keeps 64 staff in work and preserves the 3-star offer for the recovery [eval].

knowledge_max_2: discounting attracts domestic demand when household budgets are squeezed
closing underused facilities and redundancy cut fixed costs but remove value-adding capacity
application_max_2: 15% rate cut vs rivals already at 12% off and 10.2% unemployment
closing the leisure wing and 9 of 64 staff redundant vs $700,000 revenue shortfall
analysis_max_2: rate cut restores volume and add-on revenue versus deeper margin per room
closure saves costs now but weakens the hotel's offer when demand recovers
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to occupancy of 58% versus 71% before the slump
recommendation keeps facilities and staff for the recovery

scenario_stem:
Fenmarsh Food Co is a private limited company producing chilled fruit desserts, employing 11 workers. It processed 38 tonnes of strawberries and mangoes last year for $720,000 from eight retail clients, buying frozen fruit at $2,400 a tonne.

Leo Fernandes must decide whether to lease a 4-hectare orchard plot at $1,150 a month, supplying 26 tonnes a year and enabling farm fresh marketing, or keep buying frozen. The orchard needs $30,000 of irrigation equipment and ties up land and labour.

questions.question_text: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Land is the factor of production that covers all natural resources used in production, including the land area itself, minerals, water and agricultural produce grown on it. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Includes land area, minerals, water, crops/agriculture

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fenmarsh Food Co needs land.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Land provides the natural raw materials for food production [k]; Fenmarsh processed 38 tonnes of strawberries and mangoes last year and needs fertile land to grow them [app]. Reason 2: Land is needed as a site for premises and operations [k]; the company operates from a leased unit beside a wholesale market where fruit is received and desserts are packed [app].

knowledge_max_2: Land provides natural raw materials/agricultural produce
Land is needed as a site/premises for production
application_max_2: 38 tonnes of strawberries and mangoes used for desserts
Leased unit beside a wholesale market for receiving and packing

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of leasing the 4-hectare orchard plot for Fenmarsh Food Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Growing fresh fruit cuts input costs [k]; leasing at $1,150 a month costs $13,800 a year compared with $62,400 for 26 tonnes of frozen fruit [app], saving about $18,600 in the first year even after the $30,000 irrigation cost is counted [an]. Benefit 2: Fresh local fruit supports premium marketing [k]; farm fresh desserts would appeal to shoppers who currently buy frozen-fruit products [app], helping Fenmarsh raise prices and protect its $720,000 revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Own-grown inputs can cost less than bought-in inputs
Fresh/local sourcing supports premium marketing and differentiation
application_max_2: $1,150 a month = $13,800 a year vs $62,400 for 26 tonnes frozen fruit; $30,000 irrigation
farm fresh marketing appeals to shoppers vs frozen-fruit rivals
analysis_max_2: First-year saving of about $18,600 improves profit margins
Premium positioning can raise prices and protect revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenmarsh Food Co should lease the 4-hectare orchard plot? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for the lease is lower costs: 26 tonnes of frozen fruit costs $62,400 a year, while the orchard costs $13,800 a year in rent plus $30,000 irrigation [k], bringing first-year fruit supply costs to about $43,800 [app], about $18,600 cheaper than buying frozen supplies [an]. However, leasing ties up land, labour and $30,000 of capital in a single crop [k]; Leo's 11 workers would also be stretched between factory and orchard, and strawberries fail if the season is poor [app], threatening the $720,000 revenue from shop orders [an]. Overall, leasing is worthwhile because the cost saving and marketing gain outweigh the risk [eval], but Leo should phase in the orchard gradually and keep one frozen supplier as back-up [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Own-grown supply can cut input costs
Single-crop reliance creates risk; seasons fail/perishability
application_max_2: $62,400 frozen vs $13,800 rent plus $30,000 irrigation (first year about $43,800)
11 workers shared between factory and orchard; farm fresh marketing; $720,000 revenue
analysis_max_2: First-year saving about $18,600 improves profit; more thereafter
Crop failure could leave the factory short of fruit, risking revenue
evaluation_max_2: Weighs leasing vs continued frozen purchase using stem figures
Reaches a justified recommendation with a phased/back-up condition

scenario_stem:
Hollymoor Garment Co is a private limited company in Country X with 132 machinists, $3.7 million revenue and 26,000 garments monthly. The Garment Workers Union represents 98 employees. Workers face 88 decibels near cutters and poor ventilation.

The union seeks ear protection, extraction fans and a joint health and safety committee, costing $52,000. Director Elena Petrova must sign or keep basic measures, with two weeks before all 132 staff meet and no stoppages affordable.

questions.question_text: Define 'collective bargaining'.
questions.model_answer: Collective bargaining is the process by which a trade union negotiates with an employer on behalf of all its members to agree pay, working hours and conditions of employment. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Union negotiates with employer on behalf of members
Agreement covers pay/working hours/conditions for the group

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of collective bargaining for workers at Hollymoor Garment Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Collective bargaining lets the union negotiate on behalf of all members, giving workers more power than negotiating alone [k]; the 98 employees the union represents could jointly press for ear protection and extraction fans rather than complaining individually [app]. Benefit 2: Collective agreements can fix clear, agreed standards [k]; a signed deal with a joint committee would make the noise target and ventilation arrangements binding on the company [app].

knowledge_max_2: Union negotiates on behalf of members, stronger together
application_max_2: 98 employees represented; joint press for ear protection and extraction fans
Joint health and safety committee would make arrangements binding

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Hollymoor Garment Co of signing the health and safety agreement.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Signing the agreement increases short-term costs [k]; ear protection, extraction fans and a joint committee are estimated at $52,000 [app], reducing profit against annual revenue of $3.7 million [an]. Effect 2: A safer workplace can reduce accidents, absences and staff turnover [k]; cutting noise from 88 decibels and improving ventilation would make machinists healthier [app], protecting output of 26,000 garments a month [an].

knowledge_max_2: Agreed safety measures raise short-term costs
Safer workplaces reduce accidents, absence and turnover
application_max_2: $52,000 estimated cost against revenue of $3.7 million
Noise at 88 decibels; ventilation; 26,000 garments a month
analysis_max_2: Lower profit/higher costs in the short term
Healthier, more stable workforce protects output

questions.question_text: Do you think Elena should sign the collective health and safety agreement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing the agreement would address a serious, immediate risk and show the business values its workers [k]; the $52,000 for ear protection, extraction fans and a joint committee is about 1.4% of annual revenue of $3.7 million [app], which is affordable and would tackle the 88-decibel noise directly, cutting accidents, absence and possible compensation claims while protecting 26,000 garments a month [an]. However, a signed collective agreement sets a formal precedent of joint decision-making [k]; once the health and safety committee exists, the company must consult on future changes, and ongoing costs could rise beyond the $52,000 initial estimate [app], limiting management flexibility [an]. On balance, Elena should sign the agreement because the safety risk is measurable at 88 decibels and the cost is modest relative to revenue [eval]; the alternative of waiting for an injury could mean costs far above $52,000 plus reputational damage [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Safer workplace protects employees and reduces absence/accidents
Collective agreements create ongoing consultation obligations
application_max_2: 88-decibel noise; 26,000 garments a month; 98 union employees
analysis_max_2: Prevents accidents/claims and protects output and reputation
Ongoing committee costs and reduced management flexibility
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (sign vs keep current measures)
Justified recommendation (sign) with cost justification

scenario_stem:
Tandoor & Thyme is a private limited company in Country X running 12 fast-casual curry houses, with $4.2 million revenue and 210 staff. A group in Farovia offers an international franchise for 8 outlets at $75,000 each plus 5% royalties, forecasting $2.6 million sales.

The deal brings $600,000 in fees and $130,000 year-one royalties with little capital. Alternatively, 3 company-owned outlets at $900,000 each cost $2.7 million, keeping profits and control but taking 2 years to break even.

questions.question_text: Define 'franchising'.
questions.model_answer: Franchising is an agreement where a franchisor allows franchisees to use its brand, products and business methods in return for an initial fee and ongoing royalties on sales. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Franchisee pays initial fees plus ongoing royalties

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Tandoor & Thyme of international franchising in Farovia.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Fast growth with little capital [k]; 8 franchise outlets cost Tandoor & Thyme nothing to build yet bring $75,000 of fees each, worth $600,000 upfront [app]. Benefit 2: Recurring royalty income [k]; 5% of forecast $2.6 million first-year Farovia sales gives $130,000 a year with local operators running sites and staff [app].

knowledge_max_2: Franchising enables rapid expansion without large capital outlay
application_max_2: 5% of forecast $2.6 million year-1 sales = $130,000 royalties

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Tandoor & Thyme of international franchising in Farovia.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Loss of control over quality [k]; franchisees run the kitchens, so poor curries or service could damage the brand behind $4.2 million of domestic revenue [app], erasing the home market's trust in Tandoor & Thyme [an]. Problem 2: Franchise income is shared and capped [k]; Tandoor & Thyme keeps only the fees and 5% royalties, so $730,000 of year-1 income is far below what company-owned outlets would earn [app], limiting funds for further expansion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Franchisors cede operational control to franchisees
Franchisor income is limited to fees and royalties
application_max_2: Franchisees run Farovia kitchens; brand built on $4.2 million domestic revenue
$600,000 fees + $130,000 royalties = $730,000, not the outlet profits
analysis_max_2: Quality slips damage reputation and home sales
Limited income restricts reinvestment and growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Tandoor & Thyme should enter Farovia by international franchising or by opening company-owned outlets? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Franchising 8 outlets brings $600,000 of fees plus $130,000 of year-1 royalties with no capital at risk [k]; Tandoor & Thyme keeps its $4.2 million domestic business focused while partners handle Farovia's sites, with standards enforced through training [app], and expansion is fast without debt [an]. However, 3 company-owned outlets at $900,000 each cost $2.7 million [k]; they keep full profit and tight control of recipes, branding and service — vital for a cuisine-led brand — but drain cash and take about 2 years to break even [app], straining the 12 domestic houses if Farovia disappoints [an]. On balance, international franchising is the better first step for Tandoor & Thyme [eval], because $730,000 with near-zero capital beats betting $2.7 million before Farovia demand is proven [eval].

Company ownership keeps full control and full profits

analysis_max_2: Franchising funds growth from partners' capital
Owned outlets maximise long-term profit but strain cash and risk
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (franchising vs company-owned)
Justified recommendation: franchise first, own outlets later

scenario_stem:
Holloway Toys Ltd is a private limited company making toys. It made 480,000 toys, 8,000 per worker, selling at $5 per toy. 70% of sales fall in November and December, and last Christmas stockouts cost $30,000.

It forecasts 320,000 toys. It could build from August and store in a warehouse at $2,600 per month plus $500 per month insurance, or add night shifts in October and November at 25% above the $9.00 wage plus hire 15 casual workers.

questions.question_text: State the difference between production and productivity.
questions.model_answer: Production is the total output of goods or services produced, whereas productivity is the output per worker or per unit of input over a given period [2].

knowledge_max_2: production is total output of goods or services
productivity is output per worker or per unit of input

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Holloway Toys Ltd might build a finished-goods inventory before Christmas.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Building an inventory meets sudden seasonal demand [k], because the board forecasts orders of 320,000 toys in the peak two months, far above what normal production would cover [app]. Reason 2: An inventory prevents stockouts at the peak [k], because around 70% of annual sales fall in November and December and toys made from August would be ready, protecting the $30,000 of lost sales suffered last Christmas [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two costs Holloway Toys Ltd would face from building this Christmas inventory from August.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Storage and security reduce profit [k]; the warehouse costs $2,600 per month and extra insurance $500 per month, about $9,300 over three months [app], cutting the margin on 480,000 toys sold at an average of $5 [an]. Cost 2: Capital and obsolescence risk [k]; building the extra 160,000 toys beyond normal output ties up roughly $400,000 of working capital if each toy costs $2.50 to make [app], and toys that fall out of fashion cannot be sold next year [an].

knowledge_max_2: capital tied up and obsolescence risk
analysis_max_2: roughly $400,000 of working capital locked in stock

questions.question_text: Do you think Holloway Toys Ltd should build the Christmas inventory from August rather than add night shifts in October and November? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the inventory from August would secure the peak [k]; toys ready before November allow Holloway to fill the 320,000-toy forecast in the peak two months [app], where current output would meet only about half, winning the peak revenue and keeping retailers loyal [an]. However, building stock early carries costs [k]; warehouse and insurance cost $2,600 and $500 per month respectively and about $400,000 of working capital would be tied up in extra toys [app], while night shifts at 25% above $9.00 an hour plus 15 casual workers flex cost only when demand arrives [an]. Overall, Holloway should build the inventory from August [eval], because the peak represents about 70% of annual sales worth roughly $1.68 million and the $9,300 three-month holding cost is tiny against losing that revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: securing the peak versus flexible overtime
cash tied up versus lost sales
analysis_max_2: current output covers only about half of the forecast

evaluation_max_2: weighs holding cost against lost peak revenue
justified overall recommendation with reference to figures
