unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramwell Furniture Ltd is a private limited company with 52 workers making sofas and dining sets. Following 2 quarters of falling GDP, output rose 0.8%, unemployment fell 9.6% to 9.1% and confidence rose 3 consecutive months. Orders climbed $1.9 million to $2.4 million; lead times cut from 14 to 11 weeks.

Two national retailers want larger ranges. Timber up 13%, owners choose: hire 8 extra production staff and build inventory, or keep staffing at 52 before the spring retail catalogue deadline in 3 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'recovery'.
questions.model_answer: The stage of the business cycle when GDP begins to grow again after a recession or slump, and confidence and spending start to rise [2].

knowledge_max_2: the stage when GDP starts to grow after a downturn
confidence and spending begin to rise again

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Bramwell Furniture's order book recovered.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rising GDP lifts household confidence [k], and with consumer confidence improving for 3 consecutive months and GDP up 0.8%, families are more willing to replace big-ticket furniture [app]. Reason 2: Falling unemployment raises household incomes [k], and with unemployment down from 9.6% to 9.1%, orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million [app].

knowledge_max_2: recovery raises confidence, encouraging big-ticket spending
falling unemployment increases household disposable income
application_max_2: GDP rose 0.8% and confidence improved for 3 consecutive months
unemployment edged down from 9.6% to 9.1%; orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramwell Furniture of hiring 8 extra production staff and building inventory.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Extra staff shorten delivery times [k], letting Bramwell cut lead times from 11 weeks further and satisfy the two national retailers wanting larger ranges for spring [app], winning repeat orders [an]. Benefit 2: Holding inventory ahead of demand captures the early recovery [k], and with the order book already climbing from $1.9 million to $2.4 million, Bramwell can fulfil demand without delays [app], protecting its reputation with national buyers [an].

knowledge_max_2: additional staff reduce lead times and enable larger order fulfilment
holding inventory ahead of demand captures upswing orders
application_max_2: 8 extra staff needed to serve the two national retailers' spring ranges
lead times already shortened from 14 weeks to 11 weeks with orders at $2.4 million
analysis_max_2: shorter lead times win repeat spring orders and strengthen retailer relationships
inventory readiness avoids stockouts and protects revenue during the upswing

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramwell Furniture should hire 8 extra production staff rather than keep staffing at 52? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring 8 extra production staff matches output to the recovery [k]; with GDP up 0.8%, unemployment down to 9.1% and the order book climbing $500,000 to $2.4 million, Bramwell can only cut its 11-week lead times and supply the two national retailers' spring ranges if it lifts capacity [app], so revenue and market share should grow through spring [an]. However, waiting is safer if the recovery stalls [k]; recovery is only early, timber prices are 13% higher than two years ago, and if confidence slips again the extra 8 wages and unsold sofas would squeeze a margin already hit by input costs [app], so keeping staffing at 52 protects cash until orders keep rising [an]. Overall, Bramwell should hire the 8 extra staff [eval], because lead times must fall from 11 weeks to win the two national retailers' spring ranges, and the downside of a modest, reversible staffing increase is smaller than the cost of turning away growing orders [eval].

knowledge_max_2: hiring ahead of recovery wins early market share and retailer listings
holding staffing fixed protects cash if the recovery stalls
application_max_2: 8 extra staff vs keeping 52; order book up $500,000 to $2.4 million
timber prices 13% higher; lead times need to fall from 11 weeks
analysis_max_2: capacity gain versus risk of excess wages if demand softens
winning two national retailers' spring ranges versus cash protection in a fragile recovery
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the spring retail catalogue deadline in 3 weeks
recommendation weighs the fragile 0.8% GDP recovery against order momentum

scenario_stem:
Harthill Garment Co is a private limited company upcycling used denim into jackets and bags, employing 8 machinists. Last year it earned $640,000 revenue and $88,000 profit from three stockists, and has $50,000 spare for equipment this year.

Nina Kaur can afford only one option: 10 new industrial sewing machines at $5,000 each with the manual cutting table, or 1 automated cutting table at $50,000 keeping the overlockers. Orders worth $150,000 await faster cutting before winter.

questions.question_text: Define 'opportunity cost'.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. [2]

knowledge_max_2: The next best alternative that is given up/forgone
Arises because resources are scarce and choices must be made

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunity costs Harthill Garment Co faces if it buys the automated cutting table.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity cost 1: Buying the table means giving up 10 new industrial sewing machines [k]; Harthill would forgo $50,000 of added sewing capacity [app]. Opportunity cost 2: The forgone sewing machines would have raised output speed for the 8 machinists [k]; without them, jacket and bag assembly continues at the current pace [app].

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone
Choosing one use of resources means losing another
application_max_2: Loses added sewing capacity to speed up 8 machinists

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of buying the automated cutting table for Harthill Garment Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Automated cutting is much faster and more precise than manual cutting [k]; orders worth $150,000 waiting on faster cutting could be fulfilled sooner [app], unlocking revenue that manual cutting cannot reach this year [an]. Benefit 2: Consistent cutting reduces fabric waste [k]; with used denim, precise layouts squeeze more pattern pieces from each garment [app], lowering material costs and raising the $88,000 profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: Automation raises speed and precision of cutting
application_max_2: $150,000 of waiting orders could be fulfilled sooner
Used denim layouts: more pattern pieces per garment, less waste
analysis_max_2: Faster throughput unlocks waiting revenue and improves cash flow
Less waste lowers costs and increases profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Harthill Garment Co should buy the automated cutting table rather than the 10 new sewing machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for the cutting table is unlocking large orders: orders worth $150,000 are waiting specifically for faster cutting [k], and the $50,000 table would directly remove that bottleneck [app], turning part of the $88,000 profit into a much larger figure if the waiting orders are delivered [an]. However, choosing the table means giving up 10 sewing machines, which is the opportunity cost of the decision [k]; without extra sewing capacity, Harthill's 8 machinists keep sewing at the old pace [app], so cutting gains could pile up as half-finished jackets awaiting stitching [an]. Overall, the cutting table is the better choice because the immediate constraint is cutting, not sewing [eval], and Nina should reassess sewing capacity next year [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone
application_max_2: $150,000 of orders wait on faster cutting; table costs $50,000
Choosing the table means giving up 10 sewing machines at $5,000 each
analysis_max_2: Removing the cutting bottleneck unlocks waiting revenue and profit
No extra sewing capacity could create a new bottleneck downstream
evaluation_max_2: Weighs cutting table vs sewing machines using stem figures
Reaches a justified recommendation with a follow-up condition

scenario_stem:
Cove & Crumb Café is a private limited company in Country X running four cafés with 34 staff, including 11 baristas on $9.60 hourly, and $1.9 million revenue. The union wants the new $10.25 minimum wage from 1 April.

Owner Dana Whitlock must raise all 11 baristas and absorb the cost, or cut 40 staff hours weekly. July brings $310,000 revenue and 11 hours a day trading. She must decide before April.

questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: The minimum wage is the lowest hourly rate of pay that employers are legally required to pay workers, set by the government to protect low-paid employees. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage is a legal minimum hourly pay rate
Set by government to protect/benefit low-paid workers

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the minimum wage rise on workers at Cove & Crumb Café.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Low-paid workers receive higher pay [k]; the 11 baristas currently on $9.60 an hour will earn at least $10.25 from 1 April [app]. Effect 2: Higher pay can improve living standards and motivation [k]; better wages may reduce turnover among the 34 staff who rely on café wages [app].

knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage raises pay for the lowest-paid workers
Higher pay can improve living standards/motivation
application_max_2: 11 baristas rise from $9.60 to $10.25 an hour from 1 April
34 staff rely on café wages; union campaigned for the rise

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the minimum wage rise could cause for Cove & Crumb Café.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Labour costs rise [k]; raising 11 baristas from $9.60 to $10.25 adds cost across the four cafés on revenue of $1.9 million [app], which could force price increases or tighter margins [an]. Problem 2: To control costs the business may cut hours [k]; removing 40 staff hours a week across the cafés would stretch remaining staff during 11-hour days [app], causing longer queues in July and dissatisfied tourists [an].

knowledge_max_2: Businesses may respond by cutting hours/jobs/prices rise
application_max_2: 11 baristas rising from $9.60 to $10.25; $1.9 million revenue
40 staff hours a week cut; 11-hour trading days; July peak
analysis_max_2: Tighter margins or price increases reduce competitiveness
Understaffing causes queues and lost tourist sales in July

questions.question_text: Do you think Dana should absorb the minimum wage increase or cut 40 staff hours a week to offset it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Absorbing the increase shows the business values its staff and protects service [k]; in July, revenue reaches $310,000 and the cafés trade 11 hours a day on summer tourists [app], so full staffing avoids queues and protects the café's reputation at peak season [an]. However, raising 11 baristas from $9.60 to $10.25 raises costs across four cafés on $1.9 million of revenue [k]; cutting 40 staff hours a week would limit the wage rise and help keep the cafés profitable in a competitive market [app], but would stretch remaining staff in the peak summer [an]. On balance, Dana should absorb the increase through July and review rosters in quieter months [eval], because losing tourist trade in the best revenue month would cost more than the extra wages [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting hours limits the cost increase but risks service
application_max_2: $310,000 July revenue; cafés trading 11 hours a day
11 baristas to $10.25; four cafés; $1.9 million revenue; 40 staff hours a week
analysis_max_2: Full staffing in peak season protects sales/reputation
Hour cuts save money but risk understaffing and lost tourists
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (absorb cost vs cut hours)
Justified hybrid recommendation tied to seasonality

scenario_stem:
Cascabel Foods is a private limited company in Country X producing ready-to-eat meals. Double Chilli Beef sells 95,000 packs at $4.60, with $1.9 million domestic revenue and 54 workers. Zandrivia prefers milder flavours and smaller portions.

Sell the standard 500g pack at $4.20, forecasting 60,000 packs and $252,000, or localise as Zandrivia Chicken in 350g packs, costing $150,000, forecasting 140,000 packs at $3.80 ($532,000). Allergen labels in the local language are required.

questions.question_text: Define 'localising a product'.
questions.model_answer: Localising a product is adapting it to the tastes, culture, laws or conditions of a particular market, rather than selling an identical product everywhere. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Adapting a product to a specific local market
Covers taste, portion, culture or legal requirements

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Cascabel Foods might localise its meals for Zandrivia.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Local tastes differ [k]; Zandrivia shoppers prefer milder flavours, so a mild 'Zandrivia Chicken' recipe should sell better than the fiery 'Double Chilli Beef' they do not know [app]. Reason 2: Legal rules differ [k]; Zandrivia's regulator requires allergen labels in its own language, so a localised pack is needed to sell legally there at all [app].

knowledge_max_2: Markets differ in taste, culture and usage habits
Foreign markets may have product/label legal requirements
application_max_2: Zandrivia prefers milder flavours; 'Zandrivia Chicken' planned
Allergen labels required in Zandrivia's own language

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Cascabel Foods might face if it localises for Zandrivia.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Localising costs money up front [k]; the new recipe and 350g packaging need $150,000 before any Zandrivia sale is made [app], so profit is delayed and cash is tied up on two factories already running [an]. Problem 2: The sales forecast may prove wrong [k]; if the mild recipe matches only the standard pack forecast of 60,000 rather than 140,000 units, the localised range loses money despite its $532,000 vs $252,000 projected revenue [app], leaving obsolete packaging and stock [an].

knowledge_max_2: Sales forecasts for new products are uncertain
application_max_2: $150,000 reformulation and packaging cost for 350g 'Zandrivia Chicken'
analysis_max_2: Upfront cost strains cash and delays profit
If forecast is missed, the localised range makes a loss

questions.question_text: Do you think Cascabel Foods should localise its meals for Zandrivia or sell the standard 'Double Chilli Beef' pack unchanged? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Localising fits Zandrivia's milder taste preference [k]; 140,000 packs of 'Zandrivia Chicken' at $3.80 could bring $532,000 in year 1, far above the standard pack's expected 60,000 packs worth $252,000 [app], and meeting allergen-label rules protects the brand legally in Zandrivia [an]. However, the standard pack needs no new recipe or packaging, avoiding the $150,000 upfront cost [k]; it simply extends 'Double Chilli Beef', which sells 95,000 packs a year at home [app], keeping production simple but ignoring local tastes and legal labelling, so Zandrivia sales may stay slow and repeat orders may never come [an]. On balance, Cascabel should localise [eval], because the forecast $280,000 uplift in year-1 revenue comfortably exceeds the $150,000 cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Localising matches products to local tastes and laws
Standardisation is cheaper but may ignore local needs
analysis_max_2: Localising wins more Zandrivia sales and legal compliance
Standard pack saves cash but risks poor acceptance
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (localise vs standardised product)
Justified recommendation: localise; uplift exceeds cost

scenario_stem:
Dunfell Dairy Ltd is a private limited company processing milk, supplying 60 supermarkets. It processed 4 million litres, earning $3.2 million at $0.80 per litre. Fresh milk keeps only 5 days, so it holds 2 days of chilled output.

A $180,000-a-year supermarket contract prompts raising chilled inventory to 4 days. A second cold room costs $5,400 a year and $260 per week extra power; wastage, written off when unsold milk passes its date, already reached $22,000.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'obsolescence'.
questions.model_answer: When inventory can no longer be sold because it is out of date, spoiled or replaced by a newer design, so it has to be written off [2].

knowledge_max_2: inventory becomes out of date or unusable
has to be written off and cannot be sold

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dunfell Dairy Ltd holds 2 days of chilled milk inventory.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Chilled inventory ensures uninterrupted supply [k], because holding 2 days of output covers the gap between pasteurising and delivery even if a supermarket order arrives suddenly [app]. Reason 2: Chilled inventory meets sudden demand [k], because the new supermarket contract worth $180,000 a year could be supplied faster than 5 days of shelf life would allow extra production [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of raising the chilled inventory from 2 days to 4 days.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Higher running costs reduce profit [k]; the second cold room costs $5,400 a year plus $260 per week of extra power, around $18,920 a year [app], which cuts margins on 4 million litres sold at $0.80 per litre [an]. Cost 2: Greater wastage and obsolescence [k]; milk passing its 5-day date is written off and wastage already reached $22,000 last year [app], so holding 4 rather than 2 days raises the risk of unsold, date-expired milk [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher running costs of cold storage
analysis_max_2: about $18,920 a year against margins on $3.2 million of sales
longer chilled cover raises the write-off risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunfell Dairy Ltd should raise its chilled inventory from 2 days to 4 days? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising the chilled inventory would help win the supermarket contract [k]; 4 days of cover lets Dunfell supply the new customer worth $180,000 a year reliably [app], far outweighing the $18,920 of added cold-room and power costs [an]. However, higher stock risks more waste [k]; milk keeps only 5 days and wastage hit $22,000 last year [app], so if demand does not materialise, extra chilled litres could be written off rather than sold [an]. Overall, Dunfell should raise the inventory to 4 days [eval], because the potential $180,000 contract is nearly ten times the $18,920 holding cost, and the spoilage risk can be managed with strict stock rotation and sales forecasts [eval].

analysis_max_2: contract is nearly ten times the $18,920 holding cost
spoilage risk can be managed with rotation and forecasting
evaluation_max_2: justified decision to raise the chilled inventory
weighs contract value against spoilage risk

scenario_stem:
Marlborough Freight Ltd is a private limited company delivering building materials in Country X, with revenue of $3.6 million and trade receivables of $96,000, including $38,000 from one builder 60 days late, while the insurer demands payment within 30 days of renewal.

Facing an $80,000 cash shortfall for insurance renewals and repairs, with two contracts starting in February, it compares factoring its debts for a 3% fee of $2,880 with an overdraft at 10.5% interest, costing about $3,500 over 5 months.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'factoring of debts'.
questions.model_answer: Selling trade receivables to a specialist firm for immediate cash, minus a fee, rather than waiting for customers to pay [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling trade receivables to a specialist firm
provides immediate cash minus a fee

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Marlborough Freight Ltd should consider when choosing between factoring and the overdraft.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: The cost of each option [k], because factoring costs 3%, or $2,880, on the $96,000 receivables, while the overdraft costs about $3,500 over 5 months at 10.5% [app]. Factor 2: How fast the cash arrives [k], because factoring releases money within days, whereas the overdraft limit must first be agreed with the bank [app].

knowledge_max_2: the cost of each source of finance
the speed at which finance can be accessed
application_max_2: factoring costs 3%, or $2,880, on $96,000 of receivables versus about $3,500 overdraft interest
factoring releases money within days while an overdraft limit must be agreed with the bank

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of using an overdraft to cover the $80,000 shortfall.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: It keeps growing in cost [k], because 10.5% interest on $80,000 adds about $3,500 over just 5 months [app], which rises if the repairs overrun or insurance cannot be paid on time [an]. Disadvantage 2: Repayment can be demanded on short notice [k], because overdrafts are repayable on demand and the firm already has $38,000 of late paying debts [app], leaving Marlborough exposed if the bank cuts the limit [an].

knowledge_max_2: overdrafts charge interest which grows over time
application_max_2: the firm already has $38,000 of late paying debts
analysis_max_2: costs rise if repairs overrun or insurance payment is late
a reduced bank limit would leave the firm unable to pay urgent bills

questions.question_text: Do you think factoring the debts is a better option than the overdraft for the $80,000 shortfall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Factoring is quicker and cheaper [k], because the 3% fee of $2,880 beats the $3,500 five month overdraft interest, and cash can arrive within days [app], plugging the gap before insurance renewals and repairs fall due [an]. However, factoring hands over a slice of profit [k], because the factor keeps $2,880 of the $96,000 receivables and may chase the late builder aggressively for the $38,000 [app], risking a customer relationship that drives future contracts [an]. Overall, factoring is the better choice this month because it is $620 cheaper and immediate, bringing certain cash into Marlborough when the insurer demands payment within 30 days [eval], but the firm should also tighten credit checks and chase the $38,000 late payer before the next renewal [eval].

knowledge_max_2: factoring provides immediate cash at a percentage fee
overdrafts charge interest and are repayable on demand
application_max_2: 3% fee of $2,880 beats $3,500 of five month overdraft interest
the factor may chase the $38,000 late builder aggressively
analysis_max_2: plugs the gap before insurance renewals and repairs fall due
aggressive chasing could damage a customer relationship driving future contracts
evaluation_max_2: weighs the $620 saving and speed of factoring against the lost customer relationship
recommends factoring now but tightening credit control afterwards

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Windlass Recruitment Ltd is a private limited company placing staff into offices, shops and warehouses. Unemployment fell 7.8% to 6.4% and advertised vacancies rose 22% to 148,000. Temps charge $28 an hour. It filled 2,900 permanent roles and 1,100 temporary posts, reaching $3.7 million revenue, up 13%.

Directors must choose between launching a temporary-staffing division with 6 consultants for urgent warehouse demand, forecast to grow 30% next year, or opening a second northern branch costing $190,000 to fit out.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: People of working age who are willing and able to work but cannot find a job, expressed as a percentage of the workforce [2].

knowledge_max_2: people able and willing to work who cannot find jobs
measured as a percentage of the workforce

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of falling unemployment on Windlass Recruitment.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Fewer candidates are available for each vacancy [k], and with unemployment down from 7.8% to 6.4% and vacancies up 22% to 148,000, consultants must search harder to fill the 2,900 permanent roles [app]. Effect 2: Employers compete harder for talent [k], so Windlass must deliver faster shortlists and service to keep its $3.7 million revenue growing at 13% [app].

knowledge_max_2: falling unemployment shrinks the candidate pool
falling unemployment intensifies competition between employers for talent
application_max_2: unemployment fell from 7.8% to 6.4% and vacancies rose 22% to 148,000
2,900 permanent roles filled; revenue $3.7 million, up 13%

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of launching the temporary-staffing division.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Temporary placements generate recurring margin rather than one-off fees [k], and with demand forecast to grow 30% next year on top of 1,100 temporary posts already filled, recurring revenue smooths Windlass's cash flow [app], reducing reliance on a volatile placement market [an]. Benefit 2: A specialist division widens the client base [k], letting warehouses in urgent need fill gaps fast through 6 dedicated consultants charging $28 an hour [app], building larger long-term service contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: temporary staffing yields recurring revenue streams
specialist divisions deepen client relationships and win larger contracts
application_max_2: temp demand forecast to grow 30% next year; 1,100 temp posts filled last year
6 consultants and $28 an hour target urgent warehouse demand
analysis_max_2: recurring margin smooths cash flow across economic cycles
deeper warehouse relationships convert into larger, longer contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Windlass Recruitment should launch the temporary-staffing division rather than open a second branch? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The temporary-staffing division rides the strongest trend [k]; unemployment at 6.4% and vacancies up 22% to 148,000 mean firms cannot wait weeks for permanent hires, so temp demand growing 30% next year offers Windlass recurring income from 6 consultants across its existing client base [app], expanding revenue beyond the current $3.7 million without a $190,000 branch outlay [an]. However, a second branch in the industrial north would capture a new geographic market [k]; with offices, shops and warehouses all needing staff, a local presence could win both permanent and temp business where competitors are thin [app], but it duplicates overheads for an uncertain return [an]. Overall, Windlass should launch the temporary-staffing division [eval], because it builds on proven demand (1,100 temp posts, $28 an hour) at lower risk than a $190,000 new branch, and it can be scaled nationally later from head office [eval].

knowledge_max_2: temporary staffing captures urgent demand when unemployment is low
a second branch wins geographic presence but duplicates overheads
application_max_2: 6 consultants for temp demand forecast to grow 30%; 1,100 temp posts at $28 an hour
$190,000 branch fit-out vs $3.7 million revenue, vacancies up 22% to 148,000
analysis_max_2: recurring temp revenue scales without new-site costs or split management
branch option broadens reach but risks duplicated overheads and uncertain payback
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to forecast 30% temp demand growth
recommendation prefers lower-risk organic division over geographic expansion

scenario_stem:
Bramblegate Print Ltd is a private limited company printing books and magazines, employing 15 staff across design, prepress, press and dispatch on $1.9 million revenue. Binding is outsourced to a specialist 40 km away, collected weekly.

Owner Tom Herrera must decide whether to bring binding in-house with a $65,000 binding machine, cutting 3 days off delivery and keeping the value chain together, or keep outsourcing. In-house needs a binder at $27,000 a year; the outsourcer charges $0.45 per book.

questions.question_text: Define 'value chain'.
questions.model_answer: A value chain is the full series of activities a business carries out to design, produce, market, deliver and support its product, from raw inputs through to the final customer. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Series of activities/stages a business carries out
From raw inputs/design through to final customer delivery

questions.question_text: Explain two stages of Bramblegate Print Ltd's value chain.
questions.model_answer: Stage 1: Prepress turns publisher files into press-ready pages [k]; Bramblegate's 15 staff prepare pages and images before printing begins [app]. Stage 2: Printing transfers the design onto paper [k]; Bramblegate runs its press department between prepress and dispatch to produce book blocks and magazines [app].

knowledge_max_2: Prepress/design prepares files ready for printing
Printing/production converts inputs into finished goods
application_max_2: 15 staff across design and prepress prepare pages and images
Presses produce book blocks and magazines for publishers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of bringing binding in-house for Bramblegate Print Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: In-house binding removes a transport stage and delays [k]; cutting 3 days off delivery times would let Bramblegate promise faster turnaround to publishers [app], winning more orders and raising the $1.9 million revenue [an]. Benefit 2: Keeping more of the value chain in-house captures profit that currently goes outside [k]; the outsourced binder charges $0.45 per book which Bramblegate currently pays away [app], so high-volume jobs would keep that margin inside the business [an].

knowledge_max_2: In-house stages remove transport delays/improve speed of response
In-house stages keep margin/profit that would otherwise leave the business
application_max_2: Cutting 3 days off delivery improves promises to publishers
Outsourced binder's $0.45 per book fee is currently paid away
analysis_max_2: Faster turnaround wins orders and raises revenue
Retained fees improve profit on high-volume work

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblegate Print Ltd should bring binding in-house? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for in-house binding is control and speed: a $65,000 machine would cut 3 days off delivery [k], an advantage publishers value when deadlines are tight [app], helping Bramblegate win repeat work and spread the machine cost over its $1.9 million annual output [an]. However, in-house binding commits the firm to a $27,000 salary and machine breakdown risk [k]; work currently outsourced at $0.45 per book is flexible, so in-house capacity could sit idle in quiet months [app], turning a fixed cost into a burden if orders fall [an]. Overall, bringing binding in-house is justified for Bramblegate's steady book workload [eval], but Tom should hire the binder on a reviewable contract and retain the outsourcing option for peak months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: In-house production improves control and speed
Outsourcing keeps flexibility and avoids fixed costs/idle capacity
application_max_2: $65,000 machine cuts 3 days; publishers value deadline speed
$27,000 binder salary vs $0.45 per book flexible outsourcing; quiet months risk idle capacity
analysis_max_2: Faster delivery wins orders, spreading machine cost over output
Idle in-house capacity in quiet periods turns fixed costs into a burden
evaluation_max_2: Weighs in-house vs outsourced binding using stem figures
Reaches a justified recommendation with a flexible contract condition

scenario_stem:
Elmtree Dental Practice is a private limited company in Country X serving a town of 28,000 with 9 dentists, 12 dental nurses and 6 admin staff, on $2.6 million revenue. Dr Aisha Rahman sets rotas and pay. Needle-stick injuries reached 7 recorded this year from 3 last year.

The BDNA union offers representation. Dr Rahman must recognise it or create an internal staff forum with elected members for safety. Recognition would make Elmtree the town's first union practice.

questions.question_text: Identify two functions of a trade union.
questions.model_answer: Two functions of a trade union are negotiating collectively with employers on behalf of members over pay and conditions, and providing members with advice, support and representation in disputes. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Negotiates collectively with employers on pay/conditions
Provides advice/support/representation to members in disputes

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for nurses at Elmtree Dental Practice of joining the BDNA union.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The union negotiates collectively, so individual nurses gain a stronger voice on safety [k]; the 12 dental nurses could jointly press for better needle-disposal procedures after 7 needle-stick injuries this year [app]. Benefit 2: Unions support and represent members in disputes with their employer [k]; nurses could get legal advice and representation if injured at work [app].

knowledge_max_2: Collective negotiation gives members a stronger voice
application_max_2: 12 dental nurses jointly pressing for better needle-disposal procedures
7 needle-stick injuries recorded this year; support if injured

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of creating an internal staff forum instead of recognising the BDNA union.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bluefin Leisure Centres Ltd is a private limited company running 4 fitness clubs with 21,000 members and 96 staff. After 3 years of growth, GDP rose 0.4%, unemployment rose 4.9% to 5.3% and confidence fell from 112 to 104; gym visits fell 7%, revenue $8.9 million.

questions.question_text: Explain two signs that Country X is near the top of the business cycle.

Sign 2: Confidence and unemployment are turning [k], with confidence slipping from 112 to 104 and unemployment creeping up from 4.9% to 5.3%, both classic late-cycle warnings [app].

Benefit 2: Fitness demand often holds up early in a slowdown [k], and with revenue at $8.9 million across 4 clubs, a premium site could lift yield per member [app], diversifying income across locations [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluefin Leisure Centres should press ahead with the 5th premium club rather than freeze expansion? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Pressing ahead captures remaining growth before the cycle turns [k]; GDP rose 0.4% last quarter and confidence still stands at 104, so northern-suburb demand may absorb a premium club creating 30 jobs, lifting capacity beyond 21,000 members and revenue above $8.9 million [app], so Bluefin would enter any downturn as the larger, stronger operator [an]. However, freezing expansion is the prudent response to clear late-cycle signals [k]; with growth of just 0.4%, unemployment rising to 5.3%, confidence slipping from 112 to 104 and two rivals discounting memberships by 20%, a $3.6 million commitment could strain Bluefin if member numbers fall [app], whereas cutting costs by $600,000 a year shields margins through a downturn [an]. evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to late-cycle indicators (0.4% GDP, confidence 104)

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Brancott Bakery Co is a wholesale bakery supplying 24 supermarkets, with 96 production staff on three shifts making 31,000 loaves weekly. Priya Nair briefs staff daily; updated recipes hang on the canteen board.

Benefit 2: Two-way questions can be asked and answered immediately [k], so workers can clarify the content of the 15-minute briefing before starting production across the three shifts [app], preventing wasted flour, time and effort on the 31,000-loaf target [an].

scenario_stem:
Ferncombe Cheese Co is a partnership making handmade cheese. Founded 9 years ago, it has 14 staff, produces 60 tonnes, earned $630,000. Marlowe Wholesale Foods buys 70% at $9 per kg, charges 18% and supplies 45 independent shops; the farm shop sells the rest at $14.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferncombe Cheese Co of selling through Marlowe Wholesale Foods.

scenario_stem:

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Brightwick Candles is a sole trader making soy candles. Founded 3 years ago, it employs 6 staff and makes 8,000 candles a month. Of $240,000 sales, 75% came from distributors supplying 12 gift shops and 25% from craft fairs.

An e-commerce website costing $15,000 plus $400 a month to run could bring $60,000 in year one, but the owner fears postage costs, fraud and buyers unable to smell soy candles; extra craft fair pitches would cost $6,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways e-commerce could benefit Brightwick Candles.

Benefit 2: Selling online means the shop is open 24 hours a day at a running cost of only $400 a month [k], so Brightwick can take orders outside craft fair weekends without paying for extra pitches [app].

Problem 2: E-commerce exposes the business to online payment fraud and cyber-security risks [k], so Brightwick must pay for secure payment processing plus $400 a month hosting on top of the $15,000 build cost [app], diverting cash from the $6,000 extra craft fair pitches it could alternatively secure [an].

scenario_stem:
Torvion Helmets Ltd is a private limited company making reinforced cycling helmets at its Briarport factory. With 26 workers it made 40,000 helmets last year: fixed costs $240,000, variable cost $9, price $17, average cost $15.00.

Orders from European distributors exceed capacity. A $600,000 injection-moulding machine would lift capacity to 60,000 helmets, cut variable cost to $7.50 but raise fixed costs to $330,000. Alternatively, outsourcing up to 20,000 helmets costs $12 each. The board must choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'fixed costs'.
questions.model_answer: Fixed costs are costs that do not vary with the level of output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and lease payments, which must still be paid even if nothing is produced. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs do not change with the level of output in the short run
They must be paid even if output is zero (e.g. rent, leases, insurance)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages Torvion Helmets Ltd would gain from buying the new machine.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It creates technical economies of scale [k]. The machine cuts variable cost from $9 to $7.50 per helmet and lifts capacity to 60,000 helmets, so average cost falls from $15.00 to $13.00 [app]. Reason 2: It spreads fixed costs over more units [k]. Although fixed costs rise to $330,000, spreading them over 60,000 helmets gives $5.50 each instead of $6.00 at 40,000 helmets [app].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale: new machinery lowers unit production cost

application_max_2: Variable cost falls $9 to $7.50; average cost falls $15.00 to $13.00 at 60,000 helmets

Outsourcing at $12 each means Torvion pays only for the extra units actually needed, so it keeps $600,000 rather than borrowing for a machine [app], protecting cash flow while the European distributors' orders are uncertain [an]. Reason 2: It avoids the risk of excess fixed costs [k]. Fixed costs of $330,000 would still be due even if the 60,000-helmet capacity went unfilled [app], and underused machinery would push average cost back above $13.00, wiping out the expected saving [an].

analysis_max_2: Flexible output lets Torvion match supply to confirmed orders, protecting cash flow
If capacity is underfilled, fixed cost per helmet rises and the $2.00 unit saving disappears

questions.question_text: Do you think Torvion Helmets Ltd should buy the new injection-moulding machine? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the machine secures technical economies of scale [k]: variable cost falls from $9 to $7.50 and average cost from $15.00 to $13.00, adding $2.00 per helmet — about $120,000 a year at 60,000 helmets [app], more than repaying the $600,000 cost within five years [an]. However, demand could fall short [k]: if Torvion produced only 40,000 helmets a year, fixed costs of $330,000 spread over fewer units would push average cost to about $15.75 [app], worse than today's $15.00 and higher than the $12 outsourcing price for the marginal units [an]. Overall [eval], buying is justified if the two European distributors commit to volumes near 60,000 helmets; otherwise outsourcing at $12 each, which still leaves a $5.00 margin per helmet, is the safer option [eval].

Low demand spreads fixed costs over fewer units, raising average cost

At 40,000 helmets average cost would be about $15.75; outsourcing price $12 each
analysis_max_2: $120,000 annual saving would recover the $600,000 machine within five years
Underfilled capacity removes the $2.00 saving and can exceed current average cost
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and gives a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to demand commitments

scenario_stem:
Bramblefold Poultry Farm is a family partnership keeping 17,000 laying hens in two barns. It sells 5.1 million eggs yearly to supermarkets, earning $890,000 with 9 full-time employees. It lies 400 metres from Lower Ashby, with 1,150 residents.

questions.question_text: Define 'external costs'.
questions.model_answer: External costs are the costs of a business or economic activity that fall on third parties not involved in the production or consumption of the good, such as pollution, noise or odour affecting people living nearby. [2].

Reason 2: The farm imposes disruption on the community [k], as shown by 26 written complaints about flies and smells received over the past 18 months [app].

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Solmara Herbal Teas of appointing an agent in Country Y.

scenario_stem:
Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co is a private limited company producing tomato sauces and passata for 30 delicatessens. With 11 workers it makes 240,000 jars a year; variable costs are $1.10 per jar, including $0.50 tomatoes, fixed costs $66,000, selling at $2.00 per jar.

A growers' co-operative offers a two-year contract for 120 tonnes at $800 per tonne versus $1,000 per tonne weekly, saving $24,000 a year. Quarterly deliveries need cold storage at $10,000 a year, cutting the tomato portion from $0.50 to $0.40 per jar.

questions.question_text: Define 'variable costs'.
questions.model_answer: Variable costs are costs that change directly with the level of output, rising when more units are produced and falling when fewer are produced, such as raw materials, components and packaging. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Variable costs change with the level of output
Examples: raw materials, components, packaging, direct labour per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits the co-operative tomato contract could bring Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It is a purchasing economy of scale [k]. Buying 120 tonnes at $800 per tonne instead of $1,000 saves $200 per tonne, worth $24,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: It lowers the variable cost of every jar [k]. The tomato portion falls from $0.50 to $0.40, so variable cost drops from $1.10 to $1.00 per jar and average cost falls from about $1.38 to about $1.32 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Bulk purchasing earns lower prices (purchasing economies of scale)
Lower variable cost per unit reduces average cost
application_max_2: $200 per tonne saving on 120 tonnes = $24,000 a year
Tomato portion of variable cost falls $0.50 to $0.40; variable cost $1.10 to $1.00 per jar; average cost about $1.38 to $1.32

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of signing the two-year tomato contract.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: It adds a new fixed cost [k]. Leasing cold storage at $10,000 a year must be paid even if jar sales fall below 240,000 [app], so the net saving drops to $14,000 and average cost rises if output dips [an]. Disadvantage 2: It locks Marazzi into one supplier [k]. If spot prices fall below $800 per tonne or the co-operative's quality slips, Marazzi must still honour the two-year deal [app], risking higher costs or inconsistent sauces across its 30 delicatessen customers [an].

Long-term supply contracts remove flexibility if prices or quality change
application_max_2: $10,000 a year cold-storage lease; output currently 240,000 jars
Fixed price $800 per tonne for two years; supplies 30 delicatessens
analysis_max_2: Fixed lease is unavoidable, so falling sales raise average cost and shrink the saving to $14,000
Lock-in risks paying above market price or poor quality, harming margins and reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co should sign the two-year tomato contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing brings clear purchasing economies of scale [k]: the $200 per tonne saving is worth $24,000 a year, more than covering the $10,000 cold-store lease, so net costs fall by $14,000 a year [app] and profit rises from $150,000 to about $164,000, with average cost dropping to about $1.32 [an]. However, the two-year commitment is risky [k]: if tomato prices fall below $800 per tonne or demand from the 30 delicatessens weakens, the fixed lease and price would become a burden [app], and bulk quarterly deliveries could raise wastage, eroding the $0.10 saving per jar [an]. Overall [eval], the contract is worth signing because the saving exceeds the lease cost by $14,000 a year — about 9% extra profit — provided Marazzi negotiates quality guarantees and an exit clause before committing [eval].

Fixed commitments and supplier lock-in create risk
application_max_2: $24,000 annual saving versus $10,000 lease; net $14,000 saving

scenario_stem:
Starbright Toys is a private limited company selling children's toys and games online and from one shop in Country X. Annual revenue is $420,000, with 55% earned in November and December. August inflows are $6,500 against $15,800 outflows; September inflows $7,200 against $15,100 outflows, from a $9,000 opening balance on 1 August.

Marcus must decide before 1 August whether to arrange a $20,000 bank overdraft or delay paying toy suppliers $14,000 until January, when festive takings arrive.

questions.question_text: Define 'overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft is a bank facility that lets a business spend more money than it holds in its current account, up to an agreed limit, with interest paid on the amount used [2].

knowledge_max_2: overdraft allows spending beyond the current account balance
up to an agreed limit with interest on the amount used

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why festive toy retailers like Starbright prepare cash-flow forecasts before Christmas.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A forecast shows the timing of cash movements [k], so Marcus can see that August inflows of $6,500 will not cover outflows of $15,800 [app]. Reason 2: A forecast identifies borrowing needs in advance [k], letting Marcus arrange the $20,000 overdraft before the balance falls below zero [app].

knowledge_max_2: forecast shows timing of cash inflows and outflows
forecast reveals when borrowing will be needed
application_max_2: August inflows of $6,500 against outflows of $15,800
the overdraft must be arranged before the balance falls below zero

Problem 2: Suppliers may charge late fees or withdraw credit terms [k], and Starbright's forecast already shows August inflows of only $6,500 against outflows of $15,800 [app], so extra costs would deepen the shortfall [an].

late payment may trigger fees or refusal to supply

extra costs deepen the forecast cash shortfall

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should arrange the $20,000 overdraft rather than delay paying toy suppliers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arranging the overdraft would protect supplier relationships ahead of the festive peak [k], because Starbright depends on suppliers delivering festive stock against $14,000 of September invoices [app], so keeping trust secures stock this year and next [an]. However, overdraft interest will add cost [k], and inflows of $6,500 and $7,200 in August and September sit well below outflows of $15,800 and $15,100 [app], so the balance could reach about -$8,200 by the end of September before festive sales arrive [an]. Overall, Marcus should arrange the $20,000 overdraft [eval], because the interest cost is lower than the risk of empty shelves in the two months that generate 55% of annual revenue [eval].

scenario_stem:
Estwick Brick Co is a private limited company producing 9 million clay bricks yearly for housebuilders. It employs 74 workers, runs two kilns continuously and turns over $3.7 million. Estwick town, 500 metres away, has 9,000 residents downwind.

Doctors recorded 34 cases of childhood asthma; chimney particulates are 45% above the legal limit. The Agency may fine $1,500 daily or shut the oldest kiln. The board can fit $210,000 electrostatic filters, switch to low-sulphur gas at $28,000 a year, or appeal.

questions.question_text: Define 'externalities'.
questions.model_answer: Externalities are the effects of producing or consuming a good on third parties not involved in the transaction; they may be negative, such as pollution, or positive, such as jobs created for the local community. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Effects on third parties not involved in the transaction
Can be negative external costs or positive external benefits

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Environment Agency intervenes in Estwick Brick Co's operations.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To protect public health [k], since 34 cases of childhood asthma were recorded near the plant in the last year, linked to dust drifting over 500 metres into a town of 9,000 residents [app]. Reason 2: To enforce the law against pollution [k], because chimney particulates measured 45% above the legal limit, so fines of $1,500 per day are needed to force compliance [app].

knowledge_max_2: To protect public health from pollution
To enforce legal limits and standards
application_max_2: 34 cases of childhood asthma near the plant last year
Particulates 45% above the legal limit; fines of $1,500 per day

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Estwick Brick Co of fitting the electrostatic filters costing $210,000.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Emissions fall and fines stop [k], as filters capture particulates so the output stays legal and the $1,500 daily fines are avoided [app], preventing penalties that could total over $540,000 a year [an]. Effect 2: A large short-term cost [k], as $210,000 must be spent immediately, equal to about 5.7% of annual turnover of $3.7 million [app], squeezing short-term cash flow and reducing profit for the year [an].

Filters are a large one-off capital cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Estwick Brick Co should fit the $210,000 electrostatic filters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for fitting the filters is that they solve the legal problem permanently [k], removing the 45% excess particulates and stopping $1,500 daily fines while keeping both kilns running for its 9 million bricks [app], protecting turnover of $3.7 million, the jobs of 74 workers and relations with Estwick's 9,000 residents [an]. However, one argument against is the immediate cost [k], since $210,000 equals roughly 5.7% of annual turnover and the firm could instead switch to low-sulphur gas at just $28,000 a year extra, preserving cash for expansion [app], although switching fuel may not capture the heavier particulates and would delay compliance [an]. Overall, Estwick Brick Co should fit the electrostatic filters [eval], because fines of $1,500 a day would exceed the $210,000 installation cost in 5 months of breach, making compliance cheaper and safer for its licence to operate [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Upfront cost versus cheaper but partial gas switching
application_max_2: $210,000 filter cost versus $28,000 extra per year for gas
45% excess particulates; fines of $1,500 per day

Gas switching is cheaper but may not capture heavier particulates
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both fitting filters and switching fuel or appealing
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Hartfield City Hospital is a public corporation funded by the State, employing 900 staff and treating 140,000 patients a year on a $180 million budget. Waiting lists rose from 4,000 to 6,500 in 3 years.

Nearby Saracen Health is a private clinic with 120 staff charging $250 per consultation and $3,800 for minor surgery, making $4.5 million profit. The government is debating contracting it to clear Hartfield's list at 15% below public costs, or raising the hospital's budget.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'mixed economy'.
questions.model_answer: An economic system in which both private sector and public sector organisations operate side by side, with resources allocated by both markets and the State. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Both public and private sectors operate side by side
Resources are allocated by markets and by the State

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hartfield City Hospital remains in the public sector.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To provide free healthcare to all [k], the hospital treats 140,000 patients a year funded by a $180 million budget rather than charging fees [app]. Reason 2: To guarantee access for people who cannot pay [k], 6,500 patients are waiting, many of whom could not afford $250 private consultations at Saracen Health [app].

Benefit 2: The public hospital can focus on complex cases [k], since routine treatment could move to Saracen Health, freeing 900 staff and the $180 million budget for serious illness [app], improving overall service efficiency [an].

However, one argument against is that contracting private care [k] would divert public money to a firm that made a $4.5 million profit and charges $3,800 for minor surgery [app], meaning the $180 million budget grows the private sector rather than strengthening Hartfield's 900 public staff [an]. Overall, the government should agree a short-term contract [eval], because cutting the 6,500 waiting list quickly serves patients best, provided the 15% saving is properly costed and Hartfield keeps capacity for serious cases [eval].

scenario_stem:
Redmarsh Construction Ltd is building a 9-storey office block in Country X with 74 workers, including 26 contract migrants. Falls from height are the main risk and 2 scaffolders were injured. Rules use coloured posters and hazard signs plus a 20-minute weekly talk.

After 3 near-misses, the safety officer proposes toolbox talks with a translator at $60 each. The manager prefers multilingual signs for $4,800, noting accident rates fell 40% after multilingual signage elsewhere. Both start within 2 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'visual communication'.
questions.model_answer: Visual communication is the passing of information through images, such as signs, posters, charts, diagrams, photographs or videos, rather than through words alone. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication using images, symbols or diagrams
Examples include posters, signs, charts and videos

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of visual communication on the construction site.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Signs and posters communicate safety rules instantly without spoken language [k], which is vital because 26 contract migrants on site have a first language other than English [app]. Advantage 2: Visual warnings are permanent and cannot be forgotten [k], so coloured hazard signs around the site constantly remind the 74 workers of the dangers of working at height on the 9-storey block [app].

knowledge_max_2: Images communicate quickly without spoken language
Visual messages are permanent and always visible
application_max_2: 26 contract migrants have a first language other than English
Coloured hazard signs remind the 74 workers on the 9-storey block

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why visual communication alone may not be enough on the site.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Posters and signs cannot check understanding [k], so the 26 contract migrants might misread hazard warnings even in their own language [app], leaving the safety officer unable to tell whether workers understand the risks [an]. Reason 2: Visual methods cannot answer questions [k], so workers cannot clarify site rules beyond the 20-minute Monday talk without stopping work [app], meaning misunderstandings about falls from height and scaffolding could persist undetected [an].

knowledge_max_2: Visual methods are one-way and cannot check understanding
Visual methods cannot answer questions or give feedback
application_max_2: 26 contract migrants might misread existing coloured posters and hazard signs
Only the 20-minute Monday talk allows any spoken explanation of the rules

questions.question_text: Do you think the project manager should spend $4,800 on multilingual signs instead of hiring a translator for toolbox talks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the multilingual signs is that they cost $4,800 once [k] and would be on display in all areas permanently, covering the 26 contract migrants and the other 48 workers [app], so safety instructions would always be visible where the danger actually occurs on the 9-storey block [an]. However, one argument against is that signs are one-way [k] and cannot check that workers understand, as shown by the 3 near-miss incidents in one month despite existing posters [app], whereas a translator at $60 per session would let migrants ask questions and get answers face to face [an]. Overall, the site should fund both, but if only one option is possible, the multilingual signs are the better spend [eval], because they protect every worker every day, matching the 40% fall in accident rates seen on similar sites after signage was introduced [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Visual methods are permanent, always visible and cheap over time
Verbal two-way methods check understanding and allow questions
application_max_2: $4,800 once for multilingual signs covering 26 contract migrants and 48 other workers
3 near-miss incidents in one month despite existing posters and signs

scenario_stem:
Brancott Catering Co is a private limited company catering for weddings and corporate parties. Founded 4 years ago, it employs 8 staff and earned $322,000 from 46 events, averaging $7,000, with most bookings by word of mouth.

A hotel group offers wedding referrals for a 12% fee, adding 15 events at lower margins. Brancott could spend $7,500 on its own website, aiming for 2 extra corporate events monthly at $7,000 each.

questions.question_text: Define 'e-commerce'.
questions.model_answer: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet, for example through a website, app or online booking platform [2].

carried out through a website, app or online platform

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why selling services directly to customers suits a service business such as Brancott Catering Co.

Reason 2: Selling direct lets Brancott meet clients personally to plan each event [k], so each $7,000 event can be tailored to the customer's menu, budget and schedule [app].

questions.question_text: Do you think Brancott Catering Co should rely on referrals from the hotel group? Justify your answer.
