scenario_stem:
Peregrine Outdoor Co is a private limited company designing rucksacks and hiking jackets. Sales were 90,000 units ($4.5 million); fixed costs $1.8 million, variable cost $22, average cost is $42. Its two largest customers want faster northern deliveries.

The board considers a second northern factory doubling capacity to 180,000 units. Fixed costs would rise to $3.24 million, but bulk fabric buying would cut variable cost to $20. Problems include slower communication, duplicated management and integration across two sites.

questions.question_text: Define 'economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains as it increases the scale of production, so that the average cost of each unit falls as output rises. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Average cost per unit falls as the scale/output of production increases
Examples: purchasing, technical, financial, marketing and managerial economies

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Peregrine Outdoor Co would gain from economies of scale if it doubles capacity.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Purchasing economies would lower variable cost [k]. Bulk buying of fabric cuts variable cost from $22 to $20 per unit, saving $2.00 on each of 180,000 units — $360,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Fixed costs are spread over more output [k]. Fixed costs rise only to $3.24 million, so the fixed cost per unit drops from $20 to $18 and average cost falls from $42 to $38 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Purchasing (bulk-buying) economies lower variable cost per unit
Spreading fixed costs over greater output lowers average cost
application_max_2: Variable cost $22 to $20; saving $2.00 x 180,000 units = $360,000 a year
Fixed cost per unit $20 to $18 ($1.8m/90,000 vs $3.24m/180,000); average cost $42 to $38

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Peregrine might face from operating two factories.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Diseconomies of scale can emerge [k]. Slower communication between a northern site and head office, plus duplicated management, could delay decisions and cause errors [app], pushing average cost up instead of down [an]. Problem 2: Fixed costs nearly double [k]. Fixed costs rise to $3.24 million, so if demand fails to reach 180,000 units, the extra fixed cost is spread over fewer units [app], pushing average cost above $42 and reducing profit below $720,000 [an].

knowledge_max_2: Diseconomies of scale: poor communication, low morale, slow decision-making as firms grow
Higher fixed costs raise the output needed to cover them
application_max_2: Duplicated management and slower communication across two sites
Fixed costs $1.8 million rising to $3.24 million; capacity of 180,000 units
analysis_max_2: Delays and errors from weaker communication erode the cost savings of scale
If demand stays below 180,000 units, fixed cost per unit rises and the $4.00 saving is reversed

questions.question_text: Do you think Peregrine Outdoor Co should open the second northern factory? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening the factory secures economies of scale [k]: average cost falls from $42 to $38, a $4.00 saving per unit worth about $720,000 a year at 180,000 units [app], and profit could rise from $720,000 to about $2.16 million [an]. However, the gains depend on filling the extra capacity [k]: at only 90,000 units a year, fixed costs of $3.24 million would push average cost to about $56 [app], and duplicated management across two sites could cause diseconomies of scale, with slower decisions eroding the saving [an]. Overall [eval], the expansion is justified if the two largest customers commit to northern volumes and faster deliveries, since the $4.00 unit saving and delivery advantage outweigh moderate diseconomy risk; Peregrine should sign those orders before committing to the factory [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Economies of scale lower average cost as output rises
Diseconomies of scale and excess fixed costs threaten growth benefits
application_max_2: Average cost falls $42 to $38; saving worth about $720,000 a year at 180,000 units; profit could rise towards $2.16 million
At 90,000 units average cost would be about $56; fixed costs $3.24 million
analysis_max_2: $4.00 saving per unit and doubled capacity drive profit from $720,000 towards $2.16 million
Unfilled capacity makes fixed costs per unit rise, reversing the scale benefit
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and gives a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement linked to securing customer commitments first

scenario_stem:
Bramble & Board Catering Co is a private limited company offering wedding and conference catering. Annual revenue is $680,000, with 65% arriving between May and September. Fixed costs are $17,500 monthly; wedding clients pay 25% on booking and the balance 14 days before the event.

January to April inflows of $9,000, $11,000, $13,500 and $18,000 face $21,000 monthly outflows. With a $14,000 opening balance, Lena chooses between a $20,000 loan at 9% (repayable in October) and asking suppliers to wait 60 days.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash-flow forecast'.
questions.model_answer: A cash-flow forecast is a document estimating a business's cash inflows, outflows, net cash flow and opening and closing balances for each future period [2].

knowledge_max_2: estimates future cash inflows and outflows
shows net cash flow and opening/closing balances per period

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a catering company can be profitable yet still run out of cash.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit is recognised when revenue is earned, not when cash is received [k], so wedding balances paid 14 days before events may still leave Bramble & Board short in January [app]. Reason 2: Deposits of 25% arrive months before work is done [k], making some months look strong while $17,500 of fixed costs falls due every month [app].

knowledge_max_2: profit and cash differ because of timing differences
fixed costs must be paid even when inflows are weak
application_max_2: wedding balances paid 14 days before the event leave January short
25% deposits arrive early while $17,500 costs fall due monthly

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Bramble & Board of taking the $20,000 short-term bank loan instead of delaying supplier payments.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The loan protects supplier relationships [k], so flour, meat and equipment suppliers keep delivering on normal terms through the quiet first quarter [app], avoiding stopped deliveries in the busy May to September season [an]. Advantage 2: The loan gives a known repayment schedule at 9% interest [k], and October wedding receipts, part of the 65% of revenue earned between May and September, can repay it [app], so the debt is cleared from peak-season cash [an].

knowledge_max_2: a bank loan provides known, structured finance without straining suppliers
protecting supplier credit terms avoids supply disruption
application_max_2: $20,000 loan at 9% interest repayable in October
October receipts form part of the 65% of revenue earned May-September
analysis_max_2: avoids stopped deliveries heading into the peak season
debt cleared from peak-season cash rather than stretched into spring

questions.question_text: Do you think Lena should take the $20,000 short-term bank loan rather than ask suppliers to wait 60 days? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Taking the loan secures supplies and preserves goodwill with the two largest suppliers [k], at a known cost of 9% interest on $20,000 until October [app], so Lena keeps full reliability for the May to September peak [an]. However, asking suppliers to wait 60 days costs nothing in interest [k], and outflows of $21,000 a month against January inflows of $9,000 show a first-quarter gap that extra patience could bridge [app], so the loan could be unnecessary if suppliers agree [an]. Overall, Lena should take the loan [eval], because wedding clients book a year ahead and one failed delivery would cost more than the interest saved by stretching suppliers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a short-term loan preserves supplier goodwill at a known interest cost
delaying payments to suppliers avoids interest but risks goodwill
application_max_2: outflows of $21,000 a month against January inflows of $9,000
analysis_max_2: reliance on suppliers without informing them risks hidden damage
the first-quarter gap could alternatively be bridged by 60-day patience
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing certain interest against vague supplier goodwill risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kongwe Plantations Ltd is a private limited company growing oil palm across 2,600 hectares. It earns $4.6 million exporting 80% of its 7,400 tonnes of crude palm oil, used in 3,000 supermarket products.

Earthwatch Alliance reports 640 hectares of native forest cleared in 4 years, releasing carbon and destroying habitat. Buyers in Country Y now demand certified sustainable palm oil; certification costs $85,000 yearly plus a $140,000 mill upgrade, while losing two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year is a risk.

questions.question_text: Define 'deforestation'.
questions.model_answer: Deforestation is the clearing or removal of forests and trees from land, usually so the land can be used for agriculture, logging, mining or settlement. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Clearing or removal of forests or trees
For agriculture, logging, mining or settlement

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why clearing native forest harms the environment.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Habitats and biodiversity are destroyed [k], as clearing 640 hectares of native forest in the last 4 years removes homes for wildlife and reduces species diversity [app]. Reason 2: Forests store carbon, so their removal worsens climate change [k], and clearing on this scale across the 2,600-hectare plantation adds to greenhouse gas emissions [app].

knowledge_max_2: Releases stored carbon, worsening climate change
application_max_2: 640 hectares of native forest cleared in the last 4 years

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Kongwe of gaining sustainable palm oil certification.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Continued access to export markets [k], because buyers in Country Y now demand certified sustainable palm oil, and certification protects two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year [app], safeguarding the export revenue stream the business depends on [an]. Benefit 2: A stronger public image [k], as certification shows Kongwe takes environmental responsibility seriously after the Earthwatch Alliance report [app], attracting buyers who value sustainability and reducing the risk of consumer boycotts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Certification keeps export market access open
Certification improves public image and reputation
application_max_2: Country Y buyers now demand certified sustainable palm oil
Two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year at risk
analysis_max_2: Lower risk of boycotts from sustainability-minded buyers

questions.question_text: Do you think Kongwe should pay for sustainable palm oil certification? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for certification is that it secures the company's markets [k], protecting two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year by meeting Country Y buyers' demands, at a cost of $85,000 a year plus a $140,000 one-off mill upgrade [app], so annual certification fees absorb only about 4.5% of the protected revenue [an]. However, one argument against is the ongoing cost [k], since certification costs $85,000 a year indefinitely and $140,000 for traceable mills, reducing profit for a business earning $4.6 million in exports [app], and Kongwe could instead plant only on degraded land to rebuild trust without the audit burden [an]. Overall, Kongwe should pay for the certification [eval], because preserving $1.9 million of export contracts far outweighs $225,000 of first-year costs and protects its position in the 3,000 supermarket products that rely on its palm oil [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Certification carries ongoing costs and audits
application_max_2: $85,000 a year plus $140,000 one-off mill upgrade; first year $225,000
Two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year at stake
analysis_max_2: Annual fees are only about 4.5% of protected revenue
Degraded-land replanting rebuilds trust without audit costs
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both certifying and avoiding certification costs
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Sterling National Airways (SNA) is a public corporation owned by the State, operating 28 aircraft on 45 routes with 3,600 staff and carrying 4.8 million passengers. Its fleet averages 19 years, and renewal costs $650 million.

The government proposes selling SNA for $900 million to fund renewal and cut the $1.1 billion transport debt. The union warns of 500 redundancies, and island campaigners fear 3 remote island routes serving 40,000 residents will go; rivals hold 40% of the domestic market.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'nationalisation'.
questions.model_answer: The transfer of a business or industry from private ownership to state (public) ownership, usually by the government buying shares or taking over assets. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Transfer from private to public ownership
The state buys the business or its assets

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government wants to sell Sterling National Airways.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To fund the fleet renewal [k], the $900 million sale would pay for the $650 million cost of replacing the 19-year-old aircraft [app]. Reason 2: To reduce public debt [k], the proceeds would help clear part of the $1.1 billion transport debt while rivals already hold 40% of the domestic market [app].

knowledge_max_2: Sale raises funds for major investment
application_max_2: $900 million sale price vs $650 million fleet cost
$1.1 billion transport debt; rivals hold 40% of the market

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the sale of SNA could cause for island communities and employees.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Island residents may lose their air links [k], since a private owner seeking profit would likely cut the 3 remote island routes serving 40,000 residents [app], isolating communities and making it harder to reach mainland hospitals and jobs [an]. Problem 2: Employees may lose their jobs [k], as the union warns of 500 redundancies among catering and ground services to cut costs [app], lowering household incomes and weakening service standards on remaining routes [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cost cutting may lead to redundancies
application_max_2: 3 remote island routes serving 40,000 residents at risk
500 redundancies warned of by the union
analysis_max_2: Isolation makes access to hospitals and jobs harder
Job losses cut incomes and weaken remaining services

questions.question_text: Do you think the government should privatise Sterling National Airways? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for privatising SNA is that the $900 million sale [k] would fund the $650 million fleet renewal and reduce the $1.1 billion transport debt [app], giving SNA modern aircraft to compete with low-cost rivals who already hold 40% of the domestic market [an]. However, one argument against is that a private investor group [k] would likely cut the 3 remote island routes serving 40,000 residents and make 500 of SNA's 3,600 staff redundant [app], damaging the public service role SNA was nationalised to provide [an]. Overall, the government should keep SNA in public ownership [eval], because connectivity for 40,000 islanders and 3,600 jobs outweigh the $900 million price, and efficiency savings plus a smaller state equity injection could part-fund the 28 aircraft [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Privatisation raises funds for fleet investment
Public ownership protects remote routes and jobs
application_max_2: $900 million sale funding $650 million fleet renewal against $1.1 billion debt; rivals hold 40% of the market
3 remote island routes serving 40,000 residents; 500 of 3,600 staff facing redundancy
analysis_max_2: Modern fleet restores competitiveness and capacity
Route cuts and redundancies undermine the public service role
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the case for sale and the case against
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Northlight Software Ltd is a private limited company in Country X with 43 staff; 19 work from home in 5 different countries. It builds software for 11 hospitals, so 14 deadlines slipped last quarter and complaints reached 31, blamed on email chains.

Teams use email, a weekly video meeting and a shared chat channel, with builds on a spreadsheet. The director proposes a project management platform at $1,150 per month; the technical lead warns of message overload and wants video contact kept.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'electronic communication'.
questions.model_answer: Electronic communication is the passing of information using electronic devices and digital technology, such as email, video conferencing, messaging apps, intranets and websites. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication using electronic devices and digital technology
Examples include email, video calls, chat apps and intranets

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of electronic communication for Northlight Software.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: It allows instant communication across long distances [k], so the 19 staff working from home in 5 different countries can message colleagues in seconds [app]. Advantage 2: It creates shareable written records [k], so task boards and shared files would replace the single spreadsheet now updated by one senior developer [app].

knowledge_max_2: Instant, low-cost communication across long distances
Creates permanent, shareable records of messages and files
application_max_2: 19 staff work from home in 5 different countries
Shared task boards would replace the spreadsheet updated by one senior developer

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with relying on email chains for coordination.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Email threads become long and unclear, creating a barrier to understanding [k], which is why client complaints reached 31 last quarter while 14 project deadlines slipped [app], so work is delayed and errors go unnoticed until hospital clients complain [an]. Problem 2: Email is slow for urgent decisions [k], so the 19 staff working from home across 5 different countries must wait hours for replies instead of seeing tasks and deadlines on a shared board [app], reducing productivity and morale [an].

knowledge_max_2: Long email chains are unclear and create barriers to understanding
Email is slow for urgent decisions compared with live tools
application_max_2: 14 project deadlines slipped and client complaints reached 31 last quarter
19 remote staff across 5 different countries wait on email replies rather than a shared board
analysis_max_2: Delayed, unclear work hurts the 11 hospitals waiting on the software
Slow replies and poor visibility reduce productivity and morale

questions.question_text: Do you think the operations director should adopt the project management platform? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the platform is that it costs $1,150 per month [k] but gives every team member the same live task boards, deadlines and shared files, replacing slow unclear email chains blamed for 14 slipped deadlines and 31 client complaints [app], so coordination would become faster and more transparent [an]. However, one argument against is that staff already suffer 'message overload' [k], and the platform would add another channel on top of the shared chat and email rather than removing them [app], which could reduce attention and cut the personal contact of the weekly video meeting [an]. Overall, Northlight should adopt the platform but make it the single source of task truth and keep the weekly video meeting [eval], because the platform's transparency outweighs its $1,150 monthly cost if it replaces rather than adds to email [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Centralised task boards improve clarity and accountability
Too many communication channels create overload
application_max_2: $1,150 per month platform versus slow unclear email chains
14 deadlines slipped and 31 complaints blamed on email last quarter
analysis_max_2: Live shared task visibility makes coordination faster and clearer
Adding a channel without removing email worsens message overload
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the platform's clarity and the risk of overload
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Torncliffe Kayak Co is a private limited company making touring kayaks. Founded 11 years ago, it employs 28 staff and builds 850 kayaks yearly at $1,150; revenue was $977,500, with 80% through 22 independent watersports retailers, the rest at the factory showroom.

Each kayak takes 3 weeks with a 5-year guarantee. An online marketplace charges 15% commission with 2 million visits; a $30,000 own website plus $90 per kayak delivery keeps the full price but must attract customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct to consumer'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods or services straight to the final customer without intermediaries such as wholesalers or retailers, for example through a factory shop or website [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling straight to the final consumer
no intermediaries such as wholesalers or retailers involved

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Torncliffe Kayak Co could gain from selling kayaks directly to consumers online.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Selling direct removes the retail margin built into the 80% of sales currently made through 22 independent watersports retailers [k], so Torncliffe keeps the full $1,150 average price per kayak rather than the lower trade price [app]. Benefit 2: A direct online channel reaches paddlers nationwide who never visit a watersports shop [k], expanding the market beyond the 850 kayaks a year currently built [app].

knowledge_max_2: selling direct avoids paying intermediary margins
a direct online channel widens geographic market reach
application_max_2: full $1,150 kept instead of the trade price after retailer margins
expanding beyond 850 kayaks a year and the current 80% retailer share

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Torncliffe Kayak Co might face selling through an online marketplace.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The marketplace charges 15% commission on each sale [k], so on a $1,150 kayak each sale would cost Torncliffe about $172.50, far more than the $90 delivery and packaging for its own website [app], leaving a lower margin per boat and less profit to reinvest [an]. Problem 2: Marketplace listings appear side by side with rival brands, encouraging price comparison [k], so Torncliffe may have to discount its touring kayaks to win sales [app], eroding the premium brand image built over 11 years [an].

knowledge_max_2: marketplaces charge commission on every sale, reducing margin
marketplace listings expose products to direct price comparison with rivals
application_max_2: 15% of $1,150 is about $172.50 per kayak, versus $90 delivery on its own website
pressure to discount touring kayaks on the same screen as rival brands
analysis_max_2: commission directly reduces margin and funds available for reinvestment
price-comparison pressure can erode premium positioning built over 11 years

questions.question_text: Do you think Torncliffe Kayak Co should sell through the national online marketplace rather than its own website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The marketplace already receives 2 million visits a month [k], giving Torncliffe instant access to a huge paddling audience without first spending $30,000 on its own website [app]. For a firm building about 850 kayaks a year, even a modest conversion rate could lift online volume while Torncliffe learns which models sell best without upfront promotion spend [an]. However, the 15% commission costs about $172.50 per $1,150 kayak, almost double the $90 delivery for own-site orders, and the marketplace owns the customer data and shopping experience [k]. A Torncliffe website would keep the full margin, let it retarget accessory sales and control its branding, but it would take time and ongoing promotion to attract visitors [app]; over hundreds of sales the commission bill would quickly dwarf the $30,000 build cost [an]. Overall, Torncliffe should start with the marketplace only as a 12-month trial to build awareness [eval], then shift sales to its own website once enough online orders cover the $30,000 build cost, which at about $172.50 saved per kayak needs only around 174 online sales [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a marketplace provides instant access to a large existing audience
however, its commission exceeds the per-order cost of own-site delivery and it owns customer data
application_max_2: 2 million visits a month versus an $30,000 own-website build cost
15% commission on $1,150 is about $172.50 per kayak versus $90 delivery on own website
analysis_max_2: marketplace gives fast exposure with low upfront cost and risk
commission accumulates quickly; own website keeps margin, data and brand control over time
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation: trial the marketplace for 12 months, then migrate to own website
clear judgement based on roughly 174 sales to cover the $30,000 build cost

scenario_stem:
Ironbark Furniture Co is a private limited company making flat-pack and solid-oak wardrobes at its Kilndown workshop. It made 6,500 wardrobes (revenue $2.6 million, profit $325,000, fixed costs $455,000, variable cost $280).

A national retail chain offers 2,500 wardrobes a year at $380 each. Hiring a specialist operations director for $85,000 a year would raise output to 9,000 wardrobes, or Ray stays owner-managed.

questions.question_text: Define 'total cost'.
questions.model_answer: Total cost is the complete cost of producing a given level of output, equal to fixed costs plus variable costs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Total cost = fixed costs + variable costs
It rises as more units are produced because variable costs increase

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of hiring a specialist operations director.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It creates a managerial economy of scale [k]. A dedicated operations director can plan 9,000 wardrobes a year and negotiate better buying deals for the retail chain order, relieving Ray Castellane of production decisions [app]. Reason 2: The fixed salary cost is spread over a larger output [k]. At $85,000 a year, the director costs only about $9.44 per wardrobe across 9,000 units [app].

knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale: specialist managers improve efficiency and decision-making
Fixed salary costs can be spread over greater output
application_max_2: Director manages the 2,500-wardrobe retail chain order plus current production, lifting output to 9,000
$85,000 salary spread over 9,000 wardrobes = about $9.44 per wardrobe

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of accepting the retail chain contract.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The contract price is below the current selling price [k]. At $380 per wardrobe versus the $400 Ironbark earns now, it gives up $20 on each of the 2,500 contract wardrobes [app], so profit depends on tight cost control and high volume [an]. Disadvantage 2: A national chain demands reliability [k]. Supplying 2,500 wardrobes a year means late or faulty deliveries risk penalties and contract loss [app], which could add rework costs and damage Ironbark's reputation with other buyers [an].

knowledge_max_2: A lower contract price reduces the margin earned per unit
Large customers impose strict quality and delivery requirements, with penalties for failure
application_max_2: $380 contract price versus $400 current average selling price on 2,500 wardrobes
2,500 wardrobes a year required under the retail chain contract
analysis_max_2: $20 lower price per unit means volume and efficiency must compensate to keep profit growing
Penalties or lost orders from missed deadlines could erase the extra profit entirely

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironbark Furniture Co should hire the operations director and take the contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring the director unlocks a managerial economy of scale [k]: fixed costs rise only to $540,000 while output reaches 9,000 wardrobes, so average cost falls from $350 to $340 [app] and profit rises from $325,000 to about $490,000, an extra $165,000 a year [an]. However, the chain pays just $380 per wardrobe — below the $400 Ironbark gets now [k] — and the $85,000 salary is payable even if the 2,500-unit order shrinks [app], so any cancellation or quality failure could quickly wipe out the gain and leave Ironbark with unwanted fixed costs [an]. Overall [eval], signing is justified because the $40 contract margin still beats the $340 average cost and the extra $165,000 outweighs the $85,000 salary risk, provided quality at the enlarged factory stays high enough to avoid penalties [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale improve decisions and lower average cost
Fixed commitments (salaries) and lower prices increase financial risk
application_max_2: Fixed costs rise to $540,000, average cost falls $350 to $340, profit rises $325,000 to $490,000
$380 contract price versus $400 current price; $85,000 salary; 2,500-unit order
analysis_max_2: $10 lower average cost across 9,000 units plus the extra volume lifts profit by about $165,000
Shrinkage or cancellation of the order leaves fixed costs underused, eroding profit
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified position
Clear overall judgement with an explicit condition (quality maintained)

scenario_stem:
Harvest Moon Pumpkin Farm is a partnership growing pumpkins and winter squash. Annual revenue is $230,000, with 80% earned in October and November. It hires 8 seasonal workers each October and faces $6,200 monthly fixed costs plus a $34,000 March seed bill.

From an $11,500 opening balance on 1 February, inflows of $2,000, $1,500, $4,500 and $7,000 to May face $6,200 monthly outflows. By 15 February the family must choose a $35,000 overdraft or selling an older tractor for $18,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is how easily a business can turn its assets into cash in order to pay short-term debts as they fall due [2].

knowledge_max_2: liquidity measures ease of converting assets into cash
liquidity relates to paying short-term debts as they fall due

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Harvest Moon could be profitable overall yet very short of cash in spring.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: 80% of the $230,000 annual revenue arrives in October and November [k], so cash saved then must stretch across months like March when inflows are only $1,500 [app]. Reason 2: The $34,000 seed bill falls due in March before any pumpkins are sold [k], while fixed costs of $6,200 continue every month [app].

knowledge_max_2: profit and cash differ because of seasonal timing of inflows
large outflows may fall due before any sales revenue arrives
application_max_2: 80% of $230,000 arrives in October and November
March inflows of $1,500 against a $34,000 seed bill and $6,200 monthly costs

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of arranging the overdraft instead of selling the tractor.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Keeping both tractors protects the October harvest [k], so the 8 seasonal workers can still plant, cultivate and haul pumpkins at full speed [app], avoiding crop losses that would cost more than the overdraft interest [an]. Advantage 2: An overdraft is flexible [k], because the family draws only what it needs from February to April and repays it from the 80% of revenue earned in October and November [app], whereas a tractor sale is permanent and cannot be reversed [an].

knowledge_max_2: keeping productive assets protects output and revenue
overdrafts are flexible - draw only what is needed and repay from later inflows
application_max_2: both tractors needed for the October harvest with 8 seasonal workers
repayable from the 80% of revenue earned in October and November
analysis_max_2: avoids crop losses costing more than overdraft interest

questions.question_text: Do you think the Okoro family should arrange the overdraft rather than sell the tractor? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arranging the overdraft keeps both tractors available for the October harvest [k], and the family can repay it from October and November sales worth 80% of $230,000 [app], so the seasonal cycle is funded and cleared within the year [an]. selling assets raises one-off cash but permanently reduces capacity
application_max_2: 80% of $230,000 arrives in October and November to repay an overdraft
forecast balance falls to about -$33,100 by end of April vs $18,000 tractor sale
analysis_max_2: the seasonal cycle is funded then cleared within one year
tractor proceeds only partly close the forecast gap
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the $35,000 overdraft vs a -$33,100 April trough

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Stonemill Precision Ltd is a private limited company making wind-turbine gearboxes. It plans a $6.5 million factory in Ravenfield, a mining town whose last mine closed in 2019, employing 240 workers at $34,000 and creating 110 jobs locally.

Ravenfield has 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops, so the government offers a $900,000 training grant and 5 years without business rates. Residents fear 600 lorry movements weekly near the Ravenfield Levels wetland; the board prefers its existing site 120 kilometres away.

questions.question_text: Define 'external benefits'.
questions.model_answer: External benefits are the positive effects of a business activity that accrue to third parties not involved in the transaction, such as job creation, training opportunities and the regeneration of local areas. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Positive effects on third parties not involved in the activity
Examples include jobs, training and local regeneration

questions.question_text: Explain two external benefits the Stonemill factory would bring to Ravenfield.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: New jobs would cut unemployment [k], as 240 jobs at average wages of $34,000 plus 110 supplier jobs would lift a town with a 13% unemployment rate [app]. Reason 2: Skills and regeneration would improve [k], since the government's $900,000 training grant would raise local skills and spending would help revive 27 empty shops [app].

knowledge_max_2: Training and regeneration raise local skills and spending
application_max_2: 240 jobs at average wages of $34,000 plus 110 supplier jobs
$900,000 training grant and 27 empty shops on the high street

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government offers Stonemill a $900,000 training grant and 5 years without business rates.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To regenerate a deprived area [k], because Ravenfield's 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops show the town needs private investment after the coal mine closed in 2019 [app], so public money leverages far more private spending than it costs [an]. Reason 2: To build a skilled industrial workforce [k], as training 240 workers with a $900,000 grant creates transferable manufacturing skills [app], raising local productivity and helping attract further employers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Public money levers private investment and regeneration
Grants create transferable skills in the local workforce
application_max_2: Ravenfield has 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops after the 2019 mine closure

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Define 'current assets'.

scenario_stem:
Brackenfeld Salmon Farm Ltd is a private limited company raising salmon in sea cages off Dunara Bay. It produces 1,700 tonnes yearly, earns $5.2 million in exports, and shares the bay with 60 local fishing boats and holiday cottages.

scenario_stem:

questions.model_answer: Borrowing to expand brings financial economies of scale [k]: at 7.5%, interest is $37,500 a year — far cheaper than the 11% a start-up rival would pay — and doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons cuts average cost from $0.90 to $0.81 [app], lifting profit before interest from $700,000 to about $1.58 million [an]. Overall [eval], Amberfield should proceed, because even after $37,500 interest, profit after interest of about $1.54 million comfortably exceeds $700,000 today — but it should secure the chain's order in writing before drawing the loan and phase the second plant's ramp-up to protect quality [eval].

scenario_stem:
Solace Fitness Studio is a private limited company offering personal training, group classes and a small gym. It has 320 members paying $45 a month by direct debit and monthly fixed costs of $19,800.

From a $9,300 opening balance on 1 January, January inflows are $24,500 against $21,000 outflows, February $22,000 against $20,400, and March $18,500 against $19,600. Hannah must decide whether to buy $16,000 of equipment in January or spread the cost over 12 monthly payments of $1,450.

questions.question_text: Define 'creditors'.
questions.model_answer: Creditors are suppliers or other organisations a business owes money to for goods or services received but not yet paid for [2].

knowledge_max_2: creditors are owed money by the business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hannah should still prepare a monthly cash-flow forecast even though direct debits make inflows regular.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Regular inflows can still fall below outflows [k], as March shows inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $19,600 [app]. Reason 2: One-off costs such as equipment purchases do not follow the monthly pattern [k], so a forecast tells Hannah whether $16,000 of equipment can be afforded in January [app].

knowledge_max_2: regular inflows do not guarantee every month stays positive
a forecast shows whether one-off items fit the budget
application_max_2: March inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $19,600
whether $16,000 of equipment can be afforded in January

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Solace Fitness Studio of spreading the equipment cost over 12 monthly payments instead of paying $16,000 up front.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Spreading the cost keeps the balance positive [k], since 12 payments of $1,450 avoid a one-off $16,000 hit in January [app], leaving the studio able to cover its $19,800 monthly fixed costs without borrowing [an]. Benefit 2: Spreading payments smooths cash through the quieter spring months [k], when March inflows of $18,500 already sit below outflows of $19,600 [app], so the studio is less likely to need an overdraft [an].

knowledge_max_2: spreading payments avoids a large one-off outflow
regular small payments are easier to budget around fixed costs
application_max_2: 12 payments of $1,450 instead of one $16,000 outflow
March inflows of $18,500 below outflows of $19,600
analysis_max_2: fixed costs of $19,800 a month remain covered without borrowing
less reliance on an overdraft in the quiet spring

questions.question_text: Do you think Hannah should buy the equipment in January by spreading the cost rather than paying $16,000 up front? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Spreading the cost keeps cash positive all through the first quarter [k], with the studio retaining its $9,300 opening balance and roughly $11,350 after January's payment [app], so $19,800 of fixed costs stay covered without an overdraft [an]. Overall, Hannah should spread the cost [eval], because the extra $1,400 is cheaper than overdraft interest and protects cash through the quiet March [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Amberfield Brewery Ltd is a private limited company brewing 26,000 hectolitres of ale yearly with 58 staff and $7.1 million sales. Brewing creates 340 tonnes of spent grain and 9,000 cubic metres of wastewater.

Grain goes to landfill at $31,000 a year and wastewater to the sewer for $46,000. A contractor will collect grain free as feed; a digester cuts charges 60% and yields $38,000 biogas. It needs $240,000 within 12 months as landfill tax rises 12%.

questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into new products, reducing the need for raw materials, landfill space and pollution. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Converting waste materials into new products
Reduces use of raw materials, landfill and pollution

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the digester project would benefit Amberfield Brewery.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lower sewerage charges [k], as the anaerobic digester would cut the $46,000 a year wastewater charge by 60% [app]. Reason 2: A new income stream from biogas [k], as the digester would produce gas worth $38,000 a year while landfill tax rises by 12% annually [app].

application_max_2: 60% cut in the $46,000 a year wastewater charge
Biogas worth $38,000 a year; landfill tax rising 12% each year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why reducing brewery waste matters for the environment.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Less waste goes to landfill [k], as the 340 tonnes of spent grain the brewery sends to landfill each year take valuable space and produce methane, a powerful greenhouse gas [app], so diverting it to animal feed lowers the brewery's contribution to climate change [an]. Reason 2: Cleaner local rivers [k], because 9,000 cubic metres of wastewater a year can pollute waterways if it is released untreated [app], protecting fish and river life downstream of the brewery [an].

knowledge_max_2: Landfill releases methane, a greenhouse gas
application_max_2: 340 tonnes of spent grain sent to landfill each year
9,000 cubic metres of wastewater produced annually
analysis_max_2: Diverting grain to feed lowers climate change contribution
Protecting fish and river life downstream

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfield Brewery should invest $240,000 in the digester project? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the investment is the steady annual benefit [k], as the digester cuts the $46,000 sewerage charge by 60%, about $27,600 a year, and produces biogas worth $38,000 a year, together roughly $65,600 a year [app], while free collection of spent grain separately removes the $31,000 landfill cost [an]. However, one argument against is the upfront cost and complexity [k], as $240,000 is a major outlay for a business with $7.1 million revenue and 58 staff [app], and the tanks must be maintained and the 60% saving depends on the digester running reliably [an]. Overall, Amberfield Brewery should invest in the digester [eval], because roughly $65,600 a year of savings plus income recovers the $240,000 in under 4 years, ahead of landfill tax rising by 12% each year, while cutting pollution from 9,000 cubic metres of wastewater [eval].

Upfront cost and maintenance burden for the business
application_max_2: 60% of $46,000 is $27,600; plus $38,000 biogas, together roughly $65,600 a year
$240,000 outlay versus $7.1 million revenue and 58 staff
analysis_max_2: Free grain collection separately removes the $31,000 landfill cost
Savings depend on reliable digester operation
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both investing in the digester and its costs or risks
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:

Private couriers SwiftParcel and VoltX charge 30% less and carry 45% of parcels. CXPost proposes closing 150 loss-making rural offices to save $18 million, but rural communities fear losing banking access, while SwiftParcel claims it could cover 80% of routes within 3 days.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'competition'.
questions.model_answer: Rivalry between businesses that sell similar products or services and try to win customers and market share from each other. [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why CXPost might close the 150 rural post offices.

Falling demand means fewer outlets are needed

Reason 2: To keep services affordable and accessible [k], the government grants CXPost $60 million a year so branches can offer banking and bill-paying even where losses run at $22 million [app], protecting elderly and offline households from exclusion [an].

Public funding keeps essential services affordable

analysis_max_2: Rural communities stay connected to services

However, one argument against is that rural communities would lose vital services [k], because closing half of the 300 rural branches removes last local access to banking and bill-paying, and SwiftParcel can cover only 80% of the affected routes within 3 days [app], leaving isolated households without essential support [an]. Overall, CXPost should not close all 150 branches outright [eval], because the $60 million grant exists to keep them open and the wider social cost outweighs the $18 million saving [eval].

Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Castlereagh Solicitors is a partnership law firm in Country X with 52 staff in 3 offices. It plans to merge with Trelawney & Grant, moving 30 staff 12 miles away and creating 12 new roles in a $2.4 million deal. Rumours spread via the grapevine and 7 staff resigned in 2 months.

The partner must choose an all-staff meeting plus written letters, or a press release this week that tells staff through the media. Which best steadies the firm?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'formal communication'.
questions.model_answer: Formal communication is communication sent through the official, authorised channels and methods of an organisation, such as official letters, memos, meetings and press releases issued by managers. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication via the official, authorised channels of the organisation
Examples include official letters, meetings, memos and press releases

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of formal communication for Castlereagh Solicitors.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Formal channels carry authority and accuracy [k], so an all-staff meeting followed by letters would tell all 52 staff the official merger details rather than grapevine rumours [app]. Advantage 2: Formal written records can be referred back to [k], so the 30 staff moving to premises 12 miles away would have clear written terms about their relocation and the 12 new roles [app].

knowledge_max_2: Official channels are accurate and carry authority
Written formal records can be referred back to
application_max_2: All 52 staff would hear official details instead of rumours
30 staff moving 12 miles away would have written terms on the 12 new roles

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by rumours and informal communication about the merger.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Rumours are inaccurate and uncontrolled [k], so staff imagine job losses across the 3 offices even though the plan creates 12 new roles and relocates 30 staff rather than cutting jobs [app], fuelling anxiety and resignations [an]. Problem 2: Informal communication undermines trust in management [k], which is why 7 staff resigned in 2 months without any official announcement being made [app], risking client service and jeopardising the $2.4 million deal [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rumours are inaccurate and cannot be controlled by the business
Silence from management damages trust and morale

questions.question_text: Do you think Castlereagh should tell staff first through an all-staff meeting and letters rather than issuing a press release this week? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for telling staff first is that it is honest and builds trust [k], so the 52 staff would hear directly from the managing partner before a press release, preventing more resignations like the 7 staff who left in 2 months [app], protecting morale and client service during the $2.4 million merger [an]. However, one argument against is that a press release this week would reassure clients and protect the firm's reputation sooner [k], because rival firms may already know about the merger talks [app], yet staff hearing first from the media would feel betrayed and may leave before the 12 new roles are filled [an]. Overall, the firm should hold the all-staff meeting and written letters first, then issue the press release [eval], because committed staff are essential during a merger and a one-week delay for clients is a small price compared with losing key lawyers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Telling staff first builds trust and commitment
Early public announcement reassures clients and protects reputation
application_max_2: 52 staff would hear directly, stopping the 7 resignations seen in 2 months
Press release first would reach clients sooner but staff would feel betrayed
analysis_max_2: Honesty protects morale, client service and the $2.4 million deal

evaluation_max_2: Weighs both announcing to staff first and issuing a press release first
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Saltpan Lobster Co is a family partnership landing 30 tonnes of live lobsters on 2 boats with 8 fishermen. Around 80% are sold to a wholesale fish market at $14 per kg and 20% directly to 12 local restaurants at $22 per kg.

The owners could spend $25,000 on a refrigerated van for 20 more restaurants, but landings peak in July and August. Wholesale sales need no marketing, bring reliable payment and the market buys all.

questions.question_text: Define 'intermediary'.
questions.model_answer: An independent business that helps move goods from producer to consumer, for example wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission for its role [2].

knowledge_max_2: an independent business between producer and consumer
includes wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why selling lobsters directly to restaurants suits a perishable product such as live lobsters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Live lobsters are perishable, so every hour of transit matters [k], meaning short direct trips to the 12 local restaurants keep them fresher than a longer journey through the wholesale fish market [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct removes intermediary handling and margins [k], so Saltpan can charge $22 per kg instead of $14 per kg, keeping an extra $8 per kg on every lobster sold direct [app].

knowledge_max_2: perishable goods need the shortest possible channel to stay fresh
selling direct avoids the intermediary's margin or mark-up
application_max_2: short direct trips to 12 local restaurants keep lobsters fresher than the wholesale route
$22 per kg direct versus $14 per kg wholesale, an extra $8 per kg

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why wholesale markets remain important to fishing businesses such as Saltpan Lobster Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The wholesale fish market takes the full catch whatever the volume [k], giving Saltpan a guaranteed outlet for the 24 tonnes a year that currently go through it [app], securing reliable weekly cash flow without finding 32 individual direct buyers [an]. Reason 2: Selling wholesale needs no van, extra staff or marketing [k], avoiding the $25,000 refrigerated van and the daily effort of chasing $22-per-kg restaurant orders [app], keeping overheads low and letting the 8 fishermen focus on fishing [an].

knowledge_max_2: a wholesale market guarantees an outlet for the entire catch
wholesale sales require no extra vehicle, staff or marketing spend
application_max_2: 24 tonnes a year (80% of 30 tonnes) currently go through the wholesale market
avoids the $25,000 refrigerated van and daily management of restaurant orders
analysis_max_2: guaranteed outlet secures consistent revenue and working capital
lower overheads let the business concentrate on fishing rather than distribution

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltpan Lobster Co should buy the refrigerated van and sell more lobsters directly to restaurants? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the van would let Saltpan supply 20 more restaurants directly at $22 per kg [k]; shifting 6 tonnes a year from the wholesale rate to the direct rate would add about $48,000 of revenue (6,000 kg x $8 extra per kg) without catching more lobster [app]. Fresher deliveries would also build restaurant loyalty and justify premium menu pricing [an]. However, the van costs $25,000 and brings fuel, insurance and maintenance costs, and the direct channel only works if 20 restaurants order reliably every week [k]; dropped or forgotten orders would leave perishable stock worthless [app], and the wholesale market still guarantees an outlet for any unsold catch and pays reliably [an]. Overall, Saltpan should buy the van, because moving more volume to the $22-per-kg direct channel clearly beats $14 per kg for a freshness-critical product [eval], but only after the 20 restaurants commit to standing weekly orders, with the wholesale market kept as a fallback for unsold stock [eval].

knowledge_max_2: direct supply to restaurants commands a higher price for perishable seafood
however, it requires vehicle investment and reliable weekly ordering by buyers
application_max_2: shifting 6 tonnes from $14 to $22 per kg adds about $48,000 a year (6,000 kg x $8)
the van costs $25,000 and must serve 20 more restaurants reliably each week
analysis_max_2: higher margin and fresher delivery strengthen restaurant relationships and revenue per kg
if restaurants cancel or volumes vary, perishable stock is lost and the van becomes a fixed burden
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to buy the van only with confirmed standing weekly orders
balanced judgement retaining the wholesale market as an outlet for unsold stock

scenario_stem:
Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd is a private limited company brewing elderflower and ginger cordials. It sells 750,000 bottles through 400 regional shops for $1.5 million revenue; marketing costs $90,000 a year, reaching about 120,000 households; fixed costs $420,000 and variable cost $0.80 per bottle.

A media agency proposes a national TV campaign costing $400,000 over 2 years, reaching 3 million households and possibly lifting sales 20%. Alternatively, five regional TV slots cost $120,000 each, or it could keep local promotions.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Marketing economies of scale are the cost advantages gained when advertising and promotion costs are spread over a larger output, lowering the marketing cost per unit sold. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Cost of advertising/promotion spread over more units lowers marketing cost per unit
Example: one national campaign cheaper per customer than many regional campaigns

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the national television campaign.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A wider reach at lower cost per household [k]. The $400,000 campaign reaches an estimated 3 million households for about $0.13 each, versus $0.75 per household on the current local campaign [app]. Reason 2: Sales could rise nationally [k]. If sales grow by 20% to 900,000 bottles, revenue rises from $1.5 million to $1.8 million and the fixed campaign cost is spread over more bottles [app].

knowledge_max_2: One national campaign reaches more customers at lower marketing cost per customer
Higher sales volume spreads fixed marketing costs, lowering cost per unit
application_max_2: $0.13 per household ($400,000/3 million) versus $0.75 per household local spending
20% sales rise = 900,000 bottles; revenue $1.5 million to $1.8 million

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons Larkhill might keep its local promotions instead.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The campaign may not pay back [k]. At an extra $110,000 a year above current spending, Larkhill needs roughly 92,000 extra bottles a year just to break even [app] — about 12% growth — and if the forecast 20% fails, profit falls below today's $480,000 [an]. Reason 2: National reach may be wasted without distribution [k]. Advertising to 3 million households means little while bottles sell in only 400 regional shops [app], because unavailable stock turns awareness into lost sales rather than revenue [an].

Advertising is ineffective without distribution to meet demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd should spend $400,000 on the national campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The national campaign offers marketing economies of scale [k]: it reaches 3 million households at about $0.13 each — far cheaper than $0.75 per household locally — and saves $200,000 against five separate regional slots at $120,000 each [app], so if sales rise by 20% as forecast, the extra $1.20 contribution per bottle covers the extra spend within two years [an]. However, the risk of weak returns is real [k]: at only 10% sales growth, Larkhill gains just 75,000 bottles of contribution, about $90,000 a year, which fails to cover the extra $110,000 a year above current local spending [app], leaving Larkhill worse off than continuing its $90,000 local promotions [an]. Overall [eval], Larkhill should proceed only if national retailers sign listings and the agency stages payments — the reach and $200,000 saving versus regional slots justify the spend once distribution is secured; without it, local promotion remains safer [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Marketing economies of scale: wider reach at lower cost per customer
Marketing is a fixed cost; returns depend on distribution and sales growth
application_max_2: $0.13 per household nationally versus $0.75 locally; $200,000 cheaper than five regional slots at $120,000 each

analysis_max_2: At 20% growth the extra contribution repays the additional spend within two years
Slow sales or poor distribution leaves the fixed campaign cost unrecovered
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to securing national distribution first

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fairhaven Textiles Ltd is a private limited company weaving cotton fabrics for export. It employs 210 workers across two mills, produces 3.4 million metres of cloth yearly and spends $480,000 on energy, one fifth of operating costs.

The board considers rooftop solar panels and a biomass boiler costing $720,000: they would cut energy purchases 55%, saving $264,000 a year, but take almost 3 years to recover. Two German buyers offer longer contracts for a 40% carbon cut, and the 14-year-old boilers need replacing.

questions.question_text: Define 'renewable energy'.

Examples include solar, wind, hydroelectric and biomass power

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the solar and biomass investment would benefit Fairhaven Textiles.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lower energy bills [k], as cutting purchases by 55% saves $264,000 a year against current energy costs of $480,000 [app]. Reason 2: Access to longer export contracts [k], as two German buyers have offered longer contracts if Fairhaven shows a 40% cut in carbon emissions [app].

knowledge_max_2: Solar and biomass cut energy bills

application_max_2: 55% cut saves $264,000 a year against $480,000 energy costs

Reason 2: Compliance with export market expectations [k], since two German buyers have already offered longer contracts to suppliers proving lower carbon emissions [app], making Fairhaven more competitive against suppliers who cannot demonstrate sustainability [an].

knowledge_max_2: Buyers manage reputational risk in their supply chains
Export markets increasingly require proven low emissions
application_max_2: Two German buyers offering longer contracts for proven cuts
analysis_max_2: Negative publicity risk for buyers is reduced

questions.question_text: Do you think Fairhaven Textiles should install the solar panels and biomass boiler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for installing the system is the long-term saving [k], as $264,000 a year off a $480,000 energy bill, together with replacing 14-year-old boilers, means the $720,000 cost recovers in almost 3 years [app], after which savings flow straight to profit while emissions fall 40% [an]. However, one argument against is the heavy upfront cost [k], since $720,000 must be found now, reducing cash available for wages to 210 workers and other investment [app], and the savings depend on sunlight and biomass supply, which vary between the two mills [an]. scenario_stem:
The Country X National Theatre (CXNT) is a public corporation staging drama, opera and dance in the capital, employing 340 staff. It received $38 million in funding, covering 62% of costs, with tickets covering 38%, and 900,000 people attended.

Four of its 9 productions toured, reaching 40,000 schoolchildren. The minister proposes selling CXNT to Aurora Stage Group for $75 million, but the board warns touring, education and cultural shows would end. Ticket prices could rise from $28 to $40, with 90 redundancies.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A payment of money given by the government to a business or organisation to lower its costs or support a specific activity it provides. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Money paid by the government to a business or organisation
Purpose is to lower costs or support the activity provided

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government funds the Country X National Theatre.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To widen public access to the arts [k], subsidised touring took 4 of its 9 productions to regional theatres and reached 40,000 schoolchildren last year [app]. Reason 2: To preserve culture [k], the $38 million grant covering 62% of costs funds work a profit-seeking buyer would not support [app].

knowledge_max_2: Public funding widens access to arts and culture
Public funding preserves culture not viable commercially

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for audiences and schools if CXNT is privatised.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Ticket prices would rise [k], because the buyer would lift average prices from $28 to $40 per seat to maximise profit [app], excluding lower-income audiences from the theatre [an]. Problem 2: The school education programme would end [k], since Aurora Stage Group plans to scrap the scheme reaching 40,000 schoolchildren a year [app], depriving young people of cultural education [an].

Unprofitable education programmes may be cut
application_max_2: Average ticket prices rising from $28 to $40 per seat
Education scheme for 40,000 schoolchildren a year at risk
analysis_max_2: Lower-income audiences are excluded from the theatre
Young people lose access to cultural education

questions.question_text: Do you think the government should privatise the Country X National Theatre? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for privatisation is that the $75 million sale [k] would repay the state's investment and free the $38 million annual funding for other public services [app], reducing the tax burden on citizens who rarely visit the theatre [an]. However, one argument against is that private ownership [k] would end regional touring and the education scheme for 40,000 schoolchildren a year, and raise ticket prices from $28 to $40 [app], depriving lower-income audiences among the 900,000 annual visitors of affordable, high-quality theatre [an]. Overall, the government should keep CXNT in public ownership [eval], because arts and culture are public goods whose social value exceeds the $38 million cost, and CXNT already covers 38% of its costs from ticket sales [eval].

Public ownership protects access, touring and education
