Losing subsidised culture harms low-income audiences and education
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the case for privatisation and the case against
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Wrenhill Toys Ltd is a private limited company selling the 'Sunshine Express' train set through 160 retailers in Country X; about 9,000 sold at $45 each. Loose magnets pose a choking risk and 340 sets were returned.

The marketer wants a press release and social media alert. The MD prefers phoning 160 retailers and writing to 2,100 registered buyers, costing $6,500 over 2 weeks; only retailers and media reach 6,900 unregistered buyers. A public campaign may alarm non-buyers.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'written communication'.
questions.model_answer: Written communication is the passing of information through written words, such as letters, emails, memos, reports, notices or text messages, producing a record that can be read and re-read. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Examples include letters, emails, reports and notices; creates a record

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of written communication for the product recall.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Written messages give a permanent record [k], so the 160 retailers would have the recall instructions in writing to identify and return the unsafe Sunshine Express sets [app]. Advantage 2: Written communication suits messages sent to named individuals [k], so the 2,100 buyers who registered online would receive clear return instructions by letter [app].

knowledge_max_2: Written messages create a permanent, checkable record
Written messages suit sending the same message to named individuals
application_max_2: 160 retailers would have recall instructions in writing for the unsafe sets
2,100 registered online buyers would receive return instructions by letter

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of announcing the recall through a press release and social media.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Mass electronic channels reach far more people far faster [k], alerting the 6,900 unregistered buyers who never registered online [app], so unsafe Sunshine Express sets can be returned before more magnets are swallowed [an]. Advantage 2: Posting online costs almost nothing [k], compared with about $6,500 and 2 weeks for phone calls and letters to retailers and registered buyers [app], protecting public safety and the brand at minimal cost [an].

knowledge_max_2: Mass media and social media reach huge audiences quickly
Electronic public announcements cost very little
application_max_2: 6,900 unregistered buyers would be reached instantly
Compared with about $6,500 and 2 weeks for phone calls and letters
analysis_max_2: Faster alerts return unsafe sets before more injuries occur
Minimal cost protects both public safety and the brand's reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenhill Toys should rely on the press release and social media instead of phoning retailers and writing to registered buyers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the press release and social media is speed and reach [k], which would instantly alert the owners of the remaining 6,900 unregistered units, including the 340 sets already proving defective [app], so children could be protected immediately at almost no cost [an]. However, one argument against is that mass media cannot guarantee every affected buyer acts [k], whereas phoning the 160 retailers and writing to the 2,100 registered buyers uses two-way and written channels with confirmed receipt, costing about $6,500 and 2 weeks [app], giving an auditable recall record for the safety regulator [an]. Overall, Wrenhill should use both: the press release immediately to protect children, followed by calls and letters to retailers and registered buyers to evidence the recall [eval], prioritising safety over the $6,500 cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Mass media is fast and wide-reaching but unverifiable
Two-way and written channels confirm receipt and create records
application_max_2: Press coverage reaches the 6,900 unregistered buyers instantly
Phoning 160 retailers and writing to 2,100 registered buyers costs about $6,500
analysis_max_2: Immediate public alert prevents further injuries from loose magnets
Confirmed calls and letters give an auditable record for the regulator
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the public campaign and direct two-way contact
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Tidemill Electrical is a private limited company running 2 independent electrical shops. Founded 15 years ago, it employs 26 staff and earned $1.8 million, but sales fell 12% as online discounters undercut prices; a rival sells a $700 television for $549.

A click-and-collect website costing $35,000 plus $1,500 a month could help compete. 70% of customers value expert advice and free installation of kitchen appliances, earning $300,000 a year; the directors weigh online investment against remaining specialists.

questions.question_text: Define 'click-and-collect'.
questions.model_answer: A service where a customer orders goods online and collects them in person from a shop or depot at a chosen time [2].

knowledge_max_2: order placed online, typically paid for in advance
goods collected in person from a shop or depot

questions.question_text: Explain two threats e-commerce poses to Tidemill Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Online discounters carry lower store overheads and can undercut high street prices [k], as the rival selling a $700 television for $549 shows, helping drive Tidemill's 12% sales fall over 2 years [app]. Threat 2: Customers who buy online skip the shop entirely [k], so Tidemill loses walk-in trade that supports its $300,000 a year of kitchen appliance installation business [app].

knowledge_max_2: online discounters can undercut physical shops because they have lower overheads
online buying removes the store visit, cutting walk-in trade for physical retailers
application_max_2: a $700 television sold online for $549 undercuts Tidemill's pricing
the 12% sales fall over 2 years and the $300,000 installation income both reflect store traffic

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Tidemill Electrical could gain from a click-and-collect website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Click-and-collect lets Tidemill sell online while still driving customers into its two country-town shops [k], protecting footfall and upselling the kitchen appliance installation that already earns $300,000 a year [app], defending revenue and margins [an]. Benefit 2: Click-and-collect removes home delivery costs and waiting times [k], making online buying attractive for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines at a running cost of only $1,500 a month [app], improving convenience and customer loyalty [an].

knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect combines online ordering with in-store collection
click-and-collect avoids home delivery costs and delays
application_max_2: in-store collection drives upselling of the $300,000 a year installation service
$1,500 a month running cost for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines
analysis_max_2: store visits protect add-on sales and margins that pure delivery would lose
convenience versus home delivery can win back price-checking customers and build loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Tidemill Electrical should invest in a click-and-collect website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in click-and-collect would let Tidemill compete online while keeping its two shops relevant [k]; at $35,000 build cost and $1,500 a month running cost, it is cheaper than losing 12% of a $1.8 million business, about $216,000 of revenue at risk [app], and it converts browsing into store visits where advice and installation can be sold [an]. However, Tidemill cannot match online prices such as $549 for a $700 television, so price-led buyers may still leave [k]; the website only works if stock is visible online and collection is easy, and at $18,000 a year running cost the system must win back meaningful volume [app], otherwise the investment becomes an expensive brochure [an]. Overall, Tidemill should invest, prioritising click-and-collect over price cuts because its differentiator, advice and installation valued by 70% of customers, cannot be copied by online rivals [eval], and it should review sales versus the $216,000 at risk after 12 months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect lets a physical retailer compete online while retaining store visits
however, the firm cannot match online discounters on price alone
application_max_2: $35,000 setup plus $1,500 a month ($18,000 a year) versus about $216,000 revenue at risk from a 12% fall on $1.8 million
the $549 rival television example shows price competition is unwinnable; advice and installation valued by 70% of customers is the firm's edge
analysis_max_2: click-and-collect protects footfall and installation upselling worth $300,000 a year
execution risk: poor stock visibility or collection experience would make it an expensive brochure
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to invest in click-and-collect rather than cut prices
balanced judgement requiring a 12-month review against the $216,000 revenue at risk

scenario_stem:
Kettle & Fern Tea Co is a private limited company grading and packing specialty teas. It blended 480 tonnes: fixed costs $1.44 million, variable cost $5,000 per tonne, average cost $8,000, price $9,000 per tonne.

A purpose-built plant costing $3 million would double capacity to 960 tonnes. Fixed costs rise to $2.4 million, cutting average cost to $7,500 per tonne, but confirmed orders are only 700 tonnes; beyond 1,200 tonnes poor communication and low morale push costs up.

questions.question_text: Define 'average fixed cost'.
questions.model_answer: Average fixed cost is the fixed cost of production divided by the number of units produced; it falls continuously as output rises because the same fixed costs are spread more thinly. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Average fixed cost = fixed costs / output
It falls as output increases because fixed costs are spread over more units

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the new plant would lower Kettle & Fern's average cost.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Fixed costs spread over more tonnes [k]. Average fixed cost falls from $3,000 per tonne at 480 tonnes to $2,500 per tonne at 960 tonnes [app]. Reason 2: Technical economies of scale from purpose-built machinery [k]. Doubling capacity to 960 tonnes cuts average cost from $8,000 to $7,500 per tonne [app].

knowledge_max_2: Spreading fixed costs over larger output lowers average fixed cost
Larger, modern machinery creates technical economies of scale
application_max_2: Average fixed cost falls $3,000 per tonne (480 tonnes) to $2,500 per tonne (960 tonnes)
Capacity doubles to 960 tonnes; average cost falls $8,000 to $7,500

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with building the new plant ahead of demand.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Confirmed demand is too low [k]. Orders total only 700 tonnes against capacity of 960 tonnes [app]; at 700 tonnes, average cost would be about $8,429 — higher than today's $8,000 — so the plant would lose money until sales grow [an]. Problem 2: Diseconomies of scale are threatened [k]. The economist warns that beyond 1,200 tonnes, poor communication and low morale push average cost back up [app], so costs could rise again just as the new plant reaches full capacity [an].

knowledge_max_2: Underused capacity raises average cost and erodes the benefit of expansion
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and low morale raise average cost at large scale
application_max_2: Confirmed orders of only 700 tonnes versus 960 tonnes capacity
Economist warns of diseconomies beyond 1,200 tonnes
analysis_max_2: At 700 tonnes average cost rises to about $8,429, making current volume better served by the old plant
Rising costs beyond 1,200 tonnes would reverse the falling average cost curve

questions.question_text: Do you think Kettle & Fern Tea Co should build the new plant now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building now captures technical economies of scale [k]: average cost falls from $8,000 to $7,500 per tonne at 960 tonnes, and profit could rise from $480,000 to about $1.44 million [app], making the $3 million investment recoverable within a few years [an]. However, confirmed orders are only 700 tonnes [k]: at that volume average cost would be about $8,429, worse than today, and output beyond 1,200 tonnes risks diseconomies of scale such as poor communication and low morale [app], so building ahead of demand gambles $3 million on unsigned sales [an]. Overall [eval], Kettle & Fern should delay construction until signed orders exceed roughly 800 tonnes — the point where average cost matches today's $8,000 — and meanwhile secure national distribution agreements, because proceeding at 700 tonnes would destroy the expected saving [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost and raise profit
Diseconomies of scale and underused capacity threaten large investments
application_max_2: Average cost falls $8,000 to $7,500; profit could rise $480,000 to $1.44 million; $3 million cost
Only 700 tonnes confirmed; at 700 tonnes average cost is about $8,429; diseconomies beyond 1,200 tonnes
analysis_max_2: At full capacity the $500 per tonne saving adds about $480,000 of annual profit
At 700 tonnes the higher average cost erases the gain and strains cash for loan repayments
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to achieving at least 800 tonnes of signed orders

scenario_stem:
Copperpipe Plumbing & Heating is a private limited company handling boiler repairs and installations. It employs 6 plumbers and 2 apprentices, earned $390,000 last year, and has $15,500 monthly fixed costs; winter jobs pay on completion, summer contracts after 60 days.

From a $17,200 opening balance, November inflows $48,500 and outflows $39,800 are followed by December inflows $56,000 and outflows $52,300. By 31 October Dan must choose between buying a $30,000 van now for the winter rush or waiting until spring.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash flow'.
questions.model_answer: Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over a period, shown as inflows, outflows and the resulting net cash flow [2].

knowledge_max_2: cash flow is the movement of money in and out of the business
measured as inflows minus outflows, giving net cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why winter is both the busiest and the riskiest season for Copperpipe's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Winter brings the highest job volumes [k], pushing inflows to $48,500 in November and $56,000 in December [app]. Reason 2: Winter jobs increase outflows for materials, parts and overtime [k], which explains November outflows of $39,800 and December outflows of $52,300 [app].

knowledge_max_2: peak season means high job volumes and high receipts
peak season also drives higher outflows for parts and labour
application_max_2: inflows of $48,500 in November and $56,000 in December
outflows of $39,800 in November and $52,300 in December

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Dan could cover the November shortfall if he buys the van now.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Dan could arrange an overdraft with the bank [k], covering the forecast dip to about -$4,100 after paying $30,000 for the van [app], which lets the business complete winter jobs that would otherwise be turned away [an]. Way 2: Dan could delay non-essential equipment purchases [k], protecting the November balance of $25,900 before the van payment [app], so the cash gap stays smaller and interest costs are limited [an].

knowledge_max_2: an overdraft covers short-term shortfalls up to an agreed limit
application_max_2: forecast dip to about -$4,100 after paying $30,000 for the van
protecting the November balance of $25,900 before the payment
analysis_max_2: keeps capacity to complete winter jobs that would be turned away
smaller gap means lower interest costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Dan should buy the van in November rather than wait until spring? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying now captures the winter rush [k], when inflows of $48,500 and $56,000 in November and December justify extra capacity [app], and the new van could generate enough extra jobs to pay for itself [an]. However, paying $30,000 in November drops the balance from $25,900 to about -$4,100 [k], forcing reliance on the bank through December [app], so the shortfall would need covering before spring work restarts [an]. Overall, Dan should buy the van now [eval], because missing the winter peak would lose more revenue than the modest overdraft needed to bridge two months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: buying capacity ahead of peak season captures extra revenue
large one-off purchases can push cash negative in the short term
application_max_2: November and December inflows of $48,500 and $56,000 vs a $30,000 van
balance falls from $25,900 to about -$4,100 after purchase
analysis_max_2: extra capacity could pay for itself in the winter rush
reliance on the bank until spring receipts arrive
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation comparing lost winter revenue against two months of overdraft

scenario_stem:
Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd is a private limited company formed to build an 8-turbine, $14 million wind farm on moorland. It would generate 21 megawatts for 11,000 homes, creating 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent maintenance roles.

The site is 3 kilometres from Hartham (620 residents) and 900 metres from a walking trail. Hartham Ridge Action gathered 700 signatures; 45% oppose it, citing 38 decibels and visual impact. Consent needs a $120,000-a-year community scheme and closing 2 turbines during migration, cutting output 9%.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental pressure group'.
questions.model_answer: An environmental pressure group is an organisation that campaigns to influence business and government decisions to protect the natural environment, using publicity, petitions and lobbying. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Organisation campaigning to protect the environment

questions.question_text: Explain two external benefits the wind farm would bring to Country X.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Clean electricity for homes [k], as the 8 turbines would generate 21 megawatts, enough to power 11,000 homes without burning fossil fuels [app]. Reason 2: Jobs for the local area [k], as 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent maintenance roles would be created over 14 months of building [app].

knowledge_max_2: Wind farms generate clean electricity without fossil fuels
Wind farms create jobs for local people
application_max_2: 34 construction jobs plus 9 permanent roles over 14 months

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs the Hartham Ridge wind farm may create.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Noise disturbance for villagers [k], since Hartham village, 3 kilometres away with 620 residents, faces turbine noise of about 38 decibels [app], which may disturb sleep and reduce house prices, costs falling on people who gain no direct electricity [an]. Cost 2: Harm to wildlife and the landscape [k], as shutting 2 turbines during bird migration shows a real collision risk, and the moorland skyline is a valued landscape [app], damaging a recreational asset used by walkers on the nearby trail [an].

Wind farms affect wildlife and valued landscapes

However, one argument against is the impact on Hartham [k], since 45% of 620 residents oppose the farm over noise of about 38 decibels and visual impact on the valued skyline [app], and the $120,000-a-year community fund plus a 9% output cut from shutting 2 turbines eat into returns on the $14 million project [an]. Overall, Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd should proceed under the council's conditions [eval], because clean power for 11,000 homes and 43 jobs outweigh the residual disruption, and the community fund plus migration shutdowns fairly compensate Hartham while keeping the wind farm viable [eval].

Resident opposition and compliance conditions erode returns

evaluation_max_2: Weighs both proceeding under conditions and resident opposition
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Oakhurst Precision Tools is a private limited company making precision measuring instruments in Brannock, employing 45 production workers and generating $950,000 revenue. Its customers are engineering firms across Country X.

Directors want $220,000 automated calibration machines to raise output 30% and cut unit costs, shifting from steady profit to rapid growth. The union warns automation could eliminate 18 of 45 jobs; workers voted to oppose it, and the two owners disagree.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'stakeholder'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the owners and the workers at Oakhurst may have conflicting objectives over the automation plan.

Reason 2: Workers want job security and stable wages [k], because the union warns that 18 of the 45 production roles could disappear if automation goes ahead [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Oakhurst could manage the conflict between the owners and the workers.

Point 2: Oakhurst could retrain or redeploy affected workers into new roles [k], offering the 18 workers training to operate or maintain the new calibration machines [app], which would reduce redundancies and keep skilled staff available for the 30% output increase [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakhurst should approve the $220,000 investment in automated calibration machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for approving the investment is that the new machines would raise output by 30% [k], cutting unit costs for Oakhurst Precision Tools and helping it win larger orders from toolmakers across Country X [app], which could protect the business's survival and fund future growth [an]. scenario_stem:
Hartham Bakery is a family-run private limited company in Bramfield, founded 2003, with 24 staff making artisan loaves for 3 retail outlets on $520,000 sales. Priya Raman must replace the production supervisor who ran the bakery floor for 9 years.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'job description'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hartham Bakery should carry out a job analysis before recruiting the new production supervisor.

Reason 2: Job analysis ensures the advert and selection criteria match the role [k], so Priya attracts suitable candidates within the $4,500 recruitment budget rather than wasting money on unsuitable applicants [app].

knowledge_max_2: Job analysis identifies tasks and requirements of the job

$4,500 budget and need for suitable applicants

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Hartham Bakery of producing a clear job description for the supervisor vacancy.

Benefit 2: A job description gives the interviewer a checklist for comparing candidates [k], allowing internal and external applicants to be scored against the same duties [app], making the final choice more objective and lowering the risk of a poor appointment [an].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Hallowfen Bakery is a private limited company baking artisan sourdough loaves, founded in 2018. Loaves sell at $10.00 wholesale, with variable costs of $4.00 and monthly fixed costs of $9,000. Last month it sold 2,250 loaves, making $4,500 profit.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'break-even output'.
questions.model_answer: The level of output at which total revenue exactly equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Output where total revenue equals total costs

questions.question_text: Calculate Hallowfen Bakery's break-even output in loaves per month. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Contribution per loaf = $10.00 − $4.00 = $6.00 [k]. Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution = $9,000 ÷ $6.00 = 1,500 loaves per month [app], the level at which total revenue equals total costs [k]. Revenue at break-even equals $15,000 and would exactly cover all fixed and variable costs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It shows how many loaves must be sold before profit begins [k], which for Hallowfen is 1,500 loaves a month against actual sales of 2,250 loaves [app], so the owners can see the bakery has a 750-loaf cushion before falling into losses [an]. Benefit 2: It helps the owners judge price and cost changes safely [k], for example testing whether the cheaper flour or the $12.00 price rise would keep the margin of safety positive [app], which supports calmer decisions while a rival bakery undercuts on price [an].

scenario_stem:
Brackmere Paint & Decor is a sole trader paint and decorating-supplies shop with $680,000 annual revenue. Current assets are $92,000, including $38,000 owed by trade debtors, and current liabilities $74,000, including a $30,000 bank overdraft.

questions.question_text: Define 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It measures the cash and other short-term assets available to fund day-to-day trading after short-term debts are accounted for [2].

Reason 2: Working capital keeps a business trading while it waits for money it is owed to arrive [k], as $38,000 of Brackmere's $92,000 current assets is owed by trade debtors [app].

working capital funds day-to-day trading while awaiting payment from debtors

Benefit 2: Converting $38,000 owed by trade debtors into cash more quickly would strengthen Brackmere's position [k], where current liabilities of $74,000 already exceed the cash balance and current assets of $92,000 leave only $18,000 of working capital [app], easing pressure on day-to-day payments such as wages and suppliers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should ask existing debtors to pay sooner or arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Asking debtors to pay sooner would inject cash without further borrowing [k], and it directly tackles the $38,000 owed by trade debtors that is straining Brackmere's cash while current liabilities stand at $74,000 [app]. scenario_stem:
Brackenford Dye Works is a private limited company dyeing cotton fabrics for garment makers near the River Arn. Last year's revenue was $4,300,000.

scenario_stem:
Boghall Mushroom Farm is a family business harvesting about 25,000 kg of oyster mushrooms a year. Annual fixed costs are $60,000 and variable costs are $4.00 per kg.

It must choose between two sales options: selling to three restaurants at $12.00 per kg, moving around 9,000 kg a year, or selling to a supermarket chain at $7.00 per kg, taking the full 25,000 kg harvest. It wants to compare break-even output before signing and worries the supermarket could cut prices later.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'variable costs'.
questions.model_answer: Costs that vary in direct proportion with the level of output, such as raw materials and piece-rate labour. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Costs that change as output changes

questions.question_text: Calculate the break-even output and the profit for each sales option. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Option A (restaurants): contribution per kg = $12.00 − $4.00 = $8.00 [k]; break-even = $60,000 ÷ $8.00 = 7,500 kg a year, and profit at 9,000 kg = (9,000 × $8.00) − $60,000 = $12,000 [app]. Option B (supermarket): contribution per kg = $7.00 − $4.00 = $3.00 [k]; break-even = $60,000 ÷ $3.00 = 20,000 kg a year, and profit at 25,000 kg = (25,000 × $3.00) − $60,000 = $15,000 [app].

Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit

Advantage 2: Three restaurants spread risk across several buyers [k], rather than relying on one supermarket chain for the whole 25,000 kg harvest [app], so if one buyer cuts its orders the farm is not left with tonnes of unsold mushrooms and falling revenue [an].

scenario_stem:
Rillbeck Soap Co is a private limited company making handmade soaps. Its best-selling lavender bar sells at $6.00, with variable costs of $2.00 and annual fixed costs of $14,000. Last year it sold 6,000 bars, making $10,000 profit.

The owner must choose between launching an oatmeal bar, needing a $7,000-a-year moulding contract with first-year demand of 1,500 bars at $6.00 and variable cost of $2.50, or promoting lavender to push sales towards 7,500 bars. A gift shop has asked to stock the oatmeal line.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'average cost'.
questions.model_answer: The total cost per unit produced, calculated by dividing total costs by the number of units output. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Total costs divided by units produced
Falls as output rises while fixed costs stay constant

questions.question_text: Calculate the average cost per lavender bar and the profit from selling 6,000 bars. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Total cost = $14,000 fixed + (6,000 × $2.00 = $12,000 variable) = $26,000 [k]. Average cost per bar = $26,000 ÷ 6,000 = $4.33 [app]. Revenue = 6,000 × $6.00 = $36,000, so profit = $36,000 − $26,000 = $10,000 [app], matching last year's result for Rillbeck [k].

knowledge_max_2: Average cost = total costs ÷ units produced
application_max_2: Total cost $26,000; average cost $4.33 per bar

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis if Rillbeck Soap Co launches the oatmeal bar.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: It assumes one product and one price [k], but lavender and oatmeal bars share the $14,000 fixed costs and sell at $6.00 with different variable costs [app], so splitting fixed costs between two lines can distort each line's true break-even output [an]. Limitation 2: It assumes first-year demand can be predicted [k], yet the estimated 1,500 oatmeal bars sit below the 2,000 bars needed to cover the $7,000 moulding contract [app], so the new line could lose about $1,750 in year one even if the chart looks acceptable [an].

knowledge_max_2: Assumes a single product sold at one price
Assumes forecast demand levels are achieved
application_max_2: 1,500 forecast bars vs the 2,000 needed to cover $7,000
analysis_max_2: Splitting fixed costs between lines distorts per-line break-even
Forecast shortfall yields a year-one loss of about $1,750

questions.question_text: Do you think Rillbeck Soap Co should launch the oatmeal soap bar? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for launching is that a second line spreads the $14,000 fixed costs across more bars [k], and once oatmeal sales pass the 2,000-bar break-even for the $7,000 moulding contract, each extra bar contributes $3.50 to profit [app], helping Rillbeck grow beyond its current $10,000 annual profit [an]. However, one argument against is that the forecast 1,500 bars fall below that break-even [k], so the line would lose about $1,750 in year one and divert staff from the proven lavender bar [app], while pushing lavender towards 7,500 bars could more safely lift profit to about $16,000 [an]. Overall, Rillbeck should not launch yet [eval]; it should survey its gift-shop customers and trial a market stall, launching only if pre-orders top 2,000 bars [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Extra product lines spread fixed costs
New products often lose money before reaching break-even
application_max_2: Oatmeal break-even is 2,000 bars against the $7,000 moulding contract
Forecast 1,500 bars lose ≈ $1,750; lavender at 7,500 bars could yield ≈ $16,000 profit

scenario_stem:
Fenmeadow Clothing is a sole trader menswear and womenswear retailer with two high-street stores, 17 staff and $640,000 annual sales. Current assets are $78,000, of which $45,000 is owed by employers on 60-day credit for staff uniforms, and current liabilities are $69,000.

It needs $35,000 for rent and insurance due in 3 weeks. Aisha must choose between offering uniform customers a 2.5% discount to settle invoices within 14 days, or postponing the $60,000 second-store refurbishment for a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'debtors'.
questions.model_answer: Debtors are customers or businesses that owe money to the business, usually for goods sold on credit, and they are recorded as current assets [2].

knowledge_max_2: debtors are customers or businesses owing the firm money
the debt usually arises from goods sold on credit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fenmeadow Clothing needs sufficient working capital.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to meet short-term debts on time [k], as Fenmeadow urgently needs $35,000 for rent and insurance due in 3 weeks [app]. Reason 2: Working capital supports daily retail operations [k], and 17 staff across two high-street stores must be paid from the trading cash tied to $640,000 of annual sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts and bills on time
working capital funds daily operations such as wages and stock
application_max_2: Fenmeadow urgently needs $35,000 for rent and insurance due in 3 weeks
17 staff work across two stores on $640,000 of annual sales

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Fenmeadow of postponing the $60,000 refurbishment for a year.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Postponing the refurbishment keeps $60,000 in the business [k], so the urgent $35,000 rent and insurance bill due in 3 weeks can be paid without draining the $78,000 of current assets needed for stock [app], avoiding late-payment penalties [an]. Benefit 2: Delaying the spend avoids new borrowing [k], sparing the retailer interest and leaving the $9,000 of working capital available for wages and suppliers [app], which strengthens day-to-day stability while debtors still take 60 days to pay [an].

knowledge_max_2: postponing capital expenditure keeps cash in the business
delaying major spending avoids new borrowing and interest
application_max_2: the refurbishment costs $60,000 and $35,000 is due for rent and insurance in 3 weeks
current assets are $78,000 leaving working capital of $9,000
analysis_max_2: keeping cash avoids penalties and protects stock levels
avoiding borrowing preserves the $9,000 of working capital

questions.question_text: Do you think Aisha should offer the 2.5% discount to debtors or postpone the refurbishment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Offering a 2.5% discount to settle within 14 days turns slow debtors into fast cash [k], targeting the $45,000 owed by employers on 60-day credit [app], which would directly cover the $35,000 rent and insurance due in 3 weeks [an]. However, the discount costs money on every invoice settled early [k], trimming revenue below the $640,000 annual sales level on a margin-sensitive uniform trade [app], and employers who already pay within 14 days would receive a discount for nothing [an]. Postponing the $60,000 refurbishment preserves cash without discounting, though the second store stays dated for another year. On balance, postponing the refurbishment is the safer choice because it creates no direct cost, unlike the discount which eats directly into sales revenue [eval]. It also removes the $60,000 commitment from a business whose current liabilities of $69,000 already exceed what the $9,000 of working capital can comfortably cover. Overall, Aisha should postpone the refurbishment and keep the 2.5% discount as a reserve if debtors still pay too slowly [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a settlement discount motivates debtors to pay earlier
postponing planned capital expenditure preserves cash at no direct cost
application_max_2: $45,000 is owed by employers on 60-day credit
$35,000 for rent and insurance is due in 3 weeks on $640,000 of annual sales
analysis_max_2: the discount directly reduces revenue and may reward early payers for nothing
postponing removes a $60,000 commitment and costs nothing upfront
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning
weighs certain discount cost against the zero-cost delay of the refurbishment

scenario_stem:
Amberfields Cocoa Co is a private limited company importing cocoa beans to make chocolate bars. Output is 1,300 tonnes a year; last year's revenue was $5,400,000, with profit at 12% of revenue.

A newspaper investigation alleges one of its two suppliers used child labour. Switching to certified ethical beans would raise costs by $350,000 a year, cutting the margin to 5.5%. Keeping it protects profit, but a national retailer worth $2,100,000 a year will delist its chocolate. The board decides in 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Explain two ethical issues Amberfields Cocoa Co faces.

It also ends the child labour allegations [app], lifting the threat to staff morale and the brand's reputation [an]. However, switching raises bean costs by $350,000 a year [k], cutting the profit margin from 12% to about 5.5%. scenario_stem:
Sable & Stone Leatherworks is a partnership making handmade leather belts and bags in Torvale, employing 9 craftspeople and earning $190,000 revenue shared as $54,000 profit. The partners cut, stitch and finish orders for boutiques and online customers.

Partner 1 wants growth: borrow $80,000, repaid at $1,600 a month over 5 years, for a second workshop and 6 more workers. Partner 2 wants steady profit with 9 craftspeople, as debt would erode the $54,000 profit despite healthy orders and rising costs.

knowledge_max_2: A specific target or goal for the business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the two partners want different objectives for Sable & Stone Leatherworks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The partners have different attitudes to risk [k], with Partner 1 willing to borrow $80,000 to open a second workshop and hire 6 more staff [app]. Reason 2: The partners may have different personal financial goals [k], with Partner 2 preferring to protect the $54,000 annual profit and avoid $1,600 of monthly repayments [app].

knowledge_max_2: Different attitudes to risk between owners
Different personal financial goals and priorities
application_max_2: $80,000 loan for a second workshop and 6 more staff

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Sable & Stone Leatherworks of changing its objective from steady profit to growth.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Growth could raise revenue above $190,000 [k], since a second workshop with 6 extra leatherworkers would allow larger orders for belts and bags [app], increasing total sales and potential profit for both partners [an]. Benefit 2: Growth reduces dependence on one site [k], spreading production across two workshops supplying boutiques and online customers [app], so problems at one site would no longer threaten the whole business [an].

However, one argument against is that the $1,600 monthly repayments must be paid for 5 years [k], even if the second workshop underperforms or rising wage and leather costs persist [app], which could consume Partner 2's preferred stable income and strain the partnership [an]. Overall, the partners should change only to a cautious growth objective [eval], borrowing $80,000 after a trial scale-up of part-time staff confirms order volumes, with a joint six-monthly review and the right to pause the loan if repayments bite into profit [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ferrybrook Distribution Ltd is a private limited company warehouse in Country X with 96 warehouse operatives picking 26,000 orders monthly. It needs 20 temporaries in 6 weeks as volumes rise 40%.

Marcus Boateng can run 15-minute interviews with 60 shortlisted candidates for $900, or a 45-minute aptitude test for all 60 at $14 each, $840. Last year 35% of interview hires left within 3 months.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'aptitude test'.
questions.model_answer: A test that measures a candidate's natural ability or potential to learn and perform tasks, such as numeracy, literacy or spatial awareness. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Measures natural ability or potential to learn
Covers abilities such as numeracy or spatial awareness

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the aptitude test could help Ferrybrook Distribution Ltd select the 20 temporary operatives.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: The test objectively measures job-relevant ability [k], checking whether candidates can handle numeracy and spatial tasks needed to pick 26,000 orders a month [app]. Way 2: The test is fast and uniform across all 60 shortlisted candidates [k], making results easy to compare within the 6-week hiring deadline [app].

knowledge_max_2: The test measures job-relevant abilities objectively
The test is uniform and quick to score across candidates
application_max_2: Numeracy and spatial skills needed for 26,000 monthly orders
60 candidates compared consistently within the 6-week deadline

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using aptitude tests alone for the warehouse roles.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Tests measure ability, not attitude [k], so a high-scoring candidate might still skip shifts during the Christmas peak [app], raising turnover above last year's 35% for interview-based hires and triggering re-training costs [an]. Limitation 2: Tests cannot judge teamwork or reliability [k], yet temporary operatives must work safely alongside 96 staff moving fast-moving orders [app], so poor hires may cause injuries or errors that disrupt the 26,000-order monthly flow [an].

Tests cannot judge teamwork or safety behaviour

Temporary staff working alongside 96 staff on fast orders

questions.model_answer: One argument for the aptitude test is accuracy at scale [k], scoring all 60 shortlisted candidates on job-relevant numeracy and spatial skills for $840, less than the $900 interview cost [app], which should reduce mis-hires and the 35% early turnover Ferrybrook suffered last year [an]. However, interviews reveal attitude, motivation and safety awareness [k], which the Christmas peak demands more than raw test scores [app], so replacing interviews entirely could repeat last year's 35% turnover if attitude-blind hires are made [an]. Overall, Ferrybrook should use the $840 test as the first stage and keep short 15-minute interviews for the best scorers [eval], combining objective ability data with a check on attitude within the 6-week deadline [eval].

scenario_stem:
Northquay Fitness Club is a private limited company running a gym and pool with 1,800 members, 22 staff and $540,000 revenue. Membership renewals fell 8% last year, so the manager wants to survey members before changing membership packages.

He compares random sampling, emailing a questionnaire to 300 members, with quota sampling of 300 members mirroring 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30. Software costs $300 monthly; results appear as charts in the newsletter.

questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Selecting a sample from a population in which every member has an equal chance of being chosen, for example by using a random number generator [2].

knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance
selection by chance, e.g. random number generator

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Northquay Fitness Club may face in getting accurate survey results.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A low response rate [k]; if only a fraction of the 300 emailed members reply, the reason for the 8% fall in renewals will not be explained accurately [app]. Problem 2: Biased or dishonest answers [k]; members wanting cheaper fees may exaggerate complaints about the current membership packages [app], so the results overstate the problem.

knowledge_max_2: biased or dishonest answers distort results

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using quota sampling for this survey.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Quota sampling guarantees the sample reflects key member groups [k]; selecting 300 members to match 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30 [app] ensures older members' views are heard [an]. Benefit 2: It avoids the cost and complexity of random selection [k]; picking members by quota from the 1,800-name membership list needs no separate random process [app], saving staff time for a small club [an].

knowledge_max_2: avoids the cost and complexity of random selection
application_max_2: 300 members mirroring 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30
manager wants to change membership packages
analysis_max_2: ensures older members' views are included
saves staff time at a small club

questions.question_text: Do you think Northquay Fitness Club should use quota sampling rather than random sampling for its member survey? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Quota sampling ensures both age groups are fairly represented [k]; mirroring 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30 in the sample of 300 [app] reveals whether the 8% renewal fall is driven by young or older members [an]. However, random sampling gives every member an equal chance [k]; emailing 300 members chosen by random number generator [app] avoids the manager unknowingly favouring familiar faces at the gym [an]. Overall, quota sampling is the better choice here [eval] because age-related differences in package preferences are the key question, and quotas guarantee both groups are heard [eval].

knowledge_max_2: random sampling gives every member an equal chance
application_max_2: 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30 profile

scenario_stem:
Netherfield Farm is a family business running a pick-your-own strawberry field from June to August. It charges $9.00 per kg, with variable costs of $2.00 and seasonal fixed costs of $14,000. This year's harvest may reach 6,000 kg, but direct visitor sales may be only 4,500 kg.

A jam factory has offered to buy any unsold strawberries at $4.00 per kg after the season. The family must decide whether to accept, protecting against waste, or risk the crop on bumper visitor sales.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'break-even analysis'.
questions.model_answer: Comparing fixed and variable costs with revenue to find the output at which no profit or loss is made, and to judge risk and profit at different outputs. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Comparing costs and revenue to locate break-even output
Used to judge risk, profit and pricing decisions

questions.question_text: Calculate the break-even output for Netherfield Farm and the profit if 4,500 kg are sold this season. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Contribution per kg = $9.00 − $2.00 = $7.00 [k]. Break-even output = $14,000 ÷ $7.00 = 2,000 kg of strawberries [app]. Profit if 4,500 kg are sold = (4,500 × $7.00) − $14,000 = $17,500 [app], before any surplus sales to the jam factory are counted [k].

knowledge_max_2: Contribution = price − variable cost per unit
Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis for Netherfield Farm.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: It assumes all output is sold [k], but Netherfield may pick 6,000 kg and sell only 4,500 kg to visitors [app], so the chart would overstate revenue unless the 1,500 kg surplus goes to the jam factory [an]. Limitation 2: It assumes prices and costs stay fixed [k], but heat, rain or hail can ruin crop quality and force price cuts to clear fruit [app], so the real break-even can move sharply in a bad summer [an].

knowledge_max_2: Assumes prices and costs remain constant
application_max_2: 6,000 kg harvest vs 4,500 kg of visitor sales
Weather can cut quality and force price reductions
analysis_max_2: Unsold 1,500 kg breaks the all-output-sold assumption
Weather-driven price cuts push break-even upwards

questions.question_text: Do you think Netherfield Farm should accept the jam factory's offer at $4.00 per kg? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for accepting is that it guarantees a buyer for the surplus [k], turning 1,500 kg of unsold fruit into about $3,000 of extra contribution ($4.00 − $2.00 per kg) on top of the $17,500 from visitor sales [app], lifting seasonal profit towards $20,500 and cutting waste to zero [an]. However, one argument against is that $4.00 per kg is well under the $9.00 visitor price [k], so fruit sold late to the factory earns far less than field sales would, and heavy dependence on the factory could tempt the farm to neglect visitor promotion [app], damaging the premium pick-your-own image that fills the field each summer [an]. Overall, Netherfield should accept the offer as a one-season safety net for unsold fruit only [eval]; the farm should sell at $9.00 to visitors first and send only the remaining surplus to the jam factory [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Guaranteed sales of surplus cut waste
Lower-priced bulk sales yield less per kilogram
application_max_2: $9.00 field price vs $4.00 jam factory price
analysis_max_2: Profit rises towards $20,500 with the offer in place
Over-reliance on factory sales erodes the $9.00 field margin
evaluation_max_2: Weighs guaranteed surplus sales against the lower margin
Reaches a justified judgement: visitors first, factory as safety net

scenario_stem:
Dorncliffe Fish Processing is a private limited company freezing and packing sea fish with 45 workers and $2,100,000 annual output. Current assets are $210,000 and current liabilities $165,000, giving $45,000 working capital; an export customer owing $88,000 has delayed payment until next quarter.

Tomas must find $60,000 within 2 weeks for a refrigerated truck repair and wages. He must choose between delaying fish suppliers by 45 days, or asking the export customer to pay $88,000 immediately with a 2% discount, receiving $86,240.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dorncliffe Fish Processing needs sufficient working capital.

Reason 2: Working capital keeps production running while awaiting payment [k], since $88,000 owed by an export customer will not arrive until next quarter [app].

knowledge_max_2: working capital pays wages and urgent operating bills
working capital bridges the gap between production and payment
application_max_2: Dorncliffe must find $60,000 within 2 weeks for a truck repair and wages

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Dorncliffe of asking the export customer to pay immediately with a 2% discount.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: An early payment converts a delayed debt into usable cash [k], bringing in $86,240 now instead of $88,000 next quarter [app], which gives Tomas immediate money for the refrigerated truck repair [an]. Advantage 2: Securing cash from the customer avoids delaying suppliers [k], keeping Dorncliffe in good standing with the fish suppliers behind $2,100,000 of annual output [app], so production continues without interruption [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Tomas should delay paying fish suppliers by 45 days or ask the export customer to pay immediately with a 2% discount? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Asking the export customer to pay immediately uses a discount to pull cash forward [k], securing $86,240 now to cover the $60,000 needed within 2 weeks [app], which solves the crisis without harming supplier relationships [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brinsworth Timber Co is a partnership importing hardwood and softwood. Revenue last year was $6,800,000 from 9 major customers.

Retailers demand certified wood, and the largest furniture retailer, worth $2,600,000 a year, requires independently certified sustainable forestry labels. Certified timber costs 16% more, adding about $540,000 a year. A cheaper uncertified supplier offers the old price but has unclear origin documents. The partners decide before a supply audit in 5 weeks, or lose the order to a certified rival.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental impact'.
questions.model_answer: The total effect a business's activities have on the natural environment, including pollution, deforestation, habitat loss and the use of finite resources. [2].

knowledge_max_2: The effect of a business's activities on the natural environment
Including pollution, deforestation and resource use

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brinsworth Timber Co should be cautious about the cheaper supplier.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The wood may come from illegal logging [k], its origin documents are unclear [app]. Reason 2: It could cost the largest contract [k], the furniture retailer requires certified sustainable labels for an order worth $2,600,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Risk of unclear or illegal logging
application_max_2: the retailer worth $2,600,000 a year requires certified sustainable labels

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brinsworth of buying certified sustainable timber.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It keeps the largest customer [k], certified labels meet the retailer's requirement for the $2,600,000 a year contract [app], securing future orders [an]. Benefit 2: It protects the firm from legal and reputational damage [k], certified wood replaces the unclear origin documents of the cheaper supplier [app], avoiding lost contracts and bad publicity [an].

application_max_2: certified labels secure the $2,600,000 a year contract
replaces the unclear origin documents of the cheaper supplier
analysis_max_2: Avoiding lost contracts and bad publicity

questions.question_text: Do you think Brinsworth Timber Co should buy certified timber? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying certified timber keeps the retailer [k], its $2,600,000 a year contract requires certified sustainable forestry labels on every delivery [app], protecting about 38% of the $6,800,000 revenue [an]. It also removes the risk of unclear origin documents and illegal logging [app], safeguarding the firm's reputation with all 9 customers [an]. However, certified timber adds $540,000 a year to input costs, a 16% increase [k], which would squeeze margins. Overall, Brinsworth should buy certified timber [eval], because $540,000 a year is far less than the $2,600,000 contract at risk, and one audit failure could lose the order to a certified rival permanently [eval].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Hest Bank Yoghurt Co is a private limited company selling natural yoghurt pots at $1.20 each. Annual fixed costs are $9,000 and variable costs are $0.80 per pot; it sells about 30,000 pots a year.

A supermarket chain has offered a contract for 400,000 pots a year, requiring a new potting line. Machine X has $0.40 variable cost per pot with $21,000 extra fixed costs; Machine Y has $0.70 per pot with $6,000 extra fixed costs. The owner must choose based on expected demand.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'profit'.
questions.model_answer: The amount by which revenue exceeds total costs, that is sales income minus every cost of production. [2].

knowledge_max_2: The reward that remains after all costs are paid

questions.question_text: Calculate the break-even output for Machine X and Machine Y. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Machine X: contribution per pot = $1.20 − $0.40 = $0.80 [k], so break-even = $30,000 ÷ $0.80 = 37,500 pots a year [app]. Machine Y: contribution per pot = $1.20 − $0.70 = $0.50 [k], so break-even = $15,000 ÷ $0.50 = 30,000 pots a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs combine into total fixed costs
Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of Machine X over Machine Y if Hest Bank wins the supermarket contract.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Machine X earns a stronger contribution per pot [k], at $0.80 rather than $0.50 [app], so across the 400,000-pot contract it leaves Hest Bank about $105,000 better off a year ($290,000 vs $185,000 profit) [an]. Advantage 2: Machine X's lower variable cost protects profit if milk prices rise [k], because each pot needs only $0.40 of materials instead of $0.70 [app], so a dairy price increase would squeeze margin far less on the supermarket's large order [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher contribution per unit raises profit at high volume
Lower variable costs give resilience against input price rises
analysis_max_2: About $105,000 extra profit a year at 400,000 pots
Dairy price rises hurt Machine Y margins far more

questions.question_text: Do you think Hest Bank Yoghurt Co should choose Machine X for the supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for Machine X is that its $0.80 contribution suits high volume [k], so at 400,000 pots a year it would earn about $290,000 after its $30,000 fixed costs, comfortably beyond its 37,500-pot break-even [app], making automation the right fit for a long supermarket contract [an]. However, one argument against is that Machine X's break-even is 37,500 pots [k], higher than Machine Y's 30,000 pots, and below about 50,000 pots a year Machine Y leaves Hest Bank better off [app], so if the supermarket cuts orders the extra $21,000 lease could drag the business into losses [an]. Overall, Hest Bank should choose Machine X [eval], but only after written agreement of a minimum annual order of at least 60,000 pots, so the 37,500-pot break-even is safely cleared [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed leases are risky if demand falls
application_max_2: $290,000 projected profit at 400,000 pots after $30,000 fixed costs
Machine X break-even 37,500 pots vs Machine Y 30,000 pots
analysis_max_2: Automation wins clearly above roughly 50,000 pots a year
Order cuts could leave the $21,000 lease uncovered
evaluation_max_2: Weighs high-volume reward against demand risk
Reaches a justified judgement: Machine X only with a guaranteed minimum order

scenario_stem:
Harrowmere Pharmacy is a private limited company running two community pharmacies with 23 staff and $980,000 annual revenue. Current assets are $132,000, including $58,000 of medicines inventory, and current liabilities $96,000, leaving $36,000 working capital.

The main supplier demands payment within 14 days instead of 45, and wages of $28,000 are due soon. Nadia must choose between postponing the $110,000 third pharmacy for 12 months, or taking a $75,000 bank overdraft to cover running costs and open on time.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to convert its assets into cash quickly so that it can pay its short-term debts as they fall due [2].

knowledge_max_2: liquidity is the ability to convert assets into cash quickly
liquid assets pay short-term debts as they fall due

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Harrowmere Pharmacy needs sufficient working capital.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to pay suppliers on demand [k], and Harrowmere's main supplier now demands payment within 14 days instead of 45 [app]. Reason 2: Working capital pays staff on time [k], as wages of $28,000 are due soon and 23 staff must be paid to keep both community pharmacies open [app].

knowledge_max_2: working capital funds prompt payment to suppliers
working capital funds staff wages and daily operations
application_max_2: the main supplier demands payment within 14 days instead of 45
wages of $28,000 are due soon for 23 staff

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Harrowmere of postponing the third pharmacy for 12 months.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Postponing the $110,000 opening keeps cash in the business [k], protecting the $132,000 of current assets needed to honour the new 14-day supplier terms and pay the $28,000 wages due soon [app], and avoiding overdraft interest [an]. Benefit 2: Delaying gives the business time to rebuild working capital [k], strengthening the $36,000 of working capital left between current assets and current liabilities [app], so the new branch opens on a stable financial footing [an].

knowledge_max_2: postponing expansion keeps cash inside the business
delaying allows working capital to rebuild before committing funds
application_max_2: the third pharmacy costs $110,000 and wages of $28,000 are due soon

analysis_max_2: keeping cash meets the tighter 14-day supplier terms
rebuilt working capital gives the new branch a stable start

questions.question_text: Do you think Nadia should postpone the third pharmacy or take the $75,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Postponing the third pharmacy preserves cash without any interest cost [k], protecting the $36,000 of working capital left between current assets of $132,000 and current liabilities of $96,000 [app], so the 14-day supplier terms and the $28,000 wages bill stay comfortably covered [an]. However, delaying means missing the chance to open first in the third location [k], potentially losing ground in a market that supports $980,000 of annual revenue across the two existing pharmacies [app], and a rival could secure the location during the 12 months [an]. The $75,000 overdraft would keep the January opening on track, though it adds interest and could be called in just as supplier terms tighten. On balance, postponing is the safer option because the new 14-day supplier demand makes the existing business's cash tight, and an overdraft could become a trap [eval]. Keeping to the two present pharmacies lets Harrowmere absorb the tighter terms before committing to expansion. Overall, Nadia should postpone the third pharmacy by 12 months and review the opening once the 14-day payment cycle is absorbed comfortably [eval].

weighs zero-cost delay against overdraft flexibility and competitive risk

scenario_stem:
Hollowgate Recycling Co is a private limited company sorting commercial waste from clients across three provinces. Last year's revenue was $2,750,000, and it sent 5,200 tonnes to landfill.

Landfill tax rises from $88 to $130 per tonne in April, lifting the annual bill from $457,600 to $676,000. The board has 4 months to decide.

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher operating costs [k], its tax bill would rise from $457,600 to $676,000 a year [app]. Problem 2: Pressure to raise prices [k], the extra $218,400 a year would have to be passed on to customers [app].

Benefit 2: A stronger customer offer [k], it avoids passing the $218,400 on to customers [app], helping retain price-sensitive contracts across the three provinces [an].

scenario_stem:
Fennel & Rye Bakery is a sole trader start-up in Millbrook making sourdough loaves and croissants, with 3 part-time assistants. Last month revenue was $3,400 against $5,100 costs, a $1,700 loss, after Dana Whitmore invested $9,000 of savings.

Dana needs finance for a second unit. The government offers a $12,000 grant for creating 5 jobs if she matches $6,000 and repays if targets fail; Millbrook Bank offers $15,000 at 9% over 4 years, or her supplier may give 30 days' credit.

questions.question_text: Define 'grant'.
questions.model_answer: A grant is a sum of money given to a business by the government or another organisation that does not have to be repaid, usually to support a specific aim such as creating jobs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A sum of money given to a business (usually by the government or an organisation)
Does not have to be repaid / given for a specific purpose such as job creation or supporting a start-up

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Country X government offers grants to new businesses.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Grants encourage new businesses to create jobs, so unemployment falls and more people pay taxes [k]. The $12,000 grant requires at least 5 jobs, so the government expects direct employment benefits for Millbrook workers [app]. Reason 2: Supporting start-ups boosts competition and diversifies the local economy [k]. Dana must match the grant with $6,000 of her own capital, which shares the risk and reduces the cost to the government [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Fennel & Rye Bakery of accepting the government grant instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A grant does not have to be repaid, so Dana avoids interest charges [k]. The Millbrook Bank loan of $15,000 at 9% over 4 years would cost about $5,400 in interest, whereas the $12,000 grant is free if targets are met [app]. This frees cash for flour, wages and equipment during loss-making months, improving the bakery's chance of survival [an]. Benefit 2: Winning the grant gives the bakery credibility with suppliers and banks [k]. Dana is losing $1,700 every month and relies on 30 days of flour supplier credit, so government approval would reassure creditors that she can expand safely [app]. Stronger credibility may unlock better credit terms and wholesale accounts, helping revenue recover from $3,400 per month [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Dana should accept the government grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Dana could accept the grant because it provides $12,000 with no interest, directly addressing her shortage of finance while she records a loss of $1,700 a month [k]. The money would fund a second unit and the 5-job target matches her expansion plan, and it avoids the $5,400 interest she would pay on the $15,000 bank loan [app]. Avoiding that interest directly reduces her outgoings and protects her working capital while she is loss-making [an]. Failing to create 5 jobs in time would force repayment and destroy her remaining cash, so poor planning or slow sales could make the bakery fail [an]. On the other hand, the bank loan gives full flexibility with no job conditions and a longer 4-year repayment structure [app]. Overall, Dana should accept the grant because it removes her biggest constraint, finance, and the target is realistic given the commuter demand for sourdough loaves, but only if she secures the 30 days of supplier credit first [eval]. scenario_stem:
Duskmere Appliances is a sole trader white-goods retailer with 2 stores and 22 staff. Revenue fell from $540,000 to $470,000 in 18 months as unemployment rose. Shoppers trade down from premium washing machines at $650 to budget models at $310.

Rivals run $25 weekly promotions. The owner weighs cutting the $310 budget price by 15% to protect footfall in both stores against launching an own-label budget range costing $90,000, to match new spending patterns.

Reason 2: Lower real incomes make consumers more price-sensitive [k], shifting purchases towards rival chains running $25 weekly promotions [app].

Advantage 2: Differentiates Duskmere from rivals who only run $25 promotions [k], giving shoppers a reason to choose its 2 stores and trust the own-label brand [app], which can increase long-term repeat sales [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think launching the own-label budget range is a better response to changing consumer spending patterns than cutting the price of the $310 budget washing machine by 15%? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Briarfield Conserves Co, a private limited company, makes jams and chutneys in Country X. It made 900,000 jars last year on $2.7 million revenue and $270,000 profit. Rapid expansion caused poor communication between the 3 shifts, so 140 jars are rejected daily.

Options: horizontal integration, buying rival Hearthwick Conserves (60,000 jars monthly) for $1.8 million; or organic growth, adding 2 supervisors and shift handovers to reach $400,000 profit by 2029.

questions.question_text: Define 'diseconomies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Diseconomies of scale occur when a business grows beyond its most efficient size and average costs begin to rise, for example because of poor communication, low morale or slow decision-making [2].

caused by problems such as poor communication, low morale or slow decision-making

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why poor communication between the 3 shifts is increasing rejected jars.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Messages are delayed or distorted as they travel between shifts [k], so faults in jar sealing reported by night staff are not corrected before the day shift, contributing to the 140 jars rejected daily [app]. Reason 2: Poor communication means problems are not shared or standardised [k], so quality checks are skipped or duplicated across the 3 shifts running the 900,000-jar annual output [app].

knowledge_max_2: lack of communication means faults/problems are not shared or fixed quickly

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Briarfield of horizontal integration with Hearthwick Conserves.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Horizontal integration removes a competitor from the market [k], because buying Hearthwick for $1.8 million adds 60,000 jars a month of output to Briarfield's 900,000 jars a year [app], increasing market share and spreading fixed costs over more units [an]. Benefit 2: The combined business gains purchasing and marketing economies of scale [k], as shared buying of jars and chutney ingredients and a wider distribution reach follow the merger [app], helping push the $270,000 profit towards the $400,000 target [an].

However, organic growth is cheaper and tackles the real cause of failure [k], because slowing expansion, adding 2 supervisors and a shift handover process would fix the poor communication behind the 140 jars rejected daily [app], cutting waste before scale increases further [an]. Overall, I think Briarfield should grow organically first [eval], because merging two businesses while communication between the 3 shifts is broken would likely worsen diseconomies rather than cure them [eval].

scenario_stem:
Calderwell Creamery Ltd is a private limited company pasteurising milk and making cheese for supermarkets. The directors must choose between Option 1, a special dividend of $20,000, and Option 2, investing $50,000 in a new pasteuriser to raise production capacity.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit'.
questions.model_answer: Gross Profit is the profit made after deducting the cost of producing or buying the goods sold, calculated as Revenue minus Cost of Sales, before deducting Expenses [2].

Calculated before any expenses are deducted

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit is important to Calderwell Creamery Ltd.

Reason 2: Profit rewards shareholders for their investment [k], which allowed the $30,000 dividend to be paid and supports investor confidence in the company [app].

Point 2: It shows Retained Profit of $54,000 after the $30,000 dividend [k], so the $50,000 pasteuriser is feasible from internal funds with $4,000 headroom [app], leaving directors free to reject new debt for this purchase [an].

scenario_stem:
Coral Bay Berry Farm is a sole trader growing strawberries and blueberries in Country X. Its 26 pickers harvested 120 tonnes, sold to Country X supermarkets at $4.20 per kilogram, earning $504,000; $60,000 went on refrigerated storage.

A refrigerated cargo flight cuts Country V delivery from 9 days by sea to 14 hours. Three supermarkets offer $6.50 per kilogram for 30 tonnes, but air freight is $1.40 per kilogram and certificates cost $18,000 yearly. Elena must decide whether to export or stay domestic.

questions.question_text: Define 'exports'.
questions.model_answer: Exports are goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in another country. [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation has increased, using Coral Bay Berry Farm as context.

[k] The new refrigerated cargo flight has cut the delivery journey to Country V from 9 days by sea to 14 hours by air. [app] Reason 2: The growth of multinational supermarket chains creates demand for products across many countries. [k] Three Country V supermarkets have offered Elena $6.50 per kilogram, showing overseas buyers are actively seeking Country X fruit. [app]

[app] This extra income would help cover the $60,000 invested in refrigerated storage and lift profits. [an] Opportunity 2: Selling abroad spreads risk across different markets. [k] At present all 120 tonnes of fruit go to Country X supermarkets. [app] If domestic demand fell, sales to Country V would protect the farm's income and the jobs of its 26 seasonal pickers. [an]

scenario_stem:
Brightbyte Apps is a sole trader software start-up founded by Lena Ortiz, building an inventory app from her spare bedroom. 4 shop clients pay $700 each monthly, giving $2,800 revenue against $3,100 costs, and her $14,000 savings are nearly gone.

The New Enterprise Incubator offers 12 months of free desk space, weekly training, mentoring and a $10,000 grant, but requires relocating 40 km to the capital and hiring 1 full-time developer. Lena could stay home-based with no written business plan and no support.

questions.question_text: Define 'business plan'.
questions.model_answer: A business plan is a document that describes the business, its objectives, the market, forecasts and how the business will be financed and run, used to guide the owner and persuade lenders or investors. [2]

Used to guide the business and to persuade financiers to lend or invest

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why many new businesses fail.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Many new businesses lack finance and run out of cash before they become profitable [k]. Lena's revenue of $2,800 is below her monthly costs of $3,100, so she burns through her $14,000 savings every month [app]. Reason 2: Poor planning causes failure because owners do not set objectives or forecast cash needs [k]. Lena has no written business plan, so nobody has tested whether 4 shop clients can ever cover her costs [app].

Poor planning (no business plan or objectives)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Lena may face if she rejects the incubator place.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Without the incubator's weekly training, Lena would lack bookkeeping and marketing skills, which are common causes of start-up failure [k]. She currently has no written business plan and mismanages money, so guessing instead of monitoring means she may not notice that $3,100 of monthly costs are unsustainable [app]. Poor financial control would likely force her to close within months [an]. Problem 2: Rejecting the incubator forfeits the $10,000 grant and free desk space, leaving her to fund everything herself [k]. Her $14,000 savings are nearly exhausted and she still owes money for software tools, so she cannot hire the full-time developer she needs to grow [app]. Without extra hands, app development slows, clients churn and revenue of $2,800 per month stagnates [an].

Rejecting support forfeits grants and resources needed to grow

questions.question_text: Do you think Lena should accept the incubator place? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lena could accept the incubator place because it offers 12 months of free desk space, weekly training and a $10,000 grant, which would fix her two biggest weaknesses: poor planning and lack of finance [k]. With her $14,000 savings nearly exhausted and costs of $3,100 exceeding revenue of $2,800 each month, the grant alone would extend her runway by many months [app]. That extra runway lets her fix the planning weakness before savings run dry, turning a struggling start-up into a sustainable one [an]. However, accepting means relocating 40 km to the capital and hiring at least 1 full-time developer, adding a salary she may not afford [k]. If 4 shop clients cannot grow, the extra wage pushes monthly costs up further and she may be forced to use the $10,000 to cover losses rather than development [an]. On the other hand, remaining home-based keeps overheads minimal and lets her keep control while she wins more clients [app]. Overall, Lena should accept the incubator place because the training would teach her to write a proper business plan and control cash, and the $10,000 grant plus mentoring outweigh the relocation cost, provided she can sign at least 2 new clients first [eval]. Without a written plan she risks becoming another failed start-up, so structured support is the smarter option [eval].

scenario_stem:
Voss Engineering Ltd is a private limited company making hydraulic pumps for agricultural machinery at Dunwick, with 85 production staff. It needs 6 graduate production engineers and shortlisted 18 candidates from 320 applications.

The HR director wants aptitude tests, which test reading engineering drawings and problem-solving before interview, though they cost $1,800 and half a day. The production manager prefers one-to-one interviews, revealing motivation and teamwork. The managing director must choose within three weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'aptitude test'.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using aptitude tests for the graduate engineer recruitment.

Benefit 2: Testing before interviewing filters out unsuitable candidates early [k], so the company avoids wasting interview time and fills the 6 posts within three weeks [app]. [4]

Advantage 2: Interviews are inexpensive to set up and run [k], which matters when filling 6 posts from a shortlist of 18 candidates [app], helping Voss Engineering Ltd control recruitment costs while assessing every candidate properly [an]. scenario_stem:
Fernhill Cycle Works is a family-run sole trader bicycle shop with 11 mechanics, operating 9 years. Revenue slipped from $380,000 to $325,000 in 2 years as 4 online retailers and a national chain entered. Imported bikes cost $120 less than adult mountain bikes.

questions.question_text: Define 'market competition'.
questions.model_answer: The rivalry between businesses operating in the same market to attract the same customers [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the market for bicycles in Country X has become more competitive for Fernhill Cycle Works.

Benefit 2: Differentiates the shop from price-cutting online retailers [k], because 3 free services per bike per year add ongoing value beyond the $120 import saving [app], making customers less likely to switch on price alone [an].

scenario_stem:
Highmere Distribution Ltd is a private limited company running a parcel delivery network in Country X. It expanded to 11 depots, employs 260 drivers and handles 95,000 parcels weekly on $8.4 million revenue. Late deliveries hit 14% and fuel takes 31% of costs.

The operations director proposes 4 regional divisions, each with its own manager, to cut coordination loss. Alternatively, acquire Cruxhill Couriers, a 90-driver rival in 2 southern counties, for $2.6 million, adding national coverage.

questions.question_text: Define 'organic growth'.
questions.model_answer: Organic growth is expansion achieved from within a business, such as opening new depots or investing in new vehicles, rather than by merging with or buying another firm [2].

not through mergers or takeovers (internal methods such as expansion of premises/output)

questions.question_text: Explain two growth problems Highmere faces after expanding to 11 depots.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Coordination loss [k], because 11 depots and 260 staff spread over 4 years of rapid expansion are hard to direct centrally, which is reflected in late deliveries rising to 14% [app]. Problem 2: Falling efficiency and rising costs [k], because fuel already consumes 31% of total costs and 95,000 parcels a week are harder to route and monitor across a large network [app].
