application_max_2: 11 depots and 260 staff after 4 years of expansion
14% late deliveries / 31% of total costs / 95,000 parcels a week

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Highmere of splitting into 4 regional divisions.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Faster, better-informed decisions [k], because each of the 4 regional divisions would have its own manager close to its depots [app], shortening approval chains and cutting the coordination loss that produced 14% late deliveries [an]. Benefit 2: Clearer accountability [k], because division managers would own the performance of the 95,000 parcels handled weekly within their region [app], motivating them to control fuel use and driver productivity [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Highmere should acquire Cruxhill Couriers or split into regional divisions? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Acquiring Cruxhill would add instant capacity and coverage [k], because $2.6 million buys 90 drivers across 2 southern counties, widening Highmere's national network overnight [app], lifting revenue above the current $8.4 million quickly [an]. scenario_stem:

knowledge_max_2: Final profit after all expenses are deducted from gross profit
The amount available to pay dividends and to retain in the business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the change in gross profit margin matters to Hallow Brook Mushrooms.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The margin slid from 40% to 30%, so each $100 of sales now yields only $30 of gross profit instead of $40, squeezing what is left for Expenses and dividends [k][app]. Reason 2: The slide comes from compost and substrate costs, so gross profit of $123,000 barely covers the $98,000 Expenses, leaving just $25,000 before the $12,000 dividend and only $13,000 retained [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: A falling margin leaves less profit per dollar of sales
A falling margin can threaten coverage of overheads and dividends if unchecked
application_max_2: Margin slid from 40% to 30%, $30 per $100 of sales
Gross Profit of $123,000 vs $98,000 Expenses and $12,000 dividend

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the directors could respond to profit for the year falling from $36,000 to $25,000.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Attack Cost of Sales, because the margin drop was driven by substrate costs, so Option 1, switching to a cheaper supplier, could restore gross profit without touching customer prices [k][app][an]. Point 2: Raise prices by 8% (Option 2) to lift Revenue per kilogram [k][app], but risk losing orders if buyers can switch to rival growers, so directors must judge demand sensitivity before acting [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing direct costs raises gross profit and profit for the year
Raising prices raises revenue but may reduce volumes demanded
application_max_2: Option 1 targets the compost and substrate cost rise behind the 30% margin
Option 2, an 8% price rise, lifts revenue per kilogram
analysis_max_2: Cutting input costs protects the margin without risking demand
Price rises risk losing price-sensitive buyers to rival growers

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should switch to the cheaper substrate supplier (Option 1) or raise prices by 8% (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 directly targets the cause of the margin slide, because compost and substrate costs cut the margin from 40% to 30%, so a cheaper supplier could restore gross profit without reducing volumes [k][app][an]. The risk is variable quality, which could lower mushroom yields and damage the shiitake brand [app]. Option 2 lifts Revenue per kilogram and protects profit if volumes hold, but a broad 8% rise could push buyers towards other growers [k][an]. Overall, the directors should choose Option 1 first and only add a modest price rise if the margin does not recover, because fixing the input cost protects competitiveness while a blanket rise risks demand [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Rising input costs should be addressed at source where possible
Price increases must be weighed against demand elasticity
application_max_2: Compost and substrate rise cut margin from 40% to 30%
8% price rise lifts Revenue per kilogram from January 2027
analysis_max_2: Cheaper inputs restore margin without buyer resistance
A broad 8% rise risks losing customers to competitors
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: targets the root cause and protects competitiveness
Overall: Option 1 first, with a small price rise only if margins do not recover

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Velmont Electronics Plc is a multinational public limited company assembling tablets and smartphones. In Country X it proposes a $14 million tablet factory employing 350 workers at 15% above-minimum wages, paying $2.2 million tax yearly and using local suppliers, though profits return home.

Brindleford lost its steel mill; unemployment is 11%. The council offers a 10-year tax break worth $1.5 million, but residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid, untrained work. Rival Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing staff to higher wages.

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company'.
questions.model_answer: A multinational company is a business that operates in more than one country, usually with headquarters in one country and branches, factories or offices overseas. [2].

knowledge_max_2: A business operating in more than one country [1]
Head office in one country with bases/factories overseas [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits a multinational company can bring to a host country.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Multinationals create employment in host countries. [k] Velmont's factory would employ 350 workers in Brindleford, where unemployment stands at 11%. [app] Reason 2: Multinationals bring capital investment and tax revenue. [k] The $14 million factory would pay about $2.2 million a year in corporation tax and buy from local suppliers. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals create jobs in host countries [1]
Multinationals bring investment and tax revenue / use of local suppliers [1]
application_max_2: 350 workers employed in Brindleford where unemployment stands at 11%
$14 million factory paying about $2.2 million a year corporation tax

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Brindleford of welcoming Velmont's factory.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: The factory may harm existing local employers. [k] Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing workers to Velmont's higher wages. [app] Losing skilled staff could force Darrow to cut output or close, reducing competition and choice in Country X. [an] Drawback 2: The factory may impose costs on the local community. [k] Residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid assembly work with little training. [app] These negative effects would fall on the community while most profits return to Velmont's home country, so some wealth would leave Brindleford. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals can damage local rival firms competing for scarce labour [1]
Multinationals can impose negative effects on the local community/environment [1]
application_max_2: Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing workers to 15% above minimum wages
Residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid assembly work with little training
analysis_max_2: Losing skilled workers could bankrupt Darrow, reducing local competition and choice
Community bears external costs while profits flow abroad, weakening net benefit

questions.question_text: Do you think Country X should encourage Velmont to build its factory in Brindleford? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Welcoming Velmont would deliver major economic benefits. [k] The $14 million factory would employ 350 workers and pay about $2.2 million a year in corporation tax, reviving a town with 11% unemployment. [app] Local suppliers could win steady orders, and the $1.5 million 10-year tax break costs less than one year of tax revenue. [an] However, the factory also imposes real costs. [k] Most profits would return to Velmont's home country rather than stay in Country X. [app] Traffic and noise would burden residents, assembly roles offer little training, and Darrow Components risks losing staff from its 90-strong workforce, weakening an existing Country X business. [an] Overall, Country X should welcome Velmont with conditions, such as guaranteed apprenticeships and traffic limits, rather than an unconditional commitment. [eval] On balance, the jobs and tax revenue for a town with 11% unemployment outweigh the drawbacks if firm commitments are negotiated before approval. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals bring jobs, investment and tax revenue [1]
Multinationals take profits abroad and can harm local firms/communities [1]
application_max_2: $14 million factory; 350 jobs; about $2.2 million a year corporation tax in a town with 11% unemployment
10-year tax break worth $1.5 million; Darrow Components employing 90 fears staff losses
analysis_max_2: Jobs for 350 workers plus supplier orders and tax revenue would regenerate Brindleford's economy
Profit outflow, community external costs and harm to Darrow could reduce or outweigh net local gains
evaluation_max_2: Conditional welcome with negotiated safeguards (training, traffic limits)
Weighs regeneration and tax revenue against profit outflow, community costs and harm to local business

scenario_stem:
Solder & Spark Repairs is a sole trader start-up in Redford repairing smartphones and tablets from a high-street unit with 1 part-time technician. It takes $5,600 monthly, including $2,000 of walk-by trade, while rent is $950 a month.

The council enterprise centre offers low-cost premises at $480 monthly for 2 years plus business rates relief, but the unit is 6 km away with no shopfront and half the space. Rafiq can renew the high-street lease or move before it expires on 30 September.

questions.question_text: Define 'tax incentive'.
questions.model_answer: A tax incentive is a reduction in, or relief from, tax offered by the government to encourage businesses to do something, for example investing or creating jobs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A tax reduction/relief offered by the government
Designed to encourage business behaviour such as investing or hiring

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of low-cost premises for a start-up.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Low-cost premises cut fixed costs, leaving more cash for stock and wages [k]. The council's unit costs $480 per month versus $950 on the high street, saving Rafiq $470 per month [app]. Benefit 2: Rates relief lowers the tax burden, improving cash flow in the fragile first years [k]. The enterprise centre adds business rates relief on top of the $480 rent, so a repair start-up keeps more of its $5,600 monthly take [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower fixed costs improve cash flow and survival
Rates relief reduces the tax burden
application_max_2: $480 per month council unit vs $950 high-street lease (saving $470)
Business rates relief on top of the low rent; monthly takings of $5,600

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Solder & Spark Repairs of moving into the enterprise centre.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Moving cuts rent from $950 to $480 per month, saving $470 that can fund spare parts and wages [k]. With monthly takings of $5,600, that saving is over 8% of revenue and would substantially improve cash flow during a weak trading spell [app]. Lower overheads mean the business reaches break-even sooner and is less likely to fail [an]. Benefit 2: Business rates relief and a 2-year fixed rent give certainty for planning [k]. The enterprise centre guarantees $480 per month for 2 years, whereas the high-street lease could be renegotiated upward at renewal [app]. Predictable costs let Rafiq forecast cash properly and price repairs competitively, winning more repeat business [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower rent improves cash flow / speeds break-even
Fixed rent/rates relief gives cost certainty for planning
application_max_2: Move saves $470 per month versus the $950 high-street lease
$5,600 monthly takings; 2 years of fixed $480 rent plus rates relief
analysis_max_2: Lower overheads reduce failure risk and fund growth (parts, wages)
Certainty enables accurate forecasting and competitive pricing, lifting sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Rafiq should move into the enterprise centre premises? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Rafiq could move because the unit costs $480 per month instead of $950, saving $470 — over 8% of his $5,600 monthly revenue and a large cash-flow benefit for a fragile start-up [k]. With rates relief on top, moving directly tackles the cost pressure that sinks many new businesses [app]. A cheaper base improves cash flow every month, compounding into a bigger safety buffer against slow periods [an]. However, the unit is 6 km away with no shopfront and half the floor space, so his $2,000 of monthly walk-by trade may vanish [k]. Losing passing customers to competitors while gaining only $470 per month of rent saving could easily reduce total profit, especially if delivery and remarketing costs rise [an]. On the other hand, renewing at $950 keeps the high-street location and walk-by trade but locks in high fixed costs for 2 years with uncertain takings [app]. Overall, Rafiq should renew the high-street lease if he can keep at least $3,000 of walk-by-driven revenue above the $470 rent saving, but move to the enterprise centre if he has strong online or repeat trade, because location visibility drives repair takings more than rent savings alone [eval]. A short-term town-centre pop-up advert and a strong online booking page could offset the move and make the cheaper unit viable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Low-cost premises cut fixed costs and rate burden
Location affects passing trade and revenue potential
application_max_2: $480 vs $950 (saving $470); $5,600 monthly revenue; $2,000 from walk-by trade
Unit 6 km away, no shopfront, half the floor space, 2-year term, 30 September deadline
analysis_max_2: Rent saving improves cash flow and break-even speed
Loss of walk-by trade could cut revenue by more than the $470 saving
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified recommendation weighing rent savings against location loss
Evaluation tied to visibility of trade and online/repeat customer mix

scenario_stem:
Thorncombe Bay Hotel is a private limited company, a 3-star hotel with 70 bedrooms. Occupancy is 90% in July and August but 35% from November to February. It has 12 full-time housekeepers on 40-hour weeks.

The manager proposes converting 6 full-time housekeeping roles to part-time contracts of 20 hours per week, saving $56,000 a year at $9 an hour and adding flexibility. Experienced staff may resign and part-time workers need more supervision; the decision is due in October.

questions.question_text: Define 'full-time employee'.
questions.model_answer: A full-time employee is a worker contracted for the standard full working week, typically around 35 to 40 hours, usually with regular hours throughout the year and entitlement to full pro-rata holiday and benefits. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Contracted for the standard full working week
Regular hours with full pro-rata holiday and benefits

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Thorncombe Bay Hotel of employing part-time housekeepers.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Part-time housekeepers can be rostered to match seasonal demand, such as the 90% occupancy weeks in July and August [k], so the hotel covers peaks without paying full-time wages in the quiet months [app]. Benefit 2: Converting 6 full-time roles to 20 hours per week saves an estimated $56,000 a year [k], at the $9 hourly rate [app]. [4]

application_max_2: Covers 90% occupancy peak weeks in July and August
Saves about $56,000 a year at the $9 hourly rate

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Thorncombe Bay Hotel of converting the 6 full-time housekeeping roles to part-time contracts.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Experienced full-time housekeepers may resign rather than accept fewer hours [k], meaning the hotel loses staff who know the 70 bedrooms and its standards intimately [app], so room quality could slip precisely when 90% occupancy demands speed and consistency [an]. Disadvantage 2: Part-time staff often need more supervision as more people share the work [k], increasing the housekeeping manager's workload [app], which may offset the $56,000 saving through extra supervisory hours and training [an]. [6]

knowledge_max_2: Experienced staff may resign rather than accept fewer hours
Part-time staff often need more supervision
application_max_2: Loss of knowledge of the 70 bedrooms and hotel standards
Extra supervision and induction for the reduced-hours team
analysis_max_2: Room quality risk at 90% peak occupancy
Supervision and training time may offset the $56,000 saving

questions.question_text: Do you think Thorncombe Bay Hotel should convert the 6 full-time housekeeping roles to part-time contracts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Thorncombe Bay Hotel should convert the roles because occupancy swings from 35% in November to 90% in July and August [k], so matching housekeeping hours to actual occupancy avoids paying for 40-hour weeks when few rooms are let [app]. At the $9 hourly rate, cutting 6 roles from 40 to 20 hours per week saves an estimated $56,000 a year, protecting margins through the seaside off-season [an]. However, experienced full-time housekeepers may leave rather than accept shorter hours [k], taking their knowledge of the 70 bedrooms with them, and recruiting and training new part-time staff would add costs [app], undermining service precisely when 90% occupancy demands speed and consistency [an]. Overall, on balance the hotel should offer the 6 affected housekeepers the part-time contracts first and keep those who accept, because flexibility and the $56,000 saving are real but retaining known, experienced staff protects quality [eval]. Conversions should fall back to natural wastage if too many resign, limiting the operational risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Matching labour hours to seasonal demand
Experienced staff may resign over reduced hours
application_max_2: $56,000 annual saving at the $9 hourly rate
analysis_max_2: Avoids paying idle hours in the off-season
Loss of experienced staff threatens peak-season service
evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement favouring conversion with retention safeguards
Falls back to natural wastage to limit operational risk

scenario_stem:
Tern & Thistle Outdoors is a sole trader outdoor clothing brand with 17 staff, earning $520,000 mostly from technical hiking gear. A survey of 2,000 respondents found 31% practise yoga, while athleisure grows 22% yearly.

The owner compares launching a yoga athleisure line costing $48,000, expected to yield $180,000, with extending the technical hiking range for $22,000; brand recognition is strong among hikers, not yoga users.

questions.question_text: Define 'lifestyle segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Dividing a market into groups based on shared activities, interests, opinions and values [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tern & Thistle Outdoors might segment its market by lifestyle.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lifestyle groups have distinct activities and needs [k], shown by hiking enthusiasts versus the 31% of surveyed consumers practising yoga weekly [app]. Reason 2: Lifestyle segmentation allows targeted product design and promotion [k], letting the brand choose between technical hiking gear and athleisure yoga apparel [app].

knowledge_max_2: lifestyle groups have distinct activities and needs
allows targeted product design and promotion
application_max_2: 31% of surveyed consumers practising yoga weekly

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tern & Thistle Outdoors of launching the yoga athleisure line.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Access to a rapidly growing segment [k], athleisure yoga apparel growing at 22% per year nationally [app], which could lift revenue beyond $520,000 [an]. Benefit 2: Strong year 1 sales forecast [k], with $180,000 expected against the $48,000 launch cost [app], generating a healthy contribution to overheads [an].

knowledge_max_2: access to a rapidly growing segment
application_max_2: athleisure yoga apparel growing at 22% per year
analysis_max_2: generating a healthy contribution to overheads

questions.question_text: Do you think launching the yoga athleisure line is a better decision than extending the technical hiking range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The yoga athleisure line targets an emerging lifestyle segment [k], addressing the 31% of surveyed consumers practising yoga weekly and a market growing at 22% per year [app], diversifying revenue beyond hiking and reducing dependence on one lifestyle group [an]. However, extending the hiking range builds on proven brand recognition [k], leveraging the $520,000 revenue stream and existing outdoor customers for just $22,000 [app], with far lower risk than entering an unfamiliar yoga market [an]. Overall, launching the athleisure line is the better decision because 22% annual growth outweighs incremental jacket sales [eval], provided the $180,000 year 1 forecast proves credible [eval].

knowledge_max_2: athleisure targets an emerging lifestyle segment
hiking extension builds on proven brand recognition
application_max_2: 31% of surveyed consumers practising yoga weekly
analysis_max_2: diversifies revenue and reduces dependence on one group
lower risk than entering an unfamiliar market
evaluation_max_2: weighs 22% annual growth against incremental jacket sales
conditional on the $180,000 year 1 forecast

scenario_stem:
Garside Cement Ltd is a private limited company producing cement in Country X. It employs 260 workers, supplied 480,000 tonnes and earned $14 million. A second kiln brought coordination loss between shifts, causing 2 kiln stoppages and lifting average costs from $27 to $31 per tonne.

It could buy Tarnfell Cement's neighbouring plant for $5.2 million, a horizontal integration adding capacity and removing a rival. Or stay independent: invest $800,000 in planning software and reorganise into 3 production cells to return costs to $27.

questions.question_text: Define 'fixed costs'.
questions.model_answer: Fixed costs are costs that do not vary with the level of output, such as rent and insurance, and must be paid even if nothing is produced [2].

knowledge_max_2: costs that do not change with output level
examples: rent, insurance, salaries of managers (must be paid regardless of output)

questions.question_text: Explain two diseconomies of scale affecting Garside.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Coordination loss [k], because the two shifts operating the second kiln cannot synchronise maintenance and loading, causing 2 kiln stoppages [app]. Problem 2: Rising average cost [k], because stoppages and poor coordination pushed average cost from $27 to $31 per tonne, about $1.92 million extra at 480,000 tonnes [app].

knowledge_max_2: coordination loss (failure to align across departments/shifts)
rising average costs as scale increases (diseconomies of scale)
application_max_2: average cost rose from $27 to $31 per tonne / 480,000 tonnes

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Garside of buying Tarnfell Cement's plant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Horizontal integration removes its closest rival [k], because buying Tarnfell's neighbouring plant for $5.2 million adds capacity and ends direct local price competition [app], spreading fixed costs over more tonnes [an]. Benefit 2: Potential economies of scale [k], as shared purchasing of fuel and maintenance across two plants lowers average cost from the $31 peak [app], lifting profit on the $14 million revenue towards the $27 target [an].

knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration removes a competitor/gains share and capacity
economies of scale (purchasing/technical savings) reduce average cost
application_max_2: $5.2 million for Tarnfell Cement's neighbouring plant
average cost $31 peak / $14 million revenue target of $27
analysis_max_2: fixed costs spread over more output lowers average cost
removing a rival raises pricing power and margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Garside should buy Tarnfell Cement's plant or reorganise internally? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying Tarnfell gives instant capacity and removes the closest rival [k], because $5.2 million secures a neighbouring plant and ends its competition, pushing Garside towards economies of scale [app], which could cut average cost below the current $31 per tonne [an]. However, internal reorganisation is cheaper and fixes the real cause [k], because $800,000 of shift-planning software plus 3 production cells would end the coordination loss and 2 kiln stoppages driving costs from $27 to $31 [app], saving about $1.92 million a year at 480,000 tonnes without any integration risk [an]. Overall, I think Garside should reorganise internally first [eval], because buying another plant before fixing coordination would simply double the diseconomies that are already costing it margin [eval].

knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration adds capacity/removes rival but risks importing its problems
internal reorganisation fixes coordination/communication cheaply and directly
application_max_2: $5.2 million takeover of Tarnfell Cement / 480,000 tonnes / $14 million revenue
$800,000 software and 3 production cells / 2 kiln stoppages / $27 to $31
analysis_max_2: takeover raises scale quickly to unlock economies of scale
fixing coordination restores average cost (~$1.92 million a year saving) without takeover risk
evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on takeover vs reorganisation, justified with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Farthing Poultry Ltd is a private limited company processing free-range chickens. Revenue was $650,000, Gross Profit $260,000 and Expenses $225,000, leaving Profit for the year of $35,000; a $10,000 dividend left Retained Profit of $25,000.

A new chilling unit added $54,000 to overheads and drivers' overtime rose $18,000. Though gross profit margin is 40%, profit margin is about 5%. Directors weigh Option 1, cutting overtime and Saturday processing to save $28,000, against Option 2, raising prices by 4%.

questions.question_text: Calculate the retained profit for the year.
questions.model_answer: Retained Profit = Profit for the year − Dividends = $35,000 − $10,000 = $25,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Correct method: profit for the year minus dividends paid

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Farthing Poultry's expenses are a concern.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Expenses of $225,000 absorb most of the $260,000 Gross Profit [k], leaving only $35,000 of profit despite a healthy 40% gross profit margin [app]. Reason 2: The chilling unit lease added $54,000 and drivers' overtime rose by $18,000 [k], so costs jumped sharply and could persist, threatening the $25,000 Retained Profit [app].

knowledge_max_2: High expenses consume gross profit and squeeze final profit
Sudden cost increases may persist and repeat in future years
application_max_2: $225,000 Expenses vs $260,000 Gross Profit leaving only $35,000

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a profit margin of only about 5% should worry the directors and shareholders.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Profit for the year of $35,000 is only about 5% of Revenue [k], so the business has almost no cushion if wages or feed prices rise again [app], leaving dividends and reinvestment exposed [an]. Point 2: Lower profit means smaller dividends and retention, and with just $10,000 paid out the company has limited room to fund improvements from its $25,000 Retained Profit [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A low profit margin leaves a tiny cushion against cost increases
A low profit margin restricts dividends and retained profit for reinvestment
application_max_2: Only $10,000 dividend paid from $25,000 Retained Profit
analysis_max_2: Any further cost rise could erase the thin profit
Shareholders face smaller returns and the firm faces a funding squeeze

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should cut expenses by $28,000 a year (Option 1) or raise prices by 4% (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 saves a guaranteed $28,000 a year by cutting overtime and closing Saturday processing [k][app], which would lift Profit for the year from $35,000 to about $63,000 and restore the cushion the business now lacks [an]. The risk is losing butchers and restaurants that rely on Saturday supply. Option 2 should add about $26,000 of Revenue a year at 4% and is simple to implement [k], though customers may resist rises while cheaper imported chicken exists [app][an]. Overall, the directors should choose Option 1, because removing avoidable overtime tackles the root cause of expense bloat and protects the 5% margin without alienating customers; a modest price rise can follow once service levels stabilise [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting unnecessary costs raises profit without raising prices
Price increases raise revenue but risk losing price-sensitive customers
application_max_2: $28,000 saving lifts profit from $35,000 to about $63,000
analysis_max_2: Removing overtime addresses the cause of the expense surge
Customers may switch to cheaper imports if prices rise
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: guaranteed saving, protects margin and customer relationships
Overall: Option 1 first; a modest price rise later once service stabilises

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eastvale Bicycle Works is a private limited company assembling e-bikes in Country X. It made 28,000 last year, 70% abroad, earning $11.2 million. Rising costs push production to $290 a bike versus $230 in Country Q.

Country Q offers a 10-year tax holiday, one-third lower wages and a $2 million grant. Moving cuts costs $60 a bike, but closing the Country X factory makes 140 workers redundant and adds $9 a bike for buyers. It must decide: relocate or stay.

questions.question_text: Define 'host country'.
questions.model_answer: A host country is a country in which a foreign-owned business establishes operations, such as a factory, while ownership remains based elsewhere. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Country where a foreign firm operates [1]
Firm remains owned from abroad / overseas head office [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a business might locate in a host country such as Country Q.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Host countries often offer lower labour and production costs. [k] Country Q's wages are one-third lower, cutting Eastvale's cost from $290 to about $230 per bike. [app] Reason 2: Host governments often offer financial incentives to attract foreign firms. [k] Country Q is offering a 10-year tax holiday and a $2 million grant for setting up there. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Lower labour/production costs in some host countries [1]
Host governments offer incentives such as tax breaks and grants [1]
application_max_2: Country Q wages one-third lower, cutting cost from $290 to about $230 per bike
10-year tax holiday and a $2 million grant offered to attract Eastvale

questions.question_text: Explain two impacts on stakeholders if Eastvale relocates to Country Q.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Country X employees would lose their jobs. [k] Closing the Country X factory would make 140 workers redundant. [app] Lost wages and skills would harm families and cut spending at local shops, damaging the wider community. [an] Point 2: Country X customers would pay more for their bikes. [k] Shipping from Country Q would add about $9 per bike. [app] Some buyers may switch to rival brands, cutting Eastvale's home-market sales and damaging its reputation. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Relocation can make the existing workforce redundant [1]
Customers face extra costs such as shipping from abroad [1]
application_max_2: Closing the Country X factory would make 140 workers redundant
Country X buyers would pay about $9 extra per bike in shipping
analysis_max_2: Redundancies harm household incomes, local spending and the factory town's economy
Higher prices may push customers to rivals, eroding home-market share and reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Eastvale should relocate its factory to Country Q? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relocating would make Eastvale far more competitive. [k] The move cuts production cost by $60 per bike, from $290 to $230, saving roughly $1.68 million a year on 28,000 bikes, before the $2 million grant. [app] Lower costs would protect the 70% of output sold abroad on $11.2 million revenue and keep Eastvale ahead of rivals. [an] However, relocation carries heavy costs for stakeholders. [k] 140 skilled Country X workers would lose their jobs, damaging morale and the company's local reputation. [app] Country X buyers would pay about $9 extra per bike, severance pay would be owed, and moving plant and staff could take a year, so savings would not be immediate. [an] Overall, Eastvale should relocate only after exhausting home-efficiency options, since losing 140 workers and its domestic base is hard to reverse. [eval] On balance, the $1.68 million annual saving strongly favours moving in the long run, but the board must price in redundancy and transition costs before deciding. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Relocation can cut costs and improve competitiveness [1]
Relocation harms existing workers, customers and the firm's reputation [1]
application_max_2: $60 saving per bike on 28,000 bikes (about $1.68 million a year) from $290 to $230
140 redundancies; $9 extra per bike for Country X buyers; $2 million grant and 10-year tax holiday
analysis_max_2: Savings plus incentives protect 70% overseas sales on $11.2 million revenue against rivals
Redundancy, severance, transition costs and higher customer prices could offset early savings
evaluation_max_2: Relocate only after exhausting domestic efficiency savings
Weighs long-run competitiveness against stakeholder harm and transition costs

scenario_stem:
Copperladle Street Food is a sole trader start-up in Dunmore serving jollof rice and grilled chicken from a truck, with 2 part-time assistants. It took $14,500 in its first 4 months, about $121 per trading day, and Blessing wants a second truck.

The youth enterprise grant offers $9,000 for hiring an unemployed 18–24-year-old full-time for 12 months, with a business plan within 60 days. Dunmore Bank offers $9,000 at 11% over 3 years with no conditions. Blessing has a candidate but worries about paperwork.

questions.question_text: Define 'start-up capital'.
questions.model_answer: Start-up capital is the finance needed to open a new business, for example to buy equipment, premises, stock and to cover running costs before sales begin. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Finance required to start a new business
Used for equipment, premises, stock and running costs before revenue flows

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for a start-up of receiving a grant rather than a loan.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A grant does not have to be repaid, so there is no interest and no debt burden [k]. Dunmore Bank's $9,000 loan at 11% over 3 years would add about $2,970 of interest, whereas the $9,000 youth enterprise grant is free [app]. Benefit 2: Grants often come with extra support such as mentoring or training [k]. The youth grant is tied to a written business plan, pushing Blessing to plan properly and cutting her risk of failure [app].

knowledge_max_2: Grants need not be repaid (no interest or debt)
Grants often bundle support/mentoring and force planning
application_max_2: $9,000 grant vs $9,000 loan at 11% over 3 years (about $2,970 interest)
Written business plan required within 60 days of the grant

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of taking the bank loan instead of the youth enterprise grant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The loan costs about $2,970 in interest over 3 years, an extra outgoing the young business cannot easily absorb [k]. Blessing is averaging about $121 per trading day, so loan repayments would absorb a large slice of daily takings [app]. Heavy repayments reduce working capital, increase the risk of cash-flow failure and could force her to cut the 2 part-time assistants [an]. Problem 2: Unlike the grant, the loan builds debt and offers no training or plan support [k]. The grant requires a written plan, which would discipline her growth, whereas the loan simply adds $9,000 of liability with no mentoring [app]. Without structured planning she risks repeating the errors of under-priced menus and weak records that sink most food start-ups [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest/debt increases outgoings and financial risk
Loans lack the planning support bundled with grants
application_max_2: $9,000 loan at 11% over 3 years (about $2,970 interest) on takings of about $121 per day
Grant requires a plan in 60 days and 1 unemployed 18–24-year-old full-time for 12 months
analysis_max_2: Repayments drain working capital, raising risk of cash-flow insolvency
Absence of planning support increases likelihood of avoidable failure

questions.question_text: Do you think Blessing should accept the youth enterprise grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Blessing could accept the grant because $9,000 free money would fund a second truck without adding the $2,970 interest of the bank loan [k]. Having taken $14,500 across her first 4 months at about $121 a day, the grant would let her attack the evening markets quickly rather than wait to save the money [app]. Faster expansion while momentum is strong helps her secure prime evening slots before competitors do [an]. However, the grant obliges her to employ at least 1 unemployed 18–24-year-old full-time for 12 months and file a written business plan within 60 days [k]. If the evening trade underperforms, the compulsory wage plus plan obligations could sink the business faster than a flexible loan would [an]. On the other hand, the bank loan of $9,000 at 11% over 3 years is unconditional, so she could hire anyone, keep flexible hours and restructure if evening markets fail [app]. Overall, Blessing should accept the youth enterprise grant, because the $2,970 interest saving and the structured plan discipline outweigh the hiring condition, especially as she has already interviewed a suitable young assistant [eval]. If she cannot trust the 12-month demand forecast for evening markets, the loan's flexibility is the safer fallback [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grant is free but conditional (full-time hire, plan, reporting)
Loan costs interest but is unconditional and flexible
application_max_2: $9,000 grant vs $9,000 loan at 11% over 3 years (about $2,970 interest)
Takings of $14,500 in first 4 months (about $121 per day); suitable young assistant interviewed
analysis_max_2: Avoiding interest preserves cash during fragile early months
Compulsory hire/plan obligations strain cash if evening markets disappoint
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified recommendation weighing grant savings against conditions
Evaluation tied to the hire already interviewed and demand-forecast risk

scenario_stem:
Redfen Foods Ltd is a private limited company bakery with 48 staff producing bread for supermarkets. It needs a quality control manager to check 9,000 loaves a day. The last left after 3 months, costing $11,000 in waste and a $60,000-a-month contract.

Candidates: Lena Park, a food technologist seeking $38,000, and Sam Doyle, an apprentice with 2 years' experience seeking $27,000. Faults could risk contracts worth $720,000 a year, so the director must appoint the right person.

questions.question_text: Define 'interview'.
questions.model_answer: An interview is a selection method in which an employer asks a candidate questions, face to face or remotely, to assess their suitability, experience, skills and motivation for a vacancy. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Employer asks candidates questions face to face or remotely
Assesses suitability, experience, skills and motivation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why filling the quality control manager vacancy with the right person is important for Redfen Foods Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The right quality control manager can prevent faults across the 9,000 loaves checked each day [k], avoiding repeat complaints like those that cost the $60,000 a month supermarket contract [app]. Reason 2: A poor appointment risks further waste [k], such as the $11,000 in ingredients lost after the last hire, and could threaten the remaining contracts worth $720,000 a year [app]. [4]

knowledge_max_2: Avoids waste and repeat quality failures
application_max_2: Protects the $60,000 a month supermarket contract
Prevents further $11,000 ingredient losses and risks to $720,000 a year of contracts

questions.question_text: Explain two ways interviews can help Redfen Foods Ltd choose the right quality control manager.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Interviews let managers probe food safety knowledge and how candidates handled past quality incidents [k], revealing whether Lena Park's food technologist experience or Sam Doyle's 2 years of internal exposure matches the role [app], so the director can judge real competence rather than CV claims alone [an]. Way 2: Interviews assess communication and leadership skills [k], essential for a manager who must enforce standards across 48 staff [app], reducing the risk of another appointment leaving after 3 months [an]. [6]

application_max_2: Compares Lena Park's experience with Sam Doyle's 2 years
Tests ability to lead standards across 48 staff
analysis_max_2: Judges real competence rather than claims on paper
Reduces risk of another short-lived appointment after 3 months

questions.question_text: Do you think Redfen Foods Ltd should appoint Lena Park or Sam Doyle as quality control manager? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Redfen Foods Ltd should appoint Lena Park because she is an experienced food technologist whose $38,000 asking salary is justified by proven expertise [k], and her appointment directly addresses the complaints and $11,000 ingredient waste that cost a $60,000 a month contract [app]. Protecting the remaining $720,000 a year of contracts makes her premium over $27,000 easily recoverable [an]. However, Sam Doyle is an internal apprentice asking just $27,000 with 2 years of experience [k], and hiring him rewards loyalty, signals promotion prospects to the other 48 staff and avoids repeating the external mis-hire [app], though his limited supervisory experience means faults could persist if he is promoted too quickly [an]. Overall, on balance the company should appoint Lena Park, because food safety failures threaten $720,000 a year of contracts and the previous hire failed within 3 months, so verified expertise outweighs the $11,000 salary saving [eval]. Sam should be retained as her deputy to keep his loyalty and develop him toward the role later [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Experienced food technologist versus internal apprentice
Salary difference reflects experience and risk
application_max_2: Lena directly addresses complaints and $11,000 ingredient waste
Protects $720,000 a year of remaining contracts
analysis_max_2: Premium salary is recoverable against contract losses
Sam's inexperience could perpetuate faults despite loyalty gains
evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement favouring Lena Park on verified expertise
Suggests Sam as deputy to manage risk and retain talent

scenario_stem:
Redbridge Bakery & Deli is a sole trader bakery with 8 staff, earning $265,000. Regulars are 60% of sales and average spend is $6.40. A national bakery chain opened 300 metres away and till receipts show visits down 12% in 3 weeks.

The owner weighs a stamp-card loyalty scheme where 9 stamps earn a free 10th coffee, costing $9,000 with training, against cutting all prices by 10%. Both will be reviewed after 6 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'customer loyalty'.
questions.model_answer: The willingness of customers to continue buying from the same business rather than switching to rivals [2].

knowledge_max_2: customers continuing to buy from the same business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why maintaining customer loyalty is important to Redbridge Bakery & Deli.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Loyal customers generate repeat purchases [k], with regulars accounting for 60% of $265,000 annual sales [app]. Reason 2: Retaining customers is cheaper than attracting new ones [k], which matters because a national bakery chain opened 300 metres away last month [app].

knowledge_max_2: retaining customers is cheaper than attracting new ones
application_max_2: national bakery chain opened 300 metres away

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redbridge Bakery & Deli of introducing the stamp-card loyalty scheme.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Encourages repeat visits and higher purchase frequency [k], rewarding the regulars who drive 60% of sales through the free 10th coffee offer [app], defending footfall against the new chain [an]. Benefit 2: Provides information on customer buying habits [k], as stamp-card redemptions reveal visit frequency against the $6.40 average spend [app], helping the owner target promotions more effectively [an].

analysis_max_2: defends footfall against the new chain

questions.question_text: Do you think introducing the stamp-card loyalty scheme is a better response to the new national chain opening 300 metres away than reducing all prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The loyalty scheme rewards repeat behaviour [k], strengthening relationships with the customers driving 60% of $265,000 annual sales and costing only $9,000 to set up [app], protecting margin while building long-term attachment [an]. However, reducing prices by 10% is immediate and attracts price-sensitive shoppers [k], directly countering the national chain 300 metres away across every purchase [app], though it cuts margin on the $265,000 revenue and can be matched by the chain [an]. Overall, the stamp-card loyalty scheme is the better response because it builds durable loyalty rather than starting a price war [eval], provided the chain cannot undercut on both price and convenience [eval].

knowledge_max_2: loyalty scheme rewards repeat behaviour / builds attachment
price cut is immediate and attracts price-sensitive shoppers
analysis_max_2: price cut cuts margin and can be matched by the chain
evaluation_max_2: weighs durable loyalty against an immediate price war
conditional on the chain not undercutting on price and convenience

scenario_stem:
Thornby Hotels Ltd is a private limited company running 9 mid-range hotels in Country X with 720 staff. Revenue fell from $19 million to $16 million, occupancy to 66% and satisfaction to 71%. With 6 levels of management, approvals now take 8 weeks.

Kestreldon Hotels offers 4 hotels totalling 340 rooms for $9 million, a horizontal integration promising bulk-buying economies. Alternatively, delayer by removing 2 management levels, saving $650,000 yearly to reinvest in the existing hotels.

questions.question_text: Define 'delayering'.
questions.model_answer: Delayering is the removal of one or more levels of management from a business hierarchy, shortening the chain of command and widening spans of control [2].

knowledge_max_2: removing levels of management from the hierarchy
shortens chain of command / widens span of control / speeds decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by slow decision-making at Thornby.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Lost competitiveness [k], because 8-week approval cycles for pricing and refurbishments let rivals react fast, contributing to occupancy falling to 66% and revenue dropping from $19 million to $16 million [app]. Problem 2: Falling guest satisfaction and morale [k], because 6 levels of management distance staff from decisions, and satisfaction slipped to 71% [app].

knowledge_max_2: low morale/satisfaction as decisions take too long
application_max_2: 8-week approvals and revenue fall from $19 million to $16 million / occupancy 66%
6 levels of management / satisfaction slipped to 71%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Thornby of delayering 2 management levels.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Faster decisions [k], because removing 2 of the 6 levels shortens the chain of command between 720 staff and senior managers [app], ending the 8-week approval delays for pricing and refurbishment [an]. Benefit 2: Lower overheads [k], because delayering saves an estimated $650,000 a year in management salaries [app], directly improving profit at a time when revenue has fallen to $16 million [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower overhead costs (fewer managers to pay)
application_max_2: $650,000 a year saved / 8-week delays / revenue $16 million
analysis_max_2: quicker refurbishment and pricing response improves occupancy/competitiveness
cost savings flow straight to profit when revenue is falling

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornby should buy the 4 Kestreldon hotels or delayer and invest in its existing hotels? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the hotels would add instant scale [k], because $9 million secures 4 hotels with 340 rooms, and horizontal integration could spread marketing and bulk-buying costs across 13 hotels [app], lifting revenue beyond $16 million and filling empty rooms quickly [an]. However, delayering fixes the disease, not the symptom [k], because removing 2 levels saves $650,000 a year and ends 8-week approvals before new hotels are added [app], improving satisfaction at the 9 existing hotels where it has already slipped to 71% [an]. Overall, I think Thornby should delayer and reinvest in its estate [eval], because slow decision-making would simply be amplified across a bigger group if it is not cured first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration gives instant scale and shared economies of scale
delayering saves costs and speeds up decisions at existing sites
application_max_2: $9 million for 4 Kestreldon hotels, 340 rooms / 9 existing hotels / $16 million revenue
removing 2 levels saving $650,000 a year / 8-week delays / 71% satisfaction
analysis_max_2: takeover lifts capacity and shared savings improve competitiveness fast
delayering cuts overheads and fixes approval delays, improving service at existing hotels
evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on takeover vs delayering, justified with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Quincefield Orchards Ltd is a private limited company growing quinces and apples. Profit for the year fell from $52,500 in 2025 to $44,000 in 2026, while Revenue reached $330,000; after dividends, Retained Profit was $24,000. The gross profit margin fell from 50% to 40% as orchard labour and packing costs rose.

Directors weigh Option 1, selling surplus fruit to a juice contractor at $0.80 a kilogram, against Option 2, investing $55,000 in on-site juicing equipment.

questions.question_text: Identify two items found in an income statement.
questions.model_answer: Revenue and Gross Profit are two items found in an income statement [2].

knowledge_max_2: Any two components named, e.g. revenue, cost of sales, gross profit
Any two further components, e.g. expenses, profit for the year, retained profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why comparing two years of income statements helps Quincefield Orchards.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It shows trends, with the gross profit margin sliding from 50% to 40% [k], signalling rising orchard labour and packing costs that a single year would hide [app]. Reason 2: It reveals that Profit for the year fell from $52,500 to $44,000 despite Revenue growing to $330,000 [k], so directors see that growth without profitability is possible [app].

knowledge_max_2: Comparisons reveal trends and changes over time
Comparisons separate revenue growth from profit growth
application_max_2: Gross profit margin slid from 50% to 40% on higher labour and packing costs
Profit fell from $52,500 to $44,000 while Revenue reached $330,000

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the directors could use the falling gross profit margin to make decisions.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: The margin fell from 50% to 40% as labour and packing costs rose [k], so directors should find which input costs grew and renegotiate or mechanise to restore the spread [app], protecting profit per kilogram sold [an]. Point 2: Profit for the year dropped $8,500 to $44,000 and Retained Profit fell to $24,000 [k], so directors must judge whether Option 2's juicing equipment needs a loan in addition to internal funds [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Margin analysis locates where costs rose or prices lagged
Falling retained profit constrains the funding of investments
application_max_2: Margin fell from 50% to 40% on orchard labour and packing costs
Retained Profit fell to $24,000; juicing equipment costs $55,000
analysis_max_2: Targeting the input-cost rise restores profit without price changes
A funding gap may force borrowing for the juicing equipment

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should sell surplus fruit to the juice contractor at $0.80 a kilogram (Option 1) or invest $55,000 in on-site juicing equipment (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 quickly converts surplus fruit into Revenue at $0.80 a kilogram without the $55,000 outlay, but it locks the orchard into a thin margin that does nothing to repair the 40% gross profit margin [k][app][an]. Option 2 keeps juicing in-house, should lift gross profit per kilogram and support the $330,000 Revenue base [k], but Retained Profit is only $24,000 so a bank loan would be needed alongside [app][an]. Overall, the directors should choose Option 2, because building juice capacity addresses the margin slide permanently and adds a branded revenue stream; the contractor is a short-term cash fix that keeps the orchard in low-value sales [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Selling surplus stock quickly generates cash without capital spending
In-house processing can capture higher value-added margins
application_max_2: Option 1 pays $0.80 per kilogram with no equipment spend
Option 2 costs $55,000; only $24,000 Retained Profit available
analysis_max_2: Contractor route avoids debt but keeps margins thin
In-house juicing raises value-added profit but needs external finance
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: immediate cash, no borrowing, uses surplus fruit
Overall: Option 2 builds long-term margin and a brand; contractor is only a stopgap

scenario_stem:
Northharbour Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in Country X roasting coffee. Its 32 staff roast 240 tonnes yearly, sold at $14 per kilogram for about $3.36 million; most green beans come from Country W.

A free trade agreement with Country W abolished the 15% import tariff on green beans. Costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 a kilogram, saving $192,000. But Country W roasters sell in Country X at 8% above Northharbour's prices, and two brands have taken shelf space.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff, quota or import licence, usually intended to protect domestic firms. [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the removal of trade barriers encourages globalisation.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Removing tariffs makes imported goods cheaper and more competitive. [k] Northharbour's bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram once the 15% tariff was abolished, saving about $192,000 a year. [app] Reason 2: Free trade agreements open markets to businesses from partner countries. [k] The Country X–Country W deal has let larger Country W roasters sell into Country X supermarkets. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Removing tariffs lowers import prices and increases competitiveness [1]
Free trade agreements open markets between partner countries [1]
application_max_2: 15% import tariff abolished; bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year
Country W roasters now selling into Country X under the free trade agreement

questions.question_text: Explain two threats that the tariff removal creates for Northharbour Coffee Roasters.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Foreign competitors can now enter Northharbour's home market. [k] Country W's larger roasters can sell into Country X at only 8% above Northharbour's prices. [app] Their scale lets them undercut on supermarket shelves, threatening Northharbour's sales to cafés and shops. [an] Threat 2: Competition may force Northharbour to cut its prices. [k] Two Country W brands have already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets. [app] If Northharbour matches lower prices, the $192,000 bean saving could be swallowed by a reduced margin on its $14 per kilogram coffee. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Foreign competitors can enter the home market after tariffs fall [1]
Greater rivalry puts downward pressure on price and margin [1]
application_max_2: Country W roasters can sell at only 8% above Northharbour's prices
Two Country W brands already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets
analysis_max_2: Under-cutting at 8% or less erodes Northharbour's shelf position and café/shop sales
Price matching would absorb the $192,000 saving into a lower margin on $14 coffee

questions.question_text: Do you think the tariff removal will benefit Northharbour Coffee Roasters overall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The tariff removal gives Northharbour a genuine cost advantage. [k] Bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year across 240 tonnes. [app] Northharbour can hold prices steady, protect its 32 staff and reinvest the saving in quality and promotion. [an] However, the same agreement threatens Northharbour's home market. [k] Country W's larger roasters can now undercut within 8% of Northharbour's prices, and two Country W brands already occupy supermarket shelves. [app] If forced to match lower prices, the $192,000 saving could be wiped out, and Northharbour cannot match rivals' national advertising budgets. [an] Overall, Northharbour should use the saving to differentiate, such as launching speciality single-origin roasts that mass-market foreign brands cannot easily copy. [eval] On balance, the $192,000 annual saving is real but temporary, so long-term success depends on defending loyal café customers and a distinctive quality niche. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Tariff removal cuts input costs, helping margins [1]
Tariff removal also admits foreign competitors to the home market [1]
application_max_2: Bean costs down $5.20 to $4.40, saving about $192,000 a year on 240 tonnes
Country W brands undercut within 8% and hold supermarket shelf space; current revenue about $3.36 million
analysis_max_2: Saving can fund promotion, protect 32 jobs and defend price positioning
Price war could consume the saving and erode Northharbour's share against bigger rivals
evaluation_max_2: Use the saving to differentiate into speciality/quality niches
Weighs cost benefit against competitive threat and limited marketing resources

scenario_stem:
Fallow & Forge Woodworks is a sole trader start-up in Elmridge making handmade oak tables and benches with 1 part-time helper. It earned $21,000 revenue and $3,500 profit after $17,500 costs, but orders exceed capacity by 40%.

The enterprise zone offers units at $350 monthly for 3 years plus a $6,000 relocation grant, provided each business creates 2 jobs and signs a 12-month minimum lease. Callum could hire 2 workers and meet demand, but adds $350 in monthly rent; staying grows slowly.

questions.question_text: Define 'enterprise zone'.
questions.model_answer: An enterprise zone is an area designated by the government where businesses receive incentives such as low-cost premises, tax breaks or grants to encourage them to set up there. [2]

knowledge_max_2: An area designated by the government for business incentives
Offers incentives such as low-cost premises, tax breaks or grants

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government offers low-cost premises to start-ups.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Low-cost premises remove the biggest barrier to starting, lack of affordable space [k]. The zone offers units at $350 per month for 3 years, far below normal commercial rents, helping a young firm like Fallow & Forge afford proper premises [app]. Reason 2: The policy stimulates local jobs and enterprise in targeted regions [k]. The zone pays a $6,000 relocation grant but demands at least 2 jobs, directly reducing unemployment in Elmridge [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower premises costs remove a barrier to business creation
Stimulates local employment and regional regeneration
application_max_2: Units at $350 per month for 3 years
$6,000 relocation grant tied to at least 2 jobs in Elmridge

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Fallow & Forge may face if it moves into the enterprise zone.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The move adds $350 of rent each month, an extra $4,200 a year against current zero overheads [k]. Callum made only $3,500 profit on $21,000 revenue last year, so this new fixed cost alone could wipe out his margin [app]. If orders slow after the move, the 12-month minimum lease locks him into payments he cannot escape [an]. Problem 2: The 2-job requirement means hiring and managing workers before he is ready [k]. He currently employs 1 part-time helper and may lack the cash flow or supervision skills to run a bigger team [app]. Paying 2 wages before extra sales arrive drains cash, the most common killer of fast-growing start-ups [an].

knowledge_max_2: New fixed costs raise break-even and risk in early years
Forced hiring adds wage and management burdens before sales arrive
application_max_2: $350 per month extra rent; $4,200 a year; profit only $3,500 on $21,000 revenue
12-month minimum lease; 2-job requirement; currently 1 part-time helper
analysis_max_2: Higher fixed costs reduce profit and raise failure risk if demand falls
Wage outgoings before revenue growth cause cash shortages and failure

questions.question_text: Do you think Callum should move into the enterprise zone? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Callum could move because the enterprise zone offers units at $350 per month for 3 years plus a $6,000 relocation grant, immediately boosting capacity for orders exceeding it by 40% [k]. Meeting demand now would protect his reputation and let revenue grow well beyond $21,000 without years of slow organic expansion [app]. Extra capacity plus the grant means wages are covered while he scales, reducing the danger of overstretching [an]. However, the move adds $350 a month of rent against profits of only $3,500, and forces at least 2 jobs plus a 12-month minimum lease [k]. If oak orders slip seasonally, fixed rent and 2 wages would consume the grant within months and push the business towards failure [an]. On the other hand, staying home keeps costs at zero and profit at $3,500 untouched, but his 40% capacity gap means he keeps turning down customers who may not return [app]. Overall, Callum should move, but only after using the $6,000 grant to fund the 2 workers for the first 12 months and securing written orders covering at least half of the new capacity, because the 40% unmet demand is too large to ignore [eval]. If orders cannot be pre-committed, staying home and adding a second machine part-time is the safer step [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Zone offers cheap premises and relocation grant for growth
Zone imposes rent, job and lease obligations
application_max_2: $350 per month for 3 years plus $6,000 grant; 2 jobs; 12-month minimum lease
Orders exceed capacity by 40%; profit $3,500 on $21,000 revenue; 1 part-time helper
analysis_max_2: Cheap capacity and grant enable rapid growth and competitiveness
Fixed rent/wages before sales create cash risk if orders slip
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified recommendation weighing growth opportunity against fixed-cost risk
Evaluation tied to pre-committed orders / using the grant to fund wages

scenario_stem:
Brackmere City Council is a local authority with 1,150 staff delivering waste collection, leisure centres and social care. It uses a standard application form, receiving 260 applications for 8 administrative officer posts last year.

Councillors want CVs instead, saying the form discourages younger applicants, but it supports fair shortlisting and the equal opportunities policy. Rewriting the process costs $4,500 and takes 3 months; 90% of comparable councils still use forms, which are translated into 2 community languages.

questions.question_text: Define 'curriculum vitae (CV)'.
questions.model_answer: A curriculum vitae (CV) is a written summary prepared by a job applicant listing their personal details, qualifications, work history and skills. It is sent to employers when advertisements invite applications rather than use a standard form. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Written summary listing personal details, qualifications and work history
Prepared by the applicant rather than the employer

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brackmere City Council of continuing to use a standard application form.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A standard form means every applicant supplies the same information in the same order [k], so shortlisting the 260 applications for the 8 administrative officer posts is consistent and fair [app]. Benefit 2: Using the form supports the council's equal opportunities policy [k], helping it demonstrate non-discriminatory shortlisting to staff and regulators [app]. [4]

knowledge_max_2: Every applicant supplies the same information in the same format
Supports equal opportunities and defensible shortlisting
application_max_2: Consistent shortlisting of 260 applications for 8 posts
Demonstrates non-discrimination to staff and regulators

questions.question_text: Explain two arguments for the council accepting CVs instead of application forms.
questions.model_answer: Argument 1: CVs let applicants present their experience in a modern, personal format [k], encouraging younger applicants who see the paper form as outdated [app], helping the council compete for talent in social care and leisure roles [an]. Argument 2: Accepting CVs reduces the effort needed for well-prepared applicants [k], so strong candidates in a tight labour market may be more willing to apply to Brackmere City Council [app], widening the pool beyond the 260 received last year [an]. [6]

knowledge_max_2: CVs present experience in a modern, personal format
application_max_2: May attract younger applicants put off by the paper form
Could widen the pool beyond 260 applications
analysis_max_2: Helps compete for talent in social care and leisure roles
Larger, stronger pool raises quality of appointments

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackmere City Council should continue using application forms rather than accept CVs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Brackmere City Council should continue using application forms because 260 applications for 8 administrative officer posts must be shortlisted consistently [k], and the form guarantees comparable information on every candidate, matching the council's equal opportunities policy and its 2 community languages translation [app]. Rewriting the process would cost $4,500 and take 3 months, and with 90% of comparable councils still using forms, the legal and reputational risk of changing outweighs the benefits [an]. However, accepting CVs could modernise recruitment and attract younger applicants put off by the paper form [k], which matters for filling roles quickly in social care and leisure [app], and the $4,500 cost is modest for an organisation employing 1,150 staff [an]. Overall, on balance the council should keep the application form for now because consistency, translations and legal defensibility outweigh the modernising appeal of CVs [eval].
