unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Saltwick Shrimp Co is a private limited company fishing and shelling shrimp near Port Saffron, Country X. Its 44 fishermen and 18 shellers catch 900 tonnes, sold at $5.20 per kilogram to domestic processors for $4.68 million; unemployment is 13%.

Pelagia Seafood Group offers a $9 million plant in Port Saffron within 18 months. It buys 600 tonnes at $5.80 and employs 220 local people, but demands Saltwick stop supplying domestic processors; profits go abroad. Directors must decide: accept or not.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax placed by a government on imported goods, usually charged as a percentage of their value, to protect domestic firms or raise revenue. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Used to protect domestic firms / raise government revenue [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits a multinational company can bring to a host country such as Port Saffron.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Multinationals create jobs in host countries. [k] Pelagia's plant would employ 220 local people where Port Saffron unemployment stands at 13%. [app] Reason 2: Multinationals bring capital investment into the host economy. [k] The $9 million processing plant would modernise the local seafood industry and bring new technology within 18 months. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals create employment in host countries [1]
Multinationals bring capital investment / new technology [1]
application_max_2: 220 local people employed in Port Saffron where unemployment is 13%
$9 million processing plant built within 18 months

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for stakeholders if Saltwick accepts Pelagia's offer.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Saltwick would become dependent on a single powerful buyer. [k] Pelagia wants 600 of the 900 tonnes caught each year and wants Saltwick to stop supplying domestic processors. [app] If Pelagia later cut prices or cancelled orders, Saltwick could lose two-thirds of its market overnight. [an] Point 2: Local processors would lose their raw material supply. [k] Cutting off domestic processors would leave them short of shrimp. [app] Local processors could be forced to scale down or close, costing Country X jobs and reducing supply and choice for consumers. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Dependence on one powerful buyer weakens a supplier's bargaining position [1]
Diverting supply away from local customers harms those customers and consumers [1]
application_max_2: Pelagia wants 600 of 900 tonnes a year and an end to supplying domestic processors
analysis_max_2: Two-thirds of volume lost at once if Pelagia squeezes terms, threatening viability
Processor closures reduce jobs and consumer choice in Country X

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltwick should accept Pelagia's offer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting would strengthen Saltwick's finances and Port Saffron's economy. [k] Pelagia would pay $5.80 per kilogram, about 60 cents above the domestic price, adding roughly $360,000 a year on 600 tonnes. [app] The $9 million plant would create 220 jobs for a town with 13% unemployment and guarantee demand for most of Saltwick's catch. [an] However, Saltwick would trade away its independence and loyal customers. [k] Supplying 600 of 900 tonnes to one buyer and abandoning domestic processors would leave Saltwick exposed if Pelagia drove prices down or withdrew. [app] Profits flowing abroad, possible pressure on fish stocks and lost goodwill with domestic customers could damage Port Saffron more than the jobs help. [an] Overall, Saltwick should accept only with safeguards, such as a minimum-price clause, a volume cap to protect stocks and keeping some supply for domestic processors. [eval] On balance, the extra $360,000 a year and 220 local jobs favour the deal, provided the contract protects Saltwick and the community rather than Pelagia alone. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Accepting can secure revenue, jobs and investment for a host community [1]
Accepting can cost a firm its independence, customers and negotiating power [1]
application_max_2: $5.80 vs $5.20 per kilogram, about $360,000 extra a year on 600 tonnes
600 of 900 tonnes to one buyer; 220 jobs in a town with 13% unemployment
analysis_max_2: Guaranteed volume and price lift stabilise revenue and fund growth
Dependence on one buyer, profit repatriation and stock pressure threaten long-term interests
evaluation_max_2: Accept with contractual safeguards (minimum price, caps, retained domestic supply)
Weighs short-term revenue/jobs against independence, community and environmental risks

scenario_stem:
Rosehip & Rye Bakery is a private limited company under Priya Nair, employing 14 staff on $480,000 sales of sourdough loaves, pastries and cakes. Priya is writing a business plan with a cash-flow forecast and market analysis for $85,000 of expansion.

Option one is a second branch 12 kilometres away, forecast to add $190,000 revenue but costing $3,000 monthly rent. Option two refurbishes the existing shop with $40,000 ovens. The current branch has Saturday queues and profit margin fell to 9%.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'business plan'.
questions.model_answer: A written document that outlines a business's objectives, its strategies for achieving them, and details of the finance, marketing and operations needed to succeed [2].

knowledge_max_2: written document outlining objectives and strategy
includes details of finance, marketing and operations

questions.question_text: Explain two contents of a business plan and how each helps Rosehip & Rye Bakery.
questions.model_answer: Content 1: A cash-flow forecast showing monthly inflows and outflows [k], which helps Priya see whether the second branch can afford its $3,000 monthly lease without running out of cash [app]. Content 2: A market analysis of customers and competitors in the new town [k], showing whether the expected extra revenue of $190,000 is realistic before committing $85,000 to the expansion [app].

knowledge_max_2: market analysis of customers and competitors
application_max_2: second branch and its $3,000 monthly lease

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a business plan helps Rosehip & Rye secure finance for the expansion.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: It shows the bank the business is well run and worth lending to [k], because Priya can present her cash-flow forecast demonstrating she can repay the $85,000 while sales grow toward $190,000 [app], increasing the chance of approval [an]. Way 2: It identifies risks, such as the $3,000 monthly lease if the new branch underperforms [k], so Priya can plan contingency savings before borrowing [app], reducing the chance of the business running out of cash [an].

knowledge_max_2: gives lenders confidence the business is well run
identifies risks and plans for them
analysis_max_2: increases the chance of finance being approved
reduces risk of cash shortage and failure

questions.question_text: Do you think Rosehip & Rye should open the second branch rather than refurbish the existing shop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for: opening the second branch gives access to a growing town 12 kilometres away [k], with forecast extra revenue of $190,000 a year [app], which could lift profit well above the current 9% margin [an]. Argument against: the branch commits the business to $85,000 of expansion spending and $3,000 monthly lease payments [k], straining cash if the forecast proves wrong instead of a $40,000 refurbishment [app], risking failure [an]. Overall, opening the second branch is the stronger choice because the town's growth potential outweighs the cheaper refurbishment [eval], although Priya should only proceed if her cash-flow forecast confirms she can cover the lease [eval].

knowledge_max_2: access to a new growing market
fixed lease and expansion cost risks
analysis_max_2: raises profit above the current 9% margin
cash strain if the forecast proves wrong
evaluation_max_2: weighs growth potential against lease risk; justified recommendation
conditional recommendation based on cash-flow forecast

scenario_stem:
Redmoor Refrigerated Foods Ltd is a private limited company running a cold-storage depot for 40 supermarket customers, with 84 warehouse workers and drivers. Turnover reached 28% and accident absences cost $45,000. It must train 16 new pickers before the summer season, when volumes rise 35%.

A 2-day induction covering safety and stock systems costs $400 per worker. A 5-day induction adding supervised shifts and a mentor costs $950 per worker. The operations manager must choose by 15 June.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'induction training'.
questions.model_answer: Training given to new employees when they first join a business, introducing them to the organisation's culture, policies, safety rules and their duties so they can settle in quickly [2].

knowledge_max_2: training given to new employees on joining the business
introduces policies, safety rules and the duties of the role

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Redmoor Refrigerated Foods should provide induction training for the 16 new pickers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: New staff learn the depot's safety rules and procedures from day one [k], reducing the risk of accidents like those already costing $45,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Induction helps new pickers settle quickly into their roles [k], which matters because turnover is already 28% ahead of a summer season that raises volumes by 35% [app].

knowledge_max_2: helps new staff settle and integrate quickly

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing the 5-day induction for the 16 new pickers.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A 5-day induction gives each picker supervised shifts and a mentor [k], so mistakes are caught and corrected before they affect chilled orders for the 40 supermarket customers [app], reducing costly errors and waste during the 35% summer surge [an]. Advantage 2: It shows new staff the firm values them [k], improving morale in a workforce already facing 28% turnover [app], lowering the cost and disruption of replacing pickers later [an].

knowledge_max_2: longer induction allows closer supervision and mentoring
demonstrates the employer values new employees
application_max_2: supervised shifts and a mentor for each picker
analysis_max_2: catches errors early, protecting orders and reducing waste
improves morale and retention, cutting replacement costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Redmoor Refrigerated Foods should approve the 5-day induction rather than the 2-day induction? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for: the 5-day induction costs $950 per worker [k], so 16 pickers cost $15,200, adding supervised shifts and mentors that address the safety problems behind the $45,000 absence cost [app], reducing accidents and errors during the 35% summer peak [an]. Argument against: the 2-day induction costs only $400 per worker [k], so 16 pickers cost $6,400, an $8,800 saving against the $15,200 option when turnover is already 28% [app], risking wasted spend if pickers leave soon after joining [an]. Overall, the 5-day induction is the stronger choice because the mentoring and safety benefits outweigh the $8,800 saving in an accident-hit peak season [eval], although the depot should also tackle the causes of 28% turnover to protect its investment [eval].

longer induction costs more per worker

analysis_max_2: reduces accidents and errors during the peak
savings could outweigh benefits if staff leave quickly
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing mentoring benefits against extra cost
conditional judgement linking decision to tackling 28% turnover

scenario_stem:
Millbrook Roastery is a private limited company roasting coffee with 9 staff. It sells 250 g bags online and to 12 independent cafés, with $340,000 revenue. Sales fell 8% after a supermarket launched own-label coffee at $7 against Millbrook's $12.

The director chooses: promotional pricing cutting bags to $9 at $15,000, or investing $18,000 in a premium brand image campaign with packaging and a loyalty card. The board meets 30 March.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'marketing strategy'.
questions.model_answer: A marketing strategy is a long-term plan setting out how a business will use the marketing mix to achieve its marketing objectives, such as increasing sales, market share or customer loyalty [2].

knowledge_max_2: a long-term plan for using the marketing mix
designed to achieve marketing objectives such as higher sales or market share

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Millbrook Roastery must respond to the supermarket's own-label launch.

Reason 2: Responding protects Millbrook's position against a much larger rival [k], important when revenue of $340,000 and 12 café accounts are now under threat from $7 own-label bags [app].

knowledge_max_2: failing to respond risks losing customers to rivals
a response protects market share and the business's position

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing the premium brand image campaign.

Advantage 2: New packaging, storytelling and a loyalty card strengthen the brand image and recognition [k], encouraging repeat buyers at a time when sales have fallen 8% [app], so customers return more often over the 12-month campaign rather than switching to the supermarket [an].

Argument against: the promotional pricing campaign cutting the bag to $9 for 6 months [k] costs an estimated $15,000 in lost margin but could win back price-sensitive shoppers put off since sales fell 8% in 6 months [app], although margins would thin and customers may leave once prices rise again [an]. scenario_stem:
Coraline Chocolate Co is a private limited company making chocolate truffles and gift boxes, employing 22 confectioners to produce 90,000 boxes a year on $540,000 revenue. A supermarket may delist it unless quality improves after two batches contained stale centres.

Quality control rejects 4% of output, wasting $18,000 yearly. Elena must choose between investing $60,000 in quality assurance—training staff to check ingredients and temperatures—or keeping quality control plus two extra inspectors at $2,000 each per month. The supermarket reviews the contract in 6 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'quality control'.
questions.model_answer: Quality control is checking finished products or samples during production to identify and remove faulty items before they reach customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: checking products during or after production
identifying and removing faulty items before customers receive them

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why high quality is important to Coraline Chocolate Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: High quality keeps customers satisfied [k], so shoppers who enjoyed the hand-finished truffles will keep buying from Coraline instead of rivals [app]. Reason 2: High quality protects the company's reputation [k], reducing the risk that the supermarket delists its products after the stale-centre complaints [app].

application_max_2: customers keep buying the hand-finished truffles
risk of the supermarket delisting Coraline after stale-centre complaints

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Coraline Chocolate Co of replacing quality control with quality assurance.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Quality assurance prevents faults at the source [k], so ingredients and temperatures are checked at every production stage rather than after the 4% of output is wasted [app], cutting the $18,000 annual chocolate waste [an]. Benefit 2: Quality assurance makes every worker responsible for quality [k], so Elena's 22 confectioners catch stale centres before boxes are sealed [app], building trust with the supermarket customer [an].

knowledge_max_2: prevents defects at the source / building quality into the process
makes all employees responsible for quality
application_max_2: checks ingredients and temperatures at every stage
22 confectioners catching stale centres before sealing
analysis_max_2: builds trust with the supermarket customer

However, quality assurance costs $60,000 up front plus staff training time [k], whereas two extra inspectors cost only $2,000 each per month and start catching faults immediately [app], which is safer if Elena's cash is tight [an]. Overall, quality assurance is the stronger choice because preventing faults is more reliable than catching them after they occur [eval], provided Elena can fund $60,000 without straining cash flow [eval].

knowledge_max_2: quality assurance prevents defects at source
quality control / extra inspectors catch defects after production

scenario_stem:
Kelbeck Joinery Co Ltd is a private limited company making kitchen cabinets and wardrobes in Country X. Its statement of financial position at 30 September shows non-current assets of $240,000, current assets of $112,000 and current liabilities of $64,000.

It has a $110,000 long-term bank loan and shareholders' equity of $178,000. A $90,000 CNC machine would win larger contracts. Directors must choose between borrowing $90,000 now or waiting two years and using retained profits.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, and it shows the finance available for day-to-day operations such as paying wages and suppliers [2].

knowledge_max_2: day-to-day operating finance available to the business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the bank would study Kelbeck's statement of financial position before lending $90,000.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bank wants to see if Kelbeck can repay the loan [k], because current assets of $112,000 exceed current liabilities of $64,000, giving working capital of $48,000 [app]. Reason 2: The bank wants to know how much Kelbeck already owes [k], because an existing bank loan of $110,000 is repayable after more than one year and shareholders' equity is $178,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: bank assesses ability to repay / creditworthiness
bank assesses the level of existing debt and long-term financial position
application_max_2: current assets of $112,000 against current liabilities of $64,000 (working capital $48,000)
bank loan of $110,000 repayable after more than one year and shareholders' equity of $178,000

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which Kelbeck's managers could use its statement of financial position.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Managers can monitor day-to-day liquidity [k], because the statement shows current assets of $112,000 against current liabilities of $64,000 [app], so they can check Kelbeck can pay wages and suppliers on time [an]. Way 2: Managers can judge whether Kelbeck can afford extra borrowing [k], because non-current assets of $240,000 and equity of $178,000 show what the owners have invested [app], helping them decide if a $90,000 loan is affordable [an].

knowledge_max_2: managers use the statement to monitor liquidity/working capital
managers use the statement to judge whether extra borrowing or investment is affordable
application_max_2: current assets of $112,000 against current liabilities of $64,000
non-current assets of $240,000 and equity of $178,000
analysis_max_2: surplus of current assets over current liabilities shows bills can be paid on time
owners' funds of $178,000 set the limit for sensible extra borrowing

questions.question_text: Do you think Kelbeck Joinery Co Ltd should borrow $90,000 now to buy the CNC machine? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brackenmoor Electronics is a public limited company in Country X making washing machines and dishwashers. Revenue was $3.6 million, including $900,000 exports to Country Y, which has 240 million consumers but charges an 18% import tariff on finished appliances, adding $162,000 in duty to Brackenmoor's Country Y sales.

questions.question_text: Do you think The Gilded Hanger should launch the own-label range rather than keep reselling established brands? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Ironbarrow Foundry Ltd is a private limited company casting agricultural machinery components, with 96 workers. Eight experienced casting operators run manual mills. It bought 6 CNC machines at $78,000 each that triple output per shift.

The operations director wants on-the-job training: the 16 workers selected would be coached during production, costing $5,000. The finance director prefers a 4-day off-the-job college course at $1,800 each, taking the 16 workers off the production line. A decision is due this month.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'on-the-job training'.
questions.model_answer: Training carried out at the employee's normal workplace while they perform their job, often by observing or being coached by an experienced colleague [2].

knowledge_max_2: training at the employee's normal workplace
learning while doing the job, usually with an experienced colleague

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of on-the-job training for Ironbarrow Foundry.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Workers learn on the actual machines used in production [k], so the 16 workers selected gain directly practical experience on equipment costing $78,000 each [app]. Advantage 2: Output continues while training takes place [k], avoiding the lost working time of a 4-day college course [app].

application_max_2: 16 workers selected for machines costing $78,000 each

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Training quality depends on the coaching skills of existing staff [k], and with only 8 experienced casting operators to share the role [app], bad habits may be passed on to the new CNC operators [an]. Problem 2: Training during production can slow output and distract supervisors [k], delaying the tripled output per shift the machines should deliver [app], weakening the return on the $78,000 machines [an].

can disrupt or slow production while learning

analysis_max_2: risk of passing on bad habits and poor CNC practice

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironbarrow Foundry should use on-the-job training rather than the off-the-job college course? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for: on-the-job training costs only $5,000 [k], far below the $28,800 needed for 16 off-the-job course fees at $1,800 each [app], saving the foundry $23,800 while workers learn on running machines [an]. Argument against: the college course gives structured, expert-led teaching away from production pressure [k], which is valuable for staff using $78,000 CNC machines where mistakes damage parts [app], whereas coaching from just 8 busy operators risks inconsistent learning [an]. Overall, on-the-job training is the better value option for introducing the new machines [eval], provided Ironbarrow Foundry adds short off-the-job refresher courses later to keep CNC skills up to date [eval].

scenario_stem:
Cove & Compass Travel Co is a travel agency partnership with 3,200 customers, $96,000 commission and a Keldport office. Customer records show 55% are repeat clients and average age is 58.

The owners compare 'sun and sail' cruises aimed at retired couples, promoted to the 1,760 repeat clients, with a family beach-holiday social media campaign aimed at young parents costing $4,000. A decision is needed by 30 September before winter brochures print.

Reason 2: Records help the owners point the budget at proven demand [k], rather than guess at a new segment without evidence from its 3,200 annual customers [app].

Benefit 2: Satisfying the needs of its core older market deepens loyalty [k], which fits a business already getting 55% of bookings from repeat clients aged around 58 [app], raising lifetime value and securing the $96,000 commission stream [an].

scenario_stem:
Kelvara Knitwear is a public limited company manufacturing knitted school uniforms, producing 60,000 garments a month. Its defect rate is 5%, so 3,000 garments are reworked monthly at $14,400.

An overseas retailer offers a two-year contract for 25,000 jumpers worth $900,000 a year, but requires an audited defect rate below 2%. Kelvara must choose between $45,000 quality assurance training for all supervisors—checks at every stage—and doubling end-of-line quality control with a $30,000 inspection station. The retailer's audit team visits next month.

questions.question_text: Define 'quality assurance'.
questions.model_answer: Quality assurance is a system that builds quality into every stage of production by setting standards and checking processes to prevent defects from occurring [2].

knowledge_max_2: system that builds quality into every production stage
designed to prevent defects rather than detect them

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why high quality is important to Kelvara Knitwear when winning export contracts.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: High quality earns the trust of overseas buyers [k], increasing the chance the retailer agrees the two-year contract for 25,000 jumpers [app]. Reason 2: Consistent quality strengthens Kelvara's reputation [k], helping it win repeat orders instead of losing them to rival uniform suppliers [app].

application_max_2: retailer's contract for 25,000 jumpers and $900,000 a year
rival uniform suppliers competing for the same business

questions.question_text: Explain two differences between quality control and quality assurance.
questions.model_answer: Difference 1: Quality control inspects finished garments at the end of the line [k], such as checking completed uniforms before packing [app], whereas quality assurance checks each production stage as work happens [an]. Difference 2: Quality control finds defects after money has been spent on the garment [k], so 5% of the 60,000 garments are still reworked at $14,400 a month [app], while quality assurance aims to prevent those defects arising in the first place [an].

knowledge_max_2: quality control inspects finished products, quality assurance checks processes
quality control detects defects, quality assurance prevents them
application_max_2: 5% of 60,000 garments reworked at $14,400 a month
analysis_max_2: QA checks during production rather than after it
QA avoids wasted money on defects before they occur

questions.question_text: Do you think Kelvara Knitwear should invest $45,000 in quality assurance training rather than install a $30,000 inspection station? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Quality assurance training builds quality into every stage of production [k], lowering the 5% defect rate towards the retailer's required 2% audit threshold [app], which protects the $900,000-a-year two-year contract [an]. However, the inspection station costs $30,000, saving $15,000 against training [k], and doubling end-of-line checks would catch faulty jumpers before they ship [app], though defects would still occur and rework would still cost money [an]. Overall, quality assurance training is the better investment because the retailer's audit demands a process-wide system, not just final checking [eval], although Kelvara must deliver the training quickly to pass next month's audit [eval].

knowledge_max_2: quality assurance prevents defects through process checks
inspection stations detect defects after production
application_max_2: $45,000 supervisor training to reach the 2% audit threshold
analysis_max_2: end-of-line checks catch faults late, so rework still costs $14,400 a month
evaluation_max_2: weighs prevention against cheaper detection and gives a justified recommendation
conditional recommendation linked to passing next month's audit

scenario_stem:
Vantel Fashion Stores Ltd is a private limited company running 3 fashion stores. Turnover was $2.4 million last year. Its statement of financial position shows current assets of $213,000, including inventories of $175,000, receivables of $20,000 and cash of $18,000.

Current liabilities are $140,000, including rent and wages owed. Directors debate whether to keep inventories at $175,000 to avoid empty shelves or cut them to free working capital for a fourth store next year.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'current liabilities'.
questions.model_answer: Current liabilities are debts the business must repay within one year, such as trade payables, bank overdrafts, tax owed and unpaid expenses [2].

knowledge_max_2: debts due to be repaid within one year
examples such as trade payables, overdrafts, tax owed or unpaid expenses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why managers of Vantel Fashion Stores would be concerned about inventories of $175,000.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cash is tied up in unsold stock [k], because inventories of $175,000 absorb about 82% of the current assets of $213,000, leaving only $18,000 in cash [app]. Reason 2: Fashion stock can become unsellable [k], because changing trends may force Vantel to discount $175,000 of clothing heavily to shift it [app].

knowledge_max_2: inventories tie up cash that could be used elsewhere
unsold fashion stock may lose value through obsolescence and need discounting
application_max_2: inventories of $175,000 being about 82% of current assets of $213,000 with only $18,000 in cash
changing fashion trends forcing heavy discounts on clothing stock

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Vantel of interpreting its statement of financial position regularly.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Managers can see how much cash is genuinely free [k], because current assets of $213,000 less current liabilities of $140,000 leave working capital of $73,000 [app], showing whether the fourth store can be funded without overtrading [an]. Benefit 2: Managers can track whether stock is creeping above demand [k], because the statement shows inventories of $175,000 against cash of $18,000 this year [app], revealing whether buying needs tightening before the fourth store opens [an].

knowledge_max_2: statement shows the working capital position of the business
statement shows the composition of current assets such as inventories and cash
application_max_2: current assets of $213,000 against current liabilities of $140,000 (working capital $73,000)
analysis_max_2: a clear current surplus shows the fourth store can be funded without overstretching

questions.question_text: Do you think Vantel Fashion Stores Ltd should cut its inventories below $175,000 to fund the fourth store? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting inventories would release cash for the fourth store [k], because inventories of $175,000 make up about 82% of current assets of $213,000 and cash is only $18,000 [app], so trimming slow-moving lines could free useful cash for the new shop [an]. However, deep cuts risk empty shelves [k], because Vantel runs 3 fashion stores with turnover of $2.4 million and customers buy on impulse [app], so missing popular sizes could push shoppers to rival retailers [an]. Overall, Vantel should reduce inventories gradually rather than sharply [eval], because freeing working capital suits the fourth store plan, but slashing $2.4 million of dependent sales across the 3 stores would be far too risky [eval].

scenario_stem:
Corven Apparel Group is a clothing manufacturer and retailer in Country X. It employs 640 workers, producing 1.2 million shirts and uniforms yearly on $18 million revenue. Cotton costs $4.10 a metre in Country X but $2.60 in Country Z, where wages are 40% lower.

Moving production to Country Z saves $1.5 a metre, about $3.4 million yearly, with a 10-year tax holiday, while Country X stays the design and sales headquarters. But 480 of 640 workers face redundancy as two factories close.

questions.question_text: Define 'host country'.
questions.model_answer: The country in which a multinational company locates its production, offices or sales operations, which is different from the country where the multinational was originally based [2].

knowledge_max_2: a country where the multinational locates its operations
different from the multinational's home or origin country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Corven Apparel Group of relocating production to Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Fabric and wages would be much cheaper [k], with cotton at $2.60 a metre versus $4.10 in Country X and wages 40% lower [app]. Benefit 2: Corven would pay far less tax [k], as Country Z offers foreign manufacturers a 10-year tax holiday [app].

knowledge_max_2: lower input and labour costs in the host country
tax incentives or holidays offered by host country governments

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Corven Apparel Group could face if it relocates production to Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Corven would have to dismiss most of its Country X workforce [k], making 480 of the 640 workers redundant [app], which would mean large redundancy payments and lasting damage to Corven's reputation as a local employer [an]. Problem 2: Moving production overseas lengthens the supply chain [k], as finished garments must travel from Country Z to Country X shops [app], so any delays could leave stores empty in peak seasons and disappoint customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: redundancy payments and reputational damage from closing factories
longer, more complex supply chain and logistics
application_max_2: 480 of the 640 workers would be made redundant
production moves to Country Z while Country X remains the design and sales headquarters
analysis_max_2: redundancy costs and bad publicity reduce profit and staff morale
long delivery routes risk stock shortages and lost sales in peak seasons

questions.question_text: Do you think Corven Apparel Group should relocate production to Country Z or keep it in Country X? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relocating would cut Corven's costs significantly [k], saving $1.5 a metre on fabric and an estimated $3.4 million a year, plus a 10-year tax holiday [app], which would raise profit margins and help Corven compete against cheaper imported clothing [an]. However, keeping production in Country X avoids dismissing 480 of the 640 workers [k], preserving experienced staff, local supplier links and the skilled local workforce [app]; mass redundancies could harm morale and Corven's reputation, and long delivery routes from Country Z add supply risk [an]. Overall, Corven should relocate production to Country Z, because $3.4 million of annual savings and lower wages secure the firm's survival in a price-competitive market [eval], but it should honour enhanced redundancy terms and keep a small Country X finishing unit to protect its reputation [eval].

scenario_stem:
The Salted Fig Café is a sole trader café founded 15 years ago by Marco Ruiz, employing 18 staff. Revenue fell from $520,000 to $430,000: a rival opened in 2024, customer numbers dropped 25%, and ingredient costs rose 18% since 2023.

Marco is exhausted but wants to save the café. He can relaunch with a new menu, branding and loyalty cards for $35,000, or sell to a local chain for $210,000. Known for resilience, he wants to finish well; staff fear job losses.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'resilience'.
questions.model_answer: The ability of an entrepreneur or business to cope with setbacks, adapt to difficulties and keep going despite failure or pressure [2].

knowledge_max_2: adapting to difficulties and keeping going

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why The Salted Fig Café's annual revenue fell from $520,000 to $430,000.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A popular rival opened nearby in 2024 [k], drawing customers away from The Salted Fig Café and feeding the 25% drop in customer numbers [app]. Reason 2: Ingredient costs rose by 18% since 2023, forcing Marco to raise menu prices [k], which deterred price-sensitive customers and helped cut revenue by $90,000 [app].

application_max_2: rival opened in 2024 and 25% drop in customer numbers

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why an established business like The Salted Fig Café might fail despite 15 years of success.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Complacency — long-standing firms may fail to respond to competition [k], as the café watched revenue slide from $520,000 to $430,000 while a rival nearby took market share [app], so sales keep falling year after year [an]. Reason 2: Squeezed profit margins from rising costs [k], with ingredient costs up 18% forcing higher menu prices [app], leaving too little margin to reinvest in retaining customers [an].

Selling for $210,000 gives Marco immediate cash and certainty [k], but ends a 15-year family business and forfeits future profits if the relaunch works [app], walking away from recoverable revenue [an]. scenario_stem:
Brightwire Appliance Repairs is a sole trader run by Danny Okoro with 3 technicians, repairing appliances. It fixed 1,150 appliances for $138,000. A questionnaire of 400 households found 62% would choose evening appointments.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'market-orientated business'.

uses research to guide marketing rather than personal judgement

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Brightwire Appliance Repairs of acting on the household survey.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Define 'total quality management'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why high quality is important to Aster Court Hotel.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Aster Court Hotel of introducing total quality management.

However, trialling the faster line pushed defects to 5%, breaching the 3% limit in the truck maker's contract [k], risking loss of the entire contract and costly rework at $9 per defect [app], outweighing the extra contribution [an]. Overall, Arden should keep line speed unchanged and invest $80,000 in quality assurance training, because protecting the contract matters more than short-term output gains [eval], while defects below 1% should strengthen its reputation for future orders [eval].

scenario_stem:
Vantrel Software Ltd is a private limited company developing payroll software, employing 34 programmers. Revenue was $1.66 million. Its statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $380,000 and current assets of $520,000: receivables $410,000 and cash $110,000.

Current liabilities are $240,000 and working capital $280,000; share capital is $280,000 and retained profit $250,000. Customers take 90 days to pay, so directors must choose spending $200,000 on a hosted server platform or keeping cash for slow payments.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'current assets'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets are assets the business expects to turn into cash or use within one year, such as inventories, trade receivables and bank balances [2].

knowledge_max_2: assets turned into cash or used within one year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Vantrel's managers monitor receivables in the statement of financial position.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Receivables dominate the current asset base [k], because customers owe $410,000 against cash of only $110,000, on revenue of $1.66 million [app]. Reason 2: Slow payers squeeze working capital [k], because customers take around 90 days to pay while current liabilities of $240,000 fall due within one year [app].

knowledge_max_2: receivables often make up most current assets in service businesses
slow-paying customers create working capital and cash-flow problems
application_max_2: customers owe $410,000 against cash of only $110,000, on revenue of $1.66 million
around 90 days to pay against current liabilities of $240,000 due within one year

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Vantrel might face if it spends $200,000 on the server platform now.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Cash protection would weaken [k], because cash of $110,000 and receivables of $410,000 against current liabilities of $240,000 leave working capital of $280,000 [app], so wages could go unpaid before debtors settle [an]. Problem 2: The non-current asset base would be stretched [k], because non-current assets are $380,000 with equity of $280,000 share capital and $250,000 retained profit [app], so a failed platform could exhaust modest reserves [an].

spending now increases the risk if the platform underperforms

questions.question_text: Do you think Vantrel Software Ltd should spend $200,000 on the hosted server platform now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The platform would modernise delivery and cut support costs [k], because Vantrel serves small firms with revenue of $1.66 million and 34 programmers [app], so automation could lift margins and keep clients [an]. However, waiting is safer for cash [k], because receivables of $410,000 take around 90 days to arrive and current liabilities of $240,000 are due within one year [app], leaving only $110,000 in the bank to cover wages [an]. Overall, Vantrel should delay the platform until receivables are collected [eval], because protecting working capital of $280,000 matters more than the $200,000 upgrade while debtors are outstanding [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kelvarn Dyes Ltd is a Millbrook, Country X dyeing factory owned by a European multinational. It employs 300 workers and discharges waste into the River Calder with dye at 4 times the legal limit.

New rules: closed-loop treatment by next year or $250,000 fines and closure. Kelvarn can spend $2.2 million on treatment or move to Country Z with weaker controls. Closing Millbrook costs 300 jobs among 500 unemployed adults; the town council wants the factory to stay, but farmers say the river damages crops.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: A cost of a business activity that falls on people not directly involved in the transaction, such as pollution suffered by the local community [2].

knowledge_max_2: a cost paid by third parties, not those in the transaction
for example, pollution suffered by the local community

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kelvarn Dyes Ltd of installing the treatment plant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Kelvarn would avoid fines and closure [k], eliminating the risk of $250,000 fines and being shut down under the new legal controls [app]. Benefit 2: Kelvarn would protect its reputation and licence to operate [k], as complying stops pollution of the River Calder and keeps 300 Millbrook jobs, satisfying the town council and farmers [app].

knowledge_max_2: compliance protects reputation and relations with the community
application_max_2: $250,000 fines and closure under the new controls
River Calder pollution ended; 300 Millbrook jobs kept; town council and farmers satisfied

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Kelvarn Dyes Ltd would face if it relocates production to Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Relocation would make 300 Millbrook workers redundant [k], cutting jobs from a town with 500 unemployed adults [app], meaning large redundancy payments and serious reputational damage for Kelvarn [an]. Problem 2: Moving to a country with weaker controls only helps short term [k], as the River Calder tests show how strictly Country X polices pollution [app], so if Country Z adopts similar laws Kelvarn faces the same compliance costs plus lost trust from customers and the public [an].

knowledge_max_2: closing a factory makes workers redundant and damages reputation
operating where regulation is weak may not be sustainable as laws tighten everywhere
application_max_2: 300 Millbrook workers redundant; town already has 500 unemployed adults
River Calder dye levels 4 times the legal limit show strict Country X enforcement
analysis_max_2: redundancy payments and bad publicity would harm Kelvarn's profit and image
future regulation in Country Z would strand the investment and customers may lose trust

questions.question_text: Do you think Kelvarn Dyes Ltd should install the treatment plant or relocate production to Country Z? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Installing the plant keeps Kelvarn operating [k], avoiding $250,000 fines and closure under the new legal controls while protecting 300 Millbrook jobs [app], so production continues with a safer reputation and the River Calder recovers [an]. However, the $2.2 million outlay is significant [k], and Country Z has weaker controls and possibly lower operating costs [app], yet relocation abandons Millbrook, its workers and community relationships, and risks Kelvarn being seen as polluting wherever rules are weakest [an]. Overall, Kelvarn should install the treatment plant, because compliance protects its licence, its 300 workers and its reputation for far less than the damage of fleeing [eval], and the investment secures the factory's future beyond next year's deadline [eval].

knowledge_max_2: compliance avoids fines and closure and protects reputation
relocation avoids upfront compliance costs but abandons assets and community ties
application_max_2: $250,000 fines and closure vs $2.2 million treatment plant; 300 jobs kept
Country Z has weaker controls; Millbrook town with 500 unemployed adults
analysis_max_2: compliance keeps production and community relations intact and river recovers
relocation severs community ties and damages Kelvarn's image as a responsible multinational
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on installing the plant
recognises the long-term security the investment brings beyond the deadline

scenario_stem:
The Silver Scissors Salon is a sole trader hairdressing business owned by Nina Petrova for 12 years, employing 11 stylists on $380,000 revenue. Loyal customers came until a rival opened 6 months ago offering 20% discounts, and product costs rose 15%.

Nina prioritises survival over growth. She can introduce a loyalty scheme and retrain staff in new cutting techniques for $14,000, or match the rival's 20% discounts, which she estimates would cut profit to nearly zero. Keeping all 11 stylists matters.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'business objective'.
questions.model_answer: A target or goal a business aims to achieve, such as survival, growth, profit or providing a service to the community [2].

knowledge_max_2: a target or goal for the business
examples such as survival, growth or profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why The Silver Scissors Salon might fail if Nina does nothing.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The rival salon is offering 20% discounts [k], which pulls price-sensitive customers away from The Silver Scissors Salon [app]. Reason 2: Hair product costs have risen by 15% this year [k], which cuts Nina's margin unless prices rise, further deterring customers [app].

application_max_2: rival salon opened 6 months ago with 20% discounts
hair product costs up 15% this year

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a business plan could help Nina respond to the rival salon.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: The plan can compare the $14,000 loyalty scheme against matching 20% discounts [k], so Nina protects margin instead of sliding to zero profit [app], avoiding a self-defeating price war [an]. Way 2: The plan sets clear targets for winning customers back [k], linking the retraining investment to her survival objective and keeping all 11 stylists employed [app], keeping the whole business focused on one goal [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Nina should introduce the loyalty scheme rather than match the rival's discounts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The loyalty scheme costs $14,000 but rewards repeat visits [k], strengthening relationships built over 12 years and countering the rival without cutting prices [app], protecting the salon's long-term survival and $380,000 revenue [an]. Matching 20% discounts would end that price advantage [k], and Nina estimates profit would fall to nearly zero [app], leaving no surplus to absorb 15% higher product costs [an]. Overall, the loyalty scheme is the better option because it competes on loyalty, not price [eval], and it keeps all 11 stylists employed while serving her survival objective [eval].

knowledge_max_2: loyalty scheme protects margins and relationships
price matching cuts profit to zero
application_max_2: 20% discount would cut profit to nearly zero
analysis_max_2: no surplus to absorb rising product costs
evaluation_max_2: weighs competing on loyalty vs price; justified recommendation
supports survival objective and staff employment

scenario_stem:
Brinmoor Engineering Co is a private limited company making pumps, with 75 machinists, fitters and welders and $4.7 million revenue. After losing a $900,000 export contract, directors must make 15 workers redundant from 75 workers by March.

The shortlist of 30 workers includes ages 19 to 58 and 6 women. Option one is last-in-first-out, removing those with shortest service; option two selects on skills, attendance and performance, keeping newer skilled welders. Selection must comply with discrimination law.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'dismissal'.
questions.model_answer: When an employer ends an employee's employment, usually because of the employee's conduct, capability or a serious breach of contract [2].

knowledge_max_2: usually due to conduct, capability or breach of contract

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Brinmoor Engineering should consider when deciding which 15 workers to make redundant.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Skills and performance of each worker [k], keeping the machinists and welders the workshops need to fulfil the remaining order book [app]. Factor 2: Length of service [k], since last-in-first-out would remove the 15 workers with the shortest service first [app].

knowledge_max_2: skills and performance of each worker
application_max_2: keeping needed machinists and welders for remaining orders
last-in-first-out would remove the shortest-service workers

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brinmoor Engineering must avoid discrimination when selecting the 15 workers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Selection by age or gender is unlawful [k], so choosing by the shortlist's ages 19 to 58 or targeting the 6 women would break discrimination law [app], exposing the firm to tribunal claims and compensation [an]. Reason 2: Using objective criteria such as skills, attendance and performance [k], applied consistently across all 30 shortlisted workers [app], builds trust and protects the morale of the remaining workforce [an].

knowledge_max_2: age and gender discrimination are unlawful
objective, consistent criteria reduce legal risk
application_max_2: criteria applied across all 30 shortlisted workers
analysis_max_2: avoids tribunal claims and compensation costs
protects morale and trust among remaining staff

questions.question_text: Do you think Brinmoor Engineering should use last-in-first-out rather than skills-based selection? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for: last-in-first-out is simple, transparent and quick [k], removing the 15 workers with the shortest service and saving management time at a difficult moment [app], reducing disputes over how choices were made [an]. Argument against: it ignores skills and performance [k], so capable new welders could leave while weaker long-serving staff remain [app], leaving the workshops unable to deliver orders after losing the $900,000 export contract [an]. Overall, skills-based selection is fairer and better protects the business [eval], provided Brinmoor applies the criteria consistently, with an appeal process, to comply with discrimination law [eval].

application_max_2: $900,000 export contract lost; newer skilled welders at risk
analysis_max_2: simple method cuts disputes and admin time
retains skills needed to keep the order book moving
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring skills-based selection
conditional judgement requiring consistent criteria and appeal

scenario_stem:
Peregrine Bookshop is an independent partnership with 4 staff, stocking 25,000 titles. Sales are $190,000, but revenue fell 12% as a national chain and an online retailer discount bestsellers by 25%.

The owners compare a community hub with readings and a loyalty stamp card for $3,000, against matching the 25% discount on 40 bestselling titles at $18,000. A decision is due before summer holidays.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'marketing mix'.
questions.model_answer: The combination of marketing decisions — product, price, place and promotion — used together by a business to satisfy customers and achieve its objectives [2].

knowledge_max_2: the combination of product, price, place and promotion
used together to satisfy customers and meet objectives

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why matching the 25% discount may not save Peregrine Bookshop.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Matching the 25% discount means giving up margin on the 40 bestselling titles [k], costing an estimated $18,000 over the year against sales of only $190,000 [app]. Reason 2: An online retailer can sustain discounting far better than a small shop [k], so a price war Peregrine cannot afford could drag on regardless of the 12% revenue fall already seen [app].

knowledge_max_2: larger competitors can outlast small firms in price wars
application_max_2: 40 bestsellers at 25% off; $18,000 estimated lost margin
$190,000 sales; online retailer discounting; 12% revenue fall

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the community hub strategy.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Readings and a children's story hour give people a reason to visit that price cannot match [k], drawing families into the shop during the school summer holidays [app], lifting footfall and sales of non-book items such as stationery and gifts [an]. Advantage 2: A loyalty stamp card encourages repeat custom [k], building lasting relationships with the local market rather than one-off bargain hunters [app], creating a defensible position the online retailer cannot easily copy at any discount [an].

knowledge_max_2: experiential marketing attracts customers beyond price
loyalty schemes build repeat custom and relationships
application_max_2: story hour and readings timed for the school summer holidays
loyalty stamp card aimed at local repeat buyers
analysis_max_2: footfall lifts sales of higher-margin non-book items
relationships create loyalty rivals cannot buy with discounts

questions.question_text: Do you think Peregrine Bookshop should become a community hub rather than match the 25% discount? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for: the community hub costs $3,000 to set up [k], creating events and a loyalty stamp card that build reasons to visit beyond price [app], defending the $190,000 revenue without destroying margin across the 40 bestselling titles [an]. Argument against: matching the 25% discount [k] could win back price-driven buyers quickly and stem the 12% revenue decline [app], but it costs an estimated $18,000 in lost margin and teaches customers to buy only on discount [an]. Overall, the community hub is the better strategy because differentiation, not price-matching, protects an independent bookshop [eval], although the owners should promote events heavily and review sales monthly through the holiday period [eval].

discounting buys volume at the expense of margin and habits
application_max_2: $3,000 hub setup with loyalty stamp card versus $18,000 estimated lost margin on 40 bestsellers

analysis_max_2: differentiation protects margin and builds loyal demand
discounting likely triggers an unwinnable war with the online rival
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring differentiation and loyalty over discounting

scenario_stem:
Eldertree Furniture Co is a partnership making sofas and dining sets with $700,000 sales. Customer complaints rose 35%, and 3 of every 100 sofas were returned for broken frames or loose joints, while profit margin slipped to 7%.

Two big retailers paused orders until quality improves. The partners must choose between $28,000 quality assurance—redesigning the frame-gluing process and training staff to prevent faults—and $12,000 for stronger end-of-line quality control, adding a final inspection bench and two-person repair team. Orders must return within 6 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'brand reputation'.
questions.model_answer: Brand reputation is the overall opinion customers and the public hold about a business and its products, built over time through experience and word of mouth [2].

knowledge_max_2: overall opinion customers hold about a business
built over time through experience and word of mouth

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of poor quality on Eldertree Furniture Co's reputation.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Poor quality leads to complaints and returns [k], as shown by complaints rising 35% and 3 out of every 100 sofas being returned [app]. Effect 2: A damaged reputation deters retailers and customers [k], which is why two big retailers have paused orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: loss of buyer confidence and orders
application_max_2: complaints rose 35% with 3 out of every 100 sofas returned

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Eldertree Furniture Co of quality control.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Quality control catches faulty sofas before they leave the workshop [k], so broken frames and loose joints are fixed before delivery [app], reducing costly returns [an]. knowledge_max_2: detects faults before products reach customers
application_max_2: broken frames and loose joints fixed before delivery

questions.question_text: Do you think Eldertree Furniture Co should invest $28,000 in quality assurance rather than $12,000 for end-of-line quality control? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Quality assurance redesigns the frame-gluing process and trains staff to prevent faults during assembly [k], attacking the root cause of broken frames rather than just catching them late [app], which should cut the 3 out of 100 sofa returns and reverse the 35% complaint rise [an]. However, quality assurance costs $28,000, more than double the $12,000 inspection bench [k], so the partnership must weigh this against the six-month deadline to reinstate the paused retailers' orders [app], and quality control would start catching faults immediately [an]. Overall, quality assurance is the better long-term choice because preventing faults protects brand reputation more effectively than reworking bad furniture [eval], provided the partners can fund it without halting production [eval].

knowledge_max_2: quality assurance prevents faults at source
quality control detects faults at the end of the line

scenario_stem:
Alderheath Pharmacies Ltd is a private limited company operating 8 community pharmacies. Revenue was $9.5 million. Its statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $1,250,000 and current assets of $980,000, including inventories of $620,000.

Current liabilities are $530,000; debentures of $300,000 are repayable after more than one year, and share capital is $900,000. To open 2 more pharmacies costing $800,000, the board must choose between issuing new shares and borrowing through additional debentures.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'non-current liabilities'.
questions.model_answer: Non-current liabilities are debts the business does not have to repay for more than one year, such as long-term bank loans and debentures [2].

knowledge_max_2: debts not due for repayment within more than one year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Alderheath's board would compare debt and equity before financing the expansion.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways lenders use the statement of financial position when judging Alderheath.

Way 2: Lenders check working capital [k], because current assets of $980,000 against current liabilities of $530,000 leave working capital of $450,000 [app], indicating whether cash flows can service more debentures [an].

lenders assess working capital and cash-flow strength

current assets of $980,000 against current liabilities of $530,000, working capital $450,000

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderheath Pharmacies Ltd should finance the $800,000 expansion with new shares or debentures? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: New shares would avoid extra interest [k], because Alderheath already carries debentures of $300,000 and current liabilities of $530,000, while equity stands at $1,400,000 [app], keeping future cash free for pharmacy operations [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Baltica Mart Plc is a public limited company supermarket chain with 210 stores in 9 countries, planning to enter Country X's $900 million grocery market. Country X chain Castleton Retail Co has offered a joint venture using its 25 stores and distribution depot.

The board must choose between this venture and 12 stand-alone megastores. Castleton would hold 40%, and Country X competition authorities review it. Megastores could close 40 local shops; the venture keeps 480 staff and local purchasing but halves Baltica's market share gains.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical issue'.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Baltica Mart Plc of choosing the joint venture with Castleton Retail Co.

Benefit 2: Baltica would protect its reputation [k], as the joint venture would keep Castleton's 480 staff and local purchasing, avoiding accusations that it forces 40 local shops to close [app].

However, opening 12 megastores could force 40 local shops to close [k] and puts the plans under review by competition authorities [app], risking conditions, delays or a blocked launch, plus reputational damage that slows sales [an]. scenario_stem:
Ironfen Brewery is a craft brewery partnership founded by Tom and Bess Riley, employing 16 staff, brewing 9 cask ales and earning $700,000. It has a strong local following among pubs and restaurants, with orders doubling since 2023, and dreams of national distribution.

scenario_stem:
Fenhallow Construction Ltd is a private limited company building housing estates. Revenue was $7.2 million last year. Its statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $3,400,000 and current assets of $1,150,000, including receivables of $640,000 and cash of $250,000.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'net assets'.

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bank wants security for any loan [k], because non-current assets of $3,400,000 could be sold if Fenhallow defaulted on further borrowing [app]. Reason 2: The bank wants to see repayment capacity [k], because receivables of $640,000 against current liabilities of $780,000 and a bank loan of $1,800,000 already outstanding test cash-flow strength [app].

Benefit 2: Owners can check short-term headroom before big spending [k], because working capital is $370,000 from current assets of $1,150,000 less current liabilities of $780,000 [app], showing whether a $600,000 purchase needs new borrowing [an].

scenario_stem:
Clearspan Contact Centre is a private limited company handling telecom providers' billing queries, with 140 agents and $4.2 million revenue. Agents earn $1,150 a month; turnover is 22% and customer satisfaction 78%. An average agent makes 3,000 calls a month at 7 minutes each.

Two options: a 'Star Agent' scheme costing $25,000 a year, or output pay of $400 a month plus $0.25 per call, paying an average agent $1,150 and a top performer making 3,600 calls $1,300.

questions.question_text: Define 'salary'.
questions.model_answer: A fixed regular payment to an employee, usually expressed as an annual amount paid monthly [1], which does not vary with the number of hours worked or the output produced [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Clearspan Contact Centre might introduce the output-based pay option.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Output-based pay links an agent's earnings directly to productivity [k], so an agent completing 3,600 calls would earn $1,300 a month instead of the fixed $1,150 [app]. Reason 2: Agents who complete more calls are financially rewarded for their effort [k], which should motivate the 140 agents to raise call output above the current 3,000 calls a month [app].

However, the salary option gives income stability [k], agents keep a certain $1,150 a month and the $25,000 Star Agent scheme recognises effort without encouraging rushed calls [app], helping retention and satisfaction above 78% [an]. scenario_stem:
Fern & Fable Bookshop is a sole trader with 9 staff, earning $620,000 from 40,000 members spending $18. Owner Daniel Herrera considers a second branch in Ashford (48,000 people), with 3 existing bookshops, and budgets $85,000 for research.

He compares Option 1: 300 names from the electoral register, costing $4,800 over 3 weeks, with Option 2: a quota sample of 300 people on the high street, costing $2,600 in 1 week. Daniel will show charts.

questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Random sampling is a way of choosing people for research in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected [1]. Names are drawn at random from a complete list, such as an electoral register [1].

knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
names drawn at random from a complete list such as an electoral register

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fern & Fable Bookshop should carry out market research before opening in Ashford.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Market research would show whether demand in Ashford can support another bookshop alongside the 3 existing bookshops [k], helping Daniel judge whether his $620,000 revenue could be repeated in a town of 48,000 people [app]. Reason 2: Research reduces the risk of wasting the $85,000 budget [k], because the findings would reveal what Ashford's 48,000 residents want before he commits to a lease or stock [app].

knowledge_max_2: research reveals demand and customer preferences

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with using the quota sample instead of the random sample for Ashford.

Problem 2: Quotas usually only match age and gender [k], not income or reading habits, so a sample of 300 high-street visitors may not reflect all 48,000 residents [app], which could lead to the wrong decision about opening the branch [an].

However, Option 2 is cheaper and far faster [k]: interviewing 300 high-street shoppers with age and gender quotas costs $2,600 and takes 1 week, against $4,800 and 3 weeks for Option 1 [app], giving Daniel quicker answers before the lease decision is due [an]. scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Define the term 'raw materials'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why locating at Site A could reduce Redvale's production costs.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Redvale of choosing Site B.

scenario_stem:
Alderley Opticians Ltd is a private limited company running 4 optician practices. Revenue was $840,000, cost of sales $504,000, gross profit $336,000 and profit $92,400, with capital employed $660,000; last year revenue $720,000, gross profit $237,600, profit $57,600, capital employed $576,000.

The owner plans to invest $150,000 in digital measuring equipment for premium lenses, or hold prices for budget-conscious customers. Rival Clearglass Opticians has a 45% gross profit margin and 17% ROCE. The bank wants latest accounts before approving a loan.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Gross profit margin is the ratio of gross profit to revenue, expressed as a percentage (gross profit / revenue x 100), showing how much of each $1 of sales remains after the cost of sales has been deducted. It indicates how efficiently a business buys or makes its goods. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit as a percentage of revenue (gross profit / revenue x 100)
Shows how much of each $1 of sales remains after cost of sales is deducted / indicates efficiency of buying or production

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Alderley Opticians' gross profit margin may have risen from 33% to 40%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The owner could have raised retail prices or shifted the product mix towards premium lenses, which carry higher mark-ups than standard lenses [k]. Selling more premium lenses within revenue of $840,000 (up from $720,000) supports the rise in gross profit to $336,000, a 40% margin [app]. Reason 2: The firm may have reduced its cost of sales, for example by renegotiating supplier terms or bulk-buying lens blanks more cheaply [k]. A lower cost of sales of $504,000 against higher revenue lifts gross profit from $237,600 to $336,000 and explains the improvement from 33% last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher selling prices or sales mix shifted to higher-margin premium products
Lower cost of sales (cheaper suppliers, bulk buying, better trade terms)
application_max_2: Revenue rose from $720,000 to $840,000 and gross profit is $336,000 (40%)
Cost of sales $504,000 leaves $336,000 gross profit; last year 33% ($237,600 of $720,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for the bank when deciding whether to approve the loan.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Return on capital employed shows how effectively profits are earned on capital, helping the bank judge whether the business can generate enough surplus to repay interest and principal [k]. Alderley's ROCE rose to 14% from 10% ($92,400 on $660,000, up from $57,600 on $576,000), supporting its application to borrow $150,000 [app]. This means the bank can see rising returns on capital rather than relying on the balance sheet alone, reducing default risk [an]. Point 2: Profit margin shows how much profit remains from each $1 of sales after expenses, indicating whether the business generates enough surplus to cover new finance costs [k]. The profit margin improved to 11% from 8% ($92,400 profit on $840,000 revenue), so the bank can expect healthy cover for loan repayments if the trend continues [app]. The bank should still compare these ratios with rival Clearglass Opticians at 17% ROCE to judge competitive risk [an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE shows how effectively capital is used to generate profit / ability to service debt
Profit margin shows profit per $1 of revenue, indicating cover for finance costs
application_max_2: Profit margin rose from 8% to 11% ($92,400 profit on $840,000 revenue); rival Clearglass Opticians achieves 17% ROCE
analysis_max_2: Rising ratios reduce perceived default risk and support the loan decision
Comparing with the rival's 17% ROCE indicates Alderley still trails on capital efficiency

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderley Opticians should invest $150,000 in the digital measuring equipment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I believe Alderley should invest in the $150,000 digital measuring equipment. Premium lenses carry higher mark-ups, so the equipment would lift the gross profit margin above the current 40% and improve the profit margin above 11%, generating the cash to service a bank loan [k]. The firm's returns are already improving, with ROCE up from 10% on $576,000 capital employed to 14% on $660,000, which gives the bank confidence to lend and funds the investment [app]. Stronger margins would also give Alderley an advantage against Clearglass Opticians, protecting market share in premium lenses and reducing reliance on price competition [an]. However, keeping current prices would protect the budget-conscious customers who generate reliable footfall, and $150,000 is a heavy commitment when Clearglass Opticians still leads on a 45% gross profit margin and 17% ROCE [k]. If premium demand disappoints, Alderley would face higher interest costs with no guarantee of extra sales, whereas price stability preserves the volume that underpins revenue of $840,000 [app]. Although the safer option protects existing trade, it locks in the gap to the competitor and slows margin growth [an]. Overall, I recommend the investment, because the improving trend suggests premium lens demand exists and, provided the loan terms are manageable, the reward outweighs the risk of defending prices alone [eval]. The main risk is over-committing to debt, so the board should agree stage payments with the bank and track premium lens sales monthly [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Premium lenses carry higher mark-ups; equipment lifts gross profit and profit margins
Keeping prices protects budget customers; $150,000 is a large commitment
application_max_2: ROCE improved from 10% ($576,000) to 14% ($660,000); PM improved to 11%
Rival Clearglass Opticians holds a 45% GPM and 17% ROCE; revenue $840,000
analysis_max_2: Stronger margins give a competitive edge and reduce price-competition reliance
Guarding volume protects revenue but cedes ground to the rival
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation justified against both options with figures
Acknowledges risk (debt, demand) and adds conditions (stage payments, monthly tracking)

scenario_stem:
Ravensworth Creamery is a private limited company in Country X making mature cheddar in two maturing rooms. It exports 420,000 kilograms a year to Country W at $15 a kilogram, earning $6,300,000; the dollar has appreciated from $1.50 to $1.25 per euro.

Carla Jimenez must set export prices. Option A cuts the price to $12, so Country W buyers pay €9.60. Option B keeps $15, accepts falling orders and seeks domestic listings. It employs 38 workers and has $500,000 of bank loans due this year.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is an increase in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys more of a foreign currency than it did before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A rise in the value of one currency
Compared with other currencies / buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the appreciation on Ravensworth Creamery.
questions.model_answer: First, appreciation makes exports more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. At $1.25 per euro, the same $15 kilogram now costs Country W supermarkets €12 instead of €10, so they may baulk at renewing the contract or demand discounts [app]. Second, demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper locally produced cheddar [k]. The 420,000 kg Country W order book, worth $6,300,000 a year, could shrink if supermarkets delist Ravensworth in favour of domestic suppliers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports more expensive abroad
Demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper alternatives
application_max_2: €12 at $1.25 per euro vs €10 at $1.50 per euro for the $15 kilogram
420,000 kg / $6,300,000 Country W order book at risk of delisting

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ravensworth Creamery might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the price shrinks the revenue earned on every kilogram [k]. At $12 instead of $15, Ravensworth forgoes $3 per kilogram across 420,000 kilograms, about $1,260,000 a year of lost revenue [app]. That leaves less cash to repay the $500,000 bank loans this year, raising the risk of refinancing at worse terms or missing repayments [an]. Second, a sharp price cut can provoke rival suppliers into cutting prices too [k]. Country W rivals may match the €9.60 shelf price to defend their own listings [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across the category, so Ravensworth struggles to fund the two maturing rooms and its 38 workers even after winning orders back [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting price reduces revenue earned per unit
Lower prices can trigger a price war with rival suppliers
application_max_2: $3 per kilogram x 420,000 kg is about $1,260,000 of lost revenue
Reference to €9.60 shelf price being matched by Country W rivals
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to lower revenue to difficulty repaying $500,000 bank loans
Chain from price war to permanently lower margins and funding pressure on maturing rooms and staff

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensworth Creamery should cut the export price to $12 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the price by 20% to $12 a kilogram [k]. At the new rate Country W buyers pay €9.60, below the €10 they paid before the appreciation, so the 420,000 kg order book worth $6,300,000 is far more likely to hold [app]. Keeping the Country W contract fills both maturing rooms, protects the jobs of 38 workers, and avoids the slow, risky push into delicatessens in Country X where volumes are much smaller [an]. However, Option B holds the $15 price [k]. Refusing to discount avoids forgoing $1,260,000 a year, keeping cash flow stronger for the $500,000 bank loan repayments, and it bets on higher-margin delicatessen listings instead [app]. The danger is that Country W supermarkets, now facing €12 per kilogram, delist Ravensworth altogether and leave it with idle capacity and falling sales [an]. Overall, I think Ravensworth should choose Option A [eval]. The appreciation was driven by currency markets, not by anything Ravensworth failed to do, so protecting volume and shelf space in Country W matters more than squeezing the margin per kilogram, and the price can be reviewed if the dollar weakens next season [eval].

Option B: hold the $15 price and pursue Country X delicatessen listings
application_max_2: €9.60 at $1.25 per euro vs €12 at the held $15 price / €10 before the appreciation

analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to retained Country W volume and filled maturing rooms
Chain from holding the price to preserved margin but risk of delisting and idle capacity
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Define 'piece rate'.
questions.model_answer: A payment system where workers are paid a fixed amount for each unit of output they produce [1], so pay rises directly with the quantity of goods made or picked [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the piece rate option for Torr Vale Distribution Centre.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Pay would be linked directly to output [k], so a picker completing 18 orders an hour would earn $17.10 compared with $14.50 an hour now [app]. questions.question_text: Do you think Torr Vale Distribution Centre should introduce the piece rate instead of keeping hourly pay with the weekly $300 team recognition award? Justify your answer.
