scenario_stem:
Oakhanger Furniture Co is a partnership making oak dining tables, with $744,000 annual revenue. It buys 1,100 tonnes of oak and uses 480,000 kWh of electricity yearly.

Site 1 lies beside a sawmill whose private substation supplies power at $0.09 per kWh, with rent of $9,000 a year. Site 2 is on an industrial estate beside the motorway: power costs $0.14 per kWh and rent $26,000, but deliveries are 35 km shorter. Which site should they choose?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'industrial estate'.
questions.model_answer: An industrial estate is a planned area of land designed for industrial businesses, offering serviced units, utilities and transport links [2].

knowledge_max_2: serviced units with utilities and transport links

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Site 1 could reduce Oakhanger's costs.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Site 1 lies beside a sawmill [app], cutting transport costs for the 1,100 tonnes of oak Oakhanger buys each year [k]. Reason 2: Power at Site 1 costs $0.09 per kWh [app], cheaper than Site 2's $0.14, so the firm saves $24,000 a year on electricity [k].

knowledge_max_2: reduced transport costs for raw materials/oak

questions.question_text: Analyse two advantages of Site 2 for Oakhanger Furniture Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Site 2 sits beside the motorway [app], so deliveries to furniture customers are 35 km shorter [k], reducing fuel costs and delivery times for bulky tables [an]. Advantage 2: Site 2 is on a national industrial estate [app], giving reliable access to grid power and services [k], which lowers the risk of production stoppages compared with a private substation [an].

knowledge_max_2: better transport links/shorter delivery to customers
reliable grid power/services on industrial estate
analysis_max_2: reduces fuel costs and delivery times

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakhanger should choose Site 1 or Site 2? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Site 1 could cut costs sharply [k]: power at $0.09 per kWh saves $24,000 a year and rent of $9,000 is $17,000 below Site 2 [app], protecting margins on $744,000 of revenue [an]. However, Site 2 sits beside the motorway [k], so deliveries to customers are 35 km shorter [app], supporting reliable service and lower fuel costs [an]. Overall, Site 1 is the better choice because the combined $41,000 yearly saving is guaranteed, whereas the 35 km delivery advantage matters less given modest table volumes [eval]; locking in cheap power and rent protects profits in a competitive furniture market [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Site 1 saves power and rent costs
analysis_max_2: supports reliable service and lower fuel costs
evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed power and rent savings against delivery-time advantage in furniture context

scenario_stem:
Dovetail Kitchens Ltd is a private limited company fitting kitchens. This year revenue was $1,150,000, gross profit $345,000 and profit $69,000, with capital employed $460,000; last year revenue $980,000, gross profit $235,200 and profit $39,200. Profit margin rose from 4% to 6%, helped by a shared buying group and energy-efficient workshop lighting.

The owners debate switching to premium German appliance suppliers to sell higher-priced ranges, or retaining value ranges to stay price-competitive. Rival ValueBuilt Homes reports a 35% gross profit margin.

questions.question_text: Define 'profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin (net profit margin) expresses the profit a business makes as a percentage of its revenue, calculated as profit / revenue x 100. It shows how much profit remains from each $1 of sales after all costs, expenses and tax have been deducted. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Profit as a percentage of revenue (profit / revenue x 100)
Shows profit remaining per $1 of sales after all costs, expenses and tax

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dovetail Kitchens' profit margin rose from 4% to 6%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A shared buying group would have lowered the cost of materials and workshop overheads, so a greater share of each sales dollar remained as profit [k]. With profit rising from $39,200 on $980,000 revenue to $69,000 on $1,150,000, the margin improved from 4% to 6% [app]. Reason 2: Energy-efficient workshop lighting cuts electricity bills, reducing expenses and lifting profit [k]. Lower lighting costs help explain why profit rose by $29,800 even though revenue rose by only $170,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower cost of sales/materials via a shared buying group (bulk discounts)
application_max_2: Revenue rose by $170,000 while profit grew by $29,800, so margins improved

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for the owners of Dovetail Kitchens.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Profitability ratios let the owners judge how efficiently the business converts revenue into profit, guiding pricing and cost-control decisions [k]. With profit margin up from 4% to 6% and gross profit margin up from 24% to 30% ($345,000 of $1,150,000), the owners can see their current approach is working [app]. This evidence helps them justify continuing margin-focused decisions when agreeing supplier contracts [an]. Use 2: Profitability ratios highlight relative performance and guide future investment decisions [k]. Return on capital employed improved from 10% to 15% ($69,000 on $460,000), showing owners their capital is working harder than last year [app]. Comparing their own 30% gross profit margin against the 35% achieved by ValueBuilt Homes shows where improvement is still possible, guiding the decision on whether to switch suppliers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Measure efficiency of converting revenue into profit; guide pricing/cost control
Compare performance over time and with competitors to guide investment decisions
application_max_2: ROCE rose from 10% to 15% ($69,000 on $460,000); ValueBuilt Homes achieves 35% GPM
analysis_max_2: Improvement validates and supports the current strategy and supplier decisions
Gap to the rival identifies where to focus improvement before switching suppliers

questions.question_text: Do you think Dovetail Kitchens should switch to premium German appliance suppliers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Dovetail Kitchens should switch to premium German appliance suppliers. Premium ranges carry higher selling prices and mark-ups, which would lift the gross profit margin above the current 30% ($345,000 of $1,150,000) towards the 35% achieved by ValueBuilt Homes, improving the profit margin above 6% [k]. Improved margins would strengthen return on capital employed beyond 15% ($69,000 on $460,000), justifying the owners' plans and helping fund future growth [app]. Higher-quality kitchens can also differentiate the business from the national chain, winning customers who value design over lowest price [an]. However, the owners could instead keep the value ranges, because switching carries risks: premium stock costs more to hold, and if sales volumes fall, revenue growth could slip back from the $1,150,000 level achieved this year [k]. Keeping the value offer protects price-sensitive customers and avoids being undercut on price by ValueBuilt Homes, whose appeal is high volume at keen prices [app]. A wrong switch could dent the 6% profit margin if premium demand proves weak, whereas the current strategy already delivered an improvement from 4% [an]. Overall, I recommend the switch, but phased: trial premium lines in a small number of projects first and track gross profit margin monthly, since the upward trend and stronger ROCE suggest the premium market is reachable [eval]. The main risk is demand uncertainty, so supplier agreements should protect Dovetail against unsold premium stock [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Premium ranges carry higher mark-ups and prices; lift GPM
Switching carries risks: premium stock costs, demand uncertainty
application_max_2: Value strategy already improved PM from 4% to 6%; revenue now $1,150,000
analysis_max_2: Premium positioning differentiates from the national chain and can raise order values
Phased trial limits risk; track monthly GPM to confirm viability
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation justified with figures; conditions attached (trial, monthly tracking)
Weighs both options; demand-uncertainty risk acknowledged

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Netherfield Glassworks is a private limited company in Country X making toughened glass panels. It imports 500 tonnes of blanks from Country W at €4,000 a tonne; the dollar fell from $1.30 to $1.56 per euro, lifting the $2,600,000 bill to $3,120,000, a $520,000 rise.

Priya Nair must cover the rise. Option A uses the $380,000 reserve. Option B raises prices 12% across $4,400,000 of sales, adding $528,000. Three big customers hold fixed-price contracts worth $1,900,000; the firm employs 26 technicians.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of 500 tonnes of glass blanks before and after the rate change.
Explain two effects of the depreciation on Netherfield Glassworks.
questions.model_answer: First, imports become more expensive when the currency weakens [k]. The annual glass blank bill rises from $2,600,000 to $3,120,000, an extra $520,000 a year for exactly the same 500 tonnes of inputs [app]. Second, higher input costs squeeze the profit margin [k]. The $380,000 retained-profit reserve is not enough to absorb a $520,000 rise, so Netherfield must cut costs, raise prices or eat into the reserve [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency
application_max_2: $380,000 reserve is insufficient to cover the extra $520,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of choosing Option B, to raise prices by 12%.
questions.model_answer: First, customers may resist a double-digit price rise and switch to cheaper rivals [k]. The three big customers' contracts are fixed-price worth $1,900,000, so the 12% rise cannot touch them; the full $528,000 must come from smaller and new customers, who are the most price-sensitive [app]. If they defer or cancel orders, sales fall below $4,400,000 and the expected $528,000 gain shrinks fast [an]. Second, raising prices may trigger wider price competition in the office-tower market [k]. Rival glassworks may hold prices to grab Netherfield's share, leaving it with fewer orders to spread fixed costs across [app]. Falling volumes raise unit costs, cutting profit at a time when the $380,000 reserve is already stretched by the $520,000 import rise [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices risk losing customers to cheaper rivals
Price rises can trigger competitive price cuts / lost volume
application_max_2: Fixed-price contracts worth $1,900,000 cannot be repriced, so the rise falls on smaller customers
Reference to $528,000 expected gain vs $4,400,000 sales and the $380,000 reserve
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to lost orders to sales below $4,400,000 and a shrinking gain
Chain from competition on price to lower volume to higher unit costs and lower profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Netherfield Glassworks should raise prices by 12% (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B raises prices by 12% across $4,400,000 of annual sales, adding $528,000 a year [k]. That more than covers the extra $520,000 import bill and leaves $8,000 spare, restoring the $380,000 reserve for genuine emergencies such as a machine breakdown [app]. Holding real prices up protects the margin needed to keep the 26 technicians busy and avoids eating into reserves that took years to build [an]. However, Option A absorbs the $520,000 from the $380,000 reserve [k]. This keeps Netherfield fully competitive on price and protects relationships with the three fixed-price customers while their contracts run, which may win follow-on work after next summer [app]. The danger is that the reserve is wiped out entirely and still leaves $140,000 unfunded, so the firm enters winter with no cushion if the dollar weakens further or if repairs arise [an]. Overall, I think Netherfield should choose Option B [eval], because absorbing a $520,000 rise it cannot afford is riskier than the possible loss of price-sensitive orders; the firm should apply the rise to new work first and soften it if order volumes fall sharply [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option B: 12% price rise adding $528,000 a year
Option A: absorb the extra $520,000 from the $380,000 reserve
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to covered import bill to restored reserve and financial safety
Chain from absorbing the cost to exhausted reserve and no cushion for further depreciation
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and notes linking the rise to new work first

scenario_stem:
Greythorn Taxis is an unincorporated partnership owned by Femi and Ada Balogun for 5 years. It runs 4 licensed taxis and generated $260,000 revenue with $45,000 profit.

The Baloguns want a wheelchair-accessible minibus costing $70,000 but cannot raise the full amount from savings. Converting to a private limited company would let them sell shares to family members and approach banks as a separate legal entity. Ada prefers staying unincorporated to avoid registration costs and paperwork.

questions.question_text: Define 'unincorporated'.
questions.model_answer: An unincorporated business is not a separate legal entity from its owners [1], so the owners are personally liable for the debts of the business [1].

knowledge_max_2: not a separate legal entity from its owners
owners personally liable for business debts

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Greythorn Taxis of keeping the business unincorporated.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Fewer legal formalities and low running costs [k], so the Baloguns avoid registration fees and annual filings while earning $260,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Complete privacy of financial affairs [k], since accounts are not published, keeping the $45,000 profit figure away from competitors and the public [app].

knowledge_max_2: fewer legal formalities and lower costs

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the Baloguns converting to a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Limited liability protection [k], so Femi and Ada risk only their investment if the business cannot repay finance taken for the $70,000 wheelchair-accessible minibus [app], protecting the family home and savings [an]. Benefit 2: Corporate status makes raising finance easier [k], as the company could sell shares to family members and approach banks as a separate legal entity [app], unlocking the funds needed to buy the minibus quickly [an].

knowledge_max_2: limited liability protects owners' personal assets
separate legal entity can raise finance more easily
analysis_max_2: personal assets are protected from business debts
share issues and bank loans unlock the $70,000 purchase

questions.question_text: Do you think Greythorn Taxis should become an incorporated private limited company rather than remain an unincorporated partnership? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Incorporating would create a separate legal entity [k] able to sell shares to family members to raise the $70,000 needed for the minibus [app], enabling faster expansion while protecting both owners through limited liability [an]. However, remaining unincorporated avoids registration fees and paperwork [k], saving money and keeping the $260,000 revenue and $45,000 profit private [app], which suits a small two-owner partnership with modest plans [an]. Overall, Greythorn Taxis should incorporate as a private limited company [eval], because limited liability matters far more than the minor compliance costs when committing to a $70,000 asset [eval].

knowledge_max_2: incorporation creates a separate legal entity with limited liability
unincorporated business has lower costs and more privacy
analysis_max_2: separate legal status unlocks finance and share issues
privacy and low costs suit a small partnership
evaluation_max_2: weighs limited liability against compliance costs
recommendation linked to the $70,000 minibus purchase

scenario_stem:
Brightspur Field Sales is a private limited company with 24 field sales representatives selling office furniture across 3 regions. Last year's $9.6 million sales averaged $33,000 per representative monthly. They earn $1,400 base plus 3% commission, about $2,400 total, and turnover reached 20%.

Priya Nair proposes 5% commission only, paying about $1,650, or keeping the present scheme and adding a 'Star Performer' recognition programme with awards, parking and a directors' dinner, costing $8,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'commission'.
questions.model_answer: A payment made to an employee based on the value of the sales they make, usually a percentage of each sale [1], so earnings rise when sales rise [1].

knowledge_max_2: payment based on value of sales made

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the current salary-plus-commission scheme at Brightspur Field Sales.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The base salary gives representatives a stable income [k], so they still receive $1,400 a month in quiet periods when sales fall below the $33,000 average [app]. Advantage 2: The 3% commission links pay to performance [k], adding about $1,000 a month on top of salary and motivating representatives to close more sales above the current average [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with switching to 5% commission only.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Representatives would face serious income risk in quiet months [k], earning only about $1,650 at the current average and far less in slow months, compared with a certain $1,400 base today [app], which could push turnover above 20% [an]. Problem 2: Aggressive selling may result if pay depends entirely on sales [k], so representatives might pressure customers into orders they cannot afford [app], damaging Brightspur's reputation across its 3 regions [an].

knowledge_max_2: pay linked purely to sales can encourage pressure selling

questions.question_text: Do you think Brightspur Field Sales should switch to 5% commission only instead of keeping the present scheme and adding the Star Performer recognition programme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Commission-only pay would sharply reward top performers [k], with 5% on $33,000 of monthly sales paying about $1,650 and unlimited upside above that [app], likely pushing representatives to sell harder and lift revenue beyond $9.6 million [an]. However, it removes the income floor and stability [k], risking resignations among the 24 representatives and turnover above 20%, while the $8,000 Star Performer scheme costs very little and rewards loyalty without income risk [app], protecting customer relationships and morale [an]. Overall, Brightspur should keep the salary-plus-commission scheme and add the recognition programme [eval], because $8,000 a year is tiny against $9.6 million in sales and retention protects regional customer relationships [eval].

knowledge_max_2: commission-only pay rewards and motivates top sellers
recognition motivates at low cost without income risk
analysis_max_2: commission-only could lift sales but risks resignations
recognition protects morale and relationships cheaply
evaluation_max_2: weighs short-run selling incentive against retention risk
justified recommendation tied to stem figures

scenario_stem:
Briarwood Artisan Bakery is a private limited company supplying 45 shops and 12 school canteens. Owner Marcus Adebayo researches a gluten-free range; 23 out of 60 Saturday morning queuers, roughly 38%, said they would buy it.

His daughter's survey reaches only loyal buyers, so Marcus prefers a random sample of 250 from his loyalty card database of 9,500 members for $900. He worries the 60 results are unrepresentative.

questions.question_text: Define 'bias'.
questions.model_answer: Bias is a factor that distorts research findings away from the true picture [1]. It can arise when the sample is unrepresentative or when questions are worded to push respondents towards a particular answer [1].

knowledge_max_2: bias distorts research findings away from the true picture
causes include unrepresentative samples and leading questions

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Saturday-morning survey may be biased.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The Saturday survey only reaches loyal, regular customers [k], so the 60 people queuing on Saturday morning are not representative of the customers of all 45 shops and 12 school canteens [app]. Reason 2: The sample is self-selecting [k], as only people who happened to visit on that Saturday were asked, so the 23 out of 60 figure may not reflect the wider customer base [app].

knowledge_max_2: bias arises when the sample is not representative of the population
self-selecting samples over-represent the most engaged people
application_max_2: 60 Saturday-morning queue customers versus 45 shops and 12 school canteens
23 out of 60 interested in the gluten-free range

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of Marcus's gluten-free research.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: The sample size affects accuracy [k], so the views of only 60 Saturday customers are less reliable than those of a random sample of 250 from the loyalty database [app], making the roughly 38% figure less dependable [an]. Factor 2: Who is in the sample affects accuracy [k], because Saturday shoppers may be unusually loyal or health-conscious [app], unlike a random sample of the 9,500-member loyalty database, so demand for the gluten-free range could be overestimated [an].

knowledge_max_2: sample size affects the reliability of the results
sample selection affects representativeness and can introduce bias
application_max_2: 60 Saturday customers versus 250 loyalty members drawn at random
analysis_max_2: small sample makes the roughly 38% figure less dependable
unrepresentative sample could overestimate demand for the gluten-free range

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should rely on the Saturday survey instead of the loyalty-card random sample? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Saturday survey costs nothing and gives immediate results [k], with 23 out of 60 customers, roughly 38%, already showing interest in a gluten-free range [app], which could save the bakery time and the $900 mailing cost [an]. However, the sample is small and biased towards loyal customers [k], whereas a random sample of 250 from the 9,500 loyalty members would better represent his wider customer base across 45 shops [app], giving a more accurate picture before investing in new equipment and ingredients [an]. Overall, Marcus should use the loyalty-card random sample [eval], because spending $900 now is worthwhile to avoid producing a gluten-free range that his wider customers may not buy [eval].

knowledge_max_2: small, self-selected samples are cheaper but unrepresentative
random sampling from a full customer list is more representative
application_max_2: 23 out of 60 Saturday customers, roughly 38%, interested in gluten-free
250 random customers from 9,500 loyalty members, costing $900
analysis_max_2: Saturday survey saves money but risks a wrong launch decision
larger random sample gives a truer picture of wider demand across 45 shops
evaluation_max_2: weighs free quick results against the value of representative data
justified recommendation tied to the $900 cost and gluten-free launch risk

scenario_stem:
Netherby Garments is a private limited company producing school uniforms. It pays 96 sewing machinists $4.80 an hour, dispatches 70% of output by road to capital retailers and will hire 30 more machinists next year.

Tarrin offers wages of $4.10 an hour and a $60,000 new-jobs grant. Bramford pays $5.90 an hour, but 40 trained machinists seek work there and the capital is just 45 minutes away by motorway. Which town should the factory choose?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'labour supply'.
questions.model_answer: Labour supply is the number of workers available to be hired in a particular area, industry or occupation [2].

knowledge_max_2: number of workers available to hire

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tarrin might be an attractive location for the factory.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Tarrin offers wages averaging $4.10 an hour [app], 70 cents below the current $4.80 [k]. Reason 2: Tarrin's council offers a $60,000 new-jobs grant [app], which lowers the cost of hiring the 30 more machinists expected next year [k].

questions.question_text: Analyse two benefits of choosing Bramford.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Bramford has 40 trained machinists seeking work [app], so the factory can fill the 30 planned posts quickly [k], avoiding production delays and idle machines [an]. Benefit 2: Bramford is only 45 minutes from the capital [app], so the 70% of output dispatched to retail chains can arrive same-day [k], reducing transport costs and tightening delivery times [an].

application_max_2: 70% of output by road to retail chains
analysis_max_2: reduces transport costs and tightens delivery times

questions.question_text: Do you think Netherby should locate in Tarrin or Bramford? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Tarrin offers wages of $4.10 an hour [k], saving 70 cents per hour against the current $4.80 plus a $60,000 grant [app], cutting the cost of hiring 30 more machinists [an]. Bramford provides 40 trained machinists and is only 45 minutes from the capital [k], protecting delivery of the 70% of output going to retail chains [app], which keeps uniforms arriving on time for schools [an]. Overall, Bramford is the better choice because skilled labour and same-day access to the capital protect revenue, even though wages are $1.80 an hour higher than Tarrin [eval]; delivery reliability matters more than a slightly cheaper wage bill [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Tarrin cheaper wages and grant support
Bramford offers skills and proximity to market
analysis_max_2: cuts cost of hiring 30 more machinists
keeps uniform deliveries on time for retail chains
evaluation_max_2: weighs wage savings and grant against skill availability and delivery reliability in uniform-supply context

scenario_stem:
Larkhill Garden Centres Ltd is a private limited company operating 2 garden centres. This year revenue was $2,400,000, gross profit $912,000 and profit $144,000, with capital employed $1,200,000; last year revenue $2,100,000, gross profit $756,000 and profit $105,000 on $1,050,000 capital. Gross margin rose 36% to 38% and ROCE 10% to 12%.

Rival Hillview Gardenworld reports 42% gross margin and 15% ROCE. The company must choose between a third $300,000 centre with bank funding, or refurbishing its 2 stores for $150,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'return on capital employed'.
questions.model_answer: Return on capital employed (ROCE) measures how effectively a business uses its capital to generate profit. It is calculated as profit / capital employed x 100 and shows the percentage return earned on the long-term funds invested in the business. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Profit divided by capital employed, expressed as a percentage (x 100)
Shows how effectively long-term capital is used to generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Larkhill Garden Centres' ROCE rose from 10% to 12%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit grew faster than the capital employed, since profit rose from $105,000 to $144,000 while capital employed increased only modestly from $1,050,000 to $1,200,000 [k]. This produces a ROCE of 12% ($144,000 on $1,200,000), up from 10% ($105,000 on $1,050,000) [app]. Reason 2: New high-margin landscaping and cafe lines lifted the gross profit margin from 36% to 38%, so more of each dollar of revenue reached the bottom line [k]. Gross profit rose to $912,000 on revenue of $2,400,000, and this improvement flows through to a higher ROCE [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit growing faster than capital employed raises ROCE
Improved margins (cost control and sales mix) raise profit and ROCE
application_max_2: Profit $105,000 to $144,000; capital employed $1,050,000 to $1,200,000; ROCE 10% to 12%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of comparing Larkhill's profitability ratios with those of Hillview Gardenworld.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Comparison against a rival shows whether Larkhill's performance is competitive, not merely improving in isolation [k]. Hillview Gardenworld reports a 42% gross profit margin and 15% ROCE versus Larkhill's 38% and 12%, so managers can see they still trail on both measures [app]. This tells the board where effort is most needed, such as lifting margins on cafe and landscaping lines, before committing to expansion [an]. Benefit 2: Rival benchmarking helps set realistic targets and supports decisions on where to allocate scarce capital [k]. Closing even half the 4-percentage-point gap to Hillview's 42% margin would add about $96,000 to gross profit on revenue of $2,400,000 [app]. This quantifies the prize from improvement and helps prioritise investment between the two options facing the company [an].

knowledge_max_2: Benchmarking shows competitiveness vs rivals, not just trend improvement
Benchmarks set targets and guide where capital is best allocated
application_max_2: Hillview Gardenworld 42% GPM and 15% ROCE vs Larkhill 38% and 12%
Half the 4-point margin gap is worth about $96,000 on revenue of $2,400,000
analysis_max_2: Gap shows where to focus (cafe and landscaping margins) before expanding
Quantifying gains enables prioritisation between a new centre and refurbishment

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkhill Garden Centres should open a third garden centre? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Larkhill should open the third garden centre, but only with cautious debt funding. Opening a $300,000 third centre would add a new revenue stream and lift profit beyond the current $144,000, and Larkhill's ROCE of 12% is rising towards the 15% reported by Hillview Gardenworld [k]. Returns are improving, with ROCE up from 10% on $1,050,000 to 12% on $1,200,000, and a successful new site would spread fixed costs and strengthen its competitive position [app]. A third site would also reduce dependence on 2 locations and capture demand the existing centres cannot serve [an]. However, the safer choice is to refurbish the existing 2 stores for $150,000, because it costs half as much and should lift margins at proven locations [k]. Refurbishment fits the improving trend (profit margin up from 5% to 6%, gross profit margin up from 36% to 38%) and avoids new debt while Hillview Gardenworld still leads on 42% margin and 15% ROCE [app]. Spending only $150,000 protects the balance sheet and could raise returns on the current $1,200,000 capital employed more safely than untested new-site demand [an]. Overall, I recommend opening the third centre, provided the bank agrees affordable terms, because Larkhill's upward trajectory shows it can convert capital into profit efficiently and refurbishment would cap growth [eval]. If early trading disappoints, the board should fall back on the $150,000 refurbishment plan for the existing stores [eval].

knowledge_max_2: New site adds a revenue stream and spreads fixed costs; lifts profit
Refurbishment is cheaper, lower risk, proven locations, avoids new debt
application_max_2: Refurbishment $150,000 suits improving trend (GPM 36% to 38%, PM 5% to 6%); Hillview leads at 42% and 15%
analysis_max_2: New site diversifies location risk but adds untested demand risk
Refurbishment lifts returns on current capital more safely
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation justified with conditions (bank terms) and weighed against refurbishment
Fallback plan acknowledged; balanced overall judgement

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Whinmoor Wool Exports is a partnership in Country X dyeing wool tops. It sells 70% of 120,000 kg yearly to Country W at €18 a kilo: 84,000 kg, €1,512,000. The dollar fell from $1.25 to $1.50 per euro, lifting receipts from $1,890,000 to $2,268,000.

The partners must decide. Option A chases 25 new Country W accounts while wool tops are cheap abroad. Option B signs a three-year fixed-dollar domestic contract. They employ 19 dyers and expect sheep prices up 10% next year.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys less of a foreign currency than it did before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of one currency
Compared with other currencies / buys less foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the weaker currency for Whinmoor Wool Exports.
questions.model_answer: First, a weaker currency means each euro of Country W sales converts into more dollars [k]. The 84,000 kg exported at €18 per kilogram bring in €1,512,000, worth $2,268,000 now instead of $1,890,000 at the old rate — an extra $378,000 for no extra output [app]. Second, a weaker currency makes Whinmoor's wool tops cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. Country W garment factories can now buy the same combed, dyed yarn for fewer euros, which should help Whinmoor win the 25 new accounts it is chasing [app].

scenario_stem:
Snowdrift Ice Cream Co is a private limited company selling ice-cream tubs through 180 shops and 25 hotels, with $950,000 revenue. Owner Sofia Almeida considers a vegan gelato, researching in January before Easter.

A January survey of 200 shoppers in a covered market found 22% interested, 44 people. Sofia can launch at Easter or repeat research in July with 250 beach-goers for $1,300, delaying 5 months. The board sees a bar chart.

questions.question_text: Define 'primary research'.
questions.model_answer: Primary research is the collection of new, first-hand information directly from consumers [1]. Examples include questionnaires, interviews, focus groups and observation [1].

knowledge_max_2: collection of new first-hand information directly from consumers
examples include questionnaires, interviews, focus groups and observation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the timing of Snowdrift's market research matters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer behaviour changes with the seasons [k], so a January survey in a covered market would understate demand from people buying ice cream at the beach in July [app]. Reason 2: Research at the wrong time can mislead [k], as the 22% of 200 shoppers (44 people) found in winter may be far lower than peak summer demand for a new vegan gelato [app].

knowledge_max_2: consumer behaviour and demand vary with the seasons
mis-timed research can understate peak demand
application_max_2: January survey in a covered market
22% of 200 shoppers, 44 people, low winter demand

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that could make the January research data inaccurate.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Where and when people are asked affects who responds [k], so interviewing shoppers in a covered market in January reaches a different crowd from the 250 beach-goers she would meet in July [app], giving a biased picture of annual demand [an]. Factor 2: The sample size affects reliability [k], so 200 respondents in winter may not reflect the customers of the 180 shops and 25 hotels Snowdrift supplies [app], so the bar chart could misjudge interest in the vegan gelato [an].

knowledge_max_2: timing and location of the survey shape who responds
sample size affects the reliability of the findings

However, the survey was taken in winter when ice cream demand is lowest [k], so a repeat survey of 250 beach-goers and market-stall visitors in July would cost $1,300 but reflect true peak-season demand [app], reducing the risk of the Easter launch flopping [an]. scenario_stem:
Maplehurst Physiotherapy Clinic is a private limited company treating 1,400 patients a year and earning $380,000. Its town-centre site is a 5-minute walk from the bus station with 2,200 passersby a week, but rent is rising to $21,000.

A suburban medical centre unit offers 40 free parking spaces and rent of $9,000, but it is 4 km from the town centre with lower passing trade. Should the clinic relocate there?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'footfall'.
questions.model_answer: Footfall is the number of people passing through or past a particular location, such as a shopping street or clinic entrance [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the town-centre site for the clinic.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The town-centre site is a 5-minute walk from the bus station [app], making it easy for patients without cars to attend appointments [k]. Benefit 2: With 2,200 passersby a week [app], the clinic gains visibility that can attract new walk-in patients [k].

questions.question_text: Analyse two benefits of the suburban medical centre site.

questions.question_text: Do you think Maplehurst Physiotherapy Clinic should relocate to the suburban medical centre? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Marston Fish Smokery Ltd is a private limited company smoking salmon and mackerel. Revenue was $950,000, gross profit $304,000 and profit $76,000, with capital employed $475,000; last year revenue $880,000, gross profit $264,000 and profit $61,600 on $440,000 capital. Gross margin rose 30% to 32% and ROCE 14% to 16%.

Rival Clifftop Smokehouse reports 36% gross margin but 12% ROCE. Marston plans to borrow $180,000 for a second kiln to serve a supermarket contract, or continue small-batch artisan production for direct customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital employed'.
questions.model_answer: Capital employed is the total long-term funds invested in a business, usually calculated as non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities). It represents the capital base that generates the business's profit and is the denominator of the ROCE ratio. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities)
Equals total assets minus current liabilities; the base that generates profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marston Fish Smokery's ROCE rose from 14% to 16%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit rose from $61,600 to $76,000, a proportionally larger increase than capital employed, lifting the return [k]. Return on capital employed is profit / capital employed x 100, so Marston's ROCE rose from 14% ($61,600 / $440,000) to 16% ($76,000 / $475,000) [app]. Reason 2: The gross profit margin improved from 30% to 32% ($304,000 of $950,000), showing tighter control of production costs relative to prices [k]. This extra profit flows directly into ROCE, which is calculated on the $475,000 capital employed [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit rising faster than capital employed raises ROCE
Higher gross profit margin (cost control) raises the profit feeding ROCE
application_max_2: ROCE rose from 14% to 16%; profit $61,600 to $76,000; CE $440,000 to $475,000

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for Marston's managers.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Profitability ratios show managers how efficiently the firm converts sales into profit, guiding pricing and cost decisions [k]. Marston's profit margin rose from 7% to 8% ($76,000 on $950,000), with gross profit at 32% ($304,000 of $950,000), confirming the artisan strategy is adding value [app]. This evidence supports continuing to focus on premium direct customers rather than discounting [an]. Use 2: ROCE helps managers assess whether investments earn satisfactory returns [k]. The 16% ROCE (up from 14%) and the comparison with Clifftop Smokehouse's 12% show Marston is using its $475,000 capital more productively than its rival [app]. This supports expansion decisions, such as whether to build the second smokehouse kiln [an].

knowledge_max_2: GPM/PM track pricing and cost-control performance
ROCE assesses returns on investment decisions
application_max_2: ROCE 14% to 16% vs Clifftop Smokehouse 12%; capital employed $475,000
analysis_max_2: Confirms artisan premium strategy and supports its continuation over discounting
Strong relative ROCE supports the expansion decision on the second kiln

questions.question_text: Do you think Marston Fish Smokery should borrow $180,000 to build a second smokehouse kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Marston should proceed with the second smokehouse kiln. Building the kiln would let Marston serve the supermarket contract and lift revenue beyond the current $950,000, while its 16% ROCE already beats Clifftop Smokehouse's 12%, showing it uses new capital productively [k]. Profit rose to $76,000 (8% profit margin) this year, so a larger output base should raise the cash available to service loan repayments [app]. Extra capacity also diversifies Marston beyond local delicatessens and online sales, reducing reliance on its limited direct-customer base [an]. However, staying artisan keeps costs low and avoids new debt entirely [k]. Local delicatessens and online customers give predictable cash flow, and borrowing $180,000 adds repayment pressure if supermarket volumes or payment terms disappoint, squeezing the 8% margin [app]. The rival comparison is instructive: Clifftop Smokehouse earns a 36% gross profit margin at only 12% ROCE, suggesting scale alone does not guarantee strong returns on capital [an]. Overall, I recommend borrowing for the kiln, because the improving trend (margins and ROCE all rising) indicates Marston can profit from extra capacity, provided the loan is tied to the supermarket contract [eval]. The board should phase the build and monitor ROCE and profit margin quarterly so the expansion can pause if returns fall below 14% [eval].

knowledge_max_2: New capacity enables volume/revenue growth; loan funds it
Staying artisan avoids debt and protects healthy margins and cash flow
application_max_2: ROCE 16% vs Clifftop 12%; profit $76,000 (8% PM) on $950,000; GPM 32%
$180,000 loan adds repayment pressure; rival GPM 36% at only 12% ROCE
analysis_max_2: Diversification beyond direct customers reduces reliance risk
Scale alone does not guarantee returns - Clifftop evidence
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation weighs trend against debt risk; conditional on contract
Phased build with quarterly ROCE monitoring set as a safeguard

scenario_stem:
Holmfirth Surgical Instruments is a private limited company in Country X exporting bone drills to Country W hospitals. It sells 320 sets yearly at €2,400 each, worth €768,000. Rates swung between $1.20 and $1.50 per euro, moving receipts from $921,600 to $1,152,000, a $230,400 gap.

Yusuf Rahman must set next year's prices. Option A invoices in dollars at $3,000 a set, shifting risk to buyers. Option B invoices in euros at €2,400, carrying the uncertainty. The firm employs 17 machinists.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'exchange-rate fluctuation'.
questions.model_answer: Exchange-rate fluctuation is when the value of one currency against another rises and falls over time rather than staying fixed, so the price of foreign currencies changes frequently [2].

knowledge_max_2: The value of one currency against another changes over time
Rates are not fixed / they move up and down frequently

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the fluctuation creates for Holmfirth Surgical Instruments.
questions.model_answer: First, export earnings in dollars become unpredictable [k]. The 320 sets sold each year at €2,400, worth €768,000, can yield $921,600 at the low point of the range or $1,152,000 at the high point, a swing of $230,400 on identical orders [app]. Second, the firm finds budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult [k]. It cannot fix monthly dollar inflows, making it hard to schedule wages for 17 machinists or to plan equipment purchases with confidence [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fluctuations make budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult
application_max_2: Reference to $921,600 at the low point and $1,152,000 at the high point
Reference to the $230,400 gap / 320 sets / €768,000 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to invoice in Country X dollars at $3,000 a set.
questions.model_answer: First, dollar invoicing removes the exchange-rate risk from Holmfirth entirely [k]. At $3,000 a set the firm knows it will receive about $960,000 a year for 320 sets, whatever happens between $1.20 and $1.50 [app]. Predictable receipts let it budget wages, materials and the clearing-bank account without guessing each month's conversion, cutting financial stress and borrowing costs [an]. Second, invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and management reports [k]. All 320 export invoices are written and collected in dollars, so no conversion work or foreign-currency bank charges apply to each deal [app]. Management can compare monthly performance directly against equivalent euro figures, improving control and the speed of decision-making [an].

knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the home currency removes exchange-rate risk for the seller
Invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and administration
application_max_2: $3,000 x 320 sets is about $960,000 a year regardless of the rate between $1.20 and $1.50
Reference to 320 sets a year / Country X clearing bank
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed dollar receipts to reliable budgeting to lower stress and borrowing costs
Chain from dollar invoicing to simpler administration to faster, better-informed decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Holmfirth Surgical Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in dollars at $3,000 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A invoices in Country X dollars at $3,000 per set, fixing annual revenue at about $960,000 for 320 sets [k]. It removes the $230,400 swing between the low and high points of the dollar-euro range, making wages for 17 machinists and loan repayments easy to plan, and it spares the firm conversion fees and extra paperwork [app]. The trade-off is that Country W hospitals face a euro price that moves with the rate — at $1.50 the price is €2,000 and at $1.20 it is €2,500 — so buyers may push back or compare rival quotes, which could cost Holmfirth orders [an]. However, Option B invoices in euros at €2,400 per set [k]. Buyers see a stable euro price, which they prefer, and it may help Holmfirth win and keep hospital contracts against rival suppliers whose quotes also move with the rate [app]. The cost is that Holmfirth carries the full currency risk itself, so a year of adverse rates could cost $230,400 of margin, out of earnings of between $921,600 and $1,152,000 [an]. Overall, I think Holmfirth should choose Option A [eval], because the swing is worth about $230,400 a year — too large to gamble on hospital loyalty, and the firm can discount individual deals if a buyer complains, whereas it cannot recover euro invoices already written; it should review the $3,000 price each quarter as the rate moves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: dollar invoicing at $3,000 fixes revenue at about $960,000
Option B: euro invoicing at €2,400 gives buyers price stability but Holmfirth carries the risk
application_max_2: Reference to $921,600–$1,152,000 range and the $230,400 gap
Reference to 320 sets / €2,400 / $3,000 / 17 machinists / Country W hospitals
analysis_max_2: Chain from dollar invoicing to revenue certainty to easier wages and loan planning
Chain from euro invoicing to buyer price stability but $230,400 of currency risk for Holmfirth
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes quarterly price review

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Redhill Stationery Wholesalers Ltd is a private limited company supplying schools and offices. This year revenue was $5,200,000, cost of sales $4,160,000, gross profit $1,040,000 and profit $156,000, with capital employed $1,300,000; last year revenue $4,800,000, gross profit $960,000 and profit $240,000.
