Competitor Paperline Wholesale reports 24% gross profit margin. A national school supply contract of $700,000 a year is offered at a lower margin, or it could focus on profitable local retailer customers.

questions.question_text: Calculate the profit margin for Redhill Stationery Wholesalers Ltd. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin = profit / revenue x 100 = $156,000 / $5,200,000 x 100 = 3%. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit fell from $240,000 to $156,000 despite revenue rising.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Sharp increases in warehouse energy prices and staff wages pushed up operating expenses, so more of the extra revenue was absorbed by running costs [k]. Revenue rose to $5,200,000 from $4,800,000, yet profit fell by $84,000, meaning expenses grew faster than sales [app]. Reason 2: Cost of sales stayed proportional at 80% of revenue ($4,160,000 of $5,200,000), reflecting little room to raise wholesale prices in a competitive market [k]. The gross profit margin held at 20% ($1,040,000) while the profit margin dropped to 3%, showing rising operating costs drove the squeeze [app].

knowledge_max_2: Rising operating expenses (energy, wages) absorb revenue and reduce profit
Cost of sales high and stable limits scope to protect margin
application_max_2: CoS $4,160,000 = 80% of revenue; GP $1,040,000; GPM flat at 20%

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for Redhill's managers.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Profitability ratios highlight where profits are leaking, prompting targeted cost control [k]. The 3% profit margin ($156,000 on $5,200,000) signals expenses are rising too fast, so managers can act on energy and wage efficiencies [app]. Acting on this could restore the margin towards the previous 5% and protect cash flow [an]. Use 2: Ratios support decisions on which contracts to accept [k]. The national school supply contract is offered at a lower margin, and comparing it against the current 20% gross profit margin and 12% ROCE ($156,000 on $1,300,000) shows whether the added volume justifies thinner returns [app]. This prevents Redhill from diluting returns on its $1,300,000 capital employed [an].

knowledge_max_2: Identify leakages: margin compression signals cost-control action
Evaluate contract/investment decisions via ROCE and margins
application_max_2: ROCE 12% ($156,000 of $1,300,000); GPM 20%; Paperline Wholesale benchmark 24%
analysis_max_2: Cost control could restore margin and protect cash flow
Comparison prevents accepting a dilutive contract below acceptable returns

questions.question_text: Do you think Redhill Stationery Wholesalers should accept the national school supply contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Redhill should accept the contract, but only after negotiating better terms. Accepting a $700,000 annual contract would lift revenue above the current $5,200,000 and keep warehouse volumes high, spreading fixed costs over more units [k]. Higher throughput may reduce average handling costs per parcel, partly offsetting the lower margin, and Redhill already runs a 20% gross profit margin and 12% ROCE with capacity to improve [app]. A national schools presence would also raise brand recognition in a sector where Paperline Wholesale reports 24% margins, potentially winning further profitable work [an]. However, the lower margin would cut the profit margin below 3%, extending a steep fall from 5% last year, and profit could fall again even with revenue up [k]. Local retailers give Redhill better margins and shorter payment cycles, while the school contract could stretch cash flow [app]. Every extra dollar of low-margin sales consumes working capital, so profits of $156,000 on $1,300,000 capital employed could shrink further if service failures trigger penalties [an]. Overall, I recommend accepting only if the board can negotiate revised pricing or volume rebates, because the contract secures scale that will help it keep pace with Paperline Wholesale, but margin protection matters most right now [eval]. If terms cannot improve, declining and serving profitable local customers is the better path [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Contract lifts revenue and volume, spreads fixed costs
Lower margin dilutes the profit margin further
application_max_2: $700,000 contract on top of $5,200,000 revenue; GPM 20%, PM 3%, ROCE 12%
PM already fell from 5% ($240,000) to 3% ($156,000); Paperline 24% benchmark
analysis_max_2: Scale improves brand and may bring profitable follow-on work
Low-margin sales consume working capital and risk penalties, shrinking returns
evaluation_max_2: Conditional recommendation justified; both options weighed
Clear fallback if terms cannot improve

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brayford Marine Engines is a private limited company in Country X importing outboard motors from Country W at €3,100. It sells 240 yearly at $5,400, earning $1,296,000. The dollar fell from $1.25 to $1.50 per euro, raising the bill from $930,000 to $1,116,000, an extra $186,000.

Mark Davison must set spring prices. Option A raises them 20% to $6,480, adding $259,200. Option B holds $5,400, absorbing the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 reserve. The firm employs 9 fitters and uses 4 dealers.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of 240 outboard motors at €3,100 each before and after the rate change.
Explain two effects of the depreciation on Brayford Marine Engines.
questions.model_answer: First, imported motors become more expensive in local currency [k]. The 240 motors a year rise from a $930,000 to a $1,116,000 import bill, an extra $186,000 a year for the same stock [app]. Second, margins are squeezed if prices are held at $5,400 [k]. Holding price absorbs $186,000 of the $260,000 profit reserve, leaving just $74,000 of cover for the whole year [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency
Holding prices squeezes profit margins / cash reserves
application_max_2: $260,000 reserve left with only about $74,000 after absorbing $186,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of choosing Option A, to raise prices by 20% to $6,480.
questions.model_answer: First, a 20% price rise may drive fishing crews to rival importers or the used-motor market [k]. Moving from $5,400 to $6,480 adds $1,080 to each motor, and crews working on tight margins may simply delay replacing engines [app]. Every ten motors lost cuts $64,800 of revenue, so losing more than forty motors a year would wipe out the $259,200 gain from the rise [an]. Second, the rise may trigger retaliatory discounting across the small-engine market [k]. Brayford's nine fitters could be left with idle workshop hours if demand falls away [app]. Idle capacity spreads fixed workshop costs over fewer units, pushing up unit costs and eroding the very margin the price rise was meant to protect [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices risk losing price-sensitive customers to rivals
Price rises can trigger competitor discounting and lower volume
application_max_2: Reference to $1,080 increase per motor / 240 motors a year / $259,200 expected gain
Reference to fishing crews being price-sensitive and 9 fitters facing idle hours
analysis_max_2: Chain from lost sales to revenue falling to the point that $259,200 gain is erased
Chain from lower volume to fixed costs spread over fewer units to higher unit costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Brayford Marine Engines should raise retail prices by 20% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises the retail price by 20% to $6,480, adding $1,080 per motor and about $259,200 a year at 240 motors [k]. That more than covers the extra $186,000 import cost and would rebuild the profit reserve, a strong position if the dollar falls further [app]. The margin of safety is also comfortable: Brayford can lose about forty motor sales a year, roughly one sixth of volume, before the rise loses its benefit [an]. However, Option B holds the $5,400 price and absorbs the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 profit reserve [k]. Holding prices protects goodwill with fishing crews and ferry operators who buy on reputation and aftercare, keeping the order book and workshop utilisation stable [app]. The risk is that the reserve falls to about $74,000, leaving almost no cover if the rate weakens again or if warranty claims arrive, which could force an emergency loan at painful interest [an]. Overall, I think Brayford should choose Option A [eval], because the price rise stays well ahead of the reserve cushion even after realistic customer losses, and absorbing a permanent $186,000 cost into a $74,000 reserve would be reckless; it should monitor weekly orders and soften the rise if sales collapse [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 20% rise to $6,480, about $259,200 extra a year
Option B: hold $5,400 and absorb $186,000 from the $260,000 reserve
application_max_2: $259,200 gain vs $186,000 extra cost / margin of safety of about forty motors
Reference to $260,000 reserve falling to about $74,000 under Option B / 240 motors / $1,296,000 sales
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to covered import bill to rebuilt reserve and resilience
Chain from holding price to exhausted reserve to risk of emergency borrowing
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring weekly orders

scenario_stem:
Vinecourt Bottling Co is a private limited company in Country X bottling fruit juices and soft drinks. It employs 60 workers, fills 12,000 bottles daily and earned $5.5 million revenue last year.

Seeking exports to Country Y but lacking distribution experience, Vinecourt can accept French firm BleuRiviere SA's 50/50 joint venture: a $2 million plant splitting costs, risks and profits. Going alone costs $5 million, takes longer but keeps 100% of profits. The board decides in 3 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'joint venture'.
questions.model_answer: An agreement in which two or more businesses work together on a particular project [1] while remaining separate companies, sharing the costs, risks and profits [1].

knowledge_max_2: two or more businesses collaborate on a project
partners share costs, risks and profits but remain separate

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Vinecourt of the proposed joint venture with BleuRiviere SA.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Costs and risks are shared [k], so Vinecourt's share of the $2 million plant is $1 million instead of the $5 million needed alone [app]. Benefit 2: Local market knowledge and distribution [k], as BleuRiviere SA knows Country Y's retailers, helping place Vinecourt's fruit juices on shelves quickly [app].

knowledge_max_2: costs and risks are shared between partners
partner provides local knowledge and distribution

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Vinecourt might face in the joint venture.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Profits must be split equally [k], so Vinecourt would surrender 50% of Country Y earnings instead of keeping 100% [app], reducing the overall return on its investment [an]. Problem 2: Potential conflict between partners [k], because a 50/50 structure can stall decisions on the $2 million plant and its 12,000-bottles-a-day output [app], causing management clashes and costly delays [an].

knowledge_max_2: profits must be shared with the partner
conflicting priorities can cause deadlock and delays
analysis_max_2: lower retained profit from Country Y sales
deadlock and clashes slow decisions and cost money

questions.question_text: Do you think Vinecourt should form a joint venture with BleuRiviere SA rather than invest alone? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Forming the joint venture halves Vinecourt's capital commitment to $1 million [k], sharing the $2 million plant cost and its risk with BleuRiviere [app], preserving cash for the 12,000-bottles-a-day home operation [an]. However, investing alone would keep 100% of Country Y profits [k] and give Vinecourt full control over its strategy [app], but costs $5 million and demands building distribution expertise from scratch [an]. Overall, Vinecourt should proceed with the joint venture [eval], because the shared risk and immediate local knowledge outweigh the halved profit share for a first export venture [eval].

knowledge_max_2: joint venture halves capital commitment and risk
sole investment keeps 100% profit but costs more and takes longer
analysis_max_2: shared $1 million commitment protects home cash flow
sole control avoids deadlock but demands $5 million and expertise
evaluation_max_2: weighs risk sharing against profit sharing
recommendation tied to first export market decision

scenario_stem:
Copperline Hotels Group is a private limited company with 2 hotels, 180 guest rooms and 45 housekeepers, generating $2.4 million revenue. Housekeepers earn $11 an hour, clean 14 rooms and take home $88. Turnover is 21%.

Carla Reyes compares $6.50 per room, paying $91 for 14 rooms, with hourly pay plus an enriched role: welcome packs, linen ordering and training new starters, plus a 'Housekeeper of the Month' $150 voucher costing $1,800 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'job enrichment'.
questions.model_answer: Giving workers more responsibility and a wider variety of tasks in their jobs [1], so work becomes more challenging and rewarding rather than routine [1].

knowledge_max_2: more responsibility and wider variety of tasks
work becomes more challenging and rewarding

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of job enrichment for Copperline Hotels Group.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: More responsibility makes work more satisfying [k], with housekeepers taking charge of welcome packs, linen ordering and training new starters across the 2 hotels [app]. Benefit 2: Enriched jobs develop employees' skills [k], so experienced housekeepers can cover a wider range of duties without extra supervisors [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with the piece rate option for Copperline Hotels Group.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Housekeepers may rush rooms to maximise earnings [k], so the $6.50 per room rate could cut corners when cleaning the 180 guest rooms [app], harming cleanliness, guest satisfaction and reviews [an]. Problem 2: Income would vary with the number of rooms to clean [k], as quiet nights mean fewer than 14 rooms and pay below the $88 daily wage [app], so morale and retention could fall and the 21% turnover could worsen [an].

knowledge_max_2: piece rate encourages rushing and lower quality
analysis_max_2: poor cleaning damages guest satisfaction and reviews

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperline Hotels Group should introduce the piece rate instead of keeping hourly pay with the enriched role and monthly award? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The piece rate directly rewards output [k], with $6.50 per room giving $91 a day for 14 rooms, $3 more than the hourly wage, and should speed up cleaning [app], helping the 2 hotels turn rooms faster for new guests [an]. However, it risks rushed cleaning and unstable pay [k], whereas enriched duties let housekeepers run welcome packs, linen ordering and starter training, and the $150 monthly award costs just $1,800 a year [app], building motivation, skills and loyalty beyond pay [an]. Overall, Copperline should enrich the role and keep hourly pay with the monthly Housekeeper of the Month award [eval], because satisfied guests and lower turnover matter more than a $3 daily incentive [eval].

knowledge_max_2: piece rate links pay directly to output
job enrichment and recognition build loyalty and skills
analysis_max_2: piece rate speeds cleaning but risks quality and pay dips
enrichment builds skills, loyalty and guest satisfaction
evaluation_max_2: weighs immediate output incentive against loyalty and quality
justified recommendation tied to stem figures

scenario_stem:
The Drifting Goose Restaurant is a private limited company with $1.05 million turnover and 900 email subscribers. Owner Theo Brandt compares extending opening hours until 11pm, costing $48,000, with investing $30,000 in a loyalty scheme.

A questionnaire of 320 customers found 58% would visit for a late menu, and evening revenue rose 12% last summer, but a focus group of 14 warned of complaints and subscriber emails have a 35% open rate. Theo recommends on Friday.

questions.question_text: Define 'market research'.
questions.model_answer: Market research is the collection and analysis of information about customers, competitors and the market [1]. It helps a business identify and satisfy customer needs and reduces the risk of poor decisions [1].

knowledge_max_2: collection and analysis of information about customers, competitors and markets
helps identify and satisfy customer needs and reduces risk

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the questionnaire results could help Theo decide.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The questionnaire shows what customers want [k], so the finding that 58% of 320 customers would visit for a late menu directly informs the opening-hours decision [app]. Reason 2: Research data supports better decisions [k], as till data showing evening revenue rose 12% last summer backs up the survey evidence [app].

knowledge_max_2: questionnaires reveal customer preferences and intentions
research reduces uncertainty when choosing between options
application_max_2: 58% of 320 customers would visit for a late menu

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Theo could use the research findings in making his decision.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: The findings can estimate demand for late opening [k], with 58% of 320 customers and summer evening revenue up 12% both pointing to profitable extra trading hours [app], so the owners can judge whether the $48,000 annual cost would be recovered [an]. Use 2: The findings can highlight risks [k], as the focus group of 14 warned that a late menu could upset nearby residents [app], so Theo could balance this against the $30,000 loyalty scheme, which spreads benefits across all customers and both meal times [an].

knowledge_max_2: research findings can estimate the demand for a proposed change
research findings can reveal risks and downsides before acting
application_max_2: 58% of 320 customers and a 12% rise in evening revenue
focus group of 14 concerned about nearby residents
analysis_max_2: the owners can assess whether extra sales cover the $48,000 annual cost
the focus group warning informs a cautious or alternative decision

questions.question_text: Do you think Theo should extend opening hours until 11pm instead of investing $30,000 in the loyalty scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Extended hours would build on demonstrated demand [k]: 58% of the 320 surveyed customers support a late menu and summer evening revenue already rose 12% [app], so the extra trading could generate enough extra sales to recoup part of the $48,000 annual cost [an]. However, the focus group raised concerns about nearby residents and the loyalty scheme offers broader gains [k], since $30,000 targeting all 900 subscribers could lift repeat visits across both lunch and dinner without licence or noise risks [app], potentially growing loyalty more safely than late hours [an]. Overall, Theo should extend opening hours until 11pm [eval], because two independent sources of evidence, the questionnaire and till data, both point to real late-evening demand, though he should monitor complaints from residents [eval].

knowledge_max_2: primary research evidence can justify extending trading hours
loyalty schemes can raise repeat purchasing across all customers
application_max_2: 58% of 320 customers support a late menu; evening revenue up 12% last summer
$30,000 loyalty scheme targeting 900 subscribers, 35% email open rate
analysis_max_2: extra hours could recover part of the $48,000 annual cost
loyalty scheme spreads benefits more safely but less directly measured
evaluation_max_2: weighs direct late-evening demand evidence against broader loyalty benefits
recommendation justified with stem figures and a residual risk noted

scenario_stem:
Bramble Row Delicatessen is a sole trader selling fresh deli counters and household groceries, with $260,000 annual sales. It must relocate when the lease ends.

Shop A is near the university: 11,000 students within 1 km, footfall of 2,900 and rent of $17,500, but two rival delis and a discount supermarket trade there. Shop B is on a suburban estate of 900 households, 70% retired couples, with footfall 1,400, no competition and rent $9,200. Which shop offers better prospects?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'demographics'.
questions.model_answer: Demographics are the statistical characteristics of a population, such as age, income, gender and occupation, used to identify customer groups [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why demographics should influence Bramble Row's choice of shop.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Shop A sits near 11,000 students [app], a young, price-sensitive market with strong demand for quick meals [k]. Reason 2: Shop B is on an estate where 70% are retired couples [app], a group likely to value fresh deli counters and regular loyal shopping [k].

questions.question_text: Analyse two risks of choosing Shop A near the university.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Two rival delis and a discount supermarket already trade near Shop A [app], so the delicatessen faces intense competition for students [k], which could force price cuts and reduce profit margins [an]. Risk 2: Shop A's rent is $17,500 a year [app], nearly double Shop B's $9,200 [k], so the business carries higher fixed costs before selling a single basket [an].

application_max_2: two rival delis and a discount supermarket
analysis_max_2: could force price cuts and reduce profit margins
higher fixed costs before selling a single basket

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramble Row Delicatessen should choose Shop A or Shop B? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Shop A offers footfall of 2,900 a week from 11,000 students [k], a large young market within 1 km of campus [app], which could drive strong sales of snacks and groceries [an]. However, two rival delis already compete there and rent is $17,500 a year [k], so margins could be squeezed in a price-sensitive market [app], threatening profitability [an]. Overall, Bramble Row should choose Shop B because the lower rent of $9,200, a loyal retired customer base and zero competition make profits more secure [eval], even though weekly footfall of 1,400 is under half that of Shop A [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Shop B offers lower rent/no competition
analysis_max_2: could drive strong sales of snacks and groceries
evaluation_max_2: weighs student volume and competition against lower rent and loyal retired base in deli context

scenario_stem:
Northcott Leisure Ltd is a private limited company running a family fun centre. This year revenue was $1,350,000, gross profit $675,000 and profit $135,000, with capital employed $750,000; last year revenue $1,200,000, gross profit $540,000 and profit $84,000. Stronger cafe margins and arcade income lifted gross margin from 45% to 50%.

Rival Starplay Leisure reports 55% gross profit margin. The company must choose between an indoor trampoline arena costing $400,000, or upgrading the cafe and party rooms for $80,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit'.
questions.model_answer: Gross profit is the profit a business makes after deducting the cost of sales from its revenue (Gross Profit = Revenue minus Cost of Sales). It shows what remains to cover operating expenses before other costs of running the business are deducted. [2]

knowledge_max_2: The margin available to cover operating expenses/overheads

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Northcott Leisure's gross profit margin rose from 45% to 50%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Stronger cafe margins, probably from higher prices or better supply deals, mean each cafe sale now retains more gross profit [k]. Gross profit rose to $675,000 on revenue of $1,350,000 (50% margin), up from $540,000 on $1,200,000 (45%) [app]. Reason 2: Growth in arcade income, which carries high margins because games have a low ongoing cost per play [k]. Higher-margin arcade revenue pushed gross profit up by $135,000 year-on-year, lifting the overall margin to 50% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices / better input deals in the cafe raise its margin
High-margin arcade income mix lifts overall GPM
application_max_2: Arcade mix improvement added $135,000 to gross profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why analysing Northcott Leisure's profitability ratios over time is useful.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Trend analysis shows whether performance is improving or deteriorating, not just what the ratios are today [k]. Northcott's profit margin rose from 7% ($84,000 on $1,200,000) to 10% ($135,000 on $1,350,000), and ROCE rose from 14% to 18% ($135,000 on $750,000), both clear positive trends [app]. This demonstrates the fun centre is increasingly efficient, giving the owners confidence to invest [an]. Reason 2: Comparing ratios year-on-year reveals whether changes come from revenue growth or better cost control [k]. Revenue grew by $150,000 while gross profit grew by $135,000, meaning margins, not simply sales volume, drove the improvement [app]. This tells the board that pricing and mix improvements are working and should be extended to the party rooms and cafe [an].

knowledge_max_2: Trend analysis reveals improving/deteriorating performance over time
Year-on-year comparison separates revenue growth from cost control
application_max_2: Revenue grew $150,000 while GP grew $135,000 - margin-led improvement
analysis_max_2: Positive trends give confidence to invest (trampoline arena)
Identifies margins as the driver - informs extending pricing/mix to cafe and party rooms

questions.question_text: Do you think Northcott Leisure should build the indoor trampoline arena costing $400,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Northcott should build the trampoline arena. Building the arena would capture the growing family entertainment market and build on current momentum: revenue rose to $1,350,000, profit margin reached 10% and ROCE improved to 18% ($135,000 on $750,000) [k]. A $400,000 investment that lifts footfall would raise revenue and spread the fun centre's fixed costs over more visitors, strengthening returns [app]. A distinctive attraction can also outflank rival Starplay Leisure (55% gross profit margin) on experience rather than price, defending and growing the local market [an]. However, upgrading the cafe and party rooms for $80,000 is the lower-risk option, because it invests in the proven highest-margin parts of the business [k]. The cafe and parties already drove the margin improvement to 50%, so spending $80,000 there would compound gains quickly with minimal debt [app]. Spending only $80,000 also protects the balance sheet and could lift ROCE further, given $750,000 capital employed and attractive returns [an]. Overall, I recommend the trampoline arena, because the improving trend and strong ROCE indicate the business can service new investment, and an indoor trampoline park would differentiate Northcott from Starplay Leisure [eval]. If visitor projections prove weak, the board should stage the build and commit the $80,000 upgrade project first as a fallback [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Arena captures growth market and spreads fixed costs, lifting revenue
Cafe/party upgrade invests in highest-margin areas at much lower risk
application_max_2: Cafe/parties drove margin rise; $80,000 vs $400,000; Starplay rival at 55% GPM
analysis_max_2: Differentiation on experience vs price-led rival
Lower spend protects balance sheet and can still lift ROCE
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation justified with conditions; staged fallback included
Both options weighed with figures; overall judgement balanced

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ossett Digital Stores is a sole trader electronics retailer in Country X with 6 shops. It imports 20,000 tablets from Country W at €150 each; the dollar rose from $1.60 to $1.28 per euro, cutting unit cost from $240 to $192, saving $48.

Nadia Hussain must plan the promotion amid online rivalry. Option A cuts prices 8% across $6,000,000 of sales, forgoing $480,000. Option B holds prices, using the saving to open a 7th shop. It employs 34 staff and made $410,000 profit.

questions.question_text: State two ways consumers benefit when their country's currency appreciates.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods and foreign products become cheaper, so consumers get more for their money [1]. Holidays and purchases abroad cost less in local currency, stretching consumers' budgets further [1].

knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper for consumers
Purchasing power rises / foreign spending costs less in local currency

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Ossett Digital Stores.
questions.model_answer: First, the imported tablets it sells cost less to buy in [k]. Each of the 20,000 tablets falls from $240 to $192, saving $48 each — about $960,000 across the year's purchases [app]. Second, Ossett's margins improve if it holds prices while costs fall [k]. The $48 saving on every unit drops straight to profit on $6,000,000 of tablet sales, comfortably lifting profit beyond the $410,000 made last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: A stronger currency makes imports cheaper to buy
Lower import costs improve profit margins
application_max_2: Tablet cost falls from $240 to $192 (saving $48 each)
Reference to $6,000,000 of tablet sales / $410,000 profit last year / 20,000 tablets

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to cut shelf prices by 8%.
questions.model_answer: First, lower prices attract value-hungry shoppers away from rivals [k]. Cutting 8% off $6,000,000 of sales returns $480,000 to customers as savings, a strong headline claim for in-store and local advertising [app]. If footfall and basket sizes rise even modestly, tablet and accessory sales together could far outweigh the $480,000 given up [an]. Second, passing on part of the saving builds goodwill and defends market share [k]. Consumers benefit directly from cheaper tablets, strengthening Ossett's value image across the midlands [app]. A reputation for passing on savings makes future promotions more trusted, supporting volume ahead of the 7th shop and spreading fixed costs over more sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower prices attract customers and grow sales volume
Passing on savings builds goodwill and loyalty
application_max_2: Reference to 8% off $6,000,000 = $480,000 returned to shoppers
Reference to the $48 per-tablet import saving / 6 shops across the midlands
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower prices to higher footfall to sales outweighing the $480,000 given up
Chain from passed-on savings to goodwill to defending share ahead of the 7th shop

questions.question_text: Do you think Ossett Digital Stores should cut shelf prices by 8% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts shelf prices by 8% across $6,000,000 of tablet sales, giving up $480,000 of revenue [k]. The import saving is larger, at about $960,000 a year, so even after the price cut Ossett keeps roughly half the benefit, and lower shelf prices can lift volume and footfall in all 6 shops ahead of opening a 7th store [app]. Winning midlands shoppers now — before rivals respond — builds loyalty, and accessory sales typically follow tablet purchases, compounding the gain [an]. However, Option B holds prices and uses the saving to fund a 7th shop in the northern suburbs [k]. Retaining the full margin grows profit comfortably beyond last year's $410,000 and funds expansion without borrowing, the bigger long-term prize [app]. The danger is that rivals cut prices first, and Ossett, holding price, loses volume and carries excess tablet stock through the crucial winter season [an]. Overall, I think Ossett should choose Option A [eval], because the $480,000 cut is affordable from a $960,000 saving and the extra share and loyalty are what the northern expansion will live or die by; it should run the promotion for the autumn only, review sales weekly, and bank the surplus toward the 7th shop if the uplift is weak [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 8% price cut costing $480,000 to drive volume and share
Option B: hold prices and use the saving to fund a 7th shop
application_max_2: $480,000 of the about $960,000 annual saving returned to shoppers
Reference to $6,000,000 tablet sales / $410,000 profit / 6 shops / 20,000 tablets
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to higher footfall and loyalty to compounding accessory sales
Chain from holding prices to banked margin but lost volume if rivals cut first
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes a time-limited promotion

scenario_stem:
Bramley Ridge Roofing is a sole trader business owned by Tom Ellery for 8 years. With 4 roofers, it handles roof repairs and re-roofing for households and farms, generating $340,000 turnover last year.

A ladder slip caused an injury and a $60,000 claim, but insurance covers only $25,000. Tom is considering forming a private limited company to gain limited liability, or staying a sole trader and paying the $7,000 annual premium. The case goes to court next month.

questions.question_text: Define 'limited liability'.
questions.model_answer: Limited liability means shareholders can only lose the money they invested in the business [1], because the company is a separate legal entity and owners' personal assets are protected [1].

knowledge_max_2: shareholders only risk the money invested
company is a separate legal entity; personal assets protected

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Tom of converting to a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Limited liability [k], so Tom's home and savings are protected if the business cannot pay the $60,000 claim after only $25,000 of insurance coverage [app]. Benefit 2: Greater credibility with lenders and customers [k], because a limited company can pass credit checks when bidding for larger roofing contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: limited company has more credibility with lenders and customers

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of Tom forming a private limited company.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Extra legal costs and paperwork [k], including registration fees and annual filings on top of the $7,000 insurance premium [app], increasing Tom's fixed costs and administrative burden [an]. Problem 2: Less privacy [k], because limited companies must file accounts publicly, exposing the $340,000 turnover [app], allowing competitors to see his pricing and margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: extra registration costs and annual paperwork
public filing of accounts reduces privacy

questions.question_text: Do you think Tom should form a private limited company rather than remain a sole trader? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Forming a private limited company gives Tom limited liability [k], so the $35,000 uninsured remainder of the $60,000 claim (after $25,000 of insurance) cannot touch his personal assets [app], removing the threat to his family's financial security [an]. However, staying a sole trader avoids registration fees and keeps accounts private [k], suiting a small 4-roofer business that pays only the $7,000 premium [app], preserving Tom's full control and simplicity [an]. Overall, Tom should convert to a private limited company [eval], because the $35,000 uninsured exposure outweighs the minor compliance costs of incorporation [eval].

knowledge_max_2: limited liability protects personal assets against claims
sole traders avoid compliance costs and keep privacy
analysis_max_2: claim shortfall threatens personal assets without limited liability
low compliance costs suit a small business
evaluation_max_2: weighs $35,000 uninsured exposure against compliance burden
recommendation linked to the injury claim figures

scenario_stem:
Calderwood Telesales is a private limited company with 60 outbound agents selling energy contracts. Last year 1.08 million calls at 2% closed 21,600 sales worth $6.5 million. Agents earn $1,250 monthly; turnover reached 24%.

Owen Doyle compares a 2-day off-the-job training course costing $18,000, or $300 per agent, aiming to lift conversions from 2% to 3%, about 32,400 sales, with output pay of $700 basic plus $18 per sale: 45 sales earn $1,510, while 20 earn $1,060.

questions.question_text: Define 'training'.
questions.model_answer: The process of developing an employee's skills and knowledge [1], so they can perform their current job more effectively and adapt to new tasks [1].

knowledge_max_2: improves current job performance and adaptability

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the off-the-job training option for Calderwood Telesales.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Off-the-job training develops agents' selling techniques away from the desk [k], targeting a rise in the success rate from 2% to 3%, worth about 32,400 sales a year [app]. Benefit 2: Time on the 2-day course is an investment in all 60 agents at $300 each [k], and raising the whole team's skills protects the $6.5 million in sales the business depends on [app].

knowledge_max_2: off-the-job training builds new skills away from work pressures
training improves capability across the whole team

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with the output-based pay option for Calderwood Telesales.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Agents may use pressure selling to win commission [k], as the $18 per sale rewards volume over quality [app], leading to complaints and cancelled energy contracts [an]. Problem 2: Weaker agents would be pushed below the present salary [k], as an agent closing only 20 sales a month would earn $1,060 against today's $1,250 [app], so morale may fall and the 24% turnover could rise further [an].

knowledge_max_2: commission per sale encourages pressure selling
output pay is insecure for weaker performers
analysis_max_2: pressure selling damages reputation and contracts
poor earners may quit, worsening turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Calderwood Telesales should fund the off-the-job training course instead of introducing output-based pay? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Training tackles the root cause of weak results [k], lifting the success rate from 2% to 3%, around 10,800 extra sales a year, a permanent gain for all 60 agents [app], which protects and could grow the $6.5 million in sales revenue [an]. However, the $18,000 cost is certain while the 3% target is not [k], whereas output pay costs nothing until agents actually close sales and rewards high performers up to $1,510 a month [app], though it risks pressure selling and income anxiety [an]. Overall, Calderwood should fund the 2-day training course [eval], because it raises the whole team's ability without risking the 24% turnover climbing higher [eval].

knowledge_max_2: training addresses root cause and builds permanent capability
output pay rewards only realised sales but risks behaviour
analysis_max_2: pressure selling risk could worsen turnover
evaluation_max_2: weighs certain training cost against uncertain conversion gain
justified recommendation tied to stem figures

scenario_stem:
Harbour & Circuit Electronics Ltd is an electronics retailer with 3 stores and $1.8 million revenue. Rowan Ellison researches a trade-in scheme before the Christmas quarter, which brings 30% of sales.

He compares a national trade-in report for $2,400, published last year covering 2,000 consumers, with a quota sample of 350 shoppers costing $600. He recommends one option to the board by the end of the month.

questions.question_text: Define 'secondary research'.
questions.model_answer: Secondary research is the use of information already collected by others, such as government statistics, market research reports or a business's own internal records [1]. It is usually cheaper and quicker than collecting primary research [1].

knowledge_max_2: use of information already collected by others
cheaper and quicker than primary research

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Harbour & Circuit might prefer the secondary research report.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The report uses a much larger sample [k], covering 2,000 consumers nationwide against the 350 shoppers the store survey would question [app]. Reason 2: Secondary research is quick to obtain [k], costing $2,400 and available immediately, which helps Rowan decide before the Christmas quarter, when 30% of annual sales are made [app].

knowledge_max_2: secondary research can offer large, broad samples
secondary research is quick and immediately available
application_max_2: available before the Christmas quarter, 30% of annual sales

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of relying on the secondary research report for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: The report is national, not local [k], so its findings on 2,000 consumers may not reflect the customers of Harbour & Circuit's 3 stores [app], making the recommendation less relevant to the trade-in scheme's prospects [an]. Limitation 2: The report is already a year old [k], so it may miss this year's Christmas trading patterns in a market where the quarter brings 30% of sales [app], meaning the data could be out of date when Rowan makes the decision [an].

knowledge_max_2: secondary research may not match the business's specific local context
secondary research can be out of date
application_max_2: national report on 2,000 consumers versus 3 local stores
published last year, before this Christmas quarter (30% of sales)
analysis_max_2: national findings may not predict performance in the 3 stores
out-of-date data could mislead the trade-in decision

questions.question_text: Do you think Rowan should buy the secondary research report instead of running the in-store quota sample? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The report gives a broad national picture [k]: 2,000 consumers' views on phone trade-ins would be available immediately for $2,400 [app], so Harbour & Circuit would understand the whole market before launching in the Christmas quarter, when 30% of sales are made [an]. However, the quota sample of 350 store shoppers costing $600 shows exactly what its own customers want [k], directly matching the 3 stores where the scheme must succeed [app], which matters more than national trends for a decision made this month [an]. Overall, Rowan should run the in-store quota sample [eval], because store-specific evidence for $600 is better value than a generic $2,400 report for this immediate, local decision [eval].

knowledge_max_2: secondary research provides broad, immediately available evidence
primary quota sampling gives specific, store-level evidence
application_max_2: national report: 2,000 consumers, $2,400, published last year
in-store quota sample of 350 shoppers, costing $600, specific to its own customers
analysis_max_2: report informs the overall market before the Christmas quarter
store-specific data better predicts scheme success in the 3 stores
evaluation_max_2: weighs breadth and speed of secondary data against local relevance
recommendation justified by cost and the local nature of the decision

scenario_stem:
Kessler Metal Finishing Ltd is a private limited company electroplating steel components for 40 trade customers. Legal controls demand it relocate from the residential area within 18 months or install a $150,000 filtration system, following smell and wastewater complaints.

Site A, on the Eastgate Industrial Estate, offers mains drainage, rent of $30,000 and a $50,000 relocation grant. Site B is a rural depot at $11,000 a year, 40 km from most customers, with no mains drainage or grant. Which site should the firm choose?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'planning permission'.
questions.model_answer: Planning permission is the formal approval from a local authority required before a business can build premises or change their use [2].

knowledge_max_2: formal approval from a local authority
required before building/change of use of premises

questions.question_text: Explain two ways legal controls on location could affect Kessler Metal Finishing.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Legal controls require Kessler to relocate within 18 months [app], forcing an urgent and costly move from the residential area [k]. Way 2: The alternative is installing a $150,000 filtration system [app], a large one-off expense that reduces the funds available for relocation [k].

knowledge_max_2: forces urgent relocation from residential area

questions.question_text: Analyse two benefits of Site A on the Eastgate Industrial Estate.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Site A has mains drainage [app], so wastewater from electroplating can be discharged legally [k], avoiding fines and protecting the firm's licence to operate [an]. Benefit 2: Site A includes a $50,000 green relocation grant [app], which offsets one-third of the $150,000 compliance cost [k], reducing the financial burden of the move [an].

analysis_max_2: reduces financial burden of the move

questions.question_text: Do you think Site A or Site B is the better location for Kessler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Site A is a serviced industrial unit with mains drainage and a $50,000 green relocation grant [k], meeting the legal controls on wastewater within 18 months [app], which avoids fines and keeps 40 trade customers supplied [an]. Site B costs only $11,000 a year in rent [k], saving $19,000 against Site A's $30,000 [app], but without mains drainage the firm risks breaching environmental law again [an]. Overall, Site A is the better location because compliance certainty and the grant protect the firm's future [eval], even though rent is higher, since illegal discharge could close the business [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Site A meets legal controls/grant support
Site B cheaper but non-compliant risk
analysis_max_2: avoids fines and keeps 40 trade customers supplied
without mains drainage the firm risks breaching environmental law again
evaluation_max_2: weighs compliance certainty and grant against rent saving in polluting-industry context

scenario_stem:
Chippendale & Rose Auctioneers Ltd is a private limited company running a saleroom. Revenue was $900,000, gross profit $630,000, profit $225,000, capital employed $1,500,000 after a freehold purchase; last year revenue $820,000, gross profit $533,000, profit $205,000, capital $1,025,000. Gross margin rose 65% to 70%, but ROCE fell 20% to 15%.

Rival Bramley Auction House reports 72% gross margin and 18% ROCE. The partners weigh a $600,000 second saleroom in Rennick, or moving more business to a $120,000 online platform.

questions.question_text: Calculate the return on capital employed (ROCE) for Chippendale & Rose Auctioneers Ltd. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100 = $225,000 / $1,500,000 x 100 = 15%. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why ROCE fell from 20% to 15% even though revenue and gross profit rose.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Capital employed grew faster than profit - the freehold purchase raised capital employed from $1,025,000 to $1,500,000, while profit rose only from $205,000 to $225,000 [k]. Because ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100, the $475,000 extra capital dilutes the ratio to 15% despite a higher profit [app]. Reason 2: The new premises generate little immediate auction income, so in the short term they add capital without adding returns [k]. Gross profit margin actually improved to 70% ($630,000 of $900,000), so the fall reflects the timing of the investment, not weaker trading [app].

knowledge_max_2: Capital employed grew faster than profit (freehold purchase)
Investment timing: premises add capital before generating income
application_max_2: ROCE fell 20% to 15%; GPM improved 65% to 70% ($533,000 to $630,000 of $900,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using profitability ratios for the stakeholders of Chippendale & Rose.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Ratios help shareholders and partners judge whether the business gives a good return on the capital they support [k]. The 15% ROCE (down from 20%) tells partners the freehold purchase is diluting returns, which matters when weighing whether to pay for a second saleroom from retained profits [app]. This lets partners hold management accountable for restoring ROCE before committing more capital [an]. Benefit 2: Ratios help the partners benchmark efficiency against rivals when planning strategy [k]. Bramley Auction House achieves a 72% gross profit margin and 18% ROCE, against Chippendale's 70% and 15%, showing the firm is competitive on margins but behind on capital efficiency [app]. This guides the choice between a $600,000 second saleroom and a $120,000 online platform [an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios show stakeholders returns on capital; accountability for dilution
Ratios benchmark vs rivals to guide strategy
application_max_2: ROCE fell to 15% (from 20%); profit $225,000 on CE $1,500,000
Bramley Auction House 72% GPM, 18% ROCE vs Chippendale 70% GPM, 15% ROCE; $600,000 vs $120,000 options
analysis_max_2: Accountability lever: partners can demand a ROCE-recovery plan before new capital
Benchmark gap focuses strategy on capital efficiency, not just margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Chippendale & Rose Auctioneers should open a second saleroom in Rennick? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Chippendale & Rose should not open the second saleroom yet; it should move more business online first. Opening a $600,000 saleroom would raise capital employed well beyond $1,500,000, and with ROCE already down to 15% from 20%, further dilution would worry the partners [k]. The business earns a 25% profit margin ($225,000 on $900,000 revenue), yet a second room adds fixed costs and relies on unproven auction demand in Rennick [app]. Physical expansion also commits the firm to premises, staff and marketing before testing whether local demand covers those costs [an]. However, a second saleroom could tap a new catchment and lift revenue beyond $900,000, mirroring the gains made this year [k]. Gross profit margin improved to 70% and profit margin held at 25%, so the business could support careful expansion if bidding volumes hold and the $600,000 were financed sustainably [app]. Rival Bramley Auction House earns an 18% ROCE, so a physical presence may be needed to defend market share against local competitors [an]. Overall, I recommend the $120,000 online auction platform instead, because it is far cheaper, extends reach without duplicating fixed costs and protects the balance sheet while the premises investment seasons [eval]. If online auctions lift bidding volumes, the board can revisit a Rennick saleroom with clearer evidence and restore ROCE towards 20% first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Second saleroom raises capital employed and risks further ROCE dilution
Physical expansion can tap new catchment and lift revenue
application_max_2: GPM 70%; Bramley 18% ROCE benchmark; $600,000 saleroom vs $120,000 platform
analysis_max_2: Premises commit fixed costs before local demand is proven
Rival physical presence may be needed to defend market share
evaluation_max_2: Online platform cheaper and balance-sheet protective; staged revisit proposed
Recommendation justified with both options weighed and figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Garrowby Grain Co is a partnership in Country X milling flour for Country W while importing fertiliser from there. It exports 9,000 tonnes at $420 a tonne, worth $3,780,000, and imports €700,000 of fertiliser; the dollar fell from $1.30 to $1.56 per euro.

Edward Garrowby must set pricing. Option A signs a two-year deal at $420, fixing dollar revenue. Option B quotes Country W buyers in euros. The partnership employs 23 staff and farms 2,600 hectares.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a weaker currency on a business that both imports and exports.
questions.model_answer: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, so export orders and sales may rise [1]. Imports become more expensive in local currency, so the cost of raw materials and parts rises [1].

knowledge_max_2: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers / export demand may rise
Imports become more expensive in local currency / input costs rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Garrowby Grain Co.
questions.model_answer: First, its flour exports become cheaper for Country W buyers [k]. At $420 a tonne, flour now costs buyers about €269 per tonne instead of €323, so the 9,000-tonne offer becomes more attractive against Country W domestic mills [app]. Second, imported inputs become more expensive for the partnership [k]. The €700,000 fertiliser and tractor parts bill rises from $910,000 to $1,092,000, an extra $182,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers
A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency
application_max_2: Reference to €269 vs €323 per tonne at $420 a tonne / 9,000 tonnes of flour
Reference to the €700,000 fertiliser bill rising from $910,000 to $1,092,000

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to sign a two-year export deal at $420.
questions.model_answer: First, a two-year deal at $420 a tonne fixes dollar revenue [k]. With 9,000 tonnes a year, the partnership is guaranteed $3,780,000 in each of the two years, regardless of how the rate moves [app]. Predictable inflows make it far easier to plan cash for the higher fertiliser bills and tractor-part purchases, cutting the risk of short-term borrowing [an]. Second, it removes the risk of an unfavourable move in the exchange rate against the partnership [k]. If the dollar rebounds towards $1.30, euro-quoted revenue under Option B would shrink, but Option A pays out the agreed $420 per tonne in dollars [app]. Certainty also strengthens the partnership's case for credit with suppliers and its bank, easing investment across its 2,600 hectares [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixing the price gives revenue certainty over two years
Fixing the price removes exposure to adverse exchange-rate moves
application_max_2: Reference to $420 x 9,000 tonnes = $3,780,000 a year guaranteed
Reference to $1.30 rebound scenario / 2,600 hectares / fertiliser bills
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed revenue to reliable cash planning to avoiding short-term borrowing
Chain from removed rate risk to stronger credit standing to easier investment

questions.question_text: Do you think Garrowby Grain Co should sign the two-year export deal at $420 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A fixes export revenue at $420 a tonne — $3,780,000 a year for two years on 9,000 tonnes [k]. It guarantees cash far above the extra $182,000 fertiliser cost and lets management plan drilling, buying and 23 staff wages with confidence through 2027 and 2028 [app]. The trade-off is giving up the upside: if the dollar weakens further beyond $1.56, an euro-quoted deal would have paid more dollars, so signing now caps the benefit just when the currency is most favourable [an]. However, Option B quotes Country W buyers in euros and lets revenue float with the rate [k]. If the dollar stays weak or weakens further, euro-invoiced sales could bring in well over $3,780,000, but if it strengthens back towards $1.30, dollar revenue falls and margins compress exactly when input costs stay high [app]. The partnership would carry the full currency risk with no certainty, which is uncomfortable for a 23-staff business farming 2,600 hectares with thin cash cover [an]. Overall, I think Garrowby should choose Option A [eval], because certainty on $3,780,000 a year matters more to a partnership facing a certain $182,000 rise in import costs than speculative gains from further depreciation; it can revisit currency terms when the two-year deal expires [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: two-year deal fixes $420 per tonne ($3,780,000 a year)
Option B: euro-quoted pricing lets revenue float with the exchange rate
application_max_2: Reference to $3,780,000 annual revenue / 9,000 tonnes / $420 a tonne
Reference to $1.56 and $1.30 per euro / $182,000 extra fertiliser cost / 23 staff / 2,600 hectares
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed deal to predictable cash to confident planning of wages and inputs
Chain from euro quoting to either gains above $3,780,000 or falling dollar revenue and squeezed margins
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and the extra fertiliser cost

scenario_stem:
Alder & Vine Plastering is a partnership founded 6 years ago by Daniela Costa and Ruth Anselm. Employing 7 plasterers and decorators, it completed $520,000 of work, with both owners handling quoting and invoicing themselves.

They want a third partner to fund plastering machines costing $45,000, but their solicitor warns of unlimited liability: each partner is personally liable for all business debts. Alternatively each owner could lend the business $25,000, keeping the partnership. They meet tomorrow to decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'unlimited liability'.
questions.model_answer: Unlimited liability means the owners are personally and fully responsible for all the debts of the business [1], with no legal limit on what they can lose, including personal assets [1].

knowledge_max_2: owners personally responsible for all business debts
no legal limit on losses, including personal assets

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Alder & Vine of operating as a partnership.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Partners can share the workload and supervise staff jointly [k], so Daniela and Ruth can split responsibility for the 7 plasterers and decorators between them [app]. Benefit 2: More capital is available than for a sole trader [k], which could help fund the $45,000 fleet of plastering machines without heavy borrowing [app].

knowledge_max_2: partners share workload and supervision of staff
partnerships can raise more capital than sole traders

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the solicitor warned about unlimited liability.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Every partner is fully liable for all business debts [k], so if the partnership cannot repay money borrowed for the $45,000 machines, Daniela or Ruth could each lose personal savings to cover the full debt [app], threatening their homes and financial security [an]. Reason 2: Joint and several liability means one partner's mistake affects everyone [k], so a single reckless decision on a $520,000 workload could bankrupt both owners [app], creating deep mistrust within the business [an].

knowledge_max_2: each partner fully liable for all business debts
joint and several liability affects all partners
analysis_max_2: personal assets of both owners are at risk
one partner's behaviour can bankrupt everyone

questions.question_text: Do you think the partners should add a third partner rather than each lend the business $25,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Adding a third partner would bring in fresh capital and share the workload [k], fully funding the $45,000 machines and easing supervision of the 7 plasterers [app], strengthening the business without owners lending their own money [an]. However, lending $25,000 each would raise $50,000 in total, more than covering the $45,000 machines [k], while keeping only two owners and limiting each person's exposure to their own loan [app], avoiding the unlimited liability risks of an extra partner [an]. Overall, the partners should each lend $25,000 instead of adding a third partner [eval], because protecting themselves from unlimited liability matters more than the convenience of outside capital [eval].

knowledge_max_2: third partner injects capital and shares workload
owner loans keep structure simple and exposure limited
analysis_max_2: fresh capital eases machine purchase and staff supervision
new partner extends unlimited liability exposure to all three
evaluation_max_2: weighs extra capital against unlimited liability spread
recommendation linked to the $45,000 machine cost and $25,000 loans

scenario_stem:
The Saltworks Kitchen is a partnership providing event catering for weddings, conferences and festivals, with 9 chefs and 12 event staff. It serves 60 events a year, generating $1.35 million revenue and $210,000 profit. Chefs earn $2,000 a month and morale is high.

The partners weigh profit sharing of 10% of annual profit, about $2,333 each, against non-financial rewards: teamworking days, peer-voted 'Brigade of the Month' certificates and a $900 cookery course per chef, costing $8,100 in total.

questions.question_text: Define 'teamworking'.
questions.model_answer: Organising employees into groups that work together towards shared goals [1], so members support and rely on one another to complete tasks [1].

knowledge_max_2: employees organised into groups working towards shared goals
members support and rely on each other

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the non-financial rewards option for The Saltworks Kitchen.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Peer recognition makes staff feel valued [k], so the 'Brigade of the Month' certificates would reinforce excellent service across the 9 chefs [app]. Benefit 2: Working as a brigade builds cooperation and teamwork [k], which is essential when the kitchen serves around 60 events a year where timing dishes is critical [app].

knowledge_max_2: peer recognition makes staff feel valued

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with the profit-sharing option for The Saltworks Kitchen.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The reward depends on profit, not just effort [k], so a weak festival season could cut the $2,333 each chef expects despite working hard [app], creating disappointment and resentment in the kitchen [an]. Problem 2: Profit sharing rewards annual results, not daily behaviour [k], so it gives little reason to fix mistakes during service across the 60 events a year [app], meaning standards could still drift under pressure [an].

knowledge_max_2: profit-linked rewards depend on external factors
annual profit rewards do not shape daily behaviour
analysis_max_2: weak effect on day-to-day service standards

questions.question_text: Do you think The Saltworks Kitchen should introduce profit sharing instead of the teamworking days, peer certificates and cookery courses? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Profit sharing gives chefs a clear financial stake [k], with $21,000 distributed from the $210,000 profit, about $2,333 per chef, aligning the kitchen with the business's success [app], which could motivate better cost control and effort [an]. However, it is distant, uncertain and backward-looking [k], while the $8,100 package of teamworking days, peer certificates and $900 cookery courses builds morale and skills now across the 9 chefs [app], sustaining service quality at around 60 events a year [an]. Overall, The Saltworks Kitchen should choose the non-financial package [eval], because chefs already have high morale to protect, and course-and-recognition rewards cost a predictable $8,100 a year [eval].

knowledge_max_2: profit sharing aligns staff with business success
non-financial rewards build morale and capability
analysis_max_2: profit share motivates cost control but is uncertain
package sustains morale and quality at events
evaluation_max_2: weighs financial stake against morale and skill building
justified recommendation tied to stem figures

scenario_stem:
The Arncliffe Bay Hotel is a private limited company with 120 rooms generating $2.6 million. Carla Jensen wants to know why occupancy fell from 74% to 61% last year.

Option 1 is an online survey to 2,000 past guests, expecting 15% response (300 replies) for $300. Option 2 is observation with short interviews of 120 departing guests over 4 weeks for $1,900, but captures mostly leisure guests. Carla uses a table and bar chart.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation'.
questions.model_answer: Observation is a method of primary research in which researchers watch how people behave rather than asking them questions [1]. It records real behaviour, such as what customers choose or how they move around a business [1].

knowledge_max_2: researchers watch how people behave rather than asking questions
records real behaviour to inform decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the expected 15% response rate matters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A low response rate shrinks the sample [k], so only about 300 of the 2,000 emailed guests may reply, which weakens the reliability of the findings [app]. Reason 2: A low response rate may bias the results [k], as only guests motivated enough to reply answer, so their views may not represent all past guests of the Arncliffe Bay Hotel [app].

knowledge_max_2: low response rate reduces the effective sample size
respondents may be unrepresentative, introducing bias
application_max_2: about 300 of 2,000 emailed guests expected to reply
Arncliffe Bay Hotel's 120 rooms and falling occupancy

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of either option.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Sample size affects reliability [k], so 300 online replies give more data than 120 departing-guest interviews, though the smaller sample allows deeper questions [app], influencing how confidently the owners interpret the fall from 74% to 61% [an]. Factor 2: Who is included affects accuracy [k], as the interviews capture mainly leisure guests while the online survey hears only from past guests bothered to reply [app], so both samples are biased in different ways and neither fully represents everyone who might book [an].

knowledge_max_2: larger samples generally give more reliable findings
biased samples distort findings and do not generalise
analysis_max_2: sample size shapes confidence in interpreting the 74% to 61% fall
each option is biased differently, so neither is fully representative

questions.question_text: Do you think Carla should use the online survey instead of observing and interviewing departing guests? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The online survey is far cheaper and reaches more people [k]: 300 replies from 2,000 past guests at a cost of $300 would give a broad spread of views on why occupancy fell [app], letting the owners analyse trends across room types and seasons before the summer [an]. However, option 2's observation of departing guests shows real, immediate behaviour and detail [k], interviewing 120 leisure guests would reveal in depth why they rated the hotel as they did [app], whereas the 15% online response rate risks hearing only from already-disappointed guests and misdiagnosing the 74% to 61% drop [an]. Overall, Carla should use the online survey [eval], because 300 responses at $300 give the widest and cheapest evidence, and the owners can always commission follow-up interviews if the table and bar chart raise questions [eval].

knowledge_max_2: online surveys are cheap and reach large numbers
observation and interviews yield richer but narrower evidence
application_max_2: 300 replies expected from 2,000 past guests, costing $300
120 departing leisure guests observed over 4 weeks, costing $1,900
analysis_max_2: online breadth supports trend analysis across the whole past customer base
low response rate risks hearing only from disappointed guests
evaluation_max_2: weighs breadth and cost of online data against depth of interviews
recommendation justified with stem figures and practical follow-up

scenario_stem:
Aldercott Dairy Foods Ltd is a private limited company exporting cheese and yoghurt, earning $3.4 million a year, with 60% of sales to the Austral Trade Bloc. Its factory is in member Country X; Country V is outside the bloc.

Country V offers machinists at $3.10 an hour versus $5.40 in Country X and a $200,000 investment grant, but exports into the bloc face a 12% tariff. Should the board move production to Country V or stay in Country X?

questions.question_text: Define the term 'trade bloc'.

scenario_stem:
Kingsmead Family Butchers Ltd is a private limited company operating 3 butchers' shops. Revenue was $1,600,000, gross profit $560,000 and profit $48,000, with capital employed $400,000; last year revenue $1,500,000, gross profit $540,000 and profit $75,000. Wholesale meat costs rose 12% and gross margin eased from 36% to 35%.

Wellworth Supermarkets discounts meat, reporting 28% gross margin and 18% ROCE. The directors consider investing $70,000 in an in-store kitchen for higher-margin ready meals, or cutting counter prices to match it and defend footfall.

questions.question_text: Identify two stakeholders who might use profitability ratios.
questions.model_answer: Owners and shareholders use profitability ratios to judge the return on their investment, such as profit margin and ROCE. Banks and other lenders use them to assess whether Kingsmead can generate enough profit to repay loans and interest. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Owners/shareholders judge returns on their investment
Banks/lenders assess ability to repay loans and interest

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Kingsmead Family Butchers' profit margin fell from 5% to 3%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Wholesale meat costs rose by 12%, so the cost of sales climbed faster than the prices Kingsmead could charge [k]. Gross profit margin eased to 35% ($560,000 of $1,600,000) from 36% ($540,000 of $1,500,000), squeezing the profit remaining after costs [app]. Reason 2: Nearby Wellworth Supermarkets discounts meat prices, forcing Kingsmead to keep prices competitive and limiting its ability to pass on cost increases [k]. Profit fell to $48,000 from $75,000 even though revenue grew, confirming that margins rather than demand were the problem [app].

knowledge_max_2: Input cost inflation (meat +12%) outpaces price increases
Supermarket price competition prevents passing on cost increases
application_max_2: Profit fell from $75,000 to $48,000 (PM 5% to 3%) despite revenue growth

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why comparing Kingsmead's profitability ratios with Wellworth Supermarkets is useful.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Comparison shows whether Kingsmead's weakness is sector-wide or specific to Kingsmead [k]. Wellworth achieves a 28% gross profit margin at scale, while Kingsmead matches a solid 35% locally, showing its product economics are healthy and price competition is the pressure point [app]. This directs managers towards differentiation, such as ready meals, rather than a price war [an]. Reason 2: Benchmarks help set targets and evaluate strategic options [k]. Wellworth's 18% ROCE on supermarket scale shows what disciplined volume can deliver, while Kingsmead's smaller 12% ROCE ($48,000 on $400,000) is reasonable for 3 shops [app]. Comparing ROCE helps the directors judge whether investing $70,000 in a ready-meals kitchen is realistic [an].

knowledge_max_2: Distinguishes industry-wide weakness from firm-specific problems
Benchmarks set targets and assess feasibility of strategy options
application_max_2: Wellworth 28% GPM at scale vs Kingsmead 35% locally
Wellworth 18% ROCE vs Kingsmead 12% ($48,000 on $400,000); $70,000 kitchen option
analysis_max_2: Points towards differentiation rather than a price war
Benchmark quantifies headroom for the ready-meal investment decision

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsmead Family Butchers should invest $70,000 in the in-store kitchen? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Kingsmead should invest the $70,000 in the in-store kitchen. Ready meals carry higher margins than fresh meat, so the kitchen would lift the gross profit margin above the current 35% and the profit margin above 3%, reversing the fall from 5% last year [k]. Profit fell to $48,000 from $75,000 and ROCE slipped to 12% from 15%, so a margin-rich range is what Kingsmead needs to rebuild returns [app]. Differentiated artisan ready meals also give customers a reason to choose Kingsmead over Wellworth Supermarkets on quality rather than price [an]. However, cutting counter prices to match the supermarket would defend customer numbers and protect revenue of $1,600,000 in the short term [k]. But matching a supermarket's discounting would typically force margins below 3% and risk deeper losses, since Kingsmead cannot buy meat at Wellworth's scale [app]. A price war would erode ROCE further and delay any recovery towards the 15% achieved last year [an]. Overall, I recommend the $70,000 kitchen investment, because differentiation is more sustainable than chasing prices down against a supermarket, and improved margins would strengthen both profit and ROCE [eval]. The board should pilot 6 popular ready-meal lines first and track gross profit margin weekly before scaling up [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Ready meals carry higher margins than fresh meat
Price cuts defend volume but compress margins further

Wellworth 28% GPM/18% ROCE scale benchmark; revenue $1,600,000

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Amberfell Instruments is a private limited company in Country X building laser levels for Country W construction firms. It exports 1,500 units at $380 each, worth $570,000. The dollar swung between $1.25 and $1.60 per euro, making profit hard to forecast.

Lena Kovac must invoice 2027 orders. Option A bills in dollars at $380, shifting risk to buyers. Option B bills in euros at €304: $570,000 at $1.25 or $729,600 at $1.60. The firm employs 24 specialists and buys €96,000 of lenses.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar revenue at $1.25 and $1.60 per euro if 1,500 units are invoiced at €304 each.
Explain two problems the exchange-rate swing creates for Amberfell Instruments.
questions.model_answer: First, it makes annual revenue unpredictable [k]. Invoicing in euros could yield $570,000 at $1.25 per euro or $729,600 at $1.60 per euro — a difference of $159,600 on exactly the same sales of 1,500 units [app]. Second, the firm finds costing and pricing very difficult [k]. It cannot set firm budgets for wages for 24 specialists or for imported lenses when the payout for identical orders can swing by six figures in a single year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Exchange-rate swings make budgeting and pricing decisions difficult
application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 vs $729,600 at $1.60 per euro
Reference to the $159,600 swing / 1,500 units / 24 specialists

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option B, to invoice in euros at €304.
questions.model_answer: First, euro invoicing appeals strongly to Country W buyers [k]. A fixed €304 per unit removes currency risk for the construction firms, so their purchasing departments can approve orders without worrying about monthly rate moves [app]. Lower buyer risk should win repeat orders against rivals who quote in volatile currencies, keeping the workshop fuller [an]. Second, if the dollar weakens further, euro invoices convert to more dollars [k]. At $1.60, 1,500 units at €304 yield $729,600 — $159,600 above the $570,000 floor — while the imported lenses at €96,000 a year also cost more dollars at the same time [app]. This partial natural offset protects margin without any special financial instruments [an].

knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the buyer's currency removes buyer risk and can win orders
A weaker dollar raises the local-currency value of foreign earnings
application_max_2: Reference to €304 fixed unit price appealing to Country W construction firms
Reference to $729,600 at $1.60 vs $570,000 at $1.25 and €96,000 lenses rising in dollar terms
analysis_max_2: Chain from buyer price certainty to more repeat orders and fuller capacity
Chain from euro invoicing to revenue and lens costs moving together to protected margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfell Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in euros at €304 (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B invoices in euros at €304 per unit, so Country W buyers face a stable price and no currency risk [k]. That should help Amberfell win and keep contracts in a market where buyers prefer simplicity, and at $1.60 the same invoices yield $729,600, comfortably covering the €96,000 lens cost and lifting margin well above the $570,000 floor [app]. The trade-off is that if the dollar strengthens towards $1.25, Amberfell receives only $570,000 from the same orders, with zero upside if the dollar weakens further [an]. However, Option A invoices in dollars at $380, fixing Amberfell's annual revenue at $570,000 whatever happens to the rate [k]. That gives complete certainty for budgeting 24 specialists' wages and removes the $159,600 swing, but it pushes all currency risk onto buyers: at $1.60 they would pay just €237.50, while at $1.25 they pay €304, which buyers will resist [app]. The risk is losing price-sensitive orders to suppliers who quote in euros [an]. Overall, I think Amberfell should choose Option B [eval], because revenue and lens costs are both priced in euros, so euro invoicing creates a natural balance that a dollar invoice cannot match; it should monitor the rate monthly and raise the €304 price if the dollar strengthens persistently [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option B: euro invoicing at €304 gives buyers price certainty
Option A: dollar invoicing at $380 fixes revenue but shifts risk onto buyers
application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 and $729,600 at $1.60 per euro
Reference to $380 dollar price / €96,000 lenses / 24 specialists / Country W buyers
analysis_max_2: Chain from euro invoicing to buyer certainty to more orders and natural offset of euro costs
Chain from dollar invoicing to fixed $570,000 but buyers resisting a swinging euro price
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring the rate monthly

scenario_stem:
Tallow Tree Bakery is an incorporated private limited company founded by James Whitmore. It owns 3 bakeries, employs 26 staff and earns $1.1 million revenue selling sourdough bread and pastries.

James wants 2 more bakeries within 18 months. He can choose franchising, collecting an $8,000 fee and 6% of sales, or keep them company-owned, funding each $150,000 set-up from retained profit and a bank loan. He reports to the board next month.

questions.question_text: Define 'incorporated'.
questions.model_answer: An incorporated business is a separate legal entity from its owners [1], with its own rights and liabilities, so owners typically benefit from limited liability [1].
