owners usually benefit from limited liability

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Tallow Tree Bakery of franchising the two new outlets.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Expansion with minimal capital outlay [k], because franchisees fund the $150,000 set-up of each bakery while James receives the $8,000 fees and 6% royalties [app]. Benefit 2: Franchisees are motivated owner-operators [k], so each keeps profits from their outlet and personally drives sales of the sourdough bread and pastries [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tallow Tree Bakery of keeping the new bakeries company-owned.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The company keeps all the profits [k], since no royalties leak out, so both new bakeries contribute fully to the $1.1 million revenue base [app], boosting funds for future growth [an]. Benefit 2: Full control over quality and pricing [k], so standards stay consistent across the existing 3 bakeries and the 2 new ones [app], protecting the jobs of the 26 staff and the brand reputation [an].

consistent standards protect reputation and staff

However, company-owned bakeries keep 100% of profits [k] and guarantee James complete control over quality, prices and brand standards [app], avoiding any franchisee disputes that could damage reputation [an]. Overall, Tallow Tree Bakery should franchise the two new bakeries [eval], because the 18-month target is met faster and cheaper while generating immediate fee income [eval].

scenario_stem:
Elmridge Fulfilment Co is a private limited company with 120 full-time pickers and 80 seasonal workers for the 8-week peak. Revenue was $5.6 million. Pickers earn $13 an hour and handle 140 items a day against 100 items; turnover is 23%.

Option one: $0.30 per item above 100, adding $12 a day on average, $18 at 160. The other keeps hourly pay with job rotation between picking, packing and loading, plus 'Peak Hero' weekly $50 vouchers, costing $5,000.

questions.model_answer: Moving employees between different tasks or roles on a planned basis [1], so work becomes more varied and staff develop a wider range of skills [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of job rotation for Elmridge Fulfilment Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Variety reduces boredom and fatigue [k], as pickers move between picking, packing and loading during the demanding 8-week peak [app]. Benefit 2: Rotation makes workers multi-skilled [k], so full-time and seasonal staff can cover absent colleagues anywhere in the warehouse without slowing order processing [app].

However, speed focus risks picking errors and excludes slower or newer staff [k], whereas rotation plus $50 Peak Hero vouchers cost only $5,000 and motivate all 120 full-time pickers and 80 seasonal workers through variety and peer recognition [app], supporting morale and accuracy at a critical time [an]. scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Talbot & Graves Solicitors Ltd is a private limited company of solicitors. questions.question_text: Define 'profit'.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the surplus remaining after all costs and expenses have been deducted from a business's revenue (Profit = Total Revenue minus Total Costs). It is the reward to the owners, which can be retained in the business or distributed as dividends, and it is the starting point for calculating profitability ratios. [2]

Direct costs rose against revenue of $2,500,000, producing gross profit of $1,875,000 (75%) versus $1,600,000 on $2,000,000 (80%) the previous year [app]. Reason 2: Increasing salaries in a fixed-fee environment means each additional instruction adds cost faster than fee income [k]. Profit still rose to $500,000, so the fall in the gross profit margin reflects cost inflation at fee-earner level rather than weaker demand [app].

ROCE held at 20% ($500,000 on $2,500,000, the same as last year), telling partners growth so far has not diluted returns, a key test before committing $600,000 to a second office [app]. If planned investment fails to lift ROCE above 20%, it should not proceed [an]. Use 2: Comparing ratios with competitors highlights strategic gaps [k]. Brereton & Co achieves an 82% gross profit margin and a 25% ROCE, so Talbot & Graves can see its 75% GPM and 20% ROCE trail a rival, prompting action on fees or costs [app]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Larkhill Brewery Co is a private limited company in Country X brewing craft ale. It exports 30% of 480,000 litres to Country W at $6 a litre: 144,000 litres, $864,000, importing €320,000 of hops; the dollar fell $1.30 to $1.56 per euro.

Sofia Almeida must set 2027 strategy. Option A expands exports: ale is €3.85 a litre to Country W, not €4.62. Option B raises domestic prices 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 against dearer hops. It employs 14 and made $290,000 profit.

questions.question_text: State two effects of a depreciation on a business that imports its raw materials.
questions.model_answer: Imports become more expensive in the local currency, so raw material costs rise [1]. Profit margins are squeezed because prices cannot always be raised to cover the higher input costs [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of a clear chain of command for Caspian Bay Hotels Group.

questions.question_text: Do you think Caspian Bay should give hotel managers authority to spend up to $3,000 locally? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Marlowe & Bright Biscuits is a private limited company baking biscuits with 58 staff, supplying 320 supermarkets and earning $5.4 million. After a social media complaint, sales fell 11%; the batch was certified 200g but averaged 187g.

The director has $25,000 to repair its image, choosing a public relations campaign, an open day for 40 food retailers plus a press release, costing $16,000, or advertising in 8 regional papers for $22,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'public relations'.
questions.model_answer: The part of marketing that builds a favourable image and goodwill with the public through unpaid coverage such as press events, open days and news stories, rather than paid advertising [2].

knowledge_max_2: building a favourable image and goodwill with the public
gaining publicity through events, press coverage and press releases, not paid adverts

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Marlowe & Bright Biscuits of the public relations campaign rather than newspaper advertising.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Coverage earned through the open day and press release carries more credibility than paid advertising [k] because 40 food retailers and journalists would experience the bakery first-hand [app]. Benefit 2: The campaign costs $16,000 against $22,000 for newspapers [k], saving $6,000 while reaching the decision-makers behind 320 supermarket listings [app].

knowledge_max_2: earned coverage is more credible than paid advertising
public relations is cheaper than press advertising
application_max_2: 40 food retailers and journalists experiencing the bakery first-hand
$16,000 PR cost versus $22,000 newspaper adverts, reaching 320 supermarket decision-makers

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks to Marlowe & Bright Biscuits of relying on public relations to repair its image.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Marlowe & Bright cannot control what journalists write [k] after the open day [app], so coverage could rehash the 187g pack-weight story instead of celebrating the bakery, deepening distrust rather than repairing it [an]. Drawback 2: Public relations reaches only the 40 attending retailers and journalists [k] compared with 8 regional papers [app], so most supermarket buyers never hear the company's side and sales may keep falling [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowe & Bright Biscuits should run the public relations campaign rather than the newspaper advertising? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The PR campaign would rebuild credibility [k] by letting 40 food retailers and journalists see the bakery and the 200g pack quality first-hand [app], which could win back the 320 supermarket listings lost after an 11% fall in quarterly sales [an]. However, newspaper advertising across 8 regional papers [app] would reach far more of the public at once with a message the company fully controls [k], though at $22,000 it costs $6,000 more than the $16,000 PR option [an]. Overall, Marlowe & Bright should choose the PR campaign [eval] because trust, not awareness, is the problem this 187g batch created, so third-party voices will persuade sceptical shoppers better than paid adverts [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs controlled wide reach against credible third-party persuasion
justified recommendation to choose PR because the problem is trust, not awareness

scenario_stem:
Marlowcrest Tableware Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing hand-decorated ceramic plates and bowls. Its 120 workers exported $7.4 million to Country Z through 340 stores. A 22% import tariff now costs about $1.628 million a year.

Directors weigh a $5.5 million Country Z factory employing 95 local workers against staying in Country X and raising wholesale prices by 15%. Capacity is 1.1 million pieces; demand grows 8% annually, and retained profits are $6.0 million.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tax placed by a government on goods imported into a country, which raises the price of those goods [2].

knowledge_max_2: a tax or duty on imported goods
raises the price of imports and protects domestic producers

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the 22% tariff encourages Marlowcrest to produce tableware inside Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Avoiding the tariff protects competitiveness [k], because exporting from Country X would add about $1.628 million a year in duty on $7.4 million of sales [app]. Reason 2: Local production reaches buyers without import restrictions [k], because plates made in Country Z sell freely through 340 stores [app].

local production gains unrestricted access to the importing market

plates made in Country Z sell freely through 340 stores

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Marlowcrest may face if it builds the Country Z factory.

Problem 2: Training and quality risk [k], because 95 new local workers must learn Marlowcrest's hand-decoration standards [app], and faults would damage the brand in its 340 stores [an].

questions.model_answer: Building the factory removes the tariff burden [k], because production in Country Z means the $1.628 million annual duty disappears while demand grows at 8% annually across 340 stores [app], protecting Marlowcrest's $7.4 million market more securely than a price rise would [an]. However, raising prices by 15% avoids the $5.5 million outlay [k], because it keeps all 120 workers in Country X and preserves the $6.0 million profit cushion [app], but higher prices could push buyers towards rival plates and sales may fall [an]. Overall, Marlowcrest should build the Country Z factory [eval], because avoiding $1.628 million of duty each year plus 8% annual market growth outweighs the $5.5 million set-up cost over time [eval].

scenario_stem:
Copperthwaite Hotel Group is a private limited company operating a 45-room boutique hotel, managed by Sofia Marchetti. Revenue was $2.3 million and profit $310,000. Current assets are $150,000 (inventories $30,000, receivables $30,000, bank balance $90,000); current liabilities $75,000 (payables $45,000, overdraft $30,000). Occupancy falls to 35% in winter.

Sofia plans to refurbish 12 rooms for $220,000 using a 7-year, 11% bank loan to attract winter wedding parties, or keep cash for the slow season. Shareholders want a dividend and staff a pay rise before Christmas.

questions.question_text: Define 'acid test ratio'.
questions.model_answer: (Current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities; it measures the ability to pay short-term debts quickly without relying on selling inventories, expressed as x:1 [2].

knowledge_max_2: measures ability to pay short-term debts without selling inventories, expressed as x:1

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Copperthwaite's shareholders use its final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Shareholders use final accounts to decide whether to hold or sell their shares [k]; profit of $310,000 on revenue of $2.3 million suggests the hotel is trading well, which could support confidence in keeping their investment [app]. Use 2: Shareholders use final accounts to judge whether a dividend can be paid [k]; current assets of $150,000 against current liabilities of $75,000 give a current ratio of 2.0:1, so short-term debts are covered and part of the $310,000 profit could be distributed [app].

knowledge_max_2: shareholders use accounts to decide whether to hold or sell shares
shareholders use accounts to judge whether a dividend is affordable
application_max_2: profit of $310,000 on revenue of $2.3 million
current assets $150,000 and current liabilities $75,000 give a current ratio of 2.0:1

questions.question_text: Explain two ways employees use Copperthwaite's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Employees use final accounts to assess job security [k]; revenue of $2.3 million and occupancy falling to 35% between November and March show the slow season is the risky period, so staff may fear winter hours even though the year closed with a $310,000 profit [app][an]. Use 2: Employees use final accounts to support a pay claim [k]; the $310,000 profit and a current ratio of 2.0:1 suggest the hotel can afford a pay rise, strengthening the case staff put to Sofia Marchetti before Christmas [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: employees use accounts to assess job security
employees use accounts to support pay negotiations
application_max_2: occupancy falls to 35% between November and March; revenue $2.3 million
profit of $310,000; current ratio 2.0:1; pay rise wanted before Christmas
analysis_max_2: winter low season threatens winter hours despite annual profit
liquidity and profit give weight to a pay claim before Christmas

questions.question_text: Do you think Sofia should take the bank loan to refurbish the 12 rooms? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Taking the loan could transform winter trade [k]; refurbishing 12 rooms for $220,000 could attract wedding parties in the November to March season when occupancy is just 35%, lifting revenue beyond $2.3 million [app][an]. However, the loan has 11% interest for 7 years and cash is already stretched [k]; current assets of $150,000, an acid test of 1.6:1 and the $90,000 bank balance leave little slack, while staff still want a pay rise and shareholders a dividend [app][an]. Overall, Sofia should take the loan only if the bank agrees an interest-only first year and the $220,000 refit finishes before the wedding season [eval], because winter demand is unproven and she must keep enough cash for the slow season and for wages [eval].

the loan adds long-term interest cost and reduces cash headroom in winter

acid test 1.6:1; bank balance $90,000; overdraft $30,000; 11% interest over 7 years

interest for 7 years strains cash during the thin winter season alongside pay and dividend demands

scenario_stem:
Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd is a family-owned private limited company chicken farm and processing business selling 9,000 chickens weekly at $4.50 per kilogram to supermarket chains, with $6,000,000 revenue and housing at 85% capacity.

The government will cut the chicken import quota from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes, making imported frozen chicken at $3.20 per kilogram scarcer. Hollinbrook must decide whether to invest $1,200,000 in two new sheds for 2,500 more birds weekly or maintain current output.

questions.question_text: Define 'import quota'.
questions.model_answer: A physical limit on the quantity of a good that a country allows to be imported [2].

knowledge_max_2: A limit on the quantity/amount of an import
Restricts how much of the good may enter the country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd of the government cutting the chicken import quota from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Reduced competition from imports [k], so supermarkets seeking chicken at around $4.50 per kilogram are more likely to contract Hollinbrook's 9,000 weekly birds [app]. Benefit 2: Opportunity to raise price or output [k], as scarce supply lets the farm push up margins or fill its 85% capacity with extra orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: Limiting import supply reduces foreign competition for domestic firms
Domestic firms can sell more and/or charge higher prices when imports are capped
application_max_2: 9,000 chickens a week at $4.50 offered to supermarkets
Farm only at 85% capacity so room to raise sales

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of relying on the import quota for Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd's success.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: The quota could be relaxed later [k], so demand for Hollinbrook's chicken could fall back to supermarkets' previous import mix [app], leaving the farm with half-empty sheds and falling capacity utilisation [an]. Limitation 2: Protection reduces pressure to improve efficiency [k], so the farm may not tackle its $6,000,000 cost base as it would under import competition [app], meaning it struggles on price if the 3,000-tonne protection ends [an].

Revenue of $6,000,000 without cost pressure from cheaper $3.20 imports

questions.question_text: Do you think Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd should invest $1,200,000 in two new sheds to increase output or maintain its current output? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing $1,200,000 in two new sheds would raise capacity by 2,500 birds a week [k]; with imported chicken capped at 3,000 tonnes a year, supermarket demand is likely to shift to domestic suppliers such as Hollinbrook's 9,000-bird weekly output [app], lifting revenue above $6,000,000 and pushing capacity past 85% [an]. However, maintaining current output avoids the $1,200,000 cost and any debt risk [k]; if the quota is relaxed or demand softens, the extra sheds would sit empty and cut profit [app], leaving the farm with weak cash flow [an]. Overall, investing in the sheds is the better option because the quota cut from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes is a confirmed government policy and the gain comes through sales of 2,500 extra birds a week [eval], although the board should secure supermarket contracts before building begins [eval].

scenario_stem:
Haverstock Furniture Ltd is a private limited company making wooden office desks and chairs. It employs 40 workers, reporting $2.6 million revenue and $310,000 profit.

It buys 900 cubic metres of oak timber from Suncrest Sawmills at $240 per cubic metre, costing $216,000. The sawmill owners offer to sell for $1.5 million. Founder Daniel Whitmore must decide whether to buy it or invest $300,000 in a larger showroom, fearing the strain of running a sawmill.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'backward vertical integration'.
questions.model_answer: When a business merges with or takes over a supplier at an earlier stage of production, for example a furniture maker buying a sawmill [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Haverstock Furniture of buying Suncrest Sawmills.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Guaranteed timber supply [k], because the 900 cubic metres of oak Haverstock needs each year would come from its own sawmill instead of a single outside supplier [app]. Benefit 2: Lower net costs [k], because the $240 per cubic metre paid to Suncrest includes its profit margin, which Haverstock would now capture inside the integrated business [app].

knowledge_max_2: secure / guaranteed supply of raw materials
eliminates supplier's profit margin / lower input costs

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Haverstock Furniture might experience if it buys Suncrest Sawmills.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Large capital outlay [k], because paying $1.5 million for the sawmill would absorb nearly five years of its $310,000 annual profit and block the $300,000 showroom alternative [app], stretching the business's finances severely [an]. Problem 2: Lack of expertise and management strain [k], because Daniel Whitmore is already concerned about managing a sawmill as well as a furniture factory [app], so mistakes in both operations could reduce quality and profit [an].

However, the $1.5 million price equals nearly five years of its $310,000 annual profit [k], and Daniel lacks sawmill management experience while the $300,000 showroom would directly boost furniture sales [app], so the integrated business could lose money for years while he learns an unfamiliar operation [an]. scenario_stem:
Emberfall Leisure Group is a private limited company running 38 casual dining restaurants with 1,450 staff. In its flat structure, the operations director oversees 6 area managers, each over 6 or 7 restaurant managers and 8 to 10 team leaders, with 3 layers above serving staff.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of Emberfall's flat structure.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Mango Flash Snacks of the viral video campaign rather than television advertising.

scenario_stem:
Steadham Speakers Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling 240,000 Bluetooth speakers a year with 96 workers. Dollar-priced components cost $4.1 million, but the currency fell 18% against the dollar, pushing them to $4.84 million, about $740,000 more.

It sells 60% at home and exports 40%, worth $3.3 million, to Country R in dollars. The board weighs moving component sourcing and final assembly to a $2.7 million Country D factory with wages 25% lower against raising Country X prices by 9%.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: The price of one currency in terms of another, for example how many local units equal one US dollar [2].

knowledge_max_2: the price of one currency in terms of another
it determines how much local money is paid or received in foreign trade

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the 18% fall in the Country X currency affects Steadham Speakers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Imports become more expensive [k], because dollar-priced components rose from $4.1 million to about $4.84 million, an extra $740,000 [app]. Reason 2: Exports become more price-competitive [k], because the 40% of output worth $3.3 million is invoiced in dollars, so dollar receipts convert into more local currency [app].

knowledge_max_2: a fall in the currency makes imports more expensive
a fall in the currency makes exports cheaper and more competitive abroad
application_max_2: components rose from $4.1 million to about $4.84 million, an extra $740,000
40% of output worth $3.3 million is dollar-invoiced, so receipts buy more local currency

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why exchange rates influence Steadham's decision to locate production abroad.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Relocation removes import-cost risk [k], because buying components in Country D's currency avoids another $740,000 of losses if the Country X currency falls again [app], giving stable, predictable costs [an]. Reason 2: Matching costs and revenue in dollars [k], because the $3.3 million export income is dollar-priced and Country D wages are 25% lower [app], so a natural hedge protects profit margins whichever way the rate moves [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Steadham Speakers Ltd should move assembly to Country D? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Duncannon Timber Homes Ltd is a private limited company making timber-frame house kits. Revenue rose from $3.0 million to $3.4 million. Current assets are $260,000 (inventories $140,000, receivables $85,000, cash $35,000) against liabilities of $130,000; last year assets were $200,000 (inventories $90,000) and liabilities $100,000.

A housing association offers a $900,000 contract for 60 timber-frame kits but needs far more timber from March. Adam must choose between this and private housebuilders paying within 30 days, as inflation has sharply raised timber prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'ratio analysis'.
questions.model_answer: The use of financial ratios calculated from a business's final accounts to assess its performance, liquidity and position, and to compare it with other periods or businesses [2].

knowledge_max_2: financial ratios calculated from final accounts
used to assess performance, liquidity or position and to compare over time or with other businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of ratio analysis for Adam and his fellow directors.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Directors use ratio analysis to monitor liquidity and spot a deteriorating trend [k]; Duncannon's acid test has fallen to 0.92:1 this year, from 1.1:1 last year, even though the current ratio is stable at 2.0:1 in both years [app]. Use 2: Directors use ratio analysis to help decide whether to accept the housing association contract [k]; if required stocks of timber rise well beyond $140,000, the acid test could fall sharply, so Adam can insist on phased deliveries before signing [app].

knowledge_max_2: directors use ratio analysis to monitor liquidity trends
directors use ratio analysis to support decisions on large contracts and stock levels
application_max_2: acid test fell from 1.1:1 to 0.92:1; current ratio stable at 2.0:1 ($260,000 / $130,000)
inventories rose from $90,000 to $140,000; contract needs far more stock from March

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of comparing Duncannon's ratios over the last two years.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Ratios are historic figures and say nothing certain about the future [k]; the 0.92:1 acid test reflects revenue of $3.4 million earned at the year end, not whether the $900,000 contract will strain cash when it is delivered from March [app][an]. Limitation 2: Comparisons over time are distorted by inflation and price changes [k]; timber prices have pushed inventories from $90,000 to $140,000, so higher stock value does not necessarily mean more timber in real terms [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: ratios are historic and cannot predict future performance
comparisons over time are distorted by inflation and price changes
application_max_2: acid test now 0.92:1 against revenue of $3.4 million and a $900,000 contract under consideration
inventories rose from $90,000 to $140,000 due to timber price inflation
analysis_max_2: historic figures cannot show how the contract will actually affect liquidity
price rises inflate inventory values, so the deterioration may be smaller than it looks

questions.question_text: Do you think Adam should accept the housing association contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The contract could secure two years of work [k]; at $900,000 it is worth about a quarter of last year's $3.4 million revenue and would keep Duncannon's kit factory running at full capacity [app][an]. However, liquidity is already stretched, and comparisons over time can mislead [k]; the acid test has slipped from 1.1:1 to 0.92:1 and inflation has swollen inventories to $140,000, so the true position may be weaker than the figures suggest [app][an]. Overall, Adam should accept the contract only with milestone payments and staged timber deliveries [eval], because the $900,000 prize outweighs the risk if cash arrives before large inventory bills fall due, protecting the 0.92:1 acid test [eval].

the acid test is deteriorating; historic ratio comparisons can mislead

evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to accept only with milestone payments and staged deliveries

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Willow & Whistle Toys is a sole trader independent toy shop in Country X, a founding member of the Orin Trade Bloc, with $2,100,000 annual revenue. Around 70% of stock comes from outside the trade bloc.

An 18% import tariff plus a 200,000-unit annual quota now applies to non-bloc imports. Bloc-made toys enter tariff-free but cost 12% more wholesale and offer less choice, so the average imported toy shelf price rises from $50 to $59.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade bloc'.
questions.model_answer: A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members to encourage trade [2].

knowledge_max_2: A group of countries trading together
Trade barriers between members are reduced or removed

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 18% import tariff on Willow & Whistle Toys.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Higher cost of imported stock [k], since the average shelf price of an imported toy rises from $50 to $59 under the 18% tariff [app]. Effect 2: Greater appeal of bloc-made toys [k], which enter the Orin Trade Bloc tariff-free and so become more price-competitive in the shop's range [app].

knowledge_max_2: A tariff raises the price of imported goods
Tariffs improve the competitiveness of goods from inside the bloc
application_max_2: Average imported toy price rises from $50 to $59
Bloc-made toys enter tariff-free and become comparatively cheaper

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the import quota of 200,000 toy units could affect the shop's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Fewer toys available on the shelves [k], as only 200,000 non-bloc units may enter Country X each year [app], so popular imported lines may sell out as families shop for birthdays [an]. Way 2: Less product choice for shoppers [k], because the shop cannot restock its usual import-heavy range and must narrow the 70% of stock sourced from outside the Orin Trade Bloc [app], leaving customers with fewer styles and brands [an].

knowledge_max_2: A quota caps the volume of imports available

70% of stock comes from outside the Orin Trade Bloc

questions.question_text: Do you think Willow & Whistle Toys should switch to mainly bloc-made toys or keep its current import-heavy range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to mainly bloc-made toys removes the 18% tariff cost [k]; since tariff-free bloc toys are only about 12% more expensive at wholesale, the shop's shelf prices would stay closer to $50 levels while protecting margins [app]. This also strengthens ties with bloc suppliers and guarantees supply under the quota [an]. However, keeping the import-heavy range preserves the variety customers value, with 70% of stock from outside the Orin Trade Bloc [app]; the 200,000-unit quota and the $59 price point will squeeze sales and margins [an]. Import duties raise consumer prices and reduce choice when stocked goods come from outside a trade bloc [k]. Overall, switching to mainly bloc-made toys is better because the quota and 18% tariff are confirmed, whereas the 12% wholesale premium is modest against avoiding a $9 price rise per toy [eval], although the shop should keep a small import range for loyal customers [eval].

Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice
application_max_2: Tariff-free toys only 12% dearer at wholesale vs $59 price point
70% of stock from outside bloc; 200,000-unit quota confirmed
analysis_max_2: Secures supply and protects margins within the quota

evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified overall recommendation with figures

scenario_stem:
Merrow Vale Cider Ltd is a private limited company in Country X pressing apples from 30 orchards into bottled cider for supermarkets. With 22 staff it makes 600,000 bottles a year at $2.10 each, earning $1.26 million revenue and $180,000 profit.

Supermarkets add a 50-cent mark-up, charging $2.60. Founder Rosa Merrow chooses between 2 own shops at $320,000 each selling direct at $2.60, keeping the margin, or a $500,000 pressing line raising output to 800,000 bottles.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'forward vertical integration'.
questions.model_answer: When a business takes over or merges with a firm at a later stage of production, such as a producer opening its own shops to sell directly to consumers [2].

knowledge_max_2: takes over / merges with a firm at a later stage of production
moves closer to the final consumer (e.g. own retail outlets)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Merrow Vale Cider of opening its own shops.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Higher margin per bottle [k], because selling at $2.60 direct would keep the 50 cents supermarkets currently add on top of the $2.10 paid to Merrow [app]. Advantage 2: Direct customer relationships [k], because own shops would let Merrow build brand loyalty and gather feedback instead of relying on supermarket shelf space [app].

knowledge_max_2: captures the retailer's margin / higher revenue per unit
direct contact with customers / brand control

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Merrow Vale Cider might face operating its own shops.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: High set-up cost [k], because 2 shops at $320,000 each would cost $640,000 at once [app], well above the $500,000 pressing-line alternative and likely straining cash reserves while sales build up [an]. Problem 2: Lack of retailing experience [k], because Merrow knows pressing cider, not running tills, displays and shop staff [app], so poor retail management could leave the shops loss-making and damage the brand [an].

lack of retailing expertise / new risks

questions.model_answer: Own shops would keep the 50-cent mark-up on every bottle sold direct [k], because selling at $2.60 rather than receiving $2.10 would raise revenue from the 600,000 bottles and build direct customer loyalty [app], potentially lifting profit well above $180,000 [an]. However, the shops cost $640,000 against the $500,000 pressing line [k], and raising output to 800,000 bottles would grow revenue to $1.68 million through proven supermarket channels, while Merrow has no retail experience [app], so slow-selling stock and high running costs could erase the saving [an]. Overall, Merrow Vale Cider should install the second pressing line rather than open shops [eval]; it builds on existing supermarket demand with less risk than the $640,000 retail venture [eval].

analysis_max_2: keeping the 50-cent mark-up could lift profit per bottle

scenario_stem:
Hartley Vale Couriers is a private limited company with 9 regional depots, 1,150 drivers and 320 warehouse staff. Depot managers average 8 years' service, yet head office approves every vehicle repair over $500, every hire and route change over 40 kilometres.

Approvals take 4 days, leaving 26 vans off the road and costing about $38,000 a month. The board decides whether to delegate repairs up to $2,500, hiring and route changes to depot managers, or keep central control.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'delegation'.
questions.model_answer: Passing authority and responsibility for tasks from a manager to a subordinate, while the manager remains accountable for the result [2].

knowledge_max_2: transferring authority / responsibility for tasks to subordinates
the manager remains accountable for the outcome

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of delegating repair authority to depot managers.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Faster repairs return vans to work [k], because depot managers could approve the 26 vans currently off the road without waiting 4 days for head office for any repair over $500 [app]. Advantage 2: Depot managers develop and feel trusted [k], because with 8 years' average service they have the experience to judge repairs up to $2,500, and the added authority motivates them to contribute more [app].

knowledge_max_2: delegation speeds up decisions / returns resources to work sooner
application_max_2: 26 vans off the road waiting 4 days for head office approval

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of delegating hiring and route decisions to depot managers.

Problem 2: Inconsistent standards between depots [k], because each depot manager may hire and change routes differently across the 9 depots and 1,470 staff [app], so service quality and delivery times may vary for customers [an].

questions.model_answer: Delegating would turn 4-day approvals into same-day decisions [k], so the 26 vans currently off the road could return to work and the $38,000 monthly loss could fall sharply [app], protecting revenue and delivery contracts across all 9 depots [an]. However, weaker central control could raise costs and inconsistency [k], because authority to approve up to $2,500 repairs and local hiring could loosen discipline across 1,470 staff [app], and hiring mistakes are hard to reverse once made [an]. Overall, Hartley Vale should delegate repair and route authority up to $2,500 but keep hiring centralised [eval], because repairs drive the immediate $38,000 monthly loss while hiring errors are far harder to undo [eval].

scenario_stem:
Scarlet Meadow Fashion is a private limited company designing streetwear for 18-30 year-olds with $7.2 million revenue. It won a design award and wants online sales in Country V and Country W, where clothing sales grow 15%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Scarlet Meadow Fashion of the global mega-influencer campaign.

scenario_stem:
Westmarch Snack Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing tortilla chips and corn puffs. It exports $5.2 million of snacks to Country P. Country P's 1,900-tonne import quota is below Westmarch's 2,300-tonne exports, and no local maker matches its 14 flavours.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'quota'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why market access encourages Westmarch to consider opening in Country P.

Benefit 2: Reliable local supply [k], because a factory employing 60 Country P workers sets production next to the supermarkets Westmarch serves [app], cutting transport times so shelves stay stocked when exports would be capped [an].

scenario_stem:
Starrow Retail Group Plc is a public limited company listed on the Country X Stock Exchange, running 24 fashion stores. Revenue was $9.5 million, profit $640,000; it employs 1,150. Current assets of $550,000 include cash $130,000; liabilities of $250,000 include taxation payable $70,000.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

However, remaining in Country X avoids the $6,500,000 set-up cost [k], keeps the 210 existing workers in place and preserves relations with national government [app], but the tariff would keep eroding margins every year [an]. Overall, Vesper should build the Country W plant because the annual tariff saving and bloc market access justify the investment over time [eval], although a phased relocation that keeps a small Country X line would reduce disruption [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ferndell Coffee Co is a private limited company founded by Amara Diallo. It runs 4 busy cafés, employs 36 staff and reports $1.9 million revenue with $240,000 profit, despite lunchtime queues at full capacity.

Amara wants to expand into 2 new districts. She can open 2 more cafés costing $110,000 each from retained profit, or buy Bronze Bean Coffee Co, with 3 cafés and 28 staff, for $850,000 via a bank loan, risking control of her brand.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'internal growth'.
questions.model_answer: Growth achieved by expanding the business's own existing operations, such as opening new outlets or increasing output, rather than by taking over another firm [2].

knowledge_max_2: growth from the business's own existing operations
e.g. opening new outlets / increasing output (not by merger or takeover)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Ferndell Coffee Co of growing internally rather than buying Bronze Bean Coffee Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Retained control [k], because opening 2 cafés from Ferndell's own funds would let Amara keep her menu, style and management approach unchanged [app]. Advantage 2: No new debt or interest [k], because internal growth from retained profit avoids the bank loan needed for the $850,000 Bronze Bean purchase [app].

knowledge_max_2: keeps control of decisions / brand / culture
application_max_2: $850,000 Bronze Bean price needing a bank loan
Amara wants to avoid losing control of her brand

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of internal growth for Ferndell Coffee Co.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Slower expansion [k], because opening 2 cafés requires finding, fitting out and staffing sites while Bronze Bean's 3 cafés would be trading from day one [app], delaying Ferndell's entry into the new districts [an]. Disadvantage 2: Drains retained profit [k], because Ferndell's annual profit is only $240,000 against the $220,000 needed for 2 cafés [app], leaving almost nothing in reserve if sales prove slow [an].

knowledge_max_2: internal growth is slower than acquisition
application_max_2: Bronze Bean's 3 cafés trading from day one
$240,000 annual profit vs $220,000 needed for 2 cafés
analysis_max_2: delay in entering new districts cedes ground to rivals
thin reserves leave the business vulnerable if sales are slow

questions.question_text: Do you think Ferndell Coffee Co should buy Bronze Bean Coffee Co instead of opening 2 new cafés? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying Bronze Bean would give Ferndell an instant footprint [k], because 3 ready-made cafés with 28 staff and a customer base would be added to Ferndell's own 4 cafés and 36 staff immediately [app], pushing revenue well beyond $1.9 million [an]. However, the $850,000 price must be funded by a bank loan [k], and interest would burden a business earning only $240,000 profit a year, while Ferndell would inherit Bronze Bean's staff, leases and working practices [app], risking cultural friction and reduced control of the brand [an]. Overall, Ferndell should open the 2 new cafés rather than buy Bronze Bean [eval], because the internal $220,000 route from retained profit avoids loan risk and overstretching a business with $240,000 annual profit [eval].

knowledge_max_2: takeover gives instant scale / customer base
loan-funded acquisition adds debt and integration risk
application_max_2: Ferndell: 4 cafés, 36 staff, $1.9 million revenue, $240,000 profit
analysis_max_2: instant scale could lift revenue quickly
loan interest and integration friction could erode profit and control
evaluation_max_2: weighs speed and convenience of takeover against cost and control of organic growth with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Truepoint Engineering Group is a private limited company making pumps at 5 factories, employing 2,300 people. Its functional chart has a production, sales and finance director at head office, each overseeing all 5 factory managers.

The 2 Country Y factories complain weekly about parts delays that idle lines. The board chooses between this functional chart, with 3 directors above 5 factory managers, and a geographic chart with a Country X and a Country Y director, adding a layer.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'organisational chart'.
questions.model_answer: A diagram that shows how a business is structured, displaying the levels of hierarchy, departments and the reporting relationships between posts [2].

knowledge_max_2: a diagram of the structure of a business
shows levels of hierarchy, departments and reporting (who answers to whom)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the functional organisational chart for Truepoint.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Specialists lead each function [k], because a production director oversees all 5 factories, giving consistent technical standards across Country X and Country Y [app]. Advantage 2: Clear responsibilities and no duplication [k], because with only 3 directors above 5 factory managers across 2,300 employees everyone knows their role [app].

knowledge_max_2: functional charts put specialists in charge of each function
functional charts clarify roles and avoid duplicated departments
application_max_2: a production director overseeing all 5 factories
3 directors above 5 factory managers for 2,300 employees

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of keeping the functional chart.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Slow decisions for overseas factories [k], because Country Y plants must ask the production director at head office before acting on parts delays flagged weekly [app], so lines sit idle for days while approval is awaited [an]. Problem 2: Poor coordination between functions [k], because the production director prioritises factory output while the sales director pushes orders, with no Country Y leader to balance them [app], so conflicting instructions can reach the 5 factory managers [an].

knowledge_max_2: functional charts slow decisions for remote / overseas units
functions can conflict without a coordinator between them
application_max_2: Country Y factories wait on head office for parts delay decisions flagged weekly
no Country Y leader between 3 directors and the 5 factory managers
analysis_max_2: idle lines raise costs and hurt delivery performance
factories receive mixed signals, hurting output and morale

questions.question_text: Do you think Truepoint should adopt the geographic organisational chart? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A geographic chart would give Country Y its own director [k], so parts delays flagged weekly could be approved locally instead of crossing the border to head office [app], cutting downtime across the 2 Country Y factories [an]. However, it adds one layer of management [k], increasing overheads for only 2,300 staff and risking duplicated production and finance posts in both countries [app], which could weaken the functional coordination the group relies on [an]. Overall, Truepoint should adopt the geographic chart with monthly head office reviews [eval], because local control over 2 overseas factories outweighs one extra layer given weekly parts delays are losing output [eval].

knowledge_max_2: geographic charts give overseas units local authority
extra layers raise overheads and risk duplication
application_max_2: Country Y director supervising 2 overseas factories
head office sits over 5 factories and 2,300 employees with weekly parts complaints
analysis_max_2: local approval cuts downtime and speeds problem solving
extra layer raises costs and may duplicate roles
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to weekly parts delays and overseas control

scenario_stem:
Alderwick Preserves Co is a partnership of two brothers making jams with 19 staff. It sells 95,000 jars at $6.40 for $608,000, but domestic sales grew only 2% in 2 years and two supermarkets demanded a 12% price discount.

A distributor in Country V offers 30,000 jars yearly at $5.10 if labelling meets rules within 6 months, on a 3-year deal. Exporting adds $24,000 freight and $9,000 certification. The brothers must decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods produced in one country to customers in another country, extending a business's market beyond its domestic borders [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling goods produced in the home country to overseas customers
extending the market beyond domestic borders

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Alderwick Preserves Co of exporting to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: The order would add sales beyond the stagnant domestic market [k] — 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 is about $153,000 of new revenue [app]. Opportunity 2: Entering Country V spreads risk [k], so if two domestic supermarket chains force the 12% discount, the brothers still have a second market to sell into [app].

knowledge_max_2: exporting adds sales beyond the domestic market
selling into a second country spreads risk
application_max_2: 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 is about $153,000 of new revenue
a second market cushions the 12% discount demanded by supermarket chains

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Alderwick Preserves Co of exporting to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The brothers must meet Country V food-safety labelling within 6 months [k], so failure would waste the $9,000 certification fee before a single jar ships [app], delaying entry and straining the Lakeside factory's cash flow [an]. Problem 2: Freight adds $24,000 a year [k] and the $5.10 jar price is $1.30 below the domestic $6.40 [app], squeezing margins so the order may add little profit even when the factory is full [an].

knowledge_max_2: export markets impose labelling and certification requirements
freight costs and lower overseas prices squeeze margins
application_max_2: $9,000 certification and 6-month labelling deadline for Country V
$5.10 export price versus $6.40 domestic, plus $24,000 freight
analysis_max_2: failure to certify wastes the fee and strains cash flow
thin margins mean the order may add little profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderwick Preserves Co should start exporting to Country V? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting would open a Country V market while domestic sales crawl at 2% [k], with 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 worth about $153,000 even after $24,000 freight — roughly $129,000 before certification [app]. However, the $5.10 price is $1.30 below domestic $6.40 [app] and the $9,000 certification carries a real risk of rejection within 6 months [k], so refusal would waste the fee and six months of planning [an], while the domestic slide continues unchecked [an]. Overall, Alderwick should accept the export order [eval] because a second market reduces dependence on supermarkets demanding 12% discounts, and the numbers still add up after certification [eval].

knowledge_max_2: exporting opens overseas markets when domestic demand stagnates
certification deadlines and lower export prices carry real risk
application_max_2: $153,000 of export revenue at $5.10 after $24,000 freight
analysis_max_2: rejected paperwork would waste the $9,000 certification fee
evaluation_max_2: weighs overseas growth and reduced supermarket dependence against price and certification risk
justified recommendation to export because the numbers work after costs

scenario_stem:
Brinvale Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing wooden railway sets and toy trains. Its 88 workers sell $6.3 million a year, 70% at home. Strict safety rules demand $380,000 of annual testing before sale.

Country Q's basic checks cost about $60,000 a year and wages are 35% lower, but a move costs $2.4 million. Its courts are slow with contracts, and Country X import checks stay strict wherever toys are made.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'quality assurance'.
questions.model_answer: A system of checking quality at every stage of production so that faults are prevented rather than found at the end [2].

knowledge_max_2: quality is checked throughout the production process
aims to prevent faults rather than detect them at the end

questions.question_text: Explain two ways legal controls influence where Brinvale locates its factory.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Compliance costs differ between countries [k], because Country X requires $380,000 a year of laboratory testing and certification while Country Q checks cost about $60,000 [app]. Reason 2: Selling rules dictate market choice [k], because Country X import checks apply wherever toys are made, so relocation does not remove legal duties [app].

knowledge_max_2: legal requirements raise or lower compliance costs
legal controls apply based on where the product is sold, not where it is made
application_max_2: Country X testing costs $380,000 a year vs $60,000 in Country Q
Country X import checks remain in force wherever the toys are manufactured

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brinvale may face if it relocates to Country Q.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Brand and safety risk [k], because Country X import checks remain strict, so any toy failing them would embarrass Brinvale in front of its $6.3 million customer base [app], destroying the trust its wooden railway sets rely on [an]. Problem 2: Legal uncertainty [k], because Country Q resolves contract disputes slowly, so suppliers may exploit weak enforcement [app], adding costs and risk to the relocated 88-worker operation [an].

knowledge_max_2: products must still pass import checks where they are sold
a weak legal system makes contracts hard to enforce
application_max_2: Country X import checks stay strict despite relocation
Country Q's courts resolve disputes slowly
$6.3 million sales base would be exposed to brand damage
analysis_max_2: a failed check would destroy trust behind the $6.3 million sales base
slow dispute resolution raises risk and cost for the 88-worker relocated operation

questions.question_text: Do you think Brinvale Toys Ltd should relocate to Country Q? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relocating would cut legal and wage costs [k], because Country Q checks cost $60,000 a year instead of $380,000 and wages are 35% lower [app], saving around $320,000 a year plus payroll savings that could offset the $2.4 million move within a few years [an]. However, relocation would not relax Country X rules [k], because 70% of sales depend on passing strict import checks, and Country Q's slow legal system threatens contracts [app], so a quality or legal failure could cost far more than the $320,000 annual saving [an]. Overall, Brinvale should not relocate to Country Q simply to escape its legal duties [eval], because its $6.3 million reputation rests on safe, certified toys and Country X market access matters more than the compliance saving [eval].

knowledge_max_2: relocation can reduce compliance and wage costs
relocation cannot remove legal controls where products are sold
application_max_2: 70% of sales are in Country X under strict import checks
$2.4 million relocation cost against a $6.3 million sales base
analysis_max_2: $320,000 annual compliance saving plus wage savings could repay the $2.4 million move within a few years
a failed check or legal dispute could destroy far more value than $320,000 a year

scenario_stem:
Hollowbrook Artisan Bakery is a partnership between Adele and Maura Byrne supplying bread and pastries to 11 shops and its own cafe. Revenue was $520,000 with profit $48,000. Current assets are $75,000 (inventories $45,000, receivables $18,000, cash $12,000); current liabilities $60,000 (overdraft $30,000, trade payables $30,000).

The bank may renew its $40,000 overdraft in June. The partners want a $90,000 loan for a second oven to double capacity and win a supermarket own-label contract, or keep the overdraft and delay expansion for two years.

questions.question_text: Define 'stakeholders'.
questions.model_answer: Individuals or groups who have an interest in, and are affected by, a business's activities and financial performance, such as owners, employees, banks, suppliers, government and customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: individuals or groups with an interest in the business
examples include owners, employees, banks, suppliers, government and customers

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons the bank uses Hollowbrook's final accounts before lending.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bank uses the final accounts to judge whether the business can repay the $90,000 loan [k]; with a profit of only $48,000 last year on revenue of $520,000, the loan looks large relative to annual profit unless the supermarket own-label contract delivers [app]. Reason 2: The bank uses the final accounts to judge short-term liquidity before renewing the overdraft [k]; the current ratio is 1.25:1 and the acid test a weak 0.5:1, so Hollowbrook relies on selling flour, butter and bread quickly, which is risky for a perishable baker [app].

knowledge_max_2: the bank uses accounts to judge ability to repay before lending
the bank uses accounts to assess liquidity risk before renewing an overdraft
application_max_2: profit of $48,000 on revenue of $520,000; requested loan $90,000
current ratio 1.25:1; acid test 0.5:1; overdraft $30,000 with renewal of $40,000 due in June

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ratio analysis to judge Hollowbrook's liquidity.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Ratios are historic figures and cannot prove the business will repay the loan [k]; the 1.25:1 current ratio and working capital of $15,000 ($75,000 - $60,000) reflect last year, not whether the supermarket own-label contract will lift revenue above $520,000 [app][an]. Limitation 2: The acid test can exaggerate the weakness of a perishable business [k]; excluding $45,000 of flour and butter stock makes liquidity look far worse than it is, because bakery inventories usually sell within days [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: historic ratios cannot predict future repayment ability
the acid test unfairly depresses liquidity where inventories sell quickly
application_max_2: $45,000 inventories of flour, butter and finished goods; acid test 0.5:1
analysis_max_2: ratios say nothing about the future contract income from the own-label deal
perishable stock sells within days, so the acid test overstates the risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Adele and Maura should borrow the $90,000 for the second oven? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The second oven would double capacity [k]; if the supermarket own-label contract is won, revenue should rise well above $520,000 and the $48,000 profit could service the new loan over a few years of stronger margins [app][an]. However, liquidity is fragile [k]; the acid test is just 0.5:1, the overdraft of $30,000 expires in June, and a further $90,000 loan would leave Hollowbrook paying interest from working capital of only $15,000 [app][an]. Overall, the partners should take the loan only if the bank renews the $40,000 overdraft and the supermarket signs a firm own-label contract first [eval], because the contract revenue would service the $90,000 loan, whereas expansion without it would stretch the 1.25:1 current ratio beyond comfort [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a second oven could double capacity and secure the supermarket contract
weak liquidity makes extra debt risky
application_max_2: revenue $520,000, profit $48,000, working capital $15,000, acid test 0.5:1
$90,000 loan on top of a $30,000 overdraft expiring in June; renewal of $40,000 requested
analysis_max_2: the own-label contract would service the loan from higher revenue
expanding without the contract would overstretch the 1.25:1 current ratio
evaluation_max_2: conditional justified recommendation: borrow only with a signed contract and overdraft renewal

scenario_stem:
Orchard & Oak Preserves Co is a private limited company producing jam and chutney in Country X, with $1,800,000 revenue. It exports 30% of output tariff-free to Country Y in the Trident Trade Bloc, where free trade applies.

Country Z, outside the bloc with 60 million consumers, charges a 12% tariff adding $1.80 to each $15 case. Country Y offers 25 million consumers and a distributor doubling orders to 48,000 cases a year. Directors must choose where to focus export growth.

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade'.
questions.model_answer: Trade between countries without restrictions such as tariffs or quotas [2].

knowledge_max_2: No tariffs or quotas are charged on imports/exports

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Orchard & Oak Preserves Co of free trade within the Trident Trade Bloc.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: No tariff on exports to members [k], so the 30% of output sent to Country Y enters without duty on each case [app]. Benefit 2: Easier access to bloc markets [k], helping Orchard & Oak negotiate larger orders, such as Country Y's distributor doubling purchases to 48,000 cases a year, lifting sales beyond the $1,800,000 revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: No tariffs within the bloc lowers export costs
Bloc membership improves market access / negotiation power
application_max_2: 30% of output exported to Country Y tariff-free
Distributor doubling orders to 48,000 cases a year; revenue $1,800,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Orchard & Oak Preserves Co of exporting to Country Z instead.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The 12% tariff adds $1.80 to each $15 case [k], raising the delivered price for Country Z retailers and squeezing Orchard & Oak Preserves Co's export margin [app], which may force the firm to raise prices and lose competitiveness against local makers [an]. Problem 2: No established distributor in Country Z [k], meaning distribution, promotion and transport must be built from scratch in a market of 60 million consumers [app], increasing start-up costs and delaying break-even on export sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: An import tariff raises the price of foreign goods
Entering a new foreign market has set-up costs / needs distribution
application_max_2: $1.80 added to each $15 case at 12% tariff
60 million consumers; no named distributor unlike Country Y
analysis_max_2: Higher shelf prices lose sales to local competitors
Slower break-even / higher start-up cost burden

questions.question_text: Do you think Orchard & Oak Preserves Co should focus export growth on Country Z despite the 12% tariff, or increase sales in Country Y? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Country Z offers 60 million consumers [k], potentially dwarfing Country Y's 25 million, and even after the 12% tariff adds $1.80 to each $15 case, the larger market could absorb big orders and lift export revenue above the current $1,800,000 turnover [app]; however, entering from scratch means distribution costs and no guarantee of listings [an]. Increasing sales in Country Y keeps tariff-free free trade access and a distributor ready to double orders to 48,000 cases a year [app], raising reliable export volume with no duty risk [an]. Tariffs raise export costs and can make promising foreign markets unprofitable [k]. Overall, Orchard & Oak should prioritise Country Y because tariff-free access and the named distributor give the safest growth [eval], although it can test Country Z with a small pilot order before committing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Large markets with tariffs still carry price/margin penalties
Tariffs raise export costs and reduce profitability
application_max_2: Country Z: 60 million consumers; $1.80 added to each $15 case
Country Y: tariff-free; distributor ready to double to 48,000 cases
analysis_max_2: Country Z entry costs and no listing guarantee
Country Y offers reliable, risk-free volume growth
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall recommendation supported by figures
Qualifies the recommendation with a measured alternative

scenario_stem:
Stornaway Appliances Ltd is a private limited company selling washing machines and refrigerators. In 3 years it grew from 4 stores to 26 by buying 3 rival chains; it employs 380 staff and reports $14.5 million revenue.

Profit fell from $1.3 million to $700,000, complaints rose 40% and absenteeism has also doubled. The board is choosing between buying Halcyon Retail, 8 stores with 95 staff, for $2.0 million, or pausing takeovers for 2 years to improve training.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'external growth'.
questions.model_answer: Growth achieved by merging with or taking over another business, rather than by expanding the business's own internal operations [2].

knowledge_max_2: growth by merging with / taking over another business

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Stornaway Appliances gained from growing externally.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Rapid expansion [k], because buying 3 rival chains took Stornaway from 4 stores to 26 in just 3 years, far faster than building shops itself [app]. Benefit 2: Established customer bases [k], because acquiring 3 chains brought their stores, staff and shoppers overnight rather than starting each outlet from scratch [app].

knowledge_max_2: fast growth / saves time vs organic expansion
acquires existing outlets, customers and staff
application_max_2: 4 stores to 26 in 3 years via 3 rival chains

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Stornaway Appliances is experiencing from its rapid growth and how each might be overcome.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Poor communication across 26 stores and 380 staff [k], because decisions no longer reach shop floors quickly, shown by customer complaints rising 40% [app], so regular written briefings and store manager meetings should be introduced [an]. Problem 2: Low morale and rising absenteeism [k], because rapid change has doubled absence and squeezed profit from $1.3 million to $700,000 [app], so staff training and standardised procedures should be used to rebuild engagement [an].

knowledge_max_2: low morale / absenteeism / control problems from rapid growth
analysis_max_2: clearer briefings and meetings would cut errors and complaints
training and standardised procedures would restore morale and profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Stornaway Appliances should pause acquisitions and consolidate instead of buying Halcyon Retail for $2.0 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Consolidating would fix Stornaway's problems directly [k]: pausing for 2 years to improve training, standardise procedures and rebuild morale would tackle the 40% rise in complaints and doubled absenteeism across 26 stores [app], restoring profitability back toward the $1.3 million previously earned [an]. However, buying Halcyon Retail would add 8 stores and 95 staff for $2.0 million [k], quickly growing revenue and market share while rivals may be expanding too, and the profits from fixing the core business would not arrive until later [app], whereas waiting 2 years may permanently cede ground to competitors [an]. Overall, Stornaway should pause acquisitions and consolidate [eval], because acquiring Halcyon before fixing communication and morale would simply repeat the same failures on a larger, $2.0 million scale [eval].

knowledge_max_2: consolidation / pausing growth to fix internal problems
acquisition adds scale but also integration risk
application_max_2: 40% rise in complaints and doubled absenteeism
analysis_max_2: fixing communication and morale could restore profitability
buying Halcyon now multiplies integration problems on a larger scale
evaluation_max_2: weighs pausing to consolidate against buying Halcyon, using stem figures, with a justified recommendation

scenario_stem:
Corvane Construction Group is a private limited company building at 7 sites with 980 people. Its hierarchy has 5 levels: board, managing director, 3 regional contracts managers, 7 site managers and 28 trade team leaders.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a clear hierarchy helps Corvane Construction Group.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Clear authority on every site [k], because 7 site managers each control their own site with 3 regional contracts managers above them, so crews know whose instructions to follow [app]. Reason 2: Discipline and control across the workforce [k], because 5 levels mean instructions are checked before reaching crews, helping the board enforce standards across 980 employees [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of the current 5-level hierarchy for safety messages.

Opportunity 2: Sharing the $1.2 million cost means half the capital at risk [k] instead of $3.5 million for its own plant, preserving cash for product development [app].

scenario_stem:
Fenber Furniture Co is a private limited company making solid-oak tables and chairs for 30 shops. Revenue was $2.1 million. Current assets are $390,000 (inventories $210,000, receivables $140,000, cash $40,000); current liabilities $150,000 (payables $110,000, overdraft $40,000). Last year's inventories were $140,000, current ratio 2.4:1 and acid test 1.28:1.

A German retailer offers a $600,000 annual export order, needing $140,000 of imported timber upfront. The timber merchant offers 60-day credit rather than 30 days, or a 4% discount for payment within 10 days.

questions.question_text: Calculate the current ratio of Fenber Furniture Co.
questions.model_answer: Current assets / current liabilities = $390,000 / $150,000 = 2.6, so Fenber's current ratio is 2.6:1 [2].

Reason 2: The merchant uses the accounts to set the amount and length of credit [k]; an overdraft of $40,000 and existing payables of $110,000 show Fenber already uses 30-day credit, so extending to 60 days raises the merchant's risk if the export order fails and $140,000 of timber is delivered before the retailer pays [app].

Use 2: Managers use ratio analysis to plan for the export order [k]; if inventories climb above $210,000 for the $600,000 order, the acid test will fall further, so they can choose the 60-day credit or the 4% discount for payment within 10 days [app][an].

scenario_stem:
