questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of comparing Redburn's ratios over the last two years.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Changed stock mix makes the two years hard to compare [k]; inventories have risen from $130,000 to $150,000 partly because the stores added chilled fresh lines with slower turnover, so the higher figure alone does not prove poorer stock control [app][an]. Limitation 2: Historic figures ignore the new supermarket opening in March [k]; the steady 2.0:1 current ratio reflects the 2 stores trading as usual, but the third store decision depends on future footfall near the railway station, which past ratios cannot show [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: changes in stock mix or accounting methods distort year-on-year comparison
historic ratios ignore future events and market changes
application_max_2: inventories rose from $130,000 to $150,000 as chilled lines were added
new supermarket 10 minutes away opens in March; third store planned near the railway station
analysis_max_2: higher stock value may reflect range change, not worse management
past stability cannot predict competition or third-store trade

questions.question_text: Do you think the Whitmore family should open the third store or refurbish the 2 existing stores? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The third store would capture railway-station trade before the new supermarket settles [k]; $350,000 for a station-side store could keep revenue growing beyond $1.4 million and offset trade being lost to the supermarket 10 minutes away [app][an]. However, the family would carry a $250,000 loan against current liabilities of only $105,000 and an overdraft of $20,000 [k]; the acid test of about 0.57:1 and working capital of $105,000 show cash is already tied up in chilled stock, and repaying the loan from $88,000 annual profit would be tight for the first years [app][an]. Overall, the family should refurbish the 2 existing stores for $90,000 rather than open the third store now [eval], because revenue of $1.4 million may fall when the supermarket opens, and cutting costs before adding debt is safer for a partnership whose acid test is just 0.57:1 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a third store could defend revenue against the new supermarket
a $250,000 loan would be a heavy debt burden for this business
application_max_2: $350,000 cost; $250,000 loan plus $100,000 savings vs $90,000 refit
acid test about 0.57:1; working capital $105,000; profit $88,000
analysis_max_2: station footfall could secure revenue before the supermarket opens
interest and repayments from $88,000 profit would be tight in early years
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to refurbish now and delay the third store until the competitive position is clear

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kingsley Motor Group Plc is a multinational public limited company building 24,000 vehicles a year at its Country X plant with 1,800 workers. Country X is in the Valdonia Customs Union, charging 12% on parts imported from outside.

Engines and gearboxes from Country F cost $60,000,000 yearly, including $7,200,000 in tariffs. A union-based supplier quotes 15% more, about $69,000,000, tariff-free with faster delivery, while the tariff may reach 20% within 2 years. The board must decide whether to switch.

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company (MNC)'.
questions.model_answer: A company that has operations or facilities in two or more countries [2].

knowledge_max_2: A company operating in more than one country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Kingsley Motor Group Plc of switching to union-based parts suppliers.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: No tariff on parts [k], avoiding the $7,200,000 a year the 12% tariff costs on $60,000,000 of imports [app]. Benefit 2: Faster, more reliable delivery [k], as union-based suppliers quoted tariff-free delivery with shorter lead times, reducing stock needs for the 24,000 vehicles built each year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Buying inside a customs union avoids the import tariff
Local/bloc sourcing shortens delivery times and improves reliability
application_max_2: 24,000 vehicles a year; union suppliers quote faster lead times

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Kingsley Motor Group Plc of switching to union-based suppliers.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher parts prices [k], with union-based suppliers quoting about $69,000,000 a year, roughly $9,000,000 more than Country F imports [app], squeezing margins unless vehicle prices rise [an]. Problem 2: Limited supplier choice and quality risk [k], as the union has few qualified engine and gearbox makers [app], creating dependence on a small number of suppliers and possible delivery delays [an].

knowledge_max_2: Bloc-based inputs may cost more than non-bloc imports
Fewer qualified suppliers raises dependence and supply risk
application_max_2: Engines and gearboxes; few union-based manufacturers
analysis_max_2: Margins squeezed unless vehicle prices increase
Supply delays / over-reliance on a few suppliers hurt output

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsley Motor Group Plc should switch parts sourcing to union-based suppliers inside the Valdonia Customs Union? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching removes the 12% tariff [k], saving $7,200,000 a year on parts worth $60,000,000 and shielding the plant if the tariff rises to 20% within 2 years, when the duty would cost $12,000,000 [app]; this would improve margins and protect the 1,800 jobs at the Country X plant [an]. However, staying with Country F keeps the lowest quoted price but relies on imports facing $7,200,000 to $12,000,000 of tariff costs [app], weakening competitiveness over time [an]. Free trade within a customs union lowers the cost of member-based sourcing [k]. Overall, Kingsley should switch to union-based suppliers because the saving beats the 15% price premium if the tariff rises to 20% [eval], although it should negotiate phased contracts to manage quality risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Sourcing inside a customs union avoids the common external tariff
Free trade agreements lower the cost of trade between members
application_max_2: $7,200,000 now rising to $12,000,000 if tariff hits 20%
Union quote $69,000,000 vs Country F $60,000,000; tariff-free delivery
analysis_max_2: Margins improve and 1,800 jobs are protected
Staying with Country F weakens competitiveness as tariffs rise
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement with quantitative reasoning
Qualifies the switch with a risk-management condition

scenario_stem:
Darrowfield Engineering Ltd is a private limited company formed by the merger of two engineering firms. It employs 140 workers, up from 35 before the merger, and reports $7.8 million revenue.

Margin has fallen 11% to 7%, three plant managers have resigned and clients report slow responses. The board is choosing between a second factory costing $2.5 million and consolidating for a year: delegating to store-level managers, holding weekly briefings and launching a staff newsletter.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'merger'.
questions.model_answer: An agreement between two businesses to join together and form a single combined business, sharing ownership, assets and control [2].

knowledge_max_2: two businesses agree to join together
form a single combined business / share ownership and control

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of growth Darrowfield Engineering is facing.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Poor communication [k], because with 140 workers across two merged firms the old informal channels no longer work and clients complain of slow responses [app]. Problem 2: Falling morale and loss of key staff [k], because rapid change since the merger drove three plant managers to resign and cut the profit margin from 11% to 7% [app].

knowledge_max_2: communication breaks down as firms grow larger
low morale / loss of key managers / control problems
application_max_2: three plant managers resigned; margin fell from 11% to 7%

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Darrowfield Engineering could overcome its problems of growth.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Improve communication [k], because weekly briefings and a staff newsletter would keep all 140 staff informed across both former firms [app], reducing errors, delays and the client complaints about slow responses [an]. Way 2: Delegate decision-making to store-level managers [k], because pushing decisions down would speed up responses and reduce the overload on the owners [app], restoring morale and helping lift the profit margin back toward 11% [an].

knowledge_max_2: delegation empowers managers and speeds decisions
application_max_2: weekly briefings and a staff newsletter proposed
140 staff across the two merged firms
analysis_max_2: better communication cuts errors and client complaints
delegation speeds decisions and rebuilds morale and margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Darrowfield Engineering should open a second factory costing $2.5 million now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening a second factory would add capacity for growing order books [k], letting Darrowfield serve more clients and raise revenue beyond $7.8 million while competitors remain at single sites [app], spreading fixed costs and building scale advantages [an]. However, the merged business is not yet stable [k]: the margin has fallen from 11% to 7%, three managers resigned and clients complain of slow responses across 140 staff [app], so a $2.5 million commitment would stretch finances and multiply the management problems before they are fixed [an]. Overall, Darrowfield should consolidate for a year rather than open the second factory now [eval]; delegation, briefings and a clear structure would help restore the 11% margin and a sound base for expansion later [eval].

knowledge_max_2: growth adds capacity and scale advantages
growth on an unstable base multiplies management problems
application_max_2: margin fell from 11% to 7%, three managers resigned
analysis_max_2: extra capacity could raise revenue and spread fixed costs
expanding before fixing problems risks bigger losses and failure
evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion now against consolidation first, with stem figures, and recommends consolidation

scenario_stem:
Fenwillow Steel Plc is a public limited company employing 5,200 people at 5 plants in 3 countries, making steel girders. Communication is mostly top-down, with bottom-up feedback only through annual staff surveys.

After a Near Miss, an operator revealed he reported a crane fault 3 weeks earlier to his supervisor, who never forwarded it; the line stopped two hours. The board chooses a bottom-up reporting and suggestion scheme across 5 plants or annual surveys and top-down memos.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'bottom-up communication'.
questions.model_answer: Communication that flows from employees up to managers, such as feedback, reports and suggestions [2].

knowledge_max_2: communication flowing from lower to higher levels
examples include employee feedback, reports and suggestions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of an effective bottom-up reporting and suggestion scheme for Fenwillow Steel Plc.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Hazards are caught early [k], because the crane fault reported 3 weeks before the Near Miss would have been logged and fixed across the 5 plants [app]. Benefit 2: Workers feel valued and involved [k], because a formal scheme gives all 5,200 employees a regular voice instead of waiting for the annual staff surveys [app].

knowledge_max_2: bottom-up feedback reveals hazards before accidents happen
bottom-up schemes make employees feel valued / increase involvement
application_max_2: crane fault reported 3 weeks before the Near Miss
5,200 employees across 5 plants rarely heard via annual surveys

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Fenwillow may face when introducing a bottom-up scheme across 3 countries.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Managers may be overwhelmed by reports [k], because 5 plants in 3 countries could send many notes and the head office team must sift every one [app], so genuine hazards could be missed in the volume [an]. Problem 2: Ideas may be ignored, demotivating staff [k], because if the board keeps issuing top-down targets and rarely adopts suggestions [app], employees conclude the scheme is fake and stop reporting, like the paper note ignored 3 weeks before the Near Miss [an].

knowledge_max_2: volume of feedback can overwhelm managers
suggestions ignored by management destroy trust and participation
application_max_2: 5 plants across 3 countries reporting to head office
paper note ignored 3 weeks before the crane Near Miss
analysis_max_2: overload hides the serious reports among routine ones
perceived tokenism kills the scheme's safety value

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenwillow should introduce the formal bottom-up reporting and suggestion scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A formal scheme would ensure faults like the crane failure reach the board before accidents happen [k], because the paper note ignored 3 weeks earlier would instead be logged with action deadlines across the 5 plants [app], cutting downtime and preventing injury [an]. However, it costs money and management time [k], because running it across 3 countries and 5,200 employees needs a dedicated coordinator and budget [app], diverting funds from existing channels [an]. Overall, Fenwillow should introduce the scheme with a named coordinator [eval], because the 3-week-old unread warning shows memo-only communication is failing on safety [eval].

knowledge_max_2: formal schemes ensure reports are logged and acted on
coordination across sites requires dedicated staff and budget
application_max_2: crane fault reported 3 weeks before the Near Miss by paper note
analysis_max_2: logged faults prevent accidents and reduce downtime
extra cost and time needed to run the scheme properly
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation based on the ignored warning and safety risk

scenario_stem:
Tarrow Tandoor is a private limited company running 7 tandoor restaurants with $3.1 million revenue. Country X sales grew 9%. Investors want Tarrow restaurants in Country Z, where 2 million residents have none.

The board chooses international franchises, with a $35,000 fee plus 5% of sales, or one company-owned restaurant costing $420,000 needing two managers for 2 years. Imported spices cost 15% more in Country Z.

questions.question_text: Define 'franchise'.
questions.model_answer: A legal arrangement where a franchisor sells the right to trade under its brand name to a franchisee, who pays fees and runs the outlet under agreed standards [2].

knowledge_max_2: franchisor sells the right to trade under its brand name
franchisee pays fees and must follow agreed operating standards

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Tarrow Tandoor of the international franchise option.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Franchises need no $420,000 capital outlay [k]; two franchisees would pay $35,000 each plus 5% of sales, giving Tarrow brand presence in Country Z with minimal investment [app]. Advantage 2: Local franchisees understand Country Z's market and staffing [k], so Tarrow can open two restaurants faster than relocating two managers for 2 years [app].

knowledge_max_2: franchising expands with little capital investment by the franchisor
local franchisees bring local market knowledge and motivation
application_max_2: two franchisees paying $35,000 each plus 5% of sales instead of $420,000
faster entry than relocating two Country X managers for 2 years

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Tarrow Tandoor of international franchising into Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Tarrow keeps only 5% of franchisee sales [k]; the two franchisees pocket most of the profit from their restaurants [app], so the cheapest route may earn the least over the long term [an]. Drawback 2: Quality control is harder at a distance [k]; poor spicing or service from a franchisee in Country Z would tarnish the Tarrow name built across 7 restaurants [app], risking complaints that travel back to Country X [an].

knowledge_max_2: franchisors retain only a small share of outlet profits
quality control is harder to maintain at a distance
application_max_2: only 5% of sales plus set-up fees while franchisees keep the rest
poor Country Z service would tarnish the 7-restaurant Tarrow name
analysis_max_2: the low-cost route may earn the least long-term profit
brand damage from one franchisee could spread back to Country X

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarrow Tandoor should expand into Country Z through international franchises? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Franchises would open Tarrow in Country Z without the $420,000 cost [app] and bring in local partners who handle staffing, advertising and daily operations [k], so the brand could reach 2 million residents in months rather than years [an]. However, franchising pays only $35,000 fees plus 5% of sales [app] and cedes day-to-day control [k], so weak franchisee cooking or service could stain the Tarrow name in both countries [an]. Overall, Tarrow should franchise [eval] because two motivated local partners beat one distant, costly outlet, and the $420,000 stays available for opening restaurant 8 back in Country X [eval].

knowledge_max_2: international franchising enables fast, low-capital overseas expansion
franchising cedes day-to-day control and most outlet profits
application_max_2: no $420,000 outlay; local partners handle staffing and operations
only $35,000 fees plus 5% of sales retained by Tarrow
analysis_max_2: reach 2 million Country Z residents within months
weak franchisee standards could damage the brand in both countries
evaluation_max_2: weighs fast, low-capital reach against lost control and profit share
justified recommendation to franchise while keeping $420,000 for domestic growth

scenario_stem:
Pennywell Wholesale Co is a private limited company in Country X supplying rice, sugar and lentils to 240 corner shops, two wanting weekly deliveries. It buys 900 tonnes of rice at $640 a tonne. Orders above 250 tonnes earn a 6% discount, saving $34,560 yearly on quarterly buying.

Its warehouse holds 280 tonnes at peak, costing $5,200 monthly, $62,400 a year; a burst pipe once damaged $38,000 of sugar. Directors weigh half-yearly buying for a 9% discount against monthly deliveries to cut storage.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: The fall in average cost per unit as a business increases the scale of its operations, for example by buying in bulk [2].

knowledge_max_2: average cost per unit falls as scale increases
purchasing (bulk-buy) economies give discounts for large orders

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Pennywell buys 900 tonnes of rice in bulk.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To earn bulk-buy discounts [k], because orders above 250 tonnes get a 6% discount, saving about $34,560 a year on rice at $640 a tonne [app]. Reason 2: To guarantee supply for shops [k], because 240 corner shops rely on rice deliveries and peak stock of about 280 tonnes prevents empty shelves [app].

knowledge_max_2: bulk buying earns purchasing economies and lower unit costs
large inventory guarantees continuity of supply
application_max_2: 6% discount above 250 tonnes; about $34,560 saved a year on $640 a tonne rice
240 corner shops rely on deliveries; peak stock of about 280 tonnes

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of holding the larger inventory.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Storage and handling charges [k], because rent, insurance and handling cost $5,200 a month, $62,400 a year [app], which eats into the $34,560 bulk-buy saving [an]. Cost 2: Risk of damage or spoilage [k], because a burst pipe destroyed $38,000 of stored sugar last year [app], showing that holding more stock raises the chance of losing goods and money [an].

knowledge_max_2: holding inventory incurs storage, insurance and handling costs
stored goods risk damage, spoilage or loss
application_max_2: $5,200 a month, $62,400 a year in rent, insurance and handling
a burst pipe damaged $38,000 of stored sugar last year
analysis_max_2: $62,400 a year of storage costs absorb much of the $34,560 saving
greater stored volume increases exposure to damage like the $38,000 sugar loss

questions.question_text: Do you think Pennywell Wholesale Co should switch to half-yearly bulk buying for the 9% discount? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Half-yearly bulk buying would deepen the discount [k], because raising the saving from 6% to 9% adds about $17,280 a year on rice at $640 a tonne, and two shops already want weekly deliveries [app], strengthening Pennywell's margins on its $34,560 existing saving [an]. However, larger half-yearly stocks would raise storage and risk [k], because rent and insurance already cost $5,200 a month, and a burst pipe once destroyed $38,000 of sugar [app], so doubled stock could raise holding costs and potential losses above the $17,280 gain [an]. Overall, Pennywell should keep its quarterly 6% bulk buying rather than switch to half-yearly orders [eval], because the extra $17,280 a year does not cover the added storage, insurance and damage risk on much larger stock [eval].

knowledge_max_2: larger bulk orders deepen purchasing discounts
larger stocks raise storage cost and damage risk
application_max_2: 9% vs 6% discount: about $17,280 extra a year on $640 a tonne rice
$5,200 a month for rent, insurance and handling; $62,400 a year
$38,000 of sugar lost to a burst pipe last year
analysis_max_2: extra $17,280 a year improves margins on rice sales
doubled stock raises $62,400 a year baseline storage and the chance of repeat losses above the saving
evaluation_max_2: weighs the extra $17,280 a year discount against higher storage cost and damage risk ($38,000 precedent) — decides to keep quarterly 6% buying

scenario_stem:
Volantis Electronics Plc is a public limited company assembling printed circuit boards, employing 640, listed on the Country X Stock Exchange. Revenue was $18 million, profit $1.35 million. Current assets of $1,250,000 include cash $170,000; liabilities of $500,000 include payables $320,000 and taxation payable $180,000.

Current ratio rose from 2.2:1 to 2.5:1; acid test from 0.90:1 to 1.1:1. After two modest years the board must choose a $400,000 dividend or a $1.1 million automated line to cut unit costs; $180,000 tax is due 30 April.

questions.question_text: Define 'final accounts'.
questions.model_answer: The financial statements prepared at the end of a trading period, the income statement and the statement of financial position, showing a business's revenue, costs, profit and financial position [2].

knowledge_max_2: statement of financial position (assets, liabilities, equity)

questions.question_text: Explain two ways shareholders use Volantis's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Shareholders use final accounts to decide whether to buy, hold or sell their shares [k]; revenue of $18 million and a profit of $1.35 million, with the current ratio improved from 2.2:1 to 2.5:1, suggest Volantis is strengthening, encouraging shareholders to hold [app]. Use 2: Shareholders use final accounts to judge whether the special dividend of $400,000 is affordable [k]; with taxation of $180,000 due by 30 April and cash of only $170,000, shareholders can see most of the dividend must come from retained earnings rather than bank balances [app].

knowledge_max_2: shareholders use accounts to decide whether to buy, hold or sell shares
shareholders use accounts to judge the affordability of dividends
application_max_2: revenue $18 million; profit $1.35 million; current ratio improved from 2.2:1 to 2.5:1
$400,000 special dividend proposed; $180,000 tax due by 30 April; cash $170,000

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the government uses Volantis's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: The government uses final accounts to check that Volantis pays the correct tax [k]; the $180,000 taxation payable lets the tax authority verify it against the stated $1.35 million profit and $18 million revenue before collecting it by 30 April [app][an]. Use 2: The government uses final accounts to monitor large employers and public accountability [k]; with 640 people employed and shares traded on the Country X Stock Exchange, the accounts show whether Volantis is healthy enough to keep paying wages and taxes [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: government uses accounts to verify and collect taxes due
government uses accounts to monitor large employers and their compliance
application_max_2: $180,000 taxation payable against profit of $1.35 million and revenue of $18 million; due 30 April
640 employees; listed on the Country X Stock Exchange
analysis_max_2: an incorrect profit figure would change the $180,000 assessed, so verification protects public revenue
the accounts signal whether jobs and wage taxes are sustainable for a 640-person employer

questions.question_text: Do you think Volantis should pay the special dividend or reinvest in the automated line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A special dividend would attract investors [k]; $400,000 after two modest years would reward shareholders and could support the share price on the Country X Stock Exchange, and the improved 2.5:1 current ratio (up from 2.2:1) shows the business can spare it [app][an]. However, the automated line is the bigger prize [k]; $1.1 million would cut unit costs across $18 million of revenue, defending it against overseas rivals and protecting 640 jobs without borrowing [app][an]. Overall, Volantis should reinvest in the automated line and skip the special dividend this year [eval], because profit of $1.35 million is worth more as a durable cost advantage, though the board could review a dividend next year once the 1.1:1 acid test strengthens further [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a dividend rewards shareholders and can support the share price
reinvestment in automation cuts unit costs and defends revenue
application_max_2: $400,000 special dividend; two modest years; current ratio 2.5:1 vs 2.2:1 last year
$1.1 million automated line vs revenue of $18 million and profit of $1.35 million; acid test 1.1:1; 640 jobs
analysis_max_2: reinvestment improves competitiveness without new debt and spreads savings across every unit sold
paying the dividend now would forgo compounding cost savings on $18 million of revenue
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to reinvest and revisit the dividend next year once the acid test strengthens

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fernhollow Biscuit Co is a family-run private limited company biscuit manufacturer in Country X, with $2,750,000 revenue. Some 80% of sales are home-market, across 1,200 retail outlets.

A Country B supermarket chain in the Orin Trade Bloc offers to list its shortbread in 300 stores, ordering 40,000 cases a year at $9.00 each, worth $360,000 tariff-free. Country B has three rival makers and transport/insurance adds $18,000 yearly. Directors must choose this contract or expand into 400 more domestic outlets.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods or services to buyers in another country [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Fernhollow Biscuit Co of exporting shortbread to Country B.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Tariff-free entry to Country B [k], because the Orin Trade Bloc removes duties between members, so Fernhollow's 40,000 cases a year at $9.00 per case arrive without added charges [app]. Advantage 2: New customer base [k], adding Country B's 300 stores to income alongside its $2,750,000 home-market sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: Exports to bloc members enter without tariffs
Exporting adds a new customer base / diversifies sales
application_max_2: 40,000 cases a year at $9.00; tariff-free within the Orin Trade Bloc
300 Country B stores to add to $2,750,000 home sales

questions.question_text: Explain two challenges for Fernhollow Biscuit Co of serving Country B.
questions.model_answer: Challenge 1: Strong local competition [k], as three established biscuit makers already supply Country B [app], forcing Fernhollow to spend heavily on promotion or undercut on price to win shelf space [an]. Challenge 2: Extra logistics costs [k], with transport and insurance adding $18,000 a year to the contract [app], cutting into the net gain from the $360,000 deal [an].

knowledge_max_2: Foreign markets have established local competitors
Exporting adds transport and insurance costs
application_max_2: Three established biscuit makers already supply Country B
$18,000 a year transport and insurance cost
analysis_max_2: Higher promotion spend or lower prices needed to win distribution
Net revenue from the $360,000 deal is reduced

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernhollow Biscuit Co should accept the Country B export contract or expand domestic distribution into 400 more outlets? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the Country B contract gives Fernhollow Biscuit Co guaranteed $360,000 of tariff-free export revenue [k], selling 40,000 cases at $9.00 into 300 stores and diversifying beyond its 80% home-market reliance [app]; exporting spreads risk and builds the brand overseas [an]. However, domestic expansion into 400 more outlets reaches familiar shoppers with none of the $18,000 transport and insurance costs [app], protecting margins while the firm learns foreign trade [an]. Successful exporting widens markets and can lift output and profit [k]. Overall, Fernhollow should accept the Country B contract because bloc membership makes the trade tariff-free and the chain is committed to 300 stores [eval], although it should pilot the stores before any wider export push [eval].

Exporting widens markets and can raise output and profit
application_max_2: Domestic push adds 400 outlets; avoids $18,000 logistics cost
analysis_max_2: Lower-risk margins from domestic growth before exporting widely
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified choice with evidence from the stem
Qualifies recommendation with a cautious first step

scenario_stem:
Elmridge Precision Tools Ltd is a private limited company employing 48 workers making drill bits. It reports $2.9 million revenue, $3.1 million value of output and $4.4 million capital employed; rival Halstead Tools Plc employs 620 workers.

Revenue per worker is about $60,000 here and about $45,000 at Halstead. For an award directors must choose a size measure. They weigh $500,000 of automated lines cutting 18 jobs but raising value of output from $3.1 million to $4.5 million.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'value of output'.
questions.model_answer: The total monetary worth of the goods and services produced by a business over a period of time, whether or not they have been sold [2].

knowledge_max_2: total monetary worth of goods/services produced
over a period of time, including unsold output

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using value of sales to measure business size.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: It ignores production and unsold output [k], because Elmridge's output of $3.1 million exceeds its sales of $2.9 million, so sales understate the size of its production [app]. Limitation 2: It says nothing about assets or investment [k], because Elmridge's $4.4 million of capital employed is completely invisible in a sales figure [app].

knowledge_max_2: sales exclude unsold output / production scale
sales ignore capital employed / asset base
application_max_2: $4.4 million capital employed never appears in sales

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why value of output may be a better measure of business size than number of employees for Elmridge.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It shows productivity and automation [k], because Elmridge's 48 workers produce $3.1 million of drill bits, a highly productive output-per-worker figure [app], so headcount would make the firm look far smaller than it really is [an]. Reason 2: It gives a fairer comparison with Halstead Tools Plc [k], because Halstead's 620 workers against Elmridge's 48 hides the fact that Elmridge earns about $60,000 revenue per worker versus Halstead's about $45,000 [app], so output reveals efficiency, not just headcount [an].

knowledge_max_2: output reflects productivity / automation, not headcount
output allows fairer like-for-like comparison between firms
application_max_2: Halstead: 620 workers, about $45,000 revenue per worker
analysis_max_2: headcount makes capital-intensive Elmridge look smaller than it is
output reveals relative efficiency and effective scale

questions.question_text: Do you think Elmridge Precision Tools Ltd should invest $500,000 in automated drilling lines, cutting 18 jobs but raising value of output to $4.5 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Automation would raise Elmridge's value of output from $3.1 million to $4.5 million [k], an increase of about 45% that would strengthen its regional award application and competitiveness against Halstead [app], improving efficiency, output quality and profit despite the $500,000 cost [an]. scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Calculate the acid test ratio for Caldmoor Bay last February.
questions.model_answer: (Current assets - inventories) / current liabilities = ($190,000 - $60,000) / $150,000 = $130,000 / $150,000 = 0.87, so the acid test ratio was 0.87:1 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways employees use Caldmoor Bay's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Employees use final accounts to assess job security, especially in winter [k]; February current assets of $190,000 against current liabilities of $150,000 (an acid test of 0.87:1) show how tight cash gets out of season, explaining why only 25 staff keep full-time jobs while 35 are seasonal [app]. Use 2: Employees use final accounts to support a pay claim or a case for year-round hours [k]; revenue of $1.9 million, earned mostly between May and September, and summer current assets of $320,000 show the camp depends on peak-season trade, strengthening the case for seasonal pay supplements [app].

Limitation 2: Comparisons over time ignore how cash moves during the year [k]; ratios are only a snapshot, so they cannot show how the May to September surplus pays for pool repairs and winter wages, meaning a strong summer acid test can mask a winter squeeze [app][an].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The supplier keeps raising prices [k], because the announced 12% rise adds about $850,000 a year to the $7.08 million import bill [app]. Reason 2: Quality has slipped [k], because complaints now affect 6% of units arriving from the single Country G supplier [app].

knowledge_max_2: rising supplier prices squeeze margins and push firms to produce themselves
poor supplier quality threatens the brand and retail relationships
application_max_2: 12% price rise adds about $850,000 a year to the $7.08 million bill
complaints affect 6% of units from the single Country G supplier

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of building Willowfen's own factory in Country G.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The investment is heavy [k], because $3.9 million is over three times the firm's $1.1 million annual profit [app], so profits would take several years to repay the factory [an]. Problem 2: Managing from afar is hard [k], because 85 local workers must reach Country X quality standards for 95 retailers [app], and distance raises the risk of continued faults [an].

knowledge_max_2: building a factory abroad requires major capital investment
managing a workforce in a distant country is difficult
application_max_2: $3.9 million factory cost vs $1.1 million annual profit
85 local workers must meet standards for 95 retailers
analysis_max_2: about 3.5 times annual profit means a slow payback and stretched liquidity
distance and a new workforce raise the risk of persistent quality faults reaching 95 retailers

questions.question_text: Do you think Willowfen Furniture Ltd should build its own factory in Country G? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the factory would control cost and quality [k], because it removes the 12% rise costing about $850,000 a year and the 6% fault rate from the current single supplier [app], letting Willowfen set standards for its 95 retailers and keep the 4 years of reduced business taxes [an]. However, it would strain finances and focus [k], because $3.9 million is over three times the $1.1 million annual profit and 85 local workers must be recruited and trained abroad [app], and if Country G demand shifts, the factory cost may never be recouped [an]. Overall, Willowfen should build the Country G factory [eval], because the $850,000 annual saving, better quality and 4-year tax reduction outweigh the $3.9 million outlay over time [eval].

knowledge_max_2: owning production removes supplier mark-ups and improves quality control
a factory abroad is costly and carries execution risk
application_max_2: 12% rise adds about $850,000 a year; 6% of units faulty from the current supplier
$3.9 million cost vs $1.1 million annual profit
4 years of reduced business taxes on the new factory
analysis_max_2: removing the $850,000 rise and faults protects margins and the 95 retailer relationships
$3.9 million is about 3.5 times annual profit, so a slow payback strains liquidity and execution must succeed
evaluation_max_2: weighs $850,000 annual saving, quality control and 4-year tax cut against the $3.9 million outlay and 85-worker execution risk — decides for building the factory

scenario_stem:
Nordell Dental Supplies Ltd is a private limited company distributing dental consumables to 90 dental practices. Revenue was $4.6 million and profit $390,000. Current assets are $540,000 (inventories $300,000, cash $75,000); current liabilities $240,000 (payables $190,000, overdraft $50,000).

A 120-practice group offers Nordell exclusive supply worth $1.1 million a year, but needs $120,000 more high-value stock. Priya must choose between accepting using cash reserves or staying with the 90 practices, which pay within 30 days.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: The ability of a business to pay its short-term debts when they fall due, using current assets such as cash and items that can quickly be turned into cash [2].

knowledge_max_2: ability to pay short-term debts when they fall due
relates to current assets that can quickly be turned into cash

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the dental practices use Nordell's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: The 90 dental practices use Nordell's final accounts to judge whether Nordell will remain a reliable supplier [k]; a current ratio of 2.25:1 and an acid test of 1.0:1 (computed from $540,000 current assets less $300,000 inventories) show Nordell can cover its short-term bills and keep supplying implants and composites [app]. Use 2: The practices use final accounts to judge Nordell's staying power for emergency resupply and warranty support [k]; revenue of $4.6 million and profit of $390,000 show a substantial, profitable distributor likely to honour after-sales commitments [app].

knowledge_max_2: customers use accounts to judge reliability of supply (going concern)
customers use accounts to judge after-sales and warranty support
application_max_2: current ratio 2.25:1; acid test 1.0:1 derived from current assets $540,000 and inventories $300,000

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the government uses Nordell's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: The government uses final accounts to check that Nordell pays the correct corporation tax [k]; the $390,000 profit on $4.6 million revenue lets the tax authority verify the assessed tax and chase any shortfall, supporting public services [app][an]. Use 2: The government uses final accounts to assess whether Nordell is a safe public-sector supplier [k]; with current assets of $540,000 comfortably above current liabilities of $240,000, the accounts signal a stable business to keep in healthcare supply chains [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: government uses accounts to verify and collect taxes due
government uses accounts to assess businesses as employers or public-sector suppliers
application_max_2: current assets $540,000 against current liabilities $240,000; acid test 1.0:1
analysis_max_2: the profit figure is the base for the corporation tax assessment, so verification protects revenue
comfortable cover of liabilities makes Nordell a low-risk supplier for public contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should accept the 120-practice group contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The group contract would transform Nordell's scale [k]; $1.1 million a year on top of $4.6 million revenue would lift it by almost a quarter and secure exclusive supply to 120 practices [app][an]. However, buying about $120,000 more high-value implants with cash would cut the acid test sharply [k]; inventories would rise from $300,000 to $420,000 against current liabilities of $240,000, so the acid test would fall from 1.0:1 to 0.5:1, leaving thin cover if the overdraft of $50,000 is called in [app][an]. Overall, Priya should accept the group contract only with staged stock deliveries or supplier credit for the extra $120,000 [eval], because the exclusive $1.1 million deal could entrench Nordell in the market, provided she does not fund it entirely from cash and strain supply to the 90 existing practices [eval].

knowledge_max_2: the exclusive $1.1 million contract would transform scale
extra stock funded in cash would halve the acid test
application_max_2: $1.1 million contract against revenue of $4.6 million; 120-practice group vs 90 practices
inventories would rise from $300,000 to $420,000; acid test falls from 1.0:1 to 0.5:1; overdraft $50,000; liabilities $240,000
analysis_max_2: exclusive supply could entrench Nordell and add almost a quarter to revenue
halving the acid test leaves little room if suppliers tighten terms or the overdraft is called
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to accept only with supplier credit or staged deliveries, weighing market gain against cash risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Aldercombe Footwear Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing leather shoes in Country X, employing 75 workers to make 85,000 pairs a year with $5,200,000 revenue. Its best-seller retails at $65, above the $58 price of Country F rivals.

A 22% tariff now puts those imports at about $71 at the border. The tariff is temporary, reviewed after 3 years, and some ministers warn protection breeds inefficiency. Directors must choose between $1,100,000 in new lasting machines to cut costs or relying on the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: Any government measure that restricts international trade, such as a tariff or quota [2].

knowledge_max_2: A government measure restricting international trade

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the 22% tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Removes price undercutting [k], as imported rivals from Country F will now retail at about $71, above Aldercombe's $65 price [app]. Benefit 2: Higher sales volumes [k], as price-sensitive shoppers shift to the domestic 85,000 pairs Aldercombe can supply with 75 workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises import prices so domestic goods win on price
Domestic firms gain market share / higher sales volumes
application_max_2: Country F imports now about $71 vs Aldercombe's $65
Capacity of 85,000 pairs a year with 75 workers

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of relying on the tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd's success.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Complacency risk [k], as shelter from competition may let inefficient working practices persist [app], weakening the firm before the government reviews the tariff after 3 years [an]. Drawback 2: Reduced consumer choice may shrink the market [k], as shoppers face higher prices and fewer imported styles [app], cutting total footwear demand in Country X and Aldercombe's own sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: Protection reduces the incentive to improve efficiency
Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice
application_max_2: Tariff review after 3 years; inefficient practices may persist
Imported styles cost about $71, above Aldercombe's $65
analysis_max_2: Firm weakened / uncompetitive once the review happens
Total footwear demand falls / firm's own sales reduced

questions.question_text: Do you think the 22% import tariff is likely to benefit Aldercombe Footwear Ltd in the long run? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The 22% tariff lifts Aldercombe Footwear Ltd above Country F imports, which now retail at about $71 against Aldercombe's $65 [app], lifting orders and protecting $5,200,000 revenue and 75 jobs in the short term [an]; tariffs are designed to protect domestic producers from cheaper foreign competition [k]. However, shelter can breed inefficiency, letting firms delay cutting costs [k]; the tariff is temporary, facing a review after 3 years [app], so Aldercombe could struggle if protection ends while its costs stay high [an]. Overall, the tariff will benefit Aldercombe in the long run only if it invests the $1,100,000 in new lasting machines during the 3-year protection [eval], because protection will expire and competition from Country F imports will return [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Tariffs protect domestic producers from foreign competition
Protection can breed inefficiency / delay cost-cutting
application_max_2: $71 Country F imports vs $65 price; $5,200,000 revenue; 75 jobs
Tariff temporary with review after 3 years; $1,100,000 machine investment
analysis_max_2: Short-term protection of orders, revenue and employment
Competitiveness lost after the review if costs stay high
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement on long-term benefit
Recognises conditions (investment) for tariff to bring lasting gains

scenario_stem: Thistleby Apiaries is a partnership of two beekeepers in New Zealand. It sells honey in glass jars to 14 independent farm shops and earns $96,000 revenue a year from 1,600 jars at $60 each. Bought-in jars and wax cost $31,000, while wages and transport come to $38,000 a year. The partners are considering a second extraction line costing $24,000 to raise output by 30%.

questions.question_text: Define 'partnership'.
questions.model_answer: A business owned by two or more people who share the capital, profits and losses, and who each have unlimited liability [2].

knowledge_max_2: Owners share capital, profits and losses

questions.question_text: Calculate the added value of Thistleby Apiaries.
questions.model_answer: Added value = revenue minus the cost of bought-in materials = $96,000 - $31,000 = $65,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Added value = revenue minus cost of bought-in materials

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the partners of Thistleby Apiaries of operating as a partnership rather than as sole traders.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: More capital can be raised [k], because two beekeepers can each put in savings, so Thistleby Apiaries could afford the $24,000 extraction line more easily than one owner [app], and the cost and risk are shared between them [an].

Point 2: Shared workload and specialist skills [k], as one partner can manage the 14 independent farm shops while the other handles production of 1,600 jars [app], so decisions are better and illness or holidays can be covered [an].

knowledge_max_2: Work and skills can be shared between owners
application_max_2: Two owners could fund part of the $24,000 line
One partner manages the 14 farm shops, the other makes 1,600 jars
analysis_max_2: Risk and cost of expansion are spread, so each owner risks less
Cover for illness and better decisions raise the chance of survival

questions.question_text: Do you think the partners should invest $24,000 in the second extraction line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The extra line could raise output by 30%, taking sales from 1,600 jars towards 2,080 jars at $60 each [app], which would help cover the $38,000 wages and transport bill and lift profit above the current level [an].

Against: $24,000 is a large commitment for a business with $96,000 revenue, and demand from only 14 farm shops may not absorb a 30% rise in output [app], leaving idle capacity and a shared debt to repay [an].

Conclusion: The investment is only justified if the farm shops have already agreed to take the extra jars, because otherwise the risk of unsold stock outweighs the possible gain.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement on whether the $24,000 line should be bought
Conclusion weighed against the risk of unused capacity
analysis_max_2: 30% extra output could add sales at $60 a jar
Only 14 farm shops may not buy the extra 480 jars

scenario_stem: Cranbourne Bindery is a private limited company in Italy that restores and rebinds old books. Last year it earned $180,000 from 900 binding jobs at $200 each, plus $20,000 from selling handmade paper. It employs 11 bookbinders and buys leather and thread from a tannery in the primary sector. The owner is deciding whether to open a repair workshop for walk-in customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'secondary sector'.
questions.model_answer: The part of the economy that turns raw materials into manufactured goods, such as the binding work done by Cranbourne Bindery [2].

knowledge_max_2: Businesses that manufacture or process raw materials
Output is a finished or semi-finished product

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage of Cranbourne Bindery's total revenue that comes from selling handmade paper.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage share = part / total revenue x 100

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the tertiary sector has grown in Italy.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Rising incomes [k], so households in Italy buy more services such as book repairs rather than replacing goods [app], which is why Cranbourne Bindery can consider a walk-in repair workshop [an].

Point 2: Greater specialisation [k], as firms contract out tasks like book restoration instead of employing staff to do them [app], creating demand for the 900 binding jobs the company already completes each year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher incomes raise spending on services
Specialisation and outsourcing create service jobs
application_max_2: Italy households can pay for repairs
Cranbourne Bindery already completes 900 binding jobs a year
analysis_max_2: Service demand grows as people prefer repair to replacement
Outsourcing gives specialist firms a larger market

questions.question_text: Do you think Cranbourne Bindery should open the walk-in repair workshop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A workshop would sell repairs directly to local people [app], adding a third income stream beside the $180,000 from binding and $20,000 from paper and reducing reliance on business orders [an].

Against: The company has only 11 bookbinders, so staff would be pulled away from the 900 contract jobs [app], and rent and tools for a shop could cost more than the extra trade it attracts [an].

Conclusion: Opening the workshop is worthwhile only if extra staff are hired; otherwise the loss of contract capacity and the fixed cost of a shop make the move too risky for a firm with $200,000 revenue.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement on opening the walk-in workshop
Conclusion balances extra income against lost contract work
analysis_max_2: A shop adds direct sales and diversifies income
11 bookbinders cannot serve both contracts and walk-ins

scenario_stem: Tamarisk Foods is a private limited company in United Kingdom making chilled soups. It sold 2.4 million cartons last year in a market where total sales were 16 million cartons. Revenue reached $3,600,000 and profit after tax was $270,000. Its two rivals each hold about 20% of the market. The directors want to raise market share to 18% by cutting prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'market share'.
questions.model_answer: The proportion of total sales in a market held by one business, usually expressed as a percentage; Tamarisk Foods currently holds 15% [2].

knowledge_max_2: Share of total market sales held by a business
Expressed as a percentage of the market

questions.question_text: Calculate Tamarisk Foods' current market share.
questions.model_answer: Market share = (2.4 million / 16 million) x 100 = 15% [2].

knowledge_max_2: Market share = business sales / total market sales x 100

questions.question_text: Explain two possible benefits to Tamarisk Foods of increasing its market share to 18%.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Greater bargaining power with retailers [k], since selling more of the 16 million cartons gives Tamarisk Foods a stronger position to negotiate shelf space and prices [app], which can protect its $3,600,000 revenue [an].

Point 2: Lower average costs through economies of scale [k], as spreading fixed costs over a larger output reduces cost per carton [app], so the $270,000 profit could grow even if prices are cut to win share [an].

knowledge_max_2: More market power over retailers and rivals
Economies of scale lower unit costs
application_max_2: Fixed costs spread over more cartons
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs can offset price cuts and raise profit

questions.question_text: Do you think cutting prices is the best way for Tamarisk Foods to reach an 18% market share? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A lower price is a quick way to attract buyers in a crowded market [app], and moving from 15% to 18% of 16 million cartons would add 480,000 cartons of sales [an], which could use spare capacity and spread fixed costs.

Against: Price cuts squeeze the margin on every carton, so profit could fall below $270,000 even with higher volume [app], and the two rivals holding 20% each may simply match the cut, leaving shares unchanged and all three worse off [an].

Conclusion: Cutting prices alone is not the best route; Tamarisk Foods should invest in promotion and product quality, using a modest price cut only if rivals are unlikely to retaliate.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement on price cutting as the best route to 18%
Conclusion recommends a mix of methods
analysis_max_2: Extra 480,000 cartons could spread fixed costs
Rival retaliation and thinner margins threaten profit

scenario_stem: Oakhanger Metals is a sole trader run by Marek Oakhanger, recycling scrap metal in Poland. Last year the business made $210,000 revenue and $46,000 profit, but a customer is suing it for $75,000 after a damaged delivery. Marek has no business insurance and personal savings of $52,000. He is thinking of converting to a private limited company.

questions.question_text: Define 'sole trader'.
questions.model_answer: A business owned and run by one person, who keeps all profits but has unlimited liability for its debts [2].

knowledge_max_2: One owner who runs the business
Owner keeps profit and bears unlimited liability

questions.question_text: Calculate the maximum amount of the $75,000 claim that could be taken from Marek's personal savings.
questions.model_answer: As a sole trader Marek has unlimited liability, so the whole $52,000 of personal savings could be taken; the remaining $23,000 of the claim would still be owed [2].

knowledge_max_2: Unlimited liability means personal assets can be used
application_max_2: All $52,000 of savings could be taken

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Marek of converting Oakhanger Metals into a private limited company.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Limited liability [k], so if the $75,000 claim succeeds only the company's assets are at risk and Marek's $52,000 savings are protected [app], which reduces the personal risk of trading [an].

Point 2: Easier access to finance [k], because a company can sell shares to new investors and borrow in its own name [app], giving funds to expand the recycling yard beyond its current $210,000 revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Limited liability protects the owner's personal assets
A company can raise capital by selling shares
application_max_2: $52,000 of savings would be protected from the claim
Share capital could fund yard expansion
analysis_max_2: Lower personal risk makes expansion less dangerous
Extra finance allows growth beyond $210,000 revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Marek should convert Oakhanger Metals into a private limited company? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Conversion would separate his personal savings from business debts [app], so a claim like the $75,000 one would no longer threaten the $52,000 he owns, and he could bring in shareholders to fund growth [an].

Against: A company must publish accounts and file returns, adding cost and losing privacy, and Marek would have to share the $46,000 profit with other shareholders [app], while the paperwork takes time away from running the yard [an].

Conclusion: He should convert, because protection from a claim larger than his savings matters more than the extra administration for a business of this size.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement for or against conversion
Conclusion weighs liability protection against administration
analysis_max_2: Sharing $46,000 profit and publishing accounts are drawbacks

scenario_stem: Highmarsh Digital is a private limited company in Estonia providing website design to 240 small clients. Revenue is $1,250,000 a year and profit $180,000. The two shareholders want higher dividends, but the 18 staff have asked for a 6% pay rise and two senior designers have been offered jobs by a rival. The board must choose between paying a dividend and funding the pay rise, and it meets next week.

questions.question_text: Define 'dividend'.
questions.model_answer: A share of a company's profit paid to its shareholders, usually based on the number of shares they own [2].

knowledge_max_2: Part of profit paid to shareholders

questions.question_text: Calculate the dividend each shareholder would receive if the whole $180,000 profit were paid out and the two shareholders own equal shares.
questions.model_answer: $180,000 divided between two equal shareholders = $90,000 each [2].

knowledge_max_2: Dividend = total distributed profit / number of equal shares

questions.question_text: Explain two possible conflicts between the shareholders and the employees of Highmarsh Digital.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Profit versus pay [k], because a 6% pay rise for 18 staff would reduce the $180,000 profit available as dividends [app], so owners wanting income clash with staff wanting higher wages [an].

Point 2: Spending on retention versus returns [k], as two senior designers have rival job offers and matching them costs money that shareholders would rather receive [app], so the board must trade off staff stability against shareholder income [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shareholders want profit; employees want pay
Retaining key staff costs money that reduces returns
application_max_2: A 6% rise for 18 staff cuts the $180,000 profit
Two senior designers have rival offers
analysis_max_2: Higher wages reduce the dividend paid to owners
Losing designers could damage service to 240 clients

questions.question_text: Do you think Highmarsh Digital should pay the $180,000 profit out as dividends rather than fund a 6% pay rise? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Shareholders put up the capital and expect a return, so paying $90,000 each rewards them and encourages future investment [app], which keeps the company able to fund growth [an].

Against: The 18 staff have asked for a 6% rise and two senior designers already have rival offers, so losing them could damage service to 240 clients [app], cutting revenue from $1,250,000 and reducing future profit for shareholders too [an].

Conclusion: A full payout is unwise; the board should fund the 6% rise for key staff and pay a smaller dividend, because protecting $1,250,000 of revenue matters more than a one-off gain.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement on dividends versus pay rise
Conclusion recommends a compromise
analysis_max_2: Dividends reward capital and attract investment

scenario_stem: Marrowgate Bakery is a sole trader in Denmark baking sourdough loaves for 22 cafes. It makes 1,900 loaves a week at a price of $3.20 and pays $2,100 a week for flour, yeast and packaging. The owner works 62 hours a week and has turned down a salaried job paying $44,000 a year. She is considering buying a second oven for $18,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'opportunity cost'.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity cost is the benefit given up when one option is chosen instead of the next best alternative, such as the $44,000 salary the owner forgoes [2].

knowledge_max_2: The next best alternative given up
The benefit lost from choosing one option

questions.question_text: Calculate the weekly added value of Marrowgate Bakery.
questions.model_answer: Weekly revenue = 1,900 loaves x $3.20 = $6,080; added value = $6,080 - $2,100 = $3,980 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Added value = sales revenue minus bought-in costs

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Marrowgate Bakery adds value to the flour and yeast it buys.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Processing the ingredients into fresh loaves [k], turning flour and yeast costing $2,100 a week into 1,900 loaves sold at $3.20 each [app], so the finished bread is worth far more than the inputs [an].

Point 2: Convenience and regular supply for 22 cafes [k], as baking early each morning and delivering daily saves customers the time and cost of making bread themselves [app], which supports the price charged and keeps repeat orders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Processing raw materials into a finished product
Service and convenience add value for customers
analysis_max_2: Finished loaves sell for more than the input cost
Reliability supports price and repeat custom

questions.question_text: Do you think the owner of Marrowgate Bakery should buy the second oven for $18,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A second oven would raise weekly output beyond 1,900 loaves [app], and with sales already at $6,080 a week the extra bread could add profit and make the 62-hour week more manageable [an].

Against: The $18,000 cost equals about 4.5 weeks of current revenue [app], and demand from 22 cafes may be met already, so the owner risks taking on debt while giving up the $44,000 salary for no extra return [an].

Conclusion: She should buy the oven only after securing orders from new cafes, because extra capacity without extra customers would add cost without raising added value.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement on buying the second oven
Conclusion sets a condition of new orders
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity could raise output and profit
$18,000 outlay and limited cafe demand create risk

scenario_stem: Quillfen Ceramics is a partnership in Vietnam that extracts clay from its own pit and makes garden pots. Sales rose from $340,000 to $425,000 over two years, and the six partners share profit equally. Clay extraction now provides 20% of revenue, down from 35% two years ago. The partners are debating whether to stop extraction and buy clay from a supplier.

questions.question_text: Define 'primary sector'.
questions.model_answer: The primary sector is the part of the economy that extracts raw materials from the land or sea, such as the clay Quillfen Ceramics digs from its pit [2].

knowledge_max_2: Examples include mining, farming, fishing and quarrying

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage increase in Quillfen Ceramics' sales over the two years.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage change = change / original figure x 100

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the importance of the primary sector has fallen in Vietnam.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Cheaper imports of raw materials [k], so Vietnam firms can buy clay from abroad instead of digging it, which is why Quillfen Ceramics now takes only 20% of revenue from its pit [app], reducing demand for domestic extraction [an].

Point 2: Rising incomes and demand for services [k], as households spend more on tertiary activities rather than basic materials [app], so jobs and output shift away from the 35% share extraction once held [an].

knowledge_max_2: Competition from cheaper imported raw materials
Higher incomes shift demand towards services
application_max_2: Clay extraction now only 20% of revenue, down from 35%
Vietnam consumers spend more on services
analysis_max_2: Import competition reduces domestic primary output
Service demand draws labour and capital away from extraction

questions.question_text: Do you think the partners should stop extracting their own clay and buy it from a supplier instead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Buying clay would remove the cost of running a pit and free the partners to concentrate on potting, where sales have already grown to $425,000 [app], and a supplier would give consistent quality [an].

Against: Extraction still provides 20% of revenue [app], and buying clay adds a supplier's margin to every pot, so costs rise and the partners lose control over quality and delivery [an].

Conclusion: They should keep extracting while it earns 20% of revenue, because the security of supply and the saved cost outweigh the convenience of outsourcing.

evaluation_max_2: Judgement on stopping extraction
Conclusion supports keeping the pit for now
analysis_max_2: 20% of revenue and supply control would be lost

scenario_stem: Vellacott Printworks is a private limited company in Netherlands printing leaflets and posters for 380 business customers. Revenue is $940,000 a year and profit $120,000, and it employs 34 staff. A larger rival, Halden Press, has offered $600,000 to take over the business. One shareholder wants to retire. The three shareholders must decide whether to accept the offer.

questions.question_text: Define 'takeover'.
questions.model_answer: A takeover is when one business buys a controlling interest in another, such as Halden Press buying Vellacott Printworks [2].

knowledge_max_2: The buyer gains control of the target business

questions.question_text: Calculate how many years of Vellacott Printworks' profit are represented by Halden Press's $600,000 offer.

knowledge_max_2: Offer divided by annual profit gives years of profit

questions.question_text: Explain two possible benefits to Vellacott Printworks of accepting the takeover by Halden Press.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Economies of scale [k], as combining with Halden Press could spread the cost of printing equipment over a larger output [app], lowering the cost of each leaflet for the 380 customers [an].

Point 2: Financial security for the shareholders [k], because the $600,000 offer gives each of the three owners a certain return instead of relying on a $120,000 profit that may fall in a recession [app], reducing their risk [an].

knowledge_max_2: Merging can create economies of scale
A takeover gives shareholders a certain payment
application_max_2: Shared equipment costs across a larger customer base

questions.question_text: Do you think the shareholders should accept Halden Press's $600,000 offer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:

Point 1: New staff learn shop layout and delivery routes quickly [k], so they can pick the correct organic produce and avoid wrong orders [app], which addresses the rising complaints [an].

Point 2: Induction explains health, safety and food hygiene rules [k], reducing the risk of accidents and spoilage in the farm shop [app], and helps new employees feel welcome, which may lower the 18% turnover [an].

analysis_max_2: New staff feel welcome and stay

questions.question_text: Do you think Ormside Organics should pay $11,500 for the external customer service course? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Rising complaints about wrong orders suggest staff need better customer service and order-checking skills. An external course brings expertise the sole trader does not have, and $11,500 could be recovered if complaints fall and the 18% turnover improves, since replacing staff and refunding orders is costly.

Against: The owner employs only 38 staff, so $11,500 is a large sum and may train people who then leave. Much of the problem may be poor induction or unclear picking procedures, which could be fixed internally at far less cost; the $2,250 already spent on training 5 new staff shows a cheaper route exists.

Conclusion: Improve induction and order checks first, then send only the delivery team on a short external course, because a full $11,500 programme is too broad for the stated problem.

questions.question_text: Define 'oral communication'.

knowledge_max_2: Face to face, telephone or video call

questions.question_text: Calculate the total monthly mobile phone cost for the 22 tuners at Pinnock Piano Tuning.

questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Details can be misheard [k], such as a customer's address or the type of piano, when a booking is given by phone [app], so a tuner may travel to the wrong home and lose a fee [an].

Point 2: There is no written record [k], so if a customer disputes a booking or a tuner forgets a message, the partnership cannot check what was agreed [app], which damages its reputation across 6 regions [an].

analysis_max_2: Tuner travels to the wrong home

questions.question_text: Do you think Pinnock Piano Tuning should buy the scheduling app at $8,900? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: An app would give every booking a written record, send addresses and piano details directly to the tuner's phone, and reduce misheard instructions. With 22 tuners across 6 regions and 1 vacancy, better scheduling could fit more jobs into each day and cut the $572 monthly phone bill.

Against: $8,900 is a large cost for a partnership of 22 staff, and older tuners may find the app difficult. Customers may still prefer to phone, so staff would have to enter bookings twice, and the money could pay for a part-time administrator instead.

scenario_stem: Quarrydale Quilts is a private limited company making bedding in Pakistan. Its 70 staff each lose 6 days a year through absence, and average daily pay is $88. questions.question_text: Define 'bonus'.
questions.model_answer: A bonus is an additional payment made to an employee on top of their normal wage or salary, usually as a reward for good performance or meeting a target [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of absence at Quarrydale Quilts.
questions.model_answer: Absence cost = 70 staff x 6 days x $88 = $36,960 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two financial motivators Quarrydale Quilts could use to improve attendance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: An attendance bonus [k], paid to staff who complete a month without absence [app], would reward reliable machinists and could cut the 6 days lost each year and the $36,960 absence cost [an].

Point 2: A production bonus for meeting bedding targets [k], so the 70 staff gain when output is high [app], encourages cover when 4 posts are vacant and makes absence feel costly to the team [an].

application_max_2: Reward for a month without absence
Bonus when bedding targets are met

questions.question_text: Do you think Quarrydale Quilts should introduce profit-sharing costing $52,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Profit-sharing would give all 70 staff a stake in the company's success and may improve attendance and teamwork, since absence directly reduces output and profit. At $52,000 it is more than the $36,960 absence cost, but it could also reduce the 20% turnover and help fill 4 vacancies, producing savings beyond attendance.

Against: Profit depends on sales and material costs that machinists cannot control, so the scheme may not feel like a reward for their effort. The $52,000 is a large fixed commitment and could be resented in a year with low profit, whereas a smaller attendance bonus targets the actual problem more directly.

Conclusion: Start with an attendance bonus and consider profit-sharing later, because the company needs to solve absence before adding a company-wide reward.

scenario_stem: Rookwood Restoration is a partnership repairing historic buildings in Croatia. It employs 45 craftspeople, with 3 project managers each supervising one group of 15 on different sites. questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Organising resources [k], so each manager plans labour, scaffold and materials for a site [app], which keeps restoration work on schedule despite 3 vacant posts [an].

Point 2: Controlling and monitoring quality [k], because historic buildings need careful matching of stone and timber [app], so managers check standards and correct mistakes before clients inspect the work [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Rookwood Restoration should appoint an operations director at $78,000? Justify your answer.

Against: The partnership is small, and $78,000 is a large salary that would reduce partners' profit. The 3 project managers already have narrow spans of 15, so coordination may be handled through a weekly meeting instead, which costs far less.

scenario_stem: Sedgefield Saddlery is a sole trader making riding saddles in Uruguay. It employs 16 staff, including 2 apprentices who attend a college day release costing $7,200 a year in total. questions.model_answer: Off-the-job training is training that takes place away from the normal workplace, such as at a college or training centre, so the employee is not producing output while learning [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the average annual college cost per apprentice at Sedgefield Saddlery.
questions.model_answer: Cost per apprentice = $7,200 / 2 apprentices = $3,600 each [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Sedgefield Saddlery of off-the-job training for its apprentices.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Apprentices learn up-to-date saddle-making theory and leather science [k], which a small workshop may not teach [app], so they bring new techniques back and improve the quality of riding saddles [an].

application_max_2: Leather science not taught in the workshop

questions.question_text: Do you think Sedgefield Saddlery should end college day release and train the apprentices only in the workshop? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Thornby Tiles is a private limited company making wall tiles in Vietnam. It employs 112 staff across 2 factories, and a survey found that 25% did not understand the new quality instructions. Labour turnover is 21%, absence averages 6 days per employee and 7 posts are vacant. Managers may appoint a communications officer at $41,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'internal communication'.
questions.model_answer: Internal communication is the exchange of information between people within a business, such as between managers and staff or between different departments [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate how many staff did not understand the quality instructions at Thornby Tiles.
questions.model_answer: Staff who did not understand = 25% of 112 = 28 employees [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Thornby Tiles could reduce internal communication barriers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Use face-to-face briefings with demonstrations [k], so the 28 staff who misunderstood can see how to check tile quality [app], and questions can be answered immediately [an].

Point 2: Ask supervisors to confirm understanding [k], rather than assuming a notice has been read [app], so feedback reaches managers and the 7 vacancies do not spread confusion across shifts [an].

application_max_2: Shows how to check tile quality
Supervisors confirm the message was understood

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornby Tiles should appoint a communications officer at $41,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A specialist could coordinate messages across 2 factories, produce clear quality instructions and train supervisors to check understanding. With 28 staff misreading the last instruction and 21% turnover, better communication could reduce errors and help fill 7 vacancies, making the $41,000 worthwhile.

Against: Communication is a core management responsibility, and appointing an officer may let supervisors neglect it. The salary is high for a tile manufacturer, and the money could pay for short briefing training for all supervisors or translated visual instructions, which address the immediate problem.

Conclusion: Train supervisors first and appoint the officer only if misunderstandings continue, because a single person cannot replace daily contact between managers and staff.

scenario_stem: Ulverston Umbrellas is a private limited company making rainwear in Bangladesh. It employs 58 staff; 12 left last year, absence averages 5 days per employee and 7 posts are vacant. Staff say pay is below the local average and that supervisors rarely explain changes. Directors may raise pay by 5% at a cost of $63,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'piece rate'.
questions.model_answer: A piece rate is a payment system in which an employee is paid a fixed amount for each unit of output they produce, rather than a fixed wage per hour [2].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed amount for each unit produced
Pay depends on output, not hours

questions.question_text: Calculate the labour turnover of Ulverston Umbrellas.
questions.model_answer: Labour turnover = 12 leavers / 58 staff x 100 = 20.7% [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why high labour turnover is a problem for Ulverston Umbrellas.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Recruitment and training costs rise [k], because each of the 12 leavers must be replaced and taught to make rainwear [app], diverting money from materials and equipment [an].

Point 2: Output and quality suffer [k], since 7 posts are already vacant and new staff are slower [app], so delivery of umbrellas may be delayed and customers may go elsewhere [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ulverston Umbrellas should raise pay by 5% at a cost of $63,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Pay is below the local average, which helps explain why 12 staff left and 7 posts remain vacant. A 5% rise could make the company more competitive, reduce the 20.7% turnover and cut the cost of repeated recruitment; $63,000 may be recovered if production and quality improve.

Against: Staff also complain that supervisors rarely explain changes, so pay alone may not solve the problem. The $63,000 is a permanent increase that reduces profit, and the company could instead improve communication and offer a smaller bonus tied to attendance and quality.

Conclusion: Raise pay modestly and train supervisors to communicate, because the evidence points to both pay and management as causes of turnover.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $63,000 against recruitment savings

scenario_stem: Vantryck Vending is a private limited company supplying vending machines in South Africa.
