questions.question_text: Define 'decentralised organisation'.
questions.model_answer: A decentralised organisation is one in which decision-making authority is spread to regional or local managers rather than being concentrated at the top [2].

knowledge_max_2: Decisions not concentrated at the top

questions.question_text: Calculate the average span of control of the 6 regional managers at Vantryck Vending.
questions.model_answer: Average span = 84 staff / 6 regional managers = 14 subordinates each [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Vantryck Vending of decentralising price decisions.
questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Managers feel trusted and gain responsibility [k], which raises motivation and prepares them for senior roles [app], helping reduce the 18% turnover and fill 5 vacancies [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Vantryck Vending should let regional managers set local prices despite losing $33,000 in discounts? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Whitlock Watch Repairs is a partnership repairing luxury watches in Singapore. It employs 26 staff, has 4 vacancies and spends $1,900 on recruitment for each watchmaker appointed. questions.question_text: Define 'curriculum vitae'.

questions.question_text: Do you think Whitlock Watch Repairs should use paid work trials instead of interviews? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Yarrowfield Yoghurt is a private limited company making Greek yoghurt in Bulgaria. Labour turnover is 19%, absence averages 5 days per employee and 6 posts are vacant. Managers may introduce paid daily handovers costing $9,600 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'informal communication'.
questions.model_answer: Informal communication is the exchange of information between employees outside official channels, such as a quick conversation or gossip at a shift changeover [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate how many staff missed the last production briefing at Yarrowfield Yoghurt.

questions.question_text: Do you think Yarrowfield Yoghurt should introduce paid daily handovers costing $9,600? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Do you think Birkdale Boats should remove a management layer to save $44,000? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Do you think Cragside Cranes should advertise the supervisor post externally at $12,800? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Do you think Denholm Drum Works should hold face-to-face safety briefings at $15,700 a year? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Do you think Eastmoor Engraving should introduce job rotation at $6,800 a year? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Pennock Garments is a private limited company in Vietnam employing 120 machinists who produce 3,600 shirts a week. Managers are considering paying $25,000 to a consultant who would time each operation and set standard times.

questions.question_text: Define 'scientific management'.

scenario_stem: Mvuli Blooms Ltd is a private limited company near Nairobi, Kenya, growing roses for export with 150 workers. Labour turnover is 22% a year, the absence rate is 8.4% and 11 packing posts are vacant. Pickers are paid a fixed daily wage regardless of output, and supervisors rarely thank them. Directors are deciding whether to move to piece-rate pay or to spend $54,000 a year on team bonuses and public recognition.

questions.question_text: Define 'labour turnover'.
questions.model_answer: Labour turnover is the proportion of a business workforce that leaves and is replaced over a period, usually a year [k]. At Mvuli Blooms Ltd it is 22% of 150 workers, so about 33 people leave and are replaced each year [app].

knowledge_max_2: The rate at which employees leave a business and are replaced

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the fixed daily wage and lack of thanks may demotivate pickers at Mvuli Blooms Ltd.

Point 2: Maslow's esteem needs are satisfied by recognition and praise [k], but supervisors rarely thank the 150 workers [app], so pickers feel their effort is invisible, morale falls and more of them join the 33 who leave each year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Taylor: pay should be linked to output
application_max_2: Fixed daily wage whatever the number of stems cut
analysis_max_2: No reward for extra effort so output stays low

questions.question_text: Do you think Mvuli Blooms Ltd should move to piece-rate pay rather than spend $54,000 on team bonuses and public recognition? Justify your answer.

Against: A piece rate encourages speed over care, and bruised or short stems may be rejected by export buyers, so quality could fall even as output rises [app]; Herzberg also treats extra pay as a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction but does not create lasting motivation [an].

Conclusion: Team bonuses and recognition are the better choice, because $360 per worker on top of wages is unlikely to change behaviour on its own, whereas public praise and shared targets meet the esteem needs behind the 22% turnover and protect the quality that export customers demand.

Conclusion weighs $360 per worker against esteem needs and export quality

scenario_stem: Sallowfield Pottery is a partnership in New Zealand making mugs and bowls, selling 5,400 pieces a year at $18 through craft fairs and one website. Sales have stalled and the partners want to know whether to add a $45 dinner set. They can read 1,900 online customer reviews free of charge or interview 80 past buyers at $12 each.

questions.question_text: Define 'market research'.
questions.model_answer: Market research is the process of collecting and analysing information about customers, competitors and the market [2]. Sallowfield needs it to judge whether a $45 dinner set would sell.

knowledge_max_2: Gathering information about customers and the market
The information is analysed to support decisions

questions.question_text: Calculate the cost of interviewing 80 past buyers at $12 each.
questions.model_answer: 80 buyers x $12 = $960 [2]. Working shown: 80 x 12 = 960.

knowledge_max_2: Cost = number of buyers x cost per interview

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks to Sallowfield of relying on the 1,900 online reviews.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Reviewers are not a fair sample of all buyers [k]. People who write reviews often feel strongly, either very pleased or very angry, so their comments may not reflect the 5,400 pieces sold a year through craft fairs [an]. The partners could misjudge demand for a $45 dinner set.

Point 2: Reviews say little about price or buying intentions [k]. A customer may praise the glaze on a mug but never mention whether they would pay $45 for a dinner set, so the reviews answer a different question from the one Sallowfield is asking [an]. Relying on them is free but weak evidence.

knowledge_max_2: Reviewers are self-selected and may be unrepresentative
Reviews rarely answer questions about price or future buying
application_max_2: 5,400 pieces sold at $18 through craft fairs
analysis_max_2: Strong-view bias distorts the picture of demand
Comments do not test willingness to pay $45

questions.question_text: Do you think Sallowfield should interview the 80 past buyers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Past buyers already know the pottery, so 80 interviews can test whether they would pay $45 for a dinner set. At $960 the cost is modest, and direct questions reveal price limits that online reviews never mention.

Against: $960 is a real cost when sales have stalled, and 80 buyers may not represent customers who shop only at craft fairs. Interviews also take time, and people may overstate what they would buy.

Conclusion: The interviews are worth doing because they ask the right question about a $45 set, but Sallowfield should keep the sample spread across both craft fair and website buyers before committing to production.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $960 cost against evidence on willingness to pay $45
Judges direct interviews against free but weak reviews
analysis_max_2: Existing buyers can judge the new dinner set
Stated intentions may overstate actual purchases

scenario_stem: Morwenna Seaweed Snacks Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand making 180,000 packs of seaweed crisps a year, sold at $1.65, with revenue of $297,000. At a food fair the company can question 150 visitors using random sampling from the entrance list or quota sampling of 50 visitors from each of three age bands.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Quota sampling selects a set number of people from each chosen group until the sample is complete [2]. Morwenna would question 50 visitors from each of three age bands.

knowledge_max_2: A fixed number is selected from each group
Selection continues until each quota is filled

questions.question_text: Calculate Morwenna's revenue from 180,000 packs if the price is cut to $1.40.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue = packs sold x price per pack

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Morwenna of quota sampling at the food fair.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quotas make sure each age band is covered [k]. With 50 visitors from each of three age bands, Morwenna can see whether teenagers or older shoppers prefer seaweed crisps, which matters for a product selling 180,000 packs a year [an]. A random sample of 150 might miss a whole group.

Point 2: Quotas are quick to fill at a busy event [k]. Researchers simply approach visitors until each group reaches 50, so the company gets 150 usable responses during the fair without needing the entrance list [an]. That speed keeps research costs low at a launch event.

knowledge_max_2: Quotas guarantee coverage of each chosen group
Quota samples are quick and simple to collect
application_max_2: 50 visitors from each of three age bands
150 visitors questioned at the food fair
analysis_max_2: Age comparisons show which group likes the snack
Fast fieldwork keeps costs low and fits the event

questions.question_text: Do you think Morwenna should use random sampling instead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Random selection from the entrance list gives every visitor an equal chance, so the 150 responses would reflect the fair's visitors and avoid researchers choosing people who look approachable.

Against: A random sample of 150 may contain very few teenagers, so the company could miss the age group that buys most snacks. Quotas of 50 from each of three age bands guarantee a comparison, which is the purpose of the research.

Conclusion: Quota sampling is better here because Morwenna needs views from each age band rather than a perfect cross-section, but the company should record visitors' ages honestly so the quotas are not filled with the easiest people to approach.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs unbiased selection against guaranteed age coverage
Judges the method by the purpose of comparing age bands
analysis_max_2: Random selection represents visitors but may miss teenagers
Quotas guarantee enough responses in every age band

scenario_stem: Bluewharf Ferries Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand carrying 1,100,000 passengers a year on two routes, with revenue of $6,600,000. Passenger complaints about the onboard café rose to 640 last year. Managers can pay a researcher $2,400 to make 12 mystery-shopping trips or survey 900 passengers online for $700.

questions.question_text: Define 'interview'.
questions.model_answer: An interview is a conversation in which a researcher asks a customer questions to collect their views, either face to face or by telephone [2]. Bluewharf could interview passengers about the café.

knowledge_max_2: A spoken conversation to collect opinions
It can be face to face or by telephone

questions.question_text: Calculate the cost per mystery-shopping trip if 12 trips cost $2,400.
questions.model_answer: $2,400 / 12 trips = $200 per trip [2]. Working shown: 2400 / 12 = 200.

knowledge_max_2: Cost per trip = total cost / number of trips

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Bluewharf of mystery shopping rather than a passenger survey.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Mystery shoppers see the service as it really is [k]. A researcher posing as a passenger records waiting times, cleanliness and food quality on the two routes, which explains why complaints about the café reached 640 [an]. A survey only reports what passengers remember.

Point 2: It tests staff behaviour, not just customer opinion [k]. Crew do not know they are being observed, so the report shows whether service standards are actually followed and identifies training needs [an]. Twelve trips at $200 each also cost less than many large surveys.

knowledge_max_2: Mystery shopping records actual service quality
It observes staff behaviour without their knowledge
analysis_max_2: Observed service explains the complaint figures
Findings identify specific staff training needs

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluewharf should pay for the mystery shopping? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The problem is the service itself, so 12 mystery trips at $200 each show exactly what passengers experience, including waiting times and food quality. At $2,400 the cost is small against revenue of $6,600,000.

Against: Twelve trips cannot cover 1,100,000 passengers, and one researcher's view may be personal. The online survey costs only $700 and reaches 900 passengers, giving a much broader picture of the café complaints.

Conclusion: The mystery shopping is worth $2,400 because it identifies the cause of the 640 complaints, but Bluewharf should run the cheap online survey as well to measure how widely passengers share the same experience.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $2,400 against revenue and $700 for the survey
Judges cause-finding against measuring scale
analysis_max_2: Mystery trips reveal specific service failures
900 online responses show how widespread the problem is

scenario_stem: Rookwood Garden Centre is a sole trader in New Zealand, taking $540,000 a year from 60,000 customers. The owner wants to test a $6.50 delivery charge and plans to question shoppers. A random sample of 250 customers from the loyalty list would cost $1,100, while quota sampling of 250 shoppers at the tills costs nothing but excludes online buyers.

questions.question_text: Define 'questionnaire'.
questions.model_answer: A questionnaire is a set of written questions used to collect information from customers [2]. Rookwood would use one to test reactions to a $6.50 delivery charge.

knowledge_max_2: Used to gather data from a number of people

questions.question_text: Calculate the average annual spend per customer at Rookwood.
questions.model_answer: $540,000 / 60,000 customers = $9.00 per customer a year [2]. Working shown: 540,000 / 60,000 = 9.

knowledge_max_2: Average spend = annual revenue / number of customers

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the quota sample at Rookwood Garden Centre's tills might give misleading results.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It leaves out online buyers completely [k]. Rookwood's sample would contain only shoppers who visit the store, so the views of customers who order online are missing even though they would pay the $6.50 delivery charge [an]. The result would overstate resistance to delivery charges.

Point 2: Researchers tend to approach shoppers who look willing [k]. Filling quotas at the tills depends on who is available and friendly, not on chance, so the 250 shoppers may not reflect all 60,000 customers [an]. A free sample is therefore cheaper but less trustworthy.

knowledge_max_2: The sample excludes a whole group of customers
Quota selection depends on researcher choice, not chance
analysis_max_2: Missing online buyers skew views on a delivery charge
Researcher choice makes the sample unrepresentative

questions.question_text: Do you think Rookwood should pay $1,100 for the random sample? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A random sample of 250 customers from the loyalty list includes online buyers, so it tests the $6.50 delivery charge on the people who would actually pay it. Spending $1,100 avoids a decision based only on shoppers at the tills.

Against: $1,100 is a noticeable cost for a sole trader, and the loyalty list may still miss customers who shop occasionally. The free till sample could be adequate if the owner only wants a quick reaction.

Conclusion: The $1,100 is worth paying because the delivery charge mainly affects online buyers, who are excluded from the till sample. Rookwood should then compare the responses with its existing online order figures.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,100 against free but biased till sampling
Judges coverage of online buyers as the decisive factor
analysis_max_2: The loyalty list reaches customers who would pay delivery
A biased sample risks pricing the service wrongly

scenario_stem: Sandhaven Surf School is a partnership in New Zealand teaching 1,800 lessons a year at $38, with revenue of $68,400. It wants to add paddleboard hire. Local council data shows 24,000 visitors tried paddleboarding last summer, but the data covers a 40km coast. A survey of 200 past students would cost $750.

questions.question_text: Define 'sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Sampling is selecting a small group of people from a larger population so that their views can represent the whole group [2]. Sandhaven would sample 200 past students from all its customers.

knowledge_max_2: Choosing a small group from the whole population
The group is used to represent the wider population

questions.question_text: Calculate the cost per student surveyed if 200 past students cost $750.
questions.model_answer: $750 / 200 students = $3.75 each [2]. Working shown: 750 / 200 = 3.75.

knowledge_max_2: Cost per student = total cost / number surveyed

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the council data may not help Sandhaven decide.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The data covers a 40km coast, not Sandhaven's own beach [k]. It shows 24,000 visitors tried paddleboarding, but those people may be spread across many resorts, so the number available to Sandhaven could be small [an].

Point 2: The data records people who tried the activity, not what they paid or whether they would hire [k]. Sandhaven needs to know if customers would pay for hire alongside its 1,800 lessons, which the council count cannot show [an]. Using it alone could lead to buying boards nobody hires.

knowledge_max_2: The data's area is wider than the business's market
Numbers of participants do not show willingness to pay
analysis_max_2: Visitors spread along the coast are not Sandhaven's customers
Trial numbers say nothing about hire demand or price

questions.question_text: Do you think Sandhaven should carry out the survey of 200 past students? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Past students already know the school and can say whether they would hire a paddleboard, so 200 responses at $3.75 each give direct evidence for the new service. $750 is small against the cost of buying a fleet of boards.

Against: Past students may say yes to be helpful and never hire, and the school's customers are surfers rather than paddleboarders. The council's 24,000 figure at least proves the activity is popular locally.

Conclusion: The survey is worth doing because it tests willingness to pay, but Sandhaven should combine it with the council data and hire a few boards for one season before buying a full fleet.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $750 against the cost of unsold board capacity
Judges stated interest against proven local popularity
analysis_max_2: Existing students can judge hire demand
Polite yes answers may not turn into bookings

scenario_stem: Bramblecote Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand launching a 12-piece luxury box that costs $4.20 a box to make. It expects to make 60,000 boxes in the first year. Directors can launch at $14.50 to recover $180,000 of development costs quickly, or at $9.90 to win shelf space in 320 shops.

questions.question_text: Define 'price skimming'.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming sets a high launch price to earn a large profit from early buyers before lowering it later [2]. Launching the luxury box at $14.50 would be price skimming.

knowledge_max_2: A high price is set when a product is launched
The price is reduced later to attract more buyers

questions.question_text: Calculate the profit per box at a launch price of $14.50 when each box costs $4.20 to make.

knowledge_max_2: Profit per box = price - cost per box

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Bramblecote of launching at $9.90 rather than $14.50.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A lower price is more likely to win space in 320 shops [k]. Retailers prefer a box that shoppers will try, and $9.90 sits closer to everyday gift prices than $14.50, so more stores may stock it [an]. Wider distribution supports the 60,000 boxes planned.

Point 2: It builds sales volume quickly, which matters for a new brand [k]. At $9.90 more customers will try the chocolates, so Bramblecote can win repeat buyers before rivals copy the product [an]. Even with a smaller margin per box, higher volume helps cover the $180,000 development cost.

knowledge_max_2: A lower price helps gain retailer shelf space
Volume sales build awareness for a new brand
analysis_max_2: Retailers prefer products shoppers will try
Higher volume spreads the $180,000 development cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblecote should launch at $14.50? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: At $14.50 each box earns $10.30, so 60,000 boxes would contribute $618,000, enough to recover the $180,000 development cost quickly. A high price also signals luxury, which suits a 12-piece gift box.

Against: $14.50 may keep the product out of 320 shops and discourage trial, and rivals can copy a luxury box quickly. If volume falls well below 60,000, the high price will not cover costs.

Conclusion: Launching at $14.50 is defensible only as a short skimming phase. Bramblecote should start high to recover development spending, then cut towards $9.90 within a few months to win shelf space.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $10.30 margin against lost shelf space and trial
Judges skimming as a short phase before a lower price
analysis_max_2: High price limits distribution and invites copying

scenario_stem: Gorsefield Outdoor Clothing is a partnership in New Zealand making waterproof jackets that cost $46 to produce, sold at $130 through 22 specialist shops that take a 45% margin. Output is 9,000 jackets a year. The partners can sell directly online at $112, keeping the margin, but would need $70,000 of stock and a website.

questions.question_text: Define 'distribution channel'.
questions.model_answer: A distribution channel is the route a product takes from the producer to the final customer [2]. Gorsefield now uses 22 specialist shops as its distribution channel.

knowledge_max_2: The path a product follows from producer to customer
It may involve wholesalers, retailers or direct selling

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue Gorsefield receives from one jacket sold at $130 when the shop keeps a 45% margin.
questions.model_answer: Gorsefield keeps 55% of $130 [1]. $130 x 0.55 = $71.50 per jacket [1].

knowledge_max_2: Producer receives retail price minus the retailer's margin

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Gorsefield of selling directly online rather than through specialist shops.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Gorsefield would keep the whole selling price instead of losing a 45% margin [k]. At $112 online it receives $40.50 more per jacket than the $71.50 it gets from a shop selling at $130, so each of the 9,000 jackets earns more [an].

Point 2: Direct selling gives the partners control of the customer relationship [k]. They can collect emails, learn which sizes sell and promote new jackets themselves, rather than depending on 22 shops to push the brand [an]. That information supports better stock decisions.

knowledge_max_2: Direct selling removes the retailer's margin
The producer controls customer data and promotion
application_max_2: 22 specialist shops and 9,000 jackets a year
analysis_max_2: Keeping the margin raises revenue per jacket
Customer data improves stock and promotion decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Gorsefield should start selling online? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Online sales at $112 keep the full margin instead of the $71.50 left by shops, and the partners would own the customer relationship. The extra revenue per jacket could repay the $70,000 stock and website cost within a season.

Against: $70,000 is a heavy outlay for a partnership, and stock held for online orders may sit unsold. The 22 specialist shops also give advice and let buyers try jackets on, and they may drop the brand if Gorsefield competes with them.

Conclusion: Gorsefield should sell online but keep the specialist shops, using a slightly higher online price to protect retailers. Cutting off 22 shops to chase margin would remove the fitting service that sells a $130 jacket.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $40.50 extra margin against $70,000 outlay
Judges direct selling against losing specialist retailers
analysis_max_2: Higher margin per jacket speeds up repayment
Shops provide fitting advice that supports the premium price

scenario_stem: Pinfold Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand producing 4,500,000 litres of milk a year at $0.62 a litre. It wants to launch a lactose-free range and has a $220,000 promotion budget. Directors can spend it on 40 radio adverts at $2,400 each or on 90,000 money-off coupons at $1.10 each plus free in-store tastings.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Sales promotion is a short-term incentive, such as money-off coupons or free samples, used to encourage customers to buy [2]. Pinfold's 90,000 money-off coupons would be a sales promotion.

knowledge_max_2: Examples include coupons, samples or competitions

questions.question_text: Calculate the cost of the 40 radio adverts at $2,400 each and how much of the $220,000 budget remains.

knowledge_max_2: Advertising cost = number of adverts x price each
Remaining budget = total budget - advertising cost

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Pinfold of using money-off coupons rather than radio adverts.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Coupons encourage shoppers to try the lactose-free milk immediately [k]. A discount at the shelf lowers the risk of buying an unfamiliar product, so customers who might never respond to a radio advert are tempted to put a carton in the basket [an]. Trial is important for a new range.

Point 2: It is easier to see whether the promotion worked [k]. Pinfold can count how many of the 90,000 coupons are redeemed, whereas a radio advert's effect on sales is hard to separate from other influences [an]. Coupons also reach shoppers at the moment of choice.

knowledge_max_2: Coupons lower the risk of trying a new product
Redemptions give measurable evidence of response
application_max_2: Launch of a lactose-free milk range
analysis_max_2: Shelf discounts convert browsing shoppers into triers
Redemption counts show whether the spend worked

questions.question_text: Do you think Pinfold should spend the budget on the radio adverts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Radio can explain what lactose-free milk is to a wide audience, which coupons cannot do on their own. The 40 adverts cost $96,000, leaving $124,000 for other activity, and repeated mentions build awareness before shoppers reach the shelf.

Against: Radio reaches many people who never buy lactose-free milk, and Pinfold cannot tell which sales came from the adverts. Coupons and tastings put the product in shoppers' hands, which is more persuasive for a new range.

Conclusion: Radio alone is the weaker choice. Pinfold should use the $96,000 of adverts only to support a coupon and tasting campaign, because trial at the shelf is what converts a curious shopper into a repeat buyer.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs broad awareness against targeted trial
Judges radio as support for, not a substitute for, coupons
analysis_max_2: $96,000 of adverts leaves $124,000 for other promotion
Tastings and coupons generate measurable first purchases

scenario_stem: Wexley Printworks is a sole trader in New Zealand printing wedding stationery, with 1,400 orders a year at an average $95, giving revenue of $133,000. Orders have fallen 18% in two years as couples design cards online. The owner can add personalised printed photo albums at $140 each or spend $12,000 on a new website and social media adverts.

questions.question_text: Define 'product life cycle'.
questions.model_answer: The product life cycle shows the stages a product passes through from launch to decline: development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline [2]. Wexley's wedding stationery is in decline as orders fall.

knowledge_max_2: The stages a product passes through over its life
Stages run from introduction through growth and maturity to decline

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in orders if Wexley's 1,400 orders drop by 18%.
questions.model_answer: 1,400 x 0.18 = 252 orders lost [1]. Orders would fall to 1,400 - 252 = 1,148 [1].

knowledge_max_2: Fall = original orders x percentage fall

questions.question_text: Explain two ways adding photo albums might extend the life of Wexley's product range.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Albums create a second sale from the same customer [k]. A couple buying stationery at $95 could return after the wedding for a $140 album, so each wedding generates more revenue and the range stays relevant for longer [an].

Point 2: Albums compete with the online design services that caused the 18% fall [k]. Couples may design a card on a screen but still want a printed album they can hold, so Wexley offers something the websites handle less well [an]. That gives the business a new reason for customers to visit.

knowledge_max_2: New products can generate repeat sales from existing customers
Products that rivals cannot easily copy extend a range
application_max_2: Stationery orders average $95, albums sell at $140
Orders have fallen 18% in two years
analysis_max_2: A second purchase raises revenue per wedding
Printed albums answer a gap left by online design tools

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexley Printworks should spend $12,000 on the website and social media adverts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The 18% fall happened because couples now design cards online, so the answer must be online visibility. A modern website and social media adverts put Wexley in front of those couples and can showcase albums and stationery together.

Against: $12,000 is a heavy spend for a sole trader earning $133,000, and social media adverts compete with thousands of other wedding suppliers. The money might earn more from photo albums, which add revenue without chasing online traffic.

Conclusion: The website is the better use of the money because the cause of the decline is online competition, but Wexley should photograph the new albums for the site so the investment sells a product that online card tools cannot match.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $12,000 spend against the online cause of decline
Judges digital promotion against adding album revenue
analysis_max_2: The fall is digital, so online visibility addresses the cause
Albums give the website a product rivals cannot copy

scenario_stem: Cobbleford Shoes Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand making leather boots that cost $38 a pair to produce, selling 26,000 pairs a year at $72. A rival has cut its boots to $64. Directors can set a cost-plus price with a 50% mark-up, or match the rival at $64 and spend $95,000 on a quality campaign.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing adds a fixed percentage mark-up to the cost of producing a product to set its selling price [2]. A 50% mark-up on Cobbleford's $38 cost would give a price of $57.

knowledge_max_2: A mark-up is added to the unit cost
The mark-up is usually a set percentage

questions.question_text: Calculate the cost-plus price using a $38 cost per pair and a 50% mark-up.
Explain two reasons why matching the rival at $64 might reduce Cobbleford's profits.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The contribution from each pair falls [k]. At $72 Cobbleford keeps $34 above its $38 cost, but at $64 it keeps only $26, which is $8 less on every one of the 26,000 pairs [an]. Unless sales rise sharply, total profit drops.

Point 2: The quality campaign adds $95,000 of costs [k]. Matching a lower price while spending $95,000 means Cobbleford must sell far more boots just to stand still, and the campaign may not persuade shoppers who are comparing prices [an]. Profit could fall on both price and cost.

knowledge_max_2: A lower price reduces contribution per unit
analysis_max_2: $8 less per pair across 26,000 pairs cuts profit
Higher fixed costs demand much greater volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Cobbleford should use cost-plus pricing at $57? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A $57 price guarantees a $19 mark-up on every pair and keeps Cobbleford comfortably below the rival at $64, which could increase the 26,000 pairs sold without any campaign spending.

Against: $57 is $15 below the current $72 and would give up profit on customers who already pay $72. Pricing from cost ignores what shoppers think the boots are worth and may signal lower quality beside the rival's $64 boots.

Conclusion: Cost-plus at $57 is the wrong choice. It undercuts a rival Cobbleford could match and gives away margin; the company should hold $72 and defend the price with quality rather than set it from a formula.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs guaranteed $19 mark-up against $15 given away
Judges cost-based pricing against customer perceptions of quality
analysis_max_2: $57 forgoes profit on buyers willing to pay $72
Cost-plus ignores demand and may signal lower quality

scenario_stem: Willowby Hampers is a partnership in New Zealand packing 7,200 food hampers a year at $85 each, with revenue of $612,000. Most orders arrive in December. The partners have $30,000 to promote a new summer picnic hamper and can sponsor a local food festival for $30,000 or pay a specialist $30,000 for six months of social media content.

questions.question_text: Define 'sponsorship'.
questions.model_answer: Sponsorship is when a business pays to be linked with an event or person in return for having its name promoted [2]. Willowby would pay $30,000 to be linked with the local food festival.

knowledge_max_2: A business pays to support an event or person
The business gains publicity or brand association

questions.question_text: Calculate Willowby's average monthly revenue if $612,000 were spread evenly across 12 months.
Explain two advantages to Willowby of sponsoring the food festival.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The festival puts the hampers in front of people who already enjoy local food [k]. Visitors can see and taste the summer picnic hamper, so the $30,000 reaches an audience interested in exactly that kind of product [an].

Point 2: Being named as a sponsor builds local credibility [k]. A partnership selling 7,200 hampers a year gains trust when the festival advertises its support, and local press may mention the name at no extra cost [an]. That reputation helps during the quiet summer months, when orders are far below December levels.

knowledge_max_2: Sponsorship puts products before a relevant audience
Being associated with an event builds credibility and publicity
application_max_2: $30,000 sponsorship of a local food festival
analysis_max_2: Tasting reaches buyers interested in local food
Local press coverage adds free promotion and trust

questions.question_text: Do you think Willowby should spend the $30,000 on social media content instead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Six months of content keeps hampers visible through the quiet summer, when a single festival weekend is quickly forgotten. Hampers are visual products, and photographs and short videos can reach buyers far beyond one town for the same $30,000.

Against: Social media is crowded and needs consistent skill to work, while a festival offers direct tasting and local goodwill. The partners can also see and count every visitor who stops at their stall.

Conclusion: The social media content is the better spend because Willowby needs interest across the whole summer, not one weekend, and the hampers photograph well. A small unpaid stall at the festival could then support the campaign.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs six months of reach against one weekend of tasting
Judges visual product appeal against local goodwill
analysis_max_2: Content covers the quiet summer months
Social media reaches buyers beyond the festival town

scenario_stem: Thornleigh Garden Rooms Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand building insulated garden offices, with 34 installations last year at $31,000 each and revenue of $1,054,000. Customers wait 14 weeks, and 9 have cancelled. Directors can add a second four-person team costing $180,000 a year or open a $60,000 showroom to attract more enquiries.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing mix'.
questions.model_answer: The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion that a business uses to sell its products [2]. Thornleigh's mix includes a $31,000 garden office sold from a showroom.

knowledge_max_2: The four elements: product, price, place and promotion
They are combined to meet customer needs and sell the product

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue lost from the 9 cancelled installations at $31,000 each.
questions.model_answer: 9 cancellations x $31,000 = $279,000 of lost revenue [2]. Working shown: 9 x 31,000 = 279,000.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = cancellations x price per installation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a 14-week waiting time may damage Thornleigh Garden Rooms.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Long waits cause cancellations and lost revenue [k]. Nine customers have already cancelled, which at $31,000 each means $279,000 of work lost, and customers who stay may demand discounts to accept the delay [an].

Point 2: Bad word of mouth damages a premium brand [k]. A buyer paying $31,000 for a garden office tells neighbours about the experience, so a 14-week wait and cancelled orders can put off the next customer before the showroom even sees them [an]. Repeat and recommended business then falls.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs new-segment reach against immediate trial
Recognises taste drives repeat purchase

scenario_stem: Corrimore Bike Hire is a partnership with three shops that hires out 1,900 bikes a month at $18 a day to tourists. A hotel group has offered a contract for 500 corporate guests a month at $26 a day, including delivery and helmets. Taking it would mean moving staff and bikes away from the tourist trade that provides most of Corrimore's revenue.

questions.question_text: Define 'mass market'.
questions.model_answer: A mass market is a large market in which products are sold to many different types of customer [2]. Corrimore hires bikes to tourists at all three of its shops rather than to one specialised group.

knowledge_max_2: Products aimed at a wide range of buyers

questions.question_text: Calculate Corrimore's monthly revenue from 1,900 hires at $18 a day.
Explain two reasons why Corrimore might target the mass tourist market rather than the hotel contract.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Tourists are many and varied, so a single $18 daily price and three convenient shops can fill 1,900 hires without special delivery or helmet fitting [an]. That keeps operations simple for a partnership with limited staff.

Point 2: The tourist trade is spread across the season, while 500 corporate guests a month would depend on one hotel group. If that contract ended, Corrimore would have moved bikes and staff away from customers who can still be served every day [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large customer group supports simple, standard service
application_max_2: 500 corporate guests at $26 from one hotel group
analysis_max_2: Dependence on one contract raises risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Corrimore should accept the hotel contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The contract pays $26 a day, $8 more than the tourist rate, and 500 guaranteed hires would add $13,000 a month. Corporate guests also hire on weekdays when tourist demand is quieter, so the contract could use idle bikes rather than take trade from tourists.

Against: Delivery, helmets and staff would raise costs, and 500 bikes taken from the tourist trade could lose $18 hires that are already reliable. Putting a fifth of monthly capacity behind one hotel group leaves Corrimore exposed if the contract is not renewed.

Conclusion: Accept the contract only for bikes that are idle on weekdays, keeping the three shops fully stocked for tourists; that gains the $26 rate without sacrificing the core trade.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $26 with $18 and uses spare weekday capacity
Notes dependence on a single hotel group
analysis_max_2: Costs of delivery and helmets reduce the gain

scenario_stem: Mirevale Garden Centre is a private limited company with 1,200 loyalty-card customers. It is testing later opening hours and selected 80 customers at random from the card list; 52 said they would shop after 7pm. Extending hours would cost $2,400 a month in wages and lighting. The manager must decide whether to extend or to survey 300 customers at a cost of $1,900 first.

questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected for the sample [2]. Mirevale picked 80 customers at random from its 1,200 loyalty-card holders.

knowledge_max_2: Every member has an equal chance of selection
Sample drawn without bias from the whole population

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage of the 80 sampled customers who would shop after 7pm.
questions.model_answer: 52 / 80 x 100 = 65% [2]. Working: 52 out of 80 replies.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage = number in favour / sample size x 100

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a random sample of 80 may give Mirevale reliable evidence.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Because every one of the 1,200 card holders had an equal chance of selection, the 80 should include busy workers, retired gardeners and families rather than only the manager's acquaintances [an]. That reduces the risk of a result that reflects one type of customer.

Point 2: A sample of 80 is large enough to show a clear majority, and 65% saying they would shop after 7pm is a margin the manager can act on without asking all 1,200 [an]. The saving in time and cost matters for a single garden centre.

knowledge_max_2: Random selection avoids choosing only convenient customers
A sample can represent a larger population at lower cost
analysis_max_2: Mix of customer types reduces bias
Clear majority allows a decision without a census

questions.question_text: Do you think Mirevale should extend its opening hours now or spend $1,900 on a survey of 300 customers first? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The random sample already shows 65% support, a clear majority, and extending costs $2,400 a month, which can be reviewed after one month if trade disappoints. Waiting for another survey delays a decision that could win sales from rivals who close at 6pm.

Against: Saying they would shop after 7pm is not the same as doing it, and 80 replies still leave uncertainty about how many would spend enough to cover $2,400. A survey of 300 costing $1,900 could ask about basket size and preferred days, making the decision far safer.

Conclusion: Extend for a four-week trial rather than paying $1,900 for more opinions; real takings will show demand more reliably than another survey.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs a clear 65% majority against stated rather than actual behaviour
Prefers a cheap trial over another survey
analysis_max_2: Larger survey could test spending, not just intention

scenario_stem: Dunvane Furniture is a partnership that makes sofas and sells 340 a year at $1,150 through two own showrooms. An online furniture retailer has offered to stock the range but takes 25% commission on every sale. Alternatively, Dunvane could open a third showroom costing $140,000, which the partners would fund from retained profit. They must choose one route before the spring buying season.

questions.question_text: Define 'distribution channel'.
questions.model_answer: A distribution channel is the route a product takes from the producer to the final customer [2]. Dunvane currently sells through its own showrooms and is considering an online retailer as a second route.

knowledge_max_2: Route taken by a product to reach the customer
May involve wholesalers, retailers or direct selling

questions.question_text: Calculate the commission Dunvane would pay on 340 sofas at $1,150 if the online retailer takes 25%.

knowledge_max_2: Commission = sales value x percentage rate

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Dunvane should consider when choosing its distribution channel.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The cost of each route matters. Selling through the online retailer costs $97,750 in commission on 340 sofas, while a third showroom needs $140,000 upfront, so the partners must compare a repeated charge with a large one-off investment [an].

Point 2: Control over how sofas are presented is also important. Own showrooms let customers sit on the sofa and meet staff, whereas an online retailer decides the photographs and may discount, weakening the $1,150 price [an].

knowledge_max_2: Degree of control over presentation and price
analysis_max_2: Compares variable commission with fixed investment
Online selling reduces control of price and display

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunvane should sell through the online retailer or open a third showroom? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The online retailer reaches customers far beyond the two showrooms without $140,000 of capital, and 25% commission only arises when a sofa sells. At 340 sofas the $97,750 cost is covered by extra volume, and the partnership keeps its retained profit for stock.

Against: The third showroom keeps the full $1,150 from every sofa and lets buyers try the product, which matters for a high-price purchase. Commission of $97,750 a year is permanent, and an online retailer may demand discounts that damage the brand.

Conclusion: Open the third showroom if the partners can afford it, because control of the buying experience protects the $1,150 price; use the online retailer only as a trial in one region.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $97,750 recurring commission against $140,000 once
Considers brand control for a high-price product
analysis_max_2: Online route adds reach without capital
Own showroom keeps margin and allows trial

scenario_stem: Elmhallow Interiors is a partnership that completes 45 office design projects a year at $3,200 each in Marland. It is considering opening a studio in neighbouring Brenna, where a $18,000 research report suggests demand for 20 projects a year at $4,000. Staff would have to split their time between two countries, and the partners have no contacts in Brenna.

questions.question_text: Define 'target market'.
questions.model_answer: A target market is the specific group of customers a business aims its products and marketing at [2]. Elmhallow's target market would change from Marland offices to include businesses in Brenna.

knowledge_max_2: Chosen by the business for its marketing efforts

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual revenue Elmhallow expects from 20 projects at $4,000.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue = projects x price per project

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why entering Brenna may be risky for Elmhallow Interiors.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The partners have no contacts in Brenna, so winning 20 projects a year depends on an $18,000 report rather than known clients [an]. If the forecast is wrong, the studio's rent and travel costs still have to be paid.

Point 2: Splitting staff between two countries spreads a small team thinly. The 45 projects in Marland at $3,200 already need designers, so travel and different building rules could delay existing work and damage the reputation built at home [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reliance on unfamiliar customers and forecast data
analysis_max_2: Unproven demand leaves fixed costs exposed
Divided staff risk delays to core work

questions.question_text: Do you think Elmhallow should open the studio in Brenna? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Brenna projects pay $4,000 against $3,200 at home, so 20 projects would add $80,000 of revenue at a better rate. Entering early could establish Elmhallow before local designers copy its style, and the $18,000 report is already paid for.

Against: The partners have no contacts, and a forecast is not a contract. Splitting a team that already handles 45 projects risks the reliable $3,200 work, while Brenna rent, travel and unfamiliar regulations could absorb the extra $80,000.

Conclusion: Do not open a studio yet; instead run two or three Brenna projects from Marland to test demand, keeping the fixed costs of a studio out of the risk.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $80,000 potential against disruption to 45 projects
Prefers a low-cost test before fixed investment
analysis_max_2: Higher price per project raises revenue
Unfamiliar market and divided staff raise risk

scenario_stem: Dunsterly Home Bakery is a sole trader selling 620 loaves a week at $2.90 from one shop. A rival bakery opened 300 metres away and the owner expects sales to fall by 15% unless she responds. She is considering a loyalty card costing $3,600 a year or cutting the loaf price to $2.50. Her regulars have bought from her for over ten years.

questions.question_text: Define 'customer loyalty'.
questions.model_answer: Customer loyalty is when customers keep buying from the same business because they are satisfied with its products or service [2]. Dunsterly's regulars have bought its loaves for over ten years despite a new rival nearby.

knowledge_max_2: Repeated buying from the same business

questions.question_text: Calculate the weekly revenue Dunsterly would lose if sales fall by 15% from 620 loaves at $2.90.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage fall applied to sales volume
Lost revenue = lost loaves x price

questions.question_text: Explain two ways customer loyalty may help Dunsterly against the new rival.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Loyal customers do not switch on price alone, so ten years of regular buying may protect much of the 620-loaf volume even if the rival charges less [an]. That gives the owner time to respond instead of losing 93 loaves a week immediately.

Point 2: Loyal customers also recommend the shop. In a small catchment a reputation for fresh bread brings new buyers without advertising, which matters because a sole trader cannot match a rival's promotion budget [an].

application_max_2: 620 loaves a week and a rival 300 metres away
Regulars buying for over ten years
analysis_max_2: Retains volume while a response is planned
Word of mouth substitutes for advertising

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunsterly should introduce the loyalty card or cut the loaf price to $2.50? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A loyalty card rewards the regulars who already buy, costs $3,600 a year and protects the $2.90 price. Cutting to $2.50 would reduce revenue on all 620 loaves, effectively paying every customer including those who would never switch.

Against: A 40-cent price cut is immediate and visible to shoppers comparing the two shops, while a loyalty card may take months to change habits. At $2.50 the bakery still earns a margin and keeps its volume, whereas $3,600 is a fixed cost whatever sales do.

Conclusion: Keep the price and launch the loyalty card, because the ten-year regulars are the shop's main defence; a price cut would give away margin without securing their loyalty.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $3,600 fixed cost with a 40-cent cut on all loaves
Judges which response protects the core regulars
analysis_max_2: Price cut is simple and immediate

scenario_stem: Ryehollow Bakery is a private limited company with 3,100 customers and wants to test a breakfast range. Its customer records show 30% are under 35, 45% are 35 to 60 and 25% are over 60. The owner plans a quota sample of 120 customers and will survey people in the shop until each group is filled. A market research agency would charge $2,800 for a random sample of 300.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Quota sampling selects a fixed number of respondents from each identified group so the sample matches the population profile [2]. Ryehollow will survey 120 customers in groups based on its 30-45-25 age profile.

knowledge_max_2: Fixed number chosen from each group
Sample reflects the known structure of the population

questions.question_text: Calculate how many under-35 customers Ryehollow should include in a quota sample of 120 if they are 30% of customers.
questions.model_answer: 30% of 120 = 36 customers [2]. Working: 0.30 x 120 = 36.

knowledge_max_2: Quota = group percentage x sample size

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why quota sampling may suit Ryehollow's breakfast research.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The quotas force the survey to include under-35s, who are only 30% of customers but may be the group most likely to buy breakfast on the way to work [an]. A simple shop survey might otherwise fill up with retired customers who have more time to talk.

Point 2: Quota sampling is cheap and quick because the owner can stand in the shop and fill each group, leaving the $2,800 agency fee for ingredients or promotion [an]. For a small bakery testing a range, speed matters more than a perfect sample frame.

knowledge_max_2: Ensures small but important groups are represented
Cheaper and quicker than agency research
analysis_max_2: Saves money for a small launch

questions.question_text: Do you think Ryehollow should use its own quota sample or pay $2,800 for the agency's random sample of 300? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The quota sample is free, quick and guaranteed to include the under-35 group that matters for breakfast. The owner can ask about price and portion size directly and start baking test batches within a week.

Against: Quota sampling can be biased because the interviewer chooses who to approach, and 120 customers is small. The agency's random sample of 300 would allow proper comparisons between age groups and cost only $2,800, less than the waste from a failed range.

Conclusion: Use the quota sample first to shape the range, then pay for the agency only if the results are close; $2,800 is better spent once the product is nearly right.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs free, fast quota data against a more rigorous sample
Considers the cost of a failed launch
analysis_max_2: Quota guarantees coverage of key groups

scenario_stem: Carrowdore Cider is a partnership producing 8,400 bottles a year at $6.80, sold through farm shops. Sales have been flat and the partners have $7,500 for promotion. They are considering a buy-one-get-one-half-price offer in 20 shops or a radio campaign across the county. A poor harvest has raised apple costs, so every discount now comes straight out of margin.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as discounts, offers or competitions to encourage customers to buy [2]. Carrowdore is considering a buy-one-get-one-half-price offer in 20 farm shops.

knowledge_max_2: Examples include discounts, offers and competitions

questions.question_text: Calculate Carrowdore's annual revenue from 8,400 bottles at $6.80.
Explain two reasons why a sales promotion may increase Carrowdore's sales.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: An offer gives shoppers a reason to choose Carrowdore now rather than another cider on the shelf, so a buy-one-get-one-half-price deal can lift sales in the 20 participating shops quickly [an]. Flat sales suggest the brand is being overlooked rather than rejected.

Point 2: A promotion encourages trial by customers who have never paid $6.80 for a premium bottle. If they enjoy it, some become regular buyers, which matters because 8,400 bottles a year depend on repeat trade through farm shops [an].

analysis_max_2: Immediate lift in a crowded shelf

questions.question_text: Do you think Carrowdore should run the buy-one-get-one-half-price offer or spend $7,500 on radio advertising? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The offer produces an immediate reason to buy and can be measured shop by shop, while radio may be heard by thousands of people who never shop in farm shops. With flat sales, a short offer on 8,400 bottles could clear stock before the next harvest.

Against: Rising apple costs mean a half-price second bottle cuts margin on every pair sold, and shoppers may wait for the next offer instead of paying $6.80. Radio builds the brand over time and reaches the whole county for a fixed $7,500.

Conclusion: Choose radio, because the harvest has already squeezed margin and a discount teaches buyers to expect lower prices; the brand needs reach, not cheaper bottles.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs immediate volume against margin lost on each pair
Considers long-term brand building versus discount habit
analysis_max_2: Offer lifts short-term sales and clears stock
Discounts erode margin and price expectations

scenario_stem: Kittisoe Candles is a private limited company with three lines: 5,200 jar candles a year at $9, 800 gift sets at $24 and 11,000 tealights at $3. Each gift set uses three hours of staff time and the line makes a loss after packaging. The directors meet next week to decide whether to drop gift sets, raise their price or invest in cheaper packaging.

questions.question_text: Define 'product portfolio'.
questions.model_answer: A product portfolio is the full range of products a business sells, often at different prices and stages of popularity [2]. Kittisoe's portfolio contains jar candles, gift sets and tealights at three different prices.

knowledge_max_2: The range of products a business offers
Products may differ in price and market segment

questions.question_text: Calculate Kittisoe's total annual revenue from the three lines.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue for each line = units x price

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Kittisoe should review its product portfolio.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The gift sets use three hours of staff time each and still make a loss, so 2,400 hours a year are tied up in the weakest line [an]. Moving that time to jar candles or tealights could raise profit without any extra staff.

Point 2: The portfolio is unbalanced. Tealights earn $33,000 but at only $3, while 5,200 jar candles at $9 carry the brand, so the directors need to know which lines justify promotion and shelf space [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shows balance of sales and contribution across lines
application_max_2: 800 gift sets using three hours each
analysis_max_2: Staff time is scarce and could earn more elsewhere
Promotion can be targeted at stronger lines

questions.question_text: Do you think Kittisoe should drop the gift sets? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The line makes a loss even at $24 and absorbs three hours of staff time per set, so dropping it frees 2,400 hours and removes a product that weakens overall profit. The other two lines already produce $79,800 of the $99,000 total.

Against: Gift sets are the highest-priced item at $24 and bring new customers who may later buy jar candles, especially at Christmas. The loss may come from packaging rather than the product, so cheaper packaging could turn the line around without losing its prestige.

Conclusion: Do not drop the line yet; renegotiate packaging and raise the price to $27, keeping the gift set as the brand's premium entry point while removing its loss.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs 2,400 staff hours against the line's role in the brand
Distinguishes packaging cost from product weakness
analysis_max_2: Dropping frees capacity for profitable lines
Gift sets attract new and seasonal buyers

scenario_stem: Vellthorne Garden Rooms is a partnership building 26 garden offices a year at $28,000. The founder designs each model from his own sketches and has never surveyed buyers. Customers keep asking for planning help, insulation and a finish that matches their house, and two rivals now advertise these features. Research with 120 past customers would cost $12,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'market-oriented business'.
questions.model_answer: A market-oriented business designs its products around the needs and wants of customers rather than around what it finds easiest to make [2]. Vellthorne has designed from the founder's sketches instead of asking buyers about planning help and insulation.

questions.question_text: Calculate Vellthorne's annual revenue from 26 garden offices at $28,000.
Explain two benefits to Vellthorne of becoming more market-oriented.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Customers are asking for planning help and insulation, so building those into the design would make each $28,000 office easier to sell and reduce the need for discounts [an]. At 26 offices a year, even one extra sale adds $28,000.

Point 2: Research with 120 past customers could reveal which feature buyers value most, so the $12,000 is spent on changes that win orders rather than on the founder's preferences [an]. It also gives Vellthorne evidence to answer rivals who already advertise these features.

knowledge_max_2: Design matches what customers ask for
Research directs spending to valued features
application_max_2: $28,000 per office and 26 offices a year
120 past customers and a $12,000 research cost
analysis_max_2: Better fit reduces discounting and lifts sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Vellthorne should spend $12,000 on customer research before designing its next model? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Customers already mention planning help, insulation and matching finishes, so structured research can rank those features and show what buyers will pay. $12,000 is less than half the price of one $28,000 office, and a better model could raise sales across all 26.

Against: The founder has run the business for years and the requests are already clear, so $12,000 may simply confirm what he knows. That money could pay for the insulation and planning service directly, giving customers the features now rather than after another design cycle.

Conclusion: Skip the full study and interview 20 recent buyers at almost no cost, then spend the $12,000 on insulation and planning support that customers have already requested.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $12,000 with the value of one office
Notes the requested features are already known
analysis_max_2: Research ranks features and willingness to pay

scenario_stem: Vantorre Cosmetics is a private limited company selling 9,600 lipsticks a month at $12. A survey of 250 users found that 68% thought the colour lasted all day, but a focus group of eight regular buyers said the cases felt cheap and the shades suited only younger customers. Testing a new case would cost $9,400 before production.

questions.question_text: Define 'quantitative data'.
questions.model_answer: Quantitative data is information that can be measured and expressed as numbers, such as a percentage of users [2]. The finding that 68% of 250 users thought the colour lasted all day is quantitative.

knowledge_max_2: Can be counted, measured or compared statistically

questions.question_text: Calculate how many of the 250 surveyed users thought the colour lasted all day.
Explain two reasons why Vantorre should collect both quantitative and qualitative data.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The survey shows that 170 of 250 users were satisfied with colour, which measures how widespread the strength is and allows Vantorre to track changes after a redesign [an]. Numbers alone, however, cannot explain the cheap feel of the case.

Point 2: The focus group explains why eight regular buyers were unhappy, pointing to the case and the shade range rather than the colour [an]. That detail guides the design of a new case, which a percentage could never reveal.

knowledge_max_2: Quantitative data measures scale and allows comparison
Qualitative data explains reasons and feelings
application_max_2: Eight regular buyers criticised case and shades

questions.question_text: Do you think Vantorre should spend $9,400 testing a new case, or commission a national survey of 1,500 users costing $4,800? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The focus group has already identified the case as the problem, so testing a better case turns feedback into a product change that could raise sales of 9,600 lipsticks at $12. A national survey would only confirm opinions Vantorre has already heard.

Against: Eight buyers are too few to justify $9,400, and the shade complaint may matter more than the case. A survey of 1,500 costing $4,800 would show how many of the 9,600 monthly buyers share each concern before money is committed to tooling.

Conclusion: Run the $4,800 survey first, because the case complaint rests on eight people; if a large share agree, the $9,400 tooling spend is then justified.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs a small focus group against a large sample
Sequences spending to reduce risk
analysis_max_2: Case redesign could lift sales at $12
Survey measures how widespread the complaint is

scenario_stem: Stanniford Watches is a partnership that has sold classic watches for 14 years. Sales have fallen from 30,000 units a year to 21,000 at $85 each as smartwatches take younger buyers. The partners have $60,000 and are considering a smart strap that links to a phone, or a cheaper classic watch at $45 aimed at students. Their factory can tool up for only one.

questions.question_text: Define 'product life cycle'.
questions.model_answer: The product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from development and launch to growth, maturity and decline [2]. Stanniford's classic watch has reached decline, with sales falling from 30,000 to 21,000 units.

knowledge_max_2: Sales and profit change at each stage

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage fall in Stanniford's unit sales from 30,000 to 21,000.
Explain two reasons why Stanniford should use an extension strategy for its watches.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The classic watch is in decline, with sales down 30% to 21,000 units, so an extension such as a smart strap could attract younger buyers before the line becomes unprofitable [an]. The factory and brand already exist, which is cheaper than starting again.

Point 2: Extension protects the $85 price and the 14-year reputation. A smart strap keeps the classic face that older customers trust while adding a feature students and younger workers expect [an], so Stanniford need not compete only on price.

knowledge_max_2: Extension uses existing brand and facilities
analysis_max_2: Keeps premium position instead of discounting

questions.question_text: Do you think Stanniford should invest the $60,000 in a smart strap or launch a cheaper watch at $45? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A smart strap adds a reason to buy without abandoning the $85 classic, and the existing factory and 14-year brand support it. It targets the younger buyers who have moved to smartwatches while keeping older customers who value the classic face.

Against: The $45 watch meets younger buyers at a price they can afford and uses simpler technology than a smart strap, so the $60,000 goes further. Stanniford's cost base may suit a cheaper volume product better than a complex electronic accessory.

Conclusion: Choose the smart strap, because a $45 watch competes directly with cheap fashion brands on price, while the strap uses Stanniford's strength in classic design to justify a higher price.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs added feature against a low-price volume strategy
Considers where the brand can avoid direct price competition
analysis_max_2: Strap extends the classic line into a new segment
Cheap watch needs high volume to earn profit

scenario_stem: Dunlough Pottery is a private limited company selling 7,200 mugs a year at $14 and 900 vases at $48 through gift shops. Its $22,000 promotion budget is spent almost entirely on mugs, yet vases carry a much higher margin and are bought by hotels and restaurants. The marketing manager wants to shift most of the budget to vases, while the sales team fears losing mug volume.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing mix'.
questions.model_answer: The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion used to meet the needs of a target market [2]. Dunlough must decide how its $22,000 promotion spend fits with the $14 mug and $48 vase prices.

knowledge_max_2: Four elements: product, price, place, promotion
Combined to satisfy a target market

questions.question_text: Calculate Dunlough's total annual revenue from mugs and vases.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue per line = units x price

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dunlough's marketing mix should be consistent.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Vases at $48 are a premium product for hotels, so promotion should show them in a restaurant setting and place them through hospitality suppliers rather than gift shops [an]. If the same budget advertises cheap mugs, buyers receive a confused picture of quality.

Point 2: Consistency supports the price. A $48 vase needs packaging, display and service that feel expensive, while the $14 mug can sell on value; mixing the two messages weakens both and may force discounts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Each element should support the same positioning
Consistency justifies the price to buyers
analysis_max_2: Wrong channel and message confuse the buyer
Packaging and service must match a premium price

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunlough should shift most of the $22,000 promotion budget to vases? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Vases earn a much higher margin at $48 and sell to hotels and restaurants that buy in larger orders, so each promotion pound can return more than on a $14 mug. The mug market is already served and may only need repeat trade.

Against: Mugs bring $100,800 of the $144,000 revenue and their 7,200 units keep the kiln busy all year. Cutting their promotion could reduce that reliable volume, while hotels buy seasonally and may demand long payment terms.

Conclusion: Split the budget rather than shifting it, giving vases enough to win hotel buyers while keeping mug promotion; losing the 7,200-unit base would leave Dunlough dependent on a few large customers.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs vase margin against mug volume
Notes seasonal hotel demand and payment terms
analysis_max_2: Higher margin per sale rewards promotion

scenario_stem: Ardmere Pet Nutrition is a private limited company selling 4,800 bags of dog food a month at $16. Its loyalty list holds 6,400 customers, and 22% of them own dogs aged over eight. Those owners often ask for joint care and softer kibble, which the current recipe does not provide. A senior-dog range would sell at $24 but needs $8,600 of research and new production equipment.

questions.question_text: Define 'market segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Market segmentation is dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics [2]. Ardmere could segment its 6,400 customers by the age of their dogs and target owners of dogs over eight.

knowledge_max_2: Dividing a market into distinct groups
Groups share similar needs, age or income

questions.question_text: Calculate how many of Ardmere's 6,400 customers own dogs aged over eight.
