knowledge_max_2: Expressed as sales, share or new markets

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue if Ugborough sells 4,000 additional umbrellas at the corporate price of $14.
questions.model_answer: 4,000 x $14 = $56,000 [2]. The 4,000 spare umbrellas would add $56,000 of revenue.

knowledge_max_2: Additional units x price per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why launching a winter range may help Ugborough Umbrellas.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A winter range uses the factory in months when 80% of sales are absent [k]. Insulated umbrellas suit cold, wet weather, so production and sales can continue after September instead of leaving equipment idle [app]. Spreading fixed factory costs over more months lowers the cost of each umbrella [an].

Point 2: Winter sales even out cash flow and employment [k]. The company can keep skilled staff rather than lay them off and rehire, and shop orders arrive when umbrella shelves are otherwise empty [app]. That steadier income makes it easier to pay for materials before the May peak [an].

knowledge_max_2: Uses idle capacity outside the peak season
Smooths cash flow and protects skilled staff
application_max_2: 80% of sales between May and September
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over more months
Steadier cash flow before the summer peak

questions.question_text: Do you think Ugborough Umbrellas should target corporate clients at $14 rather than launch a winter range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Corporate umbrellas sell at $14 against $9.50, adding $4.50 on each unit [k]. If the 4,000 spare units go to businesses, revenue rises by $56,000 with no new machinery and no winter design work [app]. Logo umbrellas also bring repeat orders when firms rebrand or hold events [an].

Against: However, corporate buyers negotiate hard, demand credit and may order only once a year, so $14 may not hold [k]. The logo market is still seasonal around summer events and does nothing for the winter idle period that the directors want to fix [app]. A winter range creates a product the company controls and can sell through its existing shops [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Ugborough should target corporate clients first [eval]. The $14 price and $56,000 of extra revenue use spare capacity immediately, and winter products can follow once that order book is secure [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of corporate clients
Justifies with price and capacity, sequencing the winter range
analysis_max_2: Corporate orders are seasonal and buyer-dominated

scenario_stem: Breage Beds Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 45 beds a month and sells them at $620 each through one showroom. The national bed market is growing by 6% a year, but two chains hold 55% of sales. Directors must decide whether to target hotels with a contract model or keep selling only to households. Household sales have been flat at 45 beds for three years.

questions.question_text: Define 'market share'.
questions.model_answer: Market share is the percentage of total sales in a market held by one business [2]. The two chains hold 55% of bed sales between them, leaving Breage a small share.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage of a market's sales held by one firm
Measured by value or by volume

questions.question_text: Calculate Breage Beds Ltd's monthly revenue from 45 beds at $620 each.
Explain two ways the two national chains may affect Breage Beds Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The chains hold 55% of sales, giving them buying power over suppliers and the ability to advertise nationally [k]. Breage's 45 beds a month cannot match their prices or their showroom presence, so households may visit a chain first [app]. Breage then has to compete on service or design rather than price, which raises its own costs [an].

Point 2: The market is growing 6% a year, but most of that growth may go to the chains [k]. Breage's household sales have been flat at 45 beds, so it is missing the expansion rather than sharing it [app]. Offering hotels a contract model could give it a share of growth that does not depend on winning shoppers from the chains [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large rivals have scale and buying power
Market growth may bypass a small firm
analysis_max_2: Breage must compete on service, raising costs
Hotels offer growth away from the chains

questions.question_text: Do you think Breage Beds Ltd should target hotels rather than continue selling only to households? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Hotels order in batches, so one contract could lift output above the flat 45 beds a month [k]. A contract model also needs less consumer advertising, and repeat orders can be planned in advance [app]. With the market growing 6% but the chains holding 55%, hotels give Breage a route to growth it can control [an].

Against: However, hotels demand trade discounts and long credit, so each bed may earn less than the $620 retail price [k]. A contract model is plain and could weaken the design reputation Breage has built in its showroom [app]. Losing one hotel client would also remove a large share of output, replacing the present dependence on households with a new dependence [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Breage should target hotels [eval]. Household sales have been flat for three years, and contract work uses capacity that the two chains will not surrender, provided Breage keeps a small retail range [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation to enter the hotel segment
Justifies growth but guards against new dependence
analysis_max_2: Contracts lift output beyond flat household sales
Trade discounts reduce the price per bed

scenario_stem: Fowey Fudge is a sole trader in Marland who makes 900 boxes of fudge a month and sells them at $12 a box from one shop. Tourists provide most sales in summer, while regular local customers buy 220 boxes a month. The owner is considering a sugar-free line and must choose between handing out 120 questionnaires in the shop or buying a $250 trade report on sugar-free confectionery.

questions.question_text: Define 'secondary research'.
questions.model_answer: Secondary research uses data that already exists, collected by someone else for a different purpose [2]. The $250 trade report on sugar-free confectionery would be secondary data.

knowledge_max_2: Uses data already collected by others
Gathered for another purpose, then reused

questions.question_text: Calculate Fowey Fudge's monthly revenue from 900 boxes at $12 each.
Explain two limitations for Fowey Fudge of handing out only 120 questionnaires in the shop.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The 120 replies come only from people who already visit the shop [k]. Tourists and local regulars are not the same as shoppers who avoid fudge, so the answers may overstate demand for a sugar-free box [app]. The owner could launch the line on evidence from customers who would have bought anyway [an].

Point 2: A sample of 120 from a shop selling 900 boxes a month is small and easily dominated by a few enthusiastic replies [k]. Shoppers also answer quickly at the counter, so questions about taste and price may be rushed [app]. The results could be unreliable at exactly the point where $12 a box is being tested [an].

knowledge_max_2: Sample only covers existing shop visitors
application_max_2: Tourists and regulars are not all shoppers

questions.question_text: Do you think Fowey Fudge should buy the $250 trade report rather than use the 120 questionnaires? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The report costs only $250 and draws on data from across the confectionery trade [k], so it can show whether sugar-free demand is rising before the owner spends on ingredients and labels [app]. It also needs no staff time at the counter during the busy tourist season [an].

Against: However, the report covers the whole trade, not Fowey's shop or its $12 box [k]. It may be based on supermarket sales, where sugar-free products sell at very different prices and volumes [app]. The 120 questionnaires, though small, ask local customers directly and can include a taste test, which the report cannot [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Fowey should buy the $250 report first [eval]. It is cheap and gives a market-wide view, and the owner can then use a short questionnaire to check local willingness to pay $12 [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Conditional recommendation of the trade report
Sequences secondary then primary research

scenario_stem: Ravensmoor Apiaries is a partnership in Marland that jars 6,400 jars of honey a year and sells them at $7.80 each to farm shops. The partners are launching a premium jar in gift packaging that adds $1.40 to the cost of each jar. They are choosing between keeping the price at $7.80 or charging $9.90. Farm shops take a 30% margin on the retail price.

questions.question_text: Define 'premium pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Premium pricing sets a high price to signal superior quality and appeal to image-conscious customers [2]. Ravensmoor's $9.90 gift jar would be premium priced above its $7.80 standard jar.

knowledge_max_2: High price used to signal quality
Targets buyers who value image or rarity

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage increase in price if Ravensmoor moves from $7.80 to $9.90.

knowledge_max_2: Difference divided by the original price

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Ravensmoor Apiaries might charge $9.90 for the gift jar.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The gift packaging adds $1.40 to the cost of every jar, and $9.90 covers that while keeping a margin [k]. At $7.80 the partners would absorb the extra cost and earn less on each jar than before [app]. The higher price protects the income from 6,400 jars even if gift sales are only part of the total [an].

Point 2: Gift buyers are usually less sensitive to price because they are buying for someone else [k]. A wooden-style presentation at $9.90 looks more suitable as a present than a $7.80 jar, and farm shops taking 30% need a retail price that still leaves them a margin [app]. A premium price also separates the gift jar from the everyday honey sold in the same shop [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher price covers the added packaging cost
Gift buyers are less price sensitive
analysis_max_2: Premium price separates the gift from everyday honey

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensmoor Apiaries should charge $9.90 rather than keep the price at $7.80? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Charging $9.90 adds $2.10 a jar, more than the $1.40 packaging cost, so each gift jar earns $0.70 more than before [k]. Gift buyers expect to pay more, and the price covers the farm shop's 30% margin without squeezing the partners [app]. The 26.9% rise is easier to justify because the jar is visibly different [an].

Against: However, a rise of 26.9% may shock regular customers who buy several jars at $7.80 [k]. Farm shops may refuse to stock a $9.90 honey when cheaper local jars sit beside it, leaving the partners with unsold gift stock [app]. Honey is easy to compare, and a premium price may simply send buyers to the standard jar [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Ravensmoor should charge $9.90 for the gift jar [eval]. The $1.40 packaging must be recovered, gift buyers are less price sensitive, and keeping the standard jar at $7.80 protects regular sales [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of the premium price
Protects the standard product alongside the gift jar

scenario_stem: Jacobstow Juices Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that bottles 240,000 juices a year and sells them at $1.80 each. Three supermarket chains buy 75% of output. Directors are deciding whether to launch their own cold-pressed line at $2.60 a bottle or accept a supermarket own-label contract at $1.35 a bottle for 100,000 extra bottles. Spare capacity is 120,000 bottles a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'product differentiation'.
questions.model_answer: Product differentiation means making a product seem different from and better than rivals' products [2]. A cold-pressed line at $2.60 would be differentiated from Jacobstow's $1.80 standard juice.

knowledge_max_2: Making a product distinct from rivals
Achieved through design, quality or branding

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue from the own-label contract: 100,000 bottles at $1.35 each.
questions.model_answer: 100,000 x $1.35 = $135,000 [2]. That is guaranteed revenue from the extra 100,000 bottles.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why dependence on three supermarket chains may be a weakness for Jacobstow Juices.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Three chains buy 75% of output, so each one can demand lower prices or threaten to delist [k]. Jacobstow would lose most of its sales if one chain moved to a rival supplier, and 240,000 bottles cannot be sold elsewhere quickly [app]. The company would then cut output and spread its fixed costs over fewer bottles [an].

Point 2: Supermarkets control the shelf and the customer data [k]. Jacobstow never learns who drinks its juice or why, so it cannot build a brand that shoppers would ask for by name [app]. Without that brand strength, it has little defence when a chain presses for a lower price [an].

knowledge_max_2: Few buyers hold most of the sales
Supplier loses brand and customer contact
analysis_max_2: Lower output raises cost per bottle
No brand loyalty to protect the price

questions.question_text: Do you think Jacobstow Juices should launch its own cold-pressed line at $2.60 rather than accept the $1.35 own-label contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The cold-pressed line sells at $2.60, nearly double the $1.35 contract price [k]. It uses up to 120,000 bottles of spare capacity and gives Jacobstow a product shoppers can ask for by name [app]. Building a brand reduces the 75% dependence on three chains, which is the real weakness in the business [an].

Against: However, a new premium line needs marketing spending that the contract does not [k]. Demand at $2.60 is unproven, while the own-label contract guarantees $135,000 and uses the spare capacity at once [app]. If the cold-pressed launch fails, Jacobstow has still paid for development and may have damaged its relationship with the chains [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Jacobstow should launch the cold-pressed line [eval]. The contract locks it further into low prices and supermarket control, whereas $2.60 uses spare capacity to build a brand that supports future margins [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of the cold-pressed line
Weighs brand building against guaranteed contract revenue

scenario_stem: Sennen Skincare is a partnership in Marland that fills 2,400 bottles of face oil a year and sells them at $18 each online. Customers aged 18 to 25 provide 65% of sales. A new rival brand aimed at older buyers has entered the market, and the partners are deciding whether to launch an anti-ageing range or extend the existing brand to body oils.

questions.question_text: Define 'market segment'.
questions.model_answer: A market segment is a group of customers with similar needs or characteristics within a larger market [2]. Sennen's 18-to-25 buyers are one segment providing 65% of sales.

knowledge_max_2: Group of buyers with shared characteristics
One part of a larger market

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual revenue from 2,400 bottles at $18 each.
Explain two reasons why Sennen Skincare might extend its brand to body oils.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The existing brand is already known to the 18-to-25 buyers who provide 65% of sales [k]. A body oil sold at $18 can appear beside the face oil on the same website, so customers need no new reason to trust it [app]. The launch cost is lower than starting an unknown brand because the name and design already exist [an].

Point 2: Body oils use similar ingredients and filling equipment [k]. Sennen can add a line without new machinery and spread its fixed costs over more bottles than the current 2,400 [app]. That raises revenue from customers it already has rather than fighting for a new age group [an].

knowledge_max_2: Existing brand recognition carries the new product
Shared inputs and equipment lower launch cost
analysis_max_2: Cheaper than an unknown brand launch

questions.question_text: Do you think Sennen Skincare should launch an anti-ageing range rather than extend the brand to body oils? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The new rival is aimed at older buyers, a segment Sennen does not serve [k]. An anti-ageing range would reduce dependence on the 18-to-25 group that provides 65% of sales and could carry higher prices than $18 [app]. Older buyers also spend more on skincare and are growing as a market [an].

Against: However, Sennen's brand is unknown to older buyers, so it would have to spend on promotion to be noticed [k]. Anti-ageing products raise questions about ingredients and claims that body oils do not, adding cost and risk [app]. Body oils fit the existing 18-to-25 customers and the $18 price point, making a faster return likely [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Sennen should extend the brand to body oils first [eval]. It uses existing customers and equipment with low risk, while an anti-ageing range demands a new audience and a marketing budget the partnership may not have [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of the body-oil extension
Explains why the safer option comes first
analysis_max_2: Anti-ageing range reaches a new segment
Body oils fit existing buyers and price

scenario_stem: Idless Instruments Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 260 laboratory instruments a year and sells them at $1,150 each to schools. It is redesigning its best-selling model and wants teachers' views. Managers can interview 18 science teachers by video call or post a questionnaire to all 900 schools that bought equipment last year. Each instrument costs $780 to build.

questions.question_text: Define 'qualitative data'.
questions.model_answer: Qualitative data is information about opinions, reasons and feelings rather than numbers [2]. The 18 video interviews would show why teachers like or dislike the redesigned model.

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue from 260 instruments at $1,150 each.
questions.model_answer: 260 x $1,150 = $299,000 [2]. This is the revenue from a full year's production.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Idless Instruments of interviewing 18 teachers rather than surveying 900 schools.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Interviews let managers ask follow-up questions and discover why a feature fails [k]. A teacher can demonstrate how the instrument is used in a lesson, which a posted questionnaire cannot capture [app]. That depth is valuable when redesigning a product costing $1,150 [an].

Point 2: Eighteen video calls are quick to arrange and cost far less than printing and posting to 900 schools [k]. The response rate is also close to 100%, whereas a postal survey of 900 may bring only a small fraction of replies [app]. Idless gets usable evidence before the design is fixed rather than waiting weeks for forms [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interviews reveal reasons and allow follow-up
High response rate at low cost
application_max_2: Postal survey of 900 may get few replies
analysis_max_2: Faster, more reliable evidence before redesign

questions.question_text: Do you think Idless Instruments Ltd should interview 18 teachers rather than post a questionnaire to 900 schools? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Eighteen detailed interviews show why teachers value or reject features, which is what a redesign needs [k]. Video calls are cheap and get a reply from almost every teacher approached, unlike a postal survey [app]. The instrument sells at $1,150, so a design mistake would be far more costly than the interviews [an].

Against: However, 18 teachers cannot represent all 900 schools, and the sample may be chosen from convenient contacts [k]. A questionnaire to 900 gives a wider picture of how often the instrument is used and which subjects need it [app]. Numbers from a large sample are easier to defend when managers approve the final design and its $780 build cost [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Idless should interview the 18 teachers [eval]. Depth and a high response rate matter more than breadth at the redesign stage, and a short questionnaire can follow once the main problems are known [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of the interviews
Justifies depth over breadth at design stage

scenario_stem: Oakhurst Kitchens Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that installs 96 kitchens a year at an average price of $9,500. It sells through its own showroom, which costs $84,000 a year to run. Directors are considering selling through five independent retailers instead, which would take a 25% margin on the retail price and widen coverage across the region. Installation costs average $6,300 a kitchen.

questions.question_text: Define 'distribution channel'.
questions.model_answer: A distribution channel is the route a product takes from the producer to the final customer [2]. Oakhurst's showroom is a direct channel, while five retailers would form an indirect channel.

knowledge_max_2: Route from producer to final customer
May be direct or use intermediaries

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue Oakhurst receives per kitchen if a retailer sells at $9,500 and keeps a 25% margin.
questions.model_answer: $9,500 x 0.75 = $7,125 [2]. The retailer keeps $2,375 of the $9,500 retail price.

knowledge_max_2: Retailer margin deducted from the retail price
application_max_2: $7,125 received from a $9,500 kitchen at 25% margin

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why using five independent retailers may increase Oakhurst's sales.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Five retailers widen coverage across the region, so more homeowners see a kitchen than in one showroom [k]. Each retailer already has local customers and a display space, which Oakhurst would otherwise have to fund itself [app]. The showroom's $84,000 annual cost could then support fewer sites while sales grow [an].

Point 2: Retailers can provide installation leads and hold stock of finishes [k]. Customers often visit several shops before buying a $9,500 kitchen, and being in five of them raises the chance of being chosen [app]. Oakhurst still installs the kitchens, so it keeps control of quality while retailers handle the selling [an].

knowledge_max_2: Wider regional coverage through existing shops
Retailers bring local customers and display space
analysis_max_2: Being in more shops raises the chance of selection
Oakhurst keeps installation and quality control

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakhurst Kitchens Ltd should sell through five independent retailers rather than its own showroom? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Retailers sell at $9,500 and leave Oakhurst $7,125, which still covers the $6,300 installation cost [k]. Five shops reach far more homeowners than one showroom, and Oakhurst avoids opening new sites itself [app]. The margin of $825 a kitchen is small, but extra volume through five retailers could add more than enough to cover it [an].

Against: However, $7,125 is $2,375 less than selling direct, so each kitchen earns much less [k]. Retailers control the customer conversation, and a poor display or pushy sales staff could damage Oakhurst's reputation for quality [app]. The company also still pays $84,000 for its showroom while giving margin away to shops that may stock rival kitchens [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Oakhurst should use the five retailers as well as keeping the showroom [eval]. The $7,125 still covers installation, and wider coverage addresses the limited reach that holds sales at 96 kitchens a year [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Recommendation to use retailers alongside the showroom
Weighs $825 margin against wider coverage

scenario_stem: Pendeen Pens Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 1.6 million printed pens a year and sells them at $0.55 each, mainly to small firms. Each pen costs $0.31 to print. The marketing budget is $9,000. Directors are choosing between sponsoring a regional business awards event for $9,000 or sending a direct mail pack to 20,000 firms at $0.42 each.

questions.question_text: Define 'sponsorship'.
questions.model_answer: Sponsorship is paying to be linked with an event or person in return for publicity [2]. Pendeen would pay $9,000 to have its name on the regional business awards.

knowledge_max_2: Payment to be associated with an event

questions.question_text: Calculate the total cost of mailing 20,000 firms at $0.42 each.
questions.model_answer: 20,000 x $0.42 = $8,400 [2]. This leaves $600 of the $9,000 marketing budget.

knowledge_max_2: Cost = number mailed x cost per pack

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sponsorship may be suitable promotion for Pendeen Pens Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The awards event brings together owners and managers of small firms, who are exactly the buyers of printed pens [k]. Pendeen's name on the programme reaches them in a setting where business suppliers are expected [app]. That is more targeted than advertising to the general public [an].

Point 2: Sponsorship creates local press coverage and goodwill that a mail pack cannot [k]. Being associated with a respected regional award makes the brand look established, which helps when a firm chooses a supplier for 1.6 million pens [app]. The effect lasts through the event and the publicity that follows [an].

application_max_2: Pens sold mainly to small firms
analysis_max_2: Targeted at buyers rather than the public
Association with a respected event builds trust

questions.question_text: Do you think Pendeen Pens Ltd should sponsor the awards for $9,000 rather than mail 20,000 firms for $8,400? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The awards put Pendeen in front of small-firm owners who buy pens in bulk [k], and the sponsorship builds a reputation that supports a $0.55 price with a $0.24 margin [app]. Local press coverage may reach more buyers than 20,000 mail packs, most of which are thrown away [an].

Against: However, sponsorship gives no guaranteed orders, while direct mail can be measured by replies [k]. Mailing 20,000 firms costs $8,400 and leaves $600 of the budget, whereas the sponsorship uses all $9,000 [app]. At a $0.24 margin, Pendeen needs only 35,000 pens sold from the mailing to cover its cost, which is a modest share of 1.6 million [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Pendeen should choose the direct mail campaign [eval]. It is cheaper, reaches far more named firms and can be judged by actual orders, whereas the sponsorship's benefit is hard to measure [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of direct mail
Justifies measurability and reach over prestige

scenario_stem: Porthleven Pies is a sole trader in Marland who bakes 1,500 pies a week and sells them at $3.20 each to twelve cafes. A rival chain has opened four outlets nearby and Porthleven's orders have fallen 8%. The owner is deciding whether to supply two supermarkets at $2.45 a pie or protect quality and keep selling only to cafes. Ingredients cost $1.30 a pie.

questions.question_text: Define 'customer loyalty'.
questions.model_answer: Customer loyalty is when buyers repeatedly choose the same business or brand [2]. Porthleven's twelve cafes have stayed with the baker despite the rival's four outlets.

knowledge_max_2: Repeat purchasing from the same business

questions.question_text: Calculate the weekly revenue from 1,500 pies at $3.20 each.
Explain two ways the rival chain's four outlets may affect Porthleven Pies.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Four nearby outlets give cafe owners and shoppers an alternative supplier [k]. Porthleven's orders have already fallen 8%, which is about 120 pies a week at 1,500 [app]. Losing that volume leaves the baker with the same oven and delivery costs spread over fewer pies, raising unit cost [an].

Point 2: The chain can charge prices Porthleven cannot match because it buys ingredients in bulk [k]. Porthleven may be forced to hold its $3.20 price and accept lower sales, or cut the price and reduce the $1.90 margin on each pie [app]. Either way, the owner has less money to invest in quality or new recipes [an].

knowledge_max_2: Bulk buying gives the chain a price advantage
application_max_2: 8% fall equals about 120 fewer pies a week
analysis_max_2: Fixed oven and delivery costs spread over fewer pies
Margin or volume must be sacrificed

questions.question_text: Do you think Porthleven Pies should supply two supermarkets at $2.45 a pie? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Supermarkets would replace the volume lost to the rival chain and may order far more than 1,500 pies a week [k]. At $2.45 a pie with ingredients costing $1.30, each sale still adds $1.15 towards wages and overheads [app]. Bulk supermarket orders also use the bakery's spare capacity and spread its fixed costs [an].

Against: However, $2.45 gives a much thinner margin than $3.20, so Porthleven must sell many more pies to earn the same profit [k]. Supermarkets demand low prices and can delist a small supplier quickly, which would leave the bakery with even less security [app]. Selling cheap pies under a supermarket label may also convince the twelve cafes that Porthleven is no longer a quality baker [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Porthleven should supply the supermarkets [eval]. The 8% fall shows the cafes alone cannot fill capacity, and $1.15 contribution per pie is better than an idle oven, provided the cafe range keeps its quality image [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation to supply supermarkets
Balances contribution against brand risk

scenario_stem: Nancarrow Nursery Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that grows 14,000 garden plants a year and sells them at $9 each. It is considering opening a cafe beside its plant sales area, which has space for 40 seats. Managers can observe 400 visitors over four weekends or survey a random sample of 300 holders of its loyalty card at a cost of $1,100.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation' as a method of market research.
questions.model_answer: Observation is a research method that records what customers actually do rather than what they say [2]. Staff could count how many of the 400 visitors sit down and for how long.

knowledge_max_2: Does not rely on asking questions

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue from 14,000 plants at $9 each.
Explain two advantages for Nancarrow Nursery Ltd of observing visitors rather than surveying loyalty-card holders.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Observation records what visitors really do, not what they claim they would do [k]. Staff can count how many of the 400 visitors use the seating area or carry plants to the till [app]. That evidence is more reliable than opinions about a cafe that does not yet exist [an].

Point 2: Observation includes every visitor, not only loyalty-card holders [k]. Day-trippers and casual gardeners may be the people most likely to buy a drink, and they are invisible in a loyalty list [app]. It also avoids the cost and low response of a survey, so managers get evidence within four weekends [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shows actual behaviour rather than stated intent
Covers all visitors, not just loyal customers
analysis_max_2: Better evidence for a cafe that does not exist yet

questions.question_text: Do you think Nancarrow Nursery Ltd should observe visitors rather than survey its 300 loyalty-card holders? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Observation shows whether visitors actually linger and where they go, which is what decides if 40 cafe seats will be used [k]. Counting 400 visitors over four weekends gives real behaviour at the site rather than guesses [app]. It also costs little and can be done by existing staff [an].

Against: However, observation cannot show how much customers would pay for a coffee or what food they want [k]. The 300 loyalty-card holders are repeat customers who visit often and would use a cafe regularly, so their views matter for year-round trade [app]. A survey costing $1,100 is small against $126,000 of plant revenue and can ask about prices directly [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Nancarrow should survey the 300 loyalty-card holders [eval]. The cafe's success depends on spend per visit, which only asking can reveal, and four weekends of observation may not represent the quieter months [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of the survey
Justifies price evidence over behaviour counts

scenario_stem: Egloskerry Eco Homes Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that builds 18 low-energy houses a year and sells them at an average of $210,000 each. questions.question_text: Define 'after-sales service'.
questions.model_answer: After-sales service is the help a business gives customers after a purchase, such as repairs, advice and warranty work [2]. Egloskerry wants feedback on this part of its offer.

questions.question_text: Calculate the contribution per house at $210,000 with a build cost of $165,000.
Explain two reasons why interviewing 12 recent buyers may give better feedback than surveying 400 non-buyers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The 12 buyers have lived in the houses and can describe how the design works in daily use [k]. They can explain whether rooms are warm, noisy or awkward, which a non-buyer can only guess [app]. That detail is valuable when each house sells for $210,000 [an].

Point 2: Twelve interviews cover two-thirds of the 18 houses sold last year [k]. A home visit also lets managers see the finish and any repairs, and buyers are likely to agree because they already own the house [app]. The views are therefore detailed and based on real experience rather than intention [an].

knowledge_max_2: Buyers have real experience of living there
12 interviews cover two-thirds of annual sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Egloskerry Eco Homes Ltd should interview 12 recent buyers rather than survey 400 non-buyers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The buyers can explain how the design and after-sales service perform in practice [k]. Twelve interviews cover two-thirds of the 18 houses sold, and each house contributes $45,000, so improving the design protects a large margin [app]. Personal visits also strengthen relationships that may bring referrals [an].

scenario_stem: Lanreath Lavender is a sole trader in Marland who distils 9,600 bottles of lavender oil a year and sells them at $12.50 each at farmers' markets. Each bottle costs $4.60 to produce. questions.question_text: Define 'product range'.

knowledge_max_2: May share a brand and target customer

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from one gift set compared with one bottle of oil, using $19.90 and $12.50.
questions.model_answer: $19.90 - $12.50 = $7.40 [2]. Each gift set earns $7.40 more than a bottle.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the gift sets may increase Lanreath Lavender's sales.
questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Gift sets attract buyers at Christmas and other occasions when the single bottle is less suitable [k]. They also use the same lavender oil, so Lanreath does not need a new production process [app]. Selling both lines lets customers choose between an everyday bottle and a gift, widening the range without abandoning the original product [an].

knowledge_max_2: Gift set appeals to present buyers
analysis_max_2: Same oil, no new production process

questions.question_text: Do you think Lanreath Lavender should launch the gift sets rather than keep selling single bottles? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Each gift set brings $7.40 more revenue than a single bottle [k]. The extra $2.10 packaging is far below the price difference, and the soap adds value without new distilling equipment [app]. Gift buyers are less price sensitive at $19.90 and may buy several sets at once [an].

Against: However, gift sets need soap from another supplier and extra assembly time, which a sole trader may not have [k]. Unsold gift stock after the season would tie up cash and packaging that cannot be reused [app]. Loyal market customers may still prefer the $12.50 bottle and see the set as expensive [an].

Keeps the single bottle alongside

scenario_stem: Curgurrell Cakes Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that bakes 520 celebration cakes a month and sells them at $34 each through one shop and Instagram. Defined by needs, age or occasion

questions.question_text: Calculate the commission paid to the venue on one $210 wedding cake at 12%.

Compares contribution with celebration cakes

scenario_stem: Warbstow Watches is a partnership in Marland that assembles 600 mechanical watches a year and sells them at $340 each to collectors. questions.question_text: Calculate the contribution per watch at $340 with a cost of $210.
Explain two reasons why competing with the $190 smartwatch on features may fail.

Point 2: Warbstow's buyers are collectors who value mechanical engineering, not fitness tracking [k]. questions.question_text: Do you think Warbstow Watches should add fitness tracking rather than market heritage craftsmanship? Justify your answer.

Against: However, the $60,000 development adds $100 to each of 600 watches, leaving only $30 of the $130 contribution [k]. Warbstow cannot match the smartwatch brand's technology or $190 price [app]. Marketing heritage craftsmanship instead protects the $130 margin and sells to buyers who value something the smartwatch cannot offer [an].

scenario_stem: Ruan Ropes Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 42,000 metres of marine rope a year and sells it at $2.10 a metre to boatyards in three countries. questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue from 42,000 metres at $2.10 a metre.
Explain two limitations of customs export data for Ruan Ropes Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The data covers all rope and cordage exports, not the stronger marine rope at $3.40 [k]. It may show rising exports while saying nothing about whether boatyards would pay the higher price [app]. Ruan could invest in production for a market that does not want its specific product [an].

Point 2: Customs records are published after a delay and group countries together [k]. questions.question_text: Do you think Ruan Ropes Ltd should buy the $550 export data rather than phone 80 boatyards? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Morvah Marquees is a partnership in Marland that hires out 140 marquees a year at an average of $420 per event. Most bookings come from word of mouth. questions.question_text: Define 'promotion'.

questions.question_text: Calculate the commission paid on one $420 marquee booking at 10%.
questions.model_answer: $420 x 0.10 = $42 [2]. The planner keeps $42 and Morvah receives $378.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the wedding planner may bring more bookings than the magazine advertisement.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The planner meets couples who are actively choosing suppliers for a date [k]. Her recommendation comes at the moment of decision, when a marquee is needed, rather than when a magazine is flicked through [app]. That relevance should produce more enquiries from the $3,800 budget [an].

Point 2: The commission is paid only when a booking occurs, so the partners risk nothing upfront [k]. Each $420 booking costs $42, leaving $378, and the planner has an incentive to recommend Morvah because she earns from it [app]. The magazine charges for space whether or not anyone calls [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Morvah Marquees should pay the wedding planner commission rather than buy the magazine advertisement? Justify your answer.

Each $420 booking costs $42, leaving $378, and her recommendation reaches couples when they are choosing [app]. That is a measurable return on promotion, unlike an advertisement that may bring no calls [an].

Against: However, the planner may recommend several marquee firms, so Morvah still competes for each booking [k]. A magazine advertisement reaches hundreds of couples and builds a brand that works even when the planner is not involved [app]. Paying 10% also reduces the margin on every booking and may encourage the planner to push higher-priced rivals [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Morvah should use the wedding planner [eval]. Payment follows results, $42 on a $420 booking is affordable, and her recommendation reaches couples at the moment they book [eval].

Justifies pay-on-results over paid space
analysis_max_2: Magazine reaches many but may bring no calls

scenario_stem: Trevone Trunks Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 4,600 suitcases a year and sells them at $96 each through 18 luggage shops. Each suitcase costs $61 to make. Point 2: Online advertising can be measured and changed quickly [k]. Directors can see how many clicks become orders and move the $30,000 to the search terms that work [app]. That flexibility matters because each suitcase contributes only $35, so wasted spending is hard to recover [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Trevone Trunks Ltd should sponsor the travel programme rather than run the online campaign? Justify your answer.

Against: However, 62% of suitcase sales happen online, where Trevone is unknown [k]. The $30,000 must produce at least 858 extra suitcases at $35 contribution just to cover its cost [app]. Online advertising can be measured and adjusted, while a sponsorship's effect on sales is hard to prove [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Trevone should run the online campaign [eval]. It targets the channel where 62% of sales occur and can be judged by orders, whereas the same $30,000 needs 858 extra suitcases to justify itself whichever promotion is chosen [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation of the online campaign

analysis_max_2: Online is where 62% of sales happen

scenario_stem: Gweek Gallery is a sole trader in Marland who sells 40 paintings a month at an average price of $250 and takes a 30% commission. questions.question_text: Define 'commission'.

questions.question_text: Calculate the commission Gweek Gallery earns from one painting sold at $250 with a 30% rate.
questions.model_answer: $250 x 0.30 = $75 [2]. Gweek keeps $75 of the $250 selling price.

questions.question_text: Do you think Gweek Gallery should invest $5,500 in an online viewing room rather than run evening events at $1,800 a month? Justify your answer.

Events also build local relationships that support the $225 rent, whereas a website may attract browsers who never buy [an].

scenario_stem: Harrowgate Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Leeds making handmade oak tables to order. scenario_stem: Tarnbeck Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Sheffield machining steel parts for pump makers. questions.question_text: Do you think Tarnbeck Engineering Ltd should spend $180,000 on the robotic loading arm? Justify your answer.

chapter: 4.3 Sustainable production of goods and services
scenario_stem: Greenhaugh Packaging Ltd is a private limited company near Derby making cardboard boxes from recycled board for online retailers. questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.

knowledge_max_2: Margin of safety = output minus break-even output

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Hartlebury Toys could increase its margin of safety.

questions.question_text: Define 'economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Economies of scale are the falls in average cost that come from producing on a larger scale [2]. If Blyford made more than 1,550 sails, its $299,000 of fixed costs would be spread over more units.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Blyford Sailmakers could benefit from economies of scale.

Point 1: Buying cloth in larger quantities is one source of economies of scale [k]. A bigger order of sailcloth could reduce the $410 variable cost, raising contribution above $230 on each $640 sail [an].

Against: $590 is $50 below the normal $640 price. Yacht owners who hear of the deal may ask for the same terms, and building 400 extra sails could delay full-price orders in the peak spring season.

Conclusion: Blyford should accept if the sails are a simple charter specification and the price stays confidential; otherwise the $72,000 gain is outweighed by damage to its $640 market.

scenario_stem: Minsterley Toffee is a partnership in Chile that produces 28,000 boxes of toffee a year for farm shops. Point 2: Flow production is inflexible and suits identical boxes [k]. questions.question_text: Do you think Minsterley Toffee should install the flow-production line? Justify your answer.

analysis_max_2: Cost recovered in about two and a third years

chapter: 4.2 Technology and production of goods and services
scenario_stem: Hartsgrove Furniture is a private limited company in Indonesia that produces 13,000 oak chairs a year for hotels. Designs can be tested and modified on screen

questions.question_text: Calculate Hartsgrove Furniture's break-even output.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways CAD could improve Hartsgrove Furniture's production.

Point 2: Designs can pass directly from CAD to the manufacturing equipment [k]. That shortens the time between a hotel's order and the first chair, so Hartsgrove can quote for smaller custom orders without losing the efficiency of its normal runs, although staff need training and the software carries a licence cost that adds to the $162,000 of fixed costs [an].

Decision rests on securing custom order volume
analysis_max_2: Cost recovered in about two and a third years

chapter: 4.4 Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
scenario_stem: Aldermarsh Bicycles is a private limited company in Morocco that produces 3,000 electric bicycles a year for commuters, 600 below its capacity of 3,600. questions.model_answer: Contribution per bicycle = $400 - $310 = $90 [1]. Break-even output = $198,000 / $90 = 2,200 bicycles [1]. Current output of 3,000 is 800 above break-even.

knowledge_max_2: Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Aldermarsh Bicycles' average cost per bicycle may fall if it raises output towards 3,600.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $198,000 of fixed costs is spread over more bicycles [k]. At 3,000 units fixed cost is $66 a bicycle, but at 3,600 it is $55, so average cost falls by $11 even if nothing else changes, which widens the margin above the $310 variable cost [an].

Point 2: Buying components in larger quantities may earn trade discounts [k]. If bulk ordering cuts the variable cost below $310, each bicycle costs less to build and the $90 contribution rises, so the company can compete on price or keep more profit; however, storage and handling for the extra parts must not cancel the gain [an].

Bulk buying of components earns discounts

analysis_max_2: Spare capacity means no extra fixed costs

scenario_stem: Pinehallow Toys is a partnership in Thailand that produces 20,000 wooden toys a year for independent shops. Reputation and legal safety are protected

scenario_stem: Colburn Chemicals Ltd makes industrial cleaning fluids for 85 factories. questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why leasing the press might be better than buying it.

questions.question_text: Do you think Wyverstone Packaging Ltd should buy the press with a bank loan? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Rillbank Fisheries Ltd operates four trawlers and sells catch to 30 fish merchants. questions.question_text: Do you think Rillbank Fisheries Ltd should delay the $22,000 engine overhaul? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Odcombe Footwear Ltd makes leather boots and sells to 75 independent shoe shops. Last year revenue was $680,000 and cost of sales was $408,000, including $150,000 of leather. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kelmarsh Furniture Ltd is a private limited company making office chairs in Brazil, employing 140 staff and earning $8,400,000 a year. questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services [2]; Brazil's 4.8% rate means Kelmarsh Furniture Ltd pays more each year for timber, glue and wages.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general/average price level
Money buys fewer goods as costs and prices climb

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Kelmarsh Furniture Ltd would pay on a $2,500,000 loan at 14.75%.
Explain two effects of the 14.75% interest rate on Kelmarsh Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Financing the cutting line becomes expensive [k]. Borrowing $2,500,000 at 14.75% costs $368,750 a year in interest [app], which is $58,750 more than the lease and must be paid before the line earns anything [an].

Point 2: Office customers buying on credit reduce spending [k]. Higher repayments squeeze Brazilian firms refitting their premises [app], so chair orders fall just as Kelmarsh needs volume to cover its fixed costs [an].

analysis_max_2: Interest absorbs profit before the investment earns
Lower orders leave fixed costs spread over fewer chairs

questions.question_text: Do you think Kelmarsh Furniture Ltd should borrow $2,500,000 for the cutting line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Buying the line ends the $310,000 annual lease and gives Kelmarsh an asset it could sell if trade turns down. Automated cutting should reduce waste and raise output per worker, spreading the $8,400,000 revenue over fewer labour hours.

Against: At 14.75% the loan costs $368,750 a year before any principal is repaid, which is $58,750 more than leasing. With inflation at 4.8% eroding office budgets, chair orders may fall and leave the business short of cash.

evaluation_max_2: Judges borrowing against the $310,000 lease

scenario_stem: Brancock Bakery Ltd is a partnership running 14 bakery shops in Kenya, selling 1,800,000 loaves a year at $1.20. questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of a business activity paid by people outside the business [2]; Brancock Bakery Ltd's 1,800,000 plastic bags create litter that Kenyan councils must clear.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual cost to Brancock Bakery Ltd of switching all 1,800,000 bags to biodegradable ones.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the packaging levy might affect Brancock Bakery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise on every plastic bag [k]. The 8% levy is added to the existing bag price across 1,800,000 loaves [app], so the partners may lift the $1.20 loaf price and lose customers who compare prices closely [an].

Point 2: It encourages a switch to biodegradable bags [k]. Paying $0.09 instead of $0.04 adds $90,000 a year [app], but shoppers in Kenya may reward the greener choice with loyalty and the levy no longer applies [an].

application_max_2: 8% levy on bags used for 1,800,000 loaves
analysis_max_2: Price rise risks losing price-sensitive customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Brancock Bakery Ltd should switch to biodegradable bags at $0.09 each? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The switch removes the levy from every bag and answers growing concern about plastic litter in Kenya. A greener image could lift sales above the current 1,800,000 loaves and protect the partnership from further regulation.

Against: The change adds $90,000 a year, equal to 4.2% of the $2,160,000 revenue, at a time when 6.5% inflation is already raising flour costs. Passing the cost to shoppers risks losing custom to rival bakeries.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Thornvale Textiles plc is a public limited company in Vietnam making T-shirts for European retailers, with 900 workers and revenue of $14,000,000. questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in another currency [2]; Thornvale Textiles plc would convert its $36,000 order at 25,100 dong per dollar.

It changes with supply and demand for currencies

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 8% fall in the dong on Thornvale Textiles plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: T-shirts become cheaper for European buyers [k]. With the dong 8% lower, the same dollar price converts into more dong [app], so Thornvale can win extra orders while still covering its 900 workers' wages [an].

Point 2: Imported materials cost more [k]. Cotton, dyes and machinery bought abroad now need more dong for the same dollar invoice [app], squeezing the margin on the $14,000,000 of revenue [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornvale Textiles plc should quote its next order in dollars rather than dong? Justify your answer.

For: A dollar quote gives the European buyer a fixed price and removes their currency risk, making Thornvale easier to deal with. At 25,100 dong per dollar the $36,000 order is worth 903,600,000 dong, which is a large sum for a Vietnamese textile firm.

Against: If the dong falls further, Thornvale receives the same dollars but fewer dong in real terms, while its 900 workers are paid in dong. Quoting in dong would let the company share any further gain.

Conclusion: Quote in dollars for this customer. The certainty helps win repeat orders, and the 8% fall has already improved the dong value of dollar sales.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Oakmere Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Poland producing wall tiles, with 210 staff and sales of 4,200,000 square metres a year. Directors must decide whether to raise tile prices by 6% or absorb the wage increase.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level [2]; at 5.2% in Poland it raises the cost of clay, glaze and the wages of Oakmere Ceramics Ltd's 210 staff.

knowledge_max_2: Reduces the purchasing power of money

questions.question_text: Calculate the new labour cost per square metre after an 11% wage increase on $8.40.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 11% wage growth on Oakmere Ceramics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Unit costs rise [k]. Labour accounts for $8.40 of the $27.00 cost per square metre, so an 11% rise adds about $0.92 and takes labour to $9.32 [app], cutting the margin on 4,200,000 square metres unless prices change [an].

Point 2: Directors may substitute machinery for labour [k]. Higher wages make automated pressing and glazing more attractive [app], which could cut the 210-strong workforce but protect profits as inflation stays at 5.2% [an].

application_max_2: 210 staff and 4,200,000 square metres of output
analysis_max_2: Automation may cut jobs but protect profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakmere Ceramics Ltd should raise tile prices by 6%? Justify your answer.

For: A 6% rise adds $1.62 to the $27.00 cost per square metre, more than covering the $0.92 wage increase. With inflation at 5.2%, customers expect prices to move, and the extra revenue protects the margin on 4,200,000 square metres.

Against: Builders and retailers in Poland are price-sensitive and imports remain available. A 6% rise could lose volume, leaving fixed costs spread over fewer tiles and wiping out the gain.

Conclusion: Raise prices by 6% but review after three months. The increase covers the wage bill, yet the risk of lost volume means Oakmere must watch sales closely.

evaluation_max_2: Compares the 6% price rise with the $0.92 cost increase
Sets a review point to manage volume risk
analysis_max_2: Price-sensitive builders may switch to imports

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Dunrobin Brewing Co Ltd is a private limited company in Portugal brewing craft beer, filling 6,500,000 bottles a year. questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Dunrobin Brewing Co Ltd of exceeding the 70% refillable target.

Point 2: It builds a green brand [k]. Portuguese drinkers and bars increasingly choose low-waste suppliers [app], so refillable bottles may lift sales and secure listings that would otherwise go to rivals [an].

knowledge_max_2: Avoids the levy on one-way bottles

analysis_max_2: Green image wins bar listings and loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunrobin Brewing Co Ltd should spend EUR 1,200,000 refitting the line now? Justify your answer.

For: Refitting meets the 2028 law early and avoids the EUR 390,000 annual levy, so the EUR 1,200,000 outlay is recovered in roughly three years. Refillable glass also cuts bottle purchases and strengthens the brand with Portuguese bars.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

Point 2: Export revenue and cash flow come under pressure [k]. If Fenwick keeps its own price at $2,400 it absorbs $360 a tonne across 9,000 tonnes [app], cutting the margin needed to pay Chilean dairy farmers [an].

evaluation_max_2: Compares a full price cut with a partial reduction

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a 3,500,000 cedi loan at 22%.

Point 1: Input costs climb faster than prices can be changed [k]. Board, ink and glue bought for 18,000,000 cedis of sales cost more each month [app], so the margin on each box shrinks unless customers accept frequent price rises [an].

analysis_max_2: Net gain only 130,000 cedis a year

scenario_stem: Loxley Printing Ltd is a private limited company in Malaysia printing labels for food brands, using 900 tonnes of paper a year at $640 a tonne. questions.question_text: Define 'carbon tax'.

Point 2: It pushes the firm towards cleaner energy [k]. Replacing older presses or buying renewable electricity would cut taxable emissions [app], lowering the $16,200 bill and supporting the green image the client is demanding [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marrendale Footwear plc is a public limited company in Turkey making leather shoes, exporting 700,000 pairs a year at EUR 22 a pair. The lira has fallen 25% against the euro, and the EU has imposed a 16% tariff on Turkish shoes. Directors must decide whether to cut euro prices to EUR 19 to defend market share or hold EUR 22 and accept lower volumes.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation of a currency'.
questions.model_answer: A depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency against another on the foreign exchange market [2]; the lira's 25% fall means each euro now buys more Turkish lira.

knowledge_max_2: Fall in a currency's value against another
Makes exports cheaper and imports dearer

questions.question_text: Calculate the EU price of a EUR 22 pair of shoes after the 16% tariff is added.
questions.model_answer: EUR 22 x 16% = EUR 3.52. Price after tariff = EUR 22 + EUR 3.52 = EUR 25.52 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 25% fall in the lira on Marrendale Footwear plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Turkish costs fall in euro terms [k]. Leather, wages and rent are paid in lira, so a 25% fall cuts the euro cost of making each of the 700,000 pairs [app], widening the margin even at EUR 22 [an].

Point 2: Imported inputs become dearer [k]. Machinery, dyes and some hides are bought abroad, and their lira price rises by roughly a quarter [app], offsetting part of the export gain [an].

knowledge_max_2: Weaker lira raises imported input costs
application_max_2: Costs paid in lira across 700,000 pairs
Imported machinery and dyes cost more lira
analysis_max_2: Euro margin widens on each pair
Import cost inflation offsets the gain

questions.question_text: Do you think Marrendale Footwear plc should cut its euro price to EUR 19? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The 16% tariff lifts a EUR 22 pair to EUR 25.52 for EU buyers, so a cut to EUR 19 restores competitiveness. The 25% weaker lira has lowered euro costs, so a EUR 19 price may still earn a margin and keep 700,000 pairs of capacity busy.

Against: Cutting EUR 3 a pair gives up EUR 2,100,000 of revenue, and EU retailers may see the cut as a temporary discount rather than value. Holding EUR 22 protects revenue if volumes fall only slightly.

Conclusion: Cut selectively, to EUR 20.50 for large retailers. That answers the tariff without giving away the full lira advantage across 700,000 pairs.

evaluation_max_2: Compares the tariff-neutral price with a partial cut

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a 60,000,000 pound loan at 19.25%.
Explain two effects of 28% inflation on Selby Fashion Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise faster than the firm can reprice [k]. Fabric and wages for 320 staff climb throughout the season [app], so garments sold at old prices may make a loss before the range reaches shops [an].

Point 2: Workers demand higher pay [k]. With prices up 28%, staff press for rises to protect their living standards [app], adding to the 240,000,000 pounds of costs and making the 60,000,000 pound factory harder to afford [an].

application_max_2: Wage claims add to costs at 240,000,000 pounds revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Selby Fashion Ltd should borrow 60,000,000 pounds now? Justify your answer.

Against: Interest at 19.25% is 11,550,000 pounds a year, which must be found before any profit. With costs rising 28% and customers resisting a 15% price rise, the business could run short of cash.

questions.model_answer:

questions.question_text: Do you think Pilmuir Toys Ltd should raise the toy price by $3? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Wrenfield Sports Ltd is a private limited company in Indonesia making sportswear, exporting 1,200,000 shirts a year to the United States at $18 each. questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any government measure that restricts imports or exports [2]; the 20% US tariff on Wrenfield Sports Ltd's shirts is one example.

questions.question_text: Calculate the US price of an $18 shirt after the 20% tariff is added.
Explain two reasons why Wrenfield Sports Ltd might build a factory in Vietnam instead of exporting from Indonesia.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It avoids the US tariff [k]. Shirts made in Vietnam face a lower US duty than the 20% now charged on Indonesian clothing [app], so the landed price falls below $21.60 and orders are easier to win [an].

Point 2: It spreads risk across countries [k]. A second site means a flood, strike or new tariff in Indonesia cannot stop all 1,200,000 shirts [app], protecting revenue for US customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Production inside a country facing lower tariffs
application_max_2: Current output of 1,200,000 shirts from one country
analysis_max_2: Lower landed price wins US orders
Supply continues if one country is disrupted

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenfield Sports Ltd should spend $4,000,000 on a factory in Vietnam? Justify your answer.

Against: $4,000,000 is a large commitment when the rupiah has fallen 6%, which already makes Indonesian costs cheaper in dollar terms. Building abroad also means managing a new workforce and losing control of quality.

Conclusion: Do not build yet. The weaker rupiah offsets part of the tariff, so Wrenfield should first renegotiate US prices and test Vietnamese production through a local partner.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ashcombe Cycles Ltd is a private limited company in Norway assembling e-bikes, selling 12,000 units a year at $1,450. questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $1,800,000 loan at 4.5%.

Point 1: Borrowing for the line is relatively cheap [k]. Interest on $1,800,000 is $81,000 a year [app], which the saving on 12,000 imported frames can cover if assembly costs fall [an].

Point 2: Customers still delay big purchases [k]. E-bikes at $1,450 are often bought on credit, and higher repayments discourage buyers when GDP growth is only 0.8% [app], so sales may fall just as new capacity arrives [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ashcombe Cycles Ltd should borrow $1,800,000 for the assembly line? Justify your answer.

Against: GDP growth of 0.8% and inflation of 3.2% suggest cautious buyers, so 12,000 sales are not guaranteed. A fixed interest charge and a large loan could strain cash if e-bike demand dips.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Vellacott Motors plc is a public limited company in Spain making car parts, using 6,000 tonnes of steel a year at EUR 700 a tonne. questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Imported steel becomes more expensive [k]. The levy adds EUR 154 a tonne, taking the cost to EUR 854 against EUR 820 for EU steel [app], so the 6,000 tonnes now cost EUR 924,000 more than before [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Vellacott Motors plc should switch to EU steel at EUR 820 a tonne? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation of a currency'.

Makes imports cheaper and exports dearer

questions.question_text: Calculate the euro value of the $1,200,000 US orders at $1.20 per euro.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of higher fuel duty on Nordhaven Logistics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Older lorries become less viable [k]. With fuel taking a larger share of cost, the 30 least efficient vehicles may be retired early [app], pushing the firm towards the $6,000,000 electric replacement [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Nordhaven Logistics Ltd should borrow $6,000,000 for electric lorries? Justify your answer.

For: Electric lorries would remove diesel duty from 30 vehicles, saving a share of the $216,000 annual bill and shielding the firm from future duty rises. At a 5.25% bank rate, the interest cost is predictable and the vehicles cut emissions for green-minded clients.

Against: $6,000,000 is a heavy debt for a haulier, and electric lorries have limited range for long Canadian routes. Charging points and driver retraining add further cost before any saving appears.

Conclusion: Replace only the 30 lorries on short urban routes. That captures fuel savings where range is not a problem, while leaving long-haul work on diesel until charging infrastructure improves.

Against: Borrowing 40,000,000 baht commits Pellumbra for many years, and animation demand can fall sharply if clients cut budgets. The rented studio keeps the company flexible and avoids a large debt at a time of 1.5% inflation.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Everloop Recycling Ltd is a private limited company in the Netherlands processing 30,000 tonnes of plastic waste a year into pellets sold at EUR 620 a tonne. questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the percentage charged on borrowed money over a year [2]; Everloop Recycling Ltd would pay 4.0% on a EUR 3,200,000 sorting line.

knowledge_max_2: Set by lenders and central banks

questions.question_text: Calculate the new price per tonne of recycled plastic after a 12% fall from EUR 620.
questions.model_answer: EUR 620 x 12% = EUR 74.40. New price = EUR 620 - EUR 74.40 = EUR 545.60 a tonne [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 12% fall in recycled plastic prices on Everloop Recycling Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue per tonne drops [k]. The price falls from EUR 620 to EUR 545.60 [app], so 30,000 tonnes bring in EUR 16,368,000 instead of EUR 18,600,000 [an].

Point 2: The sorting line becomes harder to justify [k]. Lower pellet prices mean each tonne processed earns less [app], so the EUR 3,200,000 investment takes longer to repay while inflation at 3.3% raises running costs [an].

analysis_max_2: EUR 3,200,000 line takes longer to repay

questions.question_text: Do you think Everloop Recycling Ltd should invest EUR 3,200,000 in the sorting line now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A sorting line would lower the cost per tonne and let Everloop handle dirtier waste, protecting margins when pellets sell at EUR 545.60. Borrowing at 4.0% is relatively cheap, and better sorting could command a premium from packaging customers.

Against: Prices have fallen 12% and may stay weak, while the line costs EUR 3,200,000 and inflation adds 3.3% to running costs. Committing now risks a low return if pellet prices fall further.

Conclusion: Delay for six months. The 4.0% rate is attractive, but Everloop should wait for evidence that prices have stopped falling before spending EUR 3,200,000.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs cheap finance against falling prices
Recommends waiting for price stability

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Do you think Clearsight Waste Ltd should build the EUR 7,000,000 sorting plant? Justify your answer.

Against: The plant needs reliable waste volumes and skilled staff, and recovered materials may sell at low prices. A EUR 7,000,000 commitment is large for a collection business facing rising costs.

Changes as currencies are bought and sold

Against: The franc has already risen 8.5%, so Humblebee receives CHF 255,000 for EUR 250,000 of plants. Giving away 4% reduces a margin that is already exposed to weather and transport costs.

questions.question_text: Do you think Windrow Orchards Ltd should borrow CHF 1,200,000 for the bottling line? Justify your answer.

Against: Borrowing CHF 1,200,000 adds fixed debt just as inflation of 1.2% raises other costs. If apple harvests are poor, the company still pays interest and principal on equipment it cannot fully use.

questions.question_text: Do you think Cockerell Poultry Ltd should spend $2,400,000 on automated deboning machines? Justify your answer.

analysis_max_2: Lower volume cuts revenue and spreads fixed costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Driftwood Furniture Ltd should open a factory in China? Justify your answer.

analysis_max_2: Local plant avoids quota and freight costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sableford Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Egypt running 6 hotels with 1,800 rooms, earning $54,000,000 a year from European tourists. questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A subsidy is a payment by government to a business to reduce its costs, such as the fuel subsidy whose removal raised Sableford Hotels Ltd electricity bills by 40% [2].

knowledge_max_2: A government payment to reduce business costs
It lowers prices or helps firms stay viable

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual revenue if Sableford Hotels Ltd raises room prices by 15% and occupancy stays at 68%.
questions.model_answer: Extra revenue = 15% of $54,000,000 = $8,100,000 a year, giving total revenue of $62,100,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Extra revenue = percentage price rise x current revenue
Assumes the same number of rooms is sold

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the pound's 22% depreciation on Sableford Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Dearer imported supplies [k], as imported food, drink and spare parts cost more pounds [app], adding to costs when inflation is already 29% [an].

analysis_max_2: Higher visitor numbers raise room revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Sableford Hotels Ltd should raise room prices by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:

Against: higher prices may deter price-sensitive tour operators [app], and cutting 120 staff would reduce service quality and could deter them more than a modest price rise [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Elmswood Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Poland making 1,200,000 wooden puzzles a year, exporting 55% to Germany at $12 each. Germany has imposed a 12.5% tariff on imported toys and the zloty has appreciated 8% against the dollar. A German rival sells similar puzzles at $13. Directors must decide whether to cut their price so importers still pay $12 or keep $12 and let importers pay the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, such as the 12.5% charge Germany now adds to Elmswood Toys Ltd puzzles priced at $12 [2].

knowledge_max_2: It raises the price paid by importers

questions.question_text: Calculate the price Elmswood Toys Ltd must charge so that Germany importers still pay $12 after the 12.5% tariff.
questions.model_answer: Importers pay price + 12.5%, so price = $12 / 1.125 = $10.67, which with the tariff comes to $12 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Divide the target border price by 1 + tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the zloty's 8% appreciation on Elmswood Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer puzzles in dollars [k], because each $12 puzzle now needs fewer zloty to make the same margin [app], so Elmswood must charge more or accept lower profit on 55% of its 1,200,000 puzzles [an].

Point 2: Cheaper imported wood and paint [k], as inputs bought in dollars cost fewer zloty [app], which partly offsets the tariff pressure at $12 a puzzle [an].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports less price competitive
analysis_max_2: Higher dollar prices risk losing market share
Cheaper inputs cushion the effect on margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Elmswood Toys Ltd should cut its price to $10.67? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: cutting to $10.67 keeps the border price at $12 despite the 12.5% tariff [app], so Germany buyers face no increase while a German rival charges $13 [an]; holding volume on 660,000 exported puzzles protects the factory's capacity use [k].

Against: a cut from $12 to $10.67 reduces unit revenue by $1.33 [app], and the 8% appreciation plus higher zloty costs means margin falls twice [an]; buyers may accept the tariff because $13.50 is close to the German $13 price [k].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement on holding the price
Weighs permanent price cut against temporary tariff
analysis_max_2: Price cut absorbs the tariff and protects volume
Cut costs $1.33 per puzzle while appreciation compresses margin

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Thistledown Bakeries Ltd is a private limited company in Kenya baking 90,000 loaves a day, sold at $0.60 each. questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.

Set by government and binding on employers

questions.question_text: Calculate the increase in Thistledown Bakeries Ltd's monthly wage bill.

The new bill is the old bill plus the increase

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 28% rise in wheat prices on Thistledown Bakeries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:

knowledge_max_2: Raw material costs are a large part of food costs
Firms may reduce quantity to avoid raising price
application_max_2: Wheat up 28%; 90,000 loaves a day at $0.60
analysis_max_2: Margin squeezed between rising costs and capped prices

questions.question_text: Do you think Thistledown Bakeries Ltd should raise the price to $0.70 a loaf? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the pollution fine and boycott on Millbrook Poultry Ltd.

questions.question_text: Do you think Millbrook Poultry Ltd should build the $5,400,000 treatment plant? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company'.

Production or sales take place outside the home country

questions.question_text: Calculate the value of exports lost if the quota cut removes 25% of Foxglove Fashion Ltd's 1,440,000 dresses sent to France.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the dirham's 19% depreciation on Foxglove Fashion Ltd.

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxglove Fashion Ltd should accept the contract and build a factory in France? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ulverton Textiles Ltd is a private limited company in Cambodia weaving 30,000,000 metres of cloth a year, with revenue of $96,000,000. questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.

Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Calculate the value of orders cancelled if 18% of Ulverton Textiles Ltd's $96,000,000 revenue is lost.
questions.model_answer: Cancelled value = 18% of $96,000,000 = $17,280,000 a year, leaving revenue of $78,720,000 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising unemployment in its main market on Ulverton Textiles Ltd.

analysis_max_2: Lower sales volume reduces revenue and capacity use

questions.question_text: Do you think Ulverton Textiles Ltd should switch production to medical uniforms for hospitals? Justify your answer.
