unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ironbridge Tools Ltd is a private limited company in Taiwan making 900,000 power drills a year, exporting 65% to America at $42 each. America has raised its tariff on imported tools from 8% to 20% and the Taiwan dollar has appreciated 6% against the US dollar. An American distributor wants 300,000 drills a year but only at $35 each. Directors must decide whether to accept the distributor's price or keep $42 and export fewer drills.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation' of a currency.
questions.model_answer: An appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency against another, such as the Taiwan dollar rising 6% against the US dollar for Ironbridge Tools Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: A rise in a currency's value against another currency
It buys more units of foreign currency

questions.question_text: Calculate the total tariff paid on Ironbridge Tools Ltd's 585,000 drills at 20% of the $42 price.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff per unit = rate x price
Total tariff = units x tariff per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the Taiwan dollar's appreciation on Ironbridge Tools Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer drills in dollars [k], as each $42 drill now needs to earn more Taiwan dollars to hold its margin [app], so America buyers may switch to local suppliers [an].

Point 2: Cheaper imported components [k], because motors and switches bought in US dollars cost fewer Taiwan dollars [app], which reduces the cost of the 900,000 drills made each year [an].

application_max_2: 6% appreciation against the US dollar; $42 price
analysis_max_2: Higher dollar prices reduce export competitiveness
Cheaper components partly protect unit cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironbridge Tools Ltd should accept the distributor's price of $35? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: 300,000 drills at $35 guarantees volume worth $10,500,000 [app], replacing sales lost to the 20% tariff and the 6% appreciation [an]; a large order also spreads fixed factory costs over more units [k].

Against: $35 is $7 below the current price, cutting revenue by $2,100,000 on those 300,000 drills [app], and it may force similar discounts on the other 585,000 exported drills [an].

Conclusion: Ironbridge should accept only as a separate own-brand contract, because extra volume is useful but a general $35 price would destroy margin across its whole export range [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement with a condition on the deal
Distinguishes a separate contract from general pricing
analysis_max_2: Bulk order offsets tariff-related volume loss
$7 discount risks spreading to all exports

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Westmere Garden Centres Ltd is a private limited company in the Netherlands running 12 garden centres, with sales of $88,000,000 a year. Inflation has fallen to 1.4% from 5.2%, unemployment is 3.1%, and the central bank has cut interest rates to 2.75%, raising house sales. Sales of garden furniture have risen 9%. Directors must decide whether to open 3 new centres for $24,000,000 or expand the existing 12 centres with $9,000,000 of refits.

questions.question_text: Define 'disposable income'.
questions.model_answer: Disposable income is the money households have left after tax to spend or save, such as the income supporting Westmere Garden Centres Ltd's $88,000,000 of sales [2].

knowledge_max_2: Income remaining after direct taxes are paid
It is the amount available for spending or saving

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual sales if the 9% rise in garden furniture continues on $88,000,000 of sales.
questions.model_answer: Extra sales = 9% of $88,000,000 = $7,920,000, giving total sales of $95,920,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Extra sales = growth rate x current sales
New sales = current sales plus the increase

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of falling inflation and interest rates on Westmere Garden Centres Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Rising demand [k], because cheaper mortgages raise house sales and 3.1% unemployment supports spending [app], so garden furniture sales grow 9% on $88,000,000 [an].

Point 2: Lower borrowing costs [k], as interest rates at 2.75% make the $24,000,000 expansion cheaper to finance [app], improving the expected return on new centres [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower inflation raises real incomes and confidence
Lower interest rates cut the cost of borrowing
analysis_max_2: Higher disposable income boosts garden sales
Cheaper finance makes investment more affordable

questions.question_text: Do you think Westmere Garden Centres Ltd should open 3 new centres? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: falling inflation and rates at 2.75% support demand and cheap finance [app], and 9% growth in furniture sales suggests the market can absorb new capacity [an]; new centres reach customers beyond the existing 12 sites [k].

Against: $24,000,000 is nearly three times the $9,000,000 refit option [app], and a new site takes time to build a customer base while 3.1% unemployment means labour is scarce and wages may rise [an].

Conclusion: Westmere should refit first, because $9,000,000 improves the existing 12 centres quickly while $24,000,000 on new sites carries more risk if growth slows [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement preferring refits
Weighs cost and risk of new sites against quick gains
analysis_max_2: New centres add capacity but need time to win customers
Refits cost less and lift sales at existing sites

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pinegrove Apparel Ltd is a private limited company in Bangladesh making 8,000,000 T-shirts a year for European brands, with a wage bill of $11,400,000. A television investigation found workers paid below the legal minimum and a pressure group has urged 4 brands to leave. One brand cancelled orders worth $3,600,000. Raising pay to the legal minimum would add $2,100,000 a year. Directors must decide whether to raise pay and keep the brands or relocate to a cheaper region.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical business behaviour'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical business behaviour means acting in ways that customers and society regard as fair and right, such as Pinegrove Apparel Ltd paying workers the legal minimum [2].

knowledge_max_2: Acting fairly and responsibly towards stakeholders
Doing what society regards as morally right

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage increase in Pinegrove Apparel Ltd's wage bill if pay rises by $2,100,000 from $11,400,000.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage increase = rise / original bill x 100
The new bill is the original plus the rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the television investigation on Pinegrove Apparel Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lost orders [k], because brands fear bad publicity and one has already cancelled $3,600,000 of work [app], cutting output below 8,000,000 T-shirts [an].

Point 2: Higher wage costs [k], as the firm must pay the legal minimum to restore its reputation [app], adding $2,100,000 a year to an $11,400,000 wage bill [an].

knowledge_max_2: Firms must raise standards to keep customers
analysis_max_2: Lost contracts cut volume and revenue
Compliance raises costs and squeezes margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Pinegrove Apparel Ltd should raise pay to the legal minimum? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: it would answer the pressure group and protect contracts with the 4 brands [app], after $3,600,000 of orders were already cancelled [an]; ethical sourcing is increasingly required by European buyers, so paying legally is a condition of trade [k].

Against: $2,100,000 a year is an 18.4% rise in the wage bill when margins are already thin [app], and relocating to a cheaper region could cut costs more [an].

Conclusion: Pinegrove should raise pay, because losing the remaining brands would cost far more than $2,100,000 and relocation would repeat the same reputation risk [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement to raise pay
Compares wage cost with the value of brand contracts
analysis_max_2: Wage rise of 18.4% against thin margins

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Jasmine Bay Resorts Ltd is a private limited company in Thailand operating 4 resorts with 950 rooms, earning $46,000,000 a year, mostly from European guests. The baht has depreciated 11% against the euro, from 44 to 48.84 baht per euro, and the government has cut tourist visa fees by 50%. A rival in Vietnam has cut room rates by 8%. Directors must decide whether to cut room rates by 8% or invest $3,200,000 in a spa for higher-spending guests.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in another currency, such as 48.84 baht per euro now faced by Jasmine Bay Resorts Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: The price of one currency in terms of another
It changes with supply and demand for currencies

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in the euro price of a 4,884 baht room night when the rate moves from 44 to 48.84 baht per euro.
questions.model_answer: A 4,884 baht room night at 44 baht per euro = 4,884 / 44 = €111. At 48.84 baht per euro = 4,884 / 48.84 = €100. Fall = €11 per room night [2].

knowledge_max_2: Euro price = baht price / baht per euro
The fall is the difference between the two prices

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the baht's depreciation on Jasmine Bay Resorts Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Cheaper holidays for Europeans [k], as a room night falls from €111 to €100 [app], attracting more guests and lifting occupancy across 950 rooms [an].

Point 2: Higher costs for imported supplies [k], because imported food and wine cost more baht at 48.84 per euro [app], reducing the margin on $46,000,000 of revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation makes a destination cheaper for foreigners
analysis_max_2: Higher occupancy raises total room revenue
Costlier imports erode the gain in margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Jasmine Bay Resorts Ltd should cut room rates by 8% to match the Vietnam rival? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: an 8% cut would match the rival and, with the baht 11% weaker, euro prices are already €100 a night [app], so undercutting could fill the 950 rooms in the low season [an]; higher occupancy spreads the fixed cost of 4 resorts [k].

Against: cutting rates by 8% reduces revenue on $46,000,000 by about $3,680,000 if occupancy is unchanged [app], and the $3,200,000 spa would attract guests who spend more rather than less [an].

Conclusion: Jasmine Bay should invest in the spa instead, because the weaker baht already makes it cheaper than Vietnam in euro terms without giving away room revenue [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement preferring the spa investment
Recognises depreciation already improves price competitiveness
analysis_max_2: Rate cut costs about $3,680,000 in revenue
Spa raises spend per guest and differentiates the resort

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Yarrowfield Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand producing 120,000,000 litres of milk a year, with revenue of $180,000,000. A recession has cut GDP by 1.2% and unemployment has reached 6.4%, while farm input costs have risen 17%. Two supermarket buyers demand a 5% price cut. Directors must decide whether to reduce the farmgate price paid to 40 supplier farms or cut the dividend and accept lower profit.

questions.question_text: Define 'GDP'.
questions.model_answer: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year, such as the 1.2% fall now affecting Yarrowfield Dairy Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: Total value of output produced in a country
Measured over a year, usually in money terms

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in revenue if Yarrowfield Dairy Ltd accepts a 5% price cut on $180,000,000 of sales.

knowledge_max_2: Fall = percentage cut x current revenue
New revenue is the original less the fall

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession on Yarrowfield Dairy Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lower demand for milk [k], because unemployment at 6.4% reduces household spending [app], so the 120,000,000 litres may sell more slowly and buyers demand 5% cuts [an].

Point 2: Pressure on supplier prices [k], as falling revenue forces the firm to look for savings [app], possibly cutting the farmgate price paid to 40 farms and risking future supply [an].

knowledge_max_2: Firms seek cost savings from suppliers
application_max_2: Input costs up 17%; 5% price cut demanded
analysis_max_2: Lower sales volume reduces revenue and cash flow
Squeezing farm prices may harm long-term supply relationships

questions.question_text: Do you think Yarrowfield Dairy Ltd should reduce the farmgate price paid to its 40 supplier farms? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: revenue is under pressure from a 5% price cut worth $9,000,000 [app] and input costs are up 17% [an], so cutting farmgate prices protects profit and the dividend [k].

Against: 40 farms may switch to rival processors if paid less [app], and milk supply of 120,000,000 litres would fall, raising average costs [an]; cutting the dividend instead preserves the supply base [k].

Conclusion: Yarrowfield should cut the dividend first, because a secure supply of 120,000,000 litres matters more than one year's payout and farmers can leave permanently [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement prioritising supply security
Compares dividend cut with farmgate cut
analysis_max_2: Dividend cut preserves supply and long-run capacity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bedrock Aggregates Ltd is a private limited company in South Africa producing 2,400,000 tonnes of crushed stone a year. Dust and blasting noise have led to 38 complaints from nearby residents, and the local council has imposed a $6 per tonne levy on quarry output to fund road repairs. A pressure group wants the quarry closed. Directors must decide whether to install $4,300,000 of dust suppression and quieter blasting or move the quarry 15 kilometres away.

questions.question_text: Define 'corporate social responsibility'.
questions.model_answer: Corporate social responsibility is a business accepting a duty to act in the interests of society, such as Bedrock Aggregates Ltd cutting dust for nearby residents [2].

knowledge_max_2: A business taking responsibility for its impact on society
Acting beyond legal minimums for stakeholders

questions.question_text: Calculate Bedrock Aggregates Ltd's annual levy on 2,400,000 tonnes at $6 per tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Levy = tonnes produced x rate per tonne
The levy is based on total quarry output

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the complaints and levy on Bedrock Aggregates Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher operating costs [k], because the $6 per tonne levy takes $14,400,000 a year from revenue [app], reducing profit on 2,400,000 tonnes of stone [an].

Point 2: Risk of closure or restriction [k], as 38 complaints and a pressure group campaign may persuade the council to limit blasting hours [app], cutting output and delaying deliveries [an].

knowledge_max_2: Public complaints can lead to tougher operating conditions
analysis_max_2: Levy reduces profit per tonne sold
Restricted hours lower output and customer service

questions.question_text: Do you think Bedrock Aggregates Ltd should install the $4,300,000 dust suppression equipment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: it addresses the 38 complaints directly and reduces the chance of the council restricting blasting [app], protecting output of 2,400,000 tonnes against a levy already costing $14,400,000 [an]; staying open also keeps 15 kilometres of local haulage jobs [k].

Against: $4,300,000 may not satisfy a pressure group that wants closure [app], and moving the quarry 15 kilometres would remove the nuisance entirely and end the complaints [an].

Conclusion: Bedrock should install the equipment, because relocation is slower and costlier than $4,300,000 and the levy will continue wherever it operates in the region [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement on the equipment
Compares with relocation as the alternative
analysis_max_2: Relocation removes nuisance but is slower and costlier

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kingsmoor Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in Ireland processing 450,000,000 litres of milk a year into butter and cheese, exporting 60% to America. America has imposed a 25% tariff on dairy imports and the euro has weakened 8% against the dollar. American buyers now pay $2,500 per tonne instead of $2,000. Directors must decide whether to cut the price to $1,600 per tonne to keep the border price at $2,000 or find new buyers in Canada.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is a government measure that restricts trade between countries, such as the 25% tariff America places on Kingsmoor Dairy Ltd exports [2].

knowledge_max_2: A measure that restricts international trade
Examples include tariffs, quotas and embargoes

questions.question_text: Calculate the price per tonne Kingsmoor Dairy Ltd must charge so that American buyers still pay $2,000 after the 25% tariff.
questions.model_answer: Price = $2,000 / 1.25 = $1,600 per tonne, which with the tariff returns to $2,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Divide the target border price by 1 + tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the euro's 8% weakening on Kingsmoor Dairy Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Cheaper exports for dollar buyers [k], because a euro buys fewer dollars, so butter and cheese priced in euros cost American buyers less [app], supporting sales of 60% of 450,000,000 litres [an].

Point 2: Dearer imported inputs [k], as packaging and machinery bought in dollars cost more euros [app], raising costs just as the 25% tariff squeezes the border price [an].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency makes exports cheaper abroad
analysis_max_2: Lower dollar prices help offset the tariff
Higher import costs reduce the benefit to margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsmoor Dairy Ltd should cut its price to $1,600 per tonne? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: it keeps the border price at $2,000, so American buyers see no increase despite the 25% tariff [app], protecting export volumes built on 60% of 450,000,000 litres [an]; the weaker euro partly offsets the $400 cut in euro terms [k].

Against: $400 a tonne is a large permanent reduction in revenue [app], and America may keep raising tariffs, so repeated cuts would leave no margin [an].

Conclusion: Kingsmoor should not cut to $1,600; it should share the tariff at about $1,800 and develop Canada, because tariff policy is outside its control [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement rejecting the full cut
Proposes partial absorption plus diversification
analysis_max_2: Full cut protects volume but cuts revenue permanently
Dependence on one market leaves the firm exposed

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Zephyrline Couriers Ltd is a private limited company in Peru delivering 14,000,000 parcels a year, with revenue of $60,000,000 and fuel costs of $16,800,000. Fuel prices have risen 23%, inflation is 5.4%, and the government has raised VAT from 16% to 19%, increasing delivery charges for customers. Two large online retailers are reviewing their contracts. Directors must decide whether to add a 6% fuel surcharge to every delivery or absorb the cost and cut the marketing budget.

questions.question_text: Define 'indirect tax'.
questions.model_answer: An indirect tax is a tax charged on spending rather than income, such as the VAT rise from 16% to 19% affecting Zephyrline Couriers Ltd customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: A tax on goods and services rather than income
Collected by sellers and passed to government

questions.question_text: Calculate the increase in Zephyrline Couriers Ltd's annual fuel cost if fuel prices rise 23% on $16,800,000.

knowledge_max_2: Increase = percentage rise x current fuel cost
The new cost is the old cost plus the increase

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the fuel price rise on Zephyrline Couriers Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lower profit per parcel [k], because fuel costs $3,864,000 more while revenue is $60,000,000 [app], so the margin on 14,000,000 deliveries falls [an].

Point 2: Pressure from retail clients [k], as online retailers reviewing contracts may move to cheaper couriers [app], reducing parcel volumes and spreading fixed depot costs over fewer deliveries [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fuel is a variable cost that rises with price
Cost increases make customers consider rivals
analysis_max_2: Higher costs reduce margin on each delivery
Lost contracts lower volume and raise average cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Zephyrline Couriers Ltd should add a 6% fuel surcharge? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: a 6% surcharge raises about $3,600,000 on $60,000,000 of revenue [app], almost covering the $3,864,000 fuel increase and protecting profit [an]; customers already accept VAT at 19%, so a visible fuel charge may be understood [k].

Against: the two online retailers are reviewing contracts and may switch to rivals [app], and absorbing the cost by cutting marketing could reduce future parcel volumes [an].

Conclusion: Zephyrline should add the surcharge, because it links cost recovery to fuel use and can be removed when prices fall, unlike losing the retailers permanently [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement on the surcharge
Notes the surcharge is reversible
analysis_max_2: Surcharge recovers most of the fuel increase
Client loss risks volume and fixed cost recovery

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Redfern Chemicals Ltd is a private limited company in Belgium making 900,000 tonnes of industrial solvents a year. A leak sent 12 tonnes of solvent into a canal, killing fish, and the regulator has fined the firm $2,700,000. New rules require double-walled storage tanks by 2028, costing $6,000,000, and insurance premiums of $4,200,000 have risen 34%. Directors must decide whether to install the tanks now or reduce output by 20% and delay.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental legislation'.
questions.model_answer: Environmental legislation is laws protecting the natural environment that businesses must obey, such as the double-walled tank rule facing Redfern Chemicals Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: Businesses must comply or face fines and closure

questions.question_text: Calculate the increase in Redfern Chemicals Ltd's annual insurance premium after a 34% rise on $4,200,000.

knowledge_max_2: Increase = percentage rise x current premium
The new premium is the old premium plus the increase

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the leak and fine on Redfern Chemicals Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher costs [k], because the $2,700,000 fine and a $1,428,000 insurance rise must be paid from profit [app], reducing funds for the $6,000,000 tanks [an].

Point 2: Damaged reputation [k], as killing fish in a canal alarms customers and regulators [app], so buyers may switch to greener suppliers and output of 900,000 tonnes may fall [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fines and insurance are direct financial penalties
analysis_max_2: Penalties reduce internal funds for compliance
Reputational loss risks contracts and future sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Redfern Chemicals Ltd should install the double-walled tanks now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the leak already cost a $2,700,000 fine and added $1,428,000 to insurance [app], so early compliance cuts the risk of a second incident before 2028 [an]; the tanks also reassure customers and may lower future premiums [k].

Against: $6,000,000 is a large outlay when output is 900,000 tonnes and margins are under pressure [app], and reducing output by 20% would lower the volume exposed to any leak at far less cost [an].

Conclusion: Redfern should install the tanks now, because a second leak would threaten its licence to operate, which matters more than the timing of a $6,000,000 spend [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement on early installation
Weighs licence risk against capital cost
analysis_max_2: Early compliance reduces repeat incident risk
Output cut lowers exposure but loses sales volume

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Larkspur Software Ltd is a private limited company in Israel selling data security software to 2,800 firms worldwide at $9,000 a year. The shekel has appreciated 9% against the dollar and a US rival has cut its price by 12%. The Israeli government has raised corporation tax from 23% to 26%. Directors must decide whether to cut the annual price to $8,100 or keep $9,000 and invest $1,600,000 in new features.

questions.question_text: Define 'corporation tax'.
questions.model_answer: Corporation tax is a tax on the profits of a company, such as the rise from 23% to 26% now facing Larkspur Software Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: Paid to government on taxable profit

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in annual revenue if all 2,800 firms pay $8,100 instead of $9,000.

knowledge_max_2: The fall is the difference between the two totals

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the shekel's 9% appreciation on Larkspur Software Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer software in dollars [k], as each $9,000 licence converts into fewer shekels [app], so Larkspur must raise dollar prices or accept lower margins on 2,800 customers [an].

Point 2: Cheaper overseas development costs [k], because programmers and servers bought abroad cost fewer shekels [app], which partly offsets the price pressure from the US rival's 12% cut [an].

knowledge_max_2: Foreign costs become cheaper in home currency
analysis_max_2: Higher dollar prices risk losing customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkspur Software Ltd should cut its price to $8,100? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: a 10% cut responds to the US rival's 12% reduction and the 9% appreciation [app], helping keep 2,800 customers who could switch [an]; software has low marginal cost, so lost revenue is partly offset by retained subscriptions [k].

Against: the cut reduces revenue by $2,520,000 a year [app], and corporation tax is rising to 26%, leaving less profit to fund development [an].

Conclusion: Larkspur should keep $9,000 and invest $1,600,000 in features, because competing on value avoids a price war while the rival's discount is only 12% [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement preferring investment
Rejects matching the rival's price cut
analysis_max_2: Price cut costs $2,520,000 and invites a price war
New features differentiate against the rival

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Brantmoor Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Indonesia making 180,000 wooden chairs a year, with revenue of $27,000,000. Inflation has reached 6.2% and interest rates have risen to 7.5%, while unemployment is 5.3%. A large retailer has cancelled a $4,050,000 order and timber costs are up 19%. Directors must decide whether to cut the workforce by 15% of 620 employees or reduce the price by 10% to win new retailers.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, such as the 6.2% rate now raising costs for Brantmoor Furniture Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: A sustained rise in the general price level
It reduces the purchasing power of money

questions.question_text: Calculate the number of employees remaining if Brantmoor Furniture Ltd makes 15% of its 620 employees redundant.
questions.model_answer: Redundancies = 15% of 620 = 93 employees. Remaining = 620 - 93 = 527 employees [2].

knowledge_max_2: Remaining staff = original workforce minus redundancies

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising interest rates and inflation on Brantmoor Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher borrowing and input costs [k], as rates at 7.5% and timber up 19% raise the cost of each chair [app], cutting the margin on 180,000 chairs [an].

Point 2: Weaker demand [k], because 6.2% inflation reduces households' real incomes and a retailer has cancelled a $4,050,000 order [app], leaving capacity idle [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates raise finance costs
Inflation raises input costs and cuts real incomes
analysis_max_2: Costs rise faster than prices can be raised
Lost orders leave fixed factory capacity underused

questions.question_text: Do you think Brantmoor Furniture Ltd should cut its workforce by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: an order worth $4,050,000 has been cancelled and timber is up 19% [app], so making 93 workers redundant saves wages quickly and protects cash [an]; lower output needs fewer staff [k].

Against: cutting 93 jobs removes skills that are costly to replace when demand returns [app], and a 10% price cut might win new retailers and keep capacity used [an].

Conclusion: Brantmoor should cut the workforce only after trying the 10% price reduction, because demand may recover and rehiring trained staff is expensive [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement sequencing price cuts before redundancies
Weighs quick cost savings against lost skills
analysis_max_2: Redundancies cut costs but reduce capacity and morale
Price cut may restore volume and protect jobs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Silverdale Fisheries Ltd is a private limited company in Norway catching 95,000 tonnes of mackerel a year. A marine certification body has suspended its sustainable label after 3 breaches, and two supermarket chains in Germany have stopped buying. Regaining certification requires a $2,800,000 investment in monitoring equipment. A cod quota cut has also reduced its allowed catch by 18%. Directors must decide whether to invest in certification or sell to processors without the label.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable fishing'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable fishing means catching fish at a rate that lets stocks replace themselves, such as the standard Silverdale Fisheries Ltd has just lost [2].

knowledge_max_2: Allows future catches and protects the ecosystem

questions.question_text: Calculate the reduction in Silverdale Fisheries Ltd's allowed catch if 95,000 tonnes is cut by 18%.
questions.model_answer: Reduction = 18% of 95,000 = 17,100 tonnes. New allowed catch = 95,000 - 17,100 = 77,900 tonnes [2].

knowledge_max_2: Reduction = percentage cut x current catch
New catch = current catch minus the reduction

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of losing the sustainable label on Silverdale Fisheries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lost sales [k], because two German supermarket chains have stopped buying [app], so much of the 95,000 tonnes must find other buyers [an].

Point 2: Lower prices [k], as processors buying unlabelled fish know the firm has fewer outlets [app], forcing discounts that reduce revenue per tonne [an].

knowledge_max_2: Certification is required by many retailers
Loss of a label weakens bargaining power
application_max_2: Two German supermarket chains stopped buying
analysis_max_2: Lost retail contracts cut sales volume
Fewer buyers force lower prices per tonne

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverdale Fisheries Ltd should invest $2,800,000 in regaining certification? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: certification would reopen sales to the two German supermarket chains [app], and the 18% quota cut means every tonne must earn a higher price [an]; certified fish usually sells at a premium that improves margin [k].

Against: $2,800,000 is a large sum when the allowed catch has fallen to 77,900 tonnes [app], and processors without the label will still buy the fish, perhaps at only a small discount [an].

Conclusion: Silverdale should invest, because retail chains increasingly demand certification and losing them permanently would matter more than $2,800,000 [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement on certification investment

Against: $496,000,000 is a huge commitment for a firm with $4,200,000,000 revenue and falling petrol car demand [app], and the grant may not be repeated [an].

Conclusion: Whitlock should retool, because the annual penalty of $392,000,000 would exceed the net retooling cost within two years [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement to retool
Compares annual penalty with net retooling cost
analysis_max_2: Penalty recurs annually while retooling is one-off

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quillmark Publishing Ltd is a private limited company in Spain selling 5,600,000 textbooks a year at $14 each, with 30% of sales in Poland. The Polish currency has depreciated 15% against the euro and Poland has imposed a 10% tariff on printed books. Printing costs in Spain have risen 6% after a paper shortage. Directors must decide whether to print locally in Poland under licence or keep printing in Spain.

questions.question_text: Define 'licensing'.
questions.model_answer: Licensing is allowing another firm to produce your product in return for a fee, such as the local printing arrangement Quillmark Publishing Ltd is considering in Poland [2].

knowledge_max_2: Giving another firm the right to produce your product
The licensee pays a fee or royalty to the owner

questions.question_text: Calculate the total tariff on the 1,680,000 textbooks sold in Poland at 10% of the $14 price.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff per unit = rate x price
Total = books sold in Poland x tariff per book

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the Polish currency's 15% depreciation on Quillmark Publishing Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer textbooks in Poland [k], because each $14 book now costs more of the local currency [app], so the 10% tariff adds to an already higher price [an].

Point 2: Lower value of Poland sales in euros [k], as 30% of 5,600,000 books earn weaker currency [app], reducing euro revenue even if the same number is sold [an].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker foreign currency makes exports dearer there
Foreign sales convert into less home currency
analysis_max_2: Lower conversion value cuts euro revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Quillmark Publishing Ltd should print locally in Poland under licence? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: local printing avoids the 10% tariff and the 15% currency depreciation [app], saving $2,352,000 in tariff alone on 1,680,000 books [an]; local production also shortens delivery times and cuts freight [k].

Against: licensing means sharing revenue with a Poland printer and losing control of quality [app], while Spanish printing costs are only up 6% and the firm knows the process well [an].

Conclusion: Quillmark should license only its Poland titles, because local printing removes tariff and currency risk on 30% of sales without giving up control of the rest [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement on partial licensing
Balances tariff savings against loss of control
analysis_max_2: Local printing avoids tariff and currency exposure
Licensing shares revenue and risks quality

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Glenvale Pharmaceuticals Ltd is a private limited company in India making 60,000,000 packets of medicine a year, with revenue of $240,000,000. Government health spending has been cut by 12% and inflation is 5.8%, while the central bank has raised interest rates to 6.5%. A public hospital tender worth $18,000,000 has been postponed. Directors must decide whether to cut the price of its best-selling drug by 15% or reduce the research budget by $9,000,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'public expenditure'.
questions.model_answer: Public expenditure is government spending on goods, services and projects, such as the 12% cut now affecting Glenvale Pharmaceuticals Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: Spending by government on public goods and services
Funded mainly from taxation and borrowing

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in revenue if Glenvale Pharmaceuticals Ltd cuts its price by 15% on $240,000,000 of sales.

knowledge_max_2: Fall = percentage price cut x current revenue
New revenue = original revenue minus the fall

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the cut in government health spending on Glenvale Pharmaceuticals Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lost hospital sales [k], because public hospitals buy less medicine when budgets fall 12% [app], and a tender worth $18,000,000 has already been postponed [an].

Point 2: Pressure on prices [k], as hospitals and clinics use their buying power to demand discounts [app], reducing the margin on 60,000,000 packets sold each year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower government spending reduces public sector demand
Buyers gain bargaining power when budgets are tight
application_max_2: Health spending cut 12%; tender postponed worth $18,000,000
analysis_max_2: Lost tenders reduce revenue and capacity use
Discount pressure cuts margin on every packet

questions.question_text: Do you think Glenvale Pharmaceuticals Ltd should cut the price of its best-selling drug by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: a 15% cut may win back hospital and clinic orders after the 12% spending cut [app], and cutting the $9,000,000 research budget would weaken future products [an]; medicine has steady demand, so lower prices can raise volume [k].

Against: the cut costs $36,000,000 of revenue [app], and inflation at 5.8% plus interest at 6.5% is already raising costs [an]; reducing research saves $9,000,000 without touching revenue [k].

Conclusion: Glenvale should cut the price only on the best-selling drug, not across all 60,000,000 packets, because that targets the lost hospital business while protecting research [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement targeting a single product
Compares price cut with research reduction
analysis_max_2: Price cut may restore public hospital volume
Research cut saves less but harms long-term products

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Yewfield Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Greece running 5 coastal hotels with 1,100 rooms, each using 220,000 litres of water a day. A drought has led the council to cap use at 180,000 litres a day per hotel and to raise water charges by 35%. An eco-certification scheme costs $480,000 and tour operators now favour certified hotels. Directors must decide whether to join the scheme and install water-saving showers or keep the present system and pay higher charges.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable tourism'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable tourism is travel that meets visitors' needs without damaging the environment or local communities, such as Yewfield Hotels Ltd cutting water use across 5 hotels [2].

knowledge_max_2: Tourism that limits harm to the environment
Protects resources and communities for the future

questions.question_text: Calculate the total annual reduction in water use if each of the 5 hotels cuts from 220,000 to 180,000 litres a day.
questions.model_answer: Reduction per hotel = 40,000 litres a day. For 5 hotels = 200,000 litres a day. Annual = 200,000 x 365 = 73,000,000 litres [2].

knowledge_max_2: Reduction per hotel = current use - cap
Annual saving = daily saving x 365 days

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the water cap on Yewfield Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher operating costs [k], because water charges have risen 35% across its 5 hotels while use must fall to 180,000 litres a day [app], and installing water-saving showers would cost part of $480,000 [an].

Point 2: Risk of losing tour operator bookings [k], as operators favour certified hotels [app], so guests may move to rivals if Yewfield stays uncertified [an].

knowledge_max_2: Water scarcity raises the cost of supply
Environmental standards affect bookings from tour operators
application_max_2: Cap of 180,000 litres a day; charges up 35%
analysis_max_2: Compliance raises costs but avoids restrictions
Uncertified status threatens a key distribution channel

questions.question_text: Do you think Yewfield Hotels Ltd should join the eco-certification scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: certification keeps tour operator bookings and answers the 180,000 litre cap [app], while the $480,000 cost is spread across 5 hotels and 1,100 rooms [an]; certified hotels can charge more and face fewer restrictions [k].

Against: $480,000 is significant when water charges are already up 35% [app], and showers alone may not cut use enough to meet the cap every day [an].

Conclusion: Yewfield should join the scheme, because tour operators increasingly require certification and losing bookings would cost more than $480,000 [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement to join the scheme
Weighs certification cost against lost bookings
analysis_max_2: Cost spread across 1,100 rooms is modest per room

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Redwood Components Ltd is a private limited company in Mexico making 1,800,000 car parts a year for export to America at $26 each. America has imposed a 15% tariff on imported components and the peso has appreciated 9% against the dollar. A Japaneseese manufacturer offers to buy 450,000 parts a year at $22. Directors must decide whether to accept the Japanese order or cut the American price to $22.61 to offset the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'international competitiveness'.
questions.model_answer: International competitiveness is a firm's ability to sell against rivals in world markets, such as Redwood Components Ltd facing a 15% tariff on its $26 parts [2].

knowledge_max_2: The ability to compete with foreign suppliers
Depends on price, quality, costs and trade barriers

questions.question_text: Calculate the price Redwood Components Ltd must charge so that America importers still pay $26 after the 15% tariff.
questions.model_answer: Price = $26 / 1.15 = $22.61 per part, which with the tariff returns to $26 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Divide the target border price by 1 + tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the peso's 9% appreciation on Redwood Components Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer parts in dollars [k], as each $26 part now converts into fewer pesos [app], so Redwood must charge more abroad or accept a lower peso margin on 1,800,000 parts [an].

Point 2: Cheaper imported steel [k], because raw material bought in dollars costs fewer pesos [app], which partly offsets the 15% tariff pressure [an].

analysis_max_2: Higher dollar prices weaken export competitiveness
Cheaper steel cushions the effect on unit cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Redwood Components Ltd should accept the Japanese order at $22 a part? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the order for 450,000 parts is worth $9,900,000 [app] and reduces reliance on America and its 15% tariff [an]; the peso's 9% appreciation makes $22 convert into a workable peso price [k].

Against: $22 is $4 below the current price, so the order earns $1,800,000 less than the same parts sold to America [app], and Japanese buyers demand strict quality standards [an].

Conclusion: Redwood should accept the order, because diversifying away from a tariff-affected market is worth more than $4 a part on 450,000 units [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement to accept the order
Values diversification above the unit discount
analysis_max_2: Order reduces dependence on tariff-hit America
Discount of $1,800,000 compared with existing price

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Hollowbrook Toys Ltd is a private limited company in China making 12,000,000 soft toys a year, with revenue of $96,000,000. A recession in its main markets has cut GDP by 1.5% and unemployment there has reached 7.7%, while the central bank has cut interest rates to 2.0%. Retail orders are down 22% and 1,400 of its 3,200 staff are on short-time hours. Directors must decide whether to close one of two factories or cut prices by 10% to win discount retailers.

questions.question_text: Define 'short-time working'.
questions.model_answer: Short-time working is when employees work fewer hours and earn less to avoid redundancies, such as the 1,400 Hollowbrook Toys Ltd staff now affected [2].

knowledge_max_2: Employees work fewer hours and receive less pay
Used to cut costs and avoid job losses

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in revenue if retail orders fall 22% on $96,000,000 of sales.

knowledge_max_2: Fall = percentage decline x current revenue
New revenue = original minus the fall

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession in its main markets on Hollowbrook Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Much lower sales [k], because GDP is down 1.5% and unemployment is 7.7% [app], so orders fall 22% and revenue drops by $21,120,000 [an].

Point 2: Excess capacity and higher unit costs [k], as 12,000,000 toys can no longer be sold [app], so fixed factory costs are spread over fewer units and 1,400 staff are on short-time hours [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recession reduces consumer spending on toys
Lower output raises average fixed cost per unit
application_max_2: Orders down 22%; 1,400 of 3,200 staff on short time
analysis_max_2: Falling orders cut revenue and cash flow
Underused factories raise cost per toy

questions.question_text: Do you think Hollowbrook Toys Ltd should close one of its two factories? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: orders are down 22%, so one factory could make the 9,360,000 toys still demanded [app], cutting fixed costs and ending short-time working for 1,400 staff [an]; interest rates at 2.0% make borrowing cheap but do not create demand [k].

Against: closing a factory is hard to reverse when recovery comes [app], and a 10% price cut could win discount retailers and use the spare capacity [an].

Conclusion: Hollowbrook should keep both factories for now and cut prices, because toy demand returns quickly in recovery and a closed plant cannot be reopened cheaply [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement keeping both factories
Weighs reversibility against short-term cost saving
analysis_max_2: Closure cuts fixed costs but loses capacity
Price cut can use spare capacity and win volume

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ashcombe Printing Ltd is a private limited company in Czechia printing 40,000,000 magazines a year, using 18,000 tonnes of paper. A new extended producer responsibility rule makes printers pay $210 per tonne for paper waste, and only 55% of its paper is recycled. Recycled paper costs 16% more and its paper bill is $14,400,000. Directors must decide whether to switch to 80% recycled paper or pay the waste charge and keep virgin paper.

questions.question_text: Define 'extended producer responsibility'.
questions.model_answer: Extended producer responsibility makes producers pay for the waste their products create, such as the $210 per tonne charge now facing Ashcombe Printing Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: Producers are made responsible for product waste
Usually through charges for collection or recycling

questions.question_text: Calculate Ashcombe Printing Ltd's annual waste charge on the 8,100 tonnes of paper that is not recycled.
questions.model_answer: Waste = 45% of 18,000 tonnes = 8,100 tonnes. Charge = 8,100 x $210 = $1,701,000 a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Waste = non-recycled percentage x paper used
Charge = waste tonnes x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the new rule on Ashcombe Printing Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Extra waste cost [k], because only 55% of 18,000 tonnes is recycled [app], so the charge is $1,701,000 a year [an].

Point 2: Pressure to change materials [k], as recycled paper avoids the charge but costs 16% more than the $14,400,000 bill [app], forcing a trade-off between waste charges and material costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: Waste charges add to production costs
Recycled inputs can reduce future waste charges
analysis_max_2: Waste charge is a recurring cost
Higher material cost must be weighed against the charge

questions.question_text: Do you think Ashcombe Printing Ltd should switch to 80% recycled paper? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: recycling 80% would cut waste to 3,600 tonnes and the charge to $756,000 [app], saving $945,000 against the present $1,701,000 [an]; recycled paper also meets retailer expectations for 40,000,000 magazines [k].

Against: recycled paper costs 16% more, adding $2,304,000 to a $14,400,000 bill [app], which is more than the waste charge saved [an].

Conclusion: Ashcombe should keep virgin paper for now, because the $1,701,000 charge is cheaper than the extra $2,304,000 material cost, and should switch only if the charge rises or recycled prices fall [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement not to switch at current prices
Sets a condition under which switching would pay
analysis_max_2: Higher recycling cuts the waste charge to $756,000

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Dunhollow Plastics Ltd is a private limited company in Turkey making stackable plastic crates for warehouses, with 260 staff and revenue of $12,500,000 a year. Inflation has climbed to 24.6% and the central bank has raised interest rates to 31.5%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $3,000,000 for a new moulding machine or delay the investment.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services [2]; Turkey's 24.6% rate means Dunhollow Plastics Ltd pays more for resin, power and the wages of its 260 staff.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general or average price level
Money loses purchasing power as prices climb

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Dunhollow Plastics Ltd would pay on a $3,000,000 loan at 31.5%.

knowledge_max_2: Interest = amount borrowed x interest rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 31.5% interest rate on Dunhollow Plastics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The machine loan becomes very costly [k]. Borrowing $3,000,000 at 31.5% adds $945,000 of interest a year [app], which must be paid before the moulding machine makes a single crate and takes 7.6% of the $12,500,000 revenue [an].

Point 2: Trade customers buy less on credit [k]. Higher rates make Turkish warehouse operators reluctant to finance new racking and crates [app], so orders may fall just as Dunhollow needs volume to spread its fixed costs [an].

analysis_max_2: Interest is paid before the machine earns anything
Falling orders leave fixed costs spread over fewer crates

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunhollow Plastics Ltd should borrow $3,000,000 for the moulding machine? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A new machine should cut reject rates and lift output per worker, helping Dunhollow spread its fixed costs and defend sales of $12,500,000. Buying now also fixes the machinery price before 24.6% inflation pushes it higher.

Against: At 31.5% the interest bill is $945,000 a year, about 7.6% of revenue, and Turkish warehouse demand is weak while inflation erodes customers' budgets. If crate orders fall, the repayments still fall due.

Conclusion: Delay the investment. The interest cost is high against the $12,500,000 revenue and 24.6% inflation leaves too little margin for error.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs the $945,000 interest bill against the efficiency gain
Recommends delay because demand is uncertain
analysis_max_2: 24.6% inflation raises costs and squeezes customer budgets

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Veremont Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in Portugal bottling milk and yoghurt, with 120 staff and 18,000,000 bottles sold a year. A new packaging levy charges $0.03 on every plastic bottle, while inflation of 3.4% is raising glass and transport costs. Directors must decide whether to switch to returnable glass bottles costing $0.09 each instead of $0.05 plastic.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of business activity paid by third parties rather than the business itself [2]; Veremont Dairy Ltd's 18,000,000 plastic bottles create litter that Portuguese councils must collect and dispose of.

knowledge_max_2: A cost borne by people outside the business
Examples include pollution, litter and congestion

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual cost to Veremont Dairy Ltd of switching all 18,000,000 bottles from $0.05 plastic to $0.09 glass.

knowledge_max_2: Find the difference in cost per bottle

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the packaging levy might affect Veremont Dairy Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The levy raises the cost of every plastic bottle [k]. At $0.03 across 18,000,000 bottles it adds $540,000 a year [app], so Veremont must accept a lower margin or lift prices and risk losing shoppers in Portugal [an].

Point 2: It makes returnable glass more attractive [k]. Glass escapes the levy but costs $0.09 against $0.05, an extra $720,000 [app]; directors must weigh that against the $540,000 levy and the goodwill gained from cutting plastic waste [an].

knowledge_max_2: Levy raises the cost of plastic packaging
Levy encourages a switch to reusable packaging
analysis_max_2: Higher costs squeeze margins or force a price rise
Glass costs more but avoids the levy and builds goodwill

questions.question_text: Do you think Veremont Dairy Ltd should switch to returnable glass bottles at $0.09 each? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Glass escapes the $0.03 levy, which alone costs $540,000 a year on 18,000,000 bottles, and a returnable bottle can be used many times. The greener image may win shelf space with Portuguese retailers who face pressure over plastic waste.

Against: The switch adds $720,000 a year, so the net cost is $180,000 even after saving the levy. Glass is heavier to transport and breaks, and 3.4% inflation is already lifting costs while milk prices stay competitive.

Conclusion: Switch only with a deposit scheme that recovers bottles. The environmental gain is real, but the $180,000 net cost is hard to justify unless return rates are high.

evaluation_max_2: Sets the $720,000 extra cost against the $540,000 levy saved
Makes the recommendation conditional on high return rates
analysis_max_2: 3.4% inflation and heavy glass raise distribution costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kestrelbay Marine Ltd is a private limited company in Thailand making stainless boat fittings for American buyers, with 180 staff and export revenue of $6,400,000. The baht has fallen 9% against the dollar to 35.32 baht per dollar, and a US tariff of 5% now applies to fittings. Directors must decide whether to quote a new $48,000 order in dollars or baht.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in another currency [2]; Kestrelbay Marine Ltd converts its $48,000 order at 35.32 baht per dollar.

knowledge_max_2: Price of one currency in terms of another
It is set by supply and demand for currencies

questions.question_text: Calculate the baht value of the $48,000 order at 35.32 baht per dollar.
questions.model_answer: Working: $48,000 x 35.32 = 1,695,360. The order is therefore worth 1,695,360 baht [2].

knowledge_max_2: Multiply the dollar value by the exchange rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 9% fall in the baht on Kestrelbay Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Fittings become cheaper for American buyers [k]. With the baht 9% lower, the same dollar price converts into more baht [app], so Kestrelbay can win extra orders and still cover the wages of its 180 staff [an].

Point 2: Imported stainless steel costs more [k]. The 5% US tariff already trims margins on $6,400,000 of sales, and a weaker baht makes every imported coil dearer in baht [app], so the export gain may be cancelled out [an].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency makes exports cheaper
A weaker currency raises import prices
application_max_2: US tariff of 5% on $6,400,000 of sales
analysis_max_2: Extra American orders at better baht margins
Dearer imported steel offsets the export gain

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrelbay Marine Ltd should quote the $48,000 order in dollars rather than baht? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A dollar quote gives the American buyer a fixed price, removing their currency risk and making Kestrelbay easier to deal with. At 35.32 baht per dollar the order is worth 1,695,360 baht, a useful sum while the baht is weak.

Against: If the baht recovers, the same $48,000 will buy fewer baht and Kestrelbay loses income while its 180 staff are paid in baht. The 5% US tariff is also fixed in dollars, so a dollar quote locks in both effects.

Conclusion: Quote in dollars for this order. The 9% fall has already improved the baht value of dollar sales, and price certainty should help win repeat business.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs currency certainty against a possible baht recovery
Accepts dollar invoicing while the baht is weak
analysis_max_2: Wages are paid in baht, so recovery would hurt

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Jarrowfield Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Mexico producing canned beans, with 310 staff and profit before tax of $4,800,000. The government has raised corporation tax from 30% to 33%, and inflation of 4.7% is pushing up tinplate and fuel. Directors must decide whether to raise prices by 5% or cut 20 jobs.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct tax'.
questions.model_answer: A direct tax is a tax paid on income or profit by the person or business that earns it [2]; Jarrowfield Foods Ltd pays 33% corporation tax on its $4,800,000 profit.

knowledge_max_2: Paid directly by the earner and cannot be passed on

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual tax Jarrowfield Foods Ltd pays because corporation tax rises from 30% to 33% on $4,800,000 profit.
Explain two effects of the higher corporation tax on Jarrowfield Foods Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit falls [k]. The 3 point rise takes an extra $144,000, leaving less of the $4,800,000 profit for new canning lines or to repay debt [app], so expansion may be postponed [an].

Point 2: Directors may lift prices to protect profit [k]. A 5% rise on canned beans would pass the $144,000 to Mexican supermarkets [app], but shoppers facing 4.7% inflation may switch to cheaper brands [an].

knowledge_max_2: Business may raise prices to protect profit
application_max_2: A 5% price rise is being considered
analysis_max_2: Price rise risks losing inflation-hit customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Jarrowfield Foods Ltd should raise prices by 5% rather than cut 20 jobs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 5% price rise spreads the extra $144,000 tax across many customers instead of losing the skills of 20 staff. Keeping the workforce protects output and morale, and canned beans are a basic food that shoppers still buy during hard times.

Against: With inflation at 4.7%, a 5% rise leaves customers no better off and may push them to cheaper own-brand beans. Cutting 20 jobs from 310 staff saves wages immediately and avoids a permanent price increase.

Conclusion: Raise prices, but only by about 3%. The full 5% risks volume, while losing 20 trained staff would slow production when demand recovers.

evaluation_max_2: Compares a price rise with the loss of 20 jobs
Recommends a smaller price rise as a compromise

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Plovercrag Cement Ltd is a public limited company in Egypt producing cement, with 480 staff and output of 240,000 tonnes a year. A carbon tax of $18 per tonne of emissions has been introduced, and energy inflation has reached 11.2%. Directors must decide whether to invest $2,600,000 in a more efficient kiln or pay the tax.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of production borne by third parties rather than the business [2]; Plovercrag Cement Ltd's 240,000 tonnes of emissions damage air quality for people living near the plant.

knowledge_max_2: A cost paid by third parties, not the producer
Pollution and health damage are common examples

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual carbon tax bill for 240,000 tonnes at $18 per tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Tax = tonnes emitted x tax per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the carbon tax on Plovercrag Cement Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise sharply [k]. At $18 a tonne the tax comes to $4,320,000 on 240,000 tonnes [app], which is a large slice of cement revenue and must be recovered through higher prices [an].

Point 2: The efficient kiln becomes more attractive [k]. Energy inflation is already 11.2%, so a kiln that burns less fuel cuts both bills [app]; the $2,600,000 outlay would pay back faster as the tax continues [an].

application_max_2: Energy inflation of 11.2% and a $2,600,000 kiln
analysis_max_2: Higher costs must be passed to builders
Lower fuel use cuts both tax and energy bills

questions.question_text: Do you think Plovercrag Cement Ltd should invest $2,600,000 in the efficient kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The kiln cuts fuel use, so it lowers both the $4,320,000 carbon bill and energy costs already rising at 11.2%. Cement demand from Egyptian builders is steady, and a greener plant helps win contracts that demand lower-carbon materials.

Against: The $2,600,000 outlay is large, and the kiln may take years to repay while cement prices are held down by rivals. If the tax is reduced after the next election, the saving disappears.

Conclusion: Invest, but in stages. The tax plus 11.2% energy inflation makes the saving fairly certain, yet staging the spend protects cash flow if construction slows.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs the $4,320,000 tax saving against the $2,600,000 cost
Supports a staged investment to protect cash flow
analysis_max_2: Fuel savings cut both tax and energy bills

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marlowe Bend Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Indonesia making teak garden chairs for Dutch retailers, with 220 staff and export sales of $2,800,000. The European Union has imposed a 12% tariff on wooden furniture, inflation is 5.1%, and the next shipment is worth $250,000. Directors must decide whether to absorb the tariff or raise European prices by 9%.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax charged on imported goods [2]; the European Union's 12% tariff adds $30,000 to Marlowe Bend Furniture Ltd's $250,000 shipment.

knowledge_max_2: It raises the price of foreign goods in the importing country

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff payable on a $250,000 shipment at 12%.
questions.model_answer: Working: $250,000 x 12% = $30,000. The tariff payable on the shipment is $30,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff = value of shipment x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 12% tariff on Marlowe Bend Furniture Ltd.

questions.question_text: Do you think Brindlemoor Dairy plc should switch to the recyclable film costing EUR 240,000? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sablecrest Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Morocco running a 240-room resort, selling 24,000 room-nights a year at an average rate of $85. questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.

Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising unemployment on Sablecrest Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Bookings fall as incomes weaken [k]. With unemployment at 13.4% and arrivals down 15%, the hotel loses about 3,600 room-nights worth $306,000 [app], leaving rooms empty while fixed costs such as the 240-room building still have to be paid [an].

Point 2: Recruitment becomes easier and cheaper [k]. Higher unemployment in Morocco means more applicants for housekeeping and kitchen roles at $85 a night room rates [app], so wage pressure eases even though revenue is falling [an].

knowledge_max_2: Demand falls with lower household income
analysis_max_2: Empty rooms still carry fixed costs
Lower wage pressure partly offsets lost revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Sablecrest Hotels Ltd should make 30 staff redundant rather than cut rates by 12%? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising energy prices and efficiency rules on Orlestone Appliances plc.

questions.question_text: Do you think Orlestone Appliances plc should approve the $150,000 smart sensors? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Drayholt Timber Ltd is a private limited company in Finland sawing softwood, selling 45,000 cubic metres a year to United Kingdom builders at $210 a cubic metre. questions.question_text: Define 'quota'.

questions.question_text: Do you think Drayholt Timber Ltd should build the UK sawmill for $8,000,000? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Mirefield Poultry Ltd is a private limited company in Poland processing chicken, employing 320 staff on an average wage of $1,150 a month. questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: A minimum wage is the lowest hourly or monthly pay that employers are legally allowed to give workers [2]; Poland's 9% increase lifts the floor under Mirefield Poultry Ltd's average wage of $1,150 a month.

knowledge_max_2: Set by government to protect low-paid workers

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra monthly wage bill for Mirefield Poultry Ltd from a 9% rise on 320 staff paid $1,150 a month.
questions.model_answer: 9% of $1,150 = $103.50; 320 x $103.50 = $33,120 extra a month on the wage bill [2].

knowledge_max_2: Rise per worker x number of staff

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 9% minimum wage rise on Mirefield Poultry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Labour costs increase [k]. The rise adds $33,120 a month, about $397,440 a year, to a payroll of 320 staff [app], which cuts the margin on chicken portions sold at supermarket prices agreed months earlier [an].

Point 2: The case for automation strengthens [k]. Spending $700,000 on deboning equipment replaces tasks now costing $33,120 a month extra [app], and machines do not need wage rises, though 320 staff may fear losing work [an].

knowledge_max_2: Pressure to substitute capital for labour
analysis_max_2: Machines cut future wage exposure but affect morale

questions.question_text: Do you think Mirefield Poultry Ltd should spend $700,000 on automated deboning equipment? Justify your answer.

Against: $700,000 is a large outlay when orders are not growing, and the firm must still pay redundancy and retraining costs for staff [an]. Polish labour remains cheaper than machines in some roles, and breakdowns could halt production [ev].

evaluation_max_2: $397,440 annual saving against $700,000
Outlay risk with flat orders

Risk that shortage eases

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

Older vessels raise fuel and repair costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Nordvik Ferries Ltd should postpone the $9,000,000 vessel order? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem: Willowgarth Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Portugal making wall tiles, exporting EUR 1,500,000 a year to United States distributors and invoicing in euros. Makes exports dearer and imports cheaper

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar price of EUR 1,500,000 of tiles at $1.08 and at $1.14, and the increase.

analysis_max_2: Margin or installation price must adjust

questions.question_text: Do you think Solmara Solar Ltd should buy the Spanish cells costing 12% more? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Spanish cells avoid the EUR 162,000 duty and cut delivery times, letting Solmara fit installations faster during the sunny season [an]. Shorter supply chains appeal to customers buying green energy [ev].

Against: The Spanish price is about EUR 216,000 more, roughly EUR 54,000 worse than paying the duty, so profit falls [ev]. Asian cells are proven and available in large volumes, while a single Spanish supplier may struggle to meet demand [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

Creates external costs for third parties

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual water cost saved by a 60% cut in use of 180,000 cubic metres at $0.90.

questions.question_text: Do you think Mekong Weavers Ltd should install the $400,000 treatment plant? Justify your answer.

Makes exports cheaper and imports dearer

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Jerantut Rubber Ltd is a private limited company in Malaysia making surgical gloves, with sales of $7,500,000 a year and 1,800 workers. questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period in which national output falls for at least two consecutive quarters [2]; Malaysia's downturn is expected to cut Jerantut Rubber Ltd's hospital orders by 12%.

knowledge_max_2: Fall in national output over two quarters
Brings lower incomes, spending and employment

questions.question_text: Calculate the sales revenue Jerantut Rubber Ltd expects to lose if orders fall 12% from $7,500,000.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = sales x percentage fall

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession on Jerantut Rubber Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue falls while costs stay fixed [k]. Orders dropping 12% removes $900,000 from $7,500,000 of sales [app], so the 1,800 wages and factory overheads must be paid from a smaller income, squeezing profit [an].

Point 2: Unemployment rises and recruitment improves [k]. As Malaysian job losses spread, the firm can hire skilled machine operators more easily and at lower pay [app], but consumer and hospital spending weakens further [an].

analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over fewer gloves

questions.question_text: Do you think Jerantut Rubber Ltd should make 150 staff redundant rather than use short-time working? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:

Against: Skilled glove makers are hard to replace, and rehiring when hospitals reorder will be slow and expensive [an]. Short-time working shares the burden, keeps morale and avoids redundancy payments, even though wages stay partly fixed [ev].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Serra Verde Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Brazil roasting and packing coffee, exporting 30,000 bags a year at $180 a bag to one country that has imposed a 15% tariff on green coffee. questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff paid on 30,000 bags at $180 each when the rate is 15%.

questions.question_text: Do you think Serra Verde Foods Ltd should switch to the market charging 4%? Justify your answer.

Against: New packaging and buyer approval take time and money, and the existing buyers already accept Brazilian coffee [an]. The tariff may be temporary, and leaving could lose shelf space permanently [ev].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on the $4,000,000 loan at 9.5%.
Explain two effects of the 9.5% interest rate on Wardha Cotton Ltd.

Point 1: Buying looms becomes expensive [k]. Interest on $4,000,000 reaches $380,000 a year, which is $80,000 more than leasing at $300,000 [app], so the lease looks cheaper on annual cost alone [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Wardha Cotton Ltd should lease the looms instead of buying them? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual cost if Makassar Cocoa Ltd's $3,200,000 of costs rise by 5.9%.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 5.9% inflation on Makassar Cocoa Ltd.

questions.question_text: Do you think Makassar Cocoa Ltd should raise prices by 6% rather than cut 40 jobs? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

A carbon price of $30 a tonne now applies to emissions, and a solar farm costing $6,000,000 would cut 18,000 tonnes. Directors must decide whether to build the solar farm.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means operating without depleting resources or damaging the environment for future generations [2]; Al Waha Water Ltd would cut 18,000 tonnes of emissions and rely more on the sun.

knowledge_max_2: Meeting present needs without harming the future

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual carbon cost avoided by cutting 18,000 tonnes at $30 a tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Avoided cost = tonnes cut x carbon price

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the carbon price on Al Waha Water Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Emissions become a direct cost [k]. Paying $30 on 42,000 tonnes would cost $1,260,000 a year if none were cut [app], which is a heavy charge on a plant selling water at regulated prices [an].

Point 2: The solar farm becomes financially sensible [k]. Cutting 18,000 tonnes avoids $540,000 a year [app], so the $6,000,000 investment earns a return while also reducing exposure to future carbon prices [an].

knowledge_max_2: Adds a cost per tonne emitted
analysis_max_2: Regulated water prices limit cost recovery
Return improves as carbon price rises

questions.question_text: Do you think Al Waha Water Ltd should build the $6,000,000 solar farm? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The farm avoids $540,000 of carbon cost a year and protects the firm if the $30 price rises, while the desert site gives strong solar output [ev]. Lower emissions also support the government's green targets and the firm's licence [an].

Against: $6,000,000 is a large outlay against $540,000 a year, and water prices are regulated so the saving cannot be passed to customers [ev]. Dust and heat reduce panel output in the Gulf, raising maintenance costs [an].

evaluation_max_2: $540,000 annual saving and rising carbon price
Capital size and regulated prices

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Najd Steel Ltd is a private limited company in Saudi Arabia rolling reinforcement bar, importing 60,000 tonnes of steel scrap a year at $320 a tonne. questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods charged as a percentage of their value [2]; the 10% tariff raises the cost of Najd Steel Ltd's 60,000 tonnes of imported scrap.

knowledge_max_2: Raises the price of imported raw materials

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on 60,000 tonnes of scrap at $320 a tonne when the rate is 10%.
Explain two effects of the 10% tariff on Najd Steel Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Raw material costs rise [k]. The tariff adds $1,920,000 to a $19,200,000 scrap bill [app], pushing up the cost of every tonne of reinforcement bar rolled in Saudi Arabia [an].

Point 2: Local supply becomes more attractive [k]. The dealer's price is 7% higher, about $1,344,000 more, which is $576,000 less than the tariff [app], so switching saves money but ties the firm to one supplier [an].

knowledge_max_2: Improves the position of local suppliers
analysis_max_2: Dependence on a single local dealer

questions.question_text: Do you think Najd Steel Ltd should switch to the local scrap dealer charging 7% more? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Local scrap costs about $1,344,000 more than the old import price but $576,000 less than paying the $1,920,000 tariff [ev]. Shorter supply lines reduce freight and let the mill respond quickly to construction orders [an].

Against: Relying on one dealer weakens bargaining power and risks shortages that could stop the rolling line [an]. The tariff may be removed, leaving the firm locked into a dearer contract [ev].
