evaluation_max_2: $576,000 saving against the tariff
Single supplier risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Aqaba Marine Ltd is a private limited company in Jordan repairing boat engines, using 260,000 litres of diesel a year at $1.05 a litre in test beds. The government has removed the fuel subsidy, raising diesel prices by 18%, and hauliers are pressing for lower delivery charges. Directors must decide whether to raise charges by 4% or absorb the increase.

questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A subsidy is a payment from government to a producer that lowers its costs or the price consumers pay [2]; removing Jordan's fuel subsidy raised Aqaba Marine Ltd's diesel price by 18%.

knowledge_max_2: Shifts supply right and lowers price

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual diesel cost from an 18% rise on 260,000 litres at $1.05.
Explain two effects of removing the fuel subsidy on Aqaba Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Running costs jump [k]. Diesel for 260,000 litres now costs $49,140 more a year at $1.05 plus 18% [app], cutting the margin on every engine repaired [an].

Point 2: Prices across the economy rise [k]. Jordanian hauliers and fishermen hit by the same 18% fuel rise postpone repairs [app], so demand for Aqaba Marine's workshop falls just as its costs climb [an].

knowledge_max_2: Demand falls as customers face higher costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Aqaba Marine Ltd should raise its charges by 4%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 4% rise spreads the $49,140 diesel increase across customers instead of wiping out profit, and boat owners need repairs before the season [an]. Passing on part of the cost keeps the workshop viable without a large jump [ev].

Against: Hauliers and fishermen are themselves hit by the 18% fuel rise, so a price increase may send them to cheaper workshops [ev]. Absorbing the cost protects volume and the firm's reputation in a small port [an].

Conclusion: Raise charges by about 2%, because full recovery risks losing the customers whose engines keep the workshop busy [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Partial recovery protects margin
Customers also face 18% fuel rise
analysis_max_2: Volume loss in a small market

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Yarden Irrigation Ltd is a private limited company in Israel moulding plastic drip-line fittings, generating 900 tonnes of plastic waste a year. A new levy of $140 a tonne applies to plastic waste sent for disposal, while recycled compound would add $90,000 to annual material costs. Directors must decide whether to switch to recycled compound or pay the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is the reprocessing of waste materials into usable products instead of disposing of them [2]; Yarden Irrigation Ltd could turn 900 tonnes of plastic waste into fittings using recycled compound.

knowledge_max_2: Reduces disposal and raw material use

questions.question_text: Calculate Yarden Irrigation Ltd's annual plastic waste levy on 900 tonnes at $140 a tonne.
Explain two effects of the plastic waste levy on Yarden Irrigation Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Disposal becomes costly [k]. Paying $140 on 900 tonnes costs $126,000 a year [app], which is a direct charge on profit for waste the firm currently throws away [an].

Point 2: Recycled material looks cheaper overall [k]. Recycled compound adds $90,000 to material costs but cuts the $126,000 levy [app], so the net cost falls by about $36,000 while waste to disposal drops [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Yarden Irrigation Ltd should switch to recycled compound? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Switching cuts the $126,000 levy and adds only $90,000 of material cost, a net gain of about $36,000, and it reduces 900 tonnes of waste [ev]. Farmers buying irrigation equipment increasingly prefer suppliers with recycled content [an].

Against: The gain is small and recycled plastic can vary in strength, risking leaks in fittings that farmers rely on [ev]. The $90,000 extra cost is certain, while levy savings depend on waste actually being diverted [an].

Conclusion: Switch, because a net saving plus a stronger ethical story outweigh the small quality risk, provided the compound is tested [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Net gain about $36,000
Quality variability of recycled plastic

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Nemunas Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Lithuania making flat-pack oak furniture, with sales of $8,000,000 a year of which 60% goes to one export market. That market has imposed a 6% tariff, and opening a distribution depot there would cost $350,000 a year to run. Directors must decide whether to open the depot.

questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of world economies through trade, investment and movement of people [2]; Nemunas Furniture Ltd sells 60% of $8,000,000 of output abroad and must respond to another country's tariff.

knowledge_max_2: Rises through trade, investment and technology

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on exports of 60% of $8,000,000 at 6%.
Explain two effects of the 6% tariff on Nemunas Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export prices rise in the target market [k]. The tariff adds $288,000 to $4,800,000 of sales [app], so retailers there may reduce orders or switch to local furniture makers [an].

Point 2: A local depot becomes more attractive [k]. Holding stock inside the market would not remove the tariff but would speed delivery and support retailers [app], though $350,000 a year exceeds the $288,000 tariff [an].

knowledge_max_2: Encourages local presence in the market
analysis_max_2: Retailers may switch to local makers

questions.question_text: Do you think Nemunas Furniture Ltd should open the distribution depot costing $350,000 a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A depot shortens delivery times and lets retailers hold less stock, which can win shelf space and lift sales above the $4,800,000 now exported [an]. It also shows commitment, making buyers less likely to leave because of the 6% tariff [ev].

Against: The depot costs $350,000 a year, more than the $288,000 tariff, so it adds cost before any extra sale [ev]. A single market already takes 60% of output, so concentrating further increases risk [an].

Conclusion: Do not open the depot yet, because $350,000 exceeds the tariff and the firm should first diversify away from one market taking 60% of sales [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Service gains may raise sales
$350,000 exceeds the $288,000 tariff

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Istria Marine Ltd is a private limited company in Croatia making stainless winches for yachts, with sales of $5,000,000 and 120 skilled staff. Directors must decide whether to make 25 staff redundant or cut all hours by one day a week.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when a country's real output falls for two consecutive quarters, bringing lower incomes and spending [2]; Croatia's downturn is expected to cut Istria Marine Ltd's orders by 18%.

knowledge_max_2: Two successive quarters of falling output
Leads to lower demand and higher unemployment

questions.question_text: Calculate the sales revenue lost if orders fall 18% from $5,000,000.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = sales x percentage fall

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession on Istria Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue falls against fixed costs [k]. An 18% drop removes $900,000 from $5,000,000 of sales [app], while the workshop, machinery and 120 staff still have to be paid [an].

Point 2: Yacht buyers delay purchases [k]. In a recession, owners postpone refits and new winches [app], so orders may stay weak even after the economy turns, slowing cost recovery on any stock held [an].

analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over fewer winches
Recovery in demand lags the economy

questions.question_text: Do you think Istria Marine Ltd should make 25 staff redundant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Redundancy cuts wage costs immediately and matches the 18% fall that removes $900,000 of sales, protecting cash through the winter [an]. Keeping 95 rather than 120 staff may be enough for the reduced order book [ev].

Against: Skilled winch makers are hard to replace, and rehiring before next summer's season would be slow [an]. Cutting one day a week for all 120 staff shares the pain, keeps skills and avoids redundancy payments [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Immediate wage saving
Skill loss before seasonal recovery

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Aegean Olive Ltd is a private limited company in Greece pressing extra virgin olive oil, with revenue of EUR 2,400,000 a year. questions.question_text: Define 'fair trade'.
questions.model_answer: Fair trade is a trading arrangement that guarantees producers a minimum price and a premium, while requiring decent working conditions [2]; Aegean Olive Ltd would need certification to sell at a 12% premium to northern European retailers.

knowledge_max_2: Guaranteed price and premium for producers
Requires ethical labour and environmental standards

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from a 12% premium on EUR 2,400,000 of certified oil.
questions.model_answer: EUR 2,400,000 x 12% = EUR 288,000 extra a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Premium revenue = sales x premium rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of fair trade certification on Aegean Olive Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue rises through a premium [k]. A 12% premium on EUR 2,400,000 adds EUR 288,000 [app], which is nearly double the EUR 150,000 certification cost [an].

Point 2: Access to retailers depends on the label [k]. Northern European buyers will stock only certified brands next season [app], so refusing certification could cost the firm those listings entirely [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Aegean Olive Ltd should apply for fair trade certification? Justify your answer.

Against: Certification requires audits of pickers' pay and land use, which may force costly changes beyond the EUR 150,000 fee [ev]. Retailers might still press for discounts, eroding the premium [an].

Audit and compliance costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Valsesia Pasta Ltd is a private limited company in Italy making dried pasta, importing 4,000 tonnes of durum wheat a year at EUR 420 a tonne from Canada. questions.question_text: Define 'import'.
questions.model_answer: An import is a good or service bought from another country for use or sale in the home country [2]; Valsesia Pasta Ltd imports 4,000 tonnes of Canadian durum wheat a year at EUR 420 a tonne.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on 4,000 tonnes of durum at EUR 420 a tonne when the rate is 7%.
Explain two effects of the 7% tariff on Valsesia Pasta Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Wheat costs more [k]. The tariff adds EUR 117,600 to a EUR 1,680,000 wheat bill [app], raising the cost of every packet of pasta unless the recipe or price changes [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Valsesia Pasta Ltd should switch to Italian durum wheat? Justify your answer.

Quality change and tariff removal risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Waldviertel Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Austria making wooden toys, with sales of $3,600,000 a year and 85 employees. questions.question_text: Define 'tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax is a compulsory payment to government on income, profit, sales or assets, used to fund public spending [2]; Austria's sales tax rise from 20% to 22% reduces what Waldviertel Toys Ltd keeps from each sale.

knowledge_max_2: Used to raise revenue or change behaviour

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in net revenue if 2% is lost on sales of $3,600,000.
Explain two effects of the sales tax rise on Waldviertel Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Net revenue falls if prices are held [k]. Keeping shelf prices unchanged with tax at 22% costs $72,000 on $3,600,000 of sales [app], a direct cut in the margin on every wooden toy [an].

Point 2: Demand may fall if prices rise [k]. Passing the 2% on makes toys dearer for Austrian families [app], and wooden toys are easily replaced by cheaper plastic alternatives, so volume could drop [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Waldviertel Toys Ltd should raise shelf prices to cover the tax rise? Justify your answer.

Against: Wooden toys face close substitutes, so a price rise may shift buyers to cheaper plastic toys and lose volume worth more than $72,000 [ev]. Keeping prices stable supports the firm's value reputation before the Christmas season [an].

Volume loss from substitutes

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Vltava Glass Ltd is a private limited company in Czechia making crystal glassware, operating a gas furnace that emits 5,200 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year against a free permit allocation of 4,600 tonnes. questions.question_text: Define 'government regulation'.
questions.model_answer: Government regulation is a rule backed by law that businesses must follow, such as a cap on emissions [2]; Vltava Glass Ltd may emit only 4,600 tonnes free and must buy permits for the remaining 600 tonnes.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of permits for emissions above the 4,600 tonne allocation at EUR 70 a tonne.
Explain two effects of the permit scheme on Vltava Glass Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Excess emissions carry a price [k]. The 600 tonnes above the free allocation cost EUR 42,000 a year [app], reducing the profit on hand-cut crystal sold to hotels and shops [an].

Point 2: Replacing the furnace becomes worthwhile [k]. A EUR 900,000 electric furnace cutting 2,000 tonnes would end the permit purchase and leave 1,400 tonnes to sell [app], but the capital cost is large for a craft producer [an].

analysis_max_2: Capital cost high for a craft firm

questions.question_text: Do you think Vltava Glass Ltd should replace the furnace at a cost of EUR 900,000? Justify your answer.

Against: EUR 900,000 is more than twenty times the annual permit cost, so the financial case is weak unless energy savings are large [ev]. Crystal making is a traditional craft, and a new furnace may alter the melting process [an].

Cost is twenty times the permit bill
analysis_max_2: Process change risk in craft production

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tisza Canning Ltd is a private limited company in Hungary canning sweetcorn, exporting 1,800,000 cans a year at EUR 0.55 a can to one trade bloc. questions.question_text: Define 'trade bloc'.
questions.model_answer: A trade bloc is a group of countries that reduce or remove trade barriers among members and may set a common external tariff [2]; the bloc buying Tisza Canning Ltd's sweetcorn now charges 9% on its cans.

knowledge_max_2: Group of countries with reduced internal barriers

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on 1,800,000 cans at EUR 0.55 a can when the rate is 9%.
Explain two effects of the 9% tariff on Tisza Canning Ltd.

Point 1: The margin is squeezed [k]. Absorbing the tariff costs EUR 89,100 on EUR 990,000 of exports [app], leaving less profit from 1,800,000 cans sold at EUR 0.55 [an].

analysis_max_2: Lower volume raises unit fixed cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Tisza Canning Ltd should absorb the 9% tariff rather than cut output? Justify your answer.

Against: EUR 89,100 is a tenth of export revenue, and absorbing it may turn a profitable contract into a loss [ev]. Cutting output and finding another buyer, even at a lower price, may lose less [an].

evaluation_max_2: Keeps volume and buyer relationships
EUR 89,100 is a tenth of revenue
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over full output

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Carpathia Footwear Ltd is a private limited company in Romania making leather boots, with materials costing EUR 1,400,000 a year and 260 employees. questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, so money buys less over time [2]; Romania's 8.2% rate is raising Carpathia Footwear Ltd's leather and wage costs.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual materials cost if EUR 1,400,000 rises by 8.2%.

knowledge_max_2: Extra cost = materials bill x inflation

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 8.2% inflation on Carpathia Footwear Ltd.

Point 1: Materials costs rise [k]. An 8.2% rise on EUR 1,400,000 adds EUR 114,800 a year [app], and because leather is rising faster than wages, the squeeze is worse than the headline rate suggests [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Carpathia Footwear Ltd should raise boot prices by 5%? Justify your answer.

analysis_max_2: Partial recovery still leaves a gap
Volume protects wage cost per pair

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Rila Rose Ltd is a private limited company in Bulgaria distilling rose oil, buying 12,000 kilograms of petals a year from small growers. questions.question_text: Define 'ethical trading'.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual payment to growers from $18 a kilogram on 12,000 kilograms.

questions.question_text: Do you think Rila Rose Ltd should join the fair trade scheme? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Calculate the export revenue lost when the quota cuts sales from 4,000 to 3,200 tonnes at EUR 2,200 a tonne.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the EU quota on Morava Berry Ltd.

questions.question_text: Do you think Morava Berry Ltd should build cold storage for the surplus rather than cut growers' contracts? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Saaremaa Plywood Ltd is a private limited company in Estonia making birch plywood, with sales of $6,400,000 a year and 300 workers. Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Calculate the sales revenue lost if sales fall 14% from $6,400,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising unemployment on Saaremaa Plywood Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand for plywood falls [k]. With unemployment at 9.6% and sales down 14%, the firm loses $896,000 of revenue [app], leaving the mill with capacity it cannot use [an].

Point 2: Wage pressure eases [k]. High unemployment in Estonia means 300 workers are less likely to demand big rises and vacancies are easier to fill [app], which partly offsets the lost revenue [an].

analysis_max_2: Easier recruitment and lower pay pressure

questions.question_text: Do you think Saaremaa Plywood Ltd should make 60 of its 300 staff redundant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cutting 60 jobs matches the 14% fall that removes $896,000 of sales and protects cash through the downturn [an]. A smaller workforce is cheaper than paying 300 people for hours not needed [ev].

Against: Plywood skills take time to learn, and rehiring when construction recovers would be costly [an]. Reduced hours for all 300 keep the mill ready to raise output quickly when orders return [ev].

Conclusion: Use reduced hours first, because the fall looks cyclical and $896,000 of sales should return with construction [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Wage saving matches lost sales
Skill loss and rehiring costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kurzeme Peat Ltd is a private limited company in Latvia extracting peat for bagged garden compost, taking 240,000 cubic metres a year from protected bogs. A new nature levy of $4.50 a cubic metre applies, and a bog restoration plan costing $600,000 is required before the licence is renewed for another five years. Directors must decide whether to continue extraction.

questions.question_text: Define 'external costs'.
questions.model_answer: External costs are the harmful side effects of production felt by third parties, such as damaged wetlands [2]; Kurzeme Peat Ltd creates them by extracting 240,000 cubic metres from protected bogs.

knowledge_max_2: Harm to third parties from production
Not reflected in the firm's private costs

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual nature levy on 240,000 cubic metres at $4.50 a cubic metre.
Explain two effects of the nature levy on Kurzeme Peat Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Extraction becomes much costlier [k]. The levy adds $1,080,000 a year on 240,000 cubic metres [app], which is a large charge relative to compost sales [an].

Point 2: Restoration raises the barrier to staying [k]. The $600,000 bog restoration must be funded before the licence is renewed [app], so total compliance costs $1,680,000 in the first year and may make the site unviable [an].

analysis_max_2: Large charge relative to compost revenue
Combined costs may make the site unviable

questions.question_text: Do you think Kurzeme Peat Ltd should continue peat extraction? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Peat compost has loyal garden centre buyers, and paying $1,080,000 of levy plus $600,000 restoration keeps 240,000 cubic metres of output and protects jobs [an]. The licence and equipment have value that closing would waste [ev].

Against: The combined $1,680,000 first-year cost may exceed the profit from the bogs, and the levy could rise again [ev]. Damaged wetlands bring reputational damage as gardeners turn to peat-free compost [an].

Conclusion: Stop extraction and move to peat-free compost, because the $1,080,000 levy signals that the market is closing [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Retains output and jobs
Compliance cost may exceed profit

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Colonia Dairy Ltd is a family-owned private limited company in Uruguay making powdered milk for export, with sales of $12,000,000 a year. An Argentine dairy multinational has offered $4,000,000 for a 40% share of the company, while a local bank will lend the same amount at 9.5%. Directors must decide whether to accept the investment or borrow.

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company'.
questions.model_answer: A multinational company is a business with headquarters in one country and operations or investments in at least one other country [2]; the Argentine dairy group offering $4,000,000 for 40% of Colonia Dairy Ltd is one.

knowledge_max_2: Business operating in more than one country
Usually has headquarters in a home country

questions.question_text: Calculate the value the offer places on 100% of Colonia Dairy Ltd if $4,000,000 buys a 40% share.
Explain two effects of accepting the multinational's investment on Colonia Dairy Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The firm gains funds without debt [k]. $4,000,000 from the Argentine group avoids the $380,000 interest a year that the bank's 9.5% loan would cost [app], leaving more cash for new drying equipment [an].

Point 2: Control is shared [k]. A 40% share values the whole company at $10,000,000 but gives the multinational a strong say in pricing and exports [app], which may limit the family's independence [an].

analysis_max_2: Shared control over pricing and exports

questions.question_text: Do you think Colonia Dairy Ltd should accept the $4,000,000 investment rather than borrow? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Selling 40% raises $4,000,000 with no interest, avoiding $380,000 a year at 9.5%, and brings an experienced dairy partner with export contacts [ev]. The offer values the company at $10,000,000, a fair base for growth [an].

Against: Giving up 40% of a company worth $10,000,000 means surrendering future dividends and control over pricing [an]. A loan keeps ownership intact and interest may fall if rates ease [ev].

Conclusion: Accept the investment only if the partner brings export contracts, because $380,000 of interest is cheaper than losing 40% of a growing business [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Avoids $380,000 interest and gains partner
Loses 40% of ownership and control

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bergslagen Batteries Ltd is a private limited company in Sweden making lithium battery packs, with sales of $14,000,000 and 220 employees. The central bank has raised its policy rate from 3.25% to 4.5%, so a $9,000,000 loan for a second production line now costs more. Directors must decide whether to proceed or delay the line.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the percentage charged for borrowing money over a period, set largely by central bank policy [2]; Sweden's 4.5% rate sets the annual cost of Bergslagen Batteries Ltd's $9,000,000 loan.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on the $9,000,000 loan at 4.5%.
Explain two effects of the rise from 3.25% to 4.5% on Bergslagen Batteries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Borrowing for the second line costs more [k]. Interest on $9,000,000 reaches $405,000 a year, $112,500 more than at 3.25% [app], so the line must earn a higher return to justify itself [an].

Point 2: Customers delay electric conversions [k]. Swedish hauliers and builders facing 4.5% rates postpone battery purchases [app], weakening demand just as Bergslagen considers expanding capacity [an].

analysis_max_2: Higher hurdle for the new line

questions.question_text: Do you think Bergslagen Batteries Ltd should proceed with the $9,000,000 second production line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Demand for battery packs is growing as transport electrifies, and a second line lets the firm win contracts before rivals add capacity [an]. Interest of $405,000 is under 3% of $14,000,000 of sales [ev].

Against: Borrowing at 4.5% costs $112,500 more than before, and customers are delaying orders at these rates [ev]. Building capacity just as demand slows could leave the line idle with fixed interest still due [an].

Conclusion: Proceed but phase the investment, because long-run electrification demand is strong while $405,000 of interest is heavy if sales stall now [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Long-run demand growth
$405,000 interest if sales stall

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Calima Flowers Ltd is a private limited company in Colombia growing roses for export, with revenue of $5,600,000 a year and 900 workers. A European buyer will only sign a long-term contract if Calima joins a fair trade scheme that pays a premium of 8% of revenue to workers and the local community. Directors must decide whether to join.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical trading'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical trading means sourcing and selling in a way that treats workers and communities fairly, often verified by an independent standard [2]; Calima Flowers Ltd would pay an 8% premium to workers and the community to satisfy its European buyer.

knowledge_max_2: Fair treatment of workers and suppliers

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual fair trade premium if 8% of $5,600,000 of revenue is paid to workers and the community.
Explain two effects of joining the fair trade scheme on Calima Flowers Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A fixed premium reduces profit [k]. Paying 8% of $5,600,000 takes $448,000 a year from revenue [app], money that would otherwise cover fertiliser, cold storage and transport [an].

Point 2: The contract secures long-term sales [k]. The European buyer will sign only with certified suppliers [app], so 900 workers keep steady employment and the firm avoids the risk of losing its main market [an].

analysis_max_2: Less cash for inputs and logistics

questions.question_text: Do you think Calima Flowers Ltd should join the fair trade scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Certification secures a long-term European contract and protects the jobs of 900 workers, while the $448,000 premium builds community goodwill in the growing region [an]. Ethically certified roses increasingly command better shelf space [ev].

Against: $448,000 is 8% of revenue and comes straight off a margin already exposed to air freight and fuel costs [ev]. The buyer may still switch to cheaper certified growers in Kenya or Ecuador [an].

Conclusion: Join, because losing the European contract would be worse than the $448,000 premium, but negotiate a price increase to share the cost [ev].

evaluation_max_2: Secures contract and protects 900 jobs
$448,000 off a thin margin
analysis_max_2: Community goodwill and better shelf space

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marrowgate Steel Ltd is a private limited company in Peru rolling reinforcing bars for builders, earning $64,000,000 a year from 96,000 tonnes. Inflation has reached 7.4% and the central bank has raised interest rates to 9.25%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $9,000,000 for an electric arc furnace or keep hiring extra furnaces at $720,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services [k]. Peru's 7.4% rate means Marrowgate pays more each year for iron ore, electrodes and wages [app].

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the average price level
Money buys fewer goods and services

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Marrowgate Steel Ltd would pay on a $9,000,000 loan at 9.25%.

knowledge_max_2: Interest = amount borrowed x annual rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 9.25% interest rate on Marrowgate Steel Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The furnace loan becomes costly [k]. Borrowing $9,000,000 at 9.25% adds $832,500 of interest a year [app], which is $112,500 more than the $720,000 furnace hire and must be paid before the line earns anything [an].

Point 2: Builders who buy steel on credit cut orders [k]. Higher repayments squeeze Peruvian construction firms [app], so demand for reinforcing bars falls just as Marrowgate needs volume to cover its fixed costs [an].

analysis_max_2: Interest is paid before the investment earns revenue
Fewer orders spread fixed costs over fewer tonnes

questions.question_text: Do you think Marrowgate Steel Ltd should borrow $9,000,000 for the electric arc furnace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Buying the furnace ends the $720,000 annual hire charge and gives Marrowgate an asset it could sell if demand collapses. Electric melting should also cut energy waste and raise tonnes per worker.

Against: At 9.25% the loan costs $832,500 a year before capital is repaid, which is $112,500 more than hiring. With inflation at 7.4% eroding builders' budgets, orders may fall and leave the business short of cash.

Conclusion: Borrowing is unwise for now. The interest charge exceeds the hire cost and demand is fragile, so the furnace should wait until rates fall.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $832,500 interest with $720,000 hire
Weighs automation gains against inflation risk
analysis_max_2: Interest exceeds hire by $112,500 a year
Inflation at 7.4% may cut construction demand

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quillhaven Paper Ltd is a private limited company in Norway recycling waste into office paper, producing 42,000 tonnes a year at $780 a tonne. A carbon levy of $46 a tonne now applies to its gas dryers, while a European scheme pays $18 a tonne for paper collected. The board must decide whether to spend $3,600,000 converting the dryers to electric heat.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of production borne by a third party rather than the business [k]. Quillhaven's gas dryers emit carbon that Norwegian residents pay for through climate damage, which is why the $46 levy exists [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cost of an activity paid by a third party
Not included in the firm's private costs

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual carbon levy Quillhaven Paper Ltd would pay on 42,000 tonnes at $46 a tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Levy = tonnes x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the carbon levy may affect Quillhaven Paper Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise on every tonne dried [k]. The $46 levy adds $1,932,000 a year to a business charging $780 a tonne [app], and because paper buyers can switch supplier easily much of that cannot be passed on, so the margin on each tonne shrinks [an].

Point 2: Investment in electric dryers becomes more attractive [k]. The $18 a tonne paid for collected paper offsets part of the $3,600,000 conversion [app], reducing exposure to future carbon taxes and strengthening the recycled brand [an].

application_max_2: $18 a tonne received for collected paper
analysis_max_2: Buyers resist higher prices so margins fall
Conversion cost is partly offset by recycling income

questions.question_text: Do you think Quillhaven Paper Ltd should spend $3,600,000 converting its dryers to electric heat? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The conversion removes a $1,932,000 annual levy at today's $46 rate and shelters Quillhaven if carbon taxes rise. Electric drying also supports the recycled brand that earns $18 a tonne.

Against: $3,600,000 is a large outlay for a company earning $780 a tonne, and electricity prices may rise once the dryers depend on them. The levy could also be cut if Norway changes policy.

Conclusion: Convert only if finance is secure. The levy saving is large, but the $3,600,000 risk should be spread over several years rather than paid from one year's reserves.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,932,000 annual saving against $3,600,000 outlay
Considers future carbon policy
analysis_max_2: Levy saving repays the outlay within about two years
Electricity price risk replaces carbon price risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bluewren Seafoods plc is a public limited company in Sri Lanka freezing prawns for export, shipping 5,400 tonnes a year at $6,200 a tonne to buyers in Japan. The government has imposed a 12% export levy, and freight costs have risen by 9%. The board must decide whether to absorb the levy or raise its dollar price to Japanese importers.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: An export is a good or service sold to a buyer in another country [k]. Bluewren's frozen prawns leave Sri Lanka for Japan and earn $6,200 a tonne in foreign currency [app].

knowledge_max_2: Earns foreign currency for the seller

questions.question_text: Calculate how much revenue per tonne Bluewren Seafoods plc loses if it absorbs the 12% levy on a $6,200 tonne.
questions.model_answer: $6,200 x 12% = $744 lost per tonne [2], leaving $5,456.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the 12% export levy may reduce the competitiveness of Bluewren Seafoods plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Absorbing the levy cuts the margin on every tonne [k]. At $6,200 a tonne the levy takes $744, so Bluewren keeps $5,456 [app]; with freight already up 9%, the price it can offer Japanese buyers is squeezed against rival suppliers [an].

Point 2: Raising the price risks losing orders [k]. Japanese importers buying 5,400 tonnes compare offers closely [app], so a higher dollar price may send them to Thai exporters, leaving Bluewren's cold stores half empty [an].

analysis_max_2: Costs cannot be passed on without losing volume
Empty capacity raises unit fixed costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluewren Seafoods plc should raise its price to Japanese importers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A higher price protects the margin. Absorbing the 12% levy costs $744 on every $6,200 tonne, and with freight up 9% the business cannot pay both without eroding profit on 5,400 tonnes.

Against: Japanese buyers can switch to Thai suppliers. A price rise on top of the levy may lose volume, and Bluewren's cold-store costs would then be spread over fewer tonnes.

Conclusion: Raise the price only partly. Recovering about half the levy keeps Bluewren close to rivals while limiting the loss per tonne; a full pass-through is too risky in a price-sensitive market.

evaluation_max_2: Judges partial recovery against full pass-through
Weighs margin loss against volume loss
analysis_max_2: $744 a tonne is too large to absorb alone
Lost volume would raise unit fixed costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Harlowmoor Cement Ltd is a private limited company in Morocco producing bagged cement, selling 1,300,000 tonnes a year at $84 a tonne. The economy has entered recession with unemployment at 13.6%, and the government has cut infrastructure spending by 15%. The board must decide whether to reduce output by 200,000 tonnes or hold output and cut the price by 8%.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when a country's output falls over two successive quarters or more [k]. Morocco's downturn has pushed unemployment to 13.6%, so Harlowmoor's builders buy fewer bags of cement [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fall in national output over two quarters

questions.question_text: Calculate the price of a tonne of cement if Harlowmoor Cement Ltd cuts its $84 price by 8%.

knowledge_max_2: New price = old price x (1 - rate)

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the recession may affect Harlowmoor Cement Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand from construction falls [k]. With infrastructure spending down 15% and unemployment at 13.6%, Moroccan builders delay projects [app], so the 1,300,000 tonnes sold at $84 may not find buyers [an].

Point 2: Discounting damages revenue [k]. An 8% cut takes the price to $77.28 [app], lowering income by $8,736,000 even if volume holds, while kiln costs cannot be reduced quickly, so profit falls faster than sales [an].

analysis_max_2: Fixed kiln costs cannot be cut quickly

questions.question_text: Do you think Harlowmoor Cement Ltd should cut output by 200,000 tonnes rather than cut its price by 8%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cutting 200,000 tonnes takes pressure off the kilns and avoids selling at $77.28, which would cost $8,736,000 of revenue at current volume. Holding the price protects the margin that covers heavy fixed costs.

Against: Lower output raises unit fixed costs and may let importers take shelf space. Keeping 1,300,000 tonnes moving protects jobs in a country where unemployment is 13.6%.

Conclusion: Cut output. With infrastructure spending down 15%, defending the price matters more than defending volume, because cement margins are too thin to discount by 8%.

evaluation_max_2: Compares revenue lost by discounting with unit cost rise
Weighs jobs against margin
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs per tonne rise when output falls

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Silverbeck Laundry Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand washing linen for 60 hotels, processing 2,800,000 kilograms a year at $1.45 a kilogram. The regional council has doubled its water discharge charge to $0.06 a kilogram and set a water use limit of 2,400,000 kilograms. Directors must decide whether to install a $640,000 water recycling unit.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable production'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable production means making output while conserving resources and limiting harm so future generations can meet their needs [k]. Silverbeck must cut water use to 2,400,000 kilograms, well below its 2,800,000 kilogram throughput [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual water discharge charge Silverbeck Laundry Ltd pays on 2,800,000 kilograms at $0.06 a kilogram.
Explain two ways the water charge and limit may affect Silverbeck Laundry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The doubled charge raises operating costs [k]. At $0.06 a kilogram on 2,800,000 kilograms Silverbeck pays $168,000 a year [app], and hotels compare laundry prices closely, so most of it must be absorbed and the margin on each kilogram falls [an].

Point 2: The 2,400,000 kilogram limit caps output [k]. Silverbeck can no longer process 400,000 kilograms of linen sent by its 60 hotels [app], so it must turn work away or spend $640,000 on recycling equipment [an].

analysis_max_2: Hotels resist price rises so margin falls
Growth is blocked with the 60 hotels

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverbeck Laundry Ltd should install the $640,000 water recycling unit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The unit keeps Silverbeck within the 2,400,000 kilogram limit and preserves all 60 hotel contracts. Reusing water also cuts the $168,000 annual charge and protects against further council increases.

Against: $640,000 is almost four years of the current charge, and hotel contracts may not last long enough to recover it. If the council relaxes the limit the equipment becomes unnecessary.

Conclusion: Install it, but phase the work. The limit threatens 400,000 kilograms of throughput and the goodwill of 60 hotels, so the unit protects revenue far larger than the $168,000 annual charge.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $640,000 outlay against $168,000 annual charge
Considers contract security

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kestrelford Cycles plc is a public limited company in Bangladesh assembling bicycles, making 480,000 bikes a year at $95 each for buyers in Germany. A new trade bloc tariff of 14% has replaced duty-free access, and the taka has depreciated by 6% against the euro. The board must decide whether to build a factory inside the bloc or keep exporting.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods [k]. The 14% tariff adds $13.30 to a $95 bicycle, raising the price German buyers pay [app].

knowledge_max_2: Raises the price of imported goods

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff payable per bicycle if Kestrelford Cycles plc exports a $95 bike into the trade bloc at 14%.
Explain two effects of the 14% tariff on Kestrelford Cycles plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Each bike becomes dearer in Germany [k]. A $95 bicycle carries $13.30 of tariff [app], so German buyers comparing it with European-made bikes switch, and Kestrelford sells fewer of its 480,000 units [an].

Point 2: Building inside the bloc avoids the barrier [k]. A German factory would sell tariff-free but must match Bangladeshi costs [app]; the 6% depreciation of the taka already helps exports, so the business must weigh that against moving [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrelford Cycles plc should build a factory inside the trade bloc? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A plant inside the bloc removes the 14% tariff, worth $13.30 on every $95 bike, and protects access to the German market that takes much of the 480,000 units. Local production also shortens delivery times.

Against: Building abroad loses low Bangladeshi wage costs and the 6% currency advantage. The investment is large and the tariff may be temporary if a trade deal is agreed.

Conclusion: Do not build yet. The 6% depreciation already offsets part of the $13.30 tariff, so Kestrelford should keep exporting and press for a trade agreement before committing to a factory.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $13.30 tariff against cost of moving
Considers the 6% currency advantage
analysis_max_2: Tariff is only 14% of a $95 bike
Fixed costs of a new plant are high

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tanager Confectionery Ltd is a private limited company in Uruguay making chocolate bars, with revenue of $27,500,000 a year and 310 staff. Inflation has risen to 8.9% and the government has increased the minimum wage by 11%, while cocoa prices are up 17%. Directors must decide whether to hold prices and accept lower margins or raise prices by 6%.

questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: A minimum wage is the lowest rate an employer may legally pay a worker [k]. Uruguay's 11% rise lifts Tanager's wage bill on top of 8.9% inflation [app].

knowledge_max_2: Set by government and raises costs

questions.question_text: Calculate the price of a $2.50 chocolate bar after Tanager Confectionery Ltd raises prices by 6%.
Explain two effects of rising costs on Tanager Confectionery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Margins are squeezed [k]. Inflation at 8.9%, an 11% wage rise and cocoa up 17% all raise unit costs [app], so unless the $2.50 bar price rises, profit on the output behind $27,500,000 of revenue falls [an].

Point 2: A 6% rise may not be enough [k]. Moving the bar to $2.65 recovers only part of an 11% wage increase [app], and shoppers facing 8.9% inflation may trade down to cheaper brands, so volume falls as well as margin [an].

knowledge_max_2: Price rise is smaller than cost rise
analysis_max_2: Profit per bar falls if prices hold
Demand may fall at higher prices

questions.question_text: Do you think Tanager Confectionery Ltd should raise its prices by 6%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Costs are rising on three fronts: inflation at 8.9%, wages up 11% and cocoa up 17%. A 6% rise to $2.65 recovers part of that and protects the margin on $27,500,000 of revenue.

Against: Consumers already facing 8.9% inflation are price-sensitive, and a 6% rise may push them to rival bars, leaving factory costs spread over fewer bars.

Conclusion: Raise prices by less than 6% after cutting waste. Costs are rising faster than the proposed increase, yet a full pass-through risks volume, so a smaller rise plus efficiency savings is the safer balance.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs cost recovery against volume loss
Considers consumer price sensitivity
analysis_max_2: A smaller rise limits lost sales

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd is a private limited company in the Philippines curing leather for shoe makers, treating 18,000 tonnes of hides a year. A pollution inspector has found that its effluent kills fish in the river, and a clean-up levy of $34 a tonne is proposed. Directors must decide whether to spend $1,900,000 on a treatment plant or pay the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of an activity borne by people outside the transaction [k]. Ridgecombe's effluent damages a river used by local families, which is why a $34 a tonne clean-up levy is proposed [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cost paid by a third party
Damage not charged to the producer

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual clean-up levy Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd would pay on 18,000 tonnes at $34 a tonne.
Explain two ways the pollution may affect Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The business faces direct penalties [k]. A $34 levy on 18,000 tonnes costs $612,000 a year [app], a large sum for a tannery selling to price-sensitive shoe makers, so profit falls sharply [an].

Point 2: Reputation and orders are at risk [k]. Shoe brands audit their suppliers' water records [app], so evidence that effluent kills fish could lose Ridgecombe contracts worth more than the levy itself [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd should spend $1,900,000 on a treatment plant rather than pay the levy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The plant ends the pollution and removes a $612,000 annual levy, recovering its cost in about three years. It also keeps European shoe brands, which are tightening supplier audits, from withdrawing orders.

Against: $1,900,000 is a heavy commitment for a tannery with uncertain export demand, and the levy may never be enforced in full. The plant also adds running costs for chemicals and power.

Conclusion: Build the plant. The levy alone is $612,000 a year and reputational damage could cost far more, so treating the effluent protects both the river and future contracts.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $1,900,000 with $612,000 a year
Weighs legal and reputational risk
analysis_max_2: Cost is recovered in about three years

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Waxwing Optics plc is a public limited company in the Czech Republic grinding lenses for microscope makers, exporting 260,000 units a year at EUR 41 each. The koruna has appreciated by 11% against the euro, and a rival in Vietnam now charges EUR 35 a unit. The board must decide whether to cut its euro price or move assembly to Vietnam.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: An appreciation is a rise in the value of a currency against another [k]. The koruna's 11% rise makes Waxwing's EUR 41 lenses dearer in euro terms for its microscope customers [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate Waxwing Optics plc's annual export revenue from 260,000 lenses at EUR 41 each.
Explain two effects of the 11% appreciation on Waxwing Optics plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export prices rise in foreign currency [k]. An 11% appreciation makes each EUR 41 lens cost more euros unless Waxwing accepts a lower margin [app], and with the Vietnamese rival at EUR 35 the gap is already EUR 6 [an].

Point 2: Imported inputs become cheaper [k]. Glass blanks and coatings bought abroad cost fewer korunas [app], which softens the squeeze but is small beside the loss of competitiveness on 260,000 lenses [an].

application_max_2: EUR 41 against a rival price of EUR 35
analysis_max_2: Margin must absorb the currency rise
Input saving is smaller than lost sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Waxwing Optics plc should cut its euro price to match the Vietnamese rival? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cutting from EUR 41 to EUR 35 closes a EUR 6 gap and defends volume on 260,000 lenses. Losing orders would leave fixed grinding costs spread over fewer units.

Against: A cut of EUR 6 removes a large part of the margin, and Waxwing cannot match Vietnam's costs permanently. Matching may start a price war that only the lowest-cost producer survives.

Conclusion: Do not match EUR 35. Cut only part of the gap and sell on precision and delivery, because a full match destroys the margin Waxwing needs to fund its Czech plant.

questions.question_text: Define 'royalty'.
questions.model_answer: A royalty is a payment to a government or resource owner for the right to extract a material [k]. Ecuador charges Dunlarkin 7% of the value of every tonne of granite sold [app].

knowledge_max_2: Payment for the right to extract
Usually a percentage of sales value

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual royalty Dunlarkin Quarry Ltd would pay on 220,000 tonnes at $38 a tonne if the rate is 7%.
Explain two effects of the new royalty on Dunlarkin Quarry Ltd.

Point 1: Profit falls on every tonne sold [k]. The 7% royalty takes $585,200 from $8,360,000 of sales [app], and builders can buy granite from rival quarries, so Dunlarkin cannot easily pass it on [an].

Point 2: The case for raising the price strengthens [k]. Moving from $38 to $41 adds $660,000 of revenue on 220,000 tonnes [app], but diesel is up 22%, so the increase may only restore the margin [an].

Against: Builders can switch to rival quarries and construction demand is weak. A rise of almost 8% may lose volume, leaving fixed quarry costs spread over fewer tonnes.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Fenmoss Nursery Ltd is a private limited company in Iceland growing bedding plants in heated greenhouses, selling 950,000 pots a year at $3.80. questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable production'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable production means making output while conserving resources and limiting environmental damage [k]. Fenmoss must replace peat compost, whose extraction releases carbon, to keep selling after the 2027 ban [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual fuel cost for Fenmoss Nursery Ltd from a 5% levy on a $410,000 fuel bill.
Explain two ways the levy and the peat ban may affect Fenmoss Nursery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Energy costs rise [k]. The 5% levy adds $20,500 to a $410,000 fuel bill [app], and heat is unavoidable in Icelandic greenhouses, so the cost must come out of 950,000 pots sold at $3.80, squeezing each margin [an].

Point 2: The peat ban forces a costly input change [k]. Coconut compost costs 18% more than peat [app], raising the price of every pot while garden centres resist increases, so Fenmoss may lose price-sensitive customers [an].

analysis_max_2: Heat cannot be cut in greenhouses

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenmoss Nursery Ltd should switch to coconut compost now rather than wait for the 2027 ban? Justify your answer.

Against: Coconut compost costs 18% more and must be imported, adding transport and exchange-rate risk. Waiting keeps costs low while peat is still legal.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pikebrook Fisheries Ltd is a private limited company in Tanzania canning tuna for supermarkets in Italy, landing 3,200 tonnes a year at $2,150 a tonne. questions.question_text: Define 'quota'.
questions.model_answer: A quota is a physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported [k]. Italy allows only 2,400 tonnes of Pikebrook's tuna against the 3,200 tonnes it lands [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff Pikebrook Fisheries Ltd would pay on the surplus 800 tonnes at 20% of $2,150 a tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff = tonnage x price x rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the quota on Pikebrook Fisheries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Sales to Italy are capped [k]. The 2,400 tonne quota leaves 800 tonnes of the 3,200 tonne catch without an Italian buyer [app], so Pikebrook must find another market before the tuna spoils [an].

Point 2: Selling the surplus elsewhere lowers revenue [k]. Kenyan buyers know the fish cannot go to Italy and will offer less than $2,150 a tonne [app], while the 20% tariff above the quota makes shipping to Italy unattractive, so income per tonne falls [an].

analysis_max_2: Perishable fish must be sold quickly
Lower price per tonne cuts income

questions.question_text: Do you think Pikebrook Fisheries Ltd should freeze production at 2,400 tonnes rather than sell the surplus in Kenya? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Limiting the catch to 2,400 tonnes matches the Italian quota and avoids dumping 800 tonnes on a weak Kenyan market. It also protects tuna stocks, which matters for the fishery's future.

Against: Cutting 800 tonnes idles boats and crew for part of the year, raising the fixed cost per tonne landed. Kenyan buyers still provide revenue that contributes towards those costs.

Conclusion: Sell the surplus in Kenya but cap the catch. Losing 800 tonnes of contribution hurts more than a lower Kenyan price, provided Pikebrook agrees a floor price before the boats sail.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ashcombe Chemicals plc is a public limited company in South Korea making industrial solvents, with revenue of $118,000,000 and energy costs of $21,000,000 a year. questions.question_text: Define 'corporation tax'.
questions.model_answer: Corporation tax is a tax on the profits of a company [k]. South Korea's rise from 22% to 25% means Ashcombe keeps less of the profit earned on $118,000,000 of revenue [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Ashcombe Chemicals plc would pay on a $14,000,000 loan at 4.5%.
Explain two effects of the higher corporation tax on Ashcombe Chemicals plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit falls [k]. Paying 25% instead of 22% takes three percentage points more of profit [app], so less is left from $118,000,000 of revenue to fund the $14,000,000 expansion [an].

Point 2: The choice of finance shifts towards borrowing [k]. A $14,000,000 loan at 4.5% costs $630,000 a year [app], and although interest is a cost, the tax change makes debt relatively more attractive than using reserves, raising financial risk [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ashcombe Chemicals plc should fund the $14,000,000 expansion from retained profit rather than a bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Using reserves avoids $630,000 of annual interest and leaves profit free for dividends, which matters now that corporation tax is 25%. It also keeps debt low if interest rates of 4.5% climb.

Against: Spending $14,000,000 of reserves leaves little cushion for a chemicals business with $21,000,000 of energy costs exposed to price shocks.

Conclusion: Use retained profit but keep a loan facility open. The tax rise to 25% makes debt less attractive, yet energy volatility means Ashcombe should not empty its reserves for the whole $14,000,000.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $630,000 interest against loss of reserves

analysis_max_2: Own finance is cheaper than 4.5% debt

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company'.

questions.question_text: Calculate the price at which the rival sells its toys if it undercuts Bramblewick Toys plc's $4.80 by 15%.

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblewick Toys plc should invest $5,200,000 in automation rather than cut prices? Justify your answer.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Calderby Hotels Ltd would pay on a $5,000,000 loan at 8.75%.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Elderflower Preserves Ltd is a private limited company in Finland making jam from wild berries, producing 1,150,000 jars a year at $4.20. questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is collecting and processing waste materials so they can be used again [k]. Elderflower's glass jars can be returned under a scheme charging $0.15 for each jar not brought back [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual deposit charge Elderflower Preserves Ltd would pay if none of its 1,150,000 jars were returned at $0.15 each.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.model_answer:
For: The system keeps the existing plant, workforce and customer relationships, and meets the 40 milligram limit from January. Relocating would duplicate buildings and lose skilled dyers.

Against: $1,250,000 is heavy against $7,504,000 of revenue, and the agency may tighten the limit again, making the equipment obsolete.

Conclusion: Buy the system. Relocation leaves the same waste problem at a new site plus moving costs, whereas filtration protects a licence that the business cannot operate without.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs equipment cost against relocation cost
Considers future regulation

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pierhead Containers plc is a public limited company in Hungary making shipping containers, producing 22,000 a year at $3,150 each and exporting 70% to Germany. A trade bloc has imposed a 10% anti-dumping duty on its containers, and rail freight costs have risen 19%. The board must decide whether to open a plant in Germany or pay the duty.

questions.question_text: Define 'anti-dumping duty'.
questions.model_answer: An anti-dumping duty is a tariff imposed on imports sold below their normal price to protect domestic producers [k]. Pierhead's containers now carry a 10% duty in its main German market [app].

questions.question_text: Identify the two trade measures affecting Pierhead Containers plc.
questions.model_answer: The 10% anti-dumping duty on containers and the 19% rise in rail freight costs [2]; together they add $315 per container plus transport.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 10% duty on Pierhead Containers plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Each container costs more in Germany [k]. A 10% duty adds $315 to a $3,150 container [app], so the 70% of output sold there becomes less competitive against German-made boxes [an].

Point 2: Location decisions are affected [k]. A German plant would avoid the duty but face higher wages than Hungary [app], and with freight up 19% the saving on transport would partly offset the higher labour cost [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Pierhead Containers plc should open a plant in Germany rather than pay the duty? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A German plant removes the $315 duty on every container and cuts the 19% freight cost on 70% of output. It also gives Pierhead a local presence in its largest market.

Against: German wages and energy costs are higher than Hungarian ones, and a new plant needs capital that 22,000 containers a year may not justify.

Conclusion: Pay the duty for now. The 10% duty is $315 a container, but building in Germany adds permanent higher costs; Pierhead should negotiate a lower price with freight firms first.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs duty saving against higher German costs
Considers scale of output
analysis_max_2: Duty is only 10% of the price
German labour costs are permanently higher

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Alderney Textiles Ltd is a private limited company in Guatemala weaving cotton cloth, with 640 staff, a wage bill of 46,000,000 quetzals and revenue of 210,000,000 quetzals a year. Inflation has reached 6.2% and the government has raised the minimum wage by 9%, while the quetzal has depreciated 5% against the dollar. Directors must decide whether to buy automated looms for $8,300,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level [k]. Guatemala's 6.2% rate raises the cost of the cotton and dyes Alderney buys [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reduces the buying power of money

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual wage cost for Alderney Textiles Ltd from a 9% rise on a 46,000,000 quetzal wage bill.

knowledge_max_2: Extra cost = wage bill x rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the wage rise on Alderney Textiles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Labour costs increase [k]. A 9% rise adds 4,140,000 quetzals to a wage bill of 46,000,000 [app], which must be paid from 210,000,000 quetzals of revenue, so the margin on every metre of cloth falls [an].

Point 2: Automation becomes more attractive [k]. Looms costing $8,300,000 replace labour, and the 5% depreciation of the quetzal makes dollar-priced machines dearer [app], so the decision depends on whether savings exceed the higher import cost [an].

application_max_2: 4,140,000 quetzals added to the wage bill
analysis_max_2: Import cost rises with the exchange rate

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderney Textiles Ltd should buy the automated looms for $8,300,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Automation replaces labour that has just become 9% more expensive and protects the business from further minimum wage rises. It also raises output per worker, spreading the 210,000,000 quetzals of revenue over fewer staff.

Against: $8,300,000 is large, and the 5% depreciation makes imported looms dearer in quetzals. The 640 staff would need retraining or redundancy, which carries cost and bad publicity.

Conclusion: Buy them gradually. The 9% wage rise and 6.2% inflation make labour steadily dearer, but the 5% currency fall means Alderney should buy in stages rather than commit $8,300,000 at once.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs labour saving against import cost
Considers workforce impact
analysis_max_2: Wage rise of 9% makes looms viable

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Swallowgate Catering Ltd is a private limited company in Denmark supplying canteens at 240 schools, serving 9,600,000 meals a year at $3.40. New rules require 60% of food to be organic, which costs 24% more, and a sugar tax of $0.28 a litre applies to its drinks. Directors must decide whether to raise meal prices by 12% or cut portion sizes.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable sourcing'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable sourcing means buying inputs produced in ways that limit environmental and social harm [k]. Swallowgate must now buy 60% of its food from organic suppliers to keep its school contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: Buying inputs with limited environmental harm

questions.question_text: Calculate the new meal price if Swallowgate Catering Ltd raises its $3.40 price by 12%.
Explain two ways the new food rules may affect Swallowgate Catering Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Food costs rise [k]. Organic food costs 24% more and the sugar tax adds $0.28 a litre to drinks [app], so the cost of each of the 9,600,000 meals rises just as schools hold budgets tight [an].

Point 2: Contracts may be won or lost on compliance [k]. Schools buying at $3.40 a meal will check that 60% of food is organic [app], so complying protects 240 contracts while failing could end them [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Swallowgate Catering Ltd should raise meal prices by 12%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Costs are rising from organic food at 24% more and a $0.28 sugar tax on drinks. A 12% rise to $3.81 recovers part of that and protects the margin on 9,600,000 meals.

Against: Schools hold fixed catering budgets and may tender elsewhere. Cutting portion sizes instead avoids a price rise but risks complaints and lost contracts.

Conclusion: Raise prices by 12% but reformulate drinks to avoid the sugar tax. The organic requirement is compulsory, so schools expect higher costs, yet the $0.28 tax can be designed out rather than passed on.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs price rise against portion cuts
Considers school budgets
analysis_max_2: Organic cost of 24% cannot be avoided

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tealbrook Software plc is a public limited company in Zambia writing payroll software, earning $12,800,000 a year from 1,900 clients. A multinational has entered the market charging 25% less, and the kwacha has depreciated 18% against the dollar, raising the cost of its imported servers. The board must decide whether to cut licence fees by 15% or add a free support package.

questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of economies through trade, investment and technology [k]. The multinational now selling software in Zambia shows how quickly competition crosses borders [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual cost of Tealbrook Software plc's imported servers if they cost $1,400,000 and the kwacha depreciates 18%.
Explain two effects of the multinational's entry on Tealbrook Software plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Price competition reduces revenue per client [k]. A rival charging 25% less threatens the income from 1,900 clients that produced $12,800,000 [app], so Tealbrook may have to cut licence fees to keep them [an].

Point 2: Costs rise at the same time [k]. The 18% depreciation adds $252,000 to imported server costs [app], so the business faces lower prices and higher costs together, squeezing the margin on every licence [an].

analysis_max_2: Lower prices and higher costs combine

questions.question_text: Do you think Tealbrook Software plc should cut licence fees by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 15% cut undercuts the rival's 25% discount only partly but keeps 1,900 clients paying. Losing them would be worse than a smaller fee per licence.

Against: A cut reduces revenue on every contract while server costs have risen by $252,000 after the 18% depreciation, so profit could disappear.

Conclusion: Do not cut fees across the board. Add the free support package instead, because competing on service protects the $12,800,000 revenue without starting a price war that a multinational can win.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs fee cut against service differentiation
Considers cost pressure
analysis_max_2: Support package protects revenue per client

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Millrace Joinery Ltd is a private limited company in Indonesia making wooden window frames, selling 76,000 frames a year at $118. Interest rates have risen to 11.5% and timber prices are up 14% after an export ban. Directors must decide whether to borrow $2,200,000 for a drying kiln or buy kiln-dried timber at $19 more a frame.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the percentage charged on borrowed money [k]. Indonesia's 11.5% rate makes Millrace's proposed $2,200,000 kiln loan expensive [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Millrace Joinery Ltd would pay on a $2,200,000 loan at 11.5%.
Explain two effects of the 11.5% interest rate on Millrace Joinery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Borrowing for the kiln is costly [k]. A $2,200,000 loan at 11.5% costs $253,000 a year [app], while buying kiln-dried timber instead adds $19 to each of 76,000 frames, or $1,444,000 [an].

Point 2: Customers who build houses borrow less [k]. Indonesian developers facing 11.5% rates postpone projects [app], so window frame orders fall just as timber costs rise 14% [an].

analysis_max_2: Kiln loan costs less than dried timber

questions.question_text: Do you think Millrace Joinery Ltd should borrow $2,200,000 for the drying kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The kiln costs $253,000 a year in interest, while buying kiln-dried timber adds $1,444,000 to the cost of 76,000 frames. Owning the kiln also protects Millrace from future timber price rises after the 14% increase.

Against: 11.5% is a high rate to commit to for several years, and demand for frames may fall if Indonesian builders cut projects.

Conclusion: Borrow for the kiln. The $253,000 annual interest is far below the $1,444,000 extra cost of bought-in dried timber, and the export ban makes timber supply uncertain.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $253,000 interest with $1,444,000 extra timber cost
Considers demand risk
analysis_max_2: Interest is under a fifth of the alternative cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Coppersedge Plating Ltd is a private limited company in Paraguay coating metal parts with chrome, treating 640,000 parts a year at $2.75 each. Chrome waste has contaminated groundwater, and the water authority will charge $0.40 a part from June unless the plant is sealed. Directors must decide whether to spend $310,000 sealing the plant or pay the charge.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of production paid by someone other than the producer [k]. Coppersedge's chrome waste has contaminated groundwater used by local households, so the authority will charge $0.40 a part [app].

knowledge_max_2: Damage not paid for by the firm

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual charge Coppersedge Plating Ltd would pay on 640,000 parts at $0.40 each.
Explain two ways the contaminated groundwater may affect Coppersedge Plating Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A new charge raises costs [k]. Paying $0.40 a part on 640,000 parts costs $256,000 a year [app], which is almost half the $310,000 needed to seal the plant, so the bill recurs every year until the waste stops [an].

Point 2: Reputation with industrial customers suffers [k]. Manufacturers buying plated parts audit their suppliers' environmental records [app], so a pollution case could lose contracts worth far more than $2.75 a part [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Coppersedge Plating Ltd should spend $310,000 sealing the plant rather than pay the charge? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Sealing costs $310,000 once, while the charge is $256,000 every year on 640,000 parts. The plant also stops chrome entering groundwater used by local households, protecting the licence to operate.

Against: $310,000 is a large outlay for a business earning $2.75 a part, and the sealing may interrupt production while it is installed.

Conclusion: Seal the plant. The charge exceeds $310,000 within about fifteen months, and repeated pollution would damage the contracts that keep the plating line busy.

evaluation_max_2: Compares one-off $310,000 with recurring $256,000
Considers production disruption

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Windhover Airlines plc is a public limited company in Bulgaria flying 42 routes with 26 aircraft, carrying 3,900,000 passengers a year at $74 a ticket. A rival has cut fares by 18% on its busiest routes, and aviation fuel costs have risen 23% after a carbon levy. The board must decide whether to match the fare cut or reduce routes.

questions.question_text: Define 'competition'.
questions.model_answer: Competition is the rivalry between businesses trying to sell to the same customers [k]. Windhover's rival has cut fares by 18% on the routes that carry most of its 3,900,000 passengers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Firms compete on price and quality

questions.question_text: Calculate the fare after an 18% cut from Windhover Airlines plc's $74 ticket.
Explain two ways the rival's fare cut may affect Windhover Airlines plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Passengers switch to the cheaper airline [k]. Fares fall to $60.68 against Windhover's $74 [app], so price-sensitive travellers on the busiest routes move, cutting revenue from 3,900,000 passengers [an].

Point 2: Matching the cut squeezes margins further [k]. Fuel is already up 23% after the carbon levy [app], so a fare of $60.68 leaves very little to cover the cost of each seat [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Windhover Airlines plc should match the fare cut? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Matching at $60.68 keeps passengers on 42 routes and prevents the rival from building loyalty. Empty seats earn nothing, so a lower fare still contributes to fixed costs.

Against: Fuel is up 23% and the 18% cut removes $13.32 a ticket, so matching may mean selling seats below cost.

Conclusion: Match only on the routes the rival has targeted. A selective response protects the 3,900,000 passengers where competition is direct, while leaving fares on other routes intact to cover the 23% fuel rise.

evaluation_max_2: Selective matching versus full match
Considers contribution per seat
analysis_max_2: Full match across 42 routes is too costly

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Fennick Appliances Ltd is a private limited company in Namibia assembling refrigerators, making 190,000 units a year at $430 each. The government has imposed a 15% sales tax on appliances and raised interest rates to 10.25%, while household incomes have fallen 3%. Directors must decide whether to cut output by 15% or offer interest-free credit to customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales tax'.
questions.model_answer: A sales tax is a tax charged on the price of a good when it is sold [k]. Namibia's 15% tax adds $64.50 to each $430 refrigerator Fennick makes [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tax on the sale of goods

questions.question_text: Calculate the sales tax payable on one $430 refrigerator at 15%.
Explain two ways the sales tax and higher interest rates may affect Fennick Appliances Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Refrigerators become dearer [k]. The 15% tax adds $64.50 to a $430 unit [app], and with household incomes down 3% buyers postpone replacement, so fewer of the 190,000 units sell [an].

Point 2: Credit purchases fall [k]. Interest rates at 10.25% make loans for appliances expensive [app], so customers who would buy on credit delay, cutting demand further [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Fennick Appliances Ltd should offer interest-free credit rather than cut output by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Interest-free credit answers the 10.25% rate rise directly and keeps 190,000 units selling. Cutting output by 15% would idle capacity and raise the fixed cost per refrigerator.

Against: Offering credit costs Fennick the interest it must itself pay, and with incomes down 3% some customers will default.

Conclusion: Offer credit for a limited period. It protects output and spreads fixed costs, whereas a 15% output cut would leave Fennick with idle plant just as the market recovers.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs credit cost against lost output
Considers default risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Hollowdean Creamery Ltd is a private limited company in Taiwan making butter, producing 6,800 tonnes a year at $7,100 a tonne. Directors must decide whether to switch suppliers before Christmas orders are placed.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical sourcing'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical sourcing means buying inputs from suppliers who treat workers, animals and the environment responsibly [k]. Hollowdean's palm oil supplier clears rainforest, which the supermarket chain will not accept [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual sales value of Hollowdean Creamery Ltd's 6,800 tonnes at $7,100 a tonne.
Explain two ways the palm oil allegation may affect Hollowdean Creamery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A major customer may withdraw [k]. The supermarket chain represents 22% of sales, worth about $10,621,600 of the $48,280,000 total [app], so losing it would cut volume sharply [an].

Point 2: Costs rise if suppliers are changed [k]. Certified sustainable oil costs 16% more [app], so butter margins fall on 6,800 tonnes unless the price to shoppers rises, which may reduce demand [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Hollowdean Creamery Ltd should switch to certified sustainable palm oil? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Switching protects 22% of sales, about $10,621,600, and answers a public campaign by Greenpeace. Certified oil also appeals to other retailers who check supply chains.
