analysis_max_2: Sales at risk exceed the cost increase

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Oakharrow Furniture plc is a public limited company in Mexico making oak tables, producing 58,000 a year at $740 each and exporting 45% to the United States. The peso has depreciated 13% against the dollar, and the United States has raised tariffs on Mexican furniture to 20%. The board must decide whether to raise its dollar price or absorb the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: A depreciation is a fall in the value of a currency against another [k]. The peso's 13% fall makes Oakharrow's tables cheaper in dollars for American buyers [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff payable per table at 20% of Oakharrow Furniture plc's $740 price.
Explain two effects of the 20% tariff on Oakharrow Furniture plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: American buyers pay more [k]. The tariff adds $148 to a $740 table [app], so the 45% of output sold in the United States becomes less competitive against local makers [an].

Point 2: The weaker peso softens the blow [k]. A 13% depreciation lowers the dollar cost of Mexican labour and oak [app], giving room to absorb part of the $148 without losing the whole margin [an].

analysis_max_2: Cost advantage can absorb part of the tariff

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakharrow Furniture plc should raise its dollar price to cover the tariff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Passing on the $148 tariff protects the margin on the 45% of tables sold in the United States, and American buyers may accept a rise because local tables are dearer still.

Against: A 20% increase could push buyers to local suppliers, and the 13% peso depreciation already gives Oakharrow room to absorb part of the tariff.

Conclusion: Absorb part and raise part. Sharing the $148 keeps the American orders while protecting some margin, and the 13% currency advantage makes a full pass-through unnecessary.

evaluation_max_2: Judges sharing the tariff against full pass-through
Considers local competitors

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Stonewick Pottery Ltd is a private limited company in Serbia making stoneware plates, selling 410,000 plates a year at $16.50. Directors must decide whether to raise prices by 9% or move production to a gas-fired kiln costing $560,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services [k]. Serbia's 12.4% rate raises the cost of clay, glaze and fuel for Stonewick [app].

knowledge_max_2: Falls in the value of money

questions.question_text: Calculate the price of a plate after a 9% rise from Stonewick Pottery Ltd's $16.50.
questions.model_answer: $16.50 x 1.09 = $17.99 to the nearest cent [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the electricity price rise on Stonewick Pottery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Firing costs rise sharply [k]. Electricity is up 31% while inflation is 12.4% [app], so each of the 410,000 plates costs more to produce, and a 9% price rise to $17.99 does not cover the gap [an].

Point 2: Investment in a gas kiln becomes worthwhile [k]. A $560,000 gas-fired kiln would reduce reliance on electricity [app], but the 6.5% interest rate makes any borrowing to fund it a fixed cost every year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Investment in a gas kiln considered
analysis_max_2: Price rise to $17.99 does not cover costs
Borrowing adds a fixed annual cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Stonewick Pottery Ltd should raise prices by 9%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:

Against: A 9% rise may lose customers who can buy imported plates, and it still does not cover the 31% energy increase, so profit may fall anyway.

Conclusion: Raise prices, but by more than 9% on trade customers only. Retail buyers are price-sensitive, whereas restaurants accept higher prices when quality is consistent, so a targeted rise covers the 31% energy bill without losing volume.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs price rise against volume loss

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ravensholt Vet Clinics Ltd is a private limited company in Honduras running 34 animal clinics, treating 210,000 animals a year at $28 a visit. questions.question_text: Define 'pressure group'.
questions.model_answer: A pressure group is an organisation that campaigns to change the behaviour of businesses or governments [k]. The charity urging clients to boycott clinics using the supplier's drugs is a pressure group [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual drug cost if Ravensholt Vet Clinics Ltd switches to a supplier charging 21% more than $1,600,000.
Explain two ways the boycott campaign may affect Ravensholt Vet Clinics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Switching suppliers raises costs [k]. A 21% higher drug bill adds $336,000 a year to $1,600,000 [app], cutting profit unless visit prices rise, which risks losing more clients [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensholt Vet Clinics Ltd should switch to the pricier supplier? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Brindlemoor Pumps plc is a public limited company in Sweden making water pumps, producing 96,000 a year at $1,280 each and selling 38% in India. questions.question_text: Define 'licensing'.

Usually in return for a fee or royalty

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff payable per pump at 22% of Brindlemoor Pumps plc's $1,280 price.

questions.question_text: Do you think Brindlemoor Pumps plc should license its design to the Indian firm? Justify your answer.

analysis_max_2: Licence fee is much lower than sale price

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Cobaltfen Batteries Ltd is a private limited company in Estonia making lithium battery packs, producing 540,000 packs a year at $96 each. knowledge_max_2: Money given to support a business

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Cobaltfen Batteries Ltd would pay on a $4,600,000 loan at 3.75%.

questions.question_text: Do you think Cobaltfen Batteries Ltd should fund the $4,600,000 laboratory from retained profit rather than a loan? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Yarrowfield Tea Ltd is a private limited company in Rwanda growing tea on 1,400 hectares, producing 8,200 tonnes a year at $2,050 a tonne. Directors must decide whether to seek certification costing $260,000 or expand onto woodland.

questions.question_text: Define 'fair trade'.
questions.model_answer: Fair trade is trade that guarantees producers a fair price and decent working conditions [k]. The certified buyer offers Yarrowfield 14% above the market price for its 8,200 tonnes [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue per tonne from the 14% fair-trade premium on Yarrowfield Tea Ltd's $2,050 price.
Explain two ways the forest law may affect Yarrowfield Tea Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Expansion onto woodland is blocked [k]. The ban removes the cheapest way to add hectarage beyond the 1,400 hectares already farmed [app], so output of 8,200 tonnes cannot grow that way [an].

Point 2: Certification becomes the better route to growth [k]. The fair-trade buyer pays $287 more a tonne [app], and although certification costs $260,000, the premium applies to every certified tonne sold [an].

analysis_max_2: Output cannot grow by clearing land
Premium applies to all certified tonnes

questions.question_text: Do you think Yarrowfield Tea Ltd should seek fair-trade certification rather than expand onto woodland? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Certification costs $260,000 once but earns $287 extra on every tonne, which is far more than clearing new land could return. It also complies with the forest law and protects the hillside soil that tea depends on.

Against: $260,000 is a large sum for a 8,200 tonne business, and the certified buyer may not take the whole crop.

Conclusion: Certify. The $287 a tonne premium repays the $260,000 within about a tenth of one year's output, whereas clearing woodland is now illegal and would damage the reputation the buyer is paying for.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $260,000 cost against $287 a tonne premium
Considers legal risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Clovermead Poultry plc is a public limited company in Pakistan processing chicken, producing 210,000 tonnes a year at $2,480 a tonne for buyers in the Gulf. A new trade agreement removes a 16% tariff on Brazilian rivals, and a multinational wants to buy 55% of the business. The board must decide whether to sell or invest $38,000,000 in cold storage.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods [k]. Removing the 16% tariff on Brazilian chicken lowers the price Gulf buyers pay for rival supplies [app].

knowledge_max_2: Raises the price of imported goods

questions.question_text: Calculate the price advantage Brazilian rivals gain per tonne when a 16% tariff on a $2,480 tonne is removed.
Explain two effects of the trade agreement on Clovermead Poultry plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Rivals become cheaper [k]. Removing the 16% tariff cuts Brazilian costs by $396.80 a tonne [app], so Gulf buyers may switch from Clovermead's $2,480 chicken [an].

Point 2: Investment in cold storage becomes a way to compete [k]. A $38,000,000 facility would improve quality and delivery reliability on 210,000 tonnes [app], but it cannot close a $396.80 price gap on its own [an].

knowledge_max_2: Quality investment cannot close the gap

questions.question_text: Do you think Clovermead Poultry plc should accept the multinational's offer for 55% of the business? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Selling 55% brings capital and access to markets that can offset the $396.80 a tonne advantage Brazilian rivals now enjoy. It also spreads the risk of a trade agreement that has gone against Pakistan.

Against: The board would lose control of 210,000 tonnes of output, and a multinational may cut costs by closing Pakistani plants.

Conclusion: Reject the offer and invest in cold storage. Losing 55% of the business is a permanent surrender, whereas the $38,000,000 investment keeps control while building the quality advantage that the 16% tariff change cannot remove.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs loss of control against market access
Considers rival cost advantage
analysis_max_2: 55% is a permanent loss of control

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marlinspur Marine Ltd is a private limited company in Panama repairing cargo ships, completing 240 refits a year at $310,000 each. A drought has cut canal traffic by 25%, and the government has raised port dues by 12%, while interest rates have climbed to 7.5%. Directors must decide whether to cut prices by 8% or diversify into yacht repairs.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when an economy's output falls for at least two successive quarters [k]. The drought's 25% fall in canal traffic has reduced the ship repair work Marlinspur relies on [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fall in output over two quarters

questions.question_text: Calculate the price of a refit after an 8% cut from Marlinspur Marine Ltd's $310,000.
Explain two effects of the drought on Marlinspur Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Fewer ships need repairing [k]. Canal traffic is down 25%, so refits fall below the 240 a year at $310,000 [app], leaving docks and engineers idle [an].

Point 2: Fixed costs are spread over fewer jobs [k]. Port dues are up 12% and interest rates at 7.5% add to borrowing costs [app], so the cost per refit rises just as revenue falls [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlinspur Marine Ltd should cut prices by 8% or diversify into yacht repairs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: An 8% cut to $285,200 keeps some work flowing through the docks while canal traffic is 25% lower, and ship owners will compare quotes closely in a downturn.

Against: Cutting $24,800 from every refit reduces revenue on work Marlinspur already struggles to win, and yacht owners pay more for specialist finishes.

Conclusion: Diversify into yacht repairs. A price cut only shares out shrinking canal work, whereas yachts use the same docks and skills while removing reliance on traffic that is down 25%.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs discount against new market
Considers use of existing capacity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Thistledown Wool Ltd is a private limited company in Greece spinning wool, producing 2,300 tonnes a year at $9,600 a tonne. A new landfill tax of $95 a tonne applies to its 320 tonnes of waste, and a fashion brand will only buy wool from farms meeting animal welfare standards. Directors must decide whether to pay $470,000 for waste recycling.

questions.question_text: Define 'landfill tax'.
questions.model_answer: A landfill tax is a charge on waste sent to be buried in the ground [k]. Greece charges Thistledown $95 for each of the 320 tonnes of waste it sends to landfill [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tax on waste sent to landfill

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual landfill tax Thistledown Wool Ltd would pay on 320 tonnes at $95 a tonne.
Explain two ways the landfill tax may affect Thistledown Wool Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Waste disposal becomes a cost [k]. At $95 a tonne on 320 tonnes Thistledown pays $30,400 a year [app], which reduces the margin on 2,300 tonnes of wool sold at $9,600 [an].

Point 2: Recycling equipment becomes more attractive [k]. A $470,000 recycling line would cut taxable waste [app], but the saving of $30,400 a year takes many years to recover the outlay [an].

analysis_max_2: Saving is small against the outlay

questions.question_text: Do you think Thistledown Wool Ltd should pay $470,000 for waste recycling? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Recycling cuts the $30,400 annual landfill tax and helps meet the fashion brand's animal welfare and environmental standards, protecting sales at $9,600 a tonne.

Against: $470,000 would take more than fifteen years to recover through tax savings alone, and the brand's standards concern farms rather than waste.

Conclusion: Do not buy the line for tax reasons alone. The $30,400 saving is too small, but Thistledown should first cut waste and secure the brand contract, since that protects far more revenue than the tax costs.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $470,000 cost against $30,400 saving
Considers brand contract value
analysis_max_2: Tax saving alone cannot justify the outlay

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Glenvane Pharma plc is a public limited company in Nepal making generic medicines, producing 84,000,000 tablets a year at $0.11 each and selling 30% to India. India has introduced a 12% import duty and stricter quality inspections, and a multinational has offered a licensing deal. The board must decide whether to accept the licence or build a plant in India.

questions.question_text: Define 'import duty'.
questions.model_answer: An import duty is a tax charged on goods entering a country [k]. India's 12% duty adds to the price of each of Glenvane's tablets sold there [app].

knowledge_max_2: Raises the cost of selling abroad

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue from Glenvane Pharma plc's Indian sales if 30% of 84,000,000 tablets sell at $0.11 each.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue = units x share x price

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of India's import duty on Glenvane Pharma plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Indian sales become less profitable [k]. A 12% duty reduces the margin on 25,200,000 tablets worth $2,772,000 [app], and generic medicines compete almost entirely on price [an].

Point 2: Local production becomes more attractive [k]. A plant in India would avoid the duty and the stricter inspections at the border [app], but it requires capital and may be opposed by Indian manufacturers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Glenvane Pharma plc should accept the licensing deal rather than build a plant in India? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Licensing avoids the 12% duty and the cost of a plant while earning a fee from 25,200,000 tablets of demand. It also shifts the burden of Indian inspections to the licensee.

Against: A licence gives away the formulation and earns far less than $2,772,000 of direct sales, and the licensee may become a rival in other markets.

Conclusion: Accept the licence for India only. The 12% duty and inspections make direct sales costly, but a licence limited to India keeps Glenvane's formulations for Nepal and other export markets.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs licence fee against lost direct sales
Considers competitive risk
analysis_max_2: Duty and inspections make exports costly

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quarryford Glass Ltd is a private limited company in Tunisia making bottles, producing 130,000 tonnes a year at $680 a tonne. Natural gas prices have risen 34% and the government has cut VAT on recycled glass from 19% to 7%, while interest rates stand at 8%. Directors must decide whether to build a recycled glass furnace costing $7,400,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'value added tax'.
questions.model_answer: Value added tax is a tax charged on the value added at each stage of production and on final sales [k]. Tunisia's cut from 19% to 7% lowers the tax on Quarryford's recycled glass [app].

knowledge_max_2: Charged at each stage of production

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Quarryford Glass Ltd would pay on a $7,400,000 furnace loan at 8%.
Explain two effects of the gas price rise on Quarryford Glass Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Melting costs rise sharply [k]. Gas is up 34% for a plant melting 130,000 tonnes a year [app], so the cost of each tonne of bottles rises well above the $680 price unless it is passed on [an].

Point 2: Investment in recycled glass becomes more attractive [k]. VAT on recycled glass falling from 19% to 7% lowers its effective cost [app], and recycled cullet melts at a lower temperature, cutting gas use, though the $7,400,000 furnace needs $592,000 a year in interest [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Quarryford Glass Ltd should build the recycled glass furnace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Recycled cullet melts at a lower temperature, offsetting part of the 34% gas rise, and VAT on recycled glass has fallen from 19% to 7%. The furnace also reduces reliance on imported raw materials.

Against: $7,400,000 at 8% costs $592,000 a year before any gas is saved, and glass makers elsewhere may undercut Quarryford on price.

Conclusion: Build it only with grant support. The energy saving and VAT cut make recycling sensible, but $592,000 of annual interest is too heavy for a business already facing a 34% gas rise.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs energy saving against $592,000 interest
Considers competitor pricing
analysis_max_2: Lower melting temperature cuts gas use

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Alderbush Organics Ltd is a private limited company in Ireland growing vegetables, harvesting 4,600 tonnes a year at $2,240 a tonne. A fertiliser runoff has polluted a lake, and the regulator will fine the business 3% of revenue unless buffer strips are planted. Directors must decide whether to plant 40 hectares of buffer strips or risk the fine.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of production borne by people who are not part of the transaction [k]. Alderbush's fertiliser runoff damages a lake used by local people, which the regulator is trying to stop [app].

knowledge_max_2: Environmental damage not charged to the firm

questions.question_text: Calculate the fine Alderbush Organics Ltd would pay at 3% of revenue from 4,600 tonnes at $2,240 a tonne.
Explain two ways the pollution may affect Alderbush Organics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A fine threatens profit [k]. Paying 3% of revenue from 4,600 tonnes at $2,240 costs $309,120 [app], which is a large sum for a vegetable grower with thin margins [an].

Point 2: Buffer strips take land out of production [k]. Planting 40 hectares reduces the area growing crops [app], so output and revenue fall even though the pollution stops [an].

analysis_max_2: Thin margins cannot absorb the fine

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderbush Organics Ltd should plant the 40 hectares of buffer strips rather than risk the fine? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Buffer strips stop the runoff permanently and avoid a $309,120 fine, which would recur each year the pollution continues. They also protect the lake that local customers and retailers care about.

Against: Taking 40 hectares out of production cuts output, and the fine may never be imposed in full.

Conclusion: Plant the strips. The $309,120 fine is a certain annual risk against a one-off loss of land, and organic growers sell on environmental trust that a pollution case would destroy.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs fine against lost output
Considers reputation with retailers
analysis_max_2: Fine of $309,120 recurs if nothing changes

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kingsholm Tile plc is a public limited company in Jordan making floor tiles, producing 9,200,000 square metres a year at $6.40 and exporting 26% to Egypt. Egypt has devalued its pound by 21% against the dollar and imposed a 15% tariff on imported tiles. The board must decide whether to cut its Egyptian price or withdraw from the market.

questions.question_text: Define 'devaluation'.
questions.model_answer: A devaluation is a deliberate fall in a currency's value against other currencies [k]. Egypt's pound has fallen 21% against the dollar, making Kingsholm's tiles dearer for Egyptian buyers [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff payable per square metre at 15% of Kingsholm Tile plc's $6.40 price.
questions.model_answer: $6.40 x 15% = $0.96 per square metre [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the devaluation on Kingsholm Tile plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Egyptian buyers pay much more [k]. A 21% fall in the pound plus a 15% tariff adds $0.96 to a $6.40 tile [app], so the 26% of output sold in Egypt becomes hard to shift [an].

Point 2: Cutting the dollar price protects volume but not margin [k]. Reducing the price would offset part of the devaluation [app], yet with 9,200,000 square metres to sell, the loss per tile multiplies across the whole Egyptian order [an].

analysis_max_2: Loss per tile multiplies across volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsholm Tile plc should withdraw from the Egyptian market? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 21% devaluation plus a 15% tariff makes $6.40 tiles uncompetitive in Egypt, and price cuts would destroy the margin across 26% of output. Withdrawal frees capacity for markets without those barriers.

Against: Egypt may be a long-term market once the currency stabilises, and leaving lets rival suppliers build relationships that are hard to win back.

Conclusion: Reduce presence rather than withdraw completely. Keep a small Egyptian order through a local distributor, because the 21% devaluation may reverse, while shifting most of the 26% to other markets now.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs withdrawal against staying small
Considers future currency recovery
analysis_max_2: Devaluation and tariff together are severe

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Rookhaven Buses Ltd is a private limited company in Mongolia operating 620 buses on intercity routes, selling 7,800,000 tickets a year at $1.30. A currency depreciation of 16% has raised the cost of its $2,400,000 annual order of imported spare parts, and the government has capped fares for two years. Directors must decide whether to delay replacing 90 buses until the currency stabilises.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: A depreciation is a fall in the value of a currency against another [k]. Mongolia's 16% fall raises the local cost of Rookhaven's imported spare parts [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual cost of Rookhaven Buses Ltd's imported spare parts if the bill is $2,400,000 and the currency depreciates 16%.
Explain two effects of the depreciation on Rookhaven Buses Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Maintenance costs rise [k]. Spare parts costing $2,400,000 a year become $384,000 dearer [app], and with fares capped the extra cost cannot be passed to passengers [an].

Point 2: Replacing buses becomes expensive [k]. Ninety new buses would be priced in foreign currency [app], so the fleet may have to run longer, raising breakdown risk on 620 vehicles [an].

analysis_max_2: Fares are capped so costs cannot pass through

questions.question_text: Do you think Rookhaven Buses Ltd should delay replacing 90 buses until the currency stabilises? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: New buses would be priced in a currency that has just risen 16%, and fares are capped for two years. Delaying avoids taking on foreign-currency debt while the exchange rate is unfavourable.

Against: Keeping 90 old buses raises breakdowns and fuel use, and passengers paying $1.30 expect reliable journeys across 620 vehicles.

Conclusion: Delay only part of the order. Replacing the oldest buses cannot wait, but buying all 90 at a 16% currency premium would add debt that capped fares cannot service, on top of $384,000 extra for parts each year.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs currency cost against fleet reliability
Considers fare cap

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sorrelbank Print Ltd is a private limited company in Latvia printing catalogues, producing 46,000 tonnes of paper products a year at $1,520 a tonne. A forestry certification scheme will charge $28 a tonne for uncertified paper, and a retail client wants 100% recycled stock by 2027. Directors must decide whether to buy certified paper at 9% more.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable sourcing'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable sourcing means buying materials produced in ways that protect forests and communities for the future [k]. Sorrelbank's retail client wants 100% recycled stock by 2027 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Buying materials with limited environmental harm

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual certification charge Sorrelbank Print Ltd would pay on 46,000 tonnes at $28 a tonne.
Explain two ways the certification scheme may affect Sorrelbank Print Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Uncertified paper becomes costly [k]. The $28 charge on 46,000 tonnes would total $1,288,000 a year [app], which is larger than the whole margin on paper sold at $1,520 a tonne [an].

Point 2: Certified paper raises input prices [k]. Buying certified stock costs 9% more [app], but it keeps the retail client that wants 100% recycled material by 2027, protecting long-term orders [an].

analysis_max_2: Charge exceeds the margin per tonne

questions.question_text: Do you think Sorrelbank Print Ltd should buy certified paper at 9% more? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Certified paper avoids the $1,288,000 annual charge on uncertified stock and satisfies the client's 2027 requirement. The 9% premium is far smaller than the $28 a tonne charge.

Against: A 9% rise in input costs cuts the margin on 46,000 tonnes, and the client may move to another printer anyway.

Conclusion: Buy certified paper. Nine per cent of $1,520 is about $137 a tonne against a $28 charge, but avoiding the charge and keeping the client together clearly outweigh the premium.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs 9% premium against $28 charge
Considers client retention

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Verdanthorpe Cocoa plc is a public limited company in Nigeria grinding cocoa, processing 74,000 tonnes a year at $3,300 a tonne and exporting 62% to Europe. The naira has depreciated 24% against the euro, and the European Union will cut its import quota by 10%. The board must decide whether to raise output or open a grinding plant in the Netherlands.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota'.
questions.model_answer: A quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported [k]. The European Union will cut its cocoa import quota by 10%, reducing the 45,880 tonnes Verdanthorpe currently sends there [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in tonnes if the European Union cuts its 45,880 tonne cocoa import quota by 10%.
questions.model_answer: 45,880 tonnes x 10% = 4,588 tonnes [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the quota cut on Verdanthorpe Cocoa plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: European sales are reduced [k]. Losing 4,588 tonnes of the 45,880 tonnes allowed [app] means 62% of output can no longer be sold freely, so unsold cocoa must be diverted or stored [an].

Point 2: The weaker naira softens the loss [k]. A 24% depreciation makes Nigerian cocoa cheaper in euros [app], so Verdanthorpe can compete harder for the remaining quota, though it cannot create extra quota [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Verdanthorpe Cocoa plc should open a grinding plant in the Netherlands rather than raise output? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A plant inside the European Union escapes the import quota and the 10% cut, and grinding closer to buyers cuts transport costs. It also shelters the business from future trade barriers.

Against: Building in the Netherlands brings high wage and energy costs, while the 24% naira depreciation already makes Nigerian processing cheap.

Conclusion: Do not build yet. The 24% depreciation gives Verdanthorpe a strong cost advantage in Nigeria, so it should raise output and sell the extra 4,588 tonnes to Asian buyers before investing in a European plant.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs quota avoidance against higher European costs
Considers currency advantage

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Larchmont Bikes Ltd is a private limited company in Ukraine making mountain bikes, producing 128,000 bikes a year at $290 each. Inflation has reached 15.8% and the central bank has raised interest rates to 18%, while frame steel costs have risen 21%. Directors must decide whether to raise prices by 10% or cut the workforce by 40 employees.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services [k]. Ukraine's 15.8% rate raises the cost of steel, paint and wages for Larchmont [app].

questions.question_text: Calculate the price of a bike after a 10% rise from Larchmont Bikes Ltd's $290.
Explain two effects of the 18% interest rate on Larchmont Bikes Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Borrowing for stock becomes expensive [k]. Interest at 18% makes any loan for steel and components costly [app], so the business must finance 128,000 bikes from its own cash [an].

Point 2: Customers buy fewer bikes on credit [k]. Ukrainian households facing 18% rates and 15.8% inflation postpone large purchases [app], so demand falls while steel costs are up 21% [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Larchmont Bikes Ltd should raise prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Steel is up 21% and inflation at 15.8%, so a 10% rise to $319 recovers part of the cost increase and protects the margin on 128,000 bikes.

Against: Households facing 18% interest rates are already cutting spending, and a 10% rise may reduce sales of a $290 product.

Conclusion: Raise prices but by less than steel costs have risen. A 10% rise to $319 keeps Larchmont close to competitors, whereas passing on the full 21% would price bikes out of a market where credit is expensive.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs cost recovery against demand
Considers competitor prices

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sablecove Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Oman running three desert resorts with 260 rooms, earning $11,400,000 a year. A water conservation levy of 6% has been added to its $640,000 water bill, and guests are complaining about single-use plastic. Directors must decide whether to spend $380,000 on refillable glass bottles and water meters.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means operating in a way that meets present needs without compromising resources for the future [k]. Sablecove must cut water use and plastic waste to keep its desert resorts viable [app].

knowledge_max_2: Meeting needs without harming the future
Balances economic, social and environmental goals

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra water cost for Sablecove Hotels Ltd from a 6% levy on a $640,000 water bill.
Explain two ways the water levy may affect Sablecove Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Operating costs rise [k]. The 6% levy adds $38,400 to a $640,000 water bill [app], and desert resorts cannot reduce water use much without upsetting guests, so the cost must be absorbed from $11,400,000 of room revenue [an].

Point 2: Investment in water meters becomes worthwhile [k]. Meters would show where the 260 rooms waste water [app], and the $380,000 outlay also buys refillable bottles that answer guests' complaints about plastic [an].

knowledge_max_2: Water meters and bottles become worthwhile
analysis_max_2: Water use cannot easily be cut

questions.question_text: Do you think Sablecove Hotels Ltd should spend $380,000 on refillable bottles and water meters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Meters identify waste across 260 rooms and refillable bottles answer guests' complaints about plastic, protecting the reputation that fills three desert resorts. The equipment also limits exposure to further water levies.

Against: $380,000 is nearly ten years of the current $38,400 levy, and guests may not change their habits enough to justify it.

Conclusion: Install the meters first and bottles in stages. The $38,400 annual levy alone is too small to justify $380,000, but water scarcity in Oman makes meters a necessary protection for a business earning $11,400,000 from desert resorts.

evaluation_max_2: Phases spending against the $38,400 levy
Considers water scarcity risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Veltrix Components is a private limited company in Vietnam moulding plastic housings for appliance makers, employing 180 staff and earning $6,400,000 a year. Inflation has reached 6.2% while the central bank lifted interest rates to 11.5%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $1,800,000 for automated moulding machines or continue renting equipment at $240,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services in an economy [2]. Vietnam's 6.2% rate means Veltrix Components pays more each year for polymer granules, electricity and wages.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general price level
Money loses purchasing power as prices climb

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Veltrix Components would pay on a $1,800,000 loan at 11.5%.
questions.model_answer: $1,800,000 x 11.5% = $207,000 a year [2]. This is $33,000 less than the $240,000 annual equipment rental.

knowledge_max_2: Interest = amount borrowed x interest rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 11.5% interest rate on Veltrix Components.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Servicing the loan becomes expensive [k]. Borrowing $1,800,000 at 11.5% costs $207,000 a year [app], and that cash must be found before the moulding machines earn any revenue, squeezing the $6,400,000 turnover [an].

Point 2: Appliance makers delay their own investment [k]. Higher rates raise the cost of the credit they use to refit factories [app], so orders for plastic housings may fall just as Veltrix adds capacity [an].

knowledge_max_2: Borrowing and loan servicing become more costly
Customer demand financed by credit declines
analysis_max_2: Interest must be paid before the machines generate profit
Fewer housing orders leave new capacity underused

questions.question_text: Do you think Veltrix Components should borrow $1,800,000 for the automated moulding machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the $207,000 annual interest is $33,000 below the $240,000 rental, and the company would own an asset that raises output and quality for its appliance customers.

Against: inflation of 6.2% may push the rate higher, and a 180-person payroll must still be paid if demand falls. A fixed $207,000 commitment is risky when orders are already uncertain.

Conclusion: borrowing is justified only if Veltrix signs volume contracts first; otherwise renting at $240,000 keeps flexibility.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $33,000 annual saving against fixed interest risk
Judgement depends on order security and rate movements

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Halvorsen Fjord Salmon is a partnership in Norway farming 2,400 tonnes of salmon a year, with 95 staff and revenue of $21,000,000. A carbon tax of $24 a tonne now applies to 3,200 tonnes of carbon dioxide from its diesel feed barges, while a 15% subsidy is offered on a $1,600,000 electric barge. Partners must decide whether to buy the electric barge or keep the diesel fleet.

questions.question_text: Define 'carbon tax'.
questions.model_answer: A carbon tax is a government charge on each tonne of carbon dioxide a business releases [2]. Halvorsen Fjord Salmon must pay $24 for every tonne emitted by its diesel feed barges.

knowledge_max_2: Tax based on the volume of carbon emissions
Aims to make polluters pay and discourage fossil fuel use

questions.question_text: Calculate Halvorsen Fjord Salmon's annual carbon tax bill on 3,200 tonnes of carbon dioxide at $24 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 3,200 tonnes x $24 = $76,800 a year [2]. The 15% subsidy would cut the $1,600,000 electric barge price by $240,000.

knowledge_max_2: Tax bill = emissions x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halvorsen Fjord Salmon of buying the electric barge.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It removes the carbon tax [k]. The diesel fleet emits 3,200 tonnes at $24, costing $76,800 a year [app], so the saving improves cash flow and protects the $21,000,000 revenue from future tax rises [an].

Point 2: The 15% subsidy lowers the capital cost [k]. It reduces the $1,600,000 price by $240,000 to $1,360,000 [app], making the investment easier for a partnership with only 95 staff to finance and improving its environmental reputation with Norwegian buyers [an].

application_max_2: Saves $76,800 a year on 3,200 tonnes at $24
analysis_max_2: Green reputation supports sales and finance access

questions.question_text: Do you think Halvorsen Fjord Salmon should buy the electric barge? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the barge saves the $76,800 annual carbon tax, and the 15% subsidy cuts its price to $1,360,000, so costs fall and the partnership becomes more credible with retailers wanting low-carbon salmon.

Against: $1,360,000 is a large commitment for a 95-staff partnership, and $76,800 a year recovers only a small share of it, while diesel prices and tax rules may change.

Conclusion: buying is worthwhile as a long-term signal to buyers, but the partners should secure a subsidised loan rather than fund it all from reserves.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $76,800 annual saving with $1,360,000 outlay
Considers finance risk for a small partnership
analysis_max_2: Tax avoidance lowers operating costs permanently
Reputation strengthens bargaining power with buyers

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Nimara Garments is a private limited company in Bangladesh sewing 900,000 shirts a year for European brands, with 1,300 staff and revenue of $14,400,000. The European Union now charges a 9% tariff on those shirts, and a trade bloc offers tariff-free entry if Nimara passes an audit costing $180,000. Directors must decide whether to fund the audit or absorb the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax charged on imported goods, raising their price in the destination country [2]. The 9% tariff on Nimara Garments' shirts adds cost for European buyers.

knowledge_max_2: Raises the price of foreign goods and protects domestic producers

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff Nimara Garments would pay on $14,400,000 of shirt exports at 9%.
questions.model_answer: $14,400,000 x 9% = $1,296,000 a year [2]. That is far more than the $180,000 cost of the audit.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff = export value x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why passing the audit may benefit Nimara Garments.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Tariff-free entry cuts a major cost [k]. The 9% tariff currently costs $1,296,000 a year on $14,400,000 of exports [app], so passing the $180,000 audit saves far more and lets Nimara price shirts competitively in Europe [an].

Point 2: The certificate signals acceptable labour and safety standards [k]. European brands increasingly check suppliers before ordering [app], so approved status can win new contracts and protect the jobs of 1,300 staff [an].

knowledge_max_2: Certification proves acceptable standards to buyers
analysis_max_2: Approved supplier status attracts long-term contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Nimara Garments should fund the $180,000 audit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the audit costs $180,000 but removes a $1,296,000 annual tariff, a saving of over seven times the fee, and tariff-free status could win extra European orders.

Against: the audit may reveal problems that are expensive to fix, the bloc could change its rules, and $180,000 is significant for a firm already paying 1,300 wages.

Conclusion: Nimara should fund the audit because the tariff saving is so much larger, provided the fee is staged and the standards are achievable within a year.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,296,000 tariff against $180,000 fee
Notes risk of failing or rule changes

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Orinoco Cocoa is a co-operative in Ghana processing 8,000 tonnes of cocoa beans a year, with 320 member farmers, a wage bill of $3,600,000 and revenue of $19,200,000. Inflation of 9.8% has raised fuel and packaging costs, while the central bank lifted interest rates to 13.0%. The board must decide whether to borrow $2,000,000 for a roasting line or raise member payments instead.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the percentage charged for borrowing money or paid on savings [2]. Ghana's 13.0% rate means Orinoco Cocoa would pay $260,000 a year on a $2,000,000 loan.

knowledge_max_2: Cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage
Return paid to savers or lenders

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $2,000,000 loan at 13.0%.
questions.model_answer: $2,000,000 x 13.0% = $260,000 a year [2]. This equals 7.2% of the co-operative's $3,600,000 wage bill.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 13.0% interest rate on Orinoco Cocoa.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The roasting line becomes costly to finance [k]. A $2,000,000 loan at 13.0% adds $260,000 of annual interest [app], which must be covered before the line processes a single bean, reducing the surplus shared with 320 farmers [an].

Point 2: Farmers face dearer credit for their own farms [k]. Higher rates make loans for seedlings and equipment expensive [app], so member output may fall and Orinoco's 8,000-tonne supply could shrink [an].

knowledge_max_2: Member farmers face higher borrowing costs
analysis_max_2: Interest reduces the surplus available to members
Weaker farm investment threatens bean supply

questions.question_text: Do you think Orinoco Cocoa should borrow $2,000,000 for the roasting line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: roasting beans before export adds value, and a $260,000 interest bill may be covered if the line raises the price received per tonne and cuts waste.

Against: inflation of 9.8% is pushing up fuel and packaging, so costs are already rising, and $260,000 is a fixed burden on a co-operative that must also pay $3,600,000 in wages.

Conclusion: borrowing is justified only if buyers contract to purchase the roasted output; otherwise raising member payments protects loyalty with less financial risk.

evaluation_max_2: Balances value added against $260,000 fixed interest
Considers 9.8% inflation and member loyalty
analysis_max_2: Processing raises export value per tonne

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sundarban Rice Mills is a private limited company in India milling 60,000 tonnes of rice a year, with 240 staff and revenue of $27,000,000. New rules require 40% of husk waste to be recycled, and a landfill levy of $35 a tonne applies to the 5,000 tonnes it currently dumps. Managers must decide whether to install a $600,000 briquetting plant or keep paying the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is processing waste materials so they can be used again instead of being discarded [2]. Sundarban Rice Mills would turn rice husks into briquettes rather than dump 5,000 tonnes.

knowledge_max_2: Reduces landfill and raw material use

questions.question_text: Calculate the landfill levy saved each year if 40% of the 5,000 tonnes of husk is recycled at a levy of $35 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 40% of 5,000 tonnes = 2,000 tonnes; 2,000 x $35 = $70,000 saved a year [2]. The remaining 3,000 tonnes still cost $105,000.

knowledge_max_2: Levy saved = tonnes diverted x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Sundarban Rice Mills of installing the briquetting plant.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It avoids landfill levy payments [k]. Recycling 40% of 5,000 tonnes saves $70,000 a year immediately, and processing all husks would remove the full $175,000 bill [app], lowering costs on $27,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Briquettes create a saleable product from waste [k]. The plant converts husks into fuel blocks that can be sold to brick kilns and boilers [app], diversifying income beyond rice and improving the firm's standing with regulators [an].

knowledge_max_2: Creates a new revenue stream from waste

questions.question_text: Do you think Sundarban Rice Mills should install the $600,000 briquetting plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the plant meets the 40% recycling rule, saves $70,000 a year at once and could remove the whole $175,000 levy while making briquettes to sell.

Against: $600,000 is over eight times the immediate $70,000 saving, and the plant needs power, maintenance and trained staff, with demand for briquettes uncertain.

Conclusion: the investment is justified as a licence-protecting move, but only if management confirms buyers for the briquettes so the $600,000 is recovered faster.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $600,000 cost with $70,000 to $175,000 savings
Weighs regulatory necessity against uncertain briquette demand
analysis_max_2: Compliance secures the right to operate
New product spreads risk beyond rice

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kilimani Freight is a private limited company in Kenya moving containers between Mombasa and Nairobi, with 210 trucks and revenue of $16,800,000. A new regional trade bloc removes a 12% tariff on imported truck parts, but requires emissions certificates costing $95,000 a year. The managing director must decide whether to join the bloc or keep trading outside it.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade bloc'.
questions.model_answer: A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members [2]. The bloc offering Kilimani Freight tariff-free parts also sets common rules for members.

knowledge_max_2: Group of countries with a trade agreement
Members reduce tariffs or quotas among themselves

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual saving if the 12% tariff is removed on $3,200,000 of imported truck parts.
questions.model_answer: $3,200,000 x 12% = $384,000 saved a year [2]. After the $95,000 certificate cost, the net gain is $289,000.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = import value x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kilimani Freight of joining the trade bloc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Parts become cheaper [k]. Removing the 12% tariff on $3,200,000 of imports saves $384,000 a year [app], and even after the $95,000 certificates the firm gains $289,000, which can fund fleet maintenance [an].

Point 2: Membership eases cross-border journeys [k]. Common paperwork and recognised emissions certificates reduce delays at frontiers [app], helping 210 trucks complete more trips and raise revenue above $16,800,000 [an].

knowledge_max_2: Simpler rules speed up cross-border transport

questions.question_text: Do you think Kilimani Freight should join the trade bloc? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the tariff saving is $384,000 a year, and after the $95,000 certificates the firm is $289,000 better off, while smoother borders help its 210 trucks earn more.

Against: membership brings inspections and reporting that could disrupt schedules, the $95,000 fee is payable even in a bad year, and bloc rules may limit where Kilimani can buy parts.

Conclusion: joining is worthwhile because the $289,000 net gain is substantial, but the director should confirm the certificate process will not delay urgent containers.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $384,000 saving against $95,000 compliance cost
Considers operational disruption and rule constraints

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marisol Ceramics is a family partnership in Portugal making 240,000 decorative tiles a year, with 78 staff, a wage bill of $2,184,000 and revenue of $6,720,000. Unemployment has fallen to 5.4%, forcing wages up 7.5%, while inflation of 3.2% has raised clay and glaze costs. Partners must decide whether to invest $900,000 in a second kiln or hold output and raise prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: Unemployment is the number of people who are able and willing to work but cannot find a job [2]. Portugal's 5.4% rate means Marisol Ceramics struggles to recruit skilled tile painters.

knowledge_max_2: People of working age without a job who are seeking work
Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Calculate the increase in Marisol Ceramics' annual wage bill if wages rise by 7.5% from $2,184,000.
questions.model_answer: $2,184,000 x 7.5% = $163,800 extra a year [2]. The wage bill would rise to $2,347,800.

knowledge_max_2: Increase = current wage bill x percentage rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of falling unemployment on Marisol Ceramics.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Skilled labour becomes scarce [k]. With unemployment at 5.4%, the partnership must pay 7.5% more, adding $163,800 to a $2,184,000 wage bill [app], which reduces profit on $6,720,000 of sales unless prices rise [an].

Point 2: Local demand for home tiles strengthens [k]. More employed households renovate their homes [app], so Marisol may sell more than 240,000 tiles a year, but only if it can staff a second kiln [an].

analysis_max_2: Capacity limits the ability to meet extra demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Marisol Ceramics should invest $900,000 in a second kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: falling unemployment is lifting demand for home improvements, and extra capacity would let the partnership sell beyond 240,000 tiles and spread its $163,800 wage increase over more units.

Against: wages and clay costs are rising while inflation is 3.2%, and a $900,000 kiln adds fixed costs that 78 staff must justify even in a quiet year.

Conclusion: the kiln is justified if order books show sustained demand; otherwise holding output and raising prices protects cash while the economy settles.

evaluation_max_2: Balances demand growth against $900,000 fixed cost
Considers rising wage and material costs
analysis_max_2: Price rises risk losing price-sensitive customers

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tarkine Timber is a private limited company in Australia harvesting plantation timber, with 160 staff and revenue of $32,400,000. A biodiversity levy of $6 per cubic metre applies to the 60,000 cubic metres of native logs it buys, while a new standard requires 30% of its offcuts to be reused. Directors must decide whether to spend $450,000 on a pellet plant or keep paying the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means operating so that resources are not depleted and future generations can meet their needs [2]. Tarkine Timber must reuse 30% of its offcuts to protect forest resources.

knowledge_max_2: Meeting present needs without harming future generations
Balancing economic, social and environmental impacts

questions.question_text: Calculate Tarkine Timber's annual biodiversity levy on 60,000 cubic metres at $6 per cubic metre.
questions.model_answer: 60,000 x $6 = $360,000 a year [2]. This is 80% of the $450,000 pellet plant cost.

knowledge_max_2: Levy = volume x rate per cubic metre

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tarkine Timber of building the pellet plant.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It turns a levy into a saving [k]. The plant would process offcuts instead of paying $6 per cubic metre, and the $360,000 annual levy could be avoided on the logs redirected to pellets [app], improving margin on $32,400,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: It meets the new reuse standard [k]. Reusing 30% of offcuts keeps Tarkine compliant and avoids fines or lost certification [app], which matters to builders who check the environmental credentials of their timber suppliers [an].

analysis_max_2: Certification protects sales to ethical builders

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarkine Timber should spend $450,000 on the pellet plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the $360,000 annual levy is close to the $450,000 cost, so the plant would soon pay for itself, and it secures compliance with the 30% reuse standard.

Against: $450,000 is a large outlay for a firm with 160 staff, pellet prices may be low, and the levy applies only to native logs, so the saving could shrink if sourcing changes.

Conclusion: building the plant is sensible because the levy alone nearly equals the cost, but directors should confirm a pellet buyer before committing.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $360,000 annual levy with $450,000 cost
Considers pellet market and future sourcing
analysis_max_2: Levy avoidance gives a quick financial return

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sahil Electronics is a public limited company in the United Arab Emirates assembling 500,000 set-top boxes a year, with 620 staff and revenue of $45,000,000. A trade bloc has cut its external tariff on imported components from 14% to 6% on $12,000,000 of purchases, but a quota now caps exports at 300,000 units against planned exports of 380,000. The board must decide whether to build a plant inside the bloc.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota'.
questions.model_answer: A quota is a physical limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported or exported [2]. The quota caps Sahil Electronics' exports at 300,000 set-top boxes.

knowledge_max_2: Limit on the volume of trade in a product
Restricts supply and can raise prices

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual saving from the tariff cut on $12,000,000 of imported components when the rate falls from 14% to 6%.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = import value x fall in tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 300,000-unit quota on Sahil Electronics.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Sales inside the bloc are capped [k]. Planned exports of 380,000 units are cut by 80,000 [app], leaving finished boxes unsold and spreading fixed costs over 500,000 units instead of the planned volume, which lowers profit on $45,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Scarcity may support higher prices [k]. With only 300,000 units admitted, Sahil can charge distributors more per box [app], partly offsetting lost volume but risking customers switching to local rivals [an].

knowledge_max_2: Limited supply can support higher prices
analysis_max_2: Unsold output raises average fixed cost
Higher prices may lose buyers to competitors

questions.question_text: Do you think Sahil Electronics should build a plant inside the trade bloc? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: a plant inside the bloc avoids the 300,000-unit quota, serves 380,000 planned customers and gains the $960,000 tariff saving on components.

Against: a new plant is expensive, duplicates 620 staff and capacity, and the bloc could change rules again, while the $45,000,000 revenue may not support two sites.

Conclusion: building inside the bloc is justified only if the 80,000 blocked units are profitable enough to repay the plant; otherwise Sahil should license a local assembler.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs quota-free access and $960,000 saving against plant cost
Considers rule uncertainty and duplicated capacity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Zebulon Dairy is a private limited company in Israel producing 90,000,000 litres of milk a year, with 340 staff, revenue of $108,000,000 and profit of $9,000,000. Interest rates have risen to 8.75% and corporate tax is 23%. The finance director must decide whether to borrow $14,000,000 for a bottling plant or lease equipment at $1,900,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'corporate tax'.
questions.model_answer: Corporate tax is a tax charged on the profits of a company [2]. Zebulon Dairy pays 23% on its $9,000,000 profit, which is $2,070,000.

knowledge_max_2: Levied by government on company earnings

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $14,000,000 loan at 8.75%.
questions.model_answer: $14,000,000 x 8.75% = $1,225,000 a year [2]. This is $675,000 less than the $1,900,000 annual lease.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 8.75% interest rate on Zebulon Dairy.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The bottling plant becomes cheaper to finance than leasing [k]. Interest on $14,000,000 at 8.75% is $1,225,000, which is $675,000 below the $1,900,000 lease [app], so borrowing frees cash for marketing or staff [an].

Point 2: A large fixed interest bill raises financial risk [k]. The $1,225,000 must be paid even if milk sales fall, and with profit of $9,000,000 already taxed at 23% [app], a bad year would hit retained earnings hard [an].

knowledge_max_2: Borrowing is cheaper than the lease alternative
analysis_max_2: Lower annual cost improves cash flow
Fixed commitment reduces resilience in a downturn

questions.question_text: Do you think Zebulon Dairy should borrow $14,000,000 for the bottling plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: interest of $1,225,000 is $675,000 below the $1,900,000 lease, and owning the plant gives control over quality and output for 90,000,000 litres.

Against: the $1,225,000 is fixed for years, profit of $9,000,000 is already reduced by 23% tax, and rising rates could make refinancing expensive.

Conclusion: borrowing is preferable because the annual saving is large, but Zebulon should fix the rate and keep a reserve in case milk demand dips.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $675,000 annual saving against fixed-rate risk
Considers tax and refinancing exposure

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Coralline Cosmetics is a private limited company in the Philippines making 4,000,000 bottles of suncream a year, with 260 staff and revenue of $18,000,000. A packaging levy of $0.04 per plastic bottle starts in January, and retailers want 50% of bottles refillable by 2028. Directors must decide whether to spend $720,000 on refill stations or keep current packaging and pay the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'packaging levy'.
questions.model_answer: A packaging levy is a government charge on each unit of packaging produced or sold [2]. Coralline Cosmetics would pay $0.04 for every plastic bottle it puts on the market.

knowledge_max_2: Designed to cut waste and encourage reuse

questions.question_text: Calculate Coralline Cosmetics' annual packaging levy on 4,000,000 bottles at $0.04 each.
questions.model_answer: 4,000,000 x $0.04 = $160,000 a year [2]. If half the bottles became refillable, the levy would fall to $80,000.

knowledge_max_2: Levy = units of packaging x rate per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Coralline Cosmetics of installing refill stations.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Fewer new bottles mean a lower levy [k]. Cutting bottle use by half would reduce the $160,000 annual charge to $80,000 [app], saving cash that can fund product development on $18,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Refill stations meet retailer expectations [k]. Shops want 50% of bottles refillable by 2028 [app], so early action protects shelf space and appeals to environmentally aware shoppers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Satisfies retailer and consumer environmental demands
analysis_max_2: Retail access and brand image improve

questions.question_text: Do you think Coralline Cosmetics should spend $720,000 on refill stations? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: refill stations cut the $160,000 levy, satisfy the 50% refillable target and build a greener image that retailers reward with shelf space.

Against: $720,000 is four and a half times the annual levy, and stations need cleaning, maintenance and consumer education before they attract shoppers.

Conclusion: the investment is justified as a long-term brand and compliance move, but Coralline should trial stations in a few stores before rolling out nationwide.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $720,000 outlay with $160,000 annual levy
Considers retailer pressure and maintenance costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Mapocho Wines is a private limited company in Chile exporting 2,400,000 bottles a year, with 190 staff and revenue of $21,600,000. The peso has appreciated 10% against the dollar, and European distributors expect their $6,000,000 of orders to fall 15%. An 18% tariff also applies to bottles sold in Asia. Directors must decide whether to absorb the tariff and enter Asia or cut European prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in another currency [2]. The appreciated peso makes Mapocho Wines' bottles more expensive for dollar-paying buyers.

knowledge_max_2: Value of one currency against another
Determines the price of imports and exports

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in European sales if $6,000,000 of orders drop by 15%.
questions.model_answer: $6,000,000 x 15% = $900,000 lost [2]. European revenue would fall to $5,100,000.

knowledge_max_2: Fall = order value x percentage decline

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 10% appreciation of the peso on Mapocho Wines.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Exports become dearer abroad [k]. Dollar buyers need more of their currency for each bottle, and European orders worth $6,000,000 may fall 15%, losing $900,000 [app], which lowers revenue below $21,600,000 [an].

Point 2: Imported inputs become cheaper [k]. Bottles, corks and labels bought from abroad cost less in pesos [app], partly offsetting the export loss and protecting margin if volumes hold [an].

knowledge_max_2: Export prices rise in foreign currency
application_max_2: $900,000 lost from a 15% fall in $6,000,000 of orders

questions.question_text: Do you think Mapocho Wines should absorb the 18% Asian tariff and enter Asia? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Asia offers growth while European orders fall by $900,000, and absorbing an 18% tariff could win a foothold before rivals commit.

Against: absorbing the tariff cuts margin on every bottle, 18% is a heavy cost, and Asian buyers may still prefer cheaper local wines.

Conclusion: entering Asia is worthwhile only with a premium range that can carry the tariff; otherwise Mapocho should defend Europe with modest price cuts.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs Asian growth against an 18% margin sacrifice
Compares with defending falling European sales

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ardvale Engineering is a private limited company in Scotland making wind turbine castings, with 430 staff, revenue of $58,000,000 and profit of $7,000,000. The government has cut its infrastructure budget by 8%, reducing expected orders by $4,640,000, while corporation tax will rise from 19% to 25%. Directors must decide whether to cut 60 jobs or invest $3,000,000 in new casting moulds.

questions.question_text: Define 'government spending'.
questions.model_answer: Government spending is money used by the public sector on goods, services and projects such as roads and energy schemes [2]. Scotland's 8% budget cut reduces orders for Ardvale Engineering.

knowledge_max_2: Public expenditure on goods, services and infrastructure
Funded mainly through taxation and borrowing

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra corporation tax Ardvale Engineering would pay if the rate rises from 19% to 25% on profit of $7,000,000.

knowledge_max_2: Extra tax = profit x increase in rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 8% cut in infrastructure spending on Ardvale Engineering.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Orders fall sharply [k]. Expected work drops by $4,640,000 out of $58,000,000 of revenue [app], leaving the 430-strong workforce and casting capacity underused [an].

Point 2: Cash flow comes under pressure [k]. Fewer government contracts mean slower payments and less cash to service equipment [app], just as corporation tax rises to 25%, cutting the $7,000,000 profit further [an].

analysis_max_2: Combined tax and order cuts squeeze retained profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Ardvale Engineering should cut 60 jobs or invest $3,000,000 in new casting moulds? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For investment: new moulds could win private wind-farm contracts and reduce reliance on government work, protecting skilled staff as the 8% budget cut bites.

For job cuts: removing 60 staff lowers costs quickly when $4,640,000 of orders have disappeared and tax is rising to 25%, whereas $3,000,000 may sit idle.

Conclusion: job cuts give immediate relief, but investment is better if private orders are likely; Ardvale should cut fewer jobs and phase the mould purchase.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs immediate cost savings against capacity investment
Considers diversification into private contracts
analysis_max_2: Job cuts reduce fixed wage costs
New moulds improve competitiveness and product range

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Mopane Safari Lodges is a partnership in Botswana running 12 camps with 280 staff and revenue of $24,000,000. A wildlife conservation levy of 4% on room revenue starts next season, and guests increasingly ask for proof that local staff are paid fairly. Partners must decide whether to raise room prices by 4% or absorb the levy and cut the community fund.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical business behaviour'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical business behaviour means acting in a morally acceptable way towards employees, customers, suppliers and the community [2]. Mopane Safari Lodges faces pressure to show fair pay for its 280 staff.

knowledge_max_2: Acting morally and fairly towards stakeholders

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual wildlife conservation levy on room revenue of $24,000,000 at 4%.
questions.model_answer: $24,000,000 x 4% = $960,000 a year [2]. Raising prices by 4% would add about $960,000 if bookings stayed the same.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 4% conservation levy on Mopane Safari Lodges.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A 4% price rise may reduce bookings [k]. Adding $960,000 to room prices makes Botswana trips dearer than rival destinations [app], so price-sensitive guests may choose elsewhere and revenue could fall below $24,000,000 [an].

Point 2: Absorbing the levy cuts funds for community projects [k]. The $960,000 would have to come from the community fund or profit [app], weakening the ethical story that guests value and risking criticism from campaigners [an].

knowledge_max_2: Absorbing the levy reduces community spending

questions.question_text: Do you think Mopane Safari Lodges should raise room prices by 4% to cover the levy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the 4% rise raises about $960,000, fully covering the levy while keeping the community fund intact and protecting the lodges' ethical reputation.

Against: safari guests compare prices across countries, and a 4% increase could lose bookings worth more than $960,000, especially if rivals absorb the charge.

Conclusion: raising prices is reasonable because the levy is transparent to guests, but Mopane should explain the conservation purpose and review bookings after one season.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $960,000 levy cover against possible lost bookings
Considers competitor pricing and guest sensitivity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Hikurangi Seafood is a private limited company in New Zealand exporting 18,000 tonnes of mussels a year, with 240 staff and revenue of $36,000,000. A multinational retailer now wants 40% of its output but demands a 12% price cut and exclusive supply. Meanwhile a 7% tariff on frozen seafood has been announced. Directors must decide whether to accept the retailer's contract or refuse it.

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company'.
questions.model_answer: A multinational company is a business that operates in more than one country, often with production or sales subsidiaries abroad [2]. The retailer negotiating with Hikurangi Seafood trades across many national markets.

knowledge_max_2: Business operating in two or more countries
Typically has headquarters in one country and operations elsewhere

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue lost if the retailer's 40% share of $36,000,000 is sold at a price 12% lower.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = contract value x price reduction

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of relying on one multinational retailer for 40% of output.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue becomes vulnerable to one buyer [k]. The contract covers 40% of $36,000,000, or $14,400,000 [app], so a decision to switch suppliers would remove nearly half of Hikurangi's sales overnight [an].

Point 2: Bargaining power shifts to the retailer [k]. It can demand a 12% price cut, costing $1,728,000 [app], and exclusive supply would stop Hikurangi selling to other chains that might pay more [an].

knowledge_max_2: Concentration risk from one large buyer
analysis_max_2: Loss of the buyer threatens survival

questions.question_text: Do you think Hikurangi Seafood should accept the multinational retailer's contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the contract guarantees sales for 40% of output and gives access to the retailer's global distribution, which may outweigh the $1,728,000 price concession.

Against: exclusivity blocks other buyers, the 12% cut is permanent, and a 7% tariff on frozen seafood may make exports less profitable anyway.

Conclusion: accepting is justified only with a shorter exclusivity period and a price floor; otherwise Hikurangi should keep several customers and absorb the tariff.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs guaranteed volume against $1,728,000 lost revenue
Considers exclusivity and the 7% tariff
analysis_max_2: Dependence and tariff reduce long-run margins

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Larkspur Confectionery is a private limited company in Canada making 6,000,000 chocolate bars a year, with 310 staff and revenue of $15,000,000. Inflation has reached 5.6% and sugar prices have risen 18%, adding $540,000 to annual costs. A supermarket chain wants a two-year fixed price of $2.30 a bar, below the current $2.50. Directors must decide whether to accept the contract.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-push inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Cost-push inflation is a rise in the average price level caused by increasing costs of production [2]. Larkspur Confectionery faces it as sugar prices climb 18% and costs rise by $540,000.

knowledge_max_2: Inflation caused by rising input costs
Businesses pass higher costs to customers

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue lost if all 6,000,000 bars sell at $2.30 instead of $2.50.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = units x price reduction

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising sugar prices on Larkspur Confectionery.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise faster than prices [k]. Sugar is 18% dearer and total costs are up $540,000 [app], so each $2.50 bar earns less margin unless Larkspur reformulates or raises prices [an].

Point 2: A fixed-price contract becomes risky [k]. Accepting $2.30 for two years while inflation runs at 5.6% [app] locks in a low price even if sugar climbs again, squeezing the $15,000,000 revenue base [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed prices become unprofitable during inflation
analysis_max_2: Two-year lock-in transfers cost risk to Larkspur

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkspur Confectionery should accept the supermarket's $2.30 fixed-price contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the chain guarantees volume for 6,000,000 bars, keeps the factory running and gives predictable revenue during uncertain inflation.

Against: $2.30 loses $1,200,000 a year against $2.50, and with sugar up 18% and inflation at 5.6%, two years of fixed prices could turn profit into loss.

Conclusion: accepting is unwise unless the contract covers at least the $540,000 cost rise; Larkspur should negotiate $2.40 or a one-year term.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs guaranteed volume against $1,200,000 revenue loss
Considers two-year exposure to 5.6% inflation
analysis_max_2: Fixed price transfers inflation risk to the producer

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Vistula Furniture is a private limited company in Poland making 90,000 oak tables a year, with 420 staff and revenue of $54,000,000. A new law bans timber from uncertified forests, and certification costs $260,000 a year. Campaigners claim 15% of its current oak comes from unclear sources. Directors must decide whether to certify all supplies or switch to recycled board.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical sourcing'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical sourcing means buying materials in a way that respects workers, communities and the environment [2]. Vistula Furniture must prove its oak comes from certified, legal forests.

knowledge_max_2: Avoids harm to workers, communities and habitats

questions.question_text: Calculate the certification cost per table if $260,000 is spread over 90,000 tables.
questions.model_answer: $260,000 / 90,000 = $2.89 per table [2]. On a table selling for $600, that is under 0.5% of the price.

knowledge_max_2: Unit cost = total certification cost / output

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Vistula Furniture of certifying all its timber supplies.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Certification keeps the business legal [k]. The new law bans uncertified timber, and with 15% of oak from unclear sources [app], Vistula risks fines, seized stock and lost sales on $54,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: It protects relationships with ethical buyers [k]. The $260,000 fee adds only $2.89 per table [app], a small cost that lets Vistula reassure retailers and avoid damage to its brand from campaigner claims [an].

analysis_max_2: Non-compliance risks fines and lost trade
Low unit cost makes certification affordable

questions.question_text: Do you think Vistula Furniture should certify all supplies rather than switch to recycled board? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For certification: it keeps solid oak tables, which customers pay premium prices for, and at $2.89 per table the $260,000 fee is easily absorbed while restoring legal compliance.

For recycled board: it avoids dependence on forest certification and may appeal to green buyers, but it changes the product and could require new machinery and redesign.

Conclusion: certification is better because it protects the existing oak range at low unit cost; recycled board should be a later addition, not a replacement.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $2.89 per table certification with product change
Considers brand and customer expectations
analysis_max_2: Recycled board alters quality and production

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Altiplano Quinoa is a co-operative in Peru exporting 12,000 tonnes of quinoa a year, with 640 member farmers and revenue of $30,000,000. A new importing-country standard requires pesticide testing costing $8 a tonne, and a 6% import tariff applies to unprocessed grain. Members must decide whether to build a $1,200,000 processing plant or keep exporting raw grain.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: An export is a good or service produced in one country and sold to buyers in another country [2]. Altiplano Quinoa exports 12,000 tonnes of grain from Peru each year.

knowledge_max_2: Earns foreign currency for the exporting country

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of pesticide testing on 12,000 tonnes at $8 a tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Testing cost = tonnes x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Altiplano Quinoa of building the processing plant.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Processed quinoa escapes the 6% tariff on unprocessed grain [k]. That tariff would cost $1,800,000 on $30,000,000 of exports [app], so milling and packing before shipment could keep far more value in Peru [an].

Point 2: Processing raises the price per tonne [k]. Members currently sell 12,000 tonnes raw and pay $96,000 for testing [app], but flour and flakes earn more and create skilled work for the 640 farming families [an].

analysis_max_2: Higher export value improves member incomes

questions.question_text: Do you think Altiplano Quinoa should build the $1,200,000 processing plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
