For: processing avoids the $1,800,000 tariff exposure, raises the value of 12,000 tonnes and supports 640 member farmers with steadier incomes.

Against: $1,200,000 is a heavy commitment for a co-operative, and the plant needs reliable power, trained operators and buyers for flour and flakes.

Conclusion: building is worthwhile because the 6% tariff is large, but members should secure a long-term buyer and grant funding before committing.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,200,000 investment against $1,800,000 tariff exposure
Considers co-operative finance and buyer security
analysis_max_2: Operational demands may strain the co-operative

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sablewave Audio is a public limited company in South Korea making 800,000 wireless speakers a year, with 520 staff and revenue of $64,000,000. The won has strengthened 9% against the dollar, raising the foreign price of its exports, while interest rates have climbed to 6.5%. The board must decide whether to borrow $20,000,000 to automate assembly or cut export prices by 9%.

questions.question_text: Define 'currency appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Currency appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency against another [2]. The won has risen 9% against the dollar, making Sablewave Audio's speakers dearer for foreign buyers.

knowledge_max_2: Increase in a currency's value against another
Makes exports dearer and imports cheaper

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $20,000,000 loan at 6.5%.
questions.model_answer: $20,000,000 x 6.5% = $1,300,000 a year [2]. That is 2% of the company's $64,000,000 revenue.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 9% appreciation of the won on Sablewave Audio.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export prices rise in dollars [k]. A 9% stronger won makes each speaker cost more abroad [app], so distributors may order fewer than 800,000 units and revenue could fall below $64,000,000 [an].

Point 2: Cutting prices to stay competitive squeezes margin [k]. Matching the 9% appreciation with a 9% price cut protects volume [app], but leaves less profit to cover the $1,300,000 interest on any new loan [an].

analysis_max_2: Margin sacrifice limits funds for investment

questions.question_text: Do you think Sablewave Audio should borrow $20,000,000 to automate assembly or cut export prices by 9%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For automation: robots would offset the strong won by lowering unit costs, and the $1,300,000 interest is affordable on $64,000,000 of revenue.

For price cuts: a 9% reduction directly protects export volume, but it gives away margin permanently and may not stop buyers switching.

Conclusion: automation is the stronger choice because it tackles the cost cause of uncompetitive prices, provided Sablewave fixes the interest rate and phases the $20,000,000 spend.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,300,000 interest against permanent 9% price cut
Considers cost reduction versus margin sacrifice
analysis_max_2: Price cuts are easily matched by rivals

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tazara Coffee is a co-operative in Tanzania exporting 5,000 tonnes of arabica a year, with 1,800 member farmers and revenue of $22,500,000. A fair-trade buyer offers a guaranteed price 14% above the market, but requires a $150,000 training programme and limits chemical use. Members must decide whether to join the scheme or sell on the open market.

questions.question_text: Define 'fair trade'.
questions.model_answer: Fair trade is a trading arrangement that guarantees producers a minimum price and better working conditions [2]. The buyer offers Tazara Coffee a price 14% above the market.

knowledge_max_2: Promotes fair wages and sustainable farming

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue if the fair-trade price is 14% above current revenue of $22,500,000.
questions.model_answer: $22,500,000 x 14% = $3,150,000 extra a year [2]. Revenue would rise to $25,650,000.

knowledge_max_2: Extra revenue = current revenue x price premium

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tazara Coffee of joining the fair-trade scheme.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Income becomes higher and more stable [k]. The 14% premium adds $3,150,000 a year on $22,500,000 of revenue [app], cushioning 1,800 farmers against world price swings and supporting replanting [an].

Point 2: The scheme builds skills and reputation [k]. The $150,000 training programme teaches safer, chemical-light methods [app], improving bean quality and opening access to ethical buyers who pay promptly [an].

analysis_max_2: Stable income reduces poverty and risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Tazara Coffee should join the fair-trade scheme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the 14% premium adds $3,150,000 a year, far above the $150,000 training cost, and guarantees a buyer while improving farming methods.

Against: the scheme restricts chemical use, which may lower yields, and certification rules could raise costs or limit sales to non-member buyers.

Conclusion: joining is worthwhile because the premium is twenty times the training fee, but members should trial it on part of the 5,000 tonnes first.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $3,150,000 premium with $150,000 cost
Considers yield risk from chemical restrictions

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Rivenhall Pumps is a private limited company in England making 40,000 industrial pumps a year, with 350 staff and revenue of $48,000,000. A 10% tariff now applies to the $9,000,000 of electric motors it imports, and the pound has fallen 7% against the euro, raising European parts costs. Directors must decide whether to buy motors from a local supplier at 15% more or keep importing.

questions.question_text: Define 'import'.
questions.model_answer: An import is a good or service bought from another country [2]. Rivenhall Pumps imports $9,000,000 of electric motors each year.

knowledge_max_2: Goods or services purchased from abroad

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on $9,000,000 of imported motors at 10%.
questions.model_answer: $9,000,000 x 10% = $900,000 a year [2]. Local motors at 15% more would cost an extra $1,350,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 10% tariff and weaker pound on Rivenhall Pumps.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Imported motors cost more [k]. The 10% tariff adds $900,000 to a $9,000,000 bill [app], and the 7% weaker pound raises euro-priced parts further, pushing up the cost of each of 40,000 pumps [an].

Point 2: Local suppliers gain bargaining power [k]. With imports dearer, the English supplier can charge 15% more, or $1,350,000 extra [app], leaving Rivenhall facing higher costs whichever source it chooses [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Rivenhall Pumps should buy motors from the local supplier at 15% more? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: local motors avoid the $900,000 tariff and the 7% currency risk, shorten lead times and support a reliable English supply chain.

Against: paying 15% more costs $1,350,000 extra, which is $450,000 worse than the tariff alone, and local quality may not match imported motors.

Conclusion: the local supplier is preferable only if it matches quality and can share the cost gap; otherwise Rivenhall should import, hedge the currency and pass some cost to customers.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $1,350,000 local premium with $900,000 tariff
Considers quality, lead time and currency risk
analysis_max_2: Local sourcing removes tariff and exchange exposure

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Palembang Pulp is a private limited company in Indonesia making 300,000 tonnes of paper a year, with 2,100 staff, a wage bill of $25,200,000 and revenue of $120,000,000. The minimum wage rises 8.5%, inflation reaches 4.9% and paper prices fall 3%. Directors must decide whether to automate the finishing line for $6,000,000 or raise paper prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: A minimum wage is the lowest legal rate that employers may pay their workers [2]. Indonesia's 8.5% increase raises Palembang Pulp's $25,200,000 wage bill.

knowledge_max_2: Legal floor on pay per hour or month
Set by government to protect low-paid workers

questions.question_text: Calculate the increase in the wage bill if the minimum wage raises $25,200,000 by 8.5%.
questions.model_answer: $25,200,000 x 8.5% = $2,142,000 extra a year [2]. The wage bill would reach $27,342,000.

knowledge_max_2: Increase = wage bill x percentage rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 8.5% minimum wage rise on Palembang Pulp.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Labour costs jump [k]. The wage bill rises by $2,142,000 to $27,342,000 [app], which is hard to absorb when paper prices are already falling 3% on $120,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Automation becomes more attractive [k]. Higher wages widen the saving from a $6,000,000 finishing line [app], but the firm may need fewer of its 2,100 staff, raising redundancy costs and local criticism [an].

knowledge_max_2: Incentive to substitute machinery for labour grows
analysis_max_2: Rising costs coincide with falling prices
Automation saves labour but creates redundancy costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Palembang Pulp should spend $6,000,000 automating the finishing line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: automation offsets a $2,142,000 wage increase and protects margins as paper prices fall 3%, while raising output consistency.

Against: $6,000,000 is nearly three times the annual wage rise, and cutting labour in a weak market may damage relations and demand.

Conclusion: automating is justified if the line saves more than $2,142,000 a year; otherwise Palembang should raise prices modestly and retrain staff.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $6,000,000 cost with $2,142,000 annual saving
Considers falling prices and workforce impact
analysis_max_2: Price rises may accelerate falling demand

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Oaxaca Tiles is a private limited company in Mexico producing 2,000,000 ceramic tiles a day, with 480 staff and revenue of $42,000,000. New water rules require a treatment plant costing $2,400,000, and the firm currently pays a pollution fine of $60,000 a month. Directors must decide whether to build the plant or relocate production to a region with looser rules.

questions.question_text: Define 'pollution'.
questions.model_answer: Pollution is the release of harmful substances into air, water or land [2]. Oaxaca Tiles discharges waste water that breaches Mexico's new rules.

knowledge_max_2: Contamination of the environment by harmful substances

questions.question_text: Calculate Oaxaca Tiles' annual pollution fines at $60,000 a month.
questions.model_answer: $60,000 x 12 = $720,000 a year [2]. The $2,400,000 plant equals three and a third years of fines.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the new water rules on Oaxaca Tiles.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Operating costs rise [k]. The plant costs $2,400,000, while fines already total $720,000 a year [app], reducing funds for kiln upgrades and marketing on $42,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Relocation carries its own risks [k]. Moving to a looser region disrupts 480 staff and local supply links [app], and campaigners may publicise the move, damaging the reputation of a firm selling to builders [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Oaxaca Tiles should build the treatment plant or relocate production? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For building: the $2,400,000 plant ends $720,000 of annual fines, keeps 480 jobs and protects sales to builders who check environmental credentials.

For relocating: it may avoid the capital cost, but moving kilns is expensive, disrupts production and invites negative publicity.

Conclusion: building is the better choice because fines alone repay the plant in about three and a third years, and relocation only postpones regulation.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $2,400,000 plant with $720,000 annual fines
Considers relocation costs and reputational risk
analysis_max_2: Relocation transfers rather than solves the problem

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Benbulben Pharma is a public limited company in Ireland making 60,000,000 medicine packs a year, with 900 staff and revenue of $240,000,000. A new trade-bloc rule requires imported medicines to carry local-language labels, adding $0.03 per pack, while a 5% quota limits exports to 54,000,000 packs. The board must decide whether to build a labelling plant inside the bloc.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any measure that restricts or discourages trade between countries [2]. The labelling rule and quota both limit Benbulben Pharma's access to the bloc.

knowledge_max_2: Obstacle to free trade between countries
Includes tariffs, quotas and technical rules

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of local-language labels on 60,000,000 packs at $0.03 each.
questions.model_answer: 60,000,000 x $0.03 = $1,800,000 a year [2]. The quota cuts exports by 6,000,000 packs.

knowledge_max_2: Cost = packs x cost per pack

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the labelling rule and quota on Benbulben Pharma.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Labelling adds a fixed cost per pack [k]. At $0.03 on 60,000,000 packs, the rule costs $1,800,000 a year [app], which is small per pack but large in total and delays shipments while artwork is approved [an].

Point 2: The quota caps sales [k]. Exports are limited to 54,000,000 packs, 6,000,000 below current output [app], so the extra production must be sold elsewhere or left idle, raising average cost on $240,000,000 of revenue [an].

analysis_max_2: Unsold output raises average fixed cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Benbulben Pharma should build a labelling plant inside the trade bloc? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: a plant inside the bloc avoids the $1,800,000 labelling charge and the quota, letting Benbulben serve the full 60,000,000 packs without delay.

Against: duplicating a plant is expensive for a firm with 900 staff, and the bloc could alter its rules again, while $1,800,000 a year is modest against $240,000,000 of revenue.

Conclusion: a labelling plant is justified only if the bloc is a large, stable market; otherwise paying $1,800,000 and selling the 6,000,000 excess packs elsewhere is cheaper.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs quota-free access against plant duplication cost
Compares $1,800,000 with $240,000,000 revenue
analysis_max_2: Rule uncertainty makes heavy investment risky

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kavango Breweries is a private limited company in Namibia brewing 90,000,000 litres a year, with 620 staff and revenue of $81,000,000. The government has raised excise duty on beer by 11%, adding $1,620,000 to costs, and interest rates are now 9.25%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $12,000,000 for a canning line or reduce the workforce.

questions.question_text: Define 'excise duty'.
questions.model_answer: Excise duty is a tax charged on specific goods such as alcohol, tobacco or fuel [2]. Namibia's 11% rise adds $1,620,000 to Kavango Breweries' costs.

knowledge_max_2: Usually included in the selling price

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $12,000,000 loan at 9.25%.
questions.model_answer: $12,000,000 x 9.25% = $1,110,000 a year [2]. That is $510,000 less than the $1,620,000 excise increase.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 11% excise duty rise on Kavango Breweries.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise and prices may follow [k]. The duty adds $1,620,000 [app], and if Kavango passes it on, a higher beer price may reduce sales across 90,000,000 litres [an].

Point 2: Profit margins come under pressure [k]. Absorbing the duty would cut into returns on $81,000,000 of revenue [app], leaving less to service the $1,110,000 interest on a canning line [an].

knowledge_max_2: Tax increases production and selling costs
Margin or sales volume is squeezed

questions.question_text: Do you think Kavango Breweries should borrow $12,000,000 for the canning line or reduce the workforce? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For borrowing: a canning line adds a higher-margin product and the $1,110,000 interest is less than the $1,620,000 excise increase, so growth may protect 620 jobs.

For cutting jobs: it lowers costs at once when duty is rising, but loses skills and may reduce output and morale.

Conclusion: borrowing is preferable if canned beer demand is proven, because it addresses the cost pressure through efficiency rather than shrinking the business.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $1,110,000 interest with $1,620,000 duty rise
Considers workforce morale and demand for cans
analysis_max_2: Job cuts reduce capacity and skills

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Selenge Cashmere is a partnership in Mongolia processing 800 tonnes of cashmere a year, with 240 staff and revenue of $28,000,000. A new standard limits herds to protect grasslands, cutting member supply by 20%, while an ethical brand offers a 25% price premium for certified fibre. Partners must decide whether to certify or buy extra fibre from unregulated herders.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable production'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable production means making goods without damaging resources or the environment for future generations [2]. Selenge Cashmere must limit herd sizes to protect Mongolia's grasslands.

knowledge_max_2: Minimises environmental damage over the long term

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from a 25% price premium on current revenue of $28,000,000.
questions.model_answer: $28,000,000 x 25% = $7,000,000 extra a year [2]. Certified revenue would reach $35,000,000.

knowledge_max_2: Premium revenue = revenue x percentage premium

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Selenge Cashmere of certifying its fibre.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The ethical premium raises income [k]. A 25% premium adds $7,000,000 to $28,000,000 of revenue [app], helping partners absorb the 20% fall in member supply [an].

Point 2: Certification protects the grassland resource [k]. Limiting herds now prevents overgrazing and keeps future fibre flowing [app], safeguarding the livelihood of 240 staff and the partnership's long-term name [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Selenge Cashmere should certify its fibre rather than buy from unregulated herders? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For certification: the 25% premium adds $7,000,000, offsets the 20% supply cut and preserves grasslands that support the business long term.

Against: certification limits volume and may raise inspection costs, while unregulated fibre could fill orders quickly and keep 800 tonnes flowing.

Conclusion: certifying is the better choice because the premium is large and overgrazing would eventually destroy supply, but partners should certify gradually to protect output.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $7,000,000 premium against 20% volume loss
Considers long-term resource protection
analysis_max_2: Unregulated supply risks reputational and resource damage

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marmara Auto Parts is a private limited company in Turkey making 1,200,000 brake discs a year, with 560 staff and revenue of $72,000,000. A customs union removes a 9% tariff on exports to Europe but requires EU safety testing costing $1,400,000. European sales are 45% of revenue. Directors must decide whether to pay for testing or focus on Middle Eastern markets.

questions.question_text: Define 'customs union'.
questions.model_answer: A customs union is a group of countries with free trade between members and a common external tariff [2]. It would remove the 9% tariff on Marmara Auto Parts' European exports.

knowledge_max_2: Common tariff on goods from outside

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff saving on European sales of 45% of $72,000,000 at 9%.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = European sales x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Marmara Auto Parts of paying for EU safety testing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Tariff-free access cuts a major cost [k]. European sales of $32,400,000 currently carry 9%, or $2,916,000 [app], so testing at $1,400,000 returns more than double its cost [an].

Point 2: The certificate proves quality [k]. EU approval signals reliable safety to car makers across 45% of revenue [app], supporting long contracts and protecting 560 jobs from rival suppliers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Marmara Auto Parts should pay $1,400,000 for EU safety testing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: testing costs $1,400,000 but saves $2,916,000 in tariffs on European sales, a clear net gain, and certification strengthens relationships with car makers.

Against: the fee is paid before approval is certain, EU rules may change, and Middle Eastern markets might grow faster without such testing.

Conclusion: paying for testing is justified because the tariff saving is more than double the cost, but Marmara should keep some Middle Eastern sales to diversify.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $1,400,000 fee with $2,916,000 saving
Considers approval risk and market diversification
analysis_max_2: Relying on one region adds risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ostrova Glassworks is a private limited company in Estonia making 14,000,000 glass bottles a year, with 280 staff and revenue of $19,600,000. The economy has entered recession, with GDP falling 2.4% and unemployment rising from 6.1% to 8.3%, so orders are expected to fall 12%. Directors must decide whether to cut output and 40 jobs or hold output and build inventory.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when a country's GDP falls for two consecutive quarters or more [2]. Estonia's 2.4% fall in GDP is cutting demand for Ostrova Glassworks' bottles.

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in revenue if orders drop 12% from $19,600,000.
Explain two effects of the recession on Ostrova Glassworks.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand falls [k]. Orders are expected to drop 12%, cutting revenue by $2,352,000 from $19,600,000 [app], leaving 14,000,000 bottles of capacity underused [an].

Point 2: Unemployment weakens household spending further [k]. With unemployment up from 6.1% to 8.3% [app], drink makers order fewer bottles, so the downturn reinforces itself and price cutting becomes likely [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ostrova Glassworks should cut 40 jobs or hold output and build inventory? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For job cuts: removing 40 staff quickly lowers wage costs when revenue may fall $2,352,000 and recovery is uncertain.

For building inventory: it keeps skilled workers and prepares for recovery, but unsold bottles tie up cash and may become obsolete.

Conclusion: cutting jobs gives immediate relief, but holding output is safer if the recession is short; Ostrova should cut fewer jobs, shorten hours and store only fast-selling lines.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs wage savings against inventory holding costs
Considers recession length and skill retention
analysis_max_2: Inventory supports rapid recovery but ties up cash

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Zambezi Sugar is a private limited company in Zambia refining 250,000 tonnes of sugar a year, with 3,200 staff and revenue of $110,000,000. A carbon levy of $12 a tonne applies to 18,000 tonnes of emissions, and a labour audit found unpaid overtime. Directors must decide whether to invest $900,000 in bagasse power or pay the levy and settle wage claims.

questions.question_text: Define 'fair wage'.
questions.model_answer: A fair wage is pay that reflects the work done and allows employees a reasonable standard of living [2]. Zambezi Sugar's audit found overtime that was not paid at all.

knowledge_max_2: Pay that is just for the work performed
Covers basic needs and legal entitlements

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual carbon levy on 18,000 tonnes of emissions at $12 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 18,000 x $12 = $216,000 a year [2]. The bagasse plant costs $900,000, about four times the annual levy.

knowledge_max_2: Levy = emissions x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Zambezi Sugar of investing in bagasse power.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It cuts both energy costs and the carbon levy [k]. Burning bagasse instead of coal could avoid the $216,000 annual levy on 18,000 tonnes [app], lowering costs on $110,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: It improves ethical standing after the labour audit [k]. Cleaner power and action on unpaid overtime answer the criticisms [app], protecting contracts with buyers who check supplier standards and the jobs of 3,200 staff [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reduces carbon levy and fuel costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Zambezi Sugar should invest $900,000 in bagasse power or pay the levy and settle wage claims? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For investing: bagasse power removes the $216,000 levy and cuts coal costs, and pairing it with settled wage claims rebuilds trust with 3,200 staff and buyers.

Against: $900,000 is over four times the annual levy, and the money could instead clear unpaid overtime immediately and avoid legal action.

Conclusion: the ethical priority is to settle wage claims first; bagasse power is worthwhile afterwards, funded partly from the $216,000 annual saving.

evaluation_max_2: Prioritises wage justice against $900,000 energy investment
Compares $216,000 levy saving with capital cost
analysis_max_2: Settling claims reduces legal and reputational risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Mekelle Leather is a private limited company in Ethiopia making 300,000 leather bags a year, with 700 staff and revenue of $15,000,000. A global brand offers to buy 60% of output at $38 a bag, below the current $50, but will provide design training and access to 20 countries. A 15% export tax also applies to finished bags. Directors must decide whether to accept.

questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of world markets for goods, services, capital and labour [2]. The global brand would link Mekelle Leather to buyers in 20 countries.

knowledge_max_2: Free movement of trade, investment and ideas across borders

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue lost on 60% of 300,000 bags sold at $38 instead of $50.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = bags x price difference

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the global brand's offer on Mekelle Leather.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue per bag falls [k]. Selling 180,000 bags at $38 rather than $50 loses $2,160,000 [app], which is hard to absorb on $15,000,000 of revenue and with a 15% export tax [an].

Point 2: Training and market access build capability [k]. Design skills and entry to 20 countries could raise quality and future orders [app], reducing dependence on a few local buyers and protecting 700 jobs [an].

knowledge_max_2: Access to skills and export markets grows

questions.question_text: Do you think Mekelle Leather should accept the global brand's offer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the brand buys 60% of output, provides design training and opens 20 countries, which could transform Mekelle into a recognised exporter.

Against: $38 against $50 loses $2,160,000 a year, and the 15% export tax cuts the return further, while dependence on one buyer grows.

Conclusion: accepting is justified only for a limited period and volume, so Mekelle gains skills and contacts without locking 60% of output into a low price.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $2,160,000 revenue loss against training and access
Considers export tax and buyer dependence
analysis_max_2: Skills and contacts raise future capability

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sargasso Plastics is a private limited company in Barbados moulding 25,000,000 food containers a year, with 180 staff and revenue of $12,500,000. Oil prices have risen 22%, adding $750,000 to resin costs, and interest rates have reached 7.5%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $3,000,000 for a recycling line or increase container prices by 6%.

questions.question_text: Define 'rate of interest'.
questions.model_answer: The rate of interest is the percentage charged for borrowing money, usually expressed per year [2]. Barbados' 7.5% rate would cost Sargasso Plastics $225,000 on a $3,000,000 loan.

knowledge_max_2: Also the return earned by savers

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $3,000,000 loan at 7.5%.
questions.model_answer: $3,000,000 x 7.5% = $225,000 a year [2]. A 6% price rise would add $750,000 to revenue if sales held.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 22% rise in oil prices on Sargasso Plastics.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Resin costs increase [k]. Oil-based plastic feedstock adds $750,000 to costs [app], which is 6% of $12,500,000 revenue and must be recovered through prices or efficiency [an].

Point 2: A recycling line becomes more attractive [k]. Higher virgin resin prices improve the saving from recycled material [app], but borrowing $3,000,000 at 7.5% adds $225,000 of interest [an].

knowledge_max_2: Raw material costs rise with oil prices
analysis_max_2: Recycling offsets exposure to oil prices

questions.question_text: Do you think Sargasso Plastics should borrow $3,000,000 for the recycling line or raise prices by 6%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For borrowing: recycling reduces reliance on oil-based resin and the $225,000 interest is covered by part of the $750,000 cost increase.

For raising prices: a 6% rise recovers the resin cost immediately without debt, but may lose customers in a price-sensitive food packaging market.

Conclusion: borrowing is better because it tackles the cause of rising costs, though Sargasso should also raise prices slightly to protect cash flow.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $225,000 interest against a 6% price rise
Considers customer price sensitivity
analysis_max_2: Recycling cuts long-run raw material risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kalutara Tea is a private limited company in Sri Lanka growing 9,000 tonnes of tea a year, with 1,500 staff and revenue of $27,000,000. A new forest law forbids expansion onto 400 hectares of protected land, and buyers want certification costing $210,000 a year. Directors must decide whether to certify existing estates or buy leaf from smallholders clearing forest.

questions.question_text: Define 'deforestation'.
questions.model_answer: Deforestation is the permanent removal of forests, usually to clear land for farming or building [2]. Kalutara Tea cannot expand onto 400 hectares of protected forest.

knowledge_max_2: Causes habitat loss and carbon emissions

questions.question_text: Calculate the certification cost per tonne if $210,000 is spread over 9,000 tonnes of tea.
questions.model_answer: $210,000 / 9,000 = $23.33 per tonne [2]. On 9,000 tonnes earning $27,000,000, that is less than 1% of revenue.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kalutara Tea of certifying its existing estates.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It keeps access to ethical buyers [k]. Certification costs $210,000, or $23.33 per tonne [app], a small share of $27,000,000 revenue that protects contracts with retailers who refuse uncertified tea [an].

Point 2: It avoids legal and reputational damage [k]. The forest law protects 400 hectares, and buying from smallholders who clear land could bring fines and campaigner criticism [app], threatening the jobs of 1,500 staff [an].

analysis_max_2: Forest clearance risks fines and boycotts

questions.question_text: Do you think Kalutara Tea should certify its estates rather than buy leaf from smallholders clearing forest? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For certification: $210,000 is only $23.33 per tonne, it protects $27,000,000 of revenue and avoids association with forest clearance.

Against: smallholder leaf may be cheaper and increase volume, while certification brings inspections and restricts expansion onto 400 hectares.

Conclusion: certifying is the better long-term choice because buyers increasingly reject deforestation-linked tea, but Kalutara should help smallholders certify rather than cut them off.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $23.33 per tonne cost with supply and price gains
Considers reputational risk of deforestation
analysis_max_2: Supporting smallholders builds a sustainable supply base

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Penang Circuit Boards is a public limited company in Malaysia making 4,000,000 circuit boards a year, with 850 staff and revenue of $52,000,000. A multinational rival has opened a plant nearby, cutting Penang's prices by 8% and orders by 15%. Meanwhile a 4% tariff on its exports to the United States has started. The board must decide whether to automate or move upmarket.

questions.question_text: Define 'foreign direct investment'.
questions.model_answer: Foreign direct investment is investment by a business in production or assets in another country [2]. The multinational rival's new plant in Malaysia is foreign direct investment.

knowledge_max_2: Usually involves control of overseas operations

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in revenue if orders drop 15% from $52,000,000.
Explain two effects of the multinational rival's new plant on Penang Circuit Boards.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Price competition intensifies [k]. The rival's scale has forced an 8% price cut and orders are down 15%, costing $7,800,000 of revenue [app], leaving less margin on 4,000,000 boards [an].

Point 2: Skilled staff may be poached [k]. A large foreign plant can offer higher pay to Penang's 850 workers [app], raising wage costs just as the 4% US tariff makes exports dearer [an].

knowledge_max_2: Labour market pressure from a large employer
analysis_max_2: Rising wages and tariffs raise costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Penang Circuit Boards should automate or move upmarket? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For automation: it counters the rival's scale by cutting unit costs, helping Penang survive an 8% price cut and 15% order fall.

For moving upmarket: higher-specification boards escape direct price competition and can absorb the 4% US tariff, but need research, skilled staff and new customers.

Conclusion: automation protects the current business quickly, while moving upmarket offers better long-term margins; Penang should automate first and develop premium boards alongside.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs cost reduction against product differentiation
Considers tariff and rival scale

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Alexandria Cable is a private limited company in Egypt making 18,000 tonnes of copper cable a year, with 640 staff and revenue of $76,000,000. The Egyptian pound has fallen 18% against the dollar, raising imported copper costs by $6,840,000, while interest rates are 19.25%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $10,000,000 for a rod mill or pass costs to customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'currency depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Currency depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency against another [2]. The pound's 18% fall makes Alexandria Cable's imported copper dearer in Egyptian money.

knowledge_max_2: Decrease in a currency's value against another
Raises import prices and can boost exports

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $10,000,000 loan at 19.25%.
questions.model_answer: $10,000,000 x 19.25% = $1,925,000 a year [2]. That is 28% of the $6,840,000 rise in copper costs.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 18% depreciation of the pound on Alexandria Cable.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Imported copper becomes much dearer [k]. Costs rise by $6,840,000 [app], which is 9% of $76,000,000 revenue and forces either price rises or thinner margins [an].

Point 2: Borrowing for the rod mill becomes expensive [k]. Interest on $10,000,000 at 19.25% is $1,925,000 [app], so the investment must earn a high return before it covers its financing cost [an].

analysis_max_2: High interest raises the hurdle for investment

questions.question_text: Do you think Alexandria Cable should borrow $10,000,000 for the rod mill or pass costs to customers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For borrowing: a rod mill could process copper locally and reduce exposure to imported semi-finished metal, though $1,925,000 interest is a heavy annual burden.

For passing costs on: raising cable prices recovers the $6,840,000 increase immediately, but Egyptian builders may switch suppliers or delay projects.

Conclusion: passing on part of the cost is safer now, while borrowing should wait until interest rates fall below 19.25% or a customer contract guarantees demand.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,925,000 interest against immediate price recovery
Considers customer sensitivity and rate levels
analysis_max_2: Price rises may reduce sales volume

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Atlas Argan is a women's co-operative in Morocco producing 400,000 litres of argan oil a year, with 900 members and revenue of $16,000,000. Drought has cut the harvest by 30%, and a fair-trade buyer offers a 20% premium but requires a $120,000 water-saving press. Members must decide whether to invest or sell to a cosmetics multinational at market price.

questions.question_text: Define 'co-operative'.
questions.model_answer: A co-operative is a business owned and run by its members, who share the profits [2]. Atlas Argan's 900 women members jointly own and govern the enterprise.

knowledge_max_2: Business owned and controlled by members

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from a 20% fair-trade premium on $16,000,000.
questions.model_answer: $16,000,000 x 20% = $3,200,000 extra a year [2]. The premium is over 26 times the $120,000 press cost.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Atlas Argan of investing in the water-saving press.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It protects output during drought [k]. The harvest is already 30% lower, and a press that uses less water helps members maintain oil output from 400,000 litres [app], stabilising income from $16,000,000 of sales [an].

Point 2: It secures the fair-trade premium [k]. The buyer's 20% premium is worth $3,200,000 [app], far above the $120,000 cost, and certification strengthens the co-operative's ethical image with European customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reduces water use and protects output

questions.question_text: Do you think Atlas Argan should invest in the press or sell to the cosmetics multinational at market price? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For investing: the $120,000 press unlocks a $3,200,000 premium and helps cope with a 30% harvest cut, while keeping ownership with 900 women members.

For the multinational: a large buyer may take volume quickly without capital spending, but market prices are lower and the co-operative could lose control of its brand.

Conclusion: investing is clearly better because the premium dwarfs the cost, but members should confirm the buyer will accept lower volume during the drought.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $120,000 cost with $3,200,000 premium
Considers buyer security and member ownership
analysis_max_2: Fair trade raises and stabilises income

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Valdeon Footwear is a private limited company in Spain making 600,000 pairs of shoes a year, with 420 staff and revenue of $27,000,000. A new quota limits exports to 240,000 pairs against planned exports of 300,000, and a 12% tariff applies to $6,000,000 of leather imported from outside the EU. Directors must decide whether to source EU leather at 10% more or keep importing.

questions.question_text: Define 'protectionism'.
questions.model_answer: Protectionism is the use of tariffs, quotas or other barriers to shield domestic producers from foreign competition [2]. The quota and 12% leather tariff both protect EU suppliers.

knowledge_max_2: Aims to protect domestic industries and jobs

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on $6,000,000 of imported leather at 12%.
questions.model_answer: $6,000,000 x 12% = $720,000 a year [2]. EU leather at 10% more would cost an extra $600,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the quota and tariff on Valdeon Footwear.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export sales are capped [k]. The quota allows 240,000 pairs instead of 300,000 [app], leaving 60,000 pairs to sell elsewhere or hold, which raises average cost on $27,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Leather costs rise [k]. The 12% tariff adds $720,000, while EU leather at 10% more adds $600,000 [app], so either source reduces margin on every pair of shoes [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Valdeon Footwear should source EU leather at 10% more or keep importing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For EU leather: it avoids the $720,000 tariff, costs only $600,000 more, and shortens supply lines within the single market.

For importing: the tariff is a known cost, and non-EU leather may offer quality or volume that EU suppliers cannot match.

Conclusion: EU leather is cheaper by $120,000 a year and reduces border risk, so Valdeon should switch if quality is acceptable; otherwise it should negotiate a tariff-inclusive price with importers.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $600,000 EU premium with $720,000 tariff
Considers quality and supply reliability
analysis_max_2: EU sourcing avoids tariff and delay
Imported leather may offer superior specifications

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pohjola Paper is a private limited company in Finland making 700,000 tonnes of paper a year, with 1,100 staff and revenue of $210,000,000. A carbon tax of $30 a tonne applies to 90,000 tonnes of emissions, while a government grant covers 20% of a $5,000,000 biomass boiler. Directors must decide whether to install the boiler or keep paying the tax.

questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A subsidy is a payment from government to a business to reduce its costs or encourage certain activity [2]. The grant covers 20% of Pohjola Paper's $5,000,000 biomass boiler.

knowledge_max_2: Lowers costs or encourages desired behaviour

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual carbon tax on 90,000 tonnes of emissions at $30 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 90,000 x $30 = $2,700,000 a year [2]. The 20% grant reduces the $5,000,000 boiler to $4,000,000.

knowledge_max_2: Tax = emissions x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Pohjola Paper of installing the biomass boiler.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It removes most of the carbon tax [k]. Emissions of 90,000 tonnes at $30 cost $2,700,000 a year [app], a large saving against $210,000,000 of revenue that improves profit [an].

Point 2: The subsidy lowers the investment cost [k]. A 20% grant cuts the $5,000,000 boiler to $4,000,000 [app], reducing the capital needed and making the project easier to approve with 1,100 staff to pay [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Pohjola Paper should install the biomass boiler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: the $2,700,000 annual carbon tax is close to the $4,000,000 net cost after the grant, so the boiler pays back quickly and cuts future tax exposure.

Against: biomass fuel still has a cost and supply risk, and $4,000,000 is significant even for a firm with $210,000,000 of revenue.

Conclusion: installing is justified because the tax saving is large and the grant reduces risk, provided Pohjola secures a long-term biomass supply.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $2,700,000 tax with $4,000,000 net cost
Considers fuel supply and grant conditions

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pampero Beef is a private limited company in Argentina rearing 200,000 cattle a year, with 950 staff and revenue of $64,000,000. New rules ban grazing on recently cleared forest, forcing it to buy 15,000 tonnes of feed at $320 a tonne, while an animal-welfare label costs $400,000 a year. Directors must decide whether to gain the label or sell only to local butchers.

questions.question_text: Define 'animal welfare'.
questions.model_answer: Animal welfare is the extent to which animals are kept healthy, comfortable and free from suffering [2]. Pampero Beef must improve cattle treatment to earn its animal-welfare label.

knowledge_max_2: Physical and mental wellbeing of animals
Covers housing, feed, health and handling

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of buying 15,000 tonnes of feed at $320 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 15,000 x $320 = $4,800,000 a year [2]. The welfare label would add $400,000, making $5,200,000 in total.

knowledge_max_2: Feed cost = tonnes x price per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the new forest rules on Pampero Beef.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Feed costs replace free grazing [k]. Buying 15,000 tonnes at $320 costs $4,800,000 a year [app], a new burden on $64,000,000 of revenue that lowers profit per animal [an].

Point 2: Land use must change [k]. With grazing banned on cleared forest, Pampero must farm more intensively or find new pasture [app], which may raise costs further and invite scrutiny from buyers checking deforestation [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Pampero Beef should pay for the animal-welfare label or sell only to local butchers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For the label: $400,000 is small beside the $4,800,000 feed bill, and certified welfare could open export markets and justify premium prices.

For local butchers: it avoids certification and inspection costs, but limits sales and leaves Pampero exposed if retailers demand welfare standards.

Conclusion: the label is worthwhile because it protects access to higher-value buyers, but Pampero should first confirm that premium prices cover both the $400,000 and the new feed cost.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $400,000 label cost with market access gains
Considers premium prices against local-only sales
analysis_max_2: Local-only sales reduce growth and bargaining power

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Lagos Printworks is a private limited company in Nigeria printing 45,000,000 magazines a year, with 380 staff, revenue of $18,000,000 and a paper bill of $10,800,000. The naira has fallen 15% against the dollar, raising imported paper costs by $1,620,000, and an import ban blocks foreign printing machines. Directors must decide whether to buy local paper at 8% more or keep importing.

questions.question_text: Define 'import ban'.
questions.model_answer: An import ban is a complete prohibition on bringing a particular good into a country [2]. Nigeria's ban stops Lagos Printworks from buying foreign printing machines.

knowledge_max_2: Total block on imports of a product
A severe form of trade protection

questions.question_text: Calculate the saving from buying local paper at 8% more than $10,800,000 instead of paying an extra $1,620,000 on imports.

knowledge_max_2: Compare local premium with import cost increase

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the falling naira on Lagos Printworks.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Imported paper becomes dearer [k]. The 15% fall adds $1,620,000 to a $10,800,000 paper bill [app], which is 9% of $18,000,000 revenue and threatens margins on 45,000,000 magazines [an].

Point 2: Imported machines become unaffordable [k]. The naira's fall and the import ban together prevent modernisation [app], so ageing presses may break down and raise maintenance costs [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Lagos Printworks should buy local paper at 8% more or keep importing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For local paper: it saves $756,000 a year compared with the $1,620,000 import increase and avoids exposure to further naira falls.

For importing: imported paper may be higher quality or unavailable locally in sufficient volume, and the 8% premium still leaves $864,000 of extra cost.

Conclusion: local paper is the better choice because it saves $756,000 and reduces currency risk, provided quality meets the standards of its magazine clients.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $756,000 saving with $864,000 local premium
Considers quality and supply security
analysis_max_2: Quality risk could lose publishing clients

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Indus Surgical is a private limited company in Pakistan making 12,000,000 surgical packs a year, with 780 staff, revenue of $36,000,000 and profit of $4,000,000. Interest rates have reached 15.5% and corporate tax is 29%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $5,000,000 for new hospital sterilisation equipment or instead lease it at $900,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct tax'.
questions.model_answer: A direct tax is a tax paid straight to government on income or profit [2]. Indus Surgical pays 29% corporation tax on its $4,000,000 profit.

knowledge_max_2: Paid by the person or business earning it

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $5,000,000 loan at 15.5%.
Explain two effects of the 15.5% interest rate on Indus Surgical.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Borrowing remains cheaper than leasing [k]. Interest of $775,000 is $125,000 below the $900,000 lease [app], so ownership looks attractive despite high rates, improving margin on $36,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Financial risk increases [k]. The $775,000 must be paid whatever happens, and profit of $4,000,000 is already taxed at 29% [app], leaving little cushion if hospital orders fall [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Indus Surgical should borrow $5,000,000 or lease the sterilisation equipment at $900,000 a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For borrowing: $775,000 interest is $125,000 cheaper than the lease and the company owns an asset that supports 12,000,000 packs.

For leasing: it avoids a long fixed commitment at 15.5%, keeps cash free and allows equipment upgrades as sterilisation technology changes.

Conclusion: borrowing is cheaper by $125,000 a year, but at 15.5% the risk is high; Indus should borrow only if hospital contracts guarantee the volume.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $125,000 annual saving against fixed-rate risk
Considers technology change and cash flexibility
analysis_max_2: Leasing preserves flexibility in a high-rate market

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Chao Phraya Rubber is a private limited company in Thailand processing 120,000 tonnes of natural rubber a year, with 860 staff and revenue of $96,000,000. New effluent rules require a $1,800,000 treatment system, and the firm faces a levy of $9 per tonne on 40,000 tonnes of untreated waste water. Directors must decide whether to build the system or pay the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental regulation'.
questions.model_answer: Environmental regulation is a rule set by government to control pollution or protect natural resources [2]. Thailand's new effluent rules force Chao Phraya Rubber to treat its waste water.

knowledge_max_2: Sets limits on emissions, waste or resource use

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual levy on 40,000 tonnes of untreated waste water at $9 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 40,000 x $9 = $360,000 a year [2]. The treatment system costs $1,800,000, five times the annual levy.

knowledge_max_2: Levy = tonnes x rate per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the new effluent rules on Chao Phraya Rubber.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise immediately [k]. The levy is $360,000 a year, or the system costs $1,800,000 [app], reducing funds for rubber processing on $96,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Reputation with buyers is at stake [k]. Untreated discharge could be publicised by campaigners [app], leading tyre and glove makers to switch to cleaner suppliers and threatening 860 jobs [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Chao Phraya Rubber should build the treatment system or keep paying the levy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For building: the $1,800,000 system ends the $360,000 annual levy, protects the river and avoids the risk of tougher limits or buyer boycotts.

For paying the levy: it is cheaper in the short term and preserves cash, but the levy may rise and the firm remains exposed to criticism.

Conclusion: building is the better choice because the levy alone repays the system in five years and regulation is likely to tighten, not loosen.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $1,800,000 cost with $360,000 annual levy
Considers future regulation and reputational risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Karoo Wind Energy is a public limited company in South Africa assembling 300 wind turbines a year, with 540 staff and revenue of $150,000,000. A 10% tariff now applies to the $40,000,000 of blades it imports, and a local supplier can make them for 12% more. The board must decide whether to source blades locally or keep importing.

questions.question_text: Define 'supply chain'.
questions.model_answer: A supply chain is the sequence of businesses and activities that provide materials and move a product to the customer [2]. Karoo Wind Energy's chain includes blade makers, transporters and turbine installers.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on $40,000,000 of imported blades at 10%.
questions.model_answer: $40,000,000 x 10% = $4,000,000 a year [2]. Local blades at 12% more would cost an extra $4,800,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 10% blade tariff on Karoo Wind Energy.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Turbine costs rise [k]. The tariff adds $4,000,000 to $40,000,000 of blade imports [app], reducing margin on 300 turbines and $150,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: Local suppliers gain an advantage [k]. With imports 10% dearer, the local maker's 12% premium is nearly matched [app], so Karoo may switch, cutting currency risk but losing access to specialised blade designs [an].

analysis_max_2: Local sourcing trades design choice for security

questions.question_text: Do you think Karoo Wind Energy should source blades locally or keep importing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For local blades: the $4,800,000 premium is only $800,000 more than the $4,000,000 tariff, and local supply avoids shipping delays and currency risk.

For importing: imported blades may be lighter or more efficient, and $4,800,000 is a large premium for a firm already paying 540 wages.

Conclusion: local sourcing is close to cost-neutral once the tariff is counted, so Karoo should switch if the local blades meet performance standards.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $4,800,000 local premium with $4,000,000 tariff
Considers blade performance and delivery risk
analysis_max_2: Local supply removes tariff and freight risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Medellin Flowers is a co-operative in Colombia exporting 30,000 tonnes of cut flowers a year, with 2,400 members and revenue of $84,000,000. The peso has appreciated 14% against the dollar, making exports dearer, and US buyers expect to cut their orders by 10%. Inflation of 6.7% has also raised fertiliser and fuel costs. Members must decide whether to cut dollar prices or reduce shipments.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Exchange rate appreciation is a rise in the value of a currency against another currency [2]. Colombia's peso has risen 14%, so Medellin Flowers' blooms cost US buyers more.

knowledge_max_2: Currency rises in value against another
Exports become dearer and imports cheaper

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in revenue if US buyers cut $84,000,000 of orders by 10%.
Explain two effects of the 14% appreciation of the peso on Medellin Flowers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: US orders fall [k]. A 14% stronger peso makes bouquets dearer, and buyers expect to cut 10% of $84,000,000, losing $8,400,000 [app], which strains incomes for 2,400 members [an].

Point 2: Imported inputs become cheaper [k]. Fertiliser and fuel bought abroad cost fewer pesos [app], but inflation of 6.7% is pushing other costs up faster, so the benefit is limited [an].

analysis_max_2: Lower export volume cuts member income
Cheaper imports are offset by domestic inflation

questions.question_text: Do you think Medellin Flowers should cut its dollar prices or reduce shipments to Europe? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For cutting dollar prices: it keeps US buyers ordering and protects 30,000 tonnes of sales, though it gives away margin on $84,000,000 of revenue.

For reducing shipments: it avoids selling at low prices, but leaves flowers unsold, cuts member incomes and may lose customers to Ecuadorian rivals.

Conclusion: a modest price cut is better than losing the market, but Medellin should share the burden with members by trimming costs rather than cutting prices by the full 14%.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs margin loss against volume and member income
Considers rival exporters and perishable stock

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Carpathia Software is a private limited company in Romania running 6 data centres, with 420 staff and revenue of $48,000,000. A new energy tax adds 12% to its $9,000,000 electricity bill, and a recycling rule requires safe disposal of 2,000 old servers at $75 each. Directors must decide whether to invest $2,400,000 in efficient cooling or pay the higher bills.

questions.question_text: Define 'energy efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: Energy efficiency means obtaining the same output while using less energy [2]. Carpathia Software could cut electricity use in its 6 data centres with better cooling.

knowledge_max_2: Using less energy for the same output

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual energy tax on a $9,000,000 electricity bill at 12%.
questions.model_answer: $9,000,000 x 12% = $1,080,000 a year [2]. Disposing of 2,000 servers at $75 adds $150,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the energy tax on Carpathia Software.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Operating costs rise [k]. The 12% tax adds $1,080,000 to a $9,000,000 bill [app], which is over 2% of $48,000,000 revenue and reduces funds for software development [an].

Point 2: Efficient cooling becomes more attractive [k]. A $2,400,000 system could cut both electricity use and the tax [app], lowering future bills but requiring capital that a 420-staff firm must finance [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Carpathia Software should invest $2,400,000 in efficient cooling? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For investing: it cuts the $1,080,000 energy tax as well as electricity use, and data centres run continuously, so savings accumulate every hour.

Against: $2,400,000 is more than two years of the tax, and cooling technology changes quickly, risking early obsolescence.

Conclusion: investing is justified because energy prices and taxes are likely to rise, but Carpathia should phase the rollout across its 6 data centres to limit risk.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $2,400,000 cost with $1,080,000 annual tax
Considers technology change and phased rollout

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Geysir Geoenergy is a private limited company in Iceland making 500 geothermal heat pumps a year, with 260 staff and revenue of $25,000,000. A trade bloc will require a new efficiency certificate costing $600,000, and exports worth $15,000,000 to that bloc carry a 7% tariff. Directors must decide whether to certify or focus on domestic sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'product standard'.
questions.model_answer: A product standard is a set of requirements a good must meet for quality, safety or performance [2]. The trade bloc's efficiency certificate is a standard Geysir Geoenergy must satisfy.

knowledge_max_2: Set by governments or industry bodies

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on $15,000,000 of exports at 7%.
questions.model_answer: $15,000,000 x 7% = $1,050,000 a year [2]. Certification at $600,000 would cost less than one year of the tariff.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Geysir Geoenergy of obtaining the efficiency certificate.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It protects access to the bloc [k]. Exports of $15,000,000 currently face a 7% tariff, or $1,050,000 [app], and certification is required to keep selling there at all [an].

Point 2: The certificate signals quality [k]. It costs $600,000, less than the annual tariff [app], and proves performance to buyers comparing heat pumps, supporting premium prices on $25,000,000 of revenue [an].

analysis_max_2: Compliance is a condition of trade

questions.question_text: Do you think Geysir Geoenergy should obtain the certificate or focus on domestic sales? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For certifying: $600,000 is less than one year of the $1,050,000 tariff and keeps $15,000,000 of exports open, spreading fixed costs over more pumps.

For domestic focus: Iceland is a small market, so concentrating there avoids certification and compliance, but limits growth to 500 pumps a year.

Conclusion: certifying is clearly better because the export market is large and the fee is recovered quickly, provided the pumps can meet the efficiency standard.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $600,000 fee with $1,050,000 tariff
Considers limited size of the domestic market

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Dnipro Grain is a private limited company in Ukraine exporting 900,000 tonnes of milling wheat a year, with 520 staff and revenue of $180,000,000. Freight insurance has risen 25%, adding $4,500,000 to annual costs, and bank interest rates have reached 17.0%. Directors must decide whether to borrow $8,000,000 for storage silos or sell grain immediately at harvest.

questions.question_text: Define 'insurance'.
questions.model_answer: Insurance is a contract in which a business pays a premium in return for cover against specified risks [2]. Dnipro Grain's freight insurance has risen 25% because of higher risk.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on an $8,000,000 loan at 17.0%.
questions.model_answer: $8,000,000 x 17.0% = $1,360,000 a year [2]. That is 30% of the $4,500,000 rise in insurance costs.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 25% rise in freight insurance on Dnipro Grain.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export costs increase [k]. The rise adds $4,500,000, exactly 2.5% of $180,000,000 revenue [app], reducing the margin on 900,000 tonnes of wheat [an].

Point 2: Borrowing becomes harder to justify [k]. With interest at 17.0%, silos costing $8,000,000 would add $1,360,000 a year [app], so the firm may prefer quick sales despite low harvest prices [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Dnipro Grain should borrow $8,000,000 for storage silos or sell grain immediately at harvest? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For silos: storing wheat lets Dnipro sell later at higher prices and spread $4,500,000 of insurance costs over more valuable output.

For immediate sales: it avoids $1,360,000 of interest at 17.0% and removes storage losses, but harvest prices are usually lowest.

Conclusion: silos are worthwhile only if the price gain exceeds $1,360,000 a year; otherwise selling immediately and avoiding high-interest debt is safer.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,360,000 interest against later price gains
Considers storage losses and harvest price levels

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tarcoles Fruit is a private limited company in Costa Rica growing 200,000 tonnes of bananas a year, with 3,000 staff and revenue of $120,000,000. New rules ban a pesticide used on 60% of its crop, and organic certification costs $900,000 a year but raises prices 15%. Directors must decide whether to go organic or switch to a permitted chemical.

questions.question_text: Define 'organic production'.
questions.model_answer: Organic production means farming without synthetic pesticides or artificial fertilisers [2]. Tarcoles Fruit must replace a banned pesticide on 60% of its banana crop.

knowledge_max_2: Relies on natural methods and approved inputs

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from a 15% organic price premium on $120,000,000.
questions.model_answer: $120,000,000 x 15% = $18,000,000 extra a year [2]. That is twenty times the $900,000 certification cost.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tarcoles Fruit of going organic.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The price premium raises revenue [k]. A 15% premium adds $18,000,000 to $120,000,000 of sales [app], far above the $900,000 certification fee, improving profit and funding safer equipment for 3,000 staff [an].

Point 2: It complies with the pesticide ban [k]. With 60% of the crop affected, organic methods avoid fines and keep bananas on supermarket shelves [app], protecting contracts with retailers who audit chemical use [an].

analysis_max_2: Retail contracts depend on chemical compliance

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarcoles Fruit should go organic or switch to a permitted chemical? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For organic: the 15% premium is worth $18,000,000, twenty times the $900,000 fee, and it avoids future bans on chemicals.

For a permitted chemical: it is cheaper and may protect yields, but consumers and retailers increasingly reject chemically grown fruit, and the permitted product could later be banned.

Conclusion: organic is the stronger choice because the premium is large and regulation is tightening, but Tarcoles should test yields on part of the 200,000 tonnes first.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $18,000,000 premium with $900,000 fee
Considers yield risk and future regulation

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tonle Bikes is a private limited company in Cambodia assembling 700,000 bicycles a year, with 1,100 staff and revenue of $42,000,000. A trade bloc will remove its 14% bicycle tariff only if 40% of parts are locally made, but local frames cost $6 more per bike. Directors must decide whether to meet the local-content rule or keep exporting with the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'rules of origin'.
questions.model_answer: Rules of origin are the criteria that determine which country a product comes from for trade purposes [2]. Tonle Bikes must show 40% local content to qualify for tariff-free entry.

knowledge_max_2: Criteria defining a product's national source

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual tariff on $42,000,000 of bicycle exports at 14%.
Explain two benefits to Tonle Bikes of meeting the 40% local-content rule.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Tariff-free entry cuts a large cost [k]. The 14% tariff costs $5,880,000 a year on $42,000,000 of exports [app], while local frames add only $4,200,000, so the firm saves $1,680,000 [an].

Point 2: Local suppliers strengthen the business [k]. Buying 40% of parts in Cambodia shortens lead times and reduces currency risk [app], supporting 1,100 staff and making the supply chain more resilient [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shortens and secures the supply chain

questions.question_text: Do you think Tonle Bikes should meet the local-content rule or keep exporting with the tariff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For local content: it saves $1,680,000 a year because the $4,200,000 frame cost is below the $5,880,000 tariff, and it secures tariff-free access long term.

For paying the tariff: it preserves access to cheaper imported frames and avoids dependence on local suppliers, though $5,880,000 a year is a heavy burden.

Conclusion: meeting the rule is clearly better on cost and security, provided Cambodian frame makers can supply 40% at consistent quality.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $4,200,000 local cost with $5,880,000 tariff
Considers local supplier capability
analysis_max_2: Local content gives a net saving

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Riyadh Cooling is a public limited company in Saudi Arabia installing 8,000 air-conditioning units a year, with 640 staff and revenue of $56,000,000. The government has cut electricity subsidies, raising its power bill by 30% from $4,000,000, and interest rates are 6.0%. The board must decide whether to borrow $7,000,000 for an assembly line or import finished units.

questions.question_text: Define 'energy subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: An energy subsidy is a government payment that lowers the cost of electricity or fuel for consumers and businesses [2]. Removing it raises Riyadh Cooling's $4,000,000 power bill by 30%.

knowledge_max_2: Removal exposes businesses to full market costs

questions.question_text: Calculate the increase in the power bill if $4,000,000 rises by 30%.
questions.model_answer: $4,000,000 x 30% = $1,200,000 extra a year [2]. The bill would rise to $5,200,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of removing the electricity subsidy on Riyadh Cooling.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Operating costs rise [k]. The power bill increases by $1,200,000 to $5,200,000 [app], which is over 2% of $56,000,000 revenue and lowers profit on every unit installed [an].

Point 2: Local assembly looks more attractive [k]. Higher running costs make imported finished units less competitive once shipping is added [app], so a $7,000,000 line at 6.0% interest, costing $420,000 a year, may pay off [an].

analysis_max_2: Assembly avoids import shipping and delays

questions.question_text: Do you think Riyadh Cooling should borrow $7,000,000 for an assembly line or import finished units? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For the assembly line: interest is only $420,000 a year at 6.0%, far below the $1,200,000 power increase, and local production avoids shipping and customs delays.

For importing: it needs no capital and allows the firm to switch suppliers, but leaves it exposed to freight costs and exchange rates.

Conclusion: the assembly line is worthwhile because finance is cheap and demand is steady, but Riyadh should first confirm it can sell 8,000 units at a competitive price.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $420,000 interest with $1,200,000 power rise
Considers demand certainty and import flexibility

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Riga Marine is a private limited company in Latvia building 120 fishing boats a year, with 340 staff and revenue of $30,000,000. New rules ban copper-based anti-fouling paint, forcing a switch costing $1,800 per boat, and a recycling levy of $120,000 a year applies to fibreglass waste. Directors must decide whether to redesign hulls or keep buying banned paint abroad.

questions.question_text: Define 'hazardous waste'.
questions.model_answer: Hazardous waste is waste that is harmful to human health or the environment and needs special disposal [2]. Riga Marine's banned anti-fouling paint and fibreglass offcuts require careful handling.

knowledge_max_2: Waste posing a risk to health or environment

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of the replacement paint at $1,800 per boat for 120 boats.
questions.model_answer: 120 x $1,800 = $216,000 a year [2]. This is $96,000 more than the $120,000 recycling levy.

knowledge_max_2: Cost = boats x cost per boat

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the paint ban on Riga Marine.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Input costs rise [k]. Replacement paint costs $216,000 for 120 boats [app], and with the $120,000 recycling levy the firm must absorb $336,000 on $30,000,000 revenue [an].

Point 2: Breaking the ban would be risky [k]. Buying banned paint abroad could bring fines, seized boats and lost orders from harbour authorities [app], damaging a business that depends on 340 skilled staff and fishing customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Non-compliance risks penalties and lost sales
analysis_max_2: Reputation and licences are at risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Riga Marine should redesign hulls or keep buying banned paint abroad? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For redesigning: it removes reliance on banned paint, may cut fuel use for fishing customers and avoids $216,000 of replacement paint each year.

For buying banned paint: it is cheaper now, but breaks the law, risks fines and could destroy the firm's reputation with harbour authorities.

Conclusion: redesigning is the only sustainable choice; the $216,000 paint saving plus avoided penalties justify the design work, even if it takes several seasons.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs redesign cost against $216,000 paint and legal risk
Considers customer fuel savings and reputation
analysis_max_2: Illegal paint threatens the business licence

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marlowehyde Interiors Ltd is a private limited company making fitted kitchens in Lisbon, Portugal, employing 90 staff and earning $6,200,000 a year. Inflation has climbed to 5.6% while the central bank raised interest rates to 4.25%, raising repayment costs. Directors must decide whether to borrow $1,800,000 for a computer-controlled saw or keep renting cutting equipment at $240,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services [2]. Portugal's 5.6% rate means Marlowehyde Interiors Ltd pays more for timber, fittings and labour each year.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general price level
Money loses purchasing power as prices climb

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest Marlowehyde Interiors Ltd would pay on a $1,800,000 loan at 4.25%.

knowledge_max_2: Interest = amount borrowed x interest rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 4.25% interest rate on Marlowehyde Interiors Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Borrowing for the saw becomes costly [k]. Interest on $1,800,000 reaches $76,500 a year [app], which is $163,500 less than the $240,000 rental charge, but the loan must still be repaid from uncertain kitchen sales [an].

Point 2: Customers who finance kitchens with credit buy less [k]. Higher mortgage and loan repayments squeeze Portuguese households [app], so orders for $6,200,000 of fitted kitchens may fall just as fixed costs must be covered [an].

analysis_max_2: Interest is paid before the saw earns revenue
Fewer orders spread fixed costs over fewer kitchens

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowehyde Interiors Ltd should borrow $1,800,000 for the saw? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The loan costs $76,500 a year in interest, well below the $240,000 rental bill, so buying frees cash for marketing and gives the firm an asset it can sell later. Automated cutting should also reduce waste and speed up orders.

Against: Repaying $1,800,000 plus interest is a fixed commitment, while inflation at 5.6% is eroding household budgets and kitchen orders may fall. Renting keeps the cost variable if demand weakens.

Conclusion: Borrow only if orders are already secured. The interest saving is large, but the debt risk during high inflation makes renting safer until demand is proven.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $76,500 interest against $240,000 rent
Considers inflation risk to kitchen demand
analysis_max_2: Annual saving of $163,500 before principal repayment
Debt commitment is fixed while sales are uncertain

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Cindervale Preserves Ltd is a family-owned private limited company in Chile producing 2,400,000 jars of jam a year sold at $1.80 each. A new packaging levy of $0.04 per plastic jar starts in January, while biodegradable lids would raise lid cost from $0.05 to $0.11 per jar. Directors must decide whether to switch all lids or absorb the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a harmful effect of production or consumption paid by society rather than the business [2]. Cindervale's plastic waste in Chilean rivers is an external cost borne by local people.

knowledge_max_2: Harm caused to third parties by business activity
Not paid for by the producer

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of the $0.04 packaging levy on Cindervale Preserves Ltd's jars.

knowledge_max_2: Levy cost = jars sold x levy per jar

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs of Cindervale Preserves Ltd's plastic packaging.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Plastic waste pollutes rivers and farmland [k]. With 2,400,000 jars sold yearly, discarded lids and jars reach Chilean waterways [app], raising clean-up costs for councils and harming fishing families who depend on clean water [an].

Point 2: Wildlife and tourism suffer [k]. Animals swallow plastic fragments and beaches lose visitors [app], so local hotels and guides lose income while Cindervale pays only a $96,000 levy [an].

knowledge_max_2: Harm to wildlife and local income

questions.question_text: Do you think Cindervale Preserves Ltd should switch to biodegradable lids? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Biodegradable lids address the pollution that damages Cindervale's reputation and may avoid future bans. The extra cost is $0.06 a lid, or $144,000 across 2,400,000 jars, which a premium 'green' label could recover through a higher price.

Against: The switch costs $48,000 more than the $96,000 levy and does nothing about the plastic jars themselves. Consumers in Chile may resist paying more, cutting sales volume and spreading fixed costs over fewer jars.

Conclusion: Switch only if retailers accept a higher price. Paying the levy is cheaper in the short term, but reputation damage could cost far more than $144,000.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $144,000 lid cost with $96,000 levy
Considers reputation and pricing power
analysis_max_2: Premium price could recover the cost if demand holds

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ravensholt Cycles Ltd is a private limited company in Denmark building 60,000 touring bicycles a year, exporting 45,000 of them to Australia at $220 each. Australia has imposed a 15% tariff on imported bicycles, and freight costs have risen by $18 per bike. Directors must decide whether to absorb the tariff or raise the Australian price to $250.
