questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods [2]. Australia's 15% charge on Ravensholt's bicycles makes each exported bike dearer at the border.

knowledge_max_2: Raises the price of imported goods

questions.question_text: Calculate the total annual tariff Ravensholt Cycles Ltd pays on 45,000 bicycles at $220 each.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff = value of exports x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 15% tariff on Ravensholt Cycles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Australian buyers face a higher price [k]. Each $220 bicycle gains $33 of tariff, so the landed cost before freight reaches $253 [app], making Ravensholt's bikes less attractive than local brands and cutting export volume [an].

Point 2: Profit margins are squeezed [k]. Paying $1,485,000 in tariff plus $18 extra freight per bike adds cost the firm must absorb or pass on [app], leaving less for design and marketing at home [an].

analysis_max_2: Absorbing the tax cuts retained profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensholt Cycles Ltd should absorb the tariff or raise the Australian price to $250? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For raising the price: $250 still leaves the firm short of the $33 tariff plus $18 freight, but it recovers $30 of the $51 extra cost. A premium touring brand may lose fewer sales than a price war would cause.

For absorbing it: Holding $220 protects 45,000 units of volume and keeps the Australian distributor loyal. However, $1,485,000 of tariff plus $810,000 of extra freight would wipe out much of the margin.

Conclusion: Raise the price to $250. The brand is differentiated, and absorbing $2,295,000 of external cost is too heavy for one firm.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $30 price rise with $51 extra cost
Judges brand strength against volume loss

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Whitehaven Care Homes Ltd is a private limited company in Ireland running nine care homes with 320 staff paid $13.20 an hour for 39 hours a week. Unemployment has fallen to 3.9% and the minimum wage rises by $1.00 to $14.20 an hour. Directors must decide whether to raise weekly fees from $980 to $1,050 or cut staffing hours.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: Unemployment is the number of people willing and able to work but without a job [2]. Ireland's 3.9% rate means Whitehaven struggles to recruit carers.

knowledge_max_2: People able and willing to work but jobless
Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra weekly wage cost of the $1.00 rise for Whitehaven Care Homes Ltd's 320 staff.
questions.model_answer: 320 staff x 39 hours x $1.00 = $12,480 extra each week [2].

knowledge_max_2: Extra wage = staff x hours x rise per hour

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the falling unemployment rate on Whitehaven Care Homes Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Recruitment becomes harder [k]. With unemployment at 3.9%, few carers are seeking work in Ireland [app], so Whitehaven may pay agency staff more and leave beds empty when rosters cannot be filled [an].

Point 2: Labour costs rise faster than fees [k]. The $1.00 minimum wage increase adds $12,480 a week, about $649,000 a year [app], squeezing margins unless the $70 fee rise is accepted by families and funders [an].

analysis_max_2: Agency cover raises cost per resident
Wage bill rises about $649,000 a year

questions.question_text: Do you think Whitehaven Care Homes Ltd should raise weekly fees to $1,050? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The $70 weekly rise raises revenue across every resident and covers the $12,480 weekly wage increase without cutting care hours. Adequate staffing protects the company's inspection rating and keeps occupancy high.

Against: Families and public funders may resist a 7.1% fee rise, and some residents could move to cheaper homes, leaving fixed costs spread over fewer beds. Cutting hours risks poor care and regulatory penalties.

Conclusion: Raise fees, but phase the increase. Staffing must stay safe, and the wage rise is permanent, so revenue has to rise with it.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $70 fee rise against $12,480 weekly wage cost
Considers occupancy and care quality

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ashcombe Logistics Ltd is a private limited company in Ontario, Canada, running 180 delivery vans that use 1,200,000 litres of diesel a year. The carbon tax rises from $0.11 to $0.15 per litre, and insurance premiums are up 9%. Directors must decide whether to replace 40 vans with electric models costing $2,400,000 or keep the diesel fleet.

questions.question_text: Define 'carbon tax'.
questions.model_answer: A carbon tax is a charge on the carbon content of fuel burned by businesses and households [2]. Ontario's rise to $0.15 a litre makes Ashcombe's diesel more expensive.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual carbon tax Ashcombe Logistics Ltd pays after the $0.04 rise.

knowledge_max_2: Extra tax = litres x rise per litre

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs of Ashcombe Logistics Ltd's diesel fleet.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Air pollution harms public health [k]. Burning 1,200,000 litres of diesel releases exhaust gases across Ontario [app], adding to asthma and hospital costs that taxpayers fund rather than Ashcombe [an].

Point 2: Congestion and road wear impose costs on others [k]. Heavy vans on busy routes slow other road users and damage surfaces [app], so councils spend more on repairs, far above the $48,000 tax, and deliveries take longer for every business [an].

analysis_max_2: Health costs fall on public services

questions.question_text: Do you think Ashcombe Logistics Ltd should spend $2,400,000 on 40 electric vans? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Electric vans cut diesel use by roughly 267,000 litres, avoiding about $40,000 of carbon tax a year and shielding Ashcombe from future rises. They also win 'green' contracts and reduce pollution complaints.

Against: $2,400,000 is a heavy outlay for 40 of 180 vans, and charging points and battery range may disrupt schedules. Insurance is already up 9%, so cash is tight.

Conclusion: Buy a smaller trial fleet first. The tax saving alone does not justify $2,400,000, but a staged switch manages risk while protecting reputation.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $2,400,000 against $40,000 annual tax saving
Considers staged investment
analysis_max_2: Reputation and contract gains offset cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ostermere Seafood Ltd is a private limited company in Iceland exporting 4,000 tonnes of frozen cod a year to Japan at $3,200 a tonne. The Icelandic krona has depreciated by 12% against the dollar, and fuel for its trawlers now costs $610,000 a year. Directors must decide whether to cut the Japanese price or keep prices and take more profit.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in another [2]. The krona's 12% fall against the dollar changes what Ostermere's cod earns.

knowledge_max_2: Value of one currency in terms of another
Set by supply and demand or government

questions.question_text: Calculate the 12% increase in dollar-equivalent revenue on Ostermere Seafood Ltd's $12,800,000 of exports.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue = tonnes x price per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the krona's 12% depreciation on Ostermere Seafood Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export receipts are worth more [k]. Each $3,200 tonne converts into 12% more krona [app], adding $1,536,000 of dollar-equivalent revenue and improving cash flow without extra fishing [an].

Point 2: Imported costs become dearer [k]. Fuel billed at $610,000 and imported nets and parts cost more in krona [app], so the gain on cod is partly offset and margins may not rise as much as revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Export revenue rises in home currency
analysis_max_2: Gain depends on how much is imported

questions.question_text: Do you think Ostermere Seafood Ltd should cut its Japanese price? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For cutting the price: A lower yen price could win shelf space from Norwegian rivals and raise volume above 4,000 tonnes. Because the krona buys less, a modest price cut still leaves more home-currency revenue than before.

Against: Keeping the price captures the full $1,536,000 gain and funds the $610,000 fuel bill. A price cut may also signal weakness and start a margin-destroying price war in Japan.

Conclusion: Keep prices for now. The depreciation already improves competitiveness, and the extra $1,536,000 is better used to cover rising fuel than given away.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs volume growth against $1,536,000 gain
Considers price war risk
analysis_max_2: Depreciation already lowers the yen price
Fuel bill of $610,000 must be covered

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Brackenford Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Poland making wooden toys, with revenue of $4,800,000 and profit of $420,000. The economy has entered recession with GDP falling 2.4%, and the government has raised sales tax by 3 percentage points to 23%. Directors must decide whether to cut prices by 8% or reduce the product range.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when a country's GDP falls for two consecutive quarters or more [2]. Poland's 2.4% fall signals weaker demand for Brackenford's toys.

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in Brackenford Toys Ltd's profit if it absorbs the 3 percentage point sales tax rise on $4,800,000 of revenue.

knowledge_max_2: Tax cost = revenue x tax rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession on Brackenford Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Household demand for toys falls [k]. With GDP down 2.4%, Polish families cut discretionary spending [app], so orders for wooden toys drop and $4,800,000 of revenue may not be repeated [an].

Point 2: Unsold stock ties up cash [k]. Slower sales leave toys in the warehouse and the 3-point tax rise takes $144,000 from profit [app], leaving less money to pay suppliers and keep skilled staff [an].

analysis_max_2: Stock and tax reduce working capital

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenford Toys Ltd should cut prices by 8%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: An 8% cut may keep volume up as families trade down, protecting market share and keeping the factory busy during the recession. Lower prices could also clear stock before the tax rise bites.

Against: Cutting prices by 8% removes $384,000 of revenue at current volume, more than the $144,000 tax cost. Toys are already a discretionary purchase, so cheaper prices may not overcome the 2.4% GDP fall.

Conclusion: Do not cut prices across the board. A narrower product range cuts cost without destroying margin, which matters more when profit is only $420,000.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $384,000 revenue loss with $144,000 tax
Considers price elasticity in a recession
analysis_max_2: Price cuts may not raise volume enough

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Thornleigh Fashion Ltd is a private limited company in Bangladesh making 900,000 garments a year for European brands. A pressure group claims 18% of output is unsold waste dumped in rivers, and two retailers have threatened to cancel contracts worth $2,600,000. Directors must decide whether to donate surplus stock or build a $340,000 recycling unit.

questions.question_text: Define 'pressure group'.
questions.model_answer: A pressure group is an organisation that campaigns to influence business or government behaviour without seeking office [2]. The group naming Thornleigh's river waste is pressuring retailers to act.

knowledge_max_2: Seeks to change behaviour, not win elections

questions.question_text: Calculate the number of unsold garments represented by 18% of Thornleigh Fashion Ltd's 900,000 garments.
Explain two ethical issues facing Thornleigh Fashion Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Pollution from dumped stock [k]. The claim that 162,000 garments a year enter rivers [app] harms fishing families and damages the reputation of the European brands Thornleigh supplies [an].

Point 2: Honesty towards customers [k]. Retailers spending $2,600,000 expect accurate sustainability claims [app]; if Thornleigh conceals the waste, lost contracts and legal action could follow [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornleigh Fashion Ltd should build the $340,000 recycling unit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The unit turns 162,000 unsold garments into fibre, cutting river pollution and giving retailers evidence of action. Saving $2,600,000 of contracts easily outweighs a $340,000 investment and may attract new ethical buyers.

Against: Recycling does not stop overproduction, and $340,000 is cash that a low-margin Bangladeshi supplier may not have. Donating stock is cheaper and helps poor families directly.

Conclusion: Build the unit, but also cut overproduction. Protecting $2,600,000 of contracts justifies $340,000, while donation alone would not satisfy the retailers.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $340,000 against $2,600,000 contracts
Judges recycling versus donation

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Brantwood Motors Ltd is a private limited company in Mexico assembling 25,000 pickup trucks a year for export to the United States. A new quota cuts its American sales to 18,000 trucks, and each truck earns a contribution of $2,400. Fixed costs are $21,000,000 a year. Directors must decide whether to build a Brazilian plant or accept the smaller quota.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota'.
questions.model_answer: A quota is a physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported [2]. America's limit of 18,000 trucks directly caps Brantwood's sales.

questions.question_text: Calculate the contribution Brantwood Motors Ltd loses from the 7,000 truck cut in its American quota.

knowledge_max_2: Lost contribution = lost units x contribution per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the quota on Brantwood Motors Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Contribution falls sharply [k]. Losing 7,000 trucks at $2,400 each removes $16,800,000 [app], which is close to the $21,000,000 of fixed costs and may push the plant into a loss [an].

Point 2: Capacity is left idle [k]. The Mexican plant can build 25,000 trucks but only 18,000 can enter America [app], so machinery and 25,000 units of capacity earn nothing unless another market is found [an].

analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over fewer units

questions.question_text: Do you think Brantwood Motors Ltd should build a Brazilian plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A Brazilian plant spreads risk away from the American quota and could supply South American buyers without tariffs. Using idle Mexican capacity for other markets is not possible if the quota stays.

Against: A new plant is a large fixed cost on top of $21,000,000, and Brazil has its own taxes and currency risk. $16,800,000 of lost contribution leaves little spare cash.

Conclusion: Do not build yet. First find alternative buyers for the 7,000 trucks; only if that fails should Brantwood commit to a second plant.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs diversification against plant cost
Considers alternative markets first
analysis_max_2: Brazil adds currency and tax risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tarnside Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Greece operating 12 coastal hotels with revenue of $18,400,000. The central bank has cut interest rates from 3.75% to 3.00%, while inflation is 2.1% and package holiday prices are rising sharply across Europe. Directors must decide whether to borrow $5,000,000 to refurbish three hotels or postpone the work.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the loan [2]. Greece's fall to 3.00% makes Tarnside's planned loan cheaper.

knowledge_max_2: Expressed as a percentage per period

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest saving on a $5,000,000 loan after the rate falls from 3.75% to 3.00%.
questions.model_answer: Fall = 0.75 percentage points. $5,000,000 x 0.75% = $37,500 saved a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Saving = loan x fall in rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the interest rate cut on Tarnside Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Refurbishment finance is cheaper [k]. Interest on $5,000,000 falls by $37,500 a year [app], reducing the cost of upgrading three hotels and improving the return on each room [an].

Point 2: Guest demand may rise [k]. Lower rates cut mortgage repayments for European households [app], so more families can afford holidays and Tarnside's $18,400,000 revenue may grow [an].

analysis_max_2: Lower finance cost improves project return

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarnside Hotels Ltd should borrow $5,000,000 for the refurbishment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The rate cut saves $37,500 a year and refurbished rooms can command higher prices, raising revenue above $18,400,000. Acting while rates are 3.00% locks in cheaper finance before inflation at 2.1% pushes costs up.

Against: Borrowing $5,000,000 adds a fixed interest bill when tourism demand can collapse suddenly. The saving of $37,500 is small against the debt, and building costs are rising.

Conclusion: Proceed, but borrow in stages. The lower rate helps, yet the debt should match confirmed booking growth rather than a single optimistic forecast.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $37,500 saving against $5,000,000 debt
Considers timing and tourism risk
analysis_max_2: Fixed interest is risky if demand falls

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Solberrie Estates Ltd is a private limited company in South Africa producing 2,000,000 bottles of wine a year with revenue of $2,000,000. Fairtrade certification would cost $85,000 a year, but certified wine sells at a 9% premium and two European supermarkets have asked for it by name from next season. Directors must decide whether to apply for certification.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical trading'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical trading means buying and selling goods in a way that treats workers, suppliers and the environment fairly [2]. Solberrie's Fairtrade application is an attempt to prove ethical trading to supermarkets.

knowledge_max_2: Fair treatment of workers and suppliers
Avoids harm to people and the environment

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from a 9% premium on Solberrie Estates Ltd's $2,000,000 revenue.
questions.model_answer: $2,000,000 x 9% = $180,000 extra revenue a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Premium revenue = revenue x premium rate

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Solberrie Estates Ltd of gaining Fairtrade certification.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher revenue per bottle [k]. A 9% premium on $2,000,000 adds $180,000 [app], which more than covers the $85,000 fee and leaves $95,000 to reinvest in vines [an].

Point 2: Access to ethical buyers [k]. Two European supermarkets have asked for certified wine [app], so certification can secure contracts that rivals without the mark cannot win [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Solberrie Estates Ltd should apply for Fairtrade certification? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The 9% premium adds $180,000 against an $85,000 fee, a net gain of $95,000, and the two supermarkets may place large repeat orders. Certification also protects the estate's reputation as ethical sourcing rules tighten.

Against: The premium depends on customers paying more, and certification fees and inspections may rise. South African labour costs and drought could absorb the gain, and the estate may not sell all 2,000,000 bottles at the higher price.

Conclusion: Apply. The net gain is clear and supermarket demand is already evident, but Solberrie should secure written orders before paying the fee.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $180,000 premium against $85,000 fee
Considers whether premium demand is secure

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Fennimore Appliances Ltd is a private limited company in Slovakia making washing machines, exporting $6,000,000 a year to a regional trade bloc that is growing 3.1%. The bloc has removed its 22% tariff on appliance imports, and rival brands are cutting prices. Directors must decide whether to cut prices by 10% or keep prices and retain the saving.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade bloc'.
questions.model_answer: A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members [2]. The bloc buying Fennimore's washing machines has just removed a 22% tariff.

knowledge_max_2: Group of countries with a trade agreement

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual saving to Fennimore Appliances Ltd from removing a 22% tariff on $6,000,000 of exports.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff saving = export value x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the tariff removal on Fennimore Appliances Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The landed price falls [k]. Removing 22% from $6,000,000 of exports saves $1,320,000 [app], so Fennimore can match rival price cuts without losing margin [an].

Point 2: Competition inside the bloc intensifies [k]. Other appliance makers gain the same access and the bloc is growing only 3.1% [app], so Fennimore must improve quality or service to win share [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Fennimore Appliances Ltd should cut prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 10% cut costs $600,000 of revenue, less than the $1,320,000 tariff saving, and could win buyers while rivals hesitate. Lower prices may fill capacity and spread fixed costs further.

Against: Keeping prices retains the full $1,320,000, which could fund design improvements that matter more than price in appliance sales. A price cut is easily matched and may start a damaging war in a bloc growing only 3.1%.

Conclusion: Do not cut prices by 10%. Keep the saving for quality and marketing, which are harder for rivals to copy than a discount.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $600,000 price cut with $1,320,000 saving
Considers non-price competition

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quillmere Software Ltd is a private limited company in Estonia employing 120 developers at an average salary of $38,000. Economic growth is 3.8%, but wage inflation has reached 6.4% and rival firms are hiring. Directors must decide whether to open a second office in Latvia, where developer salaries average $30,000, or raise pay by 6.4% to keep its team.

questions.question_text: Define 'economic growth'.
questions.model_answer: Economic growth is an increase in a country's output of goods and services over time, measured by GDP [2]. Estonia's 3.8% growth means more demand for Quillmere's software.

knowledge_max_2: Rise in GDP or national output

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual cost of a 6.4% pay rise for Quillmere Software Ltd's 120 developers.

knowledge_max_2: Wage rise = total wage bill x percentage

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of wage inflation on Quillmere Software Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise faster than output [k]. A 6.4% pay rise adds $291,840 to a $4,560,000 wage bill [app], so profit per project falls unless client fees rise [an].

Point 2: Skilled staff may leave [k]. With wage inflation at 6.4% and rivals hiring [app], programmers can job-hop for better pay, forcing Quillmere to spend on recruitment and lose project knowledge [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Quillmere Software Ltd should open an office in Latvia? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Latvian salaries of $30,000 are $8,000 below Estonia's, saving $960,000 a year across 120 developers even after travel and management costs. A second site also spreads risk if Estonian wages keep climbing.

Against: A new office brings recruitment, legal and coordination costs, and splitting teams can slow software projects. Paying $291,840 to retain experienced staff may cost less than rebuilding a team abroad.

Conclusion: Open a small Latvian office, not a full move. The $8,000 gap is large, but keeping core developers in Estonia protects quality.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $960,000 saving against set-up costs
Considers team coordination and quality

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Calderwick Chemicals Ltd is a private limited company in Malaysia producing 40,000 tonnes of industrial chemicals a year. The environmental agency has fined it $320,000 for discharging effluent into a river and ordered improvements within six months. A treatment plant would cost $1,100,000 and add $90,000 a year in running costs. Directors must decide whether to invest.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of production borne by people outside the business [2]. Calderwick's effluent damages river users who receive no compensation from the company.

knowledge_max_2: Not included in the firm's private costs

questions.question_text: Calculate the fine per tonne of output for Calderwick Chemicals Ltd's 40,000 tonnes.

knowledge_max_2: Fine per tonne = total fine / output

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs of Calderwick Chemicals Ltd's river discharge.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Water pollution harms fishing and drinking supplies [k]. Effluent from 40,000 tonnes of chemical output enters the river [app], so downstream families face health risks and fishermen lose catches they cannot replace [an].

Point 2: Clean-up is paid by the public [k]. The $320,000 fine may not cover the full damage [app], so taxpayers fund water treatment while Calderwick's private costs stay below the true cost of production [an].

analysis_max_2: Fine may be below the social cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Calderwick Chemicals Ltd should invest $1,100,000 in the treatment plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The plant stops pollution, removes the risk of repeat fines above $320,000 and protects the licence the company needs to keep producing 40,000 tonnes. It also improves relations with regulators and local residents.

Against: $1,100,000 plus $90,000 a year is costly against a single $320,000 fine. Cheaper filtration or paying the fine may protect profit in the short term, though a shutdown order would be far worse.

Conclusion: Invest. The fine is a warning, and losing the operating licence would destroy far more value than $1,100,000.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $1,100,000 against $320,000 fine
Considers licence loss risk
analysis_max_2: Repeat fines and shutdown threaten output

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Calderon Footwear Ltd is a private limited company in Spain making leather boots with 150,000 labour hours a year at $18.50 an hour. questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment and communication [2]. Cheap Vietnamese labour and tariff-free imports show globalisation pressuring Calderon.

knowledge_max_2: Growth of worldwide trade and investment

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual labour saving if Calderon Footwear Ltd moves 150,000 hours from $18.50 to $4.20 an hour.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = hours x difference in wage rates

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of moving production to Vietnam on Calderon Footwear Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Labour costs fall dramatically [k]. Paying $4.20 instead of $18.50 an hour saves $2,145,000 across 150,000 hours [app], which can fund lower prices or higher marketing spending [an].

Point 2: Control and reputation are at risk [k]. Managing a distant supplier makes quality checks harder, and Spanish customers may boycott a brand that cut local jobs [app], damaging sales that depend on the 'made in Spain' label [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loss of control and reputation risk
analysis_max_2: Distance raises quality and ethical risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Calderon Footwear Ltd should move production to Vietnam? Justify your answer.

For: A $2,145,000 annual saving is enormous for a footwear maker facing tariff-free rivals. The trade agreement makes importing easy, and the saving can pay for better design and marketing.

Against: Spanish craftsmanship supports the brand and protects skilled jobs. Moving risks quality problems, longer lead times from Asia and consumer backlash, which could cost more than $2,145,000 in lost sales.

Conclusion: Do not move all production. Keep a Spanish workshop for premium boots and source volume lines from Vietnam, balancing cost savings with brand value.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $2,145,000 saving against brand damage
Considers a partial move
analysis_max_2: Premium buyers pay for Spanish origin

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Drayholt Textiles Ltd is a private limited company in Morocco employing 260 workers, with unemployment in its region at 11.2%. questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: Unemployment is the number of people who are able and willing to work but cannot find a job [2]. The region's 11.2% rate means Drayholt has plenty of potential workers to hire.

knowledge_max_2: Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Calculate the net cost of the $900,000 loom after the government pays 20%.

questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hiring is easy and cheap [k]. With unemployment at 11.2%, Drayholt can recruit 40 workers without bidding up wages [app], keeping the $6,800 salary and expanding output for rising export demand [an].

Point 2: Local demand may be weak [k]. Unemployed families buy fewer goods, so domestic textile sales suffer even though exports are growing 4.5% [app], forcing Drayholt to depend on foreign buyers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Drayholt Textiles Ltd should buy the automated loom? Justify your answer.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $720,000 net cost against $272,000 wages

analysis_max_2: Hiring is cheaper upfront but recurring

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Norbury Glassworks Ltd is a private limited company in Croatia with an annual energy bill of $320,000, mostly from a gas furnace. questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means operating in a way that meets present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs [2]. Norbury's solar array would make its glass production more sustainable.

knowledge_max_2: Meeting needs without harming the future
Balances economic, social and environmental aims

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual saving from a 40% cut in Norbury Glassworks Ltd's $320,000 energy bill.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = energy bill x percentage cut

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Norbury Glassworks Ltd of installing the solar array.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Energy costs become more predictable [k]. Solar cuts $128,000 from a $320,000 bill [app], reducing exposure to the 15% gas tax and freeing cash for furnace maintenance [an].

Point 2: Environmental reputation improves [k]. Customers buying glass for green buildings prefer low-carbon suppliers [app], so Norbury can win contracts and possibly charge a premium [an].

analysis_max_2: Less exposure to fossil fuel taxes

questions.question_text: Do you think Norbury Glassworks Ltd should install the $640,000 solar array? Justify your answer.

Against: $640,000 is a large commitment for a glassworks with thin margins, and solar output varies with weather. The furnace still needs gas, so the 15% tax is not fully avoided.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $640,000 cost against $128,000 saving

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Northgate Software Ltd is a private limited company in Zurich, Switzerland, employing 80 experienced support staff at an average salary of $42,000. A partner in India offers to run the same service with 80 staff at $9,000 each, but redundancy payments will cost $700,000 in total. Directors must decide whether to offshore the support team.

questions.question_text: Define 'offshoring'.
questions.model_answer: Offshoring is moving a business process to another country [2]. Northgate would shift its support service from Zurich to India.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual salary saving from employing 80 staff at $9,000 instead of $42,000.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = staff x difference in salary

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of offshoring on Northgate Software Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Operating costs fall [k]. Replacing $42,000 salaries with $9,000 saves $2,640,000 a year [app], which can be spent on product development and lower client prices [an].

Point 2: Service quality may suffer [k]. Time zones and accents make customer calls harder, and the $700,000 redundancy bill must be paid first [app], so savings may take months to appear while complaints rise [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Software Ltd should offshore its support team? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The $2,640,000 annual saving dwarfs the $700,000 redundancy cost, recovering it in under four months. Cheaper support lets Northgate cut prices or invest in software that wins larger clients.

Against: Support quality drives renewals, and unhappy customers may leave. The Zurich redundancy damages local reputation, and managing an Indian partner adds control and data-security risks.

Conclusion: Offshore, but keep a small Swiss escalation team. The saving is too large to ignore, while a retained senior group protects service quality.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $2,640,000 saving against $700,000 cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Fenwick Rooftops Ltd is a private limited company in Hungary installing solar panels, with a diesel fuel bill of $84,000 a year for its 26 vans. questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained increase in the average level of prices [2]. Hungary's 3.2% rate is pushing up Fenwick's fuel, parts and wages.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual fuel cost from a 12% diesel tax rise on Fenwick Rooftops Ltd's $84,000 bill.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising fuel costs on Fenwick Rooftops Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Each installation becomes less profitable [k]. The 12% tax adds $10,080 to a fuel bill already rising with 3.2% inflation [app], cutting the margin on every roof completed by the 26 vans [an].

Point 2: Prices may rise and demand fall [k]. Passing costs on makes solar installation dearer [app], so price-sensitive homeowners may delay orders just as the firm needs volume [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenwick Rooftops Ltd should pass the extra fuel cost on to customers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Passing on $10,080 protects a margin already squeezed by 3.2% inflation, and a small rise per installation is unlikely to deter buyers who expect energy savings from solar panels.

Against: Solar installation is a big household purchase, and higher prices may lose jobs to rivals. Absorbing $10,080 is modest against total revenue and keeps the order book full.

Conclusion: Pass on the cost through a small surcharge. The sum is small per job, and protecting margin matters more than risking a price rise that customers can compare easily.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $10,080 against demand risk
Considers per-job size of the increase

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Greenhalgh Recycling Ltd is a private limited company in Serbia processing 9,000 tonnes of household plastic a year. It pays $40 a tonne for collection and sells 85% of the material at $210 a tonne. A $260,000 optical sorting machine would raise the saleable share to 95% within a year. Directors must decide whether to buy the machine.

questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into reusable products [2]. Greenhalgh turns 9,000 tonnes of household plastic into material it can sell.

knowledge_max_2: Reduces landfill and raw material use

questions.question_text: Calculate Greenhalgh Recycling Ltd's current sales revenue from 85% of 9,000 tonnes sold at $210 a tonne.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue = saleable tonnes x price per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Greenhalgh Recycling Ltd of buying the sorting machine.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: More material can be sold [k]. Raising recovery from 85% to 95% turns 900 extra tonnes into saleable plastic [app], adding $189,000 of revenue at $210 a tonne [an].

Point 2: Less waste goes to landfill [k]. Better sorting cuts disposal charges and strengthens Greenhalgh's bid for council contracts [app], where low contamination and high diversion rates are required [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Greenhalgh Recycling Ltd should buy the $260,000 sorting machine? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The machine adds $189,000 of revenue a year by raising recovery to 95%, so it pays for itself in under two years, and it cuts landfill charges. Better quality output helps win council contracts.

Against: $260,000 is a heavy outlay for a firm paying $40 a tonne for collection, and plastic prices can fall sharply. The machine also needs maintenance and trained operators.

Conclusion: Buy it. Recovery in under two years is attractive, and the contract advantage protects revenue even if plastic prices dip.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $260,000 against $189,000 extra revenue
Considers plastic price volatility

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ellesmere Wines Ltd is a private limited company in Argentina exporting 40,000 cases of premium wine a year to China at $60 a case. China has imposed a 20% tariff, and the Argentine peso has risen 6% against the yuan. Directors must decide whether to absorb the tariff or raise the Chinese price to $75.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax charged on imported goods [2]. China's 20% tariff adds $12 to every case Ellesmere sells there.

knowledge_max_2: Raises the price paid by importers

questions.question_text: Calculate the total annual tariff on Ellesmere Wines Ltd's 40,000 cases at $60 each.
questions.model_answer: Tariff per case = $60 x 20% = $12. Total = 40,000 x $12 = $480,000 a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff = export value x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 20% tariff on Ellesmere Wines Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Chinese buyers pay more [k]. Each $60 case carries $12 of tariff [app], so Ellesmere's wine looks expensive beside domestic brands and volume may fall below 40,000 cases [an].

Point 2: The stronger peso compounds the problem [k]. A 6% rise makes Argentine wine dearer in yuan even before the tariff [app], leaving Ellesmere with $480,000 of tariff plus a currency headwind [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ellesmere Wines Ltd should raise its Chinese price to $75? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A $75 price recovers the $12 tariff and part of the currency loss, protecting margin on premium wine. Chinese buyers of imported wine are less price-sensitive than mass-market drinkers.

Against: $75 is 25% above the old price once the tariff is added, which could hand sales to Chilean and Australian rivals. Absorbing the tariff costs $480,000 but keeps 40,000 cases flowing.

Conclusion: Raise the price, but only to $72. Full recovery risks volume, while partial recovery shares the burden and keeps Ellesmere visible in China.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $75 price against volume loss
Considers premium segment elasticity
analysis_max_2: Rivals gain if price rises too far

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Cranbourne Motors Ltd is a private limited company in Romania running a fleet of delivery vans. Leasing costs $290,000 a year, while buying the fleet outright needs a $2,200,000 loan at an interest rate of 6.5%. The economy has slipped into recession, with GDP falling 1.5%. Directors must decide whether to buy or continue leasing.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the percentage charged for borrowing money [2]. Cranbourne would pay 6.5% on a $2,200,000 loan to buy its vans.

knowledge_max_2: Cost of borrowing as a percentage

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on a $2,200,000 loan at 6.5%.
Explain two effects of the recession on Cranbourne Motors Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Delivery volumes fall [k]. With GDP down 1.5%, retailers ship fewer goods [app], so Cranbourne's vans run below capacity while lease payments of $290,000 continue [an].

Point 2: Buying becomes riskier [k]. A $2,200,000 loan at 6.5% costs $143,000 a year before repayment [app], a fixed burden that is hard to carry when revenue is falling [an].

analysis_max_2: Lease payments continue at low volumes
Debt is fixed while revenue falls

questions.question_text: Do you think Cranbourne Motors Ltd should buy the fleet? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Buying ends the $290,000 lease, and $143,000 of interest is $147,000 cheaper each year. Owning the vans gives an asset to sell if the recession deepens.

Against: The $2,200,000 loan must be repaid even if deliveries fall, and 6.5% is expensive during a 1.5% GDP decline. Leasing can be reduced if the fleet shrinks.

Conclusion: Keep leasing until the recession ends. The annual saving is real, but a fixed $2,200,000 debt in a shrinking market is too risky for a delivery firm.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $143,000 interest against $290,000 lease
Considers recession risk
analysis_max_2: Debt cannot be reduced like a lease

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kestrelbay Paper Ltd is a private limited company in Indonesia producing 50,000 tonnes of paper a year. A new emissions quota cuts its allowance to 42,000 tonnes of carbon, and excess emissions face a penalty of $95 a tonne. Filters to abate the remaining 8,000 tonnes cost $60 a tonne. Directors must decide whether to install the filters.

questions.question_text: Define 'emissions quota'.
questions.model_answer: An emissions quota is a legal limit on the amount of pollution a business may release [2]. Kestrelbay's quota has been cut from 50,000 to 42,000 tonnes of carbon.

questions.question_text: Calculate the cost of abating the 8,000 tonnes above Kestrelbay Paper Ltd's quota at $60 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 8,000 tonnes x $60 = $480,000 to abate the excess carbon [2]. Paying the $95 penalty would instead cost $760,000.

knowledge_max_2: Abatement cost = tonnes x cost per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the tighter emissions quota on Kestrelbay Paper Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Production costs rise [k]. Abating 8,000 tonnes costs $480,000, or $760,000 if the firm instead pays the $95 penalty [app], reducing profit on 50,000 tonnes of paper [an].

Point 2: Investment and reputation are affected [k]. Kestrelbay must choose between filters and lower output [app], and buyers of paper increasingly favour suppliers with low carbon emissions [an].

knowledge_max_2: Pressure to invest or cut output

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrelbay Paper Ltd should install the filters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Filters cost $480,000 against $760,000 of penalties, saving $280,000 immediately and avoiding future quota cuts. Compliance also protects contracts with environmentally conscious paper buyers.

Against: $480,000 is a large outlay on top of the cost of cutting output to 42,000 tonnes, and the filters may need maintenance. Paying the penalty keeps flexibility if quotas are later relaxed.

Conclusion: Install the filters. The $280,000 saving and contract security outweigh the flexibility of paying penalties, which are likely to rise.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $480,000 cost with $760,000 penalty
Considers future quota tightening

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kingsmoor Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Germany importing 90,000 precision electronic components a year at $18 each from next month. The euro has appreciated by 10% against the dollar, and a 6% import duty applies to the components. Directors must decide whether to switch to a local supplier charging $22 per component.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the value of one currency expressed in another currency [2]. The euro's 10% appreciation changes the dollar cost of Kingsmoor's components.

knowledge_max_2: Price of one currency in another
Changes affect import and export prices

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual cost of the 10% euro appreciation on 90,000 components at $18 each.

knowledge_max_2: Extra cost = import bill x appreciation

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the euro's appreciation on Kingsmoor Engineering Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Imported components become dearer [k]. A 10% rise adds $162,000 to a $1,620,000 bill [app], and the 6% duty is charged on the higher value, raising unit costs further [an].

Point 2: German exports become less competitive [k]. A stronger euro makes Kingsmoor's finished machinery dearer abroad [app], so foreign orders may fall just as costs rise [an].

analysis_max_2: Duty is charged on a higher value
Export demand falls as prices rise

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsmoor Engineering Ltd should switch to the local supplier at $22? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A local supplier avoids the 10% currency risk and the 6% duty, and delivery times shorten. Paying $22 is predictable, which helps quoting on long contracts.

Against: $22 is more than the current $18 plus duty, so switching raises the unit price. The euro may fall again, making imports cheaper, and the local supplier may lack capacity.

Conclusion: Do not switch yet. The appreciation may reverse, and Kingsmoor should first ask the importer to share the currency cost rather than lock into a permanently higher price.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $22 local price against $18 import plus duty
Considers currency reversal risk
analysis_max_2: Locking in $22 may be costly if euro falls

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pellumbra Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Albania employing 210 packers at $6.00 an hour for 40 hours a week. The minimum wage rises 10% to $6.60, and a packing machine costing $420,000 could replace 30 workers. Directors must decide whether to buy the machine or pay the legally required higher wage from January.

questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: A minimum wage is the lowest legal rate an employer may pay per hour [2]. Albania's 10% rise takes Pellumbra's floor from $6.00 to $6.60.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual wage bill for 210 packers working 40 hours a week for 52 weeks after a $0.60 rise.

knowledge_max_2: Extra wages = staff x hours x rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the minimum wage rise on Pellumbra Foods Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The wage bill increases [k]. A $0.60 rise across 436,800 annual hours adds $262,080 [app], cutting profit unless prices rise or productivity improves [an].

Point 2: Automation becomes more attractive [k]. With labour dearer, a $420,000 machine replacing 30 workers looks cheaper over time [app], but redundancy and training costs must be met first [an].

analysis_max_2: Automation saves labour but needs capital

questions.question_text: Do you think Pellumbra Foods Ltd should buy the packing machine? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The machine replaces 30 of 210 packers and avoids part of the $262,080 wage rise, while working consistently without breaks. It also shields Pellumbra from future minimum wage increases.

Against: $420,000 is a large outlay, and the wage rise for the remaining 180 packers still costs about $224,640. Machines need maintenance and reduce flexibility when orders change.

Conclusion: Buy the machine, but retrain rather than dismiss. Automation offsets the permanent wage rise, yet preserving skills protects quality and local goodwill.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $420,000 machine against $262,080 wage rise
Considers retraining versus redundancy
analysis_max_2: Remaining wage bill is still large

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Vandergrift Apparel Ltd is a private limited company in Vietnam supplying $3,200,000 of clothing a year to European brands. A journalist has filmed children working at a supplier that makes 25% of its orders. An independent audit would cost $70,000, while dropping the supplier would delay deliveries by ten weeks. Directors must decide what to do.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical issue'.
questions.model_answer: An ethical issue is a situation where a business must choose between profit and what is morally right [2]. Child labour at Vandergrift's supplier is a clear ethical issue.

knowledge_max_2: Conflict between profit and moral behaviour

questions.question_text: Calculate the value of orders placed with the supplier that makes 25% of Vandergrift Apparel Ltd's $3,200,000 of sales.

knowledge_max_2: Supplier orders = sales x supplier share

questions.question_text: Explain two ethical issues facing Vandergrift Apparel Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Child labour breaches basic rights [k]. Children working for the supplier making $800,000 of orders [app] are denied schooling and safe conditions, which harms the company's reputation with European buyers [an].

Point 2: Honesty with customers [k]. Brands paying for $3,200,000 of clothing expect ethical sourcing [app]; concealing the supplier's practices could trigger cancelled contracts and legal claims [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Vandergrift Apparel Ltd should drop the supplier immediately? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Dropping the supplier removes child labour at once and shows European brands that Vandergrift acts on evidence. Protecting $3,200,000 of contracts matters more than $800,000 of cheap orders.

Against: Ten-week delays could breach delivery contracts, and the children may move to worse informal work. An audit costing $70,000 could force remediation and keep production running.

Conclusion: Audit and suspend new orders rather than drop immediately. This stops the abuse, keeps deliveries, and gives the supplier a deadline to remove child labour.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs immediate exit against remediation
Considers delivery delays and children's welfare

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tideswell Marine Ltd is a private limited company in the United Kingdom making boat engines, with revenue of $8,000,000, of which 40% is exported to the European Union. New customs checks add $140,000 a year and have cut total sales by 5%. Directors must decide whether to build a warehouse in the Netherlands for $520,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: An export is a good or service produced in one country and sold to a buyer in another [2]. Tideswell exports $3,200,000 of boat engines to the European Union each year.

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue Tideswell Marine Ltd has lost from a 5% fall in $8,000,000 of sales.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = sales x percentage fall

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the customs checks on Tideswell Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue falls [k]. A 5% drop removes $400,000 of sales and slows deliveries to EU buyers [app], who may switch to suppliers inside the single market [an].

Point 2: Costs rise and cash flow tightens [k]. The checks add $140,000 a year in paperwork and delays [app], while 40% of revenue depends on exports that now take longer to clear [an].

analysis_max_2: EU buyers switch to local suppliers

questions.question_text: Do you think Tideswell Marine Ltd should build the $520,000 warehouse in the Netherlands? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A Dutch warehouse holds stock inside the EU, cutting delivery delays and helping recover the $400,000 of lost sales. It also reduces the $140,000 annual customs cost over time.

Against: $520,000 is a large fixed cost when sales are already falling, and stock held abroad ties up cash. The checks may be streamlined later, making the warehouse unnecessary.

Conclusion: Build it only if EU customers commit to volume contracts. The warehouse solves the delay problem, but $520,000 is too much to risk on hopes of recovering $400,000.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $520,000 against $400,000 lost sales
Considers customer commitments
analysis_max_2: Fixed cost during falling sales is risky

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Harrowgate Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Turkey with revenue of $5,400,000 and profit before tax of $760,000. The government has raised corporation tax from 20% to 25%, and inflation has reached 38%, pushing up clay and gas costs. Directors must decide whether to raise prices by 4% or absorb the tax increase.

questions.question_text: Define 'corporation tax'.
questions.model_answer: Corporation tax is a tax on the profits of a company [2]. Turkey's rise to 25% reduces what Harrowgate keeps from its $760,000 profit.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra corporation tax Harrowgate Ceramics Ltd pays on $760,000 of profit after a 5 percentage point rise.

knowledge_max_2: Extra tax = profit x rise in rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the tax rise on Harrowgate Ceramics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit falls [k]. An extra $38,000 of tax leaves less from $760,000 to reinvest in kilns and design [app], slowing the capacity growth needed to compete [an].

Point 2: Inflation makes planning difficult [k]. With inflation at 38%, costs change weekly and the real value of profit shrinks [app], so a 4% price rise may not even cover higher input costs [an].

analysis_max_2: Price rise may lag cost increases

questions.question_text: Do you think Harrowgate Ceramics Ltd should raise prices by 4%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 4% rise on $5,400,000 adds $216,000 of revenue, far more than the $38,000 extra tax, and helps keep pace with 38% inflation. Ceramics buyers may accept small increases spread across the range.

Against: With inflation at 38%, a 4% rise does little for real income, and customers may switch to cheaper imports. Raising prices also risks losing volume when fixed costs are already spread thin.

Conclusion: Raise prices by more than 4% or cut costs. The tax itself is small; the real threat is inflation, so a 4% rise is too timid.

evaluation_max_2: Compares $216,000 revenue with $38,000 tax
Considers 38% inflation
analysis_max_2: Volume risk if prices rise further

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Willowfen Farms Ltd is a private limited company in Kenya growing cut flowers on 1,800,000 cubic metres of irrigation water a year. A new water levy charges $0.008 per cubic metre, and a drip recycling system costing $36,000 would cut water use by 30% on the farm. Directors must decide whether to install the recycling system.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means using resources so that future generations can still meet their needs [2]. Willowfen's water recycling would make flower growing more sustainable.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual levy saving from cutting Willowfen Farms Ltd's 1,800,000 cubic metres of water by 30% at $0.008 per cubic metre.

knowledge_max_2: Saving = water saved x levy rate

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs of Willowfen Farms Ltd's water use.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Local rivers and wells are depleted [k]. Taking 1,800,000 cubic metres leaves less water for households and livestock [app], forcing families to buy water or walk further [an].

Point 2: Ecosystems and future farming suffer [k]. Low river levels harm fish and wetland plants [app], reducing biodiversity and the natural irrigation that other Kenyan farms rely on [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Willowfen Farms Ltd should install the $36,000 recycling system? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The system cuts water use by 540,000 cubic metres, saving $4,320 a year and protecting the farm if the levy rises or water is rationed. It also strengthens its ethical image with European flower buyers.

Against: $4,320 a year takes over eight years to recover $36,000, and the system needs maintenance. The levy is small, so the financial case is weak without customer pressure.

Conclusion: Install it only with a buyer grant. The levy saving alone is too slow, but water security and supermarket contracts make the investment defensible.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $36,000 cost against $4,320 saving
Considers water security and buyer pressure
analysis_max_2: Reputation and supply security add value

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Palliser Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Sweden making office desks, with sales of $14,000,000. A United Arab Emirates distributor offers a joint venture: Palliser invests $3,500,000 for a 40% share, and the venture is forecast to earn $900,000 of profit in its first year of trading in Dubai. Directors must decide whether to accept.

questions.question_text: Define 'joint venture'.
questions.model_answer: A joint venture is an arrangement where two or more businesses share ownership and control of a new project [2]. Palliser would own 40% of the venture with the UAE distributor.

knowledge_max_2: Two or more firms share a project
Costs, risks and profits are shared

questions.question_text: Calculate Palliser Furniture Ltd's share of $900,000 forecast profit from a 40% stake.
questions.model_answer: $900,000 x 40% = $360,000, Palliser's share of first-year profit [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Palliser Furniture Ltd of the joint venture.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Local knowledge reduces risk [k]. The UAE distributor understands regulations and buyers, helping Palliser sell desks in a new market [app] without building its own sales network [an].

Point 2: Profit can be earned with shared capital [k]. A 40% share of $900,000 is $360,000 [app], a 10.3% return on the $3,500,000 investment in the first year [an].

analysis_max_2: Avoids cost of a sales network

questions.question_text: Do you think Palliser Furniture Ltd should accept the joint venture? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A $360,000 share of first-year profit is a 10.3% return on $3,500,000, and the local partner supplies market knowledge Palliser lacks. Risk is shared if demand for office desks is weaker than forecast.

Against: Palliser controls only 40%, so it cannot direct pricing or design. Profit may be lower than $900,000, and political or currency problems in the UAE could trap the investment.

Conclusion: Accept, but negotiate a larger stake or board rights. The return is sound, yet 40% leaves Palliser without the control needed to protect its brand.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs 10.3% return against loss of control
Considers political and currency risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Lindisfarne Retail Ltd is a private limited company in Finland selling 8,000 winter coats a year at $45 each, with a unit cost of $32. The economy has entered recession with GDP falling 2.2%, and interest rates have risen to 3.5%. Directors must decide whether to discount all coats by 15% or hold prices and carry the stock.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period of falling national output, usually defined as two consecutive quarters of declining GDP [2]. Finland's 2.2% fall means shoppers are cutting back on coats.

questions.question_text: Calculate the revenue lost if Lindisfarne Retail Ltd discounts 8,000 coats at $45 by 15%.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue lost = units x discount per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession on Lindisfarne Retail Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand for winter coats falls [k]. With GDP down 2.2%, Finnish households delay clothing purchases [app], so 8,000 coats may not sell at $45 and stock builds up [an].

Point 2: Holding stock becomes expensive [k]. Interest at 3.5% raises the cost of financing unsold inventory [app], while each coat still costs $32, tying up cash that the business needs [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Lindisfarne Retail Ltd should discount all coats by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Discounting cuts the price to $38.25, still above the $32 unit cost, and clears 8,000 coats before winter ends. Cash released can pay suppliers and avoid interest on unsold stock.

Against: The discount gives up $54,000 of revenue and signals weakness to customers who may wait for deeper cuts. Holding prices protects margin if the recession is short.

Conclusion: Discount, but only in January. Clearing stock at $38.25 still earns $6.25 a coat, far better than carrying inventory into spring.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $54,000 revenue loss against stock cost
Considers timing of markdowns

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Oakhampton Stores Ltd is a private limited company in Australia with 140 supermarkets that give away 6,000,000 plastic bags a year. A government charge of $0.15 per bag starts next month, and reusable paper bags would cost $0.03 more each than the plastic ones. Directors must decide whether to charge customers or absorb the cost.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a harmful side effect of production or consumption that is paid by society, not the business [2]. Plastic bag litter is an external cost borne by Australian councils and wildlife.

knowledge_max_2: Not paid by the producer or consumer

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual revenue Oakhampton Stores Ltd would collect from a $0.15 charge on 6,000,000 bags.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue = bags x charge per bag

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs of Oakhampton Stores Ltd's plastic bags.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Litter pollutes land and oceans [k]. Giving away 6,000,000 bags a year means many reach Australian beaches and waterways [app], where they harm turtles and birds and cost councils money to clear [an].

Point 2: Resources are wasted [k]. Each bag is used once but made from petrochemicals [app], adding emissions and landfill that society bears rather than Oakhampton [an].

analysis_max_2: Emissions and landfill are social costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakhampton Stores Ltd should charge customers $0.15 per bag? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The charge raises $900,000 and cuts bag use sharply, reducing litter and showing environmental responsibility. Revenue can fund paper bags or community recycling schemes.

Against: Customers may resent paying for bags and shop at rivals that absorb the charge. Paper bags cost $0.03 more each, adding $180,000 across 6,000,000 bags if usage stays high.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $900,000 revenue against customer resentment

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Wexcombe Agri Ltd is a private limited company in Ukraine growing 12,000 tonnes of wheat a year for export at $260 a tonne. The government has set an export quota of 9,000 tonnes and domestic buyers offer only $210 a tonne for immediate delivery. Directors must decide whether to store the surplus or sell it at home.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota'.
questions.model_answer: A quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported or exported [2]. Ukraine's 9,000 tonne quota leaves Wexcombe with 3,000 tonnes it cannot export.

questions.question_text: Calculate the export revenue Wexcombe Agri Ltd loses because 3,000 tonnes cannot be exported at $260.

knowledge_max_2: Lost revenue = blocked tonnes x export price

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the export quota on Wexcombe Agri Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue falls [k]. Selling 3,000 tonnes at the domestic $210 rather than $260 loses $50 a tonne, or $150,000 [app], on top of the $780,000 that cannot be exported at all [an].

Point 2: Storage and cash flow are strained [k]. Holding surplus wheat needs silos and insurance [app], tying up cash until prices or rules change [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexcombe Agri Ltd should store the surplus wheat? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Storing 3,000 tonnes keeps the chance of exporting at $260 if the quota is lifted, worth $780,000 rather than $630,000 at home. Wheat can be held for months if silos are dry.

Against: Storage, insurance and interest costs erode the $50 a tonne gap, and the quota may last years. Selling now at $210 brings cash for next season's planting.
