Unemployment is 15% and the minimum wage rose 9%, lifting the monthly bill from $80,000 to $87,200 for 160 workers. Orders fell 6%. The owner must decide whether to cut workers or raise prices to protect profit.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: The situation where people who want work cannot find a job, measured at 15% in Burundi where Bujumbura Textiles Co operates [2].

questions.question_text: Verify the new monthly wage bill after the 9% rise.
Explain two ways unemployment and the wage rise could affect Bujumbura Textiles Co.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher costs [k]. The wage bill has risen to $87,200 for 160 workers [app], squeezing profit [an].

Point 2: Weaker demand [k]. With unemployment at 15%, customers buy fewer uniforms and orders fell 6% [app], so revenue falls [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Bujumbura Textiles Co should cut workers rather than raise prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cutting workers saves wages and offsets the $7,200 rise [k/app].

Against: Job cuts reduce output and morale when orders are already down 6% [k/app].

Conclusion: Raise prices selectively first, since skilled machinists are costly to replace [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Avoid job cuts first
Weighs savings against skills

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bamako Cotton Ltd is a private limited company in Mali that buys cotton from 500 farmers. Only 175 are certified as using fair labour. A sportswear brand wants 70% certified within the next year. Certifying 175 more farmers costs $180 each. Directors must decide whether to fund the certification programme.

questions.question_text: Define 'fair labour'.
questions.model_answer: Employment that pays and treats workers properly, certified for only 175 of the 500 farmers supplying Bamako Cotton Ltd in Mali [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the percentage of farmers certified for fair labour.
questions.model_answer: 175 ÷ 500 × 100 = 35% of farmers are certified [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the brand's requirement could affect Bamako Cotton Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Contract risk [k]. At 35% certified, the brand's 70% target is unmet [app], so orders may be lost [an].

Point 2: Certification cost [k]. Checking 175 more farmers at $180 each costs $31,500 [app], raising costs [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Bamako Cotton Ltd should certify all 500 farmers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Full certification secures the sportswear brand and protects farmers [k/app].

Against: Only 175 more are needed to reach 70%, so full certification costs extra [k/app].

Conclusion: Certify the 175 needed first, then expand if more buyers demand it [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Reach 70% first
Weighs requirement against cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Roseau Banana Exports Ltd is a private limited company in Dominica that exports 1,200 tonnes of bananas a year at $780 a tonne. A trade agreement removes a 6% duty in the United Kingdom, saving $56,160. A rival from Ghana offers prices 5% lower. The sales director must decide whether to expand output or differentiate the bananas.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade agreement'.
questions.model_answer: An agreement between countries to reduce trade barriers, such as the deal removing a 6% duty for Roseau Banana Exports Ltd [2].

questions.question_text: Verify the $56,160 saving from removing the 6% duty.

knowledge_max_2: Find sales value then apply rate

questions.question_text: Explain two ways external changes could affect Roseau Banana Exports Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lower costs [k]. Removing the duty saves $56,160 on $936,000 of exports [app], improving profit [an].

Point 2: Price rivalry [k]. Ghanaian bananas are 5% cheaper [app], so the saving may be needed to match prices [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Roseau Banana Exports Ltd should differentiate rather than expand output? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Differentiation reduces the impact of the 5% Ghanaian price gap [k/app].

Against: Expansion uses the $56,160 saving to win volume in the United Kingdom [k/app].

Conclusion: Differentiate first, since a price war would erode the duty saving [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Differentiate first
Weighs brand against volume

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Podgorica Metal Co is a private limited company in Montenegro that makes steel bars. Economic growth has slowed from 4.2% to 1.9%, and orders fell 11% while energy costs rose 13%. The firm holds $260,000 of stock. The owner must decide whether to cut production or seek export orders to protect cash.

questions.question_text: Define 'economic growth'.
questions.model_answer: An increase in an economy's output over time, which has slowed to 1.9% in Montenegro where Podgorica Metal Co operates [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the fall in the rate of economic growth.
questions.model_answer: 4.2% − 1.9% = 2.3 percentage points, so growth has slowed by 2.3 points [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways slower growth and higher energy costs could affect Podgorica Metal Co.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Fewer orders [k]. Growth slowing by 2.3 points contributed to orders falling 11% [app], leaving $260,000 of stock [an].

Point 2: Higher costs [k]. Energy prices rose 13% while demand weakened [app], squeezing margin on steel bars [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Podgorica Metal Co should seek export orders rather than cut production? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Exports could replace the 11% fall in orders and use spare capacity [k/app].

Against: Finding buyers costs money while energy is up 13% and cash is tied in $260,000 of stock [k/app].

Conclusion: Seek exports cautiously with small trials, since cutting production wastes fixed investment [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Cautious export attempt
Weighs opportunity against cash

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Fennimore Spices Ltd is a private limited company grinding black pepper in Kochi, India, with annual revenue of $3,600,000. Inflation has risen to 5.2%, pushing packaging and freight costs up by $210,000 a year. The board must decide whether to raise prices by 6% or absorb the increase and protect its supermarket contracts.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services over time [2]. At 5.2% in India, Fennimore Spices Ltd pays more each year for pepper bags, freight and wages.

knowledge_max_2: A sustained rise in the general price level
Money buys fewer goods as prices climb

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra annual revenue if Fennimore Spices Ltd raises all prices by 6% on its $3,600,000 sales.
questions.model_answer: $3,600,000 x 6% = $216,000 extra revenue a year [2], assuming the volume of pepper sold stays the same.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue change = revenue x percentage price rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 5.2% inflation on Fennimore Spices Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Input costs rise [k]. Packaging and freight have already added $210,000 a year [app], so gross profit falls unless prices change [an].

Point 2: Customers resist higher prices [k]. Indian supermarkets facing their own 5.2% cost rise may demand discounts [app], squeezing Fennimore Spices Ltd margins further [an].

knowledge_max_2: Costs of inputs rise with inflation
Customers may cut spending or resist price rises
analysis_max_2: Profit falls if prices are held

questions.question_text: Do you think Fennimore Spices Ltd should raise its prices by 6%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 6% rise yields $216,000 more revenue, covering the $210,000 cost increase and restoring profit.

Against: Indian shoppers are price sensitive, and a 6% increase during 5.2% inflation may push buyers to cheaper mills, losing volume and supermarket contracts.

Conclusion: Raise prices by a smaller 5% first; that nearly covers the $210,000 while limiting the risk of lost sales.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $216,000 gain against lost sales risk
Judges 5% compromise against 6%

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Dunwister Textiles Ltd is a private limited company dyeing denim in Guadalajara, Mexico, and earns $4,800,000 a year. It discharges 12,000 litres of warm effluent daily into a local river and has just been fined $85,000. Managers must choose between installing a $600,000 filter or paying the recurring penalty. The board also worries about the effect on its reputation with local fashion buyers.

questions.question_text: Define 'pollution'.
questions.model_answer: Pollution is the release of harmful substances into the natural environment [2]. Dunwister Textiles Ltd releases 12,000 litres of warm effluent into the river in Guadalajara each day.

knowledge_max_2: Release of harmful substances into the environment
Can damage air, water or land

questions.question_text: Calculate the number of litres of effluent Dunwister Textiles Ltd discharges in a 25-day month.
questions.model_answer: 12,000 litres x 25 days = 300,000 litres a month [2].

knowledge_max_2: Total discharge = daily litres x number of days

questions.question_text: Explain two consequences of the effluent discharge for Dunwister Textiles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Financial penalties [k]. The $85,000 fine cuts directly into the $4,800,000 revenue [app], and repeated offences could raise future fines [an].

Point 2: Reputation damage [k]. Dirty river water in Guadalajara may turn away fashion buyers [app], costing orders that outweigh the $600,000 filter price [an].

knowledge_max_2: Damage to reputation and customer trust
application_max_2: Buyers in Mexico may switch suppliers
analysis_max_2: Repeated fines exceed one-off filter cost
Lost orders may be larger than filter price

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunwister Textiles Ltd should install the $600,000 filter? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The filter stops the 12,000 litres of effluent, ending the $85,000 fine and protecting the river in Guadalajara, which secures the firm's licence to operate.

Against: $600,000 is a heavy cash outlay for a firm on $4,800,000 revenue, and if the fine is not repeated the money could fund new dyeing machines.

Conclusion: Install the filter. Avoiding even two $85,000 fines plus reputational harm justifies the $600,000 spend over time.

evaluation_max_2: Judges filter cost against recurring fines
Weighs ethical duty against cash constraints
analysis_max_2: Clean river protects licence and orders

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kestrelhaven Seafood Ltd is a private limited company freezing prawns in Karachi, Pakistan, and sells $2,400,000 worth to Japanese buyers each year. The Pakistani rupee has depreciated 6% against the yen, while Japan has cut its fish import quota by 15%. Directors must decide whether to seek new European customers or cut prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price at which one currency can be swapped for another [2]. A 6% depreciation means the rupee buys fewer yen for Kestrelhaven Seafood Ltd in Karachi.

knowledge_max_2: Price of one currency in terms of another

questions.question_text: Calculate the value of prawns sold to Japan after a 15% quota cut on $2,400,000 of exports.

knowledge_max_2: New sales = original less quota reduction

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 6% rupee depreciation on Kestrelhaven Seafood Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher export earnings [k]. A weaker rupee means each yen converts into more rupees [app], raising the $2,400,000 prawn income when exchanged [an].

Point 2: Dearer imports [k]. Packaging bought from abroad costs more in rupees after a 6% fall [app], offsetting the gain partly for the Karachi plant [an].

application_max_2: Yen earnings convert to more rupees
Packaging imports cost more after 6% fall

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrelhaven Seafood Ltd should seek European customers after the Japanese quota cut? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 15% quota cut removes $360,000 of Japanese sales, so Europe could replace that $2,040,000 shortfall and spread the Karachi plant's fixed costs.

Against: European buyers demand different packaging and higher quality checks, and the 6% weaker rupee raises the cost of those imported materials.

Conclusion: Pursue Europe but gradually. The lost $360,000 makes new markets necessary, yet the 6% currency fall means margins need careful control.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $360,000 lost sales against entry costs
Judges currency effect on new market margins
analysis_max_2: Weaker rupee raises imported packaging cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ravensby Joinery Ltd is a partnership making wooden doors in Riga, Latvia, with a $1,200,000 order book. Local unemployment has reached 7.4% and the central bank rate is 3.75%. Owners must decide whether to borrow $480,000 for a new sanding line or delay expansion while demand is weak. The partnership has already turned down two similar loans in the past year.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment rate'.
questions.model_answer: The unemployment rate is the percentage of the working population without a job who are seeking work [2]. In Riga it stands at 7.4%, affecting Ravensby Joinery Ltd's customer base.

knowledge_max_2: Measures unused labour in an economy

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on Ravensby Joinery Ltd's $480,000 loan at 3.75%.

knowledge_max_2: Interest = amount borrowed x interest rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 7.4% unemployment on Ravensby Joinery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Softer local demand [k]. With 7.4% out of work, Latvian households delay home improvements [app], threatening the $1,200,000 order book for doors [an].

Point 2: Easier recruitment [k]. A larger pool of jobseekers in Riga keeps wage demands modest [app], so the new sanding line can be staffed cheaply [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower consumer spending in the economy
analysis_max_2: Wage costs stay low aiding expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensby Joinery Ltd should borrow $480,000 now for the sanding line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: At 3.75% the loan costs only $18,000 a year, and cheaper Riga labour makes expansion affordable while competitors hold back.

Against: With 7.4% unemployment, the $1,200,000 order book could shrink, leaving debt on idle machinery.

Conclusion: Delay six months. The $18,000 interest is modest, but weak Latvian demand makes the $480,000 commitment risky until orders recover.

evaluation_max_2: Judges $18,000 interest against demand risk
Weighs cheap labour against weak orders

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Cartonridge Packaging Ltd is a public limited company making cardboard cartons in Brno, Czechia, with sales of $6,500,000. It sends 90 tonnes of waste to landfill annually and pays $220,000 in disposal fees. A recycling plant costing $1,100,000 would cut waste by 80%. Shareholders want lower costs. Several shareholders have questioned whether the outlay can be justified.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable production'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable production means making goods while reducing harm to the environment and using resources efficiently [2]. Cartonridge Packaging Ltd currently buries 90 tonnes of cardboard waste in Brno.

knowledge_max_2: Meeting needs without harming future resources

questions.question_text: Calculate the tonnes of waste Cartonridge Packaging Ltd would still landfill after an 80% cut.
questions.model_answer: 80% of 90 tonnes = 72 tonnes recycled; 90 - 72 = 18 tonnes still landfilled [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the recycling plant for Cartonridge Packaging Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lower disposal fees [k]. Cutting 90 tonnes to 18 tonnes should reduce the $220,000 paid to landfill [app], saving money each year [an].

Point 2: Better public image [k]. Czech retailers prefer greener suppliers [app], so recycling may protect the $6,500,000 of carton sales [an].

application_max_2: Retailers in Czechia favour green suppliers
analysis_max_2: Savings offset the $1,100,000 outlay over time

questions.question_text: Do you think Cartonridge Packaging Ltd should buy the $1,100,000 recycling plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Recycling 72 tonnes a year would slash the $220,000 landfill fee and lift the firm's green image with Brno retailers.

Against: $1,100,000 is a large upfront cost for shareholders focused on short-term profit, and full recovery takes several years.

Conclusion: Proceed if cash allows. Halving disposal fees and protecting $6,500,000 of sales gives a strong long-term return despite the slow recovery.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs long-run savings against upfront cost
Balances shareholder wishes against green gains

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Alpine Coffee Traders Ltd is a private limited company importing green coffee into Hamburg, Germany, with annual sales of $5,200,000. The government has imposed a 12% tariff on imported beans and shipping costs rose $180,000. Managers must decide whether to pass the tariff to German cafes or switch to domestic suppliers.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods [2]. The 12% tariff raises the cost of green coffee for Alpine Coffee Traders Ltd in Hamburg.

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff paid on $5,200,000 of imported coffee at 12%.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff = value of imports x tariff rate

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 12% tariff on Alpine Coffee Traders Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher costs [k]. The tariff adds $624,000 to the $5,200,000 import bill [app], squeezing profit unless prices rise [an].

Point 2: Competitive shift [k]. German cafes may buy local beans unaffected by the tariff [app], threatening the Hamburg firm's orders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Demand may switch to domestic goods
application_max_2: Cafes in Germany may switch beans
analysis_max_2: Sales lost if buyers go local

questions.question_text: Do you think Alpine Coffee Traders Ltd should pass the tariff on to German cafes? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Passing on the $624,000 tariff through a 12% price rise protects margins and keeps importing the beans cafes prefer.

Against: Dearer coffee may push Hamburg cafes toward local suppliers, losing part of the $5,200,000 sales; shipping costs also rose $180,000.

Conclusion: Pass on only half the tariff and absorb the rest. That limits lost orders while sharing the $624,000 burden with customers.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs full pass-through against lost orders
Judges partial sharing of $624,000

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Moorhen Dairy Ltd is a private limited company selling fresh milk in Kampala, Uganda, with monthly revenue of $940,000. Inflation has hit 8.1% and animal feed prices climbed $75,000 a month. The owner must decide whether to increase the milk price by 8% or reduce herd size to protect cash flow.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation rate'.
questions.model_answer: The inflation rate is the percentage rise in the general price level over a year [2]. At 8.1% in Uganda, Moorhen Dairy Ltd faces fast-rising costs in Kampala.

knowledge_max_2: Measured over a period, usually a year

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra monthly revenue if Moorhen Dairy Ltd raises milk prices by 8% on $940,000.
questions.model_answer: $940,000 x 8% = $75,200 extra revenue a month [2], roughly covering the $75,000 feed increase.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue change = revenue x price rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 8.1% inflation on Moorhen Dairy Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Rising feed costs [k]. The $75,000 monthly feed increase cuts into $940,000 revenue [app], reducing cash for the Kampala herd [an].

Point 2: Lower real demand [k]. Ugandan families hit by 8.1% inflation buy less fresh milk [app], so an 8% price rise could reduce litres sold [an].

analysis_max_2: Volume may fall after price rise

questions.question_text: Do you think Moorhen Dairy Ltd should raise milk prices by 8%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: An 8% rise brings $75,200 a month, covering the $75,000 feed increase and keeping the herd intact.

Against: With inflation at 8.1%, Kampala households may cut milk purchases, so the higher price could shrink litres sold and revenue.

Conclusion: Raise prices by about 5% and trim herd slightly. This balances the $75,000 cost rise against the risk of losing customers in Uganda.

evaluation_max_2: Judges price rise against demand fall
Balances herd cut against revenue

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Silverthorn Chemicals Ltd is a private limited company making industrial solvents in Antofagasta, Chile, with turnover of $7,100,000. It was fined $140,000 after releasing untreated waste and faces a 9% rise in water charges. Directors must decide whether to build a $950,000 treatment plant or keep paying fines and charges.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical issue' for a business.
questions.model_answer: An ethical issue is a situation where a business must choose between right and wrong conduct [2]. Silverthorn Chemicals Ltd must decide whether to stop releasing waste in Antofagasta.

questions.question_text: Calculate the new annual water charge after a 9% rise on $600,000.

knowledge_max_2: New charge = old charge x (100% + rise)

questions.question_text: Explain two consequences of the waste release for Silverthorn Chemicals Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Financial loss [k]. The $140,000 fine plus a 9% water charge rise adds pressure on $7,100,000 turnover [app], lowering profit [an].

Point 2: Community opposition [k]. Polluted water in Antofagasta may trigger protests and tighter rules [app], risking the firm's licence [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverthorn Chemicals Ltd should build the $950,000 treatment plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The plant ends the $140,000 fine and the waste that angers Antofagasta residents, protecting the $7,100,000 turnover and the licence to operate.

Against: $950,000 is a large sum for a solvent maker, and water charges rise 9% regardless, so savings may be slow.

Conclusion: Build the plant. Repeated $140,000 fines and community hostility in Chile would cost more than the $950,000 investment over time.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs plant cost against recurring fines
Judges ethical and licence risks

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Banyan Leaf Garments Ltd is a private limited company sewing shirts in Dhaka, Bangladesh, and exports $3,300,000 a year to the European Union. A new EU import quota limits shirts to 85% of last year's volume, and the taka has weakened 4%. Owners must decide whether to automate sewing or look for Asian markets.

questions.question_text: Define 'import quota'.
questions.model_answer: An import quota is a government limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported [2]. The EU quota caps shirts from Banyan Leaf Garments Ltd at 85% of last year's volume.

questions.question_text: Calculate the export value Banyan Leaf Garments Ltd keeps after an EU quota cut to 85% of $3,300,000.
questions.model_answer: $3,300,000 x 85% = $2,805,000 of shirts still exported [2].

knowledge_max_2: New exports = original x quota percentage

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the weaker taka on Banyan Leaf Garments Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Better export competitiveness [k]. A 4% weaker taka makes Dhaka shirts cheaper in euro terms [app], helping the firm keep EU buyers despite the quota [an].

Point 2: Costlier machinery [k]. Imported sewing machines cost more taka after the 4% fall [app], raising the price of automation [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Banyan Leaf Garments Ltd should automate sewing after the EU quota cut? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Automation lowers unit costs, helping the firm compete for the reduced $2,805,000 EU quota and win Asian buyers with lower prices.

Against: Imported machines cost more with a 4% weaker taka, and the 85% quota may be temporary, making heavy investment risky.

Conclusion: Delay automation and first seek Asian markets. The quota cut is real, but the 4% currency fall makes machinery expensive right now.

evaluation_max_2: Judges automation against currency cost
Weighs new markets against investment

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Osprey Wheels Ltd is a private limited company making bicycle wheels in Bratislava, Slovakia, with annual sales of $2,900,000. The government raised employer national insurance by 3% and bank rates to 5.5%. Owners must decide whether to hire 20 extra workers at $26,000 each or buy a $520,000 automated lathe.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: The interest rate is the price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage [2]. At 5.5%, Osprey Wheels Ltd pays more to finance the $520,000 lathe.

knowledge_max_2: Cost of borrowing as a percentage

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual wage bill for 20 workers at $26,000 each before the 3% employer rise.
questions.model_answer: 20 x $26,000 = $520,000 a year [2], equal to the cost of the automated lathe.

knowledge_max_2: Total wages = number of workers x wage

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 3% employer insurance rise on Osprey Wheels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher labour costs [k]. The 3% rise adds to the $520,000 wage bill for 20 workers [app], cutting profit on $2,900,000 sales [an].

Point 2: Automation becomes attractive [k]. Dearer labour makes the $520,000 lathe relatively cheaper [app], but 5.5% rates raise borrowing cost [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Osprey Wheels Ltd should buy the $520,000 lathe rather than hire 20 workers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The lathe costs the same as one year of 20 wages ($520,000) but raises output without the 3% insurance rise, cutting unit costs.

Against: At 5.5% interest, financing costs more, and machines cannot adapt to custom wheel orders as workers can.

Conclusion: Buy the lathe. The equal one-year wage sum and the 3% labour tax rise make automation the cheaper long-run choice despite 5.5% borrowing.

evaluation_max_2: Compares lathe to $520,000 wage bill
Judges 5.5% finance against 3% tax

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marigold Pottery Ltd is a private limited company making ceramic tiles in Kutaisi, Georgia, with annual sales of $1,850,000. Its glazing process releases 3,200 kg of chemical sludge a month and regulators have warned of a $60,000 penalty. Owners must decide whether to install a $340,000 filtration system or keep dumping the sludge.

questions.question_text: Define 'waste' in a business context.
questions.model_answer: Waste is unwanted material left over from production that has no value to the business [2]. Marigold Pottery Ltd produces 3,200 kg of chemical sludge monthly in Kutaisi.

knowledge_max_2: May harm the environment if discarded

questions.question_text: Calculate Marigold Pottery Ltd's annual sludge output at 3,200 kg a month.
questions.model_answer: 3,200 kg x 12 months = 38,400 kg of sludge a year [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marigold Pottery Ltd should stop dumping sludge.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Avoid the $60,000 penalty [k]. A fine would cut into the $1,850,000 sales [app], reducing profit for the Kutaisi owners [an].

Point 2: Protect the local environment [k]. Chemical sludge in Georgian waterways harms wildlife and draws complaints [app], which could close the plant [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Marigold Pottery Ltd should install the $340,000 filtration system? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Filtration ends the 3,200 kg of sludge and the $60,000 penalty, protecting the $1,850,000 tile business and the local river.

Against: $340,000 is costly relative to a single $60,000 fine, and demand for tiles in Georgia may not support the outlay.

Conclusion: Install it. Repeated $60,000 fines and environmental harm in Kutaisi would exceed $340,000 within a few years.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs filter cost against repeated fines
Balances environment against sales

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tuareg Leather Ltd is a private limited company tanning goat skins in Agadez, Niger, and exports $1,950,000 of leather to France each year. The euro has strengthened 7% against the CFA franc and French buyers demand faster delivery. Owners must decide whether to open a Paris warehouse or keep shipping directly from Agadez.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation' of a currency.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency relative to another [2]. A 7% stronger euro helps Tuareg Leather Ltd when converting French sales into CFA francs.

questions.question_text: Calculate the value in CFA francs if the $1,950,000 export is 7% more valuable after euro appreciation.

knowledge_max_2: New value = old value x (100% + appreciation)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the stronger euro on Tuareg Leather Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher franc earnings [k]. Each euro converts into more CFA francs [app], adding about $136,500 to the $1,950,000 leather income [an].

Point 2: Pressure on delivery [k]. French buyers want faster service than shipping from Agadez allows [app], so the currency gain may be lost if orders go elsewhere [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Tuareg Leather Ltd should open a Paris warehouse? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A Paris warehouse meets French delivery demands and protects the $1,950,000 of sales, while the 7% stronger euro boosts franc earnings.

Against: Running a warehouse in France is expensive and could absorb the $136,500 currency gain, especially for a small Niger tannery.

Conclusion: Open a small Paris depot. Faster delivery secures orders and the 7% euro gain helps fund it, but costs must be watched.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs warehouse cost against $1,950,000 sales
Judges use of currency gain

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Pinecroft Bakeries Ltd is a private limited company supplying bread in Wellington, New Zealand, with weekly revenue of $310,000. Inflation is 3.6% and the central bank has lifted mortgage rates, cutting shopper spending. Owners must decide whether to discount lines or keep prices and accept lower volume from 42 outlets.

questions.question_text: Define 'consumer spending'.
questions.model_answer: Consumer spending is the amount households buy goods and services with [2]. Higher mortgage rates have reduced it in Wellington, affecting Pinecroft Bakeries Ltd.

knowledge_max_2: Household purchases of goods and services

questions.question_text: Calculate Pinecroft Bakeries Ltd's monthly revenue at $310,000 a week over four weeks.

knowledge_max_2: Monthly revenue = weekly revenue x weeks

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 3.6% inflation on Pinecroft Bakeries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer ingredients [k]. Flour and power cost more with 3.6% inflation, squeezing the $310,000 weekly revenue [app] and profit across 42 outlets [an].

Point 2: Cautious shoppers [k]. Higher mortgage rates cut consumer spending in Wellington [app], so bread volumes may fall at Pinecroft Bakeries Ltd [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Pinecroft Bakeries Ltd should discount its bread lines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Discounts could hold volumes across 42 outlets as Wellington spending falls, keeping ovens busy and covering fixed costs.

Against: With 3.6% inflation raising flour costs, lower prices cut margin on the $310,000 weekly revenue, risking losses.

Conclusion: Discount only slow lines. Protecting volume helps, but blanket cuts would worsen margins when ingredients already cost more.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs volume gain against margin loss
Judges selective versus blanket discounts

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Otterbeck Fisheries Ltd is a private limited company processing cod in Bergen, Norway, with exports of $4,400,000. It throws away 26 tonnes of fish offal weekly and faces a new $95,000 levy on organic waste. Directors must decide whether to buy a $720,000 fishmeal plant or continue paying the levy and dumping offal.

questions.question_text: Define 'recycling'.
questions.model_answer: Recycling is turning waste material into a useful product rather than discarding it [2]. Otterbeck Fisheries Ltd could turn 26 tonnes of offal into fishmeal in Bergen.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual offal waste from Otterbeck Fisheries Ltd at 26 tonnes a week over 50 working weeks.
questions.model_answer: 26 tonnes x 50 weeks = 1,300 tonnes of offal a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Annual waste = weekly waste x working weeks

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the fishmeal plant for Otterbeck Fisheries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Avoid the $95,000 levy [k]. Turning offal into fishmeal removes the organic waste charge [app], saving money on $4,400,000 exports [an].

Point 2: Extra sales [k]. Fishmeal can be sold as animal feed in Norway [app], adding revenue beyond the Bergen cod business [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Otterbeck Fisheries Ltd should buy the $720,000 fishmeal plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The plant ends the $95,000 levy and sells fishmeal, while stopping 1,300 tonnes of waste harming Bergen's waters.

Against: $720,000 is steep for a firm with $4,400,000 exports, and fishmeal prices in Norway may not cover running costs.

Conclusion: Buy the plant. The annual $95,000 levy plus new fishmeal income should repay $720,000 over time and protect the environment.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $720,000 cost against levy and sales
Judges environmental benefit

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Samarkand Silk Ltd is a private limited company weaving scarves in Uzbekistan and sells $2,750,000 to Turkey each year. Turkey has placed a 14% tariff on silk imports and the sum has weakened 5% against the lira. Owners must decide whether to shift sales to Kazakhstan or lower prices to hold Turkish buyers.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation' of a currency.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in a currency's value against another [2]. A 5% weaker sum changes what Samarkand Silk Ltd receives for Turkish lira sales.

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff on $2,750,000 of silk at 14%.
Explain two effects of the 14% tariff on Samarkand Silk Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher landed price [k]. The $385,000 tariff makes Uzbek scarves dearer in Turkey [app], threatening the $2,750,000 sales [an].

Point 2: Currency cushion [k]. A 5% weaker sum partly offsets the tariff when lira are changed back [app], softening the loss [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Samarkand Silk Ltd should shift sales to Kazakhstan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 14% tariff and $385,000 cost make Turkey costly; Kazakhstan has no such tariff and could replace lost $2,750,000 sales.

Against: Kazakh buyers may prefer cheaper silk and the 5% weaker sum weakens buying power for imported materials.

Conclusion: Diversify into Kazakhstan but keep Turkish buyers. The tariff is a strong reason to expand, yet the 5% currency fall means new markets need careful pricing.

evaluation_max_2: Judges Kazakhstan against $385,000 tariff
Balances currency effect

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Windermere Tools Ltd is a private limited company making hand drills in Melbourne, Australia, with annual sales of $3,100,000. Unemployment has fallen to 4.2%, pushing wages up, while the bank rate is 4.25%. Owners must decide whether to raise drill prices 5% or automate two production lines with a $880,000 press.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: Unemployment is the state of people of working age who want a job but cannot find one [2]. At 4.2% in Melbourne, labour is scarce for Windermere Tools Ltd.

knowledge_max_2: People seeking work but without jobs

questions.question_text: Calculate extra revenue from a 5% price rise on Windermere Tools Ltd's $3,100,000 sales.
questions.model_answer: $3,100,000 x 5% = $155,000 extra revenue a year [2], if unit sales are unchanged.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 4.2% unemployment on Windermere Tools Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher wages [k]. Scarce labour in Melbourne pushes pay up, raising costs on $3,100,000 of drills [app] and squeezing margin [an].

Point 2: Stronger demand [k]. Low 4.2% unemployment means more Australians earning and buying tools [app], supporting sales volume [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Windermere Tools Ltd should buy the $880,000 press instead of raising prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The press cuts dependence on scarce Melbourne labour and the 4.2% wage pressure, lowering unit costs permanently.

Against: At 4.25% interest the $880,000 press is costly, while a 5% price rise brings $155,000 at once with no outlay.

Conclusion: Raise prices 5% this year and save for the press. The $155,000 gain is quick, while 4.25% borrowing makes the press expensive now.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs press cost against quick price gain
Judges 4.25% finance

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kirkstall Bricks Ltd is a private limited company firing clay bricks in Leeds, United Kingdom, with revenue of $5,600,000. Its kilns emit 1,800 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and the government has introduced a $48 per tonne carbon tax. Directors must decide whether to fit $1,400,000 kiln filters or pay the tax.

questions.question_text: Define 'carbon tax'.
questions.model_answer: A carbon tax is a charge on the carbon dioxide a business emits [2]. Kirkstall Bricks Ltd pays $48 per tonne on 1,800 tonnes of emissions in Leeds.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual carbon tax bill for Kirkstall Bricks Ltd at 1,800 tonnes and $48 per tonne.
questions.model_answer: 1,800 tonnes x $48 = $86,400 carbon tax a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Tax = tonnes emitted x tax per tonne

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the carbon tax on Kirkstall Bricks Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher production cost [k]. The $86,400 tax adds to costs on $5,600,000 revenue [app], reducing profit per brick [an].

Point 2: Incentive to cut emissions [k]. A $48 per tonne charge makes $1,400,000 filters look cheaper over time [app], pushing greener kilns in Leeds [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Kirkstall Bricks Ltd should fit the $1,400,000 kiln filters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Filters cut 1,800 tonnes of emissions, ending the $86,400 tax and improving the firm's image with UK builders.

Against: $1,400,000 is far more than one year's $86,400 tax, and the $5,600,000 revenue may not fund such a large project.

Conclusion: Phase in the filters. The tax at $48 per tonne will keep rising, so greener kilns are worthwhile, but the $1,400,000 should be spread over time.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs filter cost against ongoing tax
Judges phasing option

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Mekong Rice Exports Ltd is a private limited company milling rice in Can Tho, Vietnam, and ships $6,200,000 to Africa each year. The dong has depreciated 3% against the dollar and competitors in Thailand cut prices by 8%. Managers must decide whether to cut the rice price or find buyers in the Middle East.

questions.question_text: Define 'exports'.
questions.model_answer: Exports are goods sold to buyers in another country [2]. Mekong Rice Exports Ltd ships $6,200,000 of rice from Can Tho to Africa annually.

knowledge_max_2: Brings foreign currency into a country

questions.question_text: Calculate the new price of rice if Mekong Rice Exports Ltd cuts it by 8% from $500 a tonne.
questions.model_answer: 8% of $500 = $40; new price = $460 a tonne [2].

knowledge_max_2: New price = old price x (100% - cut)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 3% dong depreciation on Mekong Rice Exports Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher dollar earnings [k]. A weaker dong means each dollar converts into more dong [app], boosting the $6,200,000 African income [an].

Point 2: Tougher competition [k]. Thai rivals cut prices 8%, so a 3% currency gain may not be enough to keep buyers [app] in Can Tho's markets [an].

analysis_max_2: May need price cut despite gain

questions.question_text: Do you think Mekong Rice Exports Ltd should cut its rice price by 8%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Matching Thai's 8% cut protects $6,200,000 of African sales, and the 3% weaker dong gives room to lower prices in dollar terms.

Against: An 8% cut from $500 to $460 sharply reduces margin, and Middle Eastern buyers may pay more without a cut.

Conclusion: Cut by about 3-4% first and pursue Middle East buyers. That uses the dong gain without surrendering as much margin as 8%.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs 8% cut against margin
Judges Middle East alternative

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Harvestvale Grain Ltd is a private limited company storing and selling wheat in Saskatoon, Canada, with revenue of $8,300,000. Grain prices rose 11% after a poor harvest, but transport costs climbed $260,000. Owners must decide whether to sell grain now or hold stock hoping for a further 6% price rise.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation' as it affects a business.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a general rise in prices that reduces the buying power of money [2]. Harvestvale Grain Ltd faces higher transport costs of $260,000 in Saskatoon.

questions.question_text: Calculate Harvestvale Grain Ltd's revenue if a further 6% price rise applies to $8,300,000.
Explain two effects of the 11% grain price rise on Harvestvale Grain Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher revenue [k]. An 11% rise lifts income on wheat sold from Saskatoon [app], boosting the $8,300,000 turnover [an].

Point 2: Dearer transport [k]. The $260,000 cost increase eats into that gain [app], so net profit rises by less than the price rise suggests [an].

analysis_max_2: Revenue up but not all profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Harvestvale Grain Ltd should hold stock for a further 6% price rise? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Holding could add $498,000 to $8,300,000 revenue if the 6% rise happens, after the 11% rise already gained.

Against: Storage and the $260,000 transport rise are certain costs, while a further 6% rise is only a hope in Canadian markets.

Conclusion: Sell most grain now. The 11% rise already gives a good price, and certain costs make holding for a speculative 6% risky.

evaluation_max_2: Judges certain costs against uncertain gain
Weighs holding versus selling

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Diani Beach Resorts Ltd is a private limited company running three beach hotels in Zanzibar, Tanzania, with annual revenue of $3,800,000. Guests leave 14 tonnes of plastic waste a month and the local council has threatened a $70,000 fine. Managers must decide whether to install a $450,000 recycling unit or keep paying cleanup costs.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental issue'.
questions.model_answer: An environmental issue is harm caused to the natural world by business activity [2]. Diani Beach Resorts Ltd creates 14 tonnes of plastic waste monthly in Zanzibar.

questions.question_text: Calculate the yearly plastic waste from Diani Beach Resorts Ltd at 14 tonnes a month.
questions.model_answer: 14 tonnes x 12 months = 168 tonnes of plastic a year [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons to tackle the plastic waste at Diani Beach Resorts Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Avoid the $70,000 fine [k]. A penalty would reduce the $3,800,000 hotel revenue [app], lowering profit in Zanzibar [an].

Point 2: Protect tourism appeal [k]. Plastic on beaches damages the environment tourists come to see [app], so waste control protects future bookings [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Diani Beach Resorts Ltd should install the $450,000 recycling unit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Recycling 168 tonnes a year ends the $70,000 fine and keeps Zanzibar beaches clean, protecting $3,800,000 of tourism revenue.

Against: $450,000 is a big outlay for three hotels, and the council fine may not be repeated every year.

Conclusion: Install the unit. Clean beaches are central to the resorts' appeal, and avoiding even a few $70,000 fines helps justify $450,000.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $450,000 against fines and image
Judges tourism link

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sahara Date Exports Ltd is a private limited company packing dates in Tozeur, Tunisia, and sells $2,150,000 to Italy each year. The euro has weakened 4% against the dinar and Italian supermarkets demand organic certification. Owners must decide whether to pay $260,000 for certification or keep selling to smaller Tunisian markets.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another [2]. A 4% weaker euro changes what Sahara Date Exports Ltd receives for Italian sales.

knowledge_max_2: Price of one currency in another

questions.question_text: Calculate the dinar value of the $2,150,000 exports after a 4% weaker euro.
Explain two effects of the weaker euro on Sahara Date Exports Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lower dinar earnings [k]. A 4% weaker euro means fewer dinars from Italian buyers [app], cutting the $2,150,000 income [an].

Point 2: Buyer demands [k]. Italian supermarkets want organic certification costing $260,000 [app], and a weaker euro leaves less money to pay for it [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Sahara Date Exports Ltd should pay $260,000 for organic certification? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Certification keeps Italian supermarket contracts and the $2,150,000 sales, which a 4% weaker euro already threatens.

Against: $260,000 is costly for a Tunisian packer, and local markets need no certificate, so the spending may not repay.

Conclusion: Seek certification with a buyer subsidy. Keeping $2,150,000 of Italian sales is vital, but the 4% currency loss means the firm should not fund all $260,000 alone.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs certification cost against Italian sales
Judges shared funding

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bramblewick Hardware Ltd is a private limited company making door handles in Edmonton, Canada, with sales of $4,050,000. The central bank raised interest rates to 5.25% and building activity has slowed. Owners must decide whether to borrow $750,000 for new dies or postpone the investment until house building recovers. The owner has already delayed this decision once because of cash concerns.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing as a percentage of the loan [2]. At 5.25%, Bramblewick Hardware Ltd pays dearly for the $750,000 dies.

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual interest on $750,000 at 5.25% for Bramblewick Hardware Ltd.
Explain two effects of the 5.25% interest rate on Bramblewick Hardware Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Expensive borrowing [k]. The $39,375 interest must be paid before the new dies earn [app], reducing profit on $4,050,000 sales [an].

Point 2: Softer demand [k]. High rates slow Canadian house building [app], so fewer handles are needed in Edmonton [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblewick Hardware Ltd should borrow $750,000 for the new dies now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: New dies cut unit costs and prepare the firm for an eventual building recovery in Edmonton.

Against: At 5.25% the loan costs $39,375 a year while Canadian construction is already slow, so sales may not cover it.

Conclusion: Postpone. The 5.25% rate and weak demand make $750,000 risky now; wait until house building picks up before committing.

evaluation_max_2: Judges rate against demand
Weighs waiting option

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kisumu Dyeworks Ltd is a private limited company dyeing cotton in Kisumu, Kenya, with turnover of $2,600,000. It releases 9,000 litres of used dye daily into Lake Victoria and faces a $55,000 environmental fine. Owners must decide whether to install a $380,000 treatment tank or continue discharging the dye. Local fishermen have complained repeatedly about the colour of the water.

questions.question_text: Define 'water pollution'.
questions.model_answer: Water pollution is the contamination of water with harmful substances [2]. Kisumu Dyeworks Ltd releases 9,000 litres of dye into Lake Victoria each day.

questions.question_text: Calculate the weekly dye discharge from Kisumu Dyeworks Ltd at 9,000 litres a day over six working days.
questions.model_answer: 9,000 litres x 6 days = 54,000 litres a week [2].

knowledge_max_2: Weekly discharge = daily litres x days

questions.question_text: Explain two consequences of the dye discharge for Kisumu Dyeworks Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Financial penalty [k]. The $55,000 fine reduces profit on $2,600,000 turnover [app], and repeat offences may cost more [an].

Point 2: Damage to Lake Victoria [k]. Polluted water harms fishers and communities near Kisumu [app], creating hostility toward the factory [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Kisumu Dyeworks Ltd should install the $380,000 treatment tank? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Treatment ends 54,000 litres of weekly dye discharge and the $55,000 fine, protecting Lake Victoria and the firm's $2,600,000 trade.

Against: $380,000 is expensive for a Kenyan dyer and may exceed several years of fines.

Conclusion: Install the tank. Continued pollution of Lake Victoria risks closures and repeated $55,000 penalties that would surpass $380,000.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs tank cost against fines
Judges environmental licence risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Andes Woollen Mills Ltd is a private limited company weaving alpaca scarves in Arequipa, Peru, and exports $1,720,000 to Brazil yearly. Brazil imposed a 16% tariff on wool imports and the sol has weakened 6% against the real. Owners must decide whether to raise prices in Brazil or target Chilean buyers instead.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods [2]. Brazil's 16% tariff raises the cost of Andes Woollen Mills Ltd's scarves.

questions.question_text: Calculate the tariff on $1,720,000 of wool exports at 16%.
Explain two effects of the 6% sol depreciation on Andes Woollen Mills Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher local earnings [k]. Each Brazilian real converts into more soles [app], adding to the $1,720,000 income [an].

Point 2: Costlier imports [k]. Dyes bought abroad cost 6% more in soles [app], partly offsetting the export gain in Arequipa [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Andes Woollen Mills Ltd should target Chilean buyers instead of Brazil? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 16% tariff adds $275,200 of cost in Brazil; Chile has no such barrier, so sales there could replace lost orders.

Against: Chilean buyers may pay less for alpaca than Brazilians, and the 6% weaker sol helps only conversion, not demand.

Conclusion: Develop Chile while keeping Brazil. The tariff is a real problem, but the 6% currency gain means Brazilian orders still have value if priced carefully.

evaluation_max_2: Judges Chile against $275,200 tariff
Balances currency gain

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Orchard Vale Cider Ltd is a private limited company pressing apples in Hereford, United Kingdom, with annual revenue of $2,280,000. Inflation has reached 4.4% and apple concentrate costs rose $130,000. Owners must decide whether to raise cider prices by 5% or keep prices to protect pub contracts. A rival bakery has just opened on the same street in Hereford.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level [2]. At 4.4%, Orchard Vale Cider Ltd pays more for apples and bottles in Hereford.

questions.question_text: Calculate the extra revenue from a 5% price rise on $2,280,000 of cider.
questions.model_answer: $2,280,000 x 5% = $114,000 extra revenue a year [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 4.4% inflation on Orchard Vale Cider Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher input costs [k]. Apple concentrate rose $130,000, cutting profit on $2,280,000 sales [app] in Hereford [an].

Point 2: Pub resistance [k]. Pubs facing 4.4% inflation may reject a 5% price rise [app], risking the firm's contracts [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Orchard Vale Cider Ltd should raise prices by 5%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 5% rise gives $114,000, covering the $130,000 concentrate rise almost fully and protecting margin.

Against: With 4.4% inflation, UK pubs may cut orders, and losing contracts could cost more than $114,000.

Conclusion: Raise prices by 3%. That recovers much of the $130,000 rise while keeping pub contracts, which are vital to the Hereford business.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $114,000 against contract loss
Judges partial rise

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bluefin Canning Ltd is a private limited company canning tuna in Port Louis, Mauritius, with exports of $3,900,000. It dumps 40 tonnes of fish offal weekly and faces a $110,000 disposal levy. Directors must decide whether to spend $640,000 on a fishmeal drier or keep paying the levy and dumping waste.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means using resources so they remain available for the future [2]. Bluefin Canning Ltd must manage 40 tonnes of waste in Port Louis.

knowledge_max_2: Meeting present needs without harming future

questions.question_text: Calculate the annual waste from Bluefin Canning Ltd at 40 tonnes a week over 50 weeks.
questions.model_answer: 40 tonnes x 50 weeks = 2,000 tonnes of offal a year [2].

knowledge_max_2: Annual waste = weekly waste x weeks

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the fishmeal drier for Bluefin Canning Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Levy avoided [k]. The $110,000 disposal levy disappears when offal becomes fishmeal [app], saving money on $3,900,000 exports [an].

Point 2: New product [k]. Fishmeal can be sold to Mauritian farms [app], adding income beyond canned tuna [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluefin Canning Ltd should buy the $640,000 fishmeal drier? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The drier ends the $110,000 levy and sells fishmeal, stopping 2,000 tonnes of waste harming Mauritian waters.

Against: $640,000 is large against $3,900,000 exports, and fishmeal prices may not cover running costs.

Conclusion: Buy the drier. Repaying $640,000 is realistic given the $110,000 annual levy plus fishmeal sales and the environmental benefit in Port Louis.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $640,000 against levy and sales
Judges environmental value

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Okavango Gems Ltd is a private limited company cutting gemstones in Gaborone, Botswana, and sells $5,500,000 to buyers in Switzerland. questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is a rise in a currency's value relative to another [2]. A 5% stronger pula affects Okavango Gems Ltd's Swiss sales.

questions.question_text: Calculate sales after a 10% Swiss quota cut on $5,500,000 of gems.
Explain two effects of the 5% pula appreciation on Okavango Gems Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lower local earnings [k]. Each Swiss franc converts into fewer pulas [app], reducing the $5,500,000 income from Gaborone [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Okavango Gems Ltd should open a sales office in Dubai? Justify your answer.

For: A 10% Swiss quota cut removes $550,000 of sales, and Dubai could replace them while the stronger pula makes expansion cheaper.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs $550,000 loss against office cost
Judges currency help

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Harbourline Buses Ltd is a private limited company running city buses in Dublin, Ireland, with revenue of $7,800,000. Fuel prices rose 18% and the government cut subsidies by $420,000. Owners must decide whether to raise fares by 10% or cut services on quiet routes. Passenger groups in Dublin have warned against any increase in fares.

questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A subsidy is a government payment to a business to keep prices low or support operations [2]. Harbourline Buses Ltd lost $420,000 of subsidy in Dublin.

questions.question_text: Calculate the new annual fuel bill if Harbourline Buses Ltd paid $2,400,000 before an 18% rise.

knowledge_max_2: New cost = old cost x (100% + rise)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the fuel price rise on Harbourline Buses Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher operating costs [k]. Fuel rose 18% to $2,832,000, cutting profit on $7,800,000 revenue [app] in Dublin [an].

Point 2: Fare pressure [k]. Covering fuel plus the $420,000 subsidy cut may require 10% higher fares [app], which could reduce passenger numbers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Harbourline Buses Ltd should raise fares by 10% rather than cut routes? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 10% fare rise helps cover the $432,000 fuel increase and $420,000 subsidy loss while keeping all Dublin routes running.

Against: Higher fares may drive passengers away, while cutting quiet routes saves fuel quickly with less admin.

Conclusion: Raise fares modestly and trim only the quietest routes. A full 10% may deter riders, but cuts alone hurt communities in Ireland.

evaluation_max_2: Weighs fares against route cuts
Judges combined approach

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Redwood Furniture Ltd is a private limited company making wooden tables in Chiang Mai, Thailand, with sales of $3,350,000. Its varnish releases 2,400 litres of chemical vapour yearly and neighbours have complained. Managers must decide whether to buy $290,000 low-emission varnish equipment or keep using the cheap current process. The local council has asked the factory to reduce its emissions voluntarily.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical issue'.
questions.model_answer: An ethical issue is a decision about right and wrong conduct [2]. Redwood Furniture Ltd must weigh cheap varnish against the health of Chiang Mai neighbours.

questions.question_text: Calculate the reduction in vapour if low-emission equipment cuts 2,400 litres by 75%.
questions.model_answer: 2,400 litres x 75% = 1,800 litres removed; 600 litres remain [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons for Redwood Furniture Ltd to change its varnish process.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Community health [k]. Removing 1,800 litres of vapour reduces complaints in Chiang Mai [app], protecting the firm's reputation [an].

Point 2: Avoid future regulation [k]. Thai rules may tighten on emissions [app], so acting now avoids costly fines later [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Redwood Furniture Ltd should buy the $290,000 low-emission equipment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
